headline: President Biden Revokes Keystone XL Permit; Pelosi Send Impeachment To Senate; National Guard in DC Told To Sleep In Parking Garage
story_text: MARTHA MACCALLUM, FOX NEWS ANCHOR: Thank you very much, guys. Thank you, John, and Sandra. So, any moment now President Biden is going to roll out the reversals of the Trump economic measures, several of them focusing today on expanding food stamps, which, if you remember, was a program that was greatly expanded during the Obama administration. And it was shrunk during the economic expansion under the Trump years at the White House. So we're going to hear about a hike to the minimum wage for federal workers to $15 an hour, which is a doubling of that minimum wage. And we expect that we're going to hear a lot more student debt and other issues that we will address very soon. So it's all part of a massive wave of executive orders and actions, that in sheer numbers surpasses anything that we have seen in the early days of prior presidents. Axios describing these first three days of the first 100 as regulatory a quote, Biden's centrist words, and liberal actions, writing Biden talks like a soothing centrist, he promises to govern like a soothing centrist, but early moves show that he is keeping his promise to advance a liberal agenda. Now, President Biden has said that he could go down as quote one of the most progressive presidents in American history. And Bernie Sanders says that Democrats are ready to make sure that that happens. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) SEN. BERNIE SANDERS (I-VT): I think if we can give them the support that he needs in Congress, he can in fact, be an extremely progressive president. (END VIDEO CLIP) MACCALLUM: So for example, while Treasury went to former Fed Chair Janet Yellen who cruised through the Senate Finance Committee with a 26 to zero vote. This is a seat to watch though. Rohit Chopra will be running the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau . He helped to establish that Bureau in the post 2008 period after the financial crisis with Senator Elizabeth Warren, who was seen as too controversial to take over Treasury, but whose influence is likely to be felt in this powerful position that will have sway over a lot of rules and regulations that affect American businesses. And the banks are also likely to get a new regulator from the Obama Treasury team in Michael Barr signaling a tightening likely of government oversight there as well. President Trump's tax cuts and loosening of government control over businesses in America was cited as one of the strongest igniters of economic growth. Now, this economy, devastated by COVID lockdowns may run into ever tightening government control. So let's get some analysis on all of this from Ari Fleischer, former White House press secretary and a Fox News contributor. And Steve Hilton, host of The Next Revolution. Gentlemen, great to have both of you with us today. We are waiting. We know that the pool was called. So we expect that this economy discussion is going to get underway shortly. Ari, what you would expect to hear from President Biden when he enters this room to start talking about his next part of his agenda on day three. ARI FLEISCHER, FORMER WHITE HOUSE PRESS SECRETARY: Well, he won't put it this way. But what's happening is the heavy hand of the regulatory state is back. And that is a hand that we all know makes it very hard for people in the private sector, particularly small businesses to create jobs to grow and to pay their employees more money. Look, if there's one thing we do know about the previous economy, right prior to the pandemic, it was booming. We had the lowest poverty rate since 1959. For people without a high school degree, it was the lowest unemployment rate ever in recorded history. So why wouldn't we want to return to the economic environment that created that type of opportunity for lower income, middle income people? The heavy hand of the regulatory state is already causing people to lose jobs such as the Keystone pipeline. That's what I fear. MACCALLUM: Yes, this is a huge issue, Steve, and it's something that I've heard business owners talk about all across the country. And President Trump talked about it a lot. He used to say, Oh, you know, the tax cuts. Everybody says that was so great. But I think the regulations cutting was even better for unleashing economic growth in the country. So now all those businesses across the country are going to look at all this and they're going to see the way this is going and it's going to change I would imagine their approach to the future and how many people they hire and all of that kind of thing. STEVE HILTON, FOX NEWS HOST: That's exactly right, Martha and I take it one step even further back, because if you actually look at the economic data, what you saw was a rebound in investment, investment in new plant and machinery and job opportunities that caused jobs to rise, employment to rise, wages rise, all of that happened even before suddenly before the tax cuts, even before some of the regulatory cuts. Why? Because businesses all over the country could sense that there was a pro enterprise pro growth administration, it wasn't going to make their lives harder as Ari's quite rightly so it's going to make their life easier. That increased confidence, so much of businesses confidence, MACCALLUM: All right. Gentlemen, stick around. Let's watch this. And we'll talk on the other side. This is President Biden and Vice President Kamala Harris JOE BIDEN , PRESIDENT OF THE UNITED STATES: -- the economic crisis in modern history. And the crisis is only deepening, it's not getting better, it's deepening. Yesterday, we learned that 900,000 more Americans file for unemployment. 900,000. They join millions of Americans who through no fault of their own, have lost the dignity and respect that comes with a job and a paycheck. So many of them never thought they'd ever be out of work in the first place. And just like my dad did when he was used to lie awake at night, when I was a kid staring at the ceiling, unable to sleep, because he worried about whether or not he's about to lose his health care, or whether we were going to have the money to pay the mortgage because of the economic circumstances. And now a lot of these folks are facing eviction, or waiting hours in their cars, literally hours in their cars, waiting to be able to feed their children as I drive up to a food bank. It's United States of America, and they're waiting to feed their kids. Folks who are able to still keep their job many have seen their paychecks reduced and they've -- they're barely hanging on and wondering what's next. Sometimes the anxiety about what's going to happen next is more consequential than what actually happened. But this is happening today in America. And this cannot be who we are as a country. These are not the values of our nation. We cannot will, not let people go hungry. We cannot let people be evicted because of nothing they did themselves. They cannot watch people lose their jobs. And we have to act, we have to act now. It's not just to meet the moral obligation to treat our fellow Americans with the dignity respect they deserve. This is an economic imperative, a growing economic consensus that we must act decisively and boldly to grow the economy for all Americans, not just for tomorrow, but in the future. There's a growing chorus of top economic -- top economists that agree that at this moment of crisis, with this, with interest rates, as low as they are historic lows, it is smart fiscal investment, including deficit spending. And they're more urgent than ever. You know, and that return on these investments in jobs and racial equity is going to prevent long-term economic damage and benefits that are going to far surpass their cost. If we don't act, the rest of the world is not standing still in terms of their competitive advantage of the competitive possibilities relative to us, that our debt situation will be more stable and not less stable according to these economists and that such investments in our people is going to strengthen our economic competitiveness as a nation and help us out compete our competitors in the global economy. Because we're going to grow the economy with these investments. The COVID-19 package that passed in December was the first step. As I said at the time, it's just a down payment. We need more action, right. We need to move fast. Last week, I laid out a two-step plan of rescue and recovery, to get through the crisis, and to a better and stronger and more secure America. The first step of our American Rescue Plan is a plan to tackle the pandemic and get direct financial relief to Americans who needed the most. You know, in just a few days, it's just been a few days since outlined this plan and received bipartisan support from majority of American mayors and governors, businesses and labor organizations have together welcomed it as urgent action is needed. Even Wall Street firms have underscored its importance. In fact, an analysis by Moody's estimates that if we pass our American rescue plan, the economy would create 7.5 million jobs just in this year alone. That would be on the way to the more than 18 million, I think is 18,600,000 jobs that they believe would be created over the four-year period with our build back better recovery plan. And with our American rescue plan, our economy would return to full employment a full year faster than without the plan. Even President Trump's -- President Trump's now, not some liberal organization, President Trump's top former economic adviser, Kevin Hassett said, quote, he absolutely is in favor of this rescue plan. This almost doesn't have a partisan piece to it. We're seeing the support because this plan takes a step that we so urgently need more than just a step number steps. It funds big parts of the COVID-19 national strategy that I released yesterday -- we released yesterday. Our national strategy puts on us on a war footing to aggressively speed up our COVID-19 response, especially on vaccines and testing and reopening in our schools. I found a fascinating yesterday the press asked the question is, you know 100 million enough week before they said, Biden you crazy you can't do 100 million in 100 days. Well, we're gong to -- God Willie, not only do 100 million, we're going to do more than that. But this is we have to do this, we have to move. The American Rescue Plan also includes economic relief for most Americans who are in need. We're going to finish the job of getting a total of $2,000 in direct payments to folks, $600 which has already passed is simply not enough. If you still have to choose between paying your rent putting food on the table. We'll will extend unemployment insurance benefits for millions of workers beyond the deadline is now set. It means that 16 million Americans are currently relying on unemployment benefits while they look for work can count on these checks continuing to be there in the middle of this crisis. The American Rescue Plan also addresses the growing housing crisis in America, approximately 14 million Americans, 14 million have fallen behind on rent, and many risks of eviction. If we fail to act, there will be a wave of evictions and foreclosures in the coming months as this pandemic rages on, because there's nothing we can do to change the trajectory of the pandemic in the next several months. So look, you should overwhelm emergency shelters increased COVID-19 infections as people have to -- have nowhere to go and are socially -- can't socially distance. The American Rescue Plan ask Congress to provide rental assistance for millions of hard hit families and tenants. This will also be abridged economic recover for countless mom and pop landlords who can't afford not to have the rent. But they can't wait. So on Inauguration Day, I directed my administration to extend nationwide restrictions on evictions and foreclosures. These crises are straining the budgets of states and cities and tribal communities that are forced to consider layoffs and service reductions among essential workers, police officers, firefighters, first responders, nurses are all at the risk of losing their jobs. Over the last year, more than 600,000 educators have lost their jobs in cities and towns. The American Rescue Plan will provide emergency funding to keep these essential workers on the job and maintain essential services. Look, it will also help small businesses that are the engines of economic growth. When you say small business, most people think the major corporate entities are the ones who hire everybody. These small businesses glues that hold and they're important but these small businesses that hold the community that the glue that holds these communities together. They are hurting badly and they account for nearly half of the entire U.S. workforce. Now we have our Rescue Plan, which will provide flexible grants to help the hardest hit small businesses survive the pandemic. And low cost capital to help entrepreneurs of all backgrounds create and maintain jobs, plus provide essential goods and services that communities so desperately depend on. Look, our Recovery Plan also calls for an increase in the minimum wage at 15, at least $15 an hour. No one in America should work 40 hours a week, making below the poverty line. $15 gets people above the poverty line. We have so many millions of people working 40 hours a week working in somewhat two jobs. And they're still below the poverty line. Our plan includes access to affordable childcare, that's going to enable parents particularly women to get back to work. Millions who are not working now because they don't have that care. All told the American Rescue Plan would lift 12 million Americans out of poverty and cut child poverty in half. That's 5 million children lifted out of poverty. Our plan to reduce poverty in the black community by one-third and reduce poverty in Hispanic community by almost 40 percent. I look forward to working with members of Congress of both parties to move quickly to get this American Rescue Plan to the American people. And then we can move with equal urgency and bipartisanship to the second step of our economic plan, to build back better the Recovery Plan. It's a plan that's going to make historic investments in infrastructure, manufacturing, innovation, research and development, and clean energy and so much more. That's going to create millions more jobs, good paying jobs, not minimum wage jobs. While we work with members of both parties in the Congress, there are steps that we can and must take right now. For example, on Inauguration Day, I directed my administration to pause student loan repayments for interest -- for the interest payments for Americans with federal student loans until at least September. So they're not going to have to pay till September, they still pay the bill as it stands now. But they will not accrue interest, and they don't have to pay begin to pay until September. And we may have to look beyond that I might add. Today, I'm signing an executive order that directs the whole government. A whole government effort to help millions of Americans who are badly hurting requires all federal agencies to do what they can do to provide relief to families, small businesses and communities. And in the days ahead, I expect agencies to act. Let me touch on two ways these action can help change Americans lives. We need to tackle the growing hunger crisis in America, one in seven households in America, one in seven. More than one in five black and Latino households in America report, they do not have enough food to eat. That includes nearly 30 million adults, and as many as 12 million children. And again, in this situation through no fault of their own. It's unconscionable. The American Rescue Plan provides additional emergency food and nutrition assistance for tens of millions of children and families to address this crisis. But families literally can't wait another day. As a result of the executive order, I'm going to shortly sign it, the Department of Agriculture will consider taking immediate steps to make it easier for the hardest hit families to enroll and claim more generous benefits in the critical Food and Nutrition Assistance area. This can help tens of millions of families, especially those who can't provide meals for their kids, who are learning remotely at home or not receiving the regular meal plans that they have at school for breakfast or lunch. It's going to also -- we also need to protect the health and safety the American worker. Right now approximately 40 percent of households in America have at least one member with a preexisting condition. Just imagine, you're out of work through no fault of your own. You file for unemployment while you're looking for a job. You find one and you get an offer. But then you find out there's a high risk of you're getting infected with COVID-19. Because of your condition, you and your loved one, and you and your loved ones have ever greater risk of death and serious illness because of the preexisting conditions. So you turn it down. Right now if you did that, you could be denied unemployment insurance because you're offered a job he didn't take it. It's wrong. No one should have to choose between their livelihoods and their own health or the health of the loved ones in the middle of a deadly pandemic. Because the executive order I'm about to sign, I expect the Department of Labor to guarantee the right to refuse unemployment, employment, that will jeopardize your health. And if you do so, you'll, still be able to qualify for the insurance. That's a judgment the Labor Department will make. Look, there are just two consequential ways that the action I'm taking today will help people in need. Another way to help approximately 2 million veterans maintain their financial footing by pausing federal collections on overpayments and debts. Another make sure that federal contractors are saving taxpayers dollars, provide their workers with the pay and benefits they deserve. These are places where federal tax dollars are administered are being made available to build things from ships to staircases. And we let out the federal government let's the contract and we're going to make sure that they buy American and are made in America. There's another right now there are up to 8 million people that are eligible for direct payments from the CARES Act and a relief bill passed in December. They're entitled those payments but there's not an easy way for those folks to assess -- access them. So we're making it a priority today to fix that problem and get the relief, they're entitled to. Look, I'm going to close and summarize this way, a lot of America is hurting. The virus is surging, were 400,000 dead expected to reach well over 600,000. Families are going hungry, people are at risk of being evicted. Job losses are mounting again, we need to act. No matter how you look at it, we need to act. If, if we act now our economy will be stronger in both the short and long run. That's what economists left, right and center telling us, both liberal and conservative will be better and stronger across the board. If we act now, we'll be better able to compete with the world. If we act now, we better able to meet our moral obligations to one another, as Americans. I don't believe that people in this country just want to stand by and watch their friends, their neighbors, co-workers, fellow Americans go hungry, lose their homes and lose their sense of dignity and hope and respect. I don't believe that, especially in the middle of a pandemic that's so weakened and wrecked so much havoc and caused so much pain on America. That's not who we are. The bottom line is this. We're in a national emergency. We need to act like we're in a national emergency. So I've got to move with everything we've got. And we got to do it together. I don't believe Democrats or Republicans are going hungry and losing jobs. I believe Americans are going hungry and losing their jobs. We have the tools to fix it. We have the tools to get through this. We have the tools to get this virus under control, and our economy back on track. And we have the tools to help people. So let's use the tools. All of them use them now. So I'm going to sign this executive order, let me conclude again by saying, folks, this is one of the cases where business, labor, Wall Street, mainstream, liberal, conservative, economists know we have to act now, not only to help people are in need now. But to allow us to be in a competitive position worldwide and be the leader of the world economy in the next year or two and three and going forward. So thank you, I'm going to sign this executive order. First one is the Economic Relief related to COVID-19 pandemic reference. The second one is Protection, Protecting the Federal Workforce. Thank you very much. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: Mr. President, do you support (INAUDIBLE) timeline for February? BIDEN: I haven't heard the detail of it. But I do think that having some time to get our administration up and running we may. I want to thank the Center for passing out our Secretary of Defense, looks like our Secretary of Treasury, looks like our Secretary of State's in place. So the more time we have to get up and running and meet these crises, the better. Thank you. MACCALLUM: All right, well, there you have it. President Biden on his third round of executive order signing in the 48 hours or so that he has been President of the United States. Let's bring in Ari Fleischer and Steve Hilton once again, with reaction to this. You know, it strikes me this has been a two part program he talked about rescue is dealing with COVID-19 and recoveries getting the economy back up and running. From everything that I heard Ari, recovery means tools, which equals money out the door to a number of different entities. And we heard it going to the military, how to go into people food stamp programs, all of that kind of thing. Not a lot of discussion about reopening America businesses here. FLEISCHER: Exactly, exactly. Well, first and foremost, it does seem to me the president allergic to taking questions. Normally, presidents take a bunch of questions after an appearance like that. In terms of what the President did by executive order today, I think is absolutely accurate to say that the return of big government is back. He said, we're going to grow the economy with these investments. Big spending has never grown the economy, it's grown the government, it hasn't solved people's problems. If you want to solve people's problems now, do it by going after COVID, to reopen the economy as fast as possible. I think the ideas of doing more doing what we can on COVID even though much of it is already in the pipeline and being done. The President is empathetic, and that's good. But empathy is not what people need. They need their jobs back. Now, one other just point, Martha -- MACCALLUM: Yes. Yes, I think -- please. FLEISCHER: The President talks about raising the minimum wage and making sure no one's in poverty again, doesn't that sound good. The poverty level for one individual in America is $12,760. The President is talking about paying Americans on an annualized basis, at least $30,000 a year. That's what a $15 minimum wage translates to. So if there's two people in a family, that's 60,000, at least, and the poverty rate for a family of four is 24 -- $26,200. These are job killers, and it's big government big spending, old time liberalism. MACCALLUM: Steve, he said he wanted to treat people with the dignity and the respect that they deserve. And the first person who popped into my mind is the gym owner in New Jersey, you know, who wants to be treated with dignity and respect. He wants to open his business. He wants to feed his family and he wants to feed the workers who work with him in his business. We didn't hear one thing in any of this, about getting America back open again, so people can help themselves. HILTON: Exactly right, Martha, that was exactly my reaction. I was thinking of all the restaurant owners and bar owners and others who you've had on your show I've had on my show, the making that exact point. I listened to the president there with just a rising level of frustration, even anger. He's absolutely right about how many millions of people in this country are hurting and suffering small businesses, workers families, yes. But why are they hurting and suffering because of the lockdowns. These lockdowns are not just cruel. They're actually counterproductive, because they even make the virus worse. Here in California where outdoor dining is shut down sending people back indoors is where they catch the virus. There's a study just a couple of weeks ago, Stanford University they looked at the data from 10 countries around the world. They showed with the data that lockdowns have no impact on actually reducing the spread. And so we didn't hit anything about reopening the economy. And worse than that what we actually are getting from this administration are incentives to keep the lockdown going. It's kind of like a lockdown bailout, especially to the blue states run by Democrats like California, like New York, where they love all this. They love the big government that Ari's talking about. And Joe Biden is just giving them incentives to keep it all going instead of to reopen the country and help those people for real. MACCALLUM: Yes. You know, Ari last thought here, when he talked about deficit spending equaling economic growth. And I know you brought this up a moment ago. But this is the sort of the mentality that we heard a lot in the past in the Obama-Biden administration, that the more that you fuel, the government, the more that you give people programs, food stamps, all of those things. And we all understand that there's a compassionate need for many people in this country. We all want that need met. But the idea that that stimulates growth in the economy, which he said several times, he said lots of top economists, you know, sort of phrases like that, believe this, is that true? FLEISCHER: Well, he's actually contradicted by his own incoming Treasury Secretary Janet Yellen, who when she was the head of the Federal Reserve warned about the job killing impact of increasing the minimum wage to eye level. And so, across the board from a spending to regulations, to the heavy handed government, the answer is no. We had the highest rate of economic growth early in the Trump administration after the tax cuts were passed higher than anything in the Obama years. But we know from doing what President Obama did that now President Biden is going to continue is it led to low growth 10 years of no salary increases, particularly for middle income and low income people and economic stagnation. MACCALLUM: Yes. FLEISCHER: There's a history here. Free markets work the heavy handed government not so much. MACCALLUM: Yes, and I would just cite the individuals that I mentioned at the top of the show. I know a lot of people don't pay attention to sort of the head of the Consumer Finance Protection Bureau or the head of the Comptroller of the Currency. These sounds like the, you know, sort of obscure jobs to a lot of people, but they're going to have a heavy hand in rules and regulations on a lot of businesses across this country. So I would urge everybody to pay attention to all of these appointments and the power that they could hold in the future in this administration, the current administration, Great to have you both with us to watch all of that, very pleasure. Thank you, Steve Hilton. Thank you as always. Thanks, gentlemen. FLEISCHER: Thanks, Martha. HILTON: Thank you. MACCALLUM: So coming up, a Canadian premier of Alberta, the oil rich area of Canada goes after President Biden's "insulting," he says, cancelation of the Keystone XL Pipeline Project, and threatens legal means even sanctions against the United States. So how is this improving international relations, that's next. (COMMERCIAL BREAK) (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) DONALD TRUMP , FORMER PRESIDENT OF UNITED STATES: With regard to the construction of the Keystone pipeline, something that's been in dispute and it's subject to a renegotiation of terms by us. We're going to renegotiate some of the terms. And if they'd like, we'll see if we can get their pipelines built. A lot of jobs, 28,000 jobs. (END VIDEO CLIP) MACCALLUM: It's been nearly four years to the day since President Trump green lighted construction on the Keystone XL pipeline. You might remember at this time, his conversations with foreign leaders were being leaked on a regular basis. He was accused of ruining relationships with our closest allies. So will the same now be said potentially of President Bided. Later today, he's going to speak with the Canadian Prime Minister Justin Trudeau, after bringing us back to the Obama day is blocking the Excel project, which would have secured the transport of 830,000 barrels of oil each day, which firms up our energy independence, of course, Trudeau called this disappointment by the new President Biden "disappointing." Other officials there are going further talking about sanctions or retaliation against the United States. Joining me now exclusively Alberta Premier Jason Kenney. Premier Kenny, thank you very much. Good to have you here today. JASON KENNEY, ALBERTA PREMIER: Great to be here. MACCALLUM: So, you have some pretty strong language on this. We understand that Prime Minister Trudeau will be speaking, in the first phone call as president that Joe Biden will have with a foreign leader this afternoon. How do you -- what's the impact on the relationship between our two countries over this? KENNEY: Well, first, we congratulate President Biden on his inauguration and election, and hope to have a really close and strong relationship. We have the biggest bilateral trade relationship in world history between Canada and the United States. But the biggest part of that trade is Canadian energy exports, largely from our province here of Alberta. We have the third largest oil reserves in the world. We ship about nearly $100 billion worth of energy to the US every year. Keystone XL would have been a significant, safe, modern increase in that shipment. And it is very frustrating that one of the first acts of the new president was, I think, to disrespect America's closest friend and ally Canada, and to kill a good paying union jobs on both sides of the border. And ultimately, to make the United States more dependent on foreign oil imports from OPEC dictatorships. We don't understand it. Then at the very least, we believe that those who have invested in this project, trusting in the regulatory process in the US should be compensated by the US administration. MACCALLUM: Yes. Well, you make a lot of great points there. I want to unpack some of those with you, if I may. One of them is that one of the greatest achievements we've seen in the past several years for the United States and Canada, for all of North America, is energy independence. So if you're a Saudi Arabia and you're looking at the cancellation of this deal today, what's going through your mind? KENNEY: Exactly. This is a good day, a good decision for the OPEC producers in reducing Canadian shipments of energy to the world's largest energy consumer. In particular, Keystone XL would like the current Keystone pipeline, largely ship Alberta heavy crude. And many of the US refineries down along the Gulf Coast are keyed up to process heavy. If they don't get it from Canada, they've got to get it from places ultimately like Venezuela. And I don't see how that's in the interests of the United States. So, our plead to the Biden ministration is, please take a half step back here, get into a conversation with your closest friend and ally Canada, about how we can ensure a future for safe energy exports, continental energy independence and security between Canada and the US, while also taking very seriously, climate policy and environmental policy. You know, President Obama State Department concluded after rigorous study that Keystone XL would actually reduce carbon emissions, because the alternative will be shipping it by rail, which is higher emitting and less safe. MACCALLUM: Yes. I mean, it's a great point. I don't know how they get around that in the Biden ministration because, as you point out, five times the United States State Department evaluated the environmental aspects of the Keystone pipeline deal. And all five times the State Department said that they could not find any increase in environmental issues that would arise from this. So, you know, one of my questions for you is when you look at what happens now, right? So your country has put a billion dollars in taxpayer money into building this pipeline. It's not finished yet. So what happens now and how does this oil get from Canada to the Gulf? How will it get there? KENNEY: Well, first we hope that Prime Minister Trudeau will raise it with the President, asked him to sit down and discuss this in the broader context of energy and the environment, we are so closely integrated in our economies, that we need that kind of cooperation. Secondly, we are sending a message that there should be, the Canadian national government should stand up for our interests, just like we did against President Trump's unfair steel tariffs against our country, just like we stood up to his effort to rip up NAFTA. And so, we hope a similar position is taken here. Ultimately, we would at the very least, it demanded the US government provide a compensation to Canadian investors, including Alberta's government for having taken the US regulatory process at face value. There was a permit, it was legally approved, investments were made on that basis. But ultimately, Canadian energy continues to flow to the United States. One thing we're concerned about, our political forces trying to decommission a number of other safe pipelines that have been operating for decades. So I would call on our friends in the United States to realize Canada is your closest friend and ally, we're a much safer source of energy to fuel your economy than OPEC dictatorships. MACCALLUM: Yes. Before I let you go, you called for potential sanctions against the United States over this decision. Do you think that Prime Minister Trudeau will go that far when he speaks with President Biden on that phone call? I don't know, but all I can do is represent the interests of Albertans. We have the third largest oil reserves on Earth. We ship nearly 100 billion of that to the United States. We need that partnership. And we need to defend that as well as other efforts to decommission long standing pipelines. Doing so would be devastating to the American economy, we need to find a way to work together on these issues. MACCALLUM: I got to let you go. I know you're short on time, but just, you know, 30 more seconds here. Were you shocked by this decision? Did you look at President Biden as somebody who might say, well, let's look at this deal. Let's see how it's working, and maybe we want to pull out and maybe we don't? KENNEY: Well, I wasn't shocked because his campaign did say that they would veto the presidential permit. Having said that, I was really disappointed that the new president didn't give enough respect to America's closest friend and ally, to at least sit down with us and hear our case about how we've reduced carbon emissions from Canada's oil sands about how this pipeline would operate on a net zero carbon emitting basis about First Nations, American native communities that are taking an ownership stake in this, but the huge support of unions, the economic benefits, we have a strong case to make. And we just wish the US administration would let us make that case. MACCALLUM: Yes, very interesting. We're going to be following it closely. Premier Kenney of Alberta, thank you so much for being here today. Thank you, sir. KENNEY: Thanks for your interest. MACCALLUM: National Guard troops were sent to the Capitol in enormous numbers to protect lawmakers than they ended up on the garage floor. They have slept in worse places, of course, but the lack of respect comes on top of vetting to make sure that they weren't strong Trump supporters. So now, the governors of Texas and Florida say enough is enough. They're bringing their guards home immediately. Senator Tom Cotton an Iraq Afghanistan veteran joins us, next. I've been out working in clinical medicine and in academic medicine and then the health policy for 15 or so years. So, I'm used to being challenged. These people are sitting there. They're not used to being challenged. I welcome the Hoover Institution . There's a lot of smart people with knowledge there. If you don't know what you're talking about, you're going to be made a fool of. So, these people were sitting there unchallenged for eight months. I walked in August and I said, well, what about these research studies? What about this? I brought in famous epidemiologists and infectious disease scientists from the West Coast and the East Coast to meet with the president. And the response was, she just decided she didn't want to show up. OK, this is not the way you develop the best policy. The American people should be very thankful that other people from outside came in instead of leaving everything to people who've been in bureaucratic positions for three decades. INGRAHAM: Can I say, they are insulated from, sorry, the real world, the fact that people have to put food on the table. Their kids are getting into depression, they're not learning anything. I don't know if you were on the show, but we were talking about opening the schools on this show, and we got trashed for it, in March, OK. Because I saw what was happening. It was clear these weren't super-spreader places given Europe's experience. We went into Italy and France and Germany and Sweden. We went over the data. There were a few little upticks here and there, but they were all handled. They didn't care. This is what I'm saying. You're being way too polite, and that's why we love you, but they didn't care. Now it's a double masks, triple masks, now they are saying triple masks. Let's play it. Let's watch about the triple masking. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) CONTESSA BREWER, CNBC CORRESPONDENT: Experts say you can double up with a tight weave fabric mask for added protection. Now, Virginia Tech researchers found doubling up these cloth masks increases the efficacy from 50 to 75 percent. A three-layer mask could block up to 90 percent of the particles. (END VIDEO CLIP) INGRAHAM: Are they not wearing masks in California where you had all of the cases? They're not wearing masks in New York? Were they not wearing masks in Michigan? It seems like everyone I know is wearing masks, and they seem to be pretty good masks. I don't know. I guess we could all walk around in scuba suits all day. ATLAS: When you look at the data from all the surveys, whether it's YouGov, Gallup, this Consortium, Americans have been wearing masks for months. And so that's not the issue. I'm fine, people can wear as many masks as they want as long as we open up -- there should be choices and things. This is a free country. I think what's destructive really is not so much the masks, but what we know is killing people is keeping businesses closed, schools closed, keeping people isolated, suicides, child abuse, domestic -- INGRAHAM: Dr. Atlas, I've got to get this in. I don't want to interrupt, but I've got to get this in. Vaccinations as a percentage of population, OK, we've heard Birx or Fauci complain about this, right. Here's our percentage of vaccinations per population -- 11.3 percent, OK, 11.3 percent U.K., U.S. is 7.1 percent, Germany 2.4, Canada 2.4, France is 1.8. Only a few other countries have better percentages than we have. I think Bahrain and UAE is really good. But they were handed a really good situation with the vaccines. And now they are trying to say, we were handed a disaster. That's untrue. And they have to be held to account for that smear of the Trump administration. Close it out. ATLAS: It's inarguable, really, that Operation Warp Speed was really a tremendous success. We're thrilled -- as people, a regular person should be thrilled that they developed drugs and vaccines in that kind of record time without cutting safety corners. And it's not a political issue. I don't even know why everything has to be political. I went to Washington very naive. I had nothing to do with politics. These people are political animals, and their interested in their own image rather than the facts. You're supposed to be doing the best for the American people. And enough trashing -- it's challenging to get the vaccines, but let's get them to the people who are at risk for dying. That might be a good strategy. INGRAHAM: Bingo. As far as I can tell and looking at what the Trump people did, if Biden just went away and just followed what the Trump plan was, we would be actually by three or four months we would actually be in really good shape. (COMMERCIAL BREAK) INGRAHAM: It's time for our "Seen and Unseen" segment where we reveal the stories behind the headlines. And for that, we go to FOX News contributor Raymond Arroyo. Raymond, as we've been reporting, Biden unveiled his big climate initiatives today. RAYMOND ARROYO, FOX NEWS CONTRIBUTOR: Yes, but it wasn't only about climate regulations, Laura. It was about jobs. This is all bad. INGRAHAM: But wait a second, Raymond, I remember back in the radio days tracking Biden's promises about green jobs, I think it, what, was 2009? (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) JOE BIDEN, (D) PRESIDENT OF THE UNITED STATES: More green jobs means more money in your pocket at the end of the month. (END VIDEO CLIP) ARROYO: Yes, but the money landed in somebody else's pocket, Laura. It wasn't the taxpayers. Obama and Biden promised 5 million green jobs as part of that $787 billion stimulus package. The only thing green was the piles of cash spent on this boondoggle. They never hit their goal. And remember, they counted janitors, cleaners, and bus drivers as green jobs. This was a boondoggle from a start to finish, including Solyndra , which you mentioned. INGRAHAM: When they go back and they keep saying, well, it will all be solar, solar has so many great jobs. I'm sure there will be some jobs, but what's going to stop the solar panel manufacturers without Trump's tariffs and other trade protections in place from moving over to Asia, whether it's China or Vietnam or India. They're all going to move overseas. So we're going to be left with no oil and gas jobs, and no solar panel jobs. So I guess we'll -- I don't know what we'll do. ARROYO: You're 100 percent right. Laura, it China that put Solyndra out of business, remember that. It really is the job of the media, though, to hold these politicians accountable and call out errors, which is why it is astounding that after years of ruthlessly fact-checking Trump, "The Washington Post" has announced they are backing off of Biden and discontinuing their presidential lie tracker, Laura. Glenn Kessler tweets "We have no plans to start a Biden false or misleading claims tracker, just as we had no plans at this point to start a Trump tracker. The constant tweeting of falsehoods forced our hand. But we will have an open mind and if the need arises we will consider one. INGRAHAM: But wait a second, Raymond, Jim Acosta over at CNN, he believes the fact-checkers should not be packed away just yet. This is not a time to put away our fact-checkers in some sort of box on the shelf. They are going to be needed to fact-check this movement that is not going away. Trump may be going away, but Trumpism is not. (END VIDEO CLIP) ARROYO: So it's the movement, Laura. INGRAHAM: He reveals himself. ARROYO: The bad man at Mar-a-Lago, he needs to be fact-checked, not the guy spending billions or executive -- issuing executive orders like they are candy at Halloween. I've never seen anything like it. But fear not, Laura. The "Los Angeles Times" is stepping into the gap. They have launched a new project called, "Covering Kamala Harris," which they say is a beat dedicated to her historic rise to the White House, or at least the naval observatory. I guess they don't realize the vice president doesn't live at the White House. But maybe they know something we don't know, Laura. Who knows? INGRAHAM: Raymond, let's look at some of the penetrating coverage, and it is pretty tough from the "L.A. Times." This is from their Instagram account. OK, it's just a reposting of Harris' own social media propaganda with absolutely no comment. ARROYO: Right. Since when is hugging a spouse news? Though there are some important reports here, Laura. Here's one, "How Kamala Harris' decision to join a sorter helped her become vice president." And my favorite, "My grandmother is named Kamala. So is my vice president, why that matters." This is like the In Style magazine or Teen Beat for the political class, Laura. I've never anything like this. INGRAHAM: This is the tiger beat of politics. And poor old Jim Acosta, Jim Acosta is like Trump's gone, Trump's gone, but Trumpism isn't. Does he not understand that he's just proving to everyone that he's an ideologue on the left who hates populist conservatives. OK, then be a pundit. Don't stand there with your tie on and be some objective journalist. You just look like a fool, OK? ARROYO: Right or left, these politicians need to be held accountable by the media. That's our job. INGRAHAM: Absolutely. And how did Biden's unity message devolve into such a dystopian nightmare? Plus, a shocking poll with some interesting findings about Trump's standings right now. Senator Lindsey Graham here on deck. (COMMERCIAL BREAK) INGRAHAM: Here now, Senator Lindsey Graham, who is the Senate Judiciary Committee chairman, and we're delighted he's with us. That's up nine percent since the Capital riots. And it's being driven by a 15-point surge in support from GOP women. And then it goes on to say that, I think it's 81 percent have a positive view of President Trump. That's up from 76 percent before the impeachment vote. So he's off Twitter , he's not commenting on every news item. So has the absence made the heart grow fonder, Senator Graham? SEN. LINDSEY GRAHAM, (R-SC): Well, I've talked to him twice. So absolutely. So what have we learned? That Trump policies are universally thought to be good by every corner of the Republican Party. If you are a Reagan national security guy, Trump delivered. If you are a pro-life person, he's the best pro-life person in my lifetime, really. If you wanted order out of chaos at the border, he delivered. If you wanted your taxes cut, he did. So there's a fondness for President Trump's policies. There's a respect for what he did. And there's a backlash brewing. This effort to destroy him morning, noon, and night for four years plus, to impeach him when he's in Florida, has created a backlash not just among Republicans. But I'll make a prediction. If he'll chill out, play golf, get involved constructively with the Republican Party, by June of 2021, his numbers are going to be up all over the place. INGRAHAM: He will be more popular out of office, perhaps, then he was when he was in office. GRAHAM: Yes. INGRAHAM: But isn't that also partly because people are seeing, Senator Graham, that in many ways he was just a proxy for the American people. Jim Acosta today said that Trump is gone, but Trumpism is here, so we have to fact-check the policies, and targeting conservatives as domestic terrorists. People are seeing this now. It's becoming clearer without Trump necessarily commenting on it every day. GRAHAM: Yes, I think the reasons that people turned to Trump are even more noticeable after he left. Look at what's going on at the border. They're unraveling the border security that President Trump put in place. The caravans are forming. They are declaring war on the fossil fuel industry in America at the expense of thousands of jobs, making us less energy independent. National Security is best achieved when you don't have to buy oil and gas from people who hate your guts and are crazy. So that's all been rolled back. So I think we'll come back strong in 2022. To my Republican colleagues, there is no way in hell we're going to retake the House and the Senate without President Trump's help. If you don't understand that, you are just missing a lot. INGRAHAM: And by the way, Liz Cheney's vote to impeach Trump -- a new poll out on that. This is a Save America PAC, so people say it's not accurate. It sounds pretty accurate to me -- disapprove 69 percent, approve, 29 percent. They are not happy with this vote to impeach the president. It's not that they don't like Liz Cheney, they don't think she's a nice person. They like the fact that Donald Trump fought for the middle class. Energy prices -- he fought for the middle class. Pat Cipollone, you worked on this. McConnell got all these great judges in. People like the policies. They might not have liked some of the other things. They love the policies, and they know Trump in the end was a great president for the middle class. They know that. GRAHAM: Yes, he was. And Liz is very strong on national security. I agree with them most of the time on national security. Name a president who has been better for the military than President Trump. The problem with House impeachment, it ocurred without a witness being called within 50 hours, and the president didn't have a lawyer. So to my Republican colleagues, if you're looking for a reason to stop this impeachment and to dismiss it as soon as possible, don't legitimize basically and impeachment of the president that you get more rights with a parking ticket than you do in this impeachment. INGRAHAM: Senator, thank you so much, great to see you tonight. And up next, the Last Bite. From Russia with love? headline: White House Press Briefing Underway; Biden Signs New Exec Orders In Unprecedented Blitz; McConnell Slams Biden Executive Orders
story_text: (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) JEN PSAKI, WHITE HOUSE PRESS SECRETARY: Well, the president talked about his commitment to putting together a commission for reunifying families. He remains committed to that, and we'll have more to share on that soon. Go ahead, all the way in back. RAQUEL KRAHENBUHL, WHITE HOUSE CORRESPONDENT, GLOBO NEWS T.V., BRAZIL: Thank you so much, Jen. Raquel Krahenbuhl from T.V. Global Brazil. I have two questions. Going back to the climate crisis, during the campaign, President Biden warned of economic consequences if Brazil did not reduce deforestation on the Amazon. I'm wondering what kind of consequences he's considering, if it could hurt, for example, the trading negotiations with Brazil or the OECD support? PSAKI: Well, we just announced yesterday that we're going to be doing a climate summit coming up in the next couple of months. And, of course, this is a big priority for President Biden. And that's why he asked his good friend former Secretary Kerry to lead our climate international effort. And, certainly, Brazil will be a key partner in that. But in terms of what those negotiations and discussions look like, it's a little too early for that at this point. And I'd certainly send you to the State Department and Secretary Kerry's office for more details. KRAHENBUHL: OK, so just a follow-up. Did he invite the Brazilian president, will he invite for the summit? And is also President Biden still planning to label countries as climate outlaws? And if so, would Brazil be part of this list? PSAKI: Well, we're not quite there yet, given we just announced it. There haven't been invites or anything that went out. But we're happy to keep everybody updated. And, certainly, as the United States is a large emitter, so is Brazil, so is China, so are many large countries and large economies, and we all have a role to play in addressing this crisis. KRAHENBUHL: One more question, Jen. When does President Biden think he will be able to start doing -- or he will do his first international trip? And where it would be the first place he would go? PSAKI: I don't have anything to preview or predict for you at this point. As you know, we haven't done any domestic travel yet, given COVID. So, I certainly don't have any predictions about a foreign trip. Go ahead, Sabrina. SABRINA SIDDIQUI, WHITE HOUSE REPORTER, THE WALL STREET JOURNAL: Sure, I had a question. At her confirmation hearing yesterday, U.N. ambassador- designate Linda Thomas-Greenfield said she believed that BDS, the Boycott, Divestment, Sanctions movement to pressure Israel, is unacceptable and borders on -- or verges on anti-Semitism. Is that a characterization that the White House shares when it comes to the BDS movement ? PSAKI: I don't have anything more for you on kind of our position. It's, I think, been -- the president has spoken to this as a candidate and prior as vice president, but I don't have anything new. And I'm happy to get back to you if there's anything I can get to you from the national security team. Go ahead. ROB CRILLY, WHITE HOUSE CORRESPONDENT, THE WASHINGTON EXAMINER: Thank you. Rob Crilly with The Washington Examiner. Just to actually follow up on that, Linda Thomas-Greenfield also said she would be standing against the unfair targeting of Israel, the (INAUDIBLE) resolutions that are proposed against Israel (INAUDIBLE). Is that the position of the White House? PSAKI: You know, I didn't see her full hearing yesterday. Actually, I didn't see any of her hearing. I'm happy to review it and take a look and see if there's more we can speak to from our end. CRILLY: (INAUDIBLE) back to the executive orders, the questions we were discussing at the start. So, I'm still trying to sort of reconcile this daily -- what are we at? I think we're at 26 orders now and reconcile that with the campaign rhetoric, because, in October, Joe Biden said there were limitations on the use of executive actions, things he can't do by executive order, unless you're a dictator. We're a democracy. We need consensus. I think you said earlier that some of these executive orders were being used to roll back some of the immoral things that the previous administration had done. If you're calling these things immoral, is that seeking consensus and unity? And then also, does it suggest that President Biden sees himself as perhaps a benevolent dictator? PSAKI: Well, Rob, I'm sure this wasn't your intention, but I think you took the president's comments a bit out of context. He was asked about tax reform, and whether that could be done via executive order during the interview with George Stephanopoulos, which you're referring to. CRILLY: (INAUDIBLE) question, but I think the answer -- (CROSSTALK) PSAKI: Well, I think -- I think the question is pretty important context for everybody. And he said no. And the president also said during an interview with columnists back in December that he didn't think executive action should be used for everything. And that certainly is his point of view. But there are steps, including overturning some of the harmful, detrimental and, yes, immoral actions of the prior administration that he felt he could not wait to overturn. And that's exactly what he did. Now, any historian will tell you that he walked into the presidency at one of the most difficult moments in history. That required additional executive action in order to take -- get immediate relief to the American people. But he believes, as is law -- as everybody knows how a bill becomes a law, is that, in order to make action and policy permanent, you need to work with Congress. That's why he's also proposed a COVID relief package, a big, bold package. Some say very big -- I agree with that -- and also an immigration bill. He has not -- he has not held back or delayed putting forth legislation either. So, he is going to use the levers that every president in history has used, executive actions. But he also feels it is important to work Congress, and not just one party, but both parties to get things done. Go ahead in the back. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: Thank you, Jen. A couple of questions. One technical question on the E.O. signed today. Does the --does the E.O. on ACA open the marketplace to noncitizens, to legal residents or undocumented immigrants that may be able to benefit from the extra care? PSAKI: It doesn't change the requirements for qualifying for the Affordable Care Act. It opens it up for three months for people who would be already eligible for the Affordable Care Act. So -- but, obviously, there are -- you know, the Health and Human Services team will continue to look for ways to expand access. I will say -- you didn't ask this, but this is a common question, so I'm just going to proactively answer it -- that we do feel, as an administration, that ensuring that all people in the United States, undocumented immigrants as well, of course, should receive access to a vaccine, because that one is morally right, but also ensures that people in the country are also safe. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: And that was my second question. PSAKI: Oh, all right, good. (CROSSTALK) UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: How are you guiding the states -- PSAKI: Actually, yes. OK. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: How are you guiding the states? PSAKI: It's a common one. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: Yes. How are you guiding the states, if any -- in any way to get those undocumented communities to come forward to get vaccinated? Many of them in the states just don't have any way to prove that they're residents of those states in order to go to their local clinics and prove residency to get the vaccine. So, how are you working with the states to get that done? PSAKI: It's challenging. We have talked about this a little bit in here. I mean, there's obviously vaccine hesitancy, which certainly exists in communities of undocumented immigrants and the concern of what it will mean for their status. And -- but we are focused on ensuring we get the vaccine out broadly into communities across the country, because that will make the American people safer. And it's something we have to be both creative about, aggressive about, ambitious about. It's one of the reasons we need additional funding through the American Rescue Plan, but one -- also one of the reasons why we plan to have an aggressive public education campaign to help embolden and empower local doctors and authorities. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: Let me ask one more on Cuba. Do you guys plan on starting -- walking back all of those restrictions that were put into place under the Trump administration, after the Obama administration had opened things up with Cuba? PSAKI: Well, our Cuba policy is governed by two principles. First, support for democracy and human rights. That will be at the core of our efforts. Second is Americans, especially Cuban Americans, are the best ambassadors for freedom in Cuba. So, we'll review the Trump administration policies, as we are in a number of other areas of national security, with an eye to assure -- ensuring that our approach is aligned with that. But, you know, we will take our own path. I don't -- I don't have anything to predict for you at this point in time. Go ahead, (INAUDIBLE). UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: I wanted to clarify something. You talked a little bit about the administration's stance on school re-openings yesterday. PSAKI: Sure. (CROSSTALK) PSAKI: I wasn't -- I wasn't really clear on that. So, I got a little better information. (LAUGHTER) UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: (INAUDIBLE) indicated that he believes, that the administration believes that schools need more funding for them to be safe enough to reopen for students to go back. But there's been a number of studies, including the recent one out of the CDC, that have shown evidence that schools are perfectly safe for students to go back. And there were recommendations that they should go back. So, this seems like a bit of a dispute between teachers' unions and sort of data and the science. So, where does the administration stand in that dispute? PSAKI: Well, first, let me be absolutely clear. President Biden wants schools to open and he wants them to stay open, because it's obviously very disruptive for families -- I'm a mother -- you know, for anyone has kids, for kids to come in and out of school. But that means making sure, as you said, that every school is able to have the equipment and resources to open safely, not just rural schools or private schools, which often is where a lot of the school re-openings and schools staying open is happening. It's more of a challenge in public schools, where they don't have that funding from tuition or smaller populations, where it's easier to put in place the actions needed to keep the schools open. But the CDC study, which I know has gotten a lot -- received a lot of attention, was based on kind of an area that was more rural in Wisconsin. It was not -- and I think what Dr. Walensky has said is that -- I think she said this on CNN last night -- is that for areas where they are more populated, where schools where there is a lot more foot traffic, that there are going to need to be a lot of steps put in place in order to make the schools reopening safe. But we are committed to doing that. That's why the President signed an executive order last week supporting the safe reopening of schools. It requires the Departments of Education and CDC to provide evidence- based guidance. So, that will include things like testing, smaller class sizes, more ventilation, better cleaning, PPE, strong state and local public health guidance. But we want to provide that clarity from the federal government, because there's a lot of confusion. And public schools especially don't know what steps they need to take, how to ensure they're safe. Those are all decisions that are going to be made locally. But we want to give them the guidance. That's in process. Our team is working on that, Dr. Walensky at the CDC and our health experts. And we hope to have more specifics soon. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: Maybe two more questions. PSAKI: Go ahead. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: So, Americans' savings rate is -- has been up throughout the pandemic. And so, I'm wondering, why give all Americans a $1,400 check? And why not means test for the relief that your administration is talking about? PSAKI: Well, first, the proposed checks, I mean, the -- have the same criteria as the package that received broad bipartisan support in December, right? So, approximately, the $1,400 checks would go to families making approximately $150,000 a year. There's a scaling up, as I think you're referencing, up to about $300,000. I think you all are aware of this, but just for everybody else. And, you know, there has been some questions about that. President Biden, our economic team, we're open to discussing that. But we want to ensure that the families that need relief, that need assistance get it. And I would say, at a time where we saw the economic data today -- and this was reflected in Brian Deese's statement -- it was worse than any week -- I don't want to misquote myself here -- that we saw during the Great Recession. I mean, people are suffering. Thousands -- millions of people are out of work. People don't know how to put food on the table. These challenges are real. We -- the data shows it, but we also see long lines for food pantries. We see, you know, people who are out of work and don't know what they're going to do to make ends meet. And so that's tangible. That's real. And we want the package -- the package is going to need to be big and bold to address that. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: And then since we have been talking about women's health and access to abortion today, does the administration plan to suspend the requirement that the medication abortion pill be picked up in person? I know that that's something that advocates have been pushing for after the reversal under the Trump administration. PSAKI: Yes, I have certainly seen some reporting and questions about that. I will have to talk to our health team about that specifically. KRAHENBUHL: Can I ask one more about the travel restrictions? PSAKI: Sure. Go ahead. And, Kaitlan, then I will go to you. (CROSSTALK) KRAHENBUHL: A lot of our viewers are asking if there will be any kind of consideration for waivers for students or unmarried couple like fiances, since there is now the requirement for testing and quarantine? PSAKI: Well, I know there's been a lot of coverage of this and questions, because this is -- these are people's lives and human beings who are missing their loved ones and their family members. And just to restate what the requirements are now, so spouses of American citizens and lawful permanent residents are able to travel under these restrictions we have put in place on international travel, although they have to take part in the mandatory pre-departure testing that applies to everyone. And we are reviewing and assessing, I should say, how students and unmarried couples -- and how we can proceed with that moving forward. I don't have anything to preview for you. But we're certainly -- our team is looking into that. KRAHENBUHL: (INAUDIBLE) criteria. Why countries with high numbers like Russia or India or Mexico are not on the list? PSAKI: Well, our health and medical team takes a close look at what restrictions we need to put in place in order to keep the American people safe. And that's how we review it. It's not about geopolitics. It was at times in the prior administration. That's not how we approach things. It's about where we need to put restrictions in place to keep the American people safe. I promised Kaitlan she would get the next one. KAITLAN COLLINS, CHIEF WHITE HOUSE CORRESPONDENT, CNN: So, just to get some clarification on the CDC study about schools being good to reopen if precautions are taking, is the White House position that it needs to be further studied, since you're citing just the one school in Wisconsin, or does the White House agree with the recommendations from the CDC about schools reopening? PSAKI: Well, the CDC hasn't issued the formal recommendations or requirements on how all schools across the country can open.
