Source telling Fox Business, the director of the agency's Office of Vaccine Research and Review, and her deputy director resigned after the Biden administration went ahead with the booster program starting the week of September 20th without FDA approval. Idaho's Republican governor is calling in 220 medical workers available through federal programs and mobilizing 150 Idaho National Guard soldiers to deal with overwhelmed state hospitals. Governor Brad Little says the moves are a last-ditch effort at avoiding -- to avoid activating for the first time statewide crisis standards of care that could force medical professionals to decide who lives and who dies. Yesterday, Governor Little said there were only four adult ICU beds still available in the state of Idaho. State officials in Georgia say more residents are being diagnosed with COVID than ever before. Georgia's rolling seven-day average for positive tests rose more than 9,600 per day Tuesday. That tops the previous high from January. Meantime in Texas, the Texas law banning most abortions in the state is now in effect. Opponents have asked the U.S. Supreme Court to intervene. Fox News chief legal correspondent, anchor of "FOX NEWS @ NIGHT" Shannon Bream joins us from New York with the latest. Good evening, Shannon. Where does this request with the Supreme Court stand right now? SHANNON BREAM, FOX NEWS CHANNEL ANCHOR (on camera): Well, Brett, it's a bit of a wait and see at this point. It is true that inaction by the Supreme Court meeting it didn't issue anything in response to a request to block the law before it went into effect today means just that, it's now in effect. BREAM (voice-over): The initial request to block it went to Justice Alito. Now, that's solely based on geography. He can decide this alone or refer to the full court. He did ask the opposing side to file a response to the emergency request. They did that yesterday, along with a final reply by the abortion clinics and groups seeking to block the law. So, those of us who watch the court thought, hey, there's a good chance we get an order or decision before midnight last night. Both sides of the abortion debate are now standing by. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: What we're seeing in Texas is frankly, chaos. Patients are scared. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: We've already seen an uptick in the number of pregnant women seeking assistance going to pregnancy resource centers because abortion clinics in Texas have announced that they can no longer offer abortions after six weeks. (END VIDEO CLIP) BREAM (on camera): So, just because it didn't happen -- I was getting something for the Supreme Court, doesn't mean we might not still get something from them, Bret. I'm glued to my phone. BAIER: Yes. You know, obviously, it's controversial, but what are the critic's main objects -- objections to this bill? And really, what are the odds it survives legal scrutiny? BREAM: Yes, well, it bans most abortions in Texas after six weeks. But it's this enforcement mechanism that is getting the real attention because it allows average private citizens to sue abortion providers or those who assist in an illegal abortion, they can recover a minimum of $10,000 in damages plus their attorney's fees. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) UNIDENTIFIED MALE: Private citizens enforce the law. The government has no role in enforcing it. So basically, every Texas citizen is now a private attorney general. (END VIDEO CLIP) BREAM: President Biden now says that the law he thinks is blatantly violating the constitution. And he calls this private citizen component of it, outrageous. It's definitely unique. So, we'll see how it stands up under scrutiny. BAIER: Yes, a lot of pro-life groups have been planning different aspects of this. How does this fit in with that strategy, number of red states making a run at overturning Roe v. Wade? BREAM: Yes, over the last couple of years, a number of states have passed laws that many elected officials are openly saying or specifically about trying to overturn Roe v. Wade. Nearly all of them immediately entangled in legal proceedings. BREAM (voice-over): And now everyone is watching and waiting for this case over Mississippi's law to be argued at the Supreme Court this fall. That law bans nearly all abortions in the state after 15 weeks. And no matter how the case is decided, it's likely that the underlying issue for the most part is going to revert to the states. BREAM (on camera): Many of them already passed laws saying that the right to abortion is secured. Now, others have these so-called, trigger laws. Meaning, if the actual underpinning of Roe v. Wade is overturned, there will be no right to an abortion in those states. This court, as we know, under the guidance of Chief Justice John Roberts has been reticent to issue, big sweeping decisions. I'd expect most likely whatever comes down from that Mississippi case could be very narrow. Bret. BAIER: We will see if you get a ruling before "FOX NEWS @ NIGHT". See you then. BREAM: We'll let you know. BAIER: "BREAKING TONIGHT", a manhunt has concluded in North Carolina after a student was killed in a shooting at a high school in Winston Salem. The Forsyth County Sheriff's Office just tweeting the shooting occurred around noon at Mount Tabor High School. The sheriff says the suspect is now in custody. Up next we go live to Louisiana to check on the devastation from Hurricane Ida. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) UNIDENTIFIED MALE: Absolutely the worst storm I've ever seen. I hope I don't see another one. Not like this. South Louisiana in a whole is destroyed. (END VIDEO CLIP) (COMMERCIAL BREAK) BAIER: The remnants of Hurricane Ida are causing problems in the East tonight. 20 homes knocked off their foundations in Western Virginia. Heavy rain pouring down from the central Appalachians to New England. Meanwhile, the devastation is keeping many people in Louisiana from returning to their homes and huge numbers are still without power tonight. President Biden will travel to the region on Friday. Senior correspondent Mike Tobin is in Metairie, Louisiana tonight. Good evening, Mike. MIKE TOBIN, FOX NEWS CHANNEL SENIOR CORRESPONDENT (on camera): Good evening, Bret. That food distribution point is one of 17 operated by the National Guard in eight different parishes across Louisiana. At last tally, the guard had given out almost a quarter-million meals ready to eat, 300,000 boxes of water, and almost 20,000 Tarbes (PH). This, as the Gulf Coast is on the long hot miserable road back to normal. TOBIN (voice-over): Countless communities along the Gulf Coast and further inland face days, weeks, and months of rebuilding. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) UNIDENTIFIED MALE: Coming to a third world country, no water, no gas, no lights. TOBIN: On the barrier island of Grand Isle, around half the homes were destroyed by Hurricane Ida. SCOOTER RESWEBER, POLICE CHIEF, GRAND ISLE, LOUISIANA: In my neighborhood, I lost my home. My grandson lost his home. I have a deputy had lost his home. TOBIN: In New Orleans, officials know they are in a race to restore services to the half of the population that decided not to evacuate. LATOYA CANTRELL , MAYOR OF NEW ORLEANS, LOUISIANA: Primary objectives today are getting our people what they need. We know they need food, water, cool air. TOBIN: With paramedics, firefighters, and EMT responding to call volumes 185 percent above normal, the dusk to dawn curfew began yesterday will remain in place until further notice. SHAUN FERGUSON, POLICE CHIEF, NEW ORLEANS: So, it is totally unsafe. And I would like to encourage each and everyone to please remain calm and vigilant. TOBIN: But progress is happening. A small number of residents finally getting power turned back on. DEANNA RODRIGUEZ, PRESIDENT, ENTERGY, NEW ORLEANS: Lights came on around 1:02 a.m. And this is the first step, again, in returning to normal. TOBIN: Shortages continued throughout the regions. Even for blood, this donation center in Baton Rouge has less than a day supply in the shelves and some transfusions have already been delayed. ALEX COHEN, PLASMA DONOR: Well, everybody has got to do their part. I mean, these tough times right now. TOBIN: And help from across America is also ramping up fast. Donations are piling up in places like Atlantic Beach, North Carolina where locals know exactly what folks further south are going through. CASEY, ARTHUR, DEPUTY CHIEF, ATLANTIC BEACH FIRE DEPARTMENT: I know how I felt when we started receiving items after Hurricane Isabel. It really meant a lot to me to just see that people cared and that we were not alone in the situation. (END VIDEO CLIP) TOBIN (on camera): Sheriff Marlin Gusman of Orleans Parish tells me, 55 people have been arrested since the storm, most of them for looting or vandalism. But there was a taskforce of guardsmen, sheriff's deputies, and metro police out in the street. And they learn from the mistakes that lead to chaos after Katrina. Bret, back to you. BAIER: Mike Tobin, live in Louisiana. Mike, thanks. We're getting a new look tonight at the damage left behind from Hurricane Ida. This look from the sky. Senior correspondent Casey Stegall is in Baton Rouge tonight. Good evening, Casey. CASEY STEGALL, FOX NEWS CORRESPONDENT: Bret, good evening. We spent the better part of the day up in a Blackhawk helicopter with the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers , and the purpose of the mission was really twofold, to give the top brass of the Corps of Engineers an up close and personal look at the damage, but also to survey the levee system, for example, and get better sense of what specific communities need to help speed up their recovery. Like in LaPlace, they now plan on cutting some of the levees to allow standing water to drain back into Lake Pontchartrain. South of New Orleans in Lafitte they have decided to bring in additional pumps and let gravity pull the water back into the gulf. But one thing is clear -- when you see the damage by the air, it is sobering, because you see stretches of hundreds and hundreds of miles that look like they have been wiped off the map along the southeast Louisiana coast. Row after row of home and businesses blown apart, boats in streets, nearly every power or communication line down and crumbled. It really puts it into perspective and the scope of this disaster, Bret, and that the rover will take weeks, if not months or even years for some people. Back to you. BAIER: Quite a view. Casey Stegall in Baton Rouge. Casey, thanks. Another disaster is growing worse out west. A massive wildfire is threatening thousands of structures in South Lake Tahoe. And that's where we find national correspondent William La Jeunesse tonight. (BEGIN VIDEO TAPE) UNIDENTIFIED MALE: Oh, yes. We don't want to go any further. WILLIAM LA JEUNESSE, FOX NEWS NATIONAL CORRESPONDENT: High winds, a record drought. The Caldor fire turning this California playground into a ghost town. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: So I promised my kid I would be out of here as soon as I saw any flames anywhere. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: I'm hoping at some point I can just nab that cat and be out of here like a shot. LA JEUNESSE: And 53,000 forced to evacuate, some now sheltering in tents, others fill California and Nevada hotels. JIM DUDLEY, METEOROLOGIST: We are in red flag conditions. And those red flag conditions are for low relative humidity and strong gusty winds, especially up over the ridges. LA JEUNESSE: Over the past 18 days, the Caldor fire burned more than 300 square miles and 544 homes. Moving west to east, firefighters struggle to keep it south of the homes and businesses around Lake Tahoe. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: I'm getting out as soon as I secure this area, which is my business. As soon as I secure it, I'm getting out of here. LA JEUNESSE: Tahoe is America's largest alpine lake, pristine waters surrounded by pines, clean mountain air now a billowing blanket of ash stretching hundreds of miles. DAVE LAUCHNER, SACRAMENTO FIRE DEPARTMENT: Basically, a flame or an ember lands on the dry brush, and it ignites. It's not stopping it. LA JEUNESSE: Torching pine needles in an overgrown forest that hasn't burned in decades, add in 40 mile-per-hour winds, you get this. STEVE VOLLMER, FIRE BEHAVIOR ANALYST: They create what's called an active crown fire run where the fire actually goes from treetop to treetop. When it does that, those ember casts that it throws out are going over a mile in distance. LA JEUNESSE: Containment lines held overnight, giving crews optimism the fire could spare the Tahoe Basin. STEVE SISOLAK , (D) NEVADA GOVERNOR: We are usually all of our resources, everything we have at our disposal, coordinating closely with CalFire. (END VIDEO TAPE) LA JEUNESSE: So winds are expected to improve tonight and tomorrow, but big picture, California has a problem. Six of the states' seven largest fires ever have burned in the last 12 months. And southern California's Santa Ana fire season is just starting, Bret, which is one reason why every national forest in California is closed for the next two weeks. BAIER: La Jeunesse live in South Lake Tahoe. William, thanks. Up next, where are all the refugees from Afghanistan going? We'll take you to one of the processing centers next. (COMMERCIAL BREAK) BAIER: Refugees from Afghanistan are passing through the massive U.S. military complex in Germany tonight. Senior foreign affairs correspondent Greg Palkot reports from Ramstein Air Base. (BEGIN VIDEO TAPE) GREG PALKOT, FOX NEWS SENIOR FOREIGN AFFAIRS CORRESPONDENT: The flights out of Kabul might be finished, but the evacuation of Afghan refugees continues through the major transit hub of Ramstein Air Base in Germany. Some 15,000 are now here, grateful to be out of the clutches of the Taliban , but, in the wake of the U.S. withdrawal, concerned about those left behind. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: We have history with the Taliban . We saw them once before. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: My whole family are there, and I'm worried about them a lot. PALKOT: You are looking at what has been the workhorse of this Afghanistan evacuation, massive C-17 cargo plane. On average it's been bringing out something like 450 people, one flight in the early days brought out over 800. In the latest 12 hour period, 1,800 people have come from other bases. After being checked out, they fly to the States on chartered commercial flights. CAPT. JAMES DIMMICK, 8TH AIRLIFT SQUADRON: It's been pretty much nonstop. We have been running 24 hours every day of the week so far, just getting as many people in and out of here as we possibly can. PALKOT: Have you ever handled this size of operation with so many moving parts? DIMMICK: I've never seen anything like this in my entire life. PALKOT: And like the service members injured in last week's terror attack, some come back in bad shape. That's when the military turns C-17s into intensive care units. On board one mission to Kabul, Major Joshua Thomas, he says they handle it all. MAJ. JOSHUA THOMAS, 10TH EAEF, RAMSTEIN AIR BASE: From battle injuries, blast injuries, gunshot wounds, just regular medical illnesses. PALKOT: This week basically marks the end of the U.S. war in Afghanistan. Some at Ramstein has been through it all. Despite the debate, service members are convinced they are doing the right thing. Was it all worth it? LT. COL. ELIZABETH DWYER, CRITICAL CARE PHYSICIAN: Absolutely. PALKOT: All worth it. Saving lives? DWYER: That's what we do. (END VIDEO TAPE) PALKOT: Saving lives, that's what we do. One officer at the base told us their part of the mission could go on for days, a lot of lives hanging in the balance. Bret? BAIER: Greg Palkot in Germany. Greg, thanks. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) JOE LIEBERMAN, FORMER CONNECTICUT SENATOR: I'm disappointed and I think we're all going to pay for it, first of all, the people of Afghanistan. But we, too, because there's no question, notwithstanding all the sweet talk from some of the Taliban leaders, that's not who they are. They are a radical Islamist terrorist group, and they're going to welcome other radical Islamist terrorist groups to Afghanistan who will aim to strike us from there as Al-Qaeda did on 9/11. It's just tragic and totally unnecessary. (END VIDEO CLIP) BAIER: Former Democratic vice presidential nominee, former Senator Joe Lieberman, talking about the situation now in Afghanistan. Let's bring in our panel, Mollie Hemingway, senior editor at "The Federalist," Leslie Marshall, Democratic strategist, and Bill McGurn, columnist for "The Wall Street Journal." Bill, let me start with you. Your thought? "The Wall Street Journal" had a really scathing editorial today about this situation, but a lot of lawmakers up on Capitol Hill on both sides of the aisle have been very critical of this administration messaging and action. BILL MCGURN, COLUMNIST, "THE WALL STREET JOURNAL": Yes, I think it's not just the messaging. It's the reality. We've just surrendered 9/11 forever to the Islamic jihadists. It is now a double victory celebration for them. First, the original Al-Qaeda strike on America, and second the Taliban victory that we see right now in Kabul. It just seems to me we are back to that pre-9/11 thinking. Remember when people used to say Al-Qaeda was at war with us long before we were at war with Al-Qaeda. And I think Joe Biden 's spin that somehow the world watches the spectacle of us leaving fellow Americans behind enemy lines and concludes that America has greater resolve and greater capabilities going forward is just farcical. BAIER: And Leslie, the State Department conceding today that most of the SIVs, most of the Afghans who helped the U.S. in the war, actually did not get out, and the numbers are pretty staggering. Here is the State Department on the safe passage that they are trying to coordinate right now. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) VICTORIA NULAND, UNDER SECRETARY OF STATE: We are looking at all possible options, air routes, land routes, to continue to find ways for them to help evacuate. And to support them in that, we're trying to ascertain who precisely still wants to leave, who their dependent family members are, what routes may or may not feel comfortable to them. NED PRICE, STATE DEPARTMENT SPOKESMAN: Half the world's countries, all of the most important stakeholders have signed on to the idea that the Taliban must uphold their commitments of safe passage. (END VIDEO CLIP) BAIER: It's just tough to believe that that's going to be smooth sailing with the Taliban knowing their history, Leslie. LESLIE MARSHALL, DEMOCRATIC STRATEGIST: Well, if we just look at what is happening with the Taliban , Bret, I think I mentioned on your podcast, the problem here is not only are they an uneducated group of men that run the Taliban , but the Taliban is used to running a terrorist organization, and running a country is very different. They could be without food in a couple of weeks. They don't have air traffic control. They have people landing right now as we speak from Qatar to try and handle that so that they can open commercial airways in two days, and hopefully more people, including those Afghans that assisted us here in the United States and abroad, can get out. Look, left and right, I have said it before, we should have started this earlier. We should not leave until everyone that we can help is out, is out. But we also do have to look at other realities. The State Department since April gave numerous warnings, over a dozen warnings to Americans to get out. In addition to that, everyone knew the Taliban was going to be in power, quite frankly. And I think it's the United States and all of our allies, especially the United States knew. The former administration, former Secretary of State Pompeo sat down with the Taliban , not with the president of Afghanistan. They knew who was going to be the new sheriff in town, sadly. So, it's messy right now. I certainly hope and pray that won't be the case going forward. And one last thing. Even though we can't trust them, Bret, no question, they need money from us and from others. And if we say we want a and then you get b, they might be apt to do it. BAIER: They also have hosted, obviously, radical Islamic terrorists, Al- Qaeda, others. They say they are fighting ISIS-K, but it's really a witches' brew there, Mollie. What about the who knew what when, and this leaked Reuters report, the transcript from this call between President Biden and the Afghan president Ghani? MOLLIE HEMINGWAY, SENIOR EDITOR, "THE FEDERALIST": Yes, we impeached a president for a phone call, and now we have this leak of phone call that President Biden had where he asked someone to lie in exchange for military support. It sounds like something that last year would have caused major problems for the previous president. I think we cannot lose sight of how we can never fight a war like this ever again. There was a Pew poll last week that showed that Americans are broadly supportive of the departure from Afghanistan. That's the Trump policy that Biden supported. They have even more agreement that the manner in which we fought this war was a failure. You don't see people talking about World War II the way we talk about this war. This war has been prosecuted poorly, according to the American people, for decades. And then there is even more agreement that the manner in which Biden departed was a complete debacle. That's not really up for debate. It was a debacle. It was a national humiliation and a disgrace. And the proper response to that is to clean out our military like we did after Bay of Pigs and make sure that people are replaced with people who know how to do their jobs. Unfortunately, the current president who was involved in this phone call is incompetent and unable to replace the military leadership who failed. And so it remains to the American people in their elections to replace him and the woke generals who cannot do basic jobs like winning wars or exiting a country. BAIER: All right, strong letter to follow. Up next, the panel on the Texas abortion law. (COMMERCIAL BREAK) (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) JEN PSAKI , WHITE HOUSE PRESS SECRETARY: The president's focus is to reiterate our deep commitment to the constitutional right, of course established by Roe v Wade nearly five decades ago, and to continue to call for the codification of Roe. (END VIDEO CLIP) BAIER: Jen Psaki following up, talking about this Texas abortion law now in effect. The president put out a statement today, says "This extreme Texas law blatantly violates the constitutional right established under Roe v. Wade and upheld as precedent for nearly half a century. Outrageously, it deputizes private citizens to bring lawsuits against anyone who they believe has helped another person get an abortion, which might even include family members, healthcare workers, front desk staff at a healthcare clinic, or strangers with no connection to the individual." And in fact, if you look at the bullet points, that is accurate. The state doesn't enforce it. Citizens can sue providers in any way involved in aiding or abetting an abortion after heartbeat is detected, and, again, six weeks here. Citizen plaintiffs are entitled to $10,000 plus legal fees if they win. We're back with the panel. Bill, this seems designed to be part of the challenge to Roe in the Supreme Court. MCGURN: Yes, it is part of -- it is a challenge, like many challenges, to the Supreme Court. But it poses a lot of legal questions on procedural ground that haven't been at the courts before. And, again, the pro-choice side is trying to get the court, that's their favorite legislature, just to dismiss it early on. They may still do it. But if they were going to do it, you would have thought it would have went into effect before today. I'm hoping -- I believe it's both a moral and constitutional victory if we get this back to the states. If we want to codify Roe, let the states do it as New York has done it. But look, the existing regime is just out of touch with the American people. The American people want limits. The Democratic Party has been able to oppose those limits because it's been done so undemocratically. I am with Justice Scalia. The Supreme Court has no business umpiring the abortion business, and they should get out of it. We would be a lot healthier, and we would return that debate to the states where it belongs. BAIER: Leslie, it seems like this administration would want to go through Congress to codify Roe, but there is no way the numbers are anywhere close to being there. MARSHALL: No, but what's really concerning here, Bret, is not only the constitutional violation of the rights of anyone with a uterus in the state of Texas, but when you just look deeper at this law, if you are a 13-year- old rape victim and you don't realize you are pregnant because you don't have a regular menstrual cycle and you come in after six weeks, you're going to be forced to carry that child. Speaking of rape, a rapist could actually sue their victim and get $10,000 if they feel that individual is trying to abort that child outside the six- week limit. And to Bill's point, you know, the American people are not looking for a six-week limit on abortion. When you look at the majority of polls out there, the majority of people in the United States support Roe v Wade, and even if they call themselves pro-life, support a woman's right to choose. Most Americans don't want, myself included, long-term abortions. Six weeks is not late term. BAIER: Mollie? HEMINGWAY: Yes, the Texas legislature passed this law that protects children who have a detectable heartbeat. And this is important that this was allowed to stand even this long because that's what Roe v Wade took away from people was the right of people to determine their own view -- what the state law should be on abortion. But the Supreme Court has a history of having had bad decisions. Roe v Wade is just one of the noteworthy bad decisions that takes an entire class of humans and dehumanizes them. And so it is incumbent upon the court to correct mistakes like that, like they did after the Dred Scott decision or Korematsu or Roe v. Wade. And they have an excellent opportunity with this case that has risen to the Supreme Court level this year with Dobbs to correct some of these problems. We have a radical abortion regime. It is violent oppression of women and their children. It is predatory, and it's just not what humans should do to each other. And we have an opportunity to allow it to come back to the states where people can set appropriate limits and protect these unborn children and their mothers. BAIER: We'll see what the court does. We'll be following it. It could happen tonight. Thanks, panel. When we come back, more of the panel with tomorrow's headlines. (COMMERCIAL BREAK) BAIER: Finally tonight, a look at tomorrow's headlines with the panel. Mollie, first to you. HEMINGWAY: Democrats continue to fight one another as they oppose the nomination by Biden of Obama's former chief of staff Rahm Emanuel to be the ambassador to Japan. BAIER: OK, we will follow that. Leslie? MARSHALL: Larry Elder, who is running in the California gubernatorial election, has a come to Jesus moment and gets out, saying talk show hosts shouldn't be running a big state in the midst of a pandemic. BAIER: I don't think that one is happening, but we are going to look into it tomorrow. All right, Bill. MCGURN: Joe Biden gives us a preview of his 9/11 speech. Despite everything you have seen with your own eyes, I have made no mistakes, and the retreat from Afghanistan was in fact the biggest American military victory since the Normandy landing. BAIER: All right, panel, thank you very much. Tomorrow on SPECIAL REPORT, we'll get the latest on the efforts to get Americans out of Afghanistan, plus, good timing, an update on the California governor recall, September 14th, Californians already voting. We will lay it all out for you and explain it. Thanks for inviting us into your home tonight. That's it for the SPECIAL REPORT, fair, balanced, and still unafraid. headline: Concerns Over Americans And Allies Left In Afghanistan; Unclear Guidance For Those Stuck In Afghanistan; U.S. Relationship With Taliban Unclear After War Ends; Hurricane Ida Devastates Parts of Louisiana; Some Republicans Call for Impeach or Resignation of President Biden over Military Withdrawal from Afghanistan
story_text: DAGEN MCDOWELL, FOX NEWS HOST: Alienate all your girlfriends before they get married so you don`t have to be in the wedding. SPECIAL REPORT is up next. Hi, Bret. BRET BAIER, FOX NEWS ANCHOR: Hi, Dagen, thank you. Good evening. Welcome to Washington. I`m Bret Baier. Breaking tonight, growing concern about Americans and those who helped Americans still stranded in Afghanistan, as anecdotes of new Taliban atrocities are filtering out of that country. The Biden administration is trying its best to turn the page from the issue that is fueling accusations of broken promises from the president. We`ll take a closer look at that in a few minutes. Also tonight, dozens of Republicans are now calling for the president`s impeachment over his actions and this phone call with the Afghan president before the fall of Kabul. But impeachment is something the top GOP senator says will not happen. White House Correspondent Jacqui Heinrich starts us off tonight, live in the North Lawn. Good evening, Jacqui. JACQUI HEINRICH, FOX NEWS CORRESPONDENT (on camera): Good evening, Bret. On the third day since the troop withdrawal, no answer on whether any more Americans have made it out of Afghanistan or how many Green Card holders or SIV applicants remain. The White House is directing those questions to other departments. And there`s a distinct feeling President Biden is trying to move on from Afghanistan to his domestic agenda. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) JOE BIDEN , PRESIDENT OF THE UNITED STATES: There`s a lot of damage. HEINRICH (voice over): President Biden addressed the nation about storm recovery but gave no update on Afghanistan and took no questions from reporters as more than a hundred Americans and countless at-risk Afghans who helped the U.S. in the 20-year war remain behind enemy lines. JEN PSAKI , WHITE HOUSE PRESS SECRETARY: There are people who are eligible, we may not even know they`re eligible yet, right? It is very hard to define those numbers. HEINRICH: Meanwhile, accounts of reprisals those Afghans face are getting more dire. This person said they killed 12 members of special forces in Kandahar, three soldiers in Jalalabad as well. The Taliban took them out of their homes and shot them. Given this kind of reporting or hearing, is it possible that our reliance on the Taliban to keep their word in terms of our evacuation is misplaced, we`re going back on things like the amnesty promise? PSAKI: No one is saying from the federal government, no one. The president, Secretary of Defense, no one from the Intelligence Community that the Taliban are good actors. That is one of the reasons we are being so clear that we are not rushing to recognition. HEINRICH: Politico reports shame among anonymous sources inside the White House. One person telling Politico, I am absolutely appalled and literally horrified we left Americans there. Kabul`s airport remains inoperable and the White House says there are risks associated with charter flights seeking to extract Americans to U.S. military basis. PSAKI: We do not have reliable means to confirm the basic details of charter flights including who may be organizing them. We know ISIS-K has a keen interest in attacks against aviation targets and our personnel on the ground and our Air Force in our military bases. HEINRICH: Among the House GOP, growing calls for the president to resign but the top Senate Republican Mitch McConnell says President Biden will not be impeached and the ballot box is a better place to hold him accountable. (END VIDEO CLIP) HEINRICH (on camera): Still, other Republican senators want accountability now. 25 members wrote to President Biden saying while they disagree on whether troops should have remained in Afghanistan, they`re all in agreement President Biden`s chaotic withdrawal caused this crisis, Bret. BAIER: Jacqui, obviously, the administration, the president want to focus on domestic agenda items, but you have this human infrastructure bill that`s kind of sitting out there, the 3.5 trillion, a key Senate Democrat is pretty much blocking that path. HEINRICH: That`s right. West Virginia Senator Joe Manchin said there is no way he will support that $3.5 trillion social infrastructure package that Democrats want to pass along party lines. He dragged his colleagues for what he called a strange belief, there`s an infinite amount of money to go around. He wrote, Democratic congressional leaders proposed to pass the largest single spending bill in history with no regard to rising inflation, crippling debt, or the inevitability of future crises. Ignoring the fiscal consequences of our policy choices will create a disastrous future for the next generation of Americans. Without Manchin`s vote, Biden`s agenda really seems to go nowhere and it appears that Manchin is dug in, Bret. BAIER: All right, we`ll follow that. Jacqui, thank you. We`re hearing tonight from an Afghan interpreter who helped save then- Senator Biden 13 years ago and is now pleading for rescue himself. That man and his family are joined by as we mentioned, Americans and thousands of Afghans who helped the U.S. through the 20 years of war who today still cannot leave that country. Correspondent Griff Jenkins has the story. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) NED PRICE , STATE DEPARTMENT SPOKESMAN: We will provide them a tailored guidance but that is not something we will provide to all of you. And we won`t do that for their safety. GRIFF JENKINS, FOX NEWS CORRESPONDENT (voice over): For those stuck behind enemy lines, the plan to get them out is unclear. With the Kabul airport shut down, dangerous ground routes appear to be the only option. The State Department also won`t say if any American citizens have gotten out since the last flight out of Kabul on August 30th. Leaving behind 100 to 200 Americans, tens of thousands of Afghan allies, including the majority of SIV applicants, and even the State Department`s own journalists. Also, among those stranded, an interpreter known as Mohammed, who helped rescue then-Senator Joe Biden in 2008 when his helicopter made an emergency landing in the snow-covered mountains of Afghanistan. BIDEN: If you want to know where Al-Qaeda lives, you want to know where bin Laden is, come back to Afghanistan with me. Come back to the area my helicopter was forced down. JENKINS: Unable to get out before the deadline, Mohammed is now pleading for President Biden to save him and his family. MOHAMMED, AFGHAN INTERPRETER: Maybe die at home. There is no way I can`t escape from my house. All borders in my country are sealed, but only I and my -- and my son have a U.S. passport. The rest of the family do not have. JENKINS: The State Department`s other focus is resettling and vetting the tens of thousands of refugees arriving on American soil amid growing concerns that individuals were extremists could slip through the cracks. State Department spokesman Ned Price says there`s a plan for those who get flagged. PRICE: In cases where that vetting may take longer, we do have options available to us. But I`m just not in a position to detail. JENKINS: This as a new diplomatic mission for Afghanistan, headquartered in Doha must decide how they will work with as soon to be formed Taliban government and if they can trust them. (END VIDEO CLIP) JENKINS: And Bret, any moment now, we expect Secretary of State Antony Blinken to arrive here to the Dulles Expo Center behind me. It`s one of the major processing centers for arriving refugees as State Department says that more than 31,000 of the total 124,000 people evacuated have made it to the U.S. soil with about 77 percent of those being at risk Afghans, Bret. BAIER: Griff Jenkins in Chantilly, Virginia. Griff, thanks. The shockwaves continued tonight over the admission by the nation`s top military officer that the U.S. may actually have to cooperate with the Taliban in counterterrorism operations. The terror group is solidifying its control over Afghanistan tonight. National security correspondent Jennifer Griffin is at the Pentagon. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) JENNIFER GRIFFIN, FOX NEWS NATIONAL SECURITY CORRESPONDENT (voice over): Taliban fighters took on the role of the police in Kabul today helping with traffic at checkpoints and issuing a statement like this one urging calm. AMANULLAH, TALIBAN BARDI SPECIAL FORCES: Everyone should go to work and live. Offices, shops and companies should start operating and have no fear of anyone. GRIFFIN: Pentagon leaders raised eyebrows when asked Wednesday about working with the Taliban in the future. GEN. MARK MILLEY, CHAIRMAN, JOINT CHIEFS OF STAFF: In war, you do what you must in order to reduce risk to mission and force, not what you necessarily want to do. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: Any possibility of coordination against ISIS-K with them? Milley: It`s possible. GRIFFIN: Dan Hoffman, a former CIA Chief of Station spent years hunting Al Qaeda and says such an intelligence relationship would be complicated. DAN HOFFMAN, FORMER CHIEF OF STATION, CIA: We would need to corroborate everything the Taliban is telling us on our own before we would launch any strikes. And whatever information we provided to them, we`d have to be very careful that they are not going to take it and then go out and conduct operations which violate human rights of innocent civilians. GRIFFIN: Former Defense Secretary William Cohen explained how the U.S. could leverage the Taliban`s need for U.S. Intelligence. WILLIAM COHEN , FORMER DEFENSE SECRETARY: They may come under severe attack from Al-Qaeda and from ISIS-K or ISIS-Z. They`ll need intelligence that they don`t have that we may be able to provide them under certain conditions. GRIFFIN: A difficult reality for the 800,000 veterans of the past 20 years and Gold Star families like this one, the last American soldier to die in Afghanistan, Staff Sergeant Ryan Knauss. He died of his wounds after the suicide bombing at Abbey Gate. His wife Elena was tiling her shower floor when she received the knock at the door. She told NPR she began screaming, collapsed and then stayed up all night through her tears to put their initials and date in the shower tile floor. ELENA KNAUSS, WIDOW OF STAFF SERGEANT RYAN KNAUSS: I`m in shambles and I`m hurting but that no mother, father, wife, brother, sister ever has to feel such emptiness, I would be grateful to know he was the last. (END VIDEO CLIP) GRIFFIN (on camera): Of the 22 wounded in the Abby Gate attack, we`ve learned that 15 Marines are currently at Walter Reed. One is in critical condition, three are serious and 11 are stable, Bret. BAIER: Jennifer Griffin live at the Pentagon. Jennifer, thank you. At least 43 people have died in the East after massive flooding from record rain fall produced by the remnants of Hurricane Ida. Correspondent Bryan Llenas shows us the devastation tonight from Queens, New York. Good evening, Bryan. BRYAN LLENAS, FOX NEWS CORRESPONDENT (on camera): Bret, good evening. The rainfall in New York City was extraordinary and unprecedented. At least 13 people have died in New York City, 11 of them drowning in their basement apartments like this one behind me. The flash flooding, stunning residents and state officials. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) LLENAS (voice over): Tonight, New York City`s in a state of emergency after a cascading waterfall shut down the city subway trapping train cars and flooding stations Wednesday night. The historic rainfall turned the city`s highways and streets into rivers, forcing first responders to save drivers from trapped vehicles. At least 11 people in the city died in their basement apartments in Queens, New York, including a 2-year-old boy, a mother and her 22-year-old son drowned in this apartment when four feet of water rushed into a gaping hole. AMIT SHIVPRASAD, HOMEOWNER: It was devastating. I can tell you that my body`s still trembling as we talk about this right now. LLENAS: The remnants of Hurricane Ida dumped a historic 10 inches of rain over just several hours in New York City. Central Park saw 3.15 inches of rain in just one hour. Shattering an old-time record set just two weeks ago. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: Look at that tornado. LLENAS: In New Jersey, a tornado ripped through the community of Mullica Hills, destroying an estimated two dozen homes. ASHLEY THOMAS, TORNADO VICTIM: It was like a warzone. LLENAS: Ashley Thomas is eight months pregnant. Bret. BAIER: Peter Doocy in the White House briefing room. Peter, thanks. Earlier in the program, we showed you the horrific damage in the northeast from the remnants of Hurricane Ida. I should add one cultural point -- the very thought that there could still be POWs and MIAs in Vietnam had a profound cultural half-life in this country for a half century. And we are going to be probably hearing stories about Americans and American allies left in Afghanistan for a long time, and I think that is going to have not only just a shameful impact on our reputation around the world, but it is also going to be part of our culture and part of the conversation for a long time to come. The people who wanted to get rid of the colorblindness provision outspent by five to one the people who wanted to keep it. But it won with California voters. In this he was very much like Bill Clinton who was just create stories about things that he did and places he had been that he never was when he was in his 40s. And Joe Biden is very much like that. SHELLENBERGER: Yes, I mean we've seen some pretty outrageous statements over the last 24 hours. There is bipartisan agreement that we need to improve the infrastructure in New York to manage heavy rains. We did that in New Orleans actually after Hurricane Katrina. I mean, if you really wanted to destroy your civilization, you'd put low IQ political extremists in charge of your power grid. Let's hope we don't do that. That's my hope anyway.
