headline: 1.7 Million Migrant Apprehensions In 2021 Fiscal Year; White House Officials Clarify Multiple Biden Comments Made During Live Town Hall; Supreme Court Moves Quickly To Hear Texas Abortion Case; Crew Member Dies After Alec Baldwin Discharges Prop Gun; Warehouse Backups Contributing To Situation; Doctors Use Nonhuman Organ In Transplant; 98,000 On National Wait List For Kidney Transplant; McAuliffe Kicks Off Virginia Bus Tour; Recent Polls Show Tight Race For Virginia Governor; President Biden's Comments On America's Commitment To Defend Taiwan From Attack From China Draw Controversy; President Biden Holds Town Hall On Possibly Supporting Changing Senate Filibuster And U.S. Foreign Policy; Polls Shows Close Race Between Democrat Terry McAuliffe And Republican Glenn Youngkin In Virginia Gubernatorial Election.
story_text: DAGEN MCDOWELL, FOX NEWS CHANNEL HOST: She had a bottle of bourbon in her backpack and I had two cans of Seltzer in my sweatpants pockets. JESSICA TARLOV, FOX NEWS CHANNEL CONTRIBUTOR: To see a very important movie though. MCDOWELL: The Silence of the Lambs. LISA KENNEDY MONTGOMERY, FOX NEWS CHANNEL HOST: The Silence of the Lambs 30th anniversary. JESSE WATTERS, FOX NEWS CHANNEL HOST: Wait, you guys drink hard seltzer smuggled to watch Silence of the Lambs together? TARLOV: Maybe. WATTERS: That's crazy. I'll see you guys here on Monday and get to the bottom of it. BRET BAIER, FOX NEWS CHANNEL HOST: Good evening. I'm Bret Baier. Coming to you tonight from Dallas, about 460 miles from the U.S. Mexico border. We will go there live shortly. But breaking tonight, it's official, a record 1.7 million apprehensions of illegal immigrants along the southern border according to just released Customs and Border Patrol statistics. That's in one year. Again, that's the most on record. The next highest number of apprehensions happened 35 years ago. That does not include the hundreds of thousands of so called got-aways that evaded apprehension. The stats paint a dire picture of the border crisis, something former and current border officials have been raising an alarm about for months. This occurs as President Biden says he has been to the border and probably should go back. Fact checkers then went into action after his town hall last night. And today, the White House press secretary attempted to clarify her boss's remarks on the border issue and several others. We have Fox team coverage tonight, Peter Doocy is at the White House with efforts to set the record straight the day after that presidential town hall. But we start off with correspondent Bill Melugin back in La Joya, Texas tonight with staggering new immigration numbers that paint a bleak picture for Border Patrol officials. Good evening, Bill. BILL MELUGIN, FOX NEWS CHANNEL CORRESPONDENT (on camera): Bret, good evening to you. Those numbers are staggering and literally just a couple of minutes ago, you can take a look at our Fox drone right now, we had groups of migrants just come walking right past us right now. They just crossed the Rio Grande and they have officially entered the United States illegally ready to turn themselves in. But late this afternoon, CBP officially released their September encounter numbers for the month of September that were just over 192,000 encounters with migrants here at the southern border. That adds up for the grand total of the 2,021 fiscal year, a staggering 1.73 million, that is an all-time record high, beating the previous high record of 1.69 million back in 1986. This border crisis is making history and it is not slowing down. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) MELUGIN (voice over): Another day, another human smuggling pursuit here at the border. This time, near Del Rio, Texas where DPS troopers give chase. The driver eventually loses control and slams into a parked vehicle, pinning the passengers inside. The driver was arrested and four illegal immigrants inside were turned over to Border Patrol. In Mission, Texas early Friday morning, another suspected human smuggling crash left two people dead and five others hospitalized. Texas DPS tells us a local police department was chasing this vehicle when it rolled over while filled with suspected migrants, two men were ejected and both died on scene. In La Joya Friday morning, we witnessed this group of single adult migrants being taken into custody by Border Patrol. Some of the men were wearing camouflage, something we often see with runners. That includes this group of illegal immigrants arrested by Texas DPS for criminal trespassing on a ranch in Kinney County, all of the men wearing camouflage trying to evade. And in Border Patrols Tucson sector, agents arrested Mexican national Felix Perez-Torres after he crossed illegally. He was previously convicted of felony sexual assault in the State of Wyoming. The vice president of the Border Patrol union tells Fox News it's the hundreds of thousands of illegal immigrants who aren't caught who are the biggest concern. ART DEL CUETO, NATIONAL BORDER PATROL COUNCIL: When you have so much lawlessness going on in the border and you have an administration that pretty much has opened the door for criminal behavior, those that are going that extra step not to get apprehended, not to get detected, what kind of criminal backgrounds do they really have? (END VIDEO CLIP) MELUGIN (on camera): And Bret, that criminal element is constantly trying to make it through the border here. Just here in the Rio Grande Valley alone on Wednesday, Border Patrol reports that just in a matter of a few hours, they arrested three confirmed gang members here after they crossed illegally. That includes two MS-13 gang members, one of whom had homicide charges in the state of New York. The other has a homicide arrest down in El Salvador. We'll send it back to you. BAIER: And Bill, I just want to clarify this, 1.7 million apprehensions but we don't really have a number on the so called got-aways. It could be 300,000 400,000 according to former Border Patrol Chief Rodney Scott. MELUGIN: Exactly, former Chief Scott says their latest numbers are there are at least 400,000 known got-aways but the key part of that is known, those are the ones they see on the cameras, they see on the sensors and they're just never able to get to. The key question is, what about the unknown got-aways? How many of those are there because agents can't be everywhere at once out on this border, Bret. BAIER: OK, Bill Melugin along the border tonight. Bill, thanks. President Biden is spending the weekend at his home in Delaware and his staff may spend a lot of time during that weekend trying to continue to clean up from a series of mistakes and misstatements during a cable news town hall Thursday night. It all occurs as the president's domestic agenda really hangs in the balance because of continued Democratic Party infighting. White House Correspondent Peter Doocy has that part of the story tonight live from the North Lawn. Good evening, Peter. PETER DOOCY, FOX NEWS CHANNEL CORRESPONDENT (on camera): Good evening, Bret. The president is trying to keep people focused on $2 trillion worth of progressive proposals and not on issues he says are out of his control. There at the border and also at the gas pump where he admits prices will remain high through next year. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) JOE BIDEN , PRESIDENT OF THE UNITED STATES: I don't have a near term answer. DOOCY (voice over): Staffers don't either. JEN PSAKI , WHITE HOUSE PRESS SECRETARY: There are limitations to what any president can do as it relates to gas prices. DOOCY: Same for the supply chain. BIDEN: 40 percent of all products coming into the United States of America on the West Coast go through Los Angeles and -- what am I doing here? ANDERSON COOPER, CNN HOST: Is it Long Beach or-- BIDEN: Long Beach. Thank you. DOOCY: President Biden floated activating the National Guard. COOPER: Would you consider the National Guard to help with the supply chain issue? BIDEN: Yes, absolutely, positively. I would do that. DOOCY: It turns out that's not true. PSAKI: It's not something under active consideration. DOOCY: The president's COVID policy could make things worse. A letter published by Politico from the leader of a union representing UPS, FedEx and DHL workers warns: We have significant concerns with the employer mandates announced on September 9th 2021 and the ability of industry members to implement the required employee vaccinations by December 8th 2021. PSAKI: We don't actually anticipate these disruptions. DOOCY: The President's top priority is finalizing a deal with trillions of taxpayer dollars for social programs. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: But you feel like a deal is close? REP. NANCY PELOSI , (D-CA): I think it's very possible. DOOCY: The vice president pitched the plan in the northeast today. KAMALA HARRIS , VICE PRESIDENT OF THE UNITED STATES: I have a motto. I drink, I eat and drink no for breakfast. DOOCY: She's been much less visible handling her most high-profile assignment, immigration. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: Do you have any plans to go to the border before the end of the year? HARRIS: I don't have any at this moment, no. DOOCY: President Biden claimed he's already been. COOPER: Do you have plans to visit the southern border? BIDEN: I've been there before and I haven't -- I mean, I know it well. I guess I should go down. DOOCY: But there's no proof of any trip where he actually got out of the car, just a motorcade from Texas to New Mexico 13 years ago. PSAKI: He did drive through the border when he was on the campaign trail in 2008. DOOCY: He said I've been there before. You're saying he drove by for a few minutes, does that count? PSAKI: What do you -- what is the root cause? Where are people coming from who are coming to the border, Peter? People come from Central America and Mexico to go to the border. The president has been to those countries 10 times to talk about border issues. There is a focus right now on a photo op. DOOCY: That's not what he said either. He said I guess I should go down. So, does he think that he needs a photo op? Is that what he's saying? PSAKI: He doesn't. (END VIDEO CLIP) DOOCY (on camera): Most of the drive officials here are saying counts as a Biden trip to the border from El Paso to Las Cruces is straight North away from the southern border, which means that if then Delaware Senator Joe Biden had much of a view of the border that trip, it was in the rearview mirror, Bret. BAIER: Peter, I have one question, back to the gas prices. In the town hall, he said he doesn't have much control, but it's up to Saudi Arabia, and he kind of trailed off. Did the White House follow up on that today? DOOCY: There's not much of a follow up. Something else the president said though, is that a lot of people in the Middle East want to talk to him and he doesn't know if he is going to answer the call. They're basically saying that if they tap the Strategic Petroleum Reserve here in the United States to get some more gas into the interior of the country, he thinks that it could lower prices by about just a little bit in the near term. But he says through 2022, expect some pain at the pump. Not his word pain at the pump but higher prices. BAIER: Right, Peter Doocy live in the North Lawn. Peter, thanks. More on this with the panel. Now to a story that is getting a lot of attention here in Texas, but obviously has implications for the nation. The U.S. Supreme Court is allowing the Texas law banning most abortions to remain in place for now. But justices have agreed to hear arguments in the case November 1st. Fox News Chief Legal Correspondent, anchor of "FOX NEWS @ NIGHT" Shannon Bream is here with the details. Good evening, Shannon. SHANNON BREAM, FOX NEWS CHIEF LEGAL CORRESPONDENT (on camera): Good evening, Bret. It is fair to characterize what happened today as rare and unusual for a body (PH) that is very deliberative with a detailed framework about how these cases proceed, this one is on the fastest of the fast tracks. The court has ordered initial briefs to be in by Wednesday, reply briefs due by Friday and then arguments that following Monday. Texas law SBA bans most abortions after a heartbeat is detected around roughly six weeks into a pregnancy. And though the justices will hear a dispute over the law on November 1st, it's much more procedural in nature about whether the Justice Department can actually sue a state, state officials or private individuals in an attempt to keep the law from being enforced. It's not about the merits. White House Press Secretary Jen Psaki saying today, she reiterated the president's position on this that the Texas law they say is "blatantly unconstitutional". In the meantime, the justices elected not to put the law on hold. Justice Sotomayor objected to that today writing this "These women will suffer personal harm from delaying their medical care and as their pregnancies progress, they may even be unable to obtain abortion care altogether". She added, every day the court fails to grant relief is devastating, both for individual women and for our constitutional system as a whole. While pro-life group by Live Action called the court's decision not to block the law "A victory for life that will save the lives of innocent preborn boys and girls." The as for actually getting to the abortion debate on the merits, that's going to happen December 1st, the date the justices will hear arguments over Mississippi's law banning most abortions after 15 weeks. A case -- a decision in that case is going to be due in June, late June. And Bret, of course, that puts it right in the middle of all those midterm elections and campaigning. BAIER: Yes, a lot of things to watch at the Supreme Court. Shannon, as always, thank you. We'll see you tonight. Stocks were mixed today, the Dow gained 74 to close at a new record. The S&P 500 lost five, the NASDAQ gave back 125-1/2 today. For the week, the Dow rose about one percentage point, the S&P 500 gained 1-2/3, the NASDAQ picked up 1-1/3. Investigators in New Mexico are looking for answers tonight about what caused the tragic fatal accident on a movie set. Actor Alec Baldwin apparently discharged a prop firearm, resulting in the death of one crew member and wounding another. Chief Correspondent Jonathan Hunt tells us what we know tonight from Los Angeles. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) UNIDENTIFIED MALE: We have a -- two people have been shot accidentally. JONATHAN HUNT, FOX NEWS CHANNEL CHIEF CORRESPONDENT (voice over): That 911 call brought police to the Bonanza Creek Ranch outside Santa Fe New Mexico Thursday afternoon after Alec Baldwin apparently fired a prop gun on the set of his new Western Rust hitting two people. 42-year-old Halyna Hutchins, the director of photography on the movie was killed and director Joel Souza who's 48 was injured. Baldwin made his first public comments today via social media, saying his heart is broken and tweeting, "There are no words to convey my shock and sadness regarding the tragic accident that took the life of Halyna Hutchins, a wife, mother and deeply admired colleague of ours. I'm fully cooperating with the police investigation to address how this tragedy occurred. The Sheriff's Department issued a statement saying in part "This investigation remains open and active. No charges have been filed in regard to this incident. Witnesses continue to be interviewed by detectives." Those witnesses include the 63-year-old Baldwin, who was seen seemingly distraught and in tears outside the sheriff's office yesterday. The shooting recalls a similar tragedy back in 1993, when 28-year-old Brandon Lee, son of the martial arts icon Bruce Lee was shot and killed with a prop gun. Those who handled weapons on movie sets say safety protocols introduced since then should now prevent any accidental shooting. SAM DORMER, SUPERVISING ARMOURER AND DIRECTOR, ALAMO ARMS: There are lots of checks in place, for instance, in the Brandon Lee incident, there was an obstruction in the barrel which came out once the blank was put behind it. And nowadays, all weapons are checked, the barrel is checked before any blanks are put into the weapon. (END VIDEO CLIP) HUNT (on camera): And tonight, the L.A. Times is reporting that the prop gun fired by Baldwin had previously misfired several times on set, also reporting that there were safety concerns among crew members and that hours before the shooting, a half dozen camera crew workers had walked off set to protest working conditions, Bret. BAIER: Tragic. Jonathan, thank you. Up next, the ships keep coming but there's no place for them to offload. We'll take you to the supply chain crisis. First, here's what some of our Fox affiliates around the country are covering tonight. Fox 5 in New York where real estate mogul Robert Durst is charged with the death of his wife, Kathie Durst who vanished in 1982. Durst is accused of second degree murder. Durst was sentenced last week in California to life in prison for killing a friend in 2000. Fox 2 in Detroit as hundreds of filters are distributed to residents of Hamtramck due to high lead results in drinking water samples. The mayor there says outdated service lines are leaching lead into the water of individual homes. The city says another 900 water filters will be distributed next week. And this is a live look in Seattle from Fox 13. One of the big stories there tonight. A record number of humpback whales have been born this season. Whale watchers and researchers have recorded 21 calves documented throughout inland Washington and British Columbia. One expert says it is the highest annual number on record. That's tonight's live look "OUTSIDE THE BELTWAY" from SPECIAL REPORT. We're outside the beltway too. We'll be right back. (COMMERCIAL BREAK) BAIER: A New York jury has convicted a former associate of Rudy Giuliani of making illegal campaign contributions to influence politicians, and advance his business interests. Lev Parnas was accused of using other people's money to pose as a powerful political broker and influence some of the nation's star Republican political figures. The case had drawn interest because Parnas has had been involved in Giuliani's efforts to get Ukrainian officials to investigate President Biden's son, Hunter. Giuliani was not charged in that case. Fingers are being pointed tonight as the supply chain crisis worsens. It is a complex problem with many possible culprits. National correspondent William La Jeunesse shows us from the Port of Los Angeles . (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) UNIDENTIFIED MALE: Being a truck driver, I think it's all in the ports. WILLIAM LA JEUNESSE, FOX NEWS CHANNEL NATIONAL CORRESPONDENT (voice-over): 10 days after President Biden promised to speed things up, congestion at the ports is worse. GENE SEROKA , EXECUTIVE DIRECTOR, PORT OF LOS ANGELES: That's like compressing 10 lanes of freeway traffic into five. LA JEUNESSE: On the water and off, that traffic piles up at America's largest port. A record 109 ships, wait to offload their cargo, half don't even have an assigned place to anchor just outside the ports, forcing the rest to simply drift in waters well outside San Pedro Bay. Going to 24/7 operations was supposed to jumpstart improvements in the supply chain, right now, there's no evidence it has. LANCE CUNNINGHAM, FREIGHT COMPANY PRESIDENT: 24/7 is just basically placating the public to saying that we're actually maybe doing something. LA JEUNESSE: Truckers say a shortage of warehouse workers is one problem. The other, a lack of chassis to haul containers. CUNNINGHAM: The extra, you know, four or five hours of the -- that the ports are being open, they're not -- I can't return an empty when that -- when that -- in that extra time that we're doing there. They're only allowing -- they're only allowing containers to go out that are already on chassis on wheels. That's my whole problem, I don't have a chassis to bring in. LA JEUNESSE: While containers stack up at the ports, the economy slows, businesses get hurt. KURT GEORGE, SUPPLY CHAIN EXPERT: Companies are losing money, because they're not able to get products on the shelves. LA JEUNESSE: As losses increase, so do insurance claims on spoiled food and time-sensitive deliveries. GEORGE: There is no creative way or quick fix to this problem right now. Until the goods, both the end-user goods and the components get into the country and get into the factories and the manufacturers' hands. Until then, we're going to start running out of things. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: Who do you think can do more? DAVID CRUZ, TRUCK DRIVER: I leave it up to the ports and Mr. President. (END VIDEO CLIP) LA JEUNESSE (on camera): So, the container ship really revolutionize the way the world moves cargo. It fueled the rise of China and our dependence on it. What we're seeing right now is the global supply chain overwhelmed and there are no silver bullets, we're told, to end it anytime soon. Bret. BAIER: William La Jeunesse, in the water off Port of Los Angeles . William, thanks. Now, to some good news for a change. There is renewed hope tonight for people with kidney problems. Doctors in New York have pulled off a breakthrough procedure involving the use of a non-human organ. Fox News contributor Dr. Marc Siegel has the breaking details tonight on this. Good evening, Dr. Siegel. DR. MARC SIEGEL, FOX NEWS CHANNEL MEDICAL CONTRIBUTOR (on camera): Hi, Bret. Dr. Robert Montgomery, chief of surgery and founding director of the Transplant Institute at NYU, and my colleague at NYU, has a long passionate history as a kidney transplant pioneer, driven by his own personal need for a heart transplant. We could up -- we caught up with Dr. Montgomery and got a look at the groundbreaking surgery that was performed. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) DR. ROBERT MONTGOMERY, DIRECTOR, TRANSPLANT INSTITUTE, NEW YORK UNIVERSITY , LANGONE MEDICAL CENTER: We want to make sure that as many people as possible have that opportunity. SIEGEL: Dr. Montgomery pioneered a lottery system for mixing and matching donors and recipients that has saved 1000s of lives. MONTGOMERY: Unfortunately, nearly half of the people who are waiting for an organ won't make it. We came up with this idea that, that person would give their kidney to someone who had been living but incompatible donor, and then that donor would give to someone else. And so, you can form this single, you know, act of altruism. SIEGEL: But the massive organ shortage continues. So, the first 2-1/2 day successful transplant of a genetically altered pig kidney to a human recipient is clearly groundbreaking. Montgomery says the surgery was no more difficult than a human operation, with the pig gene that would have caused rejection deleted. Immunosuppression, then, worked. MONTGOMERY: We can say that -- you know, it's -- it functioned well, it did all the things that a kidney is supposed to do. It acted like a human kidney transplant. And we didn't see any evidence of you know, a rapid rejection. So, the kidney did make urine almost immediately like moments after we joined blood vessels. SIEGEL: Montgomery says that the next phase will be studying longer periods after transplant to make sure that the pig kidney isn't rejected. I asked him which organ came next. MONTGOMERY: I think you know, the closest organ to the kidney in terms of being kind of ready for primetime is the heart. (END VIDEO CLIP) SIEGEL (on camera): He calls it a game-changer, pig kidney, and then the heart. Bret? BAIER: That's a great story. Dr. Siegel, thanks. SIEGEL: Thanks, Bret. BAIER: Up next, we're entering the home stretch in the Virginia governor's race and it's down to the wire. We'll have a live report there. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) TERRY MCAULIFFE (D), GUBERNATORIAL CANDIDATE, VIRGINIA: Glenn Youngkin has done nothing but run down the state since he announced. He doesn't know anything about the state. GLENN YOUNGKIN (R), GUBERNATORIAL CANDIDATE, VIRGINIA: Terry McAuliffe is seeing the sunset on his 43-year political career. (END VIDEO CLIP) (COMMERCIAL BREAK) BAIER: We are about to enter the final full week of campaigning in the Virginia governor's race. Democrat Terry McAuliffe and Republican Glenn Youngkin are neck-and-neck in recent polling. Democrats are bringing in some of the party's biggest stars to try to help McAuliffe. Former President Obama will be in Virginia tomorrow. Last night, it was Vice President Kamala Harris . Here is correspondent Alexandria Hoff. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) MCAULIFFE: We'll let's go get him. ALEXANDRIA HOFF, FOX NEWS CHANNEL WASHINGTON CORRESPONDENT (voice-over): Democrat Terry McAuliffe kicked off his Get Out The Vote tour in Arlington, Virginia, showing off new wheels and a sharpened tongue. MCAULIFFE: I'm running against a Trump wannabe. I like to say Trump and khakis. HOFF: A recent slip in the polls has put the former governor vying to win back his position in a dead heat against Republican Glenn Youngkin. Youngkin is banking on support from frustrated parents struggling to find their voice in school policies and curriculum. YOUNGKIN: This race is so clearly moving our direction is because Virginians recognize that Terry McAuliffe is all about big government imposing its view on individual liberties. HOFF: If Youngkin were to pull ahead, he would be the first Republican in 12 years elected to a statewide seat. With hopes to spark enthusiasm among Democrats, President Biden is set to hit the campaign trail in Virginia next week, despite low approval numbers. Vice President Kamala Harris lobbied for McAuliffe last night. KAMALA HARRIS , VICE PRESIDENT OF THE UNITED STATES: This race is tight. And what happens here, I promise you is about the people of the state and the people of our country. HOFF: Harris also lent her voice to a video message playing out in black churches across the commonwealth. HARRIS: I believe that my friend Terry McAuliffe is the leader Virginia needs at this moment. HOFF: Critics have questioned the legality of the video given that IRS rules prohibit church involvement with political campaigns. On the push for minority voters, Democrat Doug Wilder, Virginia's only black governor, wrote this when McAuliffe announced his run, quote, "Why should he expect that vote to be there for him in 2021 having shown such little appreciation for it." Former President Barack Obama will campaign with McAuliffe in Richmond tomorrow as Glenn Youngkin's bus tour will kick off as well some 115 miles away in northern Virginia's Fairfax County. (END VIDEO TAPE) HOFF (on camera): New early voting data shows that nine-and-a-half percent of registered voters have so far returned their ballot, with registered Democrats largely outnumbering Republicans. Bret? BRET BAIER, FOX NEWS ANCHOR: Alex, thank you. A religious organization whose 17 members were kidnapped in Haiti is asking supporters to pray tonight and share stories with the victims' families of how their faith helped them through difficult times. Ohio based Christian Aid Ministries issued the statement a day after a video was released showing the leader of the kidnappers threatening to kill those abducted if his demands are not met. Haitian officials have said the gang is seeking $1 million ransom per person. China is urging the U.S. to avoid what it calls sending any wrong signals about Taiwan. This comes after President Biden said at that town hall the U.S. would come to the defense of Taiwan in the event of a Chinese attack. The White House clarified that as well today, too. Senior foreign affairs correspondent Greg Palkot tells us where things stand tonight. (BEGIN VIDEO TAPE) GREG PALKOT, FOX NEWS SENIOR FOREIGN AFFAIRS CORRESPONDENT: Has the U.S. taken one step closer to being involved in a clash between China and the island of Taiwan. President Biden appeared to last night. JOE BIDEN , (D) PRESIDENT OF THE UNITED STATES: I don't want a cold war with China. I just want to make China understand that we are not going to step back. We are not going to change any of our views. GOV. ROY COOPER, (D) NORTH CAROLINA: So are you saying that the United States would come to Taiwan's defense if China attacked? BIDEN: Yes, we have a commitment to do that. PALKOT: Taiwan officials who have seen Chinese military aircraft enter their region cited America's rock-solid support. China, which assert Taiwan as its own, was also quick to react. WANG WENBIN , CHINESE FOREIGN MINISTER: We urge the U.S. to be cautious with its words and actions on the Taiwan issue and not to send any wrong signals. PALKOT: America's Taiwan relations act is purposefully vague, stating "the United States shall make available to Taiwan such defense articles and defense services in such quantity as may be necessary to enable Taiwan to maintain a sufficient self-defense capacity." Experts say tampering with this strategic ambiguity risks war with China. DEAN CHENG, HERITAGE FOUNDATION: Providing a blank check, so to speak, creates then a misimpression on Taiwan that maybe they can declare independence, which would absolutely destabilize the Taiwan Straits situation. PALKOT: At a NATO meeting in Brussels, Defense Secretary Austin appeared to be doing damage control. LLOYD AUSTIN, DEFENSE SECRETARY: No one wants to see strait issues come to blows, and certainly not President Biden. And there is no reason that it should. PALKOT: For the immediate future, analysts say Chinese President Xi will hold back on any Taiwan invasion, not wanting to disrupt next year's Winter Olympics in Beijing and the Chinese Communist Party conference which Xi should get a new mandate. (END VIDEO TAPE) PALKOT (on camera): White house spokesperson Jen Psaki also said today President Biden was not announcing any change in America's Taiwan policy. Experts say it was China threatening the island, that's a safe way to go. Bret? BAIER: Greg Palkot in London. Greg, thanks. Up next, the panel on why White House officials would not mind a few do- overs on some of President Biden's answers last night. (COMMERCIAL BREAK) (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) GOV. ROY COOPER, (D) NORTH CAROLINA: Do you have plans to visit the southern border. JOE BIDEN , (D) PRESIDENT OF THE UNITED STATES: I have been there before, and I haven't -- I know it well. I guess I should go down, but the whole point of it is I haven't had a whole hell of a lot of time to get down. JEN PSAKI , WHITE HOUSE PRESS SECRETARY: There has been reporting that he did dry through the border when he was on the campaign trail in 2008. He does not need a visit to the border to know what a mess was left by the last administration. (END VIDEO CLIP) BAIER: The White House saying he drove past the border during the 2008 campaign, and saying even though he said that maybe he should go down, that he didn't really mean, the president didn't in that town hall, that he would go down. Town hall needed to be cleaned up today by the White House press secretary in a couple of different points. Meantime Gallup, the approval analysis for Gallup says that the Biden's average third quarter job approval rating is down eight points from his second quarter 53 percent, 11 points from his first quarter rating of 56 percent. This 11-point decline is larger than any prior president registered between first and third quarters, although it is similar to those for the last three Democratic presidents, Barack Obama , Clinton, and Carter. So let's bring in our panel, Ben Domenech, publisher of "The Federalist," Harold Ford Jr., former Tennessee Congressman, CEO of Empowerment and Inclusion Capital, and Jason Riley, "Wall Street Journal" columnist and senior fellow at the Manhattan Institute. Jason, there were a number of incidents that the White House had to clarify. We pointed them out here. The border, the situation about gas prices, and maybe most importantly, about Taiwan. JASON RILEY, COLUMNIST, "WALL STREET JOURNAL": Yes, there are a number of issues going on here. I would add to that, Bret, the spending debate going on in Congress right now. And I think Joe Biden 's problem is that he is trying to present as a Democrat versus Republican issue when, in reality, particularly with regard to this spending bill, it's a Democrat versus Democrat problem. He can't get his own ducks in a row. And you have a debate going on between progressives in the Democratic Party and more moderates in the Democratic Party on how to spin this spending bill that they want to unleash. And it frankly boils down to their ambitions being greater than their actual mandate, that the American people did not elect a progressive president to pursue a progressive agenda, and Biden is trying to slip one by the American people. BAIER: "The Washington Post," Harold, writes it this way about that town hall, "President Biden had one central message for disappointed progressives at his CNN town hall last night -- please be patient. The problem with Biden's promises to come back to progressive priorities is that his razor thin Democratic majorities in the House and Senate won't be any bigger and Republicans won't be any more inclined to go along, which is why progressives have been urging him for months to fight to get rid of the filibuster," something he said he might actually be for now. HAROLD FORD JR., FORMER TENNESSEE REPRESENTATIVE: Well, thanks for having me on. This is -- I think Jason nailed it with the frame. Progressives didn't and don't have a massive majority in the House or even a comfortable majority in the House, for that matter, the Senate. I think when we elected President Biden, the country did, they were electing someone they thought would bring a level of stability and maturity and experience to decision- making and to the White House. And to Jason's point, the president has spent most of his time trying to referee disputes between and amongst his own party members. I have said for some time, Democrats take the victory. Give the country what they have asked for, which is an infrastructure bill. Demonstrate that you can govern and lead and then come back and do the other things, which I think at some point President Biden is going to have to say to Democrats in a forthright way. I hope he doesn't have to say in a forthright way with an outcome in Virginia that is detrimental to my party. Terry McAuliffe has asked for Democrats to give us this victory and give us a chance to lead and to govern in the lead majority, which is the way you actually enact policy. BAIER: Yes. FORD : Until they do that, I think it's going to be hard for my party. BAIER: I don't see how it's going to get done before that Virginia election, but we'll see. They may try to put the pedal to the metal, but it seems like there are really big sticking points. I mentioned the filibuster change and the evolution of the president, how he has talked about it. Take a listen to that evolution. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) JOE BIDEN , (D) PRESIDENT OF THE UNITED STATES: I'm trying to bring the country together, and I don't want the debate to only be about whether or not we have a filibuster. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: If it's a relic of Jim Crow, it's been used to fight against civil rights legislation historically, why protect it? BIDEN: There's no reason to protect it other than you are going to throw the entire Congress into chaos and nothing will get done. Nothing at all will get done. And there's a lot the stake. I also think we are going to have to move to the point where we fundamentally alter the filibuster. That remains to be seen exactly what that means in terms of fundamentally altering it, whether or not we just end the filibuster straight up. (END VIDEO CLIP) BAIER: That's quite an evolution, Ben. BEN DOMENECH, PUBLISHER, "THE FEDERALIST": How different your attitude is when you move from the Senate to the White House toward the filibuster, an essential defense of American representative politics or just a nuisance to be wiped away. Look, I think that what Harold said is correct in the sense that progressives don't have a majority here. They don't even have anything close to it. And yet, what this represents, what this massive spending package represents at this point is an attempt to try to satisfy virtually every progressive priority even in ways that are sloppy and don't make sense from fiscal policy perspectives. If you add a smaller policy package, you might be able to have something that was more permanent, more longstanding. Instead you are likely to end up, if anything ends up passing at all, with a package that is more easily swept away potentially by a future Republican majority. And I think that Democrats are really waking up to the fact that, while individual parts of this plan may test well when they are polled and when they are asked of the American people, as a whole, this plan is not something that the American people are all that excited about, and they don't really believe it's going to satisfy the problems that they see every day when this comes to inflation, when it comes to their pocketbook, and certainly when it comes to the increasingly controversial issues related to education, which are so key in this Virginia race. BAIER: Jason, I only have a few seconds here, but I was struck by the gas answer from President Biden last night at that town hall and that essentially his hands are tied and that gas prices are going up into next year, saying that a lot depends on OPEC and Saudi Arabia. Republicans would point out that a lot happened in the previous administration to free the U.S. from foreign oil, and that we're back in the place we were before that. RILEY: You're right. And what Biden isn't telling you that his progressives are happy with high energy costs to the extent that it pushes people towards renewables, towards green new deal type policies, and so forth. They have no problem with fossil fuel energy prices going up. But the American people do, the voters do. And, again, Joe Biden was not elected to transition us off fossil fuel even if that's what the progressives want. BAIER: Which is a big contention in that last debate. I got run. GLENN YOUNGKIN, (R) VIRGINIA GUBERNATORIAL NOMINEE: What we see on the other side is sun setting on Terry McAuliffe 's 43-year political career. MCAULIFFE: My opponent a Donald Trump wannabe. YOUNGKIN: Terry McAuliffe when he was governor saw the states grow around us grow 120 percent faster economically. MCAULIFFE: When I took office the last time our state was in chaos. I worked with everybody, built a robust economy. YOUNGKIN: The first thing I will do as governor is declare Virginia open for business. We won't have lockdowns. (END VIDEO CLIP) BAIER: Democratic strategist James Carville said this week he is scared to death about this race in Virginia from a Democratic point of view. If you look at the RCP average, Real Clear Politics, it is very tight, 48.8 to 47. The recent Monmouth poll just out this week had it at a dead heat at 46. We're back with the panel. Ben, your thoughts? DOMENECH: Virginia should scare every Democrat because Terry McAuliffe 's approach has been to nationalize this, to bring in all these different national figures to back him up, and to try to make this an election where Glenn Youngkin is viewed as a stocking horse for Donald Trump . Youngkin's approach has been to localize it and to make it primarily about the education issue. And in that same Monmouth that you've talked about, we have seen Youngkin creep up and up and up steadily over several months to the point where he actually has an advantage. The idea that a Republican could win in the commonwealth of Virginia on the education issue should absolutely terrify Democrats going into next year's midterms. BAIER: Harold? FORD : I think Ben nailed it there, too. I wouldn't count Terry McAuliffe out. He is the best retail politician in the party. He will nationalize this race, as a lot of governor's races are. He's got President Obama coming in, reminding Virginians that they voted Democrat over the last few cycles, and we'll have to see. It's a jump ball there, but I wouldn't count Terry McAuliffe out by any stretch. BAIER: I want to turn just really quickly to China and what the president said about Taiwan, defending Taiwan. The White House had to then walk that back and say the policy hasn't changed. China jumped all over it. It seems like sometimes the China policy for this administration is a little ambiguous. Jason? RILEY: Well, Biden is right. We need a presence in that part of the world. We're essentially in a cold war battle with China right now, not only militarily, but also economically. Trump administration liked to talk about it. The left called it bluster. But now that Biden's office are taking it seriously, I applaud them. But anyone who is paying attention knew that this was an issue. BAIER: All right, Winners and Losers. Ben, really quick. DOMENECH: Two sides of the coin, Loudoun County parents versus the Loudoun County school board. The revelations of what that superintendent of that school board hid about what they knew about a bathroom sexual assault coming clear this week, an incredible story that is terrifying parents across the country. BAIER: Harold, winner and loser? FORD : My winner is a little different but serious to me. Tom brady at 44 years old is leading the NFL in passing yards. And my loser could be the Brooklyn Nets if Kyrie Irving does not play because he won't get vaccinated. BAIER: We can always catch you in the sports winners and losers. All right, Jason, bring it home, winner and loser? RILEY: My winner is former secretary of state Condi Rice for talking about Critical Race Theory in schools and saying that black children are not helped by making white children feel guilty for being white. Amen to that. My loser is the New York City political class which is removing a statue of Thomas Jefferson from city hall. So we're now erecting statues of George Floyd and taking down statues of Thomas Jefferson . The world has gone mad, Bret. BAIER: They took down a statue of Ulysses S. Grant in San Francisco. Yes, the world has gone mad. OK, thank you all. When we come back, "Notable Quotables." (COMMERCIAL BREAK) BAIER: It's Friday, and you know what that means "Notable Quotables." (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) UNIDENTIFIED MALE: The world lost one of the greatest leaders that we have ever witnessed. SEN. LINDSEY GRAHAM , (R-SC): The Joe Biden greatest hit list, you can now put on the list nuclear arms race with China. JOE BIDEN , (D) PRESIDENT OF THE UNITED STATES: Freedom. I have the freedom to kill you with my COVID. No, I mean, come on, freedom. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: I don't know where my old friend became such a toy totalitarian. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: Investigators found what appear to be human remains such as a backpack and notebook belonging to Brian Laundrie. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: The Justice Department supports and defends the First Amendment right of parents to complain as vociferously as they wish. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: Mr. Bannon will comply with our investigation or he will face the consequences. BIDEN: All of a sudden hear bam, bam, bam, this banging on my door. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: And remember, we winnowed. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: We are talking. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: We're talking. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: This donkey on donkey fighting here is something to watch. BAIER: So your biggest issue is truck drivers and warehouse space? UNIDENTIFIED MALE: We have tightened capacity, labor shortages. BIDEN: The cost of Build Back Better bill in terms of adding to the deficit is zero, zero, zero. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: Mr. Attorney General, who buys Hunter Biden 's art? UNIDENTIFIED MALE: And what he is doing is brining everybody into this commonwealth of Virginia who has nothing to do with Virginia. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: I'm ready to go. I have got more energy today than the day I was born. (END VIDEO CLIP) BAIER: One week. Monday on SPECIAL REPORT, Democrats flood the zone over the weekend in the Virginia governor's race. As you know, we've been covering this race really closely. Will all of that work as we close in on Election Day 2021? The CDC director will be with Chris Wallace. I will be there as well on the panel. Please remember, if you are so inclined, to pick up my new book, "To Rescue the Republic, Ulysses S. Grant, the Fragile Union, and the Crisis of 1876." It is available wherever you buy books. I have an event in Dallas tonight, and then I am back to D.C. starting all next week. My thanks to the crews and staff in New York, Los Angeles, and here in Dallas for hosting me over the past two weeks. It's been a good ride. Thank you very much, everybody. story_text: JESSICA TARLOV, FOX NEWS HOST (on camera): It takes a lot of time for her to make each of these, but she called it a labor of love. Then, I just -- (CROSSTALK) GREG GUTFELD, FOX NEWS HOST (on camera): Get it? Labor? That's funny. TARLOV: I do get it, Greg. I didn't -- I didn't -- It's so sweet. Anyway -- and everyone trick or treat, do so safely. Have a great holiday weekend. SHANNON BREAM, FOX NEWS ANCHOR (on camera): Yes, I want to see pics of all of your costumes. TARLOV: Yes. BREAM: OK, I'll see you again at midnight. That is it for us here on THE FIVE. Have a great weekend. BRET BAIER, FOX NEWS ANCHOR (on camera): Good evening, I'm Bret Baier. Breaking tonight, President Biden calls a major diplomatic blunder by his own administration, clumsy. But does not apologize to one of our oldest allies on this the first day of his trip to Europe, where the president will attend major conferences on the economy and the climate. The second Catholic president in U.S. history visited the pope today at the Vatican amid calls from some bishops, that President Biden be denied communion. All of this comes amid the political chaos surrounding the president's domestic tax and spend agenda back home. White House correspondent Peter Doocy is traveling with the president starts us off in Rome tonight. Good evening, Peter. PETER DOOCY, FOX NEWS CHANNEL WHITE HOUSE CORRESPONDENT (on camera): Good evening, Bret. The President is in for the night after a day of meetings all over Rome and Vatican City. On foreign trips like these, he wants his foreign policy motto to be America is back. But today it was more like America did not stab you in the back. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) JOE BIDEN , PRESIDENT OF THE UNITED STATES: What we did was so clumsy. It was not done with a lot of grace. DOOCY: Hoping to smooth things over with the French President Macron, the president now claims, when the U.S. made a deal to sell nuclear powered subs to Australia, costing France a valuable contract, he didn't know Paris was in the dark. BIDEN: I was under the impression that France was informed long before. DOOCY: Now, the presidents are patching things up. KATE BEDINGFIELD , WHITE HOUSE COMMUNICATIONS DIRECTOR: Well, the breach such as it was is healing. President Biden obviously values this relationship tremendously. DOOCY: But Biden is not saying sorry. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: You have to apologize Mr. President. BIDEN: No. DOOCY: Just after 2:00 a.m. local, Air Force One landed, carrying a president whose agenda at home is being held up by his own party's most progressive members. REP. JAMES COMER (R-KY): To think that, that bill wasn't enough spending for them shows just how far left they are. DOOCY: The Bidens visited the Vatican. BIDEN: Thank you. I'm Jill's husband. DOOCY: And met with Pope Francis , where "The Parties focused on the joint commitment to the protection and care of the planet." Notable because the president arrived in a longer than usual motorcade with dozens of vehicles. Domestic politics crept into Biden's 90 minute meeting with the pope, including the stalled Build Back Better plan. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: Did you addressed the cuts to climate in build back better? BIDEN: Yes. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: What did you discuss about climate and Build Back Better with him? BIDEN: If you have half an hour, I'll tell you. About the need and moral responsibility we have to deal with it. BIDEN: Abortion did not come up. Even though a number of American Catholic leaders believe Biden's position that a woman should have a right to choose to terminate a pregnancy makes him ineligible to receive communion. BIDEN: He was happy I was a good Catholic and I should keep receiving communion. DOOCY: Later, comparing the pope to American servicemen and women. BIDEN: You are the most significant warrior for peace I've ever met. DOOCY: The President gifted him a challenge coin. BIDEN: Next time I see you, you don't have -- you have to buy the drinks. I'm the only Irishman you've ever met you ever had to drink. (END VIDEO CLIP) DOOCY: At one point, while the leader of the free world was joking with the leader of the Catholic Church, the President drew upon one of his most familiar Bidenisms to tell the pope something he may have heard a time or two before. God love you, man. Bret. BAIER: Peter Doocy live in Rome. Peter, thanks. While I have you, what are we learning from this updated report about the COVID-19 origins came out late this afternoon? DOOCY: Yes, it expands on that 90-day review of the COVID origins that the president ordered a few months back, and what they found in this 18-page update is one Intel agency is saying they believe COVID came from a lab accident. They say they have moderate confidence in that. Four other Intel agencies say, COVID came from exposure to an infected animal, but they have low confidence. Three other Intel agencies are saying they need more info. And the director of National Intelligence has concluded they don't think China was making a bioweapon, but the DNI is concluding that unless China comes forward with more information to help them fill in the blanks, then, we will probably never know the origin of COVID for sure. Bret. BAIER: We'll keep asking questions. Peter, thank you. Progressive Democrats back here at home are once again preventing the president's social spending measures from getting through the Democrat-run Congress. Congressional correspondent Chad Pergram live on Capitol Hill with that part of the story. Chad, we saw what happened last night, but how much blood -- bad blood is there between moderate and progressive Democrats? CHAD PERGRAM, FOX NEWS CHANNEL CONGRESSIONAL CORRESPONDENT (voice-over): Well, Bret, progressives are demanding assurances from moderates Kyrsten Sinema and Joe Manchin in the United States Senate that they will vote for the social spending bill. There is also distrust between the House and Senate that's why liberals are forcing leaders to do the infrastructure bill and the social spending bill in tandem. Both President Biden and House Speaker Nancy Pelosi failed to close the deal. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) PERGRAM: What's your response when you hear that sort of dissension in your caucus about where you stand, when you present a very positive picture of where you are? REP. NANCY PELOSI (D-CA): I have respect for all of our members on, in the full spectrum of the big tent that is our Democratic Party. Everybody has the chance to say what they wish. PERGRAM (voice-over): Or mad because they believe moderates prevailed reducing the overall cost of the bill. Plus, they nixed family leave and beefed up Medicare. Liberals are flexing their muscles. MICHAEL HARDAWAY, FORMER HOUSE DEMOCRAT LEADERSHIP AIDE: They are coming into their power in terms of understanding just how much power they willed on the Hill, and how much power they willed with throughout the Democratic Party. (END VIDEO CLIP) PERGRAM (on camera): But which side has the upper hand? Moderates control the policy. That's because Democrats hold narrow margins in the House and Senate. That dictates what can pass. But liberals control the politics. There is strength in numbers, Bret. BAIER: Chad, what's the timeline here? PERGRAM: The best case scenario is probably two weeks, even if they had a deal today, then you're into Thanksgiving. They are a long ways off from final language. The other major deadline is December 3rd. That's when lawmakers must fund the government to avoid a shutdown and there will be another Donnybrook over the debt ceiling. And they could enroll all this into a big bill in early December, the other deadline which -- of course, there's always a big deadline here on Capitol Hill. This Christmas. Bret. BAIER: All right, Chad. We'll follow it. Thank you. An election may many feel is a harbinger of things to come in next year's midterms is just four days away. The Virginia gubernatorial race has seen the Republican overtake the favorite Democrat in recent polling, sending a shiver through much of the bluish purple state. We have "FOX TEAM COVERAGE" tonight. Rich Edson is in Norfolk tonight where Democrat Terry McAuliffe has spent much of the day. First up though, correspondent Alexandria Hoff with the Glenn Youngkin campaign in Warrenton, Virginia. Good evening, Alexandria. ALEXANDRIA HOFF, FOX NEWS CHANNEL WASHINGTON CORRESPONDENT (on camera): Good evening, Bret. Yes. Glenn Youngkin has absolutely been peppering this state. This event tonight will be his fifth of the day. That's about average for his bus tour and all this voter outreach may be paying off. HOFF (voice over): According to the latest Fox News poll of likely Virginia voters, it shows Republican Glenn Youngkin now leading Democratic opponent Terry McAuliffe by eight points, 53 to 45 percent with two percent undecided. That is a major shift from just two weeks ago. The latest Washington Post poll puts Youngkin one point behind McAuliffe well within the margin of error. As part of his 50-stop tour across the state, Youngkin started the day with two stops in Charlottesville, celebrated the poll findings but added this. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) GLENN YOUNGKIN (R), GUBERNATORIAL CANDIDATE, VIRGINIA: Polls don't elect governors, voters do. Voters do. So, now it's time for all of us to go to work. (END VIDEO CLIP) HOFF: The latest Fox News poll also shows Youngkin has an eight percent lead over McAuliffe when likely voters in Virginia were asked who they trust to do a better job on education, which has been a major talking point for Youngkin. On the economy, a tie from two weeks ago was broken. McAuliffe lost a percent as Youngkin gained 10. And with these new numbers in hand, Youngkin has called McAuliffe's campaign desperate. Earlier today, members of McAuliffe's team claimed that a photo taken at a Youngkin event today in Charlottesville showcased white nationalist carrying torches. Youngkin's team fired back, calling it a disgusting and desperate stunt by the opposition. For more on that, let's turn to our Rich Edson . He has been following the McAuliffe trail and he is live in Norfolk tonight. Rich. RICH EDSON , FOX NEWS CHANNEL WASHINGTON CORRESPONDENT (on camera): Yes. Thanks and good evening, Alex. And Terry McAuliffe just left the stage here. We're all waiting for Vice President Kamala Harris to step up and address the crowd. The McAuliffe campaign has commented on that. Says they had no involvement in that group that met Youngkin's bus earlier today. And now we're hearing from The Lincoln Project, that anti-Trump group, we'll they are now claiming in a statement, "Today's demonstration was our way of reminding Virginians what happened in Charlottesville four years ago, the Republican Party's embrace of those values, and Glenn Youngkin's failure to condemn it." EDSON (voice over): McAuliffe and Democrats are accusing Youngkin of deploying what they call racist dog whistles and trying to tie the Republican to former President Donald Trump . Youngkin has countered that he is focused on local issues like education, crime, and the economy. Also, one of our foxnews.com reporters, Tyler O'Neil, he e-mailed a McAuliffe spokesperson for a response to the campaign spending more than $50,000, hiring the Elias Law Group that started by Mark Elias. He is an attorney who previously challenged elections, was Hillary Clinton 's campaign general counsel, and hired the research firm that produced the dossier with claims of connection between Russia and Trump. A campaign spokesperson e-mail that reporter back, apparently, mistakenly saying, can we try to kill this? The story is now up on foxnews.com. McAuliffe canceled campaigns this weekend. He'll be with Bruce Smith to be NFL Hall of Famer, also with a number of politicians like Senator Tim Kaine from Virginia, and representatives, Barbara Lee, and Jim Clyburn . Bret? BAIER: And Rich, quickly, I see that crowd behind you. But what have the crowds look like for McAuliffe around the state? EDSON: No, it's been hit or miss. He was in Charlottesville yesterday, the crowd at a few dozen people there and that's against a stronghold in the middle of the state, we're they're trying to get people out. This room is largely filled, and say there's a few 100 people here. But as you get to the back, it begins to empty out a little bit. Republicans have been talking at least among themselves about what they perceive as a much smaller group of people who are showing up to these McAuliffe events. They feel like they've got the momentum and the excitement going their way. BAIER: We'll see. I mean, that's what the polls show. Rich Edson on the trail. Rich, thanks. Well, the superintendent of Northern Virginia School District is comparing parental protests at school board meetings to the Capitol riot on January 6th, and his experience seeing people drinking at the beach. The comments by Loudoun County School Chief Scott Ziegler came as part of a court hearing for a man arrested at a June school board meeting. Ziegler's actions in recent months have led parents in that area to demand his resignation. Markets today, three major stock markets closed at record highs today. The Dow gained 89. "BREAKING TONIGHT", the Food and Drug Administration has approved the Pfizer vaccine for emergency use in children ages 5 to 11. The kids' doses are one-third the amount for adults and teens. Up to 28 million additional American children could be eligible for vaccinations as early as next week. The process next goes to the CDC for final approval. Meantime, New York City employees who have not yet been vaccinated are in limbo tonight. Really, right now, the mayor is threatening their jobs. City residents are worried about what will happen if they need some kind of emergency assistance in coming days if the numbers dwindle down. Correspondent David Lee Miller is in New York tonight with the latest. Good evening, David Lee. DAVID LEE MILLER, FOX NEWS CHANNEL CORRESPONDENT (on camera): Good evening, Bret. New York City's vaccine mandate took effect a little more than one hour ago. That means virtually all New York City employees must now be vaccinated, or on Monday morning, they will be placed on leave without pay. This evening, union leaders for New York City firefighters held a news conference warning that fewer people on the job could endanger lives. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) ANDREW ANSBRO, UNIFORMED FIREFIGHTERS ASSOCIATION: We need everyone we can to keep the city running and keep it safe. We're trying to avoid what is going to be an inevitable disaster by design on Monday morning. MILLER (voice over): New York is bracing for a shortage of first responders and other workers who refuse to comply with the city's vaccine mandate. Throughout the week, city employees opposed to the policy marched and rally. AMERICAN CROWD: We (INAUDIBLE) people will not comply! MILLER: Many in attendance said they were not anti-vax, but anti-mandate. KIERAN BURKE, FORMER NEW YORK CITY FIRE MARSHALL: I think at the root of it, and today especially, it's about people's right to choose. MILLER: The fire department has admit morning, said the mandate compliance rate is 71 percent. The commissioner in a written statement say there is a plan if there is a worker shortage. "We will use all means at our disposal including mandatory overtime, mutual aid from other EMS providers, and significant changes to the schedules of our members." According to the city's police commissioner, yesterday, 1,000 cops received their first dose. Raising the number of those vaccinated to 80 percent. If there is a shortage of cops, the NYPD says it is ready. DERMOT SHEA , POLICE COMMISSIONER, NEW YORK CITY: New Yorkers should not -- should not be worried about this. A contingency plans are in place there. So, this will not affect cops on the street. MILLER: Across the country, vaccine mandates have met with opposition. The L.A. County sheriff on Thursday said the Board of Supervisors decision to require vaccinations led to a mass exodus within the department, resulting in an "imminent threat to public safety". And in Chicago, multiple court battles are brewing. Both cops and firefighters are refusing to comply with the mayor's mandate, requiring city workers to disclose their vaccination status and either get a shot or undergo regular COVID testing. (END VIDEO CLIP) MILLER: And back here in New York City, even though the 5:00 p.m. mandate deadline has now passed, city workers who do get a shot over the weekend will be able to report to work on Monday and will not lose any pay. However, they will not be eligible for a $500 vaccination bonus. Bret. BAIER: David Lee Miller in Manhattan. David Lee, thank you. Also breaking tonight, the U.S. Supreme Court has rejected an emergency appeal from health care workers in Maine, seeking religious exemptions for a vaccine mandate. That went into effect today. The justices rejected a request for -- from injunctive relief that would have temporarily blocked enforcement of the state mandate for hospital and nursing home employees. Justices Gorsuch, Thomas, and Alito dissented. Up next, a Republican member of the committee investigating the Capitol riot is retiring from Congress. Plus, lawmakers investigating the riot hear from some of the defendants, we'll have a live report. (COMMERCIAL BREAK) BAIER: Illinois Republican Congressman Adam Kinzinger says he will not seek reelection next year. Kinzinger is a critic of former President Trump and he is on the panel investigating the Capitol riot. The announcement came after Illinois announced redistricting plans for his district. The military veteran was one of 10 House Republicans who voted to impeach then-President Trump on a charge of inciting the insurrection. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) REP. ADAM KINZINGER (R-IL): In Congress, I've witnessed how division is heavily rooted. It has also become increasingly obvious to me that in order to break the narrative, I cannot focus on both a reelection to Congress and a broader fight nationwide. I want to make it clear, this isn't the end of my political future, but the beginning. (END VIDEO CLIP) BAIER: Kinzinger called it the insurrection, the Capitol riot, January 6th. He is the second Republican who voted for impeachment to announce he will not seek reelection. Today, some of the hundreds of people charged in connection with that incident on January 6th, spoke with the committee looking into it. But many of the people lawmakers most want to talk with are not showing up so far. National security correspondent Jennifer Griffin is at the Pentagon tonight with details of one -- of where this investigation is headed. JENNIFER GRIFFIN, FOX NEWS CHANNEL NATIONAL SECURITY CORRESPONDENT (voice over): The January 6th Select Committee conducted more interviews today with some of the 650 defendants charged with storming the U.S. Capitol. The committee has subpoenaed 13 people, but former Trump officials continue to refuse to testify. The Justice Department is now deciding whether former Trump strategist Steve Bannon will face jail time after the House voted to hold him in contempt. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) REP. LIZ CHENEY (R-WY): He attempted to assert some sort of vague executive privilege which, of course, he doesn't have the right to assert. GRIFFIN: At the center of the investigation, is Bannon's presence at a so- called war room in the Willard Hotel, a block from the White House in the days before the riot. CHENEY: So, the war room in the Willard seems to have been established some days before the 6th itself, and was active also on the 6th, and we are, of course, very interested in talking to people who were in the war room. headline: Virginia Gubernatorial Nominees Final Campaign Push; Education Top Concern In Virginia Race; Democrats Make Final Push For Black Votes; Experts View Virginia Gubernatorial Race; Joe Biden Highlights Climate Investments In Stalled Bill; Supreme Court Hears Texas Abortion Law Challenge; West Virginia Democratic Senator Joe Manchin Criticizes Framework For Senate Reconciliation Bill; Polls Show Close Race In Virginia Gubernatorial Election Between Republican Glenn Youngkin And Democrat Terry McAuliffe ; California's Homelessness Problem Examined; Falling Poll Numbers For President Biden Possibly Affecting Democratic Prospects In Virginia Gubernatorial Race
story_text: HAROLD FORD J.R., FOX NEWS CHANNEL POLITICAL CONTRIBUTOR (on camera): (INAUDIBLE) guy, didn't have to do this. Donating all of his salary. Made me feel good to see that and read that story yesterday. JESSE WATTERS, FOX NEWS CHANNEL HOST (on camera): Yes, but he yells at all the kids. Did you hear about that? FORD : I don't -- (CROSSTALK) WATTERS: Screams at -- SANDRA SMITH, FOX NEWS CHANNEL ANCHOR (on camera): We need it. It's good. WATTERS: That's right. All right, that is it for us. "SPECIAL REPORT" -- why are you laughing so much? You got to get it together. GREG GUTFELD, FOX NEWS CHANNEL HOST (on camera): I am sorry. WATTERS: "SPECIAL REPORT" is up next with Bret Baier. BRET BAIER, FOX NEWS CHANNEL ANCHOR (on camera): Hey, Jesse, we've got a big election here in Virginia. So, I'm outside. It means -- (CROSSTALK) WATTERS: Thank you for explaining. BAIER: OK. All right, good evening. I'm Bret Baier. We are coming to you tonight from Leesburg, Virginia, the hub of Loudoun County, the county that might tell us who the next governor will be here in the Commonwealth. Later tonight, Republican Glenn Youngkin will wrap up what he hopes will be a successful come-from-behind campaign against Democrat Terry McAuliffe . Also, tonight, President Joe Biden is on the world stage trying to sell his climate change policy, while back home, one moderate Senator, a Democrat, is pumping the brakes on the president's tax and spend social agenda. We'll bring you that. But the race here in Virginia has centered in recent weeks on the issue of education and ties to current and former presidents. Those themes continued in this final day of campaigning. McAuliffe has been in Roanoke and Richmond so far today. He finishes up later in Fairfax. Youngkin was also in Roanoke and Richmond along with a stop in Virginia Beach. He'll be here in Leesburg later this evening. We'll have analysis from our political panel on this race shortly. We have "FOX TEAM COVERAGE" tonight. Rich Edson is in Fairfax, Virginia with the McAuliffe campaign. But we begin with correspondent Alexandria Hoff with us here in Leesburg, Virginia. Good evening, Alexandria. ALEXANDRIA HOFF, FOX NEWS CHANNEL WASHINGTON CORRESPONDENT (on camera): Good evening, Bret. This final rally, its location, its emphasis, it's really a full-circle moment for Glenn Youngkin, who found his footing on the issue of education. HOFF (voice-over): Tonight, Loudoun Parents Matter Rally here in Leesburg comes on the heels of a 40 plus stop bus tour in 38 counties. But it is here in Loudoun County where many have watched fiery parent versus school board debates play out. Youngkin's message of fighting what he sees as government overreach in schools helped him gain momentum statewide that seemed unlikely early on. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) MIKE RUDD, YOUGKIN SUPPORTER: When you have the school systems in jeopardy like they are, you know, if you don't want to inject racism, you should not have it in the -- have it as a subject into school or anywhere else as far as that goes. If you don't want hate, don't teach it. Everybody's upset around here because of the way the school systems -- HOFF: And that is a sentiment we have been hearing over and over again. According to the latest Washington Post poll, education has become the number one issue for voters in Virginia. That is above the economy and COVID-19. Today, Youngkin said voter enthusiasm is on his side. GLENN YOUNGKIN (R), GUBERNATORIAL CANDIDATE, VIRGINIA: Tomorrow, Virginians will go to the polls, and we will make a decision about our future. And let me tell you what's going to happen. We are going to sweep our statewide offices. (END VIDEO CLIP) HOFF: So, if that were to happen, Youngkin would become the first Republican elected statewide in office in Virginia in 12 years, likely helping to write the GOP playbook for running midterm races across the country. Now, absent on this race, former President Trump. He will be holding a tele-rally this evening. But Youngkin is not taking part in that. He has made it a point of keeping big names off of the campaign trail. Meanwhile, his Democratic opponent Terry McAuliffe , has taken a different approach. For more on that side, we turn it over to Fox News's Rich Edson . He is live in Fairfax tonight. Hi, Rich. RICH EDSON , FOX NEWS CHANNEL WASHINGTON CORRESPONDENT (on camera): Hey, good evening, Alex. And Terry McAuliffe will have the final event of his election-eve here in Northern Virginia, where he spent a good deal of time campaigning. This is Fairfax, Virginia at a beer garden. They're still setting up the event here. As you mentioned, Northern Virginia is still that area of the state where they had some of those contentious school board meetings as education has become a major issue in this race. In fact, the recent Washington Post poll has found that Terry McAuliffe standing among education voters has fallen dramatically in just the past couple of weeks. EDSON (on camera): He's been closing his campaign hitting the Democratic areas of the state, trying to get his supporters to the polls. Just the past few days, he's been in Roanoke, Richmond, the suburbs of Richmond, Hampton, and the Norfolk area. And around here in Northern Virginia. While McAuliffe denied to us he was trying to turn this race into a referendum on former President Trump. He has been mentioning Trump at nearly every stop, including just a couple of hours ago when he borrowed a line from President Biden last week. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) TERRY MCAULIFFE (D), GUBERNATORIAL CANDIDATE, VIRGINIA: I am running against -- I like to say Donald Trump and khakis, or sweater vest. What is he going to do with all those sweater vests at the end of this campaign? But Trump has now endorsed him for the 10th-time today. (END VIDEO CLIP) EDSON: Several Democratic activists have warned about turnout in this election, especially among African American voters. One of his most high- profile surrogates is South Carolina Congressman Jim Clyburn An aide close to Clyburn tells us that he accepted the invitation to campaign for McAuliffe because he knows the black vote is a huge factor in Virginia, and Clyburn wanted to do everything he could to get out that vote. EDSON (on camera): A fifth of the electorate has already voted in early in- person voting that some 1.1 million returns. McAuliffe says all of that early voting gives him the early advantage. Bret. BAIER: Hey, Rich, you know, there's a sound bite from McAuliffe that he's been making on the campaign trail actually many times that's getting some pushback. Let's take a listen. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) MCAULIFFE: In Virginia, 1,142 of our precious children have gone to ICU beds and hospital beds with COVID. We just had two 11-year olds die of COVID -- just happened. (END VIDEO CLIP) BAIER: OK. So, according to the Virginia Department of Health 's web site, through October 23rd, you've got 134,000 kids cases, 976 hospitalizations, 10 deaths. That's it since the beginning of COVID. What's the campaign saying about this? EDSON: The campaign has no comment on that, Bret. And the Washington Post looked into this last week and got a response from the campaign that said that sometimes he tends to misspoke or misspeak on the campaign trail when it comes to these COVID statistics that the Washington Post found that it just happens way too often that he tends to inflate them. And as The Post characterizes it, wildly inflated figures for child hospitalizations, Bret. BAIER: OK, Rich. We'll follow it. Final hours here. Thank you. Let's bring in our political panel to get a sense of where things are. Mo Elleithee is executive director, Georgetown Institute of Politics, and former White House Chief of Staff. Former Republican Party chief Reince Priebus joins us as well. All right, gentlemen, where do you see this race? Reince, first to you. REINCE PRIEBUS, FORMER WHITE HOUSE CHIEF OF STAFF: Well, it's going to be very, very close. Obviously, both sides are debating where we're at an early voting. I think most people agree -- obviously, there's been about 1.1 million people that have voted. The average of what people think is going to turn out tomorrow is going to be two more million people maybe a little bit more than that. Most people think that Terry McAuliffe has an early vote, absentee ballot advantage anywhere from 100 to 250,000 votes, let's say 150,000. Take the middle part -- middle ground. That would mean that Glenn Youngkin would need about 54-55 percent of the turnout tomorrow to win. That's very doable for the Republican on Election Day. Glenn Youngkin. Has the momentum in this race. Clearly, Independents are going to Youngkin. He's got the enthusiasm. And the messaging seems to be flowing Youngkin's way on education, on taxes, on all of the things that are being debated right now, Glenn has that momentum. And now, he's got the late money rush too. So, when you have the message, you've got the momentum, you've got the money -- by the way, on this turnout issue for tomorrow, 55 percent is not a huge number for Republicans. Donald Trump got over 60 percent of the vote on Election Day. Much different. Much different, because a lot of people voted early. I get it. But things do look pretty good for Glenn Youngkin. But cautiously optimistic, RNC chairwoman has done a great job. I think it's going to be very, very, very close. BAIER: You know, Mo, obviously this election like others will see a lot of mail in ballots. The early vote is a big deal here. And you're over 20 percent of the Commonwealth already voting early. Where do you see ground zero here as your head until tomorrow? MO ELLEITHEE, FOX NEWS POLITICAL CONTRIBUTOR (on camera): Yes, and I think I would agree with just about everything Reince said in terms of where we are. I do think that early vote number is critical. And I do think McAuliffe has a pretty big advantage. The numbers I've seen show that he has a -- that Democrats have a bigger advantage in the early vote this time than they did in the last governor's race. And there are a lot more votes. So, that I think is going to matter quite a bit. But I think it's going to be close tomorrow. I think there's a couple of areas to watch. You're in one of them, Bret. Loudoun County is going to be pivotal. It is a purple County, and it's gone to Democrats for a couple of elections in a row. But by no means is it a Democratic stronghold, and that seems to be ground zero. I'm going to be looking at a couple of other key areas. I'm going to be looking at the Richmond suburbs, Henrico County and Chesterfield County. Not long ago, both of those were solidly red. Henrico is solidly blue now, but Chesterfield can go either way. And so, what those numbers look like? I'm going to be looking at Virginia Beach which is also a pivotal jurisdiction. And what's the turnout? BAIER: Yes. ELLEITHEE: At the end of the night going to look like in Fairfax County. Largest county in the state, about as big of a Democratic stronghold. If turnout is high there, that's a good thing for McAuliffe. If it is low, it's going to be a longer night. BAIER: We'll explain, you know, how this state -- this Commonwealth breaks down. And a lot of times Republicans obviously rely on the southern part of the state to turn out big numbers, but there aren't bigger cities down there. So, around Washington, D.C. has been a Democratic stronghold, Reince, but it seems like this education issue has broken through and has kind of chipped away at some of those suburban voters. At least that's according to polls. But here is the New York Times in this editorial. "Recent school board wars have been a battle of subcultures. A lot of parents have trouble knowing what's going on in their kids' classrooms. When they challenge what they sense is happening, they meet a few common responses. They are told, as by Virginia's Democratic gubernatorial candidate that parents shouldn't tell schools want to teach. They are told they are racist. Or they are blindly assured that there is nothing radical going on -- when, in fact, there might be. When people sense that those culture power -- cultural power are imposing ideologies on their own families, you can expect the reaction will be swift and fierce." Is that what's happening here, Reince? Is that why some of these blue strongholds are being chipped away at? PRIEBUS: Well, I think so. But, you know, what Mo said is also I agree. You know, look, when you're talking about how Loudoun County comes down, Ed Gillespie in 2017 got more votes than any Republican in a statewide race ever got, but he still lost by 20,000. Glenn Youngkin, if he wins, Loudoun County, it's over. If Glenn Youngkin gets one-third of Fairfax County, maybe needs 36-37 percent, Fairfax County, Glenn Youngkin wins. But what's happening to your question, Bret, is that these school issues that the mask and the -- and the -- and the vaccine mandates, and who's teaching our kids and CRT? What's happened is it's nationalizing this race. And what's -- what -- this is why it's important for tomorrow. Because all the early vote is over. McAulliffe's got a slight advantage there. But if the 2020 electorate comes out, meaning the presidential vote people, not the governor voting people, but the people who only vote in a presidential election. BAIER: Yes. PRIEBUS: If they turn out -- and this is what juices up that vote. That means that Republicans that normally wouldn't bother in a Virginia governor's race, they turn out. That's why that issue is deadly for Terry McAuliffe . BAIER: All right. Mo, I got 20 seconds here. ELLEITHEE: Yes, look, for that level of turnout to happen -- I mean, look, I don't -- Donald Trump was able to draw out Republicans that no other Republican was able to draw out. Youngkin has had a tortured relationship here with Donald Trump . Trying to juice his supporters when the cameras aren't on, but keeping arm's length when they are on. So, I question whether or not he is going to be able to excite the Republican base the way it happened in 2020. But McAuliffe is making sure that every Democrat gets excited by Donald Trump 's shadow on this race. So, I -- look -- BAIER: Yes. ELLEITHEE: I think it's a roll of the dice, and I think Reince and I are going to be up late tomorrow, poring over these numbers. It's going to be an exciting night. BAIER: Well, hey, we're excited. We're excited. ELLEITHEE: Yes. BAIER: Mo, Reince, we appreciate -- we appreciate it. We'll see you tomorrow and see how it all turns out. Thank you.
