(BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) SHANNON BREAM, FOX NEWS CHANNEL CHIEF LEGAL CORRESPONDENT (voice over): The Supreme Court's fast track fight over S.B. 8 Texas has banned on most abortions after roughly six weeks into a pregnancy sparked nearly three hours worth of arguments Monday as both a group of abortion providers and the U.S. Justice Department argued to convince the justices that they have the legal right to sue to stop the law. Today's arguments were primarily procedural in nature, mostly because of the law's unique enforcement mechanism, giving private citizens and not state officials the power to enforce the laws ban on most abortions after a fetal heartbeat is detected. Justice Kagan questioned whether the law was specifically crafted to get around relevant Supreme Court precedent the case Ex parte Young. ELENA KAGAN, ASSOCIATE JUSTICE, SUPREME COURT: Some geniuses came up with a way to evade the commands of that decision, as well as the command that the broader -- the even broader principle that states are not to nullify federal constitutional rights and to say, oh, we've never seen this before, so we can't do anything about it. STEPHEN BREYER , ASSOCIATE JUSTICE, SUPREME COURT: Is it that the federal government, no matter who's in charge, without a statute, whatever party, whatever president, can just go and intervene in any case, can bring a federal case whenever they think a state law affecting private people is unconstitutional. BREAM: The Justice Department argued it has the right to go after S.B. 8 because it was designed to "chill the exercise of a constitutional rights" prompting pointed questions from Justice Gorsuch. NEIL GORSUCH , ASSOCIATE JUSTICE, SUPREME COURT: We don't get to pick and choose among our rights. We're supposed to enforce them all equally. Why does this one get special treatment? BAIER: And that's really the big one, right, Shannon? BREAM: It is. That is the one that's got talk of Roe v. Wade, what happens to those precedents, so all eyes will be watching. BAIER: To be fair to Manchin, he has been saying this all along about the kind of nebulous reconciliation bill, he needs to see it. PERGRAM: It was thought the progressives overplayed their hand asking for too much. They have now backpedaled. BAIER: December, that will be something if it all comes out. PERGRAM: December to remember. BAIER: On the way out the door, that's right, on the way out the door to Christmas. BAIER: So that issue of education that we were talking about earlier with Mo Elleithee Reince Priebus. It does seem to cross party lines. INGRAHAM: The one group that the Democrats could not afford to alienate were the suburban women. They were critical to their election victory in 2020. They were a deficit for Trump in 2020. The Democrats managed nationally, I think, and in Virginia, slowly but surely are eroding their majority base among suburban women. Education, whether you are a minority voter, a nonminority voter, it matters. You want a quality education. To kind of just teach racial polarization and gender bending, it works in college campus seminars on a Thursday night. It doesn't work for Monday through Friday in the classroom. BAIER: There is another state that Republicans have not given up on, and that is California. They haven't had the success that Virginia has seen in the Republican party in the past. You have this special coming up. INGRAHAM: Yes, on FOX Nation right now. It's called California on the edge. And I spent the better part of a week going up and down the California coast. And what we saw was both illuminating, a little scary, sad, frightening. But there are pockets of hope, and I think we captured that. BAIER: We have a clip with your ride along with police. Take a listen. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) UNIDENTIFIED MALE: When you talk about spikes in crime, this is our hotspot. And you see those boxes of food back there? INGRAHAM: Yes. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: So you have people, churches, that come here and they give them food, which, I get it. Everybody needs to eat. But the problem is, it encourages them just to stay here. And now you have old food that's trash with the rats. INGRAHAM: Everywhere. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: And then they go into these houses right here. INGRAHAM: Oh boy. What percentage of the people who are homeless are on drugs? If you had to guess. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: If I had to guess 80 percent. INGRAHAM: Yes. San Francisco police told me 90. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: Yes. (END VIDEO CLIP) BAIER: That's pretty amazing. INGRAHAM: Ron Kingi is a sergeant there and does a community safety partnership. He has a multiracial, really cool background. He is someone who hasn't given up on his neighborhood. He grew up there. He is in there. And they are making a difference. It's incremental, Bret. And just to bring you back to politics for a moment. I think what we will see tomorrow and then Wednesday is this lesson that Republicans cannot write off entire sections of the country and hope to cobble together a victory. Virginia, Colorado, New England, even California, it's got to be a 50 state campaign in 2024. Youngkin ran a smart campaign throughout the entire commonwealth of Virginia. He didn't give on Fairfax County, Loudoun County where we are tonight, really, really smart campaigner. BAIER: That's interesting. So you can stream it now on FOX Nation? INGRAHAM: Absolutely. BAIER: All right, thanks so much. INGRAHAM: Great to see you, Bret. BAIER: Up next, the panel on the Virginia governor's race and President Biden in Europe. We are also hearing Virginia, obviously, ahead of tomorrow's big governor's election. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) UNIDENTIFIED MALE: Usually I vote for Republicans, but I couldn't do it this time. BAIER: So the linkage to Trump really stuck with you. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: Yes. Yes, it did. I thought he wasn't a very nice man. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: I'm a small business owner, so wanting to make sure that Virginia gets back to being active and small business friendly and keep our economy moving. BAIER: Can I ask you how you voted? UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: You certainly can. I voted Republican. Yes. BAIER: And so do you think that there is a tide changing here? Do you feel something heading that way? UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: I do. I think that people are tired. I think that people are wanting things to get back to normal. (END VIDEO CLIP) (COMMERCIAL BREAK) (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) JOE BIDEN , (D) PRESIDENT OF THE UNITED STATES: I believe we will pass my Build Back Better plan, and I believe we will pass the infrastructure bill. Maybe it won't work, but I believe we will see by the end of next week at home that it's passed. SEN. JOE MANCHIN, (D-WV): The political games have to stop. For the sake of the country, I urge the House to vote and pass the bipartisan infrastructure bill. Holding this bill hostage is not going to work in getting my support for reconciliation bill. REP. PRAMILA JAYAPAL , (D-WA) CHAIR, PROGRESSIVE CAUCUS: We are ready to get this transformational change to people. I would just urge everybody to keep tempers down. (END VIDEO CLIP) BAIER: Well, it doesn't seem like it's moving that fast. We don't know if it's going to come together this week. It doesn't appear that way with what Senator Joe Manchin said today as these two bills are up on Capitol Hill. Meantime, asked about those bills in an ABC poll, here's how people responded. If they become law, would it help people like you, 25 percent, hurt people like you, 32 percent. That's just over the past couple of days. We'll start there with our panel. Let's bring them in, "Washington Post" columnist Marc Thiessen, Leslie Marshall, Democratic strategist, and Kimberley Strassel, a member of the editorial board at "The Wall Street Journal." Kimberley, let me start with you. It's not surprising that Joe Manchin comes out and says I want to see the specifics. I want to see what the impact is going to be. And I'm not just going to pass something without knowing what's in it. He has kind of been saying that all along. But where does this go? KIMBERLEY STRASSEL, "WALL STREET JOURNAL": He did actually make some news today, Bret, because if you drill down into what he said, a lot of attention to these buzz words about shell games and gimmicks. But he got more specific in that. He said look, if you have all these programs and you only have them run a couple of years and you claim that they are going to end when they don't, the bill is actually like twice the amount of $1.75. And I said $1.75. Well, if you extrapolate that, it means stuff is going to have to come out of this bill, like big programs. He also expressed some concern about the climate provisions. He is not close to a yes, and major modifications are going to have to happen from what they have talked about in the House. Yet, still, the question is how much will progressives swallow of that, and when will they say no themselves? BAIER: Yes. And progressives seem to be saying, OK, we'll trust the president and the administration, and let's move forward, Leslie. I'm not sure it's going to hold, but we will see. LESLIE MARSHALL, DEMOCRATIC STRATEGIST: Well, actually, Kimberley and I don't rarely agree, but today would be one day where progressives have to make a decision. I'm a democrat. I have said it before. These should not have been married, these two pieces of legislation. And I feeling as a moderate centrist that the progressive caucus is holding us hostage. And I think that all Democrats, whether it's a Manchin, a Sinema, or a Sanders have to decide do they want to have a lost gubernatorial election tomorrow in Virginia? Do they want to lose more seats in the House and Senate and lose majority in both the House and Senate and perhaps in the White House in 2024? We have to work together. And big programs have already gone to the wayside, one of which Senator Sanders will not let go of, because you have 15 Democrats that are very vulnerable in their districts that are promised lower drug prices. That's something Manchin doesn't like, and Sanders seems to require, and he definitely heads the progressive caucus. BAIER: Marc, the president is facing pretty bad poll numbers in recent days. You look at this NBC poll, his approval stands at 42 percent approval, disapprove 54 percent. On the internals of that poll, there's all kinds of questions where Republicans are really up. If the Marist poll, election confidence, better chance of winning 2024, Biden at 36 percent, someone else at 44 percent. Here's the president talking about polls this weekend. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) JOE BIDEN , (D) PRESIDENT OF THE UNITED STATES: The polls are going to go up and down and up and down. Look at every other president. It's the same thing that's happened. But that's not why I ran. I didn't run to determine how well I'm going to do in the polls. I said that I would make sure that we were in a position where we dealt with climate change, where we moved in a direction that significantly improved the prospects of American workers being able to have good jobs and good pay. And further that, I would make sure that we dealt with the crisis that was caused by COVID. We have done all of those. (END VIDEO CLIP) BAIER: Polls do go up and down, Marc, but they have been going down, and even Terry McAuliffe here in Virginia has acknowledged that that is a significant headwind. MARC THIESSEN, COLUMNIST, "WASHINGTON POST": Going down like a rock. He's right that approval rating go up and down. But it's very hard to recover when only 37 percent of the American people say that you are competent. When people make a decision that you are incompetent, it is very hard to recover from that. And that is the most devastating number in that poll, 50 percent of the American people think he is incompetent. And just the Joe Manchin press conference today is evidence of that incompetence. And Joe Manchin isn't just another stakeholder in this debate. He's got a veto. Let's be straight about it. If he doesn't agree to it, it's not going to get passed. So why would you release a framework that you haven't cleared with Joe Manchin yet, and have this whole debacle unfold over the last week? You need to sit down with Joe Manchin and Kyrsten Sinema , figure out what they're willing to accept, what they are willing to not accept, craft that as a framework, and say to the other Democrats this is it. If you want the Build Back Better, this is what it is, and you're going to have to live with it, and get their votes locked in before you start releasing it. BAIER: The White House even after that press conference said no, we will have Senator Manchin's approval eventually. They need to talk to Senator Manchin, perhaps, about that. One last poll heading into Election Day, Kimberley, this is the RCP poll, Youngkin and McAuliffe, Real Clear Politics, Youngkin up 1.7 heading into Election Day. That is a significant turnaround from where this race was at the beginning. STRASSEL: Yes, and you know, just to continue this theme, it has to be related to the White House. Obviously, McAuliffe has made some mistakes on education. But this is about what's going on in D.C. And you have to wonder how things would look different, Bret, if Biden had taking the win on that infrastructure bill at the beginning of September, said I'm a bipartisan president, and moved on. I think things might look better both in terms of those polling numbers and in terms of that Virginia race. BAIER: All right, when we come back with the panel, tomorrow's headlines from Virginia. (COMMERCIAL BREAK) BAIER: Finally tonight, a look at tomorrow's headlines with the panel. Kim, first to you. STRASSEL: Despite wild predictions of the imminent demise of Roe v. Wade, a majority of Supreme Court justices look skeptically on what is in fact a pretty technically and legally complex Texas abortion law. BAIER: Leslie? MARSHALL: Despite headlines that Democrats are infighting and can't get it together, the progressive caucus and the centrist moderate Democrats come to an agreement on both having the infrastructure and reconciliation bills go forward. And, yes, they will pass. BAIER: OK. Let's see. Marc? THIESSEN: Mine is not from tomorrow but from 2100. Glasgow climate conference wrong, climate change was not existential threat, the world did not end. We are still here. (LAUGHTER) BAIER: All right, Marc. Thank you. Tomorrow on SPECIAL REPORT, complete coverage of Election Day. Shannon Bream will have the first FOX News voter analysis on the Virginia governor's race. We'll have that for you at 6:00, then a special at 7:00 p.m. coverage. We'll also hear from former House Speaker Newt Gingrich weighing in on this race and its impact around the nation. This should be interesting to watch. We also have races, obviously a big race for governor in New Jersey. And races around the country that we haven't talked that much about, but we will touch on all of those. Thanks for inviting us into your home tonight from Virginia. That's it for the SPECIAL REPORT, fair, balanced, and still unafraid. "FOX NEWS PRIMETIME" hosted by Rachel Campos-Duffy this week starts right now. Hey, Rachel. headline: President Joe Biden At U.K. Climate Summit As Approval Dives At Home; Rep. Nancy Mace (R-SC) Is Interviewed About Joe Manchin Not Ready To Support Biden Spending Plan; Supreme Court Hears Arguments On Texas Abortion Law; New Jersey Governor's Race Tightens In Home Stretch; Baldwin Eagerly Awaiting Shooting Probe Results; Attorney For "Rust" Assistant Director On Baldwin Shooting Probe; Final Push For Votes In Virginia Governor's Race
story_text: News; Domestic President Joe Biden At U.K. Climate Summit As Approval Dives At Home; Rep. Nancy Mace (R-SC) Is Interviewed About Joe Manchin Not Ready To Support Biden Spending Plan; Supreme Court Hears Arguments On Texas Abortion Law; New Jersey Governor's Race Tightens In Home Stretch; Baldwin Eagerly Awaiting Shooting Probe Results; Attorney For "Rust" Assistant Director On Baldwin Shooting Probe; Final Push For Votes In Virginia Governor's Race Martha MacCallum, Shannon Bream, Kayleigh McEnany, Guy Benson, Jonathan Hunt, Rich Edson 8,223 words 1 November 2021 Fox News Channel: The Story with Martha MacCallum HUNDD English Copyright 2021 VIQ Solutions, Inc. JOHN ROBERTS, FOX NEWS HOST: There are times to post photos on Instagram and times not to. SANDRA SMITH, FOX NEWS HOST: Maybe a little insensitive. We'll see what happens next with the investigation, John, and great to be with you as we begin a brand-new week. Thanks for joining us. I'm Sandra Smith. ROBERTS: And I'm John Roberts. We will see you again tomorrow for another episode of "AMERICA REPORTS". THE STORY with Martha starts right now. MARTHA MACCALLUM, FOX NEWS ANCHOR: Thank you, Sandra and John. Good afternoon, everybody. I'm Martha MacCallum in New York right now on THE STORY. President Biden in Glasgow as Senator Joe Manchin says that they're essentially no closer to a deal on the president's agenda. And as Democratic infighting continues, so during this trip abroad, he was asked about the large picture of all of that and the mounting issues back home by A.P. reporter, Zeke Miller, watch this. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) ZEKE MILLER, REPORTER, A.P.: You've tried to showcase that America is back, but back at home, your poll numbers have fallen, your party's nominee for governor in Virginia is facing a very tougher than expected race, your party spent months trying to negotiate the centerpiece of your Democratic - - of your domestic legislative agenda. So, why should the world, you know, believe that when you say America is back, that really it's here to stay? JOE BIDEN, PRESIDENT OF THE UNITED STATES: Because of the way they reacted. You were here. They listened. Everyone sought me out. They wanted to know what our views were and we helped lead what happened here. I didn't run to determine how well I'm going to do in the polls. I ran to make sure that I followed through on what I said I would do as President of the United States. (END VIDEO CLIP) MACCALLUM: Rough patch to be sure for President Biden, when you look at polls like these, these are brand new numbers that we just got from Marist today. Democrats and Democrat leaning independents were asked, do you think better that Democrats have a better chance of winning the presidency in 2024 if Joe Biden is the president's nominee -- party's nominee, or if it's somebody else? 44 percent said someone else. 36 percent say Joe Biden. 20 percent say they are not sure if they want it to be the current president or another nominee from the Democrat Party when they look ahead to 2024. So, let's bring in Kayleigh McEnany, former White House press secretary and co-host of "OUTNUMBERED" and Guy Benson, political editor at Town Hall, host of the "GUY BENSON SHOW" and a Fox News contributor. Great to have both of you with us today. Kayleigh, obviously, the White House is in one of those difficult phases. And you know what it feels like to stand up at the podium and have reporters sort of come after you and tell you that things aren't going well. Your thought on what you just heard from Zeke there from A.P. and from the president, from Zeke Miller. KAYLEIGH MCENANY, FOX NEWS CHANNEL ANALYST: Yes, that was a -- that was a fantastic question by Zeke Miller of A.P., well said. Factual and really tough for Biden to answer. Look, there's one thing I can say about when I stood at the podium, we never lost the support of our party, President Trump had a base that is famously very loyal even to this day. We never saw a poll like that where you had essentially more than 60 percent of the party questioning whether you should be the nominee. Now, that's one poll. But in other polls, we've seen Democrats give President Biden low marks on the direction of the country, not necessarily tied to him. But that generic right direction, wrong direction, upwards of 40 percent of Democrats saying we're heading in the wrong direction. When you have those kinds of numbers within your own party and I have not even gotten to independents who he's underwater with that very key group. But when it's within your party, that's not something we experienced in the Trump administration. It's something they're very, very real having to deal with in a -- in a practical way. MACCALLUM: Yes, absolutely. So, right track wrong track, which Kayleigh just mentioned, Guy, 71 percent say that we're on the wrong track. I went back to look at the most recent time we've seen a number like that and it was during the heat of COVID. So, as a pandemic was sweeping the entire country, it would be understandable that the country would feel like things weren't going in the right direction. And now we have that in this environment. So, what do you attribute that wrong track number to? GUY BENSON, FOX NEWS CHANNEL CONTRIBUTOR: So many different factors, Martha, and that comes from the NBC poll. I know the president said he didn't campaign to do well in the polls, but he certainly is not doing that right now. In that poll, he's underwater by double digits overall on approval. One number that I thought was very interesting in the NBC survey, Martha, was strong approve versus strong disapprove. He only has 18 percent of the country, strongly approving of his job performance. 46 percent strongly disapprove, that goes to an intensity gap as well. We'll see if that plays out, for example in Virginia. So, I understand Biden, the president, what else can you say, when your poll numbers are this bad in a given moment, saying I'm not governing for the polls. What he did say, though, was I want to do the things that I promised for the country. Well, he promised to be truthful. He promised to be competent, and he promised to unify the country. And in that exact same poll, he is failing on those metrics as well. So, I don't really know where you go from there, but it's a bit ugly for the Democratic Party. And that's why I think some partisans on that side are starting to look around and saying maybe we need to interchange some different options, looking all the way ahead to 2024? Not a great sign. MACCALLUM: Yes, that number that Guy was just referring to Kayleigh, how would you rate Joe Biden -- this is an NBC poll, I should point out on being competent and effective as president, 20 percent give him a very good rating. 42 percent give a very poor rating. And one of the things that strikes me is these are the same kinds of things that we heard voters saying during the election period that they wanted, right? They wanted calm, sort of competent, efficient leadership. And, you know, that was one of the major issues that we saw in the last election. But now we're seeing in these numbers that they're watching nine months of this presidency, and they feel a little bit at sea. They don't feel like they're getting what they wanted. MCENANY: Yes, that's exactly right. And I think the definite turning point for this presidency was Afghanistan. And when I say that, you know, some analysts say, well, foreign policy doesn't really sink into the souls of the American voter. But this did in a real way, because I think it fed into this general understanding or a general, I guess, discernment that this presidency is an incompetent presidency. Only 37 percent gave Joe Biden a four or a five on his ability to handle a crisis. I can tell you, I go all across the country, from Oregon to Washington to Virginia, twice. And Afghanistan is one of the things I hear mainly from voters, it was far bigger than just the collapse of a country. It was the general feeling of an incompetent presidency. MACCALLUM: (INAUDIBLE) quickly here if you can, you know, Americans expect efficiency. We expect stuff to be on the shelves, we don't expect there to be huge backup at the ports, you expect, you know, monetary policy to work in terms of inflation and the border and all of that. And I think there's like an unsettling feeling right now, when people say, well, you know that this is the stuff that happens in other countries, like crazy lines at the airport and all kinds of things that you can't get your arms around and stuff doesn't work. BENSON: Joe Biden basically in the campaign against Donald Trump promised normalcy, right? He ran a basement campaign, he popped up occasionally, and he stayed out of sight, out of mind and he won. Does this feel like normalcy right now? Most Americans say absolutely not. And you can't run a basement presidency as much as he might be trying. MACCALLUM: Not when there's all this stuff going on. That's for sure. Guy, thank you. Guy Benson always great to see you. Kayleigh McEnany, always great to see you. Thank you both for being here. MCENANY: Thank you. BENSON: You bet. MACCALLUM: All right, so we are getting some brand-new feedback from the White House responding to Senator Joe Manchin, who says that he cannot support this President Biden spending bill without more clarity on how it would be paid for and he says he doesn't really care about deadlines. He wants to figure out how this will be paid for in an efficient way that they can sell to the country. We're going to show you what the White House is now saying on this, which is very important on that beautiful day, beautiful fall day at the White House. So, still ahead this hour, candidate for Virginia Governor Glenn Youngkin on the eve of Election Day in Virginia as Democrat Terry McAuliffe fights to stave off the Republicans advanced. We will speak with Glenn Youngkin clearly a rising star in this Virginia race. We'll talk about how he's feeling tonight before all of this gets underway when we come back. (COMMERCIAL BREAK) MACCALLUM: Well, I guess it all depends on who you ask. Moments ago, Senator Joe Manchin said that he is "not ready to support President Biden's social spending bill" that's a paraphrase I should say. Even after the president cut the $3.5 trillion price tag in half. Just a few moments ago, Senator Manchin stepped in front of the microphone. He said he needs to know more about what this bill will do to the economy and to the national debt. Here he is in his own words. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) SEN. JOE MANCHIN (D-WV): What I see are shell games, budget gimmicks that make the real cost of the so-called $1.75 trillion bill estimated to be almost twice that amount, if the full time has run out if you extended it permanently. (END VIDEO CLIP) MACCALLUM: So, the White House says that the plan is fully paid for, costs zero, you've heard this a lot. And it will reduce the deficit. They're confident they say that Senator Manchin will end up supporting the legislation. Joining me now Republican congresswoman Nancy Mace from South Carolina. Good to have you with us this afternoon, Congresswoman. It's interesting to note that we also just heard from Congresswoman Jayapal who said that she wants to get prescription pricing and immigration sorted out in the House bill on your side of the building there. And then she said this. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) REP. PRAMILA JAYAPAL (D-WA): We'll be happy to vote both those bills, both the infrastructure bill and the Build Back Better bill through the House. And I'm hoping that can happen as soon as tomorrow or the next day. We are ready to get this transformational change to people. (END VIDEO CLIP) MACCALLUM: So, sounds like there's going to be a vote in her mind. Is that what you're hearing? REP. NANCY MACE (R-SC): We're not hearing that at all. And I think Congressman Jayapal is probably high as a kite right now. Looking at what's going on with Senator Joe Manchin where just a few moments ago, finally, we have a Democrat on the Hill calling reconciliation. MACCALLUM: What do you mean she's high as a kite right now? What do you mean? MACE: Well, they want to have additional immigration in the bill. We haven't had time to make all these modifications, amendments and edits to the spending because clearly, it's not good enough for progressives. I don't know when they're going to do that. I don't see it happening and you have this huge race tomorrow in Virginia. I doubt you're going to get moderates on board if Youngkin wins the governor's race tomorrow. This is a bellwether for the rest of the country on where the country is particularly on these kinds of very touchy issues where you have progressives and socialists against moderates, I don't think it happens. MACCALLUM: So, you know, we know that Nancy Pelosi says all the time that she's not going to bring anything to the floor unless she believes that she can get an up -- yes vote on it. And you know, we have heard Congresswoman Jayapal has been indicating, you know, since the weekend that she felt like this was moving towards a vote. So, if -- on both of the bills. So, do you think that Nancy Pelosi will go forward if she thinks she can get yeses in the House on both of those? And how good do you think your feel is for how close they are to actually having a vote? MACE: Well, I would never bet against Nancy Pelosi but twice now she's trying to bring both bills, or at least one of the bills or both bills to the floor two different times now and has failed, because the progressives and socialists cannot strike a deal with moderate Democrats. Meanwhile, Republicans are totally out in the cold on all of the above. So, seeing what Senator Manchin's comments were today, I don't see how it happens. And he's right, I mean, this is in shell game, when you start digging in the kind of spending that they're talking about, there are limitations and dates on the spinning that end. But there would be need to be additional spending maybe two or three times as much to fulfill the programs that they're talking about. So, it really is a shell game. It really is a gimmick. And finally, I'm really grateful that Senator Manchin is calling it what it is. Inflation will rise, taxes will go up on the middle class, jobs will leave the United States and now they want -- they want illegal immigrants to have mass amnesty, spending billions of dollars on that. I just -- I just it's not going to happen the way that it's going right now. MACCALLUM: So, when you just referenced the election tomorrow, the biggest races that everybody's watching is Virginia, of course and New Jersey, keeping an eye on that as well. In fact, we're going to speak to a couple of those candidates in just a few moments. But what impact you think that might have on the fortitude behind this agenda from the next day? MACE: If Glenn Youngkin wins Virginia tomorrow, then reconciliation crumbles. It is no longer on the table. I don't know how you are a moderate Democrat and support the kind of spending that they're talking about when Republicans may very well and it's looking likely will win the governor's race in a Democrat seat for the first time in over a decade. It means the Build Back Better agenda is dead. MACCALLUM: We will see. We'll watch it closely. Thank you for weighing in today. Congressman Mace, nice to see you as always. MACE: As always. MACCALLUM: So, we have a story exclusive this hour with the attorney for Dave Halls, who is the Assistant Director on Alec Baldwin's movie Rust where the tragedy happened just a short while -- short time ago. He handed the gun to Alec Baldwin, who then fired the gun and shot and killed the cinematographer on that set. So, we're going to talk to his attorney because he said some very interesting things to the investigators. And we will ask her about that right after this. Stay with us. (COMMERCIAL BREAK) MACCALLUM: The most strict abortion law in the United States faces two challenges today at the Supreme Court. The Texas law bans abortions after a heartbeat is detected usually around six weeks. It makes exceptions for medical emergencies, but not for rape or incest. The question today is not whether the law is constitutional but who has the standing to challenge that law. "FOX NEWS @ NIGHT" anchor and Chief Legal Correspondent Shannon Bream was in the courtroom today watching all of this play out as the justices asked questions and discussed and she joins us live from the Supreme Court who better to answer these questions for us. Shannon, what did you learn in there today? SHANNON BREAM, FOX NEWS CHANNEL CHIEF LEGAL CORRESPONDENT: Hi, Martha. Well, you're right, this debate today or the Texas law was much more about procedure than it was substance. But it's a huge deal that this case was fast tracked and put on the schedule today because the justices so far have declined to put that restrictive abortion law on hold, meaning, it is still in effect right now in Texas. About three hours worth of arguments today and there were two groups including the U.S. Justice Department and a group of abortion providers, they're arguing that they should be able to sue to challenge the law and shut it down. Justice Kagan seemed very skeptical of the Texas laws' unique enforcement mechanism. It allows private citizens to be the ones who go out and bring lawsuits, not state officials or law enforcement. She asked whether this is trying to go around an important precedent. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) ELENA KAGAN, ASSOCIATE JUSTICE, SUPREME COURT: And the fact that after all these many years, some geniuses came up with a way to evade the commands of that decision, as well as the command that the broader -- the even broader principle that states are not to nullify federal constitutional rights and to say, oh, we've never seen this before, so we can't do anything about it. I guess I just don't understand the argument. (END VIDEO CLIP) BREAM: The Justice Department seemed to have a tougher hurdle today. Several of the justices expressed concern about what would happen if any administration and any president decide to simply that the feds did not like a law, that the states, any state had passed, here's Justice Breyer. STEPHEN BREYER , ASSOCIATE JUSTICE, SUPREME COURT: Is it that the federal government, no matter who's in charge, without a statute, whatever party, whatever president, can just go and intervene in any case, can bring a federal case whenever they think a state law affecting private people is unconstitutional. (END VIDEO CLIP) BREAM: So, no word on when this fast track case when we could get a decision. I've expect it to be pretty quick. Now, on December 1st, a few weeks from now, that's the really big abortion case on substance. That's Mississippi's law banning most abortions after 15 weeks. It will be held and heard here. That case, the ruling is due by the end of June, which of course, Martha, puts it right in the middle of the midterm elections. MACCALLUM: Yes, fascinating. Thank you so much, Shannon Bream at the Supreme Court. So, Election Day is upon us as you have seen us talking about this or the past several weeks, and we're going to talk about the two big races that are coming tomorrow. Big one in Virginia. Big one in New Jersey. We have two of the candidates from those races here, coming up next. (COMMERCIAL BREAK) MACCALLUM: Interesting night for tomorrow night shaping up and one of the states that we're going to be watching very closely is New Jersey. Governor Phil Murphy ahead in the polls, but Republican Jack Ciattarelli may have history on his side, a Democrat governor has not won reelection in New Jersey since 1977. We invited Governor Murphy, he's been on the show before, we invited him to come back and talk to us today. We hope that he'll take advantage of that open invitation to him. But joining us right now is his Republican challenger Jack Ciattarelli who is with us today. Sir, thank you very much. It's good to have you here. You know, 24 hours away here. Where do you think this race is going? We've seen some polls that are tight. And then we see the one that's got you at 39 percent to his 50 right now, how do you see this shaping up? JACK CIATTARELLI (R), GUBERNATORIAL CANDIDATE OF NEW JERSEY: Internal polls, Martha, out of both camps has it as a dead heat. I like our positioning, we're surging. The energy momentum up and down the state as I barnstorm all 21 counties have been phenomenal. We're going to continue to do over the next 24 hours what we've done for the -- done for the past 22 months and I'm looking forward to the outcome. MACCALLUM: I know taxes has been one of the big issues. You say that Governor Murphy said basically, if taxes are your issue, we're not your state. And you know, we do hear a lot of voters saying that they think it's really expensive to live in New Jersey, which it is and taxes are the number one issue at 27 percent. But he's also tried to paint you as too conservative for New Jersey, which is obviously generally a blue state and sort of purpley at times, but he says that you're against raising the minimum wage. He says you voted against legalizing weed. He wants to loosen the gun laws, he said about you, and that you waffle on whether or not you'll even protect women's health. What do you say to that? JACK CIATTARELLI, CANDIDATE FOR NEW JERSEY GOVERNOR: Well, if it was up to Governor Murthy, Martha. We mortgage our future with unnecessary borrowing and then we all go home and get high. And he thinks that what New Jersey is all about, it's not. Property taxes is an issue, the worst business climate in the nation, particularly for small business is an issue. A bloated, inefficient state government corrupted by special interests as an issue, a lack of support for police. He's been the most anti-cop governor we've ever had. And then, of course, we want to get our public school curriculum back on track. He's made some drastic changes to the public school curriculum that is of great concern to great many parents across the state. He's the extremist. He's more extreme than Jim Florio, Jim McGreevey and John Corzine combined, and none of them were reelected. He's not going to be reelected tomorrow. MACCALLUM: It'd be interesting to watch. One of the things obviously that's such a hot topic. And we see the closures are the temporary shuttering of fire departments here in New York City. There was sort of an undercover tape done that suggested that somebody in his camp said, we won't put in vaccine mandates until right after the election. Here's what Governor Murphy's folks said about that. Listen, (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) PHIL MURPHY, NEW JERSEY GOVERNOR: We have no plans to do that, in terms of mandate. I'm not going to "commit" to something because, as I said, the virus has taken so many turns that none of us expected. It's very humbling. But we have zero, I have zero expectation that's going to happen. We just don't, at the moment, we just don't need to. (END VIDEO CLIP) MACCALLUM: What about that? CIATTARELLI: New Jersey is very scared, Martha. This guy isn't being transparent with us. It wouldn't be the first time. He wasn't transparent with us with regard to what happened in nursing homes. New Jersey leads the nation in nursing home deaths because he didn't follow the CDC advice not to send COVID-19 patients there. So it's one of the things that certainly driving the turnout and I think the energy. The fact that they feel it, Phil Murphy is not being transparent with them about what his true intentions are. I've been clear. I'm vaccinated. I promoted my vaccination. I encourage people to get vaccinated. But I'm not going to force a vaccine mandate on any adult or any child here in New Jersey. MACCALLUM: Well, it'll be interesting to see what happens tomorrow, Jack Ciattarelli, Thank you very much. Good to have you here today, sir. CIATTARELLI: Thank you, Martha. MACCALLUM: So we are also going to be joined in moments by Virginia Republican candidate for governor Glenn Youngkin, who is out storming in the barnstorming in the southwestern part of the state. Today, we'll ask him why he's focused there right now, as he looks at tomorrow's big election. But next, an exclusive that you don't want to miss with the attorney for this man, Dave Halls, he was the assistant director on the movie "Rust." He handed the gun to Alec Baldwin that killed crew member Halyna Hutchins. What his attorney wants to tell you about what happened that day when we come back. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) HILARIA BALDWIN, ALEC BALDWIN'S WIFE: You, guys -- what know what, no details. ALEC BALDWIN, ACTOR: I'm mean -- do me a favor, I'm going to ask the question. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: Well, I appreciate that he was probably very upset. BALDWIN: The guy is overwhelmed with grief. This is something that that, you know, there are incidental accidents on film sets from time to time, but nothing like this. This is a one in a trillion episode, so one in a trillion. (END VIDEO CLIP) (COMMERCIAL BREAK) MACCALLUM: Alec Baldwin making his first comments on camera about the movie set shooting that killed cinematographer Halyna Hutchins. Baldwin is also a producer of the movie "Rust" and he defended the crew. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) BALDWIN: There are incidental accidents on film sets from time to time, but nothing. This is a one trillion episode, so one in a trillion. (END VIDEO CLIP) MACCALLUM: Interesting appearance by he and his wife yesterday by him and his wife yesterday. But the LA Times reports that there were three other accidental shootings on this movie set including a woman from the props department shooting herself in the foot. In Baldwin's case, investigators say the assistant director admitted that he should have checked the gun more carefully before saying it was cold, meaning that it was safe, that it had no live rounds in it. The lawyer for assistant director Dave Halls joins me exclusively in a moment, but first to chief correspondent Jonathan Hunt reporting live from LA. Jonathan. JONATHAN HUNT, FOX NEWS CHIEF CORRESPONDENT: Martha it's perhaps not surprising that Alec Baldwin and his wife Hilaria seemed tense after they stopped on a rural road in Vermont to talk to journalists looking for Baldwin's perspective on the day he shot and killed cinematographer Halyna Hutchins on the set of the movie "Rust." (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) BALDWIN: She was my friend. She was my friend. The day I arrived in Santa Fe to start shooting, I took her to dinner with Joel, the director. We were a very, very -- excuse me. We were a very, very, you know, well-oiled crew shooting a film together and then this horrible event happened. (END VIDEO CLIP) HUNT: Now, Baldwin has described the shooting as an accident. The LA Times reported this weekend that when the gun went off, he repeatedly asked what just happened. And he told reporters in Vermont he is cooperating with investigators and in regular contact with the Santa Fe sheriff. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) BALDWIN: We're eagerly awaiting for the Sheriff's Department to tell us what their investigation has yielded. (END VIDEO CLIP) HUNT: Now the LA Times also reported what it says are heard were Halyna Hutchins last words. According to people on the set at the time she apparently said "that was no good, that was no good at all" after being hit by the bullet. The Santa Fe district attorney told us last week Alec Baldwin could yet face criminal charges. He is one of three people investigators want to question further. The others are the armorer, Hannah Gutierrez-Reed, who in a statement released by her attorney blamed lacks safety standards onset. And perhaps most critically, they want to talk to the assistant director, David Halls, once again, who investigators say when they first talked to him, admitted he did not properly check the gun before handing it to Baldwin. Martha. MACCALLUM: Jonathan, thank you very much. So, assistant director David Halls' attorney Lisa Torraco joins me now exclusively. Lisa, thank you very much for being here. Obviously, this is a very tragic situation and you heard in Jonathan's report that what we have learned from the investigation, the early discussion that Mr. Halls had with the investigators, he said that he should have checked, he should have checked that gun more thoroughly to make sure that there were no live rounds in it. Do you stand by that statement of your client? LISA TORRACO, ASSISTANT DIRECTOR DAVID HALLS' LAWYER: Well, before we start on that note, I just want to say that this tragedy is overwhelming to all of us. I mean, it's deeply saddening to my client, it's overwhelming to our community here, the film community, and our condolences go out to the Hutchins family. And I think it's extra hard for my client, because not only is he so overwhelmed with sadness, but now the target of the investigation. People are starting to point fingers at him, and it's overwhelming. MACCALLUM: Isn't it true that there had been a couple of other incidences on other sets where his oversight was questioned in other movies, and will that be relevant in this investigation? MACCALLUM: Well, let me go back to your very first question. And your first question had to do with the responsibility. Anyone to start with the fact that in the affidavits, it states that my client grabbed the gun off of a prop cart, and handed it to Baldwin. That absolutely did not happen. That absolutely did not happen. In addition to me presenting not only what Mr. Halls has told me, but we, our defense team, has interviewed witnesses and some of those witnesses that we've talked to, when we talked to them, they hadn't even been interviewed by the police yet. And those witnesses also confirm that they remember that the armorer, or armors assistant brought in the firearm, brought it on to the set. So this idea that my client grabbed the gun off of a prop cart and handed it to Mr. Baldwin, absolutely did not happen. And I think the needs to be straight right away. MACCALLUM: OK. So what you're saying is -- hold on, let me just pause on that for a second. So are you saying that Hannah Gutierrez-Reed handed the gun to him or that another assistant handed the gun to him? And if so, who handed the gun to him? TORRACO: OK. One of the problems that some of the witnesses have had is that most of the crew knew each other, but not all of the crew knew the armorers. So the armorers were relatively new to this particular crew. And both of the armorer and the assistant armorer were women in their 20s. And so some of the witnesses are getting confused whether the armorer came in or the assistant armorer. But regardless whether it was the armorer that brought the firearm on the set, or the assistant armorer that brought the firearm on set, my client did not bring the firearm -- MACCALLUM: But the point is that someone handed it to him -- did someone -- does he know who handed him the gun before he handed it to Alec Baldwin? TORRACO: Well, I think you're twisting the facts just a little bit. And let me just back up just a little bit if I may. The armorer brings the gun in. And another really important fact that we found out is that there was another member of the crew who also checked the firearm. Because when Mr. Halls gives a safety meeting, he announces to the group, we're going to, you know, there's going to be a firearm on set. Everyone has the right to inspect the firearm as soon as it comes on set before we begin to rehearse or begin to shoot. And so, there was another crew member who our team has spoken to who confirms that he also checked the firearm at the time when the armorer brought the firearm, MACCALLUM: OK. But I need to just nail something down here. Did Dave Halls hand the gun to Alec Baldwin? That's a very straightforward question. Did he hand the gun that was used and that killed Halyna Hutchins? Did he hand it to Alec Baldwin or not? TORRACO: Here's, here's what I'm trying to tell you. When I answer a question, I want to make sure that it's consistent with all of the facts. I don't want to answer a question to you and later be proven wrong. So we've tried -- that's why we haven't spoken out for over a week because I want to make sure that I've got the facts right. I have received information from crew members that the armorer handed it directly to Baldwin. And then, Baldwin put it inside where his holster would be. And then at some point, he pulled the firearm out and he wanted to adjust the holster. And then he hands the firearm to Mr. Halls, who immediately hands it right back after he's adjusted the holster. Other witnesses have said that the armorer brought the firearm in, that they checked the firearm, that my client checked the firearm. There was another crew member that checked the firearm. And that she handed it to him like a pass through. And that he then handed immediately over to Baldwin because he was between the two. So I can't tell you verbatim what happened. These people are overwhelmed by the grief and the shock. My client went through something that was such a freak accident that he's in shock. I mean, he's having a hard time sorting. MACCALLUM: You're saying he doesn't know whether or not he handed the gun to Alec Baldwin? Is that what you're telling us right now? He doesn't know if he handed it to him? TORRACO: No, of course. No, I'm not saying that. But what I'm saying is I want to put all the facts together. MACCALLUM: OK, but you're -- TORRACO: I want to deal with evidence. MACCALLUM: You said you cannot confirm that it didn't go directly from the armorer to Baldwin. So that's what -- this is a very direct question. Did your client hand the gun to Alec Baldwin right before he fired the gun and shot Halyna Hutchins? Did he hand it to him? Was he the last person to touch it before Baldwin? TORRACO: First of all, I wasn't there. MACCALLUM: No, what did he tell you. What did he tell you. TORRACO: -- what my client remembers -- MACCALLUM: -- about what happened. Did he say I handed it to Alec Baldwin? Or did he say I didn't hand it to him? TORRACO: I've explained what has happened on set. The armorer brought the firearm into the scene. The armorer is responsible to make sure the firearm is safe. The armorer opens the revolver, open surround, my client didn't load the firearm. My client didn't point the firearm at anyone and my client didn't pull the trigger. So the armorer comes in, the armorer opens the firearm, my client looks at it. And one of the other crew members also checks it. Whether or not he handed the firearm directly to Alec Baldwin at that moment, or whether the armorer handed it directly to Alec Baldwin at that moment doesn't really matter because he didn't load it. He's not response -- MACCALLUM: OK. That can be your perspective on it but, you know, what we're hearing from all these other armorers and specialists who handle weapons is that every single person in the chain of custody of the weapon has the responsibility to spin it, to look at it, to check it from Alec Baldwin, to the assistant director to the armorer. Now, you're leaving a lot of, I mean, I understand why is his attorney you're leaving, you know things as sort of open as you can as this investigation goes forward. But there's also testimony from the investigators that said that he advised them that he should have checked it. Can you confirm or deny that part of the story before I let you go? TORRACO: OK. What I can tell you is that expecting an assistant director to check a firearm is like telling the assistant director to check the camera angle, or telling the assistant director to check sound or lighting. That's not the assistant director's job. If he chooses to check the firearm because he wants to make sure make sure that everyone's safe, he can do that but that's not his responsibility. It's just like he's not the camera operator. He's not the sound operator. He's not the armorer. So that I disagree with the other reports that are coming out. And I think that this is such a tragedy. This is something that is a deviation of norm. Yes, it's awful. MACCALLUM: We got to leave it there. I hope you'll come back because, you know, we obviously have conflicting reports here. And conflicting reports about the responsibility of the assistant director, and what his duty is with regard to these weapons on the set, and why there would even be something on the set. This was not a prop gun. This was a real gun. So why that would even be allowed on the set, why any live ammo would be allowed anywhere near the set, all our questions for your client, for the assistant director on the set. So obviously we're just at the beginning of this investigation, I hope you'll come back as we move forward. Thank you very much, Lisa. Thanks for coming in. TORRACO: Thank you. MACCALLUM: Appreciate it. All right. Live look at Richmond, Virginia where Democrat Terry McAuliffe is campaigning before the big day tomorrow, now trailing by two points behind Republican Glenn Youngkin as he gets ready to take the podium there. Mr. Youngkin will join us live as both candidates try to fit in as much as they can today in the sprint to the finish when we come back. (COMMERCIAL BREAK) MACCALLUM: Probably the biggest race that we are watching tomorrow night is the battle to for the Virginia governor's seat. Democrat Terry McAuliffe is campaigning right now in Richmond. There's a live shot of the scene where he's spending his time in the last hours here. And he's fallen behind in our latest Fox News poll., interesting to look at all the polls out there. And you see that Youngkin has pulled ahead. In several of them, McAuliffe ahead and a couple. McAuliffe now trails Glenn Youngkin by eight points in this Fox News poll among the likely voters in Virginia. McAuliffe was leading by five just two weeks ago. We invited him here today to speak to us on "The Story." His campaign said that he could not make it. Glenn Youngkin is here joining make us live in just a moment but first a correspondent Rich Edson reporting live from Fredericksburg, Virginia on the campaign trail. Hi, Rich RICH EDSON, FOX NEWS CORRESPONDENT: Hey, good afternoon, Martha. We're waiting on television on Terry McAuliffe to head to the northern part of the state. He spent plenty of time up here. Right now he's down in Virginia. He's running a little bit behind schedule waiting to take the stage at a brewery in that area. He spent earlier today in Roanoke in the central part of the state. This is how McAuliffe is ending it. His schedule is taking him to more of the Democratic areas of the state. He's trying to turn out the Democratic vote. He's been trying to paint his opponent Glenn Youngkin as extreme on social and economic issues. And while he denied to us that he was trying to make this campaign a referendum on former President Donald Trump, McAuliffe seems to mention Trump at nearly every event. Now, the former president lost Virginia by more than 10 percentage points last year, and now McAuliffe finds himself either essentially tied or behind depending on the poll. National Democrats have fanned out across the street. They're trying to boost McAuliffe's chances here. Last week, it was President Biden and Vice President Kamala Harris. Over the weekend, Congressional Democrats joined up like House Majority Whip Jim Clyburn and Senator Tim Kaine. Now, there's another dynamic here, Martha, and that is early in-person voting. It ended on Saturday but it started in mid-September, and about a fifth of the electorate has already cast their votes, much of that time, the polls have changed dramatically. In the beginning, it was a McAuliffe lead. And as you mentioned, those polls have either tightened or McAuliffe is now losing depending on which one you look at. So that's another dynamic with a fifth of the electorate already having voted before election day here with this changing polling situation in the race. Back to you. MACCALLUM: That is a great point, Rich, thank you very much. And that's exactly where I want to start with Glenn Youngkin, who joins us now. As I mentioned, we invited Chairman McAuliffe as well and we are here if he wants to hop on and talk to us as well. Mr. Youngkin, good to see you today. You heard Rich Edson's report. He talks about the early vote, which went all the way back to September 16th people started voting, and about a fifth of the Virginia electorate already voted before you started to take off in the polls. Are you concerned that that could sort of throw things in Terry McAuliffe direction tomorrow night? GLENN YOUNGKIN, CANDIDATE FOR VIRGINIA GOVERNOR: No. I felt like the early voting was very much representative of our strength. In fact, turnout for my opponent was really light and soft and we had strong turnout, and so we expect to do very well with the early voting. And the momentum that we're seeing on the campaign trail is just huge, I got to be honest. Everywhere we go, the crowds are giant and we have had this 10-day bus door. We've been all over the Commonwealth. And we've been standing room only as people fallen out the doors. And it's so exciting to watch Virginians come together because it's no longer Republicans against Democrats. This is Virginians coming together for a platform that they can believe in, with low taxes and safe schools, and safe neighborhoods, and education that works for our children and, by the way, a job market that's really growing. MACCALLUM: You know, we've seen those crowds. It's pretty evident on the video when we see those crowds, but I think it's at 51% of the early vote is Democrat. So why do you say that you feel like, you know, you would have done well in that early portion of the vote? YOUNGKIN: Well, historically, early voting has been, you know, 75% to 80% Democrat. And so, for us to be so strong in the early voting just reflects the fact that there's not any enthusiasm on my opponent side, and we've had a lot of enthusiasm. And then we expect to do really well, tomorrow. You know, Virginians are coming together and this is why we see so much momentum going into tomorrow, but also the early voting is going to be, I think, surprisingly good for us. MACCALLUM: We'll see. I mean, it's fascinating to watch. Here's what Terry McAuliffe said in the closing hours here. Watch this. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) TERRY MCAULIFFE, CANDIDATE FOR VIRGINIA GOVERNOR: We don't want a Trump wannabe, someone who's been endorsed by Donald Trump 10 times tonight, closing his campaign is Donald Trump. I mean, we don't need the hatred, the Division. (END VIDEO CLIP) MACCALLUM: Teller rally by the former president, are you -- as he says closing your campaign with President Trump? YOUNGKIN: We've had help from everybody and there is a teleconference tonight that that President Trump is hosting and we're going to be off holding a rally in Loudoun County. We've been getting help from everybody. We had governors from all over the United States hosting tella calls yesterday to get the vote out from Idaho and Arizona, and South Carolina, and Iowa. It was fabulous to see the whole Republican Party come together And oh, by the way to see Independents, we're winning, we're winning the independent vote by double digits. We've got Democrats walking across the aisle. This is what unity looks like. And this is why we're going to win on Tuesday, but we got to get the vote out. Polls don't win elections votes do, and so we're encouraging everybody to get out and vote. MACCALLUM: And I know you've been doing that in the southwest part of the state today. It's been fun to watch this race, and we look forward to covering it tomorrow. Glenn Youngkin, thank you very much, sir. Good to have you with us today. YOUNGKIN: Thank you so much. You can follow us on youngkinforgov.com and we're going to be in Virginia Beach. And we're going to be, tonight, in Loudoun County. MACCALLUM: OK, we'll be in Loudoun County tomorrow doing our show. headline: Interview with U.S. Surgeon General, Dr. Vivek Murthy; Interview with Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton
story_text: CHRIS WALLACE, FOX NEWS ANCHOR: I'm Chris Wallace. Public health officials warned of a winter surge as COVID cases rise across the country. And the Biden administration's vaccine mandate faces challenges in court. (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) WALLACE (voice-over): States and private businesses suing the government over rules requiring shots or testing for tens of millions of workers. KEN PAXTON (R), TEXAS ATTORNEY GENERAL: The president does not have the authority to force people to get a vaccine and then threatened them with their jobs. KARINE JEAN-PIERRE, WHITE HOUSE DEPUTY PRESS SECRETARY: We're confident in our authority to protect American workers. WALLACE: We'll ask surgeon general, Dr. Vivek Murthy, about the debate over public health versus personal freedom. Then, we'll get reaction from Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton , whose state is at the forefront of legal battles over vaccines, masks, abortion, and voting rights. Plus, Trump advisor Steve Bannon hit with contempt of Congress charges for refusing to provide to the House committee investigating the January 6 attack on the Capitol . We'll ask our Sunday panel about the test of a president's executive powers. And our Power Player of the Week, Virginia's incoming lieutenant governor, Winsome Sears, and how she made history. WINSOME SEARS (R), VIRGINIA INCOMING LT. GOVERNOR: I think they wanted to take a chance on me. They're tired of politicians who won't let the wounds of the past heal. WALLACE: All right now on "FOX News Sunday". (END VIDEOTAPE) WALLACE (on camera): And hello again from FOX News in Washington. There's a new spike in COVID cases across the country. Just as a federal appeals court has blocked one of the main ways President Biden wants to fight the virus. The court ruled for the second time against a new administration rule that businesses with more than 100 workers must mandate vaccines or weekly tests or face thousands of dollars in fines. The court says that the rule grossly exceeds the government's authority and rejects the argument stopping the mandate could cost dozens or even hundreds of lives per day. In a moment, we'll speak with U.S. surgeon general, Dr. Vivek Murthy, and we'll get reaction from Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton who is suing the administration. But, first, let's bring in David Spunt at the White House with the latest on the administration's fight against COVID and against its critics -- David. DAVID SPUNT, FOX NEWS CORRESPONDENT: Chris, during his first few months in office, President Biden pushed back against vaccine mandates. But COVID infections rose and that all changed. (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) SPUNT (voice-over): The Biden White House receiving another blow from a federal court, halting the vaccine and testing requirements pending review. A judge on the Fifth Circuit Court of Appeals in New Orleans in an opinion late Friday wrote that the public is maintaining our constitutional structure and maintaining the liberty of individuals to make intensely personal decisions according to their own convictions even or perhaps particularly when those decisions frustrate government officials. White House officials insists the mandate is literally a lifesaver. JEAN-PIERRE: We are confident in our authority to protect American workers as this virus is killing 1,100 -- approximately 1,100 Americans a day. SPUNT: The Department of Justice prepared to fight all the way to the Supreme Court, writing in part: The department will continue to vigorously defend the standard and looks forward to obtaining a definitive resolution following consolidation of all the pending cases for further review. The mandate lost in federal court to a growing list of supply chain issues and the highest inflation rate in 30 years and it spells trouble ahead for a president not even a year into his term. JOE BIDEN , PRESIDENT OF THE UNITED STATES: Even though wages are going up, we still face challenges that we have to tackle on. We have to tackle them head-on. (END VIDEOTAPE) SPUNT (on camera): Tomorrow, President Biden will sign the bipartisan infrastructure package into law, Chris. Then he'll head out on the road in Michigan and New Hampshire to tout the plan -- Chris. WALLACE: David Spunt reporting from the White House -- David, thanks. And joining us now, U.S. surgeon general, Dr. Vivek Murthy. Doctor, welcome back to "FOX News Sunday". DR. VIVEK MURTHY, U.S. SURGEON GENERAL: Thanks so much, Chris. It's good to see you again. WALLACE: COVID cases are up 11 percent over the last two weeks and you can see the spike across the country. The virus is on the rise in 26 states from California to Maine. In some states, increases of more than 50 percent. And the CDC says 68 percent, two-thirds of U.S. counties, now have, quote, high community transmission. As the weather gets colder and people spend more time indoors, what are the chances that we're going to see another winter surge? MURTHY: Well, Chris, the good news is that we are certainly well down from the peaks that we hit during the delta wave earlier, we see in the late summer. But as winter does approach, people do go indoors, and virus is also better able to transmit in cold dry air. So, we know that increases up the possibility that there will be spread. A couple of things that are critical, though, for people to keep in mind. And number one is if you are vaccinated, your chances of both getting sick and transmitting the virus to someone else are much, much lower. So, this makes it all the more important as winter approaches to get vaccinated. And second, if you are eligible to get a booster shot, it's especially helpful if you can go ahead and do that now as winter approaches again, and as people get prepared for the holidays. So, we should be prepared for the fact that there may be an uptick in cases that we see in various parts of the country with cold weather. But what has held true for the last year is so true, which is vaccines still give you a high degree of protection, especially against the worst outcomes of COVID like hospitalization and death. WALLACE: You talk about being eligible for the booster. Three states, California, Colorado, and New Mexico, have jumped ahead of federal authorities and said that anyone, everyone above the age of 18 can now get a booster. Do you have a problem with that? MURTHY: I certainly understand, Chris, why these states are doing that. You know, they are looking at what's happening in their own states, that they are seeing cases go up and they want to have broad protection for the entire state. And I get that. What people should know, though, is that the FDA has already made millions of people eligible for booster shots -- people who are above 65 who have other illnesses that put them at higher risk and who are at higher risk of exposure based on where they live or where they work. Millions of people are eligible who have not yet gone their booster shot and we want to focus on that. What people should also know, though, is that the FDA is considering broadening that eligibility after a request from Pfizer to do so. But what they're going to do is take a close look at the data. They want to make, you know, especially sure that the booster shots are both safe and effective for the populations that are not currently eligible. And once they determined that, then they will make a recommendation there. But the bottom line is that millions of people can get boosted right now and we want them to get boosted, because that will both extend and enhance the protection that they've already been getting from the vaccines. WALLACE: There is reportedly a split inside the Biden administration between folks like Dr. Fauci and you who, reportedly, favor making boosters available to all adults, and CDC director, Dr. Walensky, who is reportedly not as persuaded that young, healthy adults need the extra protection. Does the split inside the administration add to the public confusion about vaccinations? MURTHY: Well, Chris, I'm glad you ask that question because the reality is that there is much more agreement here than I think people appreciate. In August, in fact, all three of us, Dr. Fauci, Dr. Walensky, myself, as well as other medical leaders within the administration, including the FDA commissioner, the NIH director and others, all signed a letter saying that we believe that protection was starting to wane and that boosters would be needed at some point later in the year for people across the age spectrum, you know, 18 and above. What we also said, though, in that letter was that we wanted the CDC and the FDA to weigh in on both the efficacy and the safety of booster shots. And all that actually remains true. And so, you know, while we haven't millions of people eligible for booster shots, we are going through an FDA process and we'll go through a CDC process to see if that eligibility should be widen. But the bottom line is all of us are in the same page about the strong protection that the vaccines afford and we know that where boosters are indicated, that they will be hopeful to extending people's protection against COVID-19. WALLACE: On Friday, the Fifth Circuit Court of Appeals in New Orleans for the second time continued to block the Biden administration's mandate that all businesses with more than 100 employees vaccinate their workers or get a test. SEARS: Wow. How awesome is this. WALLACE: The power of the moment was not lost on her. But court after court continues to say there are a number of problems with this vaccine mandate for the private sector and for the government. story_text: MICHAEL MCCABE, OAKLAND COUNTY UNDERSHERIFF: So, I'll just give you a quick brief and I'll answer whatever questions I can answer. And we'll ask for comments or anything, the chief can fill us in about EMS and all that. Around 12:51 today, we received a 9-1-1 call of an active shooter at the high school. The deputies immediately responded, and we received over a hundred 9-1-1 calls into our dispatch center, over 100. The deputies took a suspect into custody within five minutes of the original 9-1-1 call. They recovered a handgun from the suspect. The suspect fired multiple shots, there are multiple victims. It's unfortunate, I have to report that we have three deceased victims right now, who are all believed to be students. We have six others that were shot. One was a school teacher. They're all at local hospitals being treated for various injuries. Again, multiple shots were fired. He did not give us any resistance when he was taken into custody. He's currently being transported back to Pontiac, for potential now like -- he's already, already invoked his right to not speak so he wants an attorney. He's not telling us anything at this point in time. It's a very tragic situation, obviously. We will brief you again later. Maybe around 5:00. We can give you ages of the victims, conditions of the victims, where they live, things of that nature. Behind us in the mire, they close the store down for us and helped us with reunification with the parents. We got a lot of upset parents want to know the, what's going on with their kids. There was an orderly evacuation. The school did everything right. Everybody remained in place, they barricaded themselves. And Tim here has done a great job in terms of preparing. You never want to prepare for something like this, but you have to, and the school district's done a wonderful job preparing all the doors over there and marked at the high school if you've seen them, deputies responded, they knew where to go. We've had assistance from other police agencies nearby. Lapeer County Sheriff, Oxford Police Department, other local police departments, the response has been overwhelming. We're still doing a secondary and ordered a third search of the high school just to make sure there's no other victims out there. If there's anything else I missed, I can answer, I will answer and I'll defer to students. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: (INAUDIBLE) was a student? MCCABE: Yes, it's a 15-year-old student who is a sophomore at the high school. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: As he said -- before he invoked attorney, did he say anything about what precipitated this? MCCABE: I'm not going to get into that. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: Was there any warning, Mike, ahead of time? Or was there any messaging? Did he put out anything? MCCABE: that's all under investigation at this time? We have literally probably a hundred different detectives and support out here right now. We're going to talk to everybody, we're going to go through everything. But at this point in time, I can't tell you that we have that or we don't have that. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: Any reason to believe the initial victims were targeted directly, or was it? MCCABE: I don't know at this point in time, still under investigation UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: Have notification then made to parents yet or do parents still not know? MCCABE: I believe all the parents know but I can't say that for certain, but I believe they do. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: So, you're saying three deceased, and how many injuries? MCCABE: We have three deceased, six others that were shot one of the six is a teacher. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: One of the witnesses I talked to said she heard shots and pause she heard shots again, do you have any idea how long he was in the school? MCCABE: He fired multiple shots; I can tell you that. We've recovered multiple shell casings in the school. Somewhere in the area, obviously with that many people shot, we're thinking, you know, 15 to 20 shots that were fired. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: So, what kind of weapon was used? UNIDENTIFIED MALE: How long was he -- MCCABE: It's a handgun. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: How long is he in this school? MCCABE: It's a semi-automatic handgun. That's all I can tell you at this point. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: Did he have more than one magazine? MCCABE: I'm not going to get it -- obviously, if he fired up multiple shots more than 15, he'd have more than one magazine. Yes. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: How did he got apprehended? MCCABE: Deputies took him into custody, he responded. I can't tell you the exact circumstances of how that occurred, but deputies confronted him. He had the weapon on him, they took him into custody. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: In school. MCCABE: Yes, sir. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: Was it the child, the child that had the issue last week and weeks to go back, with your head? MCCABE: I'm not aware of that, so I can't answer that. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: Over the course of like, 15-20 minutes, do we know how long -- MCCABE: Five minutes. The whole thing lasted five minutes. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: Was it a (INAUDIBLE) or in the common area? MCCABE: I'm not sure on that. I'll have to get back to you. And we'll do another briefing later on when we get more details. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: Any indication that he was targeting a certain room for these students and the specific teacher? MCCABE: I can't tell you that because I don't know. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: You told us a lot and we appreciate it. MCCABE: OK. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: Can we talk to the superintendent for a moment, please? MCCABE: That's up the Tim. TIM THRONE, SUPERINTENDENT OF OXFORD COMMUNITY SCHOOLS: I really don't have anything, I really don't have anything more to say other than that you certainly can pray for our families here in Oxford, and our students. I'm learning information real time just as you all are so I really don't have any more info to add -- UNIDENTIFIED MALE: Do you have any light on who the student is, a 15-year- old? THRONE: I can't, no. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: What's your reaction to this? THRONE: Of course, I'm shocked. It's devastating/ UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: Superintendent, can you say and spell your name, please Sir? THRONE: Tim Throne, T-H-R-O-N-E.
