headline: NBC NIGHTLY NEWS for September 12, 2022, NBC
story_text: [19:00:00] (COMMERCIAL BREAK) LESTER HOLT, NBC NEWS ANCHOR (on camera): Tonight the emotional outpouring of Scotland bids farewell to Queen Elizabeth. (voiceover): The Queen`s children, King Charles and his three siblings leading the solemn procession as crowds lining the streets of Scotland`s capital. The moving service. The 500-year-old crown of Scotland placed on the Queen`s casket. Thousands lining up for hours to pay tribute as the Queen lies in rest for 24 hours before her final journey to London. And Prince Harry breaking his silence. His powerful tribute to the woman he called granny. Also tonight, Ukraine saying its lightning advance has retaken more than 1000 square miles from Russia. In just 48 hours Russia retaliated by striking Ukraine`s power grid. Is the war at a turning point? Donald Trump`s legal team objecting to the DOJ`s special master candidates to review the classified documents ceased from Mar-a-Lago. What they are asking the judge to do? Extreme weather in the West. Heavy rain triggering mudslides. More than 50 people rescued as dozens of wildfires rage in the region. Caught on camera, Jeff Bezos ` unmanned Blue Origin rocket bursting into flames after liftoff. And the tributes for the Queen and what officials are now asking mourners to stop leaving behind. ANNOUNCER: This is NBC NIGHTLY NEWS with Lester Holt. Good evening. The coffin of Queen Elizabeth II lies at rest tonight in Edinburgh, Scotland where thousands have lined up to pay their respects. Tonight, the Queen`s daughter and three sons led by Charles holding a vigil for their mother at St. Giles cathedral. It was a day filled with powerful and poignant images including a quiet stately procession of the Queen`s coffin down the cobblestone streets of Edinburgh`s Royal Mile to the Cathedral. The crown of Scotland placed atop her coffin. Her children walking behind the hearse, as it slowly made its way past a silent crowd gathered to say goodbye. Scotland, a country adored by the Queen and in fact the place she died on Thursday. The newly crowned king meantime making several appearances today including addressing parliament as he both grieves and consoles the nation. Keir Simmons starts our reporting tonight from London. (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) KEIR SIMMONS, NBC NEWS SENIOR INTERNATIONAL CORRESPONDENT (voiceover): It was a powerful tribute. The Queen`s daughter and sons including King Charles walking slowly behind her cortage. Thousands lining Edinburgh`s famous Royal Mile. Crowd so quiet, you could hear the hooves of the horses on the cobbled streets of Scotland`s capital. Queen Elizabeth loves this country. The silence speaking volumes about their respect for her. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: I can`t find my words. It`s -- I`m so sorry. SIMMONS: The Queen helps plan every detail of today`s service and the many days of remembrance ahead. From the pageantry, like the precise military choreography, carrying her coffin inside the 12th-century Cathedral, to the intensely personal. In church, the Queen`s children looking on as the nearly 500-year-old Scottish crown is laid on her oak casket, taking its place alongside a wreath of flowers, including some of her favorites picked from her Balmoral garden, all on top of Scotland`s Royal Standard. CHARLES III, KING, UNITED KINGDOM: The tangible connections to my darling late mother, we see all around us. SIMMONS: Earlier, King Charles speaking to the British Parliament . CHARLES III: She set an example of selfless duty which, with God`s help and your counsels, I am resolved faithfully to follow. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: Andrew, you`re a sick (BLEEP). SIMMONS: Not everything was scripted today. One person protesting Prince Andrew was quickly removed from the crowd. Today`s events in Edinburgh capping off that solemn weekend journey that carried the Queen through 180 miles of stunning Scottish countryside after leaving her beloved Balmoral Castle. People on horseback paying respects along the road. These tractors a tribute to her from local farmers. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: We`re proud to be Scottish and we`re proud to be British. And it`s nice to say goodbye. SIMMONS: And another poignant moment in this long goodbye. The Queen`s children mounting a vigil standing on all sides of her casket heads bowed. Even as many thousands of mourners kept coming, each given just a few minutes to say goodbye to a queen who gave them her life. (END VIDEOTAPE) [19:05:10] HOLT: Keir, it was quite a day. I know tomorrow, the focus of the solemn ceremonies will turn to London. SIMMONS (on camera): That`s right, Lester. The Queen`s body will be brought here to Buckingham palace tomorrow. Then, on Wednesday, move to Westminster for four days where hundreds of thousands are expected to wait in line. And then, a week today, that historic State Funeral. Lester? HOLT: Keir Simmons, thank you. And NBC is Tom Llamas has been on the ground for us in Edinburgh, the last few days. And Tom, you walk the Royal Mile today. TOM LLAMAS, NBC NEWS SENIOR NATIONAL CORRESPONDENT (on camera): Lester, that`s right. The scene down there was remarkable because of the size of the crowd. It was double, if not triple what we experienced when the Queen`s hearse first pulled into Edinburgh on Sunday. But tonight, that solemn procession uphill through the medieval street with the king and the Queen`s children marching along through a sea of people so many onlookers were pouring over staircases on some corners. But the impact of Queen Elizabeth`s reign, it hit us afterwards, Lester, it`s what many didn`t see, the line nine hours long in some cases to see the Queen`s casket up close. I spoke to several people in the crowd, some who said they wanted to witness history but so many other saying the Queen earned that devotion with her 70 years on the throne. Two female veterans told me they were waiting all that time to personally salut the coffin. And tonight, Lester, this is a live image of the scene outside St. Giles Cathedral. The sun has gone down. It is chilly here. It`s very late. People are tired and yet they still wait to say goodbye. If you have any doubt of how the Queen touched people, look at that right there, Lester. HOLT: Yes, remarkable but not surprising outpouring tonight. Tom, thanks. And one of the more striking scenes as these events unfolded, King Charles ` sons William and Harry emerging together with their wives over the weekend in a rare reunion. Here`s Molly Hunter. (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) MOLLY HUNTER, NBC NEWS FOREIGN CORRESPONDENT (voiceover): It was a welcome reunion that took the country by surprise. Getting out of the same car, the new Prince and Princess of Wales, William and Kate, alongside Harry and Meghan. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: We didn`t imagine all four of them to be together, but I think that was the Queen`s last wish. HUNTER: We now know it was Prince William, who reportedly offered the olive branch reaching out to Harry and Meghan inviting them to greet the crowds at Windsor, a suggestion perhaps coming from the new king before such a critical week. DAISY MCANDREW, NBC NEW ROYAL COMMENTATOR: I firmly believe it was Charles who tried to metaphorically bang their heads together and say please, for me, for the future of the monarchy for your father, can you put on a brave face and go out and give us a sign of unity? HUNTER: And unity, at least for that brief hour, was seen and felt by the lucky thousands. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: That was really special, actually. I was really surprised all four of them were together. And yes, that`s quite emotional, I think, being a Brit seeing them, the two brothers side by side. HUNTER: Since Harry and Meghan famously left behind their Royal duties, fueling the brotherly rift, Prince William has moved into the role he was born for assuming his father`s former title. As the heir apparent, his official state responsibilities now a world away from Harry`s new life and California. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: Growing up Princess Diana famously really wanted Harry and William to be equally important. Even though William`s destiny was very different, he was always going to be the monarch, she didn`t want Harry to feel less important, less significant. HUNTER: In a new tribute to granny, Harry says he`s forever grateful for my earliest childhood memories to meeting you for the first time as my commander-in-chief. But the brothers strike different notes. While Harry pledges to honor his father`s new role, William says he`ll be supporting my father the king in every way I can as the next in line. And now it`s William and Kate, the new Princess of Wales, Princess Diana`s former title, who are the most popular members of the Royal Family, stepping into the spotlight, shouldering the responsibility of modernizing this monarchy. (END VIDEOTAPE) HUNTER: Now, looking ahead, there are a number of opportunities where we might see the two brothers together again. What`s clear, though, is they don`t want it to distract from the critical week ahead for the Royal Family. Lester? HOLT: Molly, thank you. The Queen has been mourned well beyond Great Britain. She was also the official head of state and 14 other nations, including some that carry memories of a painful past. Kerry Sanders reports tonight from Jamaica. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) KERRY SANDERS, NBC NEWS SENIOR NATIONAL CORRESPONDENT (voiceover): In former British colonies around the world, flags at half-staff including in India, once part of the sprawling British Empire. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: I remember her in such a way that she`s that`s like our mother`s figure. SANDERS: The Queen often visited Britain`s colonies and former colonies. Today, there are 14 Commonwealth realms where the king is still recognized as the head of state including here in Jamaica. Are you mourning the Queen`s death? CLIFF HUGHES, JAMAICA HISTORIAN: No. SANDERS: No. HUGHES: Because her passing is regrettable but she`s not that close to us for us to be mourning. [19:10:10] SANDERS: Jamaica historian Cliff Hughes says this country`s beautiful shores hold an ugly past, slavery. The enslaved forced to the West Indies by the Royal-African company. They harvested sugar known as green gold. FAE ELLINGTON, RESIDENT, KINGSTON, JAMAICA: It built England. It built the streets. It built the big businesses. SANDERS: That`s the value of sugar at the time. ELLINGTON: Yes. SANDERS: The New King, Charles III, now inherits that legacy. HUGHES: When slavery was finally abolished, those who were the enslavers were paid 20 million pounds, which was 40 percent of Britain`s annual budget. SANDERS: And how much were the slaves themselves who were now free given? HUGHES: Not one cent. SANDERS: Which is why reparations remained a hot topic. When the now-Prince and Princess of Wales visited Jamaica in March, there were protests and demand for an official apology. Some now hope that comes from the new King. (END VIDEOTAPE) SANDERS (on camera): Under the court system here which mirrors England`s, if there were an official apology, that could well open the door to reparations. Lester? HOLT: All right, Kerry Sanders tonight in Jamaica, thank you. We`ll turn now to another major story, the lightning advance by Ukraine`s military reclaiming more ground against Russian forces in the northeast as Russia retaliates by striking Ukraine`s power grid. Our Megan Fitzgerald is in Kyiv. (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) MEGAN FITZGERALD, NBC NEWS FOREIGN CORRESPONDENT (voiceover): In a fast and furious reaction, Russia launching missiles and Ukraine`s east, striking critical infrastructure plunging millions into the dark. The strike seen as retaliation as Ukraine sweeps through the Russian front line in a shocking advance. Ukraine now claims in the last 12 days, they`ve taken back 2300 square miles of Russian-held territory in the northeastern Kharkiv region. Ukraine putting out this video, an incredible scene as the Ukrainian flag is raised in a village east of Kharkiv, as many residents overcome with emotion thanking the Ukrainian soldiers for liberating them. Ukraine releasing images showing Russian artillery and tanks left behind, as they say Russian soldiers were forced to withdraw. Ukraine`s President Zelenskyy thanking his troops, saying the world is impressed and the enemy is panicking. UK`s ministry of defense describes the territory Ukraine says it took back as twice the size of London, though Russia still controls the south and the east. Russia`s President Putin not commenting on Ukraine`s counter- offensive so far. A spokesperson only saying the Russian military operation is ongoing and will achieve its objective. But the question tonight, is this a turning point in the war. (END VIDEOTAPE) FITZGERALD (on camera): And tonight, Ukraine is claiming that it`s not just Russian equipment they`ve captured, it`s also Russian soldiers, saying they have so many POWs they`re running out of room. Lester? HOLT: OK, Megan Fitzgerald in Ukraine, thank you. Back home now to the battle over the FBI search at Mar-a-Lago. Attorneys for former President Trump objecting to the candidates the Justice Department proposed to serve as special master to review the classified documents seized by the FBI . Mr. Trump`s team disputing the documents classified status and asking the judge to reject the DOJ -- the DOJ`s request to continue reviewing the files. In 60 seconds, parts of the West can`t catch a break. The threat of more extreme weather after dozens are rescued in mudslides and wildfires raged on. (COMMERCIAL BREAK) HOLT: Back now with the extreme weather in the West. Flood watches in effect after mudslides forced dozens of rescues on the heels of record heat. Here`s Miguel Almaguer. [19:15:07] (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) MIGUEL ALMAGUER, NBC NEWS NATIONAL CORRESPONDENT (voiceover): Tonight, a year of extremes in just a matter of days, historic heat fires, floods, and now mudslides. The volatile Western weather creating havoc for first responders and dangerous conditions for those suddenly in harm`s way. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: All these vehicles are stuck in about two feet of -- 20 mile an hour debris flow. ALMAGUER: Outside Los Angeles, firefighters rescued more than 50, including young families who suddenly became trapped and caked in debris as a mudslide covered a canyon road. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: It was terrifying. ALMAGUER: On the heels of record-shattering heat, the remnants of Tropical Storm Kay brought flash flooding that`s soaked the region. Downed trees, swamp neighborhoods, and sidewalk rescues. From floods to fires, there`s been little relief. Across the West, more than 90 large wildfires are burning in a region mired in drought. Some 800,000 acres scorched from active fires as crews battle to gain the upper hand. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: The flames are 300 feet in the air, the trees were exploding. ALMAGUER: With entire communities under evacuations, in recent days, four have been killed trying to escape the flames. And now, after this crash, three firefighting personnel nearly lost their lives also trying to battle them. Tonight, the West can`t catch a break from a sudden season of extremes. Miguel Almaguer, NBC news. (END VIDEOTAPE) HOLT: A spectacular rocket failure today for Blue Origin , a company owned by Jeff Bezos . It happened about a minute into the launch, flame scene shooting out of the rocket. Luckily, there were no people on board. The capsule was able to separate and parachute to Earth. This is the same type of rocket that sends paying customers to the edge of space but the capsule is different. Up next tonight, after Roe, abortion is rewriting November ballots. Ahead, one swing state`s looming battle in our series power of the vote. (COMMERCIAL BREAK) [19:20:00] HOLT: We`re back now with our series power of the vote. With less than two months until Election Day, in Michigan, voters will decide if abortion rights should be protected by the state constitution. Here`s Yamiche Alcindor. (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) YAMICHE ALCINDOR, NBC NEWS WASHINGTON CORRESPONDENT (voiceover): Lifelong Republican Jessica Leech was devastated when the Supreme Court overturned Roe v. Wade. JESSICA LEECH, LIFELONG REPUBLICAN: I cried for weeks. I cried for my daughter. I always considered myself pro-life. ALCINDOR: Now, she changed her mind and her party. Jessica got pregnant at 19 and visited an abortion clinic to weigh her options. She decided to have her son who`s now 17 and says being able to make that choice is something every woman deserves. What do you say to people who think your story is an example of why abortion shouldn`t be an option? LEECH: I would tell those people that until recently, it was always a hypothetical. I would beg them to understand that having these options paved the way for me to be a good mother. ALCINDOR: In Michigan, residents will vote on a ballot referendum in November that would enshrine abortion rights into the state constitution. GOV. GRETCHEN WHITMER (D-MI): You`re a doctor. ALCINDOR: Incumbent Democratic Governor Gretchen Whitmer is also up for reelection. What is at stake in this election and in the ballot referendum? WHITMER: Well, abortion and the right to be a full American citizen with agency of your body is on this ballot. ALCINDOR: Her views are also shaped by her experiences. WHITMER: In college, in the days after I was raped, it dawned on me. Oh, my God, I might be pregnant. And the only thing that gave me a little bit of relief is knowing that I could make a decision that was right for me if that happened. ALCINDOR: Her opponent, Republican Tudor Dixon, supports banning abortion with no exception for rape or incest. I wonder if you could just talk a bit more about your own views and talk to people who are worried about your views being too extreme. I have shared my own pro-life story. I lost a baby 18 weeks. When I lost the baby and the doctor said this baby probably died in the womb at 16 weeks, I held a beautiful baby girl. ALCINDOR: Dixon also does not believe abortion is a top issue for voters. DIXON: They`re concerned with how to get their kids back on track after they were kept out of school. And if you look at our crime rates in the past couple of years, it`s just continued to rise. And why our businesses are being crushed by the government? ALCINDOR: Both supporters and opponents of the referendum are mobilizing like anti-abortion rights activist Christen Polo, now working overtime after voters in Kansas recently voted to keep abortion protections in its state constitution. CHRISTEN POLO, ACTIVIST: I`m very concerned. Frankly, the policies that are being put forth in this abortion amendment here in Michigan are some of the most extremist policies we`ve seen in the entire country. ALCINDOR: Meantime, Jessica hopes sharing her story helps keep abortion legal in Michigan. Her son Cameron sent her a text on the day of our interview. Your life experiences, our relationship, after you decided to keep me and change your life around me, and now your perspective of life is what the world needs most. ALCINDOR: Yamiche Alcindor, NBC News, Michigan. (END VIDEOTAPE) HOLT: And up next, the tributes from everyday people honoring the Queen. (COMMERCIAL BREAK) [19:25:00] HOLT: Finally, beyond the formal tributes, the tokens people have left to honor the Queen, small gestures adding up to a powerful message. Here`s Kelly Cobiella. (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) KELLY COBIELLA, NBC NEWS FOREIGN CORRESPONDENT (voiceover): The ordinary, the extraordinary, messages and memories. Many shedding a tear for the Queen leaving a token. A small way just to say thank you for a life of service. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: She means a lot to all the people here and she`s done so much for everyone. So, we kind of need to honor her. COBIELLA: And a way to say goodbye, drawings cards, notes. Thank you for being the best Queen ever, one read. Another, with her beloved Corgi. Tributes for mourners around the world marking Queen Elizabeth`s extraordinary life. Katarina Mostova (PH) and her family fled the war in Ukraine and brought her country`s national flower, the sunflower, for the queen. Why did you come? UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: Because we want to make honor to Queen. This is so important for us. COBIELLA: Mountains of flowers and marmalade sandwiches, a nod to the Queen`s surprise skit with the children`s character Paddington Bear in June. Now, so many sandwiches and stuffed bears, they`re begging the public just to bring flowers. Members of the royal family are deeply touched. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: Have you seen the messages? WILLIAM, PRINCE OF WALES: Yes, amazing. It`s the little 7-year-olds and 11- year-olds messages get straight through every time. COBIELLA: Notes from children have only been alive for a fraction of the Queen`s long reign like this one: "Thank you for showing the world how strong a woman can be." Kelly Cobiella, NBC News, Edinburgh Scotland. (END VIDEOTAPE) HOLT: Messages from the heart. That`s NIGHTLY NEWS for this Monday. Thank you for watching, everyone. I`m Lester Holt. Please take care of yourself and each other. Good night. (COMMERCIAL BREAK) END Content and programming copyright 2022 NBCUniversal. ALL RIGHTS RESERVED. headline: Meet The Press for September 18, 2022, NBC
story_text: [09:00:00] (COMMERCIAL BREAK) CHUCK TODD, NBC HOST MEET THE PRESS: This Sunday Poll Vault. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) PRESIDENT JOE BIDEN : People are back to work. (END VIDEO CLIP0 TODD: Our new NBC News Poll shows a jump in President Biden`s approval ratings. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) PRESIDENT JOE BIDEN : We`re making progress. We`re getting places done as well. (END VIDEO CLIP) TODD: And signs that Democrat standing may be improving ahead of November. One explanation the overturning of Roe v. Wade. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) UNKNOWN: We`re moving backwards. We`re taking one step forward, three steps back. (END VIDEO CLIP) TODD: Another the high profile presence of former President Trump. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) PRESIDENT DONALD TRUMP: We may have to do it again. Stay tuned everybody. Stay tuned. (END VIDEO CLIP) TODD: My guest this morning, the number two Democrat in the Senate, Dick Durbin of Illinois and Republican Senate candidate Joe O`Dea running to flip a Colorado seat. Plus, the Senate will look into charges by a former U.S. attorney that Mr. Trump tried to use the Justice Department to punish his enemies and protect his friends. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) GEOFFREY BERMAN , FORMER U.S. ATTORNEY: Pissing off the president is not a Federal crime. (END VIDEO CLIP) TODD: Geoffrey Berman joins me this morning. Also, border wars amid a surge at the southern border. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) UNKNOWN: Some of them have been through, really horrific things. (END VIDEO CLIP) TODD: Florida Governor Ron DeSantis ships four dozen unsuspecting Venezuelan migrants from Texas to Martha`s Vineyard in Massachusetts. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) GOVERNOR RON DESANTIS (R-FL): Every community in America should be sharing in the burdens. It shouldn`t all fall on a handful of red states. UNKNOWN: (Inaudible) is so cruel, so depraved that someone would do that. (END VIDEO CLIP) TODD: Joining me for inside and analysis are New York Times Chief White House Correspondent Peter Baker, former Obama White House Senior Advisor Stephanie Cutter, Republican Strategist Al Cardenas and Leanne Caldwell of the Washington Post . Welcome to Sunday. It`s Meet the Press. ANNOUNCER: From NBC News in Washington, the longest running show in television history this is Meet the Press with Chuck Todd. TODD: Good Sunday morning. President Biden is finally getting his polling bump. A spade of news from anger over the overturning of Roe v. Wade to falling gas prices, has helped push the president`s poll numbers to their highest point in almost a year, and it`s thanks mostly to Democrats coming home. In fact, among all registered voters Mr. Biden`s job approval in our new NBC News Poll is sitting at 45 percent, 52 disapproving. The big jump really was from Democrats, particularly younger ones, happy about the passage of the agenda, perhaps student loans as well, but those are hardly robust numbers and they`re a jump from last months 42-55 split. And the race for control of Congress is dead even, 46 percent for Democrats, 46 percent for Republicans. The remarkable thing about Mr. Biden`s numbers is how he even manages to get to 45 percent. On issue after issue, his approval ratings are actually consistently below 45 on foreign policy, it`s just 42 percent. The economy even lower 40, border lower than that 36 and on cost of living even lower at a paltry 30 percent. So what`s happening? One is, of course, the Dobbs decision. It`s clearly energizing voters and not just Democrats. Only 37 percent approve of the Supreme Court`s decision to overturn Roe. Sixty-one percent disapprove of that decision, but just as important to President Biden is getting a lift from simply Donald Trump`s presence. The high-profile investigations, all of it, is preventing Republicans from turning the mid-terms into a referendum on Mr. Biden, and he loves to say judging by the alternative not the almighty and he may be benefiting from that right now. Voter feelings towards Mr. Trump are just 34 percent positive, 54 percent negative, 20 points underwater. It`s lowest point in a year and a half. Compare that to President Biden`s current personal ratings, 42 percent positive, 47 percent negative. Not great, but that`s only five points underwater. So where are we? The bottom line is this, less than two months from the mid-terms each political party is running the campaign they want to run. Republicans on crime, economy and immigration and they`re winning with that battle with the voters. Democrats are running on Mr. Trump and abortion rights and they`re winning that battle with the voters. So, what`s going to happen? Joining me now is the number two Democrat in the Senate Dick Durbin of Illinois. Senator Durbin, welcome back to Meet the Press. SEN. DICK DURBIN (D-IL): Good to be with you Chuck. TODD: So I`m going to start with the -- the stunt I guess is the best way to call it that Governor DeSantis did when trying to fund the flight of migrants in Texas, that he claimed might have been coming to Florida. He - - you know and sent them to Massachusetts. Here was his rational for it and then I want to ask you more on the other side. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) GOV. RON DESANTIS (R-FL): We are not a sanctuary state and it`s better to be able to go to a sanctuary jurisdiction. [09:05:00] And yes, we will help facilitate that transport for you. (END VIDEO CLIP) TODD: All right, do you think these bus, whether it`s these bus tickets to the Naval Observatory, New York, D.C. or Martha`s Vineyard, do you think the Federal government should stop them and prevent them from happening? CARDENAS: -- to say, I`m going to appoint these people to give me recommendations on border security, and run with that. TODD: Yeah. CARDENAS: He`s very passive on an issue that`s hurting his party a lot. TODD: Peter, I`ve gotten a few people wondering if we`re just getting played by DeSantis. He`s pulling a Trump on us, right? We`re sitting here. This is not the center of attention, but boy, he changed the subject and we all went to it. It`s like, it`s hard to -- you can`t -- we know it`s a political stunt. We know it`s for media attention, but these are human beings. We couldn`t ignore it. PETER BAKER, NBC NEWS POLITICAL ANALYST: Yeah. Yeah. I mean, you could say, obviously, he`s getting criticized for exploiting people for a political purpose, but he`s got us talking about it. He`s got us talking about it. And the point that he`s making is, you know, a rational one to talk about, what level of responsibility do states that are not at the border have to help out? Fair enough. Obviously, to do it in this way is not actually solving the problem. But look, this is the playbook we`ve seen now the last three election cycles. In the midterms last time, he tried to make immigration a big issue. TODD: Claire McCaskill would disagree. I mean -- BAKER: It obviously worked in some places. TODD: I was just going to say -- BAKER: Yes. Yes. TODD: -- it does work in red areas. BAKER: Right, exactly. CUTTER: But it -- but what it also did, it might get the Republican base all riled up, but it also has the effect, just like many other issues that we`re talking about today, of driving independent voters -- TODD: Yeah. CUTTER: -- particularly independent women, to Democrats. People are ashamed about what DeSantis did. TODD: Well, this gets to though -- because DeSantis is clearly trying to borrow from Trump. And I want to -- I want to do one excerpt from your book here, Peter. And it`s Lindsey Graham , who probably is the best symbol of sort of the folks that are trapped by Trump. BAKER: More for Trump than for the Republican Party. That`s the lowest number since you guys have been asking that question. TODD: Yeah. BAKER: So there is, I think, some disconcerting feeling -- TODD: Yeah. BAKER: -- for a lot of Republicans about whether they really want to be involved with him or not. CALDWELL: I noticed that in that poll -- CARDENAS: Except that in primaries, the -- TODD: Yes. Well, that`s the problem -- BAKER: Yeah. CARDENAS: -- numbers are -- TODD: That 33 percent is more than 50 percent -- CARDENAS: Exactly. TODD: -- in a primary electorate and that`s the issue. Very quick, and I`ve got to wrap. CALDWELL: You`re starting to see that in these -- TODD: Yeah. CALDWELL: -- general election campaigns. People are distancing themselves from Trump, even the MAGA-ers. TODD: Oh. Our New Hampshire friend is probably the most 180. CALDWELL: Yeah. TODD: We don`t have time for that quote, but we`ll see. Anyway, when we come back, Democrats own the cities and Republicans own rural America. But the most persuadable voters are concentrated in the outer suburbs -- call them the exurbs -- and they may well determine the outcome of this year`s midterms. That`s next. (COMMERCIAL BREAK) [09:46:00] TODD: Welcome back. Data Download time. In every election, there are solid Democratic voters, solid Republican voters. And then there are voters who defy easy categorization, those persuadable voters. Sometimes we call them "soccer mom" or "office-park dads". But this time, we`re going to talk about them geographically. They`re often the difference between winning and losing. And our new NBC News poll has some clues about who they are, and most importantly, where they live. So we want to do this geographically. Persuadable voters, we define that as people that have voted both Republican and Democrat at least once in the last four years. And as you could see where they live, nearly half of them, a plurality, live in what we call the outer suburbs or exurbs. You could see combined, the number of persuadable voters in cities or those close in urban suburbs basically collectively add up to what the exurbs have. And you could see in rural America, not too many persuadable voters. So what are the places where these persuadable voters could impact the battle in the midterms? Well, in House races, you`ve got Arizona`s first Congressional district. It`s a huge, the eleventh largest Congressional district in the country. It`s parts of Phoenix, and north. You`ve got Colorado 08. It starts in the suburbs of Denver, goes all the way up to Fort Collins. North Carolina 13. It`s part of the research triangle and farther out, tipping some rural parts of that area. Michigan 07 goes from the western suburbs of Detroit, all the way to Lansing. And then you`ve got here in Minnesota 02, which is St. Paul, and it goes nearly all the way down to the southern border. It`s this mix of districts. So why are they persuadable? Well, because they sort of fall on both sides of some issues. A potential Democratic edge with these voters? 51 percent want Trump investigations to continue. 54 percent of these folks disapprove of the Dobbs decision. But there`s some potential that they`re also Republican voters. 53 percent of them favor a GOP-controlled Congress. And 63 percent of them disapprove of Biden`s handling of the economy. Look, we`re always in search of who`s this year`s swing voter? Well, here`s what I can tell you. I don`t know who they are. I can tell you where they live. They live in exurban America. When we come back, the growth of Christian nationalism in the United States and the pastor who says it`s time to break down that wall between church and state. Stay with us. ELIZABETH STEVENS, UNITARIAN UNIVERSALIS CHURCH OF THE PALOUSE: In the public square, I don`t see them representing Christianity. I don`t see them representing the values that I find in the Bible. Take a look. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) REP. LAUREN BOEBERT (R-CO): And I`m tired of this separation of church and state junk. DOUG MASTRIANO (R), PENNSYLVANIA GUBERNATORIAL CANDIDATE: In November, we`re going to take our state back. My God, we`ll make it so. We will. REP. BAKER: Well, he`s very opportunistic, of course. Obviously, it`s not saying anything surprising to say that Donald Trump is not exactly the most religious person in the world. That was something therefore he needed to pay attention to. [09:55:01] He once told in fact, Lindsey Graham , and you played that clip from him earlier. He once told Lindsey Graham about these pastors who called him to tell him they were praying for him in the middle of impeachment. He says, those F`ing Christians just love me. I mean, he`s very opportunistic and kind of cynical about it, but he recognizes that it`s important to his political success. And they have recognized it`s the important -- that his success is important to them because he gave them a lot of what they wanted, in terms of judges, in terms of policies. He was the most overtly anti-abortion president and arguably the one most responsible for the overturning of Roe v. Wade. TODD: You know, look, some of this is reactionary, Leigh Ann. TODD: You know, Stephanie, there`s like -- we`ve noticed in our show for the most part there is one voting group in the Democratic coalition that does want to see, you know, religious texts sometimes be fused with public politics, and that`s churchgoing African Americans in particular. And he`s going and he`s very comfortable preaching from the pulpit about why he`s running for office, how his faith informs what he believes politically. And that`s exactly what Democrats need to keep doing because we should not cede the faith issue to Republicans. TODD: You know, Al, the Republican Party over the last 30 years was very much tied to many churchgoers-- CARDENAS: Ronald Reagan became a -- TODD: Is this going to become a liability? CARDENAS: Probably. You know, I`m saddened by the fact that America is becoming more secular just from a spiritual point of view. I also am saddened by the fact that my Catholic Church and the non-Evangelical Protestants have weakened themselves to the point where they`re not as relevant. And so the most relevant political group in the religious movement right now are Evangelicals. And they have always had a different perspective than my Catholic Church or non-Evangelical Protestants. headline: Katie Couric`s Message On The Importance Of Those Yearly Mammograms As She Reveals Her Own Breast Cancer Diagnosis
story_text: [07:41:32] CRAIG MELVIN: We are back. It is 7:41. We`re back with In-Depth Today. And this morning, an important story that`s really close to our hearts. HODA KOTB: Yes, every two minutes, a woman in this country is diagnosed with breast cancer and yesterday, our friend and our former colleague Katie Couric revealed she is now one of them. SAVANNAH GUTHRIE: And of course Katie has been on the frontlines of cancer awareness for decades, she lost her husband to cancer. And she`s using her story now to urge all women to get checked and to advocate for themselves. Sheinelle is here with more on that. Hi, good morning. SHEINELLE JONES, NBC NEWS ANCHOR: Good morning. As she battles breast cancer, Katie is turning her story into a cautionary tale in hopes of saving lives. She wants to educate women not only on the importance of screening but also about something called dense breast tissue. It affects nearly half of women in this country including Katie. And doctors say knowing you have it and how to ask for proper screenings could be lifesaving. (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) JONES (voice-over): Former today anchor Katie Couric has revealed that for the past several months, she has been privately battling cancer. COURIC: Thank you all for your support. JONES (voice-over): In an essay titled "Why Not Me?" the 65-year-old journalist says she was stunned by a stage one breast cancer diagnosis in June after missing her annual mammogram. I`m normally vigilant, bordering on neurotic, about taking care of my health. COURIC: I want to make sure that you all don`t put off your mammograms. JONES (voice-over): Katie is among nearly half of women over 40 in the U.S. who have dense breast tissue, which makes it more difficult to detect abnormalities on a mammogram and also increases your risk of breast cancer. Armed with this knowledge, her mammogram was followed by additional screening using an ultrasound, doctors biopsied a mass. The next day, Katie received the shocking results. It`s cancer. You`re going to be fine, but we need to make a plan. I felt sick and the room started to spin. What does this mean? What will the next weeks, months, even years look like? This isn`t the first time cancer has touched her life. Katie has long been an advocate for cancer awareness and screenings ever since her husband, Jay, was diagnosed with colon cancer and died of the disease at the age of 42. COURIC: Words of course will never describe how devastating this loss has been. JONES (voice-over): She famously underwent an on air colonoscopy on Today to encourage others to get checked. As a result, screenings went up by 20 percent, some dubbing it the Couric effect. COURIC: I have a pretty little colon. JONES (voice-over): She also lost her sister, Emily, to pancreatic cancer and 2001. The deaths of her loved ones prompting Katie to co found Stand Up to Cancer. COURIC: And I just realized I had to do something about this. JONES (voice-over): But with no family history of breast cancer, her own diagnosis came as a particular shock. Katie`s surgeon Dr. Lisa Newman. DR. LISA NEWMAN, KATIE COURIC`S SURGEON: More than three quarters of the breast cancers that we diagnose occur in women that do not have any established risk factors for breast cancer. JONES (voice-over): Katie`s cancer was caught early. She underwent a lumpectomy along with radiation and says she`ll need to take medication for the next five years. NEWMAN: It is wonderful that Katie has gone public with her experience and early detection of breast cancers will save millions of lives. JONES (voice-over): Now as she`s done before, Katie is determined to shine a light once again, on the importance of screening for cancer. Please get your annual mammogram. I was six months late this time. I shudder to think what might have happened if I had put it off longer. (END VIDEOTAPE) [07:45:08] JONES: Just six months late, here`s what we know for sure. When we do stories like this, our hope is that a woman watching or maybe a family member, that we give you a little nudge to go ahead and get that checkup. That`s what`s most important. KOTB: Six months is nothing, I mean especially with COVID and people not going in for a checkups. GUTHRIE: Yes, and you know, you kind of think, when I feel something -- KOTB: I did that. She thought she did it. She`s like, oh, it`s been that long. GUTHRIE: Really, for a mammogram or any of those screening, I actually made an appointment yesterday for a yearly physical I need. And it`s like because you remember, like, oh, yes, you know what, I`m going to do it. I`m not going to put it off another day. JONES: These kinds of stories save lives. MELVIN: We`re going to hear from Katie too, right? GUTHRIE: Yes, she`s going to join us on Monday. It`ll be her first live interview since sharing her diagnosis. It`ll be good to see Katie and give her a hug. And obviously she`s got a really important message to share. KOTB: We look forward to that. We`re going to get another check of the weather from Bill Karins. He`s in for Al. And some people have been wondering during the storm, where is Al, Al happen to test positive for COVID. We`re happy to say he`s feeling fine, just mild symptoms. He`s home. KARINS: He`s been sending us notes like he`s, you know, he wants to be here, he feels well. I can only imagine a step count in his house just like going back before, just like, you know, it`s like, yes. GUTHRIE: Disengage. KARINS: But Al has help us build an incredible weather team here at NBC News. And, you know, we`re getting you through this storm. And Al we`ll see you back here very soon. So concerns for today, the one thing I`m going to be watching is the storm surge. We have a storm surge warning still in effect for areas of northeast Florida. We`re not done yet. Irma really surprised us with the storm surge in the Jacksonville area. And here`s what we`re going to watch, the St. Johns River is one of the few rivers in our country that actually flows from south to north so that water that`s now falling in Orlando is going to trickle northwards up through the river at the same time. We`re going to see the storm surge coming in this afternoon at high tide about noon. This is all going to meet near Jacksonville. So we`re going to watch that area closely for the possibility of the four to six feet of storm surge. Right now they`ve already got a surge of about two feet. That`s look at your national weather. Now here`s a look at the weather outside your window. (LOCAL NEWS) KARINS: And that`s your Thursday forecast. MELVIN: All right. Thank you, Bill. Up next, he did it. Homerun history overnight, and we`re going to hear from Yankee`s superstar Aaron Judge after belting that 61st of the season to officially join baseball royalty. But first, these messages. headline: Today for September 29, 2022, NBC
story_text: (COMMERCIAL BREAK) [07:00:16] SAVANNAH GUTHRIE, NBC NEWS ANCHOR: Hi everybody. It`s Thursday. Millions in Florida waking up to catastrophic damage from Ian. HODA KOTB, NBC NEWS ANCHOR: Yes, the full impact being revealed as the sunrises this morning. It is September 29th. This is Today. Path of destruction, massive flooding and power outages as Ian barrels across Florida crashing ashore as one of the strongest hurricanes to ever hit the state. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: All the sudden I felt something and then heard like a train coming right to the house. (END VIDEO CLIP) KOTB: Nearly 3 million people in the dark, the devastating storm surge leaving entire neighborhoods underwater, homes and cars floating down streets. This hospital swapped from above and below, losing part of its roof, its ground floor flooded, crews still carrying out emergency rescues on land and at sea. We`re live across the state with complete coverage and what millions need to know as the threat moves up the East Coast. Get out, the urgent security alert for all Americans in Russia to leave the country immediately. And the new warning that anyone there with dual citizenship couldn`t be drafted into the Ukraine war, we`ll have the very latest. Breast cancer battle, well wishes pouring in for Katie Couric this morning after she revealed her diagnosis. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) KATIE COURIC, AMERICAN JOURNALIST: Thank you all for your support. (END VIDEO CLIP) KOTB: Just ahead, her decision to speak out and what she wants all women to know. Those stories, plus, historic blast. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) UNIDENTIFIED MALE: Judge keep the left field. This could be it. See you. (END VIDEO CLIP) KOTB: Yankee`s superstar Aaron Judge crushes his record tying 61st homerun of the season, cementing his place among baseball royalty. Today, Thursday, September 29th, 2022. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: From NBC News, this is Today with Savannah Guthrie and Hoda Kotb live from Studio 1A in Rockefeller Plaza. KOTB: Good Thursday morning. So happy you`re joining us today. Good to see you. GUTHRIE: Yes. The sun is coming up in Florida and we`re getting a closer look now at the widespread devastation left behind by Ian. KOTB: Yes, there are two major concerns right now there, the flooding of course and the power outages. Nearly 3 million people across the state woke up this morning and could not turn the lights on, no electricity. GUTHRIE: Ian made landfall yesterday as a major category four packing 150 mile an hour winds and causing massive storm surges across Florida`s Gulf Coast. KOTB: So right now, Ian is making its way east toward the eastern side of Florida. We have a live look at some of the conditions going on. This is Orlando. And while the storm did weakened overnight, it still remains a serious threat. GUTHRIE: Yes, it`s a rain story there. And then once Ian heads away from Florida, it is expected to then curve back toward the Georgia, South Carolina coastlines impacting millions across the South in the coming days. KOTB: Yes, we got it all covered for you this morning. We`re going to start off with NBC`s Sam Brock. He is in Venice, Florida. That`s just north of where Ian made landfall. Hi, Sam, what`s the assessment this morning? SAM BROCK, NBC NEWS CORRESPONDENT: Yes, Hoda, Savannah, good morning. It is terrifying to think what we`re going to see in the light of day. I was just talking to a police officer here in Venice. They resume search and rescue operations at 2 o`clock this morning looking for critically injured people. But he said look, I got to warn you, block to block, there`s dead wire, there`s live wire. As you look behind me right now, you`ll see splintered signs and power lines down all through here. Now when East Naples guys, there were 30 rescue missions yesterday as the urgent efforts right now are underway to find those imperiled by Ian. (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) BROCK (voice-over): It`s devastation that was predicted with the grim reality of this storm`s warped power defies imagination. Ian now with tropical storm hit the coast as a fierce hurricane shredding homes apart and Placida, Florida, tearing off roofs and splintering trees. While in the Tampa area, extremely causing this tree to crash through a home. In one of the hardest hit areas, Fort Myers, there were storm surges nearly seven feet high, nearly double the previous record more than 20 years ago. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: Oh my God. BROCK (voice-over): The massive surge of water leaving entire communities completely underwater. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: Do you want me to come out? BROCK (voice-over): Roads looking more like the ocean for block after block. Ian packed catastrophic 150 mile an hour winds knocking out power to more than 2 million customers. GOV. RON DESANTIS (R-FL): We have seen life threatening storm surge as was predicted. We`ve also seen major flooding, but that`s going to rank as one of the top five hurricanes to ever hit the Florida peninsula. BROCK (voice-over): This team of emergency responders unable to respond, a massive wall of water swamping their fire truck. [07:05:06] UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: Now we have a truck issue and the guys are pushing the truck out of the bay. BROCK (voice-over): In Port Charlotte, hospital staff working through the storm to protect patients. Other first responders struggling to help those in need, unable to start rescues until after life threatening conditions subsided. Despite repeated warnings to leave, some people did not or could not evacuate. They found themselves stranded by a 12 foot storm surge. Mark and Elizabeth living in an apartment in Venice Island, Florida but at the last minute, grab their air mattresses and hunker down in this Sarasota office when her boss offered it to them. (on camera): Here you are with air mattresses in an office space. Your home is 50 or 100 miles away. But you consider yourself lucky. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: We are. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: Yes. BROCK: Is that because you`re saved from the storm? UNIDENTIFIED MALE: Yes, yes, because somebody helped us. BROCK (voice-over): Others stayed behind in the flood zone, trying to help those who were unable to leave. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: I want to help the people in here because they`re good people here in paradise. BROCK (voice-over): This morning, the destruction left behind by this massive blow from Mother Nature is just starting to come into focus. (END VIDEOTAPE) KOTB: Well, hats off to those first responders, all those helpers out there, Sam. There were some viral images in Tampa that were just shocking. It was actually Tampa Bay, and it looked dry. It looked like you could walk on it. People were taking video and pictures of it. What`s the after effects there? BROCK: Yes, so here`s the deal, Hoda, you`re seeing all this water being really sucked out. It`s called negative storm surge. And the reason behind it, you have counterclockwise winds and hurricanes. So on the northern edge of the eye wall, the water was being pulled out of Tampa Bay, into the Gulf of Mexico. The problem with this, Hoda, is the fact that it can then refill when wind directionality change. And it can happen in a matter of minutes. So if you see this, it might be tempting to go out there on the sand and check it out. Don`t do it for your own safety. Hoda? KOTB: All right, Sam Brock for us there in Venice, Sam, thanks. GUTHRIE: Yes. These conditions can change in a split second, the water has finally stopped rising in Fort Myers. But this morning, the impact of the catastrophic flooding there is being felt across the city. And joining us now Fort Myers Mayor Kevin Anderson. Mr. Mayor, good morning. We`re glad to have you on the phone with us this morning. Have you been able to assess damage? I know it`s still early there. What`s your sense of how bad it was? MAYOR KEVIN ANDERSON, FORT MYERS, FL: We haven`t had a full assessment obviously with the sun just coming up, but it is pretty bad. I`m standing on a floating concrete dock. I`m down in the River District of downtown. The problem is the dock is in the middle of an intersection, a block, two blocks away from the water. This is about a piece of concrete that weighs a ton. And it was moved this far away. It shows you how powerful the waters were last night. KOTB: I know one of the things, that`s most concerning in a moment like this is what happened to the people who decided to stay or who were left behind. Have you guys been able to conduct rescues? Do you know how many people are still out there and in need of your help? ANDERSON: We would estimate several dozen people who stayed behind were in need of some assistance. Our teams have been working on that. I`m happy to report at this time. I`ve been not -- I haven`t been told of any loss of life in the city. Now keep in mind, we have a metropolitan area and there may be some outside, but inside the city there`s been no reports to my knowledge. Without a doubt, we`re watching one of the greatest hitters having one of the greatest seasons of all time. By the way, in case you`re wondering about what happened to that ball, look at this, Judge got it back, gifted it to his number one fan, his mom, Patty, real quick, the fan who dropped it, the Blue Jays grabbed it, they sort of pass it around they finally gave it to the Yankees . It`s worth somewhere between 200,000 to $2 million. GUTHRIE: But that`s mom`s got it. (CROSSTALK) LLAMAS: She deserves it. GUTHRIE: Yes.
