TODD: We could keep going on crime, but I want to pivot to the Achilles` heel issue on the other side, and it is abortion. Here`s some answers how Walker, Johnson and Oz are handling the abortion issue. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) HERSCHEL WALKER (R), GEORGIA SENATE NOMINEE: I`m a Christian, but I`m also representing the people of Georgia, and that`s who I represent. So what the people of Georgia stand for, I`m going to stand with them. SEN. RON JOHNSON (R-WI): I proposed a one-time, single-issue referendum to decide at what point does society has the responsibility to protect life? DR. MEHMET OZ (R), PENNSYLVANIA SENATE NOMINEE: I`m giving you a bigger answer than yes or no. I`m telling you I don`t want any federal rules limiting what states do with abortion. It should be up to the states. (END VIDEO CLIP) TODD: Eugene, we`re all over the place here. Even Evan McMullin kind of like, maybe I`ll do -- I mean, nobody knows on this issue what to do if you`re on the -- what was originally the pro-life side of this issue. DANIELS: Right. That was always going to happen. We talked about this on "Meet the Press" last year when we were talking about this issue. And it was very clear that they had caught the car. They were going to catch the car, and what was going to happen after? And this is what happens, kind of this hodgepodge of different ideas of what voters might want to hear at that time. And you know, when you look at abortion versus economy, versus crime, versus -- this is a very choose your-own-adventure election, right? TODD: Isn`t it? Yeah. DANIELS: People can just pick and choose whatever they want, even within the issue themselves. TODD: The five swing voters, what do you think they care about: crime or abortion? WALTER: Right. Although what we`re seeing too, the Kaiser Foundation had polling on this that found if you`re in a state with abortion restrictions -- TODD: You care about it more. WALTER: - you are much more motivated than if you`re in a state that doesn`t. And so if you`re in a traditional blue state, Oregon, California, et cetera, you`re less motivated by it than some of these other states. TODD: All right. I`m just going to pause the discussion. We`re going to come right back. Up next, though, why the state of Wisconsin best represents our deep divide that plays out in our national politics. A little taste of my reporting from the ground and what`s driving the red and blue divisions in a state that I like to call patient zero for polarization. (COMMERCIAL BREAK) [09:46:49] TODD: Welcome back. It is no secret the country is polarized. All you have to do is look at Washington by the numbers. Take a look at the U.S. Senate here, 50/50. The House is almost as close, 220-212. And here`s a number that should really be a bit disturbing to folks -- believe it or not, 44 states have voted for the same party for president in five of the last six elections. Take a look at the six states that don`t fit that category. So to better understand these national divisions, I traveled to Wisconsin, a state that truly represents political polarization in our country, and what we`ve undergone in recent years. I sat down with two former Wisconsin governors of opposite parties who both knew how to win big in this divided state back in the `90s and the early aughts. In 1994, incumbent governor Tommy Thompson , he won by more than 35 percentage points and all but one of Wisconsin`s 72 counties. And this came in between two presidential wins in the state for a Democrat -- Bill Clinton at the time. In 2002, Democrat Jim Doyle`s margin was narrower than Thompson. But he still carried 43 counties, including many in the rural north of the state, something that would be basically unheard of in this current political climate. So what`s changed? What does it tell us about the nation as a whole? (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) TOMMY THOMPSON (R), FORMER WISCONSIN GOVERNOR: Jim and I, you know, are friends, but I would never -- in modern-day politics -- I would not want to debate him. I wouldn`t even want to talk to him because I`m afraid somebody from my right would run against me. Jim would feel the same way. Somebody from the George Soros left would come against him. So we have become paralyzed because we have redistricted to such an extent that a Republican state`s going to be a Republican state, a Democrat - except on a statewide ballot -- but individual districts. And that has become the partisan parochialism that it is today. TODD: Sir, would you disagree with anything he just said there? JAMES DOYLE (D), FORMER WISCONSIN GOVERNOR: No, I agree. But I would add this: One of the reasons Wisconsin is so much the center of this now is you look at the demographics of the state and the big divisions that have happened in the country -- rural and small town against cities; big, expanding economies like Madison against rural economies that are struggling -- those have happened all over. It`s just in Wisconsin when you add those up, it`s a 50/50 state. So, you know, I was the attorney general when Governor Thompson was governor, and we certainly had our fights. But there were times that he would win 60 percent of the vote at the top of the ballot and then the next line down would be me and I`d win 60 percent of the vote. That is never going to happen again-- THOMPSON: Fifty-nine percent. You`ve never gotten 60. DOYLE: I got 60 in that -- TODD: It`s now, there are no swing voters. It`s two states in one. That`s what Dan Balz calls it. It`s really two states, right? THOMPSON: It has become so partisan and so divided that I would have to say it`s almost two states. (END VIDEO CLIP) TODD: So to give you an idea of where things stand today, check out Wisconsin`s nationally-watched race for governor. It is almost dead even. And, by the way, you want more of my reporting from Wisconsin? [09:50:01] Check out our latest episode of Meet the Press Reports, "Wisconsin: Ground Zero for Polarization." It`s on demand right now on Peacock, YouTube , or MeetThePress.com. When we come back, we`re going to look at the role former President Trump is playing in the midterms and beyond. (COMMERCIAL BREAK) TODD: Welcome back. Well, Mr. Trump had quite a few legal challenges this week. He chose to respond to the subpoena the January 6th Committee hearing. He didn`t say what he would do, but he did write this, complaining about a lack of one focus of the investigation. He said: It was indeed one of the largest crowds I`ve ever spoken before -- talking about his speech on the Ellipse. It was a very wide swath, stretching all the way back to the Washington Monument. The massive size of this crowd and its meaning has never been a subject of your committee. It is true, Amy, that they have never investigated the size -- WALTER: The size. TODD: -- of the January 6th crowd. I -- you know -- it`s sort of, it`s sort of I guess not shocking that he came into office talking about his crowd sizes and he`s still complaining about his crowd sizes. WALTER: Well, he would like the 2022 election to continue to be about him, which, of course, Republicans would like it not to be about him. And I think the only thing that is helping Republicans right now is that while he is still trying to put himself in the center of the conversation, he`s really not. This is in the background. I think January 6th, especially what happened this week, didn`t generate the kind of headlines and the kind of wall-to-wall coverage -- [09:55:06] TODD: Subpoenas wasn`t a headline enough for you-- WALTER: Subpoena, no. I think voters expect, of course, he`s going to get subpoenaed. If they said, we`re indict -- we believe that he should be indicted. We know that the real issue here is, until there is some legal action taken, this is still all background noise. TODD: We got defamation testimony this week in that defamation lawsuit that apparently the former president, Jean Carroll, that, that he`s worried about. That happens Wednesday, Eugene. DANIELS: Yeah. I mean, it`s just over and over and over and over again. WALTER: Yeah. DANIELS: Right? It`s January 6th. It`s Mar-a-Lago. It`s this defamation case. We talk to Republicans, and you probably would feel the same way, it`s that they`re like, it`s just too much chaos, and, we don`t want -- we want you gone. Please go away, and he wants to be at the center of attention all the time. TODD: All right. Well, I`ve got to play for you what Paul Ryan said earlier this week, because he said something that both seems obvious and yet I want to say naive at the same time. Take a listen. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) PAUL RYAN , FORMER SPEAKER OF THE HOUSE: I think Trump`s unelectability will be palpable by then. We all know that he`s so much more likely to lose the White House than anybody else running for president on our side of the aisle. So why would we want to go with that? (END VIDEO CLIP) TODD: I`m old enough to remember, Pat, when that was Scott Walker`s argument in 2015 about why people need to rally around somebody other than Donald Trump . MCCRORY: Well, there are about 20 Republican - TODD: Yeah. MCCRORY: - candidates for the presidency that are running right now. TODD: Who really believe this too, right? MCCRORY: Who really believe this, too, and they can`t say it because they don`t want to upset the core 30 percent who are with Trump regardless. And, by the way, the Democrats are running away from Biden in this election, too. They do not want -- the Democrats don`t want Biden on the stage. TODD: Well, no, no, no. Oregon Democrats do. MCCRORY: Yeah, and the Oregon governor`s race is now close-- TODD: I know. Right. MCCRORY: Democrats don`t want Biden or Harris either, and Republicans frankly don`t want Trump. And they`re the ones trying to consume the TV time. TODD: Well, I don`t think Biden`s actually -- (CROSSTALK) KUMAR: I think -- TODD: -- White House seems to be fine -- KUMAR: Yeah. Yeah. TODD: -- with this. I`ve talked to folks at the White House like, hey, we`re all on the same message. We`ll go to Oregon and Florida? Okay. (CROSSTALK) DANIELS: It doesn`t matter. KUMAR: Yeah. KUMAR: You tell us where to go. But, I also think that with Biden, his challenge is that he hasn`t been able to communicate to the American people what he`s done. I mean, we can say that the difference between Donald Trump and the difference within Biden is Biden is a policy president. So he has - - he`s going to make fundamental changes for a generation. And we`re talking about student loan relief. We`re talking about bringing back manufacturing. And the list goes on. But the difference with Trump is that his consequence is not policy. TODD: Right. KUMAR: It`s his legacy of undermining elections. MCCRORY: Biden -- KUMAR: And it`s not just him, it`s not him, but he actually has a cadre of individuals right now seeking office that are election deniers. MCCRORY: But -- but -- but -- KUMAR: And that legacy is far more dangerous for a modern-day president than any other thing -- MCCRORY: But Biden can`t go on-- TODD: Last word. KUMAR: -- because it believes in undermining our democracy. MCCRORY: Biden can`t go on TV because 401(k)s are down 20-25 percent, because the price of eggs is more than we`ve ever paid in our lifetime, because of gas is going up. headline: Conversation With Elizabeth Heiskell About Her Breast Cancer Journey
story_text: HODA KOTB: We are back. 8:13. The "Pink Power TODAY". And this morning story hits close to home for us. SAVANNAH GUTHRIE: Yes, our beloved "TODAY" food contributor Elizabeth Heiskell was diagnosed with stage two breast cancer this past summer. KOTB: Like a lot of women this can happen, too. She was in the best shape of her life. She has no family history. She says breast cancer wasn`t just -- well, not on her radar. Elizabeth, we love you. You are here with us. ELIZABETH HEISKELL, " TODAY" FOOD CONTRIBUTOR: Yes. KOTB: We are going to talk to you in a second. OK. But first, let`s check out her story. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) HEISKELL: I was diagnosed with stage two breast cancer. KOTB (voiceover): Elizabeth found a lump by chance. HEISKELL: I went to just scratch my chest and I found a lump. I thought that I had had a mammogram eight months ago. I wasn`t that concerned, honestly. KOTB (voiceover): But she had the lump checked by her doctor. HEISKELL: She felt around and she started to look very panicked. We got to get a mammogram. We got to get an ultrasound. We need to get a biopsy. KOTB (voiceover): Elizabeth thought she was up to date with her mammogram screenings but the doctor informed her otherwise. HEISKELL: She said, Elizabeth it`s been two years, almost two and a half years since you had it. KOTB (voiceover): The news she had breast cancer came as a complete shock. HEISKELL: When my doctor did call me and told me that I had invasive ductal carcinoma, I didn`t know invasive or ductal meant but I knew carcinoma. I knew that was cancer. It was like the wind had been knocked out of me, like somebody punched me. I was not prepared for this. I was in the best shape of my life. I had just lost a good amount of weight. Breast cancer was not on my radar at all. It took me to my knees. [08:15:00] I have no family history of breast cancer. That was another reason I was so blindsided by this. As hard as it is for somebody to tell you that you have cancer, as hard as that is to hear, it is impossible to say the words to your family. Honestly, I didn`t think I was going to be able to process it to say that sentence to my family. It took weeks and weeks for it to even sink in. I just finished my third chemo treatment. I am just now grasping the fact that I have cancer. KOTB (voiceover): Cooking brought some comfort. HEISKELL: I must have made meat loaf, mashed potatoes, and sort of green peas with cream sauce. This was what -- what my mother made for me. I don`t even know how many times I made that meal because it did, it brought me such comfort. I was diagnosed three weeks before mama passed away. So, it`s been a lot. We are going to do these great easy salads that we can -- KOTB (voiceover): As a well-known chef and "TODAY" contributor, Elizabeth says she is passionate about cooking and taking care of others, but cancer has forced her to focus on herself. HEISKELL: It`s not my nature. I bring the casseroles. I bring the food. I am the doer. I am the one that makes sure that everyone else is OK. And it`s easy to let that take over and you forget to take care of yourself. You just have to take it step by step, day by day. But you will, you will get there. You will get to the top of the mountain. (END VIDEO CLIP) KOTB (on camera): Yes, you will. Yes, you will, Elizabeth. GUTHRIE: yes. KOTB: We are so happy that you are sitting here on this couch. We want to know all about it. But just in this moment, like, how are you -- tell me the prognosis. How are you feeling today? HEISKELL: You know, I am so unbelievably grateful. So, we went back to MD Anderson and that little tumor has shrunk 78 percent. GUTHRIE: Wow. Wow. Wow. KOTB: Come on. HEISKELL: That was only -- that was after three chemo treatments. KOTB: Wow. HEISKELL: I mean, it`s unbelievable. And I`m just -- I am -- I`m so grateful that I`m almost -- I feel guilty at times, you know, because I have the most amazing support system. I have you all. I have family and friends. And, you know, an incredible health care. And, you know, it`s good. It`s good. GUTHRIE: So, you`re halfway through your chemo. You`ll have your surgery. But -- I mean, to have that kind of, it`s working? HEISKELL: Yes. GUTHRIE: The feeling must be such, such a -- you know, just an inspiration? HEISKELL: It was unbelievable. And the lady that did my ultrasound, she -- her -- my mother`s name was Sheila (ph). Her name was Sheila (ph). She spelled it just like my mother did. And then her daughter`s name was Elizabeth and we have the same birthday. GUTHRIE: Oh, my gosh. HEISKELL: So, if you don`t tell me that my mama wasn`t all up in that room. GUTHRIE: Oh, wow. HEISKELL: But you know, the thing is, is that this is -- it is a journey. You know, it is a climb. And I`m leaning in and I`m learning. You know, I`m learning so much. And, you know, it`s -- I had worked myself up. When I was getting ready for that first chemo treatment, honey, fear had taken over. It was driving the bus. You would have thought that I was going to go in there and they were taking off all my fingers, all my toes. Like, I was petrified. KOTB: Yes. HEISKELL: And so, I got through that day and Luke was with me and I literally -- everything they did, I said, oh, that wasn`t so bad. KOTB: Yes. HEISKELL: Well, I mean, that wasn`t so bad. So, by the time I got home, I called my girls and I said, look -- I said, fear is not going to drive this bus. It -- to dream, it`s -- you use the same exact brain, the same exact creativity to make those horrible nightmares as you do to dream. And I am not doing it any more. KOTB: That`s it. HEISKELL: I am not holding back. You all think that I`ve always been 100 percent. There is something that I have been holding back and I`m not going to do it anymore. I am not fearing. KOTB: You said there are things that cancer could -- is teaching you that nothing else could have taught you. Because everyone knows that adage of God only gives you as much as you can handle. HEISKELL: Yes. KOTB: You actually don`t believe that? HEISKELL: No, I don`t think that`s the case. I think it`s time for you to lean in and learn something new. And, you know, the lessons that I have learned -- I mean, it`s look for silver linings even in this mess. There was this sweetest lady when I was at the clinic. And, you know, they give us these warm robes. So, it -- kind of, for five minutes you feel like you are at a spa, until they take your boob and they stick it into a vice grip. For that minute, you know -- and so, as she looked at me and she is sitting there with her bald head and sunken eyes, and she said, oh -- she said, aren`t these robes just the silver lining? And I had just been diagnosed, and I thought silver lining my butt. We are sitting here, you know. And then it came to me. And then she said, you know, where you live? And I said, I live in Oxford. She said, bus -- but my sister-in-law lives here in Houston so I have a place to stay. She goes, another silver lining. And it was almost like she was catching butterflies. I am not kidding you. And so, if you stay there in that silver lining, that silver lining is going to be the thing that you`re going to wrap yourself in. That`s all you`re going to see is the silver. And I`m telling you, these are the lessons that I would have -- I mean, and I know we talk about it and we say, you know. But to really believe -- KOTB: Believe it. GUTHRIE: Yes. HEISKELL: -- and every day you are looking for the silver lining butterflies. [08:20:00] KOTB: One of your silver linings is standing over there. You talked about your tribe. HEISKELL: Yes. KOTB: Your people. Who do we have? HEISKELL: So, I have my daddy, who I love more than life itself. And it`s his birthday tomorrow. And then I have Mindy and my sweet husband, Luke who -- let me tell you something, Luke looked at me in my first cancer treatment. And he looked over and I was sitting there and he had tears in his eyes when they went to put the first chemo drug in my body. And he looked at me and I know he was thinking, if only I could just take this and put this in me right now. He has been everything. You cannot even imagine. And my girls. Oh, my gosh, and my friends. KOTB: Is that one of your brothers? HEISKELL: And my friends -- no. And that`s Molly. And we have Margie (ph) and Peter. And -- you know, I do. I have a whole tribe. I have a little boy that every day when he goes to school, he tells his dad to honk the horn and -- so that I know that they are praying for me that morning. I mean, there is -- you cannot imagine. I have somebody who sent me a night light because I`d said that when the fear was taking -- driving the bus, I was up late nights. I mean, it was tough. And so, she sent me a night light that I could turn on when I was up scared at night. I mean, these are the people that I have. And, you know, I hope that people that, if you know somebody that has breast cancer or cancer or that`s struggling, please go out of your way. It doesn`t have to be much. KOTB: Right. HEISKELL: A honk of the horn or a night light, anything. KOTB: And sometimes people think, well, you know what, they may want their family time. They may want their privacy. But reach out, right? HEISKELL: Lean into them. KOTB: Lean in, yes. HEISKELL: Get under them. KOTB: Yes. HEISKELL: Hold them up. KOTB: Hold them. HEISKELL: And carry them up that mountain. I mean -- KOTB: Yes. GUTHRIE: Call, don`t text. KOTB: Yes. HEISKELL: Yes. And they did call me. You all they called me. KOTB: Of course. HEISKELL: And of course, when I was driving back from Memphis, we had been to the oncologist when you called, and I was like, oh God. Lord. Look, Hoda`s on the phone. Stop the car. Because we were about to go through a dead area. I was like, Hoda never calls me. Just stop the car. And then Savannah called. And it was just amazing. KOTB: Well, we -- GUTHRIE: We love you. KOTB: You`re our family. GUTHRIE: You are our family. KOTB: We`re part of your tribe, too. HEISKELL: Well, that -- I have been looking forward to being back here with you all so much. And you are -- I mean, I am. I`m back with family. I`m with Debbie and my producer, who I -- who really, I mean, she is my family. KOTB: Well, we adore you. You need to -- all of this is, like, the most inspirational. GUTHRIE: I know. It really is. KOTB: I`m sure you helped a ton of people today. We love you. HEISKELL: Go get your mammograms. KOTB: Yes. HEISKELL: I literally thought it was eight months. It had been two years people. KOTB: Yes. GUTHRIE: Yes. HEISKELL: It had been two years people. KOTB: You got it. HEISKELL: You put it on your calendar right now. You stop what you`re doing. I`m serious. KOTB: Yes. GUTHRIE: Yes, absolutely. KOTB: We love you. We love you. GUTHRIE: We love you. By the way, Elizabeth wrote a beautiful and personal essay, shares more of her story, and you should read it. Check it out today.com. And we just love you. KOTB: Yes. HEISKELL: I love you. GUTHRIE: Al, over to you. ROKER: Silver lining butterflies. Oh, I`ll remember that. KOTB: We love that. ROKER: That and hotter than the hinges of hell. GUTHRIE: Yes. ROKER: All right. Let`s show you what we got going on. Heavy snow in the U.P. of Michigan today. Some showers in the northeast. Look for some wet weather also down through the Florida Peninsula. Heavy rain down through Southern Texas. Warm and dry out west. That`s what`s going on around the country. Here`s what`s happening in your neck of the woods. (LOCAL NEWS) ROKER: I`ve got to say, that was the best part of the morning. JONES: My goodness, absolutely. ROKER: But, yes. We love you. GUTHRIE: We really do. ROKER: Anyway, "POP Start." KOTB: "POP Start" too. GUTHRIE: OK. JONES: "POP Start" is good too. ROKER: Yes, it is. JONES: All right. We`re going to try to give you some good stuff today. First up, Robbie Coltrane. Tributes are pouring in after the beloved actor died at the age of 72 over the weekend. He was best known for his role as Hagrid in the "Harry Potter" movie franchise. His agent shared in a statement that he would, "Be best remembered for decades to come as Hagrid in the Harry Potter films. A role which brought joy to children and adults alike all over the world. Prompting a stream of fan letters every week for 20 years." Coltrane`s "Harry Potter" co-star Daniel Radcliffe also paid tribute in a statement writing, Robbie was one of the funniest people I`ve met and used to keep us laughing constantly as kids on set. I feel incredibly lucky that I got to meet and work with him and very sad that he has passed. All right. Next up, Carrie Underwood. As we mentioned on Friday, the country superstar is hitting the road for her "Denim and" -- I was going to say diamonds -- "Rhinestones" tour. Highlighting her greatest hits and new music from her latest album. Underwood kicked off her tour with a sold-out show in Greenville, South Carolina, over the weekend. Here`s a look at one of her epic opening night performances. [08:25:00] (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) CARRIE UNDERWOOD, SINGER: Yes, I`m one of those crazy angels. Tilted halo with a neon shine. Call me one of those crazy angels. (END VIDEO CLIP) JONES: Pretty cool. KOTB: Wow. JONES: She said she wanted to do something new and she certainly did. Underwood plans to make stops in 43 U.S. cities. That`s a lot of shows. Next up is Indianapolis, Indiana. You can catch the "Denim and Rhinestones" tour through March 20th through the 23rd. All right. Next up, Savannah and Hoda. Rumor has it our favorite duo had some fun over the weekend, taking the stage at this year`s BravoCon. The fan of it celebrates some of Bravo`s biggest TV shows and reality stars. And you guys, you sat down with our pal, Andy Cohen, to ask him all the burning questions submitted by Bravo fans. Andy even recruited you to do the infamous shotski. Check it out. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) ANDY COHEN, RADIO AND TELEVISION TALK SHOW HOST: OK. One, two, three. GUTHRIE: One, two, three. COHEN: One, two, three. GUTHRIE: One, two, three. (END VIDEO CLIP) JONES: How was it? ROKER: How many did you do? GUTHRIE: Just one. KOTB: One, two, three. One, two, three. GUTHRIE: I mean, it wasn`t even, like -- well, I don`t know. We`re like, yes, sure. Let`s bring it on. JONES: Yes, exactly. KOTB: Because it`s Friday and that`s the way -- KOTB: There you go. I love that. GUTHRIE: New "Steals & Deals" just ahead. But first your local news. (LOCAL NEWS) (COMMERCIAL BREAK) [08:30:00] HODA KOTB, NBC NEWS ANCHOR: We are back, it`s 8:30. It`s a beautiful Monday morning. We`re greeting our Rockefeller Center Plaza crowd. So many smiling faces, so many birthdays, anniversaries. We`re so happy that y`all came and that you`re joining us today. AL ROKER, NBC NEWS ANCHOR: All right. And just ahead, Sheinelle, you got to go back to Philadelphia -- SHEINELLE JONES, NBC NEWS ANCHOR: I did. ROKER: -- home of the Eagles, Savanna`s Eagles, and saw some of the work you did during last night`s game. JONES: I was so nervous. I`m like please win, please win. So they won, yes. So before their win over the Cowboys, I joined their team of groundskeepers and learn what goes into creating the perfect field. There`s truly an art to it. I can`t wait to share this story with you. KOTB: Cool. SAVANNAH GUTHRIE, NBC NEWS ANCHOR: All right. Also ahead awesome, guys, it`s cozy season already. Jill Martin wants to make sure we`re all prepared. So she brought Steals and Deals to keep warm inside and outside of your house. KOTB: And then Harry Smith, he`s taking us inside the new home of the iconic New York Philharmonic, how a few changes are making the sound even better for musicians and their audiences. ROKER: And then just ahead on the 3rd Hour of Today, our new Consumer Confidential about scams being on the rise. From Social Security to student loans, those bad guys are getting creative and getting their hands on our money. We`re going to tell you what to look out for and how we can protect ourselves. GUTHRIE: All right, Al, let`s check the weather. Looks like it`s like -- KOTB: Yes it does. ROKER: (Inaudible) some sprinkle, some wet weather here, but let`s show you what we`re looking at week ahead. Winter chill around the Great Lakes today, some winter storms coming on in, look for heavy rain down through Texas, warm out west. We got that Jetstream dipping way down. Records possible in 18 states from Texas, Kansas, on into Kentucky, in the east southeast and down to the Gulf. And then next week, warmer in the east, colder out west. Andrea Mitchell has the latest. (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) ANDREA MITCHELL, NBC NEWS CHIEF FOREIGN AFFAIRS CORRESPONDENT (voiceover): Tonight, another Iranian woman in the spotlight. Elnaz Rekabi, a 33-year- old elite rock climber, the first female athlete on an Iranian team known to have competed without her country`s mandatory headscarf or hijab. During international competition in South Korea, Rekabi`s long hair flowing uncovered, prompted concerns for her safety. Hours later, a post on her Instagram account read, I encountered a problem with my cover during the final. Adding, she was returning to Iran with her team as planned. The circumstances under which it was posted remain unclear. Human rights activists are worried about her fate and around where women and girls have been beaten and jailed for not following the dress code. What are your concerns about the fate of the woman climber who took off the hijab in competition in South Korea? NAZANIN BONIADI, IRANIAN-BORN ACTRESS AND ACTIVIST: We`re very concerned that she`s going to end up in solitary confinement and be tortured into making a false confession. NANCY PELOSI (D-CA): Well, we can make sure everyone is paying attention to it. This is organic. It`s initiated by the women, and we should all take great pride in that. LISA MONACO, U.S. DEPUTY ATTORNEY GENERAL; Corporate crime that has reached a new low and a very dark place. DILANIAN: French cement company Lafarge , which operates plants in dozens of countries and 43 U.S. states pleading guilty to paying terrorists in Syria between 2013 and 2014 so it could keep a cement plant running as ISIS and other groups fought for control. Payments made at the same time the terror group was capturing and beheading U.S. hostages, including James Foley and Steven Sotloff. Prosecutors say the company sent ISIS and the al-Qaeda-linked Nusra Front more than $10 million, then tried to cover it up. BREON PEACE, U.S. ATTORNEY, NEW YORK EASTERN DISTRICT: Lafarge made a deal with the devil, foreign terrorists who pledged to in fact did harm the United States, its people, and its national security. DILANIAN: The company agreed to pay a settlement of nearly $800 million to the U.S. government . French authorities in 2018 charged eight former Lafarge executives with financing terrorism. The company now owned by a Swiss firm said today it deeply regretted what happened, adding that the executives involved no longer work there and that none of the conduct involve us employees. (END VIDEOTAPE) DILANIAN (on camera): In a disturbing twist, court documents show Lafarge was doing business with ISIS and al-Qaeda at the same time, its concrete was being used to build One World Trade Center on the site where terrorists destroyed the Twin Towers in 2001. Lester? HOLT: Ken Dilanian, thank you. In Ukraine tonight the crippling impact of Russia`s attacks over the last week. President Zelenskyy warning today that 30 percent of Ukraine`s power stations had been destroyed, causing massive blackouts. New airstrikes today left hundreds of thousands of people without power or water. Concern is growing as cold weather sets in. Now to our reporting from inside Russia and the impact of President Putin`s partial draft. We`ve seen the traffic jams of young men fleeing the country to avoid it. Keir Simmons with some who have left. (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) KEIR SIMMONS, NBC NEWS SENIOR INTERNATIONAL CORRESPONDENT (voiceover): Tonight, as Russia`s President Putin attempts to force Ukrainians into capitulation with deadly drone strikes, he`s under pressure at home with many Russian men deciding to leave. We traveled to Kazakhstan to meet some of the thousands who came here to escape the partial draft. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: I don`t want to kill people. I don`t want to die. SIMMONS : With their possessions on their back, these men not wanting their faces on camera. This is the bag that you left Russia with? UNIDENTIFIED MALE: Yes. SIMMONS : Just this? UNIDENTIFIED MALE: Yes. SIMMONS: Dimitri, not his real name, is homeless and heartbroken. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: I feel very sad about it because I feel a connection with my motherland. SIMMONS : You love your country. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: Of course. Of course, I love -- I love Russia. SIMMONS : We met a group of Russian artists putting on street performances as a thank-you to the people of Kazakhstan for welcoming them. Alexander`s friend got his draft papers, and they decided to leave that same day, just grab anything they could. And what happened on the border? We flew, then found a car, he says. But there was 10 miles of traffic at the border. So, we walked. No longer facing life on the front line, but their lives changed forever. What do you see in the future? UNIDENTIFIED MALE: I can tell you nothing about my future because I see like only in two weeks. SIMMONS: Back in Russia, the only independent pollster here tells us support for President Putin remains strong but the partial mobilization is having an impact. DENIS, VOLKOV, DIRECTOR, LEVADA POLLING CENTER: More than half our population feel anxious about it. SIMMONS : What are they anxious about that? VOLKOV: That the husbands, sons, might be recruited. (END VIDEOTAPE) SIMMONS : The Kremlin says the partial draft will soon be over with 300,000 enlisted. But ultimately, it`s President Putin`s decision. Lester? HOLT: All right, Keir Simmons, thank you. In 60 seconds, companies making it tougher to earn those customer loyalty rewards. The well-known brands making you spend more in the "PRICE YOU PAY." (COMMERCIAL BREAK) [19:15:00] HOLT: Back now with the "PRICE YOU PAY" and the loyalty points you earn for everything from your morning coffee to your hotel stays with inflation running hot. Many companies are making big changes. Tom Costello explains. (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) TOM COSTELLO, NBC NEWS CORRESPONDENT (voiceover): For Americans earning reward points for every gallon of gas, rental car, airline ticket, and cup of coffee, loyalty may not be worth what it once was, as companies rewrite their reward rules, often requiring more purchases, not fewer. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: I`m very disappointed in Dunkin. COSTELLO: Dunkin Donuts has faced a social media backlash after raising the cost of earning a free cup of coffee from $40 to $50 and doing away with free birthday drinks. There is drama in the Dunkin world right now tweeted one customer. I no longer run on Dunkin. But Dunkin says its revamped program gives customers more options and a wider variety of food and beverages. Chipotle is also requiring more purchases to earn a free burrito. P.F. Chang`s now offers extra reward points for a monthly fee. As inflation drives up restaurant costs, forcing many to trim expenses. R.J. HOTTOVY, HEAD OF FINANCIAL RESEARCH, PLACER.AI: We`ve seen from Chipotle. We`ve seen it from Dunkin. We`ve -- probably we`ll see it for many others before we`re all set and done. COSTELLO: For many customers, the points make the difference. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: Yes, big difference. They save -- they save a lot of people a lot of money. COSTELLO: Meanwhile, you can now earn a mile on Delta Airlines for each dollar you spend at Starbucks , just as Delta will require passengers to spend more on tickets to earn top tier status and free upgrades. The advice if you`ve been gathering points -- TED ROSSMAN, SENIOR INDUSTRY ANALYST, BANKRATE: You don`t want to hoard these just for hoarding sake. You want to earn and burn strategically. COSTELLO: Use them or lose them. Tom Costello, NBC News, Washington. (END VIDEOTAPE) HOLT: Up next, a terrifying scene. The deadly plane crash slamming into a car dealership. And the controversy over a drug meant to prevent premature births. Why the FDA wants to pull it. (COMMERCIAL BREAK) [19:20:00] HOLT: Fiery images out of Ohio today when a small plane crash into a car dealership parking lot in Marietta. Investigators say the pilot and a passenger were both killed when the plane went down about 30 minutes after takeoff from Columbus. No injuries were reported on the ground. Also, tonight, the battle over a controversial pregnancy drug. The FDA wants to take it off the market but some doctors and moms say it`s a lifesaver for babies born prematurely. We get more now from Ann Thompson. (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) ANNE THOMPSON, NBC NEWS CORRESPONDENT (voiceover): They are the littlest Americans. Nearly 400,000 children born prematurely each year, 10 percent of all births, 14 percent in the African American community. Tony Blake delivered her first two children at 28 and 32 weeks. TONY BLAKE, MOTHER OF PREMATURE BABIES: I didn`t want another kid in the NICU. Like you just don`t want that because you want to have that bonding time. THOMPSON: So, her doctor prescribed McKenna for her third pregnancy, a synthetic version of the hormone progesterone. She carried her daughter Rain to 33 weeks. BLAKE: It helped me to not actually go into labor. THOMPSON: Now the FDA wants to pull McKenna from the market saying trials show Tony story is the exception, not the rule. DR. PATRIZIA CAVAZZONI, DIRECTOR, FDA CENTER FOR DRUG EVALUATION AND RESEARCH: Based on the evidence available today, McKenna is not shown to be effective. Its benefit-risk profile is unfavorable, and it shouldn`t be withdrawn from the market. THOMPSON: Once fast track for approval, regulators say, along with no benefits, there are risks to mothers, including blood clots and depression. But Dr. Kristin Lyerly wants to keep prescribing McKenna to her patients. DR. KRISTIN LYERLY, OB/GYN: Why not leave it on the market while we are investigating further? Because the potential to reduce preterm birth has an incredible impact on patients and their families for their entire lives. THOMPSON: Especially, she says, for African American moms with higher rates of premature birth. Others disagree. Is there any evidence that African American women benefit from this drug? DR. MICHAEL CAROME , DIRECTOR, PUBLIC CITIZEN HEALTH RESEARCH GROUP: The available evidence based upon data reviewed by the FDA doesn`t support that the drug is effective for those patients. THOMPSON: McKenna`s manufacturer says the drug should be kept on the market while additional study is undertaken. The advisory committee will vote tomorrow, but the final decision is still months away. Anne Thompson, NBC News. (END VIDEOTAPE) HOLT: Up next, raising the profiles of women and minority scientists. Her mission to tell their stories. (COMMERCIAL BREAK) [19:25:00] HOLT: Millions turn to Wikipedia for answers but as Stephanie Gosk reports, when one physicist noted there were few entries on women and minorities in science, she got writing. (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) STEPHANIE GOSK, NBC NEWS CORRESPONDENT (voiceover): From the Boxer Rebellion to the history of the banana. Wikipedia has instant information on everything. At least that`s what British physicists Jess Wade believed until she noticed a gaping hole in the online encyclopedia`s content. JESS WADE, BRITISH PHYSICISTS: Women is so underrepresented, and people of color are so underrepresented. GOSK: And then, the 33-year-old got to work. How many entries do you have in Wikipedia? WADE: 1757 or 1756, but who`s counting? GOSK: She`s dedicated on top of a day job spent in the lab. WADE: I get home, I have my dinner, and I have my designated Wikipedia time where I just kind of research and then write and then read and then edit and then write some more. GOSK: Writing bios on women like Gladys West. WADE: She was born in Virginia in 1930. She went to a historically black College and university. She studied Math. She became a math teacher at high school and then she worked for the U.S. government on GPS. GOSK: Jess Wade plucked her story out of forgotten history, leading to West`s 2018 induction into the U.S. Air Force Hall of Fame. It`s nice to think that you were able to give her just a little bit of nudge. WADE: Like, I don`t -- I didn`t do anything, right? She`s the magic. I just -- I`m just that person who just kind of taps it closer to the goal line, and then she shoots, and she scores. GOSK: Wade says society is doing better getting young women interested in math and science but it`s not enough. WADE: We`re not doing enough to retain them in the system. And part of that is because we`re not celebrating them. GOSK: Now, with her help, everyone can type in a search and give a round of applause. Stephanie Goss, NBC News. (END VIDEOTAPE) HOLT: That`s NIGHTLY NEWS for this Tuesday. Thank you for watching. I`m Lester Holt. Please take care of yourself and each other. Good night. We`re so happy that you`re with us. GUTHRIE: Oh, yes, and burr, that cold snap affecting much of the country, we started talking about it yesterday. Well today, it`s here. KOTB: More specifically it is here. The snow really whipping up this morning in northern Michigan near the shores of Lake Superior and while it may not be snowing where you live, the chances are it is getting cold. GUTHRIE: Yes nearly 100 million Americans under frost and freeze warnings this morning with that winter like weather extending from Colorado all the way up and down the East Coast. So I had to go back to work last week. It works. It`s great. ROKER: You look rested. DALY: Well, yes, I had some time to sit around and do that. But it feels great. There`s a long road ahead -- JONES: I was just about to ask you, so what`s the prognosis? I mean, because before you were dealing with pain, and people didn`t realize it. DALY: Well, I hope I get a chance to do a story on it because what I realized now it`s like the iceberg effect. I mean, this is just a story about people who have back pain, and they how do you fix it? There`s a subtext underneath it all. It`s very complex that so many of us have to deal with. When you`re in pain, you`re looking to just feel good. And that changes your relationship with food and drink and your life. And then when they fix the pain, you`re left with these other complex areas of your life that you need to deal with and realign relationships with. So when I say I`m getting better, I`m getting better in a multitude of ways, which is great, which is really great. GUTHRIE: And one of the parts of your recovery is walking. So you`ve been doing this like long walk about it from your neighborhood. DALY: I`m the Forrest Gump of Long Island. It`s crazy. I walk -- I`m like, yes, you would be so proud now. Inspired but I would love that. ROKER: Let`s do that. And so how far -- how long before since it`s the Tiger Woods surgery, before you going to be going for the green jacket? DALY: So he says I can ship and put a 13 week so I`m still another six weeks out from that. And then I`ll probably get a condo in Alaska -- in Augusta, Georgia first, start visiting and then I`ll start, you know, getting to win master`s hopefully in maybe four years. GUTHRIE: Carson we have -- (CROSSTALK) DALY: It`s great to be back. Thanks for all the love and time. (CROSSTALK) DALY: All right, I have to do this again now. ROKER: Yes. DALY: PopStart still on. headline: Today for October 20, 2022, NBC
story_text: (COMMERCIAL BREAK) [07:00:16] SAVANNAH GUTHRIE, NBC NEWS ANCHOR: Good Thursday morning from Washington and New York. Our top story, all eyes once again on Ukraine. HODA KOTB, NBC NEWS ANCHOR: Tension there building after new attacks and new threats. It is October 20th. This is Today. Leave immediately, this morning, thousands of residents in southern Ukraine being forced to flee their own homes. Mass evacuations underway after a warning of imminent attacks and martial law declared by Vladimir Putin . And this morning, mounting concern over power outages ahead of a harsh winter, we`ll have the very latest and a live report straight ahead. On the road, President Biden hits the campaign trail today in the closely watched battleground of Pennsylvania. Can he move the needle for the undecided voters with less than three weeks to go? Feeling the freeze, another day of bitter cold across much of the country, parts of the south waking up two record lows, but Al says, hang in there, a big warm ups on the way. They`ll have your full forecast. Consumer alert, the new warning from police after a string of robberies in cities across the country tied to popular online marketplaces. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) CMDR. RODNEY G. HILL, CHICAGO POLICE DEPARTMENT ENGLEWOOD DISTRICT: Nine times out of 10, if you see a deal that is too good to be true, it is. (END VIDEO CLIP) KOTB: This morning what you need to know before you click. Those stories, plus, "The Crown" and the controversy. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) UNIDENTIFIED MALE: It is with regret, the Prince and Princess of Wales are separating. (END VIDEO CLIP) KOTB: The growing backlash against the hit show`s upcoming storyline. Why an Oscar winner wants it to come with a disclaimer and how "The Crown`s" creator is responding. And smash hit. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) UNIDENTIFIED MALE: At the wall looking up, see you later. (END VIDEO CLIP) KOTB: The Astros defeat the Yankees in game one of the ALCS while the Padres rally to tie up their series with the Phillies in a game for the record books. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) UNIDENTIFIED MALE: Aaron Nola against Austin Nola, little brother against big brother. (END VIDEO CLIP) KOTB: The battle of the brothers going down in history, today, Thursday, October 20th, 2022. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: From NBC News, this is Today with Savannah Guthrie live from Washington, D.C. and Hoda Kotb live from Studio 1A in Rockefeller Plaza. KOTB: Well good morning. Good to see you. So happy you`re joining us on a Thursday morning. Savannah is joining us in D.C. And SG, can you imagine being the mom and dad you`re like, I`m cheering for both my sons. You go, no you go. It`s got to be a tough one. GUTHRIE: I know. Yes, moms are always like, no, I don`t have a favorite. No really, I don`t. Well, a lot more of those highlights in just a bit. Plus nearly two thirds of the country waking up to another morning of bitter cold, I know you`re feeling it there in New York, here Washington too. Record low temps expected in the south today. Al is tracking it and he has some good news on when it`ll feel a little more like fall. KOTB: But we are going to start this morning in Ukraine where new evacuations are being ordered. It comes as residents are being told to charge their devices after drone strikes knocked out key power stations, rolling blackouts now common. And this is just as the brutal Ukraine winter is approaching. NBC`s Cal Perry is in Ukraine for us. Cal, good morning. Give us the latest. CAL PERRY, NBC NEWS CORRESPONDENT: Hey, good morning to you, Hoda. Fresh strikes overnight, the target once again that vital energy infrastructure of Ukraine. It is what has prompted the mayor here to tell people turn off your electricity, save power. All the while as you mentioned, the bitter cold from the winter has arrived, the temperatures plunging overnight, all the while the strikes continue across Ukrainian cities. (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) PERRY (voice-over): This morning, the people of Kherson are caught in the middle. Thousands in the port city that has been under Russian occupation for months, now being ordered to evacuate by Russian installed leaders. Some getting text messages that read, dear residents, evacuate immediately. There will be shelling of residential areas by the armed forces of Ukraine. The evacuations and apparent reaction to Ukraine`s counter offensive in the region, recapturing villages and farmland in recent weeks, Ukrainian officials accusing Russia of trying to create hysteria. It comes on the same day Russian`s President Putin declared martial law in the four Ukrainian regions currently occupied by Russia. I have signed a decree, he said, introducing martial law into these four entities of the Russian Federation. Under the order Russia can, it says, legally seize Ukrainian homes and property, move civilian populations and create local militias, meaning Moscow may try to force Ukrainians to fight against their own country. JOE BIDEN, PRESIDENT OF THE UNITED STATES: It seems his only tool available to him is to brutalize individual citizens in Ukraine. PERRY (voice-over): From Mykolaiv and the south to Kyiv and the north, the Russian bombardment continues. In just over a month, at least 239 drones have been shot down by air defenses, according to the Ukrainian military. The ones that make it past those air defenses are frequently striking infrastructure targets, 30 percent of power plants have been destroyed. [07:05:17] Other times, civilians pay the price. Here in the capital of Kyiv, eight dead in 24 hours, all the while the threat of a nuclear attack looms. Children drill in a nearby school here in Kyiv. And while bulletproof vests are necessary on the battle front, swim caps and goggles must do here on the home front. (END VIDEOTAPE) PERRY: Now Ukraine is asking countries around the world to help with its air defense system. Israel the latest to offer hands saying it will help provide that very important early alert system. But holding back on the ammunition needed to actually shoot down the drones. Officials here are hoping to get that from the United States. Hoda? KOTB: We`re counting those young kids with swim caps and goggles, it`s just -- it`s also unsettling. Thank you so much. We appreciate your report there. Let`s move on back here at home. We`ve got another morning of cold temperatures and a lot of the country, record setting in parts of the South. Let`s bring in Mr. Roker to get a first check of the forecast. Good morning, Al. AL ROKER, NBC NEWS ANCHOR: All right, good morning, Hoda. Good morning, everybody. The good news is if you are one of the 76 million people under these frost advisory, freeze warnings, we`ve got some relief coming for you, so hold on. For this morning though, Memphis 39 degrees, Tallahassee right now 32, Orlando 55 degrees, Norfolk 39. But we are going to see a little bit of a change. For today though, it is going to stay cold but we are going to see a little relief. But for today, about 12 degrees below average in Buffalo behind where the Jetstream dips to the south. We`re looking at Pier 75 degrees, that`s 15 degrees above normal, Boise, Idaho 77. For tomorrow, those temperatures still a little on the chilly side from New York, Charlotte on into Jacksonville. But the warmth is coming, Little Rock 81, San Antonio 86, Dallas, it`s going to be 88 degrees. And as we get into early next week, temperatures moderate, look at this, we`ll be in the 60s in New York right on into early next week, 70s in Raleigh and in Cincinnati, Chicago as well. And hot springs Arkansas into the 80s. We have that record warmth out west, record cold in the east. However, it`s because of this jet stream that`s really been amplified. The good news is if you`re here in the east, we`re going to see a flip, cooler air with rain and snow, which is good news for Seattle and Portland. They have right now the worst air quality in the world because of all the heat and the wildfires. They`re going to see temperatures drop 10 to 25 degrees below normal here in the East, much warmer as we get into next week with temperatures 10 to 20 degrees above normal. So Savannah, we`re all getting some good news back to you. GUTHRIE: All right, I like that Al. Thank you. Well, this morning, new data is out. And it reveals more about the effects of inflation on families all across this country, and the Federal Reserve`s efforts to get it under control. This is some top business leaders are voicing big concerns about the months ahead. NBC`s Tom Costello here with us in Washington tracking it again. Not good news that we`re hearing from business leaders. TOM COSTELLO, NBC NEWS CORRESPONDENT: Not good news. And we`ve been talking for months about persistent sky high inflation. And now, the head of one of the country`s biggest banks, Goldman Sachs is warning about a possible volatile period as we head into 2023. Listen, when Goldman talks, people listen, for the average family, there`s less concern right now about whether we are entering a recession or already there, but rather, when will things improve and how do we cope right now. (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) COSTELLO (voice-over): From Main Street, USA to Wall Street, Americans are still staring down red hot inflation that shows no signs of cooling off. Now some top executives are warning of potentially tough times in the months ahead. DAVID SOLOMON , GOLDMAN SACHS CEO: I think it`s a time to be cautious. That doesn`t mean for sure that we have a really difficult economic scenario. But in the distribution of outcomes, there`s good chance we could have a recession. COSTELLO (voice-over): And Amazon founder, Jeff Bezos , also issuing a warning earlier this week tweeting, the probabilities in this economy tell you to batten down the hatches. With less than three weeks before the midterm elections, President Biden denies that the move to continue tapping into the nation`s emergency oil supply is politically motivated, calling on oil companies to increase production and their refining operations. BIDEN: You still make a significant profit. Your shareholders will still do very well. And the American people catch a break they deserve and get a fair price at the pump as well. COSTELLO (voice-over): But gas is just one part of the global inflation picture. In the U.K. inflation is running even hotter, above 10 percent. Food up a staggering 14.6 percent while the average American family now spends nearly $450 more per month to buy the same goods as last year. The head of the country`s largest retailer, Walmart , tell Savannah it`s hitting people in different ways. [07:10:00] GUTHRIE: Do you feel like consumers are hitting that point where they`re done paying those high prices? JOHN FURNER , WALMART U.S. CEO: I think it depends on the personal situation that consumers are in, really different depending on where you are around the country. COSTELLO (voice-over): For Stephanie Lane`s (ph) family of six living off a single income in Pennsylvania, it`s meant cutting back across the board. STEPHANIE LANE (ph), PENNSYLVANIA RESIDENT: It`s a hard pill to swallow when you have to really change everything you`ve done. And do it everything differently because you can`t afford it. COSTELLO (voice-over): Despite the challenging times, Stephanie (ph) says she and her family are looking forward. LANE (ph): We don`t know when it`s going to get better. But I do know it will. I have faith that it will. (END VIDEOTAPE) GUTHRIE: Tom, we`ve been talking so much about the Fed`s interest rates hikes and how it`s going into effect. And sometimes it takes time to see if they`re working. We`re already seeing some leading indicators right now turning up and affect in the economy. COSTELLO: Last week, you and I talked about a lagging indicator. The unemployment rate is a lagging indicator of what the economy is like right now. We have a new leading indicator, this is concerning. New home building fell 8 percent last month, the lowest since the earliest days of the pandemic, that`s a concern. Mortgage rates, of course, now up to 7.2 percent on a 30 year, that`s double in a year. As a result, existing home sales, we expect are going to be sliding dramatically when we get that data in and price is expected to fall dramatically. All of that is not good for the economy. GUTHRIE: All right, Tom, thank you so much. And, of course, another big focus here in Washington, the midterm elections, which is 19 days to go. Early voting already underway, President Biden is hitting the campaign trail in the battleground of Pennsylvania today. And that brings us over here to Kristen Welker, who`s been covering politics, of course. Well, let`s start here with gas prices. We talked to Tom about the economy, gas prices, is a leading indicator, both economically and politically for the White House. KRISTEN WELKER, NBC NEWS CHIEF WHITE HOUSE CORRESPONDENT: That`s absolutely right. And there`s no doubt that there`s a lot of concern about gas prices, which have ticked up a bit over the past month. They`re down significantly, though, from their high in the summer over $5 a gallon. Yesterday, President Biden announced they`re releasing another 15 million barrels from the Strategic Petroleum Reserve. But look, this is really the tail end of an announcement that was made several months ago to release 180 million barrels. And Savannah, it`s not clear it`s going to have a big impact on gas prices. What it does is it allows the President to make the case that he is working on this issue, which 44 percent of Americans say is their top issue right now heading into these midterms. I talked to the White House Chief of Staff Ron Klain , what`s the first thing he does every morning? Check gas prices. And it underscores, Savannah, the fact that what happens in November could very much be determined by the price of the pump. GUTHRIE: Yes, because it`s something that absolutely everyone feels and it creates a ripple through the economy. Let`s talk about the issue of abortion. Democrats thought they had a lot of momentum with that issue right on the heels of the Dobbs decision in June. Now, it doesn`t seem that it`s having as much of a sway with independent voters. WELKER: That`s right. And you look at the swing that we`re seeing among independent women in particular, who said that they favored Democrats in September. Now, huge swing over to Republicans, you saw abortion as an energizing factor in races in Kansas in special election in New York in the primaries, but I think Democrats are concerned that they need to be having a broader appeal. You saw President Biden talking about the issue of abortion earlier this week. He said remember, basically the outrage that you felt on the day that Roe v. Wade was overturned, trying to turn back the clock in essence, Savannah, but there`s a real awareness and I think a message from the White House. Yes, we need to talk about abortion. But we need to talk about issues including the economy and crime that voters care about in this election cycle, too. So that`s why the President is going to be in Pennsylvania talking about infrastructure today, for example. GUTHRIE: Yes, the polls have shown that the Republicans appeared to have some momentum going into these midterms. The control of the Senate, control of the House is on the table, Pennsylvania, where the President will be today is a key Senate race and it`s tight. WELKER: It`s very tight. It`s basically a statistical dead heat, Savannah. And what`s notable about the President stop in Pennsylvania today, he`s going to be talking about infrastructure. And here you can see these polls between John Fetterman and Dr. Oz. He`s going to talk about infrastructure and then hold a fundraising event with John Fetterman . So not the typical rally that you would usually see a President hold in these closing weeks of a campaign. Why? Well, his approval ratings are low. And I think a lot of Democrats are concerned that he will hurt, he will hinder them instead of helping them. And so that`s why I think you`re not seeing these traditional rallies. But I spoke to an administration official who said, look, the bottom line is, we think it`s more effective to have him out talking about things like infrastructure, talking about things like abortion, gas prices, the things that he has worked on, instead of basically shouting at a crowd. They point to Obama, they point to Trump, they say, look, they had big losses in their midterms as well. So they don`t necessarily see that as an effective strategy. They`re also saying he will be holding typical events getting closer. GUTHRIE: All right, Kristen Welker here in Washington with me. Thank you so much. Hoda to 14 minutes after the hour, I`ll send it over to you. [07:15:01] KOTB: All right, thank you SG. Now to the rising health concern for families across the country just as flu season is getting underway, doctors are seeing an alarming rise in cases of RSV. Now that`s a common respiratory illness that`s left some children in need of hospitalization. So the surge, so severe one Children`s Hospital in Connecticut is now using temporary units to handle their patients and is considering asking for national help. So what is going on? What`s causing it? Why now? NBC News medical contributor Dr. Natalie Azar is here with everything we need to know. Well, first of all, that sounds scary what`s happening in Connecticut. Let`s break it down. Tell us about RSV. And why is it exploding in this moment? DR. NATALIE AZAR, NBC NEWS MEDICAL CONTRIBUTOR: Right, so Hoda, so RSV is a typical seasonal respiratory virus, right? It is, by the time children are two years old, most of them will have been infected with RSV. But it does and it can cause a close to 60,000 hospitalizations every year in children. And the majority of people, it causes a mild cold like illness. So we`re talking runny nose, a low grade fever, a cough, sneezing. KOTB: How long does it last? AZAR: Usually lasts about one to two weeks, sometimes the symptoms can peak at day five. KOTB: OK. AZAR: But in certain individuals, when it goes from the upper respiratory tract into the lungs, it can actually cause more severe disease. And I think it`s very important, especially for caregivers out there of young ones who can`t communicate, the symptoms of more severe disease would be things like poor feeding, irritability, wheezing, or shortness of breath. Those are the kinds of symptoms and signs that you`d want to reach out to your pediatrician immediately. KOTB: So sometimes you wouldn`t know if your child has a cold or has this but either way, like, how do you treat it? What do you suppose to give them? AZAR: Well, that`s the thing. And so you mentioned a very good point, it`s actually indistinguishable, you know, from cold or flu or things like a COVID, you would actually need to get tested. You have to get tested, though in the doctor`s office, there are no home tests for this. In terms of treatment for the majority of people, the treatment is supportive. So that means rehydrating, managing the airway. There is a treatment, however, for people who are at risk, and that group includes premature infants, kids under the age of six months, heart lung problems, weakened immune systems, older folks. It`s a monthly injection that can actually prevent severe disease. KOTB: Just a last quick thing. There was a headline in -- here in New York that said COVID cases in some pockets of New York were up 20 percent. Is that a bellwether? Are we expecting like this big bounce in numbers? AZAR: Right, Hoda. So we`re talking about new strains, and they are descendants of the Omicron strain. This is not unexpected. This is what we expect the virus to do. At this point, it doesn`t appear that it`s causing more severe disease. But remember, more infections could lead to more hospitalizations, and then the convergence of flu. We worry about hospital capacity and of course, cases of lung COVID. So we`re certainly keeping an eye on it. KOTB: And that 20 percent is pretty alarming even in -- AZAR: It`s a pretty significant doubling time. That`s what`s making experts concerned. KOTB: All right, Dr. Azar, thank you. We appreciate it. It is 17 minutes after the hour. Hello, Craig. CRAIG MELVIN, NBC NEWS ANCHOR: Hello, good morning, Hoda. Good morning Dr. Natalie as well and good morning to you. October best part of the year for baseball fans, major league baseball playoffs underway right now. The Houston Astros came out swinging in game one of the ALCS. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) UNIDENTIFIED MALE: Drive into right, well hit, Judge on the run, and Chas McCormick, opposite field home run. (END VIDEO CLIP) MELVIN: And there you have it. Chas McCormick with Houston second home run of the inning there, they would go on to beat the Yankees four to two. Game two is tonight. Over to the National League now, the San Diego Padres scoring five runs in the fifth inning to take the lead there. They would hold on to that lead to win it, eight to five. That series all tied up at one game apiece. There was some history made in that game as noted at the top of the show here, Phillies pitcher Aaron Nola is facing his brother Austin Nola, who is a catcher for San Diego. You see their parents looking on there to the farm, right. It`s the first time in MLB postseason history that a pitcher faced his brother at the plate. Austin Nola getting the big RBI single there. That was smart the Padres in the fifth inning. And I heard you and SG in the top of the show about which, you know, as a parent watch. KOTB: -- you do, you know, who -- MELVIN: I`ll tell you who`s the favorite child, it`s Austin, the oldest child is always the favorite. KOTB: But, you know, I was just -- I was thinking of Peyton and Eli Manning`s mom and dad. How many times have they watch their two kids and there were one point they were in the Super Bowl together. It`s like, oh my, oh my, oh my. GUTHRIE: And guys, I was like either they put the split screen up of the parents so it`s like the brothers and the parents have to keep the neutral face, like game face. Yes, we like everyone. KOTB: Look at them, I can`t the jerseys, I see a Phillies Jersey maybe the mom`s got a Padres on. MELVIN: But if you look at the Phillies jersey, it looks like he`s got a Padres jersey on underneath and a Padres hat. KOTB: OK. All right, fair enough. Let`s go guys, time for the weather. Mr. Rocker we`re talking about some brutal cold. [07:20:01] ROKER: Although, Craig, I hope Sibby is not watching. MELVIN: I hope she`s not either. That`s just -- ROKER: -- you said the older is the favorite. MELVIN: Not in my house. Not in my house. ROKER: Nice clarification. I`ll do what I can to help you. MELVIN: Thank you. Anyway, for today, we do have that fire risk continuing in the western plains. So we`re watching that sunny and warm out west. It`s going to be another gorgeous day. They do really need the rain. We`re going to look at that in the next half hour and easing chill coming into the East. So that`s good news there. We`re going to get to your local forecast in the next 30 seconds. (COMMERCIAL BREAK) (LOCAL NEWS) ROKER: And that`s your latest weather. You know it`s cold when we got the hand warmers out. KOTB: SG, I got hand warmers in here, girl. GUTHRIE: Oh my gosh. But you know who`s happy Craig Melvin, he likes it when that thermostat is breezing cold. KOTB: Exactly. MELVIN: Fall and winter in 1A. KOTB: All right, coming up, it`s a big hit. But Kelly Cobiella, we got some controversy surrounding the upcoming season of "The Crown ." Tell us about it. KELLY COBIELLA, NBC NEWS ANCHOR: That`s right, Hoda. In fact Oscar winner Dame Judi Dench is now joining a chorus of critics calling some depictions in the new season, cruelly unjust. We`ll take a look at what all the controversy is about and also what the show`s creator is saying coming up. GUTHRIE: Well, that`s a good one. We`ll find out about that. Also, guys, if you buy or sell stuff online don`t want to miss this story, especially as we`re heading into the holidays, the new warning about criminals using popular sites to find their next victims. We`re going to break down the red flags to look for and give you advice for staying safe. But first, this is Today on NBC. (COMMERCIAL BREAK) MELVIN: Still ahead, the inspiring high school football player making sports history with her touchdown. [07:24:41] KOTB: Indeed. But first, your local news. (COMMERCIAL BREAK) (LOCAL NEWS) (COMMERCIAL BREAK) (LOCAL NEWS) (COMMERCIAL BREAK) (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) [07:30:18] UNIDENTIFIED MALE: Let`s please welcome the 2022 Caregiver Champion, it is not a better word to describe her, Savannah Guthrie. GUTHRIE: Thank you hidden heroes for this beautiful honor. And thank you most of all to caregivers for the privilege of knowing you. (END VIDEO CLIP) KOTB: We are back. Boy, that was beautiful. I have even seen the whole speech and I`m in. This is the reason Savannah is in D.C. She was honored with this year`s Caregiver Champion Award. And as Tom Hanks said, there`s no better descriptor than that. That was at the Elizabeth Dole Foundation`s heroes and history makers gala. Savannah, what a night, man, I mean, that looks beautiful. We`re so proud of you. GUTHRIE: Well, it was so cool. I mean, the caregivers were out in force. They just -- it was their special night. And I think we raised a lot of money for a really great cause. Senator Elizabeth Dole was there. This is her mission that she started 10 years ago. And coming up, we`re going to introduce you to the very first, so I call her the original kind of the OG caregiver that met Mrs. Dole in the hospital at Walter Reed 11 years ago and told the story of her experience. And boy that got Mrs. Dole on a mission and that mission is going strong. We`ll have more on that coming up. MELVIN: Maybe become such an important part of that mission, so more on that coming up in just a few minutes put. But right now, a check of your 7:30 headlines on this Thursday morning. Former President Donald Trump answering questions under oath yesterday in a defamation lawsuit that was brought by a writer who claims that Trump raped her in the mid-1990s, the deposition gave E. Jean Carroll`s lawyers a chance to interrogate Trump about the assault allegations, as well as statements he made in 2019 when she told her story publicly for the first time, Trump has called Carroll`s allegation quote, a hoax and a lie. KOTB: Less than three weeks after Hurricane Ian destroyed Florida Sanibel Island causeway, the bridge reopened yesterday. It was initially scheduled to reopen at the end of this month but crews worked around the clock to get the repairs done ahead of schedule. That entire road was completely washed out by floodwaters late last month. Crews used more than 8,000 loads of dirt, 2,400 loads of rock, and 4,000 tons of asphalt to finish those temporary repairs. KOTB: Wow, incredible. All right, in New York City tradition getting ready to make its return. Oh yes, the Radio City Rockettes, they`re busy gearing up for the Christmas Spectacular. This year, the show is promising new songs, new dances, new costumes, new everything and with all the old traditions, the Radio City Christmas Spectacular runs November 18th through January 2nd, it`s always on our list of things we do every single year. GUTHRIE: And I was enjoyed it when they come to the plaza as well to give us a little preview. Now to one of the most popular shows on Netflix and the growing controversy around it, Savannah, we`re talking about that Emmy winning drama "The Crown ." GUTHRIE: Yes, we all love it. Fans go crazy for waiting for next season. But this morning some prominent figures from the worlds of politics and Hollywood are publicly criticizing the series for how it depicts the royal family this season. NBC`s Kelly Cobiella is at Buckingham Palace with more on that. Kelly this got a lot of eyebrows raised. COBIELLA: It does. And you know this has come up in the past and Adam -- and Netflix has always been adamant that this show is fictitious but as they deal with more recent history, controversial times in the royal family like the marriage and divorce of Charles and Diana, some are saying it just hits too close to home for an already grieving royal family.
