headline: Meet the Press for October 23, 2022, NBC
story_text: (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) [09:00:19] CHUCK TODD, HOST, NBC`S "MEET THE PRESS WITH CHUCK TODD": This Sunday, polarized and energized. PRESIDENT JOSEPH R. BIDEN, JR.: The election is not a referendum; it`s a choice. TODD: Sixteen days until Election Day. Our new NBC News poll reveals voter interest is at an all-time high, with the potential for record turnout. REP. KEVIN MCCARTHY, HOUSE MINORITY LEADER & (R) CALIFORNIA: I want this election to be about ideas. TODD: But both sides now see the opposing party as a threat to America as we know it. FORMER VICE PRESIDENT MIKE PENCE: The American people are going to grab the reins back. FORMER PRESIDENT BARACK OBAMA: Don`t sit this election out. TODD: Majorities of Americans are worried about the economy and believe the country is heading on the wrong track. While GOP enthusiasm is growing, voters are evenly split on which party should control Congress. Plus, ordered to testify, the January 6th Committee officially issues a subpoena for former President Trump to testify, as his former advisor Steve Bannon is sentenced to prison for defying a January 6th subpoena. (UNKNOWN): Lock him up! Traitor! TODD: My exclusive guest this morning, Republican congresswoman Liz Cheney of Wyoming, vice chair of the January 6th Committee. REP. LIZ CHENEY , VICE CHAIR OF THE U.S. HOUSE SELECT COMMITTEE ON THE JANUARY 6 ATTACK & (R) WYOMING: The solution for conservatives cannot be that we`re going to torch the Constitution. TODD: I`ll ask her about the direction of the Republican Party, growing threats to the democracy and her own political future. Joining me for insight and analysis are NBC News chief White House correspondent Kristen Welker; Washington Post senior national political correspondent Ashley Parker; Democratic pollster Cornell Belcher; and Danielle Pletka of the American Enterprise Institute . Welcome to Sunday. It`s "Meet the Press." ANNOUNCER: From NBC News in Washington, the longest-running show in television history, this is "Meet the Press" with Chuck Todd. TODD: A good Sunday morning. Just 16 days until elections. Seven million Americans have already voted, and we have some brand-new NBC poll numbers to share with you that indicate interest in this election is at an all-time high. Look at this. We record 70 percent of voters saying that interest in this election`s a 9 or 10. That is higher than 18, higher than 14, higher than 10. And what`s significant about 2018? That was the highest midterm turnout in 100 years. This indicates we`re going to be even higher than that. Overall, the battle for congressional control, it`s a dead-even 47-46. But if you go under the hood of our poll, this brand-new poll, you will see that, among likely voters, Republicans have an advantage. And among the final group of persuadable voters, Republicans have the advantage. That is why it feels as if the wind has shifted a little bit here. We asked them, "What message would you send with your vote to Congress?" Democrats, the number one message clearly is "Protect women`s rights." It goes along with all of those abortion rights ads we`ve been seeing among Democratic candidates. When you ask Republicans what message would they send, it`s a bit mixed, quite a few of them. One that does stand out, though, is "Fix the economy/ reduce the cost of living," on that front. Now, presidential job approval is one of those numbers that seems to be indicative of which way the wind is blowing. So President Biden sits at 45 percent. Where does that stand contextually? It`s two points lower than Barack Obama in 2010. It`s two points lower than Donald Trump in 2018. Both were wave elections against the party in the White House. Digging deeper here, we`ve got some all-time midterm highs that should serve as red flags for the Democrats. "The wrong track," 71 percent, all- time midterm high since we`ve been polling. How about presidential disapproval on the economy? Sitting at 57 percent. Again, we hadn`t recorded that ever that high in our poll. And the third one, the direction of the economy, in the next year is it going to get better or worse? Fifty percent say it`s going to get worse. Again, an all- time high in midterm polling. Going further here, this interest in the election. We told you, it`s high on both sides. This 69 percent number for Democrats is astonishing. It`s 78 percent among Republicans. That is an extra-astonishing number, if you will. And the big gap here? African-American interest among Democrats, this is why you`re going to see a lot of Barack Obama in the next two weeks. If the Democrats don`t get interest in the election up among African-Americans, they`re going to have some problems, particularly in some of those key Senate races. There is one lone bright spot here for Democrats. Biden is seen as a bit more -- his agenda a bit more agreeable than Trump`s, though everybody is negative here. Do you agree with Joe Biden most of the time, 45 percent, mirrors his job rating; 50 percent disagree with his agenda most of the time. How about Donald Trump ? Thirty-six percent agree; 56 percent disagree most of the time. If you want to call that a bright spot, there is one there for the Democrats. Here`s another one here. Most important issue facing this country, number one, for the second poll out of three, threats to democracy. [09:05:02] Number two and three are both economic-related, jobs and the economy and cost of living, but this issue of threats to democracy rose to number one this summer after the start of the January 6th hearings. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) CHENEY: Our institutions only hold when men and women of good faith make them hold, regardless of the political cost. We have no guarantee that these men and women will be in place next time. Any future president inclined to attempt what Donald Trump did in 2020 has now learned not to install people who could stand in the way. (END VIDEO CLIP) TODD: And joining me now is Republican Congresswoman Liz Cheney of Wyoming, vice chair of the Select Committee investigating January 6. Welcome back to "Meet the Press." CHENEY: Great to be back with you, Chuck. TODD: I don`t want to presume anything, but is your number one issue threats to democracy, as a voter? CHENEY: It is. I think that, when you look at the extent to which we`re facing challenges now that threaten to unravel the fundamental institutions and structures of our election system and process, that -- that is the basis and the foundation on which we can have all of these other debates. So it absolutely is the number one issue. TODD: On the Wyoming ballot, we know of at least two election deniers, the woman that defeated you in the primary, and the -- a gentleman by the name of Chuck Gray, running for secretary of state. I assume they did not earn your vote? CHENEY: No, they will not. And I think no one of any party should be voting for people who are election deniers. And I think we have to be clear what it means to be an election denier. It means, in the case, for example, of Kari Lake and Mark Finchem in Arizona, they have both said, "We`ve looked at all of the facts; we`ve looked at the results of the election in 2020; we`ve looked at the law; we`ve looked at the fact that these -- the courts all ruled against Donald Trump ; we`ve looked at the audits and the recounts; we are willing to ignore all of that, and we are saying we would not have certified that election." They`re telling you that they`ll only certify an election they agree with. And that -- that -- there`s not much graver threat to the democracy that you can imagine than that. TODD: I want to play for you something. You brought up Kari Lake. I want to play for you, Virginia Governor Glenn Youngkin was campaigning with her. He was specifically asked by my colleague Garrett Haake about your critique of Republicans that were campaigning with Kari Lake. Here was his response. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) GOV. GLENN YOUNGKIN, (R) VIRGINIA: I believe that every state deserves a Republican governor, and Arizona deserves another Republican governor. (END VIDEO CLIP) TODD: A lot of Republicans in the last three weeks, that I would describe as empathetic to what you`ve been doing, have suddenly found themselves deciding, "Hey, party over country." What do you make of those decisions? CHENEY: You know, I think they -- they are really indefensible decisions. And, you know, I`ve said I think that Glenn Youngkin has done a good job as governor of Virginia, but nobody should be out advocating for the election of people who will not honor the sanctity of our elections process. And, you know, people who do that are in fact putting politics ahead of the Constitution and ahead of the country. TODD: I`ve noticed Dan Cox is the Republican nominee in Maryland. It`s been pretty easy for Republicans to ignore him. It seems like it`s been harder for them to ignore Kari Lake in Arizona, a battleground state, even -- you`ve seen some even campaign with Doug Mastriano in Pennsylvania. It - - this -- this "Win it, whatever it takes to win, winning trumps everything," how do you -- how do you blow that up in the party? CHENEY: Well, I think you`ve got to remind people that everybody has an obligation -- an obligation to defend the Constitution, an obligation to do what`s right. And so right now you`ve got a lot of Republicans, in particular -- Democrats do the same thing; it just happens that our candidates are more dangerous right now. But you have got a lot of Republicans who are saying, "You know what? It just -- I`m going to ignore the threat posed by a former president who attempted to use force to stop -- to overturn an election, to stop the count of electoral votes; I`m going to ignore that; I`m going to ignore these people who embrace him; I`m going to ignore the danger and I`m just going to focus on the near term, is the Republican Party going to prevail?" TODD: Why do you think more Republicans can`t -- look, I just came back from Georgia. Brad Raffensperger , the secretary of state; Brian Kemp , the governor, both beat back Trump challenges. Now, they didn`t use anti-Trump rhetoric to do it, but they won. And they look like they`re pretty -- they`re going to be in better shape. Why do you think other Republicans can`t look at that and say, "Oh, it`s good politics, not bad politics?" CHENEY: You know, I -- my hope is that ultimately our party will come back to that. I think it may take a couple of election cycles to do that. But I think, you know, people need to understand they`re not bystanders. They`re accountable for their actions. The people who are excusing and appeasing and enabling are also responsible for the -- the impact of that. And -- and words matter. And when you support and endorse somebody who`s said that they only will honor results if they win, then you are responsible and accountable for that. TODD: Well, somebody who has been walking this line has been Mitch McConnell . On one hand, I think on Trump, you and him see eye to eye on some things, the danger of Trump and all of this. But I want to bring up an excerpt in a book that Jonathan Martin and Alex Burns wrote. [09:10:03] And that -- this is about McConnell. "McConnell found the whole Liz Cheney saga confusing. In his mind, she was committing a cardinal sin, relinquishing power. Why, he wondered aloud, would Cheney willingly jeopardize her leadership post by continually condemning Trump? "Just ignore him like I do," he said. What`s your response to McConnell? And I think you`ve probably had this conversation. CHENEY: Yeah, look, I think, obviously, the idea that we could simply ignore Donald Trump and the threat would go away is clearly wrong. And I think that, you know, Leader McConnell and Leader McCarthy obviously have taken slightly different approaches to Donald Trump . Leader McCarthy is embracing him; Leader McConnell has thought we can ignore him and -- and go forward as a party without him continuing to have power and authority. That`s clearly not the case. And my view from the beginning has been, you know, we have to, as a party, reject insurrection; we have to reject what he stands for. I don`t think this is an issue about which you can make a political calculation. I think it matters too much. So, clearly, you know, Leader McConnell and I do not see eye to eye on this. TODD: He had a -- he had a chance to vote to convict Donald Trump . Do you think -- how much of a mistake do you think that vote -- his decision not to vote to convict was? CHENEY: Well, I think that it was a mistake. I think it was the wrong decision. I think, you know, the fact that -- that all of the Republicans who did not vote to convict -- some did, but not enough -- you know, we were in a situation where I would have liked to have seen that trial take place immediately. I don`t think that the article of impeachment should have been held. I think there were a number of people responsible for the delay in that trial, but that was a mistake. And I think clearly this was an impeachable offense for which Donald Trump should have been convicted. TODD: Has it made you think less of McConnell? CHENEY: I -- I don`t -- he and I do not agree on this issue, and I -- I would not like to characterize it beyond that. TODD: All right. Let`s talk about a Speaker Kevin McCarthy. You clearly think this is a mistake, that he will -- you are concerned about his speakership. What specifically concerns you? CHENEY: Well, look, the speaker is second in line to the presidency. And at every moment since, frankly, the aftermath of the election in 2020, when Minority Leader McCarthy has had the opportunity to do the right thing or do something that serves his own political purpose, he always chooses to serve his own political purpose. And, you know, that extends to what we`ve seen just in the last few days with this comments about aid to Ukraine, the idea that somehow the party is now no longer going to support the Ukrainian people, which, you know, for somebody who has a picture of Ronald Reagan on the wall of his office in the Capitol, the notion that now Kevin McCarthy is going to make himself the leader of the pro-Putin wing of my party is just a stunning thing. It`s dangerous. He knows better. But the fact that he`s willing to go down the path of suggesting that America will no longer stand for freedom, I think, tells you he`s willing to sacrifice everything for his own political gain. TODD: Do you think at all this is just gamesmanship; he just wants the Democrats to do it in the lame duck, or do you think this is a reflection of an isolationalist streak that`s actually taking hold inside the Republican Party? CHENEY: We certainly have isolationists inside our party. We have isolationists inside the Democratic Party as well. But -- but leaders have to lead. And when you have the leader of the Republican Party suggesting that -- that we can play with the fire of isolationism, suggesting that somehow the American people will not support the fight for freedom, which is the front lines of freedom, right now, happening in Ukraine, the battle between Putin and Zelensky, and the notion that he would be willing to embrace that, to enable it, tells you he`s just not fit for the office. TODD: I want to ask you a little bit more about what`s going on. We have Iran now on the ground in Ukraine helping the Russians. CHENEY: Yeah. TODD: At the same time, Iran sits on OPEC. Our supposed ally, Saudi Arabia, who doesn`t like Iran, is sitting here making decisions that essentially are helping the Russians, helping the Iranians, hurting the West. What kind of -- what should our foreign policy be to Saudi Arabia right now, consider the current circumstances? CHENEY: Well, look, I think, first of all, we ought to absolutely and clearly walk away from the negotiating table with the Iranians. The notion that the Iranians have -- are now providing these drones to the Russians to use in Ukraine, if nothing else, has convinced us yet to walk away from the table, that should. It also tells us the Russians are having a hard time replenishing their supplies. And so the sanctions are working. We ought to do more. We ought to do more with respect to sanctions against Iran. But across the board, you know, I think that there -- there are too many people around the world who no longer think that they can count on the United States; they no longer think that they can trust us, that we`ll stand with our friends and that we will ensure that we`re standing against our adversaries. TODD: I hear you. The Middle East, though, is really -- it looks problematic from a U.S. -- when some of our closest allies are, kind of, neutral in this war, right? CHENEY: Yeah. [09:15:07] TODD: Israel has been, sort of, neutral, kind of, helping late, obviously Saudi Arabia. How much of a problem do you view this? CHENEY: Well, it`s a big problem, and I think it`s a problem of American leadership. We need to be doing more, faster, in terms of what we`re providing to the Ukrainians. We need to be very clear -- you know, when Kevin McCarthy suggests that the Republicans are not going to support aid to Ukraine, that is incredibly damaging to America`s standing in the world. It`s damaging to the effort that the Ukrainians are engaged in. We need to demonstrate that the United States of America recognizes we have to be a leader in the world. We`re not going to go back to the days of isolationism, which has been a threat in this country, you know, ever since the end of World War II. TODD: Before we go -- on the other side of the break, we`re going to go deep into January 6th and your investigation. But I`m curious. For four years you publicly were supportive of the Trump administration. You were never a big Trump fan. That was pretty clear. And you would disagree with him on things when you thought it was time. But you voted with him 93 percent of the time. Do you look back and think of any moment, and think, "Boy, maybe I should have spoke out sooner, maybe I should have confronted him sooner?" CHENEY: At the time, I was confronting him on the policies when I disagreed with him. They tended to be mostly national security policies. TODD: Right. CHENEY: I`m a conservative. As you said, I voted with him 93 percent of the time. But I think that there`s no question that his election as president in 2016 began something that`s been very dangerous for this nation. And we now see he`s willing to do everything he needs to do, everything within his power, to stop a peaceful transition of power. And he can never be president again. TODD: All right. Let me pause our conversation here. When we come back, we`re going to go deeper into the January 6th Committee, which officially issued a subpoena of the former president to testify and hand over documents. Why did they wait until now? We`ll have more with the congresswoman, after this break. (COMMERCIAL BREAK) TODD: Welcome back. On Friday Donald Trump was officially subpoenaed by the January 6th Committee, ordered to turn over documents related to the insurrection by November 4th. And he`s ordered to appear before the panel by November 14th. All this came just hours after Steve Bannon , the president`s former adviser, was sentenced to four months in prison for contempt of Congress, for disobeying a similar subpoena. The sentence was stayed, pending appeal. The congresswoman is back. So let me start with the subpoena. I`ve got to start with Steve Bannon first. You both successfully showed that your subpoenas were enforceable. He`s going to serve time. But he`s still not going to turn over documents, is he? CHENEY: Well, I think Steve Bannon is one of a number of individuals who clearly have something to hide. You know, he actually, as you`ve seen, was convicted of contempt and has been sentenced to -- to prison. Others have come in front of the committee and taken the fifth. And I think it leads the American people to ask, "What is it all of these people, including Donald Trump , are attempting to hide about January 6?" [09:20:07] TODD: You`ve issued the subpoena. And I -- I assume you -- you`re going to let it play out. So what happens on November 5th if you don`t have any materials? headline: Missed Cases Of Breast Cancer: The Detection Delayed In Dozens Of Patients And The Hospital At The Center Of The Controversy
story_text: [19:15:00] LESTER HOLT: There`s no question that mammograms save lives were the early detection of breast cancer, but a review of cases at one hospital showed many cancers were initially missed even though they appeared on the scans. Kristen Dahlgren has our investigation. (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) KRISTEN DAHLGREN, NBC NEWS CORRESPONDENT (voiceover): Jim and Pat Ratliff had a 54-year love story. JIM RATLIFF, WIFE HAD BREAST CANCER: We were attached at the hip. DAHLGREN: Through ups and downs, including Pat`s breast cancer more than a decade ago, which is why she was so diligent about screening and concern when she noticed changes in her other breast. She had imaging at a nearby hospital, part of NIH Northern Arizona Health Care. And they told her what? RATLIFF: They couldn`t find anything. DAHLGREN: Eventually, Pat saw breast surgeon Beth DuPree. DR. BETH DUPREE, BREAST SURGEON: I literally couldn`t believe what I was seeing. It was screaming cancer. DAHLGREN: Advanced breast cancer. Two years later, Pat was gone. Dr. DuPree had just moved to Sedona to develop a state-of-the-art Breast Center at NIH . Pat was just the first patient she says who came to her with a cancer missed on previous scan. DUPREE: These were misses that are not subtle. DAHLGREN: The hospital has an exclusive contract with Northern Arizona Radiology. DuPree who says she continued to flag misread mammograms push them to hire dedicated breast imagers, including Mike Ulissey who couldn`t believe some of what he says was missed. MIKE ULISSEY, BREAST IMAGER: I said my god, Beth. That`s the size of a tangerine. I don`t understand how they can call it normal. DAHLGREN: The hospital requested the radiology group have those new breast imagers review more than 6000 patients whose scans had initially been read by a particular general radiologist. Ulissey says they found cancer in an additional 25 women. CHRISTIE GALLO, HAD BREAST CANCER: The recommendation was returned to me here. DAHLGREN: Among them Christie Gallo (PH). GALLO: My question was, how can I go from normal to having three tumors in one year? That didn`t make sense to me. DAHLGREN: Dr. DuPree believes the number of patients with missed cancers was much greater than the 25 detected in the review. She made a poster with all of her patients whose diagnoses she says were delayed, hoping to show it to the hospital board. We`re only showing those who gave us permission. It must be hard to look at their faces. DUPREE: It is. DAHLGREN: NBC News obtained an email from one of the breast imagers to the radiology group sent before the review was complete, warning of the gravity of the situation. After the review, there was still concern. ULISSEY: We thought that there were a significant chance that additional patients were in harm`s way. We need to expand our investigation. DAHLGREN: But Dr. Ulissey says the radiology group did not. In his statement to NBC, NIH points out the radiology group is a separate entity and says in part, "The hospital quickly acted to address these concerns. We ensured these mammograms were reread specifically by a team of breast fellowship-trained radiologists, saying very few required any follow-up. And since this review, all mammograms are read by specialized breast radiologists." The hospital`s Chief Counsel spoke on a Zoom with community advisors. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: So, the quality process works. There was an error. We`re humans. Doctors are human. GALLO: They messed up and they don`t want to fess up to it. DAHLGREN: Northern Arizona radiology called the review results well within national standards. In a statement, it says, "All radiologists are board certified and meet all requirements, including those under the Mammography Quality Standards Act. DuPree and three out of four new breast imagers including Dr. Ulissey have now left. NBC News has learned the general radiologist who was the subject of the review is now working in another state. As for Gallo, her cancer is in remission, but she`s not sure the questions will ever go away. GALLO: Maybe if they had caught it sooner, it could have been a just a lumpectomy instead of a whole mastectomy choice, but I didn`t get that choice. DAHLGREN: Kristen Dahlgren, NBC News, Sedona, Arizona. (END VIDEOTAPE) HOLT: And up next for us, late news about today`s earthquake in California. headline: NBC NIGHTLY NEWS for October 25, 2022, NBC
story_text: [19:00:00] (COMMERCIAL BREAK) LESTER HOLT, NBC NEWS ANCHOR (on camera): Tonight, the chilling new details of the deadly shooting at a St. Louis High School. (voiceover): Investigators revealing today the 19-year-old gunman had an AR-15-style rifle and 600 rounds of ammunition. That disturbing handwritten note he left behind. What we`re learning about the victims, the stories of survival, and what police a prevented even more bloodshed. Also, tonight the spike in children hospitalized with RSV as flu season ramps up and President Biden getting his Omicron booster. His warning to Americans ahead of another potential winter COVID surge. WNBA star Brittney Griner losing her appeal in a Russian court. Where does that leave negotiations for a prisoner swap? What the White House is saying? Just two weeks until the Midterms and the high stakes showdown tonight in Pennsylvania. Democrat John Fetterman and Republican Dr. Mehmet Oz facing off in their first and only debate with control of the Senate on the line. Adidas dropping its deal with Kanye West after his antisemitic comments caused a firestorm. NBC News investigates the breast cancer diagnoses missed in more than two dozen women. How did it happen? And the mission to rescue tourists stranded in the Grand Canyon Caverns 200 feet underground. ANNOUNCER: This is NBC NIGHTLY NEWS with Lester Holt. HOLT (on camera): Good evening. We will never know exactly how much higher the death toll would have been in yesterday`s school shooting in St. Louis had police not killed the attacker. But today, there is chilling new evidence the 19-year-old killer intended it to be a bloodbath. Today, police revealing the gunman used an AR-15-style rifle to shoot his victims. A teacher and a student were both killed, four others were wounded. In addition, three people were injured during the chaos at Central Visual and Performing Arts High School. Authorities also saying the shooter, a former student, was carrying 600 rounds of ammunition. But the most revealing evidence may be what police say they found in his car, entries in a notebook that may offer a disturbing roadmap into his state of mind. Emilie Ikeda is in St. Louis tonight with new details. (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) EMILIE IKEDA, NBC NEWS CORRESPONDENT (voiceover): Tonight, a trove of evidence shedding light on what may have driven a 19-year-old to storm his alma mater, gunning down a sophomore and teacher and injuring at least seven. LOUIS METROPOLITAN POLICE DEPARTMENT: He spoke about his desire to engage in this incident to conduct the school shooting. IKEDA: The handwritten note reads in part, "I don`t have any friends. I don`t have any family. I`ve never had a girlfriend. I`ve never had a social life. I`ve been an isolated loner my entire life. This was the perfect storm for a mass shooter." A mass shooter that claimed the lives of beloved health and physical education teacher Jean Kuczka and sophomore Alexandria Bell. The student`s father calling her death a nightmare. ANDRE BELL, FATHER OF ALEXANDRIA BELL: No matter how I felt, I can talk to her and it was -- it was alright. That was my baby. IKEDA: Armed with an AR 15 style weapon and 600 rounds of ammunition, police say the suspect Orlando Harris` shooting rampage could have been even worse. SACK: Oh, this could have been a horrific scene. It was not by the grace of God and that the officers were as close as they were. IKEDA: Officers who already happened to be in the area for another event, said they arrived on scene within five minutes of the first 911 call, and made it to the government on the third floor within another eight minutes. The suspect shot dead. Police would not say how the team broke into the school or obtained a long gun plus a stockpile of ammunition. When you got there, what did you see? MICHAEL BISHOP, STUDENT PARENT: It was chaos. IKEDA: Student parent Michael Bishop applauds the police`s rapid response, but knows the trauma will follow his daughter and her classmates. BISHOP: She`s going to second guess going into any school, any building with people for who knows how long and it`s heartbreaking. (END VIDEOTAPE) HOLT: Emilie, there`s going to be a lot of looking back at this point. Were there any red flags in the gunman`s history? IKEDA (on camera): Lester, police say the suspect did not have a criminal history but may have been suffering from a mental illness. Law enforcement underscoring the importance of see something, say something, encouraging people to speak up if someone makes concerning comments or is struggling. Tonight, a community still in shock as school officials say that it may be weeks before students can return for in person instruction here. Lester? HOLT: OK, Emilie, thank you. headline: Herschel Walker Facing A New Allegation Of Paying For An Abortion Of A GOP Senate Candidate Is Responding Tonight
story_text: LESTER HOLT: Let me turn now to Kristen. Kristen, there`s a new headline in that tight Georgia Senate race, an anonymous allegation against Herschel Walker . What do we know? KRISTEN WELKER, NBC NEWS CHIEF WHITE HOUSE CORRESPONDENT (on camera): Lester, that`s right. This latest allegation comes from an anonymous woman who spoke on Zoom without showing her face in a press conference arranged by Attorney Gloria Allred, an allegation Herschel Walker is strongly denying tonight. Now, the woman claims she had an affair with Walker, the football star turned Republican Senate candidate, and got pregnant nearly 30 years ago. Now, Walker fired back today calling the claims foolishness and a lie, saying his Democratic opponent Senator Raphael Warnock "lost the debate and Democrats will now say anything to win." headline: The Fallout From A High Stakes Showdown In Pennsylvania With Control Of Congress Hanging In The Ballots
story_text: [19:00:00] LESTER HOLT, NBC NEWS ANCHOR (on camera): Tonight, the fallout from a high stakes showdown in Pennsylvania with control of Congress hanging in the ballots. (voiceover): Democrat John Fetterman and Republican Dr. Mehmet Oz facing off in their first and only debate. Fetterman`s health struggles in the spotlight months after he suffered a stroke. Oz under scrutiny for an answer he gave on abortion. The reaction from voters just 13 days before the Midterms. Also, tonight, Herschel Walker facing a new allegation of paying for an abortion of a GOP Senate candidate is responding tonight. The verdict in the trial of a Wisconsin man who killed six people when he plowed his SUV into a Christmas parade. The deadly school shooting in St. Louis. The warning the shooters family gave to police and they`re pleas to take a gun away from him months before the rampage. Vladimir Putin overseeing nuclear drills as Russia pushes unproven dirty bomb allegations against Ukraine. And the American fighter killed in Ukraine two months ago finally on his way back home. Hospitals filling up with children infected with RSV. What parents need to know. The critical shortage in a medication millions used to treat ADHD. And he went from homeless to shooting college hoops. The basketball star inspiring America. ANNOUNCER: This is NBC NIGHTLY NEWS with Lester Holt. HOLT (on camera): Good evening. Just 13 days before the Midterm Elections, and a flood of political ads are saturating the airwaves on the heels of another marquee debate reminding just what is at stake in hard-fought congressional races, power and control of Congress. In the House, Democrats trying to defend their majority with all 435 seats of the body up for election. Dems facing the same challenge in the U.S. Senate with 35 seats are up for election. The balance of power in the Senate could be determined by a handful of tight races, including Pennsylvania where last night`s debate pitted Republican Mehmet Oz against Democrat John Fetterman sparring over abortion, fracking, and immigration. But not before Fetterman call out what he described as the elephant in the room, his health. Dasha Burns starts us off tonight with the latest. (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) DASHA BURNS, NBC NEWS CORRESPONDENT (voiceover): Tonight, Pennsylvania Republican Dr. Mehmet Oz back on the campaign trail following last night`s critical one and only face-off. MEHMET OZ (R-PA), SENATE CANDIDATE: Pennsylvania deserves better than Fetterman. BURNS: His opponent, Democrat John Fetterman , not yet making any public appearances after the fierce clash. JOHN FETTERMAN (D-PA), SENATE CANDIDATE: It`s something called the Oz rule that if he`s on TV, he`s lying. OZ: And this is the only debate I could get you to come to talk to me on and I had to beg. BURNS: A debate the Fetterman`s health front and center. Fetterman whose campaign says suffers from auditory processing challenges after a stroke six months ago, requesting these closed captioning monitors in the studio. FETTERMAN: I had a stroke. He`s never let me forget that. And I might miss some words during this debate. Mush two words together, but it knocked me down, but I`m going to keep coming back up. BURNS: Fetterman did miss some words during the hour-long showdown, at times of struggling to answer questions, including this moment. Fetterman was asked about his changing position on fracking, which he now says he supports. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: There is that 2018 interview that you said, "I don`t support fracking at all." So, how do you square the two? FETTERMAN: I do support fracking. And I don`t --I don`t -- I support fracking and I stand -- and I do support fracking. BURNS: Fetterman would not commit to releasing his full medical records. FETTERMAN: My doctor believes that I`m fit to be serving, and that`s what I believe is where I`m standing. BURNS: And in one of the biggest clashes of the night going after Dr. Oz on abortion rights. FETTERMAN: He celebrated when Roe v. Wade went down and my campaign would fight for Roe v. Wade, and if given the opportunity, to codify it into law. BURNS: And tonight, the Fetterman campaign zeroing in on this response from Oz. OZ: I want women, doctors, local political leaders letting the democracy that`s always allowed our nation to thrive to put the best ideas forward so states can decide for themselves. Local political leaders. Local political leaders. BURNS: Turning it into a campaign ad against his opponent. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: Oz is too extreme for Pennsylvania. BURNS: But Oz calling Fetterman the extreme candidates throughout the night, especially on the issue of crime. OZ: We have taken away the ability of police to do their job and that son John Fetterman . BURNS: The momentous matchup coming just two weeks before Election Day. Voters with strong reactions about Dr. Oz. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: His comment about political leaders, you know, determining what a woman -- a woman can and cannot do with her body is -- was very telling. [19:05:09] BURNS: And Fetterman. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: I just don`t think he`s capable at this time to be in that position. I mean, if you have somebody that can`t even handle a debate that has to, you know, read from this prompter. (END VIDEOTAPE) HOLT: And Dasha, some big names could soon be campaigning there on both sides. BURNS (on camera): Yes, Lester. Plans are coming together for both President Biden and former President Obama to campaign with Fetterman, and the Democratic candidate for governor. And former President Trump will campaign with Dr. Oz and the Republican gubernatorial candidate. Lester? HOLT: Dasha Burns, thank you. Let`s bring in Andrea Mitchell and Kristen Welker. Andrea, first to you. What are you hearing there in Pennsylvania about the impact of that debate? ANDREA MITCHELL, NBC NEWS CHIEF WASHINGTON CORRESPONDENT (on camera): Lester, Democrats here are telling me that they think Fetterman will be OK, given his labor support and Oz`s missteps on abortion and the minimum wage. But they acknowledge that this format did not work for Fetterman. Republicans say they`re pleased with how it went. The fact that this race is even close, though, tells you Republicans have momentum right now and it`s happening nationwide. In the Senate, enough incumbent Democrats could lose, giving Republicans several chances to take control. And in the House Democrats are in trouble in states like Oregon and New York, which are normally safe. Last night there was a debate for New York Governor where Republican Trump ally Congressman Lee Zeldin is within striking distance of Democratic Governor Kathy Hochul , which is remarkable in a solid blue state. Lester? HOLT: Andrea, thanks. END Content and programming copyright 2022 NBCUniversal. ALL RIGHTS RESERVED. Transcription Copyright 2022 VIQ Media Transcription, Inc. She says Walker pressured and paid for her to have an abortion, but she did not provide any evidence to support those claims. Now, Walker fired back today calling the claims foolishness and a lie, saying his Democratic opponent Senator Raphael Warnock "lost the debate and Democrats will now say anything to win." The woman`s claim comes after another woman accused Walker of paying for her abortion which Walker also strongly denied. The Georgia race is a toss-up that could determine Senate control. Lester? Brooks guilty of first-degree intentional homicide. MIGUEL ALMAGUER, NBC NEWS NATIONAL CORRESPONDENT (voiceover): The verdict was a clean sweep for prosecutors. Darrell Brooks guilty of all 76 criminal charges including intentional homicide, reckless endangering safety, and hit and run causing death. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: Are those your true verdicts? UNIDENTIFIED MALE: Yes. ALMAGUER: After just three hours of deliberation, the chaotic three-week trial came to an end as Brooks sat slumped over. SUSAN OPPER, DISTRICT ATTORNEY, WAUKESHA COUNTY: We are satisfied that this defendant has been held accountable for his actions. ALMAGUER: It was last year at this Christmas Parade in Waukesha, Wisconsin when Brooks plowed his car through the crowd, killing six and injuring dozens. Among the victims, the elderly and children. TYLER PUDLEINER, SURVIVOR: Were stronger than him and it`s been proven today. Just another step forward in the process. ALMAGUER: Maintaining his innocence -- DARRELL BROOKS, DEFENDANT: I am a lot of things. A murderer is not one of them. ALMAGUER: Brooks, who represented himself, showed a range of emotions in what became a circus-like trial, deciding to plead not guilty by reason of mental defect. JENNIFER DOROW, JUDGE, WAUKESHA COUNTY CIRCUIT COURT: Mr. Brooks, you`re interrupting me yet again. BROOKS: No, you weren`t just speaking, so -- DOROW: All right, Mr. Brooks, you are now going to be removed to the courtroom. BROOKS: I don`t concent to that. ALMAGUER: Brooks repeatedly interrupted the trial, at one point removing his shirt and staring down the judge who removed him from court. DOROW: I need to take a break. This man right now is having a staredown with me. Frankly, it makes me scared. (END VIDEOTAPE) ALMAGUER (on camera): In Wisconsin, conviction of first-degree intentional homicide carries a mandatory life sentence. Darrell Brooks will be formally sentenced in the coming weeks. Lester? HOLT: All right, Miguel Almaguer, thank you. Tonight, new details emerging about the 19-year-old gunman who killed two people and injured seven others at a St. Louis high school on Monday. Emilie Ikeda has the latest. (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) EMILIE IKEDA, NBC NEWS CORRESPONDENT (voiceover): Months before storming a St. Louis high school with a long gun and 600 rounds of ammunition, police said the accused killer`s family worked with law enforcement to have his gun removed from their home. MICHAEL SACK, INTERIM COMMISSIONER, ST. LOUIS METROPOLITAN POLICE DEPARTMENT: It`s -- and it`s hard to tell when somebody is going to be violent or act out or if they`re just struggling. [19:10:06] IKEDA: His family played an active role in getting a medical help involving therapy, medication, and committing him on several occasions according to police. Was the family aware of the arsenal of ammunition he had? SACK: They were aware that he had acquired a firearm. IKEDA: The ATF is still tracing where he originally bought the gun and how it landed back in his possession after law enforcement had transferred it to another adult. SACK: How he acquired it after that, you know, we don`t know. IKEDA: It`s believed to be the same AR-15-style weapon used to gun down sophomore Alexandria Bell and teacher Jean Kuczka, both of whom Ashley Wrench knew well. ASHLEY WRENCH, TEACHER: And you can hear just pop, pop, pop, pop. IKEDA: The longtime math teacher walking by her classroom for the first time since the shooting spree. What do you remember from Monday? WRENCH: Everything. The terror, the intruder trying to get in my room two, three, four times. IKEDA: That day, the school doors were locked, and seven unarmed security guards were on site. But authorities say the government managed to avoid the school`s checkpoints. Can you tell us if he had to break glass to get into the building though? SACK: You did have to force entry. And that`s good for us because that buys us time. (END VIDEOTAPE) IKEDA: And Lester, we`re learning tonight authorities believe the gunman was targeting the school and certain individuals. But the rapid police response and a potentially not functioning gun helps prevent even more bloodshed. Lester? HOLT: And the details that keep coming out are stunning. Thank you. A show of force in Russia. President Vladimir Putin observing annual drills led by Russia`s strategic nuclear forces as Russia continues with unfounded claims that Ukraine intends to use a dirty bomb in the war there. Also, today, Russian authorities returned the body of an American man killed in August while fighting for Ukraine. The remains of 24-year-old Joshua Jones were handed over to Ukrainian officials in a Russian- controlled part of Ukraine. Let`s turn to that big increase now in cases of RSV infections in children, with many hospitals saying they`re in crisis mode now. Tom Costello has the warning signs for parents. (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) TOM COSTELLO, NBC NEWS CORRESPONDENT (voiceover): 3-year-old Izzy Bankey is today almost back to her old self, but she`s been through rough few weeks. Homesick, a two-hour wait in an urgent care clinic, a second urgent care visit, an ambulance ride to Children`s National Med Center as she struggled to breathe. Then, admitted with RSV-caused pneumonia. KATE FOSTER-BANKEY, MOTHER OF IZZY BANKEY: Nobody wants to like, hold their kid down and hold a mask on their face. And so, she`s screaming and trying -- and trying to rip the breathing tubes out. And that breaks your heart as a parent. COSTELLO: RSV is an ever-present respiratory virus but especially serious in kids with low immunity after isolating during the pandemic. Now, hospitals nationwide say they`re overwhelmed with sick kids. 74 percent of pediatric hospital beds nationwide are occupied. 89 percent in Missouri, 91 percent in Texas, 99 percent in Rhode Island. Seattle Children`s tells NBC News it`s a 200 percent capacity in the ER. At UW Health Kids in Madison, Wisconsin, the chief medical officer is urging parents to stay on top of the symptoms before kids have to go to the ER. DR. JOSHUA ROSS, PEDIATRIC EMERGENCY MEDICINE PHYSICIAN, UW HEALTH -KIDS: Suctioning the nose, nasal passages, staying well hydrated, using anti- fever medications usually do the trick. We really want to pay attention to as kids under about 18 months of age that can develop more significant respiratory symptoms. COSTELLO: Seek immediate help if a child is in respiratory distress, breathing fast, nose flaring, using their shoulders or pulling under their ribs to breathe, and turning blue. DR. RICK PLACE, PEDIATRIC MEDICAL DIRECTOR, INOVA L.J. MURPHY CHILDREN`S HOSPITAL: If you think your child is in danger, you need to go to the E.R. I mean that`s a flat-out message. COSTELLO: Trust your gut, say doctors. Tom Costello, NBC News, Washington. (END VIDEOTAPE) HOLT: In 60 seconds, the nationwide shortage of Adderall, a key medicine that helps kids and adults with ADHD. What`s behind it and what families are doing to bridge the gap. (COMMERCIAL BREAK) [19:15:00] HOLT: Back now with a disorder that impacts so many Americans, including more than six million children, ADHD. For those who treat it with Adderall, a nationwide shortage has them scrambling to fill prescriptions. Anne Thompson explains. (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) ANNE THOMPSON, NBC NEWS CORRESPONDENT (voiceover): Giovanni is the center of Lyon and Kandy Flood`s world. KANDY FLOOD, SON HAS ADHD: Oh, nice. THOMPSON: It turned upside down by the Adderall shortage. When they told you the prescription wasn`t available, I mean, did your heart sink? K. FLOOD: Absolutely. My anxiety went up and my heart sank, and I was at a loss. THOMPSON: For a week, the third-grader had no Adderall manage his ADHD. Giovanni, what was it like for you to go without your medicine? GIOVANNI FLOOD, HAS ADHD: Uncomfortable. LYON FLOOD, SON HAD ADHD: His teacher came to us, threw her hands up and said, can you do something because he was way out of control, doing cartwheels in the class, and rolling on the floor. K. FLOOD: Rolling on the floor, yes. DR. LENARD ADLER, PSYCHIATRIST, NYU LANGONE: We`re fielding several phone calls a day. THOMPSON: Dr. Lenard Adler leads the adult ADHD program at NYU Langone Health. ADLER: I`ve had a patient having to call about 15 pharmacies before they finally got to -- THOMPSON: 15? ADLER: 15 pharmacies before they got their prescription filled. THOMPSON: This month, the FDA revealed the shortage blaming increased demand for the control substance and manufacturing issues at Teva , the largest drug maker. In a statement, Teva says the shortages are temporary and it expects inventory recovery in the coming months. ADLER: If you`re at the end of your prescription, I wouldn`t suggest doing anything on your own. I would have a discussion with your physician. Sometimes that means trying a new pharmacy. It can be. If necessary, trying a new medication. THOMAS: Kandy`s daily phone calls to her pharmacy paid off. They got a month`s refill, but there`s no guarantee they won`t face this again and soon. Anne Thompson, NBC News. (END VIDEOTAPE) HOLT: And up next, the verdict in the case against three-man accused of supporting the plot to kidnap Michigan`s governor. Plus, voter intimidation and efforts to combat it in our series "POWER OF THE VOTE." (COMMERCIAL BREAK) [19:20:00] HOLT: In Michigan today, three men were found guilty in state court for supporting a plot to kidnap Governor Gretchen Whitmer out of anger over her COVID restrictions. Two other men were convicted on federal conspiracy charges in August. Whitmer said, today`s verdicts are quote further proof that violence and threats have no place in our politics. Also, tonight, less than two weeks to the midterms, Arizona election officials are stepping up security after what they call vigilantes were spotted near ballot drop boxes. Gabe Gutierrez is there. (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) GABE GUTIERREZ, NBC NEWS NATIONAL CORRESPONDENT (voiceover): Amid complaints of armed masked groups wearing tactical gear and recording voters, the sheriff in Maricopa County, Arizona has now stepped up security near ballot drop boxes. PAUL PENZONE, SHERIFF, MARICOPA COUNTY: It troubles me that suddenly others feel compelled to act out in a way that is potentially criminal intimidation or criminal threats, trying to undermine democracy under this cloak of patriotism. And in doing so, what they`re doing is they`re destroying the most important institution in our nation, you know, the freedom and the right to vote. GUTIERREZ: He also says his office is investigating this incident captured on cell phone video where a woman tried to take a picture of one of their license plates and was pushed. We spoke to the woman. She asked us not to use her name or show her face for fear of backlash. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: You know, a lot of people are intimidated. And when people are standing around, you know, with handguns on them and sometimes tactical gear, you know, it really does scare the average person. GUTIERREZ: At least six complaints of alleged voter intimidation here have now been referred to the State Attorney General`s Office and the Department of Justice. Across the country, election threats are ramping up ahead of the Midterms. LEIGH CHAPMAN, ACTING SECRETARY, PENNSYLVANIA COMMONWEALTH: A lot of these threats are fueled by missing disinformation. GUTIERREZ: Law enforcement Nationwide is on alert. MERRICK GARLAND , U.S. ATTORNEY GENERAL: The Justice Department has an obligation to prevent to guarantee a free and fair vote. GUTIERREZ: Back in Arizona where early votes are already been counted, Republican election officials have called these armed drop box watchers uninformed vigilantes. As a Republican, how frustrating is it to you that some of these groups have latched on to conspiracy theories? STEPHEN RICHER, MARICOPA COUNTY RECORDER: Well, it`s been an interesting last two years. And you know, for the party of facts and logic, at times, we have fallen short from, in my estimation, on facts and logic. (END VIDEOTAPE) GUTIERREZ (on camera): Voter rights organizations have now sued to temporarily block at least some of these groups from monitoring these ballot drop-off boxes. Lester? HOLT: All right, Gabe, thank you. Coming up, at $700 million, it`s one of the biggest Powerball jackpots in history. Could there be a winner tonight? Plus, he was homeless before he found his place on the court. "INSPIRING AMERICA" is next. (COMMERCIAL BREAK) [19:25:00] HOLT: Tonight`s Powerball jackpot has grown to a massive $700 million, the fifth largest in the game`s history. No one has won since August. The odds are one in 293 million. If you bought your tickets, good luck to you. And finally, the student-athlete beating formidable odds with a former NBA point guard coaching them on. Kathy Park with tonight`s "INSPIRING AMERICA." (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) KATHY PARK, NBC NEWS CORRESPONDENT (voiceover): Jeremiah Armstead picked up a basketball at 14, the same age he realized life wasn`t a game. JEREMIAH ARMSTEAD, BASKETBALL PLAYER: I felt like I wasn`t in at 14. That`s what I feel like. Because that`s when they really picked up homeless and stuff like that. PARK: For years, Jeremiah says he moved from shelter to shelter with his mom and two siblings. ARMSTEAD: I was living off food stamps. PARK: What would you say were some of the darkest times in your life? ARMSTEAD: Sleeping at bleachers. People walking by, looking in the car. Stuff like that builds character, so I can`t be mad to stuff like that. PARK: Homelessness pushed Jeremiah to fight harder for his goals. ARMSTEAD: Can`t is not in my vocabulary. PARK: He excelled as a student in California and as an athlete, a winning combination that got him into Fisk University in Nashville, and a spot on the basketball team. KENNY ANDERSON, FORMER NBA PLAYER: The grit definitely sets him apart. PARK: Former NBA point guard Kenny Anderson now coaches a rising star and sees a lot of himself in Jeremiah. ANDERSON: My best year of my high school career, I was -- I have the way to live. We got evicted. PARK: The NBA legend beat the odds and believes Jeremiah can too. Meanwhile, his cheering squad couldn`t be prouder. MINDY BROOKS, MOTHER OF JEREMIAH: This is a child who deserves to just show what he can do. PARK: What`s the end game for you? ARMSTEAD: My first goal which is get my mom and my sister out to shelter that they`re in. PARK: Family first while making moves on and off the court. Kathy Park, NBC News, Nashville. (END VIDEOTAPE) HOLT: Good for him. That`s NIGHTLY NEWS for this Wednesday. Thank you for watching. I`m Lester Holt. Please take care of yourself and each other. Goodnight, everyone. headline: Democrat John Fetterman And Republican Dr. Mehmet Oz Face Off
story_text: [07:00:17] HODA KOTB, NBC NEWS ANCHOR: Good morning. It`s Wednesday, all eyes were on Pennsylvania overnight. SAVANNAH GUTHRIE, NBC NEWS ANCHOR: Yes. The first and only Senate debate there with control of Congress hanging in the balance. It is October 26th, this is Today. Center Stage, Democrat John Fetterman and Republican Dr. Mehmet Oz face off on the issues. JOHN FETTERMAN (D), PENNSYLVANIA SENATE CANDIDATE: My campaign would fight for Roe v. Wade. MEHMET OZ (R), PENNSYLVANIA SENATE CANDIDATE: John Fetterman picks everything to an extreme and those extreme positions hurt us all. GUTHRIE: And ongoing concerns over Fetterman`s fitness to serve. FETTERMAN: I had a stroke, he`s never let me forget that. GUTHRIE: This morning the candidates in their own words and the takeaways in one of the nation`s most important midterm contests. Now previous research has linked video games with depression and aggressive behavior, but the latest study found that there were no significant differences in behavior. MELVIN: There are a lot of young kids right now listen to the TODAY SHOW getting ready to go to school who are saying right now. You see mom, I told you. I told you. GUTHRIE: I know. MELVIN: We turn now out to that growing scandal that`s engulfing the Miss USA pageant. KOTB: Yes. A winner was crowned earlier this month. But in the weeks that have followed, several contestants have come forward and they claim the competition was rigged. GUTHRIE: NBC`s Stephanie Gosk is here with the details. Stephanie, good morning. GOSK: Hey, guys, good morning. Accusations this year`s winner did not earn her crown. The president of the Miss USA Organization, a former winner herself, has been suspended, leaving the future of the pageant in doubt. (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: Miss USA is Texas. GOSK (voice-over): After R`Bonney Gabriel was crowned this year as Miss USA, the first Filipino-American to ever win the prestigious pageant, there were immediate signs of trouble. Many of her rivals can be seen leaving the stage without the usual congratulatory hugs for the winner. The Miss Universe Organization which oversees the pageant now looking into claims by several contestants that the contest was rigged by Miss USA President Christy Stewart and her company Miss Brand. In a statement to NBC, the Miss Universe Organization writing in part, "It has decided to suspend Miss Brand immediately, adding the Miss Universe Organization will be taking over the Miss USA program while a comprehensive third party investigation is conducted." Gabriel`s crowning moment some say was no surprise. According to Insider, more than a dozen Miss USA contestants said this year`s pageant was either rigged or heavily favored Gabrielle. So I`m saying that Gabriel allegedly had connections to pageant sponsors and a pageant judge from a previous competition. Miss Montana Heather Lee O`Keefe convinced the fix was in. HEATHER LEE O`KEEFE, MISS MONTANA: I truly think that she could have won fair and square, but there`s just too much evidence of favoritism to let this go unnoticed. GOSK (voice-over): O`Keefe says while Miss USA sponsored all of the contestants, she believes pageant officials and sponsors are more generous to Gabriel who went on to win. Gabriel denied any favoritism in a recent interview with him. R`BONNEY GABRIEL, MISS TEXAS: I want to start by saying it was not rigged because I would never enter any pageant or any competition that I know I would win. I have a lot of integrity. GOSK (voice-over): Stewart has also denied any wrongdoing, telling insider before she was suspended the allegations against the Miss USA Organization are misleading and against everything I stand for personally and professionally. As a Miss USA contestant herself in 2008, Stewart tripped on stage but bounced back to win the competition. [07:35:12] Now after a different kind of fall from Miss USA, pageants crown may be forever tarnished. (END VIDEO CLIP) GOSK: NBC News has reached out to Crystle Stewart and the Miss USA Organization for comment. They said they had no comment at this time. KOTB: Yes. When you saw that none of the girls went over to congratulate her when it was over, and she just kind of wandered off the stage you thought something had to be up among them. GOSK: Yes. KOTB: All right. MELVIN: Thank you, Steph. KOTB: Thank you. GOSK: Thank you. KOTB: Still ahead, we got new details on Sir Elton John`s final US concert ever and how you can watch it live. MELVIN: First, Vicky Nguyen is here to break down apparently a new and timely strategy to save our next vacation. VICKY NGUYEN, NBC NEWS SENIOR CONSUMER INVESTIGATIVE CORRESPONDENT: Hi, good morning. Are you ready to get away, you would not be alone. Fall is quickly becoming the new summer when it comes to family travel. I`m going to tell you where to find the best deals right now. That`s coming up next right here on TODAY. (COMMERCIAL BREAK) GUTHRIE: Welcome back this morning on Consumer Confidential. A travel trend that could save you a lot of money on your vacation. MELVIN: Yes. For growing number of families, fall is apparently the new summer, pulling kids out of school to take advantage of seasonal deal. KOTB: Indeed. NBC senior consumer investigative correspondent Vicky Nguyen is here. She`s got everything we need to know. Hey, Vicky. Hey, good morning, Hoda, Savannah and Craig. [07:40:00] NGUYEN: Travel experts are calling fall the shoulder season. It`s that period after Labor Day but before Christmas, and vacation prices in a lot of places typically go way down. In this tough economy, many families who put off their summer vacations are now taking advantage. This morning we have the trips you can book right now to get the most bang and family fun for your buck. (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) NGUYEN (voice-over): Move over summer vacation fall is now the hot season for family getaways. More than a quarter of American travelers say they plan to take a trip in October. Travel agency sales for vacation airline tickets up 9% this fall, and average ticket prices way down for many family friendly destinations. Flights to Honolulu now 30% less, Denver down 20%, and Fort Lauderdale 15% less, with working remotely making vacations easier than ever for working parents. Many are itching to get away after being homebound during the pandemic. DANNY GENUNG, CEO, HARR TRAVEL: Compared to last fall, we`re seeing an almost 500% increase in families booking close and travel. NGUYEN (voice-over): Mom Stacy Mackenzie from Maine is actually pulling her three kids out of school this week for a long postponed vacation to Disney World and Universal Studios in Orlando. STACY MACKENZIE, MOTHER: We decided to go in the fall just because I thought it would be cooler weather and less people. NGUYEN: This vacation was too good to pass up after all that time cooped up. MACKENZIE: Yes, yes. And I`m one of those that cries at Disney commercials because I want to go so bad. So we are so excited to be going I`m so excited. If you want the best vacation deals for your family, experts say consider getting onboard a cruise. Book a future trip this week on Royal Caribbean and Norwegian, and your kids can sail for free. Blackout dates excluded. With COVID vaccine requirements now eliminated, families are signing up in droves. Nebraska mom, Miriam Hamilton, her husband and twin boys just went on an eight day Caribbean cruise for 50% off the regular price. MIRIAM HAMILTON, MOTHER: Prices are always better for traveling in the fall. It`s usually quieter for the kids. The activities are not as full for kids so they get better chances at doing things and doing them more often. (END VIDEOTAPE) KOTB: All right, Vicky. And there are some people who do not want to pull their kids out of school. Is there an option for them for a cheaper fall vacation? NGUYEN: Well, definitely if you don`t want to pull your kids out of school, Thanksgiving week going overseas for that dream European vacation. That`s the time to go because they don`t celebrate over there, great prices. If you want to go this month, Hoda, October, San Diego is your destination. KOTB: Oh is it? NGUYEN: All kinds of deals on restaurants, attractions, hotels for kids. You (inaudible) the kids out. GUTHRIE: I love San Diego. It`s a good city. OK, cool. KOTB: Thank you, Vic. MELVIN: So this time of the year. GUTHRIE: All right. Let`s check the weather outside the answer. ROKER: You know, a lot of folks take Mississippi River cruises. Well guess what, hey, those have been delayed or some canceled. Take a look at the Mississippi River. The not so mighty Mississippi, it`s dry and it`s causing big problems for shipping. This was late September last year. You can see how lush it is. This year, October of 2020, look at how dry it is. And that is continuing. And in fact we are looking at record low river levels. Memphis reaching its lowest river level since 1954. And the big problem is the drought. When this is an economic lifeline, the Mississippi River, $13 billion in shipping, a 35,000 related jobs. It accounts -- get this, 92% of our nation`s agricultural exports. So it is a lifeline literally, and the big problem has been the extensive drought in the western half of the Mississippi River basin. Problem is going into the winter, doesn`t look like we`re going to get much relief, so going to continue to have problems along the Mighty Mississippi. For Today, we`re looking at sunshine returning through the southeast into the gulf, plenty of sun from Texas on up into the plains, some mountain snows where they`re going to use that for those great ski resorts and we`re looking at sunshine from San Diego, some showers in Seattle. That`s what`s going on around the country. Here`s what`s happening in your neck of the woods. (LOCAL WEATHER) ROKER: And that is your latest weather. Guys? GUTHRIE: Thank you, Al. By the way, you`re about to hit the road for a very special lend-a-hand. ROKER: Yes. We`re really, really thrilled to be doing this. We`re going to see you tomorrow morning from Fort Myers Beach, Florida. [07:45:00] This is one month after Hurricane Ian roared ashore. We`re going to give you a firsthand look at a community`s resilience and determination to rebuild. Plus, we`re going to meet some heroes who are putting their own recovery on hold just to help others. We`re looking forward to sharing their inspiring stories live from Fort Myers Beach, Florida tomorrow on Today, in our great station down there, WBBH NBC2. We`re going to be working with them as well. KOTB: Cool. MELVIN: I love that you`re doing that. I love that you`re doing that. Up next, to rake or not to rake, apparently that is the question this morning. This morning scientists have been answered that a lot of you are really going to love. We`ll have that for you right after this. (COMMERCIAL BREAK) (CLIP FROM "IT`S THE GREAT PUMPKIN CHARLIE BROWN") MELVIN: Classic, classic. KOTB: Yes. MELVIN: Back with our beloved holiday special, "It`s the Great Pumpkin Charlie Brown." And, Carson, there`s reason we picked that scene. CARSON DALY, NBC NEWS ANCHOR: There`s got to be a reason for that. That means fall is here. Pesky task of raking leaves but that chore might be a thing of the past. According to experts, leaving at least some of those leaves on the ground can actually help your lawn improving the health of grass and encouraging plant growth. Let`s discuss it and let`s predicate this by saying I don`t rake my leaves anymore. I have when you landscaping engineers to do that. MELVIN: There you go. GUTHRIE: I like that. KOTB: Carson, did you rake when you were a kid? DALY: Yes. KOTB: Did your parents make you? DALY: Yes. MELVIN: Of course. KOTB: Did your parents make you? ROKER: Absolutely. And in fact, I did -- when I was in high school, I did a whole thing. A whole research project to convince my father that we did not have to rake leaves. And that we just take the leaf catcher, that lawnmower, and mulch it (inaudible). And I`ve talked to the Queens` cooperative extension guy. He said it`s fine. But would you leave -- they`re saying you should leave all the leaves on the lawn, it`s good for it. MELVIN: Keep watching kids. GUTHRIE: It`s like no school, candy for breakfast, what`s next? MELVIN: Did you`re dad but it? ROKER: Yes, yes, he did. DALY: I`m more likely to compost. MELVIN: You`re welcome kids. You`re welcome. DALY: How long can you hold your breath for?
