story_text: (COMMERCIAL BREAK) [08:00:00] SAVANNAH GUTHRIE, NBC NEWS TODAY, CO-ANCHOR: It`s 8:00 on "TODAY." Coming up, center stage. Inside the Pennsylvania Senate race, Democrat John Fetterman facing off against Republican Mehmet Oz sparring over the issues. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) LT. GOV. JOHN FETTERMAN (D-PA): I`m running to serve Pennsylvania. He is running to use Pennsylvania. DR. MEHMET OZ (R-PA), SENATE NOMINEE: John Fetterman takes everything to an extreme. And those extreme positions hurt us all. (END VIDEO CLIP) GUTHRIE: And John Fetterman`s health. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) FETTERMAN: I had a stroke but it knocked me down. And I`m going to keep coming back up. (END VIDEO CLIP) GUTHRIE: Why this race could help decide the balance of power in Congress. Then tripling down. New warnings about that oncoming tripledemic, COVID, flu and RSV. What experts are saying this morning about keeping you and your loved ones safe. Plus, all in the family. Jenna sits down with the Queen Consort Camilla`s nephew Luke Parker Bowles. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) LUKE PARKER BOWLES, QUEEN CONSORT CAMILLA`S NEPHEW: I have this name. And if I use it for something that helps people, then all the better. (END VIDEO CLIP) GUTHRIE: What brought him to the United States and what he hopes to accomplish here. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) JENNA BUSH HAGER, HODA & JENNA HOST: If somebody had told you when you were 18, you are going to be in New Jersey when you get older, what would you say? PARKER BOWLES: I`d say what`s New Jersey? (END VIDEO CLIP) GUTHRIE: Today, Wednesday, October 26, 2022. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) UNIDENTIFIED MALE: From Vernon, Texas. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: Celebrating our golden anniversary. CROWD: Friends for 35 years. CROWD: Visiting from Irvine, California. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: Girls trip. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: From Philadelphia. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: To the "TODAY" show. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: Shout out to my daughter. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: In Merrimac, Virginia. CROWD: From Lake Charles, Louisiana. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: Because today. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: I`m turning 70. (END VIDEO CLIP) CRAIG MELVIN, NBC NEWS ANCHOR: Aw. HODA KOTB, NBC NEWS TODAY, CO-ANCHOR: Aw. GUTHRIE: Aw. Hello. Good morning. Welcome back to "TODAY." What a great crowd out there. A beautiful fall morning. Relax. You don`t have to rake your leaves today. KOTB: Yes. Exactly. GUTHRIE: That`s what we`ve learned this morning. MELVIN: So, far. Yes. KOTB: Happy birthday, Lake Charles. Cool. GUTHRIE: Let`s get to the news, 8:00 on a Wednesday morning. With control of the U.S. Senate at stake, all eyes on that Pennsylvania rates last night. And the only debate, hitting Democrat John Fetterman against Republican Dr. Mehmet Oz. And it comes amid questions concerning Fetterman`s health after his stroke six months ago. NBC`s Dasha Burns joins us with some of the key moments last night. Hi, Dasha. Good morning. DASHA BURNS, NBC NEWS REPORTER: Hey, Savannah. Good morning. This debate was highly anticipated, not just by voters here in Pennsylvania, but across the country. This is an extremely tight race. Just a couple of points separating these candidates. And in the battle against one of the most familiar faces on American television, many tuned in to see how Fetterman would fair after suffering a stroke earlier this year and the stakes could not have been higher. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) BURNS (voiceover): In a race that could help decide the balance of power in Congress, Pennsylvania Democrat John Fetterman and Republican Mehmet Oz neck-and-neck in the polls finally face to face on the debate stage. LT. GOV. JOHN FETTERMAN (D-PA): I`m running to serve Pennsylvania. He is running to use Pennsylvania. DR. MEHMET OZ (R-PA), SENATE NOMINEE: John Fetterman takes everything to an extreme. And those extreme positions hurt us all. BURNS (voiceover): Fetterman acknowledging what he called the elephant in the room. The stroke that nearly killed him five months ago. FETTERMAN: I had a stroke. He`s never let me forget that. And I might miss some words during this debate, mush two words together. I am also fighting for any forgotten community all across Pennsylvania that ever got knocked down that had to be made -- to get back up and I have made my entire career dedicating to those kinds of pursuits. BURNS (voiceover): Fetterman using closed captioning to assist with auditory processing, battling Dr. Oz. FETTERMAN: It`s about supporting and helping, you know, young earners, excuse me, young -- young, uh -- young, you know, students to give them a break. BURNS (voiceover): But experiencing some stumbles throughout the debate, particularly during an exchange over fracking, challenged by the moderators for past contradictory comments. FETTERMAN: I do support fracking and I don`t -- I don`t -- I support fracking and I stand -- and I do support fracking. BURNS (voiceover): Fetterman says he is fit to serve, citing a letter from his doctor. But he would not commit to releasing his full medical records. FETTERMAN: I believe if my doctor believes that I`m fit to serve and that`s what I believe is appropriate. BURNS (voiceover): The celebrity TV doctor never directly addressing Fetterman`s health, but saying this during an exchange on education. OZ: I visited vocational schools. I have an answer. But, John, because you -- obviously, I wasn`t clear enough for you to understand this. BURNS (voiceover): One point where Oz has not been clear, how he would vote on an abortion ban introduced by Republican Senator Lindsey Graham . OZ: I want women, doctors, local political leaders leading the democracy that`s always allowed our nation to thrive to put the best ideas forward so states can decide for themselves. BURNS (voiceover): A clear difference from his opponent. [08:05:00] FETTERMAN: My campaign would fight for Roe V. Wade. And if given the opportunity to codify it into law. (END VIDEO CLIP) BURNS (on camera): And, Savannah, and speaking to media after the debate, the Fetterman spokesperson said the campaign was thrilled with the Democrat`s performance saying he won, "Multiple exchanges against Oz." We also asked the Oz spokesperson about that line you just heard there where Oz said that decisions about abortion should be made between, "A woman, her doctor, and local political leaders." The campaign said that Oz is, "Pro- life with exceptions for rape, incest and the life of the mother." Savannah. GUTHRIE: All right. Dasha Burns, thank you very much. KOTB: With fears of a winter tripledemic growing, President Biden is urging Americans to get their flu and their COVID boosters as soon as they can. The president, who tested positive for COVID twice this summer, got his updated COVID shot yesterday. He noted that the virus is constantly changing but said that nearly all COVID deaths can now be prevented if enough people get vaccinated. Meantime, three quarters of all pediatric hospital beds around the country are now full because of an outbreak of RSV among children. MELVIN: Clorox is recalling eight of its Pine-Sol disinfecting cleaning products because they could contain harmful bacteria. The recall covers 37 million containers of Pine-Sol cleaners. They were made at a plant in Georgia. The CDC says the bacteria can cause blood and lung infections in people with compromised immune systems. For more information on the recall, go to our website, today.com. GUTHRIE: The International Space Station had to do defensive driving this week to avoid a potential collision with a piece of Russian satellite debris. NASA says the ISS had to fire its thrusters for more than five minutes on Monday. That raised its altitude a bit and allowed it to dodge the space junk. MELVIN: Wow. GUTHRIE: That maneuver did not affect normal operations. The debris was created by Russia`s test-firing of a missile last year that destroyed one of its old out of commission satellites. MELVIN: Space is really getting crowded. GUTHRIE: Yes. MELVIN: Really getting crowded. KOTB: All right. Guys, we got the news covered. Now, how about a boost? MELVIN: Yes. KOTB: All right. So, a UPS driver in South Dakota is the hero of the neighborhood because he made one incredible shot after he made a delivery. So, he dropped off a package, heads back to his truck, he`s walking past a driveway basketball game. The ball rolls towards the street, picks it up, and he fires off a one-handed shot. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) UNIDENTIFIED MALE: No way. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: No way. (END VIDEO CLIP) KOTB: No way. MELVIN: Oh. KOTB: Oh, my gosh. After a brief celebration, the delivery man just climbs back in the truck, off he goes. MELVIN: Wow. KOTB: What a nice moment. MELVIN: That`s impressive. KOTB: That`s cool. GUTHRIE: So happy about the ring cameras sometimes. KOTB: I know. MELVIN: Yes. GUTHRIE: I mean, otherwise, they`d be like, no. But, seriously, I was away. KOTB: He did it. GUTHRIE: I did it. MELVIN: We got lots more ahead on a Wednesday morning, including our first look at a holiday special from the Marvel Universe. I can hear Al Roker screaming now. We`re going to show you the beloved star who is going to make a great cameo. GUTHRIE: But first, Jenna`s one-on-one with an extended member of the royal family, the queen consort`s nephew who lives right here in the northeast, New Jersey. Sharing his story for the first time. And Jenna, we`re looking forward to that conversation. Right after this. (COMMERCIAL BREAK) [08:10:00] MELVIN: And welcome back. Welcome back. In the wake of Queen Elizabeth`s death, the eyes on the world are on the new monarch, King Charles and Queen Consort Camilla. GUTHRIE: Well, I learned something new today. One of their biggest supporters lives right here in the U.S., very close to us. Camilla`s nephew Luke Parker Bowles. KOTB: And Jenna met up with him to hear his intriguing story. Who knew he lived in Jersey. JENNA BUSH HAGER, HODA & JENNA HOST: I mean, he -- you would have thought you had to go across the pond. KOTB: Yes. BUSH HAGER: I just had to go in the hole and tunnel. After growing up of Parker Bowles, he`s began a new life right here in New Jersey. He is smart, charming, lovely. And now he is sharing his story for the first time. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) BUSH HAGER (voiceover): It`s an unlikely story, an unofficial British ambassador for the royal family living among the rolling hills of picturesque Montclair, New Jersey. LUKE PARKER BOWLES, QUEEN CONSORT CAMILLA`S NEPHEW: This town is so much about film and culture. BUSH HAGER (voiceover): I met with up with Luke Parker Bowles, nephew of queen consort Camilla, while he was busy promoting the Montclair Film Festival. BUSH HAGER (on camera): I never really thought I`d find a little slice of England in New Jersey. But tell me how you came here. PARKER BOWLES: I came to America, I met a beautiful woman who is now my wife. And I was in England making movies there. One of Hugh Grant`s films, "Love Actually" and everything, and I moved over here and started doing independent film. BUSH HAGER (voiceover): The father of three has lived in the United States for more than a decade. Lured away from the U.K. by the bright shiny lights of Hollywood and big dreams of an acting career. PARKER BOWLES: And after a while I -- it would -- it became very clear that I did not have the skill set, but I loved film more than anything. And so, I realized I wanted to be behind the camera. BUSH HAGER (voiceover): Far different from his life in London. He grew up the nephew of Camilla Parker Bowles, by her first marriage to Andrew Parker Bowles. His last name often casting a large and dramatic shadow as his aunt was in the spotlight. BUSH HAGER (on camera): I read that when you were younger, you were actually sometimes bullied. PARKER BOWLES: It was a rough time. It was not a great time to be a Parker Bowles. But it hasn`t scarred me. BUSH HAGER (voiceover): His family focused on using its name for good. PARKER BOWLES: All of us, I think. My cousins, my brother, and myself, we`ve always have been involved in charity. It`s much more important to be doing charitable things, not to be holier than thou, just because it gives you a focus. BUSH HAGER (voiceover): One of the charities close to his heart is the Queen Elizabeth II Garden in Lower Manhattan which pays tribute to his countrymen lost on 9/11. PARKER BOWLES: His majesty, very kindly become our trustee and helped us get this garden going, and then her late majesty allowed us to name it after her. And it`s a place for people to go down and reflect and remember. BUSH HAGER (on camera): Your heart is here. Your kids are here. Your wife is here. Your job is here. Part of you is still there. And by giving back here, you are keeping that part of you alive. PARKER BOWLES: I think my shrink would say there is some guilt involved, maybe, that I`m not over there. It goes back to the fact that I have this name. And if I can use it for something that helps people, then all the better. BUSH HAGER (voiceover): He says, it`s an example set from the very top. He admired Queen Elizabeth and her dedication to service, working for the British people up until the very end. BUSH HAGER (on camera): Watching the outpouring of love -- PARKER BOWLES: Yes. BUSH HAGER (on camera): -- for her majesty, Queen Elizabeth, we were in Scotland. So, to get to see little girls lining the street with hand- colored papers for her. PARKER BOWLES: I think, for the most part, she left this world feeling that everything was in its right place. BUSH HAGER (on camera): And she was such an example -- PARKER BOWLES: Oh, yes. BUSH HAGER (on camera): -- of service. PARKER BOWLES: Oh, yes. BUSH HAGER (on camera): -- and dedication. PARKER BOWLES: Yes. BUSH HAGER: I mean -- PARKER BOWLES: And flinchingly and never seeking thanks or approval. It was her job and she took it very seriously. BUSH HAGER (voiceover): Now, with the next generation leading the monarchy into a new area, Parker Bowles says he is optimistic and excited for the future. PARKER BOWLES: It`s been a big change for the U.K. of late. You know, we are in a lot of trouble with our financial situation, with our political situation. [08:15:00] And I think that it`s no surprise that the one ray of light, at the moment, is -- I have to get used to the queen. BUSH HAGER (on camera): Yes. PARKER BOWLES: Is his majesty and my aunt, and also Kate and William. BUSH HAGER (on camera): Yes. PARKER BOWLES: You know. I think that the queen, before she died was very smart about making sure that the four of them were front and center to the public and were showing that they actually are working. BUSH HAGER (voiceover): Parker Bowles now focuses on his business called Cinema Lab, restoring old movie theaters in the U.S. PARKER BOWLES: And it was really spurned on by seeing my daughter and her friends and my friends` daughters and sons, all hanging out at CVS car parks, or whatever it may be. BUSH HAGER (on camera): There was no movie theater for them to go? PARKER BOWLES: There`s no center. We want to bring back the community. BUSH HAGER (voiceover): That need of community and a place to come together is universal, whether it`s in London or across the pond in a small town in New Jersey. BUSH HAGER (on camera): If somebody had told you when you were 18, you are going to live in New Jersey when you get older, what would you have said? PARKER BOWLES: I`d say, what`s New Jersey, probably? Truly. But I -- it`s the best decision I ever made. (END VIDEO CLIP) BUSH HAGER: Don`t you love that, what`s New Jersey? KOTB: Wow. BUSH HAGER: It just shows you never know where life is going to take you. MELVIN: Yes. BUSH HAGER: But he talked about how important giving back was to his family. That his dad had three rules. One of them was to be kind. One was to not get caught, what he said, that one that we couldn`t break. And the other one was to do service. And I think that those were good rules to take back to our kids. But do not get caught. MELVIN: CARSON DALY, NBC NEWS HOST: Two out of three ain`t bad. GUTHRIE: Yes. story_text: (COMMERCIAL BREAK) [07:00:16] SAVANNAH GUTHRIE, NBC NEWS ANCHOR: Good morning. It`s Thursday. Big developments overnight in two key races that kind of decides who`s in charge in Washington. HODA KOTB, NBC NEWS ANCHOR: With just 12 days to go until the midterms, we`re going to break it all down for you. It is October 27th. This is Today. New accusations, another woman comes forward claiming Herschel Walker urged her to have an abortion. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: I do not believe that Herschel is morally fit to be a U.S. senator. (END VIDEO CLIP) KOTB: While in Pennsylvania, John Fetterman addresses his debate performance. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) LT. GOV. JOHN FETTERMAN (D-PA), SENATOR CANDIDATE: During that debate wasn`t exactly easy. (END VIDEO CLIP) KOTB: We got it all covered. Crisis mode, hospitals nationwide being forced to take drastic measures to handle the tripledemic surge of flu, COVID, and RSV. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) UNIDENTIFIED MALE: Not only are there a lot of sick kids right now, there`s no place for them to go. (END VIDEO CLIP) KOTB: Just ahead, the new message from health officials all families need to hear. Breaking overnight, a new wave of protests in Iran, despite authorities intensifying a brutal crackdown, this morning the powerful scenes playing out across the country. Under pressure, Tesla reportedly facing a criminal investigation over its autopilot claims after a string of high profile crashes. So has the popular automaker misled consumers about how safe their cars really are? Those stories, plus, members only. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: Contrary to popular belief, you can be any age to join AARP. (END VIDEO CLIP) KOTB: From AARP to AAA, the surprising clubs you can sign up for to save big. And feeling lucky. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) UNIDENTIFIED MALE: Here are tonight`s winning numbers. (END VIDEO CLIP) KOTB: With no winner overnight, the Powerball jackpot jumps to a whopping $800 million, one of the largest prizes ever now up for grabs. Today, Thursday, October 27th, 2022. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: From NBC News, this is Today with Savannah Guthrie and Hoda Kotb live from Studio 1A in Rockefeller Plaza. KOTB: Well, good morning. It is so good to see you, happy that you`re here joining us. It is a Thursday morning. GUTHRIE: Well, you got it lined up if you want to get those Powerball tickets. The drawing is this weekend so you have time to get your tickets but jackpots up to 800 million. KOTB: It is. We`re going to have a lot more on jackpot fever coming up. But we`re going to start with another big countdown. We`re talking about the one to the midterm. GUTHRIE: Yes, 12 days to go now, and the spotlight is intensifying on two major races in Georgia and Pennsylvania. What happens there could impact the lives of every American. KOTB: Here`s what`s at stake, the balance of power in the Senate and the direction of key issues from the economy to abortion rights to rising crime rates, NBC`s senior Washington correspondent Hallie Jackson has the very latest for us. Hey, Hallie, good morning. HALLIE JACKSON, NBC NEWS SENIOR WASHINGTON CORRESPONDENT: Hey Hoda, hey Savannah. You have laid out the stakes and it is crunch time now, right, for candidates in these really important really close races with big guns like former presidents in both parties set to hit the campaign trail in the coming days. And the focus today turning to Georgia, where there`s a new abortion allegations surfacing, and one of the country`s most closely watched matchups. (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) JACKSON (voice-over): With less than two weeks to go this morning, the future of the Senate could hang on to key states with neck and neck races in Pennsylvania and Georgia, where there`s now another twist, Republican Herschel Walker who`s campaigned on an anti-abortion platform now denying a new allegation from a second woman who says Walker pressured her to have an abortion in the early 90s. HERSCHEL WALKER (R-GA), SENATOR CANDIDATE: What I`m saying, this is a lie and I`ve said it once and I`ve moved on my campaign. JACKSON (voice-over): The anonymous woman sharing her voice only came forward in a Zoom press conference arranged by Attorney Gloria Allred. The accuser saying after she became pregnant in 1993, Walker encouraged her to have an abortion, adding she first couldn`t go through with the procedure, but that Walker encouraged her to go back driving her to a Dallas clinic where she had the abortion. The woman explaining why she`s speaking up now. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: I am a registered Independent and I voted for Donald Trump in both elections. I do not believe that Herschel is morally fit to be a U.S. senator. JACKSON (voice-over): NBC News has not verified her allegations and the woman did not provide evidence Walker was involved in her abortion. WALKER: I`m done with this foolishness. JACKSON (voice-over): The Republican candidate and former football star also denied allegations earlier this month from another former girlfriend who says Walker paid for her abortion in 2009. In a statement the campaign for Walker`s opponent, Senator Raphael Warnock says Walker has a problem with the truth, a problem answering questions, and a problem taking responsibility for his actions. That match up, very close with recent polling showing Warnock leading by just five points. And in another closely watched race in Pennsylvania a tossup with polls ranking Democratic Lieutenant Governor John Fetterman and Republican candidate Dr. Mehmet Oz within the margin of error. [07:05:11] FETTERMAN: During that debate wasn`t exactly easy, you know, I knew it wasn`t going to be easy after, you know, having a stroke after five months. JACKSON (voice-over): Fetterman appearing at a campaign rally in Pittsburgh after raising $2 million, his team says, in the hours after his one and only debate against Republican Mehmet Oz. Fetterman facing questions about his at times halting debate performance with lingering auditory processing issues after a stroke five months ago. Oz also on the campaign trail hammering the issue of crime and on defense against a new Democratic ad highlighting his debate comments on abortion. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: This is who Dr. Oz wants in charge of women`s health care decisions. MEHMET OZ (R-PA), SENATOR CANDIDATE: I want women, doctors, local political leaders, local political leaders. (END VIDEOTAPE) GUTHRIE: Meanwhile, Hallie, the President hitting the campaign trail today, what do you expect? JACKSON: He is all about the economy, Savannah, in this kind of closing argument here trying to highlight his administration`s record on something we know that voters care about the economy plus cost of living. The top issue that voters say matters to them come Election Day. The President is going to be at Upstate New York to argue that Democrats economic policies are better than Republicans, even as many GOP candidates have pointed to high inflation in their midterm campaigns. You`ve also got the president`s cabinet fanning out across the country too. All of it is part of this full core press ahead of Election Day. Savannah? GUTHRIE: Twelve days to go. Hallie Jackson, thank you. And we turn now to growing concerns over the dangerous tripledemic of viruses nationwide flu, COVID, and the respiratory illness, RSV. With cases surging, some hospitals even in areas of warmer weather, are running out of beds. NBC national correspondent Gabe Gutierrez is inside Phoenix Children`s Hospital this morning with more. Gabe, good morning. GABE GUTIERREZ, NBC NEWS NATIONAL CORRESPONDENT: Savannah, good morning. It`s only October but doctors here and across the country are dealing with patient numbers that they usually don`t see until much later in winter. And overnight we met one mother who barely heard of RSV until she ended up here with her newborn son. (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) GUTIERREZ (voice-over): This morning, the latest wave of child respiratory illnesses is spreading prompting more concerns of a tripledemic this winter. In Arizona, RSV cases are up 344 percent over a typical season. CHEYENNE SHIELDER`S (ph), SON DIAGNOSED WITH RSV: Terrifying, this is serious illness. You know, with him being this young. He doesn`t have an immune system to fight it off. GUTIERREZ (voice-over): Cheyenne Shielder`s (ph) two-month-old son Ryder (ph) was in the hospital overnight. (on camera): What would you tell other parents? SHIELDER: Look up the symptoms of RSV and trust her gut to because I was on the border about coming or not to the hospital. And I feel like I probably should have come a little bit sooner. GUTIERREZ (voice-over): Last year and now this year, Phoenix Children`s Hospital has been dealing with an unusually high number of RSV cases, though the facility is not at capacity, it`s bracing for a rough winter DR. WASSIM BALLAN, PHOENIX CHILDREN`S HOSPITAL CHIEF OF INFECTIOUS DISEASES: COVID-19 combined with a potentially bad influenza season and now we`re seeing RSV going up at the same time, that obviously makes us concerned that we might get into this triple pandemic situation. GUTIERREZ (voice-over): This year, even western and southern states with warmer temperatures are seeing a significant rise in RSV and flu cases. In Arizona, 87 percent of pediatric hospital beds are occupied, in Texas 91 percent, Seattle Children`s tells NBC News it`s at 200 percent capacity in the ER. DR. ASHISH JHA, WHITE HOUSE COVID-19 RESPONSE COORDINATOR: Under normal circumstances, about 90 percent of kids end up getting RSV at least once, by the time there are two. Because of the pandemic, some of the kind of standard patterns have been disrupted so we`re seeing a lot of RSV at once. GUTIERREZ (voice-over): Parents now worried sick across the country from San Diego where Fernanda Costanarez (ph) is caring for baby Alejandra (ph). FERNANDA COSTANAREZ (ph), DAUGHTER DIAGNOSED WITH RSV: She was struggling to breathe. She was struggling breathing. And we got scared because she had no color at all on her skin. GUTIERREZ (voice-over): To Washington, D.C. where three-year-old Izzy Banki (ph) is recovering. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: Nobody wants to like hold their kid down and hold a mask on their face. And so she`s screaming and trying and trying to rip the breathing tubes out. And that breaks your heart as a parent. (END VIDEOTAPE) GUTIERREZ: And while COVID cases are trending downward nationwide, right now, there are concerns about new strains this winter. And of course, Savannah, concerns about that flu season that is already hitting many states hard around the country. Savannah? GUTHRIE: All right, Gabe Gutierrez, thank you. KOTB: Meantime, new unrest is rocking Iran with massive protests across the country more than a month after a young woman`s death while being held by the nation`s morality police. Some of those demonstrations turned deadly, emitted ongoing crackdown and that`s led to new sanctions from the United States, NBC`s chief international correspondent Keir Simmons has been following this story for us. Hey Keir, good morning. [07:10:00] KEIR SIMMONS, NBC NEWS CHIEF INTERNATIONAL CORRESPONDENT: Hoda, good morning to you. And we`re just getting more incredibly impactful video from the city of Mahabad in north western Iran. Take a look at this. This is a just this morning. You can see protesters targeting a building there. Later they seem to be throwing stones there. Looks like there is tear gas. The Kurdish rights group that posted this video says a number of government buildings have been taken over and that it`s also rounds the funeral of a man who was shot dead during protests yesterday. (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) SIMMONS (voice-over): This morning, a powerful image seen around the world. A young woman not wearing a headscarf stands on the roof of a car hands in the air as crowds attempt to reach the grave of Mahsa Amini. And near the cemetery, this video from an independent Kurdish human rights organization, captioned the resistance is glorious. Huge numbers across Iran determined to mourn and to protest the death of the 22-year-old, marking 40 days after she died in the hospital, the morality police targeting her for allegedly violating the country`s strict clothing code. In the capital of Tehran, clashes with the security forces and the sound of gunfire. In Mahsa`s hometown, they shouted women, life, freedom. And these demonstrators daring to chant freedom, freedom, enough of the despotism. Then images like this one, smoke rising told them another violent crackdown there. Reports say live rounds were used and tear gas. The Iranian authorities switching off the internet in the city. But a semi official news agency reporting at least 10,000 demonstrated. Thousands of miles away the White House announcing sanctions targeting more than a dozen Iranian officials. KARINE JEAN-PIERRE , WHITE HOUSE PRESS SECRETARY: Our message to Iran is very, very clear, stop killing your people and stop sending weapons to Russia to kill Ukrainians. SIMMONS (voice-over): A dramatic change from earlier this year when the Biden administration was trying to negotiate a nuclear deal with Iran. But this morning, there is no sign of compromise in Tehran and no backing down by these young female protesters and the many men out on the streets in support. (END VIDEOTAPE) SIMMONS : And just underscoring how incredibly tense it is in Iran, Hoda, a news of a shooting that was not related to the protests, 15 worshippers were killed, ISIS claiming responsibility for that. The government blaming foreign terrorists. It just emphasizes how incredible it is that these protesters are coming out on the streets day after day to support Mahsa Amini. KOTB: Yes, and worth repeating, too, that as you said, it`s not just women on those streets, it looked like equal numbers of men that we were seeing in those videos all with the same cause. All right, Keir Simmons for us in London. Kier, thank you. GUTHRIE: Back home, we`ve got new concerns about energy bills this winter. We haven`t even handed out the candy to trick or treaters. headline: MEET THE PRESS for November 6, 2022, NBC
story_text: [09:00:18] (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) CHUCK TODD, HOST, NBC`S "MEET THE PRESS WITH CHUCK TODD": This Sunday... PRESIDENT JOSEPH R. BIDEN, JR.: Vote. Get out and vote. TODD: ... battle for control. GOV. RON DESANTIS, (R) FLORIDA: I think Republicans are going to win the House and the Senate. I think they`re going to do both. TODD: Republicans need to flip just one seat to gain control of the Senate and only five seats to win control of the House. KEITH PEKAUI, CANDIDATE FOR U.S. REPRESENTATIVE, (R) ILLINOIS: I want you to watch Nancy Pelosi hand me that gavel. (APPLAUSE) TODD: This morning, the results of our final NBC News poll before the midterms and what it says about the GOP`s chances of taking complete power back on Capitol Hill. Plus, democracy at risk. BIDEN: You can`t love your country only when you win. TODD: President Biden issues a dire warning about election deniers and the risk for our electoral system. But will those warnings from Democrats resonate with economically challenged swing voters in the final push before Election Day? And, very soon... FORMER PRESIDENT DONALD J. TRUMP: I will very, very, very probably do it again, OK? TODD: Will former President Trump announce his 2024 bid before we finish counting the 2022 vote? My guest this morning, Florida`s Republican Senator Rick Scott , the chair of the GOP`s campaign arm; and New York Congressman Sean Patrick Maloney , the chair of the House Democratic campaign arm. Plus... (UNKNOWN): Are you ready to meet the press? TODD: Seventy-five years, from presidents to prime ministers, dictators to Civil Rights leaders, we mark 75 years as the destination where newsmakers come to make news. Joining me for insight and analysis are NBC News chief White House correspondent Kristen Welker; former Democratic senator from Missouri Claire McCaskill; former Republican governor of North Carolina Pat McCrory ; and Amy Walter, editor in chief of the "Cook Political Report." Welcome to Sunday. It`s "Meet the Press." ANNOUNCER: From NBC News headquarters in New York, the longest-running show in television history. This is a special edition of "Meet the Press With Chuck Todd." TODD: Well, good Sunday morning. On our 75th birthday, from our election headquarters here at Rockefeller Center in New York City, with just two days until Election Day, more than 40 million people have already cast ballots in the first national election since the January 6th attack on the U.S. Capitol. By the way, we expect a record midterm turnout, 120 million to 125 million, when all the votes are counted. At stake, all 435 House seats. Republicans need a net gain of just five to take control of that chamber. It is the smallest number of seats that the out-of-power party has needed since 1932. Thirty-five Senate seats are at stake this cycle. Republicans, of course, need just one Democratic seat to flip control of that chamber. There are also 36 governor`s races, including in some key 2024 presidential battlegrounds like Arizona, Florida, Georgia, Michigan, Nevada, Pennsylvania and Wisconsin. And in our final pre-election poll, conducted over the last three days, Republicans do appear to have the momentum. Just how big is that momentum? The question is whether Democrats can prevent what former President Obama once called a "shellacking." The president`s travel in the final stretch says it all about how the Democrats believe the election is going. Outside of the Philadelphia stop with Obama yesterday, President Biden has spent the final days of his campaign not in purple states but in blue states, California, New Mexico, Illinois and New York, where he`ll be campaigning later today in suburban New York City, Westchester County. And here`s why. Biden`s job approval rating sits at 44 percent in this final NBC News poll. By the way, all-time low with independents. His approval rating is just 28 percent. And let me put this in context for you. What does a job rating mean? Some people believe it`s the single most important indicator to understand where a midterm election is going. Bill Clinton`s 44 percent job approval rating translated into a 54-seat loss for his party. A 45 percent job approval rating for President Obama in 2010 translated to 63 lost House seats. Forty-six percent for President Trump, 40 House seat loss for his party. So what will 44 percent give us? And here`s, to me, the number you probably ought to care about the most in this poll, the state of the U.S. economy. Eighty-one percent tell us they are dissatisfied. This is the second highest number we`ve ever recorded. The last time it was this high was just before the 2010 election. And you know how that one went. All right. The generic congressional ballot here. We have it dead even, 47- 47. It`s a slight uptick for the Republicans from two weeks ago, when it was 47-46. Here`s something to keep in mind. Essentially a tie race probably gives the Republicans the five or six seats they need. [09:05:06] For every percentage point that they lead the Democrats, that`s probably anywhere from another five to 10 seats that would be added to their total. Just something to watch for on election night. All right. This is key, and this is something that should make Democrats relieved this weekend. Interest in this election, enthusiasm. Democrats have now matched the Republicans, dead even. In 2018 they had a slight lead. And of course the Democrats had the better night. But let me go inside the numbers, and why there`s still some warning signs here for the Democrats. There are two enthusiasm numbers in particular that I want to point -- I want to highlight here, African-American voters and young voters. And as you can see, remember Democrats had a good night in 2018. And right now African-American voters are not quite at their 2018 levels, and young voters are not quite at their -- at their 2018 levels, but look at seniors. Seniors are a little bit more. So this is why Republicans feel good about the end of this. We also asked folks to send us what message -- if you could send a message with your vote to Congress, what would you say with it? And here`s our word cloud response. And as you can see, "Fix Economy," the number one message that was sent from voters. And essentially tied for second here, "End Partisanship" and "Women`s Rights." So essentially the three big issues of the economy, abortion rights and the democracy, all represented here. And you can see the voters are engaged on this. By the way, given what happened to Paul Pelosi, we asked voters about the current climate of political violence. Voters are now more likely to view our political rhetoric as an important contributing factor, rather than seeing what happened as some isolated incident. And when we asked who is responsible for this elevated rhetoric, social media companies come out on top, almost universally blamed for our current political climate. Cable news media nearly matches them, then Trump, then Republican officials, Democratic officials, and President Biden there at the bottom. Let`s turn back now to the battle for the House. Because I want to point out some key numbers here for you to keep track of. In the seven times since the Truman era, when the president`s job rating has been below 50 percent in his first midterm election, which is what we`re staring at with this one, that president`s party has lost an average of 43 House seats. And guess what? This cycle, there are 44 Democratic held seats that are rated as lean or toss-up by the Cook Political Report, and there`s just 20 Republican held seats that are in those same categories in the House battleground. In 2018, you can see it was a much more lopsided battleground here, with the Republicans basically defending almost everything and Democrats barely defending anything. In this cycle, the defense for the Democrats includes the district where Congressman Sean Patrick Maloney is running after redistricting. He also chairs the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee charged with getting House Democrats elected and keeping their majority. And Congressman Maloney joins me now. Welcome back to "Meet the Press," two days before the election, sir. REP. SEAN PATRICK MALONEY , CHAIR OF DEMOCRATIC CONGRESSIONAL CAMPAIGN COMMITTEE & (D) NEW YORK: Good to be with you. TODD: I do want to remind people -- only twice this century have we had a national election without party control changing of either the White House, House, or Senate. WALTER: That`s right. TODD: So keep that in mind. KRISTEN WELKER, NBC NEWS CHIEF WHITE HOUSE CORRESPONDENT: Absolutely. Well, Democrats and those who are close to President Biden say, if we can hold Republicans to 20 seats in the House, that`s a pretty good night. Because look at how many seats former President Obama and former President Trump lost. Well, we`re talking about 60 and 40 respectively. And so I think that that`s part of why you`re seeing the president try to focus on this messaging of democracy, that democracy is on the ballot. Some Democrats scratching their heads, why is he talking about that and not the economy? The pushback is, because that`s what`s going to energize the base and try to mitigate those losses that they`re trying to stave off. It`s a risky strategy, though, Chuck, because as you`ve been talking about with all of your guests, the main issues are still inflation and the economy. TODD: You know, Claire, I`ve had Democrats quietly say, "Look, it better be only 20 seats." Because they want to be able to get it back in `24. And if it gets too big, and it becomes hard to get back in `24, that`s double for the Senate. CLAIRE MCCASKILL, NBC NEWS POLITICAL ANALYST: Well, here`s the deal. Listen, this time of year is exciting for all of us who are so close to it. But it also gives me a giant headache. I mean, it is like, so ridiculous. TODD: Well, you`ve been on the ballot. How does it feel when you`re on the ballot? MCCASKILL: I have won when the polls said I couldn`t and I have lost when the polls said I would win, so I am not a big believer in all of the horse race stuff. I think a lot of people are motivated to vote. And I think historically, to call it a wave it would have to be the same size as Donald Trump lost after his first two years in the presidency. We would have to lose more than 40 seats, more than 60 seats, for it not to be lining up with what happens historically. And inflation is really hard, but what most Americans don`t get, this is global. This is not Joe Biden . We have some of the least inflation in the developed world. But he has not been able to really get that home, because when bread costs that much and when eggs cost that much, that`s what people vote about. TODD: You know, it`s interesting, Republicans start at such a high point, though. They only need 20-25 to hit the number that they`ve had in the past on this. Pat, are your sources in North Carolina telling you? What are you hearing? Is it a polarized electorate, or do you hear, do you see a break? PAT MCCRORY, NBC NEWS CONTRIBUTOR: In North Carolina, it feels like a wave. But as Claire and I know, I`ve played this game and I`ve been played by the game. The last week or two is all about emotion, no content. In fact, most of this election has been about emotion and no content, which is a very sad commentary. TODD: By the way, do you know that 70 percent of people told us they made up their minds before Labor Day? MCCASKILL: Yes. TODD: seventy percent. MCCRORY: If the negative ads haven`t worked by now, they`re not working, if you try to hit emotionally. They`ve heard it all. They`re sick of TV ads right now. But the Dems are trying to play on the emotion of democracy, abortions, cutting Social Security, which is an old tried, sometimes very effective effort, and Trump. Although they haven`t talked about Trump as much as I thought they would. The Republicans I think still have the winners. Inflation, especially related to energy, which Rick didn`t mention. The gas prices, the price of egg, the price of turkey as Thanksgiving`s coming up. That is what everyone`s reminded of every day. That`s why I give advantage to the Republicans. Immigration. Biden and Harris are an issue also. They don`t consume a room. They don`t have standing when they walk in the room. Some people do. Obama does. Biden and Harris don`t. TODD: In fairness, nobody has standing when their approval ratings are in the low 40s. It`s amazing how much your standing gets better when you`re in the 50 percent, in fairness. Joe Biden was a 1 percent candidate, he had no standing in `08. MCCRORY: Well, I think the issue`s going to be -- TODD: You know, right? In fairness. MCCRORY: Yeah, the issue`s going to be, with Trump going to Ohio and Florida, which is a whole other issue. TODD: Well -- MCCRORY: Biden going, are they going to turn off more voters? TODD: Well, I was just going to say let me bring this up, this was Donald Trump last night. He is clearly focused on an election. MCCASKILL: Wait, wait. TODD: Just not this one. MCCASKILL: He`s focused on himself? TODD: Yeah, I know. MCCASKILL: No. No, he`s not. TODD: And he isn`t focused on this election. Here he is, rattling off poll numbers to his rally-goers the other night. Listen to this from last night. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) DONALD TRUMP , FORMER PRESIDENT: There it is, Trump at 71. Ron DeSanctimonius at 10 percent. Mike Pence at 7. Oh, Mike`s doing better than I thought. Liz Cheney , there`s no way she`s at 4 percent. There`s no way. There`s no way. But we`re at 71 to 10 to 7 to 4. (END VIDEO CLIP) [09:45:01] TODD: Ron DeSanctimonius. Okay, this idea that we were overhyping a Trump/DeSantis rivalry? No. WELKER: No, we`re not. I mean, he already has a nickname for a potential rival. Chuck, I had a conversation overnight with a high-level source who`s been in constant communication with former President Trump who said he very seriously considered announcing last night or sometime this weekend. His aides, advisors have urged him not to do that. Cooler heads prevailed, I`m told, and he didn`t. He all but said that on the record, by the way. He all but walked up to the line of announcing that he was running for president again by saying, I will very, very, very, he added a fourth "very," probably do it. He said, but I want the focus to be on these candidates. And I am told he is just itching to announce to potentially freeze the field. But the question is, will he? TODD: I`ve talked to people that said the smartest thing he could do is hurry up and announce. It would freeze the field. But, Claire, if you could have Donald Trump do one thing in the last 48 hours, is it this? MCCASKILL: Yes. TODD: That`s what I thought. MCCASKILL: Absolutely. Go for it Donald. MCCRORY: Oh, Claire. TODD: This is the last thing you want him doing, right. MCCRORY: If I`m Republican, I don`t want Trump to take away from the message that`s going to win. And I don`t want -- if I`m a Democrat, I don`t want Biden out there either. I said that-- WELKER: Yeah, Democrats are welcoming this. No doubt. TODD: When we come back, our guide to how to watch election night. With election counts that could take days, we`re going to give you some clues about where to look on Tuesday night itself. (COMMERCIAL BREAK) TODD: Welcome back. Data Download time. Even though we`re all counting down to Tuesday, let`s be realistic. It`s highly likely we will not know the full results of the midterms on election night. In fact, by 6:00 a.m., the day after Election Day 2020, look at all the battleground states where we were not at 95 percent, let alone 99 percent, right? Look, Wisconsin, Ohio, North Carolina, Georgia and Florida. We should at least know where these are trending, we should know if Georgia`s in a runoff by 6:00 a.m. But look at the problem here. Pennsylvania, 78 percent. New Hampshire, just 75 percent reporting. Arizona, Nevada. The states that are going to decide this majority, we`re not going to know the day after the election. But we`re going to get some clues about the House very early on. [09:50:00] Virginia and Indiana, their polls close by 7:00 p.m., and they`re both fast-counting states. So here`s what we`re going to learn. Elaine Luria , this should be the first district Republicans should be able to pick up. If they`re not picking this up, it`s suddenly a much better night for Democrats than people thought. Virginia 07 and Indiana 01 should be the next two that Republicans flip if they`re going to have as good of a night as they think they`re going to have. Let me add another district here. If for some reason this turns into a red tsunami, keep an eye on the 10th congressional district in Virginia. That was the one Barbara Comstock held. If that flips, then you know a huge Republican night. Now, did African Americans turn out? Two places to watch: Milwaukee County and Philadelphia County. Democrats need huge margins here. And if the African American vote shows up and it looks like 2018, then they should feel pretty good. But if those numbers are lower, then you know that there was a problem. How about young voters? Dane County`s a good place to check in Wisconsin, home of the University of Wisconsin . Centre County`s home of Penn State University . Will the Democrats get these margins and the raw vote that they need? That`s two places to look for. Now as for Republicans, they want a huge rural turnout. Well, Putnam County in Ohio, look at that. He had a 62-point margin in 2018. Will it get bigger? That`s something to watch there. Chattooga County in Georgia, this is Marjorie Taylor Greene`s district. How big will the Republican turnout be? That should matter. And then also, if Republicans are going to have a really good night, they`ve got to improve their numbers in suburban counties. Delaware County`s a place to look here. Well, this is a place Democrats have been inching and eroding the Republican gains here. Will that continue or not? Cherokee County, sort of an exurb if you will of Atlanta. Democrats have been making some progress there. Let`s see what happens in 2022. So bottom line is this -- those are the places to watch. But it`s going to be election week, not election night. Up next, we mark a milestone for this program, 75 years as the longest- running show in the history of television. (COMMERCIAL BREAK) [09:55:52] TODD: Welcome back. We are celebrating our diamond anniversary, 75 years of Meet the Press. It was November 6th, 1947 at 8:00 p.m. when NBC Television debuted this program. Now more than 3,500 episodes later, we`ve had 12 moderators. Thirteen presidents have answered questions here, including six while in office. Our legacy has evolved with the times, but the goal remains consistent: a fair exchange of views and perspective that gives our viewers important context on the issues of the day. Here`s a look at some of our memorable moments. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIPS) UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: Sir, are you ready to "Meet the Press"? UNIDENTIFIED MALE: I suppose I`m as ready as I will be. FIDEL CASTRO: Democracy is my ideal. REP. SHIRLEY CHISHOLM (D-NY): I understand that I have broken the ice. REV. MARTIN LUTHER KING , JR., CIVIL RIGHTS LEADER: We confront the fact that the Negro is still a victim. TODD: Were you bitter, ever? REP. JOHN LEWIS (D-GA): I was not bitter then. I`m not bitter now. JIMMY CARTER , FORMER PRESIDENT: Neither I nor the American people would support the sending of an American team to Moscow. FORMER SEN. JOHN KERRY (D-MA): This war can be ended, and it should be ended now. TIM RUSSERT, NBC NEWS MODERATOR: Full wrath. That`s a very strong statement to the Afghans this morning. DICK CHENEY , FORMER VICE PRESIDENT: It is, indeed. RICHARD NIXON , FORMER PRESIDENT: The Watergate matter should have been handled properly. RONALD REAGAN , FORMER PRESIDENT: Some people, when you say that word conservative, automatically think you are talking about a monster who eats his young. RUSSERT: So you want to be president. THEN-GOV. BILL CLINTON (D), ARKANSAS: I do. THEN-SEN. JOHN MCCAIN (R-AZ): Do Sarah Palin and I disagree on a specific issue? Yeah, because we`re both mavericks. COLIN POWELL, FORMER SECRETARY OF STATE: He is a new generation and for that reason I`ll be voting for Senator Barack Obama . BARACK OBAMA , FORMER PRESIDENT: We are going to be able to not just blunt the momentum of ISIL. Ultimately, we`re going to defeat `em. JOE BIDEN , THEN-VICE PRESIDENT: Men marrying men, women marrying women and heterosexual men and women marrying one other are entitled to the same exact rights. DONALD TRUMP , FORMER PRESIDENT: In four years, you`re going to be interviewing me, and you`re going to say, "What a great job you`ve done, President Trump." TOM BROKAW, NBC NEWS MODERATOR: Because if it is Sunday -- RUSSERT: If it`s Sunday -- DAVID GREGORY, NBC NEWS MODERATOR: If it`s Sunday -- TODD: If it`s Sunday, it`s Meet the Press. (END VIDEO CLIPS) TODD: Well, look. I`m going to make you guys toast. You`re not toasting me. We`re toasting everybody. WELKER: Cheers. We`re toasting -- TODD: And you`ve all picked your favorite race that you`re following on election night. We don`t have a lot of time. So, Pat, what is yours? MCCRORY: My race, my House seat, North Carolina, where I live. Jeff Jackson, Pat Harrigan. TODD: All right. MCCRORY: There -- sadly, there`s been violence. And how the public will respond to violence, possibly due to a commercial. TODD: Oh, wow. Claire? MCCASKILL: Nevada. TODD: The whole state? MCCASKILL: It`s going to tell us about the state of election deniers, Hispanic voters, and whether or not a really good incumbent can hold on. TODD: Very quick -- WELKER: Georgia Senate race. Will it go to a runoff? TODD: Yeah. Ruin our Thanksgiving. WALTER: You took mine. Of course, Virginia 7. This is a seat that went for Biden -- TODD: Yeah. AMY WALTER: - in 2020, went for the Republican governor in 2021. TODD: It`s as swingy as it gets. All right. Before we go, a quick programming note: however you join us on Tuesday for complete election coverage of election night beginning at 6:00 Eastern on NBC News Now and at 8:00 p.m. on NBC and simulcast on NBC News Now. That`s all for today and for 75 years of todays. Thanks for watching. We`ll be back next week because if it`s Sunday, it`s "Meet the Press". headline: The Governor`s Race In Georgia Too Early To Call Between Brian Kemp And Stacey Abrams
story_text: LESTER HOLT: Dozens of governors seats are also in play being driven by issues ranging from inflation to abortion. Blayne Alexander is following the key races. Blayne, what should we know? BLAYNE ALEXANDER, NBC NEWS CORRESPONDENT (on camera): Well, Lester, when I`ve spoken to voters, both of those issues came up and more. So much of it just depends on the state. And tonight, Lester, many of those key governor`s races are very tight. (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) B. ALEXANDER, NBC NEWS CORRESPONDENT (voiceover): Tonight, it`s not just control of Congress that`s at stake, also what for grabs, 36 critical Governor seats, including here in Georgia, Republican Governor Brian Kemp`s rematch against Stacey Abrams . A win would make her the first Black woman governor in U.S. history. A big focus for Kemp, his early decision to reopen Georgia during COVID. GOV. BRIAN KEMP (R-GA): She was criticizing me for just simply giving you the opportunity to go back to work or to open your business. B. ALEXANDER: Abrams, like many Democrats around the country emphasizing abortion access. STACEY ABRAMS (D-GA), GUBERNATORIAL CANDIDATE: We know for women in Georgia, this is the lethal decision. B. ALEXANDER: In Arizona, it`s a marquee matchup between Democrat Katie Hobbs and Kari Lake, a Trump-backed Republican who has repeatedly denied the 2020 election results and is already casting doubt on this election. KARI LAKE (R-AZ), GUBERNATORIAL CANDIDATE: We`re so ready for fair elections, aren`t we? I`m worried about tomorrow. KATIE HOBBS (D-AZ), GUBERNATORIAL CANDIDATE: When people like Kari Lake denied the results of the election, we stood firm. B. ALEXANDER: TWO other contests to watch feature Democratic incumbents in tight races. Michigan Governor Gretchen Whitmer in a tough fight against Republican Tudor Dixon and perhaps most surprising in deep blue New York where Governor Kathy Hochul is facing a serious challenge from Republican Lee Zeldin , who is focusing on rising crime. LEE ZELDIN (R-NY) GUBERNATORIAL CANDIDATE: Voters of all walks of life, Republicans, Democrats, and Independents, they`ve had enough. (END VIDEOTAPE) B. ALEXANDER (on camera): And Georgia officials say there have been very few lines at polling places today, they point to a record 2.5 million people who cast early votes. Lester? HOLT: Blayne Alexander, thank you. I want to bring in now our political director and moderator of "MEET THE PRESS," Chuck Todd. Chuck, you`ve been digging into the exit polls. What do voters seem to be most concerned about? CHUCK TODD, NBC NEWS POLITICAL DIRECTOR (on camera): Well, it will not surprise you. The number one issue overall, inflation. What`s interesting is that there`s only a five-point difference. Abortion came in second 27 percent. And then you see the other three issues you saw a lot in TV ads, crime, gun policy, and immigration. Inflation-breaking Republican, abortion-breaking Democrat. Crime-breaking Republican. Gun, if you pick guns, you broke Democrat and immigration by Republican. Let me show you by party. As you can see here, among Democrats, the most important issue was abortion. Among Republicans, the number one issue is inflation. And here`s the tiebreaker perhaps, the difference between getting 49 percent and 51 percent in some of the Senate races. Independents picked inflation. Now, let me give you a little teaser about some of the state polls, Lester. In two of our Senate battlegrounds, abortion topped inflation, Pennsylvania and New Hampshire. Just something to keep in mind tonight as we figure out who`s going to control the Senate. HOLT: Interesting trends starting to emerge. All right, Chuck, thanks very much. And our Chief Washington Correspondent Andrea Mitchell joins us now with some concerns that figured tough numbers about our exit polls. ANDREA MITCHELL, NBC NEWS CHIEF WASHINGTON CORRESPONDENT (on camera): Exactly. Well, as Chuck was just pointing out, the top issue was inflation. But abortion was a top concern among a lot more voters than we had expected and crime less than expected. But there`s something else that really stuck out to me. This early exit poll shows that 46 percent of voters say President Biden`s policies are hurting the country. Only 36 percent say they`re helping the country. 16 percent say his policies are not making a difference. Even some of Mr. Biden`s base voters, including Black voters and young voters, are not convinced that his policies are working. The President in the final weeks of the campaign has been saying that this election is a choice between his party and the Republicans and not a referendum on his presidency. But if voters ended up making their decision based on how they feel about his record -- his record, that`s not a good sign for Democrats. Lester? HOLT: All right, Andrea, thanks for that. Washington could look dramatically different in the days to come. How Congress have the Biden administration are strategizing for a big shift. Plus, we`ll take you inside a vote-counting center. Why it could take a while before the full picture of the elections is known. (COMMERCIAL BREAK) END Content and programming copyright 2022 NBCUniversal. ALL RIGHTS RESERVED. headline: The Issue That Turned Out To Be A Game-Changer In States Red And Blue
story_text: [19:20:00] LESTER HOLT: In the wake of the Supreme Court overturning Roe v Wade, the Midterm Elections saw a record number of abortion-related measures on the ballot. And in every state where voters had a direct say, they opted against restricting access. Here`s Yamiche Alcindor. (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) YAMICHE ALCINDOR, NBC NEWS WASHINGTON CORRESPONDENT (voiceover): Tonight, Democrats across the country are celebrating sweeping wins for supporters of abortion rights. JOSH SHAPIRO (D-PA), GUBERNATORIAL CANDIDATE: A woman`s right to choose one. SEN. MAGGIE HASSAN (D-NH): I will always, always keep fighting to protect a woman`s fundamental freedom. GOV. GRETCHEN WHITMER (D-MI): We will make Michigan a leader, a place where women make their own decisions. ALCINDOR: In Michigan, residents voted to enshrine abortion rights into the state constitution, an issue Governor Gretchen Whitmer and her running mate been a central part of their successful reelection campaign. WHITMER: This is a right that we are not going to go backwards on. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: I`m proud of my state. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: I don`t want the government in my bedroom. ALCINDOR: And abortion rights did drive people to the polls. It was the second most important issue to voters behind inflation. In addition to Michigan, voters in California and Vermont codified abortion rights into their state constitutions. And it wasn`t just blue states, voters in Kentucky and Montana shot down measures that could have restricted access. What do you make of that nationally? WHITMER: I think it`s a sign that the American public has had rights for 49 years. We`re not going to go backward. And so, whether it`s state by state we see this happen or hopefully at some point, you know, a national effort again, I think that this is where the fight is at the moment. ALCINDOR: Those against abortion rights not processing the results. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: I believe abortion is first-degree murder. ALCINDOR: Eric Scheidler from the Pro-Life Action League says he`s gearing up to continue their push. ERIC SCHEIDLER, EXECUTIVE DIRECTOR, PRO-LIFE ACTION LEAGUE: If we`ve learned anything over the past 50 years as a movement is that we`ve got to be able to take a punch. ALCINDOR: Still, Americans in five states send a clear message about reproductive rights. Yamiche Alcindor, NBC News, Detroit. (END VIDEOTAPE) HOLT: Coming up, their new mission: training troops to become teachers in "THOSE WHO SERVE." (COMMERCIAL BREAK) END Content and programming copyright 2022 NBCUniversal. headline: NBC NIGHTLY NEWS for November 9, 2022, NBC
story_text: [19:00:00] (COMMERCIAL BREAK) LESTER HOLT, NBC NEWS ANCHOR (on camera): Tonight, the Midterm Election cliffhanger. The battle for Congress still too close to call. (voiceover): The Senate and the House still up for grabs after the Democrats held off a red wave. President Biden at the White House today calling it a good day for democracy. In Georgia, the tight Senate race headed to a runoff. In Pennsylvania, John Fetterman defeating Mehmet Oz. And in Florida, a big reelection win for Governor Ron DeSantis setting up a possible 2024 showdown with Donald Trump . And what President Biden said today about his own 2024 plans. Our team across the country with a race is still in play. Also breaking tonight, Nicole strengthening into a hurricane and taking aim at Florida flooding on the coast. Buildings collapsing into the sea, mandatory evacuations ordered, the new track tonight. The potential major setback for Russia ordering a retreat from the key city of Kherson in southern Ukraine. Why Kyiv is skeptical. WNBA star Brittney Griner moved to a penal colony in Russia. How the U.S. is responding. Facebook `s parent company Meta laying off thousands. Why Mark Zuckerberg is slashing jobs on the heels of concept Twitter . And "THOSE WHO SERVE," the veterans answering a new call in the classroom. ANNOUNCER: This is NBC NIGHTLY NEWS with Lester Holt. HOLT (on camera): Good evening, everyone, again, tonight from our election headquarters in New York. It was a good day for democracy, President Biden`s first public reaction to yesterday`s Midterm Elections in which Democrats defied the gravity of broad voter dissatisfaction and history itself to avoid massive losses in that widely-predicted Republican wave. Let me tell you from the start tonight, much of our reporting this evening is framed by what we don`t know and that is which party will control Congress. At this hour, control of the Senate is still up for grabs with some races too close to call, while the Georgia Senate contest is headed toward a December runoff election. And the House still in play for both sides, though Republicans currently lead. But there is broad agreement that these were not the results most expected, an unpopular president faced with a bad economy managing to avoid the fate of his predecessors. The President`s message to voters tonight, I get it. Our team has fanned out again this evening watching the count and the issues that shaped the vote starting tonight with Kristen Welker at the White House. (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) KRISTEN WELKER, NBC NEWS CHIEF WHITE HOUSE CORRESPONDENT (voiceover): 24 hours after ballots were cast, tonight, control of Congress is still up for grabs. President Biden insisting it was a good night for Democrats. JOE BIDEN , PRESIDENT OF THE UNITED STATES: While the press and the pundits are predicting a giant red wave, it didn`t happen. WELKER: Republicans who had been hoping to take the House in a red wave now just looking for a win. The GOP still favored to take over but with a smaller margin than expected. REP. KEVIN MCCARTHY (R-CA): We will be in the majority and Nancy Pelosi will be in the minority. WELKER: Much more suspense in the Senate where Republicans still could gain the one seat they need to take control but Democrats could hang on to with NBC News projecting races that are too early to call in Nevada and in Arizona. And in Georgia, the showdown between Democratic senator Raphael Warnock and Republican Herschel Walker , NBC News Now projects will go to a runoff. SEN. RAPHAEL WARNOCK (D-GA): We always knew that this race would be close. HERSCHEL WALKER (R-GA), SENATE CANDIDATE: I`m like Ricky Bobby. I don`t come to lose. WELKER: Democrats` biggest win of the night coming in the critical Pennsylvania Senate race. Democrat John Fetterman , six months after suffering a stroke, defeating Republican Dr. Mehmet Oz. JOHN FETTERMAN (D-PA), SENATE CANDIDATE: We did what we needed to do. WELKER: Republicans with big victories too including Georgia Governor Brian Kemp easily defeating Democrat Stacey Abrams . And in the biggest win of the night, Florida Republican Governor Ron DeSantis winning reelection in a 19- point landslide, sweeping virtually every county in the state, including heavily Latino Miami Dade. GOV. RON DESANTIS (R-FL): We reject woke ideology. We will never ever surrender to the woke mob. Florida is where woke goes to die. WELKER: DeSantis seen as a possible 2024 presidential contender where he could face former President Trump who had a tough night. His endorsed candidates in Ohio and North Carolina won but several of Mr. Trump`s other handpick candidates in key races, including New Hampshire, Michigan, and Pennsylvania all lost. Meanwhile, President Biden was asked what he will do differently with most Americans saying they`re dissatisfied with the state of the country. [19:05:08] BIDEN: Nothing because they`re just finding out what we`re doing. The more they know about what we`re doing, the more support there is. WELKER: And we pressed him about running again. Two-thirds of Americans in exit polls say that they don`t think you should run for reelection. What is your message to them? And how does that factor into your final decision about whether or not to run for reelection? BIDEN: It doesn`t. WELKER: What`s your message to those two-thirds of Americans? BIDEN: Watch me. (END VIDEOTAPE) HOLT: Kristen, the President is likely facing divided government. Did he talk about working with Republicans how it would go? WELKER (on camera): Well, Lester, he did. The President says he`ll call top House Republican Kevin McCarthy tonight and says he`s hoping for bipartisanship on issues like Ukraine. The President also saying he`ll make his decision on running early next year. Lester? HOLT: Kristen Welker at the White House, thanks. That pivotal Senate race in Georgia, as we said, is neck and neck. Gabe Gutierrez is there. And Gabe, what can we expect in this coming run off? GABE GUTIERREZ, NBC NEWS NATIONAL CORRESPONDENT (on camera): Lester, this is what both campaigns and many voters did not want, another month of campaigning. But incumbent Raphael Warnock and challenger Herschel Walker are already fundraising ahead of the runoff now set for December 6. Neither managed to get 50 percent of the vote. But in the governor`s race here, Republican incumbent, Brian Kemp easily won reelection over Democrat Stacey Abrams . And that suggests some Republicans may have split their tickets in the Senate contest and voted for Warnock. Now, back in 2020, this state had to runoffs that tipped the balance of power in the Senate. And based on ad spending back then, it`s possible that we could see upwards of $200 million dollars in TV ads here over the next several weeks. Lester? HOLT: Gabe Gutierrez in Atlanta, thanks. Another key state in play. Arizona remains in flux both in the U.S. Senate race between incumbent Mark Kelly and Republican Blake Masters and in the governor`s race. Vaughn Hillyard is in Phoenix tonight. Vaughn, where do things stand right now? VAUGHN HILLYARD, NBC NEWS CORRESPONDENT (on camera): Yes, Lester, at least a half a million votes have yet to be counted here in Arizona. And as soon as we may know who wins this race for governor and Senate, may be tomorrow night. Elections officials continue to process and tabulate these mail-in votes. And there`s an important batch of votes that are expected to be released tomorrow. These results are going to be mail ballots that were hand delivered by voters instead of being mailed back. In 2018, these votes, they trended towards Democrats, but in 2020, towards Republicans. Now, one other note that if these margins remain close, this is a situation where if these -- any of these races finish with -- finished within a half a percentage point, that it would trigger an automatic recount under state law that wouldn`t begin until December. Lester? HOLT: All right, Vaughn, thanks very much for that. I want to bring in our political director and moderator of "MEET THE PRESS," Chuck Todd. Chuck, Monday night, you and I stood right here. And we talked about whether polarization could be the guiding factor in the election was it? CHUCK TODD, NBC NEWS POLITICAL DIRECTOR (on camera): Look, I don`t think -- I think it was because I don`t know if campaigns mattered. Let me show you Ohio. Tim Ryan ran up almost a perfect race for a Democrat in Ohio. And yet, it didn`t matter how well his campaign win. Look at this. He basically only performed 1.5 percentage points better than Biden. Essentially, the state reverted to its 2020 partisan norm. Let me take you to Colorado, another example but in the other direction. A Republican running a really good race in Colorado, and it got them all of less than a percentage point better than Donald Trump . The point is, it didn`t matter if it was a blue state or a red state. What the partisan makeup was in 2020 seemed to dictate what the result was in 2022. HOLT: All right, Chuck, thanks. Let me turn to Andrea Mitchell now who`s been looking at the Biden effect. How much credit does the President get for staving off this red wave? ANDREA MITCHELL, NBC NEWS CHIEF WASHINGTON CORRESPONDENT (on camera): Well, Lester, President Biden is touting the stronger than expected results. But our exit polls showed more voters believed his policies were hurting the country than helping. So, can Biden take credit for Democrats overperformance? Another one of our exit polls shows President Biden has less of an impact on voters decisions in this midterms than any other President has had in the last decade. That may explain why despite the President`s low approval ratings, Democrats won in states like Pennsylvania and Michigan and avoided the kind of shellacking President Obama suffered when he lost 63 seats in 2010. This election could be the best Midterm performance for any president`s party in the last 20 years, Lester. HOLT A lot to analyze. Andrea, thanks very much. And even though this election is still full of question marks, it`s already setting the stage for 2024 especially for former President Trump and his potential rivals. Here`s Ali Vitali. (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) ALI VITALI, NBC NEWS CAPITOL HILL CORRESPONDENT (voiceover): Technically, it`s still 2022. But politically -- DONALD TRUMP , FORMER PRESIDENT OF THE UNITED STATES: Stay tuned. VITALI: -- it`s open season on the 2024 Presidential Race. Launched to the front the Republican PAC Tuesday night, Florida Governor Ron DeSantis -- [19:10:03] GOV. RON DESANTIS (R-FL): Thank you for a historic landslide victory. VITALI: Or as the New York Post front page blared, DeFuture. DESANTIS: We`ve got so much more to do, and I have only begun to fight. VITALI: Supporters in the room chanting for two more years. His decisive win here in Florida drawing attention including from fellow Floridian Donald Trump who had his once ally turned likely rival top of mine this weekend. TRUMP: Trump at 71, Ron DeSanctimonious at 10 percent. VITALI: Trump`s handpick candidates suffering a string of losses Tuesday night. TRUMP : I think if they win, I should get all the credit. And if they lose, I should not be blamed at all. WELKER: Who do you think would be the tougher competitor, Ron DeSantis or former President Trump? And how is that factoring into your decision? BIDEN: It`d be fun to watch them take on each other. VITALI: But it`s not just DeSantis eyeing potential bids. GOV. BRIAN KEMP (R-GA): So, give him a big Georgia welcome. VITALI: Former VP Mike Pence also mulling a run, publishing a book So Help Me God out next week, possibly the same day Trump himself could cement his intentions to run again. TRUMP " I`m going to be making a very big announcement. VITALI: Other former Trump officials like Nikki Haley and Mike Pompeo , Senate allies Ted Cruz and Rick Scott , and governors from Arkansas and South Dakota all talked about as possible 2024 contenders. (END VIDEOTAPE) VITALI (on camera): And Pence releasing the first excerpt from his memoir tonight detailing his harrowing experience at the Capitol on January 6, and underscoring his indelible differences with Donald Trump over that day. Lester? HOLT: Ali Vitali, thank you. And meanwhile, Florida is bracing once again for a hurricane. Dylan Dreyer is here. Dylan, Hurricane Nicole is gaining steam. DYLAN DREYER, NBC NEWS METEOROLOGIST (on camera): Yes, it is a hurricane now as it moves through the Bahamas and will likely maintain that category one status as it moves to the west, right now at 12 miles per hour. And then we are looking for the chance of about eight inches of rain across parts of Florida. And this is going to make landfall tonight into early tomorrow morning. And then it`s going to race across the state of Florida, perhaps making another landfall, as it moves its way towards the Gulf of Mexico and then it takes this rapid turn to the north. It`s going to bring all of this rain up into the Northeast where we could see about three to four inches of rain. However, it`s the storm surge down through Daytona Beach and the Jacksonville and the Fort Pierce, the three to five-foot storm surge that could lead to more beach erosion and also some significant flooding right along the coastline. The only saving grace Lester is that the storm hits during low tide. It`s tomorrow morning`s high tide that we`ll worry about. HOLT: All right, Dylan, thanks very much. Let`s get the view from the ground. We want to head to Florida. That`s where NBC Sam Brock is watching as things turn for the worst. Sam? SAM BROCK, NBC NEWS CORRESPONDENT (on camera): Lester, good evening. The size of the storm is massive just six weeks after Ian. And while many people saw Ian did its damage on the west side of Florida, here on the East Coast, it caused all kinds of erosion. Just look at this beach and how it`s dwindled, exposing the coastline to a direct hit. (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) BROCK (voiceover): Tonight, it`s a state of emergency across nearly 50 Florida counties as ocean waters swell from the Space Coast to Daytona Beach. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: We watched a huge chunk of this backyard just dissolve and fall into the ocean this morning. BROCK: Dramatic images show a public restroom sliding into the ocean in Volusia County, while a couple of hours south, the ground literally crumbling beneath a home on Hutchinson Island as Florida getting slammed by the first November hurricane in almost 40 years. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: I just can`t believe that we`re having a storm in November. BROCK: These restaurant owners taking stock of the situation and considering closing down as plywood adorns the Cocoa Beach Pier along with caution tape. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: We boarded up the house and we have our generator. BROCK: Moms like Margaret Lever are on the move but not leaving the storm zone even after Hurricane Ian delivered some harsh lessons only weeks earlier. Did hurricane and changed the mentality for anyone. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: A little bit, not too much. BROCK: Instead of passengers boarding, airport gates are boarded up and school districts across the state are closing even as far south as Miami and Broward. WAYNE IVEY, SHERIFF, BREVARD COUNTY: You know you and you know your place where you live and where you take refuge. BROCK: This historically rare event -- UNIDENTIFIED MALE: The storms are coming later, storms are coming bigger. BROCK: -- ready to potentially wreak havoc on a state still in recovery mode. Sam Brock, NBC News Jensen Beach, Florida. (END VIDEOTAPE) HOLT: In 60 seconds, the major retreat ordered by Russia in Ukraine, a troubling new turn for basketball superstar Brittney Griner in Russia, and what Mark Zuckerberg just said about cuts at Facebook `s parent company. After weeks of Ukrainian advances, the Russian military announced it is retreating from Kherson, the first major city that fell after the invasion began in February. Kyiv is skeptical, however, fearing the announcement could be a ruse to lead Ukrainian troops into a trap. And in Russia, WNBA star Brittney Griner has been moved to a penal colony in an undisclosed location according to her attorneys. Griner was sentenced in Russia in August to nine years in prison on drug possession charges. Despite the stalled efforts to free Griner, President Biden said today he is determined to bring her home.
