MARK ZUCKERBERG , CEO, FACEBOOK : I want to say, you know, upfront that I take full responsibility for this decision. COSTELLO: The CEO of Facebook parent company, Meta , announcing the company would be laying off 11,000 employees, a stunning 13 percent of the workforce, saying the company needs to become leaner and more efficient. ZUCKERBERG: It is one of the hardest calls that I`ve had to make in the 18 years of running the company. COSTELLO: The trouble, Meta ramped up hiring during and after the pandemic while spending billions on Zuckerberg`s vision of a virtual reality future called the Metaverse. But the metaverse may now have to wait Mehta stock is down 70 percent this year, profits down 50 percent in the third quarter. With the economy slowing, Meta is the latest tech companies squeezed by a sharp decline in advertising revenue. JULIA BOORSTIN, CNBC SENIOR MEDIA AND TECH CORRESPONDENT: This is Mark Zuckerberg saying we grew too fast. We assumed that the boom times would continue. COSTELLO: And they haven`t. BOORSTIN: This is a really tough time right now for any ad-supported platform. COSTELLO: Meta employees took to social media of course to vent. "The inevitable has happened to me. I woke up today to news I was being laid off," wrote one. Another wrote, "Gutted, devastated, sobbing all morning." (END VIDEOTAPE) COSTELLO (on camera): Meanwhile, Tesla stock closed near a two year low today after Elon Musk sold nearly $4 billion dollars-worth of stock following his purchase of Twitter . And tonight, President Biden said Musk`s relationship with other countries should be looked into. Lester? HOLT: OK, Tom, thanks. Up next, the issue that turned out to be a game-changer in states red and blue. (COMMERCIAL BREAK) [19:20:00] HOLT: In the wake of the Supreme Court overturning Roe v Wade, the Midterm Elections saw a record number of abortion-related measures on the ballot. And in every state where voters had a direct say, they opted against restricting access. Here`s Yamiche Alcindor. (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) YAMICHE ALCINDOR, NBC NEWS WASHINGTON CORRESPONDENT (voiceover): Tonight, Democrats across the country are celebrating sweeping wins for supporters of abortion rights. JOSH SHAPIRO (D-PA), GUBERNATORIAL CANDIDATE: A woman`s right to choose one. SEN. MAGGIE HASSAN (D-NH): I will always, always keep fighting to protect a woman`s fundamental freedom. GOV. GRETCHEN WHITMER (D-MI): We will make Michigan a leader, a place where women make their own decisions. ALCINDOR: In Michigan, residents voted to enshrine abortion rights into the state constitution, an issue Governor Gretchen Whitmer and her running mate been a central part of their successful reelection campaign. WHITMER: This is a right that we are not going to go backwards on. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: I`m proud of my state. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: I don`t want the government in my bedroom. ALCINDOR: And abortion rights did drive people to the polls. It was the second most important issue to voters behind inflation. In addition to Michigan, voters in California and Vermont codified abortion rights into their state constitutions. And it wasn`t just blue states, voters in Kentucky and Montana shot down measures that could have restricted access. What do you make of that nationally? WHITMER: I think it`s a sign that the American public has had rights for 49 years. We`re not going to go backward. And so, whether it`s state by state we see this happen or hopefully at some point, you know, a national effort again, I think that this is where the fight is at the moment. ALCINDOR: Those against abortion rights not processing the results. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: I believe abortion is first-degree murder. ALCINDOR: Eric Scheidler from the Pro-Life Action League says he`s gearing up to continue their push. ERIC SCHEIDLER, EXECUTIVE DIRECTOR, PRO-LIFE ACTION LEAGUE: If we`ve learned anything over the past 50 years as a movement is that we`ve got to be able to take a punch. ALCINDOR: Still, Americans in five states send a clear message about reproductive rights. Yamiche Alcindor, NBC News, Detroit. (END VIDEOTAPE) HOLT: Coming up, their new mission: training troops to become teachers in "THOSE WHO SERVE." (COMMERCIAL BREAK) [19:25:00] HOLT: Finally, as we approach Veterans Day, how some of our military men and women are preparing for their next careers in the classroom. Here`s Courtney Kube. (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) COURTNEY KUBE, NBC NEWS PENTAGON (voiceover): After more than two decades in the Navy, John Altman still wanted to serve. He swapped his years at sea for days in the classroom. JOHN ALTMAN, U.S. VETERAN: I`m on the frontlines of developing America`s number one natural resource. What`s that? I teach high school. KUBE: John discovered a program called Troops To Teachers supporting men and women leaving the military to become educators, providing money, counseling, and job referrals with a focus on science, math, and special education in low-income communities. What is it that you hope that you instill upon your students? ALTMAN: You got to work hard if you want something. That you can google your way through life. KUBE: Life lessons his students at Paradise Valley High School take to heart. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: He`s definitely taught me to get stuff done on time and not put it off. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: People from the military could basically go and do anything and he chose to come be a teacher. KUBE: With a need for teachers -- UNIDENTIFIED MALE: The teacher shortage that you hear about is real. I`m in the trenches trying to find teachers. KUBE: Programs like Troops To Teachers are more critical than ever. ALTMAN: I`m glad I found the program. I think it`s important for me to be an example just as when I wore the uniform. KUBE: For Altman, a new battle rhythm with the same mission. ALTMAN: I think that`s my duty assignment. I believe in that. Where`s my force? These youngsters are our tomorrow. I really love my Navy and I love teaching. KUBE: Courtney Kube, NBC News Paradise Valley, Arizona. (END VIDEOTAPE) HOLT: And that`s NIGHTLY NEWS for this Wednesday. Thank you for watching, everyone. headline: Today for November 9, 2022, NBC
story_text: (COMMERCIAL BREAK) [07:00:17] HODA KOTB, NBC NEWS ANCHOR: Good Wednesday morning. After an election night of midterm surprises for both parties. SAVANNAH GUTHRIE, NBC NEWS ANCHOR: And we are still awaiting many of the results. It is November 9th. This is Today. Too close to call key races still to be decided control of Congress hanging in the balance as votes are still being counted in key battlegrounds this morning. In Pennsylvania Democrats pick up a hard fought Senate seat. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) JOHN FETTERMAN (D-PA), SENATOR-ELECT: I`ll be the next U.S. senator from Pennsylvania. (END VIDEO CLIP) GUTHRIE: In Florida, Governor Ron DeSantis wins big, grossing back to the State House and turning Florida decidedly red. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) GOV. RON DESANTIS (R-FL): The people have delivered their verdict. Freedom is here to stay. (END VIDEO CLIP) GUTHRIE: But across the country controversial Republican candidates aligned with former President Trump disappoint. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) SEN. LINDSEY GRAHAM (R-SC): Definitely not a Republican way that`s for darn sure. (END VIDEO CLIP) GUTHRIE: This morning suspense over who will control the House and Senate and the results still rolling in today, Wednesday, November 9th, 2022. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: From NBC News, this is a special edition of Today with Savannah Guthrie and Hoda Kotb live from Studio 1A in Rockefeller Plaza. GUTHRIE: Well, hi, everybody. Good morning and welcome to Today. It is nice to have you with us on a Wednesday morning, the morning after election night. KOTB: One, two, three cups of coffee and one more for you, a long night. But election results by the way, SG, still coming in right now. GUTHRIE: Absolutely. Big night for the NBC News team all-nighters but we still have the question that we headed into the night with, will there be a shift in the balance of power in Congress? It`s unknown at this hour so let`s break it down where things stand, 218 seats are needed to claim majority control in the House. And right now our projection for the House is essentially still a tossup. Now let`s go to the Senate, both parties still neck and neck there as well. KOTB: Yes, Democrats have flipped one seat. NBC News projecting Democrat John Fetterman has won his Pennsylvania seat defeating Dr. Mehmet Oz in a closely watched an extremely expensive race. GUTHRIE: Let`s go down to Georgia, neither Democrat Raphael Warnock or Republican Herschel Walker have met the 50 percent threshold yet necessary to be declared an outright winner. So it could be that they will go to a runoff election in December. KOTB: Yes, it`s still too early to call. The Senate battle in Arizona, that`s between incumbent Senator Mark Kelly and Republican Blake Masters. GUTHRIE: And in Nevada it is just after 4:00 a.m. and we`re starting to see some results in the race between the incumbent Senator Catherine Cortez Masto and Republican challenger Adam Laxalt . So put it this way, we get a lot to get to. Our correspondents, they`ve been up all night they are spread out from coast to coast. Let`s get it started with NBC`s Peter Alexander in Philadelphia this morning. Hi, Peter, good morning. PETER ALEXANDER, NBC NEWS CHIEF WHITE HOUSE CORRESPONDENT: Hey, Savannah and Hoda, good morning to both of you. What a night. The crucial Senate seat here in Pennsylvania was a top target for both parties. But now the Democrats have secured a huge flip with John Fetterman`s win. Historically in a midterm, the party in power loses dozens of seats. But Democrats this go around defied history and expectations. And with plenty of votes still to be counted, this remains a country that is deeply divided. (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) ALEXANDER (voice-over): This morning, controlled of Congress up in the air with both the House and Senate still hanging in the balance. Republicans acknowledging the expected red wave never materialized. GRAHAM: Definitely not a Republican wave that`s for darn sure. SEN. TED CRUZ (R-TX): That hasn`t been as big of a wave as I`d hoped it would be. ALEXANDER (voice-over): While the battle for the Senate may not be decided for days, Democrats are celebrating a critical Senate pick up in Pennsylvania, where Lieutenant Governor John Fetterman just months removed from a stroke, defeated his Republican rival, celebrity T.V., Dr. Mehmet Oz. FETTERMAN: Yes, this campaign has always been about fighting for everyone who`s ever been gotten knocked down that ever got back up. ALEXANDER (voice-over): Georgia`s Senate showdown appears headed to a run off next month if neither incumbent Democratic Senator Raphael Warnock nor Republican Herschel Walker can reach the 50 percent threshold. SEN. RAPHAEL WARNOCK (D-GA), SENATE CANDIDATE: You all just hang in there. I`m feeling good. HERSCHEL WALKER (R-GA), SENATE CANDIDATE: I told you he`s going to be tough to beat. You got to roll in Georgia here on. ALEXANDER (voice-over): Democrats showed signs of strength in a number of key races. GRAHAM: So you know, you got hats off to the Democrats. They perform well in a lot of these swing districts. ALEXANDER (voice-over): Two Democratic senators who`d been considered vulnerable New Hampshire`s Maggie Hassan and Colorado`s Michael Bennet, both fending off challenges overnight and in some of the country`s most competitive House races Democrats touting narrow victories including in Virginia. [07:05:04] REP. ABIGAIL SPANBERGER (D-VA): Thanks to your commitment and hard work we have won this race. ALEXANDER (voice-over): But some critical wins for the GOP holding on to a key Senate seat in North Carolina. And in Ohio, Republican political novice author J.D. Vance beating Democrat Tim Ryan . Vance was endorsed by former President Trump. J.D. VANCE (R-PA), SENATOR-ELECT: I will never forget where I came from, and I will never forget the great people of Ohio. ALEXANDER (voice-over): A major bright spot for the GOP Florida, Governor Ron DeSantis and Senator Marco Rubio cruising to reelection. Across the country, voters send a message that they`re dissatisfied with President Biden and particularly worried about the economy, with nearly a third saying in exit polls that rising inflation mattered most to them this year, but abortion rights was the second most important issue and a huge motivating factor for Democrats, now both parties facing a deeply divided electorate ahead of the next presidential election. (END VIDEOTAPE) ALEXANDER: And here in Pennsylvania, according to the NBC News exit poll, voters were confident in John Fetterman`s ability to serve this state effectively despite his health challenges. Dr. Mehmet Oz fell short of convincing those same Pennsylvanians that he had lived in this state long enough to serve it. Savannah and Hoda? GUTHRIE: All right, Peter Alexander leading us off. Thank you. KOTB: All right, let`s focus on that closely watched Senate battle in Georgia. It remains too close to call it this hour. NBC`s Gabe Gutierrez spent the night in Atlanta. His watching those results still coming in, have we seen any movement overnight, Gabe? GABE GUTIERREZ, NBC NEWS NATIONAL CORRESPONDENT: Hi, Hoda, good morning. Well, it was a long night here in Georgia. And we`re still at it, no clear winner. And NBC News has not projected this race but a runoff is appearing more and more likely at least that`s according to the Georgia Secretary of State`s office. Now incumbent senator Raphael Warnock is holding that slight lead over his challenger, football legend Herschel Walker . But there`s a third party candidate in this race. And according to Georgia State law, if no candidate reaches that 50 percent threshold, we`ll see a runoff here next month. Now this has been a wild race with more than a quarter billion dollars flowing into the state. And now voters in Georgia are preparing for the possibility of another four weeks of campaigning. Voters I`ve spoken with weren`t too thrilled about that. But in a second race, there was a clear victory. NBC News projects Republican Governor Brian Kemp defeating his Democratic challenger Stacey Abrams for the second time. And the vote tally so far is signaling that at least some Republicans may have voted for Kemp but then voted for the Democrat, Warnock. But again, this Senate race is still too close to call here. And depending on how a few other races go across the country. If we do head to a run off, it could be another several weeks before we know the balance of power in the Senate. Hoda? KOTB: All right, Gabe Gutierrez for us there in Atlanta. Gabe, thank you. GUTHRIE: Let`s go to another pivotal battleground, Arizona, the ballots in that state`s Senate and governor`s race still being counted. NBC`s Vaughn Hillyard is up early in Phoenix. Mark Kelly, the Senate incumbent holds the lead there, but we`re expecting these race results to tighten up. VAUGHN HILLYARD, NBC NEWS CORRESPONDENT: Yes, that`s right, Savannah. There are still hundreds of thousands of ballots to be counted here in this race. And it`s going to be challenger Blake Masters who is trying to take down incumbent Democratic Senator Mark Kelly. And you see that he`s down by about six percentage points right now though, but it`s important to note there is as much as one-third of the vote that is still outstanding, and much of that vote is expected to skew toward the GOP. Now election workers are returning here this morning in the Phoenix area to begin signature verifying these mail ballots that were received in recent days. This is going to be a slow process. We should also note the governor`s race, Kari Lake the Republican who is taking on Democratic Katie Hobbs , she well outpacing Masters. She is also losing at this hour to the Democrat. However, overnight, we saw the gap here shrink, and that is what the Republicans are hoping continuous here by weeks and that they are ultimately able to eclipse their Democratic opponent. Savannah? GUTHRIE: All right, Vaughn Hilliard in Arizona. Thank you. KOTB: As we mentioned earlier, we`re still waiting for results out of Nevada`s Senate race too. NBC`s Jacob Soboroff standing by in Vegas, Jacob this race was considered one of the most vulnerable for Democrats. So where do things stand this morning? JACOB SOBOROFF, NBC NEWS CORRESPONDENT: It is still on the line, Hoda. Good morning to you. And Savannah to borrow a line from you last night, what happened in Vegas is going to stay in Vegas, at least for now. It`s not going to Washington, D.C. just quite yet. It was a nail biter out here. That`s what they expected and that is exactly what Senator Catherine Cortez Masto and her Republican challenger, the former state attorney general, Adam Laxalt got. They thought it was going to be a close race. That race is maybe even closer than they thought. Senator Cortes Masto acknowledged as much in a speech to supporters last night. We were there when she told those supporters that this race that hinged on the issues of abortion and the economy is now going to hinge on the pace with which with -- with which, excuse me, those ballots are ultimately going to be counted. And that is because state law here dictates a slow pace of count to ensure a fair and accurate election. [07:10:19] Now the question will be what is Adam Laxalt do? You`ll remember after the 2020 election here, he came out on behalf of President Trump and preemptively challenged the results of the election with baseless conspiracy theory election claims, saying that the election was stolen. That of course was debunked, proven as false by the Republican secretary of state here. Now that he`s in the lead. He took the lead overnight last night. Will he do the same thing? I guess we`ll have to find out today. Meanwhile, the vote count continues out here, guys. KOTB: All right, Jacob Soboroff in Vegas, Jacob, thank you. GUTHRIE: Well, let`s get to our national political correspondent, Steve Kornacki who`s been working the big board throughout the night. He`s back at it this morning. OK. I don`t think 24 hours ago we would have predicted that we wouldn`t know what is going to happen in the House yet. STEVE KORNACKI, NBC NEWS NATIONAL POLITICAL CORRESPONDENT: It`s amazing when you consider Republicans only needed a net gain of five seats to get control of the House. That was the closest a minority party was to winning the House coming into a midterm in nearly a century. And yet this morning, as you say, this is what our NBC News house model is showing. Our projection 218 is what you need to get a majority in the House. Our projection right now is that the Republicans will land at 220 critically plus or minus 10 seats. So in other words, there is very much a universe right now where Republicans could move north of 220 and end up with a majority somewhere around 10 seats or so. There is also a universe where the Democrats could retain control of the House. It remains undecided at this hour. GUTHRIE: And same goes for the Senate. Can we do the same thing on the Senate side? What`s the path to control there for both parties? KORNACKI: Yes, so let`s take a look at it. You heard some reports in the key states there. The big call over night was that Democrats picked up Pennsylvania. That means the Republicans need to gain two Democratic seats if they`re going to get control of the Senate. You see in yellow, what`s uncalled here. Ron Johnson is leading in Wisconsin. Let`s say Ron Johnson holds on to that Republicans would hold that seat. You got the report from Georgia where a runoff is a distinct possibility. Let`s say they do go to a runoff in Georgia, what that would mean is that between Arizona and Nevada, where you just heard those two reports, Republicans would for a moment need to win one of those two, their candidate is trailing in Arizona, their candidate has a lead in Nevada. So between those two, I think the Republicans if they`re going to win one, their prospects are probably better in Nevada than in Arizona. So let`s say the Democrats were to get Arizona, the Republicans were to get Nevada under a scenario like that. This Georgia, the runoff would end up being what decides control of the Senate. That runoff would be held on December 6th. And if the Democrats instead were to sweep Nevada in Arizona, that be it. They control the Senate. GUTHRIE: Well, can we go back to the House for a minute, let`s drill down on what exactly happened and where the Democrats are vulnerable at this hour. We saw what happened in Florida, it was basically a red sweep in Florida. It makes a huge difference for the Republicans. But there`s another place where Democrats are very vulnerable. KORNACKI: This is the surprise. All right, so Democrats have done vastly better than they imagined anyone imagined they would do. And yet look at New York State, right, one of the big blue states. What happened in New York State is the governor`s race, Kathy Hochul , the Democrat gets reelected, but it`s a close race and the Republican Lee Zeldin ran up huge numbers on Long Island and huge numbers upstate. And what that`s done is there`s just a whole bunch of House races in New York State in areas where Zeldin did well, where the Republicans are leading. Look at this one, Sean Patrick Maloney is the chairman of the DCCC, the committee that organizes the Democrats campaign strategy nationally. He is trailing in his own district. Democrats are trailing in two seats on Long Island. Democrats could lose five House seats out of New York. So we`re going through all that math right now, ironically enough, the biggest batch of outstanding results this morning is in New York. And there`s the prospect that Democrats could lose five of them there. That could end up being the difference in the House, New York. GUTHRIE: That`s fascinating to see how this is developing. Steve, thank you very much. Great job. KOTB: Let`s bring in NBC`s senior Washington correspondent Hallie Jackson had a very long night tracking results too. HALLIE JACKSON, NBC NEWS SENIOR WASHINGTON CORRESPONDENT: Are you ready for another month of this? KOTB: Well, sounds like it. Let`s talk about what was expected overnight. The polls expected that people were going to vote on inflation and crime that there was going to be a red wave. Yet, a lot of folks probably waking up at this hour going what happened to that red wave? So what did happened? headline: What We Learned From Voters In This Week`s Elections About The Issues That Really Matter To Them And Where The Country May Be Headed From Here
story_text: [08:15:00] WILLIE GEIST: On election day, all of the polls, the punditry, the focus groups, and the tea leaves give way to voters. Energized by a swirl of issues, inflation, abortion, crime, immigration, and the very foundations of democracy, Americans turned out in near record midterm numbers to make a loud statement about what they`re seeing in the country and what needs to change. NBC News Capitol Hill Correspondent Ali Vitali looks closer in our "Sunday Focus". (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) ALI VITALI, NBC NEWS CAPITOL HILL CORRESPONDENT (voiceover): They were the midterms that few saw coming. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: What happened to the red wave, Congresswoman? VITALI (voiceover): History defying results. BIDEN: We lost fewer seats and House representatives in any democratic president`s first elected midterm, at least 40 years. VITALI (voiceover): Near record turnout and a twist in where the competitive seats really were. Dems holding on in red states like Kansas. While losing key seats in blue New York. REP. SEAN PATRICK MALONEY (D-NY): I don`t like to lose, but my opponent won this race. And he won it fair and square. VITALI (voiceover): The economy and inflation, the top issue for voters, and a weak point for Democrats who struggled to offer a clear response. But issues like abortion and threats to democracy acted as a dam to the previously predicted red wave for Republicans. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: I`m out to say where democracy. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: I don`t think that a body of strangers should tell us what our choices should be. VITALI (voiceover): In crucial states like Michigan and Pennsylvania, abortion rights surpassed inflation as voters` number one concern, allowing Democrats to notch key governor and Senate race wins and quiet gains on the state level. Dems not losing a single state legislative chamber for the first time in nearly 90 years. Back in Washington, Republicans now grappling with how it could have gone so wrong. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: Look, I`m frustrated that it didn`t turn out well for us. VITALI (voiceover): From once predicting a more than 20-seat margin in the House of Representatives to just being happy with a majority. REP. KEVIN MCCARTHY (R-CA): What`s was our mission? To win the majority, to stop Biden`s agenda, and fire Nancy Pelosi . All of that is accomplished. VITALI (voiceover): Maybe, but if Republicans do take the House, it`ll be very slim margins. Giving all members more power. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: I think it`s wonderful because everybody`s voice needs to be considered. [08:20:00] VITALI (voiceover): And GOP Leader Kevin McCarthy. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: Oh, I think there`s some questions about leadership. VITALI (voiceover): His future as house speaker now thrown into flux. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: I expect there will be a challenge. VITALI (voiceover): But amid a week of surprises, one important traditional hallmark, candidates who lost saying so. TIM MICHELS (R-WIS) GUBERNATORIAL CANDIDATE: Unfortunately, the math doesn`t add up. I just called Governor Evers and conceded. I wish the Evers family well. VITALI (voiceover): Not necessarily a given. With nearly 300 election deniers on the ballot and a former president insisting they make election denialism a central focus. KARI LAKE (R-AZ) GUBERNATORIAL CANDIDATE: Trump won, you`re right. VITALI (voiceover): That said, more than half of election denying candidates won their races, many coming to Congress now in 2023. And in the aftermath, Republicans also reckoning with the Trump of it all. Many of his hand-picked candidates lost. DONALD TRUMP , FORMER U.S. PRESIDENT: Well, I think if they win, I should get all the credit. And if they lose, I should not be blamed at all. VITALI (voiceover): While pro-democracy candidates won in key states. KELLY: No one party has a monopoly on good ideas. VITALI (voiceover): One of the Democrat`s strongest voting blocs, Gen Z. young voters showing up in record numbers. Rallying around things like student loan forgiveness. Among them, 25-year-old Maxwell Frost who won his election in Florida, making him the first Gen Zer elected to Congress. CROWD: Maxwell. Maxwell. VITALI (voiceover): And in a midterm election full of firsts, another. A record $17 billion spent on campaigns and ads. All for the country to wake up Wednesday pretty much how it went to bed on election night, divided down the middle. (END VIDEO CLIP) GEIST: And Ali joins me now live. Ali, good morning. It`s great to see you. So, after the stunning midterm elections, there`s been a lot of talk about Republicans walking away from Donald Trump , but we`ve heard that before. VITALI (on camera): Yes. GEIST: And the former president made it very clear again this week, he will not go quietly or perhaps at all. VITALI: Yes, that`s right, because Mr. Trump is expected to announce another run for president this week down at Mar-a-Lago. But it comes as the party that he`s controlled for the last six years has spent the last week actively pondering a future or as "The New York Post" said, a defuture without him. One of the names that keeps coming up for 2024 is Florida Governor Ron DeSantis . But we know that former V.P. Mike Pence , former Ambassador Nikki Haley, former Secretary of State Mike Pompeo , also others, they all likely have their eyes on the presidential prize this coming cycle. And while Mr. Trump`s had a bad political week, we have seen this time and again, Willie, Republicans end up going back and sticking by the former president. So, time will tell if this moment is actually any different. Willie. GEIST: Yes, see you January 6th for that. VITALI: Yes, exactly. GEIST: Meanwhile, we wake up this morning Democrats in control of the Senate. And as Steve Kornacki told us again last night, the house still very much in play. VITALI: Yes. GEIST: Extraordinary. Ali, thank you very much. Coming up next a new "Sunday Sitdown" with Daniel Radcliffe on the fun of playing "Weird Al" Yankovic in a new movie and the rocket ride of being "Harry Potter". And then a life well-lived, the pioneering journalist who broke down the locker room door for the women who came after her. And as we head to break, our photo of the week. The iconic Dolly Parton performing at last weekend`s Rock and Roll Hall of Fame induction ceremony in Los Angeles. After initially saying she did not think belonged in that hall, Dolly finally relented to the fans and accepted the honor. She even wrote and performed a new song for the occasion called "Rockin`". Dolly joined in this year`s class by Duran Duran, Eminem, Lionel Richie, Carly Simon, among others. Congratulations to Dolly, our national treasure. (COMMERCIAL BREAK) [08:25:00] (LOCAL NEWS) (COMMERCIAL BREAK) [08:30:00] (LOCAL NEWS) (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) CECILY STRONG, ACTRESS: The Maricopa County officials are incompetent. And it`s my belief that the election is rigged and the results should be thrown out. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: It sounds like new numbers coming in which has you taking a narrow lead over Katie Hobbs . STRONG: Which is why I have always said, this is democracy. Trust the system. Trust the voters. (END VIDEO CLIP) GEIST: That is Cecily Strong as Arizona Republican Gubernatorial candidate Kari Lake on last night`s new episode of "Saturday Night Live." story_text: [09:00:00] (COMMERCIAL BREAK) CHUCK TODD, NBC HOST (voiceover): This Sunday, my interview with Former Vice President Mike Pence . PENCE: All I know is that what the president asked me to do, I would have violated my oath to the Constitution. TODD: What he thinks should happen now that Trump is running for office again. And, Chuck, it may take as many years to restore the sanctity of life to the center of American law in every state in this country as it took to overturn Roe vs. Wade. But as long as I have breath, I`ll be on that cause. TODD: I know you`ve got passion. Are you -- you`re a limited government guy. I know this. And you really are. Are you comfortable with the idea of essentially government-mandated pregnancy? Somebody doesn`t want this child, doesn`t want this pregnancy to go through. You`re now advocating a law that essentially the government is ordering you to go through with this pregnancy. Are you comfortable with a government mandate like that? The folks in Kansas were not. PENCE: Our founding documents say we`re endowed by our creator with certain inalienable rights, and the first one mentioned is life. And I think government exists to protect life, particularly defenseless life. And I intend to be a part of this. But I think we have an opportunity, Chuck, to approach this debate in a new and in a renewed way. You know, when the Supreme Court took this issue away from the American people 49 years ago, there were strong dividing lines that have endured now for two generations. But now we have a political debate. And we have the opportunity not just to craft thoughtful protections for the unborn, but also to extend protections and support for women in crisis pregnancy and for newborns. I`d like to see us redouble our efforts to demonstrate the compassion of the American people. To live out the idea that there is no unwanted child, and that in the freest and most prosperous nation in the history of the world, we can make that the reality. TODD: Do you think the unborn have constitutional rights? PENCE: I believe in -- TODD: They don`t in our law right now, but do you believe they should? PENCE: I believe in the right to life. And I believe -- TODD: Do you believe that an unborn fetus has a constitutional right? PENCE: Look, we are protected in this country from being denied life or liberty without due process of law. And I believe those protections should extend to the born and the unborn. But this is a long-term cause. And it`ll be as much moral persuasion in America as political debates and battles. TODD: Shouldn`t that be where it is, though? Shouldn`t it be moral persuasion and not government mandate? PENCE: I think -- I really do believe now that it`s been returned to the political process, Chuck, that we have an incredible opportunity to demonstrate the real heart and compassion of the American people in this cause, to persuade our neighbors and friends to the day that abortion is not only illegal, but it`s unthinkable. And when that day comes, and we`ll someday institute, in the laws of all 50 states, protections. TODD: There are a lot of women uncomfortable with the idea that a politician will make this decision for them. PENCE: I understand that. I do. But I really do believe that restoring the sanctity of life to the center of law, in every state in this country, is at the very heart of achieving a boundless future for the American people. (END VIDEOTAPE) TODD: Still ahead, our panel is here with their thoughts on my interview with Mike Pence and the new special counsel investigation into Donald Trump . [09:45:03] Plus, our Meet the Press Minute looks back at how Ronald Reagan answered the question of how old was too old to serve as president? (COMMERCIAL BREAK) [09:48:03] TODD: Welcome back. The day after his granddaughter`s wedding on the White House South Lawn, President Biden is celebrating an important event of his own today. It`s his 80th birthday. Biden is now the oldest serving president in American history. It`s a title previously held by Ronald Reagan . In today`s "Meet the Press Minute", we look back to 1974, when then- Governor Reagan was in his early sixties. He was asked whether his age would be a factor in a presidential run. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) JAMES J. KILPATRICK, MEET THE PRESS: You will be 63 years old on February 6th, and during the campaign period, of course, would be 65. Does age seem to you, realistically, to be a factor that would operate against your candidacy for president? GOV. RONALD REAGAN (R), CALIFORNIA: Well, I think that`s got to be a determination the people are going to make. Certainly, Jim, by the time of 1976, if it should be my decision that I am going to be involved in that race, and I think it`s certainly too early to make that decision by a long way, the people will know my age and they`ll make that determination. We have had presidents that have pretty much spanned adulthood as to their age, and it has not seemed to affect the people. (END VIDEO CLIP) TODD: To dig into the Meet the Press archives, scan the code on your screen right now. Visit NBCNews.com/MTP75. It`s the website that is home to 75 of the biggest moments in "Meet the Press" history. When we come back, the panel. (COMMERCIAL BREAK) [09:53:11] TODD: We are back. Panel is here. Anna Palmer, co-founder of "Punchbowl News"; Peter Baker, chief White House correspondent for " The New York Times ", he`s also author of the book "The Divider"; Brendan Buck, former adviser to Speakers Paul Ryan and John Boehner ; and Kimberly Atkins Stohr, senior opinion writer for "The Boston Globe ". Peter, you wrote about the special counsel and sort of, almost the darned if you do, darned if you don`t moment -- PETER BAKER, CHIEF WHITE HOUSE CORRESPONDENT, THE NEW YORK TIMES: Yeah. TODD: -- that Merrick Garland was in. You know, and you saw it with Mike Pence in my interview. There`s this -- there are a lot of Republicans that want to let Trump sort of dangle out there, but they`re also not ready to jump on, jump on pushing him off either, just -- BAKER: Right. No, that`s exactly right. Look, you`re right. Garland had no choice. Probably under the rules as they are established, he felt that it was an obvious case for a special counsel. But the idea of a special counsel is to make it seem like politics is not involved. And, of course, that was never going to work. Of course, Trump was never going to let that be a nonpartisan figure. He immediately attacks the special counsel as a political, partisan witch hunter, the latest in a long stream, in his view. And therefore, we`re right back where we started, which is that the investigation is seen through the lens of partisan politics. TODD: You know, Anna, it was one of those, I guess if Garland could`ve done this differently, it would`ve been -- had it been a special counsel from the beginning. ANNA PALMER, FOUNDER, PUNCHBOWL NEWS: Right. Was the delay kind of an opening for Republicans in a lot of ways? It wasn`t just Trump. We`ve seen a lot of Republicans in the Senate, in the House saying, all right, now it`s time to impeach Merrick Garland . Now, you know, there should be a special counsel for Hunter Biden . I`m just saying these are the partisan attacks that you`re going to hear over and over again for the next several months. BRENDAN BUCK, FORMER ADVISER TO SPEAKERS RYAN BOEHNER: They`re going to do everything they can to undermine this process. And I will tell you, when I -- TODD: Who`s "they" though? BUCK: House Republicans. TODD: OK. BUCK: Newly in the majority, newly with committee hearings that they can call -- TODD: Is that a good focus? BUCK: It`s absolutely not. But I will tell you, when I was on the Hill working for Speaker Ryan, we spent an incredible amount of time behind the scenes trying to get our members not to undermine the Mueller investigation. [09:55:00] They wanted to do things. They wanted to try to meddle in that. And we had to say, hard no. Like, we can`t do this because this is important. I don`t know that the current House of Representatives is set up to, to be that disciplined. KIMBERLY ATKINS STOHR, SENIOR OPINION WRITER, THE BOSTON GLOBE : And I know that the DOJ and Merrick Garland want to keep things unpolitical. But I think that`s one of the things that he should`ve thought about in making the decision, either to do it from the beginning. I think that he didn`t need one at all. The regulations don`t mandate this. He could have continued this investigation, and it should`ve gone a little faster. TODD: Doesn`t it feel like he is a character from the pre-Trump era? ATKNS STOHR: Yes. TODD: And that`s sort of like what Garland`s -- you know, whatever you think, he`s just sort of, isn`t this the way we`re supposed to do it? BAKER: It`s the old fashioned. TODD: And you`re, like, it`s not the way in the Trump world, yeah. BAKER: It`s a new era. Right. A new era. But there is one thing that might be indicated here. Merrick Garland has made a threshold decision perhaps, that it is okay to charge a former president, or a presidential candidate, if the elements of the law are met, because otherwise, he wouldn`t have bothered to appoint a special counsel. That`s a pretty big step, if in fact that`s what`s going through his mind right now. TODD: All right, the other big event this weekend was this Republican Jewish Coalition event. You know, Anna, it was interesting. Donald Trump , he, he ended up satelliting it in because I think he realized Ron DeSantis was stealing the show no matter what. But he gave this rambling answer about the midterms, correctly noting the impact of abortion, but he never said the word. Meanwhile, Mike Pence is here telling me it`s the greatest achievement of the administration. PALMER: I mean, one of the biggest divides, right? You have Donald Trump , who was pro-choice. I mean, Mike Pence , ever since I`ve covered politics, this is very core to who he is. TODD: Yeah. PALMER: Clearly, not afraid that the American public might not be in the same place that Mike Pence is. But that`s one of the few distinguishing factors, right, when you look at the two of them. Mike Pence kind of twisting himself into a pretzel in this whole interview, where he didn`t really want to say that, that the former president was wrong, that what happened on January 6th was wrong. TODD: Brendan, he wants -- he wants to run on the Trump administration more than Trump does. BUCK: Pence is running what seems to be leading up to a campaign that would make a lot of sense if Donald Trump wasn`t still around. He`s the natural next -- next in line. All the great things that we did. I`m separating myself from him a little bit. But he refuses to actually take on Donald Trump . In reality, you know, he`s running for president. Donald Trump is going to be a candidate -- TODD: He`s going to take him on. BUCK: Exactly. TODD: Trump will take Pence on. BUCK: Exactly. And so we have a situation where, once again, you have Republicans sort of just hoping that he goes away, and unwilling to attack him. Donald Trump is going to attack Mike Pence . He`s going to attack Ron DeSantis . And to think that you can just sit there and wait for him to implode I think is a little naive. TODD: But is there a little bit of Trump fatigue? I feel like I`m sensing it in the rank and file. ATKINS STOHR: I think there`s more than a little bit. The midterms were evidence of that. But it`s not fatigue among the people, like including Mike Pence , who stood right next to -- TODD: Well because -- because they`re afraid of Trump`s base. ATKINS STOHR: Well, but it`s an opportunity to say, this is waning and we`re going to break free, and we`re going to take a different path. But instead, Mike Pence tried to excuse Trump for everything, other than trying to stop the certification of the election. It was -- it was Fauci`s fault that something, it was Mark Meadow`s fault that he talked about disinfectant. It was someone else`s fault. It was lawyers` fault that he -- PALMER: But where Mike Pence is, is very different, I think where you`re seeing a lot of the Republican Party saying, that was, you know, a three- time loser. You have members -- TODD: Pence doesn`t want to go there. PALMER: Not at all. TODD: No. PALMER: I mean, it`s pretty -- it`s stunning compared to where the rest of the Republicans are. TODD: Well, he`s self-aware in that who else was going to make him vice president? Ultimately, that`s the issue he has. All right, guys. I have to go. Enjoy your Thanksgiving weekend. You guys are terrific. There`s an unedited version of my Mike Pence interview, including approximately 30 minutes that we weren`t able to air here at MeetThePress.com. Please take a look at it. That`s all we have for today. Thanks for watching. Enjoy the Thanksgiving holiday. We`ll be back next week. We don`t bring leftovers. headline: NBC NIGHTLY NEWS for November 23, 2022, NBC
story_text: [19:00:00] (COMMERCIAL BREAK) LESTER HOLT, NBC NEWS ANCHOR (on camera): Tonight, another deadly mass shooting in America, this time at a Virginia Walmart just before Thanksgiving. (voiceover): The gunman, a store manager laughing before opening fire in the Walmart break room according to witnesses and police. At least six killed before the shooter took his own life. The horror unfolding as the store was filled with holiday shoppers. We`re on the scene. It comes just days after the massacre at an LGBTQ club in Colorado. The suspect making a first court appearance today slumped over in a wheelchair with visible facial injuries. What happened at that hearing? Also, tonight, the busiest day on the roads as nearly 55 million Americans travel for Thanksgiving. And the holiday storm threat. We`re tracking it. Russia`s new missile strikes on Ukraine. A maternity ward hit. A newborn infant killed. The first bombings in Jerusalem in years. The deadly blasts being called a terrorist attack. New details in the murders of four University of Idaho students. And now, the other unsolved stabbing case. Police are looking at it. Is there a link? The countdown to Black Friday. Where to find the best deals despite soaring inflation? And the spirit of a holiday. What kids say they`re most thankful for this year. ANNOUNCER: This is NBC NIGHTLY NEWS with Lester Holt. HOLT (on camera): Good evening. We keep ending in the same place, don`t we? Morning victims who could have been any of us, scratching our heads over possible motives, and reciting the growing list. All those places where mass violence has snuffed out or threatened to take innocent lives. Tonight, just days after the Colorado Springs attack, we`re absorbing details of the latest horrific mass shooting in this country. Six people at a Chesapeake, Virginia Walmart shot to death by a long-time store employee who opened fire with a handgun. Several others were wounded. A survivor is saying the attack in an employee break room was preceded by the gunman`s laughter. The 31-year-old took his own life before police arrived. The killer described by a senior law enforcement official as a disgruntled employee. But what that means as to a specific motive is unclear. In a statement, President Biden speaking with many are thinking tonight, there are now even more tables across the country that will have empty seats this Thanksgiving. NBC`s Cal Perry is in Chesapeake with the latest. (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) CAL PERRY, NBC NEWS CORRESPONDENT (voiceover): Tragedy in Chesapeake, Virginia. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: How many medics do we have left in the city right now? UNIDENTIFIED MALE: Currently six medics available. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: Go ahead and dispatch all of them. PERRY: 911 receiving its first call to the Walmart Supercenter at 10:12 p.m. Officers arriving within two minutes. We got a whole scene out here but it`s crazy out here right now. They everywhere. The 31-year-old shooter who police say worked at the store since 2010 came armed with a handgun and multiple magazines. One senior law enforcement official tells NBC News he was a disgruntled employee. BRIANA TYLER, WITNESS: I literally was frozen. I just stood there. I`d like I literally could be dead right now. It didn`t kick in until I looked at my coworker and she was bleeding out of her neck. PERRY: Six people were killed ranging in age from 16 to 70. At least four others were wounded before the shooter turned the gun on himself. MARK SOLESKY, CHIEF, CHESAPEAKE, VIRGINIA POLICE DEPARTMENT: The investigation is still ongoing, and we`ll be processing that scene for days. GOV. GLENN YOUNGKIN (R-VA): The most important thing we need to do is come around families and support them. It`s unimaginable what they`re dealing with today. PERRY: 24-year-old Jalon Jones had been working at the Walmart for about a year. He`s recovering at a nearby hospital. KIMBERLY SHUPE, MOTHER OF JALON JONES: He knew he was being shot. He made it to the front of the store. And then when he made it to the front door, he was shot again. PERRY: 28-year-old Jessie says it was just her fifth day on the job. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: I saw a lot of bad thing that happened to really good people. And I didn`t understand it. And it didn`t feel real. PERRY: She says she was in the break room when the shooter came in laughing and started firing. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: He got the gun pointed at me and he looks at me and he puts it up in the air. And all he said was just to go home. I ran. I didn`t look back. I want to look back. PERRY: Do you know why he let you go, Jessie? Do you have any idea? UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: No, I know. PERRY: So far, there`s no word on motive, and it`s unclear if the victims were targeted. Authorities today cordoned off this vehicle in the parking lot saying it`s a vehicle of interest. DR. JESSICA BURGESS, SENTARA NORFOLK GENERAL HOSPITAL: It`s heartbreaking. PERRY: Chesapeake, Virginia, just the latest community left grappling with yet another senseless shooting. [19:05:01] BURGESS: It was just two days ago that I was contacting one of my colleagues in Colorado Springs wishing her well and checking in to see how she was doing after she had just taken care of shooting victims. So it`s very disheartening that now I`m in the same position with my colleagues from across the country checking in on me. (END VIDEOTAPE) HOLT: Cal, what are investigators focusing on right now? PERRY (on camera): Lester, investigators are focused on any connection they can find between the victims and the shooter. For example, if any of the victims worked with the shooter, that could go a long way in finding a motive. Lester? HOLT: All right, Cal Perry tonight, thank you. In Colorado Springs today, the first court appearance by video from jail for the suspect in the killing of five people at that LGBTQ nightclub four days ago. The suspect who was subdued and beaten by club patrons was released from the hospital yesterday. The suspect, on public defenders, identify as non-binary person, was ordered held without bail and faces possible murder and hate crime charges. We have been through this so many times this year. By one count, there have been 608 mass shootings defined as four or more people shot. That`s not far from last year`s record. Here`s Tom Costello. (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) TOM COSTELLO, NBC NEWS CORRESPONDENT (voiceover): On this Thanksgiving Eve, America is reckoning with the violence that is tearing up the national fabric. This afternoon, four high school students shot in Philly. Every week, nearly 13 mass shootings, so many we too often forget those that happened last week or last month. 21 children and teachers killed in Uvalde, Texas. 10 people gunned down in a Buffalo grocery store. Five and Raleigh, four in Memphis, four in Tulsa, six in Sacramento. The list is excruciatingly long. ROB BONTA, ATTORNEY GENERAL, CALIFORNIA: We know that this is America`s disease, unique in the world. COSTELLO: David Hogg, one of the high school students from Parkland, Florida where 17 people died, tweeted at 2:24 this morning, I am tired of waking up to texts about another mass shooting in America. DAVID HOGG, PARKLAND SHOOTING SURVIVOR: It`s going to continue happening. And we have to work together to actually stop this from happening. COSTELLO: Nationwide, 49 people die in gun violence every day. STEVEN DETTELBACH, DIRECTOR, ATF: My biggest fear is that somehow as a country, we become callous or to kind of accept or think that this is OK, that this is somehow part of our national story. COSTELLO: Pediatrician Emily Lieberman was with her children in Highland Park, Illinois when a gunman killed seven people on July 4. Now, she`s leading a group of doctors demanding the Senate pass more than the gun safety measures enacted after Uvalde. EMILY LIEBERMAN, PEDIATRICIAN: Now, the number one cause of death of children in this country is gun violence. It`s time to start tackling gun violence as a public health problem and listening to people like physicians who know how to solve this problem. (END VIDEOTAPE) COSTELLO (on camera): The country holding a mirror to itself with politicians expected back in D.C. next week. And the decades-old gun control debate likely to be a dinner table topic tomorrow. Lester? HOLT: Tom Costello, thank you. We`ll take a turn out of the busy Thanksgiving travel rush. Almost 55 million Americans expected to travel this year nearly hitting pre pandemic levels. And we`re also tracking storms that could bring heavy rain to the south and Gulf Coast tomorrow. Erin McLaughlin joins us now from Los Angeles. Erin, what`s the traffic like there? ERIN MCLAUGHLIN, NBC NEWS CORRESPONDENT (on camera): Well, things are looking pretty good here, Lestrer, especially for Los Angeles. Nearly 49 million Americans are expected to hit the road this Thanksgiving. That`s slightly compared to last year with the national average price of a gas, a gallon of gas, just below that $5.00 mark we saw back in June. Meanwhile, across the nation`s airports tonight, some good news for the most part. Flights have been on time thanks largely to clear skies and good weather across the country. Here in Los Angeles at LAX airport, they`re expecting some 200,000 passengers today alone. It`s the busiest they`ve been since the beginning of the pandemic. Lester? HOLT: Erin McLaughlin in Los Angeles, thank you. Two bombings in Jerusalem today killed a teenager and injured at least 18 others including two Americans. The explosions were near bus stops during the morning rush hour. Israeli police say the bombs were left at those locations and blamed Palestinians for the attacks. It`s the latest in a surge of violence between Israelis and Palestinians. And in Ukraine, Russia launching a new barrage of missile strikes. Ukrainian officials say a newborn infant was killed when a missile hit a hospital maternity ward in the southern part of the country. Much of Ukraine without power after Russians attack the energy infrastructure in Kyiv and several other cities. Tonight, new details from the police in the killings of those four college students in Idaho. Lots of leads and progress reported in the case but still no suspect identified. Gadi Schwartz has the latest. [19:10:06] (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) GADI SCHWARTZ, NBC NEWS CORRESPONDENT (voiceover): For the 11th day in a row, investigators saying still no suspect, no motive and the killings of four Idaho university students, but trying to assure the public they are making headway. COL. KEDRICK WILLS, IDAHO STATE POLICE: At this crime scene, we collected 103 pieces of individual evidence. SCHWARTZ: But frustration is growing among family members who fear investigators fell behind during the first crucial 48 hours of the case. WILLS: No tip is too small and we would urge anybody that has any information whatsoever to please provide that to help us solve this case. SCHWARTZ: Those who live in Moscow also asking about a recent dog mutilation that happened three miles away from the murders. Jim and Pam Colbert say about a month ago, someone grabbed their dog at 2:00 a.m. and skinned him in a field in front of their home. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: Right over there. Right over -- SCHWARTZ: Took his fur but left his unbuckled collar behind. So, somebody actually had to unclasp it. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: Unclasp it right here. See, that stays. And somebody had to undo it. Because if you had a knife, wouldn`t you have cut it? SCHWARTZ: But Moscow police say they don`t think that case has anything to do with the murders. Police also asked about an unsolved murder 300 miles away in Oregon, in which a masked intruder attacked a couple with a knife in their sleep. JAMES FRY, CHIEF, MOSCOW, IDAHO POLICE: Actually, I had a tip come in on that case and I`ve ordered it to our tip line. SCHWARTZ: Meanwhile, the University of Idaho giving students the option of finishing their semester remotely while families of the victims are struggling with the thought of Thanksgiving without their loved ones and praying that the killer won`t strike again. Gadi Schwartz, NBC News. (END VIDEOTAPE) HOLT: Also tonight, the so-called tripledemic, RSV, the flu, and COVID, is already pushing hospitals to the brink. The U.S. facing shortages of pediatric beds, medical staff, and now even some medications. Here`s Gabe Gutierrez. (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) GABE GUTIERREZ, NBC NEWS NATIONAL CORRESPONDENT (voiceover): In Buffalo, some store shelves normally filled with children`s Tylenol are empty. Pharmacists say a spot shortage of the drug in Canada triggered by mounting cases of RSV is spilling over the border. DON ARTHUR, PHARMACIST: Apparently, up in Canada, the liquid forms of Tylenol are unavailable. GUTIERREZ: Johnson and Johnson , the maker of Tylenol, says there`s no overall shortage in the U.S., telling NBC News we are experiencing high consumer demand and they`re doing everything we can to make sure people have access to the products they need. Still, the FDA currently lists amoxicillin as being in short supply. And it all comes as the healthcare industry braces for a potential tripledemic this winter. RSV, flu, and COVID colliding. In New York, Ella Rose Giam (PH) is home after a week in the hospital. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: It was surreal. Like, seeing your daughter on a breathing mask and she`s only three and a half. GUTIERREZ: Adding to the strain on the system, an increasingly dire staffing shortage. More than half a million people in the healthcare and social services industries quit their positions in September. Were you burnt out? Extremely. Yes, sir. Reece Brown in Louisiana is no longer a traveling nurse. REECE BROWN, NURSE: That joy which is literally being sucked out of us. We were doing everything that we could and we just -- it was never enough. (END VIDEOTAPE) GUTIERREZ (on camera): As for COVID, the CDC says new data shows the Omicron boosters offer better protection against variants than earlier doses. Still, they are not as effective as the original COVID vaccine was against the initial virus. Lester? HOLT: All right, Gabe Gutierrez, thanks. In 60 seconds, new abortion restrictions and the agonizing decisions they are forcing some families to make. Our in-depth look at the issue coming up next. (COMMERCIAL BREAK) HOLT: The Georgia Supreme Court today reinstated a ban on abortions after six weeks of pregnancy while it considers an appeal. And while a few states including Georgia make exceptions when a fetus has life-threatening problems, most states with new abortion restrictions do not. Blayne Alexandre has more. (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) BLAYNE ALEXANDER, NBC NEWS CORRESPONDENT (voiceover): Jill Hurtle could not wait to become a mom. She still remembers the second she found out. JILL HURTLE, HAD ABORTION: I was like sobbing. I was so excited. [19:15:02] ALEXANDER: You felt like a mom. HURTLE: I felt like a mom in that -- in an instant. ALEXANDER: Her husband, Matt, dreamed of being a girl dad. They even picked out a name Ivy Grace. Every doctor`s appointment brought good news until the 18-week scan. HURTLE: And our world`s like came crashing down. She came in and she said her heart isn`t what it is supposed to look like. I think in that exact moment, my stomach dropped and I think I truly knew that it was going to be a really severe situation. ALEXANDER: It was. A condition known as hypoplastic left heart syndrome, HLHS. Doctor said her baby`s case was especially severe, and her daughter would likely not survive long after birth. HURTLE: I didn`t want her to have to go through so much pain and suffering. ALEXANDER: After more tests and more devastating news, Jill and her husband made the painful decision. HURTLE: If she were to live an hour or 10 days, I didn`t want her to just - - I didn`t want her to know nothing but pain. So, my protective instinct was to do what I knew what was best for her, which was to send her to heaven. ALEXANDER: Every year, congenital or fetal anomalies impact one in every 33 babies born in the U.S. and range from minor to life-limiting or life- threatening. Since the Supreme Court decision overturning Roe v. Wade, at least 16 states have successfully enacted laws further restricting abortion access. Only three have exceptions for lethal fetal anomalies. DR. DAVID LEVINE, NEONATOLOGIST: We`re not dealing with one size fits all. We can`t make laws for one size fits all. ALEXANDER: Dr. David Levine is a neonatologist who opposes abortion access and believes the baby should be carried to term even with a grim prognosis. LEVINE: Most families who have decided to spend time with their babies however short it might be, by and large, have benefited from it. They`ve been able to bond with their baby. ALEXANDER: Is it therefore a law to make that decision for a parent? LEVINE: There are many decisions that are taken out of our hands. Is it fair for the mother to make that decision to take a baby`s life away from him. ALEXANDER: Jill had to leave South Carolina and wait two weeks for an appointment in Washington, DC. HURTLE: Those two weeks were probably the hardest two weeks I`ve ever experienced in my life. Every time you feel her kick or move, it`s just a dagger to the heart. ALEXANDER: She believes abortion bans should have exceptions for cases like hers, giving women the chance to make a choice, however painful. HURTLE: I am a mom. I`m a mom to an angel in heaven. And I know that she`s at peace. ALEXANDER: Blayne Alexander, NBC News, Charleston, South Carolina. (END VIDEOTAPE) HOLT: And up next, as the holiday shopping rush begins, top tips on where and how you can save in our series "RACE TO DELIVER." (COMMERCIAL BREAK) [19:20:00] HOLT: As you may have noticed, many retailers have already rolled out their Black Friday deals. So, where can you save the most? NBC`s Brian Cheung has been shopping around for our series "RACE TO DELIVER." (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) BRIAN CHEUNG, NBC NEWS BUSINESS AND DATA REPORTER (voiceover): Tonight, amid a growing unease in the nation`s economy, the dash for holiday deals is on. With consumer prices up 7.7 percent compared to last season and one in three households saying their finances are worse off from a year ago, shoppers are left with tighter budgets. TRAE BODGE, SMART SHOPPING EXPERT, TRUETRAE.COM: Retailers are aware of the fact that consumers only have so much to spend. CHEUNG: That`s why even before Black Friday, many retailers are already offering deep discounts vying for your holiday dollars. The most discounted items this season, everything from TVs, laptops, to home appliances, and beauty products. For electronics, consider older models for an even better deal. Many clothing retailers are also offering extra deep discounts this season in part because of excess inventory falling supply chain lock-ups last year. BODGE: We are seeing a lot of overstock still and retailers have been spending the last couple of months trying to sell through that merchandise. CHEUNG: Which could lead to even deeper discounts. BODGE: I do expect to see discounts deeper than usual in categories like casual apparel, TVs, furniture, home decor. And so, in addition to the exciting cyber weekend sales that we`ll see, we`ll also see kind of extra discounts as retailers look to clear out all those overstocks. CHEUNG: Experts say shopping with strategy will save you big bucks. Start by creating a shopping list with a spending cap. Then compare prices online and in store. And check your credit card for additional discounts and offers. (END VIDEOTAPE) CHEUNG (on camera): And don`t forget about gift cards which are always a hot item every year. Many can actually be bought at a discount. Lester? HOLT: All right, Brian, thanks. Up next, what are you thankful for? Some children will tell us right after the break. (COMMERCIAL BREAK) [19:25:00] HOLT: Finally, a lot of news has been especially grim this week, but we thought you might be uplifted or find a smile in listening to the gratitude expressed by some New York school kids we spoke to about Thanksgiving. (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) HOLT (voiceover): At Manhattan Country School, today`s lesson is all about giving thanks. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: Thank you God for a mother. HOLT: And after two years of holidays overshadowed by COVID, many students told us they`re grateful for a Thanksgiving that feels a little more normal. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: I`m thankful for like, family and friends because like, during COVID, I wasn`t able to see -- I wasn`t able to see like, a lot of my friends. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: I`m very grateful that me and my family -- or my family and I have been healthy and happy and able to see each other. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: I`m really thankful for the school and for my teachers and my friends. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: I`m thankful for my dog. She`s good at comforting people especially me. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: I`m thankful for my family because they give me comfort and I just love them. HOLT: Of course, on Thanksgiving -- UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: I love cooking. HOLT: Comfort also comes in the form of turkey, stuffing, and potatoes. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: We bake and we coconut we have this huge feast at the end. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: We make an angel fruitcake which I really love to do with my grandma. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: I`m definitely looking forward to eating because we do cook pretty good Thanksgiving meal. HOLT: When you`re in grade school, there`s something else to look forward to. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: We get a lot of days off from school. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: The first thing I think about it is wrapped up in a blanket drinking hot chocolate and watching a movie, and I just get really excited about that. HOLT: A moment of peace with the people you love, to give thanks, isn`t that what the day is all about? UNIDENTIFIED MALE: When I think about the holidays, I think about community and spending time with the people that I love and giving back to them and hopefully receiving the same.
