headline: The Today Show for December 8, 2022, NBC
story_text: (COMMERCIAL BREAK) [08:00:00] HODA KOTB, NBC NEWS TODAY, CO-ANCHOR: It`s 8:00 on "TODAY." Coming up, flu fears. New concerns over medication shortages as cases spike from coast to coast. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: There`s hardly anything to choose from. (END VIDEO CLIP) KOTB: Coming up, what you can do to ensure your family is prepared this flu season. Plus, breast cancer breakthrough. The just-released study sparking hope for women with breast cancer who want to start a new family. What the promising new data shows about a safe path forward. And Garten`s variety. The Barefoot Contessa herself, Ina Garten, joins us for a full hour to help spruce up our holiday tables, from a new spin on some tasty treats to becoming the host with the most. Plus, a glimpse into some of our most treasured traditions. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) CROWD: Three, two -- yahey. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: Blast off. (END VIDEO CLIP) KOTB: We`ve got a fun-filled hour ahead with a few surprises along the way. Today, Thursday, December 8, 2022. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: Best friends. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: And "TODAY" super fans. CROWD: From Parkersburg, West Virginia. CROWD: From Pullman, Washington. CROWD: And Lynwood, Illinois. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: From Hagerstown, Maryland. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: Celebrating our 25th anniversary. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: Friends for 20 years. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: From El Paso, Texas. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: Here with my grandson. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: From Mechanicsville, Virginia. CROWD: Hello from Woodbine, Iowa. CROWD: And Cincinnati, Ohio. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: Celebrating Vicky`s birthday. CROWD: From Baton Rouge. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: Here to experience a magic. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: Of Christmas in New York. CROWD: From Mizpah, Minnesota. (END VIDEO CLIP) KOTB: Welcome back. How do we say thank you for coming out -- SAVANNAH GUTHRIE, NBC NEWS TODAY, CO-ANCHOR: I know. KOTB: -- every morning? This crowd, it`s like six people thick. It`s a big crowd. We cannot wait to get outside and visit with everybody in just a bit. But what do you say we get to our news at 8:00? CRAIG MELVIN, NBC NEWS ANCHOR: Yes. KOTB: An early surge in flu cases is sending more Americans to the hospital and it`s actually causing pharmacies to run out of both prescription and over-the-counter treatments. NBC Sam brock has the latest on how long this might last and what you should do in case your drugstore shelves are empty. Sam, good morning. SAM BROCK, NBC NEWS CORRESPONDENT: Yes. Hoda, good morning. The mere fact that the flu season has arrived weeks in advance, as you said, has put parents in quite a crunch, pretty much across the board from antibiotics to antivirals. It`s true in Coral Gables, Florida, where I am, in San Francisco, California, Detroit, Michigan. All over the country. Now, the owner of University Pharmacist here tells me that amoxicillin right now, she has, about, maybe four or five patients worth of supplies left here. This is so important, it`s so critical because it`s the preferred antibiotic for kids. It`s a little bit milder, fewer side effects. That`s just one example. She wants to order more, cannot right now. Check out the store shelves. When it comes to decongestants, you see some Mucinex but the rest of the shelf here is empty. Robitussin, Sudafed they were down here, that`s gone as well. As far as anti-inflammatories for kids, Tylenol and Advil, there`s empty spaces on the shelf for that as well. All of it is unavailable. Now, the ASHP is a pharmacy group that tracks short supplies for drugs. They have right now, Hoda, some 260 drugs nationally that are short at the moment that includes Tamiflu, which is the most popular drug for treating the flu for kids, certainly, for adults as well. The issue with Tamiflu says one of their manufacturers, they have enough supply. They said it`s available for pharmacies to buy, but the owner here tells me it now cost three times of what it did just a few weeks ago. So, that anecdotally, is something that we`re seeing on the ground. This problem could go on for a number of weeks, well into the holidays. One of the advice -- pieces of advice doctors have for you, make you`re your pediatricians office contacts the pharmacy ahead of time to see if they have a drug in stock and to ask if there`s a viable alternative if there`s not. But parents right now are having to get creative as they go through this period where everybody is getting sick. Hoda, back to you. KOTB: Yes, happening in my neighborhood, too. All right. Sam Brock for us. Sam, thank you. GUTHRIE: For the first time in four decades, journalists and other employees at " The New York Times " are staging a large-scale walkout. The 24-hour strike by more than 1,000 members of the news gilded New York started just after midnight. The union says it lost patience with contract talks that have gone on for two years. A spokesperson for the "The Times" denied the talks were at an impasse and said it was disappointing that the union had taken what she called an extreme action. Negotiations have stalled over wages and remote work rules. MELVIN: A new study has found that women who`ve been treated for breast cancer may be able to pause their follow-up medications long enough to have a baby. After treatment, patients often take drugs to suppress their hormones for up to 10 years, but those drugs can also make it hard to conceive. [08:05:00] The new research led by Dr. Ann Partridge looked at how to balance the need for drug therapy with the desire to complete a family. And it found that within three years of pausing their medications, women had no greater risk of their cancers returning than those who stayed on the drugs, and about two-thirds were able to conceive and have a child. GUTHRIE: Well, grownups, who can`t recall third grade English lessons, can probably still sing every word of the "Schoolhouse Rock" cartoon that aired on Saturday mornings in the `70s and `80s. Well, George Newall, the man who helped create those classis tunes has passed away. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: Conjunction junction what`s your function. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: Hooking up words and phrases and clauses. (END VIDEO CLIP) GUTHRIE: I mean, we`re just singing it right here. KOTB: Yes. Uh-huh. MELVIN: Uh-huh. GUTHRIE: Those cartoons had a generation of kids about math and science and civics and grammar. Newall was an advertising pro. He composed all of those songs including "I`m Just a Bill on Capitol Hill." Remember that one? KOTB: Uh-huh. GUTHRIE: "Three is a Magic Number", he got the idea when a colleague with children asked about putting multiplication tables to music. George Newall was 88 years old. What a legacy. KOTB: Wow. Indeed. Wow. All right. Guys, would you like a little "Morning Boost"? GUTHRIE: Yes. MELVIN: Yes. KOTB: You got it. As you probably know, a white elephant party, it`s when you get together with your friends and you exchange silly gifts, usually just for kicks. So, Baylor University volleyball player Lauren Briseno never imagined she would -- what she would unwrap during their white elephant party that her coach hosted for the team. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) LAUREN BRISENO, BAYLOR UNIVERSITY VOLLEYBALL PLAYER: Hear ye, hear ye. It is with great exclamation that this proclamation be read. Due to unwavering diligence and determination for relentlessness and execution of incredible skills at the highest levels. For you (ph) of this year proclamation has hereby earned yourself a full scholarship. (END VIDEO CLIP) MELVIN: Oh, wow. GUTHRIE: Wow. KOTB: Lauren is a sophomore, by the way. She was a walk-on on the volleyball team. That was a surprise scholarship. She said she was eternally grateful. I mean, you think you`re getting one of those white elephant gifts. GUTHRIE: I know. KOTB: And you get one of that. GUTHRIE: Exactly. It sure beats the fridge magnet or whatever. MELVIN: Yes. GUTHRIE: All right. Guys, next, this is the next best thing to actually be invited to Ina Garten`s house. KOTB: Yes. GUTHRIE: She is here. She`s in our house, and giving all of her secrets for throwing a memorable holiday party from the moment your guests walk through the door to a parting gift they will never forget. Ina, the hostess with the most will host this show. MELVIN: Yes. KOTB: Yes. INA GARTEN, BAREFOOT CONTESSA HOST: We are going to have such a great time. GUTHRIE: We are, my friend. We`re back after this. (COMMERCIAL BREAK) [08:10:00] ANNOUNCER: From NBC News, this is a Special Report. Here`s Savannah Guthrie and Hoda Kotb. GUTHRIE: Good morning, everybody. We are following breaking news at this hour out of Russia. Nearly 10 months after her arrest and incarceration there, WNBA star Brittney Griner is headed home. KOTB: Yes. Breaking and welcome news. Russia has agreed to a prisoner swap with the U.S. We`re going to go straight to NBC`s Chief Foreign Affairs Correspondent, Andrea Mitchell, she has these breaking details. Andrea, what can you tell us? ANDREA MITCHELL, NBC NEWS CHIEF WASHINGTON CORRESPONDENT: Good morning, Savannah and Hoda. Well, according to a senior administration official, Brittney Griner is free after 294 days in Russian captivity. The last month spent in Russia`s notoriously harsh penal colonies. She was traded for Russian arms dealer Viktor Bout who Vladimir Putin has been trying to get back and had served 11 years of a 25-year sentence in the U.S. President Biden signed off on the trade even though it meant leaving another American businessman, Paul Whelan, behind bars in Russia. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) MITCHELL (voiceover): Over the weekend, Secretary of State, Antony Blinken , saying the U.S. has been actively engaged in discussions with Russia about a possible prisoner swap to free Brittney Griner and Paul Whelan. ANTONY BLINKEN, U.S. SECRETARY OF STATE: We have to see if the engagements that we`ve had, the discussions that we had produced an actual result. MITCHELL (voiceover): Griner, the 32-year-old WNBA superstar has spent nearly 10 months in Russian custody. Arrested at a Moscow airport in February. She admitted to bringing less than a gram of medicinal cannabis into the country but said she never intended to break any law. Her plight sparked an outpouring from her family, teammates and fans. Griner`s wife, Cherelle. CHERELLE GRINER, BRITTNEY GRINER`S WIFE: I`m frustrated that my wife is not going to get justice. I know you all are frustrated, too, that`s why you`re here. MITCHELL (voiceover): Sentenced to nine years in prison, Griner appealed, pleading for leniency from behind bars. BRITTNEY GRINER, WNBA PLAYER IMPRISONED IN RUSSIA: This has been very traumatic experience waiting for this day. MITCHELL (voiceover): But she was denied. President Biden last month. JOE BIDEN , U.S. PRESIDENT: I`m telling you, I am determined to get her home and get her home safely. Along with others, I might add. MITCHELL (voiceover): The other American held by Russia will not be coming home. Paul Whelan, a former marine, a businessman, detained four years ago is serving a 16-year prison sentence after being accused of spying, which the U.S. strongly denies. Whelan`s family later raised concerns about his safety, which I asked the secretary of state about last week. BLINKEN: We`re working to bring him home, to bring Brittney Griner home. But this is, again, what we see Russia doing in terms of abusing the very basic understandings that countries have had when it comes to having access to our citizens who are being detained. (END VIDEO CLIP) MITCHELL (on camera): Those familiar with these very hard negotiations say that the Russians absolutely refused to release Paul Whelan without getting a Russian spy in return. But the U.S. insists it does not have any Russian spies in U.S. custody. So, the administration says, it had no one to trade to meet that Russian demand. And again, the U.S. maintains that Paul Whelan is wrongfully detained. He`s a businessman, not a spy. And just now we also got a statement from the group that has been campaigning for all of these hostages to be released from all over the world, actually, saying Paul Whelan has been let down and left behind by -- at least three times, by two American presidents. He deserves better from his government and our campaign implores President Biden to urgently secure Paul`s immediate return using all tools available. We understand the president will be speaking shortly or later this morning. GUTHRIE: Yes. Andrea, thank you very much for the breaking news. Brittney Griner has been freed. Paul Whelan left behind. Let`s go to Chief White House Correspondent Peter Alexander at the White House. What`s the word there, Peter? PETER ALEXANDER, NBC NEWS CHIEF WHITE HOUSE CORRESPONDENT AND WEEKEND TODAY CO-ANCHOR: Savannah, we do expect to hear from President Biden at 8:30, so 15 minutes from now. And we have just learned that Cherelle Griner, Brittney Griner`s wife, is right now in the Oval Office here at the white house. She`s behind closed doors with the president. [08:15:00] The two of them were able to speak by phone earlier this morning with Brittney Griner after she was returned to U.S. custody. And then as we understand it, Cherelle was able to have a private conversation with her wife, Brittney, from the president`s study. But this concludes for the Griner family what has just been a very distressing situation over the course of the last 10 months. The president has said this was a top priority. He had exchanged a letter with Griner in the past who wrote him, over the summer, saying that she was terrified she would be there forever in Russian custody. The good news this morning that the White House will certainly be celebrating today is the release of Brittney Griner. And again, to repeat, Cherelle Griner`s, the president`s -- is in the Oval Office with the president right now and had an opportunity to speak alongside the president with her wife just this morning. Savannah and Hoda. KOTB: All right. Peter Alexander, thank you so much. We are going to continue to keep a close eye on the story all morning long. We`re going to bring you updates. And of course, we`ll have coverage on "NBC Nightly News" and all day on "NBC News NOW". GUTHRIE: For now, many of our stations will return to the "TODAY" show in New York. This is Savannah Guthrie and Hoda Kotb. Good day. 8:16. We want to turn now to Dylan and get a check of the weather. She is aboard a ship, are you not? Oh, where are you now? DYLAN DREYER, NBC NEWS 3RD HOUR OF TODAY CO-HOST AND METEOROLOGIST: I am, but I brought you inside now to show you some of the extravagance here in an atrium. This staircase made of Swarovski crystals, I mean, because that`s what you need on a cruise ship after all. But let`s take a look at what`s going on outside. Here in the northeast, it is a little bit chilly but I`d say seasonable for this time of year. It`s really down through the Ohio River Valley where we`ll see a lot of that rain move in today, heavy at times. And the snow is going to move into the Upper Midwest. Temperatures, still very warm, especially down along the Gulf Coast where we`ll likely break high temperatures today. Although it is going to be quite chilly across the Northern Plains. Highs only in the teens and 20s. That`s a look at the weather across the country. Now, here`s a peek out your window. (LOCAL NEWS) DREYER: And that`s your latest forecast. Back to you guys. GUTHRIE: All right. Dylan, thank you. Well, back in Studio 1A, we have gathered to kick off our series "Ina`s Holiday Table". And we are at Ina`s holiday table right now. We`re all getting a special invite to her home as Ina Garten co-hosts this entire hour with us. KOTB: Yes. MELVIN: We are so excited. GARTEN: It`s crazy. KOTB: OK. First of all, Ina, how does it feel to be a co-anchor? GARTEN: Thank you. It`s just so fun and scary. KOTB: Well, you`re going to be amazing because I love -- you make everything simple. You`re going to make our holiday season a little brighter, a little warmer without the fuss. You got friends. But your keyword you keep talking about is simple, which is what we love the most. GARTEN: It`s so important. That`s exactly right, Hoda. I`m so excited to be here with all of you. The holidays can be so stressful. What do you make? How do you entertain? It can feel totally overwhelming, even for me. So, I`m here to show you how to simplify it and actually enjoy the holidays. How is that for a newbie? GUTHRIE: I love that. CARSON DALY, NBC NEWS HOST: Love it. GARTEN: So, before we get to drinking the cranberry martinis. MELVIN: Do it, Carson. GARTEN: Let`s hear how all of you like to celebrate the holiday season. CROWD: Cheers. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) DALY: If you get an invite to the Daly house, you`re going to be transformed right into the true spirit of Christmas. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: It`s the most wonderful time of the year. GUTHRIE: I have become a holiday decor person. I admit it. I`m buying cute little things with my name on it and the kids` names. KOTB: We have a beautiful Christmas tree that we love. CROWD: Three, two -- yahey. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: Blast off. KOTB: It`s only got decorations on the bottom because that`s where the kids could reach. MELVIN: I can`t imagine the holidays without Christmas music. I`ve been playing all of my favorites. And my son`s favorite Christmas song is the Donny Hathaway classic. KOTB: I`m going to be totally honest, I don`t host or entertain that much. I mean, if someone comes over, I`m like, I think we have cookies. Are you OK with this? DALY: I`m controversial with my Christmas holiday hosting duties because I`m a fun of eggnog. And I feel like eggnog is getting a bad rep these days. So, if you like eggnog, you`re always welcome in our house. MELVIN: When my wife twists my arm and we actually have people over for the holidays, I make a nice big cocktail. It`s sort of my take on a hot toddy and she makes everything else. GUTHRIE: I love having people over. Nothing formal. Just come on by. Everybody`s in their cozy sweaters. Everyone`s happy. It`s just beautiful time of year. (END VIDEO CLIP) GARTEN: Savannah, you said you like to have like a free-wheeling -- GUTHRIE: Yes. GARTEN: -- like a holiday party. GUTHRIE: Crazy. GARTEN: People just come and go. GUTHRIE: I do. GARTEN: You know what I love to do, I like to have a surprise guest. GUTHRIE: Yes. [08:20:00] GARTEN: Somebody everybody just adores and they`re just so happy to see. GUTHRIE: Someone that everyone will like. GARTEN: It has to be someone everyone will like. GUTHRIE: OK. KOTB: OK. GARTEN: And so, I invited a surprise guest -- KOTB: Who? GARTEN: -- to our party. KOTB: Who? MELVIN: Who is it? GARTEN: And I think he`s waiting in the wings. Willie Geist, are you here? GUTHRIE: Oh, my God. Drake (ph)? Oh, it`s Willie. KOTB: Willie -- WILLIE GEIST, SUNDAY TODAY, HOST: Are you disappointed it was me? GUTHRIE: I thought it was going to be Beyonce. DALY: I thought Santa was coming out. KOTB: Hi, Willie. GEIST: Great to see you. GARTEN: It`s so good to see you. GEIST: I bought you some coffee mugs for you and Jeffrey. But also can be used for cranberry martinis. GARTEN: Oh, yes. GEIST: Yes, yes, yes. GUTHRIE: Hi, Willie. KOTB: Come sit with us. GARTEN: How great is that? Did I nail that? KOTB: Why is willie your go-to guest, because he does bring the fun. DALY: He is a great guest. KOTB: Yes, he really is. GARTEN: He`s a funster. KOTB: He`s a funster? GARTEN: We had such a good -- GEIST: We`ve had some fun. GARTEN: We`ve had some fun together. KOTB: Really? GARTEN: Yes, really. Now, that`s really suggestive to say. GUTHRIE: Wow. Jeffrey was there. KOTB: Jeffrey was there and your wife, Christina, was there. GEIST: Exactly. Yes. We drink together, yes. GARTEN: So, we had a really good time together. So, I have so many questions to ask you about holiday. KOTB: OK. GARTEN: And it`s hard. It`s really stressful. And I try to keep it simple. And I -- so, Willie, what do you like to do? You like to make cocktails, right? GEIST: I like a cocktail. I like a big tent, like you, guys. Wide open, everybody come over, put some drinks out, put good music on. I just want everybody to have fun and be relaxed. KOTB: Yes. GUTHRIE: Yes. GARTEN: You know, one of the things I want, when people arrive at the door, I want all of your senses engaged. KOTB: Uh-huh. GARTEN: I want something delicious to eat, like caramelized pecans. Great music. And you guys are talking about having great music -- KOTB: Yes. DALY: Yes. GARTEN: -- and, you know, just really gorgeous -- GUTHRIE: On the fireplace -- DALY: Open firepit. GEIST: Fire, yes. GARTEN: -- gorgeous house. GUTHRIE: Are those your five senses, Ina, like do you kind of -- GARTEN: You want to smell something wonderful. So, it can be, like -- sometimes if I get an apple pie, I`ll just put it in the oven, even though it`s from the bakery. So, it smells like apple pie, doesn`t it? KOTB: Wow. That is brilliant. GARTEN: What are the other things that, like, smell great? KOTB: Cookies. GUTHRIE: You know, I love a candle. And Al bought us all the Harlem candle company. MELVIN: Yes. GUTHRIE: That green candle. And I`ve been lighting it all season and it`s just -- GARTEN: So, when you walk in, it just feels like a party. GUTHRIE: It smells so good. KOTB: It feels like cozy, cozy. GARTEN: Or, like if you have a fireplace, you can have a fire and it`s both smell and the fire but also the crackling. KOTB: Ina, I mean, I love Willie. I think he`s a great guest. GEIST: We can do better. KOTB: No. GUTHRIE: No. DALY: You`re good guest, but on TV you`re a terrible guest. KOTB: But I think there is someone who I think you adore -- I think you`ve been trying to get together with her for a while. It hasn`t been able to work out. GUTHRIE: Yes, schedule. KOTB: But you know what, today it will. GARTEN: Who? KOTB: Misty Copeland. MELVIN: No. KOTB: Will you please come out? MELVIN: Oh, I love that. GARTEN: A surprise guest. Oh, I`m so happy to see you. MISTY COPELAND, BALLET DANCER, AMERICAN BALLET THEATRE: I`m so happy I can be here and see you. KOTB: Hi, Misty. GUTHRIE: Hi, Misty. DALY: Hi, Misty. MELVIN: Hi, Misty. GUTHRIE: Have a seat at Ina`s table. COPELAND: Oh, thank you. KOTB: There you go, Ina. GUTHRIE: Ina, are you shocked? GARTEN: I`m shocked. KOTB: Now, tell us about -- you wanted Misty to be your guest. GARTEN: Well, she is. She was my guest on -- we spent a day together at my house. And we cooked together -- COPELAND: Yes, we did. GARTEN: -- and we talked about your unbelievable career. I mean, this is like the most amazing -- KOTB: Is she not amazing? GARTEN: Just amazing. We won`t talk about her while she`s here. GUTHRIE: Misty, do you like to host? Is that something like -- COPELAND: I do. GUTHRIE: Yes. COPELAND: And I -- we`ve talked about it. But I learned so much -- you know, moving to New York City when I was 17 years old and learning to host and to cook by watching Ina. GARTEN: You know, one of the things I think we all forget in hosting is about the people. MELVIN: Yes. GARTEN: It`s not about the food. KOTB: OK. GARTEN: I mean, you want the food to be good. But you can just go out and get, like, apple cider and put it on the stove and have cookies and -- I mean, your -- you`re always nervous about hosting. KOTB: Can I be honest? MELVIN: Yes. KOTB: Guys, you`re going to think I`m crazy. I don`t think I`ve ever hosted a party at my house. GARTEN: Just -- GUTHRIE: What? MELVIN: No. KOTB: Other than a birthday party for my kids or something or my sister -- GUTHRIE: And you were born to party. What`s this? DALY: You`re like Willie. You`re a great guest at other parties. You probably make the rounds during the holiday. KOTB: I do that. Was that kind of what weighed on you, and what do your parents think about this incredible man that you become? PUEBLO: Yes, I think, um -- it was -- it was hard. You know, it was hard seeing my parents go through this immense challenge of trying to keep our family afloat. And we were just -- you know, like I said before, we were stuck in a poverty trap. And it was quite difficult for us to come out of it until I became older until my brother became older, my little sister and now we can support ourselves, help our parents as well. And I think my parents are just they`re really grateful that the gamble paid off for all three of us. Because coming to United States it`s -- HAGER: Yes. PUEBLO: You know, it`s a bit of a risk and but it worked out for us. KOTB: Well, I have your book by my bedside, it`s one of those you can open up read one beautiful line and go to sleep and sleep really well. So -- HAGER: She actually goes to bed with your words in her head every night. KOTB: Yes. PUEBLO: Wow. HAGER: And then make her feel lighter. PUEBLO: That`s a big honor. KOTB: Big for me too. Thank you. HAGER: And then make her feel lighter. And I think if you want that light, it`s here. KOTB: Yes. And you got to get the book, Lighter. And also, your other two books are amazing. I like all three, but get this one because it`s new. (END VIDEOTAPE) KOTB: By the way, since that segment aired Yung Pueblo`s book Lighter reached number one on the New York Times bestsellers list. To check it out, head to today.com/books. HAGER: Coming up next, two tennis-playing sisters who truly understand the importance of serving after this. (COMMERCIAL BREAK) [10:50:53] KOTB: We hope you`ve been feeling inspired by the people and stories we`ve shared with you, but we are not done yet. HAGER: We want you to meet two sisters Ayanna and Amani Shah, they`re teenagers and they`ve already changed the lives of thousands of kids all over the world. Take a look. (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) HAGER: 16-year-old Ayanna and 18-year-old Amani Shah loves to serve. AMANI SHAH, CEO, SECOND SERVE: I think more could supply tennis because it`s a phenomenal way to build character. AYANNA SHAH, PRESIDENT, SECOND SERVE: Tennis has taught me so many lessons and I think the biggest one is learning how to push through obstacles. HAGER: And since 2019 their nonprofit organization Second Serve has been working to give kids around the world equitable access to tennis. AMANI SHAH: When I was 10 years old was when I really fell in love with the sport. AYANNA SHAH: The relationships that I`ve built through tennis have been just amazing. AMANI SHAH: Historically, tennis has been deemed an elitist sport because of its very high-cost entry. AYANNA SHAH: Second Serve redistributes new and gently used tennis equipment all around the world. Our mission is to create greater access, inclusion, and diversity within the sport. One of my personal favorite donations was to a young girl in Nigeria named Nana Rosie (PH). UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: I started playing tennis since I was three years old. AMANI SHAH: Nana spends four to five hours every day playing tennis and her dedication is really an inspiration for us. HAGER: Ayanna and Amani tap teams across the U.S. to make this all happen. AMANI SHAH: Our team has grown to over 90 different high school team members all across the U.S. We`ve been able to redistribute over 20,000 items in over 26 states and 14 different countries. EMMA HIGUCHI, COO, SECOND SERVE: What I was drawn to is it was a -- it`s a youth-led organization. We always have monthly meetings. Just hearing their great ideas is really great and hopefully, we can make those ideas come reality. SUSAN PRATT, TENNIS COACH, ORANGE GLEN HIGH SCHOOL: The Shah sisters of Second Serve have been an inspiration to me and also to our high school tennis team. It`s a school of 91 percent economically disadvantaged kids. Having a tennis racquet gives them that sense of ownership. DIANNA, ORANGE GLEN HIGH SCHOOL STUDENT: At first I couldn`t really hit but now I can do like everything. PRATT: Now she`s competing. She`s our number one player. I have seen her build a sense of confidence. I stopped. HAGER: Inspired to do more in their own backyard, the team started Serve Escondido. AMANI SHAH: We provide free tennis lessons for under-resourced kids in our own hometown of San Diego. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: Good job. HAGER: And in the spirit of giving back, we had a little surprise for Second Serve. AMANI SHAH: Second Serve has done incredible work to make the game of tennis accessible to all. Second Serves` mission of enhancing the lives of underserved children by fostering a love for tennis is inspirational and empowering, to support that mission Athleta is donating 100 girls` tennis dresses to Second Serve. Oh, my God. AMANI SHAH: Thank you so much. This is awesome. It`s just really special to see that other people support this vision of greater access and greater diversity for all kids. When I`m on the tennis court, I`ve experienced that what you believe is really what you can achieve. When you`re about to serve when you`re about to hit a ball if you can visualize that ball going exactly to your target. That`s often exactly what happens. (END VIDEOTAPE) HAGER: The Shah sisters are going to take over the world. A big thank you to Wilson and Athleta for helping us with that surprise. KOTB: Yes, that was awesome. headline: 50 Years After Roe v. Wade, America Is An Abortion Battleground After The Supreme Court Decision Overturning It
story_text: LESTER HOLT: We have new details on the Supreme Court`s probe into the stunning leak last year, that draft opinion overturning Roe v. Wade. The Supreme Court Marshal revealed today she spoke with each justice in addition to court employees, but investigators were not able to identify the leaker. And this weekend marks 50 years since the Roe v. Wade decision. In the months since it was overturned, the U.S. has become a patchwork of laws varying from state to state. Anne Thompson with more now on the deep impact on clinics. [19:15:07] (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) ANNE THOMPSON, NBC NEWS CORRESPONDENT (voiceover): The days are nonstop at Florida`s Jacksonville Health Center. 50 years after roe versus wade and seven months after the Dobbs ruling that overturned it, demand for abortion at this Planned Parenthood Clinic hasn`t slowed says Manager Jessica Wannemacher. JESSICA WANNEMACHER, MANAGER, PLANNED PARENTHOOD CLINIC, JACKSONVILLE: It`s getting worse. THOMPSON: What do you mean? WANNEMACHER: The amount of patient load that we need to be able to see more patients. THOMPSON: Four years ago, the clinic offered abortion services once a week. Now, it`s up to five days. Dr. Shelly Tien specializes in high-risk pregnancies. Of the 63 patients you`re seeing today, how many of those are seeking abortion services? DR. SHELLY TIEN, PLANNED PARENTHOOD CLINIC: The vast majority. THOMPSON: Has it been like that since the Supreme Court decision? TIEN: It has. THOMPSON: Florida bans abortions after 15 weeks with narrow exceptions. It also requires two in-person doctor`s visits at least 24 hours apart, but the outright bans and heartbeat bills in neighboring states have more than doubled the out-of-state patients here. For opponents of abortion rights like Andrew Shervill, it is a frustrating consequence of the Supreme Court decision. ANDREW SHIRVELL, FOUNDER AND EXECUTIVE DIRECTOR, FLORIDA VOICE FOR THE UNBORN: It`s extremely -- actually, it`s extremely infuriating because here Florida`s leading on so many other issues, but we should not be in this position at all. THOMPSON: So, what`s next? SHIRVELL: What`s next? Here in Florida, we`re pushing for a complete abortion ban. THOMPSON: But at the clinic Dr. Tien believes any restrictions come with dire consequences. TIEN: Women are going to die because of what has happened to reproductive rights in this country. THOMPSON: A recent Commonwealth Fund study analyzed data from 2020 and found maternal death rates were 62% higher in states that had abortion restrictions. The battle is now in states like Florida. SHIRVELL: I think the Dobbs decision properly returned the public policy fight to the states, and that for the foreseeable future is where activists on both sides are going to be engaged. THOMPSON: Should medical doctors have a role in crafting abortion law? SHIRVELL: No, I don`t believe so. THOMPSON: Dr. Tien disagrees. TIEN: It must be shared decision-making between the patient, her family and her healthcare team. THOMPSON: Do politicians have a role in this? TIEN: Absolutely not. Absolutely not. THOMPSON: Rulings may change, but the debate has no end in sight. Anne Thompson, NBC News, Jacksonville. (END VIDEOTAPE) HOLT: All right, coming up, it may say organic, but is it food fraud? The new warning and crackdown next. END Content and programming copyright 2023 NBCUniversal. ALL RIGHTS RESERVED. Transcription Copyright 2023 VIQ Media Transcription, Inc. headline: On This 50th Anniversary Weekend Of The Roe Versus Wade Decision That Was Overturned Last Year
story_text: [07:00:18] JOE FRYER, NBC NEWS ANCHOR: Good morning and thanks for starting your weekend with us and it might be a good one to stay inside with another big storm impacting much of the country. KRISTEN WELKER, NBC NEWS ANCHOR: And another one is close behind. It`s January 21st. This is TODAY. Severe weather watch. Millions in the south preparing for a heavy dose of rain today with the potential of flash floods before the same storm heads up the East Coast. Threatening to bring up to a half a foot of snow in the Northeast. We`ll have the full forecast. Battle Cry. On this 50th anniversary weekend of the Roe versus Wade decision that was overturned last year, tens of thousands take to the streets of the nation`s capital as part of the March for Life rally. Where does the abortion fight go from here? Record surge. The government reporting the number of illegal border crossings at its highest level ever since President Biden took office. What can officials do to slow down the influx? Caught on camera. Police take down. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: Drop it! Drop it! WELKER: Harrowing moments inside an Indiana Wal-Mart captured on police bodycam after a former employee opened fire. This morning, the woman police are credited with helping to stop the bloodshed from getting worse. All that, plus football frenzy. Fans from coast to coast getting ready for this weekend`s NFL playoffs divisional round. Eight teams facing off including that highly anticipated rematch between the Buffalo Bills and Cincinnati Bengals . It all kicks off today, Saturday January 21st, 2023. ANNOUNCER: From NBC News, this is TODAY with Peter Alexander and Kristen Welker. WELKER: Welcome to TODAY and thank you so much for joining us on this Saturday morning. Peter is enjoying the morning off. We`ve got Joe Fryer here. And Joe, you are here for a big weekend in softball, a big weekend for my beloved Eagles taking on the Giants. FRYER: We know what you`re going to be e doing tonight. We definitely know who you`re going to be cheering for. WELKER: Fly Eagle fly. I got the whole family in town. We are ready. FRYER: I know you are and I might be jumping on your bandwagon because the Giants beat my Vikings last week and I`m still bitter. WELKER: Yes, you know where your allegiances are. FRYER: Exactly. WELKER: I like that. All right. Good. FRYER: Exactly. We`re going to talk football and a little bit. We`re going to be begin though by covering several developing stories this morning. That includes the marches planned this weekend for activists on both sides of the abortion rights debate. We`re going to hear what anti-abortion rights protesters are hoping for next today after that big March for Life rally here in D.C. WELKER: And we`ll also tell you about tough times for the tech industry. Google `s parent company announcing on Friday at slashing 12,000 jobs. They`re joining other companies like Microsoft , Amazon and Meta making mass layoffs. FRYER: But let`s begin this morning with our top story. The weather as the south prepares for intense rain today and the Northeast gets ready for a round of snow that could bring up to six inches. WELKER: Some area saw a preview of that on Friday for the very latest on all of it. Let`s bring in Somara Theodore. Somara, you`ve been tracking this. What should folks be bracing for? (LOCAL NEWS) [07:05:16] WELKER: Somara, thanks. Maybe a good weekend to stay indoors for a lot of people. We`ll get the rest of your forecast in just a few minutes. FRYER: This weekend marks the 50th anniversary of the Supreme Court`s decision on Roe v. Wade. And a half century later the debate over abortion rights still looms large, especially after the Dobbs decision last year overturning Roe. On Friday the March for life took place just one of several marches this weekend on both sides of the issue. NBC`s Marissa Parra was at the march and joins us with more. Marissa, good morning to you. WELKER: Good morning. MARISSA PARRA, NBC NEWS CORRESPONDENT: Joe and Kristen, good morning to you. Another busy day in D.C. as usual, right? WELKER: Yes. PARRA: Well crowds for the march we`re in the tens of thousands. And we know that the march was originally started to protest Roe versus Wade. So, there was a big celebratory mood in this new post Roe era, right? This is what they`ve been fighting for. But activists on both sides of the abortion debate are really galvanized in different ways, especially as we get closer to 2024. (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) PARRA (voice over): This morning, the battle over abortion access far from over. Roughly seven months after Roe v. Wade was overturned, the nation`s capital seeing the nation`s first march for life in a post Roe world. REP. STEVE SCALISE (R-LA): And today, we celebrate Roe is gone. It`s important to keep your focus on what the mission is. But every step of the way. It`s also critical that we celebrate victories along the way. PARRA: Changing the route to reflect a change country, stopping in front of both the Supreme Court and the Capitol. A symbolic nod to the role they both have and continue to play abortion law. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: It`s up to the states now so we need to raise awareness and each of the states. PARRA: Counter protesters reading their own fight to win back lost ground. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: That is why I`m here. It is to show that we will not let America be bullied out of the right to abortion. PARRA: The path to a full nationwide victory for either side an uphill battle. It`s been 50 years since Roe v. Wade was first signed into law. But in the months since its reversal last summer, almost two dozen states have either banned abortion or they`re close to it, with several legislative sessions actively debating what their laws will be on a state level. This says federal action fails to move forward. Senator Lindsey Graham`s federal abortion ban proposal failed last fall and the Biden administration`s hopes of a federal right to choose. KARINE JEAN-PIERRE , WHITE HOUSE PRESS SECRETARY: We need to codify Roe. PARRA: Unlikely and a Republican-controlled House. And with new FDA guidance making abortion bills more accessible over the counter, a new abortion battleground is headed to the pharmacy. (END VIDEOTAPE) PARRA: Now that new FDA guidance was a small victory for abortion rights activists and we know tomorrow is the 50th anniversary of that original decision. So, there are bigger than Roe pro-choice marches scheduled across the country. Joe and Kristen? FRYER: All right. Kristen -- Marissa Parra, thank you so much. Appreciate it. WELKER: Great to see you, Marissa. Really appreciate it. Well, just one day after the Supreme Court announced it couldn`t find who was behind the leak of that draft opinion of the decision to overturn Roe v. Wade. Former President Trump is calling on the journalists who revealed the leak to be jailed. And this morning the Biden administration is fighting back. NBC`s Monica Alba is tracking all of it from the White House. Monica, good morning to you. MONICA ALBA, NBC NEWS WHITE HOUSE CORRESPONDENT: Kristen, good morning. After an eight-month investigation that leaks still could not be pinpointed with former President Trump pushing stricter measures to root out the leaker. The probe led by the courts chief security officer determined hackers were likely not responsible. after interviewing 97 employees. The search found that 82 had access to digital or hard copies of the draft. But now we`re learning more about who else was questioned in the matter. The court investigator revealing Friday she spoke with each of the nine justices several on multiple occasions and all cooperated in the process. Every credible lead was explored and none of them implicated the justices or their spouses according to the court. And soon after the 20-page report came out that couldn`t identify the leak, the former president called for the reporters who broke the news to be arrested, along with possibly their editor and publisher saying they should be put in jail "until the answer is given." Within hours, the White House released a statement defending freedom of the press saying it`s the responsibility of all leaders to protect First Amendment rights. Kristen? WELKER: Yes. Just remarkable that that investigation could not determine who was behind the leak. Monica, another big headline you are tracking we`re also in the midst of this debt ceiling standoff between the White House and Republicans but we`re hearing that the President will meet with House Speaker Kevin McCarthy to discuss a path forward. What are you hearing? ALBA: That`s right, Kristen. While speaker McCarthy did accept President Biden`s offer to meet soon, no date has been set yet by the White House. But a contentious back and forth Friday about the debt ceiling show just how difficult resolving this issue may be. [07:10:07] House Republicans don`t want to increase America`s ability to borrow without promises of future spending cuts. While the President says there`s no room for negotiation when the stakes are so high. Warning of unprecedented financial calamity if the U.S. doesn`t meet its credit obligations for the first time in history. Experts say it could even lead to a recession or stock market crash if it happens, as the treasury secretary is already using extraordinary measures to keep paying the nation`s bills effectively buying time by shifting money around but that will only last until June. Kristen? WELKER: A major test and showdown for all of Washington. Monica Alba at the White House. Thank you, Monica. FRYER: Illegal crossings at the U.S.-Mexico border last month surged to a record number since President Biden took office. The government says it stopped migrants more than 250,000 times along the border. Up 40 percent from the prior December. The extraordinary influx came shortly before Mr. Biden introduced measures to deter migrants from Cuba, Haiti, Nicaragua and Venezuela. Republicans say his lacks border policies have led to the flood. END Content and programming copyright 2023 NBCUniversal. ALL RIGHTS RESERVED. headline: Meet the Press for January 22, 2023, NBC
story_text: (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) [09:00:19] CHUCK TODD, NBC HOST (voice over): This Sunday, another document discovery. The FBI searched President Biden`s Delaware home on Friday and found more classified materials. Six documents, including some from his time as a senator, were found. Biden insists he did nothing wrong. PRESIDENT JOSEPH R. BIDEN, JR.: I think you`re going to find there`s nothing there. I have no regrets. TODD: Plus, warning signs. American politics teetering on the edge, from the court to Congress, to special counsel probes and rising extremist threats. After losing an election and claiming it was rigged, a Republican candidate is arrested and charged in connection with shootings at the homes of four Democratic lawmakers. (UNKNOWN): An attack on an elected official is an attack on democracy. TODD: New Mexico, just the latest example of election denialism sparking political violence. And, post-Roe. Fifty years after the landmark Supreme Court decision granting a constitutional right to abortion, the debate over reproductive rights has shifted, with the ruling now overturned. (UNKNOWN): We didn`t learn anything after overturning of Roe v. Wade. We buried our head in the sand. TODD: But if you think either side is open to finding a middle ground, think again. My guests this morning, Democratic Senator Joe Manchin of West Virginia and Republican Congresswoman Nancy Mace of South Carolina. Plus, lasting impact. FORMER PRESIDENT WILLIAM JEFFERSON CLINTON : I did not have sexual relations with that woman. TODD: The Lewinsky scandal and its consequences still influencing American political life 25 years later. Joining me for insight and analysis are NBC News chief White House correspondent Kristen Welker; Republican strategist Brendan Buck; New York Times chief White House correspondent Peter Baker; and Kimberly Atkins Stohr, senior opinion writer for the Boston Globe . Welcome to Sunday. It`s "Meet the Press." ANNOUNCER: From NBC News in Washington, the longest-running show in television history, this is "Meet the Press With Chuck Todd." TODD: Good Sunday morning. Boy, our democracy and our politics, they feel like we`re at a breaking point. We have rising political violence fueled by election denialism, economic brinksmanship in Congress, a Supreme Court relationships between the justices so strained after an unprecedented leak, they have yet to issue an opinion this term. And trust in the court from the public never been lower. And this morning we`re waking up to reports of another mass shooting with at least 10 dead at a lunar new year event in Monterey Park, California. Details are still coming in. No need to jump to conclusions, but, let`s be honest, these events do not exactly bring comfort to our current political system. We don`t handled these well or solve these problems. And if all of this wasn`t enough, adding to this instability, we have both the current and former presidents under investigation. And on Saturday night the White House revealed more classified information was found at Biden`s Wilmington home, after what was a remarkable 13-hour FBI -led search on Friday of the home of a sitting president. It wasn`t a subpoena; it was a cooperative search. It was done with the president`s legal team acknowledging it. They said they offered to provide prompt access to his home, and that six more items with classified markings were indeed found, including documents from Biden`s time as a senator as well as vice president. And this FBI search comes just days after Biden said he had no regrets about how he`s handled the issue of classified documents and how he`s talked to the public about it. But it`s likely to prompt more comparisons between the current and former presidents, though of course Mr. Trump and his advisers are also being investigated for obstructing their probe. Then we have the issue of election denialism. That`s been fueled by Donald Trump . And, sadly, it appears it`s given some of his supporters a permission slip to commit political violence. The case in New Mexico this week is just the latest in a string of violent incidents rooted in election denialism, from the assault on Brazil`s capitol by supporters of the former president there, where Trump allies actually helped sow doubts about those election results. We had the attack on Paul Pelosi just days before the midterm elections as well. And then, finally, we have this manufactured crisis here in Washington, this escalating rhetoric over the debt limit. It`s a reminder of just how fractured right now the Republican Party is, because it`s Republicans wanting to have this fight in an attempt to re-brand themselves as the party of fiscal discipline, if you will, after they oversaw an explosive rise in the national debt under President Donald Trump . So Republicans are trying to use this debate to try to unify them around an issue, cutting spending. Democrats, of course, now see an opportunity to paint House Republicans as extremist. The reality is, of course, at the end of the day, this debt limit is going to get raised. We just don`t know how it gets done. Even Republican Senate Leader Mitch McConnell concedes this point. SENATE MINORITY LEADER MITCH MCCONNELL, (R) KENTUCKY: America must never default on its debt. It never has and it never will. QUESTION: Should we be concerned about a financial crisis? [09:05:01] MCCONNELL: No, I would not be concerned about a financial crisis. (END VIDEOTAPE) TODD: And joining me now is Senator Joe Manchin of West Virginia. Senator Manchin, welcome back... MANCHIN: Chuck, it`s always good to be with you. TODD: Look, I want to get into the debt ceiling. I want to get into all this stuff. But I -- we got some developments overnight with this classified documents, an FBI search. The White House said it was coordinated with the FBI , but we now have an FBI searching of former President Trumps`s... MANCHIN: Sure. TODD: Now we have an FBI search into President Biden`s residence. What`s your assessment of how the president has handled this situation? MANCHIN: Well, I mean, it`s just hard to believe that -- that in the United States of America we have a former president and the current president basically in the same situation. How does this happen? You know, only thing I can tell you, Chuck, is when I go into the SCIF with the secured documents, they always ask, "Are you clean," when you walk out. They want to make sure you`re not carrying anything out. You know, and there might be a mistake. You might just put it in your other papers. But you double-check right there. So that -- to be held accountable and responsible is what we all are. And to put those in unsecured spaces is irresponsible. TODD: Do you see similarities or do you see more differences in how President Trump versus how President Biden`s handled this? MANCHIN: I`m not going to make that decision, but I think that Merrick Garland did the right thing by putting a special counsel. TODD: You do? MANCHIN: And I think that we should wait until the special counsel rather than making this a political circus. Let them find out the facts. What, was one more damaging? Are they both about the same, did not cause any problem? Or is one more reckless and irresponsible than the other? I can`t answer that question, but I think the special counsel will do a better job than the politicians and the political circus that`s going to follow. TODD: President Biden said he had no regrets on how he handled this. Do you have any advice for him on how he should handle this... MANCHIN: Oh, I think he should have a lot of regrets, yeah. I would... TODD: What are they? MANCHIN: I would think that. And I`d say, whoever`s responsible -- I mean, if I hold people accountable and I use, whether it be my staff or my -- you know, my -- my staff, that we`re doing this, and I`m looking at it, then I`m going to hold someone accountable. But, basically, the buck stops with me. TODD: So you think he should be out there, and "Look, I -- I messed up." MANCHIN: That`s all. Just say... TODD: "Maybe I didn`t do it" -- just say it? MANCHIN: "I made a mistake." TODD: Just fall on your sword here? MANCHIN: We`re all human. TODD: Yeah... MANCHIN: We make mistakes. I can tell you, I don`t think anyone intended - - he sure didn`t intend for it to fall into wrong hands and use it against our country. I know they didn`t intend that to happen. Could it have happened? I don`t know. And, yeah, you just might as well say, "Listen, it`s irresponsible. It was something we should have had a better check and balance on. TODD: Now, former President Trump defied a subpoena. So, in that sense, the way each has handled is different. Do you acknowledge that? MANCHIN: Absolutely... TODD: Yeah. TODD: ... much different than the other. One`s -- one`s saying, "OK, I hope I didn`t make any mistakes. I hope no one was compromised. I hope we didn`t hurt our country." And the other says, "Oh, I`m -- believe me." Well, you know what? (LAUGHTER) What they said, verify. You have to verify? TODD: Trust, but verify. MANCHIN: Trust, but verify. Let`s find out. And that`s what the special counsel is... TODD: And that`s what you want here? Both special counsels to, sort of, resolve... MANCHIN: First of all, every one of us in our life have to be held accountable and responsible for our actions. TODD: Yeah. MANCHIN: People want accountability. And they want, basically, when you`re held accountable, are you responsible or not? If you are, would you -- can you fix that? Did you make a mistake? Fine. You know... TODD: And that`s what you think, the president needs to get out and there just get in front of it. MANCHIN: Cicero said, "To err is human." You`re a human being. You`re going to make mistakes. Did you intend to make it? Did you intend to harm somebody? Did you intend to basically do an irresponsible thing? I don`t think, hopefully, either one of them did. TODD: Right. MANCHIN: But it sure -- sure turned out to be irresponsible. TODD: Let`s talk about the debt ceiling. You`re -- as always, you`re trying to find a compromise and middle ground. MANCHIN: Yeah. TODD: I -- I know your instinct here. (LAUGHTER) But why should Republicans get the benefit of the doubt on the debt ceiling here, considering that it`s -- that they`re, sort of, manufacturing a crisis that`s a bit unnecessary right now? MANCHIN: Well, first of all, if one side thinks that the other one`s more responsible for the debt, at $31.4 trillion, that`s -- that is totally not accurate, and it`s deceptive. We`re all responsible. We`ve got a $31.4 trillion debt. It`s a runaway debt, and no one`s holding themselves accountable. And basically, I think you said it, use the budget process. And clearly, they are different -- look, Donald Trump is not the standard. You can`t set the standard by how Donald Trump handled things. TODD: That`s Biden`s biggest problem, isn`t it? BUCK: That is. And Joe Biden himself was attacking Donald Trump for the underlying infraction, not just how whether he didn`t give them back, the underlying infraction. Either that matters, or it doesn`t. TODD: Kimberly? KIMBERLY ATKINS STOHR, NBC NEWS CONTRIBUTOR: But this is a missed opportunity here because at a time when the public trust in institutions is at a very, very low point, this was an opportunity for the Biden administration to say, look, this is how it`s done. As soon as they got the information about these documents, invite the FBI in then. Search everything. Take a look. This was inadvertent. And then you can show how this is very different from saying, you know, I can un- classify it with my mind, or defying federal authorities and saying, no, I have a right to keep these things. They`re mine. That`s very different from how they`re handling it, and it was an opportunity to show that to the American public, and they missed it. TODD: I know this is a classic case of lawyers being lawyers and not wanting to get into the PR game, but it really looks like that keeping a close circle here was damaging. [09:40:03] WELKER: It has been damaging optically and again from a messaging standpoint. It`s important to point out, and Kimberly, you kind of touched on this, that in terms of this search that happened at President Biden`s Delaware home, the thinking is it`s going to be short term pain with long term gain because they are being transparent in this moment. But Chuck, I`ve been sitting in the briefings day after day after day -- TODD: Water torture. Yeah, speaking of short term gain, drip. WELKER: And yes, there`s been a drip, drip, drip. TODD: Yeah. WELKER: And not a whole lot that the press secretary can say, in large part because the White House Counsel`s Office wants to be very careful about the investigation. Now, they did start to shift their strategy, the White House Counsel`s Office providing a little bit more information. But there are key questions that still remain unanswered, including why it took two months for the world to learn about this. TODD: All right. I want to talk about another investigation and another issue of transparency. It`s the Supreme Court investigation. I want to put up there their first when they announced that basically an investigation was done. The leak was no mere misguided attempt at protest. It was a grave assault on the judicial process. And following up on all available leads, the Marshal`s team performed additional forensic analysis and conducted multiple follow-up interviews of certain employees. But the team has to date been unable to identify a person responsible by a preponderance of the evidence. Kimberly, preponderance of the evidence was a phrase of doing a lot of work in there. And to me, including it seemed to be a yellow flag. ATKINS STOHR: Well, listen. I don`t know. It`s a very legal term that we would use to judge a lot of other things. I think the big takeaway from this is that the Supreme Court as an institution has been this insular, insulated institution for so many years and that even the Marshal tasked to try to carry out this investigation worked against that fact. There were no real rules about how to handle decisions before they were publicly released. Eighty-two people had a hold of this draft opinion. And you had it -- it was even unclear in the initial report whether they even spoke to the justices because they are -- you cover that. TODD: Well, that firestorm left and right, and they put out a new statement saying, oh no, we talked to them, too. ATKINS STOHR: But in that institution, they are almost deified in a way that it seemed like doing so, or even admitting that you might have done so, might have seemed like doing something wrong. It just shows all the ways that --- talk about a lack of transparency -- there`s few places less transparent than the Supreme Court. TODD: Brendan, there was nothing illegal about the act, so there was only so much the Marshal can do. That was another problem here. BUCK: I look at all this and it just feels like the Supreme Court is starting to be like all the rest of our politics. TODD: Welcome to the club, guys. BUCK: Yeah. Stuff leaks. I mean, it used to be that the Supreme Court, you know, was read. It wasn`t heard. It certainly wasn`t seen. But now you can go to your average progressive, and they probably have a bobble head doll of Ruth Bader Ginsburg . Like, it`s just so political in every way now, it`s just starting to feel like it`s no longer this thing that you can hold aside as, you know, the high integrity institution. TODD: The black robes -- they don`t wear black robes anymore, Peter Baker. They`re red robes and blue robes. BAKER: Yeah. No, that`s right because we do refer to them now as -- in fact, for the first time really in the last few years, you see Republican- appointed justices being consistently conservative and Democratic-appointed justices being consistently liberal. In the old days, it was much more of a mix, right? Some Republicans would be more liberal and some Democrats would be more conservative. Now it feels like, you know, you`re looking at it as R this and D that. And it`s just a very different way of looking at the Supreme Court. WELKER: I do think that one of the key takeaways is that, because this was an internal investigation, it was not subject to the rigors of an FBI investigation. Could they have made the argument that a government document was seized? And so that`s the frustration. I think. TODD: Well, maybe Congress will say that draft Supreme Court rulings are classified until they`re presented to the public, because then the FBI would`ve been involved. WELKER: Exactly. But I do think the takeaway, and we were kind of getting to this, is that what needs to change? There needs to be more security around this. Fewer people may need to be read in. Listen, these people admitted to telling their spouses about the draft document. That`s problematic. TODD: Actually though, they all have one thing in common. We don`t think they`re transparent. ATKINS STOHR: Right. TODD: The Court, the presidency, the Congress, you name it, and guess what and guess what? Zero trust. WELKER: That`s the trust deficit. TODD: You`ve got to earn trust back. When we come back, who is running America`s largest city? One party is now noticeably absent from the big cities. (COMMERCIAL BREAK) [09:47:12] TODD: We are back. Data Download time. The U.S. Conference of Mayors was here in Washington this week for their annual meeting, and one group was noticeably absent among the biggest players -- Republicans. Let me show you. These are the ten most populated cities in America. Nine of the ten have elected Democrats as mayors, and the tenth -- San Antonio - - doesn`t elect mayors by party, but I can tell you that mayor is decidedly progressive. So essentially nobody right of center is a mayor of a top ten city. That`s actually quite a change from 2000. At the turn of the century, four of the top ten -- New York, Phoenix, San Diego, L.A. -- all had Republican mayors. A huge change. And overall in the 25 most populous cities, right now just three have Republican mayors, Oklahoma City, Jacksonville, and Fort Worth, Texas. That is it. In 2000, of course, that number out of 25 was just seven. So less than half of what it was in 2000. Look, these 25 major cities, they total 38 million citizens in those cities. That accounts for 12 percent of the overall U.S. population. And in fact, there are more people in these 25 cities than there are in 21 states. So, when you talk about political power, yes, governors have power, but the mayors also are political juggernauts themselves, particularly on the Democratic side of the aisle. Meanwhile, this week marks 25 years since news broke that President Bill Clinton had an extramarital affair with a young White House intern. It`s a scandal that forever transformed Washington`s politics, the media, and the American public. Monica Lewinsky`s lawyer joined this program to discuss the president`s future just after the story broke. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP, JANUARY 25, 1998) TIM RUSSERT, MODERATOR, MEET THE PRESS: Do you believe the president can survive this crisis? WILLIAM GINSBURG, ATTORNEY: I don`t know. I don`t want to call myself a country lawyer, but I certainly am not a Beltway lawyer and I`m not a political pundit. RUSSERT: Does it influence you, affect you in any way to know that the fate of the country, the fate of Bill Clinton , is in effect in your hands and in Monica Lewinsky`s hands? GINSBURG: In addition to the fact that I don`t believe that the government of the United States is in Monica Lewinsky`s hands or in my hands, short of that, you bet you it scares me. It scares me that my country could be in this kind of a crisis. I`m not political, but I am a citizen of this country and I do respect the presidency. (END VIDEO CLIP) TODD: When we come back, just how much did the Lewinsky scandal change the course of our political history? Trust me, we are still living with the consequences today. Our panel is next to discuss. (COMMERCIAL BREAK) [09:53:36] TODD: Welcome back. This week marks the 25th anniversary of an event that arguably launched our current moment in our politics, when Matt Drudge on the Internet broke the news that "Newsweek" was sitting on a story about former President Bill Clinton having an affair with a young White House intern named Monica Lewinsky . So, here`s what happened next -- a presidential lie, an investigation, disappointing Republican midterm, impeachment, Senate acquittal, round-the- clock media coverage and speculation, and the takeoff of a more partisan cable TV news environment. It remains one of the more significant forks in the road in modern political history, and it turns out we`re perhaps still living in that moment. Peter Baker, you and I were both, sort of, younger, very much reporters in this moment. And I think at the time we were all blown away. I guess looking back last week, it just sort of hit me, my God, we`re still stuck in this loop. BAKER: Yeah. We are stuck in this loop. That`s exactly right, I was just remembering. I remember walking home at night, at 2:00 in the morning after we published the first story on this in "The Washington Post " at the time, thinking, oh my God. What have we done? What have we unleashed here? This is an extraordinary story. The president of the United States, sex in the White House, investigation of lying under oath. But to your point, I think it changed our politics. It wasn`t just a one- off sex scandal, which we`ve had a number in our history. It was a moment when we made our politics more tribal, in which we decided we were going to make any investigation, any scandal about us versus them. And that`s what we`ve seen time and time again ever since. [21:25:01] We saw it with Trump. We`ve seen it with other presidents. And I think that we redefined our ideologies to suit which side are we on. TODD: You know, before 1998 we had had one impeachment in this country. Since that time, Brendan Buck, we`ve had three. I mean you just can`t -- we live in this moment constantly and the way Democrats rallied around Bill Clinton , we saw Republicans rally around Donald Trump . And you can`t help but ask yourself -- without Clinton, does Trump ever happen? BUCK: Yeah. I think the tribalism is the right point. It`s, while I don`t like what you did, you`re my guy and I would never give the other side a win. And I think that`s how everything is viewed. It`s much less, what my team is for, as being against what the other team is. It turned politics into a soap opera. And that`s what we still have today. Most -- I won`t say "most" -- a lot of politicians now are much more entertainers in their own minds than they are public servants. And it corrodes our politics, and there are so many outlets for it. Of course, the media, there are so many more platforms for them to play the role and to entertain, and it leads us to where we are now. TODD: No, you definitely saw the partisanship of cable exploded. The idea that cable news is a prime time destination didn`t exist until Monica. But, Kimberly, we also know the fact that this was an incredibly misogynist thing that happened. This was a -- you know, when we talk about Me Too -- and I`ve had younger staff. They say when they learn the history of it, they don`t understand why there was no discussion of the power dynamic. And it`s like, that`s how immature our debate was back then. ATKINS STOHR: Yeah. Two decades before Me Too. You know, over the years, I`ve had discussions with people who have said their viewpoint about Monica Lewinsky then has changed so profoundly than it is now. That someone -- this 22-year-old intern, you think about the kids that you see walking around -- TODD: Twenty-two-year-old intern. We all have 22-year-olds walking around our offices. ATKINS STOHR: Right, and the attacks that were done. I mean, just, I couldn`t imagine being a part of that. She seems to have come out of that with a lot of grace and respect now in retrospect, but it really shows the difference in how up until then --aside from Clarence Thomas -- there wasn`t a sex scandal that was this public. Now, we treat things very differently. TODD: Do we though? WELKER: Well, and -- ATKINS STOHR: No. Not differently enough. But at least there is that change. WELKER: I do think that that is one of the biggest impacts, this cultural shift. And Monica Lewinsky herself describes herself as patient zero for Internet shaming. And she has talked about being bullied and what that experience was like. And the way that she was treated by this country, by the world has not aged well. And in many ways, it is the seeds of the Me Too movement. And I think it`s been fascinating to watch her reclaim her story. And as you say, Kimberly, so many people have changed their perspectives about how they view that moment, how they viewed her and how they treated her. TODD: Peter, the question I wonder: It`s going to take some outside event to shift us to another fork in the road and get out of this doom loop we`re in, but I don`t know what that looks like. BAKER: I don`t know what that looks like. I mean, we had 9/11, and we kind of changed -- TODD: Temporary respite. BAKER: -- our politics for about a year or so, right? TODD: Yeah. BAKER: And that didn`t make a permanent difference. And I don`t know what will happen now that will be the equivalent of that. I mean, we have these big crises. We have these big issues. We have the debt ceiling issue. We have a crisis of our democracy. We have the crisis of the war in Ukraine. So many crises, and we can`t come together on things. TODD: Everything is worse since 1998 in this moment. That`s the bottom line, sadly. Before we go, sign up for our free daily newsletter, First Read. headline: Nationwide Marches On Anniversary Of Roe v. Wade
story_text: KATE SNOW: Today, the landmark abortion ruling, Roe v. Wade turns 50 years old. But the controversy surrounding last year`s reversal or Roe is heating up once again, with marches across the country. And now, more than six months after that decision, where does the battle over abortion rights stand? Marissa Para reports from Madison, Wisconsin. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: We will win. I believe that we will win. MARISSA PARRA, NBC NEWS NATIONAL CORRESPONDENT (voiceover): Tonight, on the 50th anniversary of Roe v. Wade, abortion rights activists drumming up defiance, moving their main women`s march bigger than Roe, from the capitol to the Midwest. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: This time, we move the National March to Madison in order to kick off our newfound campaign to the states, which is where battle is taking place. PARRA (on camera): So, I have the main march here in Madison, Wisconsin, that is because we are just weeks away from a primary judicial election and a state Supreme Court seat is up for grabs. And if it is filled with a pro- abortion rights candidate, then the Wisconsin abortion ban could be overturned. PARRA (voiceover): Sister marches in hundreds of cities across the country, just days after the National March for life against abortion and just seven months after Roe v. Wade was overturned in a five-four decision, sending both sides of the debate into action. The state of play, a murky patchwork. Roughly two dozen states have either a total abortion ban or are close to it. Some state laws changed immediately, like Wisconsin`s abortion ban. Some, like neighboring Illinois, later passing abortion protection. And last fall, historically red states, Kansas and Kentucky, voted down antiabortion ballot measures. Today, Vice President Kamala Harris once again calling to codify Roe. KAMALA HARRIS , U.S. VICE PRESIDENT: Congress must pass a bill that protects freedom and liberty. PARRA (voiceover): But with Republicans in control of the House, the federal abortion debate remains in a deadlock, making mobilizing on a local level more important than ever. From Madison, Wisconsin, Marissa Parra, NBC News. (END VIDEO CLIP) SNOW: Still ahead, a goodbye at Graceland, the moving tributes from celebrities and fans today for Lisa Marie Presley. How her mother remembered her. (COMMERCIAL BREAK) [18:50:00] SNOW: A violent protest in Downtown Atlanta is under investigation tonight. It happened late Saturday. A group demonstrating against a new police training center got out of hand. Police say some people smashed windows and set a patrol car on fire. Others were carrying explosive devices. Six people were arrested and charged with domestic terrorism, arson, and criminal damage. A small plane made an emergency landing northwest of Houston Today. Take a look at this. The single engine aircraft reported that it lost power and it went down, crashing on top of an 18-wheeler. The plane then caught fire. The most astonishing thing about all this, the pilot and the truck driver were not injured. END Content and programming copyright 2023 NBCUniversal. ALL RIGHTS RESERVED.
