(LOCAL NEWS AND WEATHER) [09:00:00] [09:00:00] (COMMERCIAL BREAK) AL ROKER, NBC TODAY WEATHER ANCHOR: This morning on the "3rd Hour of TODAY," deep sea discovery. New haunting video of the "Titanic" captured nearly 40 years ago. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) UNIDENTIFIED MALE: It was really literally entering a preserved museum, and the deeper you got into the ship, the more preserved it was. (END VIDEO CLIP) ROKER: Why it`s just now being released and what researchers found inside the doomed ship. Then, later, a "TODAY`s Checklist" for men and women. How to take care of your hair and what to do if you`re losing it. Plus, an icon in the house. NBA legend Kareem Abdul-Jabbar is here. How does he really feel about his all-time scoring record being broken and his important heart health message? And Taye Diggs joining us live in studio with big news for fans of his hit show, today, Thursday, February 16, 2023. ANNOUNCER: Live from Studio 1A in Rockefeller Plaza, this is the "3rd Hour of TODAY." SHEINELLE JONES, NBC NEWS 3RD HOUR OF TODAY, CO-HOST: Good morning and welcome to the "3rd Hour of TODAY." I`m Sheinelle here with our whole team. The gang`s all here this morning. Al and Craig. First of all, can we just say, I was downstairs with everybody in the concourse, is what we call it here, and we look up at the monitor -- CRAIG MELVIN, NBC NEWS ANCHOR: Yes. JONES: -- and you guys were having like a lovefest or something. What was happening? ROKER: Well, it was the "Titanic." You know, Joe Fryer, who`s about to do a story about the Titanic. JONES: OK. ROKER: And we had the video of Jack and Rose. And I just -- I was inspired. MELVIN: I was moved by the spirit. JONES: So, did you just -- you got moved by the spirit and you just decided to just -- ROKER: Yes. MELVIN: Yes. ROKER: Yes, just kind of like -- MELVIN: It was fun. ROKER: King of the world. JONES: I love it. Well, so -- DYLAN DREYER, NBC NEWS 3RD HOUR OF TODAY CO-HOST AND METEOROLOGIST: I mean, you guys have also recreated the pottery scene from "Ghost." MELVIN: The "Ghost" scene. ROKER: Yes. JONES: Oh, "Ghost" scene. DREYER: So -- ROKER: That`s right. JONES: We need to do a mash-up. ROKER: No, we are not going to recreate the "Dirty Dancing" scene. MELVIN: No. No, we`re not. JONES: Come on. MELVIN: No. JONES: That`s -- that would be the trilogy. DREYER: Yes. MELVIN: I mean, so you`re so light, I could probably do it. JONES: You could probably do it now. All right. Well, to be continued. We`ll try to make that happen and do like a mash-up. But there is a reason we`ve been talking about the "Titanic" this morning. Here`s the latest, some never-before-seen footage. It was shot back in 1986. It`s just been released. Now, at the time, this was the first expedition to actually find the Titanic. Look at this. DREYER: Look at this. JONES: The ship is so cool. It`s gone unseen at the bottom of the Atlantic for more than 70 years. So, we have NBC`s Joe Fryer here. He`s following the story for us this morning. DREYER: Oh, the chandelier. JONES: It`s like so beautiful. Why are we just now seeing it, you know, now? JOE FRYER, NBC NEWS NOW ANCHOR: Yes. So, there was this tiny little independent film made 25 years ago called "Titanic." Perhaps you heard of it. And it`s just now starting to get some buzz. This is the 25th anniversary of the Titanic. So, it kind of to commemorate that. JONES: OK. FRYER: This video is finally being released. I mean, let me give you the background here. JONES: OK. FRYER: First of all, remember, the Titanic went down in 1912. It took decades to find. It wasn`t until 1985 that a crew was able to find it, more than 12,000 feet below the surface. Robert Ballard, who you heard from at the beginning of the show, he was on that crew. So, months later, back then in 1986, they went down, they took this footage. It`s really the first-time humans laid eyes on the wreckage of the Titanic. But the footage, basically, most it has remained private until now. It was not released publicly. It`s 81 minutes. It`s uncut. DREYER: Wow. FRYER: It`s unnarrated. And you can really just stare at it. DREYER: Which is really exciting because now so much of it is disintegrating. We can`t see anything new. So, we think all of our new Titanic stuff, we can`t get anymore. And, wow. JONES: Boom. DREYER: It`s like you see chandeliers, you see things from 1986 that were still in such good condition. FRYER: Yes, you see that. And the chandelier is really one of the most haunting images. ROKER: Yes. FRYER: But you see the front of the bow of the ship. You know, you see the first officer`s cabin. There are so many details you see. And things that look different, you know, back in the `80s than they even do now because it is disintegrating. There`s this metal-eating bacteria that`s actually sort of turning the remnants of Titanic -- MELVIN: That sounds really sci-fi. FRYER: I know. -- to dust. And so, you get to see all these -- JONES: Oh, it turns it to dust. FRYER: -- incredible images, the promenade window. And it really gives you a look into early 20th century life. And this footage probably does a better job of it than some of the high-definition cameras that have gotten down there more recently. Robert Ballard says it was like a tombstone when he remembers seeing it for the first time. ROKER: Sure. DREYER: Oh, my goodness. FRYER: And one of the most haunting images for him, he remembers seeing, you know, a mother`s shoes next to a baby`s shoes. I mean, really just some images that stick with you. ROKER: Wow. DREYER: Heartbreaking. JONES: Wow. ROKER: Joe, that was haunting. JONES: It`s interesting. Joe Fryer, thank you. MELVIN: Thanks, Joe. ROKER: Appreciate it. DREYER: Yes. ROKER: All right. So, another big story we`re watching this morning, 2024 presidential race starting to take shape. We`ve got former South Carolina governor and U.N . ambassador, Nikki Haley, officially in. Craig. MELVIN: In fact, Mr. Roker had the chance to catch up with the former ambassador right after her first campaign event yesterday in Charleston, South Carolina. We talked about her decision, some of the biggest campaign issues, and the support she`s receiving from her family. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) [09:05:00] MELVIN (voiceover): Your former boss said that you had a hard time making the decision, said that you would never run against the president, he did a great job, he was the best president in my lifetime, his words, told Nikki to follow her heart. She`s polling at 1 percent. Not a bad start. Your response to that? NIKKI HALEY, FORMER U.N. AMBASSADOR: What I`ll tell you is I think he was a good president. There was so much that he did that was good. What I`m talking about -- MELVIN: Well, then why not support him this time? NIKKI HALEY: Because I think we need to have a new generation, for Republicans. We have lost the last seven out of eight popular votes for president. It means Republicans need to do something different. MELVIN: Is it the message or is it the messengers? NIKKI HALEY: I think it`s always both. It`s always got to be someone who really does listen to the people, that has their pulse on the ground of what real families are going through. But I also think it`s how you communicate. I don`t want just Republicans with me, I want everybody with me because I believe that everybody wants to be proud about America. MELVIN: Let`s talk about abortion for a moment. A senior senator from South Carolina, Lindsey Graham, has proposed a federal ban on abortion. Would you sign that? NIKKI HALEY: We need consensus on this. Our goal -- MELVIN: Consensus on abortion? Would you support a federal ban? NIKKI HALEY: I think we -- not a full out federal ban, because I don`t think that`s been put on the table. I think what Lindsey Graham has put on the table is 15 weeks. And I think, if we`re looking at 15 weeks, what we need to understand is that we are not OK with abortion up until the time of birth. And so, we should at least decide when it is OK. MELVIN: A decade ago, you supported significantly scaling back Social Security, Medicare, Medicaid. Should those social safety nets be scaled back? NIKKI HALEY: Should we reform those entitlements? Yes. But should we take anything from people who have already been promised? No. MELVIN: When you say reform, what do you mean? NIKKI HALEY: You go and everybody that`s been promised money, they get it. We don`t take it from anybody. But these new ones coming in, they know what`s going to be broke by the time they get there. Those are the ones we fix. The younger generation, we go and do a new system on how they`re going to get it. MELVIN: So, you would phase out Social Security -- NIKKI HALEY: Not phasing -- MELVIN: and Medicare and Medicaid, as we know it. As we know it now, you would phase it out? NIKKI HALEY: You would change it. You`re not phasing it out. MELVIN: Well, it seems like semantics, if you`re saying -- NIKKI HALEY: You are saying change it out. MELVIN: So, you want to reform it? NIKKI HALEY: I want to reform it, yes. MELVIN (voiceover): A plan for the future as Nikki Haley looks at a long campaign trail ahead. But she isn`t doing it alone, her husband Michael and kids Rena and Nalin are by her side. NIKKI HALEY: You can`t do this without your family. You just can`t. And so, to have them there for support, it`s everything. MELVIN (on camera): We`ve got a wedding that`s about to happen in the Haley family. So, are you helping plan a wedding and a presidential campaign simultaneously? NIKKI HALEY: We are. But this has been really sweet. We`ve had a lot of fun with this. RENA HALEY, NIKKE HALEY`S DAUGHTER: We have. NIKKI HALEY: I mean, between like picking songs and picking flowers and all of those things, it`s kind of a sweet spot to be able to do this. MELVIN: Did you go to your family before you decided to run for president and say, you know what, this is what I think I want to do? NIKKI HALEY: I did. MELVIN: How`d that conversation go? NIKKI HALEY: I did. Nalin has always been very involved in everything I do politically. He, of course, was like, yes, you should do this. And Rena`s response was, why do you want to live in someone else`s house again? Literally, it wasn`t what it was. MELVIN (voiceover): Haley`s son not only encouraged his mom to run, he`s even working on her campaign this summer. MELVIN (on camera): Do you ever provide unsolicited political advice to mom? NIKKI HALEY: Every day, all day. MELVIN: Really? NIKKI HALEY: By text message, by phone call, and everything in between. Nonstop. NALIN HALEY, NIKKI HALEY`S SON: I`m her biggest supporter, but also her biggest critic. MELVIN: Wow. NIKKI HALEY: It`s very true. It`s very true. MELVIN: What kind of mom was Nikki Haley? NALIN HALEY: A tough one, but also a very loving one and caring one. MELVIN: Rena? RENA HALEY: She was tough but loving. She always made sure to show up to any events we had, came in and supported us, but we always had our house rules we had to follow. MELVIN: Were you surprised at all when she said, you know what, I think I want to do this? MICHAEL HALEY, HALEY`S HUSBAND: No, I wasn`t surprised. MELVIN: I would imagine from time to time you would see or hear something that`s said or written about your wife and you -- M. HALEY: You know, when you wade in this water, you know, it`s going to happen. NIKKI HALEY: I think it`s tougher on them than it is on me. And they do take it personally. And politics is a blood sport. And it`s a shame that it is, but it is. They know that the key is, you know, you have your faith, you trust in the love we have as a family, and this, too, shall pass. That`s the beautiful thing about campaigns, is there`s a start and an end. And the goal is just pray every day and let`s get through it. (END VIDEO CLIP) MELVIN: So, you know, I`ve covered ambassador for a number of years now, and when I saw the kids yesterday, it was pretty interesting because I`ve seen, you know, the kids off and on for years. In fact, I think we`ve got a picture from her first inauguration as governor. DREYER: Oh, my goodness. JONES: Wow. MELVIN: So, those are the two kids there. DREYER: All grown up. MELVIN: All grown. JONES: Look how they`ve grown. ROKER: Wow. DREYER: Did you say, I remember when you were this big? MELVIN: I did. Because I`m that old guy now. ROKER: Which kids love that. MELVIN: Yes. DREYER: Yes. Of course. JONES: I know, I know. [09:10:00] MELVIN: But it`s funny because, you know, you know, she`s obviously planning a presidential campaign, but the ambassador also a wedding as well. Her daughter is getting married in April. DREYER: I wonder which is harder? MELVIN: She said -- she sort of alluded to the fact that -- at this point, sort of equally. DREYER: Equally difficult. MELVIN: Equally difficult. So -- JONES: That was good. It`s a good interview. DREYER: That was great. ROKER: Yes. MELVIN: Thank you. ROKER: Terrific. JONES: Yes, for sure. DREYER: All right. Well, still to come, it`s "TODAY`s Checklist." We`re talking hair health. How to take care of the -- ROKER: I`m out. DREYER: -- hair you have and what to do if you start to lose it. Is it too late for Al Roker ? ROKER: Yes. DREYER: We`ll find out. ROKER: Yes. MELVIN: That`s not true. ROKER: It is. DREYER: Then, later, the one and only Kareem Abdul-Jabbar. JONES: Good morning. DREYER: He is here in Studio 1A. He`s going to open up at his own heart scare. And we are going to talk about that historic moment when Lebron broke his scoring record. We`ll be right back. (COMMERCIAL BREAK) JONES: This morning on "TODAY`s Checklist," we are taking a closer look at hair and scalp health with some of the best ways to care for the hair that you have, and to help men and women struggling with hair loss. This is such an important topic. So many people are dealing with balding or maybe they`re thinning a little bit. So, joining us now, we have plastic surgeon and hair loss specialist, Dr. Michael Wolfeld. Good morning to you. DR. MICHAEL WOLFELD, PLASTIC SURGEON AND HAIR LOSS SPECIALIST: Good morning. JONES: This is a hot topic. DR. WOLFELD: It`s a very hot topic. JONES: All right. So, let`s first start with -- I mean, even just breakage. DR. WOLFELD: Right. JONES: I guess, before you get to those other things, just how do you protect the hair you have? Let`s talk about that. DR. WOLFELD: Right. So, different things may damage your hair. And here`s some very important things to keep mind of. So, if you`re going to brush your hair, be gentle. JONES: Yes. DR. WOLFELD: Anything too rough or strenuous can maybe damage and break your hair. [09:15:00] JONES: And you know there`s a thing going around where they`re telling girls, if you want your hair to be thicker and longer, to brush it. So, kids are just brush, brush, brush. And adults are brush, brush, brush and you`re making it worse. DR. WOLFELD: That`s right. JONES: Yes. DR. WOLFELD: Overbrushing can be harmful. JONES: OK. DR. WOLFELD: You want to avoid tension on your hair. So, any tight hairstyles are no good. JONES: Yes. DR. WOLFELD: Avoid any very hot treatments, hot hair blowers are not very good. And if you have split ends, it`s good to trim them so they don`t propagate and affect the rest of your hair strands. JONES: OK. So, now, let`s talk about Craig thinning. MELVIN: Yes. JONES: That`s an issue. MELVIN: Sheinelle just mentioned it, thinning, shedding as well. DR. WOLFELD: That`s right. MELVIN: Some folks, you know, you`re in the shower, look down on the drain, you get a little concern. At what point should you actually go and see a doctor like yourself. DR. WOLFELD: Yes. So, if you noticed your hair thinning and you`re losing more hair, more hair falling out that`s a good time to come in and see a specialist and to see what may be causing that. Now, genetics is one of the most common causes of hair loss. MELVIN: Is it true -- I feel like years ago I heard that if you lose your hair -- or if your mother`s father was bald, then there`s a great chance that you`re going to be bald. JONES: That`s true. I`ve heard that. MELVIN: Is there any truth to that or is that a myth? DR. WOLFELD: That`s not true. That`s a myth. JONES: What? DR. WOLFELD: So, it can`t from either side of the family. So, really have to look at both sides of the family to see where you may fall. MELVIN: So, besides genetics, where else contributes? DR. WOLFELD: Yes. So, there`s stress. Any stress around your body, whether it`s recent procedures or illnesses can cause a shedding of hair. There`s autoimmune diseases that can cause your hair to fall out. And also, vitamin deficiencies. That`s something that you should be aware of as well. MELVIN: Certain bloodwork that folks should be asking for when they go to see their doctors? DR. WOLFELD: Yes, absolutely. So, you know, we look at vitamin D, iron, zinc, but especially hormone levels may be important. MELVIN: OK. DR. WOLFELD: Especially for women, young women and older women. Thyroid deficiencies or overactive thyroid, that can also cause hair loss as well. MELVIN: OK. I`ve already learned a lot. Mr. Roker`s -- DREYER: Al needs to look. ROKER: Well, yes. I -- well, the basics. You see God only made so many perfect heads. The rest he covered with hair. So, you`ve got to take care of your scalp, right? DR. WOLFELD: That`s right. That`s right. So, taking care of your scalp is really important. So, just in your daily life, from the products you may use, from sweating, from just grime from the environment may build up in your scalp so you want to really cleans your scalp. ROKER: Right. DR. WOLFELD: You may want to exfoliate your scalp. Massaging can help to really clear your scalp. ROKER: Do you really need all of those fancy shampoos and stuff? Can you just -- I mean, what`s the deal? DR. WOLFELD: Really just a simple shampoo that cleanses your scalp and you can massage your scalp. There`s a lot of things available over the counter, in the office. We have something called -- it`s a HydraFacial, which is a facial for your scalp that can -- it`s Keravive treatment that can really cleans the scalp, exfoliate it, and really get your scalp looking -- and your hair looking much nicer. ROKER: All right. Thanks, Mike. DR. WOLFELD: All right. Thank you. DREYER: All right. Do you hit a point where it`s too late or is regrowth a possibility? DR. WOLFELD: So, when we talk about regrowth, if you have hair and it`s thinning, there are options and treatments that can really help to thicken your hair and help to preserve your hair. DREYER: OK. What kind of treatments are there? DR. WOLFELD: So, there`s some over-the-counter treatments and there`s some in-office treatments. So, over-the-counter, there`s hair supplements. DREYER: Which we have some here. DR. WOLFELD: One example is Nutrafol, which is -- this is it right here. DREYER: OK. DR. WOLFELD: It`s an over-the-counter vitamin supplement. DREYER: Oh, so you ingest it? DR. WOLFELD: You ingest it. DREYER: Yes. DR. WOLFELD: It`s oral. It`s all-natural. And it`s -- you can get it over- the-counter and it can work. There`s also Rogaine, that`s -- which is Minoxidil, that`s over-the-counter as well. DREYER: For men and women. DR. WOLFELD: For men and women. DREYER: OK. DR. WOLFELD: It`s a topical solution or a foam. They also have now oral Minoxidil that is a prescription pill. That -- the oral is off-label but it may help. So, if you`re someone that may have other medical illnesses, such as heart problems and blood pressure. DREYER: Right. Check with your doctor. DR. WOLFELD: Check with your doctor beforehand. DREYER: OK. Then there`s injections too, right? DR. WOLFELD: There are. So, there`s what`s called PRP, which is Platelet- Rich Plasma injections. That`s really a treatment -- DREYER: Oh, it actually works. DR. WOLFELD: Yes. It`s a treatment in the office. JONES: Look at that. DR. WOLFELD: And it uses were blood and the growth factors from that and it can really help to thicken your hair. DREYER: Does it hurt? DR. WOLFELD: It`s slightly uncomfortable -- DREYER: OK. DR. WOLFELD: -- but it`s manageable. DREYER: But -- JONES: And do you have to keep doing it for it to work? That`s the only thing with all of these things, like once -- DR. WOLFELD: That`s right. JONES: -- you stop, do you lose your hair again? DR. WOLFELD: That`s right. So, the key with any of these treatments is that you have to continue using it. JONES: For the rest of your life? DREYER: OK. DR. WOLFELD: Well -- DREYER: If you want hair. ROKER: Yes. DR. WOLFELD: Well, yes. If you want to keep your hair. DREYER: Or if you want to look dashing like Al here, you don`t have to. DR. WOLFELD: Yes. ROKER: Or any of our crew members. MELVIN: We got lots of them. ROKER: Here. OK. Here, here. JONES: Oh, that`s true. ROKER: You know, over here. DREYER: Dr. Wolfeld, thank you so much for joining us. JONES: Yes. DR. WOLFELD: Thank you very much for having me. MELVIN: Coming up, the aforementioned legend himself in the house. headline: Clearing Up Some Common Nutrition Myths With The Registered Dietitian
story_text: SAVANNAH JONES: Welcome back this morning on Your Health. Common myths and maybe misguiding your diet decisions. Nora Minno is a registered dietician and she`s here to clear these things up once and for all. Nora, good morning to you. NORA MINNO, REGISTERED DIETICIAN: Good morning, Sheinelle. JONES: So we have five nutrition myths that we`re going to debunk. I should say there are three of us here because congratulations. MINNO: Yes, thank you. JONES: She was so worried as nutritionist people are going to be like, oh, she`s got little (inaudible). No, no, there`s a little baby in there. MINNO: Exactly. JONES: We are girl, we don`t know, OK. First things first, I should avoid all carbs. This is a big one. MINNO: Yes. JONES: I know so many people who just -- they feel like if they touch a carb, they explode. MINNO: I agree. And I have good news for all you carb lovers. I`m pretty sure as everybody body, right? Carbs are your friend. In fact, there are a really important part of a healthy balanced diet. They do a lot for us. They are our body`s preferred source of fuel, same with our brain. They help our digestion and they actually just make us feel good. JONES: So then, what are we doing wrong then? Because a lot of people, you know, I guess obviously probably shouldn`t have carbs before bed, but where are we going wrong? MINNO: Exactly. So really, when it comes to carbs, it is just about the quality of carbs that you`re picking and the quantity that you`re consuming. That`s really where a lot of people go wrong over consuming things like refined carbs, sweets, white breads, things like that. But if you focus on portions, choose more complex carbs. JONES: What`s a good carb? Give me a couple of example. MINNO: Fruits, vegetables, whole grains, oatmeal, things like that, you should be in the clear. JONES: All right. So myth number two, fresh produce is healthier than frozen or canned. What would you say? MINNO: No. This is not true at all. In fact, sometimes your frozen or canned options can be actually more nutritious. There was a study done that found that vegetables can lose 15% to 55% of their vitamin C by the time they`re picked, by the time they make it to your grocery shelf. So frozen, they typically flash freeze right on the spot. So you`re packing a lot more nutrients. And they`re actually a little bit better for your wallet too. JONES: I was just about to say there`s a cost benefit as well. MINNO: Exactly. Less food waste, oftentimes they are more budget friendly. And then you just have some good things on hand if you want to make a smoothie, a salad, things like that. JONES: Absolutely. OK, our next myth, this is a good one. Plant milk is healthier than dairy milk. What say ye? MINNO: All right. Well, this is not always the case. This one really comes down just to preference because you know, now it just seems like there`s a million different plant milks out there. There are options galore, which is great, but cow`s milk is still a really great option. One cup of skim milk packs in 10 grams of protein and a quarter of your daily calcium needs. Whereas plant milk like an almond milk has one gram of protein per serving. JONES: You know what it is, I guess also just depends on, you know, whether you`re lactose intolerant, you know, if you have a dietary issue. MINNO: Exactly. So this one -- one is not better than the other, it`s just going to come down to choice. And if you are picking a plant milk, you want to pick varieties that have low or no added sugar, and ones that are more fortified with things like calcium, vitamin D that you might not be getting if you`re picking that -- JONES: I will admit that the plant milks, I didn`t realize some of them do have a lot of sugar. MINNO: Some do. JONES: I just didn`t realize that. MINNO: Some do. So be a savvy reader. JONES: All right. Let`s talk about fat there. Remember for a while everything was low fat this, low fat that. MINNO: Yes. MINNO: So the nutrition or the myth number four all fat is bad. Obviously it`s not. [08:45:05] MINNO: It`s not. And thank goodness that low fat craze in the `90s and thereafter is over because we know now that fats, most importantly, mono and polyunsaturated fats are really good for us. It is still American Heart Month, and we want to get those fats in from things like avocados, nuts, seeds, olive oils, and even our fatty fish to help protect our heart boost that HDL, which is our good cholesterol, and lower LDL, which is our bad cholesterol. JONES: Sounds good. And I think sometimes when you`re eating, you just don`t know which one is right. MINNO: Exactly. So we do want to avoid certain fats, there are facts called saturated fats, that the American Heart Association says we should stay at or below 13 grams a day -- JONES: Oh wait, that`s good advice. MINNO: -- for a hearth healthy diet. JONES: All right. Si when you get a package is something flipped over the back. MINNO: Yes. JONES: And if you see saturated fats, how many grams did you say it should be layered? MINNO: 13, approximately around 13 per day. JONES: Per day. MINNO: So if you have four ounces of kind of lean ground beef, you`re already at that 13 mark. So you want to be a real savvy label reader. JONES: OK, all right. Myth number five soy, I`m actually interested in what you`re going to say. Soy increases risk for breast cancer. MINNO: Yes. You know, I hear this one all the time. JONES: Me too. MINNO: And it`s still very common and abundant. So this myth really stems from the fact that soy contains something called phytoestrogens. And we know that estrogen can sometimes be linked to an increase in breast cancer. JONES: Right. MINNO: But the estrogens in soy are very different than mammalian estrogens, ones that we have in our body, and they act differently. And in fact, they can be protective against things like breast cancer, because what we`ve seen in Asian countries where they consume more soy, is that breast cancer risk is actually much lower. JONES: Does it depend on the product or what kind of soy you`re consuming? No? MINNO: Not really. And again, the American Heart Association said 25 grams of soy protein per day can actually be heart protective. So you can get your tofu, your (inaudible), your soy milk, your edamame at a sushi restaurant, right? Lots of really great options to pack some good soy protein. JONES: There you go. So you don`t have to avoid it. Nora, thank you. MINNO: That`s OK. Thank you, Sheinelle. JONES: All right. story_text: (COMMERCIAL BREAK) [08:00:00] SHEINELLE JONES, NBC NEWS 3RD HOUR OF TODAY, CO-HOST: It is 8:00 on "TODAY." Coming up, surprise visit. This is on -- in our corner of the woods here at Rockefeller Plaza. TOM LLAMAS, NBC NEWS SENIOR NATIONAL CORRESPONDENT: Yes, they came from all over the country. We always love that. JONES: Uh-huh. LLAMAS: A lot of states represented. Savannah and Hoda, you know them, will be back tomorrow, of course, and it will be a big morning here in Studio 1A. JONES: That is right. Plus, she`ll treat us to a live performance when she joins us for our 8:00, 9:00, and 10:00 hours. So, join us tomorrow. JACOB SOBOROFF, NBC NEWS CORRESPONDENT: I am not going anywhere. LLAMAS: Yes. DOWNEY: Yes, I suppose so in some ways, you know, maybe we just turn into our parents before we realize it. SHRIVER (voice-over): In her book, Roma also shares lessons from her 15 year marriage to Hollywood producer, Mark Burnett. And she talks about the value of getting older as a woman in her 60s. DOWNEY: And I`m quicker to say, I don`t really want to do that to things that I don`t really want to do. I realize a lot of my life. I was like, much more of a people pleaser, you know. SHRIVER: Age has given you the right to say no to things. DOWNEY: I think so. I don`t know about you or anybody watching but I`m a menopausal woman, and sleep and I are not the best of friends anymore. And so some nights I`m lying in my bed, you know, and the things that maybe were like little worries during the day become these Herculean things to wrestle with in the night. Anybody that follows me on social media knows I`m obsessed with the sunrise is a great sort of symbolism of a new day, a new beginning. And if you messed up yesterday, let`s try and do better today. (END VIDEOTAPE) SHRIVER: Roma`s new book "Be an Angel" comes out Tuesday and it`s a great read. Back to you. LLAMAS: OK, Maria, thank you. JONES: Thank you. Up next, our fresh veggies really healthier than canned or frozen? We are clearing up some common nutrition myths with the registered dietitian. But first, this is TODAY on NBC. [08:39:54] (COMMERCIAL BREAK) JONES: Welcome back this morning on Your Health. Common myths and maybe misguiding your diet decisions. Nora Minno is a registered dietician and she`s here to clear these things up once and for all. Nora, good morning to you. NORA MINNO, REGISTERED DIETICIAN: Good morning, Sheinelle. JONES: So we have five nutrition myths that we`re going to debunk. I should say there are three of us here because congratulations. MINNO: Yes, thank you. JONES: She was so worried as nutritionist people are going to be like, oh, she`s got little (inaudible). No, no, there`s a little baby in there. MINNO: Exactly. JONES: We are girl, we don`t know, OK. First things first, I should avoid all carbs. This is a big one. MINNO: Yes. JONES: I know so many people who just -- they feel like if they touch a carb, they explode. MINNO: I agree. And I have good news for all you carb lovers. I`m pretty sure as everybody body, right? Carbs are your friend. In fact, there are a really important part of a healthy balanced diet. They do a lot for us. They are our body`s preferred source of fuel, same with our brain. They help our digestion and they actually just make us feel good. JONES: So then, what are we doing wrong then? Because a lot of people, you know, I guess obviously probably shouldn`t have carbs before bed, but where are we going wrong? MINNO: Exactly. So really, when it comes to carbs, it is just about the quality of carbs that you`re picking and the quantity that you`re consuming. That`s really where a lot of people go wrong over consuming things like refined carbs, sweets, white breads, things like that. But if you focus on portions, choose more complex carbs. JONES: What`s a good carb? Give me a couple of example. MINNO: Fruits, vegetables, whole grains, oatmeal, things like that, you should be in the clear. JONES: All right. So myth number two, fresh produce is healthier than frozen or canned. What would you say? MINNO: No. This is not true at all. In fact, sometimes your frozen or canned options can be actually more nutritious. There was a study done that found that vegetables can lose 15% to 55% of their vitamin C by the time they`re picked, by the time they make it to your grocery shelf. So frozen, they typically flash freeze right on the spot. So you`re packing a lot more nutrients. And they`re actually a little bit better for your wallet too. JONES: I was just about to say there`s a cost benefit as well. MINNO: Exactly. Less food waste, oftentimes they are more budget friendly. And then you just have some good things on hand if you want to make a smoothie, a salad, things like that. JONES: Absolutely. OK, our next myth, this is a good one. Plant milk is healthier than dairy milk. What say ye? MINNO: All right. Well, this is not always the case. There are options galore, which is great, but cow`s milk is still a really great option. One cup of skim milk packs in 10 grams of protein and a quarter of your daily calcium needs. Whereas plant milk like an almond milk has one gram of protein per serving. JONES: You know what it is, I guess also just depends on, you know, whether you`re lactose intolerant, you know, if you have a dietary issue. MINNO: Exactly. So this one -- one is not better than the other, it`s just going to come down to choice. And if you are picking a plant milk, you want to pick varieties that have low or no added sugar, and ones that are more fortified with things like calcium, vitamin D that you might not be getting if you`re picking that -- JONES: I will admit that the plant milks, I didn`t realize some of them do have a lot of sugar. MINNO: Some do. JONES: I just didn`t realize that. MINNO: Some do. So be a savvy reader. JONES: All right. Let`s talk about fat there. Remember for a while everything was low fat this, low fat that. MINNO: Yes. MINNO: So the nutrition or the myth number four all fat is bad. Obviously it`s not. [08:45:05] MINNO: It`s not. And thank goodness that low fat craze in the `90s and thereafter is over because we know now that fats, most importantly, mono and polyunsaturated fats are really good for us. It is still American Heart Month, and we want to get those fats in from things like avocados, nuts, seeds, olive oils, and even our fatty fish to help protect our heart boost that HDL, which is our good cholesterol, and lower LDL, which is our bad cholesterol. JONES: Sounds good. And I think sometimes when you`re eating, you just don`t know which one is right. MINNO: Exactly. So we do want to avoid certain fats, there are facts called saturated fats, that the American Heart Association says we should stay at or below 13 grams a day -- JONES: Oh wait, that`s good advice. MINNO: -- for a hearth healthy diet. JONES: All right. Si when you get a package is something flipped over the back. MINNO: Yes. JONES: And if you see saturated fats, how many grams did you say it should be layered? MINNO: 13, approximately around 13 per day. JONES: Per day. MINNO: So if you have four ounces of kind of lean ground beef, you`re already at that 13 mark. So you want to be a real savvy label reader. JONES: OK, all right. Myth number five soy, I`m actually interested in what you`re going to say. Soy increases risk for breast cancer. MINNO: Yes. You know, I hear this one all the time. JONES: Me too. MINNO: And it`s still very common and abundant. So this myth really stems from the fact that soy contains something called phytoestrogens. And we know that estrogen can sometimes be linked to an increase in breast cancer. JONES: Right. MINNO: But the estrogens in soy are very different than mammalian estrogens, ones that we have in our body, and they act differently. And in fact, they can be protective against things like breast cancer, because what we`ve seen in Asian countries where they consume more soy, is that breast cancer risk is actually much lower. JONES: Does it depend on the product or what kind of soy you`re consuming? No? MINNO: Not really. And again, the American Heart Association said 25 grams of soy protein per day can actually be heart protective. So you can get your tofu, your (inaudible), your soy milk, your edamame at a sushi restaurant, right? Lots of really great options to pack some good soy protein. JONES: There you go. So you don`t have to avoid it. Nora, thank you. MINNO: That`s OK. Thank you, Sheinelle. JONES: All right. Next, a remarkable couple who made their dreams come true, opening a unique restaurant here in New York during the pandemic. How it`s become one of the hottest tickets in town, we`ll take you there. Kathy and her family, they`re visiting us from tower Minnesota to celebrate Kathy`s 63rd birthday. SOBOROFF: I love Minnesotans. I had fun getting to know David and his mom Bibi. JONES: Kevol and Ria Graham have a remarkable story when it comes to their Caribbean-inspired restaurant. They opened Kokomo in July of 2020, four months into the COVID locked down, and right before their second child. Can you imagine? [08:50:06] Now, it is one of the hottest restaurants in Brooklyn and I paid a visit to find out their recipe for success. I never thought that I would have my own restaurant. But as we look back, we kind of see that every step that we took was actually leading us to this moment. JONES (voice-over): Today, they are the parents of three young children and will celebrate five years of marriage. But it`s their journey to this point running Kokomo, a popular pan-Caribbean restaurant with Indian and Asian flavors that combines their passion for food and hospitality. (on camera): Clearly, you both had some kind of restaurant background -- K. GRAHAM: (Inaudible) on nightlife and then became our roving chefs. The guys that I grew up with. RIA GRAHAM, KOKOMO OWNER: At the time, I was a marketing manager for a Caribbean restaurant as well. So they took the social media documenting everything about acquiring and opening a restaurant. As they were just about to open, the pandemic hit. Against all odds, they officially opened in the summer of 2020. (on camera): How challenging was it? R. GRAHAM: I would say it was like mental warfare, because you really did not know what to expect. But I think because we were so open about our feelings to our social media, people wanted to genuinely support. K. GRAHAM: Something that`s very inspirational, because Ria was a part of every step during pregnancy that motivated me to even work harder. JONES (voice-over): The couple describes the menu as elevated Caribbean fare, served up in an atmosphere that feels like the Caribbean. R. GRAHAM: I would say if you`re looking for a vibe, come here. K. GRAHAM: To represent all different parts of the Caribbean. We definitely appeal to all ethnicities, you know, whether it`s Afro Caribbean, Latin Caribbean, you know, Asian Caribbean. JONES: Did you get inspiration for different recipes? I mean, how did you do it? K. GRAHAM: We were very passionate about like bringing out things that we grew up on, you know, tapping into our Caribbean heritage. JONES: Do you feel like you are blazing a trail? R. GRAHAM: Real trailblazers for us are the grandmas, man, because there`s nothing like a Caribbean grandma in that kitchen showing her stuff. And now we`re just trying to modernize it and just make it into something fresh and new. JONES (voice-over): Some of their hottest Caribbean dishes are on flatbread. K. GRAHAM: (Inaudible) flatbread or any given day, because it`s a -- it`s something that we reinvented because I think everybody comes in and like they can get that anywhere. It serve with shrimp, foxtail, chicken. R. GRAHAM: Once we saw that brick oven, we knew we had to do O to Brooklyn by having a brick oven pizza crust, and then we`d have on top of it a tomato (inaudible) sauteed shrimp with ackee, which is the national food of Jamaica. JONES (voice-over): I had to give the food a try. K. GRAHAM: So this is our Rasta balls. JONES: OK. K. GRAHAM: Crockett fry Italian Alfredo sauce that we infuse with some jerk seasoning. So Kev and Ria say their parents also helped them run the restaurant. In the spring, they`re opening up another restaurant nearby. headline: NBC NIGHTLY NEWS for February 23, 2023, NBC
story_text: [19:00:00] (COMMERCIAL BREAK) LESTER HOLT, NBC NEWS ANCHOR (on camera): Tonight, the bombshell testimony. Alex Murdaugh taking the stand at his murder trial. (voiceover): The South Carolina attorney denying he killed his wife and son, but then stunning the courtroom, admitting he lied to police about his alibi that night. The paranoid thoughts he said he thought he was having and the moment Murdaugh broke down as he described finding the bodies. Then the prosecution`s turn. The tough questions he faced under cross- examination. Also tonight, a deadly winter storm on the move. More than a million customers without power. In the Midwest, a downed power line killing a firefighter. A parking garage collapsing under snow. The new threat in the west. Rare blizzard warnings in southern California. Al Roker is here. New clues in the toxic train derailment in Ohio. The NTSB saying it was 100 percent preventable. The preliminary report finding an alarm went off just before the wreck. What investigators say about the crew`s actions and the potential cause. The shooting spree in Florida. A TV reporter and a 9-year-old girl killed. New body cam of police arresting the suspect. The new details. And the Emmy-winning star of Abbott Elementary, Sheryl Lee Ralph on the obstacles she has overcome and inspiring a new generation. ANNOUNCER: This is NBC NIGHTLY NEWS with Lester Holt. HOLT: Good evening. For the defense, accused murderer Alex Murdaugh taking the witness stand today in South Carolina. Dramatic and at times tearful testimony from the man at the center of the country`s most closely followed criminal trial. Murdaugh under questioning from his lawyers saying I didn`t shoot my wife or son. And addressing what has appeared to be some of the prosecution`s strongest evidence. Murdaugh from the witness box admitting he lied about his whereabouts the night his wife and 22-year-old son were shot to death. Shocking at the lies to an opioid addiction and paranoia. Under cross-examination, Murdaugh, a former lawyer also admitted to stealing from clients. The prosecution has maintained the murders were part of Murdaugh`s attempt to escape accountability for financial misdeeds. We begin tonight with Catie Beck reporting from Walterboro, South Carolina. (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) CATIE BECK, NBC NEWS CORRESPONDENT (voiceover): After nearly five weeks of testimony, a stunning surprise. ALEX MURDAUGH, ACCUSED OF KILLING HIS WIFE AND SON: I am going to testify. I want to testify. BECK: The trial`s most anticipated witness takes the stand. Alex Murdaugh testifies in his own defense. The first questions aimed at the heart of the case. JIM GRIFFIN, DEFENSE LAWYER: Did you take this gun or any gun like it and blow your son`s brains out on June 7th, or any day, or any time? MURDAUGH: No, I did not. GRIFFIN: Did you take another blackout such as this and fire it into your wife Maggie`s leg, torso, or any part of her body? MURDAUGH: No, I did not. BECK: Quick to confront what is perhaps the prosecution`s strongest evidence, the video taken by Paul Murdaugh at the dog kennels, placing Alex at the crime scene minutes before the murders. He`s told investigators he wasn`t there, but admits now he was lying. GRIFFIN: Alex, why did you lie? MURDAUGH: As my addiction evolved over time, I would get in these situations or circumstances where I would get paranoid. BECK: Murdaugh says he didn`t trust state law enforcers, and regrets the lie that led to many others. GRIFFIN: Did you continue lying after that night, did you not? MURDAUGH: Once I lied, I continued the lie, yes, sir. BECK: Emotional and crying throughout, Murdaugh`s testimony largely rewrites his timeline on the night of the murders, showering and changing clothes before dinner, and describing the moment he discovered the bodies, again saying he checked for signs of life. MURDAUGH: I know I tried to turn him over. GRIFFIN: When you say you tried to turn him over, why were you trying to turn him over? MURDAUGH: I don`t know. I don`t know. I don`t know why I tried to turn him over. My boy`s laying face-down. BECK: Later in testimony, Alex admits a long-time addiction to opioids, that he stole clients` funds, but denies being overly concerned about getting caught prior to the murders. CREIGHTON WATERS, CHIEF PROSECUTOR: What kind of cases did you normally do? BECK: On cross-examination, prosecutors began by pressing Murdaugh on the fraud cases, where he admits he stole money from his clients and lied to them. And prosecutors suggesting all the stolen money wasn`t going to fund his pill addiction. WATERS: You were generating millions of dollars in fees. That was not enough for you? Would you concede that? [19:05:08] MURDAUGH: If by concede that, you mean was I also stealing money that I shouldn`t have, yes, sir, I agree with that. I`ve said that, repeatedly. (END VIDEOTAPE) HOLT: Catie, what do we know about how the jury was taking all this in how they may have reacted? BECK (on camera): Well, Lester, the jury was captivated, so attentive to Alex Murdaugh`s testimony on the stand today. At times, Murdaugh was repositioning his body to face the jurors directly and answer the questions directly to them. At one point, when Murdaugh got extremely emotional, one juror that was sitting close to him actually slid a Kleenex box in his direction. Lester? HOLT: All right, Catie Beck, thank you. Let me bring in our Senior Legal Correspondent Laura Jarrett now. Laura, what was the defense strategy here, and how does it appear to be playing out? LAURA JARRETT, NBC NEWS SENIOR LEGAL CORRESPONDENT (on camera): Lester, this is the defense team going on offense. Clearly, the goal was to try to take the sting out of the damning evidence that the prosecution would raise on cross-examination, and that`s likely why he was forced to admit that he lied to police and to his family, all while trying to plant seeds of reasonable doubt. But testifying at all, it`s a risky gamble. Already the prosecution has tried to highlight his inconsistencies and also pierce through his folksy demeanor on cross-examination to try to show this jury that he is an accomplished lawyer who knows how to cover his tracks. Lester? HOLT: All right, Laura, thank you. Now to that deadly crippling winter storm that is stretching right now across the country and a separate threat here in the West. Gabe Gutierrez is watching it all from Minneapolis. (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) GABE GUTIERREZ, NBC NEWS NATIONAL CORRESPONDENT (voiceover): Tonight, devastating snow, ice, and wind pummeling even more of the country. This time knocking out power to nearly a million people across the Midwest. Most of those outages in Michigan where a volunteer firefighter was killed when a tree brought down a high-voltage line. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: A volunteer just died in here for free. He gave his life for free. GUTIERREZ: In Wisconsin, authorities say snow likely caused a partial collapse of a parking garage at a shopping mall. Today, Minneapolis under a snow emergency. Over the last few hours, we`ve seen a very rapid snowfall here. The road conditions are getting worse. Snow totals not as high as predicted earlier in the week, still around a foot blanketed the twin cities over three days. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: This is a big one. For all coming down at once, like, yes, this is a pretty big one. GUTIERREZ: Coast-to-coast, treacherous road conditions. Portland, Oregon recording its second snowiest day on record with more than 10 inches. This 20-car pileup in Southern California injuring at least eight people. A separate system now prompting the first blizzard warnings since 1989 for the mountains near L.A. The nationwide weather whiplash is remarkable even for February. Across the Mid-Atlantic and southeastern U.S., record heat, unusually high temperatures as far north as Philadelphia. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: Having a 70-degree day is just such a welcome break. (END VIDEOTAPE) GUTIERREZ (on camera): But air travel is still dicey. More than 2,000 U.S. flights canceled just today, Lester. HOLT: All right, Gabe, thank you. And that takes us to Al Roker . Al, as one storm moves out, another moves in impacting the West Coast. AL ROKER, NBC NEWS WEATHER ANCHOR: Lester, we have six million folks out west looking at winter weather advisories, winter storm warnings, blizzard warnings, including the San Bernardino Mountains. First blizzard warning ever issued there. Record lows likely. We`re looking at morning lows in Reno in the 20s. Vegas into the 30s. Even Los Angeles into the upper 30s. Salt Lake City in the 20s. We`re looking at five to eight feet of snow back through the Sierra, but also the San Bernardino Mountains and the Santa Barbara Mountains as well. We`re also looking upwards of 10 inches of rain through Southern California. Significant roadway flooding and airport delays likely. Lester? HOLT: All right, Al Roker , thank you. And new tonight, a preliminary finding about the cause of that toxic train disaster in Ohio as the Transportation Secretary visited for the first time. Ron Allen is there. (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) RON ALLEN, NBC NEWS CORRESPONDENT (voiceover): Tonight, with the scene being cleaned up, new details about what caused the fiery derailment. Federal investigators saying a preliminary investigation shows an overheated wheel bearing likely to blame. JENNIFER HOMENDY, CHAIR, NATIONAL TRANSPORTATION SAFETY BOARD : This was 100 percent preventible. ALLEN: The NTSB says the train passed over two detectors, which showed the bearing was heating up. By the time it hit a third detector, it was 253 degrees above air temperature, triggering an audible alarm to warn the crew, who then slowed and stopped the train. HOMENDY: This is a community that is suffering. This is not about politics. What I care about is figuring out how this happened. ALLEN: The NTSB chair says there is no evidence the crew did anything wrong. In a statement, Norfolk Southern says our highest priority is the safety of our people and the communities we serve. Adding, it will continue to support the NTSB `s investigation. While today, Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg visited for the first time after criticism from some residents that he should have come sooner, demanding the nation`s rail operators stop resisting safety measures to cut costs. [19:10:19] PETE BUTTIGIEG, U.S. SECRETARY OF TRANSPORTATION: Let`s get people from both sides of the aisle to the table and come to agreement on some steps that are needed, even if the rail industry is pushing back. ALLEN: Meanwhile, near the crash, this Figleys only comes back to the farm to check on things like their chickens. They`re part of a class action lawsuit that attorneys say includes over 500 residents. MARILYN FIGLEY, RESIDENT, EAST PALESTINE: I live out of my car and at my daughter`s house. It`s awful. I feel homeless. ALLEN: Why won`t you come back home? FIGLEY: Because I don`t know what I`m coming home to, and I`m 70 years old. ALLEN: Ron Allen, NBC News, East Palestine, Ohio. (END VIDEOTAPE) HOLT: Now to Florida, where a series of shootings left three people dead, including a young girl and a reporter. Two more are hospitalized. A suspect is under arrest. Guad Venegas is there for us. (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) UNIDENTIFIED MALE: Get on your (BLEEP) face! GUAD VENEGAS, NBC NEWS CORRESPONDENT (voiceover): Tonight, the Orange County Sheriff releasing bodycam footage of the arrest of Keith Moses, the 19-year-old suspect accused of a deadly shooting spree in Orlando. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: Roll him on his side real quick. VENEGAS: Three victims killed, including a news reporter and a 9-year-old girl, two others critically wounded. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: We`re getting multiple gunshots wound calls in the Hialeah Street area. VENEGAS: The first shooting happened Wednesday morning where authorities found 38-year-old Natacha Augustin dead from a gunshot wound. Officials say the victim was an acquaintance of the suspect. Hours later, a news crew covering that incident was ambushed in their car, deputies say. The gunfire killing 24-year-old Spectrum News 13 reporter Dylan Lyons and critically wounding cameraman Jesse Walden. I just happened to catch a bullet. But he kept shooting at me as I ducked behind the wheel of my car, and he walked forward and shot into my car and ended up striking our reporter. VENEGAS: Authorities say the suspect then fled the scene and entered a nearby home. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: I`ve got two more victims, 9-year-old female. VENEGAS: Deputies say he then opened fire again, killing a 9-year-old girl and critically injuring her mother. The suspect was arrested a short time later. JOHN MINA, SHERIFF, ORANGE COUNTY, FLORIDA: We recovered a Glock 40, a semiautomatic handgun from inside of his pants. That gun was still hot to the touch, meaning it had just been fired. VENEGAS: Moses is now charged with first-degree murder. (END VIDEOTAPE) VENEGAS (on camera): And tonight, officials are still investigating a motive, but they say the 19-year-old suspect had a lengthy criminal history, including eight felony and 11 misdemeanor arrests. Lester? HOLT: Guad Venegas, thank you. In 60 seconds, the battle over abortion. How an imminent court ruling about a widely used abortion drug could have an impact nationwide. (COMMERCIAL BREAK) HOLT: It could be the most consequential abortion decision since Roe v. Wade was overturned. A Texas judge will soon decide whether to block access to a commonly used abortion pill nationwide. Dasha Burns reports. (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) CROWD: We can`t go back! DASHA BURNS, NBC NEWS CORRESPONDENT (voiceover): Amarillo, Texas now at the center of America`s abortion debate. CROWD: I believe that we will win! BURNS: Here, a group of anti-abortion doctors and medical organizations are suing the FDA , challenging the approval of Mifeprex, generically known as Mifepristone, part of a two-drug regimen commonly used for abortions that has been approved by the FDA since 2000. Alliance Defending Freedom arguing the FDA didn`t adequately evaluate the drug`s safety. ERIK BAPTIST, SENIOR COUNSEL, ALLIANCE DEFENDING FREEDOM: We`re asking the court to do what is right, to follow -- and ask the FDA to follow the law by taking these dangerous drugs off the marketplace. BURNS: Presiding over the case, a conservative judge appointed by former President Trump. An injunction would set off access to Mifepristone nationwide. If the plaintiffs win this lawsuit, what will be the effects? [19:15:01] DR. SERINA FLOYD, MEDICAL DIRECTOR, PLANNED PARENTHOOD OF METROPOLITAN WASHINGTON, DC: It will be devastating. Even in places where they`ve worked very hard to secure access to abortion, states like California, New York, here in D.C. BURNS: Abortion providers like Dr. Serina Floyd say the lawsuit is based on misinformation. How dangerous is this medication? FLOYD: It`s not dangerous at all. The evidence is solid, the science is solid. The complication rate is less than one percent. BURNS: The FDA told NBC News it does not comment on ongoing litigation. But in the court filings said the claims in the lawsuit are unsupported by any evidence. Since 2000, more than five million women have taken mifepristone with 28 deaths associated with the drug reported. Millions of women have taken these drugs safely. Doesn`t that paint a contrary picture to your complaint? DR. CHRISTINA FRANCIS, AMERICAN ASSOCIATION OF PRO-LIFE OBSTETRICIANS AND GYNECOLOGISTS: I`m seeing these women in my own practice. My emergency room physicians, they`re telling me how frequently they`re seeing these complications, that women come in with retained tissue, with heavy bleeding, with serious life-threatening infections. BURNS: In a court brief, the country`s leading group of OBGYN say the mifepristone is "exceedingly safe and effective, calling the lawsuit ideological and not scientific. The result if you win is that abortion access will be significantly limited. Is that the goal of this lawsuit? BAPTIST: No, the goal of this lawsuit is to protect American women and girls from dangerous chemical abortion drugs. BURNS: There is another drug, Misoprostol, that can be used for abortions, but doctors say it can be less effective on its own. Back in Amarillo, Amanda Barnes travelled from Atlanta to protest this case. AMANDA BARNES, ACTIVIST: It`s ridiculous that just because, you know, we were born with a uterus and certain body parts that we should have to be subjected to this treatment. BURNS: The next frontier in America`s abortion battle. Dasha Burns, NBC News, Amarillo, Texas. (END VIDEOTAPE) HOLT: Coming up, our exclusive report in the flow of goods into Russia, despite sanctions. (COMMERCIAL BREAK) [19:20:00] HOLT: As the war in Ukraine approaches the one-year mark, the U.S. is pushing for more sanctions against Russia. But are the ones already in place having an impact? Keir Simmons went inside neighboring Georgia to find out how Russia is getting around them. (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) KEIR SIMMONS, NBC NEWS SENIOR INTERNATIONAL CORRESPONDENT (voiceover): If you want to know how the Russian economy is surviving amid punishing western sanctions, you might come here. We`re just across the border in Georgia, and it`s lined with trucks. President Putin`s supply line. You`re going from Turkey to Russia? To Moscow? He`s carrying xerox printer ink, he says. Since Putin`s invasion and unprecedented Western sanctions, satellite images along with international trade data shows this mountain pass becoming much busier. That`s not surprising. At the outset of the war, Russia dropped most import restrictions on things like cars. The Russian border is about 25 miles that way, but police tell us they`ve closed the road because of an avalanche risk. Business has stopped, but only temporarily. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: Hello! SIMMONS : Then hidden in the snow, a stunning discovery. Two brand-new American ram pickups. American cars, American trucks? It was never driven, he says. Take a look at this. Look, it`s still got the protection on the dashboard. Look, they`re brand-new. Where are they going? UNIDENTIFIED MALE: To the Moscow. SIMMONS: To Moscow, he tells me. The men tell us they`ve sold both vehicles for around $170,000 each. They say they are moving cars every week. Does it matter that there is a war on? Where is that war, he asks. It doesn`t matter for us. We have obtained one of the vehicle ID numbers and asked the manufacturer who told us it was legally sold to a private customer by an authorized distributor in Abu Dhabi, that they cannot prevent that customer from reselling it, and the company complies with all U.S. and international sanctions. And it`s not only Georgia. Satellite images also show lines of trucks on the roads to Russia from China. President Putin and China`s top diplomat meeting yesterday, pledging to strengthen ties. China already provides crucial economic help to Russia. Back in Georgia, the road reopens, and we pass a construction site where China is helping build a new tunnel through the mountain. The half-billion project was started before the Ukraine invasion. But the plan will be more trade with Russia. Clearly, not every country wants this to be the end of the road for moscow. (END VIDEOTAPE) SIMMONS (on camera): Despite all the sanctions, the IMF says Russia`s economy is actually set to grow this year, though only by 0.3 percent. Lester? HOLT: Keir Simmons tonight, thank you. Up next, our inspiring one-on-one with actress and singer Sheryl Lee Ralph. (COMMERCIAL BREAK) [19:25:00] HOLT: She is the star of a hit sitcom, an Emmy winner, and recently sang at the Super Bowl. Sheryl Lee Ralph now on the hurdles she overcame and why she is only just getting started. She spoke with Dana Griffin. (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) DANA GRIFFIN, NBC NEWS CORRESPONDENT (voiceover): With a career spanning nearly five decades in showbiz, Sheryl Lee Ralph is back in the spotlight. Do you still have pinch me moments, especially now when you see we`re sitting in the middle of Hollywood? SHERYL LEE RALPH, SINGER: Yes. I have real pinch me moments in life, because, you know, I`ve lived most of my life as a very regular normal human being. I will go to the 99 Cent Store, the Dollar Tree or whatever. I will do that. And now when I go, I`m like, what in the world are they staring at? And then, I`m like, oh my God, it`s me. GRIFFIN: The entertainment icon has had a whirlwind of recent success, inspiring a new generation. RALPH: Now, who took that picture of me? GRIFFIN: Last year, she won an Emmy for supporting comedy actress for her role in Abbott Elementary where she plays teacher Barbara Howard. What was that moment like for you? RALPH: First of all, I was -- I was listening to the whole thing, and I was like getting ready to be happy for somebody. And I realized, no, this is very real. She just called my name. GRIFFIN: And more recently, the critics choice awards where her message resonated with many. RALPH: When you look in the mirror, you better love what you see. GRIFFIN: Her Broadway, TV and film career dates back to the `70s. In 1981, she starred in the original Broadway cast of Dream Girls. Her latest performance, Super Bowl LVII, singing Lift Every Voice And Sing. But stealing the show hasn`t always been easy. RALPH: They used to say you`re too dark. Your lips are too big. Your hair is too nappy. Suppose I listened to them? GRIFFIN: But Ralph persevered. What else do you want to accomplish? RALPH: More. I want to tell stories that deserve to be told, characters whose voices were dimmed or dulled or muted just because they were Black. Now is the time to tell those stories. GRIFFIN: Dana Griffin, NBC News. (END VIDEOTAPE) HOLT: And that`s NIGHTLY NEWS for this Thursday. Thanks for watching, everyone. I`m Lester Holt. Please take care of yourself and each other. Good night. (COMMERCIAL BREAK) END Content and programming copyright 2023 NBCUniversal. ALL RIGHTS RESERVED. Transcription Copyright 2023 VIQ Media Transcription, Inc.
