headline: MEET THE PRESS for March 5, 2023, NBC
story_text: (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) [09:00:18] CHUCK TODD, HOST, NBC`S "MEET THE PRESS WITH CHUCK TODD" (voice over): This Sunday, crime and punishment. President Biden backs down from fighting a Republican effort to block D.C.`s more lenient`s approach to crime. PAUL VALLAS , (D) CHICAGO MAYORAL CANDIDATE: We will make Chicago the safest city in America. (APPLAUSE) TODD: Just after the perception of rising crime took down Chicago`s mayor. MAYOR LORI LIGHTFOOT, (D) CHICAGO: We fought the right fights. TODD: Can Biden`s moves help Democrats from being seen as soft on crime going into 2024? Plus, divide and conquer. Florida Governor Ron DeSantis isn`t officially in the race yet, but he`s eagerly courting Trump`s base. GOV. RON DESANTIS, (R) FLORIDA: I think there`s a strong anti-woke majority out there across the country. TODD: The primary fight has kicked into high gear as more candidates consider challenging Trump. FORMER PRESIDENT DONALD J. TRUMP: For those who have been wronged and betrayed, I am your retribution. TODD: I`ll talk to New Hampshire Republican Governor Chris Sununu , who`s considering his own White House run. And, confronting China, a bipartisan push to face the growing threats from Beijing. REP. MIKE GALLAGHER , (R) WISCONSIN: This is an existential struggle over what life will look like in the 21st Century. TODD: Tensions continue to escalate as the U.S. warns about supplying arms to Russia and new concern over COVID`s origins. CHRISTOPHER WRAY , DIRECTOR, FEDERAL BUREAU OF INVESTIGATION: The origins of the pandemic are mostly likely a potential lab incident in Wuhan. TODD: In a joint interview, I`ll talk to the chair and ranking member of the House Intelligence Committee, Republican Mike Turner of Ohio and Democrat Jim Himes of Connecticut. (on camera): Joining me for insight and analysis are NBC News senior Washington correspondent Hallie Jackson; former Homeland Security Secretary Jeh Johnson; USA Today Washington bureau chief Susan Page; and former Republican governor of North Carolina Pat McCrory . Welcome to Sunday. It`s "Meet the Press." ANNOUNCER: From NBC News in Washington, the longest-running show in television history, this is "Meet the Press with Chuck Todd." (END VIDEOTAPE) TODD: Good Sunday morning. This may be the week where we saw the 2024 presidential campaign kick into full gear, and not just on the Republican side. President Biden`s decision to block a D.C. crime law caught many Democrats off guard. Because it`s going to be the first time in 30 years that Congress has nullified a law in D.C. And it`s a Democratic president and a Democratic Senate. But if you view it through the lens of political calculation, it may make perfect sense. President Biden decided that neither he nor his party, with a big Senator map to defend with a lot of red areas to defend, could afford to look soft on crime heading into 2024. Republicans tried to make crime a central issue in the 2022 midterms, and they certainly had some success in New York State and a few other areas. But the results this week in the Chicago mayor`s race, where voters fired the incumbent, are a reminder that crime and policing are still important to urban voters as well, a huge part of the Democratic coalition. Democrats have been twisted in knots on the crime issue because it`s a problem with swing voters. And Biden is trying to provide them with a way forward. The mirror image of, sort of, being twisted in knots for Republicans is the abortion issue. But no one in the GOP, at least to date, is taking the lead to try and come up with a modified solution to that political problem for them. If anything, the Republicans are more fractured, and not just on the abortion issue but about the general direction of the party. It`s a divide that has been on full display this weekend. But there`s one issue where there is little divide these days, and it is on China, with its rising national security threats. The secretary of state, Antony Blinken , issued yet another direct warning to China about sending lethal aid to Russia for the war in Ukraine. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) SECRETARY OF STATE ANTONY BLINKEN: China can`t have it both ways. It can`t putting itself out as a force for peace in public while it, one way or another, continues to fuel the flames of this fire that Vladimir Putin started. (END VIDEO CLIP) TODD: If we want to dig deeper into this, joining me now are the chair and ranking member of the House Intelligence Committee, appearing here together, Republican Congressman Mike Turner of Ohio and Democratic Congressman Jim Himes of Connecticut. Gentlemen, welcome back to "Meet the Press," and thank you for coming on together. REP. MIKE TURNER , (R) OHIO & CHAIR OF HOUSE INTELLIGENCE COMMITTEE: Thanks for having me. REP. JIM HIMES, (D), CONNECTICUT & RANKING MEMBER, HOUSE INTELLIGENCE COMMITTEE: Thanks for having us. TODD: Before we start on this stuff, your -- this train derailment overnight happened in your congressional district. I know the shelter in place order is no longer. What -- what more can you tell us? What more have you learned, and is the federal government responding? TURNER: Sure. This truly is outrageous. You know, Ohio is really the crossroads of America, both on the road and in the rail. An unbelievable amount of goods travel through Ohio, some hazardous. What we`ve seen recently with the risk to communities is -- is unacceptable. Luckily, it seems we may have missed a bullet in this one, that this train may have been empty, and it looks like hazardous materials is not going to be a threat to the community. We`ll have to see. TODD: Is it clear -- do you think it`s clear that the freight industry isn`t well-regulated and needs to be? TURNER: Oh, absolutely. And the fact that we`re having derailment after derailment shows really the lack of investment -- the disinvestment in our infrastructure, and that needs to change. [09:05:04] TODD: Let me move to this -- Congressman Himes, I`ll -- I`ll start with this. I know both of you have been getting these briefings. Another warning to China. We heard it from the secretary of state about arming Russia. Our reporting indicates that this actually came from our intelligence inside of Russia, confirmed (inaudible). How serious is this threat, and do we know if China has made a final decision? HIMES: Well, no question it`s a serious threat. We`ve seen the Russian military obviously come apart. The Chinese could reverse in the same way that the Iranians are helping the Russians right now. I think the administration is doing the right things by saying "Don`t do this." Now, it doesn`t surprise me at all that there`s a debate inside China about whether they should do this. Hopefully, wisdom prevails. I -- I couldn`t help but note, in the Chinese proposed peace plan, the 12th point said we need to focus on rebuilding China -- rebuilding Russia. I can imagine the Chinese see a lot of business there. Obviously, if they`re part of the Russian assault on Ukraine, they will not get that business. So, no, I don`t think a final decision has been made, but I do think it`s wise for us to say "Don`t go there." TODD: Congressman Turner, you -- you`ve noted that we have a different posture now on our intelligence. We`re releasing more of it. Do you think more of it should be released to make sure the world believes us? TURNER: Right, well, and obviously you`re seen with the CIA director, even calling out to China on this issue that they`re considering it has a huge shift in policy. And what we`re seeing is the administration using intelligence to try to impact the outcome of -- of policy, right? So they`re not just saying "We happen to know this" in looking to hold someone accountable. They`re trying to thwart them, to stop them from doing this. You know, the problem with China entering this is because, you know, you`ve got the West giving weapons to Ukraine. You`ve got Russia depleting their stores. We obviously, the West together, have an ability to impact Ukraine greater than Russia alone does. It would be an inexhaustible source of weapons if China and its production capacity supported Russia. And that would change the dynamics. TODD: What kind of intel do we have on the state of the Russian army, Congressman Himes, meaning, like, we`ve seen some reports that they may be running out of munitions; they have some issues. What does our folks say? HIMES: Well, so neither Mike nor I can get too deep into any particular intel, but, you know, you don`t need to get too deep into intel. Consider the fact that you see every single day on television, which is the entire Russian army cannot take a town that nobody had ever heard of a year ago, the town of Bakhmut. Now, you know, Mike and I have been doing this long enough that we remember when we literally devoted hundreds of billions of dollars and much of our national security apparatus to this beast of a Russian military. Today we see that they can`t, even with the push of the president, Vladimir Putin , they can`t take a town. That doesn`t mean they`re not still dangerous. They have nuclear weapons. But they are not what we thought they were. TODD: I want to play something. Sergey Lavrov was at the G-20, Congressman turner. And wait -- I mean, wait until you hear the reaction to something he said here. Let me play it. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) SERGEY LAVROV , RUSSIAN FOREIGN MINISTER: The war which we are trying to stop and which was launched against us using the Ukraine... (LAUGHTER) ... Ukrainian people... (CROSSTALK) LAVROV: of course influenced -- influenced -- influenced the policy of Russia. (END VIDEO CLIP) TODD: You know, there`s nothing like being able to say the phrase, "The world was laughing" at them. HIMES: Completely. TODD: The world was laughing at them. TURNER: Spontaneously. TODD: What should -- what should the West use a moment like that for? TURNER: Well, the thing about both Putin, Lavrov and even Medvedev, although he`s supposed to be the new, new face of a new Russia, come from an era where, you know, they controlled Eastern Europe. They could say things that were not true and people believed them because they controlled information. Today information can`t be controlled. So the -- the laughability of what they`re saying, and the ridiculousness of what they`re saying is easily exposed. TODD: All right. Let me move to the issue of these classified documents. Nobody seems to be satisfied with -- with what you`ve got. Congressman Himes, does that include you? Were you satisfied with the briefing? HIMES: So we have a lot more work to do. Look, I think, as the leaders of the Intelligence Committee, our number one job is to make sure that the DNI, the FBI , whoever needs to do it, does everything they need to do to protect the sources and methods that might have been exposed were any of those documents to have been out in the wild. [09:40:03] TODD: You know, Susan, what`s fascinating here is how the mayors -- these Democratic mayors -- are being pressured -- they`re being pressured on both sides, because these city councils are way to the left of the mayors. We see it here in D.C. I mean, 12 - the veto override of Muriel Bowser was 12-1. This wasn`t -- it wasn`t like there was a big divide. The progressives have made a lot of progress on these city councils, but they haven`t been able to win mayors` races. But it`s really put mayors in the cross-hairs. SUSAN PAGE, WASHINGTON BUREAU CHIEF, USA TODAY : Well, and in fairness you`re talking a lot about social justice issues and police reform and the need for that. And we see the need for that over and over again in some of the shootings of unarmed Black men, which continues across this country. But to make it a choice between crime and social justice is a real problem for Democrats. And I think you see with Joe Biden`s decision on where he stands on this, is his -- that is his reelection announcement. On this issue of crime and on border security he has in recent weeks moved to shore up what would`ve been the strongest issues against him in a re-election campaign. TODD: And so far, the left`s been muted on this, even on immigration. JACKSON: That`s right. TODD: You hear the complaints in press releases, but you`re not hearing elected officials do it. JACKSON: Coming out on TV -- TODD: Right. JACKSON: -- doing the whole thing, doing the whole circuit. You know, and I would be curious as to Secretary Johnson`s perspective on this. I would say to your point, though, when it comes to the issue writ large, Democrats I think truly are looking to get on offense on this. You mentioned something that I`ve heard that they`re looking to do, which is talk about, for example, the assault weapons ban that President Biden wants. It has truly pragmatically, virtually no shot in Congress as it is laid out right now -- funding I`ve heard about for the COPS program, et cetera. But you also have Democrats who are pointing to, for example, Matt Gaetz going out at CPAC this weekend and saying, let`s abolish the FBI , let`s abolish the ATF -- TODD: Right. JACKSON: -- and hoping to use that as a wedge issue as well. TODD: Jeh, very quickly, what do you make so far of what Secretary Mayorkas and the Biden administration have done? It looks like it`s working, but we`ll really find out in May, I guess. JOHNSON: Well, working off what we did in Venezuela in the fall, where we provided a legal safe pathway, which will discourage people from entering unlawfully, they`ve expanded that. And it looks like it`s working, though it`s way too early to declare victory. The numbers were down in January, but January is typically a low month. TODD: Yeah, it takes a couple more months to judge. All right, we`re going to get to the good stuff when we come back. We`re going to talk a little Trump when you guys come back. But first, we`re going to talk about President Biden`s plan to cancel student loan debt and the uncertain future of that. We`re going to show you how many borrowers will be impacted and what`s really at stake here politically. (COMMERCIAL BREAK) [09:45:24] TODD: Welcome back. Data Download time. So this week, the Supreme Court heard arguments on the Biden administration`s plan to provide student loan debt relief for tens of millions of Americans. If the justices, though, strike it down, there are going to be a lot of unhappy voters across the country in 2024, including many in important battleground states. So let`s unpack this. How did we get here? Well, first, let`s look at the cost of college tuition. In over the last 30 years, the cost of a private university`s tuition has gone up 80 percent, tuition at a public university has gone up 125 percent. Those are some big jumps. For what it`s worth, the cost of both housing and cars, those numbers are -- percentages are actually higher than the cost of education. Still, this Biden student debt relief plan, if enacted, would provide up to $20,000 of relief for those that got Pell grants. Up to $10,000 for those with other types of student loans. And guess what, when this was offered, it was popular. Over 26 million people have already applied for this debt relief, even though it is not clear whether it`s going to be allowed to happen. And if you break it down by states, and you know, how we like to do it around here, by battleground states, you see, these are some big chunks of voters who might not be happy if this gets overturned. Over a million in Pennsylvania, over a million and a half in Florida. A million in Georgia. You see where this is going. This is a popular program. If it gets repealed, there are going to be some unhappy voters. Before we go, this week marks the 58th anniversary of Bloody Sunday, when police beat and tear gassed hundreds of protesters in Selma, Alabama who were marching for racial equality and voting rights. Back in 2015, I had the honor of speaking to Congressman John Lewis on the 50th anniversary of the Selma march about his experience leading the marchers that day. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) REP. JOHN LEWIS (D-GA): We were kneeling. We were knocked down. They started beating us with nightsticks, trampling us with horses, releasing the tear gas. I was hit in the head by a state trooper with a nightstick. I lost consciousness. Fifty years later, I don`t recall how I made it back across that bridge to the little church that we had left from. Apparently, a group literally carried me back to the church. TODD: It`d be perfectly understandable if you were bitter. Bitter today, bitter a week later from when it happened, bitter 20 years. Were you bitter, ever, after all this? LEWIS: I was not bitter then. I`m not bitter now. I grew up in a movement to accept the way of love, the way of peace, the way of non-violence, the way of forgiveness, as a way of life, as a way of living. (END VIDEO CLIP) TODD: John Lewis died in 2020. President Biden is in Selma today to commemorate the anniversary of Bloody Sunday, and the Reverend Al Sharpton will be leading the march alongside him. Up next, can Ron DeSantis stop Trump from the nomination while still courting the Trump voter? We`re about to find out. (COMMERCIAL BREAK) [09:52:21] TODD: Welcome back. All right. The Republican presidential primary. Donald Trump in some ways re-announced, if you will, this weekend at CPAC. Take a listen to his message. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) DONALD TRUMP , FORMER PRESIDENT: We are never going back to the party of Paul Ryan , Karl Rove and Jeb Bush. We`re not going back to people that want to destroy our great Social Security system, even some in our own party. I wonder who that might be. In 2016, I declared I am your voice. Today, I add, I am your warrior. I am your justice. And for those who have been wronged and betrayed, I am your retribution. (END VIDEO CLIP) TODD: Pat McCrory , "I am your retribution." MCCRORY: Wow. To see a lot of good Republican candidates who would make great presidents grovel or kiss up to both CPAC and Club for Growth, is, is -- it bothers me because not one of those groups has ever solved a problem. And right now, we have some complex problems in this country that have to be solved. And what Donald Trump`s going to realize is they`re going to start having infighting among those two groups because CPAC`s with Trump, but Club for Growth, who used Trump in primary commercials to push their candidate, are probably going to turn on Trump. So, we have this internal warfare which may result in a general election where the Democrats have their candidate, the Republicans have the last candidate, and it might open up the door for a third-party candidate because the independent voter, which is 40 percent of the registered voters now in America, are going to go, "Is this the only choice we have?" TODD: Susan, we did a little survey of CPAC attendees just on the issue of Ukraine. And it just shows you where the Trump base is on this. And it shows you this is a different lane than what we`re used to. Take a listen. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) BARRY MORGENSTEIN, CPAC ATTENDEE: Of course, I feel for the people of Ukraine. I would like them to beat the Russians, but we have so many problems. We have open borders here that the money could be going to. AMY SHANK, CPAC ATTENDEE: Well, I think support is okay. But I think we need to be focusing on the people here first rather than other countries. RENE CAMPBELL, CPAC ATTENDEE: Don`t take my taxpayer money and send it over to Ukraine. Enough with this, you know? Enough with this war. (END VIDEO CLIP) TODD: Susan, I think what`s remarkable here is Donald Trump`s carving out the outsider lane. I mean, this is not the mainstream Republican position these days on Ukraine. But it is Trump`s position. PAGE: It is, although -- and it`s not the mainstream Republican position, and it`s not Mitch McConnell`s view, for instance. But there is growing public concern, and not just among Trump voters, about the extent and the length and the cost of the U.S. commitment to Ukraine. [09:55:04] And there`s still majority support for continuing the effort, but it is really pressuring the administration to come up with some answers about how this war could end in a successful way and not go on forever. But it -- Trump -- we say it`s not the mainstream Republican position. This is Trump`s party. This is not the Republican Party. It`s the Trump party. Trump`s position becomes the Republican position. TODD: But has he - has he somehow been able to position DeSantis as part of the establishment? JACKSON: You said this a couple -- you said this just now. You said it to Governor Sununu. And I wrote it down because it was interesting to me, the idea that Donald Trump is trying to run as an outsider. Because, you know, from the jump I have been hearing from sources close to his team that they want a position that`s his a la 2016, obviously not as of a la 2020. And somebody said to me this weekend, well, you know, he`s doing better than he was at this point in 2016. And I said, I sure hope so. He was the president for four years. I mean, it`s almost as though they`re trying to erase the fact that he was in the White House for four years to do what you`re talking about here. Is he going to come up with a new nickname for DeSantis? How is he going to position him as the outsider? But I will tell you what is so interesting to me just in talking with people in the last 24 hours about sort of CPAC and Club for Growth. You know, Trump allies are saying this is the most important gathering of conservatives since -- that will happen in this campaign until the Republican primary debate. And then I heard somebody else, a rival campaign adviser, let`s say, say, well, wait a second. This is a bunch of MAGA misfits who are showing up -- their words, right? And I`m not quoting but paraphrasing here, showing up to be super pro-Trump here. And actually, the adults in the room are going to Club for Growth and talking about what they`re going to do on -- from a policy perspective. TODD: But you know what the difference is between the Club for Growth and CPAC? The Club for Growth - the folks at Club for Growth talk behind the cameras, behind the scenes, not to voters, but to donors, acting like establishment people. Donald Trump was talking to people. Whatever you think of it, he was talking to the public. JOHNSON: This could be wild. You could have the major candidate in the party, an indicted criminal defendant, out on bail. TODD: He said he was going to keep running if indicted. JACKSON: But do you know what the most interesting thing he said was to me? Because this is a lot of sort of similar grievances we`ve heard. You know what was new? He said people should vote by mail-in ballot. TODD: Yeah, yeah. Speaking of new, Larry Hogan is not running. I assume that has as much to do with Chris Sununu , perhaps, getting a jumpstart on him. MCCRORY: Well, they`re all looking for a lane. And he probably didn`t see a lane unless it`s a third-party potential lane which, again, could happen. TODD: You, you -- look. You`ve been to some meetings with No Labels. MCCRORY: That`s right. TODD: Joe Manchin`s been to some meetings with No Labels. He`s been flirting about this. Is this only if it`s Trump/Biden that this gets traction? MCCRORY: I think if it`s two choices where the majority of people say, the parties have failed us, there`s a better choice to be president of the United States. PAGE: And you elect -- and you elect Donald Trump because of voters who draw with the No Labels candidate come from the Democratic side. MCCRORY: And they`re getting on the ballots. They`re getting on the ballots in the states. And you`ve got to remember, ballots is a state issue, not a federal issue. It`s not a party issue. It`s a state issue. TODD: So their -- that`s their goal, that they can get ballot access to all 50 states. MCCRORY: Get on the ballot enough to win the presidency. TODD: They`ve tried this. Do you buy it? MCCRORY: It`s an insurance policy. If the majority of people do not agree with the two parties` selection, and right now the majority of Democrats don`t agree with Biden, and the majority of Republicans don`t agree with Trump. So, it`s going to be interesting -- PAGE: But there`s a significant fraction of Republican voters who will stick with Trump no matter what. MCCRORY: Oh, I know that well. PAGE: If he`s in jail, they will stick with Trump. JOHNSON: That`s right. PAGE: And that is a kind of diamond-hard support no other candidate in America would have. MCCRORY: Big money -- by the way, you mentioned -- Club for Growth is money talking. It`s big super PAC money. TODD: All right. Speaking of that, I`ve got to stop the talking because I`ve got to end the show. That`s all we have for today. Thanks for watching. story_text: [19:00:00] (COMMERCIAL BREAK) LESTER HOLT, NBC NEWS HOST (on camera): Tonight, the urgent search for four Americans kidnapped at gunpoint in Mexico. (voiceover): The terrifying video appearing to show the Americans being dragged into the back of a pickup after gunmen opened fire on their minivan. Was it a case of mistaken identity? The reward the FBI is offering and what we`re learning. Also tonight, scary moments in the air. The passenger on a United plane accused of trying to open the emergency exit and stab a flight attendant. A Southwest plane making an emergency landing in Cuba. Smoke filling the cabin. And a passenger dying after severe turbulence. California slammed with even more snow. Desperate residents trapped for more than a week. And the new winter threats we`re tracking. Protesters and police clashing in Atlanta. Nearly two dozen now facing domestic terror charges. The NTSB investigating after another Norfolk Southern train derails in Ohio. Our one-on-one with transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg. We asked, should the company be forced to pause operations? Jurors in the Alex Murdaugh double murder trial breaking their silence. What they say about his decision to take the stand. And he was the last original member of a legendary rock band. Remembering guitarist Gary Rossington. ANNOUNCER: This is NBC NIGHTLY NEWS with Lester Holt. HOLT: Good evening, everyone. And thank you for joining us. Chilling images tonight appear to show four Americans kidnapped at gunpoint moments after crossing from Texas into Mexico on Friday. Tonight, the FBI asking for the public`s help, offering a $50,000 reward to help locate the Americans who were attacked by armed men after crossing from Brownsville, Texas into Matamoros riding in a minivan bearing North Carolina plates. One woman seen being dragged into a pickup truck. A U.S. official tells NBC News the attack may have been a case of mistaken identity. Authorities say a Mexican citizen was killed during the confrontation. Gabe Gutierrez reports it happened in an area that has become increasingly dangerous. (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) GABE GUTIERREZ, NBC NEWS NATIONAL CORRESPONDENT (voiceover): These photos shared widely on social media appear to show the kidnapping`s aftermath. The FBI says the four Americans entered Matamoros, Mexico Friday in a white minivan with North Carolina license plates before armed gunmen opened fire and abducted them. A law enforcement official with knowledge of the matter tells NBC News this video depicts part of the kidnapping, appearing to show one woman walking on her own, forced into a white pickup truck. Armed men with bulletproof vests are then seen dragging other people into the vehicle. KARINE JEAN-PIERRE , WHITE HOUSE PRESS SECRETARY: We are closely following the assault and kidnapping of four U.S. citizens in Matamoros, Mexico. These sorts of attacks are unacceptable. GUTIERREZ: Authorities say a Mexican citizen was killed during the incident. A law enforcement official tells NBC News the Americans did not cross the border for any criminal purpose and that this appears to be a case of mistaken identity. Today Mexico`s president said they`d entered the country to buy medicine, although U.S. officials have not confirmed that. We visited Matamoros to report on migrant tent camps for years, but violence there has escalated. The city of about half a million people just across the border from Brownsville, Texas is home to warring factions of the gulf drug cartel. The shootouts on Friday prompted the U.S. consulate to issue another security alert. Tonight, the FBI is offering a $50,000 reward for the safe return of the Americans. (END VIDEOTAPE) HOLT: And Gabe is with me now. Do we know anything about the identities of the Americans? GUTIERREZ (on camera): Well, Lester, the FBI has not confirmed any details but I just spoke with a family member of one of those abducted and she says the group was from South Carolina but had a rental car with North Carolina plates. She says the group crossed the border for a medical procedure. A law enforcement source with knowledge of the matter tells NBC News it was cosmetic surgery. And the family is pleading for their safe return tonight, Lester. HOLT: Gabe Gutierrez, thank you. Let`s turn now to those mid-air scares. The latest, a man arrested for allegedly trying to open a plane`s emergency exit door during a flight, then stab a flight attendant. That coming after a Southwest flight was forced to land after a bird strike. Here`s Tom Costello. (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) TOM COSTELLO, NBC NEWS CORRESPONDENT (voiceover): It happened on a United flight from L.A. to Boston. Federal prosecutors say 45 minutes before landing, a male passenger attempted to open an exit door between first class and coach. When flight attendants confronted the man, he allegedly tried to stab one of them in the neck with a broken spoon. Fellow passengers tackled and subdued the passenger until the plane landed in Boston. 33-year-old Francisco Torres tonight being held on federal charges. Meanwhile, smoke and panic on Southwest flight 3923 Sunday. The 737 hit by birds as it took off from Havana, Cuba headed for Fort Lauderdale. The engine exploded and on fire and on fire. Terrified passengers donned oxygen masks as the crew circled back, making an emergency landing in Havana. [19:05:28] UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: Smoke started coming into the cabin, and they just said stay in your seats and we had to start breathing. COSTELLO: Bird strikes are common, but rarely cause serious damage. The miracle on the Hudson landing in 2009 came after a flock of geese took out both of the plane`s engines. Meanwhile, tragedy on board a private plane when a passenger, 55-year-old Dana Hyde of Maryland, was killed as the Bombardier Challenger plane hit severe turbulence. The plane flying from New Hampshire to Virginia making an emergency landing in Connecticut. The NTSB says the pilots were dealing with a trim issue at the time, suggesting they may have hit clear air turbulence in a jet stream moving 50 to 100 miles an hour faster than normal. JOHN COX, NBC NEWS AVIATION ANALYST: Clear air turbulence is not something that radar shows. So, pilots are unable to see it in advance. COSTELLO: Every year, passengers and crew members suffer head lacerations, broken bones and bruises in severe turbulence. SARA NELSON , INTERNATIONAL PRESIDENT, ASSOCIATION OF FLIGHT ATTENDANTS: This is exactly why we tell you to wear your seat belt because if you`re not wearing your seat belt when severe turbulence like this happens, it can actually be deadly. (END VIDEOTAPE) COSTELLO (on camera): The incidents are rare but they come as the FAA prepares for an aviation safety summit next week. Lester? HOLT: All right, Tom, thank you. Parts of Southern California remain under a state of emergency tonight with many residents still trapped after days of historic snowfall. First responders still trying to reach those stranded with some running out of food and medicine. Miguel Almaguer is there. (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) MIGUEL ALMAGUER, NBC NEWS NATIONAL CORRESPONDENT (voiceover): As blizzard- like conditions blanket California cities already buried under feet of snow -- ROBIN UNWIN-BASSETT, RESIDENT, TWIN PEAKS, CALIFORNIA: We have neighbors who are panicking. They`re without, you know, food, power, heat, medications. ALMAGUER: For nearly two weeks now, trapped residents near Lake Arrowhead just two hours outside of Los Angeles have been pleading for help. Today, middle school teacher Steve Gaskell is a literal lifeline. His jeep loaded with meals and insulin for Marisa Kupsak`s uncle who`s stranded at home. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: Thank you. It`s overwhelming because my husband can`t even come home. He`s stuck at the bottom of the hill. ALMAGUER: As the desperate ration food and medicine, mounds of snow are trapping the most vulnerable who can`t dig or plow their way out. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: It`s -- it`s tough. It really is. I`m sorry. ALMAGUER: The National Guard and firefighters have been called in to help. But it`s volunteers, some walking miles through waist-deep snow, making the difference. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: I think the first responders are overwhelmed with the sheer volume of calls that they`re getting. ALMAGUER: With major roads being plowed, hand crews are slowly starting to reach senior citizens like Sidney White. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: I can`t see myself getting out of here without them. ALMAGUER: But with more than nine feet of snowfall, the weight of these storms was far too great for the only grocery store in the community of crestline. The parking lot now a free food distribution site for residents like the Moncriefs, who were lucky to get past road blocks. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: People want to go to their homes. Let them home. ALMAGUER: Tonight, the sense of desperation spelled out across this community as help finally arrives for some but not all. (END VIDEOTAPE) HOLT: So, Miguel, what is the situation right now with power and water? ALMAGUER (on camera): Well, Lester, people without power and water are slowly getting it back. I want to show you a live picture from our drone overhead. It shows another major problem they`re dealing with all across this area. That heavy snowfall is collapsing roofs. Lester, the people in this area, they need help and they need it fast. Lester? HOLT: All right, Miguel, thanks. Let`s bring in Dylan Dreyer who`s tracking all this. Dylan, when will the West Coast get some relief? DYLAN DREYER, NBC NEWS METEOROLOGIST (on camera): Well, where Miguel is we`re going to get some relief, but the next storm is already making its way across central and Northern California where over the next several days we`re going to see rounds of snow. So all the way through Wednesday at least, we will see several inches of snow, and in the higher elevations of the Sierra Nevada mountain range we`ll see one to three feet of snow. Then we`ll get a bit of a break before the next big storm system makes its way on shore for Friday into Saturday. We also have a weak little system moving across Lake Erie right now. This is going to produce just enough snow to make things tricky for Tuesday morning. Heaviest amounts will be across north-central Pennsylvania. But even in New York City just north of Philly, we could end up with enough on the roads to make things slippery for tomorrow morning. HOLT: OK, Dylan, thanks very much. Alarming scenes outside Atlanta where police say they faced a coordinated attack by rioters at the site of a planned police training facility. Tonight, more than 20 people are charged with domestic terrorism. Blayne Alexander has late details. [19:10:12] (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) BLAYNE ALEXANDER, NBC NEWS CORRESPONDENT (voiceover): In Atlanta, a chaotic clash. Atlanta Police released this video that they say shows rioters throwing fireworks at officers and setting construction vehicles and a trailer on fire. In the end, 23 charged with domestic terrorism. DARIN SCHIERBAUM, CHIEF, ATLANTA POLICE: When you throw Molotov cocktails, large rocks, a number of items at officers, your only intent is to harm. ALEXANDER: Police call it a coordinated attack by violent agitators. Of the 23 arrested, only two are from Georgia. While protesters say it all started at a family-friendly music festival and that officials used excessive force to arrest some who were not involved. All of it centered around a planned public safety training center that opponents have dubbed cop city. The planned site is right here, 85 acres just outside of Atlanta. A training facility for both Atlanta Police and Fire. Now, officers have been stationed nearby but they say they`re going to increase their presence in the coming days. Officials tout it as a way to improve community policing. ANDRE DICKENS , MAYOR OF ATLANTA: This is where your community and neighborhood watch programs, will learn how to keep your neighborhood safe. ALEXANDER: But critics say it will do just the opposite. KAMAU FRANKLIN, EXECUTIVE DIRECTOR, COMMUNITY MOVEMENT BUILDERS: 90 acres of the forest are going to be destroyed right away to build cop city. So, we see this as a further militarization of the police. ALEXANDER: This is the latest flashpoint in a fight that has stretched well over a year. In January, a protester was killed. A Georgia State Patrol trooper injured. Tonight, protesters say that this is just the start of a week of demonstrations. Blayne Alexander, NBC News, Atlanta. (END VIDEOTAPE) HOLT: We turn now to Ohio and another derailment by a Norfolk Southern train. This one just a month after that toxic explosion in East Palestine. All as there is growing outrage over the response by the rail company and the federal government. Jesse Kirsch reports. (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) JESSE KIRSCH, NBC NEWS CORRESPONDENT (voiceover): Tonight, the NTSB is investigating another Norfolk Southern crash in Ohio, the company`s fourth derailment in this state in less than five months. This Springfield train wreck caught on camera. The company says 28 cars went off the track this weekend with two crew members on board. No injuries or public health threats were reported. JENNIFER HOMENDY, CHAIR, NTSB : 212 rail cars, some of which were tank cars transporting hazardous materials. KIRSCH: Norfolk Southern says the cars with hazardous materials were not among those that derailed. Today, the company promising more investment in sensors that detect overheated wheel bearings. PETE BUTTIGIEG, U.S. SECRETARY OF STATE: Even one derailment is too many. And yet the average in recent years has been several every single day. KIRSCH: Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg says railroad standards need to change. BUTTIGIEG: But it`s really the entire industry that has been pushing hard to water down or delay safety regulations. KIRSCH: Is it now time to try figuring out a way to possibly pause Norfolk Southern `s operations until these investigations are completed? BUTTIGIEG: Well, the reality is that our economy depends on a strong freight rail network operating 24/7. We shouldn`t have to shut down the rail system in this country in order to make sure that it is safe. KIRSCH: Still, some residents here don`t fully trust what they`re hearing from officials after last month`s toxic derailment in East Palestine more than 200 miles away. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: I don`t know if it`s frustrating, but it`s just kind of scary that I`m sure there`s safety protocols in place and they`re not being followed. (END VIDEOTAPE) KIRSCH (on camera): Bipartisan calls for rail safety reform growing. Meanwhile, Norfolk Southern `s trains here once again on the move. Lester? HOLT: Jesse Kirsch, thank you. In 60 seconds, jurors in the Alex Murdaugh murder trial speak out about their guilty verdict, revealing their reactions after Murdaugh took the stand. (COMMERCIAL BREAK) A lawyer for Alex Murdaugh tells NBC News he is now off suicide watch but remains in isolation in a South Carolina prison. And now we`re hearing from some of the jurors who convicted him of murdering his wife and son. Here`s Catie Beck. [19:15:12] (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) CATIE BECK, NBC NEWS CORRESPONDENT (voiceover): After six weeks of testimony and tears -- ALEX MURDAUGH, FOUND GUILTY OF KILLING HIS WIFE AND SON: Seeing my boys lay face down -- BECK: Jurors in the Alex Murdaugh trial breaking their silence about the decision to seal his fate. JAMES MCDOWELL, JUROR, ALEX MURDAUGH MURDER TRIAL: We already know that he`s a lawyer. He`s able to be emotional with cases, he`s able to be emotional with himself, so I think we were kind of able to read right through that. BECK: Murdaugh found guilty and sentenced to life for killing his wife Maggie and son Paul. Now, a convicted murderer behind bars. Alex Murdaugh will remain at the Kirkland Correctional Center for at least 30 days to be processed and evaluated. Murdaugh was on suicide watch for the first 72 hours and is now in protective custody, locked in isolation for 23 hours a day. Jurors say Murdaugh`s fate was close to decided from the first minutes inside the jury room. AMIE WILLIAMS, JUROR, ALEX MURDAUGH MURDER TRIAL: Everyone had questions, but we were able to explain everything. BECK: Jurors say Murdaugh`s decision to take the stand in his own defense hurt his case more than it helped. MCDOWELL: I think that he believes that he`s so convincing that he felt like that was his, you know, last resort. BECK: But for several, the cell phone video from the dog kennels tipped the scales to guilty. Some jurors accept they may never understand Murdaugh`s motive but have no doubt the punishment fits the crime. GWEN GENERETTE, JUROR, ALEX MURDAUGH MURDER TRIAL: He wanted to have control of everything. Some thinking it was more like greed, him being in control. BECK: Catie Beck, NBC News, Columbia, South Carolina. (END VIDEOTAPE) HOLT: And next, as we continue tonight, our exclusive reporting on a new legal challenge to the near total abortion ban in Texas. (COMMERCIAL BREAK) [19:20:00] HOLT: Back with our NBC News exclusive. A new lawsuit being filed in Texas challenging the state`s near-total ban on abortion and seeking clarity on when doctors are allowed to intervene in dangerous pregnancies without a fear of prosecution. Here`s Yamiche Alcindor. (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) YAMICHE ALCINDOR, NBC NEWS CORRESPONDENT (voiceover): When Amanda and Josh Zurawski found out they were expecting a baby girl, they were overjoyed. The name they picked for her, Willow. AMANDA ZURAWSKI, HAD AN ABORTION: I mean, it was magical. The first 17 weeks were very easy, very smooth sailing. ALCINDOR: But just before week 18, something felt wrong. Amanda`s body was preparing for labor too early. The news from her doctor was devastating. A. ZURAWSKI: She said pretty quickly, you know, all in one breath, you`re going to lose the baby. She`s not going to survive. I thought what they would do is go in and intervene immediately, but she told me that they couldn`t because the baby`s heart was still beating and I wasn`t sick. ALCINDOR: Laws in Texas ban doctors from performing abortions except when a medical emergency endangers a person`s life or major bodily function. Those who violate the law could face up to life in prison. Take me into what it was like to wait. A. ZURAWSKI: I just existed in sorrow and fear. I was really, really scared. JOSH ZURAWSKI, HUSBAND OF AMANDA: This just isn`t something that you do with any other kind of medical issue, is you have to ask am I sick enough to get treatment. It was just -- it was infuriating. ALCINDOR: Three days after the diagnosis, Amanda`s health deteriorated. Doctors performed an abortion, but serious infections led to sepsis, and Amanda spent three days in the ICU. A. ZURAWSKI: Because of the law, I very nearly died. Nothing about this is pro-life. ALCINDOR: Now, Amanda is part of a group of seven plaintiffs represented by the Center for Reproductive Rights who plan to file a lawsuit against the State of Texas tonight. A. ZURAWSKI: Until there is a legal fight, nothing`s going to change. And something has to change. ALCINDOR: But John Seago, president of Texas Right to Life, who helped craft the Texas Heartbeat Act, says the law is clear as written and that doctors like Amanda`s are misinterpreting it. JOHN SEAGO, PRESIDENT, TEXAS RIGHT TO LIFE: If they are saying they have to delay and wait the days like you`re talking about, that is medical malpractice. But if it is uncertain that this child may survive or may not, Texas is saying we don`t jump to conclusions. ALCINDOR: Doctors are saying the law is not clear, and as a result I`m going to act on the side of being cautious, and that means that I might have to wait for a woman to get sicker and sicker before I can perform an abortion that I know she needs. SEAGO: That`s the wrong conclusion. ALCINDOR: Nancy Northup is the president of the Center for Reproductive Rights. NANCY NORTHUP , PRESIDENT, THE CENTER FOR REPRODUCTIVE RIGHTS: The issue here is not that the doctors are being too cautious. The reality is without clarification of this Texas law, without a change in the circumstances that are happening today, it is going to come that women are going to die. ALCINDOR: Seago disagrees. SEAGO: The law is not putting lives in danger. The law is black and white about what a doctor can do and what he cannot do. ALCINDOR: Does it ever give you pause that there are situations that have happened after this law where women`s lives have been put at risk? SEAGO: Yes. Our mission is to save lives. So, the fact that some women`s lives have been jeopardized is something that we take very seriously. A. ZURAWSKI: Little outfit. ALCINDOR: Amanda and Josh are still grieving their loss. J. ZURAWSKI: I know. A. ZURAWSKI: Damn onesie gets me every time. ALCINDOR: They hope something changes. A. ZURAWSKI: I want nothing more than to have kids. But I`m terrified to be pregnant again. ALCINDOR: Yamiche Alcindor, NBC News, Austin, Texas. (END VIDEOTAPE) HOLT: We`ll take a short break. Up next, remembering one of rock`s legendary guitarists. (COMMERCIAL BREAK) [19:25:00] HOLT: Finally, he was the last surviving founding member of a classic southern rock band. Harry Smith now on the legendary guitarist Gary Rossington. (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) HARRY SMITH, NBC NEWS SENIOR CORRESPONDENT (voiceover): Gary Rossington was one of the original members of Lynyrd Skynyrd. He co-wrote Sweet Home Alabama. The Jacksonville, Florida-based band exemplified the blues-fused sound of southern rock. What`s Your Name was one of their biggest hits. For many, Skynyrd was the sound of the `70s. But at the peak of their popularity, the band`s chartered plane crashed, killing bandmates Ronnie Van Zant and Steve Gaines. Rossington was terribly hurt but recovered and kept playing. Rare was the performance where an audience member didn`t raise a Bic lighter and shout "free bird," Rossington`s signature solo. Today, the band posted "Gary is now with his Skynyrd brothers and family in heaven, playing it pretty like he always does." Gary Rossington was 71. Harry Smith, NBC News. (END VIDEOTAPE) HOLT: And that`s NIGHTLY NEWS for this Monday. Thank you for watching, everyone. I`m Lester Holt. Please take care of yourself and each other. Good night. headline: The Judge In Texas Who Could Ban The Abortion Pill Nationwide, Even In States Where Abortion Is Legal
story_text: LESTER HOLT: In Texas today, a federal judge heard arguments in a lawsuit aimed at banning the most prescribed pill for abortions that`s been FDA approved for more than two decades. As Dasha Burns explains, the outcome could have consequences nationwide. (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) DASHA BURNS, NBC NEWS CORRESPONDENT (voiceover): Anticipation in Amarillo building for weeks as a case in this Texas courthouse could restrict access nationwide to the abortion pill, the most commonly used method for terminating pregnancies in the country. A conservative judge appointed by Trump could soon decide whether to issue a preliminary injunction, blocking access to Mifeprex, generically known as Mifepristone. The FDA approved it as part of a two-drug abortion regimen in 2000. Both sides had two hours to present their arguments. The judge peppering attorneys with detailed questions. Now, today was the first public hearing in the case. The judge delayed adding it to the public docket to avoid a "circus-like atmosphere." The note inspiring one group of demonstrators. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: I remember before Roe v. Wade, and now I`m looking at it all over again. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: I value life. I think it`s extremely precious. BURNS: The plaintiffs are challenging the FDA`s approval of the drug, arguing the agency didn`t adequately evaluate its safety and endangered women further when they made it available through telemedicine during the pandemic. The FDA says the claims in the lawsuit are unsupported by any evidence and said in court today that a ruling in the plaintiff`s favor would amount to unprecedented action and would cause significant public harm. Since its approval in 2000, the FDA says more than five million women have taken mifepristone with 28 deaths associated with the drug. RACHEL O`LEARY CARMONA, EXECUTIVE DIRECTOR, WOMEN`S MARCH: What happens here today will be felt by all Americans no matter what your feelings are on abortion. BURNS: A ruling that could radiate nationwide. Dasha Burns, NBC News, Amarillo, Texas. END Content and programming copyright 2023 NBCUniversal. ALL RIGHTS RESERVED. headline: The New Study On Pregnant Women That Everyone Should See
story_text: [18:50:00] KATE SNOW: We`ve reported before on the dangers of pregnancy, especially for women of color. Well, tonight, a new study with startling findings that wealthy black women are dying in child birth at rates far greater than all white women. Rehema Ellis takes a closer look at why. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) REHEMA ELLIS, NBC NEWS EDUCATION CORRESPONDENT (voiceover): This is how Aziza Bowser-Clarke and her husband Jason looked this couple looked in the early weeks of her pregnancy. AZIZA BOWSER-CLARKE: It was a picture of absolute joy. ELLIS (voiceover): But for these two highly successful new Jersey Lawyers, joy soon turned to fear. BOWSER-CLARKE: We were very, very worried about making sure that we had all the information that we had, the very best doctors that we could find. ELLIS (voiceover): In her first trimester Aziza says she was exhausted. When she told her doctor she was concerned about anemia, the response? BOWSER-CLARKE: Of course you`re tired. You`re pregnant. And me, this is my first child. ELLIS (voiceover): But this very athletic 41-year-old says it got worse. By her seventh month she could barely hold her head up and demanded a blood test. The results, she was dangerously anemic and had to have infusions. BOWSER-CLARKE: It felt like my throat dropped into my stomach, because it was there and concrete that I wasn`t imagining this. ELLIS (voiceover): After 27 hours of labor, doctors abruptly decided on an emergency c-section. Her son was born healthy, but she passed out and spent about eight days in the hospital recovering. BOWSER-CLARKE: It was traumatic. ELLIS (voiceover): And she is not alone. A groundbreaking study reveals a disturbing history of unequal care. Researchers analyzed nearly all pregnancies in California over a nine-year period. For the first time factoring in both race and income. The findings? Money didn`t matter in maternal health care. And during child birth, even the richest black women are more likely to die than the poorest white women. DR. KAMEELAH PHILLIPS, NEW YORK OBSTETRICIAN AND GYNECOLOGIST: Take it as an opportunity -- ELLIS (voiceover): Dr. Kameelah Phillips is not surprised. ELLIS (on camera): What is this about? DR. PHILLIPS: This is about racism. We are still dealing with institutions, people, and their biases. ELLIS: Some people would say that`s dramatic that, how can you say that it`s racism when black women are going to the same hospitals that white women are going to in large measure and they`re receiving the same kind of care, aren`t they? DR. PHILLIPS: So, I would argue that women of color and in particular black women are not receiving the same type of care, even in the same institutions. ELLIS (voiceover): She says some doctors often don`t take black women`s concerns about their health as seriously as white women`s. ELLIS (on camera): They`re not listening, particularly to women of color. DR. PHILLIPS: Particularly women of color. There are terms that often make it into the chart as it relates to black women, difficult, challenging, disruptive. ELLIS (voiceover): That means, early warning signs can be missed, which could lead to negative outcomes. So, what can pregnant black women do right now? Experts say, identify your risk factors with your doctor. Bring someone with you to your OB-GYN appointments, and take notes. Aziza did all that and still says -- BOWSER-CLARKE: My advice for black women who are pregnant, make sure your voice is heard. ELLIS (voiceover): A powerful message when starting a family. Race matters. Rehema Ellis , NBC News, New Jersey. (END VIDEO CLIP) SNOW: Powerful story. When we come back, brotherly love. The hero kid giving his big brother a second chance at life. headline: The Cancer Survivor`s Journey To Starting A Family That Is Giving New Hope To Other Couples
story_text: SHEINELLE JONES: Back at 8:43 this morning on Your Health. One woman`s journey that`s giving hope to others facing breast cancer while also wanting to have children. CARSON DALY: NBC senior national correspondent Kate Snow joins us with that story. Kate, good morning. KATE SNOW, NBC SENIOR NATIONAL CORRESPONDENT: Hey. Good morning Carson. Good morning, guys. For many younger women diagnosed with cancer, the toxic treatment can take away their fertility. But new innovations and increased awareness have given some women the chance to preserve their fertility and build a family even after surviving cancer. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) SHELLY BATTISTA, CANCER SURVIVOR: Hi. SNOW: Which one is Nina? UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: This is Nina. SNOW: Nina? UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: Yes, she came first. SNOW: Hi, Nina. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: And then this is little Margot. SNOW (voice-over): These days, life is a bit different for Shelly and Robert Battista. They grew from a family of three to five. While the Chicago couples days are now filled with dirty diapers, crying and lots of laundry, they wouldn`t have it any other way. Three years ago, Shelly was diagnosed with an aggressive form of breast cancer and learn she has a genetic mutation that raises her risk for ovarian cancer too. (on camera): How frightening is all of that? S. BATTISTA: Yes, it was terrifying. You know, we had a six-month-old baby at home. We felt like we were just starting our life together and we get this shocking news. SNOW (voice-over): Shelly needed to start treatment immediately, but the couple had their heart set on a big family and the chemotherapy would destroy her fertility. S. BATTISTA: We were so blessed to have Emilia prior to this breast cancer diagnosis. But, you know, you still have dreams of having more children. SNOW (voice-over): Dr. Kara Goldman specializes in fertility preservation at Northwestern Medicine in Chicago. [08:45:04] KARA GOLDMAN, PHYSICIAN: Chemotherapy that is used in young patients with triple negative breast cancer is very toxic to the ovaries. This is a tremendous blow for a young woman who a day prior was healthy and had no medical diagnosis. JONES: But Dr. Goldman told the couple there was hope. Before starting chemotherapy, Shelly and Robert could create frozen embryos. GOLDMAN: We have to do it quickly. We started her fertility preservation journey two days later. She started medications and two weeks later, she had eight frozen embryos. SNOW (voice-over): Shelly had 12 rounds of chemotherapy, a double mastectomy and had her ovaries and fallopian tubes removed. A year after treatment, she was healthy enough to get pregnant even without ovaries. GOLDMAN: The ovaries and the uterus function very independently of each other. So in Shelly`s case, because she did not have ovaries producing hormones, we were able to provide her the hormones necessary for pregnancy. SNOW (voice-over): The first two trials were unsuccessful, they tried a third embryo. And eight days later, Dr. Goldman called them with the news Shelly was pregnant. S. BATTISTA: She called me herself, personally, we were both static and crying, and yelling. ROBERT BATTISTA, SHELLY`S HUSBAND: And this was just kind of like the cherry on top. It was awesome. We`re going to have another kid. Shelly`s healthy, like everything was just like behind us at that point. SNOW (voice-over): But the surprises weren`t over yet. At their first ultrasound, the technician saw something. S. BATTISTA: She was like, oh, there`s two of them. And I was like -- we both were kind of like two of what? Like -- she`s like, there`s two babies. SNOW: You didn`t implant two embryos. S. BATTISTA: We implanted one embryo and the embryo split. And so they are identical twins. SNOW (voice-over): The chance of that happening, just 1%. Nine months later, two healthy little girls were born., Margot and Nina, born on the two year anniversary of Shelly being declared cancer free. R. BATTISTA: I think it`s like the best celebration of Shelly`s cancer journey. It`s like you`ve beaten cancer and now here`s this extra, like love you get on top of it. S. BATTISTA: It`s loud, it`s tiring. We have lots of laughs, lots of cries, lots of laundry. It`s chaotic but it is -- that`s perfect. (END VIDEO CLIP) SNOW: It`s perfect. Having a baby after cancer treatment is becoming a lot more common thanks to better technology and awareness. Also important to note, guys, the Battistas live in one of just a handful of states that require insurance to cover fertility after cancer. Most states don`t do that, so they live in Chicago, they had an Illinois law. JONES: This is going to grab the attention of so many of voice because there are so many families who are dealing with this exact same challenge. MELVIN: By the way, while you`re here, folks, in addition to being our senior national correspondent, we got to talk about this exciting personal project that Kate Snow has taken on. It`s been on your bucket list for years. We`ve talked about this but I want folks to take a look. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) (MUSIC) MELVIN: You`re thinking all your colleagues, but you thinking also -- DALY: For a story? SOBOROFF: Why you`ve been keeping this from us is the real question. SNOW: I`m not, I`m not. So that was Nashville Tennessee. I`m in a vocal tracking booth there. You heard the backing band. I met with a whole bunch of great amazing musicians in Nashville through friends of friends. I`ve been a singer my whole life. Carson think it`s funny. JONES: Well because we didn`t know. DALY: I did not see this coming. SNOW: I know. Nobody -- MELVIN: But you`re putting out songs, like music. SNOW: I have three songs out now, so that was one of them that you just heard. SOBOROFF: Just wait till they turn the chairs for you on "The Voice", Kate. JONES: Kate, I love you. DALY: Are they all covers or do you write? SNOW: They all covers. DALY: OK. SNOW: So "Nothing Compares to You" is what you just heard, "Because the Night" and "Can`t Find My Way Home." DALY: Oh my God, amazing. SNOW: Three of my favorite songs. JONES: I love it, Kate. Did you just feel like you know what it`s time to - - SNOW: It was -- yes, total (inaudible) like why not? What am I waiting for? JONES: Absolutely. SNOW: And so, kind of made it happen. DALY: How can people hear the music? It`s all -- the three of them are up on any place you stream music, Spotify , YouTube -- SOBOROFF: That is amazing, just hearing that. And the range, I was going to say if range is a reporter, you got ranges of musicians. MELVIN: Right. JONES: I love it. Do it all, my friend. SNOW: You know what -- DALY: Do you have a stage name like Lady Snow or something? I mean, people just look up Kate Snow? SNOW: Just Kate Snow. DALY: OK. JONES: Kate Snow. That`s amazing. DALY: That`s awesome. SOBOROFF: Congratulation. MELVIN: So proud. SNOW: It`s stress relief too from this job. SOBOROFF: Yes. JONES: Again you can stream her new EP, how cool does that sound -- SOBOROFF: It does. JONES: -- wherever you get your music. MELVIN: Look at you. We gave you the City Music treatment there. SOBOROFF: Wow. MELVIN: Up next, he cannot sing but he can help us find some great travel deals. Spring break season is underway, Eastern is around the corner, our guy Mark Ellwood is here. He`s going to help you plan and save on that next vacation. But first, this is TODAY on NBC. [08:50:09] (COMMERCIAL BREAK) END Content and programming copyright 2023 NBCUniversal. headline: The Today Show for March 20, 2023, NBC
story_text: (COMMERCIAL BREAK) [08:00:00] CRAIG MELVIN, NBC NEWS ANCHOR: It`s 8:00 on "TODAY." Coming up, bracing for a decision. All eyes on the grand jury in the criminal case against Donald Trump, as witnesses take the stand over allegations of hush money payments. The former president says he will be arrested tomorrow. We`ll have the latest on where the case goes from here. Plus, on air scare. A meteorologist recovering this morning after suddenly collapsing during a live broadcast. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) RACHEL KIM, KCAL NEWS WEEKEND ANCHOR: Oh. NICHELLE MEDINA, CBS NEWS LA ANCHOR: You know, we`re going to go ahead and go to break right now. KIM: Yes. (END VIDEO CLIP) MELVIN: Just ahead, how she`s feeling and her message for viewers. Then, coming to America. Why a growing number of royal families from all over the world are packing up their bags to move to the states. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: These are jet-setting, successful families. (END VIDEO CLIP) MELVIN: So, who`s making the trip and where are they headed? That story is coming up. And special celebration. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: Hip, hip. CROWD: Hooray. (END VIDEO CLIP) MELVIN: Bruce Willis` family coming together for a special milestone as his wife speaks out amid the star`s battle with dementia. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) EMMA HEMING WILLIS, BRUCE WILLIS` WIFE: As much as I do it for myself I do it for you because I know how much you love my husband. (END VIDEO CLIP) MELVIN: Today, Monday, March 20, 2023. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) CROWD: Starting off the week. CROWD: From Cabot, Arkansas. CROWD: Tamarac, Florida. CROWD: Houston, Texas. CROWD: And Springfield, Illinois. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: Shout out to my dad and my brother. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: Watching in Atlanta. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: From Michigan. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: Ohio. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: And Minnesota. CROWD: We`re on a girl`s trip. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: Celebrating my 40th birthday. CROWD: From Raleigh, North Carolina. CROWD: From Ashland, Kentucky. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: And first time in New York City. (END VIDEO CLIP) MELVIN: And welcome to New York City. Look at all those smiling faces. JACOB SOBOROFF, NBC NEWS CORRESPONDENT: Hello. MELVIN: Girls trips and birthdays and anniversaries. That`s a good Monday crowd. SHEINELLE JONES, NBC NEWS 3RD HOUR OF TODAY, CO-HOST: It`s spring break time. MELVIN: That`s right. JONES: It`s all around the country, folks. It`s freezing a little bit. MELVIN: We`re going to get outside in just moment. We`ve got Sheinelle with us. We`ve got Jacob with us. With Savannah on assignment today. Hoda enjoying time off this week. Good to have you back. SOBOROFF: You know what first day of spring means? JONES: What? MELVIN: What`s that? SOBOROFF: Summer is almost here. MELVIN: There you go. JONES: Almost here. Almost here. MELVIN: That`s right. We`ll have more on the spring from Mr. Rocker in just a moment. But let`s get right your news at 8:00. In the new and unexpected witness set to testify before grand jury in the Donald Trump hush money investigation. Over the weekend the former president himself predicting he would be arrested as soon as tomorrow. NBC`s Garrett Haake is at the district attorneys` office here in Manhattan. Garrett, good morning. GARRETT HAAKE, NBC NEWS SENIOR CAPITOL HILL CORRESPONDENT: Hey, Craig. Good morning. And yes, this courthouse behind me is going to be the center of the political world later today when grand jurors are expected to hear from what could be the final witness in what`s been a yearslong probe into those alleged hush money payments from Donald Trump going all the way back to 2016. Now, Donald Trump made clear over the weekend, he believes this investigation is going to end with his arrest. He said it would come on Tuesday. Now, to be clear, there has been no formal word from the district attorney that any indictment is coming, but law enforcement officials here in New York City have been planning for that possibility and planning for the possibility that folks could listen to Mr. Trump`s call for protests if and when that happens. Now, while we wait for the legal fallout, the political fallout is already happening. We`ve heard from speaker of the house over the weekend calling for folks not to protest any decision that may come out of here. And we`ve heard from some of Donald Trump`s political rivals rallying to his defense, calling any prosecution purely political. Now, about that witness today, Robert Costello is his name. He was a legal adviser to the prosecution`s star witness in this case, but he has been called by Donald Trump`s attorneys, according to a source directly familiar. We`ll be watching very closely throw see what comes out of that grand jury room today and what decisions are made in court and on the presidential playing field here as it relates to this over the next couple of days. Craig. MELVIN: All right. Garrett Haake, for us there. Garrett, thank you. JONES: Now, to some frightening moments for a New York lawmaker and pilot forced to make an emergency landing on a Long Island Beach. Take a look at this. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) (END VIDEO CLIP) JONES: New York state assemblyman Clyde Vanel says, he was practicing some maneuvers when suddenly his engine went out. So, he had no choice but to land his plane -- MELVIN: Wow. JONES: -- right there on the beach. MELVIN: Geez. JONES: Thankfully, both Vanel and his passenger walked away with only a few cuts and bruises. SOBOROFF: Out in L.A., a meteorologist is recovering after a frightening on air moment. She suffered a medical emergency in the middle of a broadcast, leaving her co-anchors and viewers completely stunned. NBC`s Emilie Ikeda is here with that story. Emilie, good morning. [08:05:00] EMILIE IKEDA, NBC NEWS CORRESPONDENT: Jacob, good morning. It was around this time, Saturday morning, when a local CBS Meteorologist Alissa Carlson, collapsed on live TV. We`re told she`s on the mend and she`s thanking everyone for their support. A warning to viewers, some of these images may be hard to watch. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) NICHELLE MEDINA, CBS NEWS LA ANCHOR: Let`s start off with a check of your next weather. IKEDA (voiceover): An on-air scare in Los Angeles. MEDINA: She joins us live in the studio, Alissa -- IKEDA (voiceover): Local CBS Meteorologist Alissa Carlson`s eyes appearing to roll back right before she slowly leans forward and then suddenly collapses to the floor. KCAL`s co-anchors quickly tossing to commercials after realizing something was very wrong. RACHEL KIM, KCAL NEWS WEEKEND ANCHOR: Oh. MEDINA: You know, we`re going to go ahead and go to break right now. KIM: Yes. IKEDA (voiceover): According to the station, the team took immediate action to comfort Alissa and call 9-1-1. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: 78-Immediate dispatch on 4200 Radford Avenue. IKEDA (voiceover): After she was taken to the hospital, Carlson sharing a message of reassurance on Facebook . Posting, thanks for all the text, calls, and well wishes. I`m going to be OK. This isn`t the first time she has suffered a health scare during a broadcast. Back in 2014, she got sick working as the chief meteorologist for NBC`s affiliate KGET. ALISSA CARLSON, CBS METEOROLOGIST: All of a sudden, during the newscast, I threw up in the weather center. IKEDA (voiceover): Carlson later learned she had a leaky heart valve, a diagnosis that inspired her to embrace a healthier lifestyle and advocate for the American Heart Association . And later, after giving birth to her daughter, a miraculous surprise. CARLSON: The stem cells from my baby had started to heal my heart. IKEDA (voiceover): It`s not clear why Carlson fainted in this latest incident, but she told us her heart is fine. She`s not the only TV news personality to suffer an on-air medical emergency. Just last year, Julie Chin experienced what was believed to be the beginning of a stroke while anchoring for our Tulsa, Oklahoma, affiliate. JULIE CHIN, NEWS ANCHOR, TULSA NBC AFFILIATE KJRH: -- today at the -- at the -- at the event. The event features live -- I`m sorry. Something is going on with me. IKEDA (voiceover): Chin lost partial vision while her hand and arm went numb. She was unable to read the teleprompter but managed to toss back to her co-workers on live TV. Chin later reflecting on that harrowing incident on "TODAY." CHIN: And of course, I mean, I want to know what caused it. So, you know, maybe we can prevent it from happening again. (END VIDEO CLIP) IKEDA (on camera): OK. So, the good news is, Alissa Carlson tells us she is out of the hospital and even enjoying some pizza. You can tell she`s incredibly grateful for the support of her co-workers and the thoughts and prayers from viewers. She says, she is recovering from a head injury suffered in the fall and understandably is not sure when she will be back on air. But, of course, we`re rooting for her. JONES: Absolutely. SOBOROFF: I was going to say. JONES: A quick recovery. SOBOROFF: Oh, man. So scary, but glad she`s OK. IKEDA: Absolutely. SOBOROFF: Emilie, thank you. JONES: Thank you, Emilie. MELVIN: Thanks, Emilie. JONES: All right. That`s it for the news. Do you want to give us a "Boost"? MELVIN: Hoda`s not here, JONES: OK. MELVIN: But I`ll do my best. This morning, a sweet reunion between a little girl and her dog named Leo. It turns out Leo got lost back in January. But last week, their family finally got that phone call they had been waiting for. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) (END VIDEO CLIP) JONES: Oh, so sweet. MELVIN: Oh.
