headline: The Future Of The Pill Used For More Than Two Decades Uncertain After Competing Rulings By Two Federal Judges
story_text: LESTER HOLT: This evening, the divide over abortion is centered on a pill used for more than 20 years. But now the focus of competing rulings by two federal courts. Dasha Burns reports and the growing fallout. [19:05:07] (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) DASHA BURNS, NBC NEWS CORRESPONDENT (voiceover): Tonight, the fallout from dueling court rulings. The future of the abortion pill is hanging in the balance after a Texas judge invalidated the FDA`s approval of mifepristone. The Department of Justice is now appealing that decision. JENNIFER KLEIN, WHITE HOUSE GENDER POLICY COUNCIL: What this ruling effectively is a backdoor ban on abortion. BURNS: What options are available to the administration here? KLEIN: We`ve been waiting for the judge to rule. And what we did is what we believe is the best strategy which is to appeal this decision immediately. BURNS: Minutes after the Texas judge`s decision on Friday night, a federal judge in Washington State with equal authority dropping a contradictory ruling ordering the FDA to maintain access to the drug. It all sowed confusion nationwide and created a legal standoff. Use with another drug, mifepristone is the most common method for terminating pregnancies in the U.S. It`s been approved since 2000 and used safely more than five million times. But the plaintiffs in the Texas case, a group of anti-abortion doctors and medical organizations, allege the drug is dangerous and the FDA didn`t follow proper protocol when approving it. I spoke with the group behind the lawsuit before the ruling. The result if you win is that abortion access will be significantly limited. Is that the goal of this loss? ERIK BAPTIST, SENIOR COUNSEL, ALLIANCE DEFENDING FREEDOM: No, the goal of this lawsuit is to protect American women and girls from dangerous chemical abortion drugs. It`s not -- we are not seeking a nationwide abortion ban. BURNS: Meanwhile, today, lawmakers in blue states vowed to do whatever necessary to protect reproductive rights. GOV. headline: NBC NIGHTLY NEWS for April 10, 2023, NBC
story_text: [19:00:00] (COMMERCIAL BREAK) LESTER HOLT, NBC NEWS ANCHOR (voiceover): Tonight, the moments of terror inside a Louisville bank as a gunman shoots four people dead, injuring nine others, including two police officers, all while live streaming the rampage. The shooter now dead. Why investigators were saying it`s not a random act. Plus, the governor`s close connection to one of the victims. His tribute tonight. The abortion pill battle. The future of the pill used for more than two decades uncertain after competing rulings by two federal judges. The latest action by the Justice Department. A Virginia grand jury indicts the mother of that six-year-old boy who shot his first grade teacher in a classroom. What his mother is charged with? The fallout over dozens of leaked classified documents. What they reveal about Russia, the war in Ukraine, Israeli intelligence, and more, and what American intelligence officials fear tonight. President Biden making his most definitive statement yet about running for re-election. What he told our Al Roker . She fainted after getting the COVID vaccine and became the focus of a massive internet conspiracy. Now, Tiffany Dover is breaking her silence exclusively to NBC News. And his performance at Augusta as an amateur was nothing short of masterful and is inspiring America. ANNOUNCER: This is NBC NIGHTLY NEWS with Lester Holt. HOLT (on camera): Good evening and welcome everyone. It seems we can barely catch our breaths or dry the tears before another mass shooting rocks in American city. Just two weeks ago, I stood right here reporting the heartbreaking details of a school shooting in Nashville. Today, that happened at a bank in Louisville, Kentucky in what the city`s mayor calls an evil act of targeted violence after a man in his 20s armed with a rifle went on a rampage in a workplace attack streaming the horror online as he carried out the crime. Four people were killed, nine others rushed to a hospital for treatment. Officers ran to the threat confronting the gunman in an exchange of gunfire killing the shooter. Two police officers were among the wounded. Maggie Vespa is in Louisville tonight and has late details. (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) MAGGIE VESPA, NBC NEWS CORRESPONDENT (voiceover): Tonight, chaos and carnage gripping another American city. CRAG GREENBERG, MAYOR OF LOUISVILLE, KENTUCKY: Let`s be clear about what this was. This was an evil act of targeted violence. VESPA: The familiar terror unfolding in downtown Louisville, Kentucky. Around 8:30 this morning, police say a lone gunman opened fire inside this Old National Bank killing four and wounding nine. SADIQA REYNOLDS, WITNESS: This was terrifying. It was terrifying officers on the scene within three minutes. Investigators say this was not a random act. JACQUELYN GWINN-VILLAROEL, CHIEF, LOUISVILLE METRO POLICE: White male who was employed at Old National Bank . His weapon of choice was a rifle. VESPA: Authorities identifying the shooter as Connor Sturgeon who died at the scene in a shootout with police. He livestreamed the rampage according to investigators who late today executed a search warrant on his home. Victims range in age from 40 to 64 including 63-year-old Thomas Elliott, the bank`s senior vice president according to his LinkedIn account and a friend of Kentucky Governor Andy Beshear . GOV. ANDY BESHEAR (D-KY): Tommy Elliott helped me build my law career, help me become governor, gave me advice on being a good dad. VESPA: Among the wounded, two Louisville Metro Police Officers. One officer, Nickolas Wilt, shot in the head. J.D. Worley watched it happen in horror from his office across the street. J.D. WORLEY, WITNESS: Other officers grabbed him and carried him off as he was unfortunately motionless. Never could have fathomed I would ever see something like this happen. VESPA: At 26, officer Wilt is less than two weeks out of the academy. GWINN-VILLAROEL: Nick has come out of brain surgery and is in critical but stable condition as we speak. VESPA: Kentucky`s governor praising police who raced to confront the gunman and asking for time to grieve. BESHEAR: It seems like we argue so much in this country, so much anger. But I still believe that love and compassion and humanity can lead us to a better place. And this is hard. It`s really hard. (END VIDEOTAPE) HOLT: Maggie, any more details and a possible motive here? VESPA (on camera): So, Lester, according to two senior officials, authorities are investigating this as an instance of workplace violence, noting the suspect who was an employee at that bank may have suffered from mental health issues and adding they expect much more to come out in the coming days. Lester? HOLT: All right, Maggie Vespa tonight, thank you. This evening, the divide over abortion is centered on a pill used for more than 20 years. But now the focus of competing rulings by two federal courts. Dasha Burns reports and the growing fallout. [19:05:07] (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) DASHA BURNS, NBC NEWS CORRESPONDENT (voiceover): Tonight, the fallout from dueling court rulings. The future of the abortion pill is hanging in the balance after a Texas judge invalidated the FDA`s approval of mifepristone. The Department of Justice is now appealing that decision. JENNIFER KLEIN, WHITE HOUSE GENDER POLICY COUNCIL: What this ruling effectively is a backdoor ban on abortion. BURNS: What options are available to the administration here? KLEIN: We`ve been waiting for the judge to rule. And what we did is what we believe is the best strategy which is to appeal this decision immediately. BURNS: Minutes after the Texas judge`s decision on Friday night, a federal judge in Washington State with equal authority dropping a contradictory ruling ordering the FDA to maintain access to the drug. It all sowed confusion nationwide and created a legal standoff. Use with another drug, mifepristone is the most common method for terminating pregnancies in the U.S. It`s been approved since 2000 and used safely more than five million times. But the plaintiffs in the Texas case, a group of anti-abortion doctors and medical organizations, allege the drug is dangerous and the FDA didn`t follow proper protocol when approving it. I spoke with the group behind the lawsuit before the ruling. The result if you win is that abortion access will be significantly limited. Is that the goal of this loss? ERIK BAPTIST, SENIOR COUNSEL, ALLIANCE DEFENDING FREEDOM: No, the goal of this lawsuit is to protect American women and girls from dangerous chemical abortion drugs. It`s not -- we are not seeking a nationwide abortion ban. BURNS: Meanwhile, today, lawmakers in blue states vowed to do whatever necessary to protect reproductive rights. GOV. MAURA HEALEY (D-MA): It harms patients, undermines medical expertise, and takes away freedom. BURNS: Tonight, mifepristone remains legal as the battles rage on in the courts. Dasha Burns, NBC News . (END VIDEOTAPE) HOLT: Let me bring in now Senior Legal Correspondent Laura Jarrett. Laura, there was movement on both of these cases in court today. LAURA JARRETT, NBC NEWS SENIOR LEGAL CORRESPONDENT (on camera): A flurry of court filings today, Lester. The Justice Department and the pill manufacturer both hoping to convince a conservative-leaning court of appeals to hit pause on that Texas decision, to give everyone time to make their arguments without this deadline looming of the ruling set to go into effect on Saturday. The court just minutes ago asking to hear what the plaintiffs have to say about all that, but the FDA also wants Clarity from a federal judge in Washington State who ordered the drug to stay on the market about how to reconcile that order with the Texas ruling. HOLT: This feels like this could be heading to the Supreme Court. JARRETT: Yes, it really could, and fast. If the Fifth Circuit doesn`t block the Texas decision, the DOJ will take it to the Supreme Court as soon as this week. And if DOJ wins, the plaintiffs could appeal there as well. HOLT: All right, Laura, thanks very much. I want to turn now to that political drama in Tennessee. Late today, the Nashville Council voting to reinstate one of the Black state lawmakers expelled last week over a gun protest. Kathy Park reports he has just been sworn in again. (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: Thank you, vice mayor. I would like to nominate Representative Justin Jones. KATHY PARK, NBC NEWS CORRESPONDENT (voiceover): Tonight, a political showdown in Nashville. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: Ayes 36. PARK: With former Tennessee lawmaker Justin Jones back to the state house just days after his expulsion. The Metro Nashville Council voted unanimously in favor of his reappointment. FREDDIE O`CONNELL, MEMBER, METROPOLITAN NASHVILLE COUNCIL DISTRICT 19: This is a message that partisanship has gone so far as to be a force in violating basic principles of democracy. PARK: This special meeting comes after a rare move by House Republicans to remove three Democratic lawmakers after they joined a gun control rally on the House floor which Republicans say violated the rules. CAMERON SEXTON (R-TN), STATE REPRESENTATIVE: You can call it peaceful, you can call it whatever, but they had a protest against house policy on the floor. JUSTIN JONES (D-TN), STATE REPRESENTATIVE: No action -- CROWD: No peace! PARK: Among the Tennessee three, only one survived the vote, Gloria Johnson. GLORIA JOHNSON (D-TN), STATE REPRESENTATIVE: It might have to do with the color of our skin. GOP leaders say their decision was not based on race but that Johnson didn`t go as far as her two freshman colleagues. CROWD: No justice, no peace! PARK: Representative Justin Pearson will learn his fate Wednesday in his own district with a special meeting in Memphis. Meanwhile, the political battle doesn`t end for Jones as he awaits a special election and he`s vowing to return. (END VIDEOTAPE) PARK (on camera): And moments after the critical vote to reappoint Justin Jones, hundreds of his supporters began rushing out of the metro council chambers and began marching straight toward the state capitol. Lester? HOLT: All right, Kathy Park, thank you. There is growing concern tonight about whether U.S. intelligence sources were compromised by the leak of dozens of classified documents. Andrea Mitchell has the latest. (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) ANDREA MITCHELL, NBC NEWS CHIEF FOREIGN AFFAIRS CORRESPONDENT (voiceover): The leaked documents include sensitive and top secret intelligence about U.S. adversaries and allies potentially jeopardizing U.S. spies in hostile countries and electronic surveillance. JOHN KIRBY, STRATEGIC COMMUNICATIONS COORDINATOR, NATIONAL SECURITY COUNCIL: We don`t know uh who`s responsible for this and we don`t know if they have more that they intend to post. [19:10:07] MITCHELL: The documents show Ukraine running low on ammunition and using U.S. intelligence to strike a Russian target. Russia`s military is struggling in Ukraine. South Korea reluctant to help the U.S. supply artillery to Ukraine. Is the worst damage the Russian sources and methods behind the inside information from Russia on the defense ministry? JOHN BRENNAN, FORMER DIRECTOR, CIA: I think the greatest concern is that some of our sources both human as well as technical collection systems could be compromised as a result of this. Another document has the leaders of Israel`s intelligence service, the Mossad , backing anti-government protests though Israel denies it. RON DERMER, MINISTER FOR STRATEGIC AFFAIRS, ISRAEL: The senior director of the Mossad and our senior officials in the Mossad were not involved in any way. MITCHELL: The stolen intelligence first showing up on a chat server for the Minecraft video game according to open-source intelligence agency Bellingcat before appearing on other sites. The slides showing conflicting Russian casualties in Ukraine indicate some of the documents could have been doctored but officials believe most are real. (END VIDEOTAPE) MITCHELL (on camera): The Justice Department is investigating to find the source as officials fear the leak has exposed critical vulnerabilities in U.S. intelligence. Lester? HOLT: And Andrea, separately, there`s news tonight about that Wall Street Journal reporter detained in Russia. What can you tell us? MITCHELL: That`s right, Lester. Secretary of State Blinken has determined the reporter Evan Gershkovich is wrongfully detained falsely charged with spying. Now, the U.S. hostage envoy can begin working with his family to try to get him out. But in violation of Russia`s legal obligations, U.S. diplomats had still not been able to visit him almost two weeks since he was jailed. Lester? HOLT: All right, Andrea Mitchell, thank you. Former President Donald Trump is trying to block Former Vice President Mike Pence from testifying before a federal grand jury investigating Mr. Trump`s rule in efforts to overturn the 2020 election. Lawyers for Trump are asking a federal appeals court to reverse a lower court`s decision ordering Pence to appear. With nearly 600 days until the next election, President Joe Biden turned heads today with an admission on live T.V. that he plans to run again. Kristen Welker joins us from the White House. Kristen, the timing came as a bit of a surprise. KRISTEN WELKER, NBC NEWS CHIEF WHITE HOUSE CORRESPONDENT (on camera): That`s absolutely right, Lester. President Biden making his most definitive comments yet that he`s running for reelection in 2024, talking to our Al Roker during the annual White House Easter Egg Roll. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) AL ROKER, NBC NEWS WEATHER ANCHOR: Help a -- help a brother out. Make some news for me. JOE BIDEN , PRESIDENT OF THE UNITED STATES: .No, no, no. I plan on running now but we`re not prepared to announce it yet. (END VIDEO CLIP) WELKER: Top White House advisors are preparing to make final decisions on launching his re-election campaign according to several sources familiar with the discussions. Several considerations include no major Democratic Challenger has emerged despite Mr. Biden`s sagging poll numbers. Former President Trump who`s running for the GOP nomination has been indicted and is consuming the political spotlight. Still, source familiar with President Biden`s thinking tell NBC News, don`t expect to hear a final announcement until possibly next month, if not later. Lester? HOLT: Kristen Welker at the White House tonight, thanks. In 60 seconds, a grand jury indicts the mother of a six-year-old boy who shot his teacher in a Virginia classroom. The charges she faces tonight plus what her legal team is saying. (COMMERCIAL BREAK) HOLT: A Virginia grand jury has indicted the mother of that 6-year-old boy who brought a gun to his school and shot his teacher. Miguel Almaguer reports on the charges she now faces. (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) UNIDENTIFIED MALE: I have a report of a teacher shot. MIGUEL ALMAGUER, NBC NEWS NATIONAL CORRESPONDENT (voiceover): Tonight, three months after the shocking school shooting, the mother of the 6-year- old Virginia boy who shot and seriously wounded his first-grade teacher is facing criminal charges. Today, a grand jury in Newport News indicting 25- year-old Deja Taylor on charges of felony child neglect and a misdemeanor count of recklessly leaving a loaded firearm so as to endanger a child. GEORGE PARKER, FORMER SUPERINTENDENT, NEWPORT NEWS PUBLIC SCHOOLS: Who would be prepared for a 6-year-old to bring a loaded weapon onto school or a weapon on the school. [19:15:06] ALMAGUER: After authorities announced the 6-year-old would not be charged with a crime, the Commonwealth`s Attorney saying today every criminal case is unique in its facts and these facts support these charges, but our investigation into the shooting continues. ABIGAIL ZWERNER, TEACHER: I just will never forget the look on his face that he gave me while he pointed the gun directly at me. That`s something that I will never forget. It`s changed me. It`s changed my life. ALMAGUER: Abigail Zwerner who told Savannah Guthrie the bullet still remains lodged in her body is suing School administrators for $40 million alleging gross negligence. Zwerner said staff failed to act on several warnings that the 6-year-old had a gun or made threats. There were failures in accountability at multiple levels that led to Abby being shot and almost killed, writes her attorney. We will not allow school leaders to escape accountability for their role in this tragedy. (END VIDEOTAPE) ALMAGUER (on camera): A lawyer for Deja Taylor, the mother of the 6-year- old, tells NBC News she plans to turn herself in later this week. Lester? HOLT: All right, Miguel, thank you. Up next, she was the target of an Internet conspiracy theory claiming she had died after getting vaccinated. Now, for the first time, Tiffany Dover speaks out. (COMMERCIAL BREAK) HOLT: Few Americans know what it`s like to be the target of a conspiracy theory. But since the day nurse Tiffany Dover fainted while getting her COVID vaccine, life has never been the same. And tonight, she`s speaking out for the first time in an exclusive interview with NBC`s Brandy Zadrozny. (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) BRANDY ZADROZNY, NBC NEWS CORRESPONDENT (voiceover): Tiffany Dover wants the world to know one thing. TIFFANY DOVER, NURSE: My message is simple it is that I am alive. I`m well. ZADROZNY: That`s it? DOVER: I hope they believe it. ZADROZNY: They are the massive online community of conspiracy theorists who`ve been convinced she`s dead for more than two years. I made a whole podcast about it. Tiffany wasn`t ready to share her story then, but now -- DOVER: I`m ready to just put my story out there, all my story. ZADROZNY: That story begins in 2020. Tiffany was working as a nurse manager at CHI Memorial Hospital in Chattanooga, putting in grueling hours on a COVID unit. When vaccines arrived that December, Tiffany became one of the first people at her hospital to get the shot. DOVER: I felt OK during that. ZADROZNY: Then she stood up to answer questions. DOVER: I`m sorry. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: You want to sit down? DOVER: I ended up passing out. So, that created the opposite effect of what I would have wanted. ZADROZNY: But you got right back up. DOVER: I did. And this is something that`s happened to me my whole life. I do have episodes where I pass out. ZADROZNY: But in that moment, a conspiracy theory was born. DOVER: People thought that I was dead. People thought that I was an actress paid to do this, that I was paid off by a big firm. It was completely overwhelming to be honest. ZADROZNY: It snowballed fast. DOVER: I had people showing up at my house. I had people reaching out to my friends, to my family. I`ve been -- received death threats. ZADROZNY: Were you afraid for your family? DOVER: Absolutely, yes. ZADROZNY: Through it all, Tiffany kept silent. And that only made the online frenzy worse. Why not come out and dispel these rumors? DOVER: Initially that was exactly what I wanted to do. And unfortunately, I was told that that absolutely would not happen. ZADROZNY: The hospital told you not to speak out. DOVER: Correct. Yes, it would be irrecoverable damage is what I was told if I was to speak out and have another episode. ZADROZNY: Instead, the hospital put out this video intending to show she was alive. But the so-called Tiffany Truthers picked it apart and used it as fuel. Online, anti-vaxxers and the movement are sort of using you as their poster girl. DOVER: It`s hard to think that you are being used to detour somebody from getting the vaccine. And that was really hard for me to cope with. ZADROZNY: Are you saying you blamed yourself? DOVER: Yes, absolutely. I wish that we would have used it as a platform to speak out on the fact that people do pass out after getting shots, vaccines, but that is not a reason to not proceed with getting them. ZADROZNY: CHI Memorial has repeatedly denied knowledge of any directive asking Tiffany not to speak or post, including in an interview for our podcast. KAREN LONG, MEDICA COMMUNICATIONS SPECIALIST, CHI MEMORIAL: I`m not aware of anything that asked Tiffany not to respond. ZADROZNY: The hospital recently telling NBC News we have no new information. A year ago, Tiffany left CHI Memorial. and while she hopes to work as a nurse again one day, for now, she`s focused on reclaiming her life. Even after all of this, there will be people who say, we don`t believe you. What then? DOVER: At this point, you know, I`ve done what I needed to do. I`ve put it out there that I`m alive. They have to choose whether they believe that or not. And that`s all I can do is put out the truth. ZADROZNY: Brandy Zadrozny, NBC News Higdon, Alabama. (END VIDEOTAPE) HOLT: And for the bonus podcast, scan the Q.R. code on your screen or search for Tiffany Dover wherever you get your podcasts. When we come back, a masterful performance by one of golf`s rising stars. (COMMERCIAL BREAK) [19:25:00] HOLT: It`s not often you see a 23-year-old compete at the Masters, let alone outplay some of the best golfers on the planet. Stephanie Gosk with why Sam Bennett is inspiring America. (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) STEPHANIE GOSK, NBC NEWS CORRESPONDENT (voiceover): Sometimes, the significance of the moment can be lost on the young, but not this moment. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: Nothing can top this at 18. GOSK: The magic of a standing ovation at the masters on a Sunday is not lost on amateur, Sam Bennett. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: He`s overwhelmed with emotion. GOSK: The Texas A&M senior was greeted by his mother to celebrate a remarkable 16th-place finish for someone his age at Augusta National, one of the most difficult golf courses in the world. SAM BENNETT, GOLFER: I haven`t had a kid yet, so that walk up to 18 was definitely the coolest experience of my life. GOSK: Bennett stunned golf fans with his first two rounds of the tournament, shooting back-to-back 68s. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: What a start for the amateur. GOSK: Not just making the cut, the second-best start for a masters in amateur history. At the end of the day on Friday, he was alone in third place paired up with pro golfer Jon Rahm who went on to win the whole thing. BENNETT: If you would have told me I was going to be here when I was a kid, I would have -- I would have thought you were crazy. GOSK: For inspiration, Bennett has a tattoo, words from his father who died from early-onset Alzheimer`s in 2021. Don`t wait to do something, it says, right there on his left arm every time he swings. Stephanie Gosk, NBC News. (END VIDEOTAPE) HOLT: That`s NIGHTLY NEWS for this Monday. Thank you for watching, everyone. I`m Lester Holt. Please take care of yourself and each other. Good night. (COMMERCIAL BREAK) END Content and programming copyright 2023 NBCUniversal. headline: The Battle Over An Abortion Pill: Big Pharma Pushing Back Against The Ruling As Some States Start Stockpiling Drugs
story_text: LESTER HOLT: Major backlash tonight from the drug industry to that abortion pill ruling by a federal judge. And now, some states are stockpiling abortion drugs as the legal battle plays out. Laura Jarrett has the latest. (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) LAURA JARRETT, NBC NEWS SENIOR LEGAL CORRESPONDENT (voiceover): A show of force from big pharma now waiting into the battle over a widely used abortion pill. More than 600 drug makers and biotech leaders signing on to a scathing condemnation of that ruling by a federal judge in Texas invalidating the FDA`s longtime approval of mifepristone, accusing the judge of activism. DR. AMANDA BANKS, FORMER CEO, BLACKFYNN THERAPEUTICS: Now -- it`s now been shown that courts can step in and overturn a scientific decision. Dr. Amanda Banks, a former CEO of Blackfynn Therapeutics, who co-authored the letter says the judge`s ruling sets a dangerous precedent that extends beyond the abortion issue. BANKS: If one medicine is subject to this kind of outcome, really any medicine is. JARRETT: President Biden also slamming the decision today. JOE BIDEN , PRESIDENT OF THE UNITED STATES: My thoughts are completely out of bounds what the judge did. JARRETT: While the anti-abortion group that filed the Texas lawsuit is doubling down. Writing in a statement, "The FDA failed to abide by its legal obligations to protect the health, safety, and welfare of girls and women." With the Texas order is set to go into effect early Saturday unless blocked in the courts, Democratic governors are not wasting any time taking matters into their own hands. GOV. GRETCHEN WHITMER (D-MI): We`re taking a close look at all of our options. JARRETT: Massachusetts, Washington State, New York, and California all now stockpiling years` worth of mifepristone or an alternative abortion pill. GOV. KATHY HOCHUL (D-NY): So, I`m proud to announce that New York State will create a stockpile of misoprostol, another form of medication abortion. JARRETT: It`s all in preparation for a decision that would apply nationwide. (END VIDEOTAPE) HOLT: So, Laura, where does all these stand right now as far as the courts are concerned? JARRETT (on camera): So, late tonight and tomorrow, we should see more court filings from both the plaintiffs that filed the Texas lawsuit and the Justice Department, which is asking the Fifth Circuit Court of Appeals to freeze that judge`s order. Once all those are in midday tomorrow, we could see a decision from that appeals court anytime. HOLT: All right, Laura Jarrett, thanks very much. In 60 seconds, the tough new auto emission standard is about to be announced. Will they push more Americans toward electric vehicles. Plus, spring is here and already setting some record temperatures in a lot of cities, next. (COMMERCIAL BREAK) HOLT: Spring is here but much of the country is seeing record highs temperatures in places like Phoenix, and Las Vegas, even South Dakota hit the 90s. Denver broke its record and temperatures are expected to continue to climb this week bringing record highs to the northeast. END Content and programming copyright 2023 NBCUniversal. headline: NBC NIGHTLY NEWS for April 11, 2023, NBC
story_text: [19:00:00] (COMMERCIAL BREAK) LESTER HOLT, NBC NEWS ANCHOR (on camera): Tonight, the terrifying images just released of a Louisville mass shooting. (voiceover): Police body camera video showing how officers confronted the gunman who police say ambush them after shooting and killing five of his fellow bank workers using an AR-15 he bought legally. One officer shot at and getting back off to reengage. Officers being hailed as heroes for stopping him from killing more people. Were there warning signs and what his neighbors are saying? Damage control. New revelations from those leaked classified intelligence documents putting U.S. alliances in question. The Manhattan district attorney sues a top House Republican claiming interference in the investigation of Donald Trump . The battle over an abortion pill. Big pharma pushing back against the ruling as some states start stockpiling drugs. Tough new auto emission standards about to be announced, but will they push more Americans to go electric. A big upside of artificial intelligence detecting cancer much earlier and predicting when it might strike. And the young bold athletes sharing their culture and moves with skateboarding superstar Tony Hawk . ANNOUNCER: This is NBC NIGHTLY NEWS with Lester Holt. HOLT (on camera): Good evening and welcome. Once again in the tragic aftermath of a mass shooting, we`re getting a heart-stopping first person look at police risking their own lives to stop and active shooter. Late this afternoon, Louisville police releasing body cam video of officers rushing to a downtown bank yesterday. Immediately coming under fire from a bank employee. He was armed with an AR-15 assault-style rifle carrying out a murderous rampage, fatally shooting five people. The gunman killed by police. Tonight, one of those officers who rushed to stop the gunman, a rookie just days on the streets remains in critical condition. And tonight, there is a deeper understanding of just how close to home these shootings are for many Americans. A new survey out tonight finding one in five U.S. adults say they have been threatened with a gun. Maggie Vespa leads us off tonight with new details. (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) MAGGIE VESPA, NBC NEWS CORRESPONDENT (voiceover): Echoes of gunfire as officers speed up to the scene. Tonight, a firsthand look at police say seven minutes of horror playing out inside a Kentucky bank. Police body camera and cell phone video showing Louisville Metro officers view Monday morning as they race to confront a lone gunman. One taking gunfire as windows shatter, falling, then jumping right back up. Minutes later, killing the shooter. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: I think he`s down. VESPA: What was it like to watch that body camera video? JACQUELYN GWINN-VILLAROEL, INTERIM CHIEF, LOUISVILLE METRO POLICE: It is really -- it shakes the core. It shakes the core to know that life was being lost. VESPA: Investigators say Connor Sturgeon seen here on surveillance cameras was armed with an AR-15 rifle which he bought legally from a local dealership six days before the massacre, adding the 25-year-old was a current employee at Old National Bank and knew the colleagues he targeted. Overnight, officials confirming a fifth victim died, 57-year-old Deanna Eckert. Meanwhile, dispatch audio indicating the shooter may have tried to warn a friend before the attack. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: The shooter, 25-year-old white male Connor Sturgeon, 6`4. He texted a friend -- called a friend, left voicemail saying he`s going to kill everyone at the bank, feeling suicidal. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: We know he left a note. We know he texted or called at least one person to let them know he was suicidal and contemplating harm. VESPA: Neighbors of surgeons home which investigators searched yesterday shocked by the news. KERA ALLGEIER, NEIGHBOR OF THE GUNMAN: I can`t say nothing really bad about the guy. He`s very quiet, soft spoken. I just don`t understand. VESPA: Doctors also struggling. DR. JASON SMITH, CHIEF MEDICAL OFFICER, UNIVERSITY OF LOUISVILLE HEALTH: There`s only so many times you can walk into a room and tell someone they`re not coming home tomorrow. And it just breaks your heart. When you hear someone screaming mommy or daddy, it just becomes too hard. VESPA: Tonight, three remain hospitalized, including officer Nickolas Wilk still in critical condition. The chief adding Wilk was on his fourth shift less than two weeks out of the academy. His twin brother just started. Also wounded with minor injuries, officer Corey Galloway, who investigators say killed the shooter. MONESSA BARD, MOTHER OF JULIANA FARMER: I can`t hear her voice anymore. I can`t touch her. I can`t tell her how much I love her. VESPA: The details do nothing to numb Monessa Bard`s pain. Her 45-year-old daughter Juliana Farmer among the dead. Amid a successful career in banking, she was just recruited back to Louisville and Old National Bank three weeks ago. [19:05:11] How do you make sense of that? She just got back there. BARD: There is no sense to be had. I just feel like that man stole her from us. I don`t understand his reasoning. I don`t understand why she`s gone. (END VIDEOTAPE) HOLT: And Maggie, officials I know are applauding the heroism displayed by police even after the shooter was down. VESPA (on camera): Yes, Lester, that`s right. They tell us here yesterday, EMS agencies were actually short-staffed, so a Louisville police lieutenant improvised, jumping in the front seat of an ambulance and driving it to the hospital allowing EMS workers in the back to keep caring for a wounded patient. Lester? HOLT: Maggie Vespa in Louisville, thank you. And there was yet another deadly mass shooting today, this one in Washington D.C., as a new survey shows just how much Americans are affected by gun violence. Here`s Gabe Gutierrez. (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) GABE GUTIERREZ, NBC NEWS NATIONAL CORRESPONDENT (voiceover): As a funeral for a shooting victim wrapped up in D.C. today, gunfire erupted again. One man killed, three others hurt. From workplace violence to school shootings, according to a new survey from the Kaiser Family Foundation , a majority of U.S. adults have either personally or had a family member who has been impacted by a gun-related incident, including suicide. Nearly one in five Americans have lost a family member to gun violence with people of color disproportionately impacted. So, is this about mental health or is it about easy access to guns? JACKIE ROWE-ADAMS, FOUNDER, HARLEM MOTHER S.A.V.E.: It`s about both of them. GUTIERREZ: Jackie Rowe-Adams lost two sons, Anthony and Tyrone, to gun violence. She now runs a support group in Harlem. ROWE-ADAMS: When I hear about this constant shooting, it pains me. It hurt so bad because I know another family, I know the mother, father, family is hurting for the loss of their loved one. GUTIERREZ: As the nationwide debate over access to guns heats up a day after the mass shooting in Louisville, the city`s mayor fumed over a state law that requires confiscated firearms like the rifle the killer used on Monday to be resold at auction. CRAIG GREENBERG, MAYOR OF LOUISVILLE, KENTUCKY: It`s time to change this law and let us destroy illegal guns and destroy the guns that have been used to kill our friends and kill our neighbors. GUTIERREZ: While in Tennessee, Republican Governor Bill Lee today called for stronger background checks for gun purchases. GOV. BILL LEE (R-TN): The executive order will for one thing set a 72-hour clock for reporting new criminal activity. GUTIERREZ: Other states like Maryland, Washington, and Colorado are moving forward with new restrictions as gun rights advocates push back on what they consider unconstitutional overreach. DUDLEY BROWN, PRESIDENT, NATIONAL ASSOCIATION FOR GUN RIGHTS: No amount of gun control is going to stop a criminal hell bent on murder from gaining some tools to do it. (END VIDEOTAPE) GUTIERREZ: The Kaiser survey also showed that about a third of adults have avoided large crowds due to the possibility of gun violence. Lester? HOLT: All right, Gabe, thank you. Tonight, U.S. officials are scrambling to control the damage from the disclosure of intelligence secrets after dozens of classified documents were leaked online. Andrea Mitchell now with the latest. (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) ANDREA MITCHELL, NBC NEWS CHIEF FOREIGN AFFAIRS CORRESPONDENT (voiceover): Tonight, those leaked documents causing tough conversations between Washington and U.S. allies. On Ukraine, a U.S. intelligence assessment that Ukraine`s military will fall well short of retaking most of the territory it`s lost to Russia according to a document obtained by the Washington Post . And a document seen by NBC News revealing Ukrainian agents launched drone attacks against targets in Russia and its ally Belarus, including just outside Moscow despite promising the U.S. it would not strike Russia. Secretary of State Blinken spoke with Ukraine`s Foreign Minister today. Are you concerned about cross-border attacks? ANTONY BLINKEN , U.S. SECRETARY OF STATE: Ukraine has to make decisions about how it can most effectively defend itself against Russian aggression. MITCHELL: Another leaked documents says Egypt`s President El-Sisi recently ordered 40,000 rockets to be produced for Russia according to The Washington Post . Egypt denies it. Since Camp David in 1978, Egypt has received more than $50 billion in military aid and $30 billion in economic aid from the U.S. more than any other country in the Middle East except Israel. How could intelligence officials not know sooner about the leaks? Sir, why didn`t you know about it before April 6? That means that they were up for at least many weeks if not months before U.S. intelligence knew that they were in the public domain. GEN. LLOYD AUSTIN, U.S. SECRETARY OF DEFENSE: They were somewhere in the web. And in where exactly and who had access at that point, we don`t know. (END VIDEOTAPE) MITCHELL: The Pentagon is now in damage control, limiting the number of people who can see such highly classified documents. Lester? HOLT: Andrea Mitchell, thank you. In New York, the Manhattan D.A. prosecuting former President Trump is suing the House Judiciary Chairman Jim Jordan. Garrett Haake joins me now from Capitol Hill. Garrett, explain what this means. [19:10:10] GARRETT HAAKE, NBC NEWS SENIOR CAPITOL HILL CORRESPONDENT (on camera): Well, Lester, Manhattan D.A. Alvin Bragg has asked a federal judge to block a House Judiciary Committee subpoena for a former top prosecutor in his office who`s being ordered to testify next week. Now, Bragg also asked the judge to void any subpoenas that might be filed against him or his current staff. The Democratic D.A. argues that Congress has no power to supervise the state criminal prosecutions and the efforts by Republican Committee Chairman Jim Jordan to force testimony or acquired documents related to his prosecution of Donald Trump are purely political with no legislative purpose. Jordan responding tonight in part in a tweet that reads, first, they indict a president for no crime, then they sued to block congressional oversight. Lester? HOLT: Garrett Haake, thank you. Major backlash tonight from the drug industry to that abortion pill ruling by a federal judge. And now, some states are stockpiling abortion drugs as the legal battle plays out. Laura Jarrett has the latest. (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) LAURA JARRETT, NBC NEWS SENIOR LEGAL CORRESPONDENT (voiceover): A show of force from big pharma now waiting into the battle over a widely used abortion pill. More than 600 drug makers and biotech leaders signing on to a scathing condemnation of that ruling by a federal judge in Texas invalidating the FDA`s longtime approval of mifepristone, accusing the judge of activism. DR. AMANDA BANKS, FORMER CEO, BLACKFYNN THERAPEUTICS: Now -- it`s now been shown that courts can step in and overturn a scientific decision. Dr. Amanda Banks, a former CEO of Blackfynn Therapeutics, who co-authored the letter says the judge`s ruling sets a dangerous precedent that extends beyond the abortion issue. BANKS: If one medicine is subject to this kind of outcome, really any medicine is. JARRETT: President Biden also slamming the decision today. JOE BIDEN , PRESIDENT OF THE UNITED STATES: My thoughts are completely out of bounds what the judge did. JARRETT: While the anti-abortion group that filed the Texas lawsuit is doubling down. Writing in a statement, "The FDA failed to abide by its legal obligations to protect the health, safety, and welfare of girls and women." With the Texas order is set to go into effect early Saturday unless blocked in the courts, Democratic governors are not wasting any time taking matters into their own hands. GOV. GRETCHEN WHITMER (D-MI): We`re taking a close look at all of our options. JARRETT: Massachusetts, Washington State, New York, and California all now stockpiling years` worth of mifepristone or an alternative abortion pill. GOV. KATHY HOCHUL (D-NY): So, I`m proud to announce that New York State will create a stockpile of misoprostol, another form of medication abortion. JARRETT: It`s all in preparation for a decision that would apply nationwide. (END VIDEOTAPE) HOLT: So, Laura, where does all these stand right now as far as the courts are concerned? JARRETT (on camera): So, late tonight and tomorrow, we should see more court filings from both the plaintiffs that filed the Texas lawsuit and the Justice Department, which is asking the Fifth Circuit Court of Appeals to freeze that judge`s order. Once all those are in midday tomorrow, we could see a decision from that appeals court anytime. HOLT: All right, Laura Jarrett, thanks very much. In 60 seconds, the tough new auto emission standard is about to be announced. Will they push more Americans toward electric vehicles. Plus, spring is here and already setting some record temperatures in a lot of cities, next. (COMMERCIAL BREAK) HOLT: Spring is here but much of the country is seeing record highs temperatures in places like Phoenix, and Las Vegas, even South Dakota hit the 90s. Denver broke its record and temperatures are expected to continue to climb this week bringing record highs to the northeast. Tomorrow, the EPA is expected to roll out strict new emission standards that will require automakers to accelerate the transition from gas to electric, but are car makers and drivers ready? Here`s Tom Costello. (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) TOM COSTELLO, NBC NEWS CORRESPONDENT (voiceover): They`re among America`s fastest-selling cars. Average price, an eye-popping $58,000. Electric vehicles, EVs make up seven percent of new car sales. Now, the Biden administration wants to accelerate the green revolution with tougher emission standards and industry sources say requiring that EVs make up at least 54 percent of automakers new car sales by 2030, two-thirds of sales by 2032. [19:15:18] BIDEN: Running on a cleaner grid, making and inventing the technologies that are going to power the future. COSTELLO: Automakers are already investing billions to transition from gas to electric. General Motors CEO Mary Barra . MARY BARRA , CEO, GENERAL MOTORS : The quicker we can bring everyone along to EVs, the better it`s going to be for climate. COSTELLO: We`ve seen the Green Revolution firsthand from the assembly line -- 3000 pounds of lithium-ion cells helping the Hummer to accelerate from zero to 60 in three seconds. -- to the frontline. Eventually, they want to take their whole fleet electric. Just two years ago, automakers agreed that EVs would make up half their sales by 2030. Now, the industry says the new White House goals aren`t realistic, writing in a statement, this requires a massive 100-year change to the U.S. industrial base and the way Americans drive. MICHELLE KREBS, COX AUTOMOTIVE : And there are a lot of things that have to happen to get us to a full EV. COSTELLO: Including raw materials, charging stations, and the electric grid to power it. For now, sticker shock may convince many Americans to stick with their gas guzzlers. Tom Costello, NBC News, Washington. (END VIDEOTAPE) HOLT: Up next, we`ll take a look at how artificial intelligence is already making a difference in detecting cancer. (COMMERCIAL BREAK) [19:20:00] HOLT: Back now with our series A.I. revolution and the amazing advances being made in artificial intelligence technology. Tonight, Dr. John Torres shows us how A.I. is a growing weapon in the battle against cancer. DR. JOHN TORRES, NBC NEWS SENIOR MEDICAL CORRESPONDENT (voiceover): John Roberts is lucky to be alive. JOHN ROBERTS, HAD CANCER: No one ever thinks they`re at risk for developing lung cancer. TORRES: During the treatment for a kidney stone, doctors found a mass in his lung and were able to operate before the cancer spread. ROBERTS: They would never have found it, and in all likelihood, I would not be here talking with you today. TORRES: The CDC recommends people at high risk for the disease get screened with a low dose CT scan. But even with regular screening, the most skilled radiologists can`t spot everything. DR. So, we`re missing most cases of early-stage lung cancer when people don`t have symptoms. The possibilities are limitless. TORRES: Dr. Leisha Sequist is part of a team of doctors and engineers from Massachusetts General Hospital and MIT trying to revolutionize cancer detection. Meet Sybil, an artificial intelligence program. The name inspired by the oracles of ancient Greece. SEQUIST: We`ve developed Sybil, an algorithm that is able to tell who might be at risk for lung cancer one, three, five years down the road. TORRES: Lung cancer is the leading cause of cancer death in the U.S. killing more than 127,000 a year. The Mass Gen-MIT study using three sets of independent scans found that Sybil could accurately predict whether a person will develop lung cancer in the next year, up to 94 percent of the time. SEQUIST: This is an immense amount of data in a CAT scan, and we`re only scratching the surface when we just look at it with our eyes. TORRES: Usually, a radiologist is looking for nodules or a mass, but Sybil has the power to look so closely at a CT scan that can identify patterns of data associated with cancer even before a tumor appears. So, this is AI in action. What do we see here? SEQUIST: A.I. circled this area in red and said this area has a dangerous pattern. It looks like cancer might come up. Two years later, there`s a cancer right in that same spot where the AI predicted it would be. TORRES: That`s not to say A.I. will replace radiologists, but the research team in Massachusetts believes Sybil`s assistance is the future of the field. Is A.I. going to save lives? DR. FLORIAN FINTELMANN, RADIOLOGIST, MASSACHUSETTS GENERAL HOSPITAL: Yes, it will save lives because it will enable us to do more, see more, and manage better than we did without A.I. TORRES: Clinical trials for Sybil are ongoing. FDA approval likely years away. And while doctors are still studying the technology, Don Roberts, who is now cancer free, believes technology like Sybil could help him live longer. ROBERTS: You need every weapon you can possibly get to combat cancer. TORRES: And A.I. could be a powerful one? ROBERTS: Absolutely. TORRES: Dr. John Torres, NBC News, Boston. (END VIDEOTAPE) HOLT: When we come back, we`ll hit the ramps and the rails with Tony Hawk , the Navajo Nation, and the skate park inspiring America. (COMMERCIAL BREAK) [19:25:00] HOLT: Finally, tonight, for so many skateboarders, finding somewhere to skate can be as hard as landing your first Ollie. Our Steve Patterson reports Navajo Nation was no exception until now. (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) STEVE PATTERSON, NBC NEWS CORRESPONDENT (voiceover): The Navajo Nation is breathtaking, 27,000 square miles of quiet beauty. But for kids growing up here, maybe too quiet. That`s why so many are attracted to this sound. Navajo Nation loves to skate. Just check out their president doing an ollie. BUU NYGREN, PRESIDENT, NAVAJO NATION: Friends to come out to skate. You challenge one another and you keep each other accountable. PATTERSON: But the reservation itself has been a skateboarding desert. Kids had to find a ride dozens of miles away just to get their wheels running. 12-year-old Cheyenne has been doing it for years. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: I just liked doing it because it`s fun. It teaches me to be more active. AMY DENET DEAL, COMMUNITY ORGANIZER: These remote communities need more opportunities to have outdoor recreations. PATTERSON: Something skaters could call their own became a community`s cause. And with assistance from an organization called the Skate Park Project and its famous founder Tony Hawk -- NYGREN: Thank you for bringing change in this community. PATTERSON: The Dene Skate Garden was set in concrete. How important is to have an outlet, especially for kids in a community that`s been less served traditionally. TONY HAWK, SKATEBOARDER: I think it`s hugely important, especially in a community like this. When kids find skateboarding, I think they find something that speaks to them in a deeper way and something that can teach them a lot of life lessons about overcoming their goals, about overcoming challenges. PATTERSON: Now, somewhere like that exist right here. NYGREN: I`m really excited for them so that they can be here, they can be a part of the community. PATTERSON: A place of pride, a culture of tradition now embracing the great sanctuary of skate. Steve Patterson, NBC News, Navajo Nation. (END VIDEOTAPE) HOLT: They make it look so easy. That`s NIGHTLY NEWS for this Tuesday. Thanks for watching, everyone. I`m Lester Holt. Please take care of yourself and each other. Good night. headline: The Battle Over Access To Abortion Pills Headed To The Supreme Court
story_text: LESTER HOLT: Now to the escalating fight over access to an abortion pill. The Justice Department says it will now ask the Supreme Court for emergency action to stop new restrictions from taking effect. Laura Jarrett has late details. (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) LAURA JARRETT, NBC NEWS SENIOR LEGAL CORRESPONDENT (voiceover): A fierce battle over abortion now headed to the U.S. Supreme Court . The Attorney General vowing to challenge a ruling from a federal appeals court that could jeopardize access to mifepristone, a commonly used abortion pill. KARINE JEAN-PIERRE , WHITE HOUSE PRESS SECRETARY: We believe that the law is on our side. JARRETT: Overnight, that appeals court blocked a portion of a Texas ruling that invalidated the approval of mifepristone, allowing the drug to remain on the market for now. But the judges also rolled back several FDA moves in recent years that made the drug easier to obtain. If the Supreme Court doesn`t step in, women may soon be required to visit a doctor`s office in person to receive the pill instead of taking it at home. It will no longer be available through the mail. The generic version also off the table. And the pill will only be approved through seven weeks of pregnancy instead of 10. DR. LAURA MACISAAC, OBSTETRICIAN-GYNECOLOGIST, MOUNT SINAI: Having more in- person visits means women will have to take time off of work, get childcare often during the work week. If the medication can`t get into the hands of the people that need it quickly, then it isn`t available. JARRETT: Doctors like Laura McIsaac who practice for over three decades alarmed by the ruling. MACISAAC: That will absolutely increase pregnancy complications and increase maternal mortality. JARRETT: Restricting access to mifepristone at the heart of the original Texas lawsuit. ERIN MORROW HAWLEY , SENIOR COUNSEL, ALLIANCE DEFENDING FREEDOM: The FDA has basically sanctioned mail-order abortions. JARRETT: Erin Hawley represents the advocacy groups and doctors that sued the FDA . HAWLEY: The Fifth Circuit`s decision is a huge victory for women and for the rule of law. The FDA did not have a valid basis for approving that drug. JARRETT: While the fight continues in the courts, tonight, a clash at the State House. In Florida, anger erupting on the House floor. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: Show the bill passes. JARRETT: As the Republican-controlled legislature passed a six-week abortion ban headed to the governor`s desk for signature soon. (END VIDEOTAPE) HOLT: So, Laura, when do all these restrictions take effect? JARRETT (on camera): So, those restrictions should begin early Saturday. I say should because tonight a federal judge in a different case in Washington State reiterated that the Biden administration must not make any changes to the availability of this drug. The government will likely tell the U.S. Supreme Court it simply cannot comply with all these conflicting rulings. HOLT: All right, Laura, thanks very much. headline: The Supreme Court Putting A Temporary Hold On A Lower Court Ruling That Would Limit Access To An Abortion Pill Keeping It Widely Available For Now
story_text: LESTER HOLT: A late and dramatic development in the battle over that abortion pill. Late today, the Supreme Court stepping in and putting a temporary hold on a lower court ruling that would limit access. Laura Jarrett has details for us. (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) LAURA JARRETT, NBC NEWS SENIOR LEGAL CORRESPONDENT (voiceover): Tonight, the U.S. Supreme Court moving quick to block a federal judge from rolling back access to the abortion pill mifepristone at least for now. Justice Samuel Alito handing down an order within hours of the Justice Department`s emergency appeal that had warned of chaos and profound disruption if the high court didn`t step in. At issue in the case, a legal morass of complex FDA regulations over the drug that had recently been made easier to obtain. KAMALA HARRIS , VICE PRESIDENT OF THE UNITED STATES: They attacked medication that for 20 years the FDA ruled as being safe. JARRETT: But the advocacy groups and doctors that sued to ban the drug claim the FDA ignored safety risks. Those plaintiffs now have until Tuesday to submit their legal arguments to the justices. At the same time, access to abortion now largely cut off throughout much of the south. After the Supreme Court overturned Roe v Wade, many women traveled to Florida for abortions. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: Show the bill passes. JARRETT: Now, the state has banned anyone from seeking an abortion after six weeks of pregnancy though the law won`t go into effect right away. FENTRICE DRISKELL (D-FL), STATE REPRESENTATIVE: You just don`t want women to have choice. CHASE TRAMONT (R-FL), STATE REPRESENTATIVE: Here we value life from conception to the casket. JARRETT: Governor Ron DeSantis signing the bill with a private gathering overnight, a far cry from the jubilant celebration he put on for a 15-week ban passed last spring highlighting a rising tension within the GOP on the issue. As some are mindful of the public polling largely favoring abortion, other presidential hopefuls are leaning into their conservative base with eyes on 2024, including Senator Tim Scott who spoke exclusively to NBC`s Ali Vitali today. TIM SCOTT (R-SC): If I were President of the United States, I would literally sign the most conservative pro-life legislation that they can get through Congress. JARRETT: But for now, the issue of abortion access rest with the Supreme Court, with the justices poised to rule next week. Laura Jarrett, NBC News (END VIDEOTAPE) END Content and programming copyright 2023 NBCUniversal. ALL RIGHTS RESERVED. Transcription Copyright 2023 VIQ Media Transcription, Inc. headline: The Battle Over Abortion Rights Is Now Headed Back To The Supreme Court
story_text: [18:30:21] JOSE DIAZ-BALART, NBC NEWS HOST: Today tonight, the battle over abortion rights is now headed back to the Supreme Court. Protesters out in force today from Los Angeles to Washington, D.C., as the fate of access to abortion pills could be decided within days. New revelations from those leaked intel documents, reports of up to four more Chinese spy balloons and new questions about why it took authorities so long to notice the leaked documents. Terrifying moments as a bomb is thrown at Japan`s Prime minister. He is rushed to safety before it explodes. What we know about the suspect. A violent coup d`etat playing out right now in Africa. The American ambassador and his staff forced to take shelter. The deadly police mistake caught on video. Officers at the wrong address. When the homeowner opens the door with a gun, they opened fire. How could this have happened? NBC News with rare access as law enforcement busts a giant retail crime ring. Nearly $200,000 in merchandise recovered. And there`s good news tonight. The daughter who reveals to her father after his life saving kidney transplant, she was his donor. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) UNIDENTIFIED MALE: I`m really proud of her. I can`t believe she did it. (END VIDEO CLIP) UNIDENTIFIED MALE: This is NBC NIGHTLY NEWS with Jose Diaz-Balart. DIAZ-BALART: Good evening. The nation`s highest court is once again wading into the country`s most divisive issue, abortion rights. Today, there were protesters outside the Supreme Court as well as rallies across the country. The past week has been a dizzying string of competing and contradictory court decisions, some restricting access to the abortion pill, others protecting it. The Supreme Court now says it will take up the issue, setting a deadline just five days away. At stake, access to mifepristone, the abortion pill the most common way women and pregnancies in the U.S. The Supreme Court could rule to suspend its use nationwide. We begin tonight with Monica Alba. (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: And we didn`t backed down. CROWD: No. MONICA ALBA, NBC NEWS CORRESPONDENT (voice-over): Protests from coast to coast tonight. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: Standup don`t back. ALBA (voice-over): As the fate of the nation`s most commonly used abortion pill hangs in the balance. After a week of uncertainty, the Supreme Court weighing in Friday, keeping mifepristone available for at least the next four days. The temporary action allows the full court to review emergency appeals from the Biden administration and one of the drug makers and gives the plaintiffs a group of doctors and advocacy groups until Tuesday to submit their arguments. ERIN HAWLEY, ALLIANCE DEFENDING FREEDOM SENIOR COUNSEL: It`s really time that the FDA was held to account for putting politics above women`s health and safety, as well as unborn lives. ALBA (voice-over): The high court expected to rule on Wednesday as abortion rights activists expressed concern about what the conservative majority that overturned Roe v. Wade could do now. WENDY FROSH, WASHINGTON, D.C. ABORTION RIGHTS PROTESTER: The same could happen with any other medication if we allow judges to exercise this outrageous authority or misuse of authority. ALBA (voice-over): If the Fifth Circuit ruling is upheld, women would have to get the drug in person at the doctor`s office. It would no longer be available by mail and the window for prescription would be narrowed from 10 weeks to seven. The White House standing by the FDA`s, quote, evidence- based approval. JOE BIDEN , PRESIDENT OF THE UNITED STATES: I think it`s outrageous what the court has done relative to concluding that they`re going to overrule the FDA . ALBA (voice-over): With Vice President Harris making a surprise stop at the Los Angeles women`s march Saturday, vowing to stand up and fight for abortion access. KAMALA HARRIS , VICE PRESIDENT OF THE UNITED STATES: This is a moment that history will show required each of us. (END VIDEOTAPE) DIAZ-BALART: And Monica joins us now from the White House. Monica, what could the Supreme Court do Wednesday? ALBA: Well, it`s unclear how the justices will rule, but it`s possible the court could extend the temporary pause, keeping things as they were before the Texas ruling, until this can play out in the lower courts. Jose? DIAZ-BALART: Monica Alba, thank you. END Content and programming copyright 2023 NBCUniversal. ALL RIGHTS RESERVED. Transcription Copyright 2023 VIQ Media Transcription, Inc.
