At stake, access to mifepristone, the abortion pill the most common way women and pregnancies in the U.S. The Supreme Court could rule to suspend its use nationwide. We begin tonight with Monica Alba. (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: And we didn`t backed down. CROWD: No. MONICA ALBA, NBC NEWS CORRESPONDENT (voice-over): Protests from coast to coast tonight. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: Standup don`t back. ALBA (voice-over): As the fate of the nation`s most commonly used abortion pill hangs in the balance. After a week of uncertainty, the Supreme Court weighing in Friday, keeping mifepristone available for at least the next four days. The temporary action allows the full court to review emergency appeals from the Biden administration and one of the drug makers and gives the plaintiffs a group of doctors and advocacy groups until Tuesday to submit their arguments. ERIN HAWLEY, ALLIANCE DEFENDING FREEDOM SENIOR COUNSEL: It`s really time that the FDA was held to account for putting politics above women`s health and safety, as well as unborn lives. ALBA (voice-over): The high court expected to rule on Wednesday as abortion rights activists expressed concern about what the conservative majority that overturned Roe v. Wade could do now. WENDY FROSH, WASHINGTON, D.C. ABORTION RIGHTS PROTESTER: The same could happen with any other medication if we allow judges to exercise this outrageous authority or misuse of authority. ALBA (voice-over): If the Fifth Circuit ruling is upheld, women would have to get the drug in person at the doctor`s office. It would no longer be available by mail and the window for prescription would be narrowed from 10 weeks to seven. The White House standing by the FDA`s, quote, evidence- based approval. JOE BIDEN , PRESIDENT OF THE UNITED STATES: I think it`s outrageous what the court has done relative to concluding that they`re going to overrule the FDA . ALBA (voice-over): With Vice President Harris making a surprise stop at the Los Angeles women`s march Saturday, vowing to stand up and fight for abortion access. KAMALA HARRIS , VICE PRESIDENT OF THE UNITED STATES: This is a moment that history will show required each of us. (END VIDEOTAPE) DIAZ-BALART: And Monica joins us now from the White House. Monica, what could the Supreme Court do Wednesday? ALBA: Well, it`s unclear how the justices will rule, but it`s possible the court could extend the temporary pause, keeping things as they were before the Texas ruling, until this can play out in the lower courts. Jose? DIAZ-BALART: Monica Alba, thank you. The revelations keep coming from that stunning leak of highly classified documents. And there are new questions tonight about just how closely the government is watching the people tasked with protecting the nation`s top secrets. Our Justice Department correspondent Ken Dilanian has late details. (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) KEN DILANIAN, NBC NEWS JUSTICE AND INTELLIGENCE CORRESPONDENT (voice-over): New information tonight about the Chinese spy balloon shot down earlier this year. The details coming from the classified documents allegedly leaked by 21-year-old national guard airman Jack Teixeira, arrested by federal authorities this week. "The Washington Post " citing documents not seen by NBC News, reports that Chinese spy balloon carried sensors and antennas. The U.S. still had not identified more than a week after shooting it down, and that the U.S. knew of up to four additional Chinese spy balloons. [18:35:16] The paper also reporting on Taiwan`s vulnerability to a Chinese attack, citing a Pentagon assessment that China would quickly gain air superiority if it invaded Taiwan. U.S. Secretary of State Blinken today addressed fallout from the leaked documents. ANTONY BLINKEN , U.S. SECRETARY OF STATE: We have engaged with our allies and partners since these leaks came out, and we have done so at high levels, and we have made clear our commitment to safeguarding intelligence and our commitment to our security partnerships. DILANIAN (voice-over): There are also new insights tonight into why the U.S. government didn`t know for months that state secrets had been posted online. At issue, the limits on what kind of checks are done on the 1.3 million Americans with top secret security clearance. WILLIAM EVANINA, FMR. NATIONAL COUNTERINTELLIGENCE & SECURITY CENTER DIRECTOR: Right now, there is not a social media evaluation done. There`s not an appetite for that. But what they do online is not evaluated by any agency as part of their security clearance. DILANIAN (voice-over): Former counter intel chief Bill Evanina says he pushed for more social media monitoring, but privacy concerns won out. Critics say the government now can`t keep track of all the people with access to sensitive information. (on camera): Does the U.S. government have a good handle on who these people are, what they`re doing online, whether they hold extremist views, that kind of thing? UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: Well, clearly the answer is no. (END VIDEOTAPE) DIAZ-BALART: And Ken Dilanian joins me now. Ken, what`s next for the suspected leaker? DILANIAN: Airman Jack Teixeira faces a detention hearing Wednesday, Jose, where the government is likely to ask to keep him in jail. Then, he`ll have to decide whether to fight the charges or cut a plea deal that likely could carry a lengthy prison sentence. Jose? DIAZ-BALART: Ken Dilanian in Washington, thank you. Some frightening moments in Japan with the nation`s Prime Minister rushed to safety after someone threw an explosive device in his direction during a campaign stop. The attack coming less than a year after former Prime Minister Shinzo Abe was assassinated. Josh Letterman has the very latest. (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) JOSH LEDERMAN, NBC NEWS NATIONAL POLITICAL REPORTER (voice-over): The crowd reacts the moment the explosive device is thrown, taking the attacker to the ground. Prime Minister Fumio Kishida immediately evacuated just before the explosion and the smoky aftermath, Kishida safe and unharmed. Authorities telling Japanese media, the suspect threw an eight to 12-inch pipe, likely a smoke bomb, that landed near the Prime Minister. This witness says the object was silver colored and heavy, made of metal. The suspect, a young man seen with a black and gray backpack, struggling with police as he`s carried away. Prime Minister Kishida continued with campaign events later in the day, even apologizing for causing concern. He says we must carry this on together until the end. Tonight, Japan once again traumatized by political violence. The attack bringing back memories of the fatal shooting of former Prime Minister Shinzo Abe in July, also at a campaign event. While authorities investigate the motive, the suspect is reportedly not speaking with police as tonight security measures for dignitaries are being stepped up. Josh Lederman, NBC News. (END VIDEOTAPE) DIAZ-BALART: A dangerous situation unfolding in Africa at this hour with the U.S. Ambassador to Sudan, the embassy team and others in the capital sheltering in place after rebel forces unleashed a violent assault across the country. Aaron Gilchrist is tracking it all. (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) AARON GILCHRIST, NBC NEWS CORRESPONDENT (voice-over): Tonight, the East African nation of Sudan smoldering in chaos, a deadly coup killing at least 25 and injuring hundreds, the Sudanese Doctors Union telling Reuters. The country`s paramilitary rapid support services taking to Twitter , claiming control of the Army`s headquarters, public radio and television and air navigation throughout the country. It also announced a manhunt for the Army`s commander. The battles leaving smoke billowing from commercial planes at the capital city`s airport. Inside, people fell to the floor trying to take cover as shots erupted on the streets. The fighting even disrupting a Sudanese T.V. broadcast. All this as the U.S. Ambassador to Sudan tweeted he and his staff had to take shelter inside the embassy in Khartoum, the clashes prompting the U.S. to join other world and Sudanese civilian leaders in calls for an end to the violence. BLINKEN: It`s a fragile situation. This is a real opportunity to finally carry forward the civilian led transition. GILCHRIST (voice-over): For months, tensions have been rising as Sudan transitions to democracy. Disagreement lingering about how the military factions would integrate. (END VIDEOTAPE) DIAZ-BALART: Here at home, an evacuation order has been issued for parts of Georgia after a massive fire reignited at a plastic resin plant in Glenn County . The fire first broke out early this morning and was contained before reigniting later in the day. There are no reports of injuries. [18:40:11] Growing questions in New Mexico tonight after a call for help went horribly wrong. Body cam captured police showing up at the wrong house and then fatally shooting the homeowner. Shaquille Brewster has details. A caution in some of the video is disturbing. (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) SHAQUILLE BREWSTER, NBC NEWS CORRESPONDENT (voice-over): Tonight, new body camera video capturing the fatal police shooting of a homeowner in New Mexico. The videos from April 5th show three Farmington officers responding to a domestic violence report around 11:30 p.m. identifying themselves as police three times. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: Farmington police. BREWSTER (voice-over): But the department says officers went to the wrong address. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: It might have been 4308. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: Was it 43 or 53? UNIDENTIFIED MALE: Yes, it might have been 5308. BREWSTER (voice-over): Fifty-two-year-old Robert Dotson opens his front door wearing a robe, investigators say pointing a gun at police. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: Hands up. BREWSTER (voice-over): All three officers fired their weapons. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: I`m good. I`m good. I`m good. BREWSTER (voice-over): Dotson died at the scene. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: One down at the doorway. BREWSTER (voice-over): His wife is heard screaming inside. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: Please don`t. BREWSTER (voice-over): Appearing to open the door when police say she begins firing. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: Get her in cuffs. BREWSTER (voice-over): Minutes later, she surrendered. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: Where`s the gun at? UNIDENTIFIED MALE: He dropped it and she picked it up and pointed it at us. BREWSTER (voice-over): Upstairs are two children heard on a 911 call released by the Farmington Police Department. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: There were gunshots in the house and my dad is shot. BREWSTER (voice-over): The police chief offered his condolences the next day. STEVE HEBBE, FARMINGTON, NEW MEXICO POLICE CHIEF: Mr. Dotson was not the subject of the call that our officers were responding to. And this ending is just unbelievably tragic. I`m extremely sorry that we are in this position. BREWSTER (voice-over): The department is not naming the three officers who are now on paid administrative leave. CARMEN BEST, NBC NEWS LAW ENFORCEMENT ANALYST: BREWSTER (voice-over): It is a tragedy, no doubt. BREWSTER (voice-over): Former Police Chief Carmen Best, who watched the video, says the shooting appears to be consistent with police training. BEST: I would not expect my officer to have a gun pointed in their direction and not react. BREWSTER (voice-over): A reaction stemming from a mistaken address now being investigated by state police. Shaquille Brewster, NBC News. (END VIDEOTAPE) DIAZ-BALART: Still ahead, ten years after the shattering events of the Boston Marathon bombing, the survivors who never backed down. Also, a rare inside look as law enforcement takes down giant retail theft rings. Look at all the things they recovered. (COMMERCIAL BREAK) [18:45:15] DIAZ-BALART: A day of hope and healing in Boston, with the city marking 10 years since a horrific marathon bomb attack that claimed the lives of three people and injured hundreds more are. Kathy Park takes us inside the survivor`s decade long road to recovery. (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) KATHY PARK, NBC NEWS CORRESPONDENT (voice-over): A powerful tribute today as thousands gathered at the Boston Marathon finish line, a place so many have raced through. But today, everyone was still. Here 10 years ago, an unthinkable attack. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: And we heard the two explosions. And my family and I knew something was wrong right away. PARK (voice-over): Back to back explosions that killed three people and injured hundreds more. This was Michelle Blackburn 10 years ago, cheering on a friend. The blast nearly took her leg. MICHELLE BLACKBURN, BOSTON MARATHON BOMBING SURVIVOR: I think that anytime you go through a trauma, it`s very fluid. They spent many years just avoiding it altogether. PARK (voice-over): And this is Michelle today, training to run this year`s marathon until a recent injury took her out for now. BLACKBURN: But I always say forward is the only way forward. So that`s what we`re doing. It`s nothing that`s going to preclude me from running again. JEFFERSON DRISCOLL, BOSTON MARATHON BOMBING WITNESS: I actually knew them. PARK (voice-over): Jefferson Driscoll was 10 when the bombing happened. He grew up with the family of Martin Richard, the youngest victim killed at age eight. Now 20, Jefferson is running his first marathon. (on camera): What inspired you? DRISCOLL: The Richard family, their resilience, their kindness, their peace. It`s been amazing. You learn endurance and it teaches you Boston is one family, one big, strong family. PARK (voice-over): Boston strong still on full display a decade later. Kathy Park, NBC News, Boston. (END VIDEOTAPE) DIAZ-BALART: We are back in a moment with rare access as police track and catch the suspects behind a massive retail theft ring. And life-saving surprise, a father battling for his life learns of the incredible sacrifice made by his daughter. (COMMERCIAL BREAK) [18:50:03] DIAZ-BALART: A retail theft is on the rise across America. You`ve surely seen the videos of brazen thieves smashing windows and stealing merchandise. Well, police now and the stores themselves are working together to catch them. George Solis, now with a rare inside look at one operation. (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) UNIDENTIFIED MALE: What do you want me to do with it? GEORGE SOLIS, NBC NEWS CORRESPONDENT (voice-over): As the radio calls come in. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: OK. All right. Copy. SOLIS (voice-over): California Highway Patrol squads close in. The drama unfolding just before dusk in this Southern California neighborhood. Months of surveillance into an organized retail crime ring. LT. ADAM SMITH, CALIFORNIA HIGHWAY PATROL : One was going into the stores on multiple occasions over the past three months, gathering as much items as they could. SOLIS (voice-over): All leading up to this. Three suspects arrested on suspicion of organized retail theft, according to law enforcement. This is California Highway Patrol `s specialized organized retail crime task force in action recovered a handyman`s paradise worth of high end tools. (on camera): What was the dollar figure that was recovered in tools yesterday? CAPT. JEFF LOFTIN, CALIFORNIA HIGHWAY PATROL : It was about $150,000. SOLIS (voice-over): According to the CHP , this case involved two brothers who repeatedly stole power tools from Home Depots across Southern California and their fences, or the third party they were selling to. LOFTIN: They were concentrating on Milwaukee, DeWitt. You see over here, Makita. SOLIS (voice-over): This high stakes operation, first flagged to the task force by Home Depot , a partnership between law enforcement and major stores to combat the rampant rise of organized retail crime. LOFTIN: As long as we let these people get away with what they`re doing, you and I are going to pay for it. SOLIS (voice-over): Home Depot`s own investigators were on site to ID the stolen items. RORY STALLARD, HOME DEPOT WESTERN DIVISION AP INVESTIGATION SENIOR MANAGER: That makes a huge difference when we prosecute the case, because now everything`s under one umbrella. We`re dealing with one prosecutor. SOLIS (voice-over): Organized retail crime is different than shoplifting. The goal is to resell stolen items for a profit, resulting in tens of billions of dollars lost by retailers each year, many instances caught on camera nationwide, from smash and grabs at luxury stores to dragging entire displays out the door. (on camera): This is not just one battery charger. This is a whole kit of them. LOFTIN: Right, entire boxes. SOLIS (voice-over): Since its creation in 2019, the Highway Patrols` unit has recovered more than $28 million worth of stolen goods. Because of that, California Attorney General Rob Bonta has made fighting organized retail crime a priority even across state lines. ROB BONTA, CALIFORNIA ATTORNEY GENERAL: We will hold you accountable. We will bring felony charges against you. SOLIS (voice-over): The crime surge forcing retailers to drastically increase security. (on camera): Home Depot deploys a number of security measures to ensure their products stay safe from security cameras that watch your every move to products that are secured and locked in place. STALLARD: We call it hardening the target. SOLIS (voice-over): If the thieves manage to thwart these growing security measures, the task force says they won`t get far. SMITH: We`re going to be following you, and we`re going to catch you. George Solis, NBC News, Los Angeles. (END VIDEOTAPE) DIAZ-BALART: When we come back, the amazing moment, this young girl sees the world like never before. (COMMERCIAL BREAK) [18:55:53] DIAZ-BALART: There`s good news tonight about the sacrifices we make for the ones we love. (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) DIAZ-BALART (voice-over): This is a magical moment the Scarborough family in Tucson, Arizona, will never forget. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: Casey. DIAZ-BALART (voice-over): That`s Henry and Maraena`s baby girl Ireland putting on glasses for the very first time. Now clearly seen, she`s surrounded by so much love. There were other unforgettable moments too. Here`s army major Eric Cusick, a few weeks back, surprising his kids at their schools in New York after a 10-month mission overseas, a homecoming that means so much to this military family. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: Oh, my God. DIAZ-BALART (voice-over): And in St. Louis -- UNIDENTIFIED MALE: Are you kidding me? DIAZ-BALART (voice-over): That`s John Ivanowski, shocked to find out his daughter Delaney was his kidney donor. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: It`s fine. DIAZ-BALART (voice-over): It`s a secret she kept for months preparing for the procedure when his kidney disease got worse. The gift of life, helping him heal. JOHN IVANOWSKI: I think about it every day. She`s my hero. I`ll take care of her the rest of my days here. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: I need you to read something for me. OK. DIAZ-BALART (voice-over): Across the country, students were celebrating good news like Stephen Russell. STEPHEN RUSSELL, STUDENT: That you are to be admitted. DIAZ-BALART (voice-over): The multi sports star with Special Olympics, Georgia. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: Here it goes. DIAZ-BALART (voice-over): Overwhelmed when he found out he got into Kennesaw State University . UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: Way to go Stephen. DIAZ-BALART (voice-over): But this was the moment that moved everyone to tears. That`s South K High School Senior Joshua Alvarado in Los Angeles, surprised with a $50,000 scholarship. He plans to study engineering at Stanford. Joshua embraced by his mom, Erine (ph), and his two sisters. The moment bittersweet. That`s because his dad, Mario, died five years ago. Joshua prayed to him after the celebration. (on camera): What did you tell him? JOSHUA ALVARADO, SENIOR HIGH SCHOOL STUDENT: I told him that I hope he`s watching. DIAZ-BALART: He`s proud. No doubt. You should know that. ALVARADO: Thank you. DIAZ-BALART (voice-over): The family has overcome struggles, even homelessness. As a first generation son of Mexican immigrants, Joshua hopes his story inspires others.\\ (on camera): How would you define the American dream? ALVARADO: The American dream to me, has always been reaching for something more. That belief that there`s better out there and that it`s within your reach if you just work hard enough. (END VIDEOTAPE) DIAZ-BALART: That`s NBC NIGHTLY NEWS for this Saturday. I`m Jose Diaz- Balart. Thank you for the privilege of your time. Good night. headline: Meet the Press for April 16, 2023, NBC
story_text: (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) [09:00:19] CHUCK TODD, HOST, NBC`S "MEET THE PRESS" (voice over): This Sunday, supreme uncertainty. The Supreme Court keeps the abortion pill available for now, with a final decision potentially coming in days. VICE PRESIDENT KAMALA HARRIS: They attack medication that for 20 years the FDA ruled as being safe. SEN. LINDSEY GRAHAM , (R) SOUTH CAROLINA: I do believe in common-sense restrictions on abortion. That`s where America`s at. TODD: As Republican presidential hopefuls continue to struggle with the abortion issue, post-Roe. SEN. TIM SCOTT, (R) SOUTH CAROLINA: I would literally sign the most conservative pro-life legislation that they can get through Congress. QUESTION: Even if it was six weeks? SCOTT: I`m not going to talk about six or five or seven or 10. TODD: And the gun debate, after more mass shootings in Tennessee and Kentucky. (UNKNOWN): Oh, my God, there`s an active shooter there! TODD: The NRA holds its annual meeting and Republicans pledge support. FORMER PRESIDENT DONALD J. TRUMP: With me at 1600 Pennsylvania Avenue, no one will lay a finger on your firearms. TODD: Can the two parties find common ground on issues that have divided the nation for decades? My guests this morning, Democratic Senator Tammy Baldwin of Wisconsin and Republican Senator Bill Cassidy of Louisiana. Also, rising tensions. Israel is facing crises at home and criticism abroad. PRESIDENT JOSEPH R. BIDEN, JR.: They cannot continue down this road. TODD: My exclusive interview with Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu . ISRAELI PRIME MINISTER BENJAMIN NETANYAHU: People will see at the end that Israel was a democracy, is a democracy and will be even a stronger democracy after this democratic reform. TODD: Finally, how did a 21-year-old gamer, an Air National Guardsman, gain access to the nation`s top secrets? (on camera): Joining me for insight and analysis are NBC News senior Washington correspondent Hallie Jackson; former Homeland Security Secretary Jeh Johnson; Leigh Ann Caldwell of The Washington Post ; and Stephen Hayes, editor of The Dispatch. Welcome to Sunday. It`s "Meet the Press". ANNOUNCER: From NBC News in Washington, the longest-running show in television history, this is "Meet the Press With Chuck Todd." (END VIDEOTAPE) TODD: Good Sunday morning. Debates over guns and abortion have roiled this nation for decades. This week those debates feel a bit more intense than they have in a while, and there are some deepening tensions between activists who wield power inside Republican primary circles and the overall electorate. Today mark the 16th anniversary of the Virginia Tech shooting. At the time it was the deadliest mass shooting in U.S. history. Thirty-two people were killed. Now, sadly, it`s been surpassed by mass shootings in Las Vegas and Orlando. After five people were killed this week in a mass shooting in Louisville, Kentucky, six more killed two weeks ago at a school in Nashville, 2024 Republican hopefuls gathered at the NRA Convention and rejected the idea that gun restrictions could somehow limit violence -- gun violence. And the NRA continued to demand unlimited political allegiance from the GOP. (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) WAYNE LAPIERRE , CEO, NATIONAL RIFLE ASSOCIATION: Gun-hating politicians should never go to bed unafraid of what this association and all of our millions of members can do to their political careers. TRUMP : The issue is not too many guns; the issue is too many thugs, hoodlums and savage criminals on our street. GOV. KRISTI NOEM, (R) SOUTH DAKOTA: Little Miss Addie, who is almost two, I want to reassure you, she already has a shotgun and she already has a rifle. (LAUGHTER) (APPLAUSE) And she`s got a little pony named Sparkles, too, so the girl is set up. (END VIDEOTAPE) TODD: A Gallup poll conducted before the Louisville and Nashville shootings showed 63 percent of Americans are dissatisfied with the nation`s gun laws. But a majority of Republicans, 54 percent, are satisfied. And so far that overall dissatisfaction number hasn`t translated to the ballot box. Not a single pro-gun elected politician has been thrown out over the issue. But that`s not true on abortion. Nowhere is the gap between the Republican base and the overall general electorate greater than on this issue, particularly after the overturning of Roe V. Wade. On Friday the Supreme Court put a temporary hold on a lower court ruling on the abortion pill, while the court considers the Biden administration`s request to preserve FDA approval of the drug. The state keeps the abortion pill widely available for now, with perhaps another decision expected by Wednesday to try to clear some of this up. Of course, in theory, with the Dobbs decision, the court thought it was sending abortion back to the states. Clearly, that is not the case. The Dobbs decision is not popular with the public. While 61 percent of voters disapproved of the court`s decision to overturn Roe in a fall NBC News poll, 69 percent of Republicans approved of it. Republican elected leaders are well aware of the political challenges abortion presents right now. In 2024 presidential hopefuls have struggled to answer simple questions about where they stand on abortion rights and access. This week Florida Governor Ron DeSantis quickly signed a six-week abortion ban before a speech at evangelical Liberty University . [09:05:02] But he did it behind closed doors, and then he never mentioned what he did in his speech. Donald Trump has repeatedly refused to say whether he would even support a federal law that would restrict abortion. And you`ll hear Tim Scott, Nikki Haley, even Mike Pence , all of them are struggling to define their views on this issue. (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) QUESTION: Is it encouraging a culture of life, though to propose the death penalty for women who get abortions? FORMER VICE PRESIDENT MIKE PENCE: I -- I must tell you that I don`t -- I`m not familiar with those proposals, and I don`t -- I don`t -- I don`t have a way of responding to that or confirming it. SCOTT: I would literally sign the most conservative pro-life legislation that they can get through Congress. QUESTION: Even if it was six weeks? SCOTT: I`m not going to talk about six or five or seven or 10. FORMER GOV. NIKKI HALEY, (R) SOUTH CAROLINA: I don`t want unelected justices deciding something this personal. We`re not going to let this be a political football. Let`s let the states work this out, if Congress decides to do it, but don`t get into that game of them saying "How many weeks? How many weeks?" No, let`s first figure out what we agree on. (END VIDEOTAPE) TODD: And joining me now is Democratic Senator Tammy Baldwin of Wisconsin, who announced this week that she plans to run for a third term. Senator Baldwin, welcome back to "Meet the Press." SEN. TAMMY BALDWIN , (D) WISCONSIN: It`s a delight to join you. TODD: Let me start with the Supreme Court`s decision to put a temporary hold on the ruling having to do with Mifepristone and the future of medicated abortion in this country. Do you think five days is enough time to -- for the Supreme Court to get all the information they need in order to make this decision? BALDWIN: Well, who knows how long that will take, but I`m certainly glad for the five days. But, look, what we have in Texas is a -- a judge who was not guided by science but is part of an extreme Republican concerted effort to ban abortion nationwide. And we do not need judges, politicians or government telling women about what sort of healthcare they can have. It is an issue that is not only playing out in the court in Texas but in -- in the State of Florida, with the governor signing a near six-week ban, Idaho forbidding travel out of state for minors, Wisconsin, where we`ve gone back to literally 1849. That is the date our criminal abortion ban was passed. And that`s 174 years ago. We are fighting back. TODD: If the Supreme Court decides to allow the circuit`s ruling to hold, which would roll back FDA approval of Mifepristone essentially to pre-2016 regulations -- if that happens, what do you want the Biden administration to do? For instance, do you want them -- do you think they should resubmit Mifepristone to the FDA and get a new approval? BALDWIN: Yeah, so we don`t know what the ruling is going to be. We know that this is a drug that was proven safe and effective back in 2000. We know there have been further FDA regulations and -- and the drug has been made available now in a recent ruling over the counter. And I don`t think that there should be second-guessing of the scientific-based process that FDA goes. It has such repercussions beyond the drug Mifepristone to -- you know, we want to be able to rely on a science-driven process that the FDA has. TODD: Let me ask you about, sort of, federal versus state here. In Wisconsin, assuming that the newly configured Supreme Court decides that the 1800 law is essentially null and void, that it`s obsolete, it`s likely that Wisconsin`s abortion law would -- would revert to a law that was passed in the `80s that would essentially make 20 weeks, I believe, the limit on when you can get an abortion. Your bill in the Senate would be Roe v. Wade, which is essentially 24 weeks. Do you think there`s a meaningful difference between 20 and 24 weeks, as this debate moves forward? BALDWIN: Yeah, so the Women`s Health Protection Act codifies Roe v. Wade, but it takes the additional step to tell states that they can`t pass laws that unduly limit access to that right. In Wisconsin you -- you talk about the 1980s law, but there have been laws passed in the `90s and, frankly, quite recently that further restrict a woman`s access to full reproductive healthcare, whether those are waiting periods, mandatory counseling... [09:10:03] TODD: Right. BALDWIN: ... invasive ultrasounds. These are the types of state interference that the Women`s Health Protection Act would eliminate. TODD: I`m just curious, though, how rigid are you on this? In order to get two-thirds of what you`re hoping to get, and you could get 60 votes with 20 weeks, would you do it? BALDWIN: I -- I certainly would look at that, but here is what the bill does. The bill talks about pre-viability and viability and relies on medical expertise. Because that -- that time may change as medicine advances. So we recognize that from the get-go, and I think that`s the appropriate way to do it. But I do want to get this measure passed. TODD: But you are willing to have some compromise if that was the price of getting more Republicans on board? If you could get them on board at 20 weeks rather than 24? We even heard Senator Tim Scott saying that, if 20 weeks is all he could get, looking at it through the other way, that perhaps he would support that. Is that at all... BALDWIN: I`m not... TODD: ... something worth... BALDWIN: I`m not going to negotiate... TODD: I understand that. Is that all something worth at least looking at? headline: The Supreme Court Preserving Access To The Abortion Pill For Now In The Most Significant Case Since Roe v. Wade
story_text: [19:00:00] LESTER HOLT, NBC NEWS ANCHOR (on camera): Tonight, the breaking news from the Supreme Court of the future of that abortion pill. (voiceover): The Supreme Court preserving access to the abortion pill for now in the most significant case since Roe v. Wade. So, what are the next steps? We`ll break it down. The severe storm threat moving east after tornadoes ripped through Texas and Oklahoma. At least three dead, flash flooding and water rescues in Austin, golf ball-sized hail in Illinois, even a water spout in Florida. Millions at risk heading into the weekend. Charges against Alec Baldwin officially dropped. And new details about the gun that killed the Rust cinematographer as production resumes. The new images from inside the film`s Montana set. An American killed in Sudan as fighting rages on. Plus, the latest from U.S. officials on the other Americans trapped. Alarming new findings about climate change. A new report says the melting of glaciers is off the charts. Can anything be done? Is the future of food grown in a lab? It`s better for the climate but what does it taste like? And back in the groove with record sales rising. Why so many are turning to turntables this weekend. ANNOUNCER: This is NBC NIGHTLY NEWS with Lester Holt. HOLT (on camera): Good evening, everyone. Facing an 11:59 p.m. Eastern Time deadline of its own choosing and a day of high drama, the U.S. Supreme Court has just weighed in on another pivotal and consequential question in the nation`s divide over abortion. The justices tonight deciding what`s next for a Texas Court ruling that said the FDA`s 23-year-old approval of a commonly used abortion drug is no longer valid, a ruling temporarily paused from taking effect up until now. That has had the potential to impact medical abortions even in states where abortion remains legal. Senior Legal Correspondent Laura Jarrett is standing by with late details. Laura, what is the court saying here? LAURA JARRETT, NBC NEWS SENIOR LEGAL CORRESPONDENT (on camera): Hey, Lester, good evening. Just minutes ago, the U.S. Supreme Court issued an order to keep a widely used abortion pill on the market. The justices have flatly blocked that lower court decision from Texas that had invalidated the FDA`s longtime approval of Mifepristone and would have made the drugs substantially harder to obtain. Now, Justice Thomas, Justice Alito dissenting to that decision from the rest of their colleagues. The FDA and the drug maker had strongly urged those justices to step in, warning essentially if they hadn`t stepped in, all manufacturing and distribution of this drug would have come to a screeching halt. But for now, women can continue to receive the pill by mail and use it until 10 weeks into their pregnancies while this case continues to play out in the court below. Lester, the Biden Administration just issuing obviously a statement praising it. You know, the groups that had filed this suit originally had claimed that the FDA ignored safety risk, something that the FDA and the Biden Administration put -- pushed back on very strongly, Lester. HOLT: All right, so Laura, legally, what happens next? The next steps here. JARRETT: OK, so, now the case will head back to a federal appeals court for further evaluation of the merits of the lawsuit. This Supreme Court decision was just a temporary issue just because it came up so quickly. Now the case will head back to a three-judge panel on the fifth circuit. It`s made up of mostly conservatives but we don`t know who exactly on that court will hear this case now that it`s back there, Lester. HOLT: All right, Laura Jarrett on that breaking news. I`m joined now by Peter Alexander at the White House. Peter, the president as we heard just reacted to this move. What are you learning? PETER ALEXANDER, NBC NEWS CHIEF WHITE HOUSE CORRESPONDENT (on camera): Yes, Lester, that`s right. The White House has been bracing for this decision for days. Abortion medications have become an increasingly critical flash point of the states` limit or ban abortions after the Supreme Court`s ruling last year overturning Roe v Wade largely because abortion medication can be sent by mail and taken at home. As for the president, he just moments ago weighed in, releasing a statement that reads in part, Mifepristone remains available and approved for safe and effective use. While we continue this fight in the courts, the president adding, that his administration will continue to defend the FDA`s independence to review, approve, and regulate a wide range of prescription drugs. The President says the stakes for women could not be high higher and denounces what he called politically driven attacks on women`s health, Lester. The White House had warned if the court upheld the lower court`s decision, it would have put women`s health at risk and have undermined the FDA`s ability to keep safe and effective medications available for those people who need them. Lester? HOLT: All right, Peter Alexander -- Peter, thank you. END Content and programming copyright 2023 NBCUniversal. ALL RIGHTS RESERVED. Transcription Copyright 2023 VIQ Media Transcription, Inc. BALDWIN: Then, I let go of the hammer of the gun and the gun goes off. ALMAGUER: Before stepping away from the case -- Do you believe Alec Baldwin pulled the trigger? ANDREA REEB, FORMER SPECIAL PROSECUTOR: Yes. ALMAGUER: The former special prosecutor and D.A. told us they had evidence to convict. But new case attorneys writing new facts were revealed that demand further investigation. Consequently, we cannot proceed under the current time constraints. DANNY CEVALLOS, NBC NEWS LEGAL ANALYST: It defies belief that the state is only now learning about how this firearm operates when they are the only people who have had access to it exclusively for over a year and a half. ALMAGUER: While prosecutors maintain the move does not absolve Mr. Baldwin of criminal culpability, experts don`t believe charges may be refiled as the DA`s office warns. Hannah Gutierrez-Reed, the film`s armorer who plans to plead not guilty, still faces involuntary manslaughter charges. CEVALLOS: The case against Gutierrez-Reed is still viable because of her title, her role. ALMAGUER: With production resuming on the new set of Rust, NBC News has learned director Joel Souza who was also shot gave a moving speech to the cast and crew of 200. (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) ANNE THOMPSON, NBC NEWS CHIEF ENVIRONMENTAL AFFAIRS CORRESPONDENT (voiceover): Today`s U.N . report details the relentless advance of climate change on every continent. THOMPSON: The 40 glaciers tracked worldwide lost an average of more than 4.2 feet of ice in a year. In Europe, the melting of the glaciers in the Alps is off the charts. Little winter snow and a summer heat wave exacerbated by dark dust from the Saharan Desert that trapped heat accelerating the record melt. THOMPSON: In Switzerland, for the first time, no snow survived the summer melt season even at the very highest sites. Here in lower Manhattan, scientists predict the waters behind me could rise another foot by 2050. But we can slow it down. KENNEDY: Every tenth of a degree of warming is worth fighting for. THOMPSON: To survive more floods, heat waves, and droughts that inflict the lethal human toll of climate change. Anne Thompson, NBC News New York. Our Maya Eaglin went to find out. (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) MAYA EAGLIN, NBC NEWS REPORTER (voiceover): It`s Big Tech`s newest take on Big Ag. No farmland, no coops, but these labs in Silicon Valley could be the future of meat. JOSH TETRICK , CEO, EAT JUST: There are a lot of benefits in making meat in this way from 70 percent less emissions, 70 percent less water on land. But one of the biggest is you don`t need to harm an animal. Josh Tetrick is the CEO of Eat Just. It`s one of only two companies in the U.S. that`s received clearance from the FDA for human consumption of lab- grown meat. The USDA still needs to approve it for sale. UMA VALETI, CEO, UPSIDE FOODS : This is not vegan or vegetarian. EAGLIN: The other company is UPSIDE Foods headed by cardiologist Uma Valetti. Talk to me about the science here. How does it work? VALETI: The science is fascinating but it`s fairly simple. We take cells from eggs or young animals or mature animals and we identify those cells that are capable of going into fats, proteins, connective tissue. headline: NBC NIGHTLY NEWS for April 22, 2023, NBC
story_text: [18:34:30] JOSE DIAZ-BALART, NBC NEWS HOST: Ahead for us tonight, a giant massive seaweed wider than the U.S. is bearing down on Florida. And a $20 million mystery who swiped a container of gold from a North American airport, tonight on NIGHTLY NEWS. (COMMERCIAL BREAK) [18:42:05] ANNOUNCER: This is NBC NIGHTLY NEWS with Jose Diaz Balart. DIAZ-BALART: Good evening. The race to evacuate Americans from Sudan is intensifying as the situation there it gets worse by the moment. Officials in the African nation say that the evacuation of foreign nationals has begun. But the U.S. State Department and Pentagon have not confirmed any American operation. This is part of Saudi Arabia`s evacuation today. Transporting hundreds by caravan and then by boat to safety. Take a look at this. Airports are not an option. They`re totally blown out from the intense fighting between two warring military factions there. There are an estimated 16,000 American citizens currently in the eastern African country, many with dual citizenship who may not want to leave but there are plenty who do. And they`re getting more desperate by the hour. We begin tonight with Pentagon Correspondent Courtney Kube. (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) COURTNEY KUBE, NBC NEWS NATIONAL SECURITY & MILITARY AFFAIRS CORRESPONDENT (voice-over): Tonight, a glimmer of hope for some Americans trapped in Sudan following eight days of violence and bloodshed. The Sudanese military announcing the United States, Britain, France, and China will evacuate their diplomats and citizens by air with military transport aircraft belonging to their armed forces from Khartoum. Saudi Arabia completing the first civilian evacuations this morning rescuing more than 150 of its own citizens and those of other countries first by caravan and then by ship. While officials familiar with the planning say the Biden administration is leaning towards evacuating the roughly 70 U.S. government personnel in Khartoum. Today, the Pentagon saying they`re preparing for various contingencies, but declining to talk about potential operations. There are more than 16,000 other Americans currently sheltering in place, including Rebecca Winter`s (ph) sister-in-law, a teacher in the capital city of Khartoum. She`s now hiding with her infant daughter. REBECCA WINTER (ph): The city is in complete disarray. She needs to come home now. We need evacuation for U.S. citizens. And we need humanitarian aid for everyone who`s suffering in this conflict in Sudan. KUBE: This week, the U.S. military moves specially trained troops to nearby Djibouti to be ready to rescue Americans caught in the crossfire between two warring generals fighting for control of Sudan. But with the airport`s still shut down, some Americans are prepared to take things into their own hands. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: I`m keeping my hopes up but I`m also preparing for having to find my own route. KUBE: Like 1000s of Americans still caught in the middle of this deadly power struggle. (END VIDEOTAPE) DIAZ-BALART: And Courtney, the situation is going more dire every day? KUBE: Yeah, that`s right. Trapped Americans are running out of supplies. And now some are looking for their own escape route. But tonight State Department officials are warning U.S. citizens not to take private convoys to potential evacuation points, saying, they cannot guarantee anyone safety. Jose. [18:45:04] DIAZ-BALART: Courtney Kube in Washington, thank you. Last night Supreme Court decision to keep the abortion pill mifepristone available for now means the legal and political battles over access to it are just getting started. Monica Alba reports from the White House. (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) MONICA ALBA, NBC NEWS WHITE HOUSE CORRESPONDENT: Tonight, political leaders reacting to the latest development in the hot button issue of abortion access. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: Our confidence in our judiciary (inaudible). SEN. CHUCK SCHUMER , (D) NEW YORK MAJORITY LEADER: The hard right anti- choice MAGA wing in this country will keep working and working and working to take away all women`s rights. ALBA: But for now, the most commonly used abortion pill remains widely available for millions of women after the Supreme Court preserved full access to mifepristone, Friday, while the appeals process plays out over a Texas judge`s ruling that would have jeopardized access to the drug. A majority of the justices granting the Biden administration`s request for temporary relief with Clarence Thomas and Samuel Alito publicly dissenting. The case now goes back to the Fifth Circuit, where oral arguments are set for May 17. Nothing about the medications availability will change before then, and may not until the matter goes back to the High Court. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: I think it`s very highly unlikely given that we`re in April already that this case would be heard and resolved. This term that would be extraordinary, much more likely they`re going to set the matter for argument in the fall of 2023. And a ruling would come out in the spring of 2024. ALBA: The White House relieved for now, with President Biden arguing the lower court decision would have quote undermined FDA`s medical judgment and put women`s health at risk. A new NBC News poll shows 58% of adults say abortion should be legal, either always or most of the time, compared to a combined 38% who believe abortion should be illegal either with exceptions or without exceptions. The abortion debate proving to be a key issue for voters as the race for 2024 heats up. (END VIDEOTAPE) DIAZ-BALART: Monica Alba joins me now from the White House. Monica, is there any reason to think the circuit court could rule differently than it did last time around? ALBA: Well, it`s certainly possible, Jose, because the next three judge panel from the conservative leaning Fifth Circuit that will hear the case next month will be chosen at random. Jose. DIAZ-BALART: Monica Alba at the White House, thank you. And now to the new report that the Air National Guardsmen charged with leaking classified documents may have been sharing Top Secret Intelligence online for much longer than previously thought, possibly as long as a year before he was caught. Ken Dilanian has late details. (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) KEN DILANIAN, NBC NEWS NATIONAL SECURITY CORRESPONDENT: New reporting tonight that the accused leaker of classified information began posting secrets more than a year ago, shortly after Russia`s invasion of Ukraine. The New York Times says it discovered that airman Jack Teixeira allegedly began sharing military secrets as far back as February 2022 to a chat group containing 600 members, that`s 10 months before the December 2022 leaks that Teixeira is charged with. Two sources familiar with the matter tell NBC News investigators gave no indication when briefing Congress last week that they were aware of this new set of disclosures. The FBI and the Pentagon had been scrambling to assess the damage from a leak they first discovered April 5. FRANK FIGLIUZZI, NBC NEWS, NATIONAL SECURITY ANALYST: And the longer something is out there floating in the ether, in the cyber world without the government knowing, without them being able to shut it down, the more potential damage can be done. DILANIAN: Teixeira`s lawyer, the FBI , and the Pentagon, all declined to comment tonight. The Times match the new posts to Teixeira through a series of digital clues including a handle he had previously used. The newspaper quoted Teixeira boasting of his special access to secrets. I have a little more than open-source info perks of being in a USAF intel unit, he said, seemingly referring to his job as an I.T. specialist and an Air Force Intelligence wing and hinting that he used his I.T. access to get information. "The job I have lets me get privileged above most intel guys," he wrote. Teixeira claim he was hunting through classified computer networks for intelligence on the Ukraine war, including material from the National Security Agency and GCHQ, the U.K.`s digital spying department. FIGLIUZZI: This goes way beyond a kid trying to impress his buddies. DILANIAN: When one chat room member urged him not to abuse his access to secrets, he is said to have replied, too late. (END VIDEOTAPE) DIAZ-BALART: And Ken, could these new revelations lead to more charges for Teixeira? DILANIAN: Yeah, Teixeira`s alleged comments in the second chat room really do complicate his legal situation, Jose. He allegedly even offered Teixeira secrets with people outside the United States. The textbook definition of espionage. Jose. DIAZ-BALART: Ken Dilanian in Washington, thank you. It has happened again another instance of someone accidentally pulling up to the wrong address and the homeowner opening fire. This is -- this in Florida and the police say the shooter did nothing wrong. Erin McLaughlin has the latest. (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) ERIN MCLAUGHLIN, NBC NEWS CORRESPONDENT: As the nation comes to terms with a week of random shootings involving seemingly innocuous mistakes. Tonight, in South Florida questions surrounding a grocery delivery that ended in gunfire. [18:50:12] DIAMOND D`ARVILLE: I had seen him pull out a gun and I said that`s where I was like, we got to go. We got to go. MCLAUGHLIN: 18-year-old Diamond D`arville and her 19-year-old boyfriend, Waldes Thomas say last Saturday night they mistakenly drove to the wrong house to drop off a grocery order. Thomas tells NBC News they were trying to leave the property, alleging the homeowner blocked them with his truck and later opening fire. WALDES THOMAS: They shuffled behind. It wasn`t even front, they shot from behind. So it just -- it just made me feel like it was like a racist or racist thing. MCLAUGHLIN: The car was hit multiple times. D`ARVILLE: Here, right here. MCLAUGHLIN: Though neither were injured, according to the police report, the homeowner claims he told his 12-year-old son to order them to leave his property. Moments later he heard the boy calling for help. He alleges he saw Thomas driving erratically, at one point reversing and running over his right foot. He claims he opened fire fearing he or his son were going to be further injured by the vehicle and that his intention was to disable the vehicle. The homeowner has not responded to NBCs request for comment. Investigators later concluded each party appear justified in their actions based on the circumstances they perceived and no charges were filed. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: Even an innocent person who enters a home or another person`s property could potentially risk deadly force being used against them if the homeowners perception of the threat is reasonable. MCLAUGHLIN: Tonight, Thomas says his grocery delivery days are over at a time when many Americans are thinking twice before knocking on a stranger`s door. Erin McLaughlin, NBC News. (END VIDEOTAPE) DIAZ-BALART: And not a growing mystery, a shipment of gold and other valuables worth $15 million is vanished missing from the Toronto Airport. It could be the biggest heist in Canada`s history. Jesse Kirsch has the story. (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) JESSE KIRSCH, NBC NEWS CORRESPONDENT: To the north tonight Canadian authorities are trying to solve a multimillion-dollar mystery. Police after a plane landed in Toronto Monday, cargo was moved to a holding facility before someone took off with a high value container. STEPHEN DUIVESTEYN, PEEL REGIONAL POLICE INSPECTOR: It did contain gold but was not exclusive to gold can contain other items of monetary value. KIRSCH: In all, police say the cargoes worth roughly 15 million in U.S. dollars, but they aren`t sharing much else. JOHN PISTOLE, FORMER FBI DEPUTY DIRECTOR: There may be some tactical or strategic advantage for them for not disclosing, so they`re not tipping their hand to the bad guys and where the shipment might be today. KIRSCH: John Pistole is a former Deputy FBI director and a former TSA Administrator. He has many unanswered questions. PISTOLE: Was an inside job and what evidence is there of whoever committed the heist if you will, what type of access control system that they go through? Do they have a badge? KIRSCH: In a statement, the Greater Toronto Airports Authority emphasizing last week thieves access the public side of a warehouse outside of our primary security line. This did not involve access to Toronto Pearson itself and did not pose a threat to passengers. The alleged airport theft evokes memories of New York`s 1978 Lufthansa heist becoming the stuff of Hollywood legend in Goodfellas. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: Nobody knows for sure just how much was taken in the daring pre-dawn raid at the Lufthansa Cargo Terminal at Kennedy Airport. KIRSCH: Canada has its own history of high-profile heists. In 2012, thieves snatch millions of dollars` worth of maple syrup according to the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation . Police believe this latest theft was an isolated incident. But tonight its explanation is up in the air. Jesse Kirsch, NBC News. (END VIDEOTAPE) DIAZ-BALART: And now the things that go boom in the night. That, the National Weather Service believes is the sound of a meteor and here it is, streaking through the skies over Central Indiana just before 9:00 Friday night. There were sightings in Illinois, Michigan and Kentucky as well. When we come back, there`s good news tonight, the little boy taking some giant steps. (COMMERCIAL BREAK) [18:57:25] DIAZ-BALART: There`s good news tonight about defying expectations and the little boy who never gives up on his goals. (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: Are you ready? DIAZ-BALART: Look, their seven-year-old Lenny Turley born with cerebral palsy. He was determined to take some of his first steps in front of his kindergarten class at High Point Elementary near Columbus Ohio. His trial celebrated by every single student. That reaction deeply touching for Lenny`s parents, Justin and Alicia. (On camera): What was it like when you saw the video of Lenny, not once, twice, walking in front of the class? JUSTIN TURLEY, LENNY TURLEY`S FATHER: It was unreal. That kind of support that he got from them. It was overwhelming. ALICIA TURLEY, LENNY TURLEY`S MOTHER: Here we go. DIAZ-BALART: What is the bigger lesson that all of us could learn? A. TURLEY: I think the first thing that comes to mind is hope. Sorry, I told myself I`m not going to be emotional. All kids struggle with something. So if there`s people, whoever`s out there, that struggling with something, there`s always someone out there that`s going to give them support even if they feel stuck. (END VIDEOTAPE) DIAZ-BALART: And get this Lenny is excited to start baseball next month. That`s NBC NIGHTLY NEWS for this Saturday. I`m Jose Diaz-Balart reporting from New York. Thank you for the privilege of your time. Good night. (COMMERCIAL BREAK) END Content and programming copyright 2023 NBCUniversal. ALL RIGHTS RESERVED. headline: Meet the Press for April 23, 2023, NBC
story_text: (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) [09:00:18] CHUCK TODD, NBC HOST (voice over): This Sunday, the Biden-Trump rematch. As President Biden prepares to announce his re-election bid this week, our new NBC News poll finds voters don`t want him to run again, including half of Democrats. PRESIDENT JOSEPH R. BIDEN, JR.: We`ve made a lot of progress, and we`ve just got to keep it going. TODD: And our poll also shows voters don`t want to see former President Trump run again. FORMER PRESIDENT DONALD J. TRUMP: There`s no crime. I got indicted for no crime. TODD: And yet he has huge support within the GOP even after his arrest, and he`s the clear front-runner. Is America ready for a Biden-Trump sequel? I`ll talk to New Hampshire`s Republican Governor Chris Sununu , who`s considering his own presidential run in 2024. Plus, triggered. ANDREW GILLIS, FATHER OF KAYLIN GILLIS: For this man to sit on his porch and fire at a car with no threat is just -- angers me so badly. TODD: The wrong driveway, the wrong doorbell and the wrong car, simple mistakes that all ended in Americans being shot. UNKNOWN: Mr. Yarl is fighting for his life. TODD: In a nation full of guns and growing distrust, what will it take to make knocking on a stranger`s door feel safe again? And, ethics scandal, after reports revealing Justice Clarence Thomas failed to disclose real estate transactions from a wealthy Republican donor, Senate Democrats call on the chief justice to testify. SEN. DICK DURBIN, (D) ILLINOIS: They have to do something. TODD: Why does the highest court in the land have the lowest ethical standards? I`ll talk to the Senate Judiciary Committee chairman, Dick Durbin . (END VIDEOTAPE) TODD: Joining me for insight and analysis are Politico Playbook co-author Rachael Bade; Washington Post columnist Eugene Robinson; Amy Walter, editor in chief of the Cook Political Report; and Marc Short, former chief of staff to Vice President Mike Pence . Welcome to Sunday. It`s "Meet the Press". ANNOUNCER: From NBC News in Washington, the longest-running show in television history. This is "Meet the Press With Chuck Todd." TODD: Good Sunday morning. Americans are seething at their political leaders and at each other. That`s according to a brand-new NBC News poll we are releasing right now. They`re dissatisfied with what seems to be inevitable, a 2024 rematch between Joe Biden and Donald Trump . As Biden prepares to formally announce his campaign for a second term early this week, just one in four Americans believe he should run for re- election. Seventy percent say he shouldn`t run. By the way, only 35 percent believe Donald Trump should run again. Sixty percent say no. Only 5 percent of Americans actually want both of these gentlemen to run. And let me show you even more of this poll. Fifty-three percent of 2020 Biden voters say he shouldn`t run; 64 percent of Democrats who voted for Sanders or Warren in the 2020 primaries think he shouldn`t run. And 76 percent of voters under 35 think he shouldn`t run. And what`s the top concern for that? We asked voters. We didn`t prompt them. We said, "Why don`t you think he should run?" Well, these were the responses. It almost is all about his age and his ability to do the job. Again, these are among Democratic primary voters. Overall, the president`s job rating is not in a good place when you`re seeking re-election, sitting at just 41 percent, driven by the 58 percent of Americans who disapprove of how he is handling the economy right now. Just 30 percent of independents approve of the job Biden is doing overall. But as Biden is fond of saying, he is not to be judged by the Almighty, but judge him by the alternative. And guess what? The alternative is even more unpopular among the American public. Let me show you here. Here`s the feelings about Donald Trump . Just one in three Americans have positive feelings about him. A majority have negative feelings, sitting at 53 percent. Among voters overall, a majority believe that the charges in New York are - - are serious enough because he should be held to the same standard as anyone else. Forty-three percent believe he`s being unfairly targeted. And that`s approximately the number that seems to stick behind Donald Trump on almost anything. And among Republican voters, it appears that the New York indictment only galvanized his support. We asked them whether this -- these charges were a politically motivated attack and it means they`ve got to stand behind Donald Trump , or do these charges indicate that he`s got a lot of distractions in his way and that it`s important to nominate somebody else who could focus on beating Joe Biden ? Well, as you can see here, it`s no contest. Nearly 70 percent believe they`ve got to rally around Donald Trump right now because of these indictments. Only one in four Republican voters believe it is time to move on. And that translates into the Republican primary matchup here, Donald Trump with 46 percent. Now, look, Ron DeSantis , that`s a healthy number for somebody that`s never run for president before. It`s about the same spot that Barack Obama started in against Hillary Clinton back in 2007. [09:05:03] And when you combine first and second choice here, you see that Trump and DeSantis could very well end up in a neck-and-neck race here, but that`s the point. Donald Trump seems to be as strong, if not stronger, with the groups that matter the most when it comes to winning a Republican primary. Now, there`s one more major takeaway from this poll. As the Supreme Court keeps the abortion pill Mifepristone available for now, putting a stay on the Texas ruling which revoked FDA approval for the drug, abortion is energizing voters. Nearly 60 percent, as you can see here, of voters want abortion access to remain legal. And among -- ready for this? Among the 43 percent who told us that abortion is the single issue that drives them to the polls, they believe it should be legal by a 65/34 percent margin. This is another sign that the energy is on the Democratic side of this issue after Dobbs. When Roe v. Wade was law of the land, single-issue abortion voters almost universally leaned Republican. Twenty-twenty-four Republican hopefuls met in their first Iowa cattle call last night, courting the caucus`s most important demographic, religious voters. Donald Trump didn`t appear at the event. He sent a video claiming credit for the Supreme Court justices he appointed, while his former vice president took Donald Trump on, on the issue of abortion. (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) TRUMP : I faced down vile attacks to confirm our three great Supreme Court justices, Neil Gorsuch , Brett Kavanaugh and Amy Coney Barrett . FORMER VICE PRESIDENT MIKE PENCE: I do think it`s more likely that this issue is resolved at the state level, but I don`t agree with the former president who says this is a states-only issue. (END VIDEOTAPE) TODD: And joining me now is the Republican governor of New Hampshire. It`s Chris Sununu , who himself is considering a run for president. Governor Sununu, welcome back to "Meet the Press." SUNUNU: Thanks. Thanks for having me. TODD: Look, the last time you were on, and on many a program, you have made one declaration almost universal about 2024. Let me play a montage. (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) GOV. CHRIS SUNUNU , (R) NEW HAMPSHIRE: Look, Donald trump is not going to be the nominee, right? We`re just moving on as a party, as a country. He`s not going to be the nominee. That`s just not going to happen. Here`s the good news. (APPLAUSE) I`m going to give you the good news. Ready? (APPLAUSE) I love you. I`m a big fan. BILL MAHER, HOST, "REAL TIME WITH BILL MAHER": Thank you. SUNUNU: But you`re dead wrong. He`s not going to be the nominee. (END VIDEOTAPE) TODD: All those quotes were from February and March, none of them from April. You`ve seen the numbers. You`ve seen this shift. You`ve seen the energy. We`ve watched Governor DeSantis. What say you now? SUNUNU: Yeah. There`s definitely a shift, but I still don`t think he`s necessarily going to be the nominee. Look, I think your poll is spot-on in all these areas, by the way. I think that`s actually a great poll, and I hope folks listen to it. I`ll say this. Republicans are rallying; they`re supporting former President Trump over these indictments, right? And there`s a lot of support there. Now, does it actually translate into a vote? We will see. I mean, most folks don`t decide who they`re voting for until about three weeks before the election. So there`s a lot of politics to play out. There`s -- not even a single debate has been had. Other candidates are going to get in the race. So I just think it`s so far away. And at the end of the day, we want a winner, right? Republicans want someone who can win in November of `24. Donald Trump is a loser. He has not just lost once. He lost us our House seats in 2018. He lost everything in `20. We should have 54 U.S. senators right now. We don`t because of his message. So Donald Trump is positioning himself to be a four-time loser in 2024. We need candidates that can win. TODD: Isn`t the problem, though, that a majority of Republicans don`t believe what you just said, that he lost in 2020? Because it -- the loser message should work, unless you don`t believe he lost? SUNUNU: Well, it`s not just 2020, right? We got crushed in 2022. We should have 54 U.S. Senate seats. We don`t, because he is part of that message. We lost in 2018. So it`s not just about whether he won or lost in `20, which he did, of course. A former member of Congress from Michigan, David Trott, I -- called up to go on the record to use, I`m not going to repeat the word, but basically said: DeSantis is not a likable guy, and used a more colorful word. What -- the pattern is developing here. BADE: Yeah. I mean, look, self-inflicted wound here. Be nice. Say hi to people. TODD: The Mike Pence strategy. BADE: Yeah. TODD: I`m sorry, there is a, you know -- SHORT: I do think, Chuck, I do think these endorsements are grossly overvalued. I mean, in 2016, when Donald Trump was on his way to a nomination-- ROBINSON: He had no endorsements. (CROSSTALK) SHORT: -- the only two endorsements he had were Duncan Hunter and Chris Collins , who both ended up in jail, right? TODD: The first two. And then he had Jeff Sessions and Chris Christie . SHORT: So, yeah. BADE: But here`s the problem, though -- if you can`t connect with your own delegation, I mean, Steube told me -- Greg Steube told me that he had numerous times over the past five years in Congress, reached out to DeSantis to try to get a meeting to talk policy. TODD: Right. BADE: Ignored every time. Actually, you know, told to show up at campaign events and then told, you can`t take the stage with DeSantis. This is a problem for him. And if he`s going to alienate lawmakers who understand the electability argument and why that is significant, how is he going to connect with, you know, GOP voters who sort of vote with their gut? TODD: Well, Marc, let me ask you to address it this way. You know how reticent people are to talk about people. The fact that there is a comfort now coming at DeSantis, what does that tell you about DeSantis right now? SHORT: I think it tells you everything you need to know, Chuck. I think it`s where a lot of Republicans view that he`s an easier target. I guess my concern -- TODD: That`s a dangerous place to be. SHORT: It is. TODD: I mean, when we were talking about Clinton/Obama, Clinton was the easier target back then, not Obama. And you would think it should be Trump is the easier target, and in this case it`s not been. SHORT: I think that`s right. But I think at the same time, I mean, I wouldn`t be as worried about the endorsements. I think for people of principle there`s a bigger concern about what`s happening in using a big government Republican going after private-sector industries. ROBINSON: Exactly. SHORT: And I think that`s a bigger concern for principled conservatives. ROBINSON: The pursuit of Mickey Mouse is really crazy. TODD: The two of you -- ROBINSON: It`s really crazy. TODD: -- should be a producer because you`ve just segued into a terrific tease for my next segment. When we come back, Florida Governor Ron DeSantis has been picking a fight with the state`s second largest private employer. I`m going to show you how important Disney is to the overall Florida economy, and why this battle could backfire. (COMMERCIAL BREAK) [09:47:10] TODD: Welcome back. Data Download time. The feud between Ron DeSantis and Disney escalated yet again this week when the Florida governor proposed developing land near the amusement park into a state park or, even more snarkily, he suggested, a state prison. It was the latest volley in a battle that began last year when Disney executives criticized DeSantis` parental rights in education bill. It was dubbed the "don`t say gay bill" by many opponents. But it has turned into somewhat of an all-out personal feud between a sitting governor and a business that is very crucial to much of the state`s economy. Let me just show you how important Disney is to the state of Florida. This is Disney `s annual visitors to the Disney World amusement parks. Over 36 million people in 2021. And just show you know, that`s actually kind of low right now. Pre- pandemic, close to 60 million visitors. Just, you know-- it works out to about one in five of all Americans, though, of course, there`s some global visitors there. How about in tax revenue that Disney World generates? Well, Disney itself claims they collected over $1 billion in taxes in the calendar year 2022. That amount of money is more than the entire budget for many of Florida`s state agencies. That`s how crucial this is to the state of Florida. Let me go to the number of employees. It`s the second largest private employer, over 75,000. This is central Florida`s economy, if you will. Seventy-five thousand people employed Disney World, the only private company to employ more people in the state of Florida are -- is the Publix grocery store chain. And then there`s just the overall economic impact that it does for the entire central Florida region. One estimate by Oxford Economics put it at over $75 billion in economic impact to the state of Florida thanks to Disney World. This isn`t just a mouse that roars. Politically, it could become a mouse that bites as well. When we come back, this week, we saw how simple mistakes could end in gun violence. In a nation full of firearms and fear, what would it take to make knocking on a stranger`s door feel safe again? (COMMERCIAL BREAK) [09:53:01] TODD: Welcome back. More than a quarter of Americans, 28 percent, say a family member, friend, coworker, or they themselves have been a victim of gun violence. It outnumbers self-identified political independents in our poll by two to one, as more Americans become part of a shared experience that they never wanted. I`m not interested in having a debate about gun laws. It`s more of like, we have a societal and cultural problem. And I -- it seems like it`s now bigger than just a simple fight over the laws, Rachael. I mean, this feeling that you can`t go to some neighbor`s house, and you end up at the wrong door, and you might get shot. BADE: Yeah, yeah, I mean, talk about parents being afraid to send their kids to school. I mean, it is a fear that everyone has right now. And -- and I`m going to take it back to laws because here in Washington, this was story number like 25. I mean, we`re talking about everything else and, and not about this issue. President Biden was asked about it and he said, look, I can`t do anything. Democrats, you know, Sununu pointed out, they didn`t pass laws on this when they had -- TODD: That`s very true. RACHAEL BADE: -- the majorities in Congress. And now, Republicans control the House. Nobody`s talking about it up there, and yet everybody`s talking about it everywhere else. TODD: It seems that there needs to be some leadership to sort of change the culture that says, Marc, you don`t need to pull a gun first. Like that`s where we are. Like why -- people are in a, "I`ve got to have my gun first". That seems to be the uneasiness. SHORT: Well, I think that there`s a devaluation of life, honestly, in our society, Chuck. And I do think there needs to be a greater appreciation for the value of life. But I also think that there`s a lot of media focus, and rightly there should be, on these mass shootings. But respecting everyone who, who lost a life and mourn -- we mourn them, the reality is there`s been 12,800 deaths by guns this year, 169 by mass shootings. There`s a crime problem in our inner cities that we`re not addressing. We focus a lot on the mass shootings without focusing on the real problem of crime in our inner cities. And there needs to be a bigger focus there. ROBINSON: Well, it`s not just crime in inner cities. It`s crime in suburbs. It`s crime in, you know, rural areas. [09:55:03] I mean, guns are being used everywhere. It`s a gun problem everywhere. And so again, getting back to laws. I mean, Florida after Parkland passed a red, red flag law. And that has been used thousands of times, like probably 10,000 times by now, to take guns out of the hands of people who are deemed, through a process, to be a danger to themselves or others. And I -- who knows how many shootings that has stopped, but I`ll bet it`s some. It`s not -- the number is not zero. So how else do we attack this -- TODD: Yeah. ROBINSON: -- cultural issue other than through laws? TODD: Amy, I don`t even know if we have a shared North Star on this, which is the goal -- you would think a minimum goal that everybody could agree on is we should keep guns out of those who mentally aren`t capable of having it, or who could be trigger happy for whatever reason. But we don`t agree on how -- what -- WALTER: On how to judge that. TODD: What`s the -- how do you do that either, how to judge it. I don`t know if these red flag laws are constitutional. We have yet to see it tested, for what it`s worth. So that`s an issue. But it`s also -- we don`t seem to agree that, okay, we`ve got to get rid of mentally challenged people from getting guns, but we don`t know how to do it. WALTER: Well, and we don`t -- I do think also what does "mentally challenged" mean, when so many of these shootings are literally, as you pointed out, spur of the moment, heat of the moment? If you have a gun nearby, suicides are also one on that list that you put forward. Of the number of suicides that are aided by guns, how many of those would`ve been prevented if it wasn`t as easy to pick up in your area? TODD: Here`s what I`m uncomfortable with -- is that I would`ve had to say yes on that. I`ve had a family member and a work colleague touched by gun violence. I`m guessing everybody here knows somebody or has somebody. I mean, that`s the part of this that I feel like our politicians aren`t addressing this shared reality. Rachael? BADE: On mental health? I mean -- TODD: On all of it. ROBINSON: On all of it. BADE: Yes. Yeah, I mean, you talk about trying to get some sort of united joint star -- united North Star that people can go to. I mean, you would think that, you know, Republicans always want to talk about mental health, Democrats always want to talk about gun control. I mean, there has to be some sort of overlapping area here. TODD: Right. BADE: And like, you know, red flag laws have been successful in parts of the country. Could they do something more at a national level here, in terms of making sure that guns are not finding -- falling into the hands of the wrong people? ROBINSON: But what`s the one thing that every gun crime, every gun issue, incident, has in common? It`s the gun. I mean, we have more guns than people in this country. I mean, that`s the bottom line. And, now how we address that is a difficult problem. WALTER: We also live in a -- ROBINSON: But it`s the truth. WALTER: Yeah. And we live in a society where it`s heads I win, tails you lose. There`s no such thing as compromise on any issues, because somehow if there`s compromise, I`m going to lose out. TODD: But I want to do a political reality here, Marc. We`ve yet to see somebody who is seen as a Second Amendment supporter lose an election because of that issue. SHORT: Well, sure, because I think that as many as we`ve talked about families that have been touched by gun violence, we also have family members or people we know who have also been protected because they had a gun, too, Chuck. And so it`s a complicated issue. And I think you`re right, it is a bigger societal issue than saying, let`s grab everybody`s gun. TODD: Right. BADE: Politically, I mean, you talk about, you know, there hasn`t been a Republican voter -- TODD: Right. BADE: -- who has been sort of ousted because of this. And until you start to see -- or not a Republican voter, a Republican candidate, a Republican lawmaker. Until you see something like that, you`re not going to see changes. TODD: Abortion is definitely salient -- BADE: Right. TODD: -- with swing voters. It`s not clear yet that gun policy is. ROBINSON: We`ll see. TODD: Yeah. That`s all we have for today. Thanks for watching. We`ll be back next week, because if it`s Sunday, it`s "Meet the Press". END Content and programming copyright 2023 NBCUniversal. ALL RIGHTS RESERVED. headline: How More Women Are Boldly Changing The Conversation About Menopause And Money
story_text: [19:20:00] LESTER HOLT: There`s been an empowering shift in how women are talking about menopause, no longer taboo, many are having candid conversations about what they want and need, and big business is listening. Here`s Kristen Dahlgren. (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) KRISTEN DAHLGREN, NBC NEWS CORRESPONDENT (voiceover): Menopause is more than hot flashes and night sweats. A new study shows a big financial impact too, some $1.8 billion in lost work every year, $26 billion when you add in medical expenses. DR. STEPHANIE FAUBION, DIRECTOR, MAYO CLINIC WOMEN`S HEALTH CENTER: That`s not even counting the lost opportunities women might have because they didn`t take a promotion or maybe they took a lesser job. DAHLGREN: 13 percent of women reported an adverse work outcome due to menopause. 11 percent missed at least one day of work, the average missed three days per year. Do we need to rethink how we`re thinking about menopause in the workplace? FAUBION: I think we`re where we were in the 1970s with pregnancy and lactation in the workplace. Now, we need to be having these conversations about how menopause symptoms impact women. We need to educate managers and supervisors. DAHLGREN: It took a while for Lorraine Grace White to realize what she was feeling was menopause. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: I had migraines every day so intense that I could -- I could hardly focus and concentrate. And then there was the mood swings. DAHLGREN: She found Dr. Makeba Williams, an OBGYN at Washington University in St. Louis , one of a growing number of physicians focused on individualized menopause care. The number of certified menopause practitioners has increased 70 percent in the past 10 years with the potential to almost double by the end of this year. DR. MAKEBA WILLIAMS, OBGYN, WASHINGTON UNIVERSITY IN ST. LOUIS: The average age of menopause in this country is 51 which means that a woman will spend a half to a third of her life menopausal. This notion that I hear all too often that women should just grin and bear it does everyone a disservice. DAHLGREN: And symptoms can be even more severe for African-American women. WILLIAMS: An African-American woman can expect to have these symptoms for 10 years. And unfortunately, she is half as likely to be treated as a White woman who will suffer from these symptoms only about six years. DAHLGREN: Williams says there`s hope even hormone therapy once considered too risky now seen as a safe option for many. And for those who can`t take estrogen like women who have had breast cancer, new treatments are being developed. For Lorraine, seeking help has made all the difference. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: We are a different generation of women and we have things to do. I feel amazing and I can`t wait for the next chapter. DAHLGREN: Chapters being rewritten for millions as attitudes toward what was once simply called the change are changing. Kristen Dahlgren NBC News, St. Louis. (END VIDEOTAPE) HOLT: Up next tonight, songs of survival. The beautiful instruments and the stories to save them. (COMMERCIAL BREAK) END Content and programming copyright 2023 NBCUniversal.
