headline: Meet the Press for April 30, 2023, NBC
story_text: (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) [09:00:19] CHUCK TODD, HOST, NBC`S "MEET THE PRESS WITH CHUCK TODD" (voice over): This Sunday, age-old problem. PRESIDENT JOSEPH R. BIDEN, JR.: We now have to finish the job, and there`s more to do. TODD: After officially launching his 2024 campaign focusing on Donald Trump , President Biden dismisses concerns about his age. BIDEN: I can`t even say the number. It doesn`t -- it doesn`t register with me. FORMER GOV. NIKKI HALEY, (R) SOUTH CAROLINA: The idea that he would make it until 86 years old is not -- is not something that I think is likely. BIDEN: Meanwhile, Donald Trump keeps his focus on Biden and the general election. FORMER PRESIDENT DONALD J. TRUMP: He is grossly incompetent, has no idea what he`s doing. BIDEN: Are Biden and Trump in a co-dependent relationship? Do they need each other in order to succeed in 2024? I`ll talk to Vivek Ramaswamy , a millennial entrepreneur who is running for the Republican nomination. Plus, Disney versus DeSantis. Disney sues Florida`s governor, Ron DeSantis , accusing him of retaliating against the company. GOV. RON DESANTIS, (R) FLORIDA: I don`t think the suit has merit. I think it`s political. TODD: But Republicans are now distancing themselves from the issue as the battle with the entertainment giant escalates. SEN. MARCO RUBIO, (R) FLORIDA: I do worry that, if this happens too many times, businesses that are thinking about coming to Florida are saying, "Maybe we don`t want to go there." TODD: And border surge. The Biden administration is bracing for a potential wave of migrants at the southern border, when a COVID-era restrictions ends in less than two weeks. ALEJANDRO MAYORKAS, SECRETARY OF THE DEPARTMENT OF HOMELAND SECURITY: Our border is not open and will not be open after May 11th. REP. MICHAEL MCCAUL, (R) TEXAS: This is irresponsible. TODD: Will Biden`s new strategy make a difference? I`ll speak to Homeland Security Secretary Alejandro Mayorkas. Plus, "Look For Me There." Grieving for his father and trying to honor his legacy, Luke Russert has written a new book on how he dealt with the sudden loss of his dad. (on camera): Joining me for insight and analysis are NBC News Washington correspondent Yamiche Alcindor; former Democratic senator from Missouri Claire McCaskill; NBC News Capitol Hill correspondent Ryan Nobles; and Lanhee Chen, a fellow at the Hoover Institution . Welcome to Sunday. It`s "Meet the Press." ANNOUNCER: From NBC News in Washington, the longest-running show in television history, this is "Meet the Press With Chuck Todd." TODD: And a good Sunday morning. You know, it was 10 years ago this very month that the Senate`s so-called gang of eight rolled out an immigration reform plan that they believed could finally pass Congress. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) RUBIO: We all wish we didn`t have this problem, but we do, and we have to fix it, because leaving things the way they are, that`s the real amnesty. SEN. LINDSEY GRAHAM , (R) SOUTH CAROLINA: I think 2013 is the year of immigration reform. (END VIDEO CLIP) TODD: But it was not, and the laws haven`t changed. Two years later Donald Trump would launch his presidential campaign, building his entire political identity on the issue of being tough on immigration and tough on the border. Trump even promised to wall off the nation`s 2,000-mile southern border. And though the wall didn`t materialize, his administration, in an attempt at deterrence at the border, instituted policies that included separating migrant children from their parents and instituting the Remain in Mexico program, which sent migrants back to Mexico while seeking U.S. asylum. Biden endorsed a sweeping immigration plan on his very first day in office, but the plan went nowhere, even though Democrats controlled both houses of Congress at the time. Instead the administration has adopted several of the Trump policies he once criticized, including a transit ban which will force some migrants to apply for asylum from their home countries. Now, as Biden formally runs for a second term, the immigration issue, which he never mentioned this week in his announcement video, continues to be one of his toughest challenges. In 2021, more migrants crossed the southern border than in any year since at least 1960. And in 2022, the record was broken again. In two weeks, an emergency public health rule known as Title 42 that has allowed both the Trump and Biden administrations to expel migrants and block most access to asylum at the border since March of 2020, allegedly to prevent the spread of COVID, will officially expire. And the U.S. relationship with Mexico has perhaps -- the government, that is -- has perhaps never been worse, with cooperation on the drug war at its lowest point in decades, thanks to an administration in Mexico that doesn`t seem interested in dealing with the cartels. Fentanyl, which is produced in Mexico, with chemicals sourced from China, is now the leading cause of death for Americans between the ages of 18 and 49, according to our friends at The Washington Post . This week, ahead of Title 42 expiration, the Biden administration announced new steps to stem unauthorized migration, including opening new processing centers in Colombia and Guatemala, creating a new family reunification program and increasing assistance to counter smuggling. Homeland Security Secretary Alejandro Mayorkas acknowledged there would be a border surge, but he also said it does not mean more migrants should come. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) [09:05:03] MAYORKAS: The smugglers` propaganda is false. Let me be clear. Our border is not open and will not be open after May 11th. (END VIDEO CLIP) TODD: And Secretary Mayorkas joins me now. Mr. Secretary, welcome back to "Meet the Press". MAYORKAS: Good morning, Chuck. TODD: Look, before I start on this, there`s been a horrific execution- style shooting down in Texas. Authorities are now -- there`s a manhunt right now for somebody who`s armed and dangerous. I know you`ve been monitoring this. DHS is monitoring this. What can you tell us about the alleged suspect, Francisco Oropeza? MAYORKAS: Chuck, it`s a horrific crime. And I can assure you and the American people that law enforcement will deliver accountability. The case is an active one, under investigation, so I really can`t comment further. TODD: There is some question about his citizenship. He supposedly had a -- I guess they refer to it as a counselate card from Mexico, meaning he was here legally, but perhaps he`d overstayed? MAYORKAS: So, Chuck, I -- I won`t comment on it because it is an active case. The tragedy that occurred is -- you described it correctly -- just absolutely horrific. Our hearts go to the -- the victims, the victims` families, those children. And we`ll deliver accountability. TODD: Do we know if federal authorities are involved in this right now, besides FBI and the local authorities? Is DHS, are you -- is your team involved, Border Patrol, at all? MAYORKAS: So we are monitoring the situation very carefully, but the FBI is the lead federal investigative agency, and of course working with the locals there. TODD: Let me move to the announcement and what`s coming in life after 42. There is already reports in Brownsville, Texas, right now, shelters are overwhelmed. The cities of Chicago and New York are already overwhelmed. What`s May 12th going to look like, if we`re already overwhelmed before the expiration of Title 42? MAYORKAS: A few things, Chuck. First of all, this is a really tough challenge and has been, as we all recognize, for years and years. We are seeing a level of migration, not just at our southern border, but throughout the hemisphere, that is unprecedented. It is, I think, the greatest migration in our hemisphere since World War II. The president, on day one, delivered a solution. He delivered immigration reform legislation that we had hoped Congress would act on swiftly. They haven`t. Within the constraints of a broken immigration system, we are doing so much. Our approach is to build lawful pathways, cut out the ruthless smugglers, deliver lawful pathways so people can access humanitarian relief without having to take the dangerous journey from their home countries and, at the same time, if they arrive at our southern border in between ports of entry, we will deliver consequences. TODD: All right. I want to go through some specific scenarios. So, an unaccompanied minor, under 18, that comes to our southern border on May 12th, what happens? MAYORKAS: We follow the law. And the law provides... (CROSSTALK) MAYORKAS: ... that we take custody of that child, and we have 72 hours within which to transfer that child, that unaccompanied child, to the Department of Health and Human Services . Then it is for the Department of Health and Human Services , HHS , to identify a relative, a sponsor, in the United States, to whom they can transfer care of that child. TODD: Is at all -- do you accept the idea that that is all considered a loophole to get into the country? MAYORKAS: Chuck, we have to take a look at the humanitarian issue here. These are parents that are suffering such desperation, whether it`s by reason of an authoritarian regime, tremendous violence, acute poverty, persecution, that they are so desperate that they send their children to the southern border alone. We have, the law provides, for humanitarian relief for these children. And we enforce that law. TODD: All right. If a family -- when a family comes to the border, if they`ve not done any of this pre-filing, if they`ve not filed for an asylum claim beforehand, they come to the border on May 12th, what happens to a family with children under the age of 18? MAYORKAS: So we will exercise our enforcement authorities in a traditional immigration context. Remember, Title 42 is a public health authority, not an immigration authority, that was delivered in response to the COVID-19 pandemic. When that ends on May 11th, we will use our immigration authorities under Title 8 of the United States Code. That family will be placed in immigration enforcement proceedings, removal proceedings. They will make a claim -- if they make a claim for relief, we will adjudicate that claim for relief swiftly. TODD: Define "swiftly." MAYORKAS: So it could be days or weeks. It is not going to be months or years. TODD: Because we`ve seen that, in New York, migrants are getting court dates in 2033. [09:10:03] How does that happen? MAYORKAS: So we are -- what we have done now is we are going to be able to exercise our immigration enforcement authorities. We`ve been precluded from doing so by a court. We sought to end Title 42 long ago, with... TODD: OK. MAYORKAS: Title 42 does not deliver an immigration consequence. Title 8 of the United States Code does. If an individual is removed under Title 8, they will encounter an at least five-year bar on re-admission to the United States. TODD: Here`s a question I have. There are 2 million asylum cases in the backlog right now. What happens to new asylum claims on May 12th? Do they get put in line behind these 2 million cases? Do they get -- and this is why the quick adjudication, I get it in theory. How is it going to work in practice when we`re sitting on 2 million back -- a 2 million case backlog? MAYORKAS: So we`re going to focus on recent border crossers. But the -- the point, the fundamental point, is we have more than 2 million cases in an immigration backlog that has been building year over year over year. What a powerful example of a completely broken immigration system. We have got to fix it. We need legislative reform. TODD: What is a -- you know, I`ve gone through this before. I know there`s a comprehensive aspect that we need, but just for border enforcement and the migration, you need more money for what? You want more processing centers in country? Do you want, besides Colombia and Guatemala, do you want to open up centers in Honduras? Could you even open up a center in Venezuela, or do you trust that government to allow us to do that? MAYORKAS: So, Chuck, we need resources for it all, but remember, the resources will enable us to move more quickly, more efficiently within a broken immigration system. So I just want to be clear that we are working within significant constraints. We need people; we need technology; we need facilities; we need transportation resources, all of the elements of addressing the needs of a large population of people arriving irregularly at our southern border. TODD: What`s the definition of a secure border to you? MAYORKAS: It is, in the context in which we are working, it is maximizing the resources that we have available to us to deliver the most effective results. And something that is overlooked that I speak about frequently is the fact that our apprehension rates at our southern border are consistent with the apprehension rates in the prior administration. And why is that? It is because of the extraordinary, and extraordinarily heroic work of our United States Border Patrol. But -- but the challenge is enormous. TODD: I want to ask you about Border Patrol. Because the union doesn`t like you. And they make it pretty clear on social media this month, and last month, the month before. These are all from Border Patrol -- the Border Patrol Union, on you" "The chicken are going to come home to roost because of what he`s done." They call you "a national disgrace." "Remove Mayorkas," was their most recent tweet. How can you lead a group of people whose union wants you out of office? MAYORKAS: Chuck, I`m incredibly proud to work with the United States Border Patrol. I have supported them vigorously since my first day in office. I will continue to do so. A tremendous source of pride. And I will tell you this... TODD: What do you think the disconnect is? Do you think this is -- this is media perception, what? Why do you -- why do you think there -- is this a political disconnect? Is this a red/blue divide, just simply that you`re in a Democratic administration? What do you believe it is? MAYORKAS: Chuck, I`m focused on mission. That`s what I`m focused on. I look at their needs. I try to fulfill their needs. We go to Congress and seek support. You know, this is the first administration since 2011 that has plussed up the Border Patrol with more agents. Our request of Congress for fiscal year 2024 is another 350 Border Patrol agents. That hasn`t happened for over 12 years. TODD: Let`s talk about the Fentanyl issue. The biggest impediment in dealing with the Fentanyl issue, is it Americans` addiction? Is it the Mexican government`s inability or, frankly, passe -- passe relationship with the cartels, or is it the fact that -- that China so easily exports these materials? What`s the -- what`s the toughest aspect of this? MAYORKAS: Chuck, it`s a matter of supply and it`s a matter of demand, no different than the scourge of drugs that has afflicted this country for decades. But I will tell you something, because I was a federal prosecutor for 12 years. I prosecuted cocaine trafficking cases, methamphetamine, black tar heroin. We haven`t seen anything like Fentanyl, its toxicity. It is -- these cartels are peddling in death and destruction. But we have to stop the flow of Fentanyl, and we also have to address the demand. [09:15:05] TODD: You know, in the `80s, we covertly worked with the Colombian government to deal with these cartels in Colombia, and -- and we had success. Is it time to deal -- I mean, I know some people are calling for more direct military confrontation with these cartels, or to call them terrorist organizations. But is it time for a strategy that is similar to what we did with the Colombian cartels in the `80s? MAYORKAS: So, a couple things. Number one, we are taking it to the cartels with unprecedented strength and focus. And there is a misperception that Mexico is not a good partner in our fight against... TODD: Is that government an ally, or not? They don`t act like an ally these days. MAYORKAS: They are an ally. And we have a very close partnership with them. TODD: I get chills introducing you right now, I`ll be honest. RUSSERT: Thank you. TODD: You were 22 when your dad died. RUSSERT: Yeah. TODD: And it seems that you`re looking back now and realize you didn`t process it then. RUSSERT: Yeah. TODD: Talk about it. RUSSERT: Yeah. Well, he died and it was such a whirlwind of emotions. And we came back to Washington. My mother and I were actually in Italy when it happened, which turned out to be a little bit of a blessing because we had one day to ourselves together as a family, as mother and son, to begin to process what had happened. TODD: He was with you two days earlier, right? RUSSERT: Two days before he passed away, at the Vatican, which is so fitting considering my father`s Catholic upbringing. But when we came back, we thought that people would mourn him. We had no idea there was going to be such a national outpouring of grief. He had thousands of people at his wake. And I ended up giving a eulogy at Holy Trinity Catholic Church here in D.C., and then eventually the Kennedy Center. And a lot of people saw that, and that sort of catapulted me into a very public, forward-facing space. But I was still trying to sort of reconcile, what should I do? And I think in the beginning -- TODD: What were you, weeks from graduating college, right? RUSSERT: Three weeks out. (CROSSTALK) TODD: -- just finished Boston College. RUSSERT: I had graduated college, and about three weeks later I`m looking out over a set of pews at Barack Obama, John McCain , Ethel Kennedy, Joe Biden . It was -- it was a whirlwind. TODD: It`s still surreal to think about that day. RUSSERT: It is still surreal. And I look back on that, and I think about, man, 22-year-old Luke, you had so much courage, you had so much poise. But you never really dealt with, you lost your dad. You lost your best friend. And you went into this immediately public-facing role because you were trying to preserve his legacy the best you knew, and you were trying to bring comfort to people. But it ultimately did not bring comfort to you. TODD: You wrote something that I thought was pretty brave about yourself. You write this: It`s apparent that I`ve spent so much time honoring his legacy that I`ve never truly accepted his death. Worse, by honoring that legacy, I`ve failed to forge my own life. RUSSERT: Yeah. TODD: That`s a -- that`s a pretty brave thing to write publicly, buddy. RUSSERT: One of the things that I`ve found going through this process was I had written out all these journals when I was traveling around the world, and I didn`t know really what was in them. But when I took the time to read them, I realized I was looking for something. And what I was looking for on this journey was, who am I, independent of my parents? Who am I, independent of my hometown? Who am I, independent of the ways of Washington? And I never was able to truly figure that out because I was so attached to dad. He was my guiding light. He`s gone. I try to stay in that lane, but I never really ask those difficult questions of, who are you? What do you want to do? Because it was greatly uncomfortable. And to ask those questions, I would have to deal with the fact that he was really gone, which was something that I just tried to conveniently power through, and white-knuckle, and not really think about too much. TODD: So, of all people, it`s John Boehner -- RUSSERT: Yeah. TODD: -- that sort of, what did he, flip a switch in your head? What did he say to you that made you say, wait a minute, I got to rethink this? RUSSERT: I was turning 30, I had lost a good friend of mine at 27, and my father died at 58. So I saw the light at the end of the tunnel. Friends were getting married, heck, getting mortgages. So I kept thinking about it, is this everything that`s going to happen with me in my life? Is this really what I want? I was having anxiety around the position. There were so many days where I would white-knuckle it through on television, and I wouldn`t even know why. Why is that? Why am I feeling that way? Maybe I should take some time away. And out of nowhere, John Boehner , the House speaker at the time, who I covered rather aggressively, says, I need to talk to you. And I thought he was going to be angry about coverage. And he takes me into his office and he goes, what are you doing here? I said, well, you invited me into your office. What do you mean, what am I doing here? He goes, no, what are you doing here on Capitol Hill? You`ve been here eight years, you spent all your 20s here. I`m the Speaker of the House. I want to tell you something. There is a world outside of Washington. There is a world outside of this place, the Capitol. Time is a flat circle here. You could end up 50, 60 years old, and not even know that time has gone by. Make sure this is what you want to do, and go out and do something else if you want. It`s okay. Go learn how to do something. And part of it I think was that Washington can be fleeting, and the connections that you make with people can be purely political. Go out there and really understand human beings. And it was a very impactful statement, because Boehner grew up one of 12 children, Catholic upbringing in Cincinnati, very similar to my father. Rust Belt, worked his way through college. So it didn`t fall on deaf ears at all. I was -- I was really shaken up by it. TODD: So I think anybody that`s lost somebody close to them, I think this is a book that can help them. You poured yourself out in this. Not easy to write about your mom. Your mom`s still here, doing great. I mean, Maureen Orth is a force of nature. I love her to death. I know you do, too. How`s this changed things for you two? RUSSERT: When one parent dies, your relationship with the surviving one, for the children or the child, always changes. And in my case, it was this mix of, you`re now the sort of man of the house, there are all these logistical things to deal with that dad used to always take care of. But then sometimes it was, well, you`re my son. Just do it. So it was trying to navigate this pattern of, where really are you in the structure? And also as a mom, she was more sort of the disciplinarian where my dad was the sort of, you know, do a little good cop/bad cop. He was sort of the easier guy to get along with at some points. But then I realized when I started traveling -- because my mother was a Peace Corps volunteer at a very young age, when women, when they graduated college, really had limited opportunities. It was, be a paralegal or a teacher. And she said, I want to do something else. So she goes to Colombia, goes to the Peace Corps. And it`s through travel and measuring herself against the world that she really knows who she is. And she had wanted me to do that my entire life. I had never really traveled. And it was not until I did that that I understood her. She had to fight so hard for everything she got, and that is why she demanded a lot out of me. She said, you got to be tough, and you`ve got to show yourself. TODD: Feel like you`ve found yourself? RUSSERT: I think we`re always a work in progress. But as it pertains to losing my father, I`m at peace with that. I`ve accepted it, and I`m so much better for it. TODD: Where are you headed next? RUSSERT: I like storytelling, so hopefully this book does well and that opens up some opportunities in that area. TODD: All right, man. Nice to see you. RUSSERT: Thank you so much for having me, Chuck. It`s such an honor. TODD: Honor`s mine, my brother (ph). The honor is mine. RUSSERT: Appreciate it. TODD: Well, we`ll be back next week, because if it`s Sunday, it`s "Meet the Press". END Content and programming copyright 2023 NBCUniversal. ALL RIGHTS RESERVED. headline: NBC NIGHTLY NEWS for May 5, 2023, NBC
story_text: [19:00:00] (COMMERCIAL BREAK) LESTER HOLT, NBC NEWS ANCHOR (on camera): Tonight, the stunning video just released a former president Trump`s deposition in a civil trial. (voiceover): His testimony played for the jury, considering writer E. Jean Carroll`s allegations in her civil lawsuit that he raped her and defamed her. His strong denial and what he says about Carroll, a photo with her and his wife, and an infamous comment he once made about women. The Supreme Court puts the execution of an Oklahoma death row inmate on hold. My interview with Richard Glossip was said to be his last. Instead, relief for supporters who say his trial was unfair. Their reaction, the moment the news came in. The war in Ukraine, why a Russian mercenary group is threatening to quit fighting in a key city. It`s ultimatum to Russia. Is the U.S. ready for more migrants expected to come to the Southern Border? We put the question to the Homeland Security Secretary. More good news about jobs, but the new warning from President Biden about a potential government default. Will birth control pill soon be available over the counter? The FDA set to consider it. And the coronation of King Charles now just hours away. Thousands filling the streets for a royal ritual not seen in 70 years. ANNOUNCER: This is NBC NIGHTLY NEWS with Lester Holt. HOLT (on camera): Good evening and welcome everyone. Former President Trump has not testified in the civil lawsuit in which a writer accuses him of raping her more than 20 years ago and then defaming her by saying she made up the allegation. But today, a video deposition given by Mr. Trump was made public for the first time. In it, the former president strongly denies the accusation, intense questioning from E. Jean Carroll`s lawyer. Mr. Trump was also asked about comments he made about women in that infamous Access Hollywood Tape that came to light before the 2016 election. It`s where we begin tonight with Senior Legal Correspondent Laura Jarrett. (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) LAURA JARRETT, NBC NEWS SENIOR LEGAL CORRESPONDENT (voiceover): Tonight, former President Donald Trump seen under oath, blasting the rape accusation against him from writer E. Jean Carroll. DONALD TRUMP , FORMER PRESIDENT OF THE UNITED STATES: She`s accusing me of rape, a woman that I have no idea who she is. It came out of the blue. JARRETT: Released publicly for the first time today, Mr. Trump`s deposition in a civil case. Carroll is suing him for allegedly defaming her. She says he raped her in a department store dressing room more than 20 years ago. TRUMP: It`s the most ridiculous, disgusting story. It was just made up. If it did happen, it would have been reported within minutes. JARRETT: This week, a jury in Manhattan watch clips of the deposition. Carroll`s attorney turning the focus to that now infamous Access Hollywood Tape. TRUMP : You can do anything. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: Whatever you want. TRUMP: Grab them by the (BLEEP). UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: And when you`re a star, they let you do it. You can do anything. Grab them by the (BLEEP). You can do anything. That`s what you said, correct? TRUMP: Well, historically, that`s true with stars. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: It`s true with stars that they can grab women by their (BLEEP). TRUMP: Well, that`s what, if you look over the last million years, I guess that`s been largely true. Not always, but largely true, unfortunately or fortunately. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: You consider yourself to be a star. TRUMP : I think you can say that, yes. JARRETT: Mr. Trump had repeatedly said Miss Carroll was not his type. TRUMP: It`s not politically correct to say it, and I know that, but I`ll say it anyway. JARRETT: But then he mistook Carroll for his ex-wife, Marla Maples, when shown this old photo of him shaking Carroll`s hand. TRUMP : I don`t even know who the woman. Let`s say I don`t know who -- it`s Marla. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: You say Marla is in this photo? TRUMP: That`s Marla. Yes, that`s my wife. JARRETT: Throughout the deposition, Mr. Trump steadfastly denying Carroll`s accusation and going after Carroll`s attorney. TRUMP : You know, it`s not true too. You`re a political operative also. You`re a -- you`re a disgrace. JARRETT: Later, turning to her physical appearance. TRUMP : You wouldn`t be a choice of mine either, to be honest with you. I hope you`re not insulted. I would not, under any circumstances, have any interest in you. (END VIDEOTAPE) HOLT: Laura, this is the only time the jury is going to actually hear from Mr. Trump. JARRETT (on camera): Right, Lester. Mr. Trump`s attorney has opted not to put on a defense case. The judge is giving the former president until 5:00 p.m. Sunday to change his mind. If not, closing arguments are expected on Monday. Lester? HOLT: Laura Jarrett, thank you. The Supreme Court has stepped into temporarily halt the planned execution this month of an Oklahoma man whose case has drawn support from both sides of the death penalty debate. Tonight, my exclusive interview with Richard Glossip on the day a dramatic new twist in his case unfolded. [19:05:00] (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) HOLT (voiceover): Less than two weeks before his scheduled execution, Richard Glossip once again waits at death`s door, like he has so many times before. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: And incarcerated individual at Oklahoma State Penitentiary. HOLT: Richard, how many execution dates have you had? RICHARD GLOSSIP, PRISONER CURRENTLY AT DEATH ROW: Nine. HOLT: And three of those, you were within minutes of being executed. GLOSSIP: Yes, three of them. I was fed my last meals. HOLT: Each time he was given a last-minute stay. This morning, Glossip called me from Oklahoma`s death row, his last interview before his new date to die, believing he had 13 days to live. Glossip, a former motel manager, convicted of organizing the 1997 murder of his boss, Barry Van Treese, but he maintains his innocence. I think you know the question I have to start off with and that is did you have anything to do with the murder of Barry Van Treese? GLOSSIP: I did not. HOLT: And you might be surprised who believes him and is fighting for him. KEVIN MCDUGLE (R-OK), STATE REPRESENTATIVE: These people should be ashamed. They should be arrested. These two men are not Glossip`s defense attorneys. They are pro-death penalty conservative lawmakers, Oklahoma representatives J.J. Humphrey and Kevin McDugle. MCDUGLE: I don`t think they`ve got enough to convict him of Jay Walking. J.J. HUMPHREY (R-OK), STATE REPRESENTATIVE: There`s no doubt, no doubt that he`s innocent of murder. HOLT: McDugle and Humphrey are desperate to save Glossip`s life. They point to two independent reviews. Both determine the original investigation was corrupt. HUMPHREY: This is unjust. I mean, this is a case where literally the prosecution team has tried to hide everything that they`ve done. One of the prosecutors, literally, we have it in writing, that she tried to change the testimony of the actual murderer. HOLT: Even the state`s Republican attorney general doesn`t think Glossip should be put to death. And in a rare move just this week, the A.G. asked the Supreme Court to grant a stay of execution. The answer came today in the middle of our interview. None of us saw it coming. I just handed a note. The U.S. Supreme Court halts execution of Oklahoma death row inmate Richard Glossip, whose case has drawn support from state`s Republican attorney general. MCDUGLE: Yes, that`s awesome, awesome. HUMPHREY: I tell you, we thought they would do it. Oklahoma is finally going to have the opportunity to look under the hood. The decision granting a temporary stay of execution, giving the court more time to review Glossip`s case. Minutes after the decision, we spoke to Glossip`s attorney Don Knight. DON KNIGHT, ATTORNEY FOR RICHARD GLOSSIP: We are thrilled that this -- that the court granted this stay of execution. This is something that we`ve been asking for a long time. We know that Rich Glossip is innocent. HOLT: Yet another reprieve for Glossip for now, but maybe not forever. GLOSSIP: I either let this consume me or I make peace with it and try to live the best I can with what life I have left. And that`s what I try to do. I`m scared to death. Don`t get me wrong. I don`t want anybody to think that I`m taking it lightly or anything, but you have to make peace with the situation. (END VIDEOTAPE) HOLT (on camera): We have reached out to both the district attorney and the victim`s family after today`s news but have not heard back from either. However, after a recent hearing, the family members said they believe Glossip is guilty. As the war in Ukraine grinds on, tonight, a major rift has escalated between the head of a Russian mercenary group fighting in eastern Ukraine and Russia`s military leaders. And he`s given them an ultimatum. Richard Engel has the latest. (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) RICHARD ENGEL, NBC NEWS CHIEF FOREIGN CORRESPONDENT (voiceover): It`s been called the biggest land battle since World War II, Bakhmut in eastern Ukraine. For months, a group of mercenaries known as the Wagner group has been leading the charge here where Russia has gained ground. Much to the embarrassment of the Russian army, which to undercut its rival has, according to the mercenaries, been blocking the delivery of supplies. Today, the head of Wagner standing over the bodies of his fighters said he`ll quit Bakhmut next week unless his men get more ammunition. Russia is feeling the pressure. It accuses the United States of conspiring with Ukraine to carry out a drone attack against the Kremlin itself, calling it an attempted assassination on President Putin. Allegations the U.S. and Ukraine strongly deny. JOHN KIRBY, STRATEGIC COMMUNICATIONS COORDINATOR, NATIONAL SECURITY COUNCIL: One thing I can tell you for certain is that the United States was not involved in this incident in any way. ENGEL: Today, Russia`s Foreign Minister promised a response with what he called concrete actions. And negotiations aren`t going well. In Turkey, talks over access to the Black Sea got heated when a Ukrainian delegate photobombed a Russian negotiator, the frustrated Russian turn back and snatched the Ukrainian flag. Turkey condemned the behavior as undiplomatic. (END VIDEOTAPE) [19:10:06] ENGEL: When asked about the Wagner group`s potential pull out from Bakhmut, the Kremlin`s response was no comment. Lester? ENGEL: Richard Engel tonight, thank you. We have breaking news about the death of a man in a New York City subway. Jordan Neely died this week after he was put on a choke hold by another passenger. Some riders said Neely had been threatening people on board. NBC has learned that the case is expected to go to a grand jury to decide if charges will be filed against the man who put Neely in that choke hold. He was questioned by police and released. Now, to the border crisis with officials bracing for a rush of migrants when that pandemic border restriction known as Title 42 expires next week. The Biden administration facing bipartisan criticism. And tonight, the Homeland Security Secretary is responding in an interview with Julia Ainsley. (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) JULIA AINSLEY, NBC NEWS HOMELAND SECURITY CORRESPONDENT (voiceover): Tonight, just a week from the lifting of that border restriction known as Title 42, growing numbers of migrants crossing into the U.S. All as the Border Patrol expects illegal border crossings will spike to 10,000 per day when Title 42 lifts. Are you worried about Title 42 lifting next week? ALEJANDRO MAYORKAS, U.S. SECRETARY OF HOMELAND SECURITY: I`m not worried about Title 42 lifting. We recognize the challenge at the border. Our responsibility is to plan and to execute on those plans. And that is indeed what we have done and continue to do. AINSLEY: Homeland Security Secretary Alejandro Mayorkas here to talk to border agents. The Biden administration has faced criticism over its border policies amid a record number of illegal border crossings. Mayorkas insisting the policies are working. Is our border secure? MAYORKAS: Our border is secure. The border is secure because we are maximizing our resources to deliver the most effective results to our border with the most extraordinary workforce in the world. AINSLEY: But Hidalgo County Sheriff Eddie Guerra disagrees. Is our border secure? EDDIE GUERRA, SHERIFF, HIDALGO COUNTY: Well, I can tell you no. There`s a lot of places on the southwestern border that the -- our federal partners do not have control. (END VIDEOTAPE) AINSLEY: As for the bipartisan proposal in Congress to extend Title 42, Secretary Mayorkas told us that the Biden administration has already tried to end Title 42 several times, and now is the time to do so. Lester? HOLT: All right, Julia, thank you. Just ours are now, something that Britain and the world have not seen in seven decades, the core nation of a new British monarch. Keir Simmons is watching it all for us from London. (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) KEIR SIMMONS, NBC NEWS CHIEF INTERNATIONAL CORRESPONDENT (voiceover): The night before the biggest day of his life, King Charles smiling and laughing. Palace officials say he`s shown no sign of nerves. Today, the Princess of Wales pictured with two first ladies, Jill Biden and Ukraine`s Olena Zelenska . The King, William and Catherine greeting the public earlier. WILLIAM, PRINCE OF WALES: How are you doing? SIMMONS : The Princess asked how the children are feeling. Prince George will be a page of honor tomorrow. CATHERINE, PRINCESS OF WALES He`s excited, a bit nervous. Obviously with a big day ahead. But, No, can`t wait actually. SIMMONS : Even taking a cell phone to console someone`s American relative too ill to make it. CATHERINE: I hope you get back as soon. SIMMONS : The crowds have already camped along the world-famous Mall for a glimpse of history tomorrow morning. At 5:20 Eastern, a small procession will leave Buckingham Palace with the King to Westminster Abbey. Then the solemn service, not seen this century, will commence. The moment of crowning is expected around 7:00 a.m. Next, a breathtaking spectacle. From the Abbey, a 4,000-strong military parade would escort the King along this route. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: And he won`t answer questions about why. SIMMONS : But polls show enthusiasm for the monarchy waning and protesters will be out too. GRAHAM SMITH, CEO, REPUBLIC: I would think the monarchy is in a lot of trouble because they`ve lost their star player. SIMMONS : The King is looking to answer those critics by combining tradition with change tomorrow. Manju Malhi, a chef, has been invited for her charity work. MANJU MALHI, CHEF: I feel included and very inclusive and part of British history being a daughter of an immigrant. (END VIDEOTAPE) SIMMONS : Meanwhile, Prince Harry is here in London tonight. He will not play a formal role tomorrow. But Buckingham Palace is not saying who will appear on the famous balcony behind me. They say we`ll find out when it happens. Lester? HOLT: All right, Keir Simmons in London, thank you. In 60 seconds, the landmark moment in the fight against COVID. Plus, why trade schools are becoming the bold new trend in education. And the battle over birth control. The FDA is set to consider whether a pill can be sold over the counter. (COMMERCIAL BREAK) [19:15:00] HOLT: We are back with a remarkable announcement from the World Health Organization that the COVID global health emergency is officially over. It`s a milestone three years after the start of the pandemic that killed millions in upended economies across the globe. Officials say vaccines and high levels of immunity significantly cut the risk, but they caution the virus is still a threat. Turning out of the economy less than four weeks away from the country potentially defaulting if there`s no deal to raise the debt ceiling. Economists say that will be catastrophic. Still, markets close sharply higher today as the economy added 253,000 jobs last month and unemployment fell to 3.4 percent. Catie Beck now on the uncertainty that lies ahead. (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) CATIE BECK, NBC NEWS CORRESPONDENT (voiceover): President Biden today highlighting the good. JOE BIDEN , PRESIDENT OF THE UNITED STATES: Unemployment rate is at 3.4 percent, which is the lowest in 50 years. BECK: But accusing Republicans who want spending cuts of putting the economy at risk over the debt ceiling. BIDEN: They`re trying to hold the debt hostage to us to agree to some draconian cuts, magnificently difficult and damaging cuts. BECK: A possible default on the debt along with rising interest rates and ongoing turmoil among banks fueling fears of a recession. But an uncertain economic future is something Abbie Carlson is preparing for. Her decision to go to trade school wasn`t easy one. ABBIE CARLSON, STUDIES AT A TRADE SCHOOL: People are finding out that with a four-year degree, they`re not making a whole lot of money off the bat and they`re ending up with all of debt. BECK: She`ll graduate with none thanks to state funding for the program. Carlson will finish her training in welding in October. Is the common knowledge among students, we`re going to be hired right away when we leave here? CARLSON: Yes, 100 percent. If you don`t leave with a job, it`s on you. BECK: Tennessee College of Applied Technology President Nathan Garrett says there`s a waitlist to get in. NATHAN GARRETT, PRESIDENT, COLLEGE OF APPLIED TECHNOLOGY: I think at the end of the day, people are really looking at where`s the value at? BECK: Trade program enrollment is surging with big spikes in construction up almost seven percent, and mechanic and repair programs up five percent last fall, while undergraduate college enrollment has declined in recent years. CARLSON: I have hope for the future like I never did before. BECK: Hopeful for opportunity even in an uncertain economy. Catie Beck, NBC News, Nashville. (END VIDEOTAPE) HOLT: Still ahead tonight, the battle over birth control as the FDA gets sent away in and whether to sell pills without a prescription. (COMMERCIAL BREAK) [19:20:00] HOLT: A revolutionary change could be coming to birth control, pills sold without a prescription. A group of FDA advisors is set to meet next week to consider the measure. Maggie Vespa has details. (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) MAGGIE VESPA, NBC NEWS CORRESPONDENT (voiceover): In an era of historic shifts in reproductive health, a push for an American first over the counter, birth control pills. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: I think that`s great. I feel like it`s necessary. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: Without a doubt, this is a right that everybody should have access to. VESPA: Advisors to the Food and Drug Administration meeting next week to review drug maker Perrigo`s application to sell its oral contraceptive, Opil, over the counter. It`s been available for 50 years with a prescription like all birth control pills in the U.S. Perrigo aiming to offer it to all women and teens, no doctor needed. DR. KRISTYN BRANDI, FELLOW, AMERICAN COLLEGE OF OBSTETRICIANS AND GYNECOLOGISTS : I`m surprised that this hasn`t happened already. People can self-screen. People can read instructions. And so, we shouldn`t be limiting people`s access to care. VESPA: It`s unclear how much Opil would cost, whether it would be available on store shelves or behind a pharmacist counter and whether a minor would need parental consent. An initial FDA review, flagging concerns about whether adolescents can understand the label`s instructions and whether current and former breast cancer patients, who the FDA says should not be on hormonal birth control, would know to avoid it. Perrigo writing its application demonstrates that Opil is safe and effective. Experts noting any decision on Opil will have no impact on other prescription birth controls or on lawsuits over the abortion pill, Mifepristone. (END VIDEOTAPE) VESPA (on camera): The FDA`s final decision on the push to sell Opil over the counter is expected this summer. Lester? HOLT: All right, Maggie, thank you. When we come back, London`s monarchy mania. Just how far some travel to be in the middle of all the royal excitement. (COMMERCIAL BREAK) [19:25:00] HOLT: Finally tonight, the Royal fans who traveled across the pond for a front-row seat to King Charles` coronation. Here`s Kelly Cobiella. (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) KELLY COBIELLA, NBC NEWS FOREIGN CORRESPONDENT (voiceover): Tonight, the flags are flying, the horses prancing, the crowds dressed in their best red, white, and blue for the first coronation in 70 years. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: It`s just an awesome time to witness history. I mean, we haven`t done this in our lifetimes. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: Yes. COBIELLA: The monarch`s smiling face is everywhere, from windows to fridge magnets. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: He`s our king. He`s going to be our super king. COBIELLA: A super king with super fans. And we found plenty of Americans. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: I just love it. I just absolutely eat it up. COBIELLA: Braving the rain for a front-row seat to history. Cassandra Estrella Rocha from California changed her vacation plans to be here. Have you been camping here? CASSANDRA ESTRELLA ROCHA FROM CALIFORNIA, AMERICAN TOURIST: Yes. COBIELLA: Oh, my gosh. ROCHA: And I`m not a camper. COBIELLA: Why? ROCHA: I want to be a part of history. Like, I just think -- you know, in America, we don`t have things like this, right? COBIELLA: As the skies cleared, surprise handshakes from the King, telling greatest hits radio London News -- CHARLES III, KING OF THE UNITED KINGDOM: Rain`s a blessing, except for your camera. COBIELLA: A smiling king, a cheering crowd, and tomorrow, the crowning moment. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: I think he`s an amazing, amazing guy, and I`m proud to be a Brit. Long live the queen -- the king. COBIELLA: Kelly Cobiella, NBC News, London. (END VIDEOTAPE) HOLT: And NBC`s coverage of Charles` coronation starts at 5:00 a.m. Eastern tomorrow morning. That`s NIGHTLY NEWS for this Friday. Thank you for watching, everyone. I`m Lester Holt. Please take care of yourself and each other. Good night. (COMMERCIAL BREAK) END Content and programming copyright 2023 NBCUniversal. headline: New Guidelines For Breast Cancer Screening
story_text: LESTER HOLT: There is major news tonight about women in breast cancer. Government experts now say mammograms should begin much earlier, at age 40. Erin McLaughlin has details. (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) ERIN MCLAUGHLIN, NBC NEWS CORRESPONDENT (voiceover): Tonight, a leading health panel now recommending mammogram screenings for breast cancer begin for women at age 40, a full decade sooner than the panel`s previous guidelines. Experts say it`s about time. DR. MAXINE JOCHELSON, CHIEF OF BREAST IMAGING, MEMORIAL SLOAN KETTERING : The science has always been there. That`s why many of us have been recommending 40 for years. MCLAUGHLIN (on camera): So, finally this panel is listening to that science? JOCHELSON: Yes. MCLAUGHLIN (voiceover): The draft recommendations come from the U.S. preventative Services Task Force. They say the new guidelines could save 20 percent more lives across the board for all women, emphasizing the new guidelines are especially important for black women. DR. CAROL MANGIONE, US. PREVENTIVE SERVICES TASK FORCE: Black women are 40 percent more likely to die from breast cancer than white women if they get it. They also are more likely to get more aggressive forms of breast cancer. MCLAUGHLIN: The panel stopping short of recommending annual mammogram screenings, maintaining that women still screen every two years. MCLAUGHLIN (on camera): Does this recommendation go far enough? JOCHELSON: No. MCLAUGHLIN (voiceover): She argues women 40 and over should get screenings every year and says women should start talking with their doctors about risk factors at age 25. Still, experts are hopeful these new recommendations will help send a more consistent message. [19:15:13] MANGIONE: The most important thing for women to know is to begin screening at the age of 40 because it just might save your life. MCLAUGHLIN: Erin McLaughlin, NBC News. HOLT: In a moment, NBC News investigates work contracts with the nation`s largest hospital chain nurses say they`ve been a threat to their health and yours. headline: Frustrated Over Getting Quality Care: What Mothers To Be Want In The Delivery Room
story_text: [19:20:00] LESTER HOLT: As Mother`s Day approaches, we`re reminded pregnancy and childbirth can come with health risks. And for Black women, those risks are significantly higher. Zinhle Essamuah now on why more mothers are working with doulas. (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) ZINHLE ESSAMUAH, NBC NEWS CORRESPONDENT (voiceover): Kanaiah King`s (ph) first pregnancy in 2021 was traumatic. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: Good job. Everything that could go wrong went wrong. ESSAMUAH (voiceover): She went into labor early at just 24 weeks and had a serious infection. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: You know, doctors kind of use the big words, thinking you would know, but I didn`t. It was my first time. ESSAMUAH (voiceover): But the St. Louis native had support from a doula, Robin Lloyd. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: Ms. Robin would literally stop them like, hey, stop. Let me talk to her. And she would tell me exactly what it meant. ESSAMUAH (voiceover): Birthing doulas are trained nonclinical professionals who support clients through pregnancy, labor, delivery, and postpartum. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: We all are going through the same thing. ESSAMUAH (voiceover): The doulas offer one-on-one education. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: No question is a dumb question. ESSAMUAH (voiceover): And group courses for expectant and new moms. Kanaiah credits Robin for helping her get through it all? ESSAMUAH: What are you feeling? UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: I`m very grateful for her. I`m very grateful for her. Because if she wasn`t there, I don`t know what would have happened. ESSAMUAH: Do you think you would be here and your kids would be here if you hadn`t had a doula? UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: Not at all, no. ESSAMUAH (voiceover): The American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists finding doulas-improved outcomes for women and labor. They`re especially critical for Black women, who are three times more likely to die from a pregnancy-related cause than White women. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: You`re so cute. ESSAMUAH (voiceover): Kanaiah`s doula, Robin, works with the nonprofit Parents as Teachers, motivated by her own life-threatening delivery. The nonprofit received state funding, making it possible to provide doula services to families cost-free. Of the nearly 320 families they serve, many unhoused, 95 percent are people of color, and all of their doulas are Black women. ESSAMUAH: Why is it particularly important for women of color and Black women to have access to them? UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: Well, I think -- I think access is the key. We wanted to make sure that we had Black doulas serving those families that resemble them. ESSAMUAH (voiceover): Now, Kanaiah is expecting a baby boy in just a few weeks with Robin by her side. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: I`m going to be there. You know, you`re going to have that support and not to worry. ESSAMUAH (voiceover): Zinhle Essamuah, NBC News, St. Louis, Missouri. headline: A Federal Appeals Court Hearing Arguments On Limiting Access Nationwide To A Widely Used Abortion Pill, A Fight Ultimately Heading To The Supreme Court
story_text: LESTER HOLT: Now to the battle over abortion. A federal appeals court hearing arguments on limiting access nationwide to a widely used abortion pill, a fight ultimately heading to the Supreme Court, while some states restrict abortion further. Here`s Laura Jarrett. (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) LAURA JARRETT, NBC NEWS SENIOR LEGAL CORRESPONDENT (voiceover): Tonight, the most commonly used abortion pill still on the market, but its legal future uncertain. A federal appeals court appearing deeply skeptical today of arguments from the Biden administration and pill manufacturer as they try to keep Mifepristone available. JAMES HO, JUDGE: I don`t understand this theme. The FDA can do no wrong. We are allowed to look at the FDA, just like we`re allowed to look at any agency. JARRETT (voiceover): The three-judge panel must decide what to do with that controversial decision out of Texas last month, which invalidated the FDA`s longtime approval of the drug. One judge hearing the case appointed by George W. Bush , the other two by Donald Trump. All have a history of supporting abortion restrictions. Judge James Ho calling abortion a moral tragedy in a 2018 case. The stakes of what happens to a pill women can currently get in the mail even higher now with new abortion restrictions emerging at the state level. TIM MOORE, HOUSE SPEAKER, NORTH CAROLINA: We needed to take action to protect the unborn. JARRETT (voiceover): Overnight in North Carolina, a GOP supermajority banned most abortions after 12 weeks with few exceptions, overriding the governor`s veto. DR. BEVERLY GRAY, OBSTETRICS AND GYNECOLOGY ASSOCIATE PROFESSOR, DUKE UNIVERSITY : The law is incredibly arbitrary. And it was crafted by people who are not physicians. It`s really important to note that when there`s a list of exceptions, someone is always left out. JARRETT (voiceover): North Carolina had been an outlier among the sea of states that restricted access after the Supreme Court decided women don`t have a constitutional right to an abortion. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: Every pregnancy threatens the life of mothers. JARRETT (voiceover): In neighboring South Carolina, a six-week ban like Florida`s is on the horizon. (END VIDEOTAPE) [19:10:07] HOLT: So, Laura, help me understand where we are. The -- it`s for the abortion pill. The justices agreed last month to keep it on the market during the appeal process. JARRETT (on camera): That`s exactly right, Lester. And there`s no deadline for the appeals court to rule on Mifepristone. But once it makes a decision, the case is inevitably headed back to the Supreme Court for a final say. HOLT: All right, Laura Jarrett, thanks. JARRETT: Sure. HOLT: President Biden is heading to Asia tonight for the G7 summit as the U.S. inches closer to a critical default deadline. Kristen Welker is in Hiroshima. Kristen, the President with a clear message before leaving today. KRISTEN WELKER, NBC NEWS CHIEF WHITE HOUSE CORRESPONDENT: Lester, that`s right. President Biden projecting optimism with just 15 days to reach a deal to raise the debt limit or risk economic calamity. While still in Washington, the President said he`s confident the country won`t default, calling a meeting with top congressional leaders this week productive. The president has cut short part of this critical diplomatic trip to deal with the crisis. But despite that, Republican House Speaker Kevin McCarthy blasting Mr. Biden this afternoon for going overseas at all before a deal is done. Lester? HOLT: Kristen Welker, thank you. GUTIERREZ (voiceover): He then says he dropped them back off at the police precinct where a different car eventually took them home. Prince Harry , of course, has railed against the paparazzi for much of his life, accusing them of invading his privacy. HARRY, DUKE OF SUSSEX: I had to do everything I could to protect my family. Breaking news from Ukraine tonight. Another American volunteer, former Green Beret, has been killed in battle there. Molly Hunter has more on his decision to fight as new images show the immense toll of war in the east. (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) MOLLY HUNTER, NBC NEWS FOREIGN CORRESPONDENT (voiceover): Tonight, as this grinding war continues to rob young Ukrainian lives on the battlefield, the family of American volunteer soldier Nicholas Maimer telling NBC News he was killed on Ukraine`s front lines. NICHOLAS MAIMER, AMERICAN KILLED IN UKRAINE: I had that strong internal debate on whether I should, what I could contribute, you know, should I accept the risk? GOSK: So, they go to places where people are vulnerable. STERN: Drunk. People are vulnerable. They`re drunk. They`re having good time. GOSK (voiceover): Joanna Stern covers tech for the Wall Street Journal. She`s done a series of reports exposing a new crime wave. Phones being ripped off at bars leading to tens of thousands of dollars stolen and Apple accounts locked. STERN: I was blown away by how many people I heard from that had been to different cities across the U. S. GOSK (voiceover): NBC`s digital team also helped uncover a ring of thieves allegedly targeting gay bars in Manhattan. Victims are drugged. Their phones stolen. Two men John Umberger and Julio Ramirez overdosed and died. Three suspects are charged with murder. Taylor Ashie says he too was drugged and a victim of theft, waking up after a night out and realizing his phone was gone. TAYLOR ASHIE, VICTIM OF THEFT: I immediately got up, went to check my computer to see what was going on. I had about 20 to 25 fraud alert emails. GOSK (voiceover): He says the thieves changed his Apple ID password, locked him out, and then went on a shopping spree. ASHIE: They added my credit cards to Apple Pay which I had not previously used, and then they went around New York City using my phone as a credit card. GOSK (voiceover): Ashie would get roughly $15,000 back but what he couldn`t get restored was his Apple account. ASHIE: Hours of conversations with Apple , support staff. I never received my information back. GOSK: We`re talking about personal photos, contacts? ASHIE: Both. GOSK (voiceover): The key is getting the passcode. GOSK: How quickly can you change my Apple ID? STERN: All right, so I`m going to tap here at the top. This is your iCloud or Apple ID area. I`m going to password and security. I`m going to change password. I`m going to put in your passcode. It`s in. Is that right? GOSK: And you`re there. STERN: And I`m there. GOSK (voiceover): It took her 18 seconds. But there`s more. STERN: These thieves on the streets know how to enable something that`s a pretty hidden setting. It`s called this recovery key. GOSK (voiceover): The recovery key is supposed to add another layer of protection. STERN: The problem is that the thieves have the recovery key. Once you`ve changed someone`s Apple ID password and turned on this recovery key, it`s basically game over for the person whose account that is. GOSK (voiceover): In a statement, Apple says we take all attacks on our users very seriously no matter how rare. We work tirelessly every day to protect our user`s accounts and data and are always investigating additional protections. There are some steps to take. Make the passcode on the iPhone stronger like using six digits instead of four. STERN: You can also go here to passcode options and do a custom alphanumeric code. GOSK (voiceover): Another option is going to screen time, then content and privacy restrictions where there are several places you can add a four- digit code that will block access. The changes will make the phone less convenient. ASHIE: I feel like it`s Fort Knox on my phone now. GOSK (voiceover): But with life`s most important information in the palm of your hand, the hassle may be worth it. Stephanie Gosk, NBC News New York. (END VIDEOTAPE) HOLT: When we come back, the astonishing new images of the Titanic like you`ve never seen it before. (COMMERCIAL BREAK) [19:25:00] HOLT: Finally, astonishing new 3D images of a Titanic providing the most captivating view yet of the shipwreck. Here`s Tom Costello. (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) TOM COSTELLO, NBC NEWS CORRESPONDENT (voiceover): The images are breathtaking in their clarity and detail. The Titanic broken in two, 1200 feet below the North Atlantic. Too big for a single photo, the new 3D scan combining 700,000 images reveals the full scale of the disaster. The bow covered in rust. It`s anchor still attached. The boiler room where workers shoveled coal to keep the lights on. The propeller, its serial number, still legible. Scattered on the ocean floor unopened champagne bottles, shoes, hats and jewelry. 1500 people died that day in 1912. Edith Haisman was just 16 on board with her parents. We talked to her in 1996. EDITH HAISMAN, TITANIC SURVIVOR: I`ll never forget it, see all the dead bodies floating in the sea. It was terrible. COSTELLO (voiceover): A deep sea mapping company used submersibles to create this 360-degree view. Coming soon, a documentary looking at how an iceberg cut open a ship once branded unsinkable. COSTELLO: This makes the Titanic tragedy much more real. ANTHONY GEFFEN, CEO AND CREATIVE DIRECTOR, ATLANTIC PRODUCTIONS: There`s no doubt about that. People around the world will be able to walk around the Titanic for themselves and they`ll be able to see the wreck, they`ll be able to see the debris field. This is a history where we can live in the past. COSTELLO (voiceover): A virtual view preserved forever. Tom Costello, NBC News, Washington. (END VIDEOTAPE) HOLT: The fascination continues. That`s NIGHTLY NEWS for this Wednesday. Thank you for watching. I`m Lester Holt. Please take care of yourself and each other. Good night.
