headline: Joe Biden Trying To Salvage Domestic Agenda Legislation; Social Spending Bill Cost Still Uncertain; New Subpoena Issued To Clinton- Connected Law Firm; Polls Show Glenn Youngkin And Terry Mcauliffe In Tight Race; McAuliffe And Youngkin Spar In Fiery Debate; Youngkin Faces McAuliffe In Virginia Gubernatorial Race; Youngkin Relationship With Former President; Schools Nationwide Deal With Staff Shortages; Defense Department Officials Testify Before Senate Concerning Intelligence On Imminent Collapse Of Kabul Government In Afghanistan After U.S. Troop Withdrawal; North Korean Leader Kim Jong-un Makes Diplomatic Overtures To South Korea; Democrats Continue Negotiations Over Passing Bipartisan Infrastructure Bill And Budget Reconciliation Bill
story_text: MARTHA MACCALLUM, FOX NEWS CHANNEL HOST: SPECIAL REPORT is up next. Hello there, Bret Baier. BRET BAIER, FOX NEWS CHANNEL HOST: I don't know what I would do if I saw that coming down the aisle. I'm not sure. All right, Martha, thank you. Good evening, welcome to Washington, I'm Bret Baier. Breaking tonight, does she have the votes tonight or not? A question frequently heard on Capitol Hill in the past few hours, all about House Speaker Nancy Pelosi and a potential vote on a bipartisan infrastructure bill $1.2 trillion without a massive reconciliation spending bill at $3.5 trillion. Frantic phone calls, meetings at the White House and on Capitol Hill, progressives versus moderates. But Democratic Senator Joe Manchin from West Virginia put his foot down today, a $3.5 trillion bill will not get his needed vote in the Senate. So, what will? That's where we are at this hour at this minute. There was a victory for leadership today in the form of legislation to avoid a partial federal government shutdown at least until early December, punting that fiscal cliff a few months. But most things including a debt ceiling increase and the future of the Biden legislative agenda hanging in the balance tonight as SPECIAL REPORT kicks off. We have Fox team coverage, Jacqui Heinrich at the White House tells us what the administration is doing to try to get the key votes. But we begin with Congressional Correspondent Chad Pergram on Capitol Hill with where things stand. Good evening, Chad. CHAD PERGRAM, FOX NEWS CHANNEL CONGRESSIONAL CORRESPONDENT (on camera): Good evening, Bret. It's Democrat against Democrat, the left battling centrist. Moderate Democrat Joe Manchin calling 3.5 trillion in social spending "fiscal insanity". For days Manchin said he was not negotiating a price tag. But a memo obtained by Fox says Manchin has been committed to only 1.5 trillion since summertime. Manchin says he worries about the nation becoming a welfare state. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) SEN. JOE MANCHIN (D-WV): I don't fault any of them who believe that they're much more progressive and much more liberal. God bless them. And all they need to do is we have to elect more -- I guess for them to get theirs, elect more liberals. PERGRAM (voice over): That inflame the left, protesters heckling Manchin at the Capitol . UNIDENTIFIED MALE: Joe Manchin is a traitor, (INAUDIBLE). REP. ALEXANDRIA OCASIO-CORTEZ (D-NY): So, this is really about the deficit, then maybe we go after our defense spending and find our savings there instead of going after people's childcare. PERGRAM: Liberals now threatened to yank their support from the bipartisan infrastructure bill scheduled for a vote today. REP. PRAMILA JAYAPAL (D-WA): We reiterated this again to the speaker and we're in the same place that we will not be able to vote for the reconcile -- for the infrastructure bill until the reconciliation bill has passed. PERGRAM: As many as 50 progressives could vote no, more than 10 GOP members could vote yes. But the math doesn't add up. It begs the question, is the president's domestic agenda too ambitious in a split Senate and a House with a three-vote margin? REP. NANCY PELOSI , (D-CA): From what I imply from -- infer from what you say is that we should have just done nothing because we had a slim majority? That's not who we are. No, it's not too big. No, it's not too big. In fact, it will be a compromise. (END VIDEO CLIP) PERGRAM: Pelosi believes the bill will pass maybe later tonight. The House Majority Whip Jim Clyburn says he hasn't whipped the vote and some good news Congress voted to avert a government shutdown. Tonight, the lights remain on until December 3rd, Bret. BAIER: Chad Pergram up on the Hill. Chad, thanks. We'll head back for any breaking details. President Biden has taken a hit as we've told you in the polls recently, but that has not stopped him and his staff from working the phones, trying to cut deals and get those key votes on Capitol Hill. What we do know tonight is that the price tag for his agenda appears to be dropping overall. Here's White House Correspondent Jacqui Heinrich. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) JACQUI HEINRICH, FOX NEWS CHANNEL CORRESPONDENT (voice over): After days of talks brokered by the White House, a new but fluid price tag on President Biden's social infrastructure package, no longer $3.5 trillion, now somewhere in the low to mid $2 trillion range with the caveat that nothing appears to be final. Perceived progress was drowned out when a leaked memo Senator Joe Manchin sent to Chuck Schumer this summer put with the West Virginia Democrats top line number at 1.5 trillion in social spending. MANCHIN: I've never been -- I've never been a liberal in any way, shape or form. There's no one has ever thought I was. HEINRICH: Progressives patience wearing thin, feeling emboldened to tank support for the hard infrastructure bill that still needs to pass the House. The roads and bridges funding touted by the president as a bipartisan win in front of the Oval Office now hanging in the balance, adding pressure for the president who campaigned on his ability to unite people to pull his own party together. Some people say that it appears that progressives are running the show, they're banding together and making their demands. Other people are saying looks like Joe Manchin is playing president. So, who is in charge? JEN PSAKI , WHITE HOUSE PRESS SECRETARY: Well, this is how democracy works. We're not trying to paint over how messy it looks from the outside, we know that. But what the good news is, is that there is agreement that among most Democrats, if not every single one of them that we need to get something done. HEINRICH: Republicans say the food fight that's been playing out is no surprise. SEN. MARCO RUBIO (R-FL): They have these radical left-wing nut cases who basically want to -- they want it to be seven trillion, not 3.5 trillion, and they think 3.5 trillion is a compromise. Joe Biden wasn't elected because he was Joe Biden . He was elected as a vessel, right? He was -- he's there because he became sort of an instrument for the far left and now dominates the Democratic Party to pursue their agenda. (END VIDEO CLIP) HEINRICH (on camera): Now, there was some talk at the White House today that the president might go to the Hill at some point. At this point, it doesn't appear that that's going to be happening. White House aides were huddled in Speaker Pelosi is office for hours trying to strike some sort of a deal and we haven't gotten any updates from that, Bret. BAIER: OK, we'll follow it. Jacqui Heinrich live in the North Lawn. Jacqui, thank you. Stocks were off today. The Dow lost 547, the S&P 500 fell 52, the NASDAQ dropped 64. Also breaking tonight, there is more movement in the investigation into the origins of the Trump Russia collusion probe. The special prosecutor John Durham is going after another individual with connections to Hillary Clinton . Correspondent David Spunt is live tonight from the Justice Department with the latest specifics. Good evening, David. DAVID SPUNT, FOX NEWS CHANNEL CORRESPONDENT (on camera): Bret, good evening to you. The announcement of this subpoena tonight comes just a couple of weeks after a former Clinton campaign attorney from 2016 was indicted by special counsel Durham for lying to the FBI . Fox News can confirm tonight that this subpoena specifically involves a man named Rodney Joffe according to a source with knowledge of the investigation. Our sources Bret, they tell us that Joffe's name appears in the indictment of Michael Sussman. Sussman is the former Perkins Coie attorney who the special counsel says brought information to the FBI about an alleged server the Trump campaign used to communicate with the Kremlin through a Russian bank. Information Bret, that just did not pan out. Joffe's attorney denounced the allegation of Fox News saying in part, this indictment of cherry picked portions of e-mails and selective facts that gratuitously present an incomplete and misleading picture of his actions and role in the events in question. It is not clear in what capacity Michael Sussman was acting as against the Trump campaign. According to special counsel Durham, Sussman claimed he was doing it as a good citizen when he delivered the information. In 2-1/2 years, John Durham charged two people in the probes, Sussman and this man Kevin Clinesmith, a former FBI attorney who pleaded guilty to falsifying a document used to apply for the application to surveil Trump campaign aide Carter Page . (END VIDEO CLIP) SPUNT (on camera): While Clinesmith pleaded guilty, there's no indication that Sussman wants to do so. He plans to fight this case. But Bret, this subpoena tonight is significant because it shows that John Durham is still hard at work at this case. More than 2-1/2 years later, Bret. BAIER: We'll follow it. David, thank you. Former Trump campaign manager Corey Lewandowski is out of a job tonight. This follows an accusation he inappropriately touched a female Trump fundraiser during a recent charity dinner. He will no longer be leading former President Trump's Make America Great Again political action committee. Up next, we will talk with the Republican gubernatorial nominee in Virginia who's giving a former governor -- Democratic governor a tougher than expected fight for his old job. We'll also have brand new Fox News polls on this bellwether race. First, here's what some of our Fox affiliates around the country are covering tonight. Fox 4 in Dallas-Fort Worth were four firefighters and four civilians were taken to the hospital after a gas explosion at an apartment complex. The blast shattered windows on neighboring buildings, throwing debris into a nearby field. Nearly 300 people are out of their homes as firefighters investigate that incident. KHON in Honolulu where the Kilauea volcano erupts for the second time in a year. Lava fountains cover the floor of the crater on the Big Island as clouds of volcanic ash and gas rise into the air. Official say the eruption is contained to that crater and no residents are in danger there. And this is a live look at Cleveland from our affiliate Fox 8, the big story there tonight, are you feeling lucky? A gas station in Powell, Ohio sold a $2 million winning ticket in the latest Powerball drawing. The winner has 180 days from now to claim the prize, so check your tickets on that. But the Powerball jackpot is now $620 million for Saturday's drawing, the sixth highest ever. So, there you go. That's tonight's live look outside the Beltway from SPECIAL REPORT. We'll be right back. (COMMERCIAL BREAK) BAIER: The Virginia governor's race appears to be much closer than many people had expected. Our latest Fox polls has Republican Glenn Youngkin trailing by only four percentage points to former governor Democratic nominee Terry McAuliffe . The margin of error there you see is plus three, minus three. Both men have 79 percent certainty among their supporters. The top issue for McAuliffe's people, the coronavirus pandemic. Youngkin's supporters are most concerned about the economy. Tonight, we're talking with Republican nominee Glenn Youngkin. Thanks for coming in. GLENN YOUNGKIN (R), GUBERNATORIAL CANDIDATE OF VIRGINIA: Bret, thank you for having me. And I just appreciate the fact that this race is front and front and center on your mind because it's front and center in Virginian's minds and we have a chance to chart a different direction in Virginia and I'm looking forward to having voters come to the polls over the next 32 days and decide this. BAIER: You know, a lot of people look at it as a bellwether, especially in this current environment. You've had a couple of debates now, one just the other night which we -- which we covered. Polls are one thing, but where do you see the race and what issues are most important from your point of view? YOUNGKIN: Well, the race is a toss-up right now. I feel amazing amount of momentum, particularly over the last six to seven weeks as we've been talking to voters and listening to voters about cutting taxes and fixing our schools and making our communities safe again, and getting our economy moving. There's a lot of Virginians who are really concerned about whether their job is going to be there for them. And so, those are the areas that we're focused most on. And that is where Virginians are focused most on. And you're right, Bret, this race has national importance because what happens in Virginia is going to have a huge impact on what happens in congressional elections next year, and this is our chance for Virginians to come together and speak for the whole country. BAIER: You know, one of the issues, I want to talk to you about schools, because that got a lot of attention. And you made one answer into an ad right away, but I want to talk about another issue that wasn't covered as much, and that's abortion and the difference between you two. Let's take a listen to this exchange. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) YOUNGKIN: I am pro-life. I do believe in exceptions in the case where there's rape or incest, or the mother's life is in jeopardy. My opponent, on the other hand, is the most extreme abortion candidate in the country. He actually has said he's going to promote Virginia businesses to come. For companies to come to Virginia because it's the easiest place to get an abortion. I think that's shameful. TERRY MCAULIFFE (D), GUBERNATORIAL CANDIDATE, VIRGINIA: I want every woman in Virginia to listen to me closely. I was a brick wall to protect women's rights when I was governor. The businesses that I brought to Virginia, Amazon , Google , Facebook , Microsoft -- (CROSSTALK) UNIDENTIFIED MALE: OK, thank you. MCAULIFFE: They are not coming to a state that discriminates against women. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: Thank you. MCAULIFFE: They're not. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: Mr. -- MCAULIFFE: Half the stuff he said came from outer space tonight. I mean, he literally could have had a tinfoil hat on. (END VIDEO CLIP) BAIER: So, it seems like there's a big chasm on the issue of abortion. But what about his charge that, that what you were saying is not right? YOUNGKIN: Well, it's -- he's -- Terry does one thing this entire election, which is combat truth with his untruths. I mean, he said that he would sign the bill that would use taxpayer money to fund abortions up through and including birth. He said it was common-sense legislation and that he would sign it. And now he wants to try to walk away from that. This is what he does. This is what a 43-year career politician who's been working in the swamp his whole life does is defend something by saying it's untrue. The reality is that Terry McAuliffe is the most pro-abortion candidate in America. The vast majority of Virginians disagree with his position. And to say that companies are going to come to Virginia because we have the most liberal abortion laws is absolutely insanity. We just watched Ford Motor Company make a decision with four plants. They put two in Kentucky, one in Tennessee, and one in Georgia. And let me tell you, Ford was making a decision based on workforce, on site of male availability, on the ability to make sure that that state is going to maintain their right to work status. And Terry McAuliffe has threatened to get rid of right to work. He's told everybody he'll sign the bill. That will be a death blow for Virginia's business community. (CROSSTALK) BAIER: Yes. YOUNGKIN: And I'm going to protect right to work. And this is absolutely on the ballot, and Terry McAuliffe 's on the wrong side of it. BAIER: Well, listen, the most important issues according to our latest Fox poll, number one is the economy, number two is the coronavirus, and what happens with that down the line, you get to abortion, crime, education. When it comes to coronavirus, will there be an effort, if your governor to repeal rollback vaccine mandates, mask mandates that Governor Northam in Virginia has put in place? YOUNGKIN: Yes, I believe that everyone in Virginia should get the vaccine, and I'm going to work tirelessly to help people get the best information so that they can make a decision for themselves to get it. Of course, what Terry McAuliffe wants to do is have companies fire people who don't get the vaccine. I mean, here we are coming out of a pandemic. And Virginia is ranked 44th in the nation when it comes to job recovery. And Terry McAuliffe wants companies to fire their employees if they don't get the vaccine. I mean, this is what dictatorial leadership is all about. You know, if he doesn't like what the sheriff says, he yells at him the other day. If he doesn't like what she's -- what she -- what parents have to say about schools, he tells that he doesn't want you involved in their education. And in this case, when you actually want to make a decision about whether you get the vaccine or not, if you don't make the right decision for Terry McAuliffe , he wants your employer to fire you. BAIER: You know, in some places -- (CROSSTALK) YOUNGKIN: This is not leadership. This is not leadership. BAIER: In some places, President Joe Biden and his approval is a factor. In Virginia, according to our poll, it's about even: 50 to 49 approve disapprove. How much do you think what's happening federally, with the potential tax increases, other proposals affect your race come November? YOUNGKIN: Well, I think Virginians, just because of our proximity to Washington, D.C., pay a lot of attention to what's happening in Washington. But as I said earlier, I've talked to tens of thousands of Virginians and listen to their concerns. And they're worried about their jobs and the economy? Yes, they're worried that we have to manage our way through this pandemic. We want to do it together so we can protect both lives and livelihoods. They're worried about their kids' education. I mean, parents want their children to receive a great education, and they want to be involved in it. And what we've heard from Terry McAuliffe is he doesn't want them involved in it. And they're worried about public safety. I mean, we're at a 20-year high in murder rate in Virginia, shouldn't shock Terry because when he was governor, the murder rate went up 43 percent. And that's why all of the sheriffs in Virginia, I mean, 50 sheriffs have stood up for me. I was endorsed by -- I was endorsed by the FOP, I was endorsed by the Police Benevolent Association. They understand that I'm going to help Virginia have our community safe again, we're going to have the best jobs, we're going to have the best schools, we're going to cut taxes, we're going to lower the tax burden on Virginians, and that's what they're most, most important to them. BAIER: Last thing quickly, Terry McAuliffe and his campaign spent a lot of time trying to link you to Donald Trump . And he did that in the debate saying that you -- he was endorsed -- you were endorsed by Donald Trump , he said four times. If Donald Trump comes to Virginia, are you going to come campaign with them? YOUNGKIN: Well, first of all, when President Trump endorsed me, I thanked him for it. I was -- I was grateful for it. I've been endorsed by lots of Republicans, and we're bringing people together. This is a moment for us to bring Virginians together, forever Trumpers, folks that were never Trumpers, single-issue voters, but also Independents and Democrats. I think what you'll see in your poll is I'm winning amongst the Independents because they trust me. This is a moment for Virginians to come together and decide who they trust. They do not trust Terry McAuliffe . He's a 43-year-career political operative. He changes his mind every other week. He actually lies every other day or if not every other minute. BAIER: Yes. YOUNGKIN: And this is what's on the ballot. BAIER: Oh, yes. YOUNGKIN: This is why Virginians are coming together around me as the candidate. And I know Terry is seeing the polling numbers. He wishes he was running against somebody else. But it's Terry McAuliffe against Glenn Youngkin, and we are surging in momentum. And that's why I feel so good about the fact that we're going to win this fall and get Virginia move and come January. BAIER: Well, Glenn Youngkin, we appreciate your time. You're right, President Trump is not on the ballot. We will cover this race very closely. We've asked Terry McAuliffe to come on. We'll see if he does. We appreciate your time today. YOUNGKIN: Thank you so much for having me. I hope you have a great day. BAIER: Up next, pandemic vaccine mandates are creating staff shortages in schools. We'll take a look at that. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) MIGUEL CARDONA , UNITED STATES SECRETARY OF EDUCATION: It's all hands on deck. I think we have the right policy. SEN. TOMMY TUBERVILLE (R-AL): We can't shut down Alabama or some of these other states. SEN. PATTY MURRAY (D-WA): They are making denial a badge of honor. (END VIDEO CLIP) (COMMERCIAL BREAK) BAIER: Tomorrow is the deadline for New York City school staff to be vaccinated or risk losing their jobs that could lead to a major personnel problem. Many school districts throughout the country are dealing with similar issues because of the coronavirus pandemic. Rich Edson shows us tonight. RICH EDSON , FOX NEWS CHANNEL WASHINGTON CORRESPONDENT (voice-over): Teenagers on a party bus with neon lights and a stripper pole. The only ride earlier this month that a group of Boston high school students had for their field trip. Their neon substitute is just part of a nationwide campaign of impromptu fixes to major school staff shortages. Also, in Massachusetts, Governor Charlie Baker deployed about 250 National Guardsmen to drive school buses. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) CARDONA: It's all hands on deck. I think we have the right policy. EDSON: This morning on Capitol Hill, Education Secretary Miguel Cardona told the Senate committee that part of the solution is federal money for better salaries and training. CARDONA: If we're serious about reopening schools and making sure our children have the best opportunity to engage not only in the classroom, but extracurricular activities or getting to school on time, we have to make sure that we're addressing these workforce gaps boldly. EDSON: In Brooklyn, reports of staff shortages, forcing a school cafeteria to close. And starting Monday, the nation's largest school system, New York City, is requiring the bulk of its workers to show proof of vaccination. Union leaders there are warning of employee shortages. Others from states with lower vaccination rates say mandates there would create major problems in school districts. TUBERVILLE: We can't shut down Alabama or some of these other states simply for the fact that we might not be taking as many vaccines. EDSON: City officials in New York say they'll have 1000s of substitutes standing by for teachers who fail to present vaccination cards. Union officials say they're also concerned about staff beyond teachers like custodians, cafeteria workers, and safety officers. (END VIDEO CLIP) EDSON (on camera): Just this afternoon, a federal appeals court ruled New York State must temporarily allow vaccine exemptions for healthcare workers with religious objections. The judge will hear arguments in that case in a couple of weeks. Bret. BAIER: Thank you. Just in the past few minutes, we got word from our Supreme Court team Shannon Bream, Bill Mears, that some New York City teachers have filed an emergency request with the Supreme Court to block the vaccine mandate that is about to kick in based on geography alone. This filing would go to Justice Sotomayor, and she can decide alone or refer it to the full court. We will continue to watch this as it develops. The Senate Judiciary Committee is deadlocked tonight over President Biden's nominee for U.S. Attorney in Massachusetts. Suffolk County District Attorney Rachael Rollins is being opposed by Republicans who insist she is soft on crime. Senate Democrats must now hold a vote in the full chamber to bring up her nomination. The regional director of the International Red Cross is warning of a major humanitarian crisis in Afghanistan, because of severe financial shortfalls and the coming of winter. The U.S. withdrawal from that country has been a foreign policy crisis for President Biden and his team. The smoke is still clearing tonight after explosive testimony this week from the president's top defense advisors on Capitol Hill. National security correspondent Jennifer Griffin looks at the fallout from the Pentagon. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) GEN. MARK MILLEY , CHAIRMAN, JOINT CHIEFS OF STAFF: It's a real possibility in the not too distant future, 6, 12, 18, 24, 36 months, that time and timeframe for reconstitution of al-Qaeda or ISIS. JENNIFER GRIFFIN, FOX NEWS CHANNEL NATIONAL SECURITY CORRESPONDENT (voice- over): Just one of the stunning admissions from this week's hearing. Signs of collapse began in June, yet the White House did not halt the withdrawal. Documents obtained by Reuters show the Afghan Central Bank depleted its U.S. dollar reserves in the months before the Taliban took Kabul. LLOYD AUSTIN , DEFENSE SECRETARY: We didn't fully comprehend the depth of corruption. GRIFFIN: And yet that corruption was documented for more than a decade by the special inspector general for Afghan reconstruction in quarterly reports required by Congress. Defense officials testified no one anticipated the fall of Kabul in 11 days, but they had intelligence suggesting the Afghan government would fall by Thanksgiving. GEN. MARK MILLEY , CHAIRMAN, JOINT CHIEFS: We knew that when we pulled the advisers out, when we pulled the money out, that at some point in the future, most said it was in the fall, that the Afghan security forces were going to fracture and the government would collapse. GRIFFIN: Asked why they did not begin evacuating Americans and civilian allies sooner -- AUSTIN: How to do that and when to do it is really a State Department call. GRIFFIN: Today another private charter plane landed in Chicago with American citizens and green card holders on board. Eight military bases in the U.S. are housing 53,000 Afghan evacuees awaiting further screening. GEN. GLEN VANHERCK, U.S. NORTHERN COMMAND AND NORAD: One-hundred percent of the Afghans are COVID tested, and 84 percent have received COVID vaccinations to date. GRIFFIN: All received the MMR measles vaccine, 4,000 are ready for placement in American communities, among them this Afghan air force pilot currently at Fort McCoy Wisconsin. HABDUL, FORMER AFGHAN AIR FORCE PILOT: I got my pilot training in the United States. I was in San Antonio one year, one year in Alabama. Wherever I find a job, I want to live in the United States. (END VIDEO TAPE) GRIFFIN (on camera): Hundreds of U.S. military veterans have volunteered through private veterans' groups, like Save Our Allies, to provide services to these Afghan evacuees at eight U.S. military bases. Some of these Afghans may be on the military bases until spring. Bret? BAIER: Jennifer Griffin at the Pentagon. Jennifer, thank you. Tonight, Republicans are celebrating a big win over Democrats in the congressional baseball game. The GOP side won the back and forth affair by a score of 13 to 12. President Biden was on hand. He was one of four former players inducted into the congressional baseball hall of fame which also enshrined a late president George H. W. Bush. Last night's contest raised $1.2 million for local charities. Up next, North Korea's leader wants to talk with the south and wants some big changes from the U.S., but is still being provocative. (COMMERCIAL BREAK) BAIER: Two FBI agents entered the home of Brian Laundrie and his parents today in North Port, Florida. Laundrie has been identified as a person of interest in the death of his former girlfriend, Gabby Petito. He is also a federal fugitive on a charge of bank fraud. The agents, we're told, stayed for approximately 30 minutes and briefly explored the camper in the driveway at that home before leaving with a bag. After the agents departure, the Laundrie family attorney said the agents collected some of Brian's personal items to assist canines in their search for him. Also tonight, police records obtained by FOX show at least 46 911 calls or response requests related to that home between September 10 and the 27th. Overseas now, North Korea's leader says he is willing to start talking with South Korea again, but Kim Jong-un 's regime continues to conduct weapons testing, including a reported launch of a newly developed anti-aircraft missile just hours ago. Kim is also calling out the U.S. for what he says is its hostile policy. Senior foreign affairs correspondent Greg Palkot has details. (BEGIN VIDEO TAPE) GREG PALKOT, FOX NEWS SENIOR FOREIGN AFFAIRS CORRESPONDENT: North Korea's Kim Jong-un making nice with his neighbor to the south. A year since Pyongyang destroyed an office aimed at facilitating ties with South Korea in a North Korea border town. Later Kim said this week he wants to restore severed communication between the North and South, moves perhaps aimed at nudging his new nemesis, President Biden, reacting to diplomatic offers like one from Biden at the U.N . last week -- JOE BIDEN , (D) PRESIDENT OF THE UNITED STATES: We seek serious and sustained diplomacy to pursue the complete denuclearization of the Korean peninsula. PALKOT: Kim is reported to have said "It is no more than a petty trick for deceiving the international community and hiding its hostile acts." Kim also said he'd continue to bolster his nuclear arsenal, underscoring that Pyongyang continues to test nuclear capable weaponry. Just this month there's been a cruise missile launch, then train launch mobile missiles, and, this week, what the North claims is a superfast, maneuverable hypersonic missile. Experts are doubtful and say the launch was less than a success. Still, it could be a game changer. NICHOLAS EBERSTADT , AMERICAN ENTERPRISE INSTITUTE : It is significant. Exactly what the significance is I think we'll have to assess in the next few days. PALKOT: There's even talk of another summit between Kim Jong-un and South Korean President Moon Jae -in . The last time they met was at the DMZ in 2019 with then President Trump. But North Korea hit by COVID-19 restrictions, natural disasters, and U.S. backed sanctions, neighbor China is hoping for the best. HUA CHUNYING, CHINESE FOREIGN MINISTRY : We hope the relevant measure can play a positive role in improving and developing North-South relations. (END VIDEO TAPE) PALKOT (on camera): South Korean President Moon has to constitutionally step down next March, one more reason for him to push his new ally, President Trump, to make some kind of peace with longtime rival Kim Jong- un, no easy feat. Bret? BAIER: Greg Palkot in London. Greg, thank you. Up next, the panel on scaling back expectations for the Biden agenda, where things stand at this minute. First Beyond our Borders tonight. High level Russian and U.S. diplomats meet in Geneva as part of strategic talks revived by President Biden and Vladimir Putin at a June summit. Deputy Secretary of State Wendy Sherman held several hours of discussions with her Russian counterpart. They addressed, we're told, contentious issues such as nuclear weapons, artificial intelligence, and cyberspace. Coronavirus cases surged to a record high in Melbourne, Australia. Australian officials blame the spike on illegal home gatherings to watch a major soccer match. Australia's two largest cities, Sydney and Melbourne, are in a weeks-long lockdown that has resulted in mass protests against the strict virus measures. And Swedish police look for a man in connection with an explosion and fire at a large apartment building in Sweden. Sixteen people were injured in the blast, four of them seriously. Swedish media are reporting the suspect is a man in his 50s who lived with his mother in that building. A local newspaper reports the property owner had been trying to evict them from that apartment. Just some of the other stories Beyond our Borders tonight. We'll be right back. (COMMERCIAL BREAK) (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) NANCY PELOSI , (D-CA) HOUSE SPEAKER: Doubt in anyone's mind that we will not have a reconciliation. We will have a reconciliation bill. That is for sure. JENNIFER GRANHOLM , ENERGY SECRETARY: It is not some major cataclysm if there isn't a vote today. Mark my words, the infrastructure bill will be passed, and a version of the reconciliation bill will be as well. REP. PRAMILA JAYAPAL , (D-WA) HOUSE BUDGET COMMITTEE: We will not be able to vote for the infrastructure bill until the reconciliation bill has passed. So we're in the same place. SEN. JOE MANCHIN, (D-WV): It's a shame for that, because no two bills should ever be linked together to the point that we're going to let the perfect be the enemy of the good. (END VIDEO CLIP) BAIER: Senator Joe Manchin there. At this hour we are told that the House will not have any votes before 9:00 p.m. We don't know the status of whether the infrastructure bill is coming up, whether there's a deal on the reconciliation bill. We do know this -- Joe Manchin laid down a marker today, and "The Washington Post " took note, saying "Joe Manchin delivers a dagger to the heart of the progressive cause. They can huff and puff all they want, but they won't blow down the West Virginia Democrat's House because he correctly read public opinion. Reengineering the fabric of American life is modern progressivism's whole point. Its adherents believe that the nation is in crisis. Crises demand immediately and wide-ranging action, not incremental change or tinkering around the edges. Their ambitions, however, can only prevail in a democracy if they are supported by public opinion." That's where we are at this hour. Let's bring in our panel, Ben Domenech, publisher of "The Federalist," Mara Liasson , national political correspondent of National Public Radio, and Trey Gowdy , former Congressman from South Carolina. Mara, we don't know where this is going. We do know that it's going to be less than $3.5 trillion in the reconciliation bill, if it happens. MARA LIASSON , NATIONAL POLITICAL CORRESPONDENT, NATIONAL PUBLIC RADIO: Yes, it's definitely going to be less. I think we've known that for quite some time. But we just didn't know the actual parameters of the negotiation. And I think the big progress that was made today is that Joe Manchin said in public before a camera what he's been saying in private and actually on paper in this memo that he and Chuck Schumer signed, that his number, top line number is $1.5 trillion. He has some other substantive demands. He wants new entitled programs, social safety net programs to be means tested. He wants to roll back the Trump tax cuts, including carried interest. So he has a whole lot of things that he cares about. Now, he did not say that this was a hard and fast number and he wasn't flexible at all. He said, we're going to negotiate. So, somewhere between $3.5 trillion and $1.5 trillion is where they'll end up if they can get a deal among themselves. BAIER: And that's a big if, Trey, listening to progressives saying, listen, we're going to vote against this, the infrastructure, bipartisan infrastructure bill, if we don't have a deal, a vote on reconciliation. TREY GOWDY , FORMER SOUTH CAROLINA REPRESENTATIVE: Yes, Bret. I give credit to the progressives in the House. They watched very carefully as the Freedom Caucus on the Republican side proved that you can get a lot more famous opposing your own leadership than you can fighting with the other side. And fame has become the ultimate political virtue. I will say this. Jen Psaki used the word "democracy." "The Washington Post " used the world "democracy." Let's lay aside the fact that they tried to ram it through with a parliamentarian and put everything in one bill. Let's give them credit for liking democracy. Bret, you and I won the same number of counties in West Virginia that Joe Biden did. And Arizona was less than one half of a percentage point. So don't be lecturing Joe Manchin and Kyrsten Sinema about democracy. BAIER: Speaking of Jen Psaki , she was asked about the White House potentially losing control of this whole deal today. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) JEN PSAKI , WHITE HOUSE PRESS SECRETARY: This is how democracy works. I know it feels foreign because there wasn't much that happened over the last couple of years. But how it works is the American people elect their elected officials. The president of the United States puts forward a bold and ambitious proposal, and everybody negotiates about it. And they have different points of view. That's how democracy should work. We're in the midst of it right now. We're not trying to paint over how messy it looks from the outside. We know that. (END VIDEO CLIP) BAIER: Ben? BEN DOMENECH, PUBLISHER, "THE FEDERALIST": Well, we're not actually a democracy, just to point that out for a point of clarification. If we were, then we would be fine with majorities running pell-mell toward all of these types of extreme steps, even if they were slimmest of majorities. There's an important reason, and the founders really believed in it, that we are not that way, and our government does not work that way. And that's why Joe Manchin is so important in this moment. Look, he reads the politics very well. Not just in his own state, but in, I think, the broader dynamic. And I think in this moment there ought to be a lot of critiques of the approach that Nancy Pelosi used, because at the end of the day, she may have missed an opportunity to achieve a package that could be much more perhaps than what Manchin's number would be, but far less than what progressives are currently demanding. Taking the step that she did in terms of linking these measures together in the way that I think was politically unwise is coming back to bite her in a big way today. BAIER: We always knew that Senator Manchin was going to be crucial in this whole thing. We've talked to him here on this show many times and asked him specific questions. Today, Mara, you're right. With the $1.5 trillion top line that he talked about, take a listen to this and reaction on the progressive side. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) SEN. JOE MANCHIN, (D-WV): I guess for them to get theirs, elect more liberals. But I'm not asking them to change. I'm willing to come from zero to $1.5 trillion. My top line has been $1.5 trillion because I believe in my heart that what we can do and with the needs we have right now and what we can afford to do without basically changing our whole society to an entitlement mentality. REP. ALEXANDRIA OCASIO-CORTEZ, (D-NY): Which senator are we negotiating with? Is this June Manchin? Is it September Manchin? Is it August Manchin? Will December Manchin be a different -- will this be a different Senator that pops up? (END VIDEO CLIP) LIASSON: It's actually July 28th Manchin. That's the date of the memo. BAIER: Yes, that's right. LIASSON: And it hasn't changed since then. But look, what he said was just basic facts. The reason Democrats are in this fix is because they have a gigantic agenda and a miniscule majority. And they failed to win the extra seats in the House and Senate that they thought they were going to win in 2020, that Republicans thought they were going to win in 2020, and that's just reality. And as Joe Manchin said today, I have never been a liberal. He's representing a state that Trump won by, what, 29 points? So like that song in "Hamilton," they don't have the votes, and they're going to have to compromise. And that's just the way it is. BAIER: Trey, you've seen this play before. And Speaker Pelosi has pulled rabbits out of hats legislatively before. We don't know what's going to happen tonight. Do you think she could cobble this together? GOWDY: It depends. It depends on how many Republican senators continue to call Republican members of the House and ask them to vote for the infrastructure bill. So Kevin McCarthy has a job to do here, too, which is keep the Republicans coalesced. I love AOC's political strategy, which is insult the person whose vote you need. I just don't think it's going to work. BAIER: But let's take you to the flipside, Ben. What about those moderate Republicans who look at the $1.2 trillion infrastructure bill and say, this is a chance to finally build that bridge, to finally fix that road that I have been talk about fixing to my constituents forever. Maybe I should vote for it. Is the politics of the moment more important than the bridge at home? DOMENECH: I think that's the big question, but headed into a midterm year, delivery of that bridge is going to become less and less of their priority. And one more note on this. The kind of jabs that we've seen not just at Joe Manchin but today from some progressives at Arizona Senator Sinema have really become more and more aggressive during this point. The idea said by one member today that she hasn't shown us anything but a designer purse. That's not the kind of insult that's going to go across very well with someone who is navigating a situation and who, last I checked has, 40 percent popularity among Republicans in Arizona. BAIER: And either one of them could become Republicans and change the dynamic. You get Senate Majority Leader McConnell. All right, thank you all. When we come back, a look at the newly renovated Washington Bureau. (COMMERCIAL BREAK) BAIER: Fancy. Finally tonight, FOX News is marking the 25th anniversary this year. We've covered a lot of stories in that time, and a lot have come from here in our Washington Bureau, where this program originates. As we look back on the past quarter century, we're also moving forward with a special ceremony here just a short time ago. (BEGIN VIDEO TAPE) (APPLAUSE) BAIER: A state-of-the-art, all-digital newsroom, the FOX News Washington Bureau reopened after a major renovation. Two new flagship studios, a super high resolution technology platform for video and graphics, and our newsroom. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: David is replacing on two, right. BAIER: Reconfigured to allow producers and editors to easily monitor the ever-growing number of satellite video feeds on 75-inch TV screens. FOX Corporation CEO Lachlan Murdoch calls it an investment in the future for the top-rated news channel. LACHLAN MURDOCH , FOX CORPORATION CEO: And the reason is to give all of you the space and environment to continue to do your very best work. BAIER: Another behind the scenes feature of our new bureau, two very special places honoring two very special people. First, the Charles Krauthammer Green Room. If you've watched SPECIAL REPORT, you know how important he was to the show and the channel. We miss his words of wisdom every day. This plaque says in memory of our beloved colleague, friend, and patriot. This is the Tony Snow Radio Studio in honor of our friend who passed away 13 years ago, the host of FOX News Sunday. This is to remember him every day. JAY WALLACE, FOX NEWS MEDIA PRESIDENT: The heartbeat of the news operation since FOX News Sunday kicked off 25 years ago this past spring. SUZANNE SCOTT , FOX NEWS MEDIA CEO: This is also a moment to remember an extraordinary voice and gentle giant in our business. BAIER: This renovation was long in the planning. The original FOX News Washington Bureau was our home through the major news events of our time -- impeachments, wars, congressional fights, Bush v Gore, and 9/11. But an ever-evolving news environment has inspired us to redesign our new offices bigger and better to complement the latest technology along with our solid storytelling and reporting. (END VIDEO TAPE) BAIER: It's great digs, 25 years later, we'll be looking back over the next couple of weeks. Tomorrow on SPECIAL REPORT, we'll talk about the coronavirus pandemic with former Food and Drug Administration commissioner Dr. Scott Gottlieb . Thanks for watching us. Thanks for the SPECIAL REPORT, fair, balanced, and still unafraid. "FOX NEWS PRIMETIME" hosted this by Brian Kilmeade starts right now. Brian? headline: Pentagon Says Kabul Drone Strike Killed Civilians; FDA Rejects Joe Biden Plan For Booster Shots; Virginia Gubernatorial Candidates Democrat Terry McAuliffe and Republican Glenn Youngkin Hold First Debate; Biden Administration States Drone Strike in Afghanistan Aimed at ISIS-K Member Instead Killed 10 Innocent People Including Seven Children
story_text: JESSE WATTERS, FOX NEWS HOST: That's it for us. Have a great weekend, everybody. We'll see you on Monday. BRET BAIER, FOX NEWS ANCHOR: Good evening, welcome to Washington. I'm Bret Baier. Breaking tonight, three major stories developing tonight. A Food and Drug Administration advisory board has rejected the president's plan to have all Americans take a booster vaccine shot against COVID-19, at least not yet. The board is recommending Americans 65 and older and those immunocompromised get a booster shot, further confusing the administration's announcements on booster shots. More than 11,000 illegal immigrants, many of them from Haiti surged toward the southern border of the U.S. under a bridge in Del Rio, Texas. Customs and Border Patrol officers call it a situation that is out of control tonight. And the president's so-called over the horizon counterterrorism strategy in the wake of the Afghanistan withdrawal is in question this evening, real question. Senior Pentagon officials now admit a drone strike the White House celebrated at first as a major victory against the ISIS actually did kill almost a dozen civilians including an aid worker and seven children but no terrorists. Lucas Tomlinson starts us off at the Pentagon with the tragic details of this strike. Good evening, Lucas. LUCAS TOMLINSON, FOX NEWS CORRESPONDENT (on camera): Good evening, Bret. An American reaper drone orbiting high above Kabul had been tracking and shadowing a Toyota Corolla -- a white Toyota Corolla for eight hours before launching a hellfire missile. The military thought it destroyed a car filled with explosives and ISIS fighters. Instead, 10 innocent civilians including seven children were killed. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) TOMLINSON (voice over): The head of U.S. forces in Afghanistan General Frank McKenzie coined the strike on August 29th, one day before all U.S. troops left Afghanistan, a tragic mistake. The strike took place three days after 13 American troops were killed in a suicide attack in Kabul, General McKenzie said more attacks were anticipated. GEN. KENNETH "FRANK" MCKENZIE, COMMANDER, U.S. CENTRAL COMMAND: It's important that I emphasize that we did not have the luxury of time to develop pattern of life and to do a number of other things. We struck under the -- under the theory of reasonable certainty. TOMLINSON: Did you have forces on the ground that helped you conduct this strike? MCKENZIE: No, we did not. As you know, no time where our forces really away from Hamid Karzai International Airfield. So, there was nobody there -- nobody there on the ground to have to play that role. TOMLINSON: American drones must fly for hours from distant bases in the Middle East. Two days after the drone strike, President Biden touted the military's ability to strike over the horizon. JOE BIDEN , PRESIDENT OF THE UNITED STATES: We have what's called over the horizon capabilities, which means we can strike terrorists and targets without American boots on the ground, or very few if needed. We've shown that capacity just in the last week. We struck ISIS-K remotely days after they murdered 13 of our service members and dozens of innocent Afghans. TOMLINSON: The U.S. military's top officer General Mark Milley spoke earlier this month about the strike. GEN. MARK MILLEY, CHAIRMAN, JOINT CHIEFS OF STAFF: Because there were secondary explosions, there's a reasonable conclusion to be made that there was explosives in that vehicle. We think that the procedures were correctly followed and it was a righteous strike. MCKENZIE: We knew from the very beginning, there was a possibility of civilian casualties. (END VIDEO CLIP) TOMLINSON (on camera): General McKenzie also said those explosions were likely the result of a propane tank located behind the car. That's not what the military said after the strike. Officials tell me there'll be no disciplinary action taken, Bret. BAIER: Quite something. Lucas, before we learned about this drone strike, the focus really was on General Milley's calls to the Chinese in the wake of that Bob Woodward, Bob Costa book. He spoke for the first time publicly today. What did he say? TOMLINSON: Well, General Milley claims he didn't do anything wrong. Telling the Associated Press while in Greece that his calls to the Chinese was nothing out of the ordinary. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) MILLEY: These are routine calls in order to discuss issues of the day, to reassure both allies and adversaries in this case, in order to ensure strategic stability. (END VIDEO CLIP) TOMLINSON: General Milley will appear before the Senate Armed Services Committee on September 28th to discuss these calls to the Chinese and also Afghanistan including this tragic drone strike, Bret. BAIER: Number of questions there. Lucas Tomlinson at the Pentagon. Lucas, thanks. Trey Yingst is coming up with a live report from Kabul, Afghanistan, the story of an American man who traveled there to try to save his family. Also breaking tonight, a blow to President Biden's effort to have all Americans take a third vaccination shot or a booster. And FDA advisory committee is overwhelmingly rejecting a broad booster vaccine plan, but is recommending narrowing the scope who should get a third shot. White House Correspondent Peter Doocy joins us live from the North Lawn with murky messaging on boosters from this administration. Good evening, Peter. PETER DOOCY, FOX NEWS CORRESPONDENT (on camera): Good evening, Bret. President Biden likes to say the pandemic is not political but the layout of today's FDA booster hearing was because doctors debated the science for hours and then, took a vote and the result was no boosters yet. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: This vote did not pass since the majority voted no. DOOCY: Just two FDA advisors voted in favor of a third shot for the general population right now, an overwhelming 16 voted against it. Three days before the booster program was to be launched. DR. MEG SEYMOUR, SENIOR FELLOW, NATIONAL CENTER FOR HEALTH RESEARCH: It is unfortunate that the White House announced the need for an availability of boosters prior to FDA 's assessment of the data. DOOCY: And that is exactly what President Biden did. BIDEN: Just remember, as a simple rule, eight months after your second shot, get a booster shot. DOOCY: Biden officials were so confident in their plan, they bought boosters before scientists signed off. JEFF ZIENTS, COVID COORDINATOR, WHITE HOUSE: We have supply in inventory and we have also supply on order. So, supply is in good shape. DOOCY: Moderna and Johnson & Johnson boosters were not considered, only reps from Pfizer were invited to argue in favor of a third dose. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: There is clear erosion of vaccine protection over time against COVID-19. DOOCY: But experts were generally unimpressed with the presentation. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: And I just don't think we're there yet in terms of the data. DOOCY: Today was not a condemnation of COVID vaccination, more just raising questions about boosters. DR. CODY MEISSNER, MEMBER, FDA ADVISORY COMMITTEE: Everyone has to get the primary series. This booster dose is not going to make a big difference. DOOCY: One of the most common issues flagged is the risk of cardiovascular problems in young men who got the booster already. DR. JAMES HILDRETH, FDA ADVISORY COMMITTEE: I have a serious concern about myocarditis in young people. DOOCY: One advisor Marion Gruber participated today despite announcing a plan to resign amid a dispute about boosters. MARION GRUBER, OFFICE DIRECTOR OF VACCINES RESEARCH AND REVIEW, FDA: It has been a privilege to serve you. DOOCY: For now, there is unanimous agreement that the immunocompromised and senior citizens are helped by third doses. DR. ARCHANA CHATTERJEE, MEMBER, FDA ADVISORY COMMITTEE: I'd like to see more data before I would recommend it for a younger age group. But over 60 is probably OK from my standpoint. DOOCY: But not the general population. Despite the president's announcement that starting Monday, it would be easy for everybody. BIDEN: It will be easy, just show your vaccination card and you'll get a booster. (END VIDEO CLIP) DOOCY (on camera): Not unless you're 65 and up, the only age group this advisory board is recommending vaccine boosters for right now. And this is the first time White House officials have been bopped (PH) by the scientists when it comes to COVID. When White House officials pushed mask wearing, scientists said great. When the White House officials pushed vaccines, scientists said great but when they started to push boosters here, the scientists said wait, Bret. BAIER: But Peter, internally, are they now acknowledging that, you know, follow the science they got over their skis here on this one? DOOCY: That would have been a great question for the president today but he did not take any and he is now at his beach house. It would have been a great question for Jen Psaki , but there was no White House briefing and it would have been a great question for any of the White House COVID advisory board but they decided today to speak before this announcement, before this vote was taken. And so, it's hard to get them on the record on camera about something that hasn't happened yet, Bret. BAIER: Well, good try. Peter Doocy live in the North Lawn. Peter, thanks. We have some startling exclusive images tonight from the southern border. Take a look at these images, mass of illegal immigrants, thousands of them assembling along one key entry point. The numbers are really staggering and according to the Customs and Border Patrol, the fact that virtually none of them are vaccinated and they are now setting up as you see here a tent city under a bridge is concerning to authorities there. Correspondent Bill Melugin reports tonight from Del Rio, Texas. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) UNIDENTIFIED MALE: My God, look at that. BILL MELUGIN, FOX NEWS CORRESPONDENT (voice over): From a Texas DPS helicopter, Fox News is getting an exclusive look at the deteriorating situation along the border here in Del Rio, Texas and the footage is stunning. Close to 11,000 migrants all crammed under the International Bridge waiting to be processed by a completely overwhelmed Border Patrol. Some already building makeshift shelters out of grass and sticks, others erecting tents. A majority of these migrants from Haiti which has a COVID vaccination rate of under one percent. From the air, we watched as a constant stream of hundreds of people left Mexico by crossing a dam in the Rio Grande and then walked illegally into the United States, masses of them gathering on the shore after they cross. From there, we could see a lengthy line of migrants walking a dirt path towards the International Bridge where they will join the constantly growing mass of people there. Nearby, a bulldozer clears a field apparently making space for potential emergency shelters, or maybe a processing tent. Sources on the ground sent us video showing the situation from their perspective as hundreds of migrants cross illegally into the U.S. without any resistance on either side of the border. With more in wait on the Mexican side of the river, and it happens all day long. The Del Rio mayor, a Democrat declaring a local state of disaster as a result. BRUNO LOZANO, MAYOR OF DEL RIO, TEXAS: There's people having babies down there, there's people collapsing out of the heat. It's something that it's very challenging to describe in words, but it's extremely chaotic. (END VIDEO CLIP) MELUGIN (on camera): And Bret, last night, we learned that the FAA had suddenly issued a TFR, a temporary flight restriction in the area around the bridge right here. What that meant was that our Fox News drone could no longer fly in the area and bring everybody those images of the migrants under the bridge, at the time the FAA said it was for a special security reason. Well, I'm happy to give an update today. This morning, Fox News filed a waiver with the FAA to try to get our drone back in the air. Happy to report, the FAA cleared us this afternoon. We have been given clearance to fly our drone once again here at the bridge. We will continue to do so in the coming days. We'll send it back to you. BAIER: Bill Melugin live in Del Rio, Texas. Keep it up. Thanks, Bill. The Dow lost 166 today, the S&P 500 fell 41, the NASDAQ was off 138. For the week, the Dow dropped seven hundredths of a percentage point, the S&P and the NASDAQ lost about a half point. America's oldest foreign ally is furious tonight with the Biden administration. French officials are livid over a military deal between the U.S., Australia and Great Britain. So much so they have pulled their ambassador from Washington D.C. back to Paris and extremely rare move in diplomatic circles especially between allies. State Department Correspondent Rich Edson explains. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) RICH EDSON , FOX NEWS CORRESPONDENT (voice over): Allies and partners, the foundation of the Biden administration's foreign policy and a strategy openly cheered months ago in European capitals. Though a new security partnership just announced between the United States, United Kingdom and Australia has allies in Europe, especially France, irate. PHILIPPE ETIENNE, FRENCH AMBASSADOR TO U.S.: We have a feeling, yes, of not being treated like an ally. France play a key role in the Indo-Pacific Ocean. EDSON: The U.S. and U.K. agreed to provide nuclear submarine technology to Australia as American allies bolster their presence in the Indo-Pacific to counter China. The European Union 's foreign policy chief complained the United States failed to even notify the Europeans about this deal. The French also lose out on an agreement they signed with Australia in 2016, to provide tens of billions of dollars in submarines. BENJAMIN HADDAD, DIRECTOR OF THE EUROPE CENTER, ATLANTIC COUNCIL: I do think there is a sense of disappointment right now in Europe towards the Biden administration, especially after four years of disagreements and conflicts under the Trump administration, there was a hope for sort of a new age in transatlantic relations, and we've seen very little substance to show for it. EDSON: A French diplomat says France's Embassy in Washington has canceled a reception tonight to commemorate the 240th anniversary of the Battle of the Capes, a French naval victory over the British, resulting in a successful Siege of Yorktown and the creation of the United States of America. ANTONY BLINKEN , U.S. SECRETARY OF STATE: France in particular, is a vital partner on this and so many other issues, stretching back generations and we want to find every opportunity to deepen our transatlantic cooperation in the Indo-Pacific and around the world. EDSON: Blinken says the administration had spoken with the French government ahead of the Australian partnership announcement. (END VIDEO CLIP) EDSON (on camera): The French government has just announced it is recalling its ambassadors to the United States and Australia, saying this submarine deal represents unacceptable behavior among allies and partners. The White House official says the U.S. had been in close touch with French leaders, and we'll continue to try to resolve these differences, Bret. BAIER: But Rich, for people sitting at home, I mean, it's a big deal, right? They pull the ambassador. EDSON: That is a big deal. Anytime you do this, it says an awful lot about a relationship when you bring an ambassador back. It's happened with the U.S. and Russia in a number of different times. And it really is a strong diplomatic message of displeasure. BAIER: OK, Rich Edson live at the State Department. Rich, thank you. Up next, Trey Yingst reporting from inside Afghanistan brings us a remarkable story of one man's journey to try to save his family. First, here's what some of our Fox affiliates around the country are covering tonight. Fox 40 in Sacramento, where old growth trees and other structures in Sequoia National Park are threatened by another fast-moving wildfire in the area. That blaze could reach a grove of 2,000 sequoias in a matter of days. Fire crews have wrapped the base of the tallest, the 275-foot General Sherman sequoia in a flame-resistant aluminum blanket. California wildfires have scorched more than 3,500 square miles this summer, destroying hundreds of homes. Fox 5 in New York where the latest crime spree there involves victims wearing expensive jewelry, and a pair of suspects using a Mercedes getaway car. One person was shot while another had a Rolex watch stolen at an upper Eastside restaurant this week. Police are looking for links to several similar attacks in recent days in other high-end and trendy areas. And this is a live look at St. Louis from our affiliate Fox2, you see the arch there, the big story there tonight. Boeing picks MidAmerica St. Louis airport as the site to build the Navy's first carrier-based unmanned aircraft. The 15-year $200 million project is expected to bring 300 jobs or so to that region. That is tonight's live look "OUTSIDE THE BELTWAY" from SPECIAL REPORT. We'll be right back. (COMMERCIAL BREAK) BAIER: Police are warning of threats of violence ahead of a rally tomorrow here in Washington by a group supporting people arrested during the January 6th riot. Hundreds of demonstrators are expected for what is being called the Justice for J6 event. Law enforcement is being beefed up around the capital city and 100 National Guard troops are on standby nearby. A temporary fence has been installed around the Capitol . Several streets will be closed in the area and members and staff are encouraged to avoid the conflicts. There are new revelations tonight about Facebook 's unwillingness and inability to enforce its own rules, and its awareness that its products routinely fail and are harmful to consumers. The Wall Street Journal says Facebook 's own research confirms it rules favor -- its rules favor VIP clients and its platforms have negative effects on the health of their users. More with this story coming up. Tonight, we are hearing from an Afghan American who left his home here in the U.S. to try to rescue his family following the Taliban takeover. Correspondent Trey Yingst has the remarkable story tonight from Kabul, Afghanistan, where Americans and allies are still trying to get to safety. TREY YINGST, FOX NEWS FOREIGN CORRESPONDENT (voice-over): One citizens wait outside the Serena Hotel in Kabul, passports in hand. They're trying to get inside the grounds that will act as a staging point for evacuations. A Qatari official tells Fox News, 170 people left Afghanistan today on a chartered flight. The passengers included people from eight different nationalities, including the United States. Onboard was U.S. citizen Ehsanullah Muhsen, his wife, and 2-year-old daughter, Miriam. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) YINGST (on camera): You're in St. Louis last month. EHSANULLAH MUHSEN, UNITED STATES CITIZEN: Yes. Yes. YINGST: And your wife and daughter are here for a wedding. And then, the Taliban takes over, and you say to yourself -- MUHSEN: I'm going to get my family out. As simple as that, you know, because I knew one way or another, especially when the explosion happened with ISIS, and then the consequent firing upon the protesters, or whatever happened. You know, I just knew I got one way or another, I got to get my family out. YINGST (voice-over): After watching the chaotic scenes outside the airport and getting limited help from the U.S. government , Ehsanullah flew to Pakistan, and then crossed into Afghanistan by land. The Biden administration said there were contingency plans in place for the U.S. withdrawal. You experienced this firsthand. What's your reaction to that? MUHSEN: It's not true. It's not true. I mean, this -- it could have been avoided, but it's just never, you know, it's too much hectic, too much disorder. YINGST: Across the street, the reason so many are fleeing Afghanistan. YINGST (on camera): People are headed now to Friday prayers in the Afghan capital of Kabul. The imam inside this mosque chanting death to America, declaring victory for the Taliban and the Afghan people. YINGST (voice-over): Inside Muslim prayers are recited as some worshippers thank God for the Taliban victory over U.S. forces. Just over a month ago, the Taliban entered Kabul. Today, its fighters are being praised in mosques throughout the city. There's no way to tell who willingly accepts the Taliban and who is being forced. (END VIDEO CLIP) YINGST (on camera): The Taliban is already going back on their promises about what life will look like for the Afghan people, like you saw in that mosque, a dangerous preview about what is to come. Bret. BAIER: Trey Yingst, early Saturday morning, live in Kabul Afghanistan. Trey, thank you. A former campaign lawyer for Hillary Clinton is facing a federal charge tonight in what is the first legal action taken in the investigation into the origin of the Trump-Russia probe, the John Durham investigation. JONATHAN SERRIE, FOX NEWS CORRESPONDENT (voice-over): More than 1,000 tips have flooded in this investigators, trace Gabby Petito's movements on a cross-country road trip prior to her disappearance. Her boyfriend, Brian Laundrie silence, and his solo trip back home and the couple's van are raising suspicions. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) JOSH TAYLOR, SPOKESMAN, NORTH PORT POLICE DEPARTMENT: Obviously, that vehicle drove a couple of 1,000 miles to get back here to North Port. It didn't do that on one tank of gas. Gabby's family members believe Brian holds the key to her whereabouts and are increasing the pressure on him to break his silence. FLORA ROCCO, GODMOTHER OF GABBY PETITO: It's not that you're not even helping anymore, it's now hindering this investigation. It's now you're using up resources and people's time. And it's now been beyond days that you could have talked. (END VIDEO CLIP) SERRIE (on camera): Yes. And Bret, we have some breaking news from digital reporters on the ground saying that there are police inside the Laundrie house here in the city of North Port. Also, an update from authorities in Grand County, Utah, they are investigating a double homicide involving a newlywed couple. They were found shot to death near a campsite just outside the city of Moab. BAIER: And Jonathan, just to go back, to the first part of that, you said there's police activity at the Laundrie house now? SERRIE: Police activity at the Laundrie house. Justice Thomas says it's not the role of judges to make policy or base decision on personal feelings or religious beliefs. MCAULIFFE: I believe a woman ought to make a decision about her own reproductive right, and I will support those. YOUNGKIN: I'm pro-life. I believe in exceptions in the case of rape and incest and when the life of the mother is in jeopardy. HOFF: Youngkin added that he would not support a bill similar to Texas' controversial new post six week ban. (END VIDEO TAPE) HOFF (on camera): Just like we saw in California, Bret, a constant in this race has been the Trump card. The Democratic candidate criticizing his opponent for having the former president's endorsement, and a Republican trying to emerge as their own person. Bret? BAIER: Alex, thank you. And welcome to our team. HOFF: Thank you so much. I'm proud to be here. BAIER: Up next, the panel on what has turned out to be a bad day, a bad week, really, for President Biden and his administration. First, Beyond our Borders tonight. Scientists in Spain are monitoring a so- called earthquake swarm in the Canary Islands. China has also landed a space probe on Mars and a rover on the far side of the moon. Just some of the other stories beyond our borders tonight. We'll be right back. JEN PSAKI , WHITE HOUSE PRESS SECRETARY: Our over-the-horizon capacity can work and has worked in going after ISIS targets and killing people who went after our troops. GEN. MARK MILLEY, CHAIRMAN, JOINT CHIEFS: At least one of those people that were killed was an ISIS facilitator. So were there others killed? Yes, there were others killed. Who they are we don't know. GEN. KENNETH "FRANK" MCKENZIE, U.S. CENTRAL COMMAND: I am now convinced that as many as 10 civilians, including up to seven children, were tragically killed in that strike. However, when the administration came out touting this as an example of over-the-horizon and going after ISIS terrorists in the day after that, and then to find out what happened today, your reaction? TREY GOWDY , FORMER SOUTH CAROLINA REPRESENTATIVE: Yes, "over-the-horizon" apparently is a euphemism for infanticide. I want to know the layer of review before this country, the world's greatest country, decides to kill seven children. Who gets to approve it? Who reviews it? What's the quantum of evidence? And it's not lost on me, Bret, that Joe Biden was slow to pull the trigger on Usama bin Laden but quick to pull the trigger on this drone strike while he was having really bad press that resulted in the death of seven children. So, Trump gets criticized for killing the right people. Let's see what happens to Biden for killing seven children. BAIER: I will say, Harold, it was interesting to see this announcement come on a Friday afternoon. The president had already left for vacation for the weekend. The White House had pretty much shut down because of the -- there were no briefings after that, and we got this announcement from the Central Command general. HAROLD FORD JR., FORMER TENNESSEE REPRESENTATIVE: There's no question our prayers and thoughts go to the family and families that lost loved ones. This is tragic. I give the White House credit for being transparent. Questions can be asked, Bret, about whether the timing of the announcement of this, of the admission of this had to do with the fact it was Friday evening. I do think Trey raises an important point about the process has to be evaluated about how they reached this decision, and try to ensure it doesn't happen again. I would caution us although to remember the intentions of our -- of any U.S. government , U.S. military is to protect us. They made a mistake here, and I hope they learn from it. BAIER: Byron? And so the first run of this over-the-horizon capability in Afghanistan is just an absolute disaster. And the other thing is, as the president just said in that clip you played, clearly this was seen as vengeance for, or a strike back after this bombing that killed -- suicide bombing killed 13 Americans. So now we strike back afterwards, and we hit the wrong person. We hit 10 of the wrong people. So, it's just absolutely wrong all around. And I heard in Trey Gowdy 's voice the sound of a former congressional overseer. There are going to be a lot of people in Congress, hopefully Democrats and Republicans, who are going to want a detailed accounting of this. BAIER: Yes, again, chairman of the Joint Chiefs facing a lot of questions on a lot of different fronts September 28th up on Capitol Hill, and we'll carry that live. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) JOE BIDEN , (D) PRESIDENT OF THE UNITED STATES: We bought enough boosters, enough booster shots, and the distribution system is ready to administer them. As soon as they are authorized. Those eligible will be able to get a booster right away. DR. VIVEK MURTHY, U.S. SURGEON GENERAL: Our goals were to stay ahead of the virus, to lay out an additional plan based on our clinical judgment, and to ultimately ensure that the final plan would be based on the independent assessment and recommendation of the FDA and CDC. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: This vote did not pass since the majority voted no. (END VIDEO CLIP) BAIER: It wasn't even the majority, Trey. It was 16 to two against a broad booster shot for the Pfizer vaccine for the three shots, at least not yet. They did say if you are 65 and over or immunocompromised you should get it. But clearly the administration, the president was ahead on this, ahead of the science. GOWDY: Yes. We were told to follow the science. We weren't told to kind of predict it and be off by an overwhelming vote. I was surprised at the vote. I thought that I would be in line for a booster. This is what vexes people, though, Bret. I'm not a scientist. I have to rely on people to tell me whether or not the risks outweigh the reward when it comes to boosters. And they say, if you are 65 and above or immunosuppressed, go ahead and do it. But if you are looking for a job, fact checking Joe Biden 's COVID press conferences would be a really good place to start looking, because there's a lot of information. BAIER: Again, Harold, we did not hear from the COVID team today on this decision. But it is frustrating for some people, we get told again and again and again follow the science, and then it's kind of murky on the messaging. I know some of this is evolving as we learn more, but that's where people's heads are as they're waiting for what to do. FORD : Look, if you had told me a year ago today that we would have a vaccine, two shots on two of them and one shot on another, that would pretty much immunize and protect us from hospitalizations, not all together, and certainly death, and that only 54 percent of Americans would have taken it, I would have probably taken the other side of the bet, saying there is no way with President Trump leading this effort that every American, in spite of what some Democrats may have said, we all would have gotten this. And we didn't. The science and FDA can guide us on the third shot, but ultimately everyone has to get the first and second shot, and we should follow the science, too. I know I will. BAIER: OK, a lot to talk about with this in coming days. Up next, the Friday Lightning Round. It will be lightning. MCAULIFFE: This isn't a -- (END VIDEO CLIP) BAIER: Well, you can get a feel there for the debate in Virginia, Terry McAuliffe and Glenn Youngkin. We're back with the panel. Harold, this really will be an interesting race that will tell you where a lot of people maybe stand, because Virginia is pretty purple, bluish-purple, but purple. FORD : Look, Terry McAuliffe , I think, is the best retail politician in politics, certainly, in the Democratic Party, I would argue in politics. But this Virginia Republican is a strong opponent. Terry has got to continue to focus on the economy. I think he has been given a good, good issue here as the abortion issue has come to the forefront to subordinate some of the others, but this will be a tight race. And I think Virginians are going to have to tell, they're going to have to determine, do they want to go forward with the economy or not. BAIER: Glenn Youngkin is arguing that the history is not there, Byron, as far as the economic success, and that's part of the squabbling back and forth. But it really will be a test. And there's a number of issues like Critical Race Theory and the Biden administration, all kinds of things. YORK: And over it all looms Donald Trump . I think it's going to be a test of whether the Democrat McAuliffe can accuse credibly Glenn Youngkin of wanting to be a Trump wannabe or an imitator. And it's also about COVID. Their first fight last night was about COVID, with McAuliffe kind of implying that Youngkin might be a vaccine denier or something, and Youngkin came out with a strong statement in support of vaccines. So it's really going to be really interesting to see whether that label can stick. BAIER: Trey, I wanted to turn to this French response to this U.S.- Australia-U.K. deal on nuclear subs. They pulled the ambassador. It's kind of a strong letter to follow here. GOWDY: Well, you can argue there would not be a United States if it were not for France, so I'm sure they got their feelings hurt. I'm not sure if their feelings were hurt mainly at the result or the fact that they had to hear it on the radio. What struck me as weird, Bret, is Joe Biden was supposed to repair all of these relationships and Tony Blinken was supposed to be a Francophile. France has been a great ally to us. We've got to get this fixed, and we can't communicate over radio and television with our allies. BAIER: Some lightning winners and losers. Here we go, Harold, winner and loser? FORD : My winner is the U.S. Our strategic national interest are advancing because of what you and Trey just talked about. This agreement between the U.K. and Australia will help us counter China. And my loser is anyone who protests violently tomorrow. You can protest on any issue you want, but just be nonviolent in how you do it. BAIER: Byron, winner and loser? YORK: Loser, San Francisco Mayor London Breed. The city has a mask mandate, but that did not stop her from partying in a nightclub without a mask on Wednesday night. Winner is Daniil Medvedev. The Russian tennis player won the U.S. Open, but more importantly, he stopped the Grand Slam of Novak Djokovic. That's a historic thing. BAIER: There you go. Winner and Loser, Trey? GOWDY: Winner, U.S. women's tennis who outdrew the match with Djokovic and whoever Byron just mentioned, because I wasn't watching either. Loser is the FBI for botching yet another serious investigation. BAIER: All right, guys, make it a great weekend. We will see you next week. When we come back, "Notable Quotables." (COMMERCIAL BREAK) BAIER: Well, it's Friday. You know what that means, "Notable Quotables." (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) JOE BIDEN , (D) PRESIDENT OF THE UNITED STATES: I'm not out to punish anyone. I'm a capitalist. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: Pinocchio won't tell you the truth, but I will, and so will the American public. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: We had great growth under the Tax Cuts and Jobs Act. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: She wanted to make sure that this message was brought into that room. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: We said yes to the diversity. We said yes to inclusion. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: To be clear, I blame Larry Nassar, and I also blame an entire system that enabled and perpetrated his abuse. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: It's heart wrenching. She's my only daughter.
