headline: General Mark Milley Spoke To Counterpart With 15 People In Room; Thousands Of Fighters Freed After Kabul Takeover; Reports Allege Joe Biden Ignored Military Advisers; Gymnasts Detail Doctor Abuse And FBI Handling Of Case; Critical Race Theory Could Energize Virginia Voters; Democrats Include Immigration Reform In Spending Plan; Democrats Include Immigration Reform In Large Spending Bill; Car Prices Rising Due To Shortage Of Semiconductor Chips; New Book Indicates Chairman Of Joint Chiefs Of Staff General Milley Intended To Possibly Circumvent Former President Trump's Authority During Last Days Of Presidency; Democrats And Republicans Battle Over Spending Items And Taxes In Proposed Reconciliation Bill
story_text: DANA PERINO, FOX NEWS CHANNEL HOST: All right, great show. That's it for us, SPECIAL REPORT is up next with Bret Baier. Hi, Bret. BRET BAIER, FOX NEWS CHANNEL HOST: You sure? You sure Greg doesn't want more time? GREG GUTFELD, FOX NEWS CHANNEL HOST: Nobody wants me to stay here. BAIER: All right. We do. All right, thanks, Dana. Good evening. Welcome to Washington. I'm Bret Baier. Breaking tonight, we're learning new details about the bombshell allegations concerning then President Trump's top military adviser, and what the Chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff did or did not do to try to calm the Chinese, assuring them that the U.S. was not planning any military action against them in the wake of the instability after the election. And what he did or did not do to insert himself into the process for launching nuclear weapons. A decision the President of the United States makes. All of this in the wake of the January 6th riot on Capitol Hill and concern from the Speaker of the House and General Mark Milley that President Trump was acting erratically. Some Republican lawmakers are already demanding answers now. Others say General Milley should be brought in front of a military tribunal. The Pentagon is pushing back tonight essentially saying there's nothing to see here and it's out of context. National Security Correspondent Jennifer Griffin joins us from the Pentagon with the latest. Good evening, Jennifer. JENNIFER GRIFFIN, FOX NEWS CHANNEL NATIONAL SECURITY CORRESPONDENT (on camera): Good evening, Bret. The two calls made by General Milley to his Chinese counterpart were not secret. They were done with 15 people in the room including note takers in coordination with the civilian leaders of the military at the time and the interagency I'm told by current and former U.S. Defense officials. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) GRIFFIN (voice over): Unnamed sources in the Woodward and Costa book Peril contend General Milley told his Chinese counterpart General Li that he would give him a heads up if the U.S. plan to strike. Colonel Dave Butler, the Joint Staff spokesman issued the following statement: "His calls with the Chinese and others in October and January were in keeping with these duties and responsibilities conveying reassurance in order to maintain strategic stability." JOHN KIRBY, PRESS SECRETARY, PENTAGON: I can tell you, frequent communication with two countries like Russia and China is not a typical at all for a chairman of the Joint Chiefs. And those communications are their routine. They're staffed, they're coordinated, and they're transparent, as transparent as they can be. GRIFFIN: The White House defended General Milley. JOE BIDEN , PRESIDENT OF THE UNITED STATES: I have great confidence in General Milley. JEN PSAKI , WHITE HOUSE PRESS SECRETARY: The president's experience with him is that he is a man of honor. He is a man who's -- the president is confident in his leadership, his patriotism, his fidelity to the Constitution. GRIFFIN: General Milley will address these accusations under oath during testimony on September 28th. SEN. TOM COTTON (R-AR): The idea that an American military general is going to warn an adversary if an attack is coming. As you say, when Donald Trump was never even thinking about a military attack against China, the whole thing is pretty far-fetched. GRIFFIN: A former senior Trump defense official says the phone call to the Chinese was done after then-Defense Secretary Mark Esper requested his civilian policy officials to do the same. It was designed to lower the temperature and prevent the U.S. and China from stumbling into a conflict. Then-Defense Secretary Esper was so concerned about not spooking the Chinese that he asked for a delay in sending a significant number of ships and war planes to the region around the time of the election for a December exercise. Regarding allegations that General Milley attempted to usurp power from the president when it came to launching a nuclear weapon, the Joint Staff pushed back. The meeting regarding nuclear weapons protocols was to remind uniformed leaders in the Pentagon of the long-established and robust procedures in light of media reporting on the subject. A reference to Speaker Pelosi's phone call to General Milley on January 8th. (END VIDEO CLIP) GRIFFIN (voice over): Officials here at the Pentagon scoffed at the suggestion today from former acting Defense Secretary Chris Miller that he did not know about the call with Milley's Chinese counterpart. Not only was he briefed, I'm told, so were senior State Department and White House officials who General Milley called after his January 8th call with his Chinese counterpart, Bret. BAIER: We'll follow this. Jennifer Griffin live at the Pentagon. Jennifer, thank you. Tonight, we take you inside Afghanistan and inside a prison inside Afghanistan from which the Taliban has released thousands of its fighters, along with criminals since taking over that country. Correspondent Trey Yingst reports tonight from Kabul. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) TREY YINGST, FOX NEWS CHANNEL CORRESPONDENT (voice over): Right now, we are entering the Pole Charkhi Prison with the Taliban . When the group entered the Afghan capital, they came into this facility and freed thousands of their fellow fighters. These fighters came from the Logar province, and they said it was a 15-year struggle to take over Afghanistan and that they're happy they now control the country. And they say they are bringing security to the Afghan people. Tiny prison cells, handcuffs chained to bars and long dark hallways make up the grounds. The only people left here are petty criminals in jail and Taliban guards. Niaz Mohammed Halim spent four years behind bars here as a prisoner. He came back today to visit. He's now a top Taliban intelligence official. Halim thank God for the Taliban 's takeover, he then talked about reports of division among the ranks of the Taliban over how to divide power in the country. NIAZ MOHAMMED HALIM, TALIBAN INTELLIGENCE OFFICIAL, AFGHANISTAN (through translator): From individual people to top level officials, everyone obeys the rule of the Taliban Emirate. There is no infighting. What we order here in Kabul is implemented in all provinces, that is propaganda of the enemy. YINGST: The Taliban has started to implement a system of justice based on Sharia law. It bans men and women from working together, does not allow music to be played and adheres to violent punishment for crimes. This as the European Commission today expressed concern that the Taliban could target people who used to hold them accountable under the previous Afghan Government. URSULA VON DER LEYEN , PRESIDENT, EUROPEAN COMMISSION : We stand by the Afghan people, the women and children, prosecutors, journalists and human rights defenders. I think in particular of women judges, who are now in hiding from the man they jailed. They have been put at risk for their contribution to justice and the rule of law. (END VIDEO CLIP) YINGST (on camera): Tonight, evacuation flights from the Afghan city of Mazar-i-Sharif are still grounded by the Taliban . This as the U.S. State Department is telling visa applicants they'll have to either apply in a neighboring country or online. Neither positive news for those looking to leave Afghanistan, Bret. BAIER: I'd say. Trey Yingst live in Kabul early Thursday morning. Trey, thank you. Back here at home, criticism continues tonight of how President Biden conducted the U.S. withdrawal from Afghanistan, specifically allegations he ignored his military advisors. White House Correspondent Jacqui Heinrich has details. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) JACQUI HEINRICH, FOX NEWS CHANNEL CORRESPONDENT (voice over): Leaks from a classified hearing on the Hill Tuesday further make the case President Biden rebuffed his commanders and pressed on with a full Afghanistan withdrawal against military advice. SEN. JAMES INHOFE (R-OK): He did say that it's all right to acknowledge that he opposed the effort that took place. HEINRICH: Two sources in the hearing tell Fox the former commander of U.S. troops in Afghanistan, General Austin Scott Miller passed his recommendation through the chain of command that 2,500 troops should remain on the ground to maintain stability given the Taliban threat assessment. Miller's view was troops should maintain a holding pattern potentially supplemented by additional forces from allied nations giving no recommendation on how long they should stay and making clear he didn't know what the end timeline would be. But he strongly dissented with the intelligence believe Afghanistan would fall to the Taliban in one to three years. Miller saying it would go much, much faster. INHOFE: And he did not tell the president of that because the president wasn't there. HEINRICH: Fox has also learned Miller did have the chance to share his views with President Biden several times before the draw down and his assessments were included in the Chairman of the Joint Chiefs presentations to the National Security Council before Biden's decision. Senators were unclear if the president ultimately saw Miller's recommendations wanting to hear from Defense Secretary Lloyd Austin , about how much weight they were given. Was the president support Secretary Austin appearing before Congress? Would he encourage it? PSAKI: He is appearing before Congress at the end of the month. And he's already agreed to that. HEINRICH: Miller told senators once his recommendation was turned down, it became his job to execute on the withdrawal order. And eventually, decisions like abandoning Bagram were forced by constraints through the president's orders, like troop caps. Pressure is now ramping up on the Hill for more hearings. SEN. BOB MENENDEZ (D-NJ): The Congress has either been lied to, misled, or gave overly rosy projections. (END VIDEO CLIP) HEINRICH: Tonight, President Biden announced new trilateral agreement between Australia, the U.K. and the U.S. known as AUKUS. It will help Australia acquire nuclear powered submarines in an apparent challenge to China's activities in the Indo-Pacific. U.S. has only ever shared nuclear propulsion technology with one other country, the U.K. This will bolster alliances and it comes after China taunted the U.S. withdrawal from Afghanistan and also targeted U.S. allies like Taiwan, Bret. BAIER: Long military relationship with Australia but this is a big deal. Jacqui, thank you. Stocks were up, today, the Dow gained 237, the S&P 500 finished ahead 38, the NASDAQ jumped 124. Some of America's greatest young athletes were reduced to tears today on Capitol Hill describing incidents of sexual abuse at the hands of their team doctor. Olympic gold medalist Simone Biles and several others are accusing the FBI of deliberately covering up abuse by the physician during the Bureau's widely criticized investigation. They're also very upset that no one from the Justice Department came to today's hearing. Congressional Correspondent Aishah Hasnie has some of their dramatic testimony tonight. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) SIMONE BILES, OLYMPIC GYMNAST: I blame Larry Nassar and I also blame an entire system that enabled and perpetrated his abuse. AISHAH HASNIE, FOX NEWS CHANNEL CORRESPONDENT (voice over): Tearful testimony today from Olympic superstar Simone Biles, Aly Raisman, McKayla Maroney and Maggie Nichols, as they told members of the Senate Judiciary Committee how the FBI failed them when they tried to report sexual abuse by USA Gymnastics team Dr. Larry Nassar. But tears turned into anger when Department of Justice officials who can actually bring charges didn't turn up. MCKAYLA MARONEY, OLYMPIC GYMNAST: Deputy Attorney General Lisa Monaco couldn't even bring herself to be here today. And it is the Department of Justice's job to hold them accountable. HASNIE: Several senators also took issue with DOJ's no show. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: It is outrageous. When we asked them to bring someone in to explain this today, they refused. HASNIE: The comments come as lawmakers dig into a scathing Department of Justice report in June, which revealed the Indianapolis FBI office botched the case by failing to respond with urgency, falsifying statements and failing to notify state or local authorities. The report found this led to a yearlong delay that ultimately allowed Nassar to abuse dozens of more girls. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: This man is on the loose molesting children. CHRISTOPHER WRAY , DIRECTOR, FBI: I don't have a good explanation for you. It is utterly jarring to me. HASNIE: Wray said he's implementing all of the inspector general's recommendations. MICHAEL HOROWITZ, JUSTICE DEPARTMENT INSPECTOR GENERAL: We keep following up and we will keep working on this. HASNIE: And the FBI recently fired a supervisory agent for not properly pursuing tips about Nassar. But former Special Agent in Charge Jay Abbott, who the DOJ found applied for a job with USA Gymnastics while the FBI was investigating Nassar wound up retiring, leaving little justice for the women. WRAY: It is extremely frustrating that we are left with little disciplinary recourse when people retire before their cases can be adjudicated. (END VIDEO CLIP) HASNIE (on camera): And Bret, a DOJ official tells Fox tonight that A.G. Garland will appear before this very same committee next month to take questions. And that same official is telling us also that several career prosecutors have looked over this case more than once and decided that federal charges just would not be successful, Bret. BAIER: Aishah Hasnie live on Capitol Hill. Aishah, thanks. Up next, how data that could shed light on the origins of the coronavirus disappeared from the National Institutes of Health archive. You'll be surprised to hear who made that request. First, here's what some of our Fox affiliates around the country are covering tonight. Fox 26 in Houston where 98,000 customers are still without power as the remnants of Hurricane Nicholas move into Louisiana. Storm was downgraded today to a tropical depression but it is dumping heavy rain across the area still recovering from Hurricane Ida. Fox 9 in Minneapolis where the Minnesota Supreme Court has overturned a third-degree murder conviction for a police officer charged in the shooting death of an Australian woman. Mohamed Noor testified he feared he was being ambushed when Justine Damond approached his squad car. She had called earlier to report a possible assault. Noor's partner says Damond made a loud noise slapping the back of their squad car before Noor fired his gun ultimately killing the woman. And this is a live look at Cape Canaveral from Fox 35. Big story there tonight, the world's first all civilian space crew is preparing for liftoff. The four-person squad will ride aboard a SpaceX Falcon 9 rocket and Dragon Resilience spacecraft. They'll conduct research on advancing human health on earth during their three-day trip. Launch window opens just about two hours. That's tonight's live look outside the Beltway from SPECIAL REPORT. We will be right back. (COMMERCIAL BREAK) BAIER: The Los Angeles County is -- Los Angeles County is planning to require proof of vaccination or negative COVID test to attend indoor bars, nightclubs, and lounges. That's a big place, L.A. County. The order also covers sporting events. It will strongly recommend but not require verification to attend indoor restaurants. Pfizer says U.S. regulators should approve a booster dose of the COVID-19 vaccine because of decreasing effectiveness overtime of the initial shots. The company is recommending the third shot six months after the second. And FDA committee of outside experts will vote on this proposal Friday. President Biden met today with the CEOs of Walt Disney and other companies to discuss his recently announced vaccine requirement for firms that employ at least 100 people. President says he looks forward to building on that policy. And the man considered China's most famous defector reportedly warned American intelligence agencies about the coronavirus in November of 2019. That's according to a report in the New York Post. It cites a portion of a book about the Wuhan lab. The defector says he felt U.S. intelligence agencies were not taking his information seriously. China did not alert the World Health Organization to the coronavirus until December 31st of 2019. Well, the mystery surrounding the origins of the coronavirus takes another strange turn tonight. It involves the disappearance of information that could shed some light on this issue. Correspondent David Spunt picks up the story. DAVID SPUNT, FOX NEWS CHANNEL CORRESPONDENT (voice-over): The National Institutes of Health is reviewing results of an investigation into deleted coronavirus data from the early days of the pandemic. Researchers store genetic sequencing data in an archive run by the NIH . It's accessible to scientists around the world. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) DR. MARTY MAKARY, FOX NEWS CHANNEL MEDICAL CONTRIBUTOR (on camera): Those sequences are essentially the Rosetta stone that enable virologists to trace the drift or manipulation of a genetic code. SPUNT: According to the NIH , the sequences from Wuhan, China were submitted to the database in March 2020. By June of that year, a Chinese researcher asked the NIH to remove the data. MAKARY: It's very unusual for any data of genetic information in that database to be deleted. SPUNT: The NIH considers the sequences to be the property of researchers and obliged, but keeps a backup. It is not available to the public without the researcher's permission. The Wall Street Journal reported the deleted sequences in June, prompting three Republicans to question NIH Director Dr. Francis Collins about the data. SEN. MARSHA BLACKBURN (R-TN): The Chinese Communist Party once again, what are they trying to cover up? What do they want to make sure we never know? SPUNT: The NIH just days ago responded to Blackburn, announcing an investigation to "determine whether the appropriate steps were taken to assess this withdrawal request. Withdrawal makes the data undiscoverable but does not erase it." And NIH spokesperson confirms the investigation is complete, though the results are not yet public. BLACKBURN: We don't consider it case closed until we get the results of that investigation. (END VIDEO CLIP) SPUNT: This news comes just weeks after the U.S. intelligence community fail to find a definitive origin of the virus. China says the United States should look at other countries for origin information. Bret. BAIER: We continue to follow this. David, thanks. The Justice Department is asking a federal judge in Texas to temporarily halt the controversial new state law banning abortions after about six weeks. The emergency motion comes days after the agency sued Texas, claiming the law was enacted to prevent women from exercising their constitutional rights. The Texas governor's office says it is confident the court will uphold the law. The new rule went into effect September 1st after the U.S. Supreme Court refused to block it. Prosecutors say former University of Miami professor, his wife, and his sister, are facing federal charges related to purchasing genetic sequencing equipment from U.S. manufacturers, and illegally shipping it to Iran. The suspects made their initial appearances Tuesday in Miami federal court. A criminal complaint says a company operated by the family received numerous wire transfers from accounts overseas totaling almost $3-1/2 million dollars between 2016 and 2020. Up next, why Republicans think one key issue could be a game-changer in the Virginia governor's race. Plus, how Democrats are trying to make immigration reform an economic issue and bend the rules on the Senate filibuster. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) SEN. DICK DURBIN (D-IL): Fate is being decided by the Senate parliamentarian. I think we have a strong case. SEN. JOHN CORNYN (R-TX): They are trying to do something on a purely partisan basis using the budget reconciliation process. (END VIDEO CLIP) (COMMERCIAL BREAK) BAIER: California Democratic Governor Gavin Newsom easily defeated a Republican recall effort against him. Newsom is ahead by a 30 point margin with about two-thirds of the ballots counted so far in California. Newsom gets to keep his job, at least for a while. He is up for re-election next year. Well, this year the governor's race in Virginia is expected to be very close. The Republican nominee and his supporters have made critical race theory which links racial discrimination to America's foundations and legal system a key issue. The first candidate debate in this race is tomorrow. Here is Chief Washington correspondent Mike Emanuel. MIKE EMANUEL, FOX NEWS CHANNEL CHIEF WASHINGTON CORRESPONDENT (voice-over): Critical race theory is on the ballot in Virginia and Republicans see it as a potentially defining issue in the governor's race. The RealClearPolitics average of recent poll shows Democrat Terry McAuliffe leading Republican Glenn Youngkin by 5.2. 46 to 40.8, likely closer than the former Governor McAuliffe would like it to be since President Biden won Virginia by 10 points. McAuliffe is called critical race theory, "Another right-wing conspiracy." At a school board meeting in Loudoun County, Virginia, which has been ground zero in the CRT fight, parents sounded off again. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: You have implemented programs that are not creating high academic achievers. It is implementing progressive political ideologies, it's not academic. EMANUEL: Youngkin is hitting education hard, including at a recent save our schools event with former HUD Secretary Dr. Ben Carson. GLENN YOUNGKIN (R), GUBERNATORIAL CANDIDATE, VIRGINIA: Our curriculum has gone haywire. So, on day one, we are going to ban teaching critical race theory in our schools. EMANUEL: Larry Sabato from the University of Virginia says critical race theory could energies GOP voters in this off-year election. LARRY SABATO , DIRECTOR, CENTER FOR POLITICS, UNIVERSITY OF VIRGINIA : They see these issues, these curriculum issues and some of the controversy about masks, for example, is helping them to reduce the democratic margin. They might be influenced by this and might well motivate more Republicans to turn out or at least at a greater rate than Democrats turnout. That's the Republican hope. (END VIDEO CLIP) EMANUEL: This is a critical stage in the race with that first debate tomorrow night, and early voting starting on Friday, in a race that could create a playbook for next year's midterms. Bret. BAIER: It's one to watch. Mike, thanks. House Democrats are under pressure from Speaker Nancy Pelosi tonight to have language specifically ready for their massive $3.5 trillion tax and spending bill. They call it human infrastructure. Pelosi wants to pass that measure before the end of the month. Well, today, White House officials, including President Biden are putting their own pressure on too moderate Democratic senators, who so far have said they won't support the bill as proposed. Congressional correspondent Chad Pergram tells us where things stand tonight from Capitol Hill. Good evening, Chad. CHAD PERGRAM, FOX NEWS CHANNEL CONGRESSIONAL CORRESPONDENT (on camera): Good evening, Bret. Well, Kyrsten Sinema and Joe Manchin went to the White House today. They're trying to get an agreement to keep moderates on board here. The other thing to watch for is whether or not immigration reform can be a part of this reconciliation bill. Listen. PERGRAM (voice-over): Democrats are trying to stuff as much as they can into their big social spending bill. It's just not environmental policies and tax hikes. Liberals could use the multitrillion-dollar bill to pass immigration reform and create pathways to citizenship for millions. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) REP. ALEXANDRIA OCASIO-CORTEZ (D-NY): That is too precious and too important of an opportunity for us to allow to sail by. PERGRAM: Budget bills are reserved exclusively for money in taxes. Democrats are already using the special process to avoid a filibuster. The Senate can't pass immigration the regular way because of the filibuster, but it's different if Democrats can jam immigration into this bill. So, they are working the ref. SEN. DICK DURBIN, (D-IL) SENATE JUDICIARY COMMITTEE CHAIRMAN: Our fate is being decided by the Senate parliamentarian. I think we have a strong case. I hope she agrees. PERGRAM: Senate Parliamentarian Elizabeth MacDonough determines what's in and what's out. If Democrats persuade MacDonough that immigration is a money issue, it could be in. Even Senate Minority Leader Mitch McConnell admires the audacity of the Democrats, and he is resigned to an eventual McDonough decision. SEN. MITCH MCCONNELL , (R-KY) SENATE MINORITY LEADER: I can't blame the other side for trying. That's always the temptation of the majority using the reconciliation process. But abiding by the ruling of the parliamentarian is essential to the function of the Senate. PERGRAM: Democrats could use revenue from new citizens as new taxpayers to cover the cost of the bill. REP. JAMES CLYBURN, (D-SC) HOUSE MAJORITY WHIP: If we do the Dreamers and get protected workers on a pathway to citizenship, it would be, some estimate, $121 billion benefit to the GDP. PERGRAM: But some Republicans think the Democrats effort to wedge immigration into the bill shows desperation. SEN. JOHN CORNYN , (R-TX) SENATE JUDICIARY COMMITTEE : I think it speaks to their lack of seriousness at dealing with things like the border crisis. (END VIDEO TAPE) PERGRAM (on camera): If they cut the size of the bill to please moderates, the left would be hard pressed to oppose the plan if they include immigration. Also, the House has just finalized tax policy in the bill. The corporate rate 26.5 percent, and those earning more than $5 million a year are pegged with a three percent upcharge. Bret? BRET BAIER, FOX NEWS ANCHOR: Well, without Manchin and Sinema, this does not get through. There are other moderates that possibly are not voting for this because of other pieces of it, right, Chad? PERGRAM: That's right. BAIER: Or is this all negotiated down to something Schumer says, OK, we won't do this, but we are going to pass this? PERGRAM: Two things to look at here. There is so much attention focused on Kyrsten Sinema and Joe Manchin. Today in the Ways and Means Committee when they marked up the tax portion of the bill, the blue dog leader Stephanie Murphy, a moderate Democrat from Florida, she voted no. She left the door open to maybe voting yes later. And also Tom Suozzi , a Democrat from Long Island, he raised questions about whether or not they would have SALT, the state and local tax reduction, whether or not that would be in this bill. It's not in there yet. But he has said he might oppose this if they don't fix this in the end. Bret? BAIER: That's a good update. We're going to talk about more of this with the panel. Chad, thanks. Up next, that new car smell getting harder and harder to find. (COMMERCIAL BREAK) BAIER: State police in South Carolina say a prominent lawyer tried to arrange his own death earlier this month so his son would get a $10 million life insurance payment. But authorities say the plan's fatal shot only grazed Alex Murdaugh's head. The state law enforcement division says it has charged the shooter with assisted suicide, insurance fraud, and several other counts. Murdaugh has not been charged, but agents say that may change. Two days after the shooting, Murdaugh said he was resigning from his law firm and entering rehab. Murdaugh's son and wife were killed in a double shooting in June. Police investigating the disappearance of a 22-year-old woman who was on a cross-country trip with her boyfriend now say that man is a person of interest in this case. The family of Gabby Petito says Brian Laundrie is refusing to tell them where he last saw her. He has hired an attorney but so far has not spoken to police. Meanwhile, police in Utah say officers were called for an incident involving the two, but no charges were filed, and they are still following up on all leads there. If you are trying to find a new vehicle, you know prices are high, supply is scarce. Part of the reason is that shortage we have been telling you about of a key electronic component. FOX Business Correspondent Lydia Hu is at a car dealership in New Jersey to explain. Good evening, Lydia. LYDIA HU, FOX BUSINESS CORRESPONDENT: Good evening, Bret. The global shortage on semiconductor chips continues as industry groups say shipments and production are reaching an all-time high. The world's few chip manufacturers, located mostly overseas, struggle to keep up with surge in demand as supply chain bottlenecks delay shipments. Taiwan is home to the world's leading chip producer, and its tense relationship with China adds concern about America's ongoing access to chips. The shortage is pitting the auto industry against consumer electronics for the limited supply available. The car manufacturers are feeling the pinch with constrained car inventories. Estimates show more than 4 million vehicles have been lost due to the chip shortage. Those losses could reach 9.5 million as some automakers stall production without needed chips. And vehicle prices are already surging. Prices for new cars continue to climb in August, up 7.6 percent year over year. The average new vehicle transaction price for last month was more than $43,000. That's a record high for the fifth straight month. And prices on used cars and trucks came down slightly in August but are still up nearly 32 percent year over year. Average transaction prices for used cars at dealerships hit more than $28,000 last month. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) TOM MAOLI NEW JERSEY DEALERSHIP OWNER: I think it's going to stay this way for a long time because, as they start producing, the pent-up demand is going to try dry up the inventory that's being produced, and you're going to have another supply and demand issue. (END VIDEO CLIP) HU: Now, the chip shortage is expected to stretch into the beginning of next year. In the short-term car prices are expected to surge again in the aftermath of hurricane Ida as widespread flooding is believed to have destroyed thousands of cars. Bret? BAIER: Lydia, thank you. And that's not just cars. A lot of different items. Thank you. Up next, the panel on a bombshell report of then President Trump's top military adviser, what he did or didn't do, plus the reaction. Plus, what are Capitol Hill's plans for taxes? We are going to go into that. First, Beyond our Borders tonight. A post monsoon fever outbreak kills at least 115 people in the most populous state of India. The state's health minister says most cases were caused by dengue, a seasonal viral infection spread by mosquitoes. The sister of North Korean leader Kim Jong-un threatens a complete destruction of bilateral relations with South Korea. The criticism of Kim Yo-jong comes after both countries tested ballistic missiles hours apart. The rival launches underscore a return of tensions amid stalled nuclear talks there. Just some of the other stories Beyond our Borders tonight. We'll be right back. (COMMERCIAL BREAK) (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) JOE BIDEN , (D) PRESIDENT OF THE UNITED STATES: I have great confidence in General Milley. JEN PSAKI , WHITE HOUSE PRESS SECRETARY: His experience with him has been that he is a patriot. He is somebody who is -- has fidelity to the Constitution. I can't speak to anonymous, unconfirmed reports about prior conversations during the last administration. JOHN KIRBY, PENTAGON PRESS SECRETARY: It is completely appropriate for the chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff as the senior military adviser to both the secretary and the president to want to see those protocols reviewed. I see nothing in what I have read that would -- that would cause any concern. SEN. RAND PAUL , (R-KY): If it happened, he should be immediately relieved of his dues and court-martialed. If it is true, absolutely immediately needs to be removed. This is very, very dangerous. (END VIDEO CLIP) BAIER: Well, that's another day in Washington after a Bob Woodward book. This time Bob Woodward and Bob Costa with the book "Peril," reaction to charges, allegations in this book of what Chairman of the Joint Chiefs General Mark Milley did in the wake of the January 6th riots on Capitol Hill. Here's a voice we hadn't heard from in a while, retired lieutenant colonel Alexander Vindman of impeachment fame tweeting out "If this is true General Milley must resign. He usurped civilian authority, broke chain of command, violated the sacrosanct principle of civilian control over the military. It's an extremely dangerous precedent. You can't simply walk away from that. Do the right thing in the right way." Let's bring in our panel, Ben Domenech, publisher of "The Federalist," Harold Ford Jr., former Tennessee Congressman, CEO of Empowerment and Inclusion Capital, and Trey Gowdy , former Congressman from South Carolina. Trey, a lot of push back from the Pentagon today. We had our own reporting saying what General Milley did with two calls to the Chinese was to try to calm fears, and what he did, they say, with the nuclear process was to make sure the process was intact and everybody knew what was going on. The book alleges something different. Where are you on this and the significance of it? TREY GOWDY , FORMER SOUTH CAROLINA REPRESENTATIVE: Bret, I have never liked anonymous source. We certainly didn't use them in the courtroom, and there is a reason for that. And I don't like starting things by saying "if it's true," but this is television and not court. I find the whole thing bizarre that you have a U.S. general who thinks an American president is more of a threat to the country than China. I think it's really bizarre that he didn't tell anyone who could have actually done something about it, if that's what he believed. And I think it's bizarre that we call people ahead of time and warn them, hey, we may attack you. My dominant thought, Bret, is I bet that Afghan driver who was bringing some water to folks would have appreciated an advance call before an attack. BAIER: Harold, this comes, stems from in a book a transcript actually of a call between Speaker Pelosi and General Milley in the wake of the January 6th riot on Capitol Hill. I assume it's Pelosi's office who records that call and gives Woodward the transcript. But in it she says how do we prevent this president who losing it from using the nuclear football, from authorizing a nuclear strike, which, by the way, no one in the Trump administration or around them ever said that the president was even contemplating any action like that. HAROLD FORD JR., FORMER TENNESSEE REPRESENTATIVE: Look, first, thanks for having me on. I think Trey, again, has the frame about right. We have to remember, though, the last two months of President Trump's presidency was pretty chaotic. In fact, the last two weeks were the most remarkable -- the most remarkable I have seen in politics since 9/11. It appears that according to the reporting in the book, and I have not read it, just what reports are about the reporting in the book, that Senators Graham and McConnell also wanted to try to erect some guardrails around the president, and including Attorney General Barr, according to the reporting. General Milley will have to answer these questions before the Senate in a couple of weeks. And I don't know him, but what I do know of him from seeing him on television, reading his comments, he seems like a pretty straightforward guy who is not afraid to answer questions honestly. So we will see if the reporting is true. BAIER: Yes, it's important to have that context in the wake of January 6th and leading up to January 20th, Ben. There were a lot of people inside the administration who was saying the former president, now former, was acting erratically. But the actions of the chairman of the Joint Chiefs if as reported is true, and again, there is a lot of pushback, would go outside his line of command. BEN DOMENECH, PUBLISHER, "THE FEDERALIST": One think I can tell you, Bret, is that members of Congress, certainly the ones that I have spoken to, do not believe the pushback. They do not believe that this is an accurate reflection of what went on there. And they have raised significant questions, particularly those members of the Republican caucus who are themselves veterans. And I expect that we will see a continued focus on this in the days to come, particularly given that this is something that exists outside of the chain of command. This is not a situation where General Milley would ever be authorized to do something along these lines. And there are questions that are raised by this that go beyond just the normal slate of things. This is the kind of thing that can be used in many ways to run down the expectations and the respect that military members have for not just the chain of command but for the highest officers, those who are met with the greatest challenges. It does no service to them in order to see this kind of thing happen. And I think you are going to see an investigation into this, perhaps a classified one from the Intel Committee or from the Armed Services Committee in the House that continues and that digs down and that tries to get to the accurate estimation of what really was said, because I think we all deserve to know it. BAIER: Again, Milley is scheduled to testify September 28th. We have invited the chairman of the Joint Chiefs on the show if he wants to come talk about before that, and we will see how that testimony goes. Meantime, up on Capitol Hill, dealing with what is in the bill, the massive bill. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) JEN PSAKI , WHITE HOUSE PRESS SECRETARY: The president encouraged members of Congress to put things forward, things they would like to see in the package. REP. MIKE JOHNSON , (R-LA): This $3.5 trillion spending palooza includes amnesty for somewhere between 8 and 10 million illegal immigrants. STEVEN HORSFORD, (D-NV) HOUSE WAYS AND MEANS COMMITTEE: It's about making the American worker competitive. SEN. JOHN CORNYN , (R-TX): Permanent welfare with no work requirements, green new deal climate mandates. JIMMY GOMEZ, (D-CA) HOUSE WAYS AND MEANS COMMITTEE: We invest the largest amount in the history of this country in the green economy. SEN. ROB PORTMAN, (R-OH): It increases taxes on retirement accounts. It increases income taxes. REP. RO KHANNA , (D-CA): The plan means that seniors are going to get dental. They are going to get vision. REP. MIKE KELLY, (R-PA) HOUSE WAYS AND MEANS COMMITTEE: This ain't no open bar. Somebody's paying for it. Somebody is going to pay for it down the road. (END VIDEO CLIP) BAIER: So some different takes about what's in the bill. Trey, we have got moderate senators, Kyrsten Sinema and Joe Manchin up on the White House. I'm sure they are doing the hardcore press, full-court press on trying to get those moderates to come along. GOWDY: I don't know Joe Manchin, but I can tell you it won't work with Kyrsten Sinema. She ain't afraid of anything. My two dominate thoughts are, number one, how embarrassed I am. I never thought to get the parliamentarian to tell me I could put whatever I wanted in a bill and just have one bill for the entire year. Never entered my mind. We used to call that a queen. Now it's called a parliamentarian. The other thing I can't get my head around, Bret, is we are a 50-50 country. The House is close. The Senate is evenly divided. That is not the time to pursue transformational change on either side. It won't work. BAIER: Massive immigration reform in a budgetary item is really pretty brazen. But we'll see where that goes. Here's "The Wall Street Journal" on the tax plan. I just want to give a couple second to this. Expected to raise -- this is what passed out of panel today, expected to raise more than $2 trillion in new revenue over the next decade from high income households and U.S. companies, raise the corporate tax rate to 26.5 percent from 21 percent, basic top income tax rate would increase from 239.6 from 37 percent. The top bracket starting at $400,000 for individuals, $450,000 for married couples. A three percent surtax for household incomes above $5 million. It would increase long-term capital gains and dividends to 25 percent from 20 percent, prevents people from contributing to retirement plans that's Roth IRA if value exceeds $10 million, $78 billion in funding for IRS to ramp up tax enforcement. That's a lot more tax agents. Doubles the current tax rate on cigarettes, small cigars, and roll your own tobacco, just to name few. Harold, there is a lot in here. FORD : There is. Look, I am for immigration reform. But this is not the way to do it in a reconciliation package. And I would hope the parliamentarian might feel the same way, but we shall see. I would agree with Trey. Senator Manchin and Senator Sinema are probably not going to agree to too much of this. But I've got to tell you, a tax code and spending on the part of government ought to be organized around how we make America stronger and more competitive. And I think some of the ideas in this plan are not as objectionable I think to a majority of Americans as some may think, particularly when you consider that it's going to raise taxes on the highest of earners. I think the $400,000 limit the White House may have, they are going to have to shelve that. If what this plan says you are going to tax those earning over $5 million over a year a little bit more to pay for some things, I think a lot of Americans may come along with that. BAIER: Yes. I think there may be a lot of horse trading here and Chuck Schumer may know that it's not going to be $3.5 trillion. It may be $2 trillion and a lot may go in the negotiation. But they might still get something through. Ben, you will start on tomorrow's headlines when we come back after this. (COMMERCIAL BREAK) BAIER: Finally tonight, a look at tomorrow's headlines with the panel. As promised, Ben, first to you. DOMENECH: Hilarious Canadian man fights cancer to a draw. RIP to the great Norm MacDonald, the best news anchor that I know not named Bret Baier for his fight and battle against cancer. He pointed out that you never actually lose to cancer. You take it with you. So he fought it to a draw. And congratulations to him and all the happiness he has given us over the many years of life he had on this earth. BAIER: Rest in peace. Trey? GOWDY: The FBI botches another major investigation, this one involving sexually abused young girls. BAIER: Tough one. Harold? FORD : I agree with Trey. Woodward has done it again, this time with Bob Costa. He has gotten Washington's most powerful to talk about things that sell books. BAIER: That is true. Thanks, panel. Tomorrow on SPECIAL REPORT, Democrats push federal voting rights in the latest attempt to federalize elections. Will they have the votes? Thanks for inviting us into your home tonight. That's it for the SPECIAL REPORT, fair, balanced, and still unafraid. "FOX NEWS PRIMETIME" hosted by Lawrence Jones starts right now. Hey, Lawrence. headline: President Joe Biden Tours Destruction In Louisiana; Explosion And Fire At Banquet Hall And Nearby Homes; Concerns Over Stranded Americans As Taliban Seize Power; Democrats Renew Push To Pack Supreme Court; Rep. Markwayne Mullin (R-OK), Is Being Interviewed About His Effort Getting SIVs And AMCITS Out Of Afghanistan; Unending Battle To Keep Focus On Illegal Crossings; Mullin Mission Barred From Landing In Afghanistan; Mullin Disputes Claims About Rescue Effort
story_text: SHANNON BREAM, FOX NEWS ANCHOR: All right, that is it for us. Thanks for watching. Have a great Labor Day weekend, everybody. We'll see you back here Monday for fan mail Monday. BRET BAIER, FOX NEWS ANCHOR: Good evening, welcome to Washington I'm Mike Emanuel in for Bret Baier. Breaking tonight, we're following two big stories including the increasing concern over Americans and Afghans stranded in Afghanistan as the Taliban consolidate power. We will have a report from the State Department. And Bret interviews an Oklahoma congressman who has returned from a highly criticized secret effort to get to Afghanistan. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) BAIER: Why should we not think that this was, you know, bravado or testosterone or an effort to get the spot? How do you respond to that? (END VIDEO CLIP) EMANUEL: His answer, still ahead, but we begin with devastation from Hurricane Ida and its remnants in the south and the Northeast. We have Fox team coverage, Bryan Llenas is in Manville, New Jersey, where a banquet hall damaged in the storm exploded this morning, but we begin with Correspondent Jeff Paul in New Orleans with President Biden's visit to Louisiana. Good evening, Jeff. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) JEFF PAUL, FOX NEWS CORRESPONDENT (on camera): Yes, Mike, here in New Orleans, French Quarter, power is slowly flipping back on but throughout the state, hundreds of thousands of people are still without electricity, let alone water and gas and in some cases, without a place to call home. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) PAUL (voice over): Nearly a week after it ripped through Louisiana, the grip of Hurricane Ida's impact continues to tighten. Power lines toppled, lines stretched long and some houses just pieces of their original form. On Friday, President Joe Biden got his first glimpse of the widespread destruction. JOE BIDEN , PRESIDENT OF THE UNITED STATES: We also know there's a heck of a lot more work to do and that's why we're here today. PAUL: Welcomed to the State by Governor John Bel Edwards . President Biden toward one of the hardest hit communities of LaPlace, Louisiana. BIDEN: Folks, I know you're hurting -- I know you're hurting. And we're going to make sure we have someone coming through here going door to door, letting people know what's available to them right now. PAUL: The area was not only walloped by the storm's strong gusts but feet of floodwater left folks trapped and their homes partially submerged. The president also got to see the vast devastation from the sky flying above Lafayette, Port Fourchon and Grand Isle, a town where not a single home is still livable. AUSTIN LASSERE, BAYOU BOEUF, LOUISIANA FIRE CHIEF: We just got to keep pushing forward. You know, the past behind us. We got to keep going forward. Oh, what happened happened, that's the way I look at it. We just got to rebuild. PAUL: While crews work around the clock to restore power, refuel gas stations and distribute food and water, the state is now investigating several nursing homes. Investigators say hundreds of elderly patients were moved to a warehouse amidst the hurricane. They received unconfirmed reports of patients being packed together, laying on the floor, water seeping inside and without power. At least four died and 14 were hospitalized. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: This time, I didn't know if my mom was dead or alive. This is a nightmare. It's a nightmare. (END VIDEO CLIP) PAUL (on camera): Now, Biden at times joined by a Democratic governor and two Republican senators says this has nothing to do with party affiliation, this is about being an American, he says. He will be standing next to Louisiana as they rebuild but they need to Build Back Better, a nod to his massive infrastructure plan he hopes passes soon, Mike. EMANUEL: Jeff Paul starting us off from New Orleans tonight. Jeff, many thanks. At least 49 people across five eastern states have died from the remnants of Ida. A building exploded this morning in New Jersey where some neighborhoods were inundated with as much as 14 feet of water. Correspondent Bryan Llenas is in Manville tonight. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) JAYESH MEHTA, OWNER, THE SAFFRON BANQUET HALL: Invested every penny that I'd earned in my life in this property. BRYAN LLENAS, FOX NEWS CORRESPONDENT (voice over): This smoldering rubble is all that's left of The Saffron banquet hall in Manville, New Jersey. The business exploded overnight, and three other homes caught fire after being inundated with up to eight feet of water. Jayesh Mehta opened the obliterated banquet hall in 2018. Business was already tough because of COVID, now this. MEHTA: I don't know what words to use. I bet everything in my life that I had for this property. I worked too hard. I don't know what to do. Totally helpless. And I just hope everybody pray for me. LLENAS: First responders in Manville were called to 500 homes rescuing 1,000 people from floodwaters spilled over from the Raritan River, which rose to a record shattering 28-feet. THOMAS HERBST, POLICE CHIEF, MANVILLE, NEW JERSEY: It's not every year but I've been here 30 years and I think this is like I said in my eighth or 10th flood somewhere around there, and you know, this is the most catastrophic by far. LLENAS: These satellite photos show before and after the devastating flash floods in New Jersey, 10 inches of rain inundating homes and vehicles along the Delaware River. More than two dozen people died in New Jersey, several are still missing. Most of the victims drowned in their vehicles. In New York's Westchester County where floodwaters rose to 40 feet in some places, stunned residents are beginning to pick up the pieces. ALI SHEBA, STORE MANAGER: It's a disaster. It's like a hurricane was in size. It's like Ida was actually in my store. LLENAS: More than a thousand buildings suffered damage in New York City where leaders admit they were surprised by the historic rainfall. Tonight, the mayor is promising to increase warnings and evacuation orders for those living in basement apartments that became death traps for 11 people including this two-year-old boy and his parents. BILL DE BLASIO (D), MAYOR OF NEW YORK: If we are seeing this kind of rain, we have to have an evacuation mechanism that can reach them. (END VIDEO CLIP) LLENAS (on camera): The smoke is still billowing at the destroyed banquet hall behind me. Floodwaters made roadways impassable for firefighters. Flooding is still a concern for Jersey townships along the Passaic River which won't crest until tomorrow morning, Mike. EMANUEL: So many heartbreaking stories. Bryan Llenas in the Garden State tonight. Bryan, thanks a lot. There are growing questions tonight about what has happened to the Americans and Afghans who want to get out of Afghanistan but cannot. Correspondent Griff Jenkins looks for answers tonight at the State Department. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) ANTONY BLINKEN , U.S. SECRETARY OF STATE: We're in constant contact with Americans who remain in Afghanistan. GRIFF JENKINS, FOX NEWS CORRESPONDENT (voice over): It's been four days since U.S. troops left Afghanistan and Secretary of State Blinken won't say if a single American left behind has gotten out. BLINKEN: Protect the viability of the -- of our tactics, I'm not going to go into any details. JENKINS: Blinken says most of the remaining Americans are dual nationals who call Afghanistan home. And while he says the vast majority of the 124,000 evacuated were at risk Afghans, he acknowledges that a majority of SIV applicants did not make it out. This as reports pour in of the Taliban going door to door to find and punish Afghans who worked with the U.S. FATIMA, AMERICAN TRAPPED IN KABUL: They are stranded, they are left behind. Their lives are in danger. And when I talk danger, it's extreme danger. JENKINS: At the Department of Homeland Security , Secretary Alejandro Mayorkas charged with overseeing the vetting process says some of the evacuees flown out have been flagged on terror watch lists. ALEJANDRO MAYORKAS, DEPUTY SECRETARY, HOMELAND SECURITY: We deny access to individuals whose derogatory information is not resolved and we do not feel confident in the safety and security of the American people. JENKINS: Meanwhile, a group of Republican senators led by Tom Cotton, turning up the heat on the president. SEN. TOM COTTON (R-AR): He broke his promise to Americans and he's continuing to break it because there are American citizens who are trying to get out of the country right now. One of the things no one is talking about is those people are hostages, and they are going to hold Biden's policies going forward hostage. Can you do anything tough to the Taliban now when they have all these Americans? We have to leave it there, gentlemen. Thanks so much. Have a great weekend. When we come back, "Notable Quotables." (COMMERCIAL BREAK) EMANUEL: It's Friday. That means it's time for "Notable Quotables." (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) UNIDENTIFIED MALE: Do you think people should, those who call him sleepy Joe should apologize to him? JEN PSAKI , WHITE HOUSE PRESS SECRETARY: I think we are looking for allowing the president to continue to address multiple crises at a time. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: Right now what we are seeing in Texas is frankly chaos. Patients are scared. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: This is my first time in my 40 years that I ever saw something like this. I thought Katrina was bad. This is the worst one. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: We did not know that the heavens would literally open up and bring Niagara Falls level water to the streets of New York. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: This is tough stuff. War is hard. It's vicious. It's brutal. It's unforgiving. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: They died with their brothers and their sisters right next to them, doing exactly what they all wanted to do. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: The war is over, but the heartbreak continues. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: The parade of horribles are about to unfold. We are leaving thousands of Afghan allies behind who fought bravely with us. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: Do not forget me and my family at the moment in Afghanistan. It is a very hard and horrifying situation. JOE BIDEN , (D) PRESIDENT OF THE UNITED STATES: Couldn't this have been done in a more orderly manner? I respectfully disagree. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: The White House needs to get some oranges and get tougher with the Taliban . PSAKI: We're clearly need to -- sorry, that was aggressive bug. (END VIDEO CLIP) EMANUEL: Quite a week. Next week on SPECIAL REPORT, we will speak with the education secretary and surgeon general and take some of your questions. That's coming up Thursday. Coming up on FOX NEWS SUNDAY, Congressman Michael McCaul and Dr. Ashish Jha . Thank you for watching SPECIAL REPORT. FOX NEWS PRIMETIME hosted by Tammy Bruce starts right now.
