headline: President Joe Biden Tours Destruction In Louisiana; Explosion And Fire At Banquet Hall And Nearby Homes; Concerns Over Stranded Americans As Taliban Seize Power; Democrats Renew Push To Pack Supreme Court; Rep. Markwayne Mullin (R-OK), Is Being Interviewed About His Effort Getting SIVs And AMCITS Out Of Afghanistan; Unending Battle To Keep Focus On Illegal Crossings; Mullin Mission Barred From Landing In Afghanistan; Mullin Disputes Claims About Rescue Effort
story_text: SHANNON BREAM, FOX NEWS ANCHOR: All right, that is it for us. Thanks for watching. Have a great Labor Day weekend, everybody. We'll see you back here Monday for fan mail Monday. BRET BAIER, FOX NEWS ANCHOR: Good evening, welcome to Washington I'm Mike Emanuel in for Bret Baier. Breaking tonight, we're following two big stories including the increasing concern over Americans and Afghans stranded in Afghanistan as the Taliban consolidate power. We will have a report from the State Department. And Bret interviews an Oklahoma congressman who has returned from a highly criticized secret effort to get to Afghanistan. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) BAIER: Why should we not think that this was, you know, bravado or testosterone or an effort to get the spot? How do you respond to that? (END VIDEO CLIP) EMANUEL: His answer, still ahead, but we begin with devastation from Hurricane Ida and its remnants in the south and the Northeast. We have Fox team coverage, Bryan Llenas is in Manville, New Jersey, where a banquet hall damaged in the storm exploded this morning, but we begin with Correspondent Jeff Paul in New Orleans with President Biden's visit to Louisiana. Good evening, Jeff. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) JEFF PAUL, FOX NEWS CORRESPONDENT (on camera): Yes, Mike, here in New Orleans, French Quarter, power is slowly flipping back on but throughout the state, hundreds of thousands of people are still without electricity, let alone water and gas and in some cases, without a place to call home. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) PAUL (voice over): Nearly a week after it ripped through Louisiana, the grip of Hurricane Ida's impact continues to tighten. Power lines toppled, lines stretched long and some houses just pieces of their original form. On Friday, President Joe Biden got his first glimpse of the widespread destruction. JOE BIDEN , PRESIDENT OF THE UNITED STATES: We also know there's a heck of a lot more work to do and that's why we're here today. PAUL: Welcomed to the State by Governor John Bel Edwards . President Biden toward one of the hardest hit communities of LaPlace, Louisiana. BIDEN: Folks, I know you're hurting -- I know you're hurting. And we're going to make sure we have someone coming through here going door to door, letting people know what's available to them right now. PAUL: The area was not only walloped by the storm's strong gusts but feet of floodwater left folks trapped and their homes partially submerged. The president also got to see the vast devastation from the sky flying above Lafayette, Port Fourchon and Grand Isle, a town where not a single home is still livable. AUSTIN LASSERE, BAYOU BOEUF, LOUISIANA FIRE CHIEF: We just got to keep pushing forward. You know, the past behind us. We got to keep going forward. Oh, what happened happened, that's the way I look at it. We just got to rebuild. PAUL: While crews work around the clock to restore power, refuel gas stations and distribute food and water, the state is now investigating several nursing homes. Investigators say hundreds of elderly patients were moved to a warehouse amidst the hurricane. They received unconfirmed reports of patients being packed together, laying on the floor, water seeping inside and without power. At least four died and 14 were hospitalized. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: This time, I didn't know if my mom was dead or alive. This is a nightmare. It's a nightmare. (END VIDEO CLIP) PAUL (on camera): Now, Biden at times joined by a Democratic governor and two Republican senators says this has nothing to do with party affiliation, this is about being an American, he says. He will be standing next to Louisiana as they rebuild but they need to Build Back Better, a nod to his massive infrastructure plan he hopes passes soon, Mike. EMANUEL: Jeff Paul starting us off from New Orleans tonight. Jeff, many thanks. At least 49 people across five eastern states have died from the remnants of Ida. A building exploded this morning in New Jersey where some neighborhoods were inundated with as much as 14 feet of water. Correspondent Bryan Llenas is in Manville tonight. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) JAYESH MEHTA, OWNER, THE SAFFRON BANQUET HALL: Invested every penny that I'd earned in my life in this property. BRYAN LLENAS, FOX NEWS CORRESPONDENT (voice over): This smoldering rubble is all that's left of The Saffron banquet hall in Manville, New Jersey. The business exploded overnight, and three other homes caught fire after being inundated with up to eight feet of water. Jayesh Mehta opened the obliterated banquet hall in 2018. Business was already tough because of COVID, now this. MEHTA: I don't know what words to use. I bet everything in my life that I had for this property. I worked too hard. I don't know what to do. Totally helpless. And I just hope everybody pray for me. LLENAS: First responders in Manville were called to 500 homes rescuing 1,000 people from floodwaters spilled over from the Raritan River, which rose to a record shattering 28-feet. THOMAS HERBST, POLICE CHIEF, MANVILLE, NEW JERSEY: It's not every year but I've been here 30 years and I think this is like I said in my eighth or 10th flood somewhere around there, and you know, this is the most catastrophic by far. LLENAS: These satellite photos show before and after the devastating flash floods in New Jersey, 10 inches of rain inundating homes and vehicles along the Delaware River. More than two dozen people died in New Jersey, several are still missing. Most of the victims drowned in their vehicles. In New York's Westchester County where floodwaters rose to 40 feet in some places, stunned residents are beginning to pick up the pieces. ALI SHEBA, STORE MANAGER: It's a disaster. It's like a hurricane was in size. It's like Ida was actually in my store. LLENAS: More than a thousand buildings suffered damage in New York City where leaders admit they were surprised by the historic rainfall. Tonight, the mayor is promising to increase warnings and evacuation orders for those living in basement apartments that became death traps for 11 people including this two-year-old boy and his parents. BILL DE BLASIO (D), MAYOR OF NEW YORK: If we are seeing this kind of rain, we have to have an evacuation mechanism that can reach them. (END VIDEO CLIP) LLENAS (on camera): The smoke is still billowing at the destroyed banquet hall behind me. Floodwaters made roadways impassable for firefighters. Flooding is still a concern for Jersey townships along the Passaic River which won't crest until tomorrow morning, Mike. EMANUEL: So many heartbreaking stories. Bryan Llenas in the Garden State tonight. Bryan, thanks a lot. There are growing questions tonight about what has happened to the Americans and Afghans who want to get out of Afghanistan but cannot. Correspondent Griff Jenkins looks for answers tonight at the State Department. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) ANTONY BLINKEN , U.S. SECRETARY OF STATE: We're in constant contact with Americans who remain in Afghanistan. GRIFF JENKINS, FOX NEWS CORRESPONDENT (voice over): It's been four days since U.S. troops left Afghanistan and Secretary of State Blinken won't say if a single American left behind has gotten out. BLINKEN: Protect the viability of the -- of our tactics, I'm not going to go into any details. JENKINS: Blinken says most of the remaining Americans are dual nationals who call Afghanistan home. And while he says the vast majority of the 124,000 evacuated were at risk Afghans, he acknowledges that a majority of SIV applicants did not make it out. This as reports pour in of the Taliban going door to door to find and punish Afghans who worked with the U.S. FATIMA, AMERICAN TRAPPED IN KABUL: They are stranded, they are left behind. Their lives are in danger. And when I talk danger, it's extreme danger. JENKINS: At the Department of Homeland Security , Secretary Alejandro Mayorkas charged with overseeing the vetting process says some of the evacuees flown out have been flagged on terror watch lists. ALEJANDRO MAYORKAS, DEPUTY SECRETARY, HOMELAND SECURITY: We deny access to individuals whose derogatory information is not resolved and we do not feel confident in the safety and security of the American people. JENKINS: Meanwhile, a group of Republican senators led by Tom Cotton, turning up the heat on the president. SEN. TOM COTTON (R-AR): He broke his promise to Americans and he's continuing to break it because there are American citizens who are trying to get out of the country right now. JENKINS: But the fate of remaining Americans and Afghan allies depends on promises made by the Taliban in their soon to be formed government, which Blinken says needs to live up to its commitments. BLINKEN: More important still is what any government does. And that's what we're -- that's what we're really looking at. (END VIDEO CLIP) JENKINS (on camera): And Mike, Secretary Blinken departs for Doha on Sunday. And while he is there, we are told he will not be meeting with any representatives of the Taliban . An official here at State Department saying we're not at that stage yet, Mike. EMANUEL: Interesting. Griff Jenkins live at the State Department. Griff, thanks a lot. President Biden has signed an executive order directing the declassification of certain documents related to the 9/11 terror attacks. Families of victims have long sought the records in the hopes of implicating the Saudi government. The order comes about a week before the 20th anniversary of the attacks. President Biden says the Texas abortion law is an un-American vigilante system, the Supreme Court has refused to stop the new regulations and that's intensifying Democratic efforts to change the makeup of the High Court and get rid of the Senate filibuster. White House Correspondent Peter Doocy has the latest on that tonight. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) BIDEN: I have been continued to be a strong supporter of Roe v. Wade. PETER DOOCY, FOX NEWS CORRESPONDENT (voice over): And before Roe v. Wade is challenged in front of the Supreme Court, President Biden is worried because they just upheld a Texas law restricting abortions. BIDEN: The most pernicious thing about the Texas law, it sort of creates a vigilante system where people get rewards to go out to -- anyway, and it just seems -- I know this sounds ridiculous, almost un-American. DOOCY: Progressives have had it. AOC tweets, Republicans promised to overturn Roe v. Wade, and they have. Democrats can either abolish the filibuster and expand the court or do nothing. Some progressives have already outlined how they do it. SEN. ED MARKEY (D-MA): We undo the damage that Republicans have done by restoring balance. And we do it by passing the Judiciary Act of 2021, to add four seats to the court to create a 13-member Supreme Court. DOOCY: The President describes himself as a -- BIDEN: Student of history. DOOCY: And has historically been against expanding the court like when FDR tried. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: He violated no law. He was legalistically absolutely correct. But it was a bonehead idea. DOOCY: But as president, he has ordered a commission of experts to brief him on the pros and cons of court packing and his mind is open. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: The president doesn't have any new thoughts on the structure of the court? PSAKI: He is waiting for the conclusion of this report, looks forward to reviewing it, seeing where they come out. (END VIDEO CLIP) DOOCY (on camera): If the president decides he wants to add four spots to the court and fill them with progressives, he's going to have to do it while Democrats control Congress which could make the fight ahead of the upcoming midterms the equivalent of a quadruple Kavanaugh, Mike. EMANUEL: Peter Doocy in the White House Briefing Room. Peter, thanks a lot. Up next, feeling ignored at the border. One local mayor says he is fed up. Plus, Bret Baier's exclusive interview with the congressman who took matters into his own hands in what he says an attempt to get people out of Afghanistan. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) BAIER: You're a congressman from Oklahoma, you're a businessman, mixed martial arts background but no military, right? REP. MARKWAYNE MULLIN (R-OK): I wasn't trying to go over there and be a cowboy or anything like that. It was just, what else do you do, when you see a problem, how do you say no if you can be an asset? BAIER: Do you have any regrets about what you did? (COMMERCIAL BREAK) EMANUEL: President Biden is pushing hard for his massive $3.5 trillion spending package to be approved by Congress. The president is also trying to explain a hugely disappointing August jobs report showing a gain of only 235,000 jobs, about a half million jobs short of expectations. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) BIDEN: There's no question that Delta variant is why today's job report isn't stronger. I know people were looking, and I was hoping, for a higher number. And now, we need Congress to finish the job to come through for the American people. (END VIDEO CLIP) MIKE EMANUEL, FOX NEWS CHIEF CONGRESSIONAL CORRESPONDENT (on camera): West Virginia Democrat Senator Joe Manchin says he will not support that $3-1/2 trillion dollar package. Stocks were mixed. The Dow lost 75, the S&P 500 was off two, NASDAQ gained 32 for another record close. For the week, the Dow lost a quarter of a percentage point. The S&P 500 was up about a half-point. NASDAQ gained 1-1/2. The CDC does not want you to travel this Labor Day weekend if you've not been vaccinated. Some states are already dealing with hospitals at capacity. Idaho is reporting record numbers of emergency room visits, hospitalizations, and intensive care unit patients. And in South Carolina, the National Guard is sending help to a hospital system where a surge in COVID patients is overwhelming emergency departments and doctors fear it will only get worse following Labor Day gatherings. Some politicians who are not Republicans are turning on President Biden over the border crisis. The mayor of Laredo, Texas is accusing the president of abandoning border communities. Tonight, chief correspondent Jonathan Hunt shows us how the massive influx of immigrants continues to vex the people trying to deal with it. (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) JONATHAN HUNT, FOX NEWS CHIEF CORRESPONDENT (voice-over): Border Patrol agents are using every tool at their disposal. Airboats among them as they try to turn back the tide of illegal immigration that threatens to swamp our southern border. In the Laredo sector alone, they have seen a more than 130 percent increase in the number of apprehensions of immigrants crossing the Rio Grande this year compared to last. HUNT (on camera): On this side of the river, the Mexican side, those who want to cross watch and wait on that side, the U.S. side, Border Patrol agents do the same watching and waiting. But there simply aren't enough of them to cover every inch of the 136 miles of this sector. And that's where these airboats can make a real difference. HUNT (voice-over): And they do. But inevitably, they cannot stop everyone from making it to the north side of the river. MATT HUDAK, LAREDO SECTOR CHIEF PATROL AGENT: When we encounter them, it's a foot chase on the ground, it's a vehicle pursuit. But, you know, from us or from our partner agencies, so the smuggling organizations are driving that. HUNT: And so, it's dangerous. HUDAK: It's dangerous. Right. HUNT: The mayor of Laredo says he has had enough and accuses President Biden of breaking promises. PETE SAENZ, MAYOR OF LAREDO, TEXAS: We want the cavalry to arrive. We've been waiting months now for that. And unfortunately, we haven't seen much of them. HUNT: In a recent debate in the Texas State Senate. One Democrat summed it up this way. SEN. JUAN HINOJOSA (D-TX): When a nation cannot define its border, it says to be a nation. And right now we do not control a border. HUNT: Trying to take back control, the hard-pressed agents on land and on water. HUDAK: They do tremendous work, but there's no doubt that, that volume it does -- it does tire you out. (END VIDEOTAPE) HUNT (on camera): And the chief tells me Border Patrol could be even more effective here if they had more boats, more technology, and most of all more boots on the ground. But the money for all that, of course, has to come from Washington. Mike. EMANUEL: Jonathan Hunt live in Laredo. Jonathan, many thanks. Up next, Bret talks with the Oklahoma republican congressman who set out on a mission to help Americans in Afghanistan. First, here is what some of our Fox affiliates around the country are covering tonight. WFXT in Boston, where former Cardinal Theodore McCarrick pleads not guilty to sexually assaulting a 16-year-old boy during a wedding reception in Massachusetts nearly 50 years ago. McCarrick did not speak during the hearing. The court said bail at $5,000 and ordered him to stay away from the victim and have no contact with minors. Fox2 in San Francisco with reports of price gouging as a massive wildfire forces evacuations in Lake Tahoe. A rideshare company quoted a fee of more than $1500 to reach the Reno-Tahoe International Airport, an eightfold increase. Nevada Governor Steve Sisolak signed a price gouging prohibition in June but it does not take effect until October. And this is a live look at Atlanta from Fox5. One of the big stories there tonight, after going virtual in 2020, Dragon Con is soaring in person again. The convention welcomes back sci-fi fantasy and pop culture fans for five days of events and celebrity appearances. Attendance might show a proof of vaccination or a proof of a negative COVID test taken within 72 hours prior to arriving. That's tonight's live look "OUTSIDE THE BELTWAY" from SPECIAL REPORT. We'll be right back. (COMMERCIAL BREAK) EMANUEL: Tonight, we get a firsthand account of how difficult it is to get in and out of Afghanistan. My colleague Bret Baier talked with Republican Congressman Markwayne Mullin earlier today. Mullin is back from his trip to the region, which he says he paid for himself and with the help of private contributions. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) BRET BAIER, FOX NEWS ANCHOR (on camera): Mike, thank you. Joining us now, Republican Congressman Markwayne Mullin from Oklahoma. Just had an interesting trip overseas, got a lot of attention. Thanks for being here. REP. MARKWAYNE MULLIN (R-OK): Yes. Thank you for having me. BAIER: Let's start at the beginning. MULLIN: Right. BAIER: How does this start? MULLIN: Well, I want to make it very clear. I wasn't looking to try to get on Afghanistan. That wasn't what this thing started out to be. What started was people started calling me want help. And we'd been getting friends of mine that was in the service that said, can you help our interpreter get out, which we had a lot of conversations about that. Then, we started getting phone calls from people that had family members or friends that were AMCITS or Americans -- American Citizens, AMCITS for short, to get -- to get them out. And I said, let me make the phone call. And it came out that they needed a state department or a government entity to sponsor their flight going in. That's the only way they could get in. And no one would sponsor the fight, even though that it was designated to get these 20 Americans out. And so, they called me back and said would you be interested in sponsoring the flight? And I said, I mean, what do you mean financially? And they said, no, a congressman can sponsor a flight going in. And it gives one of these other departments cover because it's kind of no one wants to touch it because I personally believe ready it was because they knew this was a hot mess. And so, that's we -- that's how this thing -- whole thing started. BAIER: So, you don't actually get into Afghanistan to get people out? MULLIN: So, as this thing move forward, is they wanted -- everybody kept denying them, and then they asked, would you go with us? And these are Tier 1 operators. These are Delta guys, Special Forces. These guys are legit. I'm nobody. I'm just a congressman. BAIER: You're a congressman from Oklahoma, you're a businessman. MULLIN: Sure. BAIER: Mixed martial arts background, but no military, right? MULLIN: No, that doesn't know -- that that doesn't play well in this. I wasn't trying to go over there and be a cowboy or anything like that. It was just what else you do? When you see a problem, how do you say no, if you can be an asset? And they believe I could be an asset. We got who a humanitarian -- a flight plan from FAA . And everything was good to go. We left -- we left the United States, we had a time of arrival at HKIA -- in the Kabul, with HKIA's airport there in Kabul. And we got there and we're gone approach and it canceled our PPR. And so, we circled the airport, probably for an hour, and we had five PPRs canceled. Every time they'd cancel, the agency that would -- that was trying to get us in, would give us a new one. They actually went into the tower to say, let them land. We were on the phone with them texting, we couldn't talk, we're texting back and forth. And they kept issuing us new ones. And they would never let us in Afghanistan. And I'll tell you this, too. Unfortunately, one of our American citizens, her two-year-old son, and I believe it was her father to which I all have passports on, we lost contact of, because they were at the Abbey Gate. And a few hours later, the Abbey Gate blew up. And we haven't had -- we haven't had any contact with them since. And I believe it's because they were caught up in that. And so, what they did by playing politics on this? For whatever reason? BAIER: So, you don't know who shuts you down from landing? MULLIN: I don't know what -- I don't know who shut us down. But I think it was 100 percent directed from the State Department. BAIER: At some point, you go on to Tajikistan. MULLIN: No, I never went to Tajikistan. BAIER: You didn't go in. MULLIN: No, that is absolutely, absolutely false. We did work around the region, but Tajikistan was -- unfortunately, the Ambassador Pommersheim was not helpful at all. And a lot of misinformation was -- is going out about that. BAIER: And for the storyline that said that you possibly interrupted some covert thing that was going on or some operation Tajikistan. MULLIN: No, I don't -- I don't have a clue what they're talking about. This is what Ambassador Pommersheim told me. He says it's very sensitive right now Mark (INAUDIBLE) sensitive because Putin and Chinese -- and the Chinese governments come to take me here September 5th, it's very sensitive. I said I get it very sensitive. I don't need any of your assets. I don't need anything. I, first of all, is making you aware that we're coming in. But I also -- and I also made the point I said, but we are coming in with a large sum of cash. Why are you coming out at a large sum of cash? Sir, you do know that we got to go through 16 checkpoints, just to get from mess, each one of those charge. Someone to come through. I don't know what their requirements are. But what are the requirements to bring in this cash? And he says, I can't assist you. I can't help you. Why? I was told not to. You were told not to help an American citizen. You were told by the federal government in Washington, D.C., not to help when we're not trying to smuggle anybody over. We're trying to do a job that President Biden wouldn't do. BAIER: You know, a lot of people look at what you're trying to do as admirable. You had House Minority Leader Kevin McCarthy saying he really didn't want members doing this wrong. (CROSSTALK) MULLIN: Sorry. BAIER: Because, one, they could become hostages, two, they could become problems that the military would have to deal with. MULLIN: Sure. BAIER: Do you think about that? Whether that was worth it? MULLIN: I did. But how do you say no? I mean, how do you say no, when you have the opportunity to do something? Believe me, my wife wasn't happy about me going. BAIER: Yes, I'm sure. MULLIN: My kids wasn't happy about me going in, and be quite frank with you, all of us that was on that plane, we felt like we probably had a 50-50 chance of coming back. BAIER: Yes. Why should we not think that this was, you know, bravado -- (CROSSTALK) MULLIN: Sure. BAIER: Testosterone or an effort to get the spotlight? MULLIN: I understand that. BAIER: Like how do you respond to that? MULLIN: Well, I'm not Rambo. BAIER: Yes. MULLIN: I never pretend to be Rambo. We were surrounded by great people. Of all the guys that I was working with, I'm the low man on the totem pole. And I understood that. But they felt like I could be the assistance to them. How? Logistically maybe. Open the door for them, making phone calls, and being able to take in the SIVs and the AMCITS as they came on to the plane. And that was the plan. That plan changed, and it changed when we wasn't allowed to get into Afghanistan. We quickly realized that the president and the State Department, General Milley, General McKenzie were lying to the American people by saying everybody who wanted out could get out. That is a lie. That a boldfaced, 100 percent lie, because we were working with these individuals. BAIER: And you know today that there are just a bunch of them still stuck there? MULLIN: Right now as we speak, right before we started talking, I called the guys that are still over there, and they said there was five planes setting at Meza Sharif with Amcits, SIVs, and refugees on it. BAIER: American citizens, Special Immigration Visas. MULLIN: Special Immigration Visas, and refugees. And there may be P-1, P-2s which are levels of refugees that we can get out. But they can't get clearance to get out because no country is willing to help them. We called the State Department about this. The State Department said we are not in control of the airspace. We're not handling any of that. Well, it's our mess. I don't care which way you think about it, it's our mess. The United States created this vacuum to allow the Taliban to come in. President Biden and his horrific withdrawal has caused this to happen. BAIER: Do you have any regrets about what did you? MULLIN: Absolutely not. I would do it again tomorrow. We were saving people's lives. BAIER: What if 535 members decide to get on a plane and -- MULLIN: Everybody is helping right now. I don't care if they are Republican or Democrat. Everybody is helping. I have heard from a lot of different members that are trying to do their thing. Everybody has a different way of helping. Do you know why all those other governments were going out and picking up their individuals and bringing them back in? Because there was three Taliban checkpoints before you could get to HKIA, and all three of them could charge you a tax. And the tax was anywhere between $500 to $4,000. This one young lady and her four kids to which I have recordings of, we were recording as we were walking through because I was on the phone with the State Department for 12 hours trying to get someone from the State Department to come out of the gate to get her, for 12 hours, 12 hours. I have it recorded. Couldn't get anybody to come out. She had to come through there. It cost her $2,000. The State Department kept saying, hey, go up and talk to them. Tell them they're waiting on us. Give them your name. They know you are coming. Five times she approached this guard with the Taliban . The last time they stuck a pistol to her head with her kids there. I have it recorded with her kids screaming and crying. She goes back and she -- she is crying so hard that she begins to puke, the mother did. And the State Department sent her up there five times saying we've got clearance for her. And here we are, the United States government , and we're negotiating with the Taliban to get American citizens out, and then the president of the United States is going to go to the mic and say that every American that wanted out got out? I have a list of 50 that want out that they haven't got out. I have a list of 50 that we have ran out of Kabul and put in safe houses around Afghanistan that I promise you they wanted out. BAIER: Do you think we're going to get these people out? MULLIN: We're going to get some, but there is going to be some that's going to die because of the failure from President Biden. I promise you that. At some point they are going to lose patience and aren't going to keep letting us drive past checkpoints and paying them off. Sorry, taxes. That's what they call it, tax. And when I say that blood is on his hands, that means President Biden's hands, I mean that with everything in my heart. It's his fault. I wouldn't have been over there. I wouldn't have even thought about going if it wasn't for his failure. I wouldn't have put my life in danger. I wouldn't have put my kids and my wife through that. I wouldn't have put anybody through it. BAIER: And you'd do it again? MULLIN: Without even hesitation. BAIER: Congressman, we appreciate your time. I know you just traveled back. And the story is compelling. MULLIN: Thank you, sir. BAIER: Mike, we'll send it back to you. MIKE EMANUEL, FOX NEWS ANCHOR: Bret, thanks a lot. Up next, why many in the mainstream media are moving on from Afghanistan. (COMMERCIAL BREAK) EMANUEL: The mainstream media are concentrating on the Texas law and hurricane Ida as many try to push Afghanistan into the background. FOX News media analyst and host of FOX's "Media Buzz" Howard Kurtz takes a look tonight. (BEGIN VIDEO TAPE) HOWARD KURTZ, FOX NEWS HOST: With new polls showing public disapproval of President Biden's handling of Afghanistan, some liberal commentators are focusing on his decision to pull out U.S. forces. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: It is a fact that ending this war required a level of resolve that no one had prior to President Joe Biden . KURTZ: But a "Washington Post"-ABC poll today shows a crucial distinction. While 77 percent back Biden on getting out of Afghanistan, a striking 60 percent say they disapprove of Biden's handling of what proved to be a chaotic and violent evacuation. Only seven percent of Republicans approve of that. The obvious political damage to the president may help explain why some liberal outlets are quickly moving on from the war. One hour after Biden defended the exit from Afghanistan -- JOE BIDEN , (D) PRESIDENT OF THE UNITED STATES: Extraordinary success of this mission. KURTZ: Several MSNBC hosts started leading their programs instead with comments by freshman Republican Congressman Madison Cawthorn, who said the failure to change what he called rigged election systems could lead to bloodshed. JOY REID , MSNBC HOST: So Cawthorn, let's just reiterate, is not just some guy. He is a, yes, embarrassing, creepy, tree-punching, but sitting member of Congress. KURTZ: And since then, most of the evening MSNBC opinion shows haven't even mentioned the war. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: Meanwhile the GOP led assault on our democracy through the passage of voter suppression measures marches on. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: Two Trump Organization executives are now set to testify before a Manhattan grand jury this week. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: If you are a red state, you not only have no protection from COVID, your schools are getting sued so they can't have mask mandates. KURTZ: The media have also been covering two important stories -- deadly flooding in the northeast, and a highly restrictive Texas abortion law. The war now an afterthought. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: President Biden and the Democrats are hoping Americans have a short memory and forget all about the fiasco they unleashed. (END VIDEO TAPE) KURTZ (on camera): There's a natural tendency for war coverage to fade once U.S. soldiers are back home, though some Americans remain stranded in Afghanistan. But for the media to quickly leave the war disaster behind could ease the political fallout for President Biden. Mike? EMANUEL: Howie, thanks a lot. Up next, the panel on President Biden's bad week. First, Beyond our Borders tonight. New Zealand authorities fatally shot an extremist inspired by the Islamic State group within 60 seconds of his knife attack that wounded six people at an Auckland supermarket. Three of the shoppers were taken to hospitals in critical condition. Police had been following the suspect around the clock. Syria says it shot down Israeli missiles as they approached Damascus today. The state news agency says the weapons were launched from the area of southeast neighboring Lebanon. The Israel military is not commenting. Japanese Prime Minister Yoshihide Suga says he not run for the leadership of the governing party later this month. Suga says heading Japan's pandemic response and campaigning to lead his governing Liberal Democratic Party at the same time divided his energies. Just some of the other stories Beyond our Borders tonight. We'll be right back. (COMMERCIAL BREAK) (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) GEN. KENNETH MCKENZIE, U.S. CENTRAL COMMAND: There's a lot of heart break associated with this departure. We did not get everyone out that we wanted to get out. JOE BIDEN , (D) PRESIDENT OF THE UNITED STATES: Ninety percent of Americans in Afghanistan who wanted to leave were able to leave. REP. BUDDY CARTER, (R-GA): It starts with Joe Biden and it ends with Joe Biden . And I'm telling you, he should be impeached. SEN. MITCH MCCONNELL , (R-KY) SENATE MINORITY LEADER: There isn't going to be any impeachment, but I think they have a good chance of having a very bad election next year. BIDEN: When Congress returns this month, I'm going to press for their action on my build back better plan. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: We are coming in with a much weaker jobs report Dagen, a much weaker jobs report. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: This is terrible news for what it means for the real economy. BIDEN: I know people were looking, and I was hoping for a higher number. (END VIDEO CLIP) EMANUEL: So the week starting with the Afghan drawdown and still questions about whether Americans and Afghan partners are actually able to get out of the country, and ending with a disappointing jobs report. With that, let's bring in our panel, Byron York, chief political correspondent of "The Washington Examiner," Charles Lane , opinion writer for "The Washington Post," and Bill McGurn, columnist for "The Wall Street Journal." Gentlemen, welcome. So, Byron, obviously President Biden is not responsible for hurricane Ida, but really a double punch this week in terms of hammering Louisiana and then the Newark, New Jersey area. The president will certainly be graded on the government's response. BYRON YORK, CHIEF POLITICAL CORRESPONDENT, "THE WASHINGTON EXAMINER": He will, and it will come on top of all the other issues that you were referring to this week. And in general, President Biden is facing the consequences of his own actions. On Afghanistan, he chose to do it the way that he did. And now we're facing the issue not only of some U.S. citizens apparently still stranded in Afghanistan. We're facing the question of who the U.S. actually did evacuate, more than 100,000 people who may or may not have been vetted very well, getting stories now that the U.S. is kind of trying to find out who it just brought out of Afghanistan. Now, on COVID, the president told us during the campaign that he knew how to handle this. He had a plan, which at the time was just masks and social distancing and waiting for a vaccine. But now that you have the Delta variant, his administration has sowed confusion about the vaccine, and he specifically bungled this question of whether a booster shot is going to be needed, and, if so, when. And then on the economic effects of it, the president today tried to make it sound like it was really OK. But, in fact, you have not only the effects of COVID, you have inflation, and the president's main solution is to push this $3.5 trillion spending bill that not everybody in his own party supports. So, on all of that, he is facing the consequences of his own actions. EMANUEL: Picking up on that point, The $3.5 trillion spending package, West Virginia Senator Joe Manchin, which sometimes feels like the most powerful guy in town, says not so fast, we should pump the brakes on that. Chuck, are we looking at an all-out war on the democratic side? CHARLES LANE , OPINION WRITER, "WASHINGTON POST": I don't know about all-out war, but it certainly, maybe a switch the cliche here, it's kind of a Gordian knot. You have moderates and progressives in the party who just really don't see eye to eye on the need for that second piece. And in the middle is the already baked, so to speak, $1.2 trillion infrastructure plan. So something has got to give in the Democratic Party by September 27th when Nancy Pelosi has promised a vote to the House moderates on that issue. And honestly, I think that the Manchin thing, of all the things that happened this week, must have really come as a kind of a just when it rains it pours moment for the president, because in the middle of all of his other troubles, a member of his own party really complicated his domestic agenda. And they are going to either have to meet his demands, whatever they may be, or see that whole thing go down in flames. EMANUEL: So you have got progressives saying we are not going to do the bipartisan compromise until we gets the $3.5 trillion. Manchin pumping the brakes on that. Bill, your thoughts? BILL MCGURN, COLUMNIST, "THE WALL STREET JOURNAL": Yes. No, I agree with Charles. Look, I was in the White House when Katrina hit. We had Iraq and all sorts of things. It is the kind of thing when there's bad news it does seem to come in droves. And also, look, it's not just that the policies have not worked out, especially on Afghanistan. On Afghanistan, the American people watched their president and commander-in-chief tell them falsehoods about we're going to stay until every last person gets out there. So there's a lot of questions about the president's honestly and whether he is up to the job in addition to whether he picked the right policies. So that makes your, then that makes people reluctant to stand by you when you need them. So we'll see. I think with all these things going on in the economy, the problem is you can pull out one thread and the whole thing unravels. EMANUEL: OK, then you have got Congressman Markwayne Mullin from the great state of Oklahoma going to Afghanistan, saying he was just trying to help. Let's take a listen to this clip. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) BRET BAIER, FOX NEWS ANCHOR: Do you think we are going to get these people out? REP. MARKWAYNE MULLIN, (R-OK): We're going to get some, but there's going to be some that's going to die because of the failure from President Biden. I promise you that. At some point, they are going to lose patients and aren't going to let us keep drive past these checkpoints and paying them off -- sorry, taxes. That's what they call it, tax. And when I say that blood is on his hands, that means the President Biden's hands, I mean that with everything in my heart. It's his fault. (END VIDEO CLIP) EMANUEL: I have talked to members of Congress, the Senate who all say they are all getting bombarded by requests from people to help get people out. This congressman went there, even though leadership said don't go. Byron, your thoughts? Well, I think this is kind of odd freelance mission that Congressman Mullin went on is a product of the confusion and chaos in the Biden administration's withdrawal from Afghanistan. As you said, members of Congress are getting a lot of calls, can you help this person? Can you help that person? So it's not crazy to think that they would try to help somebody. But, at the same time, the State Department and the Defense Department were just struggling minute by minute trying to get people on planes and out of there. Then there was this terrible, deadly attack. So I think that Mullin's act was basically a product. It would not have happened if the withdrawal had been a more organized affair. EMANUEL: Chuck, is there intense pressure on the State Department to come up with a number of Americans and Afghan partners who have gotten out since the U.S. military went wheels up? LANE: Yes, there is, and they are struggling to do that. For some reasons that are understandable and some others that are probably the result of their own fault. I have to say I think what Congressman Mullin, I honestly couldn't understand what he was trying to explain, what the story or the situation exactly was. It was kind of a tangled narrative he was putting forth there. And one -- and one is led to conclude that he really shouldn't have done it. His own minority leader in the House said don't go. And he pressed ahead with something that was, perhaps well-intentioned, perhaps political, but certainly not well-advised. EMANUEL: Bill, you made a reference to bad news coming in a wave. Do you sense that any senior officials will be asked to leave to basically stop the bleeding? MCGURN: No, I don't see that. I don't see any signs of this yet. Look, I think the congressman's trip is not what's needed when you are in the midst of this chaos. However, I agree with Byron. It is a function that the commander-in-chief didn't do his job, that he told us we are going to get people out. Look, the American people wanted out of Afghanistan, but they don't like humiliation. They don't like defeat. They don't like to be driven out. And they don't like to leave people behind enemy lines. One of the things no one is talking about is those people are hostages, and they are going to hold Biden's policies going forward hostage. Can you do anything tough to the Taliban now when they have all these Americans? We have to leave it there, gentlemen. Thanks so much. Have a great weekend. When we come back, "Notable Quotables." (COMMERCIAL BREAK) EMANUEL: It's Friday. That means it's time for "Notable Quotables." (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) UNIDENTIFIED MALE: Do you think people should, those who call him sleepy Joe should apologize to him? JEN PSAKI , WHITE HOUSE PRESS SECRETARY: I think we are looking for allowing the president to continue to address multiple crises at a time. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: Right now what we are seeing in Texas is frankly chaos. Patients are scared. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: This is my first time in my 40 years that I ever saw something like this. I thought Katrina was bad. This is the worst one. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: We did not know that the heavens would literally open up and bring Niagara Falls level water to the streets of New York. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: This is tough stuff. War is hard. It's vicious. It's brutal. It's unforgiving. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: They died with their brothers and their sisters right next to them, doing exactly what they all wanted to do. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: The war is over, but the heartbreak continues. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: The parade of horribles are about to unfold. We are leaving thousands of Afghan allies behind who fought bravely with us. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: Do not forget me and my family at the moment in Afghanistan. It is a very hard and horrifying situation. JOE BIDEN , (D) PRESIDENT OF THE UNITED STATES: Couldn't this have been done in a more orderly manner? I respectfully disagree. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: The White House needs to get some oranges and get tougher with the Taliban . PSAKI: We're clearly need to -- sorry, that was aggressive bug. (END VIDEO CLIP) EMANUEL: Quite a week. Next week on SPECIAL REPORT, we will speak with the education secretary and surgeon general and take some of your questions. That's coming up Thursday. Coming up on FOX NEWS SUNDAY, Congressman Michael McCaul and Dr. Ashish Jha . Thank you for watching SPECIAL REPORT. FOX NEWS PRIMETIME hosted by Tammy Bruce starts right now. Have a wonderful Labor Day weekend and great show, Tammy. TAMMY BRUCE, FOX NEWS CONTRIBUTOR: Thank you, sir. Nice to see you, Mike. And good evening, everyone, and welcome to FOX NEWS PRIMETIME.
