headline: Concerns Over Americans And Allies Left In Afghanistan; Unclear Guidance For Those Stuck In Afghanistan; U.S. Relationship With Taliban Unclear After War Ends; Hurricane Ida Devastates Parts of Louisiana; Some Republicans Call for Impeach or Resignation of President Biden over Military Withdrawal from Afghanistan
story_text: DAGEN MCDOWELL, FOX NEWS HOST: Alienate all your girlfriends before they get married so you don`t have to be in the wedding. SPECIAL REPORT is up next. Hi, Bret. BRET BAIER, FOX NEWS ANCHOR: Hi, Dagen, thank you. Good evening. Welcome to Washington. I`m Bret Baier. Breaking tonight, growing concern about Americans and those who helped Americans still stranded in Afghanistan, as anecdotes of new Taliban atrocities are filtering out of that country. The Biden administration is trying its best to turn the page from the issue that is fueling accusations of broken promises from the president. We`ll take a closer look at that in a few minutes. Also tonight, dozens of Republicans are now calling for the president`s impeachment over his actions and this phone call with the Afghan president before the fall of Kabul. But impeachment is something the top GOP senator says will not happen. White House Correspondent Jacqui Heinrich starts us off tonight, live in the North Lawn. Good evening, Jacqui. JACQUI HEINRICH, FOX NEWS CORRESPONDENT (on camera): Good evening, Bret. On the third day since the troop withdrawal, no answer on whether any more Americans have made it out of Afghanistan or how many Green Card holders or SIV applicants remain. The White House is directing those questions to other departments. And there`s a distinct feeling President Biden is trying to move on from Afghanistan to his domestic agenda. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) JOE BIDEN , PRESIDENT OF THE UNITED STATES: There`s a lot of damage. HEINRICH (voice over): President Biden addressed the nation about storm recovery but gave no update on Afghanistan and took no questions from reporters as more than a hundred Americans and countless at-risk Afghans who helped the U.S. in the 20-year war remain behind enemy lines. JEN PSAKI , WHITE HOUSE PRESS SECRETARY: There are people who are eligible, we may not even know they`re eligible yet, right? It is very hard to define those numbers. HEINRICH: Meanwhile, accounts of reprisals those Afghans face are getting more dire. This person said they killed 12 members of special forces in Kandahar, three soldiers in Jalalabad as well. The Taliban took them out of their homes and shot them. Given this kind of reporting or hearing, is it possible that our reliance on the Taliban to keep their word in terms of our evacuation is misplaced, we`re going back on things like the amnesty promise? PSAKI: No one is saying from the federal government, no one. The president, Secretary of Defense, no one from the Intelligence Community that the Taliban are good actors. That is one of the reasons we are being so clear that we are not rushing to recognition. HEINRICH: Politico reports shame among anonymous sources inside the White House. One person telling Politico, I am absolutely appalled and literally horrified we left Americans there. Kabul`s airport remains inoperable and the White House says there are risks associated with charter flights seeking to extract Americans to U.S. military basis. PSAKI: We do not have reliable means to confirm the basic details of charter flights including who may be organizing them. We know ISIS-K has a keen interest in attacks against aviation targets and our personnel on the ground and our Air Force in our military bases. HEINRICH: Among the House GOP, growing calls for the president to resign but the top Senate Republican Mitch McConnell says President Biden will not be impeached and the ballot box is a better place to hold him accountable. (END VIDEO CLIP) HEINRICH (on camera): Still, other Republican senators want accountability now. 25 members wrote to President Biden saying while they disagree on whether troops should have remained in Afghanistan, they`re all in agreement President Biden`s chaotic withdrawal caused this crisis, Bret. BAIER: Jacqui, obviously, the administration, the president want to focus on domestic agenda items, but you have this human infrastructure bill that`s kind of sitting out there, the 3.5 trillion, a key Senate Democrat is pretty much blocking that path. HEINRICH: That`s right. West Virginia Senator Joe Manchin said there is no way he will support that $3.5 trillion social infrastructure package that Democrats want to pass along party lines. He dragged his colleagues for what he called a strange belief, there`s an infinite amount of money to go around. He wrote, Democratic congressional leaders proposed to pass the largest single spending bill in history with no regard to rising inflation, crippling debt, or the inevitability of future crises. Ignoring the fiscal consequences of our policy choices will create a disastrous future for the next generation of Americans. Without Manchin`s vote, Biden`s agenda really seems to go nowhere and it appears that Manchin is dug in, Bret. BAIER: All right, we`ll follow that. Jacqui, thank you. We`re hearing tonight from an Afghan interpreter who helped save then- Senator Biden 13 years ago and is now pleading for rescue himself. That man and his family are joined by as we mentioned, Americans and thousands of Afghans who helped the U.S. through the 20 years of war who today still cannot leave that country. Correspondent Griff Jenkins has the story. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) NED PRICE , STATE DEPARTMENT SPOKESMAN: We will provide them a tailored guidance but that is not something we will provide to all of you. And we won`t do that for their safety. GRIFF JENKINS, FOX NEWS CORRESPONDENT (voice over): For those stuck behind enemy lines, the plan to get them out is unclear. With the Kabul airport shut down, dangerous ground routes appear to be the only option. The State Department also won`t say if any American citizens have gotten out since the last flight out of Kabul on August 30th. Leaving behind 100 to 200 Americans, tens of thousands of Afghan allies, including the majority of SIV applicants, and even the State Department`s own journalists. Also, among those stranded, an interpreter known as Mohammed, who helped rescue then-Senator Joe Biden in 2008 when his helicopter made an emergency landing in the snow-covered mountains of Afghanistan. BIDEN: If you want to know where Al-Qaeda lives, you want to know where bin Laden is, come back to Afghanistan with me. Come back to the area my helicopter was forced down. JENKINS: Unable to get out before the deadline, Mohammed is now pleading for President Biden to save him and his family. MOHAMMED, AFGHAN INTERPRETER: Maybe die at home. There is no way I can`t escape from my house. All borders in my country are sealed, but only I and my -- and my son have a U.S. passport. The rest of the family do not have. JENKINS: The State Department`s other focus is resettling and vetting the tens of thousands of refugees arriving on American soil amid growing concerns that individuals were extremists could slip through the cracks. State Department spokesman Ned Price says there`s a plan for those who get flagged. PRICE: In cases where that vetting may take longer, we do have options available to us. But I`m just not in a position to detail. JENKINS: This as a new diplomatic mission for Afghanistan, headquartered in Doha must decide how they will work with as soon to be formed Taliban government and if they can trust them. (END VIDEO CLIP) JENKINS: And Bret, any moment now, we expect Secretary of State Antony Blinken to arrive here to the Dulles Expo Center behind me. It`s one of the major processing centers for arriving refugees as State Department says that more than 31,000 of the total 124,000 people evacuated have made it to the U.S. soil with about 77 percent of those being at risk Afghans, Bret. BAIER: Griff Jenkins in Chantilly, Virginia. Griff, thanks. The shockwaves continued tonight over the admission by the nation`s top military officer that the U.S. may actually have to cooperate with the Taliban in counterterrorism operations. The terror group is solidifying its control over Afghanistan tonight. National security correspondent Jennifer Griffin is at the Pentagon. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) JENNIFER GRIFFIN, FOX NEWS NATIONAL SECURITY CORRESPONDENT (voice over): Taliban fighters took on the role of the police in Kabul today helping with traffic at checkpoints and issuing a statement like this one urging calm. AMANULLAH, TALIBAN BARDI SPECIAL FORCES: Everyone should go to work and live. Offices, shops and companies should start operating and have no fear of anyone. GRIFFIN: Pentagon leaders raised eyebrows when asked Wednesday about working with the Taliban in the future. GEN. MARK MILLEY, CHAIRMAN, JOINT CHIEFS OF STAFF: In war, you do what you must in order to reduce risk to mission and force, not what you necessarily want to do. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: Any possibility of coordination against ISIS-K with them? Milley: It`s possible. GRIFFIN: Dan Hoffman, a former CIA Chief of Station spent years hunting Al Qaeda and says such an intelligence relationship would be complicated. DAN HOFFMAN, FORMER CHIEF OF STATION, CIA: We would need to corroborate everything the Taliban is telling us on our own before we would launch any strikes. And whatever information we provided to them, we`d have to be very careful that they are not going to take it and then go out and conduct operations which violate human rights of innocent civilians. GRIFFIN: Former Defense Secretary William Cohen explained how the U.S. could leverage the Taliban`s need for U.S. Intelligence. WILLIAM COHEN , FORMER DEFENSE SECRETARY: They may come under severe attack from Al-Qaeda and from ISIS-K or ISIS-Z. They`ll need intelligence that they don`t have that we may be able to provide them under certain conditions. GRIFFIN: A difficult reality for the 800,000 veterans of the past 20 years and Gold Star families like this one, the last American soldier to die in Afghanistan, Staff Sergeant Ryan Knauss. He died of his wounds after the suicide bombing at Abbey Gate. His wife Elena was tiling her shower floor when she received the knock at the door. She told NPR she began screaming, collapsed and then stayed up all night through her tears to put their initials and date in the shower tile floor. ELENA KNAUSS, WIDOW OF STAFF SERGEANT RYAN KNAUSS: I`m in shambles and I`m hurting but that no mother, father, wife, brother, sister ever has to feel such emptiness, I would be grateful to know he was the last. (END VIDEO CLIP) GRIFFIN (on camera): Of the 22 wounded in the Abby Gate attack, we`ve learned that 15 Marines are currently at Walter Reed. One is in critical condition, three are serious and 11 are stable, Bret. BAIER: Jennifer Griffin live at the Pentagon. Jennifer, thank you. At least 43 people have died in the East after massive flooding from record rain fall produced by the remnants of Hurricane Ida. Correspondent Bryan Llenas shows us the devastation tonight from Queens, New York. Good evening, Bryan. BRYAN LLENAS, FOX NEWS CORRESPONDENT (on camera): Bret, good evening. The rainfall in New York City was extraordinary and unprecedented. At least 13 people have died in New York City, 11 of them drowning in their basement apartments like this one behind me. The flash flooding, stunning residents and state officials. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) LLENAS (voice over): Tonight, New York City`s in a state of emergency after a cascading waterfall shut down the city subway trapping train cars and flooding stations Wednesday night. The historic rainfall turned the city`s highways and streets into rivers, forcing first responders to save drivers from trapped vehicles. At least 11 people in the city died in their basement apartments in Queens, New York, including a 2-year-old boy, a mother and her 22-year-old son drowned in this apartment when four feet of water rushed into a gaping hole. AMIT SHIVPRASAD, HOMEOWNER: It was devastating. I can tell you that my body`s still trembling as we talk about this right now. LLENAS: The remnants of Hurricane Ida dumped a historic 10 inches of rain over just several hours in New York City. Central Park saw 3.15 inches of rain in just one hour. Shattering an old-time record set just two weeks ago. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: Look at that tornado. LLENAS: In New Jersey, a tornado ripped through the community of Mullica Hills, destroying an estimated two dozen homes. ASHLEY THOMAS, TORNADO VICTIM: It was like a warzone. LLENAS: Ashley Thomas is eight months pregnant. THOMAS: I just couldn`t believe that everywhere the ambulance went, they was just slamming on his brakes because there was a wire down or a tree and I`m like our community has just destroyed in five seconds. That`s all it took. Heartbreaking. LLENAS: Nearly a foot of rain caused historic deadly flash flooding in New Jersey, submerging a ballpark, homes and businesses. In Pennsylvania, first responders have conducted thousands of water rescues saving people trapped on their roofs. New York Governor Kathy Hochul today said state officials were caught off guard by the flooding. GOV. KATHY HOCHUL (D-NY): We did not know that between 8:50 and 9:50 p.m. last night that the heavens would literally open up and bring Niagara Falls level water to the streets of New York. Could that have been anticipated? I want to find out. LLENAS: President Biden today blamed climate change. BIDEN: That these extreme storms and the climate crisis are here. We need to do -- we best be better prepared. We need to act. (END VIDEO CLIP) LLENAS (on camera): The death toll has shockingly risen to at least 43. Governor Phil Murphy says at least 23 people died in New Jersey, the majority people who were trapped in their vehicles as the floodwaters rose and swept them away. The bottom line is here though that the flood danger continues tonight into tomorrow as the rivers continue to rise and have yet to crest, Bret. BAIER: Yes, we`ll follow it here on Fox. Bryan Llenas live in Queens. Bryan, thanks. Stocks were up today, the Dow gained 131, the S&P 500 Rose 13 to a new record close. The NASDAQ finished ahead 22, also a new record close tonight. Up next, we take you to the southern border for a Fox News exclusive. A look at the organization and sophistication of human smuggling opera (AUDIO GAP). First, here`s what some of our Fox affiliates around the country are covering tonight. Fox 40 in Sacramento as firefighters throw all their resources into boxing a wildfire, the Caldor Fire after winds finally turn in their favor. The blaze which began August 14th has scorched more than 210,000 acres in that area. Fox 26 in Houston were veterans suffering from post-traumatic stress disorder can now legally get medical marijuana to ease those symptoms. Cancer patients can also obtain cannabis to lessen suffering and side effects particularly from chemotherapy. And this is a live look at Cleveland, Ohio from one of our affiliates Fox 8. One of the big stories there tonight, officials determined a foul odor smelled in several lakeshore communities resulted from an inversion of Lake Erie`s waters. Strong winds and large waves churned up sludge along the bottom of the lake, blowing the smell along the shore. One official says the scent pops up once or twice a year. That`s tonight`s live look outside the Beltway from SPECIAL REPORT. We`ll be right back. (COMMERCIAL BREAK) BAIER: The U.S. Supreme Court is refusing to intervene in the controversial Texas abortion law. Justice voted -- justices voted five to four to deny an emergency appeal. The law went into effect Wednesday. It bans most abortions after six weeks and allows private citizens to bring lawsuits against anyone involved in the procedure other than the patient. President Biden has condemned the decision and intends to talk to lawmakers about possible legislation. The ruling is sparking demands from progressives to codify Roe vs. Wade and end the Senate filibuster. There is a report the U.S. government has lost contact with thousands of migrant children who crossed the southern border illegally and were then released from custody into the country. Trying to confirm that with Border Patrol and other sources in the administration. But also tonight, exclusive images of a human smuggling operation in Laredo, Texas. Chief correspondent Jonathan Hunt takes us there. JONATHAN HUNT, FOX NEWS CHIEF CORRESPONDENT (voice-over): It`s a stunning glimpse into just how well organized the human smuggling operations are on our southern border. Security camera video shows a huge tractor-trailer pull up on a street in Laredo, Texas, and within seconds dozens of immigrants rushing in. Some having hidden nearby, many dropped off in a fleet of vehicles that then quickly depart. Border Patrol agents tell us up to 200 immigrants crowded into this truck, destinations unknown. It`s the final stage of a journey that begins usually at night at the Rio Grande, where Border Patrol agents play a high stakes game of cat and mouse with those trying to cross from Mexico to the U.S. HUNT (on camera) It`s 1:00 a.m. here on the banks of the Rio Grande in Laredo and all night there has been a constant flow of people from the Mexican side, trying to get across here. Border Patrol agents just intercepted a group of around 30. On this night, a congressional delegation joined the patrol. Among them, South Carolina Congresswoman Nancy Mace. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) REP. NANCY MACE (R-SC): Every time someone illegally crosses the border and they paid the cartels thousands of dollars, we`re putting that cash in the cartel`s pocket, which makes us less safe as a nation. HUNT (voice-over): On top of all, the immigrants who deliberately evade Border Patrol, it`s now emerged that the Biden administration has lost track of thousands of migrant children who first arrived seeking asylum. (END VIDEO CLIP) HUNT (on camera): Axios reports that have nearly 15,000 calls made between January and May to check on children initially processed then released to relatives or sponsors, nearly 5,000 went unanswered. Meaning, no one couldn`t trace those children or check on their welfare. Bret. BAIER: Jonathan, thank you. We`ll follow that story. We`re less than two weeks away from the final voting in California`s gubernatorial recall. 21 percent of active registered voters in the State of California have already returned those ballots. At stake, whether Democratic Governor Gavin Newsom gets to keep his job. National correspondent William La Jeunesse explains. (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) GOV. GAVIN NEWSOM (D-CA): Climate, science is on (INAUDIBLE). WILLIAM LA JEUNESSE, FOX NEWS NATIONAL CORRESPONDENT (voice-over): And so, is Gavin Newsome with his recall election just 12 days away. NEWSOM: You`d better remind people what`s at stake -- LA JEUNESSE: The latest poll shows Newsom up by nearly 20 points among likely voters. NEWSOM: Polls don`t vote, people vote. LA JEUNESSE: Of 22 million ballots mailed out, voters returned one in five. The recall ballot has two questions. One, should Newsome be recalled? Two, who should replace him? Well, that second question won`t matter if Newsome wins a majority on the first. Conservative radio host Larry Elder leads the challengers. LARRY ELDER (R), GUBERNATORIAL CANDIDATE, CALIFORNIA: I urge you all to vote to recall Gavin Newsom . LA JEUNESSE: Elder is facing an avalanche of negative media coverage following 20 years of provocative radio commentary. Along with allegations, he once use, a racial slur during a comedy sketch, and that he pulled a weapon on an ex-fiancee while high on pot. ELDER: This is not the first time the L.A. Times has attacked me. There`s another writer who also called me a black David Duke . LA JEUNESSE: Newsom`s big advantage, bags of cash from unions and liberal donors to dominate the airwaves. SEN. BERNIE SANDERS (D-VT): The last thing we need is to have some right- wing Republican governor in California. LA JEUNESSE: Yet, state Democrats are nervous. Instead of a booming economy following COVID rates and schools back to normal, Newsome faces raging fires, angry parents, rising crime, and a homeless epidemic. ELDER: They are scared to death. They know that if California can elect a conservative governor like myself, and they can, and they will on September the 14th, that any state can. (END VIDEOTAPE) LA JEUNESSE (on camera): While this latest poll shows Republicans more motivated than Democrats, they outnumber the GOP two to one. But Latino voters who have long favored Democrats could make a difference. Republicans believe, despite the polls, that they`ve lost confidence in Governor Newsome, was bringing in Senator Elizabeth Warren this weekend to campaign here in California. Bret. BAIER: All right, William, thank you. More on this with the panel. The Federal Aviation Administration says Virgin Galactic cannot launch anyone into space again until an investigation is complete into a mishap during July`s flight with founder Richard Branson . The FAA says the ship carrying Branson and five Virgin Galactic employees veered off course during its descent back to New Mexico. The deviation put the ship outside the air traffic control clearance area. The ban comes is Virgin Galactic announces plans to launch three Italian researchers to the edge of space in just a few weeks. Up next, the broken promises on Afghanistan. We`ll look at some of the criticism hounding President Biden. Plus a bird`s eye view of Ida`s wrath in Louisiana. (COMMERCIAL BREAK) BAIER: President Biden is facing increasing criticism tonight for what some critics say is clearly a broken promise about getting Americans and thousands of Afghans who helped America out of Afghanistan. White House correspondent Peter Doocy looks at the controversy tonight. PETER DOOCY, FOX NEWS WHITE HOUSE CORRESPONDENT (voice-over): Afghanistan policy has not played out as advertised. (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) JOE BIDEN , PRESIDENT OF THE UNITED STATES: If there`s American citizens left, we`re going to stay and we will get them all out. DOOCY: Turns out all out meant nine out of 10. BIDEN: 90 percent of Americans in Afghanistan who wanted to leave were able to leave. DOOCY: So, even though the administration initially claimed -- JEN PSAKI , WHITE HOUSE PRESS SECRETARY: It`s irresponsible to say Americans are stranded. They are not. DOOCY: The Pentagon later clarified. REAR ADM. JOHN KIRBY (RET.), PENTAGON PRESS SECRETARY: We have Americans that get stranded in countries all the time. DOOCY: Then, there are those who helped the U.S. in wartime. GEORGE STEPHANOPOULOS, CHIEF ANCHOR, ABC NEWS: How about our Afghan allies? Does the commitment hold for them as well? BIDEN: The commitment holds to get everyone out that, in fact, we can get out and everyone should come out. DOOCY: That didn`t happen either. PSAKI: Are there more people who want to leave Afghanistan? Absolutely. DOOCY: Early on, the president was confident in his plan. BIDEN: The likelihood there`s going to be the Taliban overrunning everything, and owning the whole country is highly unlikely. DOOCY: But they did in just 11 days. BIDEN: Afghanistan political leaders gave up and fled the country. The Afghan military collapsed sometime without trying to fight. DOOCY: Still, the president claims he felt global support. BIDEN: I have seen no question of our credibility from our allies around the world. Yet, criticism was heard, including in the British Parliament , where one M.P. took major issue with the U.S. president, criticizing the Afghan army. TOM TUGENDHAT, MEMBER, PARLIAMENT OF THE UNITED KINGDOM : To see that commander in chief call into question the courage of men I fought with, to claim that they ran, shameful. DOOCY: However, this president stands by the way he ordered the withdrawal. BIDEN: I gave him my word with all of my heart. I believe this is the right decision, a wise decision, and the best decision for America. (END VIDEO CLIP) DOOCY (on camera): As a candidate, President Biden once claimed that if you want other countries would have reason to trust and respect the word of an American president again, but so far on foreign policy, his word and the way things have gone have been different. Bret. BAIER: Peter Doocy in the White House briefing room. Peter, thanks. Earlier in the program, we showed you the horrific damage in the northeast from the remnants of Hurricane Ida. Well, Louisiana is trying to recover from even more devastation. Senior correspondent Casey Stegall is in Louisiana tonight. (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) CASEY STEGALL, FOX NEWS CORRESPONDENT: Parts of Louisiana, including metro New Orleans, are slowly coming back to life. For some, the lights are on. MAYOR LATOYA CANTRELL , NEW ORLEANS: We saw some critical success on yesterday as it relates to power restoration. We expect more to come online and gradually throughout the day and, of course, every day making and pushing for significant progress. STEGALL: FOX News got an exclusive ride with the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers as the agency`s top brass flew along with state leaders to the hardest hit areas of southeast Louisiana. The fact-finding mission was to assess the individual needs of each community, like how to best remove standing water that hasn`t yet drained outside the federal protection system. LT. GEN. SCOTT SPELLMON, U.S. ARMY CORPS OF ENGINEERS : There are other places where we need to go south of New Orleans where we`ll actually go in and we`ll cut a levee to help that water get back into the river, and then we`re going to patch it right back up again. STEGALL: In other places like Lafitte, they`ve determined pumps will work best on draining the judge along with mother nature. SPELLMON: Gravity is going to take that water over the course of the next two or three days and put that water back in Lake Pontchartrain. STEGALL: More than 948,000 are still in the dark across the region, four days after Ida`s devastating landfall. Thousands more don`t have clean drinking water. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: My wife needs it. She needs a lot of fluid and stuff because she takes a lot of medicine. STEGALL: Thomas Washington and his neighbors have had to rely on distribution sites like this one in Gramercy, Louisiana, run by the National Guard. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: This is a blessing right here, this water. STEGALL: Fuel is badly needed, too. Lines stretched for miles that only a handful of gas stations with supply and power to run pumps. There is also a sense of urgency with this recovery as we`re only halfway through the Atlantic hurricane season. (END VIDEOTAPE) STEGALL (on camera): Today we also learned of at least three new deaths here in the state of Louisiana, all residents of a nursing home that had been evacuated to a parish north of New Orleans. The state department of health is investigating that. It brings the total now to 11 people who have lost their lives in the gulf coast region. Bret? BAIER: Casey Stegall in Louisiana tonight. Casey, thanks. Up next, the panel on the politics of Afghanistan, also the California recall. First, Beyond our Borders tonight. India imposes a near total lockdown in the disputed areas of Kashmir following the death of a revered separatist leader there -- 92-year-old Syed Ali Geelani died at his home late Wednesday. He was buried quickly amid fears of anti-India protests. The family claims it was blocked from attending his burial. Ambulance drivers in Athens, Greece, joins hundreds of health care workers to protest new mandatory COVID vaccinations. The government is threatening to suspend without pay hospital personnel who refuse the vaccine. Workers warn the requirement could lead to staff shortages. And climate envoy John Kerry is in China calling for action to cut global carbon emissions. Kerry says the effort needs Beijing`s full engagement. China`s foreign minister warns the deteriorating relations between the two countries could undermine cooperation. Just some of the other stories Beyond our Borders tonight. We`ll be right back. (COMMERCIAL BREAK) UNIDENTIFIED MALE: You called for his impeachment over Afghanistan. Do you still feel he should be impeached over this? SEN. LINDSEY GRAHAM , (R-SC): I think he has been derelict in his duties as commander-in-chief. I don`t think he got bad advice and took it. I think he ignored sound advice, and this is Joe Biden being Joe Biden . He has been this way for 40 years. But now he is the commander-in-chief. SEN. MITCH MCCONNELL , (R-KY) SENATE MINORITY LEADER: The president is not going to be removed from office. It`s a Democratic House, a narrowly Democratic Senate. That`s not going to happen. There isn`t going to be any impeachment. But I think they have a good chance of an a very bad election next year. (END VIDEO CLIP) BAIER: Senate minority leader Mitch McConnell saying there is not going to be an impeachment, the president is not going to resign. But there`s a number of Republicans calling for that. If you look at Republicans calling for removal, resignation, 46 Republicans, impeachment 11, raising the 25th Amendment because of the decisions over Afghanistan, there you see three. Meantime, "The Wall Street Journal" about the Afghanistan impact on elections. At home Bidenites hope Afghanistan will be in rearview mirror long before the midterm elections. Swing district Democrats can immunize themselves by criticizing the administration over the execution of the withdrawal. All Democrats will benefit from their association with a president who, however inelegantly, is ending unpopular wars rather than starting new ones. These hopes are not completely unfounded, and Republicans who want to ride the Afghanistan issue back into power may be disappointed. History, however, always punishing failure." Let`s bring in our panel, former Education Secretary Bill Bennett, Mara Liasson , national political correspondent of National Public Radio, and Jonah Goldberg, editor in chief of "The Dispatch." Jonah, what about that analysis from "Wall Street Journal" and the lasting impact of the decisions in Afghanistan? JONAH GOLDBERG, "THE DISPATCH": Yes, I certainly think that history is going to be brutal on Joe Biden for what he has done here. And I think that if the story goes away the way it did after the fall of Saigon to a certain extent, the "Journal" might be right on that, that Americans don`t generally vote on foreign policy. The problem with this vanishing into the rearview window theory is that the Taliban and Al-Qaeda and the facts on the ground in Afghanistan in effect get a vote. And if we see ongoing executions, brutalities, if there are terrorist attacks that can be linked back to Al-Qaeda in Afghanistan , it keeps it a live issue in the way that the North Vietnamese taking over South Vietnam wasn`t. I should add one cultural point -- the very thought that there could still be POWs and MIAs in Vietnam had a profound cultural half-life in this country for a half century. And we are going to be probably hearing stories about Americans and American allies left in Afghanistan for a long time, and I think that is going to have not only just a shameful impact on our reputation around the world, but it is also going to be part of our culture and part of the conversation for a long time to come. BAIER: I think you are right. The shelf life of that, especially with Americans on the ground, plus the thousands of Afghans who helped America, and the Taliban perhaps reverting to the Taliban we know so well, at least the atrocities that we`re hearing already from the BBC and others, Mara. The tough part is that the administration really can`t get us a firm number on any of this. It seems like we are out of State, out of the Pentagon, out of the White House, we cannot get a number. MARA LIASSON , NATIONAL POLITICAL CORRESPONDENT, NATIONAL PUBLIC RADIO: Yes, a number of how many Afghan allies are SIV candidates and want to leave, how many Americans are still there, green card holders, legal residents who are there and want to leave. Yes, that number is pretty important, because the bigger it is, the more problem it is for the administration, because they`ve got to get those people out. They`ve said they would. They said that somehow there is a way to get them out even without American boots on the ground there. So we`ll see what happens. But I think in terms of what impact had has on the next election, that depends on all those things Jonah just listed. Maybe Afghanistan will fade from the headlines, but if there are stories of atrocities, stories of people being trapped, and Republicans will call them hostages, not being allowed to leave by the Taliban , that`s going to be a real problem. But I think in general, we have learned that Americans don`t really care that much about Afghanistan. BAIER: Bill? BILL BENNETT, FORMER EDUCATION SECRETARY: Well, but they do care about those stories and about those people. The numbers matter, the data matters, those individual stories have a resonance. Here is this man who helped Joe Biden and others when his helicopter was in trouble or went down in the snow. And now he is writing him directly saying help me get out. And the president seems powerless to do it. Look, Mitch McConnell is right. Impeachment here is deserved, but the currency of impeachment I think has been cheapened over the last few years. But he is not going to be impeached because of the House. I think it may be better in the long run for him to stay and to listen to the cries of these folks, these people, and to understand what a lot of us believe, that this was the most disgraceful act of foreign policy I believe a president has ever done. I don`t know if it`s the most consequential. Maybe, that depends. But disgraceful, yes. I don`t think there is a parallel, and I have been looking through the history the last three days. BAIER: You mentioned that interpreter who was among the people who saved Senator Biden and the other two senators, Senator Kerry and Senator Hagel, he spoke to FOX & FRIENDS this morning, Mohammed. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) MOHAMMED INTERPRETER WHO HELPED RESCUE BIDEN: They left me and my family and other people behind. That`s what is scary. We are under great risk. Hello, President. Do not leave. Do not forget me and my family at the moment in Afghanistan. It is a very hard and horrifying situation. There is no way to escape from here to another area. Do not leave me and my family behind. (END VIDEO CLIP) BAIER: It`s tough to listen to, Jonah. And we, again, can`t get the numbers of the people since the last flight went out who have gotten out. And we don`t have those numbers either, either Americans or Afghan allies. GOLDBERG: Yes. And it does appear that we were at least misled by the tone and tenure of President Biden`s remarks about this. He made it seem that a big chunk of those 120,000 odd people who were evacuated from Afghanistan were, in fact, Afghans and SIVs. And it turns out it is looking like the numbers are much smaller. I think Mara raises an important point here when we are talking about the rearview mirror of history and how much shelf life this is going to have. The fall of Saigon, and Joe Biden has been committed to this analogy. He talked about this with Richard Holbrooke, which Holbrooke talks about in his memoirs, that he thinks Nixon and Kissinger got away with abandoning Vietnam, we can get away with abandoning Afghanistan. The thing is that if, in fact, the Taliban takes hostages, not just the ones the Republicans call hostages, but literally rounds up these people and says open up the spigots of aid for these kinds of things, then you are not looking at a Vietnam analogy. You`re look at an Iran analogy. And Jimmy Carter`s presidency was mortally wounded by the hostage crisis, and we could have a much bigger one on our hands. We just don`t know because we don`t know the numbers of who is there and whether they can get out or not yet. BAIER: Yes, and we are going to follow it every day. We`re not going to turn the page on that. We are going to talk about the California gubernatorial recall next. But as we head to break, I want you to listen to Charles Krauthammer , our late colleague, talking about then Vice President Biden in 2012. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) CHARLES KRAUTHAMMER , SYNDICATED COLUMNIST: The vice president has been over the last 30 years holds the American record for wrong on the most issues in foreign affairs ever. And the list starts with the nuclear freeze in the early 80s against Thatcher and Reagan and Kohl, which was one of the fathers of the era. He is the Herbert Hoover of American foreign policy. (END VIDEO CLIP) (COMMERCIAL BREAK) (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) GOV. GAVIN NEWSOM , (D) CALIFORNIA: We have major candidates on the other side of this recall that have two things in common. One is they all supported Donald Trump . And, number two, none of them condemned that hate. In fact, many of them defended Donald Trump , including the leading candidate, Larry Elder. LARRY ELDER, (R) CALIFORNIA GUBERNATORIAL CANDIDATE: They are going to outspend us, but we still believe that so many people are angry about the crime, about the homelessness, about the outrageous cost of living. About the way he ignored science while his own kids were enjoying in person education, and the fact that for the very first time in this state`s 170 year history, people are leaving and they`re taking their taxpayer dollars with them. (END VIDEO CLIP) BAIER: Democratic Governor Gavin Newsom in California could be in trouble. The recall is September 14th. Here`s how it works. We`ll put up the poll numbers. You have to vote no if you want to keep Gavin Newsom in. In other words, don`t recall him. Rights now, that`s where these latest recall numbers, the average of recent polls stands. But there are some thoughts that maybe it`s going to be tighter than that. Once you get to yes, he should be recalled, then you have the GOP candidates, and there they are, John Cox, Larry Elder, who seems to be leading among these, Kevin Faulconer , and Caitlyn Jenner. And the ballot itself is fairly complex. You`ve got first the yes and no, and then it`s the other candidates, and really the other candidates could win with 25 percent of the vote depending. There is a lot of candidates listed. We`re back with our panel. Mara, you saw that big sign behind Gavin Newsom , vote no because it`s a little confusing. Some Democrats say yes, we are going to vote yes. LIASSON: Yes, we want to keep Newsom. Yes. Look. Putting aside whether Gavin Newsom is going to win or not, the polls have shown lately a tiny bit of advantage for him better than they were doing about a week or two ago. But the whole recall process is amazing. As you said, Gavin Newsom can lose his job if he gets 49.9 percent of the vote, and Larry Elder could become the governor if he gets something like 25 percent of the vote. So it`s this tool that was part of the California progressivism that was going to give populist -- give the people the chance to recall their governor, but it`s turned into this minoritarian tool, where you can get rid of the governor if he gets a hair under 50, and you can elect a new governor with a tiny, tiny sliver of the vote. So that`s why a lot of people are talking about even after this is all over, California needs to reform its recall process. BAIER: Yes. Bill, your thoughts? BENNETT: I think he`s going down. And they do a lot of goofy things in California, Mara. I know you already know that. (LAUGHTER) BENNETT: I recall Prop 16, which -- that`s the don`t count race, don`t take race into account in college admissions and other things. The people who wanted to get rid of the colorblindness provision outspent by five to one the people who wanted to keep it. But it won with California voters. So they do a lot of goofy things out there. But most of the goofy things are done by the people in charge, not by the voters. So I predict he`s out and Larry Elder is in, my former colleague in Salem Radio. BAIER: We`ll see, and we`re going to follow it very closely. I want to play this one soundbite, and it`s just happening. The president talking to Jewish leaders. The Tree of Live Synagogue in Pittsburgh is where that shooting happened. Here`s what he said, and I will tell you why I`m playing it after that. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) JOE BIDEN , (D) PRESIDENT OF THE UNITED STATES: I remember spending time at the, you know, -- going to the -- you know, the Tree of Life Synagogue, speaking with -- just, it just is amazing these things are happening, happening in America. (END VIDEO CLIP) BAIER: Now, we have no record that he has ever gone to the Tree of Life Synagogue. The "New York Post" first pointed this out. Peter Doocy says he doesn`t recall anything like that. The White House has not responded to us. Jonah, these are things that happen, that clearly was suggesting that he went there and talked to folks. GOLDBERG: Yes, I think there is a temptation to chalk this up to the idea that he is lost it, he`s old, and all that kind of thing, and I understand those kinds of arguments. But this is the kind of thing Joe Biden has done for 40 years. In this he was very much like Bill Clinton who was just create stories about things that he did and places he had been that he never was when he was in his 40s. And Joe Biden is very much like that. He is a crowd pleaser. He likes to say things to audiences and make connections with the audiences. And so maybe he went to the Tree of Life Synagogue. Maybe he didn`t. But this doesn`t shock me because this is the real Joe Biden , a guy who says what he wants to say regardless of whether the facts are with him. BAIER: Yes. And we`ll follow up and continue to. Thought we`d bring that up. All right, panel, when we come back, tomorrow`s headlines. (COMMERCIAL BREAK) BAIER: Finally tonight, a look at tomorrow`s headlines with the panel, a little lightning round. Mara? LIASSON: Mine is abortion politics return to voters. State by state battles begin. I think if Roe is truly on the way out, all of a sudden it`s not about the Supreme Court anymore. It`s about actual voters and their state legislatures. BAIER: Bill? BENNETT: Yes. President Biden will not be impeached, but despite efforts to ignore the calls of the suffering and oppressed in Afghanistan, once he hears those calls, maybe he will have the decency to resign. BAIER: Jonah? GOLDBERG: Struggling to find a winning message on Afghanistan, Joe Biden borrows a page from the Obama administration and now boasts he created or saved over 1 million refugees. BAIER: All right, thanks, guys. Next Thursday on SPECIAL REPORT, special announcement, Education Secretary Miguel Cardona and Surgeon General Vivek Murthy will be our guests. headline: Concerns Over Americans And Allies Left In Afghanistan; Unclear Guidance For Those Stuck In Afghanistan; U.S. Relationship With Taliban Unclear After War Ends; Hurricane Ida Devastates Parts of Louisiana; Some Republicans Call for Impeach or Resignation of President Biden over Military Withdrawal from Afghanistan
story_text: DAGEN MCDOWELL, FOX NEWS HOST: Alienate all your girlfriends before they get married so you don`t have to be in the wedding. SPECIAL REPORT is up next. Hi, Bret. BRET BAIER, FOX NEWS ANCHOR: Hi, Dagen, thank you. Good evening. Welcome to Washington. I`m Bret Baier. Breaking tonight, growing concern about Americans and those who helped Americans still stranded in Afghanistan, as anecdotes of new Taliban atrocities are filtering out of that country. The Biden administration is trying its best to turn the page from the issue that is fueling accusations of broken promises from the president. We`ll take a closer look at that in a few minutes. Also tonight, dozens of Republicans are now calling for the president`s impeachment over his actions and this phone call with the Afghan president before the fall of Kabul. But impeachment is something the top GOP senator says will not happen. White House Correspondent Jacqui Heinrich starts us off tonight, live in the North Lawn. Good evening, Jacqui. JACQUI HEINRICH, FOX NEWS CORRESPONDENT (on camera): Good evening, Bret. On the third day since the troop withdrawal, no answer on whether any more Americans have made it out of Afghanistan or how many Green Card holders or SIV applicants remain. The White House is directing those questions to other departments. And there`s a distinct feeling President Biden is trying to move on from Afghanistan to his domestic agenda. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) JOE BIDEN , PRESIDENT OF THE UNITED STATES: There`s a lot of damage. HEINRICH (voice over): President Biden addressed the nation about storm recovery but gave no update on Afghanistan and took no questions from reporters as more than a hundred Americans and countless at-risk Afghans who helped the U.S. in the 20-year war remain behind enemy lines. JEN PSAKI , WHITE HOUSE PRESS SECRETARY: There are people who are eligible, we may not even know they`re eligible yet, right? It is very hard to define those numbers. HEINRICH: Meanwhile, accounts of reprisals those Afghans face are getting more dire. This person said they killed 12 members of special forces in Kandahar, three soldiers in Jalalabad as well. The Taliban took them out of their homes and shot them. Given this kind of reporting or hearing, is it possible that our reliance on the Taliban to keep their word in terms of our evacuation is misplaced, we`re going back on things like the amnesty promise? PSAKI: No one is saying from the federal government, no one. The president, Secretary of Defense, no one from the Intelligence Community that the Taliban are good actors. That is one of the reasons we are being so clear that we are not rushing to recognition. HEINRICH: Politico reports shame among anonymous sources inside the White House. One person telling Politico, I am absolutely appalled and literally horrified we left Americans there. Kabul`s airport remains inoperable and the White House says there are risks associated with charter flights seeking to extract Americans to U.S. military basis. PSAKI: We do not have reliable means to confirm the basic details of charter flights including who may be organizing them. We know ISIS-K has a keen interest in attacks against aviation targets and our personnel on the ground and our Air Force in our military bases. HEINRICH: Among the House GOP, growing calls for the president to resign but the top Senate Republican Mitch McConnell says President Biden will not be impeached and the ballot box is a better place to hold him accountable. (END VIDEO CLIP) HEINRICH (on camera): Still, other Republican senators want accountability now. 25 members wrote to President Biden saying while they disagree on whether troops should have remained in Afghanistan, they`re all in agreement President Biden`s chaotic withdrawal caused this crisis, Bret. BAIER: Jacqui, obviously, the administration, the president want to focus on domestic agenda items, but you have this human infrastructure bill that`s kind of sitting out there, the 3.5 trillion, a key Senate Democrat is pretty much blocking that path. HEINRICH: That`s right. West Virginia Senator Joe Manchin said there is no way he will support that $3.5 trillion social infrastructure package that Democrats want to pass along party lines. He dragged his colleagues for what he called a strange belief, there`s an infinite amount of money to go around. He wrote, Democratic congressional leaders proposed to pass the largest single spending bill in history with no regard to rising inflation, crippling debt, or the inevitability of future crises. Ignoring the fiscal consequences of our policy choices will create a disastrous future for the next generation of Americans. Without Manchin`s vote, Biden`s agenda really seems to go nowhere and it appears that Manchin is dug in, Bret. BAIER: All right, we`ll follow that. Jacqui, thank you. We`re hearing tonight from an Afghan interpreter who helped save then- Senator Biden 13 years ago and is now pleading for rescue himself. That man and his family are joined by as we mentioned, Americans and thousands of Afghans who helped the U.S. through the 20 years of war who today still cannot leave that country. Correspondent Griff Jenkins has the story. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) NED PRICE , STATE DEPARTMENT SPOKESMAN: We will provide them a tailored guidance but that is not something we will provide to all of you. And we won`t do that for their safety. GRIFF JENKINS, FOX NEWS CORRESPONDENT (voice over): For those stuck behind enemy lines, the plan to get them out is unclear. With the Kabul airport shut down, dangerous ground routes appear to be the only option. The State Department also won`t say if any American citizens have gotten out since the last flight out of Kabul on August 30th. Leaving behind 100 to 200 Americans, tens of thousands of Afghan allies, including the majority of SIV applicants, and even the State Department`s own journalists. Also, among those stranded, an interpreter known as Mohammed, who helped rescue then-Senator Joe Biden in 2008 when his helicopter made an emergency landing in the snow-covered mountains of Afghanistan. BIDEN: If you want to know where Al-Qaeda lives, you want to know where bin Laden is, come back to Afghanistan with me. Come back to the area my helicopter was forced down. JENKINS: Unable to get out before the deadline, Mohammed is now pleading for President Biden to save him and his family. MOHAMMED, AFGHAN INTERPRETER: Maybe die at home. There is no way I can`t escape from my house. All borders in my country are sealed, but only I and my -- and my son have a U.S. passport. The rest of the family do not have. JENKINS: The State Department`s other focus is resettling and vetting the tens of thousands of refugees arriving on American soil amid growing concerns that individuals were extremists could slip through the cracks. story_text: GREG GUTFELD, FOX NEWS CHANNEL HOST: He must be on the ball. GERALDO RIVERA, FOX NEWS CHANNEL CORRESPONDENT-AT-LARGE: He was a great, great brother. GUTFELD: That's it for us. "SPECIAL REPORT" is up next. Hi, Bret. BRET BAIER, FOX NEWS CHANNEL HOST: Kurt Vonnegut for 500. Thanks, Greg. Good evening. Welcome to Washington. I'm Bret Baier. Breaking tonight, the enemy of my enemy is my friend. It's an old saying that may have new relevance tonight for U.S. counterterrorism policy. The nation's top military officer now says it is possible the U.S. will cooperate with the Taliban in taking on other terrorist groups, most notably ISIS-K. Chairman of the Joint Chiefs General Mark Milley says it's unclear whether the Taliban has changed from the ruthless group it once was. But new reports from the ground suggest the Taliban in certain parts of the country is going back to its old ways. National Security Correspondent Jennifer Griffin starts us off tonight from the Pentagon. Good evening, Jennifer. JENNIFER GRIFFIN, FOX NEWS CHANNEL NATIONAL SECURITY CORRESPONDENT (on camera): Good evening, Bret. We saw in Iraq what happened when the U.S. declared a war over and pulled out troops leaving a nascent ISIS to grow. Tonight, an admission that the U.S. isn't done with Afghanistan. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) GRIFFIN (voice over): As the Taliban continue to brandish American weapons captured from the Afghan army when the government fell 17 days ago, those fighters expressed anger the U.S. had disabled all of the military planes and helicopters at the airport before leaving. For the first time since the last American soldier left Afghanistan, the Defense Secretary and Chairman of the Joint Chiefs faced the press, they took just three questions including whether they might have to partner with the Taliban in the future. GEN. MARK MILLEY, CHAIRMAN, JOINT CHIEFS OF STAFF: I can tell you from personal experience, this is a ruthless group from the past, and whether or not they change remains to be seen. And as far as our dealings with them at that airfield, in war, you do what you must in order to reduce risk to mission and force, not what you necessarily want to do. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: Any possibility of coordination against ISIS-K with them do you think? Milley: It's possible. GRIFFIN: A stunning admission as a result of the new reality on the ground in Afghanistan, and the absence of intelligence networks which had to be rolled up as part of the hasty U.S. withdrawal. GEN. LLOYD AUSTIN , DEFENSE SECRETARY: We shouldn't expect Afghan war veterans to agree any more than any other group of Americans. I've heard strong views from many sides in recent days and that's vital. That's democracy. That's America. MILLEY: How we got to this moment in Afghanistan will be analyzed and studied for years to come. And we in the military, will approach this with humility, transparency and candor. GRIFFIN: Both were asked about lessons learned over two decades at war, how violently it ended with the deaths of 13 U.S. service members. MILLEY: I wasn't born a four-star general. I have walked the patrols and been blown up and shot at and RPG and everything else. This is tough stuff. War is hard and it's vicious, it's brutal, it's unforgiving. I'm a professional soldier. I'm going to contain my pain and anger and continue to execute my mission. (END VIDEO CLIP) GRIFFIN (on camera): That mission is to get the remaining 100 or so Americans out of Afghanistan along with U.S. allies, something that the State Department is now the lead on. But it's hard to imagine them getting very far without the Taliban and Delta Force, Bret. BAIER: You know, Jen, there are these reports, one from the BBC citing a former Afghan soldier, a Special Forces soldier hiding with his family. And quoting here, he says, since the Taliban have come to power, they haven't stopped killing. A few days ago, they killed 12 members of the Special Forces in Kandahar and three soldiers in Jalalabad as well. There were my close friends, the Taliban took them out of their homes and shot them in front of their families. I know we don't have specifics on this incident. But what are we hearing? GRIFFIN: Well, I have actually incidents that have come to my attention that I can confirm in terms of Taliban fighters taking the phones of some of those who are trying to escape overland, especially up to the north. And they -- if they find any American numbers on those phones, they'll call them and then if somebody answers, they will kill those people with the person on the other end of the line listening. So, that is very dangerous right now. We know that they are hunting female judges near the prison where many of those ISIS-K were released. And we know of many, many people in hiding tonight in Afghanistan, because the Taliban are not keeping their word. And some of their fighters are already seeking retribution. BAIER: Yes, it's amazing. We'll follow it. Jennifer Griffin at the Pentagon. Jennifer, thank you. There's increasing confusion really in Afghanistan about who is in charge now that the Taliban has taken over, that is affecting people trying to get out of the country. Meanwhile, the group continues to celebrate the withdrawal of U.S. troops showing off U.S. personnel -- U.S. material, U.S. weapons and U.S. vehicles. Correspondent Trey Yingst has the latest tonight from Doha, Qatar. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) TREY YINGST, FOX NEWS CHANNEL CORRESPONDENT (voice over): A helicopter flies overhead displaying a Taliban flag. The Group is parading their American made weapons and Humvees through the Afghan city of Kandahar. Declarations of victory continue across the country. Though in the capital of Kabul, the challenges of governing are already setting in. AHMAD RAMISH, SHOPKEEPER (through translator): We asked them the Taliban to bring peace, which develops the economy. The situation is very poor. Since the Islamic Emirate, the Taliban has entered Kabul, people have been facing more economic problems. YINGST: Today, the Taliban appointed a new central bank governor to address problems with financial institutions. Long lines at banks and withdrawal limits are creating tension among the civilian population. Market traders say the price of vegetables is up 50 percent, with the price of fuel up 75 percent. UNIDENTIFIED MALE (through translator): Before the Taliban came, the markets situation and selling were good. Although, we were dissatisfied with the government at the time as well. Now, the situation is such that we have a lot of selling, but there are no sales. YINGST: Worried about economic hardship on the horizon and the brutality of the Taliban , thousands are hoping to flee Afghanistan on foot. Neighboring Tajikistan has pledged to accept 100,000 Afghan refugees, while Pakistan is being urged to add to its refugee population that already tops 1.4 million people. (END VIDEO CLIP) YINGST (on camera): As people continue to leave Afghanistan, there are reports tonight of renewed fighting in the Panjshir Valley, the last pocket of resistance in Afghanistan against the Taliban , Bret. BAIER: Trey Yingst in Doha, Qatar. Trey, thanks. There are questions tonight about whether President Biden asked his Afghan counterpart to lie about how bad the situation was getting on the ground in Afghanistan more than a month ago. Right now, as you heard, there are still thousands of Americans and Afghans who helped the Americans throughout the 20 years of the war who do want to leave that country. White House Correspondent Jacqui Heinrich has that part of the story tonight. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) JACQUI HEINRICH, FOX NEWS CHANNEL CORRESPONDENT (voice over): Two days after troops left Afghanistan, it's still unclear if any more Americans or Afghans left behind have made it out. Is there a plan to do something else so that that movement can happen? JEN PSAKI , WHITE HOUSE PRESS SECRETARY: Well, today is September 1st, we ended our presence in Afghanistan yesterday or on the 31st in Afghanistan. HEINRICH: A key hurdle getting the Kabul airport operational again. But among those awaiting safe passage, journalists funded by the U.S. government reportedly turned away from the gates by American troops, preventing their rescue. Senior State Department officials tell Fox, communications that we're supposed to prioritize certain groups went viral. Was that a contingency that was planned for? PSAKI: Well, Jacqui, I think it's important to remember again, 120,000 people made it out of the airport and out of the country. And our commitment to people who want to evacuate want to leave, American citizens, journalists, Afghan partners who have stood by our side is enduring and remains. HEINRICH: As the Taliban 's promise of free passage is put to the test, President Biden met with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky , who like the former Afghan President is desperate for economic and military aid in Ukraine's fight against Russia. According to Reuters, Afghan President Ghani told Biden July 23rd, his country was facing a full-scale Taliban invasion. And President Biden told Ghani he needed to project an image of strength saying, "I need not tell you the perception around the world and in parts of Afghanistan, I believe, is that things are not going well in terms of the fight against the Taliban . And there is a need, whether it is true or not, there is a need to project a different picture." Was the president in any way pushing a false narrative in that call with the Afghan President? PSAKI: I think it's pretty clear. Again, I'm not going to go into details of a private conversation. But what we saw over the course of the last few months is a collapse in leadership. What the president has conveyed repeatedly privately and publicly is you need to stand up and lead your country. (END VIDEO CLIP) HEINRICH (on camera): The White House maintains nobody saw the Taliban takeover coming as quickly as it did. And while they would not comment on the call, they said the reporting also illustrates that. But at the very least, the call shows President Biden was aware of the public perception that a Taliban takeover could happen, Bret. BAIER: Jacqui Heinrich live in the North Lawn. Jacqui, thank you. Let's bring in Senior Political Analyst Brit Hume to discuss what we're learning about President Biden during this crisis. Good evening, Brit. For 30,000 feet here, what do you think this says about President Biden, his leadership and where it goes from here? BRIT HUME, FOX NEWS SENIOR POLITICAL ANALYST: Well, Bret, I think people have to begin now to assess whether this president was the man the president they thought he was and would be. After all, this is the season foreign policy expert, former chairman of the Fed Senate Foreign Relations Committee, a post he held twice. The kind of man they believe I think would not make serious foreign policy mistakes. And yet, this is the first big foreign policy issue of his presidency, the first big crisis. And the condemnation of it has been virtually unanimous across the board, including many Democrats. Not to mention that it has gotten a level of criticism from the mainstream media, one rarely sees directed at a Democratic president. Not to mention the fact that the public can see with his own eyes that all the things -- nearly all the things that President Biden told us would not happen in Afghanistan have now come to pass. Yes, indeed, it was a remarkable evacuation mission, a remarkable response to an emergency, but it was an emergency created by this administration and the way they handled the evacuation. And we know now that the president repeatedly overruled his military advisers as to how to conduct this evacuation. So, it seems to me that that there's a real chance here that people are looking at this president in an entirely new light and may not see him the same again. BAIER: You know, obviously, the focus is on the Americans on the ground, the Afghan allies who worked with us trying to get those people out who want to get out. But in the political sphere, a lot of times people just talk about Americans losing interest, turning the page, you know, closing the chapter and moving on. Obviously, the administration would like that to happen, is it going to happen with something like Afghanistan in this handling? HUME: Well, as long as there are Americans there that want to get out and cannot or have not gotten out, and there are tales of atrocities by the Taliban , which I suspect will multiply in the days ahead. So, such that even though we don't have very much in the way of news coverage coming out of there, word gets out. So, it will be hard for this issue to fade completely anytime soon. Which is not to say that over time, people's memory of it won't fade. But they will, I think, remember for a very long time the shaky character who came out and made these bogus explanations of what was happening and why it happened, said things that were probably not true and was called on them. So, the question comes, yes, people may stop thinking about Afghanistan as such, but it really is a good question whether you ever look at Joe Biden the same way again. BAIER: Brit, as always, thank you. HUME: You bet. BAIER: Stocks were mixed today. The Dow lost 48, the S&P 500 was up one, the NASDAQ gained 50 for another new record close. After being checked out, they fly to the States on chartered commercial flights. CAPT. JAMES DIMMICK, 8TH AIRLIFT SQUADRON: It's been pretty much nonstop. We have been running 24 hours every day of the week so far, just getting as many people in and out of here as we possibly can. PALKOT: Have you ever handled this size of operation with so many moving parts? DIMMICK: I've never seen anything like this in my entire life. PALKOT: And like the service members injured in last week's terror attack, some come back in bad shape. That's when the military turns C-17s into intensive care units. On board one mission to Kabul, Major Joshua Thomas, he says they handle it all. MAJ. JOSHUA THOMAS, 10TH EAEF, RAMSTEIN AIR BASE: From battle injuries, blast injuries, gunshot wounds, just regular medical illnesses. PALKOT: This week basically marks the end of the U.S. war in Afghanistan. Some at Ramstein has been through it all. Despite the debate, service members are convinced they are doing the right thing. Was it all worth it? LT. COL. ELIZABETH DWYER, CRITICAL CARE PHYSICIAN: Absolutely. PALKOT: All worth it. Saving lives? DWYER: That's what we do. (END VIDEO TAPE) PALKOT: Saving lives, that's what we do. One officer at the base told us their part of the mission could go on for days, a lot of lives hanging in the balance. Bret? BAIER: Greg Palkot in Germany. Greg, thanks. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) JOE LIEBERMAN, FORMER CONNECTICUT SENATOR: I'm disappointed and I think we're all going to pay for it, first of all, the people of Afghanistan. But we, too, because there's no question, notwithstanding all the sweet talk from some of the Taliban leaders, that's not who they are. They are a radical Islamist terrorist group, and they're going to welcome other radical Islamist terrorist groups to Afghanistan who will aim to strike us from there as Al-Qaeda did on 9/11. It's just tragic and totally unnecessary. (END VIDEO CLIP) BAIER: Former Democratic vice presidential nominee, former Senator Joe Lieberman, talking about the situation now in Afghanistan. Let's bring in our panel, Mollie Hemingway, senior editor at "The Federalist," Leslie Marshall, Democratic strategist, and Bill McGurn, columnist for "The Wall Street Journal." Bill, let me start with you. Your thought? "The Wall Street Journal" had a really scathing editorial today about this situation, but a lot of lawmakers up on Capitol Hill on both sides of the aisle have been very critical of this administration messaging and action. BILL MCGURN, COLUMNIST, "THE WALL STREET JOURNAL": Yes, I think it's not just the messaging. It's the reality. We've just surrendered 9/11 forever to the Islamic jihadists. It is now a double victory celebration for them. First, the original Al-Qaeda strike on America, and second the Taliban victory that we see right now in Kabul. It just seems to me we are back to that pre-9/11 thinking. Remember when people used to say Al-Qaeda was at war with us long before we were at war with Al-Qaeda. And I think Joe Biden 's spin that somehow the world watches the spectacle of us leaving fellow Americans behind enemy lines and concludes that America has greater resolve and greater capabilities going forward is just farcical. BAIER: And Leslie, the State Department conceding today that most of the SIVs, most of the Afghans who helped the U.S. in the war, actually did not get out, and the numbers are pretty staggering. Here is the State Department on the safe passage that they are trying to coordinate right now. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) VICTORIA NULAND, UNDER SECRETARY OF STATE: We are looking at all possible options, air routes, land routes, to continue to find ways for them to help evacuate. And to support them in that, we're trying to ascertain who precisely still wants to leave, who their dependent family members are, what routes may or may not feel comfortable to them. NED PRICE, STATE DEPARTMENT SPOKESMAN: Half the world's countries, all of the most important stakeholders have signed on to the idea that the Taliban must uphold their commitments of safe passage. (END VIDEO CLIP) BAIER: It's just tough to believe that that's going to be smooth sailing with the Taliban knowing their history, Leslie. LESLIE MARSHALL, DEMOCRATIC STRATEGIST: Well, if we just look at what is happening with the Taliban , Bret, I think I mentioned on your podcast, the problem here is not only are they an uneducated group of men that run the Taliban , but the Taliban is used to running a terrorist organization, and running a country is very different. They could be without food in a couple of weeks. They don't have air traffic control. They have people landing right now as we speak from Qatar to try and handle that so that they can open commercial airways in two days, and hopefully more people, including those Afghans that assisted us here in the United States and abroad, can get out. Look, left and right, I have said it before, we should have started this earlier. We should not leave until everyone that we can help is out, is out. But we also do have to look at other realities. The State Department since April gave numerous warnings, over a dozen warnings to Americans to get out. In addition to that, everyone knew the Taliban was going to be in power, quite frankly. And I think it's the United States and all of our allies, especially the United States knew. The former administration, former Secretary of State Pompeo sat down with the Taliban , not with the president of Afghanistan. They knew who was going to be the new sheriff in town, sadly. So, it's messy right now. I certainly hope and pray that won't be the case going forward. And one last thing. Even though we can't trust them, Bret, no question, they need money from us and from others. And if we say we want a and then you get b, they might be apt to do it. BAIER: They also have hosted, obviously, radical Islamic terrorists, Al- Qaeda, others. They say they are fighting ISIS-K, but it's really a witches' brew there, Mollie. What about the who knew what when, and this leaked Reuters report, the transcript from this call between President Biden and the Afghan president Ghani? MOLLIE HEMINGWAY, SENIOR EDITOR, "THE FEDERALIST": Yes, we impeached a president for a phone call, and now we have this leak of phone call that President Biden had where he asked someone to lie in exchange for military support. It sounds like something that last year would have caused major problems for the previous president. I think we cannot lose sight of how we can never fight a war like this ever again. There was a Pew poll last week that showed that Americans are broadly supportive of the departure from Afghanistan. That's the Trump policy that Biden supported. They have even more agreement that the manner in which we fought this war was a failure. You don't see people talking about World War II the way we talk about this war. This war has been prosecuted poorly, according to the American people, for decades. And then there is even more agreement that the manner in which Biden departed was a complete debacle. That's not really up for debate. It was a debacle. It was a national humiliation and a disgrace. And the proper response to that is to clean out our military like we did after Bay of Pigs and make sure that people are replaced with people who know how to do their jobs. Unfortunately, the current president who was involved in this phone call is incompetent and unable to replace the military leadership who failed. And so it remains to the American people in their elections to replace him and the woke generals who cannot do basic jobs like winning wars or exiting a country. BAIER: All right, strong letter to follow. Up next, the panel on the Texas abortion law. (COMMERCIAL BREAK) (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) JEN PSAKI , WHITE HOUSE PRESS SECRETARY: The president's focus is to reiterate our deep commitment to the constitutional right, of course established by Roe v Wade nearly five decades ago, and to continue to call for the codification of Roe. (END VIDEO CLIP) BAIER: Jen Psaki following up, talking about this Texas abortion law now in effect. The president put out a statement today, says "This extreme Texas law blatantly violates the constitutional right established under Roe v. Wade and upheld as precedent for nearly half a century. Outrageously, it deputizes private citizens to bring lawsuits against anyone who they believe has helped another person get an abortion, which might even include family members, healthcare workers, front desk staff at a healthcare clinic, or strangers with no connection to the individual." And in fact, if you look at the bullet points, that is accurate. The state doesn't enforce it. Citizens can sue providers in any way involved in aiding or abetting an abortion after heartbeat is detected, and, again, six weeks here. Citizen plaintiffs are entitled to $10,000 plus legal fees if they win. We're back with the panel. Bill, this seems designed to be part of the challenge to Roe in the Supreme Court. MCGURN: Yes, it is part of -- it is a challenge, like many challenges, to the Supreme Court. But it poses a lot of legal questions on procedural ground that haven't been at the courts before. And, again, the pro-choice side is trying to get the court, that's their favorite legislature, just to dismiss it early on. They may still do it. But if they were going to do it, you would have thought it would have went into effect before today. I'm hoping -- I believe it's both a moral and constitutional victory if we get this back to the states. If we want to codify Roe, let the states do it as New York has done it. But look, the existing regime is just out of touch with the American people. The American people want limits. The Democratic Party has been able to oppose those limits because it's been done so undemocratically. I am with Justice Scalia. The Supreme Court has no business umpiring the abortion business, and they should get out of it. We would be a lot healthier, and we would return that debate to the states where it belongs. BAIER: Leslie, it seems like this administration would want to go through Congress to codify Roe, but there is no way the numbers are anywhere close to being there. MARSHALL: No, but what's really concerning here, Bret, is not only the constitutional violation of the rights of anyone with a uterus in the state of Texas, but when you just look deeper at this law, if you are a 13-year- old rape victim and you don't realize you are pregnant because you don't have a regular menstrual cycle and you come in after six weeks, you're going to be forced to carry that child. Speaking of rape, a rapist could actually sue their victim and get $10,000 if they feel that individual is trying to abort that child outside the six- week limit. And to Bill's point, you know, the American people are not looking for a six-week limit on abortion. When you look at the majority of polls out there, the majority of people in the United States support Roe v Wade, and even if they call themselves pro-life, support a woman's right to choose. Most Americans don't want, myself included, long-term abortions. Six weeks is not late term. BAIER: Mollie? HEMINGWAY: Yes, the Texas legislature passed this law that protects children who have a detectable heartbeat. And this is important that this was allowed to stand even this long because that's what Roe v Wade took away from people was the right of people to determine their own view -- what the state law should be on abortion. But the Supreme Court has a history of having had bad decisions. Roe v Wade is just one of the noteworthy bad decisions that takes an entire class of humans and dehumanizes them. And so it is incumbent upon the court to correct mistakes like that, like they did after the Dred Scott decision or Korematsu or Roe v. Wade. And they have an excellent opportunity with this case that has risen to the Supreme Court level this year with Dobbs to correct some of these problems. We have a radical abortion regime. It is violent oppression of women and their children. It is predatory, and it's just not what humans should do to each other. And we have an opportunity to allow it to come back to the states where people can set appropriate limits and protect these unborn children and their mothers. BAIER: We'll see what the court does. We'll be following it. It could happen tonight. Thanks, panel. When we come back, more of the panel with tomorrow's headlines. (COMMERCIAL BREAK) BAIER: Finally tonight, a look at tomorrow's headlines with the panel. Mollie, first to you. HEMINGWAY: Democrats continue to fight one another as they oppose the nomination by Biden of Obama's former chief of staff Rahm Emanuel to be the ambassador to Japan. BAIER: OK, we will follow that. Leslie? MARSHALL: Larry Elder, who is running in the California gubernatorial election, has a come to Jesus moment and gets out, saying talk show hosts shouldn't be running a big state in the midst of a pandemic. BAIER: I don't think that one is happening, but we are going to look into it tomorrow. All right, Bill. MCGURN: Joe Biden gives us a preview of his 9/11 speech. Despite everything you have seen with your own eyes, I have made no mistakes, and the retreat from Afghanistan was in fact the biggest American military victory since the Normandy landing. BAIER: All right, panel, thank you very much. Tomorrow on SPECIAL REPORT, we'll get the latest on the efforts to get Americans out of Afghanistan, plus, good timing, an update on the California governor recall, September 14th, Californians already voting. We will lay it all out for you and explain it. Thanks for inviting us into your home tonight. That's it for the SPECIAL REPORT, fair, balanced, and still unafraid.
