story_text: GREG GUTFELD, FOX NEWS CHANNEL HOST: He must be on the ball. GERALDO RIVERA, FOX NEWS CHANNEL CORRESPONDENT-AT-LARGE: He was a great, great brother. GUTFELD: That's it for us. "SPECIAL REPORT" is up next. Hi, Bret. BRET BAIER, FOX NEWS CHANNEL HOST: Kurt Vonnegut for 500. Thanks, Greg. Good evening. Welcome to Washington. I'm Bret Baier. Breaking tonight, the enemy of my enemy is my friend. It's an old saying that may have new relevance tonight for U.S. counterterrorism policy. The nation's top military officer now says it is possible the U.S. will cooperate with the Taliban in taking on other terrorist groups, most notably ISIS-K. Chairman of the Joint Chiefs General Mark Milley says it's unclear whether the Taliban has changed from the ruthless group it once was. But new reports from the ground suggest the Taliban in certain parts of the country is going back to its old ways. National Security Correspondent Jennifer Griffin starts us off tonight from the Pentagon. Good evening, Jennifer. JENNIFER GRIFFIN, FOX NEWS CHANNEL NATIONAL SECURITY CORRESPONDENT (on camera): Good evening, Bret. We saw in Iraq what happened when the U.S. declared a war over and pulled out troops leaving a nascent ISIS to grow. Tonight, an admission that the U.S. isn't done with Afghanistan. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) GRIFFIN (voice over): As the Taliban continue to brandish American weapons captured from the Afghan army when the government fell 17 days ago, those fighters expressed anger the U.S. had disabled all of the military planes and helicopters at the airport before leaving. For the first time since the last American soldier left Afghanistan, the Defense Secretary and Chairman of the Joint Chiefs faced the press, they took just three questions including whether they might have to partner with the Taliban in the future. GEN. MARK MILLEY, CHAIRMAN, JOINT CHIEFS OF STAFF: I can tell you from personal experience, this is a ruthless group from the past, and whether or not they change remains to be seen. And as far as our dealings with them at that airfield, in war, you do what you must in order to reduce risk to mission and force, not what you necessarily want to do. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: Any possibility of coordination against ISIS-K with them do you think? Milley: It's possible. GRIFFIN: A stunning admission as a result of the new reality on the ground in Afghanistan, and the absence of intelligence networks which had to be rolled up as part of the hasty U.S. withdrawal. GEN. LLOYD AUSTIN , DEFENSE SECRETARY: We shouldn't expect Afghan war veterans to agree any more than any other group of Americans. I've heard strong views from many sides in recent days and that's vital. That's democracy. That's America. MILLEY: How we got to this moment in Afghanistan will be analyzed and studied for years to come. And we in the military, will approach this with humility, transparency and candor. GRIFFIN: Both were asked about lessons learned over two decades at war, how violently it ended with the deaths of 13 U.S. service members. MILLEY: I wasn't born a four-star general. I have walked the patrols and been blown up and shot at and RPG and everything else. This is tough stuff. War is hard and it's vicious, it's brutal, it's unforgiving. I'm a professional soldier. I'm going to contain my pain and anger and continue to execute my mission. (END VIDEO CLIP) GRIFFIN (on camera): That mission is to get the remaining 100 or so Americans out of Afghanistan along with U.S. allies, something that the State Department is now the lead on. But it's hard to imagine them getting very far without the Taliban and Delta Force, Bret. BAIER: You know, Jen, there are these reports, one from the BBC citing a former Afghan soldier, a Special Forces soldier hiding with his family. And quoting here, he says, since the Taliban have come to power, they haven't stopped killing. A few days ago, they killed 12 members of the Special Forces in Kandahar and three soldiers in Jalalabad as well. There were my close friends, the Taliban took them out of their homes and shot them in front of their families. I know we don't have specifics on this incident. But what are we hearing? GRIFFIN: Well, I have actually incidents that have come to my attention that I can confirm in terms of Taliban fighters taking the phones of some of those who are trying to escape overland, especially up to the north. And they -- if they find any American numbers on those phones, they'll call them and then if somebody answers, they will kill those people with the person on the other end of the line listening. So, that is very dangerous right now. We know that they are hunting female judges near the prison where many of those ISIS-K were released. And we know of many, many people in hiding tonight in Afghanistan, because the Taliban are not keeping their word. And some of their fighters are already seeking retribution. BAIER: Yes, it's amazing. We'll follow it. Jennifer Griffin at the Pentagon. Jennifer, thank you. There's increasing confusion really in Afghanistan about who is in charge now that the Taliban has taken over, that is affecting people trying to get out of the country. Meanwhile, the group continues to celebrate the withdrawal of U.S. troops showing off U.S. personnel -- U.S. material, U.S. weapons and U.S. vehicles. Correspondent Trey Yingst has the latest tonight from Doha, Qatar. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) TREY YINGST, FOX NEWS CHANNEL CORRESPONDENT (voice over): A helicopter flies overhead displaying a Taliban flag. The Group is parading their American made weapons and Humvees through the Afghan city of Kandahar. Declarations of victory continue across the country. Though in the capital of Kabul, the challenges of governing are already setting in. AHMAD RAMISH, SHOPKEEPER (through translator): We asked them the Taliban to bring peace, which develops the economy. The situation is very poor. Since the Islamic Emirate, the Taliban has entered Kabul, people have been facing more economic problems. YINGST: Today, the Taliban appointed a new central bank governor to address problems with financial institutions. Long lines at banks and withdrawal limits are creating tension among the civilian population. Market traders say the price of vegetables is up 50 percent, with the price of fuel up 75 percent. UNIDENTIFIED MALE (through translator): Before the Taliban came, the markets situation and selling were good. Although, we were dissatisfied with the government at the time as well. Now, the situation is such that we have a lot of selling, but there are no sales. YINGST: Worried about economic hardship on the horizon and the brutality of the Taliban , thousands are hoping to flee Afghanistan on foot. Neighboring Tajikistan has pledged to accept 100,000 Afghan refugees, while Pakistan is being urged to add to its refugee population that already tops 1.4 million people. (END VIDEO CLIP) YINGST (on camera): As people continue to leave Afghanistan, there are reports tonight of renewed fighting in the Panjshir Valley, the last pocket of resistance in Afghanistan against the Taliban , Bret. BAIER: Trey Yingst in Doha, Qatar. Trey, thanks. There are questions tonight about whether President Biden asked his Afghan counterpart to lie about how bad the situation was getting on the ground in Afghanistan more than a month ago. Right now, as you heard, there are still thousands of Americans and Afghans who helped the Americans throughout the 20 years of the war who do want to leave that country. White House Correspondent Jacqui Heinrich has that part of the story tonight. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) JACQUI HEINRICH, FOX NEWS CHANNEL CORRESPONDENT (voice over): Two days after troops left Afghanistan, it's still unclear if any more Americans or Afghans left behind have made it out. Is there a plan to do something else so that that movement can happen? JEN PSAKI , WHITE HOUSE PRESS SECRETARY: Well, today is September 1st, we ended our presence in Afghanistan yesterday or on the 31st in Afghanistan. HEINRICH: A key hurdle getting the Kabul airport operational again. But among those awaiting safe passage, journalists funded by the U.S. government reportedly turned away from the gates by American troops, preventing their rescue. Senior State Department officials tell Fox, communications that we're supposed to prioritize certain groups went viral. Was that a contingency that was planned for? PSAKI: Well, Jacqui, I think it's important to remember again, 120,000 people made it out of the airport and out of the country. And our commitment to people who want to evacuate want to leave, American citizens, journalists, Afghan partners who have stood by our side is enduring and remains. HEINRICH: As the Taliban 's promise of free passage is put to the test, President Biden met with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky , who like the former Afghan President is desperate for economic and military aid in Ukraine's fight against Russia. According to Reuters, Afghan President Ghani told Biden July 23rd, his country was facing a full-scale Taliban invasion. And President Biden told Ghani he needed to project an image of strength saying, "I need not tell you the perception around the world and in parts of Afghanistan, I believe, is that things are not going well in terms of the fight against the Taliban . And there is a need, whether it is true or not, there is a need to project a different picture." Was the president in any way pushing a false narrative in that call with the Afghan President? PSAKI: I think it's pretty clear. Again, I'm not going to go into details of a private conversation. But what we saw over the course of the last few months is a collapse in leadership. What the president has conveyed repeatedly privately and publicly is you need to stand up and lead your country. (END VIDEO CLIP) HEINRICH (on camera): The White House maintains nobody saw the Taliban takeover coming as quickly as it did. And while they would not comment on the call, they said the reporting also illustrates that. But at the very least, the call shows President Biden was aware of the public perception that a Taliban takeover could happen, Bret. BAIER: Jacqui Heinrich live in the North Lawn. Jacqui, thank you. Let's bring in Senior Political Analyst Brit Hume to discuss what we're learning about President Biden during this crisis. Good evening, Brit. For 30,000 feet here, what do you think this says about President Biden, his leadership and where it goes from here? BRIT HUME, FOX NEWS SENIOR POLITICAL ANALYST: Well, Bret, I think people have to begin now to assess whether this president was the man the president they thought he was and would be. After all, this is the season foreign policy expert, former chairman of the Fed Senate Foreign Relations Committee, a post he held twice. The kind of man they believe I think would not make serious foreign policy mistakes. And yet, this is the first big foreign policy issue of his presidency, the first big crisis. And the condemnation of it has been virtually unanimous across the board, including many Democrats. Not to mention that it has gotten a level of criticism from the mainstream media, one rarely sees directed at a Democratic president. Not to mention the fact that the public can see with his own eyes that all the things -- nearly all the things that President Biden told us would not happen in Afghanistan have now come to pass. Yes, indeed, it was a remarkable evacuation mission, a remarkable response to an emergency, but it was an emergency created by this administration and the way they handled the evacuation. And we know now that the president repeatedly overruled his military advisers as to how to conduct this evacuation. So, it seems to me that that there's a real chance here that people are looking at this president in an entirely new light and may not see him the same again. BAIER: You know, obviously, the focus is on the Americans on the ground, the Afghan allies who worked with us trying to get those people out who want to get out. But in the political sphere, a lot of times people just talk about Americans losing interest, turning the page, you know, closing the chapter and moving on. Obviously, the administration would like that to happen, is it going to happen with something like Afghanistan in this handling? HUME: Well, as long as there are Americans there that want to get out and cannot or have not gotten out, and there are tales of atrocities by the Taliban , which I suspect will multiply in the days ahead. So, such that even though we don't have very much in the way of news coverage coming out of there, word gets out. So, it will be hard for this issue to fade completely anytime soon. Which is not to say that over time, people's memory of it won't fade. But they will, I think, remember for a very long time the shaky character who came out and made these bogus explanations of what was happening and why it happened, said things that were probably not true and was called on them. So, the question comes, yes, people may stop thinking about Afghanistan as such, but it really is a good question whether you ever look at Joe Biden the same way again. BAIER: Brit, as always, thank you. HUME: You bet. BAIER: Stocks were mixed today. The Dow lost 48, the S&P 500 was up one, the NASDAQ gained 50 for another new record close. A federal bankruptcy judge says he will accept with small changes a settlement between OxyContin maker Purdue Pharma , and state and local governments over the opioid crisis. The value of the plan is estimated to be about $10 billion. It would cap years of litigation. Members of the Sackler family would give up ownership of the company and pay $4.5 billion while the company is converted to a new entity, with its profits being used to fight the epidemic. Up next, a hugely controversial abortion law is now in effect in Texas. We'll tell you what that means and where it may be going. First, here's what some of our Fox affiliates around the country are covering tonight. Fox 5 in San Diego where a search is underway for five missing crew members after a U.S. Navy helicopter crashes off the coast. U.S. Coast Guard official tells Fox debris from that helicopter has been found. One crew member was rescued and is in stable condition. A Navy spokesman says the helicopter had been operating on the deck of the USS Abraham Lincoln before it crashed into the sea. Five sailors aboard the carrier were injured. Fox 5 in New York as Governor Kathy Hochul brings back lawmakers to extend the state's eviction moratorium through January 15th, hours before the ban was set to expire. The U.S. Supreme Court ruling we told you last week allowed evictions to continue blocking a temporary ban from President Biden in his administration. And this is a live look at Salt Lake City from Fox 13. The big story there tonight, Utah joins seven other states allowing residents to add driver's licenses and state I.D.s to their Apple Wallet for iPhone and Apple Watch. The TSA will now allow customers to use the new feature at select airport security checkpoints in participating airports. That's tonight's live look outside the Beltway from SPECIAL REPORT. We'll be right back. (COMMERCIAL BREAK) BAIER: Two Food and Drug Administration senior officials are reportedly stepping down from their posts over a disagreement with the White House on the administration of booster shots. Source telling Fox Business, the director of the agency's Office of Vaccine Research and Review, and her deputy director resigned after the Biden administration went ahead with the booster program starting the week of September 20th without FDA approval. Idaho's Republican governor is calling in 220 medical workers available through federal programs and mobilizing 150 Idaho National Guard soldiers to deal with overwhelmed state hospitals. Governor Brad Little says the moves are a last-ditch effort at avoiding -- to avoid activating for the first time statewide crisis standards of care that could force medical professionals to decide who lives and who dies. Yesterday, Governor Little said there were only four adult ICU beds still available in the state of Idaho. State officials in Georgia say more residents are being diagnosed with COVID than ever before. Georgia's rolling seven-day average for positive tests rose more than 9,600 per day Tuesday. That tops the previous high from January. Meantime in Texas, the Texas law banning most abortions in the state is now in effect. Opponents have asked the U.S. Supreme Court to intervene. Fox News chief legal correspondent, anchor of "FOX NEWS @ NIGHT" Shannon Bream joins us from New York with the latest. Good evening, Shannon. Where does this request with the Supreme Court stand right now? SHANNON BREAM, FOX NEWS CHANNEL ANCHOR (on camera): Well, Brett, it's a bit of a wait and see at this point. It is true that inaction by the Supreme Court meeting it didn't issue anything in response to a request to block the law before it went into effect today means just that, it's now in effect. BREAM (voice-over): The initial request to block it went to Justice Alito. Now, that's solely based on geography. He can decide this alone or refer to the full court. He did ask the opposing side to file a response to the emergency request. They did that yesterday, along with a final reply by the abortion clinics and groups seeking to block the law. So, those of us who watch the court thought, hey, there's a good chance we get an order or decision before midnight last night. Both sides of the abortion debate are now standing by. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: What we're seeing in Texas is frankly, chaos. Patients are scared. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: We've already seen an uptick in the number of pregnant women seeking assistance going to pregnancy resource centers because abortion clinics in Texas have announced that they can no longer offer abortions after six weeks. (END VIDEO CLIP) BREAM (on camera): So, just because it didn't happen -- I was getting something for the Supreme Court, doesn't mean we might not still get something from them, Bret. I'm glued to my phone. BAIER: Yes. You know, obviously, it's controversial, but what are the critic's main objects -- objections to this bill? And really, what are the odds it survives legal scrutiny? BREAM: Yes, well, it bans most abortions in Texas after six weeks. But it's this enforcement mechanism that is getting the real attention because it allows average private citizens to sue abortion providers or those who assist in an illegal abortion, they can recover a minimum of $10,000 in damages plus their attorney's fees. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) UNIDENTIFIED MALE: Private citizens enforce the law. The government has no role in enforcing it. So basically, every Texas citizen is now a private attorney general. (END VIDEO CLIP) BREAM: President Biden now says that the law he thinks is blatantly violating the constitution. And he calls this private citizen component of it, outrageous. It's definitely unique. So, we'll see how it stands up under scrutiny. BAIER: Yes, a lot of pro-life groups have been planning different aspects of this. How does this fit in with that strategy, number of red states making a run at overturning Roe v. Wade? BREAM: Yes, over the last couple of years, a number of states have passed laws that many elected officials are openly saying or specifically about trying to overturn Roe v. Wade. Nearly all of them immediately entangled in legal proceedings. BREAM (voice-over): And now everyone is watching and waiting for this case over Mississippi's law to be argued at the Supreme Court this fall. That law bans nearly all abortions in the state after 15 weeks. And no matter how the case is decided, it's likely that the underlying issue for the most part is going to revert to the states. BREAM (on camera): Many of them already passed laws saying that the right to abortion is secured. Now, others have these so-called, trigger laws. Meaning, if the actual underpinning of Roe v. Wade is overturned, there will be no right to an abortion in those states. This court, as we know, under the guidance of Chief Justice John Roberts has been reticent to issue, big sweeping decisions. I'd expect most likely whatever comes down from that Mississippi case could be very narrow. Bret. BAIER: We will see if you get a ruling before "FOX NEWS @ NIGHT". See you then. BREAM: We'll let you know. BAIER: "BREAKING TONIGHT", a manhunt has concluded in North Carolina after a student was killed in a shooting at a high school in Winston Salem. The Forsyth County Sheriff's Office just tweeting the shooting occurred around noon at Mount Tabor High School. The sheriff says the suspect is now in custody. Up next we go live to Louisiana to check on the devastation from Hurricane Ida. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) UNIDENTIFIED MALE: Absolutely the worst storm I've ever seen. I hope I don't see another one. Not like this. South Louisiana in a whole is destroyed. (END VIDEO CLIP) (COMMERCIAL BREAK) BAIER: The remnants of Hurricane Ida are causing problems in the East tonight. 20 homes knocked off their foundations in Western Virginia. Heavy rain pouring down from the central Appalachians to New England. Meanwhile, the devastation is keeping many people in Louisiana from returning to their homes and huge numbers are still without power tonight. President Biden will travel to the region on Friday. Senior correspondent Mike Tobin is in Metairie, Louisiana tonight. Good evening, Mike. MIKE TOBIN, FOX NEWS CHANNEL SENIOR CORRESPONDENT (on camera): Good evening, Bret. That food distribution point is one of 17 operated by the National Guard in eight different parishes across Louisiana. At last tally, the guard had given out almost a quarter-million meals ready to eat, 300,000 boxes of water, and almost 20,000 Tarbes (PH). This, as the Gulf Coast is on the long hot miserable road back to normal. TOBIN (voice-over): Countless communities along the Gulf Coast and further inland face days, weeks, and months of rebuilding. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) UNIDENTIFIED MALE: Coming to a third world country, no water, no gas, no lights. TOBIN: On the barrier island of Grand Isle, around half the homes were destroyed by Hurricane Ida. SCOOTER RESWEBER, POLICE CHIEF, GRAND ISLE, LOUISIANA: In my neighborhood, I lost my home. My grandson lost his home. I have a deputy had lost his home. TOBIN: In New Orleans, officials know they are in a race to restore services to the half of the population that decided not to evacuate. LATOYA CANTRELL , MAYOR OF NEW ORLEANS, LOUISIANA: Primary objectives today are getting our people what they need. We know they need food, water, cool air. TOBIN: With paramedics, firefighters, and EMT responding to call volumes 185 percent above normal, the dusk to dawn curfew began yesterday will remain in place until further notice. SHAUN FERGUSON, POLICE CHIEF, NEW ORLEANS: So, it is totally unsafe. And I would like to encourage each and everyone to please remain calm and vigilant. TOBIN: But progress is happening. A small number of residents finally getting power turned back on. DEANNA RODRIGUEZ, PRESIDENT, ENTERGY, NEW ORLEANS: Lights came on around 1:02 a.m. And this is the first step, again, in returning to normal. TOBIN: Shortages continued throughout the regions. Even for blood, this donation center in Baton Rouge has less than a day supply in the shelves and some transfusions have already been delayed. ALEX COHEN, PLASMA DONOR: Well, everybody has got to do their part. I mean, these tough times right now. TOBIN: And help from across America is also ramping up fast. Donations are piling up in places like Atlantic Beach, North Carolina where locals know exactly what folks further south are going through. CASEY, ARTHUR, DEPUTY CHIEF, ATLANTIC BEACH FIRE DEPARTMENT: I know how I felt when we started receiving items after Hurricane Isabel. It really meant a lot to me to just see that people cared and that we were not alone in the situation. (END VIDEO CLIP) TOBIN (on camera): Sheriff Marlin Gusman of Orleans Parish tells me, 55 people have been arrested since the storm, most of them for looting or vandalism. But there was a taskforce of guardsmen, sheriff's deputies, and metro police out in the street. And they learn from the mistakes that lead to chaos after Katrina. Bret, back to you. BAIER: Mike Tobin, live in Louisiana. Mike, thanks. We're getting a new look tonight at the damage left behind from Hurricane Ida. This look from the sky. Senior correspondent Casey Stegall is in Baton Rouge tonight. Good evening, Casey. CASEY STEGALL, FOX NEWS CORRESPONDENT: Bret, good evening. We spent the better part of the day up in a Blackhawk helicopter with the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers , and the purpose of the mission was really twofold, to give the top brass of the Corps of Engineers an up close and personal look at the damage, but also to survey the levee system, for example, and get better sense of what specific communities need to help speed up their recovery. Like in LaPlace, they now plan on cutting some of the levees to allow standing water to drain back into Lake Pontchartrain. South of New Orleans in Lafitte they have decided to bring in additional pumps and let gravity pull the water back into the gulf. But one thing is clear -- when you see the damage by the air, it is sobering, because you see stretches of hundreds and hundreds of miles that look like they have been wiped off the map along the southeast Louisiana coast. Row after row of home and businesses blown apart, boats in streets, nearly every power or communication line down and crumbled. It really puts it into perspective and the scope of this disaster, Bret, and that the rover will take weeks, if not months or even years for some people. Back to you. BAIER: Quite a view. Casey Stegall in Baton Rouge. Casey, thanks. Another disaster is growing worse out west. A massive wildfire is threatening thousands of structures in South Lake Tahoe. And that's where we find national correspondent William La Jeunesse tonight. (BEGIN VIDEO TAPE) UNIDENTIFIED MALE: Oh, yes. We don't want to go any further. WILLIAM LA JEUNESSE, FOX NEWS NATIONAL CORRESPONDENT: High winds, a record drought. The Caldor fire turning this California playground into a ghost town. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: So I promised my kid I would be out of here as soon as I saw any flames anywhere. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: I'm hoping at some point I can just nab that cat and be out of here like a shot. LA JEUNESSE: And 53,000 forced to evacuate, some now sheltering in tents, others fill California and Nevada hotels. JIM DUDLEY, METEOROLOGIST: We are in red flag conditions. And those red flag conditions are for low relative humidity and strong gusty winds, especially up over the ridges. LA JEUNESSE: Over the past 18 days, the Caldor fire burned more than 300 square miles and 544 homes. Moving west to east, firefighters struggle to keep it south of the homes and businesses around Lake Tahoe. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: I'm getting out as soon as I secure this area, which is my business. As soon as I secure it, I'm getting out of here. LA JEUNESSE: Tahoe is America's largest alpine lake, pristine waters surrounded by pines, clean mountain air now a billowing blanket of ash stretching hundreds of miles. DAVE LAUCHNER, SACRAMENTO FIRE DEPARTMENT: Basically, a flame or an ember lands on the dry brush, and it ignites. It's not stopping it. LA JEUNESSE: Torching pine needles in an overgrown forest that hasn't burned in decades, add in 40 mile-per-hour winds, you get this. STEVE VOLLMER, FIRE BEHAVIOR ANALYST: They create what's called an active crown fire run where the fire actually goes from treetop to treetop. When it does that, those ember casts that it throws out are going over a mile in distance. LA JEUNESSE: Containment lines held overnight, giving crews optimism the fire could spare the Tahoe Basin. STEVE SISOLAK , (D) NEVADA GOVERNOR: We are usually all of our resources, everything we have at our disposal, coordinating closely with CalFire. (END VIDEO TAPE) LA JEUNESSE: So winds are expected to improve tonight and tomorrow, but big picture, California has a problem. Six of the states' seven largest fires ever have burned in the last 12 months. And southern California's Santa Ana fire season is just starting, Bret, which is one reason why every national forest in California is closed for the next two weeks. BAIER: La Jeunesse live in South Lake Tahoe. William, thanks. Up next, where are all the refugees from Afghanistan going? We'll take you to one of the processing centers next. (COMMERCIAL BREAK) BAIER: Refugees from Afghanistan are passing through the massive U.S. military complex in Germany tonight. Senior foreign affairs correspondent Greg Palkot reports from Ramstein Air Base. (BEGIN VIDEO TAPE) GREG PALKOT, FOX NEWS SENIOR FOREIGN AFFAIRS CORRESPONDENT: The flights out of Kabul might be finished, but the evacuation of Afghan refugees continues through the major transit hub of Ramstein Air Base in Germany. Some 15,000 are now here, grateful to be out of the clutches of the Taliban , but, in the wake of the U.S. withdrawal, concerned about those left behind. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: We have history with the Taliban . We saw them once before. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: My whole family are there, and I'm worried about them a lot. PALKOT: You are looking at what has been the workhorse of this Afghanistan evacuation, massive C-17 cargo plane. On average it's been bringing out something like 450 people, one flight in the early days brought out over 800. In the latest 12 hour period, 1,800 people have come from other bases. After being checked out, they fly to the States on chartered commercial flights. CAPT. JAMES DIMMICK, 8TH AIRLIFT SQUADRON: It's been pretty much nonstop. We have been running 24 hours every day of the week so far, just getting as many people in and out of here as we possibly can. PALKOT: Have you ever handled this size of operation with so many moving parts? DIMMICK: I've never seen anything like this in my entire life. PALKOT: And like the service members injured in last week's terror attack, some come back in bad shape. That's when the military turns C-17s into intensive care units. On board one mission to Kabul, Major Joshua Thomas, he says they handle it all. MAJ. JOSHUA THOMAS, 10TH EAEF, RAMSTEIN AIR BASE: From battle injuries, blast injuries, gunshot wounds, just regular medical illnesses. PALKOT: This week basically marks the end of the U.S. war in Afghanistan. Some at Ramstein has been through it all. Despite the debate, service members are convinced they are doing the right thing. Was it all worth it? LT. COL. ELIZABETH DWYER, CRITICAL CARE PHYSICIAN: Absolutely. PALKOT: All worth it. Saving lives? DWYER: That's what we do. (END VIDEO TAPE) PALKOT: Saving lives, that's what we do. One officer at the base told us their part of the mission could go on for days, a lot of lives hanging in the balance. Bret? BAIER: Greg Palkot in Germany. Greg, thanks. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) JOE LIEBERMAN, FORMER CONNECTICUT SENATOR: I'm disappointed and I think we're all going to pay for it, first of all, the people of Afghanistan. But we, too, because there's no question, notwithstanding all the sweet talk from some of the Taliban leaders, that's not who they are. They are a radical Islamist terrorist group, and they're going to welcome other radical Islamist terrorist groups to Afghanistan who will aim to strike us from there as Al-Qaeda did on 9/11. It's just tragic and totally unnecessary. (END VIDEO CLIP) BAIER: Former Democratic vice presidential nominee, former Senator Joe Lieberman, talking about the situation now in Afghanistan. Let's bring in our panel, Mollie Hemingway, senior editor at "The Federalist," Leslie Marshall, Democratic strategist, and Bill McGurn, columnist for "The Wall Street Journal." Bill, let me start with you. Your thought? "The Wall Street Journal" had a really scathing editorial today about this situation, but a lot of lawmakers up on Capitol Hill on both sides of the aisle have been very critical of this administration messaging and action. BILL MCGURN, COLUMNIST, "THE WALL STREET JOURNAL": Yes, I think it's not just the messaging. It's the reality. We've just surrendered 9/11 forever to the Islamic jihadists. It is now a double victory celebration for them. First, the original Al-Qaeda strike on America, and second the Taliban victory that we see right now in Kabul. It just seems to me we are back to that pre-9/11 thinking. Remember when people used to say Al-Qaeda was at war with us long before we were at war with Al-Qaeda. And I think Joe Biden 's spin that somehow the world watches the spectacle of us leaving fellow Americans behind enemy lines and concludes that America has greater resolve and greater capabilities going forward is just farcical. BAIER: And Leslie, the State Department conceding today that most of the SIVs, most of the Afghans who helped the U.S. in the war, actually did not get out, and the numbers are pretty staggering. Here is the State Department on the safe passage that they are trying to coordinate right now. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) VICTORIA NULAND, UNDER SECRETARY OF STATE: We are looking at all possible options, air routes, land routes, to continue to find ways for them to help evacuate. And to support them in that, we're trying to ascertain who precisely still wants to leave, who their dependent family members are, what routes may or may not feel comfortable to them. NED PRICE, STATE DEPARTMENT SPOKESMAN: Half the world's countries, all of the most important stakeholders have signed on to the idea that the Taliban must uphold their commitments of safe passage. (END VIDEO CLIP) BAIER: It's just tough to believe that that's going to be smooth sailing with the Taliban knowing their history, Leslie. LESLIE MARSHALL, DEMOCRATIC STRATEGIST: Well, if we just look at what is happening with the Taliban , Bret, I think I mentioned on your podcast, the problem here is not only are they an uneducated group of men that run the Taliban , but the Taliban is used to running a terrorist organization, and running a country is very different. They could be without food in a couple of weeks. They don't have air traffic control. They have people landing right now as we speak from Qatar to try and handle that so that they can open commercial airways in two days, and hopefully more people, including those Afghans that assisted us here in the United States and abroad, can get out. Look, left and right, I have said it before, we should have started this earlier. We should not leave until everyone that we can help is out, is out. But we also do have to look at other realities. The State Department since April gave numerous warnings, over a dozen warnings to Americans to get out. In addition to that, everyone knew the Taliban was going to be in power, quite frankly. And I think it's the United States and all of our allies, especially the United States knew. The former administration, former Secretary of State Pompeo sat down with the Taliban , not with the president of Afghanistan. They knew who was going to be the new sheriff in town, sadly. So, it's messy right now. I certainly hope and pray that won't be the case going forward. And one last thing. Even though we can't trust them, Bret, no question, they need money from us and from others. And if we say we want a and then you get b, they might be apt to do it. BAIER: They also have hosted, obviously, radical Islamic terrorists, Al- Qaeda, others. They say they are fighting ISIS-K, but it's really a witches' brew there, Mollie. What about the who knew what when, and this leaked Reuters report, the transcript from this call between President Biden and the Afghan president Ghani? MOLLIE HEMINGWAY, SENIOR EDITOR, "THE FEDERALIST": Yes, we impeached a president for a phone call, and now we have this leak of phone call that President Biden had where he asked someone to lie in exchange for military support. It sounds like something that last year would have caused major problems for the previous president. I think we cannot lose sight of how we can never fight a war like this ever again. There was a Pew poll last week that showed that Americans are broadly supportive of the departure from Afghanistan. That's the Trump policy that Biden supported. They have even more agreement that the manner in which we fought this war was a failure. You don't see people talking about World War II the way we talk about this war. This war has been prosecuted poorly, according to the American people, for decades. And then there is even more agreement that the manner in which Biden departed was a complete debacle. That's not really up for debate. It was a debacle. It was a national humiliation and a disgrace. And the proper response to that is to clean out our military like we did after Bay of Pigs and make sure that people are replaced with people who know how to do their jobs. Unfortunately, the current president who was involved in this phone call is incompetent and unable to replace the military leadership who failed. And so it remains to the American people in their elections to replace him and the woke generals who cannot do basic jobs like winning wars or exiting a country. BAIER: All right, strong letter to follow. Up next, the panel on the Texas abortion law. (COMMERCIAL BREAK) (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) JEN PSAKI , WHITE HOUSE PRESS SECRETARY: The president's focus is to reiterate our deep commitment to the constitutional right, of course established by Roe v Wade nearly five decades ago, and to continue to call for the codification of Roe. (END VIDEO CLIP) BAIER: Jen Psaki following up, talking about this Texas abortion law now in effect. The president put out a statement today, says "This extreme Texas law blatantly violates the constitutional right established under Roe v. Wade and upheld as precedent for nearly half a century. Outrageously, it deputizes private citizens to bring lawsuits against anyone who they believe has helped another person get an abortion, which might even include family members, healthcare workers, front desk staff at a healthcare clinic, or strangers with no connection to the individual." And in fact, if you look at the bullet points, that is accurate. The state doesn't enforce it. Citizens can sue providers in any way involved in aiding or abetting an abortion after heartbeat is detected, and, again, six weeks here. Citizen plaintiffs are entitled to $10,000 plus legal fees if they win. We're back with the panel. Bill, this seems designed to be part of the challenge to Roe in the Supreme Court. MCGURN: Yes, it is part of -- it is a challenge, like many challenges, to the Supreme Court. But it poses a lot of legal questions on procedural ground that haven't been at the courts before. And, again, the pro-choice side is trying to get the court, that's their favorite legislature, just to dismiss it early on. They may still do it. But if they were going to do it, you would have thought it would have went into effect before today. I'm hoping -- I believe it's both a moral and constitutional victory if we get this back to the states. If we want to codify Roe, let the states do it as New York has done it. But look, the existing regime is just out of touch with the American people. The American people want limits. The Democratic Party has been able to oppose those limits because it's been done so undemocratically. I am with Justice Scalia. The Supreme Court has no business umpiring the abortion business, and they should get out of it. We would be a lot healthier, and we would return that debate to the states where it belongs. BAIER: Leslie, it seems like this administration would want to go through Congress to codify Roe, but there is no way the numbers are anywhere close to being there. MARSHALL: No, but what's really concerning here, Bret, is not only the constitutional violation of the rights of anyone with a uterus in the state of Texas, but when you just look deeper at this law, if you are a 13-year- old rape victim and you don't realize you are pregnant because you don't have a regular menstrual cycle and you come in after six weeks, you're going to be forced to carry that child. Speaking of rape, a rapist could actually sue their victim and get $10,000 if they feel that individual is trying to abort that child outside the six- week limit. And to Bill's point, you know, the American people are not looking for a six-week limit on abortion. When you look at the majority of polls out there, the majority of people in the United States support Roe v Wade, and even if they call themselves pro-life, support a woman's right to choose. Most Americans don't want, myself included, long-term abortions. Six weeks is not late term. BAIER: Mollie? HEMINGWAY: Yes, the Texas legislature passed this law that protects children who have a detectable heartbeat. And this is important that this was allowed to stand even this long because that's what Roe v Wade took away from people was the right of people to determine their own view -- what the state law should be on abortion. But the Supreme Court has a history of having had bad decisions. Roe v Wade is just one of the noteworthy bad decisions that takes an entire class of humans and dehumanizes them. And so it is incumbent upon the court to correct mistakes like that, like they did after the Dred Scott decision or Korematsu or Roe v. Wade. And they have an excellent opportunity with this case that has risen to the Supreme Court level this year with Dobbs to correct some of these problems. We have a radical abortion regime. It is violent oppression of women and their children. It is predatory, and it's just not what humans should do to each other. And we have an opportunity to allow it to come back to the states where people can set appropriate limits and protect these unborn children and their mothers. BAIER: We'll see what the court does. We'll be following it. It could happen tonight. Thanks, panel. When we come back, more of the panel with tomorrow's headlines. (COMMERCIAL BREAK) BAIER: Finally tonight, a look at tomorrow's headlines with the panel. Mollie, first to you. HEMINGWAY: Democrats continue to fight one another as they oppose the nomination by Biden of Obama's former chief of staff Rahm Emanuel to be the ambassador to Japan. BAIER: OK, we will follow that. Leslie? MARSHALL: Larry Elder, who is running in the California gubernatorial election, has a come to Jesus moment and gets out, saying talk show hosts shouldn't be running a big state in the midst of a pandemic. BAIER: I don't think that one is happening, but we are going to look into it tomorrow. All right, Bill. MCGURN: Joe Biden gives us a preview of his 9/11 speech. Despite everything you have seen with your own eyes, I have made no mistakes, and the retreat from Afghanistan was in fact the biggest American military victory since the Normandy landing. BAIER: All right, panel, thank you very much. Tomorrow on SPECIAL REPORT, we'll get the latest on the efforts to get Americans out of Afghanistan, plus, good timing, an update on the California governor recall, September 14th, Californians already voting. We will lay it all out for you and explain it. Thanks for inviting us into your home tonight. That's it for the SPECIAL REPORT, fair, balanced, and still unafraid. story_text: KATIE PAVLICH, FOX NEWS HOST (on camera): Wally, this the time after -- off the coast of Southern Ireland. He spends his time between Ireland, Britain, France, and Spain. One time he fell asleep on an iceberg and floated it back to Ireland. So -- (CROSSTALK) WILL CAIN, FOX NEWS HOST (voice-over: He got in. (INAUDIBLE) PAVLICH: Wally the walrus, good job. DANA PERINO, FOX NEWS HOST (on camera): So good. All right. That is it for us. "SPECIAL REPORT" is up next. Hi, Bret. BRET BAIER, FOX NEWS ANCHOR (on camera): A lot of animals' great today. Thank you, Dana. Good evening. Welcome to Washington. I'm Bret Baier. Breaking tonight, New York Democratic Governor Andrew Cuomo is resigning amid the enormous controversy over sexual harassment allegations. The Democrats saying today that he wants to let government -- state government get back to governing and avoid months of litigation and impeachment proceedings. Governor Cuomo said he accepts full responsibility for what he calls his misinterpreted actions, but blamed politics for his persecution. We have "FOX TEAM COVERAGE" tonight. David Lee Miller in New York City tells us how Cuomo may still have legal problems despite his resignation. And correspondent Bryan Llenas is in Albany tonight with the blockbuster details of this day. Good evening, Bryan. BRYAN LLENAS, FOX NEWS CHANNEL NATIONAL CORRESPONDENT (on camera): Bret, good evening. Governor Andrew Cuomo 's reputation in Albany is infamous. A bully and a fighter who gets his way no matter what. But tonight, facing the biggest political fight of his life. Cuomo did what few believed possible, he gave up. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) GOV. ANDREW CUOMO (D-NY): The best way I can help now is if I step aside and let government get back to governing. LLENAS (voice-over): New York Governor Andrew Cuomo resigned today amid sexual harassment allegations, criminal investigations, and a looming impeachment. In a surprise speech, the governor apologize for offending women, but at the same time denied that he ever groped anyone, while also saying he's the victim of a political witch hunt. CUOMO: The most serious allegations made against me had no credible factual basis in the report. I am a fighter. And my instinct is to fight through this controversy. Because I truly believe it is politically motivated. LLENAS: Just minutes before Cuomo resigned, his attorney, Rita Glavin leveled a blistering attack via PowerPoint against last week's state attorney general report which found the governor sexually harassed 11 women, including groping. RITA GLAVIN, ATTORNEY TO GOVERNOR ANDREW CUOMO : It failed to include witnesses whose testimony did not support the narrative. LLENAS: Glavin discredited each accuser one by one including Lindsey Boylan , the former Cuomo aide who was the first to accuse him of harassment. GLAVIN: She was out for some type of revenge against the governor's office. LLENAS: In a tweet, Boylan shot back, "From the beginning, I simply asked that the governor stop his abusive behavior. It became abundantly clear he was unable to do that, instead attacking and blaming victims until the end." The question now is whether the Democrat-controlled state assembly will still move forward with impeachment. RON KIM MEMBER, NEW YORK STATE ASSEMBLY: We will get to the truth of not just the women, but all the nursing home scandals, the book deals, everything else in between. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: Andrew Cuomo -- LLENAS: Cuomo's resignation may end a storybook political career. The son and advisor of an iconic Democratic governor, he came to the national stage as President Clinton's housing and urban development secretary and was later elected as New York's Attorney General. But he had bigger ambitions to be governor like his dad. AMERICAN CROWD: Cuomo! Cuomo! Cuomo! CUOMO: Thank you. LLENAS: In 2010, he was elected and served three terms. Today, the president said he respects Cuomo's resignation and said this about the fall of one of the Democratic Party's biggest stars. JOE BIDEN , PRESIDENT OF THE UNITED STATES: But he's done a hell of a job. And I mean, both on everything from access to voting, to infrastructure. That's why it's so sad. (END VIDEO CLIP) LLENAS: The governor will step down in 14 days. Lieutenant Governor Kathy Hochul will fill the role. She will become the first female governor of the State of New York. Bret. BAIER: Bryan, thank you. The governor's resignation may actually not end his legal jeopardy. Correspondent David Lee Miller is in New York tonight with that part of the story. Good evening, David. DAVID LEE MILLER, FOX NEWS CHANNEL CORRESPONDENT (on camera): Bret, even after his resignation takes effect. Governor Cuomo's legal problems are only likely just beginning. MILLER (voice-over): Multiple investigations on the state and federal level could result in fines, the payout of monetary damages, and even the possibility of time behind bars. Prosecutors in at least four New York counties are looking into whether Cuomo's alleged sexual harassment was criminal. One of the women, Brittany Commisso has already filed a criminal complaint in Albany County, which is the home of the state capitol. The Albany County Sheriff issued a statement soon after Cuomo went public with his planned resignation, saying in part, "Today's announcement will have no effect on our investigation. We still have a complaint and an allegation of criminal conduct. Our investigation continues." Unlike the investigation by the state attorney general that sparked Cuomo's resignation, a criminal conviction would have to meet the higher standard of guilt beyond a reasonable doubt. According to a former New York prosecutor, a possible charge of forcible touching is not a felony in New York State. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) RANDY ZELIN, FORMER NEW YORK STATE PROSECUTOR: That could be argued as unfair, as outrageous as -- how can it only be a misdemeanor? Well, again, a misdemeanor still carries up to a year in jail. It still carries up to three years of probation, and it carries a criminal record. So, let's not water down the seriousness of being convicted of a misdemeanor sex offense. MILLER: Cuomo could also face possible prison time resulting from a federal investigation into his administration's handling of COVID nursing home deaths if charged with obstruction of justice. (END VIDEO CLIP) MILLER (on camera): State investigators, meanwhile, want to know if Cuomo broke the law by using state workers and other resources to write his memoir about the pandemic. Cuomo could also be sued civilly for his alleged misdeeds, as well as being held financially accountable for civil rights violations. At least one legal expert says the greatest punishment for Andrew Cuomo is sullying his reputation. Bret. BAIER: David Lee Miller in New York. David, thanks. Let's bring in our panel early. Former Education Secretary Bill Bennett. Harold Ford, Jr., former Tennessee congressman CEO of Empowerment and Inclusion Capital. And Byron York, chief political correspondent of the Washington Examiner. Bill, for some it felt like this was a long time and it dragged on. But if you look at kind of how things evolved, how do you see this resignation today that comes 14 days from now? BILL BENNETT, FOX NEWS CHANNEL CONTRIBUTOR (on camera): Well, it's over. And I think the whole country is grateful that it's over. Republicans, Democrats, everybody, listening this soliloquy today and then last week, I thought of those immortal lines from the exorcist, for God's sakes get out. And it's time that he did, and I'm glad that he did.
