headline: President Joe Biden At U.K. Climate Summit As Approval Dives At Home; Rep. Nancy Mace (R-SC) Is Interviewed About Joe Manchin Not Ready To Support Biden Spending Plan; Supreme Court Hears Arguments On Texas Abortion Law; New Jersey Governor's Race Tightens In Home Stretch; Baldwin Eagerly Awaiting Shooting Probe Results; Attorney For "Rust" Assistant Director On Baldwin Shooting Probe; Final Push For Votes In Virginia Governor's Race
story_text: News; Domestic President Joe Biden At U.K. Climate Summit As Approval Dives At Home; Rep. Nancy Mace (R-SC) Is Interviewed About Joe Manchin Not Ready To Support Biden Spending Plan; Supreme Court Hears Arguments On Texas Abortion Law; New Jersey Governor's Race Tightens In Home Stretch; Baldwin Eagerly Awaiting Shooting Probe Results; Attorney For "Rust" Assistant Director On Baldwin Shooting Probe; Final Push For Votes In Virginia Governor's Race Martha MacCallum, Shannon Bream, Kayleigh McEnany, Guy Benson, Jonathan Hunt, Rich Edson 8,223 words 1 November 2021 Fox News Channel: The Story with Martha MacCallum HUNDD English Copyright 2021 VIQ Solutions, Inc. JOHN ROBERTS, FOX NEWS HOST: There are times to post photos on Instagram and times not to. SANDRA SMITH, FOX NEWS HOST: Maybe a little insensitive. We'll see what happens next with the investigation, John, and great to be with you as we begin a brand-new week. Thanks for joining us. I'm Sandra Smith. ROBERTS: And I'm John Roberts. We will see you again tomorrow for another episode of "AMERICA REPORTS". THE STORY with Martha starts right now. MARTHA MACCALLUM, FOX NEWS ANCHOR: Thank you, Sandra and John. Good afternoon, everybody. I'm Martha MacCallum in New York right now on THE STORY. President Biden in Glasgow as Senator Joe Manchin says that they're essentially no closer to a deal on the president's agenda. And as Democratic infighting continues, so during this trip abroad, he was asked about the large picture of all of that and the mounting issues back home by A.P. reporter, Zeke Miller, watch this. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) ZEKE MILLER, REPORTER, A.P.: You've tried to showcase that America is back, but back at home, your poll numbers have fallen, your party's nominee for governor in Virginia is facing a very tougher than expected race, your party spent months trying to negotiate the centerpiece of your Democratic - - of your domestic legislative agenda. So, why should the world, you know, believe that when you say America is back, that really it's here to stay? JOE BIDEN, PRESIDENT OF THE UNITED STATES: Because of the way they reacted. You were here. They listened. Everyone sought me out. They wanted to know what our views were and we helped lead what happened here. I didn't run to determine how well I'm going to do in the polls. I ran to make sure that I followed through on what I said I would do as President of the United States. (END VIDEO CLIP) MACCALLUM: Rough patch to be sure for President Biden, when you look at polls like these, these are brand new numbers that we just got from Marist today. Democrats and Democrat leaning independents were asked, do you think better that Democrats have a better chance of winning the presidency in 2024 if Joe Biden is the president's nominee -- party's nominee, or if it's somebody else? 44 percent said someone else. 36 percent say Joe Biden. 20 percent say they are not sure if they want it to be the current president or another nominee from the Democrat Party when they look ahead to 2024. So, let's bring in Kayleigh McEnany, former White House press secretary and co-host of "OUTNUMBERED" and Guy Benson, political editor at Town Hall, host of the "GUY BENSON SHOW" and a Fox News contributor. Great to have both of you with us today. Kayleigh, obviously, the White House is in one of those difficult phases. And you know what it feels like to stand up at the podium and have reporters sort of come after you and tell you that things aren't going well. Your thought on what you just heard from Zeke there from A.P. and from the president, from Zeke Miller. KAYLEIGH MCENANY, FOX NEWS CHANNEL ANALYST: Yes, that was a -- that was a fantastic question by Zeke Miller of A.P., well said. Factual and really tough for Biden to answer. Look, there's one thing I can say about when I stood at the podium, we never lost the support of our party, President Trump had a base that is famously very loyal even to this day. We never saw a poll like that where you had essentially more than 60 percent of the party questioning whether you should be the nominee. Now, that's one poll. But in other polls, we've seen Democrats give President Biden low marks on the direction of the country, not necessarily tied to him. But that generic right direction, wrong direction, upwards of 40 percent of Democrats saying we're heading in the wrong direction. When you have those kinds of numbers within your own party and I have not even gotten to independents who he's underwater with that very key group. But when it's within your party, that's not something we experienced in the Trump administration. It's something they're very, very real having to deal with in a -- in a practical way. MACCALLUM: Yes, absolutely. So, right track wrong track, which Kayleigh just mentioned, Guy, 71 percent say that we're on the wrong track. I went back to look at the most recent time we've seen a number like that and it was during the heat of COVID. So, as a pandemic was sweeping the entire country, it would be understandable that the country would feel like things weren't going in the right direction. And now we have that in this environment. So, what do you attribute that wrong track number to? GUY BENSON, FOX NEWS CHANNEL CONTRIBUTOR: So many different factors, Martha, and that comes from the NBC poll. I know the president said he didn't campaign to do well in the polls, but he certainly is not doing that right now. In that poll, he's underwater by double digits overall on approval. One number that I thought was very interesting in the NBC survey, Martha, was strong approve versus strong disapprove. He only has 18 percent of the country, strongly approving of his job performance. 46 percent strongly disapprove, that goes to an intensity gap as well. We'll see if that plays out, for example in Virginia. So, I understand Biden, the president, what else can you say, when your poll numbers are this bad in a given moment, saying I'm not governing for the polls. What he did say, though, was I want to do the things that I promised for the country. Well, he promised to be truthful. He promised to be competent, and he promised to unify the country. And in that exact same poll, he is failing on those metrics as well. So, I don't really know where you go from there, but it's a bit ugly for the Democratic Party. And that's why I think some partisans on that side are starting to look around and saying maybe we need to interchange some different options, looking all the way ahead to 2024? Not a great sign. MACCALLUM: Yes, that number that Guy was just referring to Kayleigh, how would you rate Joe Biden -- this is an NBC poll, I should point out on being competent and effective as president, 20 percent give him a very good rating. 42 percent give a very poor rating. And one of the things that strikes me is these are the same kinds of things that we heard voters saying during the election period that they wanted, right? They wanted calm, sort of competent, efficient leadership. And, you know, that was one of the major issues that we saw in the last election. But now we're seeing in these numbers that they're watching nine months of this presidency, and they feel a little bit at sea. They don't feel like they're getting what they wanted. MCENANY: Yes, that's exactly right. And I think the definite turning point for this presidency was Afghanistan. And when I say that, you know, some analysts say, well, foreign policy doesn't really sink into the souls of the American voter. But this did in a real way, because I think it fed into this general understanding or a general, I guess, discernment that this presidency is an incompetent presidency. Only 37 percent gave Joe Biden a four or a five on his ability to handle a crisis. I can tell you, I go all across the country, from Oregon to Washington to Virginia, twice. And Afghanistan is one of the things I hear mainly from voters, it was far bigger than just the collapse of a country. It was the general feeling of an incompetent presidency. MACCALLUM: (INAUDIBLE) quickly here if you can, you know, Americans expect efficiency. We expect stuff to be on the shelves, we don't expect there to be huge backup at the ports, you expect, you know, monetary policy to work in terms of inflation and the border and all of that. And I think there's like an unsettling feeling right now, when people say, well, you know that this is the stuff that happens in other countries, like crazy lines at the airport and all kinds of things that you can't get your arms around and stuff doesn't work. BENSON: Joe Biden basically in the campaign against Donald Trump promised normalcy, right? He ran a basement campaign, he popped up occasionally, and he stayed out of sight, out of mind and he won. Does this feel like normalcy right now? Most Americans say absolutely not. And you can't run a basement presidency as much as he might be trying. MACCALLUM: Not when there's all this stuff going on. That's for sure. Guy, thank you. Guy Benson always great to see you. Kayleigh McEnany, always great to see you. Thank you both for being here. MCENANY: Thank you. BENSON: You bet. MACCALLUM: All right, so we are getting some brand-new feedback from the White House responding to Senator Joe Manchin, who says that he cannot support this President Biden spending bill without more clarity on how it would be paid for and he says he doesn't really care about deadlines. He wants to figure out how this will be paid for in an efficient way that they can sell to the country. We're going to show you what the White House is now saying on this, which is very important on that beautiful day, beautiful fall day at the White House. So, still ahead this hour, candidate for Virginia Governor Glenn Youngkin on the eve of Election Day in Virginia as Democrat Terry McAuliffe fights to stave off the Republicans advanced. We will speak with Glenn Youngkin clearly a rising star in this Virginia race. We'll talk about how he's feeling tonight before all of this gets underway when we come back. (COMMERCIAL BREAK) MACCALLUM: Well, I guess it all depends on who you ask. Moments ago, Senator Joe Manchin said that he is "not ready to support President Biden's social spending bill" that's a paraphrase I should say. Even after the president cut the $3.5 trillion price tag in half. Just a few moments ago, Senator Manchin stepped in front of the microphone. He said he needs to know more about what this bill will do to the economy and to the national debt. Here he is in his own words. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) SEN. JOE MANCHIN (D-WV): What I see are shell games, budget gimmicks that make the real cost of the so-called $1.75 trillion bill estimated to be almost twice that amount, if the full time has run out if you extended it permanently. (END VIDEO CLIP) MACCALLUM: So, the White House says that the plan is fully paid for, costs zero, you've heard this a lot. And it will reduce the deficit. They're confident they say that Senator Manchin will end up supporting the legislation. Joining me now Republican congresswoman Nancy Mace from South Carolina. Good to have you with us this afternoon, Congresswoman. It's interesting to note that we also just heard from Congresswoman Jayapal who said that she wants to get prescription pricing and immigration sorted out in the House bill on your side of the building there. And then she said this. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) REP. PRAMILA JAYAPAL (D-WA): We'll be happy to vote both those bills, both the infrastructure bill and the Build Back Better bill through the House. And I'm hoping that can happen as soon as tomorrow or the next day. We are ready to get this transformational change to people. (END VIDEO CLIP) MACCALLUM: So, sounds like there's going to be a vote in her mind. Is that what you're hearing? REP. NANCY MACE (R-SC): We're not hearing that at all. And I think Congressman Jayapal is probably high as a kite right now. Looking at what's going on with Senator Joe Manchin where just a few moments ago, finally, we have a Democrat on the Hill calling reconciliation. MACCALLUM: What do you mean she's high as a kite right now? What do you mean? MACE: Well, they want to have additional immigration in the bill. We haven't had time to make all these modifications, amendments and edits to the spending because clearly, it's not good enough for progressives. I don't know when they're going to do that. I don't see it happening and you have this huge race tomorrow in Virginia. I doubt you're going to get moderates on board if Youngkin wins the governor's race tomorrow. This is a bellwether for the rest of the country on where the country is particularly on these kinds of very touchy issues where you have progressives and socialists against moderates, I don't think it happens. MACCALLUM: So, you know, we know that Nancy Pelosi says all the time that she's not going to bring anything to the floor unless she believes that she can get an up -- yes vote on it. And you know, we have heard Congresswoman Jayapal has been indicating, you know, since the weekend that she felt like this was moving towards a vote. So, if -- on both of the bills. So, do you think that Nancy Pelosi will go forward if she thinks she can get yeses in the House on both of those? And how good do you think your feel is for how close they are to actually having a vote? MACE: Well, I would never bet against Nancy Pelosi but twice now she's trying to bring both bills, or at least one of the bills or both bills to the floor two different times now and has failed, because the progressives and socialists cannot strike a deal with moderate Democrats. Meanwhile, Republicans are totally out in the cold on all of the above. So, seeing what Senator Manchin's comments were today, I don't see how it happens. And he's right, I mean, this is in shell game, when you start digging in the kind of spending that they're talking about, there are limitations and dates on the spinning that end. But there would be need to be additional spending maybe two or three times as much to fulfill the programs that they're talking about. So, it really is a shell game. It really is a gimmick. And finally, I'm really grateful that Senator Manchin is calling it what it is. Inflation will rise, taxes will go up on the middle class, jobs will leave the United States and now they want -- they want illegal immigrants to have mass amnesty, spending billions of dollars on that. I just -- I just it's not going to happen the way that it's going right now. MACCALLUM: So, when you just referenced the election tomorrow, the biggest races that everybody's watching is Virginia, of course and New Jersey, keeping an eye on that as well. In fact, we're going to speak to a couple of those candidates in just a few moments. But what impact you think that might have on the fortitude behind this agenda from the next day? MACE: If Glenn Youngkin wins Virginia tomorrow, then reconciliation crumbles. It is no longer on the table. I don't know how you are a moderate Democrat and support the kind of spending that they're talking about when Republicans may very well and it's looking likely will win the governor's race in a Democrat seat for the first time in over a decade. It means the Build Back Better agenda is dead. MACCALLUM: We will see. We'll watch it closely. Thank you for weighing in today. Congressman Mace, nice to see you as always. MACE: As always. MACCALLUM: So, we have a story exclusive this hour with the attorney for Dave Halls, who is the Assistant Director on Alec Baldwin's movie Rust where the tragedy happened just a short while -- short time ago. He handed the gun to Alec Baldwin, who then fired the gun and shot and killed the cinematographer on that set. So, we're going to talk to his attorney because he said some very interesting things to the investigators. And we will ask her about that right after this. Stay with us. (COMMERCIAL BREAK) MACCALLUM: The most strict abortion law in the United States faces two challenges today at the Supreme Court. The Texas law bans abortions after a heartbeat is detected usually around six weeks. It makes exceptions for medical emergencies, but not for rape or incest. The question today is not whether the law is constitutional but who has the standing to challenge that law. "FOX NEWS @ NIGHT" anchor and Chief Legal Correspondent Shannon Bream was in the courtroom today watching all of this play out as the justices asked questions and discussed and she joins us live from the Supreme Court who better to answer these questions for us. Shannon, what did you learn in there today? SHANNON BREAM, FOX NEWS CHANNEL CHIEF LEGAL CORRESPONDENT: Hi, Martha. Well, you're right, this debate today or the Texas law was much more about procedure than it was substance. But it's a huge deal that this case was fast tracked and put on the schedule today because the justices so far have declined to put that restrictive abortion law on hold, meaning, it is still in effect right now in Texas. About three hours worth of arguments today and there were two groups including the U.S. Justice Department and a group of abortion providers, they're arguing that they should be able to sue to challenge the law and shut it down. Justice Kagan seemed very skeptical of the Texas laws' unique enforcement mechanism. It allows private citizens to be the ones who go out and bring lawsuits, not state officials or law enforcement. She asked whether this is trying to go around an important precedent. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) ELENA KAGAN, ASSOCIATE JUSTICE, SUPREME COURT: And the fact that after all these many years, some geniuses came up with a way to evade the commands of that decision, as well as the command that the broader -- the even broader principle that states are not to nullify federal constitutional rights and to say, oh, we've never seen this before, so we can't do anything about it. I guess I just don't understand the argument. (END VIDEO CLIP) BREAM: The Justice Department seemed to have a tougher hurdle today. Several of the justices expressed concern about what would happen if any administration and any president decide to simply that the feds did not like a law, that the states, any state had passed, here's Justice Breyer. STEPHEN BREYER , ASSOCIATE JUSTICE, SUPREME COURT: Is it that the federal government, no matter who's in charge, without a statute, whatever party, whatever president, can just go and intervene in any case, can bring a federal case whenever they think a state law affecting private people is unconstitutional. (END VIDEO CLIP) BREAM: So, no word on when this fast track case when we could get a decision. I've expect it to be pretty quick. Now, on December 1st, a few weeks from now, that's the really big abortion case on substance. That's Mississippi's law banning most abortions after 15 weeks. It will be held and heard here. That case, the ruling is due by the end of June, which of course, Martha, puts it right in the middle of the midterm elections. MACCALLUM: Yes, fascinating. Thank you so much, Shannon Bream at the Supreme Court. So, Election Day is upon us as you have seen us talking about this or the past several weeks, and we're going to talk about the two big races that are coming tomorrow. Big one in Virginia. Big one in New Jersey. We have two of the candidates from those races here, coming up next. (COMMERCIAL BREAK) MACCALLUM: Interesting night for tomorrow night shaping up and one of the states that we're going to be watching very closely is New Jersey. Governor Phil Murphy ahead in the polls, but Republican Jack Ciattarelli may have history on his side, a Democrat governor has not won reelection in New Jersey since 1977. We invited Governor Murphy, he's been on the show before, we invited him to come back and talk to us today. We hope that he'll take advantage of that open invitation to him. But joining us right now is his Republican challenger Jack Ciattarelli who is with us today. Sir, thank you very much. It's good to have you here. You know, 24 hours away here. Where do you think this race is going? We've seen some polls that are tight. And then we see the one that's got you at 39 percent to his 50 right now, how do you see this shaping up? JACK CIATTARELLI (R), GUBERNATORIAL CANDIDATE OF NEW JERSEY: Internal polls, Martha, out of both camps has it as a dead heat. I like our positioning, we're surging. The energy momentum up and down the state as I barnstorm all 21 counties have been phenomenal. We're going to continue to do over the next 24 hours what we've done for the -- done for the past 22 months and I'm looking forward to the outcome. MACCALLUM: I know taxes has been one of the big issues. You say that Governor Murphy said basically, if taxes are your issue, we're not your state. And you know, we do hear a lot of voters saying that they think it's really expensive to live in New Jersey, which it is and taxes are the number one issue at 27 percent. But he's also tried to paint you as too conservative for New Jersey, which is obviously generally a blue state and sort of purpley at times, but he says that you're against raising the minimum wage. He says you voted against legalizing weed. He wants to loosen the gun laws, he said about you, and that you waffle on whether or not you'll even protect women's health. What do you say to that? JACK CIATTARELLI, CANDIDATE FOR NEW JERSEY GOVERNOR: Well, if it was up to Governor Murthy, Martha. We mortgage our future with unnecessary borrowing and then we all go home and get high. And he thinks that what New Jersey is all about, it's not. Property taxes is an issue, the worst business climate in the nation, particularly for small business is an issue. A bloated, inefficient state government corrupted by special interests as an issue, a lack of support for police. He's been the most anti-cop governor we've ever had. And then, of course, we want to get our public school curriculum back on track. He's made some drastic changes to the public school curriculum that is of great concern to great many parents across the state. He's the extremist. He's more extreme than Jim Florio, Jim McGreevey and John Corzine combined, and none of them were reelected. He's not going to be reelected tomorrow. MACCALLUM: It'd be interesting to watch. One of the things obviously that's such a hot topic. And we see the closures are the temporary shuttering of fire departments here in New York City. There was sort of an undercover tape done that suggested that somebody in his camp said, we won't put in vaccine mandates until right after the election. Here's what Governor Murphy's folks said about that. Listen, (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) PHIL MURPHY, NEW JERSEY GOVERNOR: We have no plans to do that, in terms of mandate. I'm not going to "commit" to something because, as I said, the virus has taken so many turns that none of us expected. It's very humbling. But we have zero, I have zero expectation that's going to happen. We just don't, at the moment, we just don't need to. (END VIDEO CLIP) MACCALLUM: What about that? CIATTARELLI: New Jersey is very scared, Martha. This guy isn't being transparent with us. It wouldn't be the first time. He wasn't transparent with us with regard to what happened in nursing homes. New Jersey leads the nation in nursing home deaths because he didn't follow the CDC advice not to send COVID-19 patients there. So it's one of the things that certainly driving the turnout and I think the energy. The fact that they feel it, Phil Murphy is not being transparent with them about what his true intentions are. I've been clear. I'm vaccinated. I promoted my vaccination. I encourage people to get vaccinated. But I'm not going to force a vaccine mandate on any adult or any child here in New Jersey. MACCALLUM: Well, it'll be interesting to see what happens tomorrow, Jack Ciattarelli, Thank you very much. Good to have you here today, sir. CIATTARELLI: Thank you, Martha. MACCALLUM: So we are also going to be joined in moments by Virginia Republican candidate for governor Glenn Youngkin, who is out storming in the barnstorming in the southwestern part of the state. Today, we'll ask him why he's focused there right now, as he looks at tomorrow's big election. But next, an exclusive that you don't want to miss with the attorney for this man, Dave Halls, he was the assistant director on the movie "Rust." He handed the gun to Alec Baldwin that killed crew member Halyna Hutchins. What his attorney wants to tell you about what happened that day when we come back. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) HILARIA BALDWIN, ALEC BALDWIN'S WIFE: You, guys -- what know what, no details. ALEC BALDWIN, ACTOR: I'm mean -- do me a favor, I'm going to ask the question. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: Well, I appreciate that he was probably very upset. BALDWIN: The guy is overwhelmed with grief. This is something that that, you know, there are incidental accidents on film sets from time to time, but nothing like this. This is a one in a trillion episode, so one in a trillion. (END VIDEO CLIP) (COMMERCIAL BREAK) MACCALLUM: Alec Baldwin making his first comments on camera about the movie set shooting that killed cinematographer Halyna Hutchins. Baldwin is also a producer of the movie "Rust" and he defended the crew. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) BALDWIN: There are incidental accidents on film sets from time to time, but nothing. This is a one trillion episode, so one in a trillion. (END VIDEO CLIP) MACCALLUM: Interesting appearance by he and his wife yesterday by him and his wife yesterday. But the LA Times reports that there were three other accidental shootings on this movie set including a woman from the props department shooting herself in the foot. In Baldwin's case, investigators say the assistant director admitted that he should have checked the gun more carefully before saying it was cold, meaning that it was safe, that it had no live rounds in it. The lawyer for assistant director Dave Halls joins me exclusively in a moment, but first to chief correspondent Jonathan Hunt reporting live from LA. Jonathan. JONATHAN HUNT, FOX NEWS CHIEF CORRESPONDENT: Martha it's perhaps not surprising that Alec Baldwin and his wife Hilaria seemed tense after they stopped on a rural road in Vermont to talk to journalists looking for Baldwin's perspective on the day he shot and killed cinematographer Halyna Hutchins on the set of the movie "Rust." (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) BALDWIN: She was my friend. She was my friend. The day I arrived in Santa Fe to start shooting, I took her to dinner with Joel, the director. We were a very, very -- excuse me. We were a very, very, you know, well-oiled crew shooting a film together and then this horrible event happened. (END VIDEO CLIP) HUNT: Now, Baldwin has described the shooting as an accident. The LA Times reported this weekend that when the gun went off, he repeatedly asked what just happened. And he told reporters in Vermont he is cooperating with investigators and in regular contact with the Santa Fe sheriff. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) BALDWIN: We're eagerly awaiting for the Sheriff's Department to tell us what their investigation has yielded. (END VIDEO CLIP) HUNT: Now the LA Times also reported what it says are heard were Halyna Hutchins last words. According to people on the set at the time she apparently said "that was no good, that was no good at all" after being hit by the bullet. The Santa Fe district attorney told us last week Alec Baldwin could yet face criminal charges. He is one of three people investigators want to question further. The others are the armorer, Hannah Gutierrez-Reed, who in a statement released by her attorney blamed lacks safety standards onset. And perhaps most critically, they want to talk to the assistant director, David Halls, once again, who investigators say when they first talked to him, admitted he did not properly check the gun before handing it to Baldwin. Martha. MACCALLUM: Jonathan, thank you very much. So, assistant director David Halls' attorney Lisa Torraco joins me now exclusively. Lisa, thank you very much for being here. Obviously, this is a very tragic situation and you heard in Jonathan's report that what we have learned from the investigation, the early discussion that Mr. Halls had with the investigators, he said that he should have checked, he should have checked that gun more thoroughly to make sure that there were no live rounds in it. Do you stand by that statement of your client? LISA TORRACO, ASSISTANT DIRECTOR DAVID HALLS' LAWYER: Well, before we start on that note, I just want to say that this tragedy is overwhelming to all of us. I mean, it's deeply saddening to my client, it's overwhelming to our community here, the film community, and our condolences go out to the Hutchins family. And I think it's extra hard for my client, because not only is he so overwhelmed with sadness, but now the target of the investigation. People are starting to point fingers at him, and it's overwhelming. MACCALLUM: Isn't it true that there had been a couple of other incidences on other sets where his oversight was questioned in other movies, and will that be relevant in this investigation? MACCALLUM: Well, let me go back to your very first question. And your first question had to do with the responsibility. Anyone to start with the fact that in the affidavits, it states that my client grabbed the gun off of a prop cart, and handed it to Baldwin. That absolutely did not happen. That absolutely did not happen. In addition to me presenting not only what Mr. Halls has told me, but we, our defense team, has interviewed witnesses and some of those witnesses that we've talked to, when we talked to them, they hadn't even been interviewed by the police yet. And those witnesses also confirm that they remember that the armorer, or armors assistant brought in the firearm, brought it on to the set. So this idea that my client grabbed the gun off of a prop cart and handed it to Mr. Baldwin, absolutely did not happen. And I think the needs to be straight right away. MACCALLUM: OK. So what you're saying is -- hold on, let me just pause on that for a second. So are you saying that Hannah Gutierrez-Reed handed the gun to him or that another assistant handed the gun to him? And if so, who handed the gun to him? TORRACO: OK. One of the problems that some of the witnesses have had is that most of the crew knew each other, but not all of the crew knew the armorers. So the armorers were relatively new to this particular crew. And both of the armorer and the assistant armorer were women in their 20s. And so some of the witnesses are getting confused whether the armorer came in or the assistant armorer. But regardless whether it was the armorer that brought the firearm on the set, or the assistant armorer that brought the firearm on set, my client did not bring the firearm -- MACCALLUM: But the point is that someone handed it to him -- did someone -- does he know who handed him the gun before he handed it to Alec Baldwin? TORRACO: Well, I think you're twisting the facts just a little bit. And let me just back up just a little bit if I may. The armorer brings the gun in. And another really important fact that we found out is that there was another member of the crew who also checked the firearm. Because when Mr. Halls gives a safety meeting, he announces to the group, we're going to, you know, there's going to be a firearm on set. Everyone has the right to inspect the firearm as soon as it comes on set before we begin to rehearse or begin to shoot. And so, there was another crew member who our team has spoken to who confirms that he also checked the firearm at the time when the armorer brought the firearm, MACCALLUM: OK. But I need to just nail something down here. Did Dave Halls hand the gun to Alec Baldwin? That's a very straightforward question. Did he hand the gun that was used and that killed Halyna Hutchins? Did he hand it to Alec Baldwin or not? TORRACO: Here's, here's what I'm trying to tell you. When I answer a question, I want to make sure that it's consistent with all of the facts. I don't want to answer a question to you and later be proven wrong. So we've tried -- that's why we haven't spoken out for over a week because I want to make sure that I've got the facts right. I have received information from crew members that the armorer handed it directly to Baldwin. And then, Baldwin put it inside where his holster would be. And then at some point, he pulled the firearm out and he wanted to adjust the holster. And then he hands the firearm to Mr. Halls, who immediately hands it right back after he's adjusted the holster. Other witnesses have said that the armorer brought the firearm in, that they checked the firearm, that my client checked the firearm. There was another crew member that checked the firearm. And that she handed it to him like a pass through. And that he then handed immediately over to Baldwin because he was between the two. So I can't tell you verbatim what happened. These people are overwhelmed by the grief and the shock. My client went through something that was such a freak accident that he's in shock. I mean, he's having a hard time sorting. MACCALLUM: You're saying he doesn't know whether or not he handed the gun to Alec Baldwin? Is that what you're telling us right now? He doesn't know if he handed it to him? TORRACO: No, of course. No, I'm not saying that. But what I'm saying is I want to put all the facts together. MACCALLUM: OK, but you're -- TORRACO: I want to deal with evidence. MACCALLUM: You said you cannot confirm that it didn't go directly from the armorer to Baldwin. So that's what -- this is a very direct question. Did your client hand the gun to Alec Baldwin right before he fired the gun and shot Halyna Hutchins? Did he hand it to him? Was he the last person to touch it before Baldwin? TORRACO: First of all, I wasn't there. MACCALLUM: No, what did he tell you. What did he tell you. TORRACO: -- what my client remembers -- MACCALLUM: -- about what happened. Did he say I handed it to Alec Baldwin? Or did he say I didn't hand it to him? TORRACO: I've explained what has happened on set. The armorer brought the firearm into the scene. The armorer is responsible to make sure the firearm is safe. The armorer opens the revolver, open surround, my client didn't load the firearm. My client didn't point the firearm at anyone and my client didn't pull the trigger. So the armorer comes in, the armorer opens the firearm, my client looks at it. And one of the other crew members also checks it. Whether or not he handed the firearm directly to Alec Baldwin at that moment, or whether the armorer handed it directly to Alec Baldwin at that moment doesn't really matter because he didn't load it. He's not response -- MACCALLUM: OK. That can be your perspective on it but, you know, what we're hearing from all these other armorers and specialists who handle weapons is that every single person in the chain of custody of the weapon has the responsibility to spin it, to look at it, to check it from Alec Baldwin, to the assistant director to the armorer. Now, you're leaving a lot of, I mean, I understand why is his attorney you're leaving, you know things as sort of open as you can as this investigation goes forward. But there's also testimony from the investigators that said that he advised them that he should have checked it. Can you confirm or deny that part of the story before I let you go? TORRACO: OK. What I can tell you is that expecting an assistant director to check a firearm is like telling the assistant director to check the camera angle, or telling the assistant director to check sound or lighting. That's not the assistant director's job. If he chooses to check the firearm because he wants to make sure make sure that everyone's safe, he can do that but that's not his responsibility. It's just like he's not the camera operator. He's not the sound operator. He's not the armorer. So that I disagree with the other reports that are coming out. And I think that this is such a tragedy. This is something that is a deviation of norm. Yes, it's awful. MACCALLUM: We got to leave it there. I hope you'll come back because, you know, we obviously have conflicting reports here. And conflicting reports about the responsibility of the assistant director, and what his duty is with regard to these weapons on the set, and why there would even be something on the set. This was not a prop gun. This was a real gun. So why that would even be allowed on the set, why any live ammo would be allowed anywhere near the set, all our questions for your client, for the assistant director on the set. So obviously we're just at the beginning of this investigation, I hope you'll come back as we move forward. Thank you very much, Lisa. Thanks for coming in. TORRACO: Thank you. MACCALLUM: Appreciate it. All right. MACCALLUM: You know, we've seen those crowds. It's pretty evident on the video when we see those crowds, but I think it's at 51% of the early vote is Democrat. And then we expect to do really well, tomorrow. You know, Virginians are coming together and this is why we see so much momentum going into tomorrow, but also the early voting is going to be, I think, surprisingly good for us. MACCALLUM: We'll see. I mean, it's fascinating to watch. Here's what Terry McAuliffe said in the closing hours here. Watch this. headline: Taliban Allows Evacuation Flight Out Of Kabul; Military Vet On Private Effort To Evac Americans; DOJ Announces Civil Suit Against Texas On Abortion; Taliban Beats Afghan Journalists Covering Protests; New Docs Shed Light On US-Funded COVID Research; GOP California Governor Candidate Attacked By Protester; Debate Over Requiring COVID Vaccine For Students; Reflecting On 9/11 Attacks 20 Years Later
story_text: SANDRA SMITH, FOX NEWS HOST: Continuing coverage of 20 years after the 9/11 attacks here on the Fox News Channel throughout the weekend on Saturday, 9/11. Thanks for joining us. I'm Sandra Smith. MARTHA MACCALLUM, FOX NEWS HOST: All right, thank you, John and Sandra. Good afternoon, everybody. I'm Martha McCallum in New York. Breaking right now on THE STORY, "cooperative and business-like," that is how the White House is describing the Taliban at this moment after the terror group allowed, gave permission for 113 Americans and others included in that group to escape the Taliban rule in Afghanistan. They're now on the ground in Doha have to be very happy when they come down those steps and hit that ground after a harrowing experience. It is stunning, but this is how the relationship is described 20 years hence, from September 11th. The Taliban 's acting Prime Minister, this man you see pictured here, who by the way, has a $10 million FBI bounty on his head for terrorist acts, and maybe holding an American hostage, just told Al Jazeera that all of those tens of thousands of Afghans who helped to start the Afghan government and who worked with the United States, he says, do not leave, come back if you have left already. He says, the bloodshed is over. So tell that to the protesters who were just fired on, and women who were beaten with those short whip devices that you see them carrying around, because they came out and demonstrated and asked for freedom in the streets of Kabul. Joining me now Foreign Correspondent Trey Yingst is in Doha where that happy flight just landed a short time ago and another one maybe on the way. Trey? TREY YINGST, FOX NEWS FOREIGN CORRESPONDENT: Martha, good afternoon. Certainly some positive news here today in Doha, 113 foreigners landing here from Afghanistan, they were given permission by the Taliban . And we are learning more about how they got here. According to a source familiar with the situation, the Qataris actually set up a safety corridor for these individuals to get to Afghanistan's biggest airport, the Hamid Karzai International Airport, and then they were able to get on that flight and fly here to Doha. Now that those individuals are here, they're going to take Corona test, they'll get some food and some rest. Once they're processed they're free to return to their home countries. We do know something about the citizens on that flight, not only Americans but also Germans, British citizens and even Ukrainians. Also today, according to the Wall Street Journal, Americans who were stuck in Northern Afghanistan in the city of Mazari Sharif, were told to come to the airport for this flight, but it's unclear how many were able to actually make the journey. That's why we may see future flights like the one earlier today, eight flights into Kabul are continuing with the UAE and Pakistan delivering aid to the country, an important development with over half of Afghanistan's population relying on international aid to survive. This does come as those protests erupted once again, in the Afghan capital of Kabul some disturbing images and reports out of Afghanistan, of journalists and women being beaten by Taliban fighters. We talked about this earlier in the week, Martha, but really, it gives you a sense of what these demonstrators and civilians are facing on the ground now that the Taliban is in control. Martha. MACCALLUM: Trey Yingst, thank you so much for your reporting from Doha this evening. Joining me now is Retired Navy SEAL Jason Redmond, 10 of his 21 years as a Navy SEAL were spent leading combat efforts in Iraq and Afghanistan? He and a group of Afghanistan war veterans have helped rescue hundreds of U.S. citizens and Afghan allies and their families in the mission that they call the Pineapple Express enormously successful for these individuals. He's joined by retired Navy SEAL Commander Dave Sears, who served in Afghanistan and in Iraq. He is highly decorated for his missions in more than 40 countries around the globe as a U.S. Navy SEAL, he's also the author of "Smarter, Not Harder." Gentlemen, it's great to have you with us. So, it feels as though over the past week and a half, we've been reporting on the fact that there has been this sort of difficult relationship between the groups and the veterans who are trying to get people out. And the White House and the State Department, the State Department was charged by the president with the job of getting people out. Now, it feels like the gears are turning a little bit on this. This is General Jack Keane a short time ago, watch this. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) GEN. JACK KEANE, FOX NEWS MILITARY CONTRIBUTOR: It looks like the White House. And DOD and the Department of State is going to put together a private public partnership with these veterans groups to access the list, put them in a central data system, which would be very comprehensive. They know the status. They know where these people are. (END VIDEO CLIP) MACCALLUM: So, Jason, you know, we pulled all of the United States military out, and groups like yours tried to fill that void. So, I think the Pineapple Express has been involved in a meeting at the White House is what we're learning. Can you tell us anything about where all this stands now? JASON REDMOND, RETIRED U.S. NAVY SEAL: Yes, Martha, absolutely and thank you for the time. Dave, good to see you again. But yes, absolutely seen senior members, Lieutenant Colonel Scott Mann was invited to meet with General Milley. And that's exactly what they talked about this private public partnership with the US and other great civilian led organizations that are out there, such as Task Force Pineapple. We're still waiting on that final word, but the bottom line is Task Force pineapple from the beginning. We, we recognize the need to work with, with our government. Right now, we are trying to do everything in our power to, you know, keep these incredible Afghan veterans in our incredible Afghan allies safe on the ground. But we need the support of our government. We're looking forward to this public private relationship. And we're looking forward to work directly with Department of State and the Department of Homeland Security to make that happen. MACCALLUM: Yes. I mean, Dave, what do you think about the fact that this is sort of coming together now, and I also -- I know, the Qataris have been very helpful. We just heard in Trey Yingst's report, what they had done to literally sort of Shepherd people from one place to another with protection around them. What do you think about the timing on all this and should it have happened sooner? DAVE SEARS, AFGHANISTAN WAR VETERAN: Yes, without a doubt, I think that, you know, the fact that Jason these guys and lots of others have stood up these organizations and effort to help the Afghan people and the U.S. citizens that are there. Just really, it's a bittersweet story. I mean, the sweet part is what they're doing, but the bitter part is that this is the role of the U.S. government , it shouldn't take private citizens to step in, or veterans to step in. You know, they can come to offer their help, but the government has the resources to do this. They're supposed to protect U.S. citizens around the globe. So, there's an obvious lack of confidence and trust in what our government's willing and capable to do right now. MACCALLUM: Yes, and no doubt the military could have done it and the void was filled. In gentlemen, we got to leave it there because we have some breaking news coming in from the department justice, but I thank you both so much for your service and for being here. Attorney General Merrick Garland speaking now at the Justice Department, this is very important, announcing a lawsuit seeking to block enforcement of the Texas abortion ban. Let's listen. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) MERRICK GARLAND, ATTORNEY GENERAL: -- view for as long as possible. Thus far, the law has had its intended effect. Because the statute makes it too risky for an abortion clinic to stay open, abortion providers have ceased providing services. This leaves women in Texas unable to exercise their constitutional rights and unable to obtain judicial review at the very moment they need it. This kind of scheme, to nullify the Constitution of the United States is one that all Americans, whatever their politics or party should fear. If it prevails, it may become a model for action in other areas, by other states, and with respect to other constitutional rights and judicial precedents, nor need one think long or hard to realize the damage that would be done to our society if states were allowed to implement laws and empower any private individual to infringe on another's constitutionally protected rights in this way. The United States has the authority and the responsibility to ensure that no state can deprive individuals of their constitutional rights through a legislative scheme, specifically designed to prevent the vindication of those rights. The United States also brings this suit to assert other Federal Interests that SB-8 unconstitutionally impairs. Among other things, SB-8 conflicts with federal law by prohibiting federal agencies from exercising their authorities and carrying out their responsibilities under federal laws relating to abortion services. It also subjects federal employees and non-governmental partners to implement those laws to civil liability and penalties. Among the federal agencies and programs whose operations the statute unconstitutionally restricts, are the Labor Department's Job Corps program, the Defense Department's TRICARE health program, the Office of Refugee Resettlement , the Bureau of Prisons, the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services , and the Office of Personnel Management. The complaint therefore seeks a declaratory judgment that SB-8 is invalid under the supremacy clause, and the 14th amendment is pre-empted by federal law and violates the doctrine of inter-governmental immunity. The United States also seeks a permanent and preliminary injunction prohibiting enforcement of the statute against the state of Texas including against the state's officers, employees and agents and private parties it has effectively deputized who would bring suit under SB-8. The Department of Justice has a duty to defend the Constitution of the United States, and to uphold the rule of law. Today, we fulfill that duty by filing the lawsuit I have just described. Now, before I take some questions, I want to say a few words to the American people on the eve of the 20th anniversary of the attacks of September 11th, 2001. That day, is seared into all of our memories. Nothing we can do or say, can replace the loss so many endured that day. Nothing can change the profound way the events of September 11th altered us individually and collectively, as a nation. And let there be no doubt the threat from terrorists, from foreign terrorists, like those involved in the September 11 attack is one we must constantly guard against. But what we can do, and what we have done is learn from the past to better anticipate and prepare for the next threat and to seek to disrupt it. As we mark this anniversary, we rededicate ourselves at the Justice Department, to doing all we can to protect the American people from terrorism in all its forms, whether originating from abroad or at home, and to doing so in a manner that is consistent with our values and the rule of law. With that, I'm happy to take questions. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: Attorney General Garland, is there, is there a provision in the Texas law that you personally find especially concerning?
