story_text: SANDRA SMITH, FOX NEWS HOST: Continuing coverage of 20 years after the 9/11 attacks here on the Fox News Channel throughout the weekend on Saturday, 9/11. Thanks for joining us. I'm Sandra Smith. MARTHA MACCALLUM, FOX NEWS HOST: All right, thank you, John and Sandra. Good afternoon, everybody. I'm Martha McCallum in New York. Breaking right now on THE STORY, "cooperative and business-like," that is how the White House is describing the Taliban at this moment after the terror group allowed, gave permission for 113 Americans and others included in that group to escape the Taliban rule in Afghanistan. They're now on the ground in Doha have to be very happy when they come down those steps and hit that ground after a harrowing experience. It is stunning, but this is how the relationship is described 20 years hence, from September 11th. The Taliban 's acting Prime Minister, this man you see pictured here, who by the way, has a $10 million FBI bounty on his head for terrorist acts, and maybe holding an American hostage, just told Al Jazeera that all of those tens of thousands of Afghans who helped to start the Afghan government and who worked with the United States, he says, do not leave, come back if you have left already. He says, the bloodshed is over. So tell that to the protesters who were just fired on, and women who were beaten with those short whip devices that you see them carrying around, because they came out and demonstrated and asked for freedom in the streets of Kabul. Joining me now Foreign Correspondent Trey Yingst is in Doha where that happy flight just landed a short time ago and another one maybe on the way. Trey? TREY YINGST, FOX NEWS FOREIGN CORRESPONDENT: Martha, good afternoon. Certainly some positive news here today in Doha, 113 foreigners landing here from Afghanistan, they were given permission by the Taliban . And we are learning more about how they got here. According to a source familiar with the situation, the Qataris actually set up a safety corridor for these individuals to get to Afghanistan's biggest airport, the Hamid Karzai International Airport, and then they were able to get on that flight and fly here to Doha. Now that those individuals are here, they're going to take Corona test, they'll get some food and some rest. Once they're processed they're free to return to their home countries. We do know something about the citizens on that flight, not only Americans but also Germans, British citizens and even Ukrainians. Also today, according to the Wall Street Journal, Americans who were stuck in Northern Afghanistan in the city of Mazari Sharif, were told to come to the airport for this flight, but it's unclear how many were able to actually make the journey. That's why we may see future flights like the one earlier today, eight flights into Kabul are continuing with the UAE and Pakistan delivering aid to the country, an important development with over half of Afghanistan's population relying on international aid to survive. This does come as those protests erupted once again, in the Afghan capital of Kabul some disturbing images and reports out of Afghanistan, of journalists and women being beaten by Taliban fighters. We talked about this earlier in the week, Martha, but really, it gives you a sense of what these demonstrators and civilians are facing on the ground now that the Taliban is in control. Martha. MACCALLUM: Trey Yingst, thank you so much for your reporting from Doha this evening. Joining me now is Retired Navy SEAL Jason Redmond, 10 of his 21 years as a Navy SEAL were spent leading combat efforts in Iraq and Afghanistan? He and a group of Afghanistan war veterans have helped rescue hundreds of U.S. citizens and Afghan allies and their families in the mission that they call the Pineapple Express enormously successful for these individuals. He's joined by retired Navy SEAL Commander Dave Sears, who served in Afghanistan and in Iraq. He is highly decorated for his missions in more than 40 countries around the globe as a U.S. Navy SEAL, he's also the author of "Smarter, Not Harder." Gentlemen, it's great to have you with us. So, it feels as though over the past week and a half, we've been reporting on the fact that there has been this sort of difficult relationship between the groups and the veterans who are trying to get people out. And the White House and the State Department, the State Department was charged by the president with the job of getting people out. Now, it feels like the gears are turning a little bit on this. This is General Jack Keane a short time ago, watch this. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) GEN. JACK KEANE, FOX NEWS MILITARY CONTRIBUTOR: It looks like the White House. And DOD and the Department of State is going to put together a private public partnership with these veterans groups to access the list, put them in a central data system, which would be very comprehensive. They know the status. They know where these people are. (END VIDEO CLIP) MACCALLUM: So, Jason, you know, we pulled all of the United States military out, and groups like yours tried to fill that void. So, I think the Pineapple Express has been involved in a meeting at the White House is what we're learning. Can you tell us anything about where all this stands now? JASON REDMOND, RETIRED U.S. NAVY SEAL: Yes, Martha, absolutely and thank you for the time. Dave, good to see you again. But yes, absolutely seen senior members, Lieutenant Colonel Scott Mann was invited to meet with General Milley. And that's exactly what they talked about this private public partnership with the US and other great civilian led organizations that are out there, such as Task Force Pineapple. We're still waiting on that final word, but the bottom line is Task Force pineapple from the beginning. We, we recognize the need to work with, with our government. Right now, we are trying to do everything in our power to, you know, keep these incredible Afghan veterans in our incredible Afghan allies safe on the ground. But we need the support of our government. We're looking forward to this public private relationship. And we're looking forward to work directly with Department of State and the Department of Homeland Security to make that happen. MACCALLUM: Yes. I mean, Dave, what do you think about the fact that this is sort of coming together now, and I also -- I know, the Qataris have been very helpful. We just heard in Trey Yingst's report, what they had done to literally sort of Shepherd people from one place to another with protection around them. What do you think about the timing on all this and should it have happened sooner? DAVE SEARS, AFGHANISTAN WAR VETERAN: Yes, without a doubt, I think that, you know, the fact that Jason these guys and lots of others have stood up these organizations and effort to help the Afghan people and the U.S. citizens that are there. Just really, it's a bittersweet story. I mean, the sweet part is what they're doing, but the bitter part is that this is the role of the U.S. government , it shouldn't take private citizens to step in, or veterans to step in. You know, they can come to offer their help, but the government has the resources to do this. They're supposed to protect U.S. citizens around the globe. So, there's an obvious lack of confidence and trust in what our government's willing and capable to do right now. MACCALLUM: Yes, and no doubt the military could have done it and the void was filled. In gentlemen, we got to leave it there because we have some breaking news coming in from the department justice, but I thank you both so much for your service and for being here. Attorney General Merrick Garland speaking now at the Justice Department, this is very important, announcing a lawsuit seeking to block enforcement of the Texas abortion ban. Let's listen. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) MERRICK GARLAND, ATTORNEY GENERAL: -- view for as long as possible. Thus far, the law has had its intended effect. Because the statute makes it too risky for an abortion clinic to stay open, abortion providers have ceased providing services. This leaves women in Texas unable to exercise their constitutional rights and unable to obtain judicial review at the very moment they need it. This kind of scheme, to nullify the Constitution of the United States is one that all Americans, whatever their politics or party should fear. If it prevails, it may become a model for action in other areas, by other states, and with respect to other constitutional rights and judicial precedents, nor need one think long or hard to realize the damage that would be done to our society if states were allowed to implement laws and empower any private individual to infringe on another's constitutionally protected rights in this way. The United States has the authority and the responsibility to ensure that no state can deprive individuals of their constitutional rights through a legislative scheme, specifically designed to prevent the vindication of those rights. The United States also brings this suit to assert other Federal Interests that SB-8 unconstitutionally impairs. Among other things, SB-8 conflicts with federal law by prohibiting federal agencies from exercising their authorities and carrying out their responsibilities under federal laws relating to abortion services. It also subjects federal employees and non-governmental partners to implement those laws to civil liability and penalties. Among the federal agencies and programs whose operations the statute unconstitutionally restricts, are the Labor Department's Job Corps program, the Defense Department's TRICARE health program, the Office of Refugee Resettlement , the Bureau of Prisons, the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services , and the Office of Personnel Management. The complaint therefore seeks a declaratory judgment that SB-8 is invalid under the supremacy clause, and the 14th amendment is pre-empted by federal law and violates the doctrine of inter-governmental immunity. The United States also seeks a permanent and preliminary injunction prohibiting enforcement of the statute against the state of Texas including against the state's officers, employees and agents and private parties it has effectively deputized who would bring suit under SB-8. The Department of Justice has a duty to defend the Constitution of the United States, and to uphold the rule of law. Today, we fulfill that duty by filing the lawsuit I have just described. Now, before I take some questions, I want to say a few words to the American people on the eve of the 20th anniversary of the attacks of September 11th, 2001. That day, is seared into all of our memories. Nothing we can do or say, can replace the loss so many endured that day. Nothing can change the profound way the events of September 11th altered us individually and collectively, as a nation. And let there be no doubt the threat from terrorists, from foreign terrorists, like those involved in the September 11 attack is one we must constantly guard against. But what we can do, and what we have done is learn from the past to better anticipate and prepare for the next threat and to seek to disrupt it. As we mark this anniversary, we rededicate ourselves at the Justice Department, to doing all we can to protect the American people from terrorism in all its forms, whether originating from abroad or at home, and to doing so in a manner that is consistent with our values and the rule of law. With that, I'm happy to take questions. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: Attorney General Garland, is there, is there a provision in the Texas law that you personally find especially concerning? GARLAND: I think I've described all the provisions that I find especially concerning and this and the complaint does that in even more detail, so I wouldn't pick anyone. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: So, there's been several GOP lawmakers who said that they will follow Texas's lead. And I was wondering if you expect DOJ to be involved in similar actions against other states? Like would it would it be a leap to say that this is, this could be one of several similar actions? GARLAND: Well, as I said in my remarks, the risk here, the greater risk here, the additional and further risk here is that other states will follow similar models with respect not only to this constitutional right, but theoretically against any constitutional right and in any other state. So, if another state uses the same kind of provisions to deprive its citizens of their constitutional rights, and in particular, to deprive their citizens of the ability to seek immediate review, we will bring the same kind of lawsuit. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: So, there have been some pressure themes from Democratic lawmakers on the hill. And if you've worked in groups, and even some could argue from the White House on, on the Department of Justice to do something about this Texas law. Did you feel any of that pressure? Is that any did that play any role in this? GARLAND: The Department of Justice does not file lawsuits based on pressure? We carefully evaluated the law and the facts, and this complaint expresses our view about the law and the facts. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: Thanks, everybody. GARLAND: Thank you. (END VIDEO CLIP) MACCALLUM: All right, the Attorney General Merrick Garland, taking some questions there and laying out the suit that the Department of Justice is bringing against Texas for the bill known as SB-8, which limits abortion to prior to the period when a heartbeat is detected. Let's bring in Fox News Contributor Jonathan Turley, Constitutional Attorney, of course, and he's been watching this along with us. Jonathan, great to have you with us to respond to this. Essentially, he said, you know that this bill means that a woman can't exercise her constitutional right. We can't stand by for anything that undermines the Constitution and also he touched on the empowerment of private individuals in this case to bring, to bring suits against individuals who are receiving abortions or involved in abortions. He said you cannot empower private individuals to impinge on the constitutional rights of others. How does this case look to you the way it's been laid out? JONATHAN TURLEY, FOX NEWS CONTRIBUTOR: Well, it's hard to unpack all this because there's aspects of this that are quite breathtaking. I mean, the, among other things, he challenges the use of private attorney generals, but the type of citizen lawsuit that's involved in tend to take says abortion law, that is a common provision. It is used throughout federal law to allow citizens to enforce aspects of federal law. I've brought a number of those lawsuits. So it'll be rather hard to see how you could challenge that as a concept. What really needs to be challenged is the bass violation. That is what he's really objecting to, is this pre- viability provision of the Texas law that sets it at roughly six weeks or eight weeks, depending on who you ask. A Georgia law was just struck down last year. And most of us expect that the lower courts will strike down this law, it's already being challenged in the federal courts. But what is really odd about this is that the Department of Justice is entering as a party. Usually, the term justice is an ambiguous or a friend of the court. Here, it's saying we're a party of interest. Anytime a state law threatens constitutional rights, we have skin in the game. That's not exactly how the Department Justice has operated in the past. And I think some courts are going to ask about that. You know, for example, Garland said, we're going to say that this field is partially or wholly preempted. The Supreme Court has always recognized that states have a right to legislate in the area of abortion, the question is where to draw that line? So, this is a major assertion of federal authority and perhaps an unprecedented one. Now, the problem with that is he may have just created a new point of challenge for pro-life litigants. He could have made this the situation worse with his filing, because he's added a robust federalism issue that is quite novel in a lot of courts are likely to be somewhat uncomfortable with in this degree of federal jurisdictional authority. MACCALLUM: Yes, it's very interesting. I got to go. But I just want to ask you one quick question. You know, the interpretation was that it was the, the statute was written in a novel way that made it sort of understandable that the Supreme Court would uphold it. Can you explain that to everybody briefly? TURLEY: I'm sorry, you just broke up just slightly. MACCALLUM: So, that there was a sort of a novel writing of this bill. And that because it was sort of clever is the word that was used as well, the way it was written, you could understand how the Supreme Court would uphold it, a majority of justices. TURLEY: Well, that's, that's right, because a lot of people said, including a member of Congress that the court had just overturned Roe and upheld the Texas law. That's untrue. And this press conference proves it. If the if the Supreme Court upheld the Texas law, they wouldn't be challenging it right now. But what the court really said was you, you pick two people almost at random, a state judge and a clerk. They don't have any enforcement role here. They're not named in the law. And what the court said is you can't ask us to enjoin two people at random as a way of enjoying the law. And that was the basis. The court said it was not ruling on the merits. MACCALLUM: Yes. It can be very interesting to watch this. Jonathan, thank you, as always great to have you here to break down for us, Jonathan Turley. So, Senator Tom Cotton on the brutal crackdown on those daring to oppose the Taliban takeover in the streets of Kabul. He's next. (COMMERCIAL BREAK) MACCALLUM: So, this is going to be interesting. The Senate Armed Services Committee is going to hold hearings in a week or so where the Defense Secretary General Austin, and the Chairman of the Joint Chiefs General Milley will be questioned before Congress about their handling of the Afghanistan exit. How many troops did they want? What was their idea of how it should all work? Also the general in charge on the ground there a person that American really haven't heard too much from his general Scotty Miller, he will also testify and be asked these questions. And at the same time, this question today, this is life under the Taliban , despite what they're saying their Taliban fighters opening fire on protesters in Kabul this week, and whipping women who were protesting. They were shouting freedom. They were incredibly brave in the streets of Kabul, and they were beaten for it. These images of Afghan journalists and we warn you this is graphic, they were also whipped and beaten and this is the scars of what the Taliban did to these individuals. So, Senator Tom Cotton joins us now. He's an Afghan War veteran, and he's a member of the armed services committee. Senator, good to have you with us today. Let's first deal with what the Taliban is saying and what the Taliban is doing. Because they have said, you know, everyone's going to love life under the Taliban , as long as you understand that everything will be done under Sharia law, and under the cultural tenants that we ascribe to. And in fact, you know, this is the greatest oxymoron of all, you can protest as long as we approve of what you're protesting, of what you're saying. SEN. TOM COTTON (R-AR): Yes, Martha, we shouldn't be surprised that even though Joe Biden and Tony Blinken have been saying for weeks that this is the new and improved and moderate and inclusive Taliban , that it's the same gang of terrorist savages that we saw 20 to 25 years ago, the Secretary of State said in Europe this week, that the Taliban cabinet isn't meeting the test of inclusivity, or they have very challenging histories. That's to put it mildly, Martha. I mean, the Biden administration seems to be more worried that the cabinet in Afghanistan is full of men, rather than that it's full of terrorists. Let's just consider some of their histories. I mean, the Supreme Leader, the Emir of the Taliban, is so moderate Martha, that he blessed his own son going off to kill himself as a suicide bomber years ago. That Minister of Interior in charge of security inside of Afghanistan, so probably in charge of some of those beatings of protesters, you've seen in recent days, was designated by a terrorist, the leader of the Chi Network by none other than Barack Obama, and all of the Guantanamo detainees that Barack Obama released in return for an American traitor, have now found their way back to Afghanistan are all in senior positions of responsibility in this Taliban government. So, now, I would say that it's a little bit more than a challenging history, contrary to what the Secretary of State said. MACCALLUM: Let me ask you this. Senator, you know, is, is some of this we heard the the NSC today say that they've been dealing with the Taliban in a businesslike way. We know that the President said that, you know, eventually there might he said, you know, we recognize the Taliban will that, that's a long way off was the term that was used. Is this just to get people out, is all of this nice talk and, and sort of, you know, to play along so that we can get these people out and then the tone will change? COTTON: Well, if that were the case, Martha, you wouldn't have to say some of the praising things the administration has said in recent weeks, you just have to refrain from the criticism that the Taliban so justly deserves. What trouble is even more than what they're saying is what they're potentially doing behind closed doors, things like holding out the offer of diplomatic recognition, or even more concretely, unfreezing billions of dollars in assets that the former Afghan government had around or other financial inducements that the United States working alone or through international financial institutions can offer to the Taliban . When the Congress is back in session next week. I think that we'll be probing some of those very questions. MACCALLUM: Yes, what would be what line of questioning would you take with General Milley and with General Austin and with General Miller before I let you go? COTTON: So, with the Secretary and the chairman, I'd like to know, what were their recommendations and when did they make those recommendations to the president and how did he act? Let's take one simple case that is a very easy question to answer: Why was Bagram closed? What did our military recommend and what did the President do? I find it hard to believe that Secretary Austin and General Milley recommended that we closed Bagram in response to anything other than an arbitrary and low troop cap from Joe Biden , in the period of time from when he announced his decision to when we withdrew, those are the questions we want answered. MACCALLUM: Yes. And Millie has, has said as much if you read into what he said in terms of how many people they had, and being able to guard the embassy or let go of Kabul. So, that's going to be fascinating. Senator, thank you very much. Great to have you with us today. COTTON: Thank you. MACCALLUM: You bet. So, Senator Cotton is also calling for a probe of Dr. Anthony Fauci for what he calls a Chinese lab lie in the face of the new documents that have been outed, essentially, by the intercept that contradict Dr. Fauci's denial that his agency funded any dangerous research in Wuhan. The State Department's former lead investigator under the Pompeo State Department was digging into this a long time ago, he responds to what we've just learned. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) DR. ANTHONY FAUCI , WHITE HOUSE MEDICAL ADVISOR: The NIH has not ever and does not now fund gain of function research in the Wuhan Institute. (END VIDEO CLIP) (COMMERCIAL BREAK) MACCALLUM: A bombshell new report shows the path of nearly $600,000 going to the Wuhan Institute of Virology in China for the risky bat coronavirus research that they were doing. According to documents obtained by the Intercept, is a proposal for "understanding the risk of bat coronavirus emergence from 2014 to 2019." That was filed with Dr. Fauci's National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Disease . In a moment former State Department investigator David Asher, who was on the team that was tasked with figuring out where this virus came from and investigating the Wuhan lab in the Trump administration joins us with his take. He says this is a big deal. First, to Correspondent Rich Edson at the State Department. RICH EDSON, FOX NEWS CORRESPONDENT. Hi. Good afternoon, Martha. These documents provided detailed look into how an American organization, EcoHealth Alliance used US government money to fund Coronavirus research at a lab in Wuhan, China. The publication called the Intercept sued the National Institutes of Health for these documents. Republicans on the House Energy and Commerce Committee say they've been asking for this information for months, and it took a lawsuit from a news outlet to get it. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) REP. CATHY MCMORRIS RODGERS (R-WA): We've learned that these risky research projects make a lab leak a plausible theory as to the origins of COVID-19, and that EcoHealth Alliance . (END VIDEO CLIP) EDSON: Dr. Richard Ebright, a molecular biologist at Rutgers University , says he's reviewed these documents and tells Fox News that they confirm scientists in Wuhan created coronaviruses using a gene from one with genetic information from another that created a virus that could infect human cells. And that quote, "the documents make it clear that assertions by the NIH Director Francis Collins and the NIAID Director, Anthony Fauci , that the NIH did not support gain of function research or potential pandemic pathogen enhancement at WIV, are untruthful. Still, the NIH and the White House say that they never approved research that would make viruses more dangerous to humans. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) JEN PSAKI, WHITE HOUSE PRESS SECRETARY; A body of science produced by this research demonstrates that the bad coronavirus sequences published from network, NIH-supported, were not COVID, the strain, COVID 2 strain. So what he said was correct. (END VIDEO CLIP) EDSON: Now congressional researchers say they are still pushing for more information regarding this to figure out what exactly taxpayers were funding through these grants. Back to you to. MACCALLUM: That's a good question. Thank you very much, Rich Edson. Let's bring in David Asher. As I said he led the State Department investigation under Secretary Pompeo, worked with that team into the origins of the virus. And that probe was then halted and has never continued under this White House. David, good to have you with us. You said that there are revelations in here that are a big deal now that these documents have been exposed. What's a big deal that you see in here? DAVID ASHER: Well, did you know that Dr. Shi Zhengli, the Bat Lady, that apparently was at the center of creating what we believe to be COVID-19 itself was on the payroll essentially of the NIH for years. (Inaudible) They didn't know that we were -- yes we knew we had used the funding from the NIH through this EcoHealth Alliance to contribute to their research but they even put salary for Dr. Shi herself and line items, rather senior scientists under that. So we're basically, not only training them (inaudible) technology, but we're even paying them directly part of their salary. So the communist government, which was operating a top secret classified program from at least 2016, that Secretary Pompeo unveiled the world in January of this year, at that very lab, with those very people. With the way -- they were also being paid but at the same time they are being paid by the Chinese People's Liberation Army, by the National Institutes of Health . MACCALLUM: Yes. ASHER: Pretty interesting, huh? MACCALLUM: It's very interesting. And I know that you revealed[, your group revealed that the Chinese military was also involved in this lab. So I think any, you know, you don't have to be a scientist or an investigator to say what the heck are US dollars doing in a Chinese lab that is involved with the Chinese military, and the transparency there is zero on what was going on with this. So, you know, my other question is, we just did a 90, the White House did a 90 day investigation, which I know you said was just like an evaluation, it wasn't even close to an investigation. So why did it take the Intercept to find these documents and get them out there when supposedly 90 days of investigation was going on? Where were these then? ASHER: They'd been in the government's possession the whole time. We told that the DNI that they should be asking for them, but they said they weren't intelligence. Oh, you know, it's like the intelligence that exists between your two ears is an intelligence. These are documents that the US government knew it had its possession, and there's far more data than this. We knew about these documents when I was at the State Department but they don't class -- because it's not classified intelligence, it doesn't matter, even though it comes up to some very specific revelations very quickly. You remember in 2012, there was allegedly, according to Chinese, these miners that died of a predecessor to COVID-19 identified in a mine in Southern China, in Yunnan Province called Mojiang. Six people got sick, three of them died. It's is the first case in history of bats killing human beings directly with coronavirus. If it's true, well, there's -- that effort was run by EcoHealth Alliance with NIH funding as well. There's no mention of the miners dying in the report, which is very suspicious because either it EcoHealth is covering up for the Chinese, which is sort of a cover up of the cover up, or the miners never died and this was all part of an elaborate backstory by Chinese intelligence to cover up this military program and to suck American research dollars into (inaudible). I mean, what they were doing was creating a coronavirus that could kill humans directly. Human to humans could stretch stealthily, which is in line with Chinese doctrine and war where they were trapping the United States in our own larges (inaudible). MACCALLUM: They must have loved that they were getting money from us to fund this research. And it is absolutely stunning. Dr. Fauci has a lot of questions to answer. And we hope that there'll be a forum where he can do that, under some scrutiny and soon. David Asher, we could talk all day out, but thank you very much for being here with us today on that. OK. So, our Afghanistan coverage continues with a look at how Americans see the Biden exit from Afghanistan through the lens of the 20th commemoration of September the 11th. Senior Correspondent Claudia Cowan live on this in Sausalito, California. Stunning video, Claudia. CLAUDIA COWAN, FOX NEWS CORRESPONDENT: Yes, that's right, Martha. Things are actually getting quite ugly here in the homestretch of this recall election with recall opponents now attacking the Republican frontrunner for his conservative views going so far as invoking his race. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: He's a Trump, a black Trump basically. And yes, he's a terrible person as far as everything I've heard him say. We fight for DREAMers, we fight for women, we fight for voting rights. Elder was pelted by eggs and his staff was physically assaulted by a group that included one protester wearing a gorilla mask. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) LARRY ELDER, CALIFORNIA GUBERNATORIAL CANDIDATE: I understand the frustration. Many of them are mentally ill, and they've been trained and taught that anybody who's black, who's got an R at the end of their name is a villain, is an enemy. That's what the left has done, it divided this country. (END VIDEO CLIP) COWAN: This recall election has national implications and big name democrats including now Barack Obama are lending their support to Governor Gavin Newsom's campaign. And on Monday, election eve, Newsom will hold his final campaign rally with President Biden in Long Beach. Martha. MACCALLUM: We'll be there, cover it. Thank you very much, Claudia Cowan. Also in California, the nation's second largest school district is expected to now require students 12 and older to get the COVID-19 vaccine. Board members on the LA School District set to pass the measure less than two hours from now, which could have a snowball effect across parts of the country. Let's bring in Dr. Marty Makary, Professor at Johns Hopkins University School of Public Health, Editor in Chief of Medpage Today and a Fox News Medical Contributor. Doctor, good to see you as always. Do you think this is -- this makes good sense. MARTY MAKARY, FOX NEWS MEDICAL CONTRIBUTOR: Look, Martha, I believe in child vaccinations and I believe in the COVID vaccine for young, for adolescents. But the current dose is probably too high, and the interval is probably too short. And the reason I say that is that it never made sense that we give the same dose to a heavy 50 year old man that we give to a thin 12 year old girl. And we're seeing high rates of heart inflammation and they are clustered around this second dose, not the first dose. So the first dose provides that immune protection, 100% effective in the Israeli study of kids 12 through 15. And that's the dose that I recommend now until we get better data. And also the FDA this watch this -- MACCALLUM: I just want -- everyone needs to pay attention to what you're saying here. The same dose is looked at being given to little kids and, you know, as you put it a large 50 year old men, right? And now, do we have any studies before we impose this on everyone, on the kids under 18? And you know, I think everyone should be vaccinated. You want to get all your vaccines to go to school, MMR polio, all of them, but we need to know what the right dose is. What are we doing to find out what the right dose is for these kids before we mandate them? MAKARY: I think the FDA did rush the indication approval with the emergency use authorization for kids. They did not convene their technical experts, the VRBPAC, which is the external group of advisors, were never convened for the child indication that is the 12 to 15 indication. And the first dose is so effective, that's the dose that makes sense to me and kids who don't have natural immunity. And that's the other problem with the mandate is it discounts those kids who already have immunity from circulating antibodies from prior COVID infection. MACCALLUM: Yes. So you think that people who have had COVID already, also may fall into and we haven't -- we don't have the studies done and we need to do them. We may also fall into that category that one shot is the best dosage for them. MAKARY: It appears that one shot confers pretty good immune protection and we know that with some immunization. You get a tenfold reduction in hospitalization. That's important, that's valuable. We've got outbreaks going on right now with the Delta virus in schools around the country. MACCALLUM: Absolutely. MAKARY: But when we tell those who already have immunity to get immunized, it makes no sense. MACCALLUM: Thank you, doctor. These are all really important things for people to focus on. And we need to have CDC studies and FDA work so that we know what the right dosage is. That's why there's a children's medicine aisle in, you know, at the drugstore. Because the dosage is different depending on who you are and how old you are. Doctor, thank you very much helpful information. MAKARY: Thank you. MACCALLUM: So how Americans view the Biden exit from Afghanistan through the lens of the 20th commemoration of September 11th? How does all of this shakeout in the minds and hearts of Americans? That's next. (COMMERCIAL BREAK) MACCALLUM: 20 years ago, Wall Street Journal Editorial Writer Dan Henninger watched it close range as the Twin Towers collapsed just steps away from his office building. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) DAN HENNINGER, WALL STREET JOURNAL EDITORIAL WRITER: I looked up at the sky just because it was so blue. And when I turned my head down, I said to myself, that plane is too low. And it look black back up, and I saw a gash in the side of the World Trade Center. (END VIDEO CLIP) MACCALLUM: Unbelievable. Dan Henninger is Wall Street Journal Editorial Deputy Page Editor now and Fox News Contributor. Dan, good to have you with us today. DAN HENNINGER, FOX NEWS CONTRIBUTOR: Good to be with you, Martha. MACCALLUM: You know, what an incredible story you and your colleagues tell you found a colleague's apartment in the middle of all of this, and managed to push the paper out the next morning and write about what you saw, right? HENNINGER: Yes, that's exactly right. We hardly, of course, knew what to do with ourselves if we were there at the time. But everyone had to figure out some way to get through the day. And, Martha, we're and our journalists in the Wall Street Journal found a way to publish the newspaper. Everyone who could went down to our offices in Princeton, New Jersey. Our technicians wired up about 100 computers in ours, connected it to our publishing network. And writers who've been distributed all over New York City, some in Brooklyn, some on the Upper West Side. I was in my colleague, Dorothy Rubina (ph). Rubina's apartment on the Lower East side, and I simply sat down and wrote a first hand account of what I had seen. And all the others at the Journal were doing the same thing, and we delivered a newspaper to our readers the next day. In hindsight, it was something of a miracle but the whole day seems like a fantasy in retrospect. MACCALLUM: It sure was. And it was so potent and so immediate, obviously with your experience and all of those writings in that paper won a Pulitzer Prize for the covering of what happened that day. And I'm sure you also remember a day that we have been working on remembering on our team here at "The Story." And I want to play a piece of what happened three days later when President Bush went to ground zero. Watch this. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) UNIDENTIFIED MALE: The crushed fire truck and fading bullhorn would become the President's makeshift podium. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: They go over and say they want to hear from the President. And he said, you're right, they want to hear from me. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: And I went over and asked the president, would you be willing to say something? And he said, do you think it's appropriate? I said, if you think it's appropriate, it's appropriate. Just be you, just be yourself. And he said, OK, and I went to the Secret Service agent and said, can the President stand on this thing? UNIDENTIFIED MALE: The lead Secret Service guy is going nuts. He's like, we're not doing this. He's trying to make sure the President doesn't get visible. He's rather has (inaudible) on the ground. He doesn't want him highlighted up there. MACCALLUM: Not knowing what was about to happen or why he'd been asked to test the strength of the truck. Beckwith stayed put. BOB BECKWITH, FORMER NEW YORK FIREMAN: I didn't know who called (inaudible). But says to me, somebody is coming over here. And when they -- when they come over, you help them up, and then you get down. I said, OK. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: And I noticed Beckwith was sort of looking around at everything. He wasn't paying attention to the President's movements. BECKWITH: I see the President coming around. He gets -- they will applaud him and yelling. He comes right in front of me, and he puts his arm up. I said my God, I pull him up. I turn around. I said, you OK, Mr. President? He said, yes. I started to get down. He said, where you going? I said, I was told to get down. He said, you stay right here. MACCALLUM: When you felt him, pull his arm around you. Say, no, you're going to stay up here with me while I talk, what did you think? BECKWITH: I looked up to sky and I said look at me, ma. I'm with the president. (END VIDEO CLIP) MACCALLUM: Dan, so many thoughts got through my head when I think about that day. But I also want people to understand. The country have been attacked in three different places, right, Pennsylvania, the Pentagon, downtown, how terrifying it was for those secret servicemen and women to put the President out there have him walking through that crowd. Everybody felt at that point that there was another attack coming and that it could be anywhere at any time, right? HENNINGER: Absolutely. We all felt that way. The scale of this events were just outside human understanding. The death, simultaneously, the four airplanes, two into the World Trade Center towers, one into the Pentagon. And, you know, what George Bush did then was what the country needs at a time like that, which is leadership. And he stepped in and did what you expect from the President of the United States. And he did it in a very comfortable and secure way. He seemed very comfortable in what he was doing, which had to be overwhelmingly difficult, Martha, standing down there at ground zero, amid the rubble, the death, the odor. Many of us who are down there that day, did not return for weeks and months. But President Bush stood there and what did what the nation needed at that moment, was to comment and reassure it that we would be protected and that the government would do what was needed. And it was a very, very important thing that he did three days after the event. MACCALLUM: It sure was. And the scars for all the people that were down there continue. The things that they saw what they worked through, very hard for everybody on this 20th anniversary. But look at this poll. ABC poll nearly half, 46% say the events of 9/11 changed the country for the worse. And right after 9/11, you know, there was a feeling or, you know, in the following years, that it had strengthened the country in a way as well as the tragedy. Why do you think that number is so different now, Dan? HENNINGER: Well, you know, Martha, I look back on all this with a lot of sadness. There was such tremendous solidarity in the time after 9/11. The country really came together in a beautiful way. But we forget that just a year before that, you had the contested 2000 election between President Bush, then George W. Bush and Al Gore . It was a bitter political fight. And then the seven years after that, the George W. Bush presidency was attacked relentlessly and I think the political divisions of that time have simply widened even to our day. And that's what people recognize, and so disheartened some, that more better didn't come from that tragic event. MACCALLUM: Well said, Dan Henninger, thank you. I encourage everybody to watch the whole video with Mary O'Grady and Jason Riley. It's very, very moving the experience that all of you had down there. Thank you, Dan. Thanks for being with us today. So that is "The Story" for this Thursday, but "The Story" goes on. And tomorrow, it goes on in this way. We will be down at ground zero, near ground zero tomorrow, doing the show live from there, near the 9/11 Memorial where the Twin Towers once stood. We hope you'll join us. Neil Cavuto is up next. headline: Interview With Sen. John Kennedy (R-LA); Senate Vote On Bipartisan $1.2 Trillion Spending Bill; Cheney Speaks After GOP Pulls Pick From January 6 Committee; Pentagon: Taliban Control Half Of Afghanistan Districts; Report: U.S. And Germany Reach Deal On Russian Pipeline; Senator Paul and Dr. Anthony Fauci Spar Over Research Funding; Biden Administration Walks Back Ties To Group Pushing CRT; Education Department Cites Error After Linking To Radical Group; Protests Over Biden Event On Catholic Campus; Biden Panel Considers Possible SCOTUS Changes; Major Changes To The Supreme Court Under Review
story_text: SHANNON BREAM, FOX NEWS ANCHOR (on camera): We'll see after the Speaker kick-off two of the GOP members. McCarthy saying that if he doesn't get all five, they're done. JOHN ROBERTS, FOX NEWS ANCHOR (on camera): Kamala Harris, the vice president coming out in support of what Nancy Pelosi did a short time ago. So, we'll continue to watch all of this. Thanks for joining us today on AMERICA REPORTS. I'm John Roberts. Great to have you here today. BREAM: Thank you so much. I'm Shannon Bream. We'll see you at midnight. "THE STORY" starts right now. MARTHA MACCALLUM, FOX NEWS ANCHOR (on camera): Thank you very much, guys. Good afternoon, everybody. I'm Martha MacCallum in New York. And on Capitol Hill, they're absolutely right. There's a lot still going on as a bruising battle emerges. Nancy Pelosi blows up the January 6th commission. We're going to go there in just a moment. And breaking right now, a Senate vote any moment. We will ask the question, are we going to get roads and bridges in this country? Or maybe not? This is the first step in a several -- in several steps, I should say. It's a $1.2 trillion bill. Republicans though, say all of this is a stunt because they say the bill hasn't actually even been written yet. So, they have to take a look at it in order to see whether or not they want to move it through this process. It's a big test this moment for Senator Chuck Schumer. He has been encouraging this process to move forward, he needs to carve out all 50 Democrats, some of whom wanted an even bigger bill. And then he's got to also keep in the mix 10 Republicans to vote to move this forward. So, it's on pretty tenuous ground, we're going to watch it pretty closely, because it's going to tell us a lot about how strong the majority party is right now, with all of this. There's potential for $6.6 trillion. Wrap your head around that. In new spending in the United States, both sides see that this could be very transformative, potentially, for the United States, depending on which way this goes. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) SEN. CHUCK SCHUMER (D-NY): Coming together on what will be the most profound change to help the middle class in America in generations. Its scope is almost Rooseveltian. SEN. LINDSEY GRAHAM (R-SC): I'm for infrastructure, roads, bridges, ports paid for. And not for an explosion of the size of government. (END VIDEO CLIP) MACCALLUM: Senator John Kennedy is a member of the Senate Budget Committee . So, this is very front and center on his desk right now. He joins us now. Senator, always good to have you with us. You know, I'm struck in that sound bite that Senator Schumer said that it was almost Rooseveltian, referring to the scope of the new deal and how that truly transformed the United States government . A lot of agencies and entities that didn't even exist before existed after that. But let's put this up on the screen because it's actually a lot bigger than that. The first new deal represented 5.9 percent of the U.S. GDP. This whole kit and caboodle represent almost 30 percent, $6.6 trillion of the United States' gross domestic products. Your thoughts? SEN. JOHN KENNEDY (R-LA): Well, shouldn't a new deal. This is a bad deal. Let me -- let me be clear, Martha, what we're talking about. Senator Schumer sets the agenda in the Senate. And there are two bills that he has put before us, not formula yet. One bill is an infrastructure bill. Both senators and Republicans are both are working on that. I'll come back to it. The second bill is a tax and spend orgy of bill that will cost $3-1/2 trillion. That's $3,500 billion. I don't know a single Republican that would touch that with a barge pole. Let me move back to the infrastructure bill. We're not there yet. We have unity and uncertainty. I'll tell you what I want. I want an infrastructure bill. And by infrastructure, I mean roads, bridges, ports, flood protection, clean water that is fully paid for. That we don't have to borrow money to pay for, we don't have to raise taxes to pay for. MACCALLUM: Yes. KENNEDY: Now, I want to see the bill. And if it really does that, and it's true infrastructure and not a lot of other extraneous garbage, I'll vote for it. If it's not like that, I won't. I'm not going to buy a car to get the cup holders. But that's only maybe 25 percent of this equation. The other bill, let me say it again. It is a $3.5 trillion tax and spending orgy bill that President Biden and my Democratic colleagues have come up with. It is breathtaking. And it will we will end up with $30 trillion worth of debt. MACCALLUM: Would you vote to raise the debt ceiling? We just learned that it's going to -- the ceiling will be hit in October, November. Are you on board with that or not? KENNEDY: Let me tell you, if my Democratic friends want to spend this money, like it was -- like they were sailors on shore leave, if they want to run up $30 trillion worth of debt that we've got to pay back, by the way, if they want to do this, then let them -- let them figure that out. Let them vote to raise the debt limit. That's on them. That's their responsibility. They can't -- they can't spend like sailors on shore leave, and then come to me and say, oh, by the way, you've got to raise to -- vote to raise the debt limit so we can keep spending more and more. How long would your family last if every month -- if every month you spent -- you spent more -- (CROSSTALK) MACCALLUM: That we kept them using the credit cards? Yes. KENNEDY: Yes, you give -- you spent more and more on the credit card, and every month you just paid the minimum. MACCALLUM: Yes. All right. Senator, it's always good to see you. Thank you very much. Good to have you with us. KENNEDY: Thanks, Martha. You bet. MACCALLUM: So, here with some whiteboard wisdom on all this, Karl Rove. Former George W. Bush deputy chief of staff and a Fox News contributor. Karl, always good to see you. What are your thoughts as you listen to this conversation and you hear from the senator? KARL ROVE, FOX NEWS CHANNEL CONTRIBUTOR (on camera): Well, I think there's a lot of wisdom there. I want to disagree with him on one issue, however. MACCALLUM: OK. ROVE: This is not $3.5 trillion. That's what the Congress -- congressional Democrats in the White House say, $3.5 trillion. And he's right, that's 3500 billions of dollars. The Committee for a Responsible Federal Budget, which is a respected bipartisan group, has looked at the gimmicks written in this bill so far, written in the measure so far. It's called the American Jobs Plan. And their estimate is, is that the minimum cost is between $5 trillion and $5-1/2 trillion when you get the gimmicks out of it. For example, in order to keep the cost down, they'll say we're going to set up a benefit, social -- welfare benefit, and it's only going to last eight years. Or it's going to only last five years. Or we're going to start raising the money for it now, and we'll begin it in like year three. And because we got a head start in raising the money before we actually kick the program into effect, it's only going to cost this much over the decade. But the true cost of this plan is between $5 and $5-1/2 trillion dollars. The biggest explosion of government in the history of America. MACCALLUM: Yes, it's truly mind blowing. And we've heard from Bernie Sanders and from Senator Schumer, both senators, that they see it as transformative. That they want to transform the United States economy. (CROSSTALK) ROVE: Right. MACCALLUM: And essentially be -- you know, the cradle to grave expression is somewhat hackneyed, but it literally is that. It's preschool to eldercare to make people more and more dependent on the United States government , Karl. ROVE: Right. That's right. And look, these measures appear to not be aimed at the D.D. These are universal benefits, so everybody gets them. You could get a free community college, whether your family is a millionaire or you're from a poor family. There are no work requirements, you can get all these welfare benefits without the requirement that you'd be working or seeking work. And you're right, cradle to grave. The idea here is to make so many people dependent upon government that they will constantly support and vote for the party that promises more. MACCALLUM: Yes. ROVE: And that's the -- that brought about the end of the Roman Empire, and he would bring about the end of America as we know it if we have that kind of -- I hate to say it, socialist regime in place from cradle to grave. MACCALLUM: Karl Rove, always good to see you. Thank you, Karl. ROVE: You bet. MACCALLUM: So, coming up, Senator Rand Paul joins me also here this hour on his call to investigate Anthony Fauci's comments to Congress. He believes the Department of Justice must figure out if Dr. Fauci lied before Congress. And remember this? (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) GEN. MARK MILLEY, CHAIRMAN, JOINT CHIEFS OF STAFF: I've read Mao Zedong. I've read -- I've read Karl Marx. I've read Lenin. That doesn't make me a communist. (END VIDEO CLIP) MACCALLUM: Moments ago, the new fiery defense from the chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff on concerns over wokeness and readiness, the most important part of the United States military. We'll show you what he said, coming up next. (COMMERCIAL BREAK) MACCALLUM: All right, breaking right now, Liz Cheney on Capitol Hill speaking after House Minority Leader Kevin McCarthy pulled out of this Jan 6 commission. Let's listen to this for a moment. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) REP. LIZ CHENEY (R-WY): -- who did this and ensures that it never happens again. And the American people deserve that, and that is what we are going to do. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: If you are -- do you are -- UNIDENTIFIED MALE: Do you think you can still get that nonpartisan investigation you want given that no other Republican but yourself will participate? CHENEY: I am absolutely confident that we will have a nonpartisan investigation, that it will look at the facts, that it will go wherever the facts may lead. There are three members that the minority leader proposed that the Speaker did not object to. She has objected to two members. And the rhetoric around this from the minority leader and from those two members has been disgraceful. This must be an investigation that is focused on facts. And the idea that any of this has become politicized is really unworthy of the office that we all hold and unworthy of our republic. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: Do you personally -- did you personally urge the Speaker to take this step? CHENEY: I agree with what the Speaker has done. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: And also, McCarthy, of course wants to become speaker next year. Do you think that he deserves to be Speaker in the aftermath of his actions here? CHENEY: I think that any person who would be third in line to the presidency must demonstrate a commitment to the constitution and a commitment to the rule of law. And Minority Leader McCarthy has not done that. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: Last question -- last question. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: Are there other Republicans that you or Speaker Pelosi believes should be part of this investigation? The other three you mentioned that she did not veto are not going to participate. Are there others -- Are there other colleagues you've spoken to? CHENEY: There are many Republicans. The vast majority of the Republicans, both in the House as well as across the country recognize and understand that this was an assault on our democracy and assault on our Constitution. And that there must be a fact-based investigation so that this never happens again. And we cannot allow those voices who are attempting to prevent the American people from getting the truth to prevail. And we certainly will not -- (CROSSTALK) UNIDENTIFIED MALE: Olivia, last question. Last question, Olivia. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: Doesn't this play right into Republican messaging that this committee was going to be (INAUDIBLE) from the beginning. CHENEY: Absolutely not. This committee has been focused, and I am certainly focused on ensuring that we get to the facts. And in fact, there were 35 Republicans who supported an independent bipartisan commission, which as I've said, would have been the far preferable way to go. Minority Leader McCarthy opposed that actively and aggressively and be lobbied against it in the Senate, and the Senate blocked it. We must have this select committee investigation. This is our only option left. And people must be willing to put their oath to the Constitution above partisan politics and above party. And I am absolutely committed to doing that. I'm committed to ensuring that this investigation be one that gets to the truth of what happened here on January 6th. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: Thanks, everybody. Thanks, thanks. Thank you. Thank you. Thank you. Thank you. Thank you. (END VIDEO CLIP) MACCALLUM: All right. Liz Cheney, you saw that on the steps of Capitol Hill. I want to bring Karl Rove back in for a quick reaction to what's been going on here this afternoon. Karl, your thoughts on what she just said, and, you know, what's your take on what we have seen this thing blew up, essentially, when Nancy Pelosi removed Representative Jim Banks and minority leader -- I'm sorry, Jim Jordan -- Representative Jim Jordan from this committee. ROVE: Right. Well, first of all, let me say I'm a close friend of Liza's. I'm a contributor to her campaign, I support her reelection. I agree with her that the best way to resolve this would have been an independent commission like the 9/11 Commission or the Warren Commission, both of which were above and outside of politics. Having said that, I disagree with her. I think that Speaker of the House should not have objected to leader McCarthy's recommendations for the committee. That is -- that is immediately plunged it into politics. Look, Jamie Raskin is a very smart Democrat from Maryland, who's one of our closest nominees to this committee. He objected to the 2016 certification of Donald Trump, and yet he's on the commission. And so, I don't see why she shouldn't give the same respect into the minority leader and allow him to name his five members. I'm sure if they became unconstructive in the hearings, and in the work that committee, we know about it, and they pay a political price. But I think the assumption that right from the beginning that she was going to only allow people that she agreed with, that she approved to be on the select committee was a -- was a political act that should not have been taken. MACCALLUM: Thank you, Karl. Karl Rove, good to see you today. ROVE: Thank you. MACCALLUM: So, also breaking just a short time ago, the defense secretary and Joint Chiefs chairman were pressed on whether wokeness is infiltrating the training in the United States military, where there is one united front to defend the nation. That's the way that it should be. General jack Keane is here. First to correspondent Lucas Tomlinson who was there and fills us in on what happened today. Hi, Lucas. LUCAS TOMLINSON, FOX NEWS CHANNEL PENTAGON CORRESPONDENT (on camera): Hi, Martha. When asked about critical race theory, Defense Secretary Lloyd Austin says he doesn't want the forces distracted by it. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) GEN. LLOYD AUSTIN (RET), UNITED STATES SECRETARY OF DEFENSE: The Critical race theory is not something that this department teaches, professes, embraces. We're not going to spend too much time debating the merits of this theory or any other theory. TOMLINSON (voice-over): On Afghanistan, the U.S. military's top officer painting a dire picture. The Taliban rapidly gaining ground. General Milley says the Taliban now control half of Afghanistan's 421 districts, and are putting pressure on half the country's provincial capitals. General Milley warned momentum is now with the side of the Taliban as the U.S. military withdraws, which is now more than 95 percent complete, Martha. We also learned the first Afghan interpreters would arrive soon to Fort Lee, Virginia outside Richmond. There are currently 300,000 Afghan forces battling 75,000 Taliban . Militia, the Afghan army has the capacity to defend their country but admitted the numbers don't tell the whole story in warfare. Asked about the recent books on former President Trump, General Milley would not confirm or deny if he played any role in stopping a potential coup, Milley did offer the following. MILLEY: I always personally provided the best military professional advice to President Trump previously. We take an oath, an oath to a document an oath to the Constitution of the United States, and not one time do we violate that. (END VIDEO CLIP) TOMLINSON: General Milley also said the U.S. military will remain apolitical. Martha. MACCALLUM: Lucas, thank you very much. Lucas Tomlinson. Here now, General Jack Keane, former vice chief of staff of the Army, chairman of the Institute of the -- for the Study of war, I should say, and a Fox News, senior strategic analyst. General, always good to have you with us. This is interesting, this press conference, news conference that we saw by the defense secretary and the chairman of the Joint Chiefs. It appears that they obviously they knew they were going to get some questions on this issue of woke training to the extent that it does or does not exist in our military. What did you think of their answers and their willingness to engage on that issue today? GEN. JACK KEANE (RET.), FOX NEWS SENIOR STRATEGIC ANALYST: Well, I think the secretary of defense has been pretty clear on this, during testimony and also at the press conference today. You know, it's not going to be a part of the United States military. We're not going to teach you, we're not going to embrace you, we're not going to support it. There's no policy advocating that. And that also implies that if it's going on someplace, he expects his commanders to knock it off. It's that simple. And not anybody that's been around in the military for any bit of time knows full well that for the military to be effective on the battlefield, to advance into enemy fire, despite casualties, in spite your personal fear, the only way we can do that successfully is we must have cohesion. We have to be together. Anything that divides us and separates us, we have always been against, and will always continue to be against that. MACCALLUM: Yes. KEANE: That's my sense of it. MACCALLUM: Yes. And I think that you know, everybody in every institution has to keep their mission first. And the mission is very clear for the United States military to protect the United States of America, and to do it in a unified way, not in a way that, you know, leads us to sort of be in different factions within the military and have them, you know, commenting to any extent on how they feel about that is a question, I think that's come up a lot lately. And we certainly hope that, that mission is clear and carried out for the benefit of the whole country, as I know you do. I want to ask you also about Nord Stream 2 , and this pipeline issue, because it has surfaced today that the German Chancellor Angela Merkel spoke on the phone with President Putin of Russia. And all of this happens as they -- as the United States expresses his desire on behalf of President Biden to make sure that Ukraine is protected in this arrangement that allows Russia to become so dominant in the energy supply for Europe. What do you think about where this is right now? Tell us? KEANE: Yes. Well, these responses, I think are really quite feckless that what we're trying to dress this thing up. And the fact is this is just really bad public policy that we have here. I mean, the idea that Putin during a crisis or a conflict, would not use the pipeline and the gas distribution into Europe, as economic and strategic leverage is, is an absurdity. And the fact that somehow we're going to constrain him from doing that, having given up any leverage already, it's just not reality. Listen, this is a pattern we have seen among the Europeans in the past. Time and time again, not all the time, but far too often, they will put economic and commercial gain ahead of national security. We've seen it in the nuclear deal, and an insistence on continuing to do business with Iran, ahead of all the dangers that Iran poses. That's what this is about for Merkel. She saw the commercial benefit and she wrote off the opposition to it within her own party, within her own country, in terms of what the implications were for national security. Not just for Germany, but for all of Europe, particularly Eastern Europe, and certainly for Ukraine. MACCALLUM: Yes. We know that the Ukraine President Zelensky is going to visit with President Biden on August 30th. And we can just imagine that he's going to have a lot to say to him about the lifting of sanctions that allowed this deal to go through, because it's tough to put that genie back in the bottle at this point. General, thank you very much. It's always good to see you, sir. KEANE: Yes, great talking to you, Martha. MACCALLUM: Thank you. How about these alleged shoplifters? I'd say it's pretty clear they're shoplifters, but we don't know their identity. Just casually helping themselves to pile on (INAUDIBLE). This used to happen during looting, now, it just happens on a normal day. Brazen crime caught on camera, Greg Gutfeld joins us with a special appearance here on THE STORY taking on this. Oh my, here he comes. (COMMERCIAL BREAK) MACCALLUM: This is not another brazing crime caught on camera. Police say that a man hit a New York City police officer over the head with a bottle in an unprovoked attack. It happened just before 5:00 a.m. on Sunday in Brooklyn. Police zoomed in on the body cam video to show it this is a bottle in the guy's hand. The NYPD officer says that -- the NYPD says that the officer needed stitches and staples in his head neck, but he's going to be OK. So, I guess that's all on the line of duty these days for these New York City police officers. And in California, police say that shoplifters didn't even bother to run. They just gathered up all this stuff, and then they walked out of the store carrying piles of clothes. This video was posted three days ago. It shows the incident in Granada Hills, outside Los Angeles. One officer blames Prop 47 to measure California voters passed that lowers the jail sentences for shoplifting under $950 worth of items. So, you can bet that those guys probably got about $949. Let's bring in Greg Gutfeld, our great special guest today. Host of "GUTFELD!" and co-host of "THE FIVE" Good to see you again, Greg. GREG GUTFELD, FOX NEWS CHANNEL HOST (on camera): Good to see you. MACCALLUM: So, I mean, this is the -- it looks like looting video, but it's not. It's just like a no -- there's people inside the store and there's no looting. It's just brazing. GUTFELD: And it's -- as if it's in slow motion. First, you have to understand, it's like almost impossible to steal $950 worth of merchandise from T.J. Maxx when you can buy a suit for $10. MACCALLUM: Is there any precedent for the kind of pylon that we've seen, the buses in Washington, DC that say "Retire Breyer" on the side, and now an increasing number of senators who are coming out with Elizabeth Warren comment. And they think they have a better chance at chipping away at what Roe did back in 1973, because of all of the advances and changes in science and medicine and technology. So, it seems that, that is Governor Abbott's aim and his strategy as well. But again, this court case that they're probably going to hear in the fall maybe early next year is one that will shape the contours of where this conversation goes. And pro-choice advocates are very worried because states across the country over the last couple of years have passed a number of similar measures. They almost immediately end up in court many of them are tied up there right now. MACCALLUM: Yes, Shannon, what's the likelihood, real quick, of there being another justice on the court before that case is heard? BREAM: You know, we always do this trying to bring the tea leaves. Justice Breyer, there's a lot of pressure on him. But we see when it comes from the left, look how that turned out with the late Justice Ginsburg, she dug in her heels and said there's no way I'm leaving. I tend to get the same feeling from Justice Breyer he's giving us no signals he would leave this year. MACCALLUM: Yes. BREAM: Nor is any other justice. MACCALLUM: Yes. Thanks, Shannon. BREAM: You too. MACCALLUM: So, mask hysteria hits the House. Several defiant Republicans now fighting Pelosi-backed rules that don't line up with the president's own CDC. KENNEDY: But -- (END VIDEO CLIP) PERGRAM: Under the Constitution, the House can make its own rules. Capitol attending physician Brian Monahan just reiterated the mask requirement for the House floor. PETE AGUILAR (D-CA): We're following the exact CDC guidelines which says workplaces can be unique and different based on their conditions. BRETT GIROIR, FORMER ASSISTANT SECRETARY, HEALTH AND HUMAN SERVICES: Absolutely 100 percent yes if you've been fully vaccinated. GIROIR: Incredibly small risk. And that's why the CDC came about last week and said that if you're vaccinated, it's OK to not wear a mask even in indoor spaces, even if there are other people who are unvaccinated because the risk of you transmitting is so small. And it's actually sending the wrong message to Americans. Again, we should be inspiring confidence in the vaccine. And what Americans are seeing is that Biden administration is talking the talk, but the Speaker of the House is not walking the walk. I think this is dangerous to public health, it needs to be fixed. MARTHA MACCALLUM, ANCHOR: I don't get it. I mean, they're trying to encourage everyone to get vaccinated, they should be really proud and happy to stand up and say, we as a body, we got vaccinated. And so, we want to show you how great life can be if you can take off the mask. It makes absolutely zero sense based on your first two answers to those questions, and the fact that they have been vaccinated. Here's Dr. Fauci on the misinterpretation of the mask mandate. (END VIDEO CLIP) MACCALLUM: So who should, based on that, who should still be wearing a mask, doctor? GIROIR: People who are unvaccinated if they're in public places, especially indoors, should wear a mask to protect themselves. MACCALLUM: Well, only two Republican governors in the history of New York State, Rockefeller and Pataki, and you want to add your name to that list, so we look forward to covering the campaign, Andrew, and we thank you very much for being here and hope you'll come back soon. GIULIANI: Martha, thanks a lot. Any New Yorkers that want to fight, go to NYforgiuliani.com, spelt out. Thank you, Martha. MACCALLUM: Thank you, Andrew Giuliani, joining us today. And it always plays from the position of oppressive oppression and victimhood. And I don't think Joe Rogan is wrong, that eventually it will encompass everyone and everything. I think I'd go further than Joe Rogan. It's not going to silence just single white men, it will silence anyone who dares walk outside of whatever is deemed popular and acceptable at the moment. Because I mean, look around. I mean, people of various minorities who do not control -- Senator Tim Scott has he not been essentially attempted to be canceled or slandered throughout time. So it's everyone. It's everyone who holds a point of view this currently not acceptable to popular culture. MACCALLUM: There is pushback to this beginning. And one other example that I would just point out that just came out today, Mayor Lori Lightfoot of Chicago said that she only wants to do interviews with black and brown reporters. I mean, the idea that we have a free press that everyone can ask questions, she's saying I only want to do interviews with black and brown reporters. But I think that there is some pushback. I jumped in my car and I said we're going -- I'm going to go out on blacktop and drive around to see if I can see anything. And in court, Cristhian Rivera, the man charged with Tibbetts' death has been relatively emotionless. He has headphones on the entire time because he has a translator, and he has just been looking quietly and steadily at the witnesses. Martha. MACCALLUM: Finn, thank you very much. I don't think that's relevant to this to this case. The family profoundly asks that it not be brought up. The father, Rob, has been very, very strong about that. He wants the case tried on the evidence and the murderer, if convicted, sent to jail for life. MACCALLUM: So brutal murder, and we will continue to cover it. There's a lot of angles here that needs to be needs to be presented. Before let you go, I wanted to remember Charles Grodin, who has made me laugh so many times, who passed yesterday, just a brilliant actor and writer. The "Heartbreak Kid," "Midnight Run," "Beethoven," "King Kong." We were colleagues at CNBC. We've shared an agent, the great Jim Griffin. You know, Charles and I would get together after his show. You could never tell him he was being serious. He had that Rye deadpanned as Johnny Carson just experienced. He was a wonderful icon and he had a great run. MACCALLUM: He'll be missed. And if you played that clip for about 30 seconds longer, Randi Weingarten answer to that caller who was asking her about the way they betrayed children has been. Well, I think the union has done well for communities and families across this country. And the first thing she pointed to as evidence of that was higher wages for teachers. The mask is off. The teachers union is not looking out for our children. I'm not talking about the mask wearing for COVID, but the mask that they put out in front to pretend that our children's interest was at the forefront of their priorities. It clearly is not, the last year's exposed that. MACCALLUM: Will, she got higher wages, that's for sure. Because you got $126 billion for teachers, for education across the country as part of the COVID Rescue Bill, and they didn't even have to open up to get it. I mean, it's absolutely extraordinary. They didn't even have to, you know, everything that they got vaccines. You know, they asked for rent money, and they asked to defund the police in California. CAIN: Right, because that's connected education. MACCALLUM: Incredible, incredible. Will, always good to see you. CAIN: Good to see you. MACCALLUM: We'll watch you at night and watch you this weekend. CAIN: Yes, thank you. MACCALLUM: All the time. CAIN: 7:00 tonight. MACCALLUM: We'll watch. CAIN: Thank you. MACCALLUM: Thank you very much, Will. Good to see you. So day one of the trial of a Mexican national accused of murdering Iowa college student Mollie Tibbetts, left her body in a cornfield. We're going to take you there live, it's getting underway. (COMMERCIAL BREAK) MACCALLUM: Day one of the trial of Mollie Tibbetts accused killer has just wrapped for the day. They'll be back at it 9:30 tomorrow morning. The 20- year-old went missing after going for a run in Iowa almost three years ago. Her murder so brutal prosecutors warn potential jurors that the evidence will be very graphic. Correspondent Matt Finn reporting live from the courthouse in Davenport, Iowa today. Hi, Matt. MATT FINN, CORRESPONDENT: Martha, 24-year-old Mexican national Cristhian Rivera in the country illegally is charged with first degree murder in the brutal stabbing death of Mollie Tibbetts. He has pleaded not guilty. Today in court, the state moving rather efficiently through some of its most critical witnesses including Tibbetts' boyfriend and the woman last believed to see Mollie Tibbetts alive. Dalton Jack and Mollie Tibbetts were together for about three years. They were living together at the time of her death. Jack testified today that Mollie was the love of his life. They talked about marriage. And after Dalton jack and Mollie's sudden death, he wanted to get away so he joined the army now based at Fort Bragg. The prosecution trying to prove Tibbetts' boyfriend had an airtight alibi, working construction more than 100 miles away. The defense of Cristhian Rivera trying to poke holes in the boyfriend story and getting him to testify, he previously had a temper and cheated on Mollie Tibbetts. Dalton Jack said he would not have taken a stand today unless subpoenaed because he did not want to see Mollie's alleged killer in court today. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) UNIDENTIFIED MALE: Why do you not want to be sitting in this room with that guy? With this man? DALTON JACK, MOLLIE TIBBETTS' FORMER BOYFRIEND: I wholeheartedly believe he's guilty. (END VIDEO CLIP) FINN: Also emotional testimony from Molly's occasional hairstylist believed to be the last person to see Tibbetts alive when she drove by her the night that she went missing. The hairstylist told the court today that what she did when she found out about Mollies' disappearance. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) CHRISTINA STEWART, LAST WOMAN TO SEE TIBBETTS ALIVE: My sister had sent me a text message, asking if I heard about Mollie. My heart sank because I knew that I passed her. I jumped in my car and I said we're going -- I'm going to go out on blacktop and drive around to see if I can see anything. (END VIDEO CLIP) FINN: And that woman can testify that she never saw anything related to Tibbetts. And in court, Cristhian Rivera, the man charged with Tibbetts' death has been relatively emotionless. He has headphones on the entire time because he has a translator, and he has just been looking quietly and steadily at the witnesses. Martha. MACCALLUM: Finn, thank you very much. Let's bring in Geraldo Rivera, once again, Fox News Correspondent-at-Large and Author of "The Geraldo Show" on that and one other topic that we want to get to. Geraldo, your thoughts on this case as we watch this get started here. GERALDO RIVERA, CORRESPONDENT-AT-LARGE: It's heart-wrenching what the perpetrator did to that poor girl is horrific. What, you know, the knife wounds, 7, 8, 9, 10, knife stabbing wounds to her chest. It's just, I don't know if this person did it. The evidence seems pretty powerful. The circumstances are pretty powerful. They found her blood in his trunk and so forth. It is sad that the case is becoming such a referendum on illegal immigration. I don't think that's relevant to this to this case. The family profoundly asks that it not be brought up. The father, Rob, has been very, very strong about that. He wants the case tried on the evidence and the murderer, if convicted, sent to jail for life. MACCALLUM: So brutal murder, and we will continue to cover it. There's a lot of angles here that needs to be needs to be presented. Before let you go, I wanted to remember Charles Grodin, who has made me laugh so many times, who passed yesterday, just a brilliant actor and writer. Here just a little moment of him with Johnny Carson. Quick thought on the other side. Watch this. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) CHARLES GRODIN, ACTOR: Look at you. I mean, you don't really care what I have to say, do you honestly? JOHNNY CARSON, HOST: I got to do an hour a night. I'm looking for a warm body. GRODIN: Right. CARSON: I can get seven minutes out of you. I take a bundle I go home to Malibu. (END VIDEO CLIP) MACCALLUM: Quick thought, Geraldo. RIVERA: He's so great. The "Heartbreak Kid," "Midnight Run," "Beethoven," "King Kong." We were colleagues at CNBC. We've shared an agent, the great Jim Griffin. You know, Charles and I would get together after his show. You could never tell him he was being serious. He had that Rye deadpanned as Johnny Carson just experienced. He was a wonderful icon and he had a great run. MACCALLUM: He'll be missed. Geraldo, thank you very much. That's THE STORY of this Wednesday. We'll see you see you back here tomorrow, have a great day. END Content and Programming Copyright 2021 Fox News Network, LLC.
