headline: Sen. John Barrasso (R-WY) Is Interviewed About The Impact Of Biden's Climate Executive Orders; Biden Begins To Deliver On Progressive Demands; Two FBI Agents Killed, Three Wounded In South Florida; Chicago Teachers Union Slammed For Dancing Video; Frustrated Parents Plead For In-Person Learning; Mothers Of Murder Victims On Defunding Police; Canadian Rapper Calls Out "Woke" America
story_text: JOHN ROBERTS, FOX NEWS HOST: This is -- this is what's helping keep me warm today, my big Baffin boots. Yes. SANDRA SMITH, FOX NEWS HOST: Well, you are prepared. ROBERTS: Well, I grew up in a place that's like the Arctic, so why not? SMITH: Good to be with you, John, "THE STORY" starts now. MARTHA MACCALLUM, FOX NEWS ANCHOR: Thank you, John and Sandra. Good to see you both today. Today, a short time ago, though, in Florida, we all witnessed this awful scene. The body of an FBI agent draped in the American flag, one of two agents who were killed in a bloody gun battle that was part of a raid on a home where they were investigating violent crimes against children. It was the first time in 12 years that agents, FBI agents were killed in their line of duty. And with that, good afternoon, everybody. I'm Martha McCallum and this is THE STORY. We're going to take you to the scene there in Florida shortly as we learn more about that unfolding situation today. But first, we want to turn our attention to a major change that is underway in America. Today, workers in our energy industries are wondering where the Biden White House is leading them. We've spent decades building energy independence in this country. And that has been great news for workers, and not such great news for other big energy providers like Venezuela, or Russia, or the Middle East, we're no longer reliant on them. And we were building our own enormous energy supply. That shifted the global power dynamic in a way that was not seen, really, since the advent of the automobile. But now, that is changing, as executive orders are shutting down new leases for fracking on federal lands. And as you know, the XL Pipeline is also a casualty here. So, here's what some of those workers are saying as they react to all of this. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) UNIDENTIFIED MALE: You prepare for these -- for these large projects. And when one gets the rug yanked out from under it, I mean, you have nothing for that year, or you're going to have nothing for the next two years. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: I just can't believe that all this in one day. That a man's stroke of a pen that can sit there, it's just un-American. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: How's that guy that's had 30, 40 years of welding (INAUDIBLE) pipelines in? How does he, you know, how does he transfer that to solar? Flyover country, that's what they call us. They don't -- it's like we don't even exist. (END VIDEO CLIP) MACCALLUM: So, we've been down this road before. The Obama administration promised a plethora of green jobs. They said they would be easily transferred from canceled projects over the wind and solar work. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) BARACK OBAMA, FORMER PRESIDENT OF THE UNITED STATES: Workers in 22 states are manufacturing the supplies for this project. Workers in a dozen states are building the advanced manufacturing equipment that will power this new facility. Solyndra expects to hire 1,000 workers to manufacture solar panels and sell them across America and around the world. (END VIDEO CLIP) MACCALLUM: But that is just one example. But after receiving two years, two years after receiving their half-billion-dollar loan from the Obama White House, Solyndra filed for bankruptcy, as you probably well remember. So, fast forward today to where House Republicans went to the Houston Ship Channel, an enormously busy energy port in the United States. And they began to push back. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) UNIDENTIFIED MALE: In a time of pandemic when jobs have already been lost, you thought you would take action to help them, not cut them. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: It weakens America and empowers our enemies. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: We have to support American energy. That's what the science actually says. (END VIDEO CLIP) MACCALLUM: So, another hard hit state will be New Mexico because more than half of their oil production takes place on those federal lands. And that's where we find our Fox Business Network reporter Grady Trimble there today. Hi, Grady. GRADY TRIMBLE, FOX BUSINESS NETWORK REPORTER: Hi, Martha. This oil pump and just about every oil pump, as far as the eye can see out here, is on federal land. And as you mentioned, New Mexico is disproportionately impacted by this executive action, pausing new leases on drilling for oil on federal land. That's because about half of U.S. oil production or rather a quarter of U.S. oil production takes place on federal land. But in New Mexico, that number is closer to 56 percent. Claire Chase knows this industry well. It's a family business, Mack Energy Corporation. And tell me how this is going to impact you guys and this entire state. CLAIRE CHASE, DIRECTOR OF COMMUNITY RELATIONS, MACK ENERGY CORPORATION: It's going to be really tough for us, for our company in particular. We do about 60 percent of our production on federal lands. And at the state level, it's about 56 percent of all the oil that we produce. That represents about $1.4 billion in revenue to the State of New Mexico and north of 9 billion to the federal government. So, it's a -- it's a really huge hit. TRIMBLE: A lot of people in the industry see this as a first step to banning drilling entirely on federal lands, and that would be devastating for your industry. CHASE: Yes, it's absolutely devastating because as we look at our future and how we're going to spend money, we want to -- you know, we obviously need to be able to drill to produce this commodity that people need. And if we're not allowed to do that, we're going to have to find other areas where we can drill, places like Texas that don't have a lot of federal lands. So, I think New Mexico is looking -- it's looking really bad for us. And hopefully, our governor is able to take a stand for it. TRIMBLE: And Claire mentioned this, Martha, but 33 percent of the state revenue here in New Mexico is from the oil and gas industry, about $1.4 billion from this industry goes to public schools. So, it's not just these workers that are directly impacted by it. It's all of that trickle down all the way to school teachers and students. Martha? MACCALLUM: Very interesting. Our thanks to Claire for speaking with you today about her family's business and the larger implications for New Mexico. Grady Trimble down there today. Senator John Barrasso was a key player in passing climate legislation last year, and he is now poised to be perhaps one of President Biden's biggest opponents when it comes to this issue. He's also the ranking member of the Energy and National Resources Committee. And he's from the great state of Wyoming. Senator, great to see you today. Thank you so much for being here. SEN. JOHN BARRASSO (R-WY): Great to be with you, Martha. Thank you. MACCALLUM: So, how do you see this? What's the impact on Wyoming? BARRASSO: Well, it's a dramatic impact on Wyoming. And I stand with the workers. And these are the workers I was with this weekend in Wyoming, the people who work in oil and gas and coal and who provide affordable energy for America. You know, you can protect the environment without punishing the economy, and punishing the people who work to provide energy. But Joe Biden hasn't taken this approach. He's taken a sledgehammer to the energy workers of the country. The energy needs are going to continue to be there. But the jobs are going to go other places, whether it's to Canada, whether it's to Saudi Arabia, because we need the energy. And the people that are going to suffer aren't just the workers in this country; they're also the people that purchase energy, people that fill their cars, people that heat their homes, because we're going to see an increase in the cost of energy for consumers, because of these executive orders. You know, President Biden said he wanted to work together, but when he got to the White House, and he drew a big target on the back of American energy, and he pulled the trigger, killing the Keystone XL pipeline, you know, killing oil and gas leases, and then putting us back in the -- in the Paris Accord. MACCALLUM: Yes, I mean, when you look at the huge gains that were made, in terms of energy independence. I mean, I remember gas lines when I was a little kid. And you know, you look at all of the impact of OPEC and the power that they had over the world and over the United States through that entire period, gaining energy independence has put us in a completely different position against these countries when we go to negotiate with them and talk with them. We know that John Kerry, the former Secretary of State has now been put in charge of climate change. That's his area for the Biden administration. Watch this little snippet of an interview that he did with Fareed Zakaria. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) FAREED ZAKARIA, HOST, CNN: Canceling the Keystone Pipeline, the decision on no new fracking on new federal lands, those governmental decisions are going to put people out of work, in fact, already are doing so. What do you say to those people? JOHN KERRY, U.S. SPECIAL PRESIDENTIAL ENVOY FOR CLIMATE: We're a great nation at creating jobs, so they're going to be a massive, literally millions of jobs created over these next years. And there will be a transition in our economy. (END VIDEO CLIP) MACCALLUM: So, are there going to be million -- I just noticed on the graphic in Grady Trimble's piece, a million jobs likely lost in up to 2022. That's a very big number. But Kerry is --John Kerry is saying that there's going to be millions of jobs created in these new industries. Do you agree with that? BARRASSO: No, I do not. John Kerry is wrong. If he were standing here, I'll look him straight in the eye, and I'd say, John Kerry, you should be straight with the American people. Because even the fact checkers, The Washington Post, who endorsed President Biden for president has said of what John Kerry said, they said it was false hope and it was misleading information. At the most, you're talking about 10,000 new jobs over the next 10 years in solar and in wind. You know, the nominee to be Secretary of Energy said jobs may need to be sacrificed. That's the approach of this administration. These are climate alarmists, and they want to do things dramatically, unilaterally, immediately to no benefit to the -- to the climate, but to devastation of the economy. Energy is called the master resource for a reason. It powers our economy, jobs, the military. We are a world energy superpower, and we have been acting like it in the last four years. President Biden has now turned off the switch. MACCALLUM: So, is it legal for the President of the United States to ban energy production on federal lands because there's a question about that. Right? BARRASSO: I agree with you, Martha. When we take a look at it, there's an executive orders that have come out, there will be lawsuits, I can assure you. And with the fact that over the last four years, we've put over 200 conservative judges on the courts, I think there's a very good chance that what President Biden is trying to do will be overturned, will not be found to be legal. And there are a number of us in Congress actually on both sides of the aisle that are trying to stop Joe Biden and his climate alarmists from moving in that direction. There are a number of members of Congress who are Democrats from Texas, who are opposing what President Biden is trying to do. And I'm going to work closely with Joe Manchin, Democrat from West Virginia, who is chair of the Energy Committee, I'm the ranking member of the Energy Committee. And we both believe that we need all of the energy. We need oil and gas and coal. We need uranium for nuclear power. We do need wind and solar. But we need to make sure that American energy, and we make energy as clean as we can as fast as we can, and do it in ways that don't raise costs for American consumers. MACCALLUM: Well, it's a very big story. And it's a big political story, as well. A lot of these energy producing states are red states, but there are swing states on that list, as well. So, it's going to be interesting to see where this goes. I had the pleasure of being in your beautiful state of Wyoming all last week, Senator, and it's an amazing place that you come from. So, thank you very much. It's great to have you here today. BARRASSO: Great people, hardworking, and we produce a lot of energy. Thanks, Martha. MACCALLUM: That's for sure. Thank you, Senator. So, less than two weeks in now, how Republicans who vowed to give President Biden a fair shot are now feeling about what Rich Lowry is calling that this perhaps could be the most radical left-wing presidency in history. We break down the numbers and the actions just so far, but it is disguised, as Lowry puts it, under the mood music of moderation and unity. Marc Thiessen and Governor Huckabee, next. (COMMERCIAL BREAK) (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) JOE BIDEN, PRESIDENT OF THE UNITED STATES: And I pledge this to you, I will be a president for all Americans, all Americans. And I promise you, I will fight as hard for those who did not support me as for those who did. (END VIDEO CLIP) MACCALLUM: So, that was 13 days ago. President Joe Biden calling for unity. And hours later, he signed 17 executive orders and actions, rolling back some of President Trump's policies and he has signed dozens more executive orders, a record number actually, in the early days of his presidency. Now, Republicans who said that they would give Biden a chance appear to be at kind of a crossroads with all of this. Rich Lowry writing this in the New York Post, quote, "The dulcet tones of Biden's inaugural address already seem an artifact of a bygone era. The fact is that Biden is governing as he promised, further to the left of his own record, further to the left of his ex-boss, former President Barack Obama, and further to the left of any Democrat who made his career prior to the ascendancy of the cultural left. Let's bring in American Enterprise Institute Scholar Marc Thiessen and former Arkansas Governor Mike Huckabee. Both are Fox News Contributors. Gentlemen, great to have both of you with us today. Thanks for being here. MARC THIESSEN, FOX NEWS CHANNEL CONTRIBUTOR: Good to be with you, Martha. MACCALLUM: You know, I'm struck by a couple of things. When I look at the moves so far from President Biden. One is that he won, and that the country seems to be open to a lot of these ideas. There was a poll that showed that people generally support 13 out of the 14 of those executive orders that he did on the first day, Marc, and let me start with you. Is this becoming a country that is shifting center left, or is that a misread on President Biden's part? THIESSEN: I think all of us want to give President Biden a chance. I think most of us want to say, you know, he promised to unite the country, that what they -- what people remember as he campaign, I'm the only guy who can bring Republicans and Democrats together. I did it for years on Capitol Hill, I've spent 40 years in the Senate. I know how to do this. Nobody else can do this. So, we're all waiting for him to do that. You know, and what I -- what we need -- I think he needs to realize, and the Democrats need to realize is that unity is about more than not insulting each other. You know, it's great. I mean, I hope we can cross that bar. If we can't, God help us. But it's about compromise. It's about letting the other side get some things they want and moderating your own demands and being willing to give up some things in order to bring the other side along and reaching a consensus. And that's what Biden promised to do, and he's not doing that. He's not doing it with the executive orders. And he is not doing with legislation either. He has no major bipartisan initiative, his one first big initiative, this COVID relief bill, he's -- he, just after meeting with Republicans, said we're proceeding with budget reconciliation, I can pass this with just Republic -- with just democratic votes. So, there's no -- they're not interested in real unity. MACCALLUM: Yes, it's interesting, because, you know, he did talk about it a lot on the campaign trail, governor. And you know, he is seen as somebody who has worked with both sides. So now, he does seem to be pitching much further to the left, I think, than a lot of people ever thought he would. This is a soundbite here from Pramila Jayapal, congresswoman. Watch this. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) REP. PRAMILA JAYAPAL (D-WA): 1.9 trillion is an excellent start. It should be the floor. If anything, we should strengthen it, not weaken it. I think we could probably argue that we -- really, economists have argued that we need between 3 and 4 trillion. And so, we're continuing to work on that. But 1.9 trillion should be the floor. (END VIDEO CLIP) MACCALLUM: We've already done 4.5 trillion, governor. And I -- there's at least a trillion, I think, that's still on the table, hasn't been spent yet, but she's going for 3 or 4 trillion. So, this is what he's dealing with. MIKE HUCKABEE, FOX NEWS CHANNEL CONTRIBUTOR: Why stop there? Let's make it 25, 50 trillion. Let's just give everybody everything they've ever wanted. Let government be Santa Claus. She said, that's the floor. Heck, I'm on the floor thinking about how crazy this is. Joe Biden said he wanted to fight for me. My gosh, I'd hate to think if this is what he's doing for me what he would be doing to me, if he was fighting against me. A lot of these executive orders are killing people's jobs all over the country, especially in the energy field. And despite the fact that 58 percent of Americans don't want taxpayer funded abortions, he's pushing ahead. 77 percent of Americans, including Democrats, this isn't a bipartisan issue, don't want America to be paying for foreign abortions. He just suspended the Mexico City policy, which does exactly that. This is not a unity president, this is not a, gee, let's all come together. Joe Biden is making Barack Obama look like Ronald Reagan in terms of his leftist policies. And I think a lot of people who voted for him. Goodness, I hope they're as disappointed as they need to be over this. MACCALLUM: You know, it just raises a basic question about how the president, you know, none of us can get inside his mind and figure out why he's looking at it this way. But he seems to feel an obligation to check a ton of these boxes off for the further left part of his party, Marc. And before he knows it, he's going to be dealing with a midterm election. And he may wish when that rolls around, that he listened to some of the workers that we heard from in the first segment here from the energy sector in places that are potentially swing states. THIESSEN: No, no doubt. I mean, look, we shouldn't be surprised that a democratic president and we're representing a far-left liberal Democratic Party is doing some things by executive order that we as conservatives don't like. And you know, and if he goes too far, it's going to create a backlash, and it's going to come back -- it's going to come back to haunt him. You know, keep in mind, it was Barack Obama going and saying elections have consequences, and I won. That led to the backlash that started the Tea Party movement, and eventually over time, created Donald Trump if Joe Biden doesn't tack to the center, and to the moderate path and try working with Republicans. He just had 10 Republican Senators come to him in the Oval Office yesterday, and offer their hand outstretched and saying, let's work on a scale down COVID relief bill that we can find consensus. $618 billion, that's on top of the 900 billion we just passed a few weeks ago. So, $1.5 trillion since Biden was elected. That's real money, that's a lot of money. And he seems to be uninterested in compromising with them. And that means his whole promise of -- his whole promise of his inaugural address is a lie. MACCALLUM: I got to believe there's a lot of suburban voters across the country who if you walked out of that meeting with them and said, You know what, we're going to meet in the middle on this, and we're going to get this done right away, and we're not going to use reconciliation, and I think it would be a very interesting outcome. I do think it's what Americans want. Gentlemen, thank you very much. Great to see you both today. THIESSEN: Thank you. MACCALLUM: It's a very sad story coming out of Florida today. And we have breaking news on this killing of two FBI agents. We're going to bring you some new information on this, as they were serving a federal search warrant. It was violence against children that was being committed in that home. That was the investigation. We're going to tell you exactly what happened as we learn more about these details of this gunfight, next. (COMMERCIAL BREAK) MACCALLUM: Law enforcement officers saluting one of two FBI agents who lost their lives in action today in South Florida. Three other agents were wounded. In this operation, the FBI says that they were serving a search warrant in a case involving violent crimes against children. They are the first FBI agents to die in the line of duty in more than 12 years. Correspondent Phil Keating joins us with the breaking news in this developing story in sunrise Florida this afternoon. Hi, Phil. PHIL KEATING, FOX NEWS CHANNEL CORRESPONDENT: Hi, Martha. An absolutely devastating, dramatic, and brutal early morning here in sunrise just west of Fort Lauderdale as a suspect, who was being served a federal court ordered search warrant for child pornography and violent crimes against children, instead of opening the door to his apartment down the street. Instead, he grabbed his gun and started shooting very unusual for FBI agents to be shot and killed in the line of duty, and yet today, two of them were, both of them, and three other agents were shot and wounded. Two of them remain in stable condition. It was a dramatic and chaotic scene inside the gated apartment complex. The road here remains closed to traffic. The FBI director has named the two fallen agents as Daniel Alfin and Laura Schwartzenberger. And director William (PH) Wray did release a short statement today, and I quote, "Tragically, the FBI lost two of our own today. Special Agent Daniel Alfin and Special Agent Laura Schwartzenberger were both shot and killed in the line of duty while executing a federal court ordered search warrant in crimes against children investigation. The last time agents, as I mentioned were -- an agent was shot and killed in the line of duty was 2008. The suspect inside his apartment barricaded himself in the minutes after the shootout. That person is now dead, as well. still unclear is whether the subject of the search warrant ended up shooting and killing himself or whether crossfire from FBI agents and local law enforcement on the scene took his life. We will find out more this afternoon as the FBI in South Florida is going to have a news conference at 5:30. Sad day up here on Sunrise, Florida. Martha? MACCALLUM: All right. Absolutely. We will look ahead to that at 5:30 tonight for more information on those fallen officers. Thank you very much, Phil Keating, in sunrise, Florida today. So, coming up right here, Republicans see an opening to winning back suburban voters by helping parents and fighting the teachers' unions to get their students back into the classroom. Here's union president Randi Weingarten blaming the prior administration. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) RANDI WEINGARTEN, PRESIDENT, AMERICAN FEDERATION OF TEACHERS: We had an administration that completely failed, that distorted fact from reality. The same kind of distortions of fact versus untruths have happened when it comes to school reopening. (END VIDEO CLIP) MACCALLUM: Dr. Scott Atlas was part of that White House team, and he responds with his look at the science behind all of this, next. (COMMERCIAL BREAK) MACCALLUM: President Biden said that he hopes to have most kids back in the classroom within his first 100 days, but the clock is ticking. And, you know, by that time, you're going to be close to summer for a lot of these students. Meanwhile, you've got Catholic schools, which are celebrating National Catholic Schools Week this week and it's been quite a year for them. Because across the country they're seeing surging enrollment, they have really set the standard for safe open schools, as the unions continue to blame others for the fact that they are not going back into the classroom. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) WEINGARTEN: We had an administration that completely failed, that distorted fact from reality as everyone has seen because of the big lie and the effects on Washington, DC before January 6th, and then in the aftermath of January 6th. The same kind of distortions of fact versus untruths have happened when it comes to school reopening, and that people of goodwill don't actually even know what the science is, and how to have a roadmap in terms of safely opening. (END VIDEO CLIP) MACCALLUM: All right. Let's bring in Dr. Scott Atlas, former Special Adviser to President Trump and a Stanford University Hoover Institute Senior Fellow. Dr. Atlas, good to have you with us today. You heard Randi Weingarten, the Head of the American Federation for Teachers. She says that there's no pathway, there's no guidance, there's no science involved in the urge across the country to get these teachers back in the classroom. DR. SCOTT ATLAS, FORMER SPECIAL ADVISER TO TRUMP: Yes. Hi, Martha, thanks for having me. Well, you know, this is sort of surreal at this point. It's been known for months and months. I'm talking about eight months that the science the data has said school should be open. And there's no new information that contradicts that, the only new information is confirmatory. From Brown University from Duke University , from all over the world, we know children have very, very little risk of a significant illness. We know that children are not significant spreaders to adults. We know that teachers do not get significant cases when in schools that are open. And we know, overwhelmingly, the harms to children, not the teachers, to children of lack of in-person schools. These people are, I don't know what they're talking about with lie. These are just bizarre statements that have no fact whatsoever. There's been a complete perversion of the term "the science." There is no reason not to open schools. There is nothing special about schools except that they're low risk environments. If I had a job where I wanted to be safe from COVID, I would become a teacher. I mean, these people are just, I don't understand that. In fact, there's no reason, by the way, to prioritize teachers in vaccination programs, teachers are not at high risk. High risk teachers should be prioritized. But, you know, 82% of teachers in the United States are under 55, half of them are under 41. They're a low risk young profession. They should be back at work. I said this months ago, but aren't schools and social business -- MACCALLUM: Yes, you did. You said it on our program and, you know, people give you a hard time. I just want to play for anybody who may have missed it. This is a dance montage that was put together by Chicago teachers. They are in a cooling down period right now because they're about to strike because they don't want to go back to the classroom. But here they are dancing and talking about safety. Let's listen to this for just 20 seconds. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: Make it make sense. Safety is essential. Keep our students and our teachers safe. (END VIDEO CLIP) MACCALLUM: All right. You know that -- I know you couldn't see that, Dr. Atlas, but it's teachers dancing around in their apartments, in their homes, doing interpretive dance and talking about making teaching safe and making children safe, and listening to science. I mean, you know, as you point out, it's like we're living in parallel universes here. Quick thought. ATLAS: Well, you know, I think that at some point, if teachers don't want to work, they should get out of the way and let people do their jobs. There's plenty of people who are unemployed in the country. They are not fit to be teachers if they cannot be critical thinkers and look at the data themselves. I will say that. MACCALLUM: Yes. You know, I think everyone understands if someone has a specific health concern, then they should maybe be in a different category, but most of these people, as you point out, are not in those categories and children are suffering across the country. Dr. Atlas, thank you. Good to have you back on the show. Thanks for being here. ATLAS: Thanks. MACCALLUM: You bet. So, my next guests have been personally impacted by the shutdown of schools in Northern Virginia, Denise Warburton and her son Max, a senior at TC Williams High School join me now. Great to have both of you with us. I know you're at home because where else would you be, right, at this point given the circumstance that's going on. Max, let me start with you. What has life been like for you and do you wish that you could go back to school? MAX CONSTANDY, SENIOR, TC WILLIAMS HIGH SCHOOL: Life at home has been terrible. I have to do Zoom calls along with my barking dogs, and I would really want to go back to school so I can meet someone in-person, and have fun lunches. MACCALLUM: Yes, you want to have lunch and you want to be with your friends, and be in a room. Denise, you know, when you listen to that Chicago teachers' video and, you know, what goes through your mind as you listen to this debate? What do you want to say to these teachers? DENISE WARBURTON, VIRGINIA MOTHER: I think what's hard to see as I have one in the public school and one is in the private school, I've seen that the private schools have gone back successfully in a Hybrid model. They brought them back. None of these kids are falling ill. They're all able to have -- there's a complete change in their demeanor when the days my daughter does actually go to school versus virtual at home. I see my son isolated on home with no social interactions all day. He is on a spectrum. And for a kid with Asperger's to be home alone, with absolutely not a single social interaction all day, is completely detrimental. And to do virtually Zoom social skills groups or occupational therapy groups, they're completely ineffective and not serving these children whatsoever. It's been heartbreaking to see the fact that he's home alone all day and suffering. MACCALLUM: Yes. I know you said that he's gone and looked in the window at school just sort of dreaming about being there, right? WARBURTON: Yes. He -- the Catholic school that he used to attend for 9th and 10th grade is only a block from us. And he knows they're back, and we were pretty much pushed out of the private Catholic school because they said they couldn't serve his needs. They couldn't do enough for social skills. They couldn't do enough for executive functioning. And they kept encouraging us to go to the public school, saying they have more resources. But right now, they don't. They don't and it's been so sad that he's actually walked over to the school. And he's been found peering in their windows and inside their campus trying to interact with the kids. And when I asked him what he's doing. He says, I just want to see my friends. And I just wanted to cry. I just thought that was really poignant. And it just shows how desperate they are to be around other people. MACCALLUM: Absolutely. And, Max, you have a beautiful smile and it's so nice to meet you. And I'm sure that your friends miss you so much, too. And I hope that you can all be back together in the classroom very, very soon. I want to thank both of you for being with us today. Thank you, guys. CONSTANDY: Yes. My friends really missed me so much and desperate to see me go back to school. MACCALLUM: I know they are. And we hope everybody can go back soon. And we thank you very much for being here today, both of you. It's great to meet you. WARBURTON: Thank you, Martha. CONSTANDY: I would also like to thank the people who came and have the suffer studying at home. And I would like for them to go back to school. MACCALLUM: I hear you. I think everybody in the country hears you, Max. Thank you so much, great to have you with us. Thank you, Denise. Thank you both. So coming up, we're going talk to a group of mothers who band together to honor the lives of children lost to violence, by standing up against calls to defund the police in their communities. That is not what they want. They want safer cities. The mothers leading that charge are up next. (COMMERCIAL BREAK) MACCALLUM: A mother says that if a police officer had been at the gas station, the night a stray bullet hit her 19-year-old daughter, her daughter might still be alive today. Now 17 years later, Sylvia Bennett- Stone is leading the Voices of Black Mothers United Initiative. She says, they're coming together to honor the lives of their fallen children by spreading the message, positive police reform not defunding local law enforcement could help stop violence on America's streets. A new study discovered homicides jumped 30% last year compared to 2019, a jump that has no modern precedent in history. Let's bring in Sylvia Bennett-Stone and former civil rights activist, Robert Woodson, Founder and President of the Woodson Center and 1776 Unites. Thank you so much for being here, both of you. ROBERT WOODSON, FOUNDER, WOODSON CENTER: Thank you. SYLVIA BENNETT-STONE, DIRECTOR, VOICES OF BLACK MOTHERS UNITED: Thank you. MACCALLUM: Sylvia, I want to start with you. And tell me why you think it's so important for these mothers who have lost children the way you lost your daughter, to bond together. Because these stories don't get the kind of attention that we see other shootings in this country getting? BENNETT-STONE: Absolutely. We have a network of over 2,500 mothers thus far, and we are assured to be quiet. You bury your child, the fool goes away, and then they want you to go away as well with no resolve. So, we band together to say enough is enough. We're no longer going to be silent. We're going to take a stand, and we are going to help do whatever we can to make our communities safer. We're going to do whatever we can to help save the life of the next child that goes to the gas station. MACCALLUM: Your daughter is beautiful. We have a picture of her up on the screen right now and we are with you, and your grief that I'm sure it doesn't get any easier 17 years down the road. But you hear these calls to defund the police, and you see what happens in the aftermath of some of these shootings. What's your message on that? BENNETT-STONE: We are saying defunding the police is not even an option at all. It's not at all. However, we're coming forward with some solutions. We're saying we want police accountability, of course. No one should have to bury their child as a result of shooting. Either way, whether it's community of police, it hurts, but defunding and taking police out the community is not even an option. MACCALLUM: Robert Woodson, your thoughts on this today? WOODSON: Well, for the past four decades, the Woodson Center has worked with local leaders like Sylvia in successfully preventing youth violence in the cities. The answers are found there, and the monies that are being spent to groups who are calling for the reduction of police or defunding, it is really exacerbating the very prominent, saying that they're trying to solve. So, the Woodson Center is supporting these mothers and as a consequence of the relationship they have with law enforcement, they have increased the closure rates in homicides in cities, and their other crime prevention efforts. MACCALLUM: We thank you both so much. I hope you'll come back when we have more time. Oh, Robert Woodson, thank you so much, sir. We'll see you next time. Sylvia, thank you very much. BENNETT-STONE: Thank you. MACCALLUM: Thank you both. You might not consider yourself someone who cares about a rap song that's climbing the charts. But it is a pretty interesting cultural moment when the tune is called "Fake Woke." It attacks cancel culture, and it questions the Black Lives Matter Movement. The exclusive interview you don't want to miss, next. (COMMERCIAL BREAK) MACCALLUM: A song exploding on the music charts this week with more than 2.5 million views on YouTube in just a couple of days. The viral hit is called "Fake Woke." Canadian rapper Tom McDonald serves up a controversial take on cancel culture and much more. Fox News Headlines 24/7 Reporter Carely Shimkus has just spoken with Tom MacDonald exclusively Hi, Carely, CARELY SHIMKUS, FOX NEWS REPORTER: Hey, Martha. Yes, that's right. It was a very interesting interview. And, you know, it's common for musicians to release politically charged songs these days. But you've probably never heard one quite like this before. Rapper Tom MacDonald rails against cancel culture and censorship in his new song titled "Fake Woke" and his message has been heard by millions. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) TOM MACDONALD, RAPPER: We're ashamed to be American, you should probably love it, because you have the right to hate it and not get stoned to death in public. As children we were taught how to walk and talk, but the system wants adults to sit down and shut up. Cancel culture runs the world now, the planet went crazy. (END VIDEO CLIP) SHIMKUS: Now, McDonald's anti-censorship anthem has racked up over 2.5 million views on YouTube since it was released just four days ago. More impressively, it's currently the number one most downloaded song on iTunes, beating out this year Super Bowl performer, The Weekend and Grammy winner Ed Sheeran. MacDonald believes his music is popular because he is willing to scream what others would never say out loud. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) MACDONALD: This song was just about screaming my truth at the top of my lungs and sort of there's this performative wokeness that's going on in society today. And I think it was just important to point some fingers at the hypocrisy and the way that the world is changing not for the better. (END VIDEO CLIP) SHIMKUS: Now, the 32-year-old is no stranger to tackling hot button issues in a track released last year titled "People So Stupid." He made his feelings on abortion clear, wondering why some don't consider a heartbeat a sign of life. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) MACDONALD: Let's talk about abortion, sorry, tell me how this works. Bacteria is life on Mars but a heartbeat isn't life on Earth? Weird. (END VIDEO CLIP) SHIMKUS: In another song, he discussed Black Lives Matter calling it a valuable movement, but adding all lives matter isn't racist or stupid. Supporters call his stance refreshing but critics have accused him of racism and homophobia. One Twitter user writing, if someone listens to Tom MacDonald cut them off completely. Another tweeting, if you like Tom MacDonald, you got to be racist. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) MACDONALD: I know who I am. My friends and my family know who I am. My fans know who I am. If I see something on TV, I change the channel. If I'm reading something I don't like I close the book. Like I don't try to call the radio station and call the people who were on TV names and try to cancel them or call the publishing company that published the book that I don't like, and try and get the author cancelled. (END VIDEO CLIP) SHIMKUS: And while MacDonald has the most popular song on iTunes right now and 1.6 million followers on YouTube , he is doing it only with the help of his girlfriend who shoots all of his music videos. He does not have a manager, a record label, a publicist or PR team. He also doesn't get a lot of media attention. He attributes this to not fitting in with today's accepted narrative. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) MACDONALD: People have become allergic to opinions in North America and these last five years, and it's pretty soon like they're going to cancel everything. And all we're going to have is tall gray buildings and quiet car rides. And then, we're all going to be kicking ourselves in the butt for this craziness. (END VIDEO CLIP) SHIMKUS: And while you may think he's conservative, MacDonald says he doesn't support either political party. He thinks the most important thing is to have moderate voices instead of the political polarization facing America today, Martha. MACCALLUM: Carely, thank you, very interesting interview, a controversial rapper with a pretty strong message, interesting to hear from him. I also just want to do a shout out to my friend, Charles Gubish. She was 102 years old today. He is one of the featured veterans of Iwo Jima in my book "Unknown Valor." So that's Tuesday, February 2nd, happy birthday, Charlie. THE STORY goes on. We'll see you back here at 3:00 tomorrow. "Your World with Neil Cavuto" starts right now.
