headline: Sen. John Barrasso (R-WY) Is Interviewed About The Impact Of Biden's Climate Executive Orders; Biden Begins To Deliver On Progressive Demands; Two FBI Agents Killed, Three Wounded In South Florida; Chicago Teachers Union Slammed For Dancing Video; Frustrated Parents Plead For In-Person Learning; Mothers Of Murder Victims On Defunding Police; Canadian Rapper Calls Out "Woke" America
story_text: JOHN ROBERTS, FOX NEWS HOST: This is -- this is what's helping keep me warm today, my big Baffin boots. Yes. SANDRA SMITH, FOX NEWS HOST: Well, you are prepared. ROBERTS: Well, I grew up in a place that's like the Arctic, so why not? SMITH: Good to be with you, John, "THE STORY" starts now. MARTHA MACCALLUM, FOX NEWS ANCHOR: Thank you, John and Sandra. Good to see you both today. Today, a short time ago, though, in Florida, we all witnessed this awful scene. The body of an FBI agent draped in the American flag, one of two agents who were killed in a bloody gun battle that was part of a raid on a home where they were investigating violent crimes against children. It was the first time in 12 years that agents, FBI agents were killed in their line of duty. And with that, good afternoon, everybody. I'm Martha McCallum and this is THE STORY. We're going to take you to the scene there in Florida shortly as we learn more about that unfolding situation today. But first, we want to turn our attention to a major change that is underway in America. Today, workers in our energy industries are wondering where the Biden White House is leading them. We've spent decades building energy independence in this country. And that has been great news for workers, and not such great news for other big energy providers like Venezuela, or Russia, or the Middle East, we're no longer reliant on them. And we were building our own enormous energy supply. That shifted the global power dynamic in a way that was not seen, really, since the advent of the automobile. But now, that is changing, as executive orders are shutting down new leases for fracking on federal lands. And as you know, the XL Pipeline is also a casualty here. So, here's what some of those workers are saying as they react to all of this. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) UNIDENTIFIED MALE: You prepare for these -- for these large projects. And when one gets the rug yanked out from under it, I mean, you have nothing for that year, or you're going to have nothing for the next two years. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: I just can't believe that all this in one day. That a man's stroke of a pen that can sit there, it's just un-American. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: How's that guy that's had 30, 40 years of welding (INAUDIBLE) pipelines in? How does he, you know, how does he transfer that to solar? Flyover country, that's what they call us. They don't -- it's like we don't even exist. (END VIDEO CLIP) MACCALLUM: So, we've been down this road before. The Obama administration promised a plethora of green jobs. They said they would be easily transferred from canceled projects over the wind and solar work. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) BARACK OBAMA, FORMER PRESIDENT OF THE UNITED STATES: Workers in 22 states are manufacturing the supplies for this project. Workers in a dozen states are building the advanced manufacturing equipment that will power this new facility. Solyndra expects to hire 1,000 workers to manufacture solar panels and sell them across America and around the world. (END VIDEO CLIP) MACCALLUM: But that is just one example. But after receiving two years, two years after receiving their half-billion-dollar loan from the Obama White House, Solyndra filed for bankruptcy, as you probably well remember. So, fast forward today to where House Republicans went to the Houston Ship Channel, an enormously busy energy port in the United States. And they began to push back. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) UNIDENTIFIED MALE: In a time of pandemic when jobs have already been lost, you thought you would take action to help them, not cut them. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: It weakens America and empowers our enemies. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: We have to support American energy. That's what the science actually says. (END VIDEO CLIP) MACCALLUM: So, another hard hit state will be New Mexico because more than half of their oil production takes place on those federal lands. And that's where we find our Fox Business Network reporter Grady Trimble there today. Hi, Grady. GRADY TRIMBLE, FOX BUSINESS NETWORK REPORTER: Hi, Martha. This oil pump and just about every oil pump, as far as the eye can see out here, is on federal land. And as you mentioned, New Mexico is disproportionately impacted by this executive action, pausing new leases on drilling for oil on federal land. That's because about half of U.S. oil production or rather a quarter of U.S. oil production takes place on federal land. But in New Mexico, that number is closer to 56 percent. Claire Chase knows this industry well. It's a family business, Mack Energy Corporation. And tell me how this is going to impact you guys and this entire state. CLAIRE CHASE, DIRECTOR OF COMMUNITY RELATIONS, MACK ENERGY CORPORATION: It's going to be really tough for us, for our company in particular. We do about 60 percent of our production on federal lands. And at the state level, it's about 56 percent of all the oil that we produce. That represents about $1.4 billion in revenue to the State of New Mexico and north of 9 billion to the federal government. So, it's a -- it's a really huge hit. TRIMBLE: A lot of people in the industry see this as a first step to banning drilling entirely on federal lands, and that would be devastating for your industry. CHASE: Yes, it's absolutely devastating because as we look at our future and how we're going to spend money, we want to -- you know, we obviously need to be able to drill to produce this commodity that people need. And if we're not allowed to do that, we're going to have to find other areas where we can drill, places like Texas that don't have a lot of federal lands. So, I think New Mexico is looking -- it's looking really bad for us. And hopefully, our governor is able to take a stand for it. TRIMBLE: And Claire mentioned this, Martha, but 33 percent of the state revenue here in New Mexico is from the oil and gas industry, about $1.4 billion from this industry goes to public schools. So, it's not just these workers that are directly impacted by it. It's all of that trickle down all the way to school teachers and students. Martha? MACCALLUM: Very interesting. Our thanks to Claire for speaking with you today about her family's business and the larger implications for New Mexico. Grady Trimble down there today. Senator John Barrasso was a key player in passing climate legislation last year, and he is now poised to be perhaps one of President Biden's biggest opponents when it comes to this issue. He's also the ranking member of the Energy and National Resources Committee. And he's from the great state of Wyoming. Senator, great to see you today. Thank you so much for being here. SEN. JOHN BARRASSO (R-WY): Great to be with you, Martha. Thank you. MACCALLUM: So, how do you see this? What's the impact on Wyoming? BARRASSO: Well, it's a dramatic impact on Wyoming. And I stand with the workers. And these are the workers I was with this weekend in Wyoming, the people who work in oil and gas and coal and who provide affordable energy for America. You know, you can protect the environment without punishing the economy, and punishing the people who work to provide energy. But Joe Biden hasn't taken this approach. He's taken a sledgehammer to the energy workers of the country. The energy needs are going to continue to be there. But the jobs are going to go other places, whether it's to Canada, whether it's to Saudi Arabia, because we need the energy. And the people that are going to suffer aren't just the workers in this country; they're also the people that purchase energy, people that fill their cars, people that heat their homes, because we're going to see an increase in the cost of energy for consumers, because of these executive orders. You know, President Biden said he wanted to work together, but when he got to the White House, and he drew a big target on the back of American energy, and he pulled the trigger, killing the Keystone XL pipeline, you know, killing oil and gas leases, and then putting us back in the -- in the Paris Accord. MACCALLUM: Yes, I mean, when you look at the huge gains that were made, in terms of energy independence. I mean, I remember gas lines when I was a little kid. And you know, you look at all of the impact of OPEC and the power that they had over the world and over the United States through that entire period, gaining energy independence has put us in a completely different position against these countries when we go to negotiate with them and talk with them. We know that John Kerry, the former Secretary of State has now been put in charge of climate change. That's his area for the Biden administration. Watch this little snippet of an interview that he did with Fareed Zakaria. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) FAREED ZAKARIA, HOST, CNN: Canceling the Keystone Pipeline, the decision on no new fracking on new federal lands, those governmental decisions are going to put people out of work, in fact, already are doing so. What do you say to those people? JOHN KERRY, U.S. SPECIAL PRESIDENTIAL ENVOY FOR CLIMATE: We're a great nation at creating jobs, so they're going to be a massive, literally millions of jobs created over these next years. And there will be a transition in our economy. (END VIDEO CLIP) MACCALLUM: So, are there going to be million -- I just noticed on the graphic in Grady Trimble's piece, a million jobs likely lost in up to 2022. That's a very big number. But Kerry is --John Kerry is saying that there's going to be millions of jobs created in these new industries. Do you agree with that? BARRASSO: No, I do not. John Kerry is wrong. If he were standing here, I'll look him straight in the eye, and I'd say, John Kerry, you should be straight with the American people. Because even the fact checkers, The Washington Post, who endorsed President Biden for president has said of what John Kerry said, they said it was false hope and it was misleading information. At the most, you're talking about 10,000 new jobs over the next 10 years in solar and in wind. You know, the nominee to be Secretary of Energy said jobs may need to be sacrificed. That's the approach of this administration. These are climate alarmists, and they want to do things dramatically, unilaterally, immediately to no benefit to the -- to the climate, but to devastation of the economy. Energy is called the master resource for a reason. It powers our economy, jobs, the military. We are a world energy superpower, and we have been acting like it in the last four years. President Biden has now turned off the switch. MACCALLUM: So, is it legal for the President of the United States to ban energy production on federal lands because there's a question about that. Right? BARRASSO: I agree with you, Martha. When we take a look at it, there's an executive orders that have come out, there will be lawsuits, I can assure you. And with the fact that over the last four years, we've put over 200 conservative judges on the courts, I think there's a very good chance that what President Biden is trying to do will be overturned, will not be found to be legal. And there are a number of us in Congress actually on both sides of the aisle that are trying to stop Joe Biden and his climate alarmists from moving in that direction. There are a number of members of Congress who are Democrats from Texas, who are opposing what President Biden is trying to do. And I'm going to work closely with Joe Manchin, Democrat from West Virginia, who is chair of the Energy Committee, I'm the ranking member of the Energy Committee. And we both believe that we need all of the energy. We need oil and gas and coal. We need uranium for nuclear power. We do need wind and solar. But we need to make sure that American energy, and we make energy as clean as we can as fast as we can, and do it in ways that don't raise costs for American consumers. MACCALLUM: Well, it's a very big story. And it's a big political story, as well. A lot of these energy producing states are red states, but there are swing states on that list, as well. So, it's going to be interesting to see where this goes. I had the pleasure of being in your beautiful state of Wyoming all last week, Senator, and it's an amazing place that you come from. So, thank you very much. It's great to have you here today. BARRASSO: Great people, hardworking, and we produce a lot of energy. Thanks, Martha. MACCALLUM: That's for sure. Thank you, Senator. So, less than two weeks in now, how Republicans who vowed to give President Biden a fair shot are now feeling about what Rich Lowry is calling that this perhaps could be the most radical left-wing presidency in history. We break down the numbers and the actions just so far, but it is disguised, as Lowry puts it, under the mood music of moderation and unity. Marc Thiessen and Governor Huckabee, next. (COMMERCIAL BREAK) (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) JOE BIDEN, PRESIDENT OF THE UNITED STATES: And I pledge this to you, I will be a president for all Americans, all Americans. And I promise you, I will fight as hard for those who did not support me as for those who did. (END VIDEO CLIP) MACCALLUM: So, that was 13 days ago. President Joe Biden calling for unity. And hours later, he signed 17 executive orders and actions, rolling back some of President Trump's policies and he has signed dozens more executive orders, a record number actually, in the early days of his presidency. Now, Republicans who said that they would give Biden a chance appear to be at kind of a crossroads with all of this. Rich Lowry writing this in the New York Post, quote, "The dulcet tones of Biden's inaugural address already seem an artifact of a bygone era. The fact is that Biden is governing as he promised, further to the left of his own record, further to the left of his ex-boss, former President Barack Obama, and further to the left of any Democrat who made his career prior to the ascendancy of the cultural left. Let's bring in American Enterprise Institute Scholar Marc Thiessen and former Arkansas Governor Mike Huckabee. Both are Fox News Contributors. Gentlemen, great to have both of you with us today. Thanks for being here. MARC THIESSEN, FOX NEWS CHANNEL CONTRIBUTOR: Good to be with you, Martha. MACCALLUM: You know, I'm struck by a couple of things. When I look at the moves so far from President Biden. One is that he won, and that the country seems to be open to a lot of these ideas. There was a poll that showed that people generally support 13 out of the 14 of those executive orders that he did on the first day, Marc, and let me start with you. Is this becoming a country that is shifting center left, or is that a misread on President Biden's part? THIESSEN: I think all of us want to give President Biden a chance. I think most of us want to say, you know, he promised to unite the country, that what they -- what people remember as he campaign, I'm the only guy who can bring Republicans and Democrats together. I did it for years on Capitol Hill, I've spent 40 years in the Senate. I know how to do this. Nobody else can do this. So, we're all waiting for him to do that. You know, and what I -- what we need -- I think he needs to realize, and the Democrats need to realize is that unity is about more than not insulting each other. You know, it's great. I mean, I hope we can cross that bar. If we can't, God help us. But it's about compromise. It's about letting the other side get some things they want and moderating your own demands and being willing to give up some things in order to bring the other side along and reaching a consensus. And that's what Biden promised to do, and he's not doing that. He's not doing it with the executive orders. And he is not doing with legislation either. He has no major bipartisan initiative, his one first big initiative, this COVID relief bill, he's -- he, just after meeting with Republicans, said we're proceeding with budget reconciliation, I can pass this with just Republic -- with just democratic votes. So, there's no -- they're not interested in real unity. MACCALLUM: Yes, it's interesting, because, you know, he did talk about it a lot on the campaign trail, governor. And you know, he is seen as somebody who has worked with both sides. So now, he does seem to be pitching much further to the left, I think, than a lot of people ever thought he would. This is a soundbite here from Pramila Jayapal, congresswoman. Watch this. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) REP. PRAMILA JAYAPAL (D-WA): 1.9 trillion is an excellent start. It should be the floor. If anything, we should strengthen it, not weaken it. I think we could probably argue that we -- really, economists have argued that we need between 3 and 4 trillion. And so, we're continuing to work on that. But 1.9 trillion should be the floor. (END VIDEO CLIP) MACCALLUM: We've already done 4.5 trillion, governor. And I -- there's at least a trillion, I think, that's still on the table, hasn't been spent yet, but she's going for 3 or 4 trillion. So, this is what he's dealing with. MIKE HUCKABEE, FOX NEWS CHANNEL CONTRIBUTOR: Why stop there? Let's make it 25, 50 trillion. Let's just give everybody everything they've ever wanted. Let government be Santa Claus. She said, that's the floor. Heck, I'm on the floor thinking about how crazy this is. Joe Biden said he wanted to fight for me. My gosh, I'd hate to think if this is what he's doing for me what he would be doing to me, if he was fighting against me. A lot of these executive orders are killing people's jobs all over the country, especially in the energy field. And despite the fact that 58 percent of Americans don't want taxpayer funded abortions, he's pushing ahead. 77 percent of Americans, including Democrats, this isn't a bipartisan issue, don't want America to be paying for foreign abortions. He just suspended the Mexico City policy, which does exactly that. This is not a unity president, this is not a, gee, let's all come together. Joe Biden is making Barack Obama look like Ronald Reagan in terms of his leftist policies. And I think a lot of people who voted for him. Goodness, I hope they're as disappointed as they need to be over this. MACCALLUM: You know, it just raises a basic question about how the president, you know, none of us can get inside his mind and figure out why he's looking at it this way. But he seems to feel an obligation to check a ton of these boxes off for the further left part of his party, Marc. And before he knows it, he's going to be dealing with a midterm election. And he may wish when that rolls around, that he listened to some of the workers that we heard from in the first segment here from the energy sector in places that are potentially swing states. THIESSEN: No, no doubt. I mean, look, we shouldn't be surprised that a democratic president and we're representing a far-left liberal Democratic Party is doing some things by executive order that we as conservatives don't like. And you know, and if he goes too far, it's going to create a backlash, and it's going to come back -- it's going to come back to haunt him. You know, keep in mind, it was Barack Obama going and saying elections have consequences, and I won. That led to the backlash that started the Tea Party movement, and eventually over time, created Donald Trump if Joe Biden doesn't tack to the center, and to the moderate path and try working with Republicans. He just had 10 Republican Senators come to him in the Oval Office yesterday, and offer their hand outstretched and saying, let's work on a scale down COVID relief bill that we can find consensus. $618 billion, that's on top of the 900 billion we just passed a few weeks ago. So, $1.5 trillion since Biden was elected. That's real money, that's a lot of money. And he seems to be uninterested in compromising with them. And that means his whole promise of -- his whole promise of his inaugural address is a lie. MACCALLUM: I got to believe there's a lot of suburban voters across the country who if you walked out of that meeting with them and said, You know what, we're going to meet in the middle on this, and we're going to get this done right away, and we're not going to use reconciliation, and I think it would be a very interesting outcome. I do think it's what Americans want. Gentlemen, thank you very much. Great to see you both today. THIESSEN: Thank you. MACCALLUM: It's a very sad story coming out of Florida today. And we have breaking news on this killing of two FBI agents. We're going to bring you some new information on this, as they were serving a federal search warrant. It was violence against children that was being committed in that home. That was the investigation. We're going to tell you exactly what happened as we learn more about these details of this gunfight, next. (COMMERCIAL BREAK) MACCALLUM: Law enforcement officers saluting one of two FBI agents who lost their lives in action today in South Florida. Three other agents were wounded. In this operation, the FBI says that they were serving a search warrant in a case involving violent crimes against children. They are the first FBI agents to die in the line of duty in more than 12 years. Correspondent Phil Keating joins us with the breaking news in this developing story in sunrise Florida this afternoon. Hi, Phil. PHIL KEATING, FOX NEWS CHANNEL CORRESPONDENT: Hi, Martha. An absolutely devastating, dramatic, and brutal early morning here in sunrise just west of Fort Lauderdale as a suspect, who was being served a federal court ordered search warrant for child pornography and violent crimes against children, instead of opening the door to his apartment down the street. Instead, he grabbed his gun and started shooting very unusual for FBI agents to be shot and killed in the line of duty, and yet today, two of them were, both of them, and three other agents were shot and wounded. Two of them remain in stable condition. It was a dramatic and chaotic scene inside the gated apartment complex. The road here remains closed to traffic. The FBI director has named the two fallen agents as Daniel Alfin and Laura Schwartzenberger. And director William (PH) Wray did release a short statement today, and I quote, "Tragically, the FBI lost two of our own today. Special Agent Daniel Alfin and Special Agent Laura Schwartzenberger were both shot and killed in the line of duty while executing a federal court ordered search warrant in crimes against children investigation. The last time agents, as I mentioned were -- an agent was shot and killed in the line of duty was 2008. The suspect inside his apartment barricaded himself in the minutes after the shootout. That person is now dead, as well. still unclear is whether the subject of the search warrant ended up shooting and killing himself or whether crossfire from FBI agents and local law enforcement on the scene took his life. We will find out more this afternoon as the FBI in South Florida is going to have a news conference at 5:30. Sad day up here on Sunrise, Florida. Martha? MACCALLUM: All right. Absolutely. We will look ahead to that at 5:30 tonight for more information on those fallen officers. Thank you very much, Phil Keating, in sunrise, Florida today. So, coming up right here, Republicans see an opening to winning back suburban voters by helping parents and fighting the teachers' unions to get their students back into the classroom. Here's union president Randi Weingarten blaming the prior administration. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) RANDI WEINGARTEN, PRESIDENT, AMERICAN FEDERATION OF TEACHERS: We had an administration that completely failed, that distorted fact from reality. The same kind of distortions of fact versus untruths have happened when it comes to school reopening. (END VIDEO CLIP) MACCALLUM: Dr. Scott Atlas was part of that White House team, and he responds with his look at the science behind all of this, next. (COMMERCIAL BREAK) MACCALLUM: President Biden said that he hopes to have most kids back in the classroom within his first 100 days, but the clock is ticking. And, you know, by that time, you're going to be close to summer for a lot of these students. Meanwhile, you've got Catholic schools, which are celebrating National Catholic Schools Week this week and it's been quite a year for them. Because across the country they're seeing surging enrollment, they have really set the standard for safe open schools, as the unions continue to blame others for the fact that they are not going back into the classroom. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) WEINGARTEN: We had an administration that completely failed, that distorted fact from reality as everyone has seen because of the big lie and the effects on Washington, DC before January 6th, and then in the aftermath of January 6th. The same kind of distortions of fact versus untruths have happened when it comes to school reopening, and that people of goodwill don't actually even know what the science is, and how to have a roadmap in terms of safely opening. (END VIDEO CLIP) MACCALLUM: All right. Let's bring in Dr. Scott Atlas, former Special Adviser to President Trump and a Stanford University Hoover Institute Senior Fellow. Dr. Atlas, good to have you with us today. You heard Randi Weingarten, the Head of the American Federation for Teachers. She says that there's no pathway, there's no guidance, there's no science involved in the urge across the country to get these teachers back in the classroom. DR. SCOTT ATLAS, FORMER SPECIAL ADVISER TO TRUMP: Yes. Hi, Martha, thanks for having me. Well, you know, this is sort of surreal at this point. It's been known for months and months. I'm talking about eight months that the science the data has said school should be open. And there's no new information that contradicts that, the only new information is confirmatory. From Brown University from Duke University , from all over the world, we know children have very, very little risk of a significant illness. We know that children are not significant spreaders to adults. We know that teachers do not get significant cases when in schools that are open. And we know, overwhelmingly, the harms to children, not the teachers, to children of lack of in-person schools. These people are, I don't know what they're talking about with lie. These are just bizarre statements that have no fact whatsoever. There's been a complete perversion of the term "the science." There is no reason not to open schools. There is nothing special about schools except that they're low risk environments. If I had a job where I wanted to be safe from COVID, I would become a teacher. I mean, these people are just, I don't understand that. In fact, there's no reason, by the way, to prioritize teachers in vaccination programs, teachers are not at high risk. High risk teachers should be prioritized. But, you know, 82% of teachers in the United States are under 55, half of them are under 41. They're a low risk young profession. They should be back at work. I said this months ago, but aren't schools and social business -- MACCALLUM: Yes, you did. You said it on our program and, you know, people give you a hard time. I just want to play for anybody who may have missed it. This is a dance montage that was put together by Chicago teachers. They are in a cooling down period right now because they're about to strike because they don't want to go back to the classroom. But here they are dancing and talking about safety. Let's listen to this for just 20 seconds. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: Make it make sense. Safety is essential. Keep our students and our teachers safe. (END VIDEO CLIP) MACCALLUM: All right. You know that -- I know you couldn't see that, Dr. Atlas, but it's teachers dancing around in their apartments, in their homes, doing interpretive dance and talking about making teaching safe and making children safe, and listening to science. I mean, you know, as you point out, it's like we're living in parallel universes here. Quick thought. ATLAS: Well, you know, I think that at some point, if teachers don't want to work, they should get out of the way and let people do their jobs. There's plenty of people who are unemployed in the country. They are not fit to be teachers if they cannot be critical thinkers and look at the data themselves. I will say that. MACCALLUM: Yes. You know, I think everyone understands if someone has a specific health concern, then they should maybe be in a different category, but most of these people, as you point out, are not in those categories and children are suffering across the country. Dr. Atlas, thank you. Good to have you back on the show. Thanks for being here. ATLAS: Thanks. MACCALLUM: You bet. So, my next guests have been personally impacted by the shutdown of schools in Northern Virginia, Denise Warburton and her son Max, a senior at TC Williams High School join me now. Great to have both of you with us. I know you're at home because where else would you be, right, at this point given the circumstance that's going on. Max, let me start with you. What has life been like for you and do you wish that you could go back to school? MAX CONSTANDY, SENIOR, TC WILLIAMS HIGH SCHOOL: Life at home has been terrible. I have to do Zoom calls along with my barking dogs, and I would really want to go back to school so I can meet someone in-person, and have fun lunches. MACCALLUM: Yes, you want to have lunch and you want to be with your friends, and be in a room. Denise, you know, when you listen to that Chicago teachers' video and, you know, what goes through your mind as you listen to this debate? What do you want to say to these teachers? DENISE WARBURTON, VIRGINIA MOTHER: I think what's hard to see as I have one in the public school and one is in the private school, I've seen that the private schools have gone back successfully in a Hybrid model. They brought them back. None of these kids are falling ill. They're all able to have -- there's a complete change in their demeanor when the days my daughter does actually go to school versus virtual at home. I see my son isolated on home with no social interactions all day. He is on a spectrum. And for a kid with Asperger's to be home alone, with absolutely not a single social interaction all day, is completely detrimental. And to do virtually Zoom social skills groups or occupational therapy groups, they're completely ineffective and not serving these children whatsoever. It's been heartbreaking to see the fact that he's home alone all day and suffering. MACCALLUM: Yes. I know you said that he's gone and looked in the window at school just sort of dreaming about being there, right? WARBURTON: Yes. He -- the Catholic school that he used to attend for 9th and 10th grade is only a block from us. And he knows they're back, and we were pretty much pushed out of the private Catholic school because they said they couldn't serve his needs. They couldn't do enough for social skills. They couldn't do enough for executive functioning. And they kept encouraging us to go to the public school, saying they have more resources. But right now, they don't. They don't and it's been so sad that he's actually walked over to the school. And he's been found peering in their windows and inside their campus trying to interact with the kids. And when I asked him what he's doing. He says, I just want to see my friends. And I just wanted to cry. I just thought that was really poignant. And it just shows how desperate they are to be around other people. MACCALLUM: Absolutely. And, Max, you have a beautiful smile and it's so nice to meet you. And I'm sure that your friends miss you so much, too. And I hope that you can all be back together in the classroom very, very soon. I want to thank both of you for being with us today. Thank you, guys. CONSTANDY: Yes. My friends really missed me so much and desperate to see me go back to school. MACCALLUM: I know they are. And we hope everybody can go back soon. And we thank you very much for being here today, both of you. It's great to meet you. WARBURTON: Thank you, Martha. CONSTANDY: I would also like to thank the people who came and have the suffer studying at home. And I would like for them to go back to school. MACCALLUM: I hear you. I think everybody in the country hears you, Max. Thank you so much, great to have you with us. Thank you, Denise. Thank you both. So coming up, we're going talk to a group of mothers who band together to honor the lives of children lost to violence, by standing up against calls to defund the police in their communities. That is not what they want. They want safer cities. The mothers leading that charge are up next. (COMMERCIAL BREAK) MACCALLUM: A mother says that if a police officer had been at the gas station, the night a stray bullet hit her 19-year-old daughter, her daughter might still be alive today. Now 17 years later, Sylvia Bennett- Stone is leading the Voices of Black Mothers United Initiative. She says, they're coming together to honor the lives of their fallen children by spreading the message, positive police reform not defunding local law enforcement could help stop violence on America's streets. A new study discovered homicides jumped 30% last year compared to 2019, a jump that has no modern precedent in history. Let's bring in Sylvia Bennett-Stone and former civil rights activist, Robert Woodson, Founder and President of the Woodson Center and 1776 Unites. Thank you so much for being here, both of you. ROBERT WOODSON, FOUNDER, WOODSON CENTER: Thank you. SYLVIA BENNETT-STONE, DIRECTOR, VOICES OF BLACK MOTHERS UNITED: Thank you. MACCALLUM: Sylvia, I want to start with you. And tell me why you think it's so important for these mothers who have lost children the way you lost your daughter, to bond together. Because these stories don't get the kind of attention that we see other shootings in this country getting? BENNETT-STONE: Absolutely. We have a network of over 2,500 mothers thus far, and we are assured to be quiet. You bury your child, the fool goes away, and then they want you to go away as well with no resolve. So, we band together to say enough is enough. We're no longer going to be silent. We're going to take a stand, and we are going to help do whatever we can to make our communities safer. We're going to do whatever we can to help save the life of the next child that goes to the gas station. MACCALLUM: Your daughter is beautiful. We have a picture of her up on the screen right now and we are with you, and your grief that I'm sure it doesn't get any easier 17 years down the road. But you hear these calls to defund the police, and you see what happens in the aftermath of some of these shootings. What's your message on that? BENNETT-STONE: We are saying defunding the police is not even an option at all. It's not at all. However, we're coming forward with some solutions. We're saying we want police accountability, of course. No one should have to bury their child as a result of shooting. Either way, whether it's community of police, it hurts, but defunding and taking police out the community is not even an option. MACCALLUM: Robert Woodson, your thoughts on this today? WOODSON: Well, for the past four decades, the Woodson Center has worked with local leaders like Sylvia in successfully preventing youth violence in the cities. The answers are found there, and the monies that are being spent to groups who are calling for the reduction of police or defunding, it is really exacerbating the very prominent, saying that they're trying to solve. So, the Woodson Center is supporting these mothers and as a consequence of the relationship they have with law enforcement, they have increased the closure rates in homicides in cities, and their other crime prevention efforts. MACCALLUM: We thank you both so much. I hope you'll come back when we have more time. Oh, Robert Woodson, thank you so much, sir. We'll see you next time. Sylvia, thank you very much. BENNETT-STONE: Thank you. MACCALLUM: Thank you both. You might not consider yourself someone who cares about a rap song that's climbing the charts. But it is a pretty interesting cultural moment when the tune is called "Fake Woke." It attacks cancel culture, and it questions the Black Lives Matter Movement. The exclusive interview you don't want to miss, next. (COMMERCIAL BREAK) MACCALLUM: A song exploding on the music charts this week with more than 2.5 million views on YouTube in just a couple of days. The viral hit is called "Fake Woke." Canadian rapper Tom McDonald serves up a controversial take on cancel culture and much more. Fox News Headlines 24/7 Reporter Carely Shimkus has just spoken with Tom MacDonald exclusively Hi, Carely, CARELY SHIMKUS, FOX NEWS REPORTER: Hey, Martha. Yes, that's right. It was a very interesting interview. And, you know, it's common for musicians to release politically charged songs these days. But you've probably never heard one quite like this before. Rapper Tom MacDonald rails against cancel culture and censorship in his new song titled "Fake Woke" and his message has been heard by millions. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) TOM MACDONALD, RAPPER: We're ashamed to be American, you should probably love it, because you have the right to hate it and not get stoned to death in public. As children we were taught how to walk and talk, but the system wants adults to sit down and shut up. Cancel culture runs the world now, the planet went crazy. (END VIDEO CLIP) SHIMKUS: Now, McDonald's anti-censorship anthem has racked up over 2.5 million views on YouTube since it was released just four days ago. More impressively, it's currently the number one most downloaded song on iTunes, beating out this year Super Bowl performer, The Weekend and Grammy winner Ed Sheeran. MacDonald believes his music is popular because he is willing to scream what others would never say out loud. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) MACDONALD: This song was just about screaming my truth at the top of my lungs and sort of there's this performative wokeness that's going on in society today. And I think it was just important to point some fingers at the hypocrisy and the way that the world is changing not for the better. (END VIDEO CLIP) SHIMKUS: Now, the 32-year-old is no stranger to tackling hot button issues in a track released last year titled "People So Stupid." He made his feelings on abortion clear, wondering why some don't consider a heartbeat a sign of life. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) MACDONALD: Let's talk about abortion, sorry, tell me how this works. Bacteria is life on Mars but a heartbeat isn't life on Earth? Weird. (END VIDEO CLIP) SHIMKUS: In another song, he discussed Black Lives Matter calling it a valuable movement, but adding all lives matter isn't racist or stupid. Supporters call his stance refreshing but critics have accused him of racism and homophobia. One Twitter user writing, if someone listens to Tom MacDonald cut them off completely. Another tweeting, if you like Tom MacDonald, you got to be racist. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) MACDONALD: I know who I am. My friends and my family know who I am. My fans know who I am. If I see something on TV, I change the channel. If I'm reading something I don't like I close the book. Like I don't try to call the radio station and call the people who were on TV names and try to cancel them or call the publishing company that published the book that I don't like, and try and get the author cancelled. (END VIDEO CLIP) SHIMKUS: And while MacDonald has the most popular song on iTunes right now and 1.6 million followers on YouTube , he is doing it only with the help of his girlfriend who shoots all of his music videos. He does not have a manager, a record label, a publicist or PR team. He also doesn't get a lot of media attention. He attributes this to not fitting in with today's accepted narrative. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) MACDONALD: People have become allergic to opinions in North America and these last five years, and it's pretty soon like they're going to cancel everything. And all we're going to have is tall gray buildings and quiet car rides. And then, we're all going to be kicking ourselves in the butt for this craziness. (END VIDEO CLIP) SHIMKUS: And while you may think he's conservative, MacDonald says he doesn't support either political party. He thinks the most important thing is to have moderate voices instead of the political polarization facing America today, Martha. MACCALLUM: Carely, thank you, very interesting interview, a controversial rapper with a pretty strong message, interesting to hear from him. I also just want to do a shout out to my friend, Charles Gubish. She was 102 years old today. He is one of the featured veterans of Iwo Jima in my book "Unknown Valor." So that's Tuesday, February 2nd, happy birthday, Charlie. THE STORY goes on. We'll see you back here at 3:00 tomorrow. "Your World with Neil Cavuto" starts right now. headline: White House Press Briefing Underway; Biden Signs New Exec Orders In Unprecedented Blitz; McConnell Slams Biden Executive Orders
story_text: (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) JEN PSAKI, WHITE HOUSE PRESS SECRETARY: Well, the president talked about his commitment to putting together a commission for reunifying families. He remains committed to that, and we'll have more to share on that soon. Go ahead, all the way in back. RAQUEL KRAHENBUHL, WHITE HOUSE CORRESPONDENT, GLOBO NEWS T.V., BRAZIL: Thank you so much, Jen. Raquel Krahenbuhl from T.V. Global Brazil. I have two questions. Going back to the climate crisis, during the campaign, President Biden warned of economic consequences if Brazil did not reduce deforestation on the Amazon. I'm wondering what kind of consequences he's considering, if it could hurt, for example, the trading negotiations with Brazil or the OECD support? PSAKI: Well, we just announced yesterday that we're going to be doing a climate summit coming up in the next couple of months. And, of course, this is a big priority for President Biden. And that's why he asked his good friend former Secretary Kerry to lead our climate international effort. And, certainly, Brazil will be a key partner in that. But in terms of what those negotiations and discussions look like, it's a little too early for that at this point. And I'd certainly send you to the State Department and Secretary Kerry's office for more details. KRAHENBUHL: OK, so just a follow-up. Did he invite the Brazilian president, will he invite for the summit? And is also President Biden still planning to label countries as climate outlaws? And if so, would Brazil be part of this list? PSAKI: Well, we're not quite there yet, given we just announced it. There haven't been invites or anything that went out. But we're happy to keep everybody updated. And, certainly, as the United States is a large emitter, so is Brazil, so is China, so are many large countries and large economies, and we all have a role to play in addressing this crisis. KRAHENBUHL: One more question, Jen. When does President Biden think he will be able to start doing -- or he will do his first international trip? And where it would be the first place he would go? PSAKI: I don't have anything to preview or predict for you at this point. As you know, we haven't done any domestic travel yet, given COVID. So, I certainly don't have any predictions about a foreign trip. Go ahead, Sabrina. SABRINA SIDDIQUI, WHITE HOUSE REPORTER, THE WALL STREET JOURNAL: Sure, I had a question. At her confirmation hearing yesterday, U.N. ambassador- designate Linda Thomas-Greenfield said she believed that BDS, the Boycott, Divestment, Sanctions movement to pressure Israel, is unacceptable and borders on -- or verges on anti-Semitism. Is that a characterization that the White House shares when it comes to the BDS movement ? PSAKI: I don't have anything more for you on kind of our position. It's, I think, been -- the president has spoken to this as a candidate and prior as vice president, but I don't have anything new. And I'm happy to get back to you if there's anything I can get to you from the national security team. Go ahead. ROB CRILLY, WHITE HOUSE CORRESPONDENT, THE WASHINGTON EXAMINER: Thank you. Rob Crilly with The Washington Examiner. Just to actually follow up on that, Linda Thomas-Greenfield also said she would be standing against the unfair targeting of Israel, the (INAUDIBLE) resolutions that are proposed against Israel (INAUDIBLE). Is that the position of the White House? PSAKI: You know, I didn't see her full hearing yesterday. Actually, I didn't see any of her hearing. I'm happy to review it and take a look and see if there's more we can speak to from our end. CRILLY: (INAUDIBLE) back to the executive orders, the questions we were discussing at the start. So, I'm still trying to sort of reconcile this daily -- what are we at? I think we're at 26 orders now and reconcile that with the campaign rhetoric, because, in October, Joe Biden said there were limitations on the use of executive actions, things he can't do by executive order, unless you're a dictator. They have set a goal of getting most K through eight students back into the classroom in this first 100 days. Trace. GALLAGHER: Jeff Paul live for us in Los Angeles. Jeff, thank you. Let's bring in former Texas Congressman and Physician Ron Paul. Congressman, Dr. Paul, thank you for joining us, sir. The gentleman we showed at the top, the parent in Loudoun County, Virginia who's so upset. The reason partly he's upset is because they've got 6,000 teachers in Loudon County who have already had their first round of vaccinations, and they still won't go back to the classroom even though the CDC says the five studies that they have cited, show there is very low risk of transmission. Parents are frustrated, and a lot of people think they have a right to be. RON PAUL (R), FORMER TEXAS CONGRESSMAN: It's such a tragedy because the suicide and the death (inaudible) school is just tragic. It's preventable, and they don't change. They're even talking about maybe we will let them back in but they'll have to have the mask and the social distancing. It's not going to do it. They should look to the statistics of the states that never locked him out of their schools, and they've done quite well. It doesn't stop the disease but it stops the complication. Well, we've suffered from it the most of past year. I think 90% of it has been the lockdown. The economic crisis has come, the economic consequences. And right now, they're talking about what we have to. You know, look at what happened to the elderly in the nursing homes in New York. Everybody knows that story, but there's stories out now that the elderly are going to be the most vulnerable to get the vaccine because their immune systems are down, so government management of a delicate situation of a medical problem where it shouldn't be patient, the doctor making decisions. It's a tragedy. It was preventable. It's really sad. GALLAGHER: I know you're a doctor, I know you're concerned about these kids health, their mental health specifically. We talked about the suicide rate in Las Vegas, 18 suicides in nine months. I want to put these numbers on the screen for you, Dr. Paul, because I think it's important to know that mental health related visits for children increased during the pandemic. Ages 5 to 11 up 24%, ages 12 to 17, up 31%. There is clearly an impact on our children across the country by remote learning. R. PAUL: Oh, there's no doubt about it. And these parents are the only thing left to try to wake people up and that, you know, the dad was pretty upset than he should be. And that's what's going to have to happen, have to have a lot more people, you know, get excited about this to do something about it. But right now, it looks like it's going to continue, but there's some special interest behind so many of the problems that have come out of lockdown. And when you think about it, who's the strongest defenders of gifted kids and keep the kids out of school forever. And we know where that comes from. GALLAGHER: Sure. R. PAUL: It happens to be the teachers themselves. That's a shame, why do you want people like that being the teachers. GALLAGHER: The Teachers Unions have a great deal of influence in a lot of these states around the country. I want to play the sound bite because you're a doctor, I want to get this I want to play Dr. Fauci and the contradictory information we're getting watch. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) FAUCI: If you have a physical covering with one layer, you put another layer on it just makes common sense that it likely would be more effective. And that's the reason why you see people either double masking or doing a version of an N95. DR. ROCHELLE WALENSKY, DIRECTOR, CDC: I do think that if everybody is wearing a mask, if you're wearing it, if you're six feet apart, and you're wearing -- anybody else who you might be with is also wearing a mask, that you have enough protective efficacy in the barriers of those two masks and the space between you, then you probably don't need it. (END VIDEO CLIP) GALLAGHER: Fauci says double mask, the CDC director, the new one, says you need a single mask. Is this contradictory information we have been getting from the start? Your final thoughts about 15 seconds, Dr. Paul. R. PAUL: Well, I would say for a gentleman who's making the most money of anybody in the government in the bureaucracy, he's giving out bad information is not very scientific to talk like that. Today, there was somebody came out and says if who's good, I recommend and this was a sign, you know, because I don't call on much of assignment. He says, make it for if it's not (inaudible) a group that mask it didn't ask the mask have not prevented any significant disease. GALLAGHER: Yes. Congressman, former congressman, Dr. Paul, thank you, sir, for coming on. R. PAUL: Sure thing, thanks. GALLAGHER: Well, Lara Logan on the reversal to Trump era immigration policies in the pipeline. That's coming up next. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) JOE BIDEN, PRESIDENT OF UNITED STATES: You come to the United States and you make your case that you've seek asylum based on the following premise, why I deserve it under American law. They're sitting in squalor on the other side of the river. (END VIDEO CLIP) (COMMERCIAL BREAK) GALLAGHER: Well, several immigration orders are on the back burner until next week, including President Biden's plans for a task force to reunite families separated at the border, and an increase in the number of refugees allowed into the US. National Correspondent Jacqui Heinrich has the details from Capitol Hill. Jacqui? JACQUI HEINRICH, NATIONAL CORRESPONDENT: Good afternoon to you, Trace. Well, President Biden doesn't want to repeat President Obama's mistake of waiting too long to pursue comprehensive immigration reform with the midterms on the horizon. So now, Democrats are breaking up a bill that Biden revealed his first day in office into smaller pieces that could get bipartisan support to strike while the iron is hot. And one of the first pieces we might see is a bill dealing with TPS DREAMers and DACA. Democratic Senator Dick Durbin is working with Republican Senator Lindsey Graham on a package modeled off previous legislation they introduced in 2019 that would provide permanent residency and a path to citizenship for immigrants brought to the US as children who meet education and work requirements. Now, the proposal may include some of the items the Biden package proposed, like automatic green cards for those groups, but the talks are still early. Durbin told me the hope is that this base bill could be expedited and serve as a kicking off point for broader negotiations. And Senator Graham also told Fox he wants to work in border security provisions, but said comprehensive reform will be an uphill battle because Democrats stopped building the wall. Now, one Democratic senator told me they've got support from a few quote "hardline" Republicans who you wouldn't expect, and because the country just spent billions of dollars on border security, there's more support than previous years to do something about DACA and DREAMers. But still, there's plenty of pushback from Republicans, Senator Rick Scott wrote to the acting DHS Secretary yesterday, "Securing our border is the most important thing we can do to protect our citizens and the thousands of individuals working their way through the legal immigration process. We can make much needed reforms to our broken system, but it has to start with securing the border." And the White House tells me that Biden has not all out endorsed this but understands that immigration cannot be an all or nothing approach. And in the meantime, those executive orders Biden was expected to sign tomorrow have been delayed until next week. Future reforms include establishing that task force for families separated at the border and also increasing refugee admissions. Trace GALLAGHER: Jacqui Heinrich live for us on Capitol Hill, Jacqui, thank you. Let's bring in Fox Nation Host Lara Logan. Her new series, "Laura Logan Has No Agenda Return to the Border" starts Monday, February 1st. Lara, it's always great to see you. As always your reporting on this is exceptional, very compelling. I want to play a clip of it, and then get your response on the other side. Watch. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) LARA LOGAN, HOST: In Biden administration, you're not going have a job. MARK MORGAN, BORDER PATROL COMMISSIONER: Correct. LOGAN: There's also no deportations for 100 days, what else? MORGAN: Oh, it keeps going. If you look at the entire immigration strategy that has been talked about, it will systematically undo everything that's been done for the past four years, that has absolutely been successful. (END VIDEO CLIP) GALLAGHER: Yes. I mean, talking with Mark Morgan there, he's right. I mean, illegal immigration, they're still coming through, I mean, there's still some of the drugs coming through, but not at the levels that we have seen. Lara, what are your thoughts on this? LOGAN: Well, this is their reality, the warning orders that border agencies have been given under the new guidelines from the new administration will shut down all of the internal checkpoints. So, the last line of defense that's about, you know, 80 miles from the border, for example, will go first. It will move all of those resources, they're preparing for a surge of people. So, the new administration's plan is built around expecting, you know, thousands and thousands of people to come into the United States. The special units like hospitals, and boat units, and ATVs, those will be taken off their normal duties, their security operations. And they'll be put with, along with most of the other resources on migrant care, right? So, what you're doing is defining the border in terms of immigration, as opposed to border security, or as opposed to an approach that, you know, sort of that balances the both of them. And this is where the real issue comes in, is that for border security operations, the reality is that the cartels in Mexico, they know perfectly well how to exploit the flow and the movement of people. And they use that as a cover. So that's when they move the kind of people high value, you know, sort of people who are paying a lot more money to come in to the US undetected, whether they're spies or terrorists, or hackers or whoever it happens to be. That's when they're moving more the drugs. That's when they're moving their cash. That's when they're moving the weapons. That's when they're moving everything. They exploit that issue. And as long as it's only defined as a conversation about immigration, then you don't address the security issues. GALLAGHER: And I think we should point out that there's a reason they're coming. I mean, the whole idea is the senior national security fellow at the Center for Immigration Studies said the following here, "I've just returned from interviewing migrants in Juarez, without exception, all of them had been made expected and excited that they will be able to come into the US with no fear or possibility of rejection or later deportation." He's right. I mean, these migrants are on social media, they know what's going on in the United States. They know the climate is changing rapidly, Lara. LOGAN: Well, look at what some of the leaders are saying. I mean, that leaders -- the statement from Honduras, when the migrant caravan that's heading for the US right now, came up against Guatemalan forces, when they forced their way into Guatemala, and two people were killed. The Honduran statement was that migration is a right, is a human rights. So they're coming up with, you know, with government, given human rights versus what the US Constitution protects, which is God given rights, right? There's a distinction there, and those lines are being blurred in border policy. And yes, there are lots and lots, and lots of people being interviewed and picked up were saying, we know that Biden is coming into power. We know that now we can stay. And this is why, Trace, because this is what will change. Before border patrol agents would apprehend you, you'd be processed. It's a long process, right? That's when you'd see people in so called cages, right? GALLAGHER: Right. LOGAN: That's in detention processing centers, facilities, right? Because you're trying to figure out who they are. If you have someone coming from China, and I've seen many Chinese people trying to -- crossing the border illegally when I've been down there. And they say, this is my name, this is where I'm from, how do you prove that? How do you know who they are? You think the Chinese Communist Party is telling you, you know, everything you want to know this person has a criminal record or whatever? No. I mean, the reality is they have no idea who's coming. So there was a detailed process, now, you'll be given a notice to appear with five years, Trace, have your fingerprints and biometrics taken, and everyone except convicted felons will be led into the country. GALLAGHER: Lara, I've got about literally 15 seconds for you. LOGAN: And to be legal. When they let you go, you'll be legal. GALLAGHER: 15 seconds, what's the big takeaway from this special? 15 seconds left. LOGAN: The big takeaway is that we are really in the midst of the most unprecedented narcotics crisis. Fentanyl is a synthetic. It's the deadliest drug we've ever seen. And the quantities flooding US streets are phenomenal. They're mixed with cocaine, they're mixed with meth, they're mixed with marijuana, and they're making fake pills. Your kid is not taking Adderall if they got it on the street. GALLAGHER: Yes, got it. Look forward to it very much. Thanks for coming on. That's "The Story" for Thursday, January 26th. As always, "The Story" continues. I'll see you back here tomorrow. headline: White House Press Briefing Underway; Biden Signs New Exec Orders In Unprecedented Blitz; McConnell Slams Biden Executive Orders
story_text: (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) JEN PSAKI, WHITE HOUSE PRESS SECRETARY: Well, the president talked about his commitment to putting together a commission for reunifying families. He remains committed to that, and we'll have more to share on that soon. Go ahead, all the way in back. RAQUEL KRAHENBUHL, WHITE HOUSE CORRESPONDENT, GLOBO NEWS T.V., BRAZIL: Thank you so much, Jen. Raquel Krahenbuhl from T.V. Global Brazil. I have two questions. Going back to the climate crisis, during the campaign, President Biden warned of economic consequences if Brazil did not reduce deforestation on the Amazon. I'm wondering what kind of consequences he's considering, if it could hurt, for example, the trading negotiations with Brazil or the OECD support? PSAKI: Well, we just announced yesterday that we're going to be doing a climate summit coming up in the next couple of months. And, of course, this is a big priority for President Biden. And that's why he asked his good friend former Secretary Kerry to lead our climate international effort. And, certainly, Brazil will be a key partner in that. But in terms of what those negotiations and discussions look like, it's a little too early for that at this point. And I'd certainly send you to the State Department and Secretary Kerry's office for more details. KRAHENBUHL: OK, so just a follow-up. Did he invite the Brazilian president, will he invite for the summit? And is also President Biden still planning to label countries as climate outlaws? And if so, would Brazil be part of this list? PSAKI: Well, we're not quite there yet, given we just announced it. There haven't been invites or anything that went out. But we're happy to keep everybody updated. And, certainly, as the United States is a large emitter, so is Brazil, so is China, so are many large countries and large economies, and we all have a role to play in addressing this crisis. KRAHENBUHL: One more question, Jen. When does President Biden think he will be able to start doing -- or he will do his first international trip? And where it would be the first place he would go? PSAKI: I don't have anything to preview or predict for you at this point. As you know, we haven't done any domestic travel yet, given COVID. So, I certainly don't have any predictions about a foreign trip. Go ahead, Sabrina. SABRINA SIDDIQUI, WHITE HOUSE REPORTER, THE WALL STREET JOURNAL: Sure, I had a question. At her confirmation hearing yesterday, U.N. ambassador- designate Linda Thomas-Greenfield said she believed that BDS, the Boycott, Divestment, Sanctions movement to pressure Israel, is unacceptable and borders on -- or verges on anti-Semitism. Is that a characterization that the White House shares when it comes to the BDS movement ? PSAKI: I don't have anything more for you on kind of our position. It's, I think, been -- the president has spoken to this as a candidate and prior as vice president, but I don't have anything new. And I'm happy to get back to you if there's anything I can get to you from the national security team. Go ahead. ROB CRILLY, WHITE HOUSE CORRESPONDENT, THE WASHINGTON EXAMINER: Thank you. Rob Crilly with The Washington Examiner. Just to actually follow up on that, Linda Thomas-Greenfield also said she would be standing against the unfair targeting of Israel, the (INAUDIBLE) resolutions that are proposed against Israel (INAUDIBLE). Is that the position of the White House? PSAKI: You know, I didn't see her full hearing yesterday. Actually, I didn't see any of her hearing. I'm happy to review it and take a look and see if there's more we can speak to from our end. CRILLY: (INAUDIBLE) back to the executive orders, the questions we were discussing at the start. So, I'm still trying to sort of reconcile this daily -- what are we at? I think we're at 26 orders now and reconcile that with the campaign rhetoric, because, in October, Joe Biden said there were limitations on the use of executive actions, things he can't do by executive order, unless you're a dictator. We're a democracy. We need consensus. I think you said earlier that some of these executive orders were being used to roll back some of the immoral things that the previous administration had done. If you're calling these things immoral, is that seeking consensus and unity? And then also, does it suggest that President Biden sees himself as perhaps a benevolent dictator? PSAKI: Well, Rob, I'm sure this wasn't your intention, but I think you took the president's comments a bit out of context. He was asked about tax reform, and whether that could be done via executive order during the interview with George Stephanopoulos, which you're referring to. CRILLY: (INAUDIBLE) question, but I think the answer -- (CROSSTALK) PSAKI: Well, I think -- I think the question is pretty important context for everybody. And he said no. And the president also said during an interview with columnists back in December that he didn't think executive action should be used for everything. And that certainly is his point of view. But there are steps, including overturning some of the harmful, detrimental and, yes, immoral actions of the prior administration that he felt he could not wait to overturn. And that's exactly what he did. Now, any historian will tell you that he walked into the presidency at one of the most difficult moments in history. That required additional executive action in order to take -- get immediate relief to the American people. But he believes, as is law -- as everybody knows how a bill becomes a law, is that, in order to make action and policy permanent, you need to work with Congress. That's why he's also proposed a COVID relief package, a big, bold package. Some say very big -- I agree with that -- and also an immigration bill. He has not -- he has not held back or delayed putting forth legislation either. So, he is going to use the levers that every president in history has used, executive actions. But he also feels it is important to work Congress, and not just one party, but both parties to get things done. Go ahead in the back. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: Thank you, Jen. A couple of questions. One technical question on the E.O. signed today. Does the --does the E.O. on ACA open the marketplace to noncitizens, to legal residents or undocumented immigrants that may be able to benefit from the extra care? PSAKI: It doesn't change the requirements for qualifying for the Affordable Care Act. It opens it up for three months for people who would be already eligible for the Affordable Care Act. So -- but, obviously, there are -- you know, the Health and Human Services team will continue to look for ways to expand access. I will say -- you didn't ask this, but this is a common question, so I'm just going to proactively answer it -- that we do feel, as an administration, that ensuring that all people in the United States, undocumented immigrants as well, of course, should receive access to a vaccine, because that one is morally right, but also ensures that people in the country are also safe. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: And that was my second question. PSAKI: Oh, all right, good. (CROSSTALK) UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: How are you guiding the states -- PSAKI: Actually, yes. OK. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: How are you guiding the states? PSAKI: It's a common one. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: Yes. How are you guiding the states, if any -- in any way to get those undocumented communities to come forward to get vaccinated? Many of them in the states just don't have any way to prove that they're residents of those states in order to go to their local clinics and prove residency to get the vaccine. So, how are you working with the states to get that done? PSAKI: It's challenging. We have talked about this a little bit in here. I mean, there's obviously vaccine hesitancy, which certainly exists in communities of undocumented immigrants and the concern of what it will mean for their status. And -- but we are focused on ensuring we get the vaccine out broadly into communities across the country, because that will make the American people safer. And it's something we have to be both creative about, aggressive about, ambitious about. It's one of the reasons we need additional funding through the American Rescue Plan, but one -- also one of the reasons why we plan to have an aggressive public education campaign to help embolden and empower local doctors and authorities. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: Let me ask one more on Cuba. Do you guys plan on starting -- walking back all of those restrictions that were put into place under the Trump administration, after the Obama administration had opened things up with Cuba? PSAKI: Well, our Cuba policy is governed by two principles. First, support for democracy and human rights. That will be at the core of our efforts. Second is Americans, especially Cuban Americans, are the best ambassadors for freedom in Cuba. So, we'll review the Trump administration policies, as we are in a number of other areas of national security, with an eye to assure -- ensuring that our approach is aligned with that. But, you know, we will take our own path. I don't -- I don't have anything to predict for you at this point in time. Go ahead, (INAUDIBLE). UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: I wanted to clarify something. You talked a little bit about the administration's stance on school re-openings yesterday. PSAKI: Sure. (CROSSTALK) PSAKI: I wasn't -- I wasn't really clear on that. So, I got a little better information. (LAUGHTER) UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: (INAUDIBLE) indicated that he believes, that the administration believes that schools need more funding for them to be safe enough to reopen for students to go back. But there's been a number of studies, including the recent one out of the CDC, that have shown evidence that schools are perfectly safe for students to go back. And there were recommendations that they should go back. So, this seems like a bit of a dispute between teachers' unions and sort of data and the science. So, where does the administration stand in that dispute? PSAKI: Well, first, let me be absolutely clear. President Biden wants schools to open and he wants them to stay open, because it's obviously very disruptive for families -- I'm a mother -- you know, for anyone has kids, for kids to come in and out of school. But that means making sure, as you said, that every school is able to have the equipment and resources to open safely, not just rural schools or private schools, which often is where a lot of the school re-openings and schools staying open is happening. It's more of a challenge in public schools, where they don't have that funding from tuition or smaller populations, where it's easier to put in place the actions needed to keep the schools open. But the CDC study, which I know has gotten a lot -- received a lot of attention, was based on kind of an area that was more rural in Wisconsin. It was not -- and I think what Dr. Walensky has said is that -- I think she said this on CNN last night -- is that for areas where they are more populated, where schools where there is a lot more foot traffic, that there are going to need to be a lot of steps put in place in order to make the schools reopening safe. But we are committed to doing that. That's why the President signed an executive order last week supporting the safe reopening of schools. It requires the Departments of Education and CDC to provide evidence- based guidance. So, that will include things like testing, smaller class sizes, more ventilation, better cleaning, PPE, strong state and local public health guidance. But we want to provide that clarity from the federal government, because there's a lot of confusion. And public schools especially don't know what steps they need to take, how to ensure they're safe. Those are all decisions that are going to be made locally. But we want to give them the guidance. That's in process. Our team is working on that, Dr. Walensky at the CDC and our health experts. And we hope to have more specifics soon. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: Maybe two more questions. PSAKI: Go ahead. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: So, Americans' savings rate is -- has been up throughout the pandemic. And so, I'm wondering, why give all Americans a $1,400 check? And why not means test for the relief that your administration is talking about? PSAKI: Well, first, the proposed checks, I mean, the -- have the same criteria as the package that received broad bipartisan support in December, right? So, approximately, the $1,400 checks would go to families making approximately $150,000 a year. There's a scaling up, as I think you're referencing, up to about $300,000. I think you all are aware of this, but just for everybody else. And, you know, there has been some questions about that. President Biden, our economic team, we're open to discussing that. But we want to ensure that the families that need relief, that need assistance get it. And I would say, at a time where we saw the economic data today -- and this was reflected in Brian Deese's statement -- it was worse than any week -- I don't want to misquote myself here -- that we saw during the Great Recession. I mean, people are suffering. Thousands -- millions of people are out of work. People don't know how to put food on the table. These challenges are real. We -- the data shows it, but we also see long lines for food pantries. We see, you know, people who are out of work and don't know what they're going to do to make ends meet. And so that's tangible. That's real. And we want the package -- the package is going to need to be big and bold to address that. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: And then since we have been talking about women's health and access to abortion today, does the administration plan to suspend the requirement that the medication abortion pill be picked up in person? I know that that's something that advocates have been pushing for after the reversal under the Trump administration. PSAKI: Yes, I have certainly seen some reporting and questions about that. I will have to talk to our health team about that specifically. KRAHENBUHL: Can I ask one more about the travel restrictions? PSAKI: Sure. Go ahead. And, Kaitlan, then I will go to you. (CROSSTALK) KRAHENBUHL: A lot of our viewers are asking if there will be any kind of consideration for waivers for students or unmarried couple like fiances, since there is now the requirement for testing and quarantine? PSAKI: Well, I know there's been a lot of coverage of this and questions, because this is -- these are people's lives and human beings who are missing their loved ones and their family members. And just to restate what the requirements are now, so spouses of American citizens and lawful permanent residents are able to travel under these restrictions we have put in place on international travel, although they have to take part in the mandatory pre-departure testing that applies to everyone. And we are reviewing and assessing, I should say, how students and unmarried couples -- and how we can proceed with that moving forward. I don't have anything to preview for you. But we're certainly -- our team is looking into that. KRAHENBUHL: (INAUDIBLE) criteria. Why countries with high numbers like Russia or India or Mexico are not on the list? PSAKI: Well, our health and medical team takes a close look at what restrictions we need to put in place in order to keep the American people safe. And that's how we review it. It's not about geopolitics. It was at times in the prior administration. That's not how we approach things. It's about where we need to put restrictions in place to keep the American people safe. I promised Kaitlan she would get the next one. KAITLAN COLLINS, CHIEF WHITE HOUSE CORRESPONDENT, CNN: So, just to get some clarification on the CDC study about schools being good to reopen if precautions are taking, is the White House position that it needs to be further studied, since you're citing just the one school in Wisconsin, or does the White House agree with the recommendations from the CDC about schools reopening? PSAKI: Well, the CDC hasn't issued the formal recommendations or requirements on how all schools across the country can open. They did a report, as they do reports frequently, based on an area in Wisconsin, important -- interesting data, no doubt. But that is not reflective of every school district and community in the country. And so, they will be coming out with more specific requirements -- or more specific, I should say, guidelines for the public, because there are schools that are in much more highly populated areas. There are schools that have far more kids in classrooms, far more kids walking into the school. And they want to ensure that there's clarity on testing needs, class size needs, you know, public health guidance that people can abide by. But, you know, their recommendation is that K through 12 schools should be the last settings to close after all of these mitigation measures have been employed and the first to reopen. So, we all want schools to open and be open for good. What I'm reflecting on -- or what I'm trying to clarify, I guess, is that, you know, schools in cities are dealing with different challenges than schools in rural communities, and schools in Wisconsin may be dealing in different challenges than schools in, you know -- you know, downtown Atlanta, right? So, there needs to be kind of -- the CDC will issue more specific guidelines soon. They're focused on it now. COLLINS: OK. And last question on this. So, President Biden has said he wants all schools to reopen in his first 100 days. Is that still the goal if Congress does not pass this proposal, which has the money for schools, which Ron Klain and others have said is what they believe schools need to reopen? PSAKI: I sense skepticism about the bill getting passed. We don't feel that. Look, I think the reason -- COLLINS: We have to go through everything. PSAKI: I know. That's your job. Look, I think, Kaitlan, one of the reasons why we're so focused on the American Rescue Plan and getting it urgently passed through Congress is because we need this funding in order for schools to reopen and for them to have the support to ensure that they have proper ventilation, better cleaning, testing, PPE. That's a key component of the package. And that's one of the reasons we're not going to negotiate out that versus vaccine funding or, you know, unemployment insurance, because that's a key component. And we need that to ensure that schools will have the resources across the country to be able to reopen. And that's exactly what the President wants to happen. COLLINS: Thank you, Jen. PSAKI: Thank you. Oh, OK, we're good. She was very patient. Go ahead. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: Thank you. I just wonder if there is a general sense of frustration just about the pace of things, you know, given the vaccine distribution, you know, some of what you inherited from the Trump administration, trying to roll out executive orders, you know, working with Congress, and sort of having some lawmakers raise concerns. Is it harder to change things than you all thought it would be? (LAUGHTER) PSAKI: I'm only laughing because we're on our eighth day here. So, you know -- and in that period of time, the President has signed multiple executive orders. He has proposed several comprehensive bills. He's had many conversations with members of Congress about the urgency of getting things done. And I will say, in those conversations, there is an understanding and agreement about the urgency of addressing these issues. story_text: MARTHA MACCALLUM, FOX NEWS ANCHOR: Thank you very much, guys. Thank you, John, and Sandra. And we expect that we're going to hear a lot more student debt and other issues that we will address very soon. So it's all part of a massive wave of executive orders and actions, that in sheer numbers surpasses anything that we have seen in the early days of prior presidents. Axios describing these first three days of the first 100 as regulatory a quote, Biden's centrist words, and liberal actions, writing Biden talks like a soothing centrist, he promises to govern like a soothing centrist, but early moves show that he is keeping his promise to advance a liberal agenda.
