story_text: [19:00:00] (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) LESTER HOLT, NBC NEWS ANCHOR: Tonight, the desperate surge in the North Atlantic for a missing submersible near the Titanic. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) HOLT (voiceover): The U.S. and Canadian coast guard scouring for a sub- carrying five people. Contact lost for more than 24 hours as the tourist vessel made its way toward the Titanic 12,000 feet down. Rough seas, rain, and fog hampering the surge in rescue efforts for those on board, including a billionaire businessman and explorer. Late details just in tonight. Also tonight, the high-stakes summit between China`s President Xi Jinping and Secretary of State Anthony Blinken . A chance to reset rising tensions that have only gotten worse since the U.S. shot down a spy balloon. Our one-on-one interview with the Secretary of State. The nonstop threat of tornadoes, one dead and almost two dozen injured as multiple tornadoes tear through Mississippi. The search for survivors. A weekend of mass shooting, some of them deadly. But when it happened twice last month in another country, they took quick and decisive action. Richard Engel is there. The new boom in building, not to buy, but to rent. What`s behind it in our series "PRICED OUT." On Juneteenth, celebrations across America and a field of dreams reborn as a testament to the past. (END VIDEO CLIP) ANNOUNCER: This is NBC NIGHTLY NEWS with Lester Holt. HOLT (on camera): Good evening and welcome. Tonight, near the site of one of the 20th century`s worst ocean disasters, a new undersea drama is unfolding. Right now, the U.S. Coast Guard leading the urgent search for a group of modern-day adventurers after the submersible carrying them to the Titanic shipwreck lost contact with the surface yesterday about an hour and 45 minutes into their journey. Five people are on board the vessel which is used to carry paying passengers to see the Titanic up close. The search happening about 350 miles off the coast of Newfoundland in waters more than two miles deep. Tonight, the company that runs the deep sea charters, Ocean Gate Expeditions, saying in a statement, our entire focus is on the crew members and their families. Tom Costello has late-breaking developments for us. (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) TOM COSTELLO, NBC NEWS CORRESPONDENT (voiceover): U.S. and Canadian Coast Guard ships are this hour rushing to the North Atlantic as two U.S. C-130 planes surveyed the vast ocean surface for any signs of a private submersible and the five people on board, last seen Sunday morning as it descended to survey the wreck of the Titanic. REAR ADM. JOHN MAUGER, COMMANDER, U.S. COAST GUARD FIRST DISTRICT: During the course of the dive, they lost communications and we have not had communications with the submersible since then. COSTELLO (voiceover): The 21-foot submersible named Titan, made of titanium and carbon fiber, is owned by Ocean Gate, an operator of small subs for research, film production, and tourist trips to the Titanic for $250,000. On board a pilot and four passengers, including billionaire adventurer Hamish Harding, who had taken a submersible to the Mariana Trench and flown in space on Jeff Bezos ` Blue Origin . On his Instagram account Sunday, he signed his name on the logo as he announced he`d be diving to the Titanic. His company later tweeted, 4:00 a.m. start this morning on the RMS Titanic Mission 5. The sub had a successful launch and Hamish is currently diving. Today, Ocean Gate said our entire focus is on the crew members in the submersible and their families. We are working toward the safe return of the crew members. The CEO told our Seattle KING 5 last August he caters to Titanic enthusiasts. STOCKTON RUSH , CEO, OCEAN GATE: We have a number of people who come with us, who sometimes we referred to as Titaniacs, people who have just been consumed by the Titanic. And it was just great to take them down. COSTELLO (voiceover): The Titanic rests at treacherous depths, 12,500 feet below the surface. 1,500 people died when she sank in 1912. The missing sub was only supposed to be gone for six to eight hours with 96 hours of reserve oxygen. Already, Canadian P-8 search planes have dropped sonar buoys on the rough seas, listening for the sub in a deep, vast expanse of ocean. COSTELLO: Are they listening for voices? What could they pick up? MAUGER: We`re hoping that they can pick up any unusual sounds, maybe tapping on the hull or voices or those types of things, any signs of the vassal mare in the water. And that`s why we`ve really pressed in with the capabilities that we have. (END VIDEOTAPE) HOLT: Now, Tom as I understand it, submersible are meant to dive much deeper than say, a typical Navy sub. If the Coast Guard can locate it under the surface, can they get to it? [19:05:03] COSTELLO (on camera): They can`t. That`s the problem. They don`t have the deep-sea rescue capabilities that the Navy has. So, both the U.S. and the Canadian navies are rushing those assets to the scene as well as contacting private companies who have those capabilities. But if they find this crew, it`s going to be a very, very challenging rescue operation and the clock is ticking, Lester. HOLT: All right, Tom Castello, thank you. Let`s turn out of that critical meeting in China today between President Xi Jinping and Secretary of State Antony Blinken with relations at a low point. Blinken now touting progress at an interview with Janis Mackey Frayer. (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) ANTONY BLINKEN , U.S. SECRETARY OF STATE: Good afternoon. JANIS MACKEY FRAYER, NBC NEWS FOREIGN CORRESPONDENT (voiceover): Tonight, a high-stakes visit to Beijing, capped by a handshake. Secretary of State Antony Blinken meeting China`s President Xi Jinping for 35 minutes to stop what officials call a downward spiral in relations. BLINKEN: Direct engagement and sustained communication at senior levels is the best way to responsibly manage our differences and ensure that competition does not veer into conflict. FRAYER (voiceover): Xi`s message to Blinken, I hope that through this visit, Mr. Secretary, you`ll make more positive contributions to stabilizing China-U.S. relations. There`s no shortage of flashpoints here, tension over Taiwan, China`s role in the fentanyl crisis, unanswered questions about the origins of COVID. Chinese officials not holding back on their grievances either, like U.S. export bans on technology. Tonight, in an interview with NBC News, Blinken said the two-day visit has stabilized ties, at least for now. BLINKEN: Both China and the United States, I think, recognized that we were in an increasingly unstable place in our relationship. I think this is the start of a process to put a little more stability into it. FRAYER (voiceover): But China refused Blinken`s request to reopen military crisis lines that were cut off by Beijing nearly a year ago. Since then some close calls, including this Chinese warship sailing within 150 yards of a U.S. destroyer in the Taiwan Strait, and this Chinese fighter jet darting in front of an American surveillance plane, something we saw for ourselves when we were on board another U.S. Navy plane intercepted by a Chinese jet. BLINKEN: We`ve seen a couple of very dangerous incidents in the last couple of weeks. FRAYER (voiceover): China says the encounters are justified to protect its sovereignty. Blinken`s first trip here was called off after that Chinese spy balloon which was shot down after it flew over the U.S. Senior U.S. officials told NBC News it collected intelligence from American military sites. JOE BIDEN , PRESIDENT OF THE UNITED STATES: I think it was more embarrassing than it was intentionally. FRAYER: So, with Beijing, the balloon incident is over. It`s water under the bridge? BLINKEN: Well, we did what we needed to do to protect our interests. We said what we needed to say and made clear what we needed and made clear in terms of this not happening again. And so, as long as it doesn`t, that chapter should be closed. (END VIDEOTAPE) HOLT: Janis, Secretary Blinken insists the relationship is now stabilized, but was anything concrete accomplished? FRAYER: Lester, relations are at such a low point that even having the meeting is seen by both sides as a positive. Other high-level visits can now follow with President Xi potentially meeting President Biden in the U.S. before the end of the year. Lester? HOLT: All right, Janis Mackey Frayer in Beijing, thank you. In Mississippi, at least one person died and almost two dozen were injured by an overnight tornado, the latest in a wave of destructive storms. Blayne Alexander reports. (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) BLAYNE ALEXANDER, NBC NEWS CORRESPONDENT (voiceover): Across the South, it`s the unforgiving sound of summertime severe weather striking in the dead of night. Its latest target, Louin, Mississippi. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: Oh, that was big. ALEXANDER (voiceover): Overnight, a reported tornado tore through this community an hour outside of Jackson, where people were rushed from their mangled homes on stretchers. Daylight reveals the true scope of the devastation, trees torn to shreds, homes now unrecognizable. All of it leaving more than two dozen people injured and claiming at least one life, 67-year-old Georgine Hayes. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: She`s a good person, good church person, you know. ALEXANDER (voiceover): Her cousin, Lester, lives right across the street. He helped pull her from the rubble. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: Her house where a black Jeep at -- ALEXANDER: Right there. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: It was right there. It`s gone. There isn`t anything there. ALEXANDER: So it`s completely gone. ALEXANDER (voiceover): It`s the latest in a deadly storm system sweeping across the South and central plains, producing at least 17 confirmed tornadoes in just four days. Among the towns hit, Perryton, Texas where the storms destroyed downtown and this mobile home community, killing three people. Oscar Hernandez lost his four businesses in a matter of minutes. He spoke to NBC`s Priscilla Thompson. [19:10:02] OSCAR HERNANDEZ, BUSINESS OWNER: It`s really hard. It`s really hard. All the lost, all the people that lost their lives. ALEXANDER (voiceover): Severe weather continues to sweep the South. Today, a confirmed tornado along the Florida Panhandle and flash flooding in Alabama, an ominous sign of what`s to come. (END VIDEOTAPE) ALEXANDER (on camera): And across the region, hundreds of thousands of people remain without power in some of the very same places that are seeing triple digit highs making cleanup like this all the more difficult with threats of more tornadoes tonight. Lester? HOLT: All right, Blayne, thank you. And we have breaking news tonight about the first named storm in the Atlantic this season. Tropical Storm Bret has formed in the central Atlantic. It`s about 1,300 miles from the lesser Antilles. It is expected to strengthen to become a category one hurricane by tomorrow night and could impact Puerto Rico by the weekend. We`ll stay on top of that one. Across America, the long weekend, a string of mass shootings. Near Chicago, 23 people were shot, one of them fatally during a Juneteenth event yesterday. In Kellogg, Idaho, four people were shot and killed. A suspect was arrested. And in San Francisco, six people were injured in a shootout involving two cars. Two were hit by stray bullets and two young girls were hit by the cars. With little agreement in Washington over to how to stop the violence, tonight, Richard Engel reports on how lawmakers in Serbia responded following two mass shootings there. (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) RICHARD ENGEL, NBC NEWS CHIEF FOREIGN CORRESPONDENT (voiceover): Serbians didn`t see it coming. On May 3rd, a 13-year-old boy stormed into a school with his father`s two guns and a hitlist and killed eight classmates. The next day, a man with a history of violence opened fire in a village, killing eight more. But then came more than thoughts and prayers. Tens of thousands demanded not just tighter gun controls, but a reorientation of society away from violence. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: I think a lot of us have just had enough. ENGEL (voiceover): Zarco Svechik`s (ph) nine-year-old daughter Zora was in the school when the 13-year-old boy went on a killing spree. ENGEL: What would you say to Americans who`ve been through this and then see no change? UNIDENTIFIED MALE: I would say to them, you know, safeguard your democracy if you still have it and mobilize. ENGEL (voiceover): Within weeks of the shootings here, new laws were introduced and old ones enforced. Now all sales of new guns are banned for two years. Gun owners must submit to in-person psychological and background checks. And owning an illegal gun is punishable by up to 15 years in prison. Many Serbians are turning in their guns voluntarily. ENGEL: Here`s a lot of AKs and assault rifles. ENGEL (voiceover): There are 70,000 guns in this police warehouse surrendered under a no-questions-asked amnesty. The Deputy Interior Minister says this is only the start. ENGEL: What do you think when you see all of this? ENGEL (voiceover): I see life saved, he said. Serbia is deeply divided politically, but overhauling gun laws was universally popular. Dobrica Veselinovic, is an opposition politician. ENGEL: Why is it do you think you were able to cross political divides? DOBRICA VESELINOVIC, SERBIAN POLITICIAN: We are not having these big gun lobbies and the big industry which is behind it. (END VIDEOTAPE) ENGEL (on camera): The father we spoke, to and many others now want to push further, dialing back violence in the media and in political discourse. Lester.? HOLT: All right, Richard, thank you. In 60 seconds, tracking who gets an abortion. One state tried to make sure personal data isn`t used to follow women who are driving there for the procedure. Plus, the new housing boom in rentals. (COMMERCIAL BREAK) HOLT: It`s no secret there is surveillance almost everywhere we go these days. Now, one state is taking action to prevent the tracking of women who may be driving to get an abortion. Anne Thompson explains. [19:15:07] (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) ANNE THOMPSON, NBC NEWS CORRESPONDENT (voiceover): If it feels like you are being tracked, it may be because you are, at red lights going in and out of the office on your smartphone. But what if you could be tracked seeking a legal abortion simply by your license plate? ALEXI GIANNOULIAS, SECRETARY OF STATE, ILLINOIS: I don`t think people realize how much of their personal data is collected, that their whereabouts are tracked. THOMPSON (voiceover): That`s why Illinois Secretary of State Alexi Giannoulias backs what he says is a first-in-the-nation bill to outlaw sharing or selling license plate data for women seeking abortions. THOMPSON: Who has access to license plate trackers? GIANNOULIAS: A number of private and public entities have this personal sensitive data. THOMPSON (voiceover): Data he fears could be weaponized as some states try to criminalize helping someone get an abortion even in a state where it is legal. Three other states have passed laws aimed at protecting health data from such efforts. GIANNOULIAS: When they travel, whether it`s to an abortion clinic or the grocery store, we need to make sure this data is protected. THOMPSON (voiceover): Illinois Right to Life Executive Director Mary Kate Zander opposes abortion. THOMPSON: Do you think this bill is necessary? MARY KATE ZANDER, DIRECTOR, ILLINOIS RIGHT TO LIFE EXECUTIVE: I think it`s unnecessary. They`re trying to create a narrative around what the pro-life movement may or may not be doing. THOMPSON (voiceover): She says her organization is not trying to criminalize women seeking the procedure. THOMPSON: Is the right to life movement tracking license plates of women? story_text: [19:00:00] (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) LESTER HOLT, NBC NEWS ANCHOR: Tonight, the desperate surge in the North Atlantic for a missing submersible near the Titanic. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) HOLT (voiceover): The U.S. and Canadian coast guard scouring for a sub- carrying five people. Contact lost for more than 24 hours as the tourist vessel made its way toward the Titanic 12,000 feet down. Rough seas, rain, and fog hampering the surge in rescue efforts for those on board, including a billionaire businessman and explorer. Late details just in tonight. Also tonight, the high-stakes summit between China`s President Xi Jinping and Secretary of State Anthony Blinken . A chance to reset rising tensions that have only gotten worse since the U.S. shot down a spy balloon. Our one-on-one interview with the Secretary of State. The nonstop threat of tornadoes, one dead and almost two dozen injured as multiple tornadoes tear through Mississippi. The search for survivors. A weekend of mass shooting, some of them deadly. But when it happened twice last month in another country, they took quick and decisive action. Richard Engel is there. The new boom in building, not to buy, but to rent. What`s behind it in our series "PRICED OUT." On Juneteenth, celebrations across America and a field of dreams reborn as a testament to the past. (END VIDEO CLIP) ANNOUNCER: This is NBC NIGHTLY NEWS with Lester Holt. HOLT (on camera): Good evening and welcome. Tonight, near the site of one of the 20th century`s worst ocean disasters, a new undersea drama is unfolding. Right now, the U.S. Coast Guard leading the urgent search for a group of modern-day adventurers after the submersible carrying them to the Titanic shipwreck lost contact with the surface yesterday about an hour and 45 minutes into their journey. Five people are on board the vessel which is used to carry paying passengers to see the Titanic up close. The search happening about 350 miles off the coast of Newfoundland in waters more than two miles deep. Tonight, the company that runs the deep sea charters, Ocean Gate Expeditions, saying in a statement, our entire focus is on the crew members and their families. Tom Costello has late-breaking developments for us. (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) TOM COSTELLO, NBC NEWS CORRESPONDENT (voiceover): U.S. and Canadian Coast Guard ships are this hour rushing to the North Atlantic as two U.S. C-130 planes surveyed the vast ocean surface for any signs of a private submersible and the five people on board, last seen Sunday morning as it descended to survey the wreck of the Titanic. REAR ADM. JOHN MAUGER, COMMANDER, U.S. COAST GUARD FIRST DISTRICT: During the course of the dive, they lost communications and we have not had communications with the submersible since then. COSTELLO (voiceover): The 21-foot submersible named Titan, made of titanium and carbon fiber, is owned by Ocean Gate, an operator of small subs for research, film production, and tourist trips to the Titanic for $250,000. On board a pilot and four passengers, including billionaire adventurer Hamish Harding, who had taken a submersible to the Mariana Trench and flown in space on Jeff Bezos ` Blue Origin . On his Instagram account Sunday, he signed his name on the logo as he announced he`d be diving to the Titanic. His company later tweeted, 4:00 a.m. start this morning on the RMS Titanic Mission 5. headline: A Federal Appeals Court Hearing Arguments On Limiting Access Nationwide To A Widely Used Abortion Pill, A Fight Ultimately Heading To The Supreme Court
story_text: LESTER HOLT: Now to the battle over abortion. A federal appeals court hearing arguments on limiting access nationwide to a widely used abortion pill, a fight ultimately heading to the Supreme Court, while some states restrict abortion further. Here`s Laura Jarrett. (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) LAURA JARRETT, NBC NEWS SENIOR LEGAL CORRESPONDENT (voiceover): Tonight, the most commonly used abortion pill still on the market, but its legal future uncertain. A federal appeals court appearing deeply skeptical today of arguments from the Biden administration and pill manufacturer as they try to keep Mifepristone available. JAMES HO, JUDGE: I don`t understand this theme. The FDA can do no wrong. We are allowed to look at the FDA, just like we`re allowed to look at any agency. JARRETT (voiceover): The three-judge panel must decide what to do with that controversial decision out of Texas last month, which invalidated the FDA`s longtime approval of the drug. One judge hearing the case appointed by George W. Bush , the other two by Donald Trump. All have a history of supporting abortion restrictions. Judge James Ho calling abortion a moral tragedy in a 2018 case. The stakes of what happens to a pill women can currently get in the mail even higher now with new abortion restrictions emerging at the state level. STERN: I was blown away by how many people I heard from that had been to different cities across the U. S. GOSK (voiceover): He says the thieves changed his Apple ID password, locked him out, and then went on a shopping spree. ASHIE: They added my credit cards to Apple Pay which I had not previously used, and then they went around New York City using my phone as a credit card. GOSK (voiceover): Ashie would get roughly $15,000 back but what he couldn`t get restored was his Apple account. ASHIE: Hours of conversations with Apple , support staff. I never received my information back. GOSK: We`re talking about personal photos, contacts? ASHIE: Both. GOSK (voiceover): The key is getting the passcode. GOSK: How quickly can you change my Apple ID? STERN: All right, so I`m going to tap here at the top. This is your iCloud or Apple ID area. I`m going to password and security. I`m going to change password. I`m going to put in your passcode. It`s in. Is that right? GOSK: And you`re there. STERN: And I`m there. GOSK (voiceover): It took her 18 seconds. But there`s more. STERN: These thieves on the streets know how to enable something that`s a pretty hidden setting. It`s called this recovery key. GOSK (voiceover): The recovery key is supposed to add another layer of protection. STERN: The problem is that the thieves have the recovery key. GOSK (voiceover): Another option is going to screen time, then content and privacy restrictions where there are several places you can add a four- digit code that will block access. The boiler room where workers shoveled coal to keep the lights on. The propeller, its serial number, still legible. Scattered on the ocean floor unopened champagne bottles, shoes, hats and jewelry. 1500 people died that day in 1912. Edith Haisman was just 16 on board with her parents. We talked to her in 1996. EDITH HAISMAN, TITANIC SURVIVOR: I`ll never forget it, see all the dead bodies floating in the sea. It was terrible. COSTELLO: This makes the Titanic tragedy much more real. ANTHONY GEFFEN, CEO AND CREATIVE DIRECTOR, ATLANTIC PRODUCTIONS: There`s no doubt about that. People around the world will be able to walk around the Titanic for themselves and they`ll be able to see the wreck, they`ll be able to see the debris field. This is a history where we can live in the past. COSTELLO (voiceover): A virtual view preserved forever. Tom Costello, NBC News, Washington. (END VIDEOTAPE) HOLT: The fascination continues. And tonight, there appeared to be differing accounts about what happened next. A spokesperson for the Duke and Duchess of Sussex admonishing photographers for a relentless pursuit that lasted two hours and resulted in multiple near collisions involving other drivers on the road, pedestrians, and two NYPD officers. Adding, the near-catastrophic car chase came at the hands of a ring of highly aggressive paparazzi. ERIC ADAMS, MAYOR, NEW YORK CITY: The briefing I received, you know, two of our officers could have been injured. I thought that was a bit reckless and irresponsible. GUTIERREZ (voiceover): Though tonight, at least three law enforcement sources tell NBC News, the couple was followed, not chased, and that the incident was a bit chaotic, not near catastrophic. ADAMS: I would find it hard to believe that there was a two-hour high-speed chase. GUTIERREZ (voiceover): In a written statement, the NYPD says numerous photographers made the couple`s transport challenging, but there were no reported collisions, injuries, or arrests. GUTIERREZ: Harry and Meghan had private security as they left this venue. And two law enforcement sources tell NBC News that they wanted to return to Manhattan`s upper east side, where they were staying with a friend, and did not want the paparazzi to follow. GUTIERREZ (voiceover): So, the law enforcement sources say the couple was driven up and down Manhattan for more than an hour with a police escort. Then the pair was taken to this police precinct where a taxi picked them up. GUTIERREZ: Would you describe it as chaotic? SONNY SINGH, TAXICAB DRIVER: Yes, chaotic. You could say chaotic. With me - - GUTIERREZ: Catastrophic? SINGH: I don`t know what happened previous in the day, right? With me, it was chaotic, but not crazy, crazy, right? GUTIERREZ: Do you think the paparazzi went too far? SINGH: You know, I don`t know. When we were -- they kept their distance when they were following us in my cab. GUTIERREZ (voiceover): Sonny Singh told us he`s the taxi driver who picked up the couple. But he says they drove around for only 10 minutes before the street was blocked by a garbage truck. SINGH: People just came out of nowhere with cameras and started snapping pictures. GUTIERREZ: Did they seem worried? SINGH: They seem worried. They seem worried and nervous as well. GUTIERREZ (voiceover): He then says he dropped them back off at the police precinct where a different car eventually took them home. GUTIERREZ (voiceover): Though critics say Harry and Meghan also court the cameras and publicity pointing to their Netflix docu-series. HARRY: No one sees what`s happening behind closed doors. [19:05:02] GUTIERREZ (voiceover): It was 26 years ago this summer that his mother, Princess Diana, died during a car chase in Paris. HARRY: You get followed, photograph, chase, harassed. GUTIERREZ (on camera): Well, Lester, source close to Harry and Meghan says that there is a security video that captured the encounter, but it has not yet been publicly released, Lester. New developments this evening in the brutal killings of those four University of Idaho students. The suspect has been indicted. And as Erin McLaughlin reports, we will see him in court soon. The indictment includes four counts of murder in the first degree and one count of burglary. If found guilty, he could be sentenced to death. Kohberger has yet to enter a plea, but his previous attorney said he believes he`ll be exonerated. The indictment follows his December arrest at his family home in Pennsylvania. President Biden projecting optimism with just 15 days to reach a deal to raise the debt limit or risk economic calamity. While still in Washington, the President said he`s confident the country won`t default, calling a meeting with top congressional leaders this week productive. The president has cut short part of this critical diplomatic trip to deal with the crisis. But despite that, Republican House Speaker Kevin McCarthy blasting Mr. Biden this afternoon for going overseas at all before a deal is done. Lester? HOLT: Kristen Welker, thank you. Breaking news from Ukraine tonight. Another American volunteer, former Green Beret, has been killed in battle there. Molly Hunter has more on his decision to fight as new images show the immense toll of war in the east. And months before his death, he spoke to NBC`s Raf Sanchez, protecting his identity, going by the name Sema. The 20-year U.S. Army veteran training volunteer soldiers outside of Kyiv. NICHOLAS MAIMER, AMERICAN KILLED IN UKRAINE: I had that strong internal debate on whether I should, what I could contribute, you know, should I accept the risk? MAIMER: I signed up knowing that but with the statement that I was willing to fight. HUNTER: Ukraine says they now have the momentum in Bakhmut, fighting hard for what little remains. Maggie Vespa reports. (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) KAYLA UNBEHAUN, SIX YEARS MISSING: Hi, this is Taylor here. I have a cat. VESPA (voiceover): The tipster also crediting the hit show Unsolved Mysteries which featured Kayla`s case last fall. BROWN: The media attention that this case has received over the years up to and including the Netflix documentary most likely heightened her awareness. BROWN: She looked relatively healthy, didn`t appear to be in any type of physical trauma. VESPA: Police soon uncovered the pair`s true identities. Tonight, they say Kayla is back home in Illinois. Her mother, Heather Unbehaun charged with kidnapping. The remarkable homecoming following years of pleas from Kayla`s dad, Ryan Iskerka, on multiple true crime shows. RYAN ISKERKA, FATHER OF KAYLA UNBEHAUN: My daughter was gone. Turning now to the important warning. Thieves are stealing iPhones and passwords to hijack all your personal information. Stephanie Gosk explains how they`re doing it and how to protect yourself. [19:20:15] (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) STEPHANIE GOSK, NBC NEWS CORRESPONDENT (voiceover): Just behind the locked screen of an iPhone, a goldmine of money, memories, and connections, and thieves have found a way in. JOANNA STERN, SENIOR PERSONAL TECH COLUMNIST, WALL STREET JOURNAL: They`re stealing your passcode. GOSK: It`s so sinister. STERN: It`s so sinister but also so simple. GOSK: So, they go to places where people are vulnerable. STERN: Drunk. People are vulnerable. They`re drunk. They`re having good time. GOSK (voiceover): Joanna Stern covers tech for the Wall Street Journal. She`s done a series of reports exposing a new crime wave. Phones being ripped off at bars leading to tens of thousands of dollars stolen and Apple accounts locked. STERN: I was blown away by how many people I heard from that had been to different cities across the U. S. GOSK (voiceover): He says the thieves changed his Apple ID password, locked him out, and then went on a shopping spree. ASHIE: They added my credit cards to Apple Pay which I had not previously used, and then they went around New York City using my phone as a credit card. GOSK (voiceover): Ashie would get roughly $15,000 back but what he couldn`t get restored was his Apple account. ASHIE: Hours of conversations with Apple , support staff. I never received my information back. GOSK: We`re talking about personal photos, contacts? ASHIE: Both. GOSK (voiceover): The key is getting the passcode. GOSK (voiceover): Another option is going to screen time, then content and privacy restrictions where there are several places you can add a four- digit code that will block access. The changes will make the phone less convenient. ASHIE: I feel like it`s Fort Knox on my phone now. GOSK (voiceover): But with life`s most important information in the palm of your hand, the hassle may be worth it. Stephanie Gosk, NBC News New York. (END VIDEOTAPE) HOLT: When we come back, the astonishing new images of the Titanic like you`ve never seen it before. (COMMERCIAL BREAK) [19:25:00] HOLT: Finally, astonishing new 3D images of a Titanic providing the most captivating view yet of the shipwreck. Here`s Tom Costello. (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) TOM COSTELLO, NBC NEWS CORRESPONDENT (voiceover): The images are breathtaking in their clarity and detail. The Titanic broken in two, 1200 feet below the North Atlantic. Too big for a single photo, the new 3D scan combining 700,000 images reveals the full scale of the disaster. The bow covered in rust. It`s anchor still attached. The boiler room where workers shoveled coal to keep the lights on. The propeller, its serial number, still legible. Scattered on the ocean floor unopened champagne bottles, shoes, hats and jewelry. 1500 people died that day in 1912. Edith Haisman was just 16 on board with her parents. We talked to her in 1996. COSTELLO: This makes the Titanic tragedy much more real. ANTHONY GEFFEN, CEO AND CREATIVE DIRECTOR, ATLANTIC PRODUCTIONS: There`s no doubt about that. People around the world will be able to walk around the Titanic for themselves and they`ll be able to see the wreck, they`ll be able to see the debris field. This is a history where we can live in the past. COSTELLO (voiceover): A virtual view preserved forever. Tom Costello, NBC News, Washington. (END VIDEOTAPE) HOLT: The fascination continues. That`s NIGHTLY NEWS for this Wednesday. Thank you for watching. I`m Lester Holt. Please take care of yourself and each other. Good night. headline: Frustrated Over Getting Quality Care: What Mothers To Be Want In The Delivery Room
story_text: [19:20:00] LESTER HOLT: As Mother`s Day approaches, we`re reminded pregnancy and childbirth can come with health risks. And for Black women, those risks are significantly higher. Zinhle Essamuah now on why more mothers are working with doulas. (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) ZINHLE ESSAMUAH, NBC NEWS CORRESPONDENT (voiceover): Kanaiah King`s (ph) first pregnancy in 2021 was traumatic. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: Good job. Everything that could go wrong went wrong. ESSAMUAH (voiceover): She went into labor early at just 24 weeks and had a serious infection. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: You know, doctors kind of use the big words, thinking you would know, but I didn`t. It was my first time. ESSAMUAH (voiceover): But the St. Louis native had support from a doula, Robin Lloyd. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: Ms. Robin would literally stop them like, hey, stop. Let me talk to her. And she would tell me exactly what it meant. ESSAMUAH (voiceover): Birthing doulas are trained nonclinical professionals who support clients through pregnancy, labor, delivery, and postpartum. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: We all are going through the same thing. ESSAMUAH (voiceover): The doulas offer one-on-one education. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: No question is a dumb question. ESSAMUAH (voiceover): And group courses for expectant and new moms. Kanaiah credits Robin for helping her get through it all? ESSAMUAH: What are you feeling? UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: I`m very grateful for her. I`m very grateful for her. Because if she wasn`t there, I don`t know what would have happened. ESSAMUAH: Do you think you would be here and your kids would be here if you hadn`t had a doula? UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: Not at all, no. ESSAMUAH (voiceover): The American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists finding doulas-improved outcomes for women and labor. They`re especially critical for Black women, who are three times more likely to die from a pregnancy-related cause than White women. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: You`re so cute. ESSAMUAH (voiceover): Kanaiah`s doula, Robin, works with the nonprofit Parents as Teachers, motivated by her own life-threatening delivery. The nonprofit received state funding, making it possible to provide doula services to families cost-free. Of the nearly 320 families they serve, many unhoused, 95 percent are people of color, and all of their doulas are Black women. ESSAMUAH: Why is it particularly important for women of color and Black women to have access to them? UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: Well, I think -- I think access is the key. We wanted to make sure that we had Black doulas serving those families that resemble them. ESSAMUAH (voiceover): Now, Kanaiah is expecting a baby boy in just a few weeks with Robin by her side. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: I`m going to be there. You know, you`re going to have that support and not to worry. ESSAMUAH (voiceover): Zinhle Essamuah, NBC News, St. Louis, Missouri. (END VIDEOTAPE) HOLT: And up next, the moving reunion for one man who nearly died in a supermarket and the hero nurses who saved his life. headline: New Guidelines For Breast Cancer Screening
story_text: LESTER HOLT: There is major news tonight about women in breast cancer. Government experts now say mammograms should begin much earlier, at age 40. Erin McLaughlin has details. (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) ERIN MCLAUGHLIN, NBC NEWS CORRESPONDENT (voiceover): Tonight, a leading health panel now recommending mammogram screenings for breast cancer begin for women at age 40, a full decade sooner than the panel`s previous guidelines. Experts say it`s about time. DR. MAXINE JOCHELSON, CHIEF OF BREAST IMAGING, MEMORIAL SLOAN KETTERING : The science has always been there. That`s why many of us have been recommending 40 for years. MCLAUGHLIN (on camera): So, finally this panel is listening to that science? JOCHELSON: Yes. MCLAUGHLIN (voiceover): The draft recommendations come from the U.S. preventative Services Task Force. They say the new guidelines could save 20 percent more lives across the board for all women, emphasizing the new guidelines are especially important for black women. DR. CAROL MANGIONE, US. PREVENTIVE SERVICES TASK FORCE: Black women are 40 percent more likely to die from breast cancer than white women if they get it. They also are more likely to get more aggressive forms of breast cancer. MCLAUGHLIN: The panel stopping short of recommending annual mammogram screenings, maintaining that women still screen every two years. MCLAUGHLIN (on camera): Does this recommendation go far enough? JOCHELSON: No. MCLAUGHLIN (voiceover): She argues women 40 and over should get screenings every year and says women should start talking with their doctors about risk factors at age 25. Still, experts are hopeful these new recommendations will help send a more consistent message. [19:15:13] MANGIONE: The most important thing for women to know is to begin screening at the age of 40 because it just might save your life. MCLAUGHLIN: Erin McLaughlin, NBC News. HOLT: In a moment, NBC News investigates work contracts with the nation`s largest hospital chain nurses say they`ve been a threat to their health and yours. story_text: LESTER HOLT: There is major news tonight about women in breast cancer. Government experts now say mammograms should begin much earlier, at age 40. Erin McLaughlin has details. (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) ERIN MCLAUGHLIN, NBC NEWS CORRESPONDENT (voiceover): Tonight, a leading health panel now recommending mammogram screenings for breast cancer begin for women at age 40, a full decade sooner than the panel`s previous guidelines. Experts say it`s about time. DR. MAXINE JOCHELSON, CHIEF OF BREAST IMAGING, MEMORIAL SLOAN KETTERING : The science has always been there. That`s why many of us have been recommending 40 for years. MCLAUGHLIN (on camera): So, finally this panel is listening to that science? JOCHELSON: Yes. MCLAUGHLIN (voiceover): The draft recommendations come from the U.S. preventative Services Task Force. They say the new guidelines could save 20 percent more lives across the board for all women, emphasizing the new guidelines are especially important for black women. DR. CAROL MANGIONE, US. PREVENTIVE SERVICES TASK FORCE: Black women are 40 percent more likely to die from breast cancer than white women if they get it. They also are more likely to get more aggressive forms of breast cancer. MCLAUGHLIN: The panel stopping short of recommending annual mammogram screenings, maintaining that women still screen every two years. MCLAUGHLIN (on camera): Does this recommendation go far enough? JOCHELSON: No. MCLAUGHLIN (voiceover): She argues women 40 and over should get screenings every year and says women should start talking with their doctors about risk factors at age 25. Still, experts are hopeful these new recommendations will help send a more consistent message. [19:15:13] MANGIONE: The most important thing for women to know is to begin screening at the age of 40 because it just might save your life. MCLAUGHLIN: Erin McLaughlin, NBC News. HOLT: In a moment, NBC News investigates work contracts with the nation`s largest hospital chain nurses say they`ve been a threat to their health and yours. Mr. Trump was also asked about comments he made about women in that infamous Access Hollywood Tape that came to light before the 2016 election. It`s where we begin tonight with Senior Legal Correspondent Laura Jarrett. Jean Carroll. DONALD TRUMP , FORMER PRESIDENT OF THE UNITED STATES: She`s accusing me of rape, a woman that I have no idea who she is. It came out of the blue. JARRETT: Released publicly for the first time today, Mr. Trump`s deposition in a civil case. Carroll is suing him for allegedly defaming her. She says he raped her in a department store dressing room more than 20 years ago. TRUMP: It`s the most ridiculous, disgusting story. It was just made up. If it did happen, it would have been reported within minutes. JARRETT: This week, a jury in Manhattan watch clips of the deposition. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: And when you`re a star, they let you do it. You can do anything. Grab them by the (BLEEP). You can do anything. That`s what you said, correct? TRUMP: Well, historically, that`s true with stars. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: It`s true with stars that they can grab women by their (BLEEP). TRUMP: Well, that`s what, if you look over the last million years, I guess that`s been largely true. Not always, but largely true, unfortunately or fortunately. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: You consider yourself to be a star. TRUMP : I think you can say that, yes. JARRETT: Mr. Trump had repeatedly said Miss Carroll was not his type. TRUMP: It`s not politically correct to say it, and I know that, but I`ll say it anyway. JARRETT: But then he mistook Carroll for his ex-wife, Marla Maples, when shown this old photo of him shaking Carroll`s hand. TRUMP : I don`t even know who the woman. Let`s say I don`t know who -- it`s Marla. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: You say Marla is in this photo? TRUMP: That`s Marla. Yes, that`s my wife. JARRETT: Throughout the deposition, Mr. Trump steadfastly denying Carroll`s accusation and going after Carroll`s attorney. TRUMP : You know, it`s not true too. You`re a political operative also. You`re a -- you`re a disgrace. JARRETT: Later, turning to her physical appearance. TRUMP : You wouldn`t be a choice of mine either, to be honest with you. I hope you`re not insulted. I would not, under any circumstances, have any interest in you. (END VIDEOTAPE) HOLT: Laura, this is the only time the jury is going to actually hear from Mr. Trump. JARRETT (on camera): Right, Lester. Mr. Trump`s attorney has opted not to put on a defense case. The judge is giving the former president until 5:00 p.m. Sunday to change his mind. If not, closing arguments are expected on Monday. Lester? HOLT: Laura Jarrett, thank you. The Supreme Court has stepped into temporarily halt the planned execution this month of an Oklahoma man whose case has drawn support from both sides of the death penalty debate. Tonight, my exclusive interview with Richard Glossip on the day a dramatic new twist in his case unfolded. [19:05:00] (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) HOLT (voiceover): Less than two weeks before his scheduled execution, Richard Glossip once again waits at death`s door, like he has so many times before. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: And incarcerated individual at Oklahoma State Penitentiary. HOLT: Richard, how many execution dates have you had? RICHARD GLOSSIP, PRISONER CURRENTLY AT DEATH ROW: Nine. HOLT: And three of those, you were within minutes of being executed. GLOSSIP: Yes, three of them. I was fed my last meals. HOLT: Each time he was given a last-minute stay. This morning, Glossip called me from Oklahoma`s death row, his last interview before his new date to die, believing he had 13 days to live. Glossip, a former motel manager, convicted of organizing the 1997 murder of his boss, Barry Van Treese, but he maintains his innocence. I think you know the question I have to start off with and that is did you have anything to do with the murder of Barry Van Treese? GLOSSIP: I did not. HOLT: And you might be surprised who believes him and is fighting for him. KEVIN MCDUGLE (R-OK), STATE REPRESENTATIVE: These people should be ashamed. They should be arrested. These two men are not Glossip`s defense attorneys. They are pro-death penalty conservative lawmakers, Oklahoma representatives J.J. Humphrey and Kevin McDugle. MCDUGLE: I don`t think they`ve got enough to convict him of Jay Walking. J.J. HUMPHREY (R-OK), STATE REPRESENTATIVE: There`s no doubt, no doubt that he`s innocent of murder. HOLT: McDugle and Humphrey are desperate to save Glossip`s life. They point to two independent reviews. Both determine the original investigation was corrupt. HUMPHREY: This is unjust. I mean, this is a case where literally the prosecution team has tried to hide everything that they`ve done. One of the prosecutors, literally, we have it in writing, that she tried to change the testimony of the actual murderer. HOLT: Even the state`s Republican attorney general doesn`t think Glossip should be put to death. And in a rare move just this week, the A.G. asked the Supreme Court to grant a stay of execution. The answer came today in the middle of our interview. None of us saw it coming. I just handed a note. The U.S. Supreme Court halts execution of Oklahoma death row inmate Richard Glossip, whose case has drawn support from state`s Republican attorney general. MCDUGLE: Yes, that`s awesome, awesome. HUMPHREY: I tell you, we thought they would do it. Oklahoma is finally going to have the opportunity to look under the hood. The decision granting a temporary stay of execution, giving the court more time to review Glossip`s case. Minutes after the decision, we spoke to Glossip`s attorney Don Knight. DON KNIGHT, ATTORNEY FOR RICHARD GLOSSIP: We are thrilled that this -- that the court granted this stay of execution. This is something that we`ve been asking for a long time. We know that Rich Glossip is innocent. HOLT: Yet another reprieve for Glossip for now, but maybe not forever. GLOSSIP: I either let this consume me or I make peace with it and try to live the best I can with what life I have left. And that`s what I try to do. I`m scared to death. Don`t get me wrong. I don`t want anybody to think that I`m taking it lightly or anything, but you have to make peace with the situation. (END VIDEOTAPE) HOLT (on camera): We have reached out to both the district attorney and the victim`s family after today`s news but have not heard back from either. However, after a recent hearing, the family members said they believe Glossip is guilty. As the war in Ukraine grinds on, tonight, a major rift has escalated between the head of a Russian mercenary group fighting in eastern Ukraine and Russia`s military leaders. And he`s given them an ultimatum. Richard Engel has the latest. (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) RICHARD ENGEL, NBC NEWS CHIEF FOREIGN CORRESPONDENT (voiceover): It`s been called the biggest land battle since World War II, Bakhmut in eastern Ukraine. For months, a group of mercenaries known as the Wagner group has been leading the charge here where Russia has gained ground. Much to the embarrassment of the Russian army, which to undercut its rival has, according to the mercenaries, been blocking the delivery of supplies. Today, the head of Wagner standing over the bodies of his fighters said he`ll quit Bakhmut next week unless his men get more ammunition. Russia is feeling the pressure. It accuses the United States of conspiring with Ukraine to carry out a drone attack against the Kremlin itself, calling it an attempted assassination on President Putin. Allegations the U.S. and Ukraine strongly deny. JOHN KIRBY, STRATEGIC COMMUNICATIONS COORDINATOR, NATIONAL SECURITY COUNCIL: One thing I can tell you for certain is that the United States was not involved in this incident in any way. ENGEL: Today, Russia`s Foreign Minister promised a response with what he called concrete actions. And negotiations aren`t going well. In Turkey, talks over access to the Black Sea got heated when a Ukrainian delegate photobombed a Russian negotiator, the frustrated Russian turn back and snatched the Ukrainian flag. Turkey condemned the behavior as undiplomatic. (END VIDEOTAPE) [19:10:06] ENGEL: When asked about the Wagner group`s potential pull out from Bakhmut, the Kremlin`s response was no comment. Lester? ENGEL: Richard Engel tonight, thank you. We have breaking news about the death of a man in a New York City subway. Jordan Neely died this week after he was put on a choke hold by another passenger. Some riders said Neely had been threatening people on board. NBC has learned that the case is expected to go to a grand jury to decide if charges will be filed against the man who put Neely in that choke hold. He was questioned by police and released. Now, to the border crisis with officials bracing for a rush of migrants when that pandemic border restriction known as Title 42 expires next week. The Biden administration facing bipartisan criticism. And tonight, the Homeland Security Secretary is responding in an interview with Julia Ainsley. (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) JULIA AINSLEY, NBC NEWS HOMELAND SECURITY CORRESPONDENT (voiceover): Tonight, just a week from the lifting of that border restriction known as Title 42, growing numbers of migrants crossing into the U.S. All as the Border Patrol expects illegal border crossings will spike to 10,000 per day when Title 42 lifts. Are you worried about Title 42 lifting next week? ALEJANDRO MAYORKAS, U.S. SECRETARY OF HOMELAND SECURITY: I`m not worried about Title 42 lifting. We recognize the challenge at the border. Our responsibility is to plan and to execute on those plans. And that is indeed what we have done and continue to do. AINSLEY: Homeland Security Secretary Alejandro Mayorkas here to talk to border agents. The Biden administration has faced criticism over its border policies amid a record number of illegal border crossings. Mayorkas insisting the policies are working. Is our border secure? MAYORKAS: Our border is secure. The border is secure because we are maximizing our resources to deliver the most effective results to our border with the most extraordinary workforce in the world. AINSLEY: But Hidalgo County Sheriff Eddie Guerra disagrees. Is our border secure? EDDIE GUERRA, SHERIFF, HIDALGO COUNTY: Well, I can tell you no. There`s a lot of places on the southwestern border that the -- our federal partners do not have control. (END VIDEOTAPE) AINSLEY: As for the bipartisan proposal in Congress to extend Title 42, Secretary Mayorkas told us that the Biden administration has already tried to end Title 42 several times, and now is the time to do so. Lester? HOLT: All right, Julia, thank you. Just ours are now, something that Britain and the world have not seen in seven decades, the core nation of a new British monarch. Keir Simmons is watching it all for us from London. (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) KEIR SIMMONS, NBC NEWS CHIEF INTERNATIONAL CORRESPONDENT (voiceover): The night before the biggest day of his life, King Charles smiling and laughing. Palace officials say he`s shown no sign of nerves. Today, the Princess of Wales pictured with two first ladies, Jill Biden and Ukraine`s Olena Zelenska . The King, William and Catherine greeting the public earlier. WILLIAM, PRINCE OF WALES: How are you doing? SIMMONS : The Princess asked how the children are feeling. Prince George will be a page of honor tomorrow. CATHERINE, PRINCESS OF WALES He`s excited, a bit nervous. Obviously with a big day ahead. But, No, can`t wait actually. SIMMONS : Even taking a cell phone to console someone`s American relative too ill to make it. CATHERINE: I hope you get back as soon. SIMMONS : The crowds have already camped along the world-famous Mall for a glimpse of history tomorrow morning. At 5:20 Eastern, a small procession will leave Buckingham Palace with the King to Westminster Abbey. Then the solemn service, not seen this century, will commence. The moment of crowning is expected around 7:00 a.m. Next, a breathtaking spectacle. From the Abbey, a 4,000-strong military parade would escort the King along this route. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: And he won`t answer questions about why. SIMMONS : But polls show enthusiasm for the monarchy waning and protesters will be out too. GRAHAM SMITH, CEO, REPUBLIC: I would think the monarchy is in a lot of trouble because they`ve lost their star player. SIMMONS : The King is looking to answer those critics by combining tradition with change tomorrow. Manju Malhi, a chef, has been invited for her charity work. MANJU MALHI, CHEF: I feel included and very inclusive and part of British history being a daughter of an immigrant. (END VIDEOTAPE) SIMMONS : Meanwhile, Prince Harry is here in London tonight. He will not play a formal role tomorrow. But Buckingham Palace is not saying who will appear on the famous balcony behind me. They say we`ll find out when it happens. Lester? HOLT: All right, Keir Simmons in London, thank you. In 60 seconds, the landmark moment in the fight against COVID. Plus, why trade schools are becoming the bold new trend in education. And the battle over birth control. The FDA is set to consider whether a pill can be sold over the counter. (COMMERCIAL BREAK) [19:15:00] HOLT: We are back with a remarkable announcement from the World Health Organization that the COVID global health emergency is officially over. It`s a milestone three years after the start of the pandemic that killed millions in upended economies across the globe. Officials say vaccines and high levels of immunity significantly cut the risk, but they caution the virus is still a threat. Turning out of the economy less than four weeks away from the country potentially defaulting if there`s no deal to raise the debt ceiling. Economists say that will be catastrophic. Still, markets close sharply higher today as the economy added 253,000 jobs last month and unemployment fell to 3.4 percent. Catie Beck now on the uncertainty that lies ahead. (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) CATIE BECK, NBC NEWS CORRESPONDENT (voiceover): President Biden today highlighting the good. JOE BIDEN , PRESIDENT OF THE UNITED STATES: Unemployment rate is at 3.4 percent, which is the lowest in 50 years. BECK: But accusing Republicans who want spending cuts of putting the economy at risk over the debt ceiling. BIDEN: They`re trying to hold the debt hostage to us to agree to some draconian cuts, magnificently difficult and damaging cuts. BECK: A possible default on the debt along with rising interest rates and ongoing turmoil among banks fueling fears of a recession. But an uncertain economic future is something Abbie Carlson is preparing for. Her decision to go to trade school wasn`t easy one. ABBIE CARLSON, STUDIES AT A TRADE SCHOOL: People are finding out that with a four-year degree, they`re not making a whole lot of money off the bat and they`re ending up with all of debt. BECK: She`ll graduate with none thanks to state funding for the program. Carlson will finish her training in welding in October. Is the common knowledge among students, we`re going to be hired right away when we leave here? CARLSON: Yes, 100 percent. If you don`t leave with a job, it`s on you. BECK: Tennessee College of Applied Technology President Nathan Garrett says there`s a waitlist to get in. NATHAN GARRETT, PRESIDENT, COLLEGE OF APPLIED TECHNOLOGY: I think at the end of the day, people are really looking at where`s the value at? BECK: Trade program enrollment is surging with big spikes in construction up almost seven percent, and mechanic and repair programs up five percent last fall, while undergraduate college enrollment has declined in recent years. CARLSON: I have hope for the future like I never did before. BECK: Hopeful for opportunity even in an uncertain economy. Catie Beck, NBC News, Nashville. (END VIDEOTAPE) HOLT: Still ahead tonight, the battle over birth control as the FDA gets sent away in and whether to sell pills without a prescription. (COMMERCIAL BREAK) [19:20:00] HOLT: A revolutionary change could be coming to birth control, pills sold without a prescription. A group of FDA advisors is set to meet next week to consider the measure. Maggie Vespa has details. (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) MAGGIE VESPA, NBC NEWS CORRESPONDENT (voiceover): In an era of historic shifts in reproductive health, a push for an American first over the counter, birth control pills. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: I think that`s great. I feel like it`s necessary. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: Without a doubt, this is a right that everybody should have access to. VESPA: Advisors to the Food and Drug Administration meeting next week to review drug maker Perrigo`s application to sell its oral contraceptive, Opil, over the counter. It`s been available for 50 years with a prescription like all birth control pills in the U.S. Perrigo aiming to offer it to all women and teens, no doctor needed. DR. KRISTYN BRANDI, FELLOW, AMERICAN COLLEGE OF OBSTETRICIANS AND GYNECOLOGISTS : I`m surprised that this hasn`t happened already. People can self-screen. People can read instructions. And so, we shouldn`t be limiting people`s access to care. VESPA: It`s unclear how much Opil would cost, whether it would be available on store shelves or behind a pharmacist counter and whether a minor would need parental consent. An initial FDA review, flagging concerns about whether adolescents can understand the label`s instructions and whether current and former breast cancer patients, who the FDA says should not be on hormonal birth control, would know to avoid it. Perrigo writing its application demonstrates that Opil is safe and effective. Experts noting any decision on Opil will have no impact on other prescription birth controls or on lawsuits over the abortion pill, Mifepristone. (END VIDEOTAPE) VESPA (on camera): The FDA`s final decision on the push to sell Opil over the counter is expected this summer. Lester? HOLT: All right, Maggie, thank you. When we come back, London`s monarchy mania. Just how far some travel to be in the middle of all the royal excitement. (COMMERCIAL BREAK) [19:25:00] HOLT: Finally tonight, the Royal fans who traveled across the pond for a front-row seat to King Charles` coronation. Here`s Kelly Cobiella. (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) KELLY COBIELLA, NBC NEWS FOREIGN CORRESPONDENT (voiceover): Tonight, the flags are flying, the horses prancing, the crowds dressed in their best red, white, and blue for the first coronation in 70 years. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: It`s just an awesome time to witness history. I mean, we haven`t done this in our lifetimes. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: Yes. COBIELLA: The monarch`s smiling face is everywhere, from windows to fridge magnets. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: He`s our king. He`s going to be our super king. COBIELLA: A super king with super fans. And we found plenty of Americans. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: I just love it. I just absolutely eat it up. COBIELLA: Braving the rain for a front-row seat to history. Cassandra Estrella Rocha from California changed her vacation plans to be here. Have you been camping here? CASSANDRA ESTRELLA ROCHA FROM CALIFORNIA, AMERICAN TOURIST: Yes. COBIELLA: Oh, my gosh. ROCHA: And I`m not a camper. COBIELLA: Why? ROCHA: I want to be a part of history. Like, I just think -- you know, in America, we don`t have things like this, right? COBIELLA: As the skies cleared, surprise handshakes from the King, telling greatest hits radio London News -- CHARLES III, KING OF THE UNITED KINGDOM: Rain`s a blessing, except for your camera. COBIELLA: A smiling king, a cheering crowd, and tomorrow, the crowning moment. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: I think he`s an amazing, amazing guy, and I`m proud to be a Brit. Long live the queen -- the king. COBIELLA: Kelly Cobiella, NBC News, London. (END VIDEOTAPE) HOLT: And NBC`s coverage of Charles` coronation starts at 5:00 a.m. Eastern tomorrow morning. That`s NIGHTLY NEWS for this Friday. Thank you for watching, everyone. I`m Lester Holt. Please take care of yourself and each other. Good night. (COMMERCIAL BREAK) END Content and programming copyright 2023 NBCUniversal. AINSLEY: Homeland Security Secretary Alejandro Mayorkas here to talk to border agents. (END VIDEOTAPE) AINSLEY: As for the bipartisan proposal in Congress to extend Title 42, Secretary Mayorkas told us that the Biden administration has already tried to end Title 42 several times, and now is the time to do so. Lester? HOLT: All right, Julia, thank you. Just ours are now, something that Britain and the world have not seen in seven decades, the core nation of a new British monarch. Keir Simmons is watching it all for us from London. (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) KEIR SIMMONS, NBC NEWS CHIEF INTERNATIONAL CORRESPONDENT (voiceover): The night before the biggest day of his life, King Charles smiling and laughing. Palace officials say he`s shown no sign of nerves. Today, the Princess of Wales pictured with two first ladies, Jill Biden and Ukraine`s Olena Zelenska . The King, William and Catherine greeting the public earlier. WILLIAM, PRINCE OF WALES: How are you doing? SIMMONS : The Princess asked how the children are feeling. Prince George will be a page of honor tomorrow. CATHERINE, PRINCESS OF WALES He`s excited, a bit nervous. Obviously with a big day ahead. But, No, can`t wait actually. SIMMONS : Even taking a cell phone to console someone`s American relative too ill to make it. CATHERINE: I hope you get back as soon. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: And he won`t answer questions about why. SIMMONS : But polls show enthusiasm for the monarchy waning and protesters will be out too. MANJU MALHI, CHEF: I feel included and very inclusive and part of British history being a daughter of an immigrant. (END VIDEOTAPE) SIMMONS : Meanwhile, Prince Harry is here in London tonight. He will not play a formal role tomorrow. But Buckingham Palace is not saying who will appear on the famous balcony behind me. They say we`ll find out when it happens. Lester? Officials say vaccines and high levels of immunity significantly cut the risk, but they caution the virus is still a threat. JOE BIDEN , PRESIDENT OF THE UNITED STATES: Unemployment rate is at 3.4 percent, which is the lowest in 50 years. BECK: But accusing Republicans who want spending cuts of putting the economy at risk over the debt ceiling. BIDEN: They`re trying to hold the debt hostage to us to agree to some draconian cuts, magnificently difficult and damaging cuts. CARLSON: I have hope for the future like I never did before. BECK: Hopeful for opportunity even in an uncertain economy. Catie Beck, NBC News, Nashville. COBIELLA: Kelly Cobiella, NBC News, London. (END VIDEOTAPE) HOLT: And NBC`s coverage of Charles` coronation starts at 5:00 a.m. Eastern tomorrow morning. That`s NIGHTLY NEWS for this Friday. Thank you for watching, everyone. I`m Lester Holt. Please take care of yourself and each other. Good night. (COMMERCIAL BREAK) END Content and programming copyright 2023 NBCUniversal. headline: How More Women Are Boldly Changing The Conversation About Menopause And Money
story_text: [19:20:00] LESTER HOLT: There`s been an empowering shift in how women are talking about menopause, no longer taboo, many are having candid conversations about what they want and need, and big business is listening. Here`s Kristen Dahlgren. (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) KRISTEN DAHLGREN, NBC NEWS CORRESPONDENT (voiceover): Menopause is more than hot flashes and night sweats. A new study shows a big financial impact too, some $1.8 billion in lost work every year, $26 billion when you add in medical expenses. DR. STEPHANIE FAUBION, DIRECTOR, MAYO CLINIC WOMEN`S HEALTH CENTER: That`s not even counting the lost opportunities women might have because they didn`t take a promotion or maybe they took a lesser job. DAHLGREN: 13 percent of women reported an adverse work outcome due to menopause. 11 percent missed at least one day of work, the average missed three days per year. Do we need to rethink how we`re thinking about menopause in the workplace? FAUBION: I think we`re where we were in the 1970s with pregnancy and lactation in the workplace. Now, we need to be having these conversations about how menopause symptoms impact women. We need to educate managers and supervisors. DAHLGREN: It took a while for Lorraine Grace White to realize what she was feeling was menopause. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: I had migraines every day so intense that I could -- I could hardly focus and concentrate. And then there was the mood swings. DAHLGREN: She found Dr. Makeba Williams, an OBGYN at Washington University in St. Louis , one of a growing number of physicians focused on individualized menopause care. The number of certified menopause practitioners has increased 70 percent in the past 10 years with the potential to almost double by the end of this year. DR. MAKEBA WILLIAMS, OBGYN, WASHINGTON UNIVERSITY IN ST. LOUIS: The average age of menopause in this country is 51 which means that a woman will spend a half to a third of her life menopausal. This notion that I hear all too often that women should just grin and bear it does everyone a disservice. DAHLGREN: And symptoms can be even more severe for African-American women. WILLIAMS: An African-American woman can expect to have these symptoms for 10 years. And unfortunately, she is half as likely to be treated as a White woman who will suffer from these symptoms only about six years. DAHLGREN: Williams says there`s hope even hormone therapy once considered too risky now seen as a safe option for many. And for those who can`t take estrogen like women who have had breast cancer, new treatments are being developed. For Lorraine, seeking help has made all the difference. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: We are a different generation of women and we have things to do. I feel amazing and I can`t wait for the next chapter. DAHLGREN: Chapters being rewritten for millions as attitudes toward what was once simply called the change are changing. Kristen Dahlgren NBC News, St. Louis. (END VIDEOTAPE) HOLT: Up next tonight, songs of survival. The beautiful instruments and the stories to save them. (COMMERCIAL BREAK) END Content and programming copyright 2023 NBCUniversal. headline: NBC NIGHTLY NEWS for April 22, 2023, NBC
story_text: [18:34:30] JOSE DIAZ-BALART, NBC NEWS HOST: Ahead for us tonight, a giant massive seaweed wider than the U.S. is bearing down on Florida. And a $20 million mystery who swiped a container of gold from a North American airport, tonight on NIGHTLY NEWS. (COMMERCIAL BREAK) [18:42:05] ANNOUNCER: This is NBC NIGHTLY NEWS with Jose Diaz Balart. DIAZ-BALART: Good evening. The race to evacuate Americans from Sudan is intensifying as the situation there it gets worse by the moment. Officials in the African nation say that the evacuation of foreign nationals has begun. But the U.S. State Department and Pentagon have not confirmed any American operation. This is part of Saudi Arabia`s evacuation today. Transporting hundreds by caravan and then by boat to safety. Take a look at this. Airports are not an option. They`re totally blown out from the intense fighting between two warring military factions there. There are an estimated 16,000 American citizens currently in the eastern African country, many with dual citizenship who may not want to leave but there are plenty who do. And they`re getting more desperate by the hour. We begin tonight with Pentagon Correspondent Courtney Kube. (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) COURTNEY KUBE, NBC NEWS NATIONAL SECURITY & MILITARY AFFAIRS CORRESPONDENT (voice-over): Tonight, a glimmer of hope for some Americans trapped in Sudan following eight days of violence and bloodshed. The Sudanese military announcing the United States, Britain, France, and China will evacuate their diplomats and citizens by air with military transport aircraft belonging to their armed forces from Khartoum. Saudi Arabia completing the first civilian evacuations this morning rescuing more than 150 of its own citizens and those of other countries first by caravan and then by ship. While officials familiar with the planning say the Biden administration is leaning towards evacuating the roughly 70 U.S. government personnel in Khartoum. Today, the Pentagon saying they`re preparing for various contingencies, but declining to talk about potential operations. There are more than 16,000 other Americans currently sheltering in place, including Rebecca Winter`s (ph) sister-in-law, a teacher in the capital city of Khartoum. She`s now hiding with her infant daughter. REBECCA WINTER (ph): The city is in complete disarray. She needs to come home now. We need evacuation for U.S. citizens. And we need humanitarian aid for everyone who`s suffering in this conflict in Sudan. KUBE: This week, the U.S. military moves specially trained troops to nearby Djibouti to be ready to rescue Americans caught in the crossfire between two warring generals fighting for control of Sudan. But with the airport`s still shut down, some Americans are prepared to take things into their own hands. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: I`m keeping my hopes up but I`m also preparing for having to find my own route. KUBE: Like 1000s of Americans still caught in the middle of this deadly power struggle. (END VIDEOTAPE) DIAZ-BALART: And Courtney, the situation is going more dire every day? KUBE: Yeah, that`s right. Trapped Americans are running out of supplies. And now some are looking for their own escape route. But tonight State Department officials are warning U.S. citizens not to take private convoys to potential evacuation points, saying, they cannot guarantee anyone safety. Jose. [18:45:04] DIAZ-BALART: Courtney Kube in Washington, thank you. Last night Supreme Court decision to keep the abortion pill mifepristone available for now means the legal and political battles over access to it are just getting started. Monica Alba reports from the White House. (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) MONICA ALBA, NBC NEWS WHITE HOUSE CORRESPONDENT: Tonight, political leaders reacting to the latest development in the hot button issue of abortion access. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: Our confidence in our judiciary (inaudible). SEN. CHUCK SCHUMER , (D) NEW YORK MAJORITY LEADER: The hard right anti- choice MAGA wing in this country will keep working and working and working to take away all women`s rights. ALBA: But for now, the most commonly used abortion pill remains widely available for millions of women after the Supreme Court preserved full access to mifepristone, Friday, while the appeals process plays out over a Texas judge`s ruling that would have jeopardized access to the drug. A majority of the justices granting the Biden administration`s request for temporary relief with Clarence Thomas and Samuel Alito publicly dissenting. The case now goes back to the Fifth Circuit, where oral arguments are set for May 17. Nothing about the medications availability will change before then, and may not until the matter goes back to the High Court. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: I think it`s very highly unlikely given that we`re in April already that this case would be heard and resolved. This term that would be extraordinary, much more likely they`re going to set the matter for argument in the fall of 2023. And a ruling would come out in the spring of 2024. ALBA: The White House relieved for now, with President Biden arguing the lower court decision would have quote undermined FDA`s medical judgment and put women`s health at risk. A new NBC News poll shows 58% of adults say abortion should be legal, either always or most of the time, compared to a combined 38% who believe abortion should be illegal either with exceptions or without exceptions. The abortion debate proving to be a key issue for voters as the race for 2024 heats up. (END VIDEOTAPE) DIAZ-BALART: Monica Alba joins me now from the White House. Monica, is there any reason to think the circuit court could rule differently than it did last time around? ALBA: Well, it`s certainly possible, Jose, because the next three judge panel from the conservative leaning Fifth Circuit that will hear the case next month will be chosen at random. Jose. DIAZ-BALART: Monica Alba at the White House, thank you. And now to the new report that the Air National Guardsmen charged with leaking classified documents may have been sharing Top Secret Intelligence online for much longer than previously thought, possibly as long as a year before he was caught. Ken Dilanian has late details. (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) KEN DILANIAN, NBC NEWS NATIONAL SECURITY CORRESPONDENT: New reporting tonight that the accused leaker of classified information began posting secrets more than a year ago, shortly after Russia`s invasion of Ukraine. The New York Times says it discovered that airman Jack Teixeira allegedly began sharing military secrets as far back as February 2022 to a chat group containing 600 members, that`s 10 months before the December 2022 leaks that Teixeira is charged with. Two sources familiar with the matter tell NBC News investigators gave no indication when briefing Congress last week that they were aware of this new set of disclosures. The FBI and the Pentagon had been scrambling to assess the damage from a leak they first discovered April 5. FRANK FIGLIUZZI, NBC NEWS, NATIONAL SECURITY ANALYST: And the longer something is out there floating in the ether, in the cyber world without the government knowing, without them being able to shut it down, the more potential damage can be done. DILANIAN: Teixeira`s lawyer, the FBI , and the Pentagon, all declined to comment tonight. The Times match the new posts to Teixeira through a series of digital clues including a handle he had previously used. The newspaper quoted Teixeira boasting of his special access to secrets. I have a little more than open-source info perks of being in a USAF intel unit, he said, seemingly referring to his job as an I.T. specialist and an Air Force Intelligence wing and hinting that he used his I.T. access to get information. "The job I have lets me get privileged above most intel guys," he wrote. Teixeira claim he was hunting through classified computer networks for intelligence on the Ukraine war, including material from the National Security Agency and GCHQ, the U.K.`s digital spying department. FIGLIUZZI: This goes way beyond a kid trying to impress his buddies. DILANIAN: When one chat room member urged him not to abuse his access to secrets, he is said to have replied, too late. (END VIDEOTAPE) DIAZ-BALART: And Ken, could these new revelations lead to more charges for Teixeira? DILANIAN: Yeah, Teixeira`s alleged comments in the second chat room really do complicate his legal situation, Jose. He allegedly even offered Teixeira secrets with people outside the United States. headline: The Supreme Court Preserving Access To The Abortion Pill For Now In The Most Significant Case Since Roe v. Wade
story_text: [19:00:00] LESTER HOLT, NBC NEWS ANCHOR (on camera): Tonight, the breaking news from the Supreme Court of the future of that abortion pill. (voiceover): The Supreme Court preserving access to the abortion pill for now in the most significant case since Roe v. Wade. So, what are the next steps? We`ll break it down. The severe storm threat moving east after tornadoes ripped through Texas and Oklahoma. At least three dead, flash flooding and water rescues in Austin, golf ball-sized hail in Illinois, even a water spout in Florida. Millions at risk heading into the weekend. Charges against Alec Baldwin officially dropped. And new details about the gun that killed the Rust cinematographer as production resumes. The new images from inside the film`s Montana set. An American killed in Sudan as fighting rages on. Plus, the latest from U.S. officials on the other Americans trapped. Alarming new findings about climate change. A new report says the melting of glaciers is off the charts. Can anything be done? Is the future of food grown in a lab? It`s better for the climate but what does it taste like? And back in the groove with record sales rising. Why so many are turning to turntables this weekend. ANNOUNCER: This is NBC NIGHTLY NEWS with Lester Holt. HOLT (on camera): Good evening, everyone. Facing an 11:59 p.m. Eastern Time deadline of its own choosing and a day of high drama, the U.S. Supreme Court has just weighed in on another pivotal and consequential question in the nation`s divide over abortion. The justices tonight deciding what`s next for a Texas Court ruling that said the FDA`s 23-year-old approval of a commonly used abortion drug is no longer valid, a ruling temporarily paused from taking effect up until now. That has had the potential to impact medical abortions even in states where abortion remains legal. Senior Legal Correspondent Laura Jarrett is standing by with late details. Laura, what is the court saying here? LAURA JARRETT, NBC NEWS SENIOR LEGAL CORRESPONDENT (on camera): Hey, Lester, good evening. Just minutes ago, the U.S. Supreme Court issued an order to keep a widely used abortion pill on the market. The justices have flatly blocked that lower court decision from Texas that had invalidated the FDA`s longtime approval of Mifepristone and would have made the drugs substantially harder to obtain. Now, Justice Thomas, Justice Alito dissenting to that decision from the rest of their colleagues. The FDA and the drug maker had strongly urged those justices to step in, warning essentially if they hadn`t stepped in, all manufacturing and distribution of this drug would have come to a screeching halt. But for now, women can continue to receive the pill by mail and use it until 10 weeks into their pregnancies while this case continues to play out in the court below. Lester, the Biden Administration just issuing obviously a statement praising it. You know, the groups that had filed this suit originally had claimed that the FDA ignored safety risk, something that the FDA and the Biden Administration put -- pushed back on very strongly, Lester. HOLT: All right, so Laura, legally, what happens next? The next steps here. JARRETT: OK, so, now the case will head back to a federal appeals court for further evaluation of the merits of the lawsuit. This Supreme Court decision was just a temporary issue just because it came up so quickly. Now the case will head back to a three-judge panel on the fifth circuit. It`s made up of mostly conservatives but we don`t know who exactly on that court will hear this case now that it`s back there, Lester. HOLT: All right, Laura Jarrett on that breaking news. I`m joined now by Peter Alexander at the White House. Peter, the president as we heard just reacted to this move. What are you learning? PETER ALEXANDER, NBC NEWS CHIEF WHITE HOUSE CORRESPONDENT (on camera): Yes, Lester, that`s right. The White House has been bracing for this decision for days. Abortion medications have become an increasingly critical flash point of the states` limit or ban abortions after the Supreme Court`s ruling last year overturning Roe v Wade largely because abortion medication can be sent by mail and taken at home. As for the president, he just moments ago weighed in, releasing a statement that reads in part, Mifepristone remains available and approved for safe and effective use. While we continue this fight in the courts, the president adding, that his administration will continue to defend the FDA`s independence to review, approve, and regulate a wide range of prescription drugs. The President says the stakes for women could not be high higher and denounces what he called politically driven attacks on women`s health, Lester. It`s one of only two companies in the U.S. that`s received clearance from the FDA for human consumption of lab- grown meat. The USDA still needs to approve it for sale. (END VIDEOTAPE) HOLT: When we return, how vinyl got its groove back. The return of the record in the record store thanks to everyone from emerging artists to superstars like Taylor Swift. (COMMERCIAL BREAK) [19:25:00] HOLT: Finally tonight, the viral revival ahead of tomorrow`s Record Store Day. Sales of albums now skyrocketing thanks in part to superstars like Taylor Swift. Our Stephanie Gosk has that story. (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) STEPHANIE GOSK, NBC NEWS CORRESPONDENT (voiceover): At a time when music from any era and every genre lives invisibly in the cloud, Record Store Day is dedicated to music that can actually be held in your hand and to the independent stores that never stop selling it.
