GOSK: Record sales are on the rise for the last 16 years, up 17 percent in 2022. BECHOR: We`ve seen vinyl totally almost decimated. We thought we would close. GOSK: Rock and Soul Records Store has been in Midtown Manhattan for 50 years. How would you describe the future today for a record store? BECHOR: Super exciting. Like, we`re really excited. GOSK: Record store day gets bigger every year. Musicians fuel the hype with special releases, limited editions that sell out fast and can only be bought in the store. Last year, the big record was Taylor Swift. BECHOR: They started lining up 24 hours before. GOSK: Wow. BECHOR: So, they really wanted that Taylor Swift. GOSK: And this year, it`s also Taylor Swift. But there is a lot more. Billy Joel, Grateful Dead, Stevie Nicks. The best part about Record Store Day is that there is something for everyone, every taste, every generation, including me. It`s the 40th anniversary of Violent Femmes` debut album, Blister In The Sun, like you`ve never heard it before. And without skipping a beat -- Oh, come on. Oh, right back to high school. So, get offline, get off the couch and go to the record store. Stephanie Gosk, NBC News, New York. (END VIDEOTAPE) HOLT: Well, that sound of a needle hitting the record. That`s NIGHTLY NEWS for this Friday. Thanks for watching. I`m Lester Holt. Please take care of yourself and each other. Good night, everyone. headline: The Battle Over Abortion Rights Is Now Headed Back To The Supreme Court
story_text: [18:30:21] JOSE DIAZ-BALART, NBC NEWS HOST: Today tonight, the battle over abortion rights is now headed back to the Supreme Court. Protesters out in force today from Los Angeles to Washington, D.C., as the fate of access to abortion pills could be decided within days. New revelations from those leaked intel documents, reports of up to four more Chinese spy balloons and new questions about why it took authorities so long to notice the leaked documents. Terrifying moments as a bomb is thrown at Japan`s Prime minister. He is rushed to safety before it explodes. What we know about the suspect. A violent coup d`etat playing out right now in Africa. The American ambassador and his staff forced to take shelter. The deadly police mistake caught on video. Officers at the wrong address. When the homeowner opens the door with a gun, they opened fire. How could this have happened? NBC News with rare access as law enforcement busts a giant retail crime ring. Nearly $200,000 in merchandise recovered. And there`s good news tonight. The daughter who reveals to her father after his life saving kidney transplant, she was his donor. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) UNIDENTIFIED MALE: I`m really proud of her. I can`t believe she did it. (END VIDEO CLIP) UNIDENTIFIED MALE: This is NBC NIGHTLY NEWS with Jose Diaz-Balart. DIAZ-BALART: Good evening. The nation`s highest court is once again wading into the country`s most divisive issue, abortion rights. Today, there were protesters outside the Supreme Court as well as rallies across the country. The past week has been a dizzying string of competing and contradictory court decisions, some restricting access to the abortion pill, others protecting it. The Supreme Court now says it will take up the issue, setting a deadline just five days away. At stake, access to mifepristone, the abortion pill the most common way women and pregnancies in the U.S. The Supreme Court could rule to suspend its use nationwide. We begin tonight with Monica Alba. (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: And we didn`t backed down. CROWD: No. MONICA ALBA, NBC NEWS CORRESPONDENT (voice-over): Protests from coast to coast tonight. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: Standup don`t back. ALBA (voice-over): As the fate of the nation`s most commonly used abortion pill hangs in the balance. After a week of uncertainty, the Supreme Court weighing in Friday, keeping mifepristone available for at least the next four days. The temporary action allows the full court to review emergency appeals from the Biden administration and one of the drug makers and gives the plaintiffs a group of doctors and advocacy groups until Tuesday to submit their arguments. ERIN HAWLEY, ALLIANCE DEFENDING FREEDOM SENIOR COUNSEL: It`s really time that the FDA was held to account for putting politics above women`s health and safety, as well as unborn lives. ALBA (voice-over): The high court expected to rule on Wednesday as abortion rights activists expressed concern about what the conservative majority that overturned Roe v. Wade could do now. WENDY FROSH, WASHINGTON, D.C. ABORTION RIGHTS PROTESTER: The same could happen with any other medication if we allow judges to exercise this outrageous authority or misuse of authority. ALBA (voice-over): If the Fifth Circuit ruling is upheld, women would have to get the drug in person at the doctor`s office. It would no longer be available by mail and the window for prescription would be narrowed from 10 weeks to seven. The White House standing by the FDA`s, quote, evidence- based approval. JOE BIDEN , PRESIDENT OF THE UNITED STATES: I think it`s outrageous what the court has done relative to concluding that they`re going to overrule the FDA . ALBA (voice-over): With Vice President Harris making a surprise stop at the Los Angeles women`s march Saturday, vowing to stand up and fight for abortion access. KAMALA HARRIS , VICE PRESIDENT OF THE UNITED STATES: This is a moment that history will show required each of us. (END VIDEOTAPE) DIAZ-BALART: And Monica joins us now from the White House. Monica, what could the Supreme Court do Wednesday? ALBA: Well, it`s unclear how the justices will rule, but it`s possible the court could extend the temporary pause, keeping things as they were before the Texas ruling, until this can play out in the lower courts. Jose? DIAZ-BALART: Monica Alba, thank you. END Content and programming copyright 2023 NBCUniversal. ALL RIGHTS RESERVED. Transcription Copyright 2023 VIQ Media Transcription, Inc. headline: The Supreme Court Putting A Temporary Hold On A Lower Court Ruling That Would Limit Access To An Abortion Pill Keeping It Widely Available For Now
story_text: LESTER HOLT: A late and dramatic development in the battle over that abortion pill. Late today, the Supreme Court stepping in and putting a temporary hold on a lower court ruling that would limit access. Laura Jarrett has details for us. (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) LAURA JARRETT, NBC NEWS SENIOR LEGAL CORRESPONDENT (voiceover): Tonight, the U.S. Supreme Court moving quick to block a federal judge from rolling back access to the abortion pill mifepristone at least for now. Justice Samuel Alito handing down an order within hours of the Justice Department`s emergency appeal that had warned of chaos and profound disruption if the high court didn`t step in. At issue in the case, a legal morass of complex FDA regulations over the drug that had recently been made easier to obtain. KAMALA HARRIS , VICE PRESIDENT OF THE UNITED STATES: They attacked medication that for 20 years the FDA ruled as being safe. JARRETT: But the advocacy groups and doctors that sued to ban the drug claim the FDA ignored safety risks. Those plaintiffs now have until Tuesday to submit their legal arguments to the justices. At the same time, access to abortion now largely cut off throughout much of the south. After the Supreme Court overturned Roe v Wade, many women traveled to Florida for abortions. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: Show the bill passes. JARRETT: Now, the state has banned anyone from seeking an abortion after six weeks of pregnancy though the law won`t go into effect right away. FENTRICE DRISKELL (D-FL), STATE REPRESENTATIVE: You just don`t want women to have choice. CHASE TRAMONT (R-FL), STATE REPRESENTATIVE: Here we value life from conception to the casket. JARRETT: Governor Ron DeSantis signing the bill with a private gathering overnight, a far cry from the jubilant celebration he put on for a 15-week ban passed last spring highlighting a rising tension within the GOP on the issue. As some are mindful of the public polling largely favoring abortion, other presidential hopefuls are leaning into their conservative base with eyes on 2024, including Senator Tim Scott who spoke exclusively to NBC`s Ali Vitali today. TIM SCOTT (R-SC): If I were President of the United States, I would literally sign the most conservative pro-life legislation that they can get through Congress. JARRETT: But for now, the issue of abortion access rest with the Supreme Court, with the justices poised to rule next week. Laura Jarrett, NBC News (END VIDEOTAPE) END Content and programming copyright 2023 NBCUniversal. ALL RIGHTS RESERVED. Transcription Copyright 2023 VIQ Media Transcription, Inc. headline: The Battle Over Access To Abortion Pills Headed To The Supreme Court
story_text: LESTER HOLT: Now to the escalating fight over access to an abortion pill. The Justice Department says it will now ask the Supreme Court for emergency action to stop new restrictions from taking effect. Laura Jarrett has late details. (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) LAURA JARRETT, NBC NEWS SENIOR LEGAL CORRESPONDENT (voiceover): A fierce battle over abortion now headed to the U.S. Supreme Court . The Attorney General vowing to challenge a ruling from a federal appeals court that could jeopardize access to mifepristone, a commonly used abortion pill. KARINE JEAN-PIERRE , WHITE HOUSE PRESS SECRETARY: We believe that the law is on our side. JARRETT: Overnight, that appeals court blocked a portion of a Texas ruling that invalidated the approval of mifepristone, allowing the drug to remain on the market for now. But the judges also rolled back several FDA moves in recent years that made the drug easier to obtain. If the Supreme Court doesn`t step in, women may soon be required to visit a doctor`s office in person to receive the pill instead of taking it at home. It will no longer be available through the mail. The generic version also off the table. And the pill will only be approved through seven weeks of pregnancy instead of 10. DR. LAURA MACISAAC, OBSTETRICIAN-GYNECOLOGIST, MOUNT SINAI: Having more in- person visits means women will have to take time off of work, get childcare often during the work week. If the medication can`t get into the hands of the people that need it quickly, then it isn`t available. JARRETT: Doctors like Laura McIsaac who practice for over three decades alarmed by the ruling. MACISAAC: That will absolutely increase pregnancy complications and increase maternal mortality. JARRETT: Restricting access to mifepristone at the heart of the original Texas lawsuit. ERIN MORROW HAWLEY , SENIOR COUNSEL, ALLIANCE DEFENDING FREEDOM: The FDA has basically sanctioned mail-order abortions. JARRETT: Erin Hawley represents the advocacy groups and doctors that sued the FDA . HAWLEY: The Fifth Circuit`s decision is a huge victory for women and for the rule of law. The FDA did not have a valid basis for approving that drug. JARRETT: While the fight continues in the courts, tonight, a clash at the State House. In Florida, anger erupting on the House floor. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: Show the bill passes. JARRETT: As the Republican-controlled legislature passed a six-week abortion ban headed to the governor`s desk for signature soon. (END VIDEOTAPE) HOLT: So, Laura, when do all these restrictions take effect? JARRETT (on camera): So, those restrictions should begin early Saturday. I say should because tonight a federal judge in a different case in Washington State reiterated that the Biden administration must not make any changes to the availability of this drug. The government will likely tell the U.S. Supreme Court it simply cannot comply with all these conflicting rulings. HOLT: All right, Laura, thanks very much. headline: The Battle Over An Abortion Pill: Big Pharma Pushing Back Against The Ruling As Some States Start Stockpiling Drugs
story_text: LESTER HOLT: Major backlash tonight from the drug industry to that abortion pill ruling by a federal judge. And now, some states are stockpiling abortion drugs as the legal battle plays out. Laura Jarrett has the latest. (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) LAURA JARRETT, NBC NEWS SENIOR LEGAL CORRESPONDENT (voiceover): A show of force from big pharma now waiting into the battle over a widely used abortion pill. More than 600 drug makers and biotech leaders signing on to a scathing condemnation of that ruling by a federal judge in Texas invalidating the FDA`s longtime approval of mifepristone, accusing the judge of activism. DR. AMANDA BANKS, FORMER CEO, BLACKFYNN THERAPEUTICS: Now -- it`s now been shown that courts can step in and overturn a scientific decision. Dr. Amanda Banks, a former CEO of Blackfynn Therapeutics, who co-authored the letter says the judge`s ruling sets a dangerous precedent that extends beyond the abortion issue. BANKS: If one medicine is subject to this kind of outcome, really any medicine is. JARRETT: President Biden also slamming the decision today. JOE BIDEN , PRESIDENT OF THE UNITED STATES: My thoughts are completely out of bounds what the judge did. JARRETT: While the anti-abortion group that filed the Texas lawsuit is doubling down. Writing in a statement, "The FDA failed to abide by its legal obligations to protect the health, safety, and welfare of girls and women." With the Texas order is set to go into effect early Saturday unless blocked in the courts, Democratic governors are not wasting any time taking matters into their own hands. GOV. GRETCHEN WHITMER (D-MI): We`re taking a close look at all of our options. JARRETT: Massachusetts, Washington State, New York, and California all now stockpiling years` worth of mifepristone or an alternative abortion pill. GOV. KATHY HOCHUL (D-NY): So, I`m proud to announce that New York State will create a stockpile of misoprostol, another form of medication abortion. JARRETT: It`s all in preparation for a decision that would apply nationwide. (END VIDEOTAPE) HOLT: So, Laura, where does all these stand right now as far as the courts are concerned? JARRETT (on camera): So, late tonight and tomorrow, we should see more court filings from both the plaintiffs that filed the Texas lawsuit and the Justice Department, which is asking the Fifth Circuit Court of Appeals to freeze that judge`s order. Once all those are in midday tomorrow, we could see a decision from that appeals court anytime. HOLT: All right, Laura Jarrett, thanks very much. In 60 seconds, the tough new auto emission standard is about to be announced. Will they push more Americans toward electric vehicles. Plus, spring is here and already setting some record temperatures in a lot of cities, next. (COMMERCIAL BREAK) HOLT: Spring is here but much of the country is seeing record highs temperatures in places like Phoenix, and Las Vegas, even South Dakota hit the 90s. Denver broke its record and temperatures are expected to continue to climb this week bringing record highs to the northeast. END Content and programming copyright 2023 NBCUniversal. headline: NBC NIGHTLY NEWS for April 11, 2023, NBC
story_text: [19:00:00] (COMMERCIAL BREAK) LESTER HOLT, NBC NEWS ANCHOR (on camera): Tonight, the terrifying images just released of a Louisville mass shooting. (voiceover): Police body camera video showing how officers confronted the gunman who police say ambush them after shooting and killing five of his fellow bank workers using an AR-15 he bought legally. One officer shot at and getting back off to reengage. Officers being hailed as heroes for stopping him from killing more people. Were there warning signs and what his neighbors are saying? Damage control. New revelations from those leaked classified intelligence documents putting U.S. alliances in question. The Manhattan district attorney sues a top House Republican claiming interference in the investigation of Donald Trump . The battle over an abortion pill. headline: The Future Of The Pill Used For More Than Two Decades Uncertain After Competing Rulings By Two Federal Judges
story_text: LESTER HOLT: This evening, the divide over abortion is centered on a pill used for more than 20 years. But now the focus of competing rulings by two federal courts. Dasha Burns reports and the growing fallout. [19:05:07] (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) DASHA BURNS, NBC NEWS CORRESPONDENT (voiceover): Tonight, the fallout from dueling court rulings. The future of the abortion pill is hanging in the balance after a Texas judge invalidated the FDA`s approval of mifepristone. The Department of Justice is now appealing that decision. JENNIFER KLEIN, WHITE HOUSE GENDER POLICY COUNCIL: What this ruling effectively is a backdoor ban on abortion. BURNS: What options are available to the administration here? KLEIN: We`ve been waiting for the judge to rule. And what we did is what we believe is the best strategy which is to appeal this decision immediately. BURNS: Minutes after the Texas judge`s decision on Friday night, a federal judge in Washington State with equal authority dropping a contradictory ruling ordering the FDA to maintain access to the drug. It all sowed confusion nationwide and created a legal standoff. Use with another drug, mifepristone is the most common method for terminating pregnancies in the U.S. It`s been approved since 2000 and used safely more than five million times. But the plaintiffs in the Texas case, a group of anti-abortion doctors and medical organizations, allege the drug is dangerous and the FDA didn`t follow proper protocol when approving it. I spoke with the group behind the lawsuit before the ruling. The result if you win is that abortion access will be significantly limited. Is that the goal of this loss? ERIK BAPTIST, SENIOR COUNSEL, ALLIANCE DEFENDING FREEDOM: No, the goal of this lawsuit is to protect American women and girls from dangerous chemical abortion drugs. It`s not -- we are not seeking a nationwide abortion ban. BURNS: Meanwhile, today, lawmakers in blue states vowed to do whatever necessary to protect reproductive rights. GOV. MAURA HEALEY (D-MA): It harms patients, undermines medical expertise, and takes away freedom. BURNS: Tonight, Mifepristone remains legal as the battles rage on in the courts. Dasha Burns, NBC News . (END VIDEOTAPE) HOLT: Let me bring in now Senior Legal Correspondent Laura Jarrett. Laura, there was movement on both of these cases in court today. LAURA JARRETT, NBC NEWS SENIOR LEGAL CORRESPONDENT (on camera): A flurry of court filings today, Lester. The Justice Department and the pill manufacturer both hoping to convince a conservative-leaning court of appeals to hit pause on that Texas decision, to give everyone time to make their arguments without this deadline looming of the ruling set to go into effect on Saturday. The court just minutes ago asking to hear what the plaintiffs have to say about all that, but the FDA also wants Clarity from a federal judge in Washington State who ordered the drug to stay on the market about how to reconcile that order with the Texas ruling. HOLT: This feels like this could be heading to the Supreme Court. JARRETT: Yes, it really could, and fast. If the Fifth Circuit doesn`t block the Texas decision, the DOJ will take it to the Supreme Court as soon as this week. And if DOJ wins, the plaintiffs could appeal there as well. HOLT: All right, Laura, thanks very much. END Content and programming copyright 2023 NBCUniversal. ALL RIGHTS RESERVED. Transcription Copyright 2023 VIQ Media Transcription, Inc. Israel attacked by rockets from inside Syria. The retaliation tonight. Should this convicted killer walk free? headline: Abortion Rights Activists Vowing To Fight, Others Celebrate The Rule, As The Biden Administration Says It Will Appeal
story_text: JOSE DIAZ-BALART: President Biden is vowing to fight the Texas ruling. It`s the beginning of what`s expected to be yet another contentious round of court battles over abortion. Monica Alba reports from the White House. (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) MONICA ALBA, NBC NEWS WHITE HOUSE CORRESPONDENT: The battle over abortion rights could again be headed for the Supreme Court, with the Department of Justice planning to appeal the Texas ruling that would jeopardize access to the most commonly used abortion pill, setting up a legal showdown, less than a year after the court overturned Roe v. Wade. [18:35:07] President Biden vowed to fight the decision, writing Friday, if it were to stand, there will be virtually no prescription approved by the FDA that would be safe from these kinds of political ideological attacks. The Texas case now goes to the conservative Fifth Circuit, but in the short term, the drug is still available. It`s unclear whether the Washington State ruling which asks for the medication to be kept on the market will also be appealed. If both are heard at the circuit level, it`s unlikely this will be resolved in the courts anytime soon. CAROL LAM , FORMER SOUTHERN DISTRICT OF CALIFORNIA U.S. ATTORNEY: I would not expect there to be much change in the actual law for at least several months, perhaps upwards of a year. ALBA: With the Supreme Court, which currently has a conservative majority watching to see how that plays out. LAM: What is most likely to happen is that there will be a split in the circuits. So the Fifth Circuit will rule one way, the Ninth Circuit will rule a different way. And the Supreme Court will say now there is a conflict between two circuits. And that means we should probably hear this case and decide the issue on the merits. ALBA: As Vice President Harris, who has been the administration`s leading voice on abortion access, slammed the Texas decision as a dangerous precedent. KAMALA HARRIS , U.S. VICE PRESIDENT: There is no question that the President and I are going to stand with the women of America. (END VIDEOTAPE) DIAZ-BALART: And Monica joins us now from the White House. What else Monica, could the Biden administration do here? ALBA: Well, the Justice Department could file an emergency appeal with the High Court, while it also tries to get the Texas order blocked by the Fifth Circuit, a strategic call that likely will become apparent in the next week or so. Jose? DIAZ-BALART: Monica Alba at the White House, thank you. END Content and programming copyright 2023 NBCUniversal. ALL RIGHTS RESERVED. Transcription Copyright 2023 VIQ Media Transcription, Inc. headline: Major Fallout After A Federal Judge Suspends Approval Of The Commonly Used Abortion Pill Set To Begin Within Day
story_text: [18:30:17] JOSE DIAZ-BALART, NBC NEWS HOST: Tonight, major fallout after a federal judge suspends approval of the commonly used abortion pill set to begin within day. Abortion rights activists vowing to fight, others celebrate the rule, as the Biden administration says it will appeal. New confusion today after another judge rules in favor of the pill. Will the Supreme Court decide the issue? Is their mole in the Pentagon? The race to find out who may be leaking top secret intelligence, the Department of Justice and Pentagon now investigate. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: They put ourselves at risk, they put our allies at risk. DIAZ-BALART: China`s major escalation launching massive military drills off Taiwan`s coast just as U.S. lawmakers visit the island. Our correspondent is there. Gunfire at the beach, six people shot most of them teenagers enjoying a senior skip day. Video so the chaotic moments shots were fired. Terrifying new footage of trees falling at the Masters are these the luckiest people on earth. Watch his three trees just barely missed them. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: Trees are falling off of the ground. DIAZ-BALART: Why play was halted again today. And the need for speed. The new push across the country to raise the speed limit. How fast is too fast. ANNOUNCER: This is NBC NIGHTLY NEWS with Jose Diaz-Balart. DIAZ-BALART: Good evening, a new front has opened to the nation`s ongoing battle over abortion rights. Not even a year after Roe v. Wade was overturned leaving it up to the states to determine whether abortions are legal. A federal judge issued a ruling that would halt the use of the commonly used abortion pill nationwide. The decision came down late on a Friday of a holiday weekend. But the reaction today was swift with some small protests across the country. The suspension doesn`t go into effect for seven days. And the Biden administration is vowing to stop it. The case seems destined to rocket up the legal system possibly all the way to the Supreme Court. We have two reports tonight beginning with Dasha Burns, who has been with activists on both sides. (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) DASHA BURNS, NBC NEWS CORRESPONDENT: Tonight activist outraged over a Texas judge`s ruling late Friday, suspending the FDA approval of the abortion pill Mifeprex generically known as mifepristone. Judge Matthew Kacsmaryk writing in his opinion, the court does not second guess the FDA`s decision making lightly. But here the FDA acquiesced on its legitimate safety concerns. But he stopped short of an immediate nationwide ban, instead allowing the federal government seven days to appeal the decision. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: This is an assault on the humanity of women. This is an assault on basic reproductive rights. It`s also an assault on democracy. BURNS: The outcomes celebrated by the plaintiffs. ERIK BAPTIST, ALLIANCE DEFENDING FREEDOM LEAD ATTORNEY: This is a significant victory for the doctors and medical associations we represent. And more importantly, the health and safety of women and girls. BURNS: We sat down with Alliance Defending Freedom before the ruling the conservative group behind the lawsuit that was also instrumental in overturning Roe v. Wade. BAPTIST: The goal of this lawsuit is to protect American women and girls from dangerous chemical abortion drugs. It`s not we are not seeking a nationwide abortion ban. BURNS: The drug has been approved by the FDA since 2000. Since then, more than 5 million women have taken mifepristone with 28 deaths associated with the drug reported. It`s the most common method for terminating pregnancies in the U.S. But just minutes after the Texas ruling came down a federal judge in Washington State dropped a contradictory decision protecting access to the abortion pill in 17 states and Washington D.C., the dueling rulings now so in chaos and confusion across the country. (END VIDEOTAPE) DIAZ-BALART: And Dasha joins us now from New York City`s Washington Square Park where, Dasha, a small group of protesters have gathered? BURNS: That`s right, Jose. Activists here and nationwide criticizing the judges timing, the ruling coming ahead of a holiday weekend. Still protesters here telling me the stakes are too high to stay home as this decision could impact abortion access here in New York and nationwide. Jose? DIAZ-BALART: Dasha Burns in New York. Thank you. END Content and programming copyright 2023 NBCUniversal. ALL RIGHTS RESERVED. Transcription Copyright 2023 VIQ Media Transcription, Inc. headline: The Issue Of Abortion, In Idaho, Doctors Are Facing Difficult Decisions
story_text: LESTER HOLT: On the issue of abortion, in Idaho, doctors are facing difficult decisions. Some choosing to leave the state due to its restrictive abortion laws. Kristen Dahlgren explains. [19:10:08] (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) KRISTEN DAHLGREN, NBC NEWS CORRESPONDENT (voiceover): Not far from Idaho`s Capitol building, Dr. Kylie Cooper and her family are packing up and moving out of the state. The high-risk pregnancy specialist says she can no longer safely practice under one of the nation`s most restrictive abortion bans. DR. KYLIE COOPER, OBSTETRICIAN-GYNECOLOGIST: My husband and I are finding ourselves having conversations about what we would do if I were charged with a felony. DAHLGREN: Idaho only has exceptions for rape, incest, or averting the mother`s death. COOPER: Do I make the medically appropriate decision and commit a felony or do I follow the law and then watch as this person in front of me gets sicker and sicker? DAHLGREN: A recent survey shows about half of OBGYN`s in Idaho are considering leaving the state in the next year. All but two of those polled say the state`s abortion ban is the reason. So, you don`t think doctors are leaving the state. RAUL LABRADOR , ATTORNEY GENERAL, IDAHO: I don`t think there`s a huge outflow of doctors. DAHLGREN: GOP State Attorney General Raul Labrador . LABRADOR: I think maybe they just need more education on what the law allows. DAHLGREN: So, you`re saying the doctors are misinformed? LABRADOR: I think I`ve heard a lot of things that that borders on misinformation. But I think doctors are safe as long as they`re following the law. DAHLGREN: Many doctors say the law can be confusing. In fact, just hours after talking to us, Labrador withdrew a widely circulated letter to a state senator, in which he stated the law prohibits doctors from providing abortion pills or referring women out of state for abortions. Now saying it was not intended as a guidance document, and an updated law made it moot. For Dr. Cooper, it`s a hard day leaving patients like the one who recently asked -- DAHLGREN: Is it safe for me to be pregnant in Idaho? And my unequivocal answer was no, it`s not. DAHLGREN: But she doesn`t think it`s safe for doctors either. Kristen Dahlgren, NBC News, Boise, Idaho. (END VIDEOTAPE) HOLT: We`ll be back in 60 seconds with a chilling new video showing a tech executive moments after he was stabbed. Plus, the shocking moment that shut down the Masters. (COMMERCIAL BREAK) HOLT: At the Masters Golf Tournament in Georgia today, this is a terrifying moment high winds knocked down three trees near the 17th tee. Take a look. You can see people scrambling to get out of the way. There are no reports of injuries, but tournament play when suspended and the grounds evacuated because of dangerously high winds, lightning, and approaching thunderstorms. HOLT: And Laura, we`re also watching some breaking news about a high-stakes lawsuit in Texas over the abortion pill. What do you know? JARRETT: Yes, that`s right, Lester. This just coming down minutes ago. This decision a partial victory for a group of anti-abortion advocates and doctors that had asked a federal judge to block access to the drug most widely used to induce abortions. Now, the plaintiffs had asked that judge to remove it from the market entirely nationwide immediately, but the judge didn`t go that far. Instead, he has suspended the original approval of the drug, acknowledging the plaintiffs do have a right to sue in this case, acknowledging their arguments about safety concerns, but there`s no immediate effect of this ruling. The judge has instead giving the Justice Department seven days to appeal, something Biden administration has almost certainly going to do very quickly. They have signaled that previously. HOLT: All right, Laura Jarrett, thank you for all that. On the issue of abortion, in Idaho, doctors are facing difficult decisions. Some choosing to leave the state due to its restrictive abortion laws. Kristen Dahlgren explains. [19:10:08] (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) KRISTEN DAHLGREN, NBC NEWS CORRESPONDENT (voiceover): Not far from Idaho`s Capitol building, Dr. Kylie Cooper and her family are packing up and moving out of the state. The high-risk pregnancy specialist says she can no longer safely practice under one of the nation`s most restrictive abortion bans. DR. KYLIE COOPER, OBSTETRICIAN-GYNECOLOGIST: My husband and I are finding ourselves having conversations about what we would do if I were charged with a felony. DAHLGREN: Idaho only has exceptions for rape, incest, or averting the mother`s death. COOPER: Do I make the medically appropriate decision and commit a felony or do I follow the law and then watch as this person in front of me gets sicker and sicker? DAHLGREN: A recent survey shows about half of OBGYN`s in Idaho are considering leaving the state in the next year. All but two of those polled say the state`s abortion ban is the reason. So, you don`t think doctors are leaving the state. RAUL LABRADOR , ATTORNEY GENERAL, IDAHO: I don`t think there`s a huge outflow of doctors. DAHLGREN: GOP State Attorney General Raul Labrador . LABRADOR: I think maybe they just need more education on what the law allows. DAHLGREN: So, you`re saying the doctors are misinformed? LABRADOR: I think I`ve heard a lot of things that that borders on misinformation. But I think doctors are safe as long as they`re following the law. DAHLGREN: Many doctors say the law can be confusing. In fact, just hours after talking to us, Labrador withdrew a widely circulated letter to a state senator, in which he stated the law prohibits doctors from providing abortion pills or referring women out of state for abortions. Now saying it was not intended as a guidance document, and an updated law made it moot. For Dr. Cooper, it`s a hard day leaving patients like the one who recently asked -- DAHLGREN: Is it safe for me to be pregnant in Idaho? And my unequivocal answer was no, it`s not. DAHLGREN: But she doesn`t think it`s safe for doctors either. Kristen Dahlgren, NBC News, Boise, Idaho. (END VIDEOTAPE) HOLT: We`ll be back in 60 seconds with a chilling new video showing a tech executive moments after he was stabbed. Plus, the shocking moment that shut down the Masters. (COMMERCIAL BREAK) HOLT: At the Masters Golf Tournament in Georgia today, this is a terrifying moment high winds knocked down three trees near the 17th tee. Take a look. You can see people scrambling to get out of the way. There are no reports of injuries, but tournament play when suspended and the grounds evacuated because of dangerously high winds, lightning, and approaching thunderstorms. Police in San Francisco are combing through disturbing newly released surveillance video hoping to find new clues in the stabbing death this week of a Silicon Valley tech titan. Miguel Almaguer reports. (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) MIGUEL ALMAGUER, NBC NEWS NATIONAL CORRESPONDENT (voiceover): This Chilling surveillance video could be a key piece of evidence. The dailymail.com which obtained CCTV says after tech executive Bob Lee was stabbed multiple times, he appears to try and wave down a passing car for help before the motorists drives away, wounded and stumbling into clear view around 2:35 a.m. Tuesday. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: The location is 365 Main, across from Folsom and Harrison. There`s been stabbing. ALMAGUER: The San Francisco Standard says Lee called 911 and screamed help, someone stabbed me. BROOKE JENKINS, DISTRICT ATTORNEY, SAN FRANCISCO: That 911 call of course gives us a sense of time, but unfortunately unless someone says who did it or what happened specifically, its usefulness can be limited. ALMAGUER: San Francisco`s D.A. says she cannot confirm reports a knife was found near the crime scene, but says cellphone data is key. JENKINS: We want to know who he has been communicating with just before he was stabbed, who he was with, what cell phone towers that cell phone was hitting. Those are all critical pieces of evidence for us tracing backward to the moment that this stabbing occurred. [19:15:05] ALMAGUER: Perhaps best known for creating the mobile payment service, Cash App -- BOB LEE, TECH EXECUTIVE: We still need solutions for the unbanked. ALMAGUER: -- Lee was a tech icon who used to live near the area where he was killed. The police chief facing pressure as the city safety remains under blaring scrutiny amid a rash of negative headlines. BILL SCOTT, CHIEF, SAN FRANCISCO POLICE: We do have some good things to follow up on his case. And they are working tirelessly. ALMAGUER: Tonight, the high-profile murder mystery of a tech titan. Miguel Almaguer, NBC News. (END VIDEOTAPE) HOLT: We are back in a moment with a warning for parents about the big risks over where your baby sleeps. (COMMERCIAL BREAK) [20:20:00] HOLT: We have an important warning for parents. Doctors are reporting a jump in infant deaths linked to unsafe sleeping conditions and co-sleeping with parents. Tom Costello now with what you need to know. (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) TOM COSTELLO, NBC NEWS CORRESPONDENT (voiceover): Cook Children`s in Fort Worth calls it alarming. 30 babies in just 15 months who likely died during unsafe sleeping conditions suffocating next to the adult in the bedding or pillows. DR. GEETHA DEVDAS, EMERGENCY MEDICINE PHYSICIAN, COOK CHILDREN`S MEDICAL CENTER: Co-sleeping is not something that we recommend. We recommend that babies really have their own bed, crib, or bassinet to sleep in. COSTELLO: Last month, the CDC reported a 15 percent increase of sudden infant death cases among African Americans in 2020 during the pandemic. Providers say multi-generational homes where parents sleep with children and have poor access to health care could be contributing factors. Nationwide, each year, 3400 sleep-related infant deaths. The risk is five to 10 times higher while bed-sharing with an adult even higher on a couch or chair. Tragically, it happened to pediatric cardiologist Sam Hankey in 2010. His 3-week-old son Charlie fell asleep on his chest as Sam also slept. [19:20:30] SAM HANKE, PEDIATRIC CARDIOLOGIST: When I woke up, Charlie never did. And this tragedy is something that happens way too often in our country. COSTELLO: Pediatricians say children should sleep and PJs or sleeping sack flat on their backs on fitted sheets, no blankets, pillows or stuffed animals. Sam hanky and his wife have started Charlie`s Kids. HANKE: What we`ve learned is that we`re not alone in this tragedy. COSTELLO: Teaching safe sleep to prevent another baby from dying. Tom Costello, NBC News, Washington. (END VIDEOTAPE) HOLT: And I`ll be back with a remarkable story of forgiveness in this season of renewal. (COMMERCIAL BREAK) HOLT: Finally, tonight, in this season of grace and renewal, we have a remarkable story of forgiveness. It`s a story of a man who was willing to open himself up to the humanity and potential of a stranger who took the life of someone dear to him. [19:25:02] (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) HOLT: I`ve done a lot of interviews with newly released incarcerated people and generally they have been exonerated. That`s not your story. RANDALL BAGLEY, INCARCERATED FOR MURDER: That`s not my story. HOLT: You did it. BAGLEY: I did it. HOLT: You killed a man. BAGLEY: I did. HOLT (voiceover): In 1998, Randall Bagley shot and killed Donald Mitchell during a Maryland robbery. BAGLEY: I turn to say something to him, and the gun went off. HOLT: In an instant, a man robbed of his life and the victim`s young son robbed of a father. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: You`re the Boogeyman. HOLT: Last September, 24 years later, Idris Mitchell spoke in a Maryland court where that man who killed his dad was asking for a second chance, a reduction of his sentence. Audio recordings captured the hearing. IDRIS MITCHELL, SON OF DONALD MITCHELL: You are the nightmare. I`ve never seen you. I never knew what you look like. HOLT: But then, he stunned the courtroom. MITCHELL: I fundamentally, wholly and wholeheartedly forgive you. HOLT: Mitchell asked the judge to release Begley from his life-plus 35 years sentence. When Idris spoke, what was going through your mind? BAGLEY: I thought it was unreal. I thought it was unreal. HOLT: Mitchell even surprised himself. MITCHELL: I didn`t want to say that I forgave him. HOLT: But more than for forgive him, you also called for his release. You said -- MITCHELL: No, that was unexpected. HOLT: It was unexplained. MITCHELL: That was unexpected. I was going to stop there. And I think what changed, and even advocating for his release was again hearing what he had done. HOLT: In Bagley, Mitchell says he found things in common, both high achievers. Mitchell, a Yale grad. Bagley accepted into the first class of Georgetown University `s bachelor degree program for the incarcerated. MITCHELL: Not to be funny, but he had a better GPA than I did at Yale. So, I was like, OK, slightly better. I had a good one. But I think that he simply -- he simply dedicated himself to improvement. HOLT: Mark Howard heads Georgetown`s Prisons and Justice Initiative. MARK HOWARD, DIRECTOR, GEORGETOWN`S PRISON AND JUSTICE INITIATIVE: When he started explaining what happened in that courtroom and also the role that this program had played in his journey of getting him to that point, it was very emotional. HOLT: A judge recently slashed Bagley sentence, and he was released in January. In some ways setting two men free. MITCHELL: You wait 23 years to say something. And then when you do, you find yourself actually advocating for the man who killed your father. That`s not -- I don`t think that`s conventional, but it`s what felt right. HOLT: Did you deserve that level of forgiveness? BAGLEY: I don`t deserve anything. I took a man`s life. I don`t deserve anything. I`m grateful. Happy, but I don`t deserve anything. MITCHELL: Randall, Mr. Bagley, which do you prefer? BAGLEY: Whatever. MITCHELL: Whatever? BAGLEY: Randall, yes. MITCHELL: Randall, OK. Are you OK? BAGLEY: Yes. MITCHELL: OK. BAGLEY: Are you OK? MITCHELL: We`re working on it. We`re working on it. BAGLEY: Idris. MITCHELL: So, what`s going on? BAGLEY: I`m still trying to process it. HOLT: And as they recently met for the first time, one question lingered in the air -- why? BAGLEY: What made you do it when you could have said so many other things other than I forgive you? MITCHELL: Because I -- because I think people can change, all right. People can change. You`re 22. It`s been 24 years. BAGLEY: It takes a lot to do what you`re doing. It takes a lot. It takes a lot. MITCHELL: I appreciate that. BAGLEY: Takes a lot, bro. (END VIDEOTAPE) HOLT: A powerful moment of healing. That`s NIGHTLY NEWS for this Friday. Thank you for watching, everyone. I`m Lester Holt. Please take care of yourself and each other. Good night. (COMMERCIAL BREAK) END Content and programming copyright 2023 NBCUniversal. ALL RIGHTS RESERVED. story_text: [19:00:00] (COMMERCIAL BREAK) LESTER HOLT, NBC NEWS ANCHOR (on camera): Tonight, the dramatic showdown over guns in Tennessee. (voiceover): The state`s Republican-led house voting on removing three Democrats from office after they led a protest on the floor demanding stricter gun laws after the Nashville school shooting that killed six people. The rare punishment used only three times before since the Civil War. Outside the building, the massive protest and what happens now with the ousted Democrat seats? Also, tonight, in the new report of the U.S. withdrawal from Afghanistan, the White House largely blaming the chaos and decisions by Former President Trump and the actions it says the U.S. should have taken even sooner. The rising tensions of the Middle East. Israel striking back tonight after the biggest barrage of missiles from Lebanon in more than 16 years. Tracking severe storms on the move tonight in the Mid-Atlantic on the heels of that deadly tornado outbreak. NBC News investigates after our report on toxic air concerns near a Louisiana school. What the EPA is now doing about it. And it was 20 years ago we lost a member of our NBC News family covering the war in Iraq. Tonight, my conversation with David Bloom`s widow about the lives his story may have saved. ANNOUNCER: This is NBC Nightly News with Lester Holt. HOLT (on camera): Good evening and welcome. The tears of grief that consume Nashville, Tennessee just 10 days ago over the murders of young children and school staffers are replaced tonight by cries of anger and accusations after an extraordinary move by Tennessee House Republicans to seek the expulsion of three Democratic members for their roles in a gun safety protest on the House floor last week. All day, angry supporters and gun safety advocates crowding the state house where the GOP majority was putting the resolutions up to a vote one by one, declaring the three participated in disorderly behavior when they led supporters in chants demanding stricter gun safety measures. Expulsion, a rarely exercise right of the Tennessee House that critics on the left tonight are calling anti-democratic. NBC`s Priscilla Thompson is in Nashville following it all for us. Where do things stand right now, Priscilla? PRISCILLA THOMPSON, NBC NEWS CORRESPONDENT (on camera): Well, Lester, just moments ago, a vote to expel one lawmaker narrowly failed. And this after earlier today, another lawmaker was expelled. That third lawmaker is in the chamber pleading his case right now. (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) THOMPSON (voiceover): Outrage tonight in Nashville in reaction to Republican-led efforts to expel three Democratic lawmakers from the state legislature. CAMERON SEXTON, SPEAKER, TENNESSEE STATE HOUSE: I hereby declare of Representative Justin Jones of the 57 representative district expelled from the House of Representatives of the 113th assembly of the State of Tennessee. The three Democrats in question, state representatives Justin Jones, Gloria Johnson, and Justin Pearson were accused of disorderly behavior following their participation in a demonstration on the house floor last week. JUSTIN JONES (D-TN), STATE REPRESENTATIVE: We need action! We need action! We need action! THOMPSON: They joined advocates calling for stricter gun safety measures following the mass shooting at the Nashville private school that left six people dead on March 27th. Their chants with a bull horn from the podium in the house well led to today`s showdown. JONES: We called for you all to ban assault weapons and you respond with an assault on democracy. THOMPSON: While Tennessee`s Constitution allows for any member of the state legislature to be expelled with the two-thirds vote, it has only happened three times before. Demonstrators today filled the halls of the state capitol. But arguments from Democrats did little to sway the Republican super majority. JONES: This does not seem like America. To expel voices of opposition and dissent is a signal of authoritarianism and it is very dangerous. THOMPSON: The Republican Speaker of the House says today`s actions were about the rules. SEXTON: It did break rules by going to the well and showing that they were at the well, they were speaking, they pulled out a bull horn, and rolled out of order before there was a recess. THOMPSON: But protesters here told us they felt today`s vote was a distraction from the urgent issue of gun violence. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: What`s happening in Tennessee right now is abhorrent and our legislators are not listening to what we are saying. (END VIDEOTAPE) HOLT: Priscilla, what happens next? THOMPSON (on camera): Lester, counties will appoint interim representatives to fill the seats of those expelled lawmakers until a special election is set. And that would be set by the governor. And as for those expelled lawmakers, here in Tennessee, they are still eligible to run and could potentially be re-elected for those seats in that special election. Lester? [19:05:07] HOLT: Priscilla Thompson tonight, thank you. Tonight`s other top story, a Biden administration review partially blaming the Trump Administration for the chaotic and deadly U.S. withdrawal from Afghanistan, prompting a backlash from Republicans. Kristen Welker is at the White House with more. (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) KRISTEN WELKER, NBC NEWS CHIEF WHITE HOUSE CORRESPONDENT (voiceover): Tonight, nearly two years after the deadly and disastrous American withdrawal from Afghanistan, those stunning images of Afghans desperately chasing U.S. planes and the airport terror attack which killed 13 U.S. service members. The Biden Administration releasing its after-action review trying to pin much of the blame on Former President Trump who had left office eight months earlier including citing sharp drawdowns of U.S. troops. JOHN KIRBY, STRATEGIC COMMUNICATIONS COORDINATOR, NATIONAL SECURITY COUNCIL: It is also undeniable that decisions made and the lack of planning done by the previous administration significantly limited options available to him. WELKER: Though acknowledging the Biden Administration should have started the evacuation earlier. Despite facing withering criticism, President Biden at the time called the withdrawal a "extraordinary success." JOE BIDEN , PRESIDENT OF THE UNITED STATES: No nation -- no nation has ever done anything like it in all of history. WELKER: And today, this pushback from a White House spokesperson. KIRBY: For all this talk of chaos, I just didn`t it. Not from my perch. I just won`t buy the whole argument of chaos. It was tough in the first few hours -- WELKER: But a former top Trump official tonight firing back. MIKE POMPEO , FORMER U.S. SECRETARY OF STATE: They came in, took the plan that we had, and just botched it. It is outrageous for them to somehow try and blame anyone but Joe Biden . WELKER: We pressed the White House. Does the president take responsibility for the withdrawal and everything that happened thereafter? KIRBY: He`s the commander-in-chief. And he absolutely has responsibility for the operations that our men and women conduct and the orders that he gives. Meanwhile, in Taliban -controlled Afghanistan tonight, women face new oppression and Afghan interpreters who helped the U.S. are in hiding. We asked Jeff Phaneuf, a veteran trying to get translators out about the report. JEFF PHANEUF, VETERAN: It doesn`t do enough to take full ownership of the continued problem looking forward to save the 160 to 200,000 of our Afghan partners who were left behind. (END VIDEOTAPE) WELKER (on camera): Just last month, the CENTCOM commander warned ISIS in Afghanistan could conduct terror attacks against U.S. interests abroad in under six months. Lester? HOLT: Kristen Welker at the White House, thank you. Tonight, Israel launching new strikes in Gaza after getting hit by a wave of rocket attacks fired by militants in Lebanon. Raf Sanchez is in Tel Aviv tonight. Raf, what more do we know about this? RAF SANCHEZ, NBC NEWS FOREIGN CORRESPONDENT (on camera): Lester, in the last hour, Israeli jets have begun striking targets in Gaza belonging to the Hamas militant group. And we are hearing sirens going off in southern Israel which suggests Palestinian militants are shooting back. We don`t yet know if there are casualties, but we do know Israel blames Hamas for those rockets from Lebanon earlier in the day. And all of this comes after violent scenes yesterday between Israeli police and Palestinians at the Al-Aqsa mosque in Jerusalem, the third holiest site in Islam. Lester? HOLT: Raf Sanchez, thank you. Despite growing China tensions, a U.S. delegation is in Taiwan after talks in California between Taiwan`s President and House Speaker Kevin McCarthy. Courtney Kube reports now from Taiwan. (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) COURTNEY KUBE, NBC NEWS PENTAGON CORRESPONDENT (voiceover): Tonight, despite threats from China, including this warship seen off the coast, a top delegation of American officials arriving in Taiwan for critical high- level talks. The bipartisan group meeting with Taiwan`s Vice President Lai, and later this weekend, President Tsai after her historic visit with house Speaker Kevin McCarthy in California. TSAI ING-WEN, PRESIDENT, TAIWAN: Taiwan is grateful to have the States of America by our side. KUBE: China blasting the show of support from the U.S. for Taiwan vowing to firmly defend national sovereignty and territorial integrity. China says the island democracy of Taiwan is part of its territory. REP. MICHAEL MCCAUL (R-TX): The United States stands by you and will protect you. KUBE: Tonight, a top House Republican Michael McCall saying the U.S. needs to arm and train Taiwan`s military. While Taiwan`s Vice President says they are already on the front lines of combating China`s authoritarianism, U.S. intelligence says China`s President Xi has instructed his military to be ready to invade Taiwan by 2027. We met Enoch Wu a former Special Forces Soldier now using his training to prepare Taiwan`s civilians to be ready. ENOCH WU, FORMER TAIWANESE SPECIAL FORCES: It was important for us to stand up a volunteer corps trained in crisis response. KUBE: He believes the threat of an invasion is higher now than ever. WU: If you can`t defend it, it`s not yours. Protecting Taiwan, protecting our home is our own responsibility. [19:10:01] (END VIDEOTAPE) KUBE (on camera): Despite the sharp comments, some U.S. officials tell me Chinese President Xi Jinping is unlikely to put on a large military show of force while French President Emmanuel Macron is in China on a state visit. But once President Macron leaves, President Xi could respond more forcefully. Lester? HOLT: Courtney Kube in Taipei, thank you. We`re tracking more severe weather here at home as the storm that ripped through parts of the Midwest now pushes into the Mid-Atlantic. 10 million people are at risk. Damaging winds the main concern. Fortunately, the tornado threat has diminished. We`ll turn to abortion now and what has been a consequential week for both sides of that battle as it plays out across the country. Blayne Alexander has the story for us. (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) BLAYNE ALEXANDER, NBC NEWS CORRESPONDENT (voiceover): It`s been nearly 10 months since the end of Roe v Wade and the beginning of abortion access falling solely under state control, with major developments in four states this week. In Idaho, the governor signed a controversial new law making it a felony for non-parent adults to help a minor cross state lines for an abortion, the first law of its kind nationwide. Planned Parenthood is slamming the measure as extreme saying it will put young people in dangerous and isolating situations. What would you say to critics who call this unnecessarily cruel? TODD LAKEY (R-ID), STATE SENATOR: I think again it`s important that we protect the life of the unborn child. When it comes to minors, what the legislation requires is that parents essentially be informed. ALEXANDER: In Florida, protests and arrests after the state senate passed the so-called Heartbeat Protection Act reducing abortion access from 15 weeks to six. LAUREN BOOK, (D-FL), STATE SENATOR: If you vote for this ban, things will get worse. Women will die. ERIN GRALL (R-FL), STATE SENATOR: For 50 years, the killing of innocent children has been legal. Legal does not equate to right. ALEXANDER: It all comes amid a pair of victories for abortion rights advocates. In Michigan, Governor Gretchen Whitmer signed a repeal of the state`s abortion ban on the books since 1931. GOV. GRETCHEN WHITMER (D-MI): Abortion rights are now enshrined into our state constitution. ALEXANDER: And in Wisconsin, abortion was at the heart of Tuesday`s high- stakes election for a seat on the state supreme court now set to be filled by the liberal candidate all but ensuring abortion access in the state. JANET PROTASIEWICZ, JUSTICE-ELECT, WISCONSIN SUPREME COURT: Wisconsin voters have made their voices heard. ALEXANDER: Tonight, several more states are considering legislation that would either expand or restrict access to abortions. Blayne Alexander, NBC News. (END VIDEOTAPE) HOLT: In 60 seconds, what residents say is a long-time toxic threat to a school near a production plant in Louisiana, and what the EPA is now doing about it following our investigation, next. (COMMERCIAL BREAK) HOLT: Three weeks ago, we first reported on the Fifth Ward Elementary School in Reserve Louisiana located next to a plant emitting what the EPA has long said was a likely carcinogen. Cynthia McFadden returned with the head of the EPA who was now taking action. (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) MICHAEL REGAN , ADMINISTRATOR, EPA : Our work isn`t done. CYNTHIA MCFADDEN, NBC NEWS SENIOR LEGAL AND INVESTIGATIVE CORRESPONDENT (voiceover): 18 months ago, the newly appointed head of the EPA , Michael Regan took what he called a journey to justice tour that brought him here. REGAN: I vowed that EPA would take action. MCFADDEN: Today, he returned to make good on that promise proposing a staggering slate of emission standards for 80 toxic chemicals. REGAN: We`re sending a safety standard that we believe is the lowest you can set that is detectable with technology. MCFADDEN: Including chemicals being emitted from the Danka plant here in Reserve. On our last visit here, we met George and his great-grandmother Mary Hampton who`s been battling for years to get the Denka Plant next door to George`s elementary school to stop emitting where the EPA has long said are unsafe levels of two of those toxic chemicals. One of your neighbors says it`s like sending the kids to a gas chamber. MARY HAMPTON, RESIDENT, RESERVE, LOUISIANA: Exactly, exactly. [19:15:00] MCFADDEN: We also met Robert Taylor who had been fighting with her for years. He didn`t have much confidence the EPA would do anything. So, when the agency called the night our story aired and suggested we meet up with Michael Regan in Louisiana, we agreed. One of the things that Mr. Taylor said to me the first time I came to visit was that this was a sacrifice zone. REGAN: What I can tell you is there are none of these facilities in Beverly Hills. There`s no coincidence if you look at who`s on the front lines, most of these individuals are Black, Brown, or tribal and or low-income. So, there`s a consistent pattern here. If the new standards announced today are put into effect, they become much more enforceable. MCFADDEN: I think what angers a lot of people is though the Denka plant has been emitting at these historically high levels for years now. Why not shut the plant down while everything else is being sorted out. REGAN: We are using every tool in our toolbox. And if I have more powers, trust me, I would use them. MCFADDEN: Denka told us it`s reduced emissions and says it`s breaking no laws denying it`s putting the folks who live here at any increased risk for cancer. REGAN: I wish that we could move more expeditiously to take action to protect George, to protect Mr. Taylor, to do all the things that we want to do yesterday. MCFADDEN: As for Bob and Mary, they said today has filled them with hope. What`s the best part of today? ROBERT TAYLOR, RESIDENT, RESERVE, LOUISIANA: We got the attention of our politicians. HAMPTON: It`s not over. TAYLOR: It`s not over but we`ll be here when it ends. I tell them all the time. I was here from day one. I`ll be there till day zero. MCFADDEN: Cynthia McFadden, NBC News Reserve, Louisiana. (END VIDEOTAPE) HOLT: We`ll take a short break. Up next, sticker shock, the soaring cost of buying a new car. What`s driving it up in "THE PRICE YOU PAY." (COMMERCIAL BREAK) [19:20:00] HOLT: If you`ve been shopping for a new car, then you know that prices and monthly payments have been soaring. Miguel Almaguer reports on why and what you can do in "THE PRICE YOU PAY." (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) MIGUEL ALMAGUER, NBC NEWS NATIONAL CORRESPONDENT (voiceover): For Americans already facing sticker shock on the sales lot, tonight, car payments are also accelerating towards record levels. Admins revealed the average annual percentage rate or APR on a newly financed vehicle has now ballooned to seven percent. The typical payment for a new car in overdrive hitting $730 a month. It could be enough for Sharon Divestern to pump the brakes on buying new. SHARON DIVESTER, LOOKING TO BUY A CAR: If you find something that you like, you just save money. ALMAGUER: As car payments become more expensive than ever, tonight, one in six buyers who finance new are paying more than $1,000 a month. The staggering price to sit behind the wheel rivaling the cost of putting a roof over your head. IVAN DRURY, DIRECTOR, EDMUNDS INSIGHTS: Unless you have a lot of cash on hand to kind of mitigate those APRs, you will be looking at a number you probably have never seen before if you bought a car in the last 10 years. ALMAGUER: With more drivers going into delinquency, the average cost of a new car has nearly hit $50,000. Many buyers are no longer in the driver`s seat when it comes to monthly payments. Supply remains tight. Inflation is driving up costs and the Fed continues to raise interest rates. There is some good news though. Experts believe rates will soon stabilize. But for now, it`s a bumpy road ahead for drivers buying new. Miguel Almaguer, NBC News Los Angeles. (END VIDEOTAPE) HOLT: And next tonight, I`ll remember a beloved NBC News colleague, David Bloom, and his important Legacy 20 years later. (COMMERCIAL BREAK) [19:25:00] HOLT: This is a somber anniversary for all of us at NBC News and for journalism at large. It was 20 years ago we learned our colleague David Bloom had died while embedded with the front-line elements of the U.S. invasion of Iraq. How David died was a shock in itself and a wakeup call still impacting lives today. (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) DAVID BLOOM, FORMER NBC NEWS CORRESPONDENT: This is the U.S. Army `s third infantry division. We`re with the second brigade, the 315 Infantry. HOLT: It`s where we like to be on the big story out front. David Bloom rolling into combat on live T.V. with the Army`s 3rd Infantry Division trailed by a customized satellite truck known as the Bloom Mobile. BLOOM: Basically, what we`ve done is we`ve established the ability transmit live from this vehicle using a pretty sophisticated camera which can be outside the vehicle and take the bumps and the jars. HOLT: Paul Nassar was David`s producer on the journey. BLOOM: We`re just rolling along. It`s nighttime now. headline: NBC NIGHTLY NEWS for April 6, 2023, NBC
story_text: [19:00:00] (COMMERCIAL BREAK) LESTER HOLT, NBC NEWS ANCHOR (on camera): Tonight, the dramatic showdown over guns in Tennessee. (voiceover): The state`s Republican-led house voting on removing three Democrats from office after they led a protest on the floor demanding stricter gun laws after the Nashville school shooting that killed six people. The rare punishment used only three times before since the Civil War. Outside the building, the massive protest and what happens now with the ousted Democrat seats? Also, tonight, in the new report of the U.S. withdrawal from Afghanistan, the White House largely blaming the chaos and decisions by Former President Trump and the actions it says the U.S. should have taken even sooner. The rising tensions of the Middle East. Israel striking back tonight after the biggest barrage of missiles from Lebanon in more than 16 years. Tracking severe storms on the move tonight in the Mid-Atlantic on the heels of that deadly tornado outbreak. NBC News investigates after our report on toxic air concerns near a Louisiana school. What the EPA is now doing about it. And it was 20 years ago we lost a member of our NBC News family covering the war in Iraq. Tonight, my conversation with David Bloom`s widow about the lives his story may have saved. ANNOUNCER: This is NBC Nightly News with Lester Holt. HOLT (on camera): Good evening and welcome. The tears of grief that consume Nashville, Tennessee just 10 days ago over the murders of young children and school staffers are replaced tonight by cries of anger and accusations after an extraordinary move by Tennessee House Republicans to seek the expulsion of three Democratic members for their roles in a gun safety protest on the House floor last week. All day, angry supporters and gun safety advocates crowding the state house where the GOP majority was putting the resolutions up to a vote one by one, declaring the three participated in disorderly behavior when they led supporters in chants demanding stricter gun safety measures. Expulsion, a rarely exercise right of the Tennessee House that critics on the left tonight are calling anti-democratic. NBC`s Priscilla Thompson is in Nashville following it all for us. Where do things stand right now, Priscilla? PRISCILLA THOMPSON, NBC NEWS CORRESPONDENT (on camera): Well, Lester, just moments ago, a vote to expel one lawmaker narrowly failed. And this after earlier today, another lawmaker was expelled. That third lawmaker is in the chamber pleading his case right now. (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) THOMPSON (voiceover): Outrage tonight in Nashville in reaction to Republican-led efforts to expel three Democratic lawmakers from the state legislature. CAMERON SEXTON, SPEAKER, TENNESSEE STATE HOUSE: I hereby declare of Representative Justin Jones of the 57 representative district expelled from the House of Representatives of the 113th assembly of the State of Tennessee. The three Democrats in question, state representatives Justin Jones, Gloria Johnson, and Justin Pearson were accused of disorderly behavior following their participation in a demonstration on the house floor last week. JUSTIN JONES (D-TN), STATE REPRESENTATIVE: We need action! We need action! We need action! THOMPSON: They joined advocates calling for stricter gun safety measures following the mass shooting at the Nashville private school that left six people dead on March 27th. Their chants with a bull horn from the podium in the house well led to today`s showdown. JONES: We called for you all to ban assault weapons and you respond with an assault on democracy. THOMPSON: While Tennessee`s Constitution allows for any member of the state legislature to be expelled with the two-thirds vote, it has only happened three times before. Demonstrators today filled the halls of the state capitol. But arguments from Democrats did little to sway the Republican super majority. JONES: This does not seem like America. To expel voices of opposition and dissent is a signal of authoritarianism and it is very dangerous. THOMPSON: The Republican Speaker of the House says today`s actions were about the rules. SEXTON: It did break rules by going to the well and showing that they were at the well, they were speaking, they pulled out a bull horn, and rolled out of order before there was a recess. THOMPSON: But protesters here told us they felt today`s vote was a distraction from the urgent issue of gun violence. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: What`s happening in Tennessee right now is abhorrent and our legislators are not listening to what we are saying. (END VIDEOTAPE) HOLT: Priscilla, what happens next? THOMPSON (on camera): Lester, counties will appoint interim representatives to fill the seats of those expelled lawmakers until a special election is set. And that would be set by the governor. And as for those expelled lawmakers, here in Tennessee, they are still eligible to run and could potentially be re-elected for those seats in that special election. Lester? [19:05:07] HOLT: Priscilla Thompson tonight, thank you. Kristen Welker is at the White House with more. headline: The New Study On Pregnant Women That Everyone Should See
story_text: [18:50:00] KATE SNOW: We`ve reported before on the dangers of pregnancy, especially for women of color. Well, tonight, a new study with startling findings that wealthy black women are dying in child birth at rates far greater than all white women. Rehema Ellis takes a closer look at why. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) REHEMA ELLIS, NBC NEWS EDUCATION CORRESPONDENT (voiceover): This is how Aziza Bowser-Clarke and her husband Jason looked this couple looked in the early weeks of her pregnancy. AZIZA BOWSER-CLARKE: It was a picture of absolute joy. ELLIS (voiceover): But for these two highly successful new Jersey Lawyers, joy soon turned to fear. BOWSER-CLARKE: We were very, very worried about making sure that we had all the information that we had, the very best doctors that we could find. ELLIS (voiceover): In her first trimester Aziza says she was exhausted. When she told her doctor she was concerned about anemia, the response? BOWSER-CLARKE: Of course you`re tired. You`re pregnant. And me, this is my first child. ELLIS (voiceover): But this very athletic 41-year-old says it got worse. By her seventh month she could barely hold her head up and demanded a blood test. The results, she was dangerously anemic and had to have infusions. BOWSER-CLARKE: It felt like my throat dropped into my stomach, because it was there and concrete that I wasn`t imagining this. ELLIS (voiceover): After 27 hours of labor, doctors abruptly decided on an emergency c-section. Her son was born healthy, but she passed out and spent about eight days in the hospital recovering. BOWSER-CLARKE: It was traumatic. ELLIS (voiceover): And she is not alone. A groundbreaking study reveals a disturbing history of unequal care. Researchers analyzed nearly all pregnancies in California over a nine-year period. For the first time factoring in both race and income. The findings? Money didn`t matter in maternal health care. And during child birth, even the richest black women are more likely to die than the poorest white women. DR. KAMEELAH PHILLIPS, NEW YORK OBSTETRICIAN AND GYNECOLOGIST: Take it as an opportunity -- ELLIS (voiceover): Dr. Kameelah Phillips is not surprised. ELLIS (on camera): What is this about? DR. PHILLIPS: This is about racism. We are still dealing with institutions, people, and their biases. ELLIS: Some people would say that`s dramatic that, how can you say that it`s racism when black women are going to the same hospitals that white women are going to in large measure and they`re receiving the same kind of care, aren`t they? DR. PHILLIPS: So, I would argue that women of color and in particular black women are not receiving the same type of care, even in the same institutions. ELLIS (voiceover): She says some doctors often don`t take black women`s concerns about their health as seriously as white women`s. ELLIS (on camera): They`re not listening, particularly to women of color. DR. PHILLIPS: Particularly women of color. There are terms that often make it into the chart as it relates to black women, difficult, challenging, disruptive. ELLIS (voiceover): That means, early warning signs can be missed, which could lead to negative outcomes. So, what can pregnant black women do right now? Experts say, identify your risk factors with your doctor. Bring someone with you to your OB-GYN appointments, and take notes. Aziza did all that and still says -- BOWSER-CLARKE: My advice for black women who are pregnant, make sure your voice is heard. ELLIS (voiceover): A powerful message when starting a family. Race matters. Rehema Ellis , NBC News, New Jersey. (END VIDEO CLIP) SNOW: Powerful story. When we come back, brotherly love. The hero kid giving his big brother a second chance at life. DR. PHILLIPS: So, I would argue that women of color and in particular black women are not receiving the same type of care, even in the same institutions. ELLIS (voiceover): She says some doctors often don`t take black women`s concerns about their health as seriously as white women`s. ELLIS (on camera): They`re not listening, particularly to women of color. DR. PHILLIPS: Particularly women of color. There are terms that often make it into the chart as it relates to black women, difficult, challenging, disruptive. ELLIS (voiceover): That means, early warning signs can be missed, which could lead to negative outcomes. So, what can pregnant black women do right now? Experts say, identify your risk factors with your doctor. Bring someone with you to your OB-GYN appointments, and take notes. Aziza did all that and still says -- BOWSER-CLARKE: My advice for black women who are pregnant, make sure your voice is heard. ELLIS (voiceover): A powerful message when starting a family. Race matters. Rehema Ellis , NBC News, New Jersey. (END VIDEO CLIP) SNOW: Powerful story. When we come back, brotherly love. The hero kid giving his big brother a second chance at life. headline: The Judge In Texas Who Could Ban The Abortion Pill Nationwide, Even In States Where Abortion Is Legal
story_text: LESTER HOLT: In Texas today, a federal judge heard arguments in a lawsuit aimed at banning the most prescribed pill for abortions that`s been FDA approved for more than two decades. As Dasha Burns explains, the outcome could have consequences nationwide. (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) DASHA BURNS, NBC NEWS CORRESPONDENT (voiceover): Anticipation in Amarillo building for weeks as a case in this Texas courthouse could restrict access nationwide to the abortion pill, the most commonly used method for terminating pregnancies in the country. A conservative judge appointed by Trump could soon decide whether to issue a preliminary injunction, blocking access to Mifeprex, generically known as Mifepristone. The FDA approved it as part of a two-drug abortion regimen in 2000. Both sides had two hours to present their arguments. The judge peppering attorneys with detailed questions. Now, today was the first public hearing in the case. The judge delayed adding it to the public docket to avoid a "circus-like atmosphere." The note inspiring one group of demonstrators. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: I remember before Roe v. Wade, and now I`m looking at it all over again. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: I value life. I think it`s extremely precious. BURNS: The plaintiffs are challenging the FDA`s approval of the drug, arguing the agency didn`t adequately evaluate its safety and endangered women further when they made it available through telemedicine during the pandemic. The FDA says the claims in the lawsuit are unsupported by any evidence and said in court today that a ruling in the plaintiff`s favor would amount to unprecedented action and would cause significant public harm. Since its approval in 2000, the FDA says more than five million women have taken mifepristone with 28 deaths associated with the drug. RACHEL O`LEARY CARMONA, EXECUTIVE DIRECTOR, WOMEN`S MARCH: What happens here today will be felt by all Americans no matter what your feelings are on abortion. BURNS: A ruling that could radiate nationwide. Dasha Burns, NBC News, Amarillo, Texas. END Content and programming copyright 2023 NBCUniversal. ALL RIGHTS RESERVED.
