Jim and Pam Colbert say about a month ago, someone grabbed their dog at 2:00 a.m. and skinned him in a field in front of their home. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: Right over there. Right over -- SCHWARTZ: Took his fur but left his unbuckled collar behind. So, somebody actually had to unclasp it. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: Unclasp it right here. See, that stays. And somebody had to undo it. Because if you had a knife, wouldn`t you have cut it? SCHWARTZ: But Moscow police say they don`t think that case has anything to do with the murders. Police also asked about an unsolved murder 300 miles away in Oregon, in which a masked intruder attacked a couple with a knife in their sleep. JAMES FRY, CHIEF, MOSCOW, IDAHO POLICE: Actually, I had a tip come in on that case and I`ve ordered it to our tip line. SCHWARTZ: Meanwhile, the University of Idaho giving students the option of finishing their semester remotely while families of the victims are struggling with the thought of Thanksgiving without their loved ones and praying that the killer won`t strike again. Gadi Schwartz, NBC News. (END VIDEOTAPE) HOLT: Also tonight, the so-called tripledemic, RSV, the flu, and COVID, is already pushing hospitals to the brink. The U.S. facing shortages of pediatric beds, medical staff, and now even some medications. Here`s Gabe Gutierrez. (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) GABE GUTIERREZ, NBC NEWS NATIONAL CORRESPONDENT (voiceover): In Buffalo, some store shelves normally filled with children`s Tylenol are empty. Pharmacists say a spot shortage of the drug in Canada triggered by mounting cases of RSV is spilling over the border. DON ARTHUR, PHARMACIST: Apparently, up in Canada, the liquid forms of Tylenol are unavailable. GUTIERREZ: Johnson and Johnson , the maker of Tylenol, says there`s no overall shortage in the U.S., telling NBC News we are experiencing high consumer demand and they`re doing everything we can to make sure people have access to the products they need. Still, the FDA currently lists amoxicillin as being in short supply. And it all comes as the healthcare industry braces for a potential tripledemic this winter. RSV, flu, and COVID colliding. In New York, Ella Rose Giam (PH) is home after a week in the hospital. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: It was surreal. Like, seeing your daughter on a breathing mask and she`s only three and a half. GUTIERREZ: Adding to the strain on the system, an increasingly dire staffing shortage. More than half a million people in the healthcare and social services industries quit their positions in September. Were you burnt out? Extremely. Yes, sir. Reece Brown in Louisiana is no longer a traveling nurse. REECE BROWN, NURSE: That joy which is literally being sucked out of us. We were doing everything that we could and we just -- it was never enough. (END VIDEOTAPE) GUTIERREZ (on camera): As for COVID, the CDC says new data shows the Omicron boosters offer better protection against variants than earlier doses. Still, they are not as effective as the original COVID vaccine was against the initial virus. Lester? HOLT: All right, Gabe Gutierrez, thanks. In 60 seconds, new abortion restrictions and the agonizing decisions they are forcing some families to make. Our in-depth look at the issue coming up next. (COMMERCIAL BREAK) HOLT: The Georgia Supreme Court today reinstated a ban on abortions after six weeks of pregnancy while it considers an appeal. And while a few states including Georgia make exceptions when a fetus has life-threatening problems, most states with new abortion restrictions do not. Blayne Alexandre has more. (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) BLAYNE ALEXANDER, NBC NEWS CORRESPONDENT (voiceover): Jill Hurtle could not wait to become a mom. She still remembers the second she found out. JILL HURTLE, HAD ABORTION: I was like sobbing. I was so excited. [19:15:02] ALEXANDER: You felt like a mom. HURTLE: I felt like a mom in that -- in an instant. ALEXANDER: Her husband, Matt, dreamed of being a girl dad. They even picked out a name Ivy Grace. Every doctor`s appointment brought good news until the 18-week scan. HURTLE: And our world`s like came crashing down. She came in and she said her heart isn`t what it is supposed to look like. I think in that exact moment, my stomach dropped and I think I truly knew that it was going to be a really severe situation. ALEXANDER: It was. A condition known as hypoplastic left heart syndrome, HLHS. Doctor said her baby`s case was especially severe, and her daughter would likely not survive long after birth. HURTLE: I didn`t want her to have to go through so much pain and suffering. ALEXANDER: After more tests and more devastating news, Jill and her husband made the painful decision. HURTLE: If she were to live an hour or 10 days, I didn`t want her to just - - I didn`t want her to know nothing but pain. So, my protective instinct was to do what I knew what was best for her, which was to send her to heaven. ALEXANDER: Every year, congenital or fetal anomalies impact one in every 33 babies born in the U.S. and range from minor to life-limiting or life- threatening. Since the Supreme Court decision overturning Roe v. Wade, at least 16 states have successfully enacted laws further restricting abortion access. Only three have exceptions for lethal fetal anomalies. DR. DAVID LEVINE, NEONATOLOGIST: We`re not dealing with one size fits all. We can`t make laws for one size fits all. ALEXANDER: Dr. David Levine is a neonatologist who opposes abortion access and believes the baby should be carried to term even with a grim prognosis. LEVINE: Most families who have decided to spend time with their babies however short it might be, by and large, have benefited from it. They`ve been able to bond with their baby. ALEXANDER: Is it therefore a law to make that decision for a parent? LEVINE: There are many decisions that are taken out of our hands. Is it fair for the mother to make that decision to take a baby`s life away from him. ALEXANDER: Jill had to leave South Carolina and wait two weeks for an appointment in Washington, DC. HURTLE: Those two weeks were probably the hardest two weeks I`ve ever experienced in my life. Every time you feel her kick or move, it`s just a dagger to the heart. ALEXANDER: She believes abortion bans should have exceptions for cases like hers, giving women the chance to make a choice, however painful. HURTLE: I am a mom. I`m a mom to an angel in heaven. And I know that she`s at peace. ALEXANDER: Blayne Alexander, NBC News, Charleston, South Carolina. (END VIDEOTAPE) HOLT: And up next, as the holiday shopping rush begins, top tips on where and how you can save in our series "RACE TO DELIVER." (COMMERCIAL BREAK) [19:20:00] HOLT: As you may have noticed, many retailers have already rolled out their Black Friday deals. So, where can you save the most? NBC`s Brian Cheung has been shopping around for our series "RACE TO DELIVER." (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) BRIAN CHEUNG, NBC NEWS BUSINESS AND DATA REPORTER (voiceover): Tonight, amid a growing unease in the nation`s economy, the dash for holiday deals is on. With consumer prices up 7.7 percent compared to last season and one in three households saying their finances are worse off from a year ago, shoppers are left with tighter budgets. TRAE BODGE, SMART SHOPPING EXPERT, TRUETRAE.COM: Retailers are aware of the fact that consumers only have so much to spend. CHEUNG: That`s why even before Black Friday, many retailers are already offering deep discounts vying for your holiday dollars. The most discounted items this season, everything from TVs, laptops, to home appliances, and beauty products. For electronics, consider older models for an even better deal. Many clothing retailers are also offering extra deep discounts this season in part because of excess inventory falling supply chain lock-ups last year. BODGE: We are seeing a lot of overstock still and retailers have been spending the last couple of months trying to sell through that merchandise. CHEUNG: Which could lead to even deeper discounts. BODGE: I do expect to see discounts deeper than usual in categories like casual apparel, TVs, furniture, home decor. And so, in addition to the exciting cyber weekend sales that we`ll see, we`ll also see kind of extra discounts as retailers look to clear out all those overstocks. CHEUNG: Experts say shopping with strategy will save you big bucks. Start by creating a shopping list with a spending cap. Then compare prices online and in store. And check your credit card for additional discounts and offers. (END VIDEOTAPE) CHEUNG (on camera): And don`t forget about gift cards which are always a hot item every year. Many can actually be bought at a discount. Lester? HOLT: All right, Brian, thanks. Up next, what are you thankful for? Some children will tell us right after the break. (COMMERCIAL BREAK) [19:25:00] HOLT: Finally, a lot of news has been especially grim this week, but we thought you might be uplifted or find a smile in listening to the gratitude expressed by some New York school kids we spoke to about Thanksgiving. (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) HOLT (voiceover): At Manhattan Country School, today`s lesson is all about giving thanks. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: Thank you God for a mother. HOLT: And after two years of holidays overshadowed by COVID, many students told us they`re grateful for a Thanksgiving that feels a little more normal. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: I`m thankful for like, family and friends because like, during COVID, I wasn`t able to see -- I wasn`t able to see like, a lot of my friends. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: I`m very grateful that me and my family -- or my family and I have been healthy and happy and able to see each other. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: I`m really thankful for the school and for my teachers and my friends. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: I`m thankful for my dog. She`s good at comforting people especially me. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: I`m thankful for my family because they give me comfort and I just love them. HOLT: Of course, on Thanksgiving -- UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: I love cooking. HOLT: Comfort also comes in the form of turkey, stuffing, and potatoes. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: We bake and we coconut we have this huge feast at the end. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: We make an angel fruitcake which I really love to do with my grandma. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: I`m definitely looking forward to eating because we do cook pretty good Thanksgiving meal. HOLT: When you`re in grade school, there`s something else to look forward to. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: We get a lot of days off from school. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: The first thing I think about it is wrapped up in a blanket drinking hot chocolate and watching a movie, and I just get really excited about that. HOLT: A moment of peace with the people you love, to give thanks, isn`t that what the day is all about? UNIDENTIFIED MALE: When I think about the holidays, I think about community and spending time with the people that I love and giving back to them and hopefully receiving the same. (END VIDEOTAPE) HOLT: And thank all of you for being here tonight. That`s NIGHTLY NEWS. Be sure to tune in for the Macy`s Thanksgiving Day Parade at 9:00 Eastern here on NBC and Peacock. Thank you for watching and Happy Thanksgiving, everyone. Please take care of yourself and each other. Good night. (COMMERCIAL BREAK) END Content and programming copyright 2022 NBCUniversal. headline: The Issue That Turned Out To Be A Game-Changer In States Red And Blue
story_text: [19:20:00] LESTER HOLT: In the wake of the Supreme Court overturning Roe v Wade, the Midterm Elections saw a record number of abortion-related measures on the ballot. And in every state where voters had a direct say, they opted against restricting access. Here`s Yamiche Alcindor. (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) YAMICHE ALCINDOR, NBC NEWS WASHINGTON CORRESPONDENT (voiceover): Tonight, Democrats across the country are celebrating sweeping wins for supporters of abortion rights. JOSH SHAPIRO (D-PA), GUBERNATORIAL CANDIDATE: A woman`s right to choose one. SEN. MAGGIE HASSAN (D-NH): I will always, always keep fighting to protect a woman`s fundamental freedom. GOV. GRETCHEN WHITMER (D-MI): We will make Michigan a leader, a place where women make their own decisions. ALCINDOR: In Michigan, residents voted to enshrine abortion rights into the state constitution, an issue Governor Gretchen Whitmer and her running mate been a central part of their successful reelection campaign. WHITMER: This is a right that we are not going to go backwards on. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: I`m proud of my state. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: I don`t want the government in my bedroom. ALCINDOR: And abortion rights did drive people to the polls. It was the second most important issue to voters behind inflation. In addition to Michigan, voters in California and Vermont codified abortion rights into their state constitutions. And it wasn`t just blue states, voters in Kentucky and Montana shot down measures that could have restricted access. What do you make of that nationally? WHITMER: I think it`s a sign that the American public has had rights for 49 years. We`re not going to go backward. And so, whether it`s state by state we see this happen or hopefully at some point, you know, a national effort again, I think that this is where the fight is at the moment. ALCINDOR: Those against abortion rights not processing the results. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: I believe abortion is first-degree murder. ALCINDOR: Eric Scheidler from the Pro-Life Action League says he`s gearing up to continue their push. ERIC SCHEIDLER, EXECUTIVE DIRECTOR, PRO-LIFE ACTION LEAGUE: If we`ve learned anything over the past 50 years as a movement is that we`ve got to be able to take a punch. ALCINDOR: Still, Americans in five states send a clear message about reproductive rights. Yamiche Alcindor, NBC News, Detroit. (END VIDEOTAPE) HOLT: Coming up, their new mission: training troops to become teachers in "THOSE WHO SERVE." (COMMERCIAL BREAK) END Content and programming copyright 2022 NBCUniversal. headline: NBC NIGHTLY NEWS for November 9, 2022, NBC
story_text: [19:00:00] (COMMERCIAL BREAK) LESTER HOLT, NBC NEWS ANCHOR (on camera): Tonight, the Midterm Election cliffhanger. The battle for Congress still too close to call. (voiceover): The Senate and the House still up for grabs after the Democrats held off a red wave. President Biden at the White House today calling it a good day for democracy. In Georgia, the tight Senate race headed to a runoff. In Pennsylvania, John Fetterman defeating Mehmet Oz. And in Florida, a big reelection win for Governor Ron DeSantis setting up a possible 2024 showdown with Donald Trump . And what President Biden said today about his own 2024 plans. Our team across the country with a race is still in play. Also breaking tonight, Nicole strengthening into a hurricane and taking aim at Florida flooding on the coast. Buildings collapsing into the sea, mandatory evacuations ordered, the new track tonight. The potential major setback for Russia ordering a retreat from the key city of Kherson in southern Ukraine. Why Kyiv is skeptical. WNBA star Brittney Griner moved to a penal colony in Russia. How the U.S. is responding. Facebook `s parent company Meta laying off thousands. Why Mark Zuckerberg is slashing jobs on the heels of concept Twitter . And "THOSE WHO SERVE," the veterans answering a new call in the classroom. ANNOUNCER: This is NBC NIGHTLY NEWS with Lester Holt. HOLT (on camera): Good evening, everyone, again, tonight from our election headquarters in New York. It was a good day for democracy, President Biden`s first public reaction to yesterday`s Midterm Elections in which Democrats defied the gravity of broad voter dissatisfaction and history itself to avoid massive losses in that widely-predicted Republican wave. Let me tell you from the start tonight, much of our reporting this evening is framed by what we don`t know and that is which party will control Congress. At this hour, control of the Senate is still up for grabs with some races too close to call, while the Georgia Senate contest is headed toward a December runoff election. And the House still in play for both sides, though Republicans currently lead. But there is broad agreement that these were not the results most expected, an unpopular president faced with a bad economy managing to avoid the fate of his predecessors. The President`s message to voters tonight, I get it. Our team has fanned out again this evening watching the count and the issues that shaped the vote starting tonight with Kristen Welker at the White House. (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) KRISTEN WELKER, NBC NEWS CHIEF WHITE HOUSE CORRESPONDENT (voiceover): 24 hours after ballots were cast, tonight, control of Congress is still up for grabs. President Biden insisting it was a good night for Democrats. JOE BIDEN , PRESIDENT OF THE UNITED STATES: While the press and the pundits are predicting a giant red wave, it didn`t happen. WELKER: Republicans who had been hoping to take the House in a red wave now just looking for a win. The GOP still favored to take over but with a smaller margin than expected. REP. KEVIN MCCARTHY (R-CA): We will be in the majority and Nancy Pelosi will be in the minority. WELKER: Much more suspense in the Senate where Republicans still could gain the one seat they need to take control but Democrats could hang on to with NBC News projecting races that are too early to call in Nevada and in Arizona. And in Georgia, the showdown between Democratic senator Raphael Warnock and Republican Herschel Walker , NBC News Now projects will go to a runoff. SEN. RAPHAEL WARNOCK (D-GA): We always knew that this race would be close. HERSCHEL WALKER (R-GA), SENATE CANDIDATE: I`m like Ricky Bobby. I don`t come to lose. WELKER: Democrats` biggest win of the night coming in the critical Pennsylvania Senate race. Democrat John Fetterman , six months after suffering a stroke, defeating Republican Dr. Mehmet Oz. JOHN FETTERMAN (D-PA), SENATE CANDIDATE: We did what we needed to do. WELKER: Republicans with big victories too including Georgia Governor Brian Kemp easily defeating Democrat Stacey Abrams . And in the biggest win of the night, Florida Republican Governor Ron DeSantis winning reelection in a 19- point landslide, sweeping virtually every county in the state, including heavily Latino Miami Dade. GOV. RON DESANTIS (R-FL): We reject woke ideology. We will never ever surrender to the woke mob. Florida is where woke goes to die. WELKER: DeSantis seen as a possible 2024 presidential contender where he could face former President Trump who had a tough night. His endorsed candidates in Ohio and North Carolina won but several of Mr. Trump`s other handpick candidates in key races, including New Hampshire, Michigan, and Pennsylvania all lost. Meanwhile, President Biden was asked what he will do differently with most Americans saying they`re dissatisfied with the state of the country. [19:05:08] BIDEN: Nothing because they`re just finding out what we`re doing. The more they know about what we`re doing, the more support there is. WELKER: And we pressed him about running again. Two-thirds of Americans in exit polls say that they don`t think you should run for reelection. What is your message to them? And how does that factor into your final decision about whether or not to run for reelection? BIDEN: It doesn`t. WELKER: What`s your message to those two-thirds of Americans? BIDEN: Watch me. (END VIDEOTAPE) HOLT: Kristen, the President is likely facing divided government. Did he talk about working with Republicans how it would go? WELKER (on camera): Well, Lester, he did. The President says he`ll call top House Republican Kevin McCarthy tonight and says he`s hoping for bipartisanship on issues like Ukraine. The President also saying he`ll make his decision on running early next year. Lester? HOLT: Kristen Welker at the White House, thanks. That pivotal Senate race in Georgia, as we said, is neck and neck. Gabe Gutierrez is there. And Gabe, what can we expect in this coming run off? GABE GUTIERREZ, NBC NEWS NATIONAL CORRESPONDENT (on camera): Lester, this is what both campaigns and many voters did not want, another month of campaigning. But incumbent Raphael Warnock and challenger Herschel Walker are already fundraising ahead of the runoff now set for December 6. Neither managed to get 50 percent of the vote. But in the governor`s race here, Republican incumbent, Brian Kemp easily won reelection over Democrat Stacey Abrams . And that suggests some Republicans may have split their tickets in the Senate contest and voted for Warnock. Now, back in 2020, this state had to runoffs that tipped the balance of power in the Senate. And based on ad spending back then, it`s possible that we could see upwards of $200 million dollars in TV ads here over the next several weeks. Lester? HOLT: Gabe Gutierrez in Atlanta, thanks. Another key state in play. Arizona remains in flux both in the U.S. Senate race between incumbent Mark Kelly and Republican Blake Masters and in the governor`s race. Vaughn Hillyard is in Phoenix tonight. Vaughn, where do things stand right now? VAUGHN HILLYARD, NBC NEWS CORRESPONDENT (on camera): Yes, Lester, at least a half a million votes have yet to be counted here in Arizona. And as soon as we may know who wins this race for governor and Senate, may be tomorrow night. Elections officials continue to process and tabulate these mail-in votes. And there`s an important batch of votes that are expected to be released tomorrow. These results are going to be mail ballots that were hand delivered by voters instead of being mailed back. In 2018, these votes, they trended towards Democrats, but in 2020, towards Republicans. Now, one other note that if these margins remain close, this is a situation where if these -- any of these races finish with -- finished within a half a percentage point, that it would trigger an automatic recount under state law that wouldn`t begin until December. Lester? HOLT: All right, Vaughn, thanks very much for that. I want to bring in our political director and moderator of "MEET THE PRESS," Chuck Todd. Chuck, Monday night, you and I stood right here. And we talked about whether polarization could be the guiding factor in the election was it? CHUCK TODD, NBC NEWS POLITICAL DIRECTOR (on camera): Look, I don`t think -- I think it was because I don`t know if campaigns mattered. Let me show you Ohio. Tim Ryan ran up almost a perfect race for a Democrat in Ohio. And yet, it didn`t matter how well his campaign win. Look at this. He basically only performed 1.5 percentage points better than Biden. Essentially, the state reverted to its 2020 partisan norm. Let me take you to Colorado, another example but in the other direction. A Republican running a really good race in Colorado, and it got them all of less than a percentage point better than Donald Trump . The point is, it didn`t matter if it was a blue state or a red state. What the partisan makeup was in 2020 seemed to dictate what the result was in 2022. HOLT: All right, Chuck, thanks. Let me turn to Andrea Mitchell now who`s been looking at the Biden effect. How much credit does the President get for staving off this red wave? ANDREA MITCHELL, NBC NEWS CHIEF WASHINGTON CORRESPONDENT (on camera): Well, Lester, President Biden is touting the stronger than expected results. But our exit polls showed more voters believed his policies were hurting the country than helping. So, can Biden take credit for Democrats overperformance? Another one of our exit polls shows President Biden has less of an impact on voters decisions in this midterms than any other President has had in the last decade. That may explain why despite the President`s low approval ratings, Democrats won in states like Pennsylvania and Michigan and avoided the kind of shellacking President Obama suffered when he lost 63 seats in 2010. This election could be the best Midterm performance for any president`s party in the last 20 years, Lester. HOLT A lot to analyze. Andrea, thanks very much. And even though this election is still full of question marks, it`s already setting the stage for 2024 especially for former President Trump and his potential rivals. Here`s Ali Vitali. (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) ALI VITALI, NBC NEWS CAPITOL HILL CORRESPONDENT (voiceover): Technically, it`s still 2022. But politically -- DONALD TRUMP , FORMER PRESIDENT OF THE UNITED STATES: Stay tuned. VITALI: -- it`s open season on the 2024 Presidential Race. Launched to the front the Republican PAC Tuesday night, Florida Governor Ron DeSantis -- [19:10:03] GOV. RON DESANTIS (R-FL): Thank you for a historic landslide victory. VITALI: Or as the New York Post front page blared, DeFuture. DESANTIS: We`ve got so much more to do, and I have only begun to fight. VITALI: Supporters in the room chanting for two more years. His decisive win here in Florida drawing attention including from fellow Floridian Donald Trump who had his once ally turned likely rival top of mine this weekend. TRUMP: Trump at 71, Ron DeSanctimonious at 10 percent. VITALI: Trump`s handpick candidates suffering a string of losses Tuesday night. TRUMP : I think if they win, I should get all the credit. And if they lose, I should not be blamed at all. WELKER: Who do you think would be the tougher competitor, Ron DeSantis or former President Trump? And how is that factoring into your decision? BIDEN: It`d be fun to watch them take on each other. VITALI: But it`s not just DeSantis eyeing potential bids. GOV. BRIAN KEMP (R-GA): So, give him a big Georgia welcome. VITALI: Former VP Mike Pence also mulling a run, publishing a book So Help Me God out next week, possibly the same day Trump himself could cement his intentions to run again. TRUMP " I`m going to be making a very big announcement. VITALI: Other former Trump officials like Nikki Haley and Mike Pompeo , Senate allies Ted Cruz and Rick Scott , and governors from Arkansas and South Dakota all talked about as possible 2024 contenders. (END VIDEOTAPE) VITALI (on camera): And Pence releasing the first excerpt from his memoir tonight detailing his harrowing experience at the Capitol on January 6, and underscoring his indelible differences with Donald Trump over that day. Lester? HOLT: Ali Vitali, thank you. And meanwhile, Florida is bracing once again for a hurricane. Dylan Dreyer is here. Dylan, Hurricane Nicole is gaining steam. DYLAN DREYER, NBC NEWS METEOROLOGIST (on camera): Yes, it is a hurricane now as it moves through the Bahamas and will likely maintain that category one status as it moves to the west, right now at 12 miles per hour. And then we are looking for the chance of about eight inches of rain across parts of Florida. And this is going to make landfall tonight into early tomorrow morning. And then it`s going to race across the state of Florida, perhaps making another landfall, as it moves its way towards the Gulf of Mexico and then it takes this rapid turn to the north. It`s going to bring all of this rain up into the Northeast where we could see about three to four inches of rain. However, it`s the storm surge down through Daytona Beach and the Jacksonville and the Fort Pierce, the three to five-foot storm surge that could lead to more beach erosion and also some significant flooding right along the coastline. The only saving grace Lester is that the storm hits during low tide. It`s tomorrow morning`s high tide that we`ll worry about. HOLT: All right, Dylan, thanks very much. Let`s get the view from the ground. We want to head to Florida. That`s where NBC Sam Brock is watching as things turn for the worst. Sam? In Georgia, the tight Senate race headed to a runoff. In Pennsylvania, John Fetterman defeating Mehmet Oz. And in Florida, a big reelection win for Governor Ron DeSantis setting up a possible 2024 showdown with Donald Trump . And what President Biden said today about his own 2024 plans. Our team across the country with a race is still in play. Also breaking tonight, Nicole strengthening into a hurricane and taking aim at Florida flooding on the coast. Buildings collapsing into the sea, mandatory evacuations ordered, the new track tonight. The potential major setback for Russia ordering a retreat from the key city of Kherson in southern Ukraine. Why Kyiv is skeptical. WNBA star Brittney Griner moved to a penal colony in Russia. How the U.S. is responding. Facebook `s parent company Meta laying off thousands. At this hour, control of the Senate is still up for grabs with some races too close to call, while the Georgia Senate contest is headed toward a December runoff election. And the House still in play for both sides, though Republicans currently lead. But there is broad agreement that these were not the results most expected, an unpopular president faced with a bad economy managing to avoid the fate of his predecessors. The President`s message to voters tonight, I get it. headline: The Governor`s Race In Georgia Too Early To Call Between Brian Kemp And Stacey Abrams
story_text: LESTER HOLT: Dozens of governors seats are also in play being driven by issues ranging from inflation to abortion. Blayne Alexander is following the key races. Blayne, what should we know? BLAYNE ALEXANDER, NBC NEWS CORRESPONDENT (on camera): Well, Lester, when I`ve spoken to voters, both of those issues came up and more. BRIAN KEMP (R-GA): She was criticizing me for just simply giving you the opportunity to go back to work or to open your business. B. But if voters ended up making their decision based on how they feel about his record -- his record, that`s not a good sign for Democrats. Lester? HOLT: All right, Andrea, thanks for that. Washington could look dramatically different in the days to come. How Congress have the Biden administration are strategizing for a big shift. Plus, we`ll take you inside a vote-counting center. headline: Herschel Walker Facing A New Allegation Of Paying For An Abortion Of A GOP Senate Candidate Is Responding Tonight
story_text: LESTER HOLT: Let me turn now to Kristen. Kristen, there`s a new headline in that tight Georgia Senate race, an anonymous allegation against Herschel Walker . What do we know? KRISTEN WELKER, NBC NEWS CHIEF WHITE HOUSE CORRESPONDENT (on camera): Lester, that`s right. This latest allegation comes from an anonymous woman who spoke on Zoom without showing her face in a press conference arranged by Attorney Gloria Allred, an allegation Herschel Walker is strongly denying tonight. Now, the woman claims she had an affair with Walker, the football star turned Republican Senate candidate, and got pregnant nearly 30 years ago. She says Walker pressured and paid for her to have an abortion, but she did not provide any evidence to support those claims. Now, Walker fired back today calling the claims foolishness and a lie, saying his Democratic opponent Senator Raphael Warnock "lost the debate and Democrats will now say anything to win." The woman`s claim comes after another woman accused Walker of paying for her abortion which Walker also strongly denied. The Georgia race is a toss-up that could determine Senate control. Lester? HOLT: Kristen Welker, thank you. END Content and programming copyright 2022 NBCUniversal. ALL RIGHTS RESERVED. Transcription Copyright 2022 VIQ Media Transcription, Inc. headline: The Fallout From A High Stakes Showdown In Pennsylvania With Control Of Congress Hanging In The Ballots
story_text: [19:00:00] LESTER HOLT, NBC NEWS ANCHOR (on camera): Tonight, the fallout from a high stakes showdown in Pennsylvania with control of Congress hanging in the ballots. (voiceover): Democrat John Fetterman and Republican Dr. Mehmet Oz facing off in their first and only debate. Fetterman`s health struggles in the spotlight months after he suffered a stroke. Oz under scrutiny for an answer he gave on abortion. The reaction from voters just 13 days before the Midterms. Also, tonight, Herschel Walker facing a new allegation of paying for an abortion of a GOP Senate candidate is responding tonight. The verdict in the trial of a Wisconsin man who killed six people when he plowed his SUV into a Christmas parade. The deadly school shooting in St. Louis. The warning the shooters family gave to police and they`re pleas to take a gun away from him months before the rampage. Vladimir Putin overseeing nuclear drills as Russia pushes unproven dirty bomb allegations against Ukraine. And the American fighter killed in Ukraine two months ago finally on his way back home. Hospitals filling up with children infected with RSV. What parents need to know. The critical shortage in a medication millions used to treat ADHD. And he went from homeless to shooting college hoops. The basketball star inspiring America. ANNOUNCER: This is NBC NIGHTLY NEWS with Lester Holt. HOLT (on camera): Good evening. Just 13 days before the Midterm Elections, and a flood of political ads are saturating the airwaves on the heels of another marquee debate reminding just what is at stake in hard-fought congressional races, power and control of Congress. In the House, Democrats trying to defend their majority with all 435 seats of the body up for election. Dems facing the same challenge in the U.S. Senate with 35 seats are up for election. The balance of power in the Senate could be determined by a handful of tight races, including Pennsylvania where last night`s debate pitted Republican Mehmet Oz against Democrat John Fetterman sparring over abortion, fracking, and immigration. But not before Fetterman call out what he described as the elephant in the room, his health. Dasha Burns starts us off tonight with the latest. (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) DASHA BURNS, NBC NEWS CORRESPONDENT (voiceover): Tonight, Pennsylvania Republican Dr. Mehmet Oz back on the campaign trail following last night`s critical one and only face-off. MEHMET OZ (R-PA), SENATE CANDIDATE: Pennsylvania deserves better than Fetterman. BURNS: His opponent, Democrat John Fetterman , not yet making any public appearances after the fierce clash. JOHN FETTERMAN (D-PA), SENATE CANDIDATE: It`s something called the Oz rule that if he`s on TV, he`s lying. OZ: And this is the only debate I could get you to come to talk to me on and I had to beg. BURNS: A debate the Fetterman`s health front and center. Fetterman whose campaign says suffers from auditory processing challenges after a stroke six months ago, requesting these closed captioning monitors in the studio. FETTERMAN: I had a stroke. He`s never let me forget that. And I might miss some words during this debate. Mush two words together, but it knocked me down, but I`m going to keep coming back up. BURNS: Fetterman did miss some words during the hour-long showdown, at times of struggling to answer questions, including this moment. Fetterman was asked about his changing position on fracking, which he now says he supports. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: There is that 2018 interview that you said, "I don`t support fracking at all." So, how do you square the two? FETTERMAN: I do support fracking. And I don`t --I don`t -- I support fracking and I stand -- and I do support fracking. BURNS: Fetterman would not commit to releasing his full medical records. FETTERMAN: My doctor believes that I`m fit to be serving, and that`s what I believe is where I`m standing. BURNS: And in one of the biggest clashes of the night going after Dr. Oz on abortion rights. FETTERMAN: He celebrated when Roe v. Wade went down and my campaign would fight for Roe v. Wade, and if given the opportunity, to codify it into law. BURNS: And tonight, the Fetterman campaign zeroing in on this response from Oz. OZ: I want women, doctors, local political leaders letting the democracy that`s always allowed our nation to thrive to put the best ideas forward so states can decide for themselves. Local political leaders. Local political leaders. BURNS: Turning it into a campaign ad against his opponent. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: Oz is too extreme for Pennsylvania. BURNS: But Oz calling Fetterman the extreme candidates throughout the night, especially on the issue of crime. OZ: We have taken away the ability of police to do their job and that son John Fetterman . BURNS: The momentous matchup coming just two weeks before Election Day. Voters with strong reactions about Dr. Oz. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: His comment about political leaders, you know, determining what a woman -- a woman can and cannot do with her body is -- was very telling. [19:05:09] BURNS: And Fetterman. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: I just don`t think he`s capable at this time to be in that position. I mean, if you have somebody that can`t even handle a debate that has to, you know, read from this prompter. (END VIDEOTAPE) HOLT: And Dasha, some big names could soon be campaigning there on both sides. BURNS (on camera): Yes, Lester. Plans are coming together for both President Biden and former President Obama to campaign with Fetterman, and the Democratic candidate for governor. And former President Trump will campaign with Dr. Oz and the Republican gubernatorial candidate. Lester? HOLT: Dasha Burns, thank you. Let`s bring in Andrea Mitchell and Kristen Welker. Andrea, first to you. What are you hearing there in Pennsylvania about the impact of that debate? ANDREA MITCHELL, NBC NEWS CHIEF WASHINGTON CORRESPONDENT (on camera): Lester, Democrats here are telling me that they think Fetterman will be OK, given his labor support and Oz`s missteps on abortion and the minimum wage. But they acknowledge that this format did not work for Fetterman. Republicans say they`re pleased with how it went. The fact that this race is even close, though, tells you Republicans have momentum right now and it`s happening nationwide. In the Senate, enough incumbent Democrats could lose, giving Republicans several chances to take control. And in the House Democrats are in trouble in states like Oregon and New York, which are normally safe. Last night there was a debate for New York Governor where Republican Trump ally Congressman Lee Zeldin is within striking distance of Democratic Governor Kathy Hochul , which is remarkable in a solid blue state. Lester? HOLT: Andrea, thanks. END Content and programming copyright 2022 NBCUniversal. ALL RIGHTS RESERVED. Transcription Copyright 2022 VIQ Media Transcription, Inc. MICHAEL SACK, INTERIM COMMISSIONER, ST. LOUIS METROPOLITAN POLICE DEPARTMENT: It`s -- and it`s hard to tell when somebody is going to be violent or act out or if they`re just struggling. [19:10:06] IKEDA: His family played an active role in getting a medical help involving therapy, medication, and committing him on several occasions according to police. IKEDA: The ATF is still tracing where he originally bought the gun and how it landed back in his possession after law enforcement had transferred it to another adult. SACK: How he acquired it after that, you know, we don`t know. ASHLEY WRENCH, TEACHER: And you can hear just pop, pop, pop, pop. IKEDA: The longtime math teacher walking by her classroom for the first time since the shooting spree. What do you remember from Monday? WRENCH: Everything. The terror, the intruder trying to get in my room two, three, four times. IKEDA: That day, the school doors were locked, and seven unarmed security guards were on site. But authorities say the government managed to avoid the school`s checkpoints. Can you tell us if he had to break glass to get into the building though? SACK: You did have to force entry. And that`s good for us because that buys us time. President Vladimir Putin observing annual drills led by Russia`s strategic nuclear forces as Russia continues with unfounded claims that Ukraine intends to use a dirty bomb in the war there. GIOVANNI FLOOD, HAS ADHD: Uncomfortable. LYON FLOOD, SON HAD ADHD: His teacher came to us, threw her hands up and said, can you do something because he was way out of control, doing cartwheels in the class, and rolling on the floor. K. FLOOD: Rolling on the floor, yes. DR. LENARD ADLER, PSYCHIATRIST, NYU LANGONE: We`re fielding several phone calls a day. THOMPSON: Dr. Lenard Adler leads the adult ADHD program at NYU Langone Health. ADLER: I`ve had a patient having to call about 15 pharmacies before they finally got to -- THOMPSON: 15? ADLER: 15 pharmacies before they got their prescription filled. THOMPSON: This month, the FDA revealed the shortage blaming increased demand for the control substance and manufacturing issues at Teva , the largest drug maker. ADLER: If you`re at the end of your prescription, I wouldn`t suggest doing anything on your own. I would have a discussion with your physician. Sometimes that means trying a new pharmacy. It can be. Two other men were convicted on federal conspiracy charges in August. Whitmer said, today`s verdicts are quote further proof that violence and threats have no place in our politics. (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) GABE GUTIERREZ, NBC NEWS NATIONAL CORRESPONDENT (voiceover): Amid complaints of armed masked groups wearing tactical gear and recording voters, the sheriff in Maricopa County, Arizona has now stepped up security near ballot drop boxes. PAUL PENZONE, SHERIFF, MARICOPA COUNTY: It troubles me that suddenly others feel compelled to act out in a way that is potentially criminal intimidation or criminal threats, trying to undermine democracy under this cloak of patriotism. And in doing so, what they`re doing is they`re destroying the most important institution in our nation, you know, the freedom and the right to vote. GUTIERREZ: He also says his office is investigating this incident captured on cell phone video where a woman tried to take a picture of one of their license plates and was pushed. We spoke to the woman. She asked us not to use her name or show her face for fear of backlash. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: You know, a lot of people are intimidated. And when people are standing around, you know, with handguns on them and sometimes tactical gear, you know, it really does scare the average person. GUTIERREZ: At least six complaints of alleged voter intimidation here have now been referred to the State Attorney General`s Office and the Department of Justice. Across the country, election threats are ramping up ahead of the Midterms. LEIGH CHAPMAN, ACTING SECRETARY, PENNSYLVANIA COMMONWEALTH: A lot of these threats are fueled by missing disinformation. GUTIERREZ: Law enforcement Nationwide is on alert. MERRICK GARLAND , U.S. ATTORNEY GENERAL: The Justice Department has an obligation to prevent to guarantee a free and fair vote. GUTIERREZ: Back in Arizona where early votes are already been counted, Republican election officials have called these armed drop box watchers uninformed vigilantes. As a Republican, how frustrating is it to you that some of these groups have latched on to conspiracy theories? STEPHEN RICHER, MARICOPA COUNTY RECORDER: Well, it`s been an interesting last two years. (END VIDEOTAPE) GUTIERREZ (on camera): Voter rights organizations have now sued to temporarily block at least some of these groups from monitoring these ballot drop-off boxes. Lester? (COMMERCIAL BREAK) [19:25:00] HOLT: Tonight`s Powerball jackpot has grown to a massive $700 million, the fifth largest in the game`s history. No one has won since August. The odds are one in 293 million. If you bought your tickets, good luck to you. And finally, the student-athlete beating formidable odds with a former NBA point guard coaching them on. Kathy Park with tonight`s "INSPIRING AMERICA." (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) KATHY PARK, NBC NEWS CORRESPONDENT (voiceover): Jeremiah Armstead picked up a basketball at 14, the same age he realized life wasn`t a game. JEREMIAH ARMSTEAD, BASKETBALL PLAYER: I felt like I wasn`t in at 14. That`s what I feel like. Because that`s when they really picked up homeless and stuff like that. PARK: For years, Jeremiah says he moved from shelter to shelter with his mom and two siblings. ARMSTEAD: I was living off food stamps. PARK: What would you say were some of the darkest times in your life? ARMSTEAD: Sleeping at bleachers. People walking by, looking in the car. PARK: He excelled as a student in California and as an athlete, a winning combination that got him into Fisk University in Nashville, and a spot on the basketball team. KENNY ANDERSON, FORMER NBA PLAYER: The grit definitely sets him apart. PARK: Former NBA point guard Kenny Anderson now coaches a rising star and sees a lot of himself in Jeremiah. ANDERSON: My best year of my high school career, I was -- I have the way to live. We got evicted. PARK: The NBA legend beat the odds and believes Jeremiah can too. Meanwhile, his cheering squad couldn`t be prouder. MINDY BROOKS, MOTHER OF JEREMIAH: This is a child who deserves to just show what he can do. PARK: What`s the end game for you? ARMSTEAD: My first goal which is get my mom and my sister out to shelter that they`re in. PARK: Family first while making moves on and off the court. Kathy Park, NBC News, Nashville. (END VIDEOTAPE) HOLT: Good for him. That`s NIGHTLY NEWS for this Wednesday. Thank you for watching. I`m Lester Holt. Please take care of yourself and each other. Goodnight, everyone. headline: Missed Cases Of Breast Cancer: The Detection Delayed In Dozens Of Patients And The Hospital At The Center Of The Controversy
story_text: [19:15:00] LESTER HOLT: There`s no question that mammograms save lives were the early detection of breast cancer, but a review of cases at one hospital showed many cancers were initially missed even though they appeared on the scans. Kristen Dahlgren has our investigation. (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) KRISTEN DAHLGREN, NBC NEWS CORRESPONDENT (voiceover): Jim and Pat Ratliff had a 54-year love story. JIM RATLIFF, WIFE HAD BREAST CANCER: We were attached at the hip. DAHLGREN: Through ups and downs, including Pat`s breast cancer more than a decade ago, which is why she was so diligent about screening and concern when she noticed changes in her other breast. She had imaging at a nearby hospital, part of NIH Northern Arizona Health Care. And they told her what? RATLIFF: They couldn`t find anything. DAHLGREN: Eventually, Pat saw breast surgeon Beth DuPree. DR. BETH DUPREE, BREAST SURGEON: I literally couldn`t believe what I was seeing. It was screaming cancer. DAHLGREN: Advanced breast cancer. Two years later, Pat was gone. Dr. DuPree had just moved to Sedona to develop a state-of-the-art Breast Center at NIH . Pat was just the first patient she says who came to her with a cancer missed on previous scan. DUPREE: These were misses that are not subtle. DAHLGREN: The hospital has an exclusive contract with Northern Arizona Radiology. DuPree who says she continued to flag misread mammograms push them to hire dedicated breast imagers, including Mike Ulissey who couldn`t believe some of what he says was missed. MIKE ULISSEY, BREAST IMAGER: I said my god, Beth. That`s the size of a tangerine. I don`t understand how they can call it normal. DAHLGREN: The hospital requested the radiology group have those new breast imagers review more than 6000 patients whose scans had initially been read by a particular general radiologist. Ulissey says they found cancer in an additional 25 women. CHRISTIE GALLO, HAD BREAST CANCER: The recommendation was returned to me here. DAHLGREN: Among them Christie Gallo (PH). GALLO: My question was, how can I go from normal to having three tumors in one year? That didn`t make sense to me. DAHLGREN: Dr. DuPree believes the number of patients with missed cancers was much greater than the 25 detected in the review. She made a poster with all of her patients whose diagnoses she says were delayed, hoping to show it to the hospital board. We`re only showing those who gave us permission. It must be hard to look at their faces. DUPREE: It is. DAHLGREN: NBC News obtained an email from one of the breast imagers to the radiology group sent before the review was complete, warning of the gravity of the situation. After the review, there was still concern. ULISSEY: We thought that there were a significant chance that additional patients were in harm`s way. We need to expand our investigation. DAHLGREN: But Dr. Ulissey says the radiology group did not. In his statement to NBC, NIH points out the radiology group is a separate entity and says in part, "The hospital quickly acted to address these concerns. We ensured these mammograms were reread specifically by a team of breast fellowship-trained radiologists, saying very few required any follow-up. And since this review, all mammograms are read by specialized breast radiologists." The hospital`s Chief Counsel spoke on a Zoom with community advisors. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: So, the quality process works. There was an error. We`re humans. Doctors are human. GALLO: They messed up and they don`t want to fess up to it. DAHLGREN: Northern Arizona radiology called the review results well within national standards. In a statement, it says, "All radiologists are board certified and meet all requirements, including those under the Mammography Quality Standards Act. DuPree and three out of four new breast imagers including Dr. Ulissey have now left. NBC News has learned the general radiologist who was the subject of the review is now working in another state. As for Gallo, her cancer is in remission, but she`s not sure the questions will ever go away. GALLO: Maybe if they had caught it sooner, it could have been a just a lumpectomy instead of a whole mastectomy choice, but I didn`t get that choice. DAHLGREN: Kristen Dahlgren, NBC News, Sedona, Arizona. (END VIDEOTAPE) HOLT: And up next for us, late news about today`s earthquake in California. Plus, top brands cut ties after antisemitic comments by music and fashion mogul Kanye West. (COMMERCIAL BREAK) [19:20:00] HOLT: Back with the new troubles for Kanye West. Adidas ended its deal today with the music mogul and designer who now goes by Ye over his recent antisemitic comments. Hours later, Gap said it is immediately removing West`s clothing line from its stores. Forbes reports that without his lucrative Adidas deal, West is no longer a billionaire. Some scary moments in Northern California today when an earthquake struck near San Jose. The quake had a preliminary magnitude of 5.1 according to the U.S. Geological Survey . Seismologists say it`s the biggest quake to hit the Bay Area in more than eight years, but there are no reports of injuries or significant damage. Up next, the dramatic rescue. Tourists trapped hundreds of feet underground at a cavern in Arizona. (COMMERCIAL BREAK) END Content and programming copyright 2022 NBCUniversal. ALL RIGHTS RESERVED. headline: NBC NIGHTLY NEWS for October 25, 2022, NBC
story_text: [19:00:00] (COMMERCIAL BREAK) LESTER HOLT, NBC NEWS ANCHOR (on camera): Tonight, the chilling new details of the deadly shooting at a St. Louis High School. (voiceover): Investigators revealing today the 19-year-old gunman had an AR-15-style rifle and 600 rounds of ammunition. That disturbing handwritten note he left behind. What we`re learning about the victims, the stories of survival, and what police a prevented even more bloodshed. Also, tonight the spike in children hospitalized with RSV as flu season ramps up and President Biden getting his Omicron booster. His warning to Americans ahead of another potential winter COVID surge. WNBA star Brittney Griner losing her appeal in a Russian court. Where does that leave negotiations for a prisoner swap? What the White House is saying? Just two weeks until the Midterms and the high stakes showdown tonight in Pennsylvania. Democrat John Fetterman and Republican Dr. Mehmet Oz facing off in their first and only debate with control of the Senate on the line. Adidas dropping its deal with Kanye West after his antisemitic comments caused a firestorm. NBC News investigates the breast cancer diagnoses missed in more than two dozen women. How did it happen? And the mission to rescue tourists stranded in the Grand Canyon Caverns 200 feet underground. ANNOUNCER: This is NBC NIGHTLY NEWS with Lester Holt. HOLT (on camera): Good evening. We will never know exactly how much higher the death toll would have been in yesterday`s school shooting in St. Louis had police not killed the attacker. But today, there is chilling new evidence the 19-year-old killer intended it to be a bloodbath. Today, police revealing the gunman used an AR-15-style rifle to shoot his victims. A teacher and a student were both killed, four others were wounded. In addition, three people were injured during the chaos at Central Visual and Performing Arts High School. Authorities also saying the shooter, a former student, was carrying 600 rounds of ammunition. But the most revealing evidence may be what police say they found in his car, entries in a notebook that may offer a disturbing roadmap into his state of mind. Emilie Ikeda is in St. Louis tonight with new details. (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) EMILIE IKEDA, NBC NEWS CORRESPONDENT (voiceover): Tonight, a trove of evidence shedding light on what may have driven a 19-year-old to storm his alma mater, gunning down a sophomore and teacher and injuring at least seven. Investigators discovering a letter in the suspect`s car parked outside Central Visual and Performing Arts High School. MICHAEL SACK, INTERIM CHIEF, ST. LOUIS METROPOLITAN POLICE DEPARTMENT: He spoke about his desire to engage in this incident to conduct the school shooting. IKEDA: The handwritten note reads in part, "I don`t have any friends. I don`t have any family. I`ve never had a girlfriend. I`ve never had a social life. I`ve been an isolated loner my entire life. This was the perfect storm for a mass shooter." A mass shooter that claimed the lives of beloved health and physical education teacher Jean Kuczka and sophomore Alexandria Bell. The student`s father calling her death a nightmare. ANDRE BELL, FATHER OF ALEXANDRIA BELL: No matter how I felt, I can talk to her and it was -- it was alright. That was my baby. IKEDA: Armed with an AR 15 style weapon and 600 rounds of ammunition, police say the suspect Orlando Harris` shooting rampage could have been even worse. SACK: Oh, this could have been a horrific scene. It was not by the grace of God and that the officers were as close as they were. IKEDA: Officers who already happened to be in the area for another event, said they arrived on scene within five minutes of the first 911 call, and made it to the government on the third floor within another eight minutes. The suspect shot dead. Police would not say how the team broke into the school or obtained a long gun plus a stockpile of ammunition. When you got there, what did you see? MICHAEL BISHOP, STUDENT PARENT: It was chaos. IKEDA: Student parent Michael Bishop applauds the police`s rapid response, but knows the trauma will follow his daughter and her classmates. BISHOP: She`s going to second guess going into any school, any building with people for who knows how long and it`s heartbreaking. (END VIDEOTAPE) HOLT: Emilie, there`s going to be a lot of looking back at this point. Were there any red flags in the gunman`s history? IKEDA (on camera): Lester, police say the suspect did not have a criminal history but may have been suffering from a mental illness. Law enforcement underscoring the importance of see something, say something, encouraging people to speak up if someone makes concerning comments or is struggling. Tonight, a community still in shock as school officials say that it may be weeks before students can return for in person instruction here. Lester? HOLT: OK, Emilie, thank you. Tonight, pediatric emergency rooms around the country say they are beyond capacity because of that surge in children with respiratory viruses including RSV. It comes as they deal with COVID and flu as well. Here`s Tom Costello. [19:05:16] (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) TOM COSTELLO, NBC NEWS CORRESPONDENT (voiceover): In Northern Virginia, the respiratory virus known as RSV has made its way into 4-year-old Nova Louis`s lungs. How are you feeling? NOVA LOUIS, HAS RSV: Sick. COSTELLO: Struggling to breathe with an existing heart condition, her mom rushed her to the ER this morning. SUMMER LOUIS, MOTHER OF NOVA: It`s very troubling and worrisome because everyone`s getting sick, and she just had COVID this summer for the first time. COSTELLO: The medical director at the Inova Children`s ER says they`re in crisis mode. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: Three days of fever and cough congestion. COSTELLO: Overwhelmed like many hospitals with a dangerous viral tripledemic. headline: The New Pledge From President Biden, If Democrats Keep Control Of Congress, He`ll Immediately Move To Pass National Abortion Rights
story_text: LESTER HOLT: 21 days before the Midterms, President Biden trying to keep abortion rights front and center, but polls show voters worrying most about the economy and soaring inflation. Peter Alexander reports on the new clashes between candidates in key battlegrounds. [19:05:09] (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) PETER ALEXANDER, NBC NEWS CHIEF WHITE HOUSE CORRESPONDENT (voiceover): With just three weeks until the Midterms and Republicans slamming Democrats over the economy and record inflation, President Biden tonight trying to amplify the politically divisive issue of abortion rights, urging voters to keep Democrats in control of Congress. JOE BIDEN , PRESIDENT OF THE UNITED STATES: Here`s the promise I make to you and the American people. The first bill that I will send to the Congress will be to codify Roe v. Wade. ALEXANDER: But some Democrats fear the potency of that message may be waning. Tonight, a new poll shows 44 percent of likely voters cite the economy or inflation as the number one problem facing the country while just five percent list abortion as their top issue. And now, Republicans have a four-point lead when voters are asked which party`s candidate they`d support. In Ohio, one of several crucial races that`ll determine control of the Senate. Republican candidate J.D. Vance hammered Democrat Tim Ryan over skyrocketing prices in a heated final debate. J.D. VANCE (R-OH) SENATE CANDIDATE: That rising energy price that people see at the pump, that they see in the utility bills, that was the direct result of policies enacted by Joe Biden and Nancy Pelosi and supported 100 percent by Tim Ryan . ALEXANDER: While Ryan slammed Vance for embracing former President Trump. REP. TIM RYAN (D-OH): You were calling Trump America`s Hitler. Then he kissed his ass -- VANCE: It`s not true. RYAN: It is true. And then you kissed his ass, and then he endorsed you. And you said he`s the greatest president of all time. ALEXANDER: There are critical governor`s races too in the battlegrounds of Arizona and Michigan and a rematch in Georgia between Republican Governor Brian Kemp and Democrat Stacey Abrams . Their one and only showdown last night. STACEY ABRAMS (D-GA), GUBERNATORIAL CANDIDATE: We live in a state of fear. And this is a governor who for the last four years has beat his chest but delivered very little for most Georgians. ALEXANDER: Kemp touting his early moves to reopen the state during the pandemic and going after Abrams. GOV. BRIAN KEMP (R-GA): Miss Abrams is going to lie out my record because she doesn`t want to talk about her own. (END VIDEOTAPE) HOLT: Peter, President Biden is going to pivot to the economy tomorrow focusing on high gas prices. ALEXANDER (on camera): Yes, Lester, that`s right. Looking to lower those prices, the President is going to announce that the administration will move forward with the release of as many as 15 million additional barrels of oil from the Strategic Petroleum Reserve. It`s a controversial move that comes amid Russia`s war in Ukraine and after Saudi Arabia snub the President`s request to boost oil production. Lester? HOLT: Peter Alexander at the White House, thank you. There`s breaking news and a trial involving a murder they went unsolved for 25 years. A California man convicted late today for killing Kristin Smart, a college student who disappeared in 1996. Paul Flores, a former classmate of Smart`s wasn`t arrested for the crime until last year. Flores` father who was accused of helping move Smart`s body was found not guilty. Smart`s remains were never found. END Content and programming copyright 2022 NBCUniversal. ALL RIGHTS RESERVED. headline: NBC NIGHTLY NEWS for October 18, 2022, NBC
story_text: [19:00:00] (COMMERCIAL BREAK) LESTER HOLT, NBC NEWS ANCHOR (on camera): Tonight, the arctic blast of cold putting tens of millions on alert across the eastern half of the country. (voiceover): Frost and freeze warnings across 25 states, 86 million impacted. For many, the coldest air of the season yet. More than a foot of snow falling in parts of the Midwest less than a month into fall. Al Roker is tracking it. Also, tonight, just three weeks until the Midterms. The new pledge from President Biden, if Democrats keep control of Congress, he`ll immediately move to pass national abortion rights. Will it be enough with polls showing voter concerns focused on the economy right now? More than 25 years after the disappearance of Kristin Smart, the verdict in the murder trial or for former college classmate. Blackouts in Ukraine after officials say Russia destroyed nearly a third of its power stations in little over a week. Growing fears for an Iranian climber after she competed without a hijab. The worries about her safety tonight. The deadly crash. A plane slamming into a car dealership. The FDA pushing to take a controversial pregnancy drug off the market. Why some doctors and moms say it`s a mistake And the Wikipedia warrior fighting to get some remarkable women the recognition they deserve. ANNOUNCER: This is NBC Nightly News with Lester Holt. HOLT (on camera): Good evening. In a year defined by some of the most extreme heat we`ve ever seen, along with one of the strongest hurricanes to hit the U.S. mainland, tonight, making headlines for unseasonable cold and early snow. In the East, autumn interrupted by a sudden and dramatic detour into winter, a climate change whiplash leaving 86 million people currently under freezing alerts from the northern tip of Texas across the south and up into the Northeast. More than 40 record lows possible this evening across 18 states. Several cities in the south could see their earliest freezes on record. Al Roker will lay it out for us in a moment but first let`s go to Maggie Vespa feeling the big chill in Michigan. East of the Rockies, temperatures are 10 to 25 degrees below average. Even seasoned locals shutter. And is it a birthday gift or is it a problem. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: It`s a problem. headline: Dr. Mehmet Oz On Crime And His Campaign`s Attacks On Fetterman`s Health
story_text: LESTER HOLT: Just 25 days before the Midterms, tonight, we speak exclusively with Dr. Mehmet Oz, the Republican facing off against Democrat John Fetterman in that critical Pennsylvania Senate race. Our Dasha Burns pressing Dr. Oz on crime and his campaign`s attacks on Fetterman`s health. (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) DASHA BURNS, NBC NEWS CORRESPONDENT (voiceover): Pennsylvania Republican Senate candidate and celebrity doctor, Mehmet Oz, has focused much of his campaign on crime and blasting Democrat John Fetterman on his votes as the head of the state`s Board of Pardons. He says he believes in second chances, the former president with his First Step Act, also was about giving second chances to prisoners who deserve it. Why don`t prisoners who prove good behavior, who are modeled prisoners, why don`t they deserve second chances? MEHMET OZ (R-PA), SENATE CANDIDATE: The First Step Act had nothing to do with convicted murderers being released from prison, especially if they`ve been sentenced to life in prison. It`s a whole different game. When John Fetterman is asked, if you could wave a magic wand, what`s the one thing you would do, the one thing? And he says why get rid of life in prison? BURNS: Well, I asked him that. He actually said, it would be codifying Roe versus Wade and abolishing the Filibuster. OZ: Well, he`s answered it the way I just described in the past as well. And too often, John Fetterman seems to pay more attention to the feelings of the criminals than the innocent who were hurt. BURNS: We also asked about his campaign`s attacks on Fetterman`s health. He was off the campaign trail for months after suffering a stroke. One of your campaign staffers said that John Fetterman wouldn`t have had a stroke if he had "ever eaten a vegetable in his life." You`re a doctor. You`re a heart doctor. You of all people understand what John Fetterman is going through better than most. Why would you allow your campaign to mock him like that? OZ: I have tremendous compassion for what John Fetterman has gone through. I mean, not only do I, as a doctor, appreciate the challenges, but I know his specific ailment because it`s a specialty area of mine. BURNS: But would you ever talk to your patients like this? OZ: No. BURNS: He criticizes Fetterman for not releasing his medical records, while Fetterman accuses Dr. Oz of not being transparent on abortion rights. This is what he told us this week. JOHN FETTERMAN (D-PA), SENATE CANDIDATE: Dr. Oz likes to make fun of me that I might miss a word. But you know, he`s missed, you know, two words. And that is a yes or no on the national abortion ban. BURNS: So, we asked him about Republican Senator Lindsey Graham`s bill that would ban abortions after 15 weeks. If you win, you`re going to be a colleague of his. You`re going to have to vote on bills like this. So, can you tell us right now, yes or no on that bill? OZ: I`m giving you a bigger answer than yes or no. I`m telling you. HOLT: Blayne Alexander in Raleigh tonight, thank you. ALEXANDER LUKASHENKO , PRESIDENT, BELARUS (through translator): If you put a person or a country in a corner, there is only one way out from there, to move forward? SIMMONS : How would you describe President Putin state of mind right now? LUKASHENKO (through translator): Is that what you think in the western United States? Now, she`s dominating the sport as a professional pickleballer. BRIGHT: I probably netted between 100 and $125,000 since late February. IKEDA: So, you`ve made six figures within less than a year of playing pickleball. BRIGHT: Yes. IKEDA: Once viewed as a pastime for the older athletes among us, pickleball, with its noisy pops of plastic, is somewhere between tennis and ping pong and proving it has no bounds. This is Major League Pickleball complete with color commentary. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: Taddeo is flashing it all right now. IKEDA: Today, the first of a three-day tournament in Columbus, Ohio. 12 teams, 48 players. The top prize, $100,000. Pickleball is considered the fastest-growing sport in the U.S. with nearly five million players picking up a paddle last year. ANNE WORCESTER, STRATEGIC ADVISER AND BOARD MEMBER, MAJOR LEAGUE PICKLEBALL: There will be 40 million people playing pickleball by 2030. IKEDA: And some of the biggest names in sports are paying attention. TOM BRADY, NFL STAR: All right, Pickleball. IKEDA: Tom Brady, LeBron James, and Kim Clijsters are among the growing list of superstar pro athletes buying up professional pickleball teams. What makes pickleball appealing as an investor? KIM CLIJSTERS, FORMER PROFESSIONAL TENNIS PLAYER: The growth margin. I think it`s really cool to see that there is still so much potential. The reason why I did MLP is because it`s equal pay. Men and women are starting on an equal playing field. IKEDA: Major League money is following the fans as professional pickleball takes its swing. Emilie Ikeda NBC News, Columbus, Ohio. (END VIDEOTAPE) HOLT: It sounds like it`s time to get in the game. That`s NIGHTLY NEWS. Thank you for watching, everyone. I`m Lester Holt. Please take care of yourself and each other. Good night. headline: Top Republicans Traveling To Georgia To Campaign With Herschel Walker Amid His Abortion Controversy
story_text: LESTER HOLT: Just four weeks until the Midterms, today`s Senate Republican heavyweights rally behind Herschel Walker as he tries to weather the abortion controversy now overshadowing his campaign in all-important Georgia. Here`s Peter Alexander. (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) PETER ALEXANDER, NBC NEWS CHIEF WHITE HOUSE CORRESPONDENT (voiceover): Tonight, in Georgia, Republican reinforcements arriving to pollster embattled Senate nominee Herschel Walker . SEN. TOM COTTON (R-AR): It`s especially good to be here with the next United States Senator from Georgia Herschel Walker . ALEXANDER: Key senators Tom Cotton and Rick Scott standing by the former football great as he faces an allegation that he paid for an abortion for an ex-girlfriend more than a decade ago, while now campaigning on his opposition to abortion rights. Walker has strongly denied the accusation, but today for the first time publicly acknowledged he now knows who the woman is. The senators tonight insists the controversy will not cost Walker the race. SEN. RICK SCOTT (R-FL): Inflation, crime, parents not being involved in schools. That`s what people are going to vote on. ALEXANDER: Still, some state Republicans have criticized Walker. Lieutenant Governor Geoff Duncan writing, Walker has not yet earned my vote. He has four weeks left to change our minds. While, overnight, another critical clash over Ohio`s open Senate seat. In their first debate, Democratic Congressman Tim Ryan , accusing Republican J.D. Vance of lavishing praise on former President Trump. REP. TIM RYAN (D-OH): Ohio needs an ass-kicker, not an ass-kisser. ALEXANDER: While Vance attacked Ryan for voting 100 percent of the time with President Biden who remains unpopular with Ohio voters. J.D. VANCE (R-OH), SENATE CANDIDATE: We`re getting close to Halloween and Tim Ryan is put on a costume where he pretends to be a reasonable moderate. (END VIDEOTAPE) [19:10:07] ALEXANDER (on camera): Tim Ryan also tried to distance himself from President Biden saying he does not believe the President should run for reelection in 2024. Lester? HOLT: Peter, thank you. END Content and programming copyright 2022 NBCUniversal. ALL RIGHTS RESERVED. Transcription Copyright 2022 VIQ Media Transcription, Inc. headline: The New Twist In The Herschel Walker Firestorm
story_text: [19:05:15] LESTER HOLT: With a little over A month until the Midterms, a growing firestorm in Georgia of a Republican Senate candidate Herschel Walker . the woman who says Walker paid for her abortion is now making a new allegation which Walker is strongly denying. Yamiche Alcindor is there. (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) YAMICHE ALCINDOR, NBC NEWS WASHINGTON CORRESPONDENT (voiceover): After a campaign event in Georgia, tonight Herschel Walker defiant. HERSCHEL WALKER (R-GA), SENATE CANDIDATE: And I`m not going to back down. The stakes are way, way too high. ALCINDOR: Following the latest twist and the controversy surrounding the Republican Senate candidate and former football star. The Daily Beast reporting the unnamed woman who the legend Walker paid for her abortion more than a decade ago says she`s also the mother of one of his children. Previously, she provided the news outlet with a receipt from an abortion clinic as well as a check and a get-well card she says are from Walker. She has not revealed her name citing privacy concerns, and NBC News has not verified her story nor the documents. Walker, an abortion rights opponent, again strongly denying the accusation. WALKER: I know this is untrue. I know nothing about any woman having an abortion. ALCINDOR: But Walker`s son, Christian, has fiercely criticized his father. CHRISTIAN WALKER, SON OF HERSCHEL WALKER : Don`t lie on the lives you`ve destroyed and act like you`re some moral family man. Y`all should care about that, conservatives. ALCINDOR: Today, we pressed Walker. What`s your reaction to people so close to you, your son, a mother of your -- someone who says that she`s the mother of your kid saying that you`re lying. What`s your reaction to people so close to you saying don`t trust you? WALKER: Just like what I just said. Democrats are desperate for this seat. This seat is important. ALCINDOR: They`re your family. WALKER: They`re very desperate for to seat. I love my family. I always love my family. I`m going to win this race. ALCINDOR: The Daily Beast says the anonymous woman, a registered Democrat, who says she`d had a years-long relationship with Walker thinks his denials are quote ridiculous. Many National Republican standing by Walker slamming it, and said it`s Democratic distraction from issues like inflation and crime. SEN. TED CRUZ (R-TX): Herschel Walker is going to win that race. This is an effort from Democrats to hold on to power. ALCINDOR: But some state Republican starting to voice their unease. LT. GOV. GEOFF DUNCAN (R-GA): Even the most staunch Republicans I think are rattled at the continued flow of information. ALCINDOR: Meanwhile, voters in Georgia sounding off. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: It`s 100 percent true right now, but we don`t know a whole story. I`m voting for Herschel. I mean, he made a mistake. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: The only reason Herschel Walker is on his ballot right now is because he supports Trump. If you support Trump, you can have any kind of morals in this country. (END VIDEOTAPE) ALCINDOR: Today, Walker`s opponent, Democratic Senator Raphael Warnock called these allegations, "disturbing." And he`s reiterated his support for abortion rights. Next week, both men are scheduled to face off in a debate. Lester? HOLT: All right, Yamiche, thank you. END Content and programming copyright 2022 NBCUniversal. ALL RIGHTS RESERVED. VESPA: At 100, the retired Cincinnati engineer and great grandfather of four logs five to 10 miles three times a week. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: You are so sweet. VESPA: His 14-minute mile pace only slowed by starstruck fans. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: You`re an inspiration to a lot of people. VESPA: Does that feel weird to hear that you`re a celebrity? FREMONT: Absolutely embarrassing. VESPA: With 60 marathons under his feet, Mike boasts four world records, fastest marathons for his age at 80 and 90. Fastest half marathons at 90 and 91. Running started his therapy in his 30s after the loss of his first wife. FREMONT: So, starting to run and it worked. VESPA: Decades later, after battling cancer, Mike went vegan and with the encouragement of his second wife, Marilyn, ran marathon after marathon. What do you think is fueling it? MARILYN WALL, WIFE OF MIKE FREMONT: I think he can`t quit. VESPA: Proving her point, his other hobby, canoeing. Of course, racing goes to. VESPA: Proof no matter your age, your best time may still lie ahead. Maggie Vespa, NBC News, Cincinnati. (END VIDEOTAPE) HOLT: And he just keeps going. That`s NIGHTLY NEWS for this Thursday. Thank you for watching. I`m Lester Holt. Please take care of yourself and each other. Goodnight, everyone. (COMMERCIAL BREAK) END Content and programming copyright 2022 NBCUniversal. headline: Herschel Walker , The GOP Candidate Who Has Called For A Ban On Abortion, Denying That He Paid For An Ex-Girlfriend`s Abortion More Than A Decade Ago
story_text: LESTER HOLT: Just 35 days before the Midterms, a new allegation is rocking that very tight Senate race in Georgia. Republican Herschel Walker strongly denying an accusation that he paid for a former girlfriend abortion. Here`s Kristen Welker. (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) KRISTEN WELKER, NBC NEWS CHIEF WHITE HOUSE CORRESPONDENT (voiceover): Tonight, Republican candidate and former football star Herschel Walker forcefully denying an allegation that`s rocking the critical Georgia Senate race. A new accusation that Walker who supports an abortion ban after 15 weeks without any exceptions, paid for his then-girlfriend to have an abortion in 2009. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: Do you know the woman that is making this allegation? HERSCHEL WALKER (R-GA), SENATE CANDIDATE: I have no -- I had no idea but it is a flat-out lie. WELKER: The explosive report appearing in The Daily Beast which did not name the woman citing privacy concerns. She says she and Walker agreed she would have the abortion. The Daily Beast publishing a photo of a get-well card she says this from Walker. The news outlet also says she gave them a receipt from an abortion clinic and an image of a $700 check she says his from Walker. NBC News has not seen nor independently verified any of the documents. WALKER: I never asked anyone to get an abortion. I never pay for an abortion and that`s a lie. WELKER: But tonight, Walker is facing fierce criticism from his 23-year-old son Christian saying Walker`s family urged him not to run because we all knew some of his past. CHRISTIAN WALKER, SON OF HERSCHEL WALKER : Don`t lie about your life at the expense of me, my mom, and all of the people that you`ve affected throughout your life. You don`t get to pretend you`re some moral family guy. WELKER: Herschel Walker tweeting I love my son no matter what. And blasting the allegations as a last-minute distraction by Democrats. WALKER: There`s inflation, the border wide open, crime. They don`t want to talk about that. So, they`re making up lies now because they need this Georgia seat. WELKER: Now, top national Republicans are rallying around him from former President Trump to Senator Rick Scott tonight saying Democrats know that Herschel Walker is winning so they have cranked up this smear machine. (END VIDEOTAPE) WELKER: Incumbent Democrat Senator Raphael Warnock not weighing in on the controversy, but saying he`s been a consistent abortion rights supporter. Lester? HOLT: Kristen Welker, thanks. It appears that Elon Musk`s plan to buy Twitter is back on tonight. A lawyer for the billionaire tells federal regulators that Musk is willing to go forward with a $44 billion deal if a Delaware court ends Twitter `s lawsuit against Musk. Twitter file that soon after Musk put the deal on hold last spring. END Content and programming copyright 2022 NBCUniversal. ALL RIGHTS RESERVED. In just 48 hours Russia retaliated by striking Ukraine`s power grid. Is the war at a turning point? Donald Trump`s legal team objecting to the DOJ`s special master candidates to review the classified documents ceased from Mar-a-Lago. What they are asking the judge to do? Scotland, a country adored by the Queen and in fact the place she died on Thursday. SIMMONS: Not everything was scripted today. One person protesting Prince Andrew was quickly removed from the crowd. Today`s events in Edinburgh capping off that solemn weekend journey that carried the Queen through 180 miles of stunning Scottish countryside after leaving her beloved Balmoral Castle. People on horseback paying respects along the road. These tractors a tribute to her from local farmers. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: We`re proud to be Scottish and we`re proud to be British. And it`s nice to say goodbye. SIMMONS: And another poignant moment in this long goodbye. The Queen`s children mounting a vigil standing on all sides of her casket heads bowed. Even as many thousands of mourners kept coming, each given just a few minutes to say goodbye to a queen who gave them her life. (END VIDEOTAPE) [19:05:10] HOLT: Keir, it was quite a day. I know tomorrow, the focus of the solemn ceremonies will turn to London. SIMMONS (on camera): That`s right, Lester. The Queen`s body will be brought here to Buckingham palace tomorrow. Then, on Wednesday, move to Westminster for four days where hundreds of thousands are expected to wait in line. And then, a week today, that historic State Funeral. Lester? HOLT: Keir Simmons, thank you. And NBC is Tom Llamas has been on the ground for us in Edinburgh, the last few days. And Tom, you walk the Royal Mile today.
