It was double, if not triple what we experienced when the Queen`s hearse first pulled into Edinburgh on Sunday. But tonight, that solemn procession uphill through the medieval street with the king and the Queen`s children marching along through a sea of people so many onlookers were pouring over staircases on some corners. But the impact of Queen Elizabeth`s reign, it hit us afterwards, Lester, it`s what many didn`t see, the line nine hours long in some cases to see the Queen`s casket up close. I spoke to several people in the crowd, some who said they wanted to witness history but so many other saying the Queen earned that devotion with her 70 years on the throne. Two female veterans told me they were waiting all that time to personally salut the coffin. And tonight, Lester, this is a live image of the scene outside St. Giles Cathedral. The sun has gone down. (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) MOLLY HUNTER, NBC NEWS FOREIGN CORRESPONDENT (voiceover): It was a welcome reunion that took the country by surprise. Getting out of the same car, the new Prince and Princess of Wales, William and Kate, alongside Harry and Meghan. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: We didn`t imagine all four of them to be together, but I think that was the Queen`s last wish. HUNTER: We now know it was Prince William, who reportedly offered the olive branch reaching out to Harry and Meghan inviting them to greet the crowds at Windsor, a suggestion perhaps coming from the new king before such a critical week. DAISY MCANDREW, NBC NEW ROYAL COMMENTATOR: I firmly believe it was Charles who tried to metaphorically bang their heads together and say please, for me, for the future of the monarchy for your father, can you put on a brave face and go out and give us a sign of unity? HUNTER: And unity, at least for that brief hour, was seen and felt by the lucky thousands. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: That was really special, actually. I was really surprised all four of them were together. And yes, that`s quite emotional, I think, being a Brit seeing them, the two brothers side by side. As the heir apparent, his official state responsibilities now a world away from Harry`s new life and California. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: Growing up Princess Diana famously really wanted Harry and William to be equally important. Even though William`s destiny was very different, he was always going to be the monarch, she didn`t want Harry to feel less important, less significant. HUNTER: In a new tribute to granny, Harry says he`s forever grateful for my earliest childhood memories to meeting you for the first time as my commander-in-chief. But the brothers strike different notes. While Harry pledges to honor his father`s new role, William says he`ll be supporting my father the king in every way I can as the next in line. And now it`s William and Kate, the new Princess of Wales, Princess Diana`s former title, who are the most popular members of the Royal Family, stepping into the spotlight, shouldering the responsibility of modernizing this monarchy. (END VIDEOTAPE) HUNTER: Now, looking ahead, there are a number of opportunities where we might see the two brothers together again. What`s clear, though, is they don`t want it to distract from the critical week ahead for the Royal Family. Lester? HOLT: Molly, thank you. The Queen has been mourned well beyond Great Britain. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) KERRY SANDERS, NBC NEWS SENIOR NATIONAL CORRESPONDENT (voiceover): In former British colonies around the world, flags at half-staff including in India, once part of the sprawling British Empire. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: I remember her in such a way that she`s that`s like our mother`s figure. SANDERS: The Queen often visited Britain`s colonies and former colonies. Today, there are 14 Commonwealth realms where the king is still recognized as the head of state including here in Jamaica. Are you mourning the Queen`s death? CLIFF HUGHES, JAMAICA HISTORIAN: No. SANDERS: No. HUGHES: Because her passing is regrettable but she`s not that close to us for us to be mourning. [19:10:10] SANDERS: Jamaica historian Cliff Hughes says this country`s beautiful shores hold an ugly past, slavery. The enslaved forced to the West Indies by the Royal-African company. They harvested sugar known as green gold. FAE ELLINGTON, RESIDENT, KINGSTON, JAMAICA: It built England. It built the streets. It built the big businesses. SANDERS: That`s the value of sugar at the time. ELLINGTON: Yes. SANDERS: The New King, Charles III, now inherits that legacy. HUGHES: When slavery was finally abolished, those who were the enslavers were paid 20 million pounds, which was 40 percent of Britain`s annual budget. SANDERS: And how much were the slaves themselves who were now free given? HUGHES: Not one cent. SANDERS: Which is why reparations remained a hot topic. When the now-Prince and Princess of Wales visited Jamaica in March, there were protests and demand for an official apology. Some now hope that comes from the new King. (END VIDEOTAPE) SANDERS (on camera): Under the court system here which mirrors England`s, if there were an official apology, that could well open the door to reparations. Lester? HOLT: All right, Kerry Sanders tonight in Jamaica, thank you. We`ll turn now to another major story, the lightning advance by Ukraine`s military reclaiming more ground against Russian forces in the northeast as Russia retaliates by striking Ukraine`s power grid. Our Megan Fitzgerald is in Kyiv. (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) MEGAN FITZGERALD, NBC NEWS FOREIGN CORRESPONDENT (voiceover): In a fast and furious reaction, Russia launching missiles and Ukraine`s east, striking critical infrastructure plunging millions into the dark. The strike seen as retaliation as Ukraine sweeps through the Russian front line in a shocking advance. Ukraine now claims in the last 12 days, they`ve taken back 2300 square miles of Russian-held territory in the northeastern Kharkiv region. Ukraine putting out this video, an incredible scene as the Ukrainian flag is raised in a village east of Kharkiv, as many residents overcome with emotion thanking the Ukrainian soldiers for liberating them. Ukraine releasing images showing Russian artillery and tanks left behind, as they say Russian soldiers were forced to withdraw. Ukraine`s President Zelenskyy thanking his troops, saying the world is impressed and the enemy is panicking. UK`s ministry of defense describes the territory Ukraine says it took back as twice the size of London, though Russia still controls the south and the east. Russia`s President Putin not commenting on Ukraine`s counter- offensive so far. A spokesperson only saying the Russian military operation is ongoing and will achieve its objective. But the question tonight, is this a turning point in the war. (END VIDEOTAPE) FITZGERALD (on camera): And tonight, Ukraine is claiming that it`s not just Russian equipment they`ve captured, it`s also Russian soldiers, saying they have so many POWs they`re running out of room. Lester? HOLT: OK, Megan Fitzgerald in Ukraine, thank you. Back home now to the battle over the FBI search at Mar-a-Lago. Attorneys for former President Trump objecting to the candidates the Justice Department proposed to serve as special master to review the classified documents seized by the FBI . Mr. Trump`s team disputing the documents classified status and asking the judge to reject the DOJ -- the DOJ`s request to continue reviewing the files. In 60 seconds, parts of the West can`t catch a break. The threat of more extreme weather after dozens are rescued in mudslides and wildfires raged on. (COMMERCIAL BREAK) HOLT: Back now with the extreme weather in the West. Flood watches in effect after mudslides forced dozens of rescues on the heels of record heat. Here`s Miguel Almaguer. [19:15:07] (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) MIGUEL ALMAGUER, NBC NEWS NATIONAL CORRESPONDENT (voiceover): Tonight, a year of extremes in just a matter of days, historic heat fires, floods, and now mudslides. The volatile Western weather creating havoc for first responders and dangerous conditions for those suddenly in harm`s way. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: All these vehicles are stuck in about two feet of -- 20 mile an hour debris flow. ALMAGUER: Outside Los Angeles, firefighters rescued more than 50, including young families who suddenly became trapped and caked in debris as a mudslide covered a canyon road. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: It was terrifying. ALMAGUER: On the heels of record-shattering heat, the remnants of Tropical Storm Kay brought flash flooding that`s soaked the region. Downed trees, swamp neighborhoods, and sidewalk rescues. From floods to fires, there`s been little relief. Across the West, more than 90 large wildfires are burning in a region mired in drought. Some 800,000 acres scorched from active fires as crews battle to gain the upper hand. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: The flames are 300 feet in the air, the trees were exploding. ALMAGUER: With entire communities under evacuations, in recent days, four have been killed trying to escape the flames. And now, after this crash, three firefighting personnel nearly lost their lives also trying to battle them. Tonight, the West can`t catch a break from a sudden season of extremes. Miguel Almaguer, NBC news. (END VIDEOTAPE) HOLT: A spectacular rocket failure today for Blue Origin , a company owned by Jeff Bezos . It happened about a minute into the launch, flame scene shooting out of the rocket. Luckily, there were no people on board. The capsule was able to separate and parachute to Earth. This is the same type of rocket that sends paying customers to the edge of space but the capsule is different. Up next tonight, after Roe, abortion is rewriting November ballots. Ahead, one swing state`s looming battle in our series power of the vote. (COMMERCIAL BREAK) [19:20:00] HOLT: We`re back now with our series power of the vote. With less than two months until Election Day, in Michigan, voters will decide if abortion rights should be protected by the state constitution. Here`s Yamiche Alcindor. (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) YAMICHE ALCINDOR, NBC NEWS WASHINGTON CORRESPONDENT (voiceover): Lifelong Republican Jessica Leech was devastated when the Supreme Court overturned Roe v. Wade. JESSICA LEECH, LIFELONG REPUBLICAN: I cried for weeks. I cried for my daughter. I always considered myself pro-life. ALCINDOR: Now, she changed her mind and her party. Jessica got pregnant at 19 and visited an abortion clinic to weigh her options. She decided to have her son who`s now 17 and says being able to make that choice is something every woman deserves. What do you say to people who think your story is an example of why abortion shouldn`t be an option? LEECH: I would tell those people that until recently, it was always a hypothetical. I would beg them to understand that having these options paved the way for me to be a good mother. ALCINDOR: In Michigan, residents will vote on a ballot referendum in November that would enshrine abortion rights into the state constitution. GOV. GRETCHEN WHITMER (D-MI): You`re a doctor. ALCINDOR: Incumbent Democratic Governor Gretchen Whitmer is also up for reelection. What is at stake in this election and in the ballot referendum? WHITMER: Well, abortion and the right to be a full American citizen with agency of your body is on this ballot. ALCINDOR: Her views are also shaped by her experiences. WHITMER: In college, in the days after I was raped, it dawned on me. Oh, my God, I might be pregnant. And the only thing that gave me a little bit of relief is knowing that I could make a decision that was right for me if that happened. ALCINDOR: Her opponent, Republican Tudor Dixon, supports banning abortion with no exception for rape or incest. I wonder if you could just talk a bit more about your own views and talk to people who are worried about your views being too extreme. I have shared my own pro-life story. I lost a baby 18 weeks. When I lost the baby and the doctor said this baby probably died in the womb at 16 weeks, I held a beautiful baby girl. ALCINDOR: Dixon also does not believe abortion is a top issue for voters. DIXON: They`re concerned with how to get their kids back on track after they were kept out of school. And if you look at our crime rates in the past couple of years, it`s just continued to rise. And why our businesses are being crushed by the government? ALCINDOR: Both supporters and opponents of the referendum are mobilizing like anti-abortion rights activist Christen Polo, now working overtime after voters in Kansas recently voted to keep abortion protections in its state constitution. CHRISTEN POLO, ACTIVIST: I`m very concerned. Frankly, the policies that are being put forth in this abortion amendment here in Michigan are some of the most extremist policies we`ve seen in the entire country. ALCINDOR: Meantime, Jessica hopes sharing her story helps keep abortion legal in Michigan. Her son Cameron sent her a text on the day of our interview. Your life experiences, our relationship, after you decided to keep me and change your life around me, and now your perspective of life is what the world needs most. ALCINDOR: Yamiche Alcindor, NBC News, Michigan. (END VIDEOTAPE) HOLT: And up next, the tributes from everyday people honoring the Queen. (COMMERCIAL BREAK) [19:25:00] HOLT: Finally, beyond the formal tributes, the tokens people have left to honor the Queen, small gestures adding up to a powerful message. Here`s Kelly Cobiella. (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) KELLY COBIELLA, NBC NEWS FOREIGN CORRESPONDENT (voiceover): The ordinary, the extraordinary, messages and memories. Many shedding a tear for the Queen leaving a token. A small way just to say thank you for a life of service. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: She means a lot to all the people here and she`s done so much for everyone. So, we kind of need to honor her. COBIELLA: And a way to say goodbye, drawings cards, notes. Thank you for being the best Queen ever, one read. Another, with her beloved Corgi. Tributes for mourners around the world marking Queen Elizabeth`s extraordinary life. Katarina Mostova (PH) and her family fled the war in Ukraine and brought her country`s national flower, the sunflower, for the queen. Why did you come? UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: Because we want to make honor to Queen. This is so important for us. COBIELLA: Mountains of flowers and marmalade sandwiches, a nod to the Queen`s surprise skit with the children`s character Paddington Bear in June. Now, so many sandwiches and stuffed bears, they`re begging the public just to bring flowers. Members of the royal family are deeply touched. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: Have you seen the messages? WILLIAM, PRINCE OF WALES: Yes, amazing. It`s the little 7-year-olds and 11- year-olds messages get straight through every time. COBIELLA: Notes from children have only been alive for a fraction of the Queen`s long reign like this one: "Thank you for showing the world how strong a woman can be." Kelly Cobiella, NBC News, Edinburgh Scotland. (END VIDEOTAPE) HOLT: Messages from the heart. That`s NIGHTLY NEWS for this Monday. Thank you for watching, everyone. I`m Lester Holt. Please take care of yourself and each other. Good night. (COMMERCIAL BREAK) END Content and programming copyright 2022 NBCUniversal. ALL RIGHTS RESERVED. headline: The Cancer Survivor`s Journey To Starting A Family That Is Giving New Hope To Other Couples
story_text: SHEINELLE JONES: Back at 8:43 this morning on Your Health. One woman`s journey that`s giving hope to others facing breast cancer while also wanting to have children. CARSON DALY: NBC senior national correspondent Kate Snow joins us with that story. Kate, good morning. KATE SNOW, NBC SENIOR NATIONAL CORRESPONDENT: Hey. Good morning Carson. Good morning, guys. For many younger women diagnosed with cancer, the toxic treatment can take away their fertility. But new innovations and increased awareness have given some women the chance to preserve their fertility and build a family even after surviving cancer. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) SHELLY BATTISTA, CANCER SURVIVOR: Hi. SNOW: Which one is Nina? UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: This is Nina. SNOW: Nina? UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: Yes, she came first. SNOW: Hi, Nina. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: And then this is little Margot. SNOW (voice-over): These days, life is a bit different for Shelly and Robert Battista. They grew from a family of three to five. While the Chicago couples days are now filled with dirty diapers, crying and lots of laundry, they wouldn`t have it any other way. Three years ago, Shelly was diagnosed with an aggressive form of breast cancer and learn she has a genetic mutation that raises her risk for ovarian cancer too. (on camera): How frightening is all of that? S. BATTISTA: Yes, it was terrifying. You know, we had a six-month-old baby at home. We felt like we were just starting our life together and we get this shocking news. SNOW (voice-over): Shelly needed to start treatment immediately, but the couple had their heart set on a big family and the chemotherapy would destroy her fertility. S. BATTISTA: We were so blessed to have Emilia prior to this breast cancer diagnosis. But, you know, you still have dreams of having more children. SNOW (voice-over): Dr. Kara Goldman specializes in fertility preservation at Northwestern Medicine in Chicago. [08:45:04] KARA GOLDMAN, PHYSICIAN: Chemotherapy that is used in young patients with triple negative breast cancer is very toxic to the ovaries. This is a tremendous blow for a young woman who a day prior was healthy and had no medical diagnosis. JONES: But Dr. Goldman told the couple there was hope. Before starting chemotherapy, Shelly and Robert could create frozen embryos. GOLDMAN: We have to do it quickly. We started her fertility preservation journey two days later. She started medications and two weeks later, she had eight frozen embryos. SNOW (voice-over): Shelly had 12 rounds of chemotherapy, a double mastectomy and had her ovaries and fallopian tubes removed. A year after treatment, she was healthy enough to get pregnant even without ovaries. GOLDMAN: The ovaries and the uterus function very independently of each other. So in Shelly`s case, because she did not have ovaries producing hormones, we were able to provide her the hormones necessary for pregnancy. SNOW (voice-over): The first two trials were unsuccessful, they tried a third embryo. And eight days later, Dr. Goldman called them with the news Shelly was pregnant. S. BATTISTA: She called me herself, personally, we were both static and crying, and yelling. ROBERT BATTISTA, SHELLY`S HUSBAND: And this was just kind of like the cherry on top. It was awesome. We`re going to have another kid. Shelly`s healthy, like everything was just like behind us at that point. SNOW (voice-over): But the surprises weren`t over yet. At their first ultrasound, the technician saw something. S. BATTISTA: She was like, oh, there`s two of them. And I was like -- we both were kind of like two of what? Like -- she`s like, there`s two babies. SNOW: You didn`t implant two embryos. S. BATTISTA: We implanted one embryo and the embryo split. And so they are identical twins. SNOW (voice-over): The chance of that happening, just 1%. Nine months later, two healthy little girls were born., Margot and Nina, born on the two year anniversary of Shelly being declared cancer free. R. BATTISTA: I think it`s like the best celebration of Shelly`s cancer journey. It`s like you`ve beaten cancer and now here`s this extra, like love you get on top of it. S. BATTISTA: It`s loud, it`s tiring. We have lots of laughs, lots of cries, lots of laundry. It`s chaotic but it is -- that`s perfect. (END VIDEO CLIP) SNOW: It`s perfect. Having a baby after cancer treatment is becoming a lot more common thanks to better technology and awareness. Also important to note, guys, the Battistas live in one of just a handful of states that require insurance to cover fertility after cancer. Most states don`t do that, so they live in Chicago, they had an Illinois law. JONES: This is going to grab the attention of so many of voice because there are so many families who are dealing with this exact same challenge. MELVIN: By the way, while you`re here, folks, in addition to being our senior national correspondent, we got to talk about this exciting personal project that Kate Snow has taken on. It`s been on your bucket list for years. We`ve talked about this but I want folks to take a look. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) (MUSIC) MELVIN: You`re thinking all your colleagues, but you thinking also -- DALY: For a story? SOBOROFF: Why you`ve been keeping this from us is the real question. SNOW: I`m not, I`m not. So that was Nashville Tennessee. I`m in a vocal tracking booth there. You heard the backing band. I met with a whole bunch of great amazing musicians in Nashville through friends of friends. I`ve been a singer my whole life. Carson think it`s funny. JONES: Well because we didn`t know. DALY: I did not see this coming. SNOW: I know. Nobody -- MELVIN: But you`re putting out songs, like music. SNOW: I have three songs out now, so that was one of them that you just heard. SOBOROFF: Just wait till they turn the chairs for you on "The Voice", Kate. JONES: Kate, I love you. DALY: Are they all covers or do you write? SNOW: They all covers. DALY: OK. SNOW: So "Nothing Compares to You" is what you just heard, "Because the Night" and "Can`t Find My Way Home." DALY: Oh my God, amazing. SNOW: Three of my favorite songs. JONES: I love it, Kate. Did you just feel like you know what it`s time to - - SNOW: It was -- yes, total (inaudible) like why not? What am I waiting for? JONES: Absolutely. SNOW: And so, kind of made it happen. DALY: How can people hear the music? It`s all -- the three of them are up on any place you stream music, Spotify , YouTube -- SOBOROFF: That is amazing, just hearing that. And the range, I was going to say if range is a reporter, you got ranges of musicians. MELVIN: Right. JONES: I love it. Do it all, my friend. SNOW: You know what -- DALY: Do you have a stage name like Lady Snow or something? I mean, people just look up Kate Snow? SNOW: Just Kate Snow. DALY: OK. JONES: Kate Snow. That`s amazing. DALY: That`s awesome. SOBOROFF: Congratulation. MELVIN: So proud. SNOW: It`s stress relief too from this job. SOBOROFF: Yes. JONES: Again you can stream her new EP, how cool does that sound -- SOBOROFF: It does. JONES: -- wherever you get your music. MELVIN: Look at you. We gave you the City Music treatment there. SOBOROFF: Wow. MELVIN: Up next, he cannot sing but he can help us find some great travel deals. Spring break season is underway, Eastern is around the corner, our guy Mark Ellwood is here. story_text: (COMMERCIAL BREAK) [08:00:00] CRAIG MELVIN, NBC NEWS ANCHOR: It`s 8:00 on "TODAY." Coming up, bracing for a decision. All eyes on the grand jury in the criminal case against Donald Trump, as witnesses take the stand over allegations of hush money payments. The former president says he will be arrested tomorrow. GARRETT HAAKE, NBC NEWS SENIOR CAPITOL HILL CORRESPONDENT: Hey, Craig. Good morning. Now, Donald Trump made clear over the weekend, he believes this investigation is going to end with his arrest. He said it would come on Tuesday. Now, to be clear, there has been no formal word from the district attorney that any indictment is coming, but law enforcement officials here in New York City have been planning for that possibility and planning for the possibility that folks could listen to Mr. Trump`s call for protests if and when that happens. Now, while we wait for the legal fallout, the political fallout is already happening. headline: Clearing Up Some Common Nutrition Myths With The Registered Dietitian
story_text: SAVANNAH JONES: Welcome back this morning on Your Health. Common myths and maybe misguiding your diet decisions. Nora Minno is a registered dietician and she`s here to clear these things up once and for all. Nora, good morning to you. NORA MINNO, REGISTERED DIETICIAN: Good morning, Sheinelle. JONES: So we have five nutrition myths that we`re going to debunk. I should say there are three of us here because congratulations. MINNO: Yes, thank you. JONES: She was so worried as nutritionist people are going to be like, oh, she`s got little (inaudible). No, no, there`s a little baby in there. MINNO: Exactly. JONES: We are girl, we don`t know, OK. First things first, I should avoid all carbs. This is a big one. MINNO: Yes. JONES: I know so many people who just -- they feel like if they touch a carb, they explode. MINNO: I agree. And I have good news for all you carb lovers. I`m pretty sure as everybody body, right? Carbs are your friend. In fact, there are a really important part of a healthy balanced diet. They do a lot for us. They are our body`s preferred source of fuel, same with our brain. They help our digestion and they actually just make us feel good. JONES: So then, what are we doing wrong then? Because a lot of people, you know, I guess obviously probably shouldn`t have carbs before bed, but where are we going wrong? MINNO: Exactly. So really, when it comes to carbs, it is just about the quality of carbs that you`re picking and the quantity that you`re consuming. That`s really where a lot of people go wrong over consuming things like refined carbs, sweets, white breads, things like that. But if you focus on portions, choose more complex carbs. JONES: What`s a good carb? Give me a couple of example. MINNO: Fruits, vegetables, whole grains, oatmeal, things like that, you should be in the clear. JONES: All right. So myth number two, fresh produce is healthier than frozen or canned. What would you say? MINNO: No. This is not true at all. In fact, sometimes your frozen or canned options can be actually more nutritious. There was a study done that found that vegetables can lose 15% to 55% of their vitamin C by the time they`re picked, by the time they make it to your grocery shelf. So frozen, they typically flash freeze right on the spot. So you`re packing a lot more nutrients. And they`re actually a little bit better for your wallet too. JONES: I was just about to say there`s a cost benefit as well. MINNO: Exactly. Less food waste, oftentimes they are more budget friendly. And then you just have some good things on hand if you want to make a smoothie, a salad, things like that. JONES: Absolutely. OK, our next myth, this is a good one. Plant milk is healthier than dairy milk. What say ye? MINNO: All right. Well, this is not always the case. headline: The Today Show for February 20, 2023, NBC
story_text: (COMMERCIAL BREAK) [08:00:00] SHEINELLE JONES, NBC NEWS 3RD HOUR OF TODAY, CO-HOST: It is 8:00 on "TODAY." Coming up, surprise visit. Overnight, President Biden making history arriving in Ukraine. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) JOE BIDEN , U.S. PRESIDENT: I`m here to show our unwavering support for the nation`s independence, and sovereignty, and territorial integrity. (END VIDEO CLIP) JONES: A major sign of support from the U.S. as the war in Ukraine approaches its one-year anniversary. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) BIDEN: That`s how long we`re going to be with you, Mr. President, for as long as it takes. (END VIDEO CLIP) JONES: We`re live with the latest. Then, holiday sales. Hoping to save some money this long weekend. We have a look at all the best Presidents` Day deals, everything from furniture to appliances, electronics, and cars. Plus, the three questions you should ask yourself before making a purchase. And royal treatment. The Prince and Princess of Wales joining stars from around the world for the so-called British Oscars. We`re highlighting all the best moments including an emotional tribute to Queen Elizabeth. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) HELEN MIRREN, ACTRESS: Cinema at its best does what her majesty did effortlessly, bring us together and unite us in a story. (END VIDEO CLIP) JONES: So, what films took home the night`s biggest awards? All that and more. Today, Monday, February 20, 2023. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: Spending Presidents` Day. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: On the plaza. CROWD: From Fort Worth, Texas. CROWD: Murrysville (ph), Pennsylvania. CROWD: Huntsville, Alabama. CROWD: St. John, Indiana. CROWD: And New Lenox, Illinois. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: Celebrating milestone birthdays. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: My 30th. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: And my 60th. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: From Jacksonville, Florida. CROWD: Lea`s (ph) turning 18. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: Shout out to our NBC family. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: At KOMU 8 News. CROWD: In Columbia, Missouri. CROWD: Happy Presidents` Day. (END VIDEO CLIP) JONES: Welcome back to "TODAY." We certainly appreciate you being with us on this Monday morning. And take a look at all of these folks. We are happy to see this happy holiday crowd. This is on -- in our corner of the woods here at Rockefeller Plaza. TOM LLAMAS, NBC NEWS SENIOR NATIONAL CORRESPONDENT: Yes, they came from all over the country. We always love that. JONES: Uh-huh. LLAMAS: A lot of states represented. Savannah and Hoda, you know them, will be back tomorrow, of course, and it will be a big morning here in Studio 1A. JONES: That is right. Grammy winning superstar Pink will be here. She`s coming out with a new album and heading on tour. So, a lot to talk about. Plus, she`ll treat us to a live performance when she joins us for our 8:00, 9:00, and 10:00 hours. So, join us tomorrow. JACOB SOBOROFF, NBC NEWS CORRESPONDENT: I am not going anywhere. LLAMAS: Yes. JONES: Right SOBOROFF: I`m going to stick around for that. JONES: It`s going to be a party. LLAMAS: She always brings it. Like, live -- JONES: She does. LLAMAS: -- Pink live is always amazing. JONES: She does. And we`ll get back outside and say hi to all those folks coming up in just a bit. Meantime, it is a busy morning. So, let`s get to your news at 8:00. In an unprecedented show of support for Ukraine, President Biden took a high stakes trip to the war zone overnight. His surprise journey to Kyiv coming just days before the first anniversary of the Russian invasion. NBC`s Erin McLaughlin is in the Ukrainian capital with more on this historic visit. Erin, good morning. ERIN MCLAUGHLIN, NBC NEWS CORRESPONDENT: Good morning, Sheinelle. President Zelenskyy calling the visit historic, timely, and brave. The visit began here in the capital at the presidential palace. President Biden was greeted by President Zelenskyy and his wife, Olena. He signed a guest book and announced a $500 million military aid package and delivered this message. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) JOE BIDEN , U.S. PRESIDENT: One year later, Kyiv stands and Ukraine stands, democracy stands. America stands with you and the world stands with you. (END VIDEO CLIP) MCLAUGHLIN: From the palace, they made their way to St. Michael`s Cathedral. I watched as air raid sirens echoing in the distance. The two presidents walked out this way and paid tribute to the thousands of fallen Ukrainian soldiers in the memorial behind me. From there, President Biden made his way to the U.S. embassy where he met with staff before departing the capital. In Russia, this visit is being seen as a provocation. But here in Ukraine, it is being seen as a remarkable show of support and solidarity by America. Back to you. JONES: All right. Erin, thank you. LLAMAS: And as we just saw there, the president`s secret trip showing his unwavering support for Ukraine, even as some in NATO and in Congress are questioning the ongoing commitment. NBC`s Chief White House Correspondent and Weekend TODAY co-anchor Kristen Welker joins us now live from Poland where the president will be marking this week`s first anniversary of the war. Kristen, good morning. KRISTEN WELKER, NBC NEWS CHIEF WHITE HOUSE CORRESPONDENT AND "SATURDAY TODAY" ANCHOR: Hi, Tom. Good morning to you. That`s right. [08:05:00] This trip was so secret because of the dangers that it posed, that only a handful of the president`s inner staff was aware that he was actually traveling to Kyiv. And that keen message just adding to what Erin said, the president saying, we`re not leaving. But executing on that is going to be more challenging to keep the global community on board and Congress, with some Republicans, already saying they are not going to write a blank check to Ukraine. So, what happens now? Well, he travels here to Poland. He`s going to be meeting with the president of Poland. He will be meeting with leaders of the critical eastern flank and then he`s going to deliver his capstone address in the same location where he spoke in Warsaw when he visited when the war was just a month old. And I am told in talking to top officials, that part of his message is going to be a condemnation of Vladimir Putin building on what we heard from the vice president over the weekend, that Putin has committed crimes against humanity and should be held accountable. Now, this all comes amid new concerns about China, it`s believed that China is providing nonlethal aid to Russia. The secretary of state, over the weekend, saying that they believe China is considering providing lethal aid as well. The secretary of state warning that would be met with serious consequences, all as this war enters a pivotal new phase. Tom. LLAMAS: All right. Kristen Welker with a lot of new developments there. Kristen, thank you. SOBOROFF: Breaking overnight, North Korea fired two short-range ballistic missiles towards Japan today, it`s second weapons test in the last three days. The missiles landing in the waters off the west coast of Japan. The test prompting Tokyo to call for an emergency meeting of the United Nations Security Council . Over the weekend North Korea also launched an intercontinental ballistic missile, and in response, the U.S. military yesterday held bilateral air drills with South Korea and Japan. JONES: All right. We`ve covered the news. Now, are you ready for a "Morning Boost"? LLAMAS: Yes. SOBOROFF: Yes, please. JONES: All right. This is a good one. A young Australian basketball fan was in tears after watching his team, the Tasmanian Jackjumpers get knocked out of the playoffs during a game in New Zealand. While on his way back to the locker room the Australian captain noticed the heartbroken fan and knew that he had traveled a long way to come see the game. So, he walked over to comfort him and even gave him a pair of sneakers. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) UNIDENTIFIED MALE: How is that, mate? UNIDENTIFIED MALE: Amazing. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: Wow. CLINT STEINDL, TASMANIA JACKJUMPERS BASKETBALL TEAM CAPTAIN: As much as I try to put a smile on his face, he still had the tears. But maybe puts them up in his bedroom or something, gives him something to aspire to. And that`s what we`re trying to do in Tasian (ph), you know, I just try to help the little fella out. (END VIDEO CLIP) JONES: Oh, that`s sweet. A little classy move. Keeping in mind that the player has got to be hurting too from that season ending loss. Listen, there are fans young and old, and it hurts when you lose, you know. LLAMAS: Yes, that`s -- SOBOROFF: Shout out to the Jackjumpers. JONES: There you go. LLAMAS: Tasmanian Jackjumpers. I like those jerseys too. SOBOROFF: Nice. JONES: Learn something everything. LLAMAS: Those are pretty cool. All right. Coming up, the Prince and Princess of Wales rubbing elbows with the stars of Hollywood. We`re going to take you live to London for an inside look at the big night at the British version of the Oscars. JONES: But first, expert tips you need to hear to make the most of today`s holiday sales. We`ll get to that in a moment right after this. (COMMERCIAL BREAK) [08:10:00] JONES: Welcome back this morning on "TODAY`s Consumer". We are focusing on those Presidents` Day sales. LLAMAS: Yes, inflation is putting a strain on your budget, it could be a great day to find a few deals, but, of course, there are things you need to consider. JONES: Joining us now is CNBC`s Senior Personal Finance Correspondent Sharon Epperson. Sharon, good morning to you. SHARON EPPERSON, CNBC`S SENIOR PERSONAL FINANCE CORRESPONDENT: Good morning. JONES: All right. Before we get into it, you say, before we get to the deals, you have three questions you want people to ask themselves. EPPERSON: Very important questions to ask. JONES: OK. EPPERSON: First of all, do you need it? JONES: Fair. EPPERSON: Do you love it? And can you pay it off immediately? JONES: Fair enough. EPPERSON: And so, it`s not just can you afford it. Because you`re probably going to put it on a credit card. JONES: Yes. EPPERSON: You don`t want to carry that interest on the credit card. You want to pay that off immediately or that savings is really something you`re going to be paying for, for months and months in interest. JONES: So, can you pay it within the month before you get that bill? EPPERSON: Exactly. JONES: All right. Fair enough. LLAMAS: I feel that`s a good life lesson -- JONES: It is. LLAMAS: -- not just for Presidents` Day. JONES: It is. I know. That is good. LLAMAS: Speaking of Presidents` Day, talk about some of the deals. EPPERSON: Well, there are a lot of different deals. A lot of people look at mattresses for Presidents` Day, furniture, maybe electronics. You may think about home appliances, large ones or little gadgets for your kitchen. LLAMAS: Uh-huh. EPPERSON: Maybe even a new car. So, there are a lot of different deals out there. I think I seem to be getting messages all the time about this deal or that deal for Presidents` Day doesn`t necessarily mean it`s something that I need. JONES: Right, right. EPPERSON: So, I kind of delete that message. LLAMAS: OK. All right. JONES: So, you were saying -- what about like kitchen or -- the kitchen appliances, are we talking like coffee pots or like refrigerators, like big ticket items? EPPERSON: There are some big ticket items too that are -- that you can get. One of the things to keep in mind when you`re talking about appliances, whether they`re large or small, as you`re often sold a or asked to purchase a warranty, an extended warranty -- JONES: OK. EPPERSON: -- or sometime service agreement. JONES: OK. EPPERSON: Important thing to check out there is to make sure that you actually really need that because it`s not going to be lasting that long. And that you could use that money, perhaps, to put into a savings account to buy a new one. What`s the replacement cost of that? JONES: That`s right. EPPERSON: Do you need to buy the extended warranty or the service agreement. JONES: The service agreement. LLAMAS: All right. Let`s dig a little deeper here. I know a family shopping around for a TV. Is it -- are electronics good right now? Is it a day to shop for electronics? EPPERSON: Well, there are large electronics. Some people want TVs, some people want a laptop or maybe something else for their, you know, sound system or something like that. Again, the important thing to think about is, one, not carrying the credit card debt if you`re going to put it on the card. But also, think about how much that energy is costing on your home. I`m thinking about everything I have on in my house right now when I`m not there. Why do I have my TV on -- LLAMAS: Right. EPPERSON: -- or my laptop on -- JONES: The energy vampire. EPPERSON: The energy vampires. The energy vampires can cost $250 a year in your house if they`re sucking energy -- LLAMAS: Oh. EPPERSON: -- because you don`t use it. So, think about that. As you`re thinking about what to purchase, keep in mind that maybe you don`t need that extra TV or if you get it, don`t have it on all the time. JONES: That`s fair. LLAMAS: OK. That`s good to know. JONES: But if you`re looking for a car, is now the time? A new car. EPPERSON: Well, there are going to be deals out there for new cars. Inventory is not tremendous, so there are going to be special deals for certain models. But again, the thing to think about is how are you going to pay for this car? And shopping around to get the best loan is very important. You`re going to see perhaps six percent or more for a five-year car loan on average. You could go to a credit union and get far less than maybe you pay through the dealer in terms of the loan or even a bank. So, make sure you shop around for a car loan and look at credit unions for a good place to get that loan. LLAMAS: Real quick on that before we go, should you call first or just go on the website? What`s the best when you`re dealing with credit unions or the banks? EPPERSON: Well, I think it`s great to go on websites to kind of consolidate all of the different -- give you all the options -- LLAMAS: Yes. EPPERSON: -- to look at. And then I absolutely think you should be calling or contacting the financial institution directly. LLAMAS: All right. JONES: That`s good advice. Thank you, Sharon. LLAMAS: Yes. EPPERSON: Absolutely. JONES: Happy, I guess, shopping. I didn`t -- expect to say, I guess -- LLAMAS: Presidents` Day. JONES: Yes, Presidents` Day shopping. But you have to be smart about it. EPPERSON: Smart. Smart shopping. JONES: Exactly. For more on the holiday sales, be sure to check out today.com/shop. Now, let`s head over to Dylan for the weather. DYLAN DREYER, NBC NEWS 3RD HOUR OF TODAY CO-HOST AND METEOROLOGIST: Good morning again, everyone. We do have some pretty decent weather for today, especially across the southeast where temperatures will be well above average. We do have a little bit of light rain falling through Kentucky and into Tennessee. And little light snow about to move through Central Minnesota through Minneapolis and Saint Paul, Billings. Also seeing some of that light snow too. [08:15:00] Now, there`s a bigger storm system that`s going to make its way across the country. It`s just bringing rain to the coast of Washington State right now but that will eventually turn into a big snow maker for the Rockies, also, across the Upper Midwest by the middle of the week. So, enjoy what`s out there right now. 50s and 60s up into the Carolinas, that`s above average for this time of year. 80s down through Texas. 80s into Florida too. And we are looking for temperatures to get well up into the 90s which could break all-time record high temperatures for the month of February in Florida, especially Wednesday and Thursday. So, this cold front is going to cool things off a little bit for the northeast. Again, we`ll watch that snow system -- the stormy system begins to move eastward as we go through the middle of the week. And it also looks nice in the southwest, a bit breezy, temperatures though with that sunshine in the 60s and 70s. That`s a look at the weather across the country. Now, here`s a peek out your window. (LOCAL NEWS) DREYER: And that is your latest forecast. JONES: All right. Thank you, Dylan. Now, Jacob, you`re covering "POP Start" for Carson today? SOBOROFF: Sure am. Ladies and gentlemen, here is your "POP Start." First up, "Back to the Future". JONES: What? LLAMAS: What? SOBOROFF: Believe it or not, it`s been almost four decades since Doc Brown gave us this lesson in time travel. Watch. DREYER: Oh, that`s nice. SOBOROFF: How cool is this? Over the weekend, you see Christopher Lloyd, Michael J. Fox, Lea Thompson, Tom Wilson. Everybody reunited for a fan expo in Portland, Oregon. LLAMAS: Oh, OK. SOBOROFF: And the iconic former castmates shared a few sweet snaps -- JONES: That`s awesome -- SOBOROFF: -- from behind the scenes. Michael J. Fox said of this whole thing, some of my favorite people. JONES: I love that. SOBOROFF: One of the best. DREYER: I love it. SOBOROFF: One of the best. LLAMAS: One of the best. SOBOROFF: One of the best. LLAMAS: Yes. SOBOROFF: Yes, I miss the ride at Universal Studios. Bring it back, guys, bring it back. Next up, Rebel Wilson. Exciting announcement from the "Pitch Perfect" star. She is engaged. On Sunday, Wilson shared the happy news on social media posting this picture alongside fiance Ramona Agruma. story_text: (COMMERCIAL BREAK) [08:00:00] SHEINELLE JONES, NBC NEWS 3RD HOUR OF TODAY, CO-HOST: It is 8:00 on "TODAY." Coming up, surprise visit. Overnight, President Biden making history arriving in Ukraine. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) JOE BIDEN , U.S. PRESIDENT: I`m here to show our unwavering support for the nation`s independence, and sovereignty, and territorial integrity. (END VIDEO CLIP) JONES: A major sign of support from the U.S. as the war in Ukraine approaches its one-year anniversary. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) BIDEN: That`s how long we`re going to be with you, Mr. President, for as long as it takes. (END VIDEO CLIP) JONES: We`re live with the latest. Then, holiday sales. Hoping to save some money this long weekend. We have a look at all the best Presidents` Day deals, everything from furniture to appliances, electronics, and cars. Plus, the three questions you should ask yourself before making a purchase. And royal treatment. The Prince and Princess of Wales joining stars from around the world for the so-called British Oscars. We`re highlighting all the best moments including an emotional tribute to Queen Elizabeth. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) HELEN MIRREN, ACTRESS: Cinema at its best does what her majesty did effortlessly, bring us together and unite us in a story. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: On the plaza. CROWD: From Fort Worth, Texas. CROWD: Murrysville (ph), Pennsylvania. CROWD: Huntsville, Alabama. CROWD: St. John, Indiana. CROWD: And New Lenox, Illinois. We certainly appreciate you being with us on this Monday morning. And take a look at all of these folks. We are happy to see this happy holiday crowd. This is on -- in our corner of the woods here at Rockefeller Plaza. TOM LLAMAS, NBC NEWS SENIOR NATIONAL CORRESPONDENT: Yes, they came from all over the country. We always love that. JONES: Uh-huh. LLAMAS: A lot of states represented. Savannah and Hoda, you know them, will be back tomorrow, of course, and it will be a big morning here in Studio 1A. JONES: That is right. JONES: Right SOBOROFF: I`m going to stick around for that. JONES: It`s going to be a party. LLAMAS: She always brings it. Like, live -- JONES: She does. LLAMAS: -- Pink live is always amazing. JONES: She does. And we`ll get back outside and say hi to all those folks coming up in just a bit. Meantime, it is a busy morning. So, let`s get to your news at 8:00. In an unprecedented show of support for Ukraine, President Biden took a high stakes trip to the war zone overnight. His surprise journey to Kyiv coming just days before the first anniversary of the Russian invasion. NBC`s Erin McLaughlin is in the Ukrainian capital with more on this historic visit. Erin, good morning. ERIN MCLAUGHLIN, NBC NEWS CORRESPONDENT: Good morning, Sheinelle. President Zelenskyy calling the visit historic, timely, and brave. The visit began here in the capital at the presidential palace. President Biden was greeted by President Zelenskyy and his wife, Olena. He signed a guest book and announced a $500 million military aid package and delivered this message. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) JOE BIDEN , U.S. PRESIDENT: One year later, Kyiv stands and Ukraine stands, democracy stands. America stands with you and the world stands with you. (END VIDEO CLIP) MCLAUGHLIN: From the palace, they made their way to St. Michael`s Cathedral. I watched as air raid sirens echoing in the distance. The two presidents walked out this way and paid tribute to the thousands of fallen Ukrainian soldiers in the memorial behind me. From there, President Biden made his way to the U.S. embassy where he met with staff before departing the capital. In Russia, this visit is being seen as a provocation. But here in Ukraine, it is being seen as a remarkable show of support and solidarity by America. Back to you. JONES: All right. Erin, thank you. LLAMAS: And as we just saw there, the president`s secret trip showing his unwavering support for Ukraine, even as some in NATO and in Congress are questioning the ongoing commitment. NBC`s Chief White House Correspondent and Weekend TODAY co-anchor Kristen Welker joins us now live from Poland where the president will be marking this week`s first anniversary of the war. Kristen, good morning. KRISTEN WELKER, NBC NEWS CHIEF WHITE HOUSE CORRESPONDENT AND "SATURDAY TODAY" ANCHOR: Hi, Tom. Good morning to you. That`s right. [08:05:00] This trip was so secret because of the dangers that it posed, that only a handful of the president`s inner staff was aware that he was actually traveling to Kyiv. And that keen message just adding to what Erin said, the president saying, we`re not leaving. But executing on that is going to be more challenging to keep the global community on board and Congress, with some Republicans, already saying they are not going to write a blank check to Ukraine. So, what happens now? Well, he travels here to Poland. He`s going to be meeting with the president of Poland. He will be meeting with leaders of the critical eastern flank and then he`s going to deliver his capstone address in the same location where he spoke in Warsaw when he visited when the war was just a month old. And I am told in talking to top officials, that part of his message is going to be a condemnation of Vladimir Putin building on what we heard from the vice president over the weekend, that Putin has committed crimes against humanity and should be held accountable. Now, this all comes amid new concerns about China, it`s believed that China is providing nonlethal aid to Russia. The secretary of state, over the weekend, saying that they believe China is considering providing lethal aid as well. The secretary of state warning that would be met with serious consequences, all as this war enters a pivotal new phase. Tom. LLAMAS: All right. Kristen Welker with a lot of new developments there. Kristen, thank you. SOBOROFF: Breaking overnight, North Korea fired two short-range ballistic missiles towards Japan today, it`s second weapons test in the last three days. The missiles landing in the waters off the west coast of Japan. The test prompting Tokyo to call for an emergency meeting of the United Nations Security Council . Over the weekend North Korea also launched an intercontinental ballistic missile, and in response, the U.S. military yesterday held bilateral air drills with South Korea and Japan. JONES: All right. We`ve covered the news. Now, are you ready for a "Morning Boost"? LLAMAS: Yes. SOBOROFF: Yes, please. JONES: All right. This is a good one. (END VIDEO CLIP) JONES: Oh, that`s sweet. A little classy move. Keeping in mind that the player has got to be hurting too from that season ending loss. I like those jerseys too. SOBOROFF: Nice. JONES: Learn something everything. LLAMAS: Those are pretty cool. All right. JONES: So, can you pay it within the month before you get that bill? EPPERSON: Exactly. JONES: All right. Fair enough. LLAMAS: I feel that`s a good life lesson -- JONES: It is. LLAMAS: -- not just for Presidents` Day. JONES: It is. I know. That is good. LLAMAS: Speaking of Presidents` Day, talk about some of the deals. EPPERSON: Well, there are a lot of different deals. EPPERSON: Maybe even a new car. So, there are a lot of different deals out there. EPPERSON: So, I kind of delete that message. LLAMAS: OK. All right. JONES: So, you were saying -- what about like kitchen or -- the kitchen appliances, are we talking like coffee pots or like refrigerators, like big ticket items? EPPERSON: There are some big ticket items too that are -- that you can get. EPPERSON: -- or sometime service agreement. JONES: OK. EPPERSON: Important thing to check out there is to make sure that you actually really need that because it`s not going to be lasting that long. And that you could use that money, perhaps, to put into a savings account to buy a new one. What`s the replacement cost of that? JONES: That`s right. EPPERSON: Do you need to buy the extended warranty or the service agreement. JONES: The service agreement. LLAMAS: All right. Let`s dig a little deeper here. I know a family shopping around for a TV. Again, the important thing to think about is, one, not carrying the credit card debt if you`re going to put it on the card. But also, think about how much that energy is costing on your home. EPPERSON: Well, I think it`s great to go on websites to kind of consolidate all of the different -- give you all the options -- LLAMAS: Yes. EPPERSON: -- to look at. And then I absolutely think you should be calling or contacting the financial institution directly. LLAMAS: All right. JONES: That`s good advice. Thank you, Sharon. LLAMAS: Yes. EPPERSON: Absolutely. JONES: Happy, I guess, shopping. I didn`t -- expect to say, I guess -- LLAMAS: Presidents` Day. JONES: Yes, Presidents` Day shopping. But you have to be smart about it. EPPERSON: Smart. FRYER: First of all, remember, the Titanic went down in 1912. It took decades to find. It wasn`t until 1985 that a crew was able to find it, more than 12,000 feet below the surface. WOLFELD: It`s a topical solution or a foam. They also have now oral Minoxidil that is a prescription pill. That -- the oral is off-label but it may help. WOLFELD: And it uses were blood and the growth factors from that and it can really help to thicken your hair. DREYER: Does it hurt? DR. WOLFELD: It`s slightly uncomfortable -- DREYER: OK. DR. headline: On This 50th Anniversary Weekend Of The Roe Versus Wade Decision That Was Overturned Last Year
story_text: [07:00:18] JOE FRYER, NBC NEWS ANCHOR: Good morning and thanks for starting your weekend with us and it might be a good one to stay inside with another big storm impacting much of the country. KRISTEN WELKER, NBC NEWS ANCHOR: And another one is close behind. It`s January 21st. This is TODAY. Severe weather watch. Millions in the south preparing for a heavy dose of rain today with the potential of flash floods before the same storm heads up the East Coast. Threatening to bring up to a half a foot of snow in the Northeast. We`ll have the full forecast. Battle Cry. On this 50th anniversary weekend of the Roe versus Wade decision that was overturned last year, tens of thousands take to the streets of the nation`s capital as part of the March for Life rally. Where does the abortion fight go from here? Record surge. The government reporting the number of illegal border crossings at its highest level ever since President Biden took office. What can officials do to slow down the influx? Caught on camera. Police take down. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: Drop it! Drop it! WELKER: Harrowing moments inside an Indiana Wal-Mart captured on police bodycam after a former employee opened fire. This morning, the woman police are credited with helping to stop the bloodshed from getting worse. All that, plus football frenzy. Fans from coast to coast getting ready for this weekend`s NFL playoffs divisional round. Eight teams facing off including that highly anticipated rematch between the Buffalo Bills and Cincinnati Bengals . It all kicks off today, Saturday January 21st, 2023. ANNOUNCER: From NBC News, this is TODAY with Peter Alexander and Kristen Welker. WELKER: Welcome to TODAY and thank you so much for joining us on this Saturday morning. Peter is enjoying the morning off. We`ve got Joe Fryer here. And Joe, you are here for a big weekend in softball, a big weekend for my beloved Eagles taking on the Giants. FRYER: We know what you`re going to be e doing tonight. We definitely know who you`re going to be cheering for. WELKER: Fly Eagle fly. I got the whole family in town. We are ready. FRYER: I know you are and I might be jumping on your bandwagon because the Giants beat my Vikings last week and I`m still bitter. WELKER: Yes, you know where your allegiances are. FRYER: Exactly. WELKER: I like that. All right. Good. FRYER: Exactly. We`re going to talk football and a little bit. We`re going to be begin though by covering several developing stories this morning. That includes the marches planned this weekend for activists on both sides of the abortion rights debate. We`re going to hear what anti-abortion rights protesters are hoping for next today after that big March for Life rally here in D.C. WELKER: And we`ll also tell you about tough times for the tech industry. Google `s parent company announcing on Friday at slashing 12,000 jobs. They`re joining other companies like Microsoft , Amazon and Meta making mass layoffs. FRYER: But let`s begin this morning with our top story. The weather as the south prepares for intense rain today and the Northeast gets ready for a round of snow that could bring up to six inches. WELKER: Some area saw a preview of that on Friday for the very latest on all of it. Let`s bring in Somara Theodore. Somara, you`ve been tracking this. What should folks be bracing for? (LOCAL NEWS) [07:05:16] WELKER: Somara, thanks. Maybe a good weekend to stay indoors for a lot of people. We`ll get the rest of your forecast in just a few minutes. FRYER: This weekend marks the 50th anniversary of the Supreme Court`s decision on Roe v. Wade. And a half century later the debate over abortion rights still looms large, especially after the Dobbs decision last year overturning Roe. On Friday the March for life took place just one of several marches this weekend on both sides of the issue. NBC`s Marissa Parra was at the march and joins us with more. Marissa, good morning to you. WELKER: Good morning. MARISSA PARRA, NBC NEWS CORRESPONDENT: Joe and Kristen, good morning to you. Another busy day in D.C. as usual, right? WELKER: Yes. PARRA: Well crowds for the march we`re in the tens of thousands. And we know that the march was originally started to protest Roe versus Wade. So, there was a big celebratory mood in this new post Roe era, right? This is what they`ve been fighting for. But activists on both sides of the abortion debate are really galvanized in different ways, especially as we get closer to 2024. (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) PARRA (voice over): This morning, the battle over abortion access far from over. Roughly seven months after Roe v. Wade was overturned, the nation`s capital seeing the nation`s first march for life in a post Roe world. REP. STEVE SCALISE (R-LA): And today, we celebrate Roe is gone. It`s important to keep your focus on what the mission is. But every step of the way. It`s also critical that we celebrate victories along the way. PARRA: Changing the route to reflect a change country, stopping in front of both the Supreme Court and the Capitol. A symbolic nod to the role they both have and continue to play abortion law. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: It`s up to the states now so we need to raise awareness and each of the states. PARRA: Counter protesters reading their own fight to win back lost ground. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: That is why I`m here. It is to show that we will not let America be bullied out of the right to abortion. PARRA: The path to a full nationwide victory for either side an uphill battle. It`s been 50 years since Roe v. Wade was first signed into law. But in the months since its reversal last summer, almost two dozen states have either banned abortion or they`re close to it, with several legislative sessions actively debating what their laws will be on a state level. This says federal action fails to move forward. Senator Lindsey Graham`s federal abortion ban proposal failed last fall and the Biden administration`s hopes of a federal right to choose. KARINE JEAN-PIERRE , WHITE HOUSE PRESS SECRETARY: We need to codify Roe. PARRA: Unlikely and a Republican-controlled House. And with new FDA guidance making abortion bills more accessible over the counter, a new abortion battleground is headed to the pharmacy. (END VIDEOTAPE) PARRA: Now that new FDA guidance was a small victory for abortion rights activists and we know tomorrow is the 50th anniversary of that original decision. So, there are bigger than Roe pro-choice marches scheduled across the country. Joe and Kristen? FRYER: All right. Kristen -- Marissa Parra, thank you so much. Appreciate it. WELKER: Great to see you, Marissa. Really appreciate it. Well, just one day after the Supreme Court announced it couldn`t find who was behind the leak of that draft opinion of the decision to overturn Roe v. Wade. Former President Trump is calling on the journalists who revealed the leak to be jailed. And this morning the Biden administration is fighting back. NBC`s Monica Alba is tracking all of it from the White House. Monica, good morning to you. MONICA ALBA, NBC NEWS WHITE HOUSE CORRESPONDENT: Kristen, good morning. After an eight-month investigation that leaks still could not be pinpointed with former President Trump pushing stricter measures to root out the leaker. The probe led by the courts chief security officer determined hackers were likely not responsible. after interviewing 97 employees. The search found that 82 had access to digital or hard copies of the draft. But now we`re learning more about who else was questioned in the matter. The court investigator revealing Friday she spoke with each of the nine justices several on multiple occasions and all cooperated in the process. Every credible lead was explored and none of them implicated the justices or their spouses according to the court. And soon after the 20-page report came out that couldn`t identify the leak, the former president called for the reporters who broke the news to be arrested, along with possibly their editor and publisher saying they should be put in jail "until the answer is given." Within hours, the White House released a statement defending freedom of the press saying it`s the responsibility of all leaders to protect First Amendment rights. Kristen? WELKER: Yes. Just remarkable that that investigation could not determine who was behind the leak. Monica, another big headline you are tracking we`re also in the midst of this debt ceiling standoff between the White House and Republicans but we`re hearing that the President will meet with House Speaker Kevin McCarthy to discuss a path forward. What are you hearing? ALBA: That`s right, Kristen. While speaker McCarthy did accept President Biden`s offer to meet soon, no date has been set yet by the White House. But a contentious back and forth Friday about the debt ceiling show just how difficult resolving this issue may be. [07:10:07] House Republicans don`t want to increase America`s ability to borrow without promises of future spending cuts. While the President says there`s no room for negotiation when the stakes are so high. Warning of unprecedented financial calamity if the U.S. doesn`t meet its credit obligations for the first time in history. Experts say it could even lead to a recession or stock market crash if it happens, as the treasury secretary is already using extraordinary measures to keep paying the nation`s bills effectively buying time by shifting money around but that will only last until June. headline: On This 50th Anniversary Weekend Of The Roe Versus Wade Decision That Was Overturned Last Year
story_text: [07:00:18] JOE FRYER, NBC NEWS ANCHOR: Good morning and thanks for starting your weekend with us and it might be a good one to stay inside with another big storm impacting much of the country. KRISTEN WELKER, NBC NEWS ANCHOR: And another one is close behind. It`s January 21st. This is TODAY. Severe weather watch. Millions in the south preparing for a heavy dose of rain today with the potential of flash floods before the same storm heads up the East Coast. Threatening to bring up to a half a foot of snow in the Northeast. We`ll have the full forecast. Battle Cry. On this 50th anniversary weekend of the Roe versus Wade decision that was overturned last year, tens of thousands take to the streets of the nation`s capital as part of the March for Life rally. Where does the abortion fight go from here? Record surge. The government reporting the number of illegal border crossings at its highest level ever since President Biden took office. What can officials do to slow down the influx? Caught on camera. Police take down. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: Drop it! Drop it! WELKER: Harrowing moments inside an Indiana Wal-Mart captured on police bodycam after a former employee opened fire. This morning, the woman police are credited with helping to stop the bloodshed from getting worse. All that, plus football frenzy. Fans from coast to coast getting ready for this weekend`s NFL playoffs divisional round. Eight teams facing off including that highly anticipated rematch between the Buffalo Bills and Cincinnati Bengals . It all kicks off today, Saturday January 21st, 2023. ANNOUNCER: From NBC News, this is TODAY with Peter Alexander and Kristen Welker. WELKER: Welcome to TODAY and thank you so much for joining us on this Saturday morning. Peter is enjoying the morning off. We`ve got Joe Fryer here. And Joe, you are here for a big weekend in softball, a big weekend for my beloved Eagles taking on the Giants. FRYER: We know what you`re going to be e doing tonight. We definitely know who you`re going to be cheering for. WELKER: Fly Eagle fly. I got the whole family in town. We are ready. FRYER: I know you are and I might be jumping on your bandwagon because the Giants beat my Vikings last week and I`m still bitter. WELKER: Yes, you know where your allegiances are. FRYER: Exactly. WELKER: I like that. All right. Good. FRYER: Exactly. We`re going to talk football and a little bit. We`re going to be begin though by covering several developing stories this morning. That includes the marches planned this weekend for activists on both sides of the abortion rights debate. We`re going to hear what anti-abortion rights protesters are hoping for next today after that big March for Life rally here in D.C. WELKER: And we`ll also tell you about tough times for the tech industry. Google `s parent company announcing on Friday at slashing 12,000 jobs. They`re joining other companies like Microsoft , Amazon and Meta making mass layoffs. FRYER: But let`s begin this morning with our top story. The weather as the south prepares for intense rain today and the Northeast gets ready for a round of snow that could bring up to six inches. WELKER: Some area saw a preview of that on Friday for the very latest on all of it. Let`s bring in Somara Theodore. Somara, you`ve been tracking this. What should folks be bracing for? (LOCAL NEWS) [07:05:16] WELKER: Somara, thanks. Maybe a good weekend to stay indoors for a lot of people. We`ll get the rest of your forecast in just a few minutes. FRYER: This weekend marks the 50th anniversary of the Supreme Court`s decision on Roe v. Wade. And a half century later the debate over abortion rights still looms large, especially after the Dobbs decision last year overturning Roe. On Friday the March for life took place just one of several marches this weekend on both sides of the issue. NBC`s Marissa Parra was at the march and joins us with more. Marissa, good morning to you. WELKER: Good morning. MARISSA PARRA, NBC NEWS CORRESPONDENT: Joe and Kristen, good morning to you. Another busy day in D.C. as usual, right? WELKER: Yes. PARRA: Well crowds for the march we`re in the tens of thousands. And we know that the march was originally started to protest Roe versus Wade. So, there was a big celebratory mood in this new post Roe era, right? This is what they`ve been fighting for. But activists on both sides of the abortion debate are really galvanized in different ways, especially as we get closer to 2024. (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) PARRA (voice over): This morning, the battle over abortion access far from over. Roughly seven months after Roe v. Wade was overturned, the nation`s capital seeing the nation`s first march for life in a post Roe world. REP. STEVE SCALISE (R-LA): And today, we celebrate Roe is gone. It`s important to keep your focus on what the mission is. But every step of the way. It`s also critical that we celebrate victories along the way. PARRA: Changing the route to reflect a change country, stopping in front of both the Supreme Court and the Capitol. A symbolic nod to the role they both have and continue to play abortion law. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: It`s up to the states now so we need to raise awareness and each of the states. PARRA: Counter protesters reading their own fight to win back lost ground. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: That is why I`m here. It is to show that we will not let America be bullied out of the right to abortion. PARRA: The path to a full nationwide victory for either side an uphill battle. It`s been 50 years since Roe v. Wade was first signed into law. But in the months since its reversal last summer, almost two dozen states have either banned abortion or they`re close to it, with several legislative sessions actively debating what their laws will be on a state level. This says federal action fails to move forward. Senator Lindsey Graham`s federal abortion ban proposal failed last fall and the Biden administration`s hopes of a federal right to choose. KARINE JEAN-PIERRE , WHITE HOUSE PRESS SECRETARY: We need to codify Roe. PARRA: Unlikely and a Republican-controlled House. And with new FDA guidance making abortion bills more accessible over the counter, a new abortion battleground is headed to the pharmacy. (END VIDEOTAPE) PARRA: Now that new FDA guidance was a small victory for abortion rights activists and we know tomorrow is the 50th anniversary of that original decision. So, there are bigger than Roe pro-choice marches scheduled across the country. Joe and Kristen? FRYER: All right. Kristen -- Marissa Parra, thank you so much. Appreciate it. WELKER: Great to see you, Marissa. Really appreciate it. Well, just one day after the Supreme Court announced it couldn`t find who was behind the leak of that draft opinion of the decision to overturn Roe v. Wade. Former President Trump is calling on the journalists who revealed the leak to be jailed. And this morning the Biden administration is fighting back. NBC`s Monica Alba is tracking all of it from the White House. Monica, good morning to you. MONICA ALBA, NBC NEWS WHITE HOUSE CORRESPONDENT: Kristen, good morning. After an eight-month investigation that leaks still could not be pinpointed with former President Trump pushing stricter measures to root out the leaker. The probe led by the courts chief security officer determined hackers were likely not responsible. after interviewing 97 employees. The search found that 82 had access to digital or hard copies of the draft. But now we`re learning more about who else was questioned in the matter. The court investigator revealing Friday she spoke with each of the nine justices several on multiple occasions and all cooperated in the process. Every credible lead was explored and none of them implicated the justices or their spouses according to the court. And soon after the 20-page report came out that couldn`t identify the leak, the former president called for the reporters who broke the news to be arrested, along with possibly their editor and publisher saying they should be put in jail "until the answer is given." Within hours, the White House released a statement defending freedom of the press saying it`s the responsibility of all leaders to protect First Amendment rights. Kristen? WELKER: Yes. Just remarkable that that investigation could not determine who was behind the leak. Monica, another big headline you are tracking we`re also in the midst of this debt ceiling standoff between the White House and Republicans but we`re hearing that the President will meet with House Speaker Kevin McCarthy to discuss a path forward. What are you hearing? ALBA: That`s right, Kristen. While speaker McCarthy did accept President Biden`s offer to meet soon, no date has been set yet by the White House. But a contentious back and forth Friday about the debt ceiling show just how difficult resolving this issue may be. [07:10:07] House Republicans don`t want to increase America`s ability to borrow without promises of future spending cuts. While the President says there`s no room for negotiation when the stakes are so high. Warning of unprecedented financial calamity if the U.S. doesn`t meet its credit obligations for the first time in history. Experts say it could even lead to a recession or stock market crash if it happens, as the treasury secretary is already using extraordinary measures to keep paying the nation`s bills effectively buying time by shifting money around but that will only last until June. Kristen? WELKER: A major test and showdown for all of Washington. Monica Alba at the White House. Thank you, Monica.
