headline: TODAY WITH HODA & JENNA for Dec 26, 2022, NBC
story_text: (COMMERCIAL BREAK) [10:00:17] HODA KOTB, NBC NEWS ANCHOR (voiceover): Today, get ready to be inspired. Donna shows up at the door of a beloved neighbor and gives him the ultimate sweet surprise. Plus, writer and poet Yung Pueblo. How his millions of followers are learning and healing from his every word. And the breast cancer survivor whose personal journey is touching and saving the lives of countless women. JENNA BUSH HAGER, NBC NEWS ANCHOR (voiceover): It`s TODAY WITH HODA -- KOTB: -- & JENNA. It all starts right now. HAGER: It all starts right now. KOTB (on camera): Hey, guys, happy day after Christmas. It`s Monday, December 26th. We hope that you all had a very merry one and a happy one. All the wrapping paper the bows and all that stuff tucked away. HAGER (on camera): Waking up with family still in the house. It`s -- what were they called this day in the U.K.? Boxing Day? KOTB: Boxing Day? They do? HAGER: Yes. I`m not sure why. KOTB: Oh, just like to decorative -- HAGER: But let`s celebrate Boxing Day. Why not? KOTB: OK. I like that. HAGER: And we`ve got an amazing show today that`s going to leave you feeling inspired and feeling good. Just as this day should. KOTB: Oh my God, this is -- this is our kind of show. HAGER: It sure is. KOTB: Because we love -- loves -- love things that feel like that. HAGER: Wait, in fact, can you just talk about the way you start your day? And the way you end your day? Because Henry is reading a book called Think Like A Monk by Jay Shetty. KOTB: Jay Shetty, yes. HAGER: And he says a lot of people think about the morning routine, but people forget about the end. KOTB: You know what`s funny? The morning routine I packed with inspirational readings and quotes and prayers and writing in my journal and all these kinds of things at night. I usually read and we have Yung Pueblo on today, a couple of lines from his book. And just before I close my eyes. Like last thing in, last thing in. I also try to say -- usually you think of like three things you`re grateful for. Yes, but a twist on that and this sounds vain, but it isn`t. Three things I appreciate about myself. Now, think about for right now, just freeze for a second. In this moment, what are three things you appreciate? Not that you`re grateful for? So, what is it that you`ve done that you appreciated? And it`s only for you, you`re not bragging. But what did you -- what have you done so far that you appreciate? And sometimes they`re small things like I gave my kids space, so that they could say what they wanted to say and then I received? OK, that`s the thing. And so, that`s the way -- HAGER: Yes. Or the way you handle situations. KOTB: Yes. Yes. HAGER: Yes, it`s so -- it`s so interesting, because I think we don`t even realize the negative stuff we say to ourselves, which is constant. Why did you do that? Why did you do that for? Why did you -- KOTB: I`m telling why (INAUDIBLE) should -- HAGER: You shouldn`t have said that. KOTB: Yes. HAGER: But -- so imagine just filling that time with? Oh, look, what you did there. You know, saying nice things. And I think it really does make a difference. KOTB: You know, Michelle Obama`s book that`s been out for a little bit is so beautifully written. But she talks about in one part, how we have a rectangular-sized shield that we put between us and the world. And she`s talking about the phone. HAGER: Oh, interesting. KOTB: And she says, what we`re doing every day is we are missing micro connections. You`re in the line at the bank, but I`m playing Candy Crush, so I don`t even look up to say hello, or I`m here and I`m doing something small. What your day -- she talked about how every day a micro connection and actually matters. It shows that we`re -- we may be different, but we`re human. But if you`re -- if there`s something in your ears and something in front of you, because people keep saying why are we drifting further apart? Tiny interactions that we would normally have. HAGER: Thank you. Yes. KOTB: Please, hi on the street. HAGER: The kind of smile that kind of makes you feel good. KOTB: Yes. Yes. HAGER: Wait, do you know -- so, when I first went back to work after having Mila, she`s 9, so about nine years ago, I got assigned the story. And I swear, it was like some sort of gift. Because the story was all about how basically kids are feeling like they`re not interesting. There was this doctor at Harvard who was studying what this -- what this does to a child. So, pretend you`re saying, Mommy, mommy -- KOTB: Hey, mom, mom, I want to tell you something. No, mom, mom, mom? HAGER: Hear. Hear. Hear. So, the words -- KOTB: Right. This is more important. HAGER: This is more important than this. KOTB: Than you. Than you. HAGER: And it was the best gift because what I realized is I was putting emphasis on work everything -- KOTB: I got to get this deal. Very important. HAGER: -- and you`ll (INAUDIBLE) instead of looking into my baby`s eye. KOTB: Yes. HAGER: And well, it`s not true. I mean, no mom thinks this is more interesting than their child. KOTB: Or, we don`t even realize -- we think how of just doing one quick thing, just one quick thing. HAGER: Anyway, that`s -- that could be a New Year`s resolution for a lot of people out there, and it`d be for mine. KOTB: Yes, yes. Me, too. [10:05:05] HAGER: OK. So, there`s research that recently was published in the Economic Times. It says humor at work actually accelerate creativity, motivation, and promoting productivity. KOTB: You know what, here`s the funny thing. I`m sitting next to this one. So, here`s the funny thing about you. Sometimes, I worry as we`re sitting here, because the things you say are so crazy and funny that I`ll just lose it instantly. But here`s the funny thing. I feel like there are ways -- there are ways of connection. HAGER: Yes. KOTB: For us, we have it. I think we have a deep kind of spiritual connection. But when you make me laugh, I feel so weirdly and crazily connected. Like I am -- sometimes I think about what you say much later in the day, and I`ll literally just be like, and goes what, I got nothing. It was something -- I can`t even explain. HAGER: You called me the other day. And you go, all I have to say is pirate and hung up. KOTB: You know why? Because I thought I was wearing a pair of cute black pants, black boots, but they didn`t meet in the middle. So, Jenna goes, hey, pirate. And literally, I was -- I just laughed, but that`s the whole thing. They say, it`s the whole thing. If you have them laughing, you have them listening. HAGER: That is such a good one. KOTB: And teachers who are -- yes, teachers who are -- who make kids laugh, kids lean in, they listen. HAGER: Totally. But laughing also is so much fun. I feel like that`s -- I mean, I`m coming up with all my New Year`s resolutions. Somebody, write this down. KOTB: What is it? HAGER: My other New Year`s resolution is to laugh more. KOTB: Yes. How? HAGER: Like why are we too busy? I mean, we laugh a lot because that`s our -- KOTB: Because we have -- and we also have space too. If we didn`t, if we were rushing through, you know, the whole -- HAGER: Rushing and doing this, and -- here`s your paper. Like, laugh instead, right? KOTB: Get in the next segment. I know. HAGER: Why don`t we just laugh more? KOTB: Yes, we do. HAGER: I mean, we do. In life, why don`t we -- KOTB: We all, collectively. OK, shall we see this video that`ll make us feel good. HAGER: Yes, yes. All right, this is the father of a bride in Jersey. So, the wedding videographer mic`d up the dad for his big walk down the aisle. So, let`s take a listen. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) UNIDENTIFIED MALE: Nice and slow, honey. Look at his face. You see nothing but smiles. I love you, you know? Take care of her. Give me a hug, too. You`ll be fine, kiddo. I`ll be always by your side. You`ll never be alone, OK? (END VIDEO CLIP) KOTB: Oh my gosh. HAGER: There were so few words yet they were so beautiful. KOTB: We were talking about laughing. HAGER: It`s good, now we`re crying. But you know what I think about crying? If you`re crying, you`re listening, too. KOTB: Yes, yes, yes. It works for both. All right, coming up, if you love a surprise we got a good one for you. HAGER: And Donna shows up unannounced to surprise a beloved neighbor right after this. (COMMERCIAL BREAK) [10:10:00] HAGER: Now to our series, "KNOCK KNOCK SURPRISE!" And this is a surprise that`s going to fill your heart, for sure. KOTB: Yes. So, a few months ago, a viewer wrote in to tell us about her incredible neighbor of 20 years. His name is Ernie Mann. He lives in Rensselaer, New York. So, we sent Donna there to surprise him with something we knew he`d love. Check it out. DONNA FARIZAN, NBC NEWS HOST: This is so exciting, ladies. I`m here with Amy Mooney who nominated Ernie for National Good Neighbor Day. We`re walking up to his door right now. I`m going to leave you right there, Amy, OK? And I`m going up. I am -- we were hiding in the bushes for quite some time, a little bit nervous of what was going to happen, and how he`s going to react. Amy said that he`s going to be in shock. So, I`m going to knock on the door right now. And hopefully, Ernie will come out and be surprised. We can`t wait. There`s a crowd of over 30 here with us. This neighborhood loves him so much. And I don`t know how he`s going to react, but I`m hoping he`s going to be happy. So, let`s see what Ernie has to say. We`ve knock knocked the doors. Hi, Ernie, surprise! Ernie, come on out here. I`m Donna -- I`m Donna from the TODAY SHOW. And you are live. Come on over here with me, Ernie. It`s nice to meet you. You are so beloved as you can feel and see. And I don`t know if you know this, Ernie, but we can go right here. It is National Good Neighbor Day today. And we wanted to honor you because you are a pillar of this community. And you are just about the best neighbor that anyone could ask for. What`s going through your mind right now? ERNIE MANN, GOOD NEIGHBOR: Well, totally confused. FARIZAN: Well, let me fill you in a little bit more. Amy right here -- Amy right here nominated you. You are on live television on the TODAY SHOW right now. You can wave hi to Hoda and Jenna and millions of Americans if you want. We`re all here to honor you. MANN: Well, thank you very much. And if I had any influence in anything, I`d ask them if they`d please throw some fastballs to Aaron Judd. They walked in four times last night and a win. But anyway -- FARIZAN: So, Ernie, we know that Hoda and Jenna want to say something, too. So, we just are going to give you these earbuds, so you can listen to what`s going on. We know that you are so beloved and like a father figure to so many here. And I actually wanted to show you a little video on why Amy nominated you. Let`s take a look. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: Ernie is a local legend in Rensselaer. He is not only a phenomenal neighbor, but a true hero in our community. He was a teacher for over 30 years, and he was also an active volunteer firefighter. He was our fire chief. [10:15:09] My kids would play wiffle ball in his backyard. Ernie`s like a dad to a lot of us, and he would do anything for any of us. Ernie and his wife, Jan moved into the neighborhood. That was almost 20 years ago. And unfortunately, Jan was stricken with ovarian cancer, and it took her way sooner than any of us thought. And Ernie was crushed. He`s not having the retirement he planned on with Jan. But he still celebrates life every day. He`s infamous for his mustache. His grandchildren can celebrate his mustache. They play in the snow, and they make his face on trees. We are Boston fans. Ernie is a Yankee fan. So, there`s a healthy rivalry going on. Ernie`s sense of humor can be summed up in a card that our daughter received at Johns Hopkins Hospital, he sent her a beautiful get well card and signed it Derek Jeter . Ernie is a person who has gone above and beyond, and now it`s time for us to honor him. He`s going to be so pissed at me. You have no idea. (END VIDEO CLIP) FARIZAN: Is that true? How do you feel right now? MANN: I`m overwhelmed, honestly. FARIZAN: I`ll take -- I`ll take these out. I know -- MANN: Totally, I don`t know what to say. I don`t know -- I -- my response was, who the hell is at my door at this time of day? FARIZAN: It was us. There are a lot of -- a lot of iterations of the mustache everywhere. And I know your late wife Jan would be so proud of all you`ve done today. MANN: Thank you so much. Thank you. FARIZAN: And all the love you`re receiving today. MANN: Thank you so much. FARIZAN: Have you always loved Rensselaer this much? MANN: Yes, I have. Yes. My father was born in Rensselaer. And before it was Rensselaer, actually. And now, I`ve lived through all my life. And it`s a wonderful city. People are just great. I taught 33 years into schools, and then the fire department now pushing 60 years. And it`s just a wonderful town. FARIZAN: Well, thank you for all that you do. You`re such a great representation of not only calm but a good neighbor. MANN: Thank you so much. FARIZAN: And you know, I wanted you to put the earbuds in one more time because I heard Ernie that you are a big Yankees fan. Is that right? MANN: Yes, that`s true. FARIZAN: So, well, in honor of that, I think there`s a member of the team that wanted to say hello to you if that`s OK, let`s take a listen. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) NESTOR CORTES: Nestor Cortes here with the New York Yankees . I just want to congratulate you on being a good neighbor. We`ve heard all about you and what you`ve do -- and what you`ve done with the community. By the way, we have a special gift coming for you. So, stay tuned. And go Yankees . (END VIDEO CLIP) FARIZAN: Well, I know that you just saw Nestor Cortes, Jr. through the screen. But you know what, can we just grab some Yankees swag? OK, this is for you. I think you`re going to need it because, Ernie, we are getting you four tickets to Yankee Stadium, so you can go see Nestor (INAUDIBLE) and you have a lot of people to choose from to take with you. How do you feel? MANN: I`m, honest to God, I`m overwhelmed. And I totally didn`t see any of this coming. I don`t know -- FARIZAN: Well, you know, thank you so much for being a great neighbor. MANN: Well, I`ve had great neighbors around me. It`s been pretty easy. All the people around me, they`re wonderful people. FARIZAN: As we send it back to Hoda and Jenna, is there one piece of advice you would give people to become a better neighbor? MANN: If you just look out for each other, if you look and see if somebody`s up against it, try to help them a little bit. You can do it quietly. You don`t have to make a big fuss. And if just people are nicer to each other all over. It`s easy to do. FARIZAN: Thank you, Ernie. It`s easy to do with you. KOTB: Oh my gosh, how much do we love Earnie. HAGER: We love Earnie. He`s such a sweet, sweet man, and what a great group of neighbors, a beautiful community. KOTB: Incredible. Incredible. Coming up next, a mother of two who wouldn`t let breast cancer beat her, and now she`s helping other women get a fighting chance coming up after this. [10:20:00] (COMMERCIAL BREAK) HAGER: All morning long, we`re celebrating people whose stories inspire us to live our very best life. KOTB: Breast cancer survivor Ricki Fairley is one of those people. After defying the odds, she created a brand new life for herself with a very important mission. Take a look. (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) RICKI FAIRLEY, BREAST CANCER SURVIVOR: I try to like let everything go and just paddle and just feel the water and see that -- feel the sun or the wind. Feel God around me. KOTB (voiceover): Ricki Fairley starts most of our days like this, alone and at peace on the Chesapeake Bay. But this mother of two didn`t always know how to slow down. Like most caregivers, Ricki was constantly on the go. FAIRLEY: I was a crazy, busy typical mom, working mom. I actually had been married for 30 years, and I was the breadwinner for our family, traveling every week on the road. KOTB: After a routine mammogram, the words triple negative breast cancer stopped her in her tracks. FAIRLEY: My doctor said we found five spots on your chest wall. You are now metastatic. You have two years to live. Get your affairs in order. We don`t have anything for you. And I said, well, I can`t really die right now. I have a daughter at Dartmouth. I have to pay for her tuition. So, me, you and gotten some drugs or something. We got to work this out. KOTB: It was a long road of surgeries, chemotherapy, radiation, and experimental drugs, but it worked. And Ricki was cancer free. She decided to quit her old life and start fresh. [10:25:03] FAIRLEY: I knew I had to get rid of all the cancers in my life. I divorced my husband of 30 years. I quit my business partner of 10 years. I sold my house in Alpharetta, Georgia with a pool and two acres, and I moved to my little one-bedroom condo on the beach. KOTB: She also did a lot of research and learned about the disparity in breast cancer for black women. FAIRLEY: This disease for black women is a different disease. And now, we have a growing body of data that validates that a black breast cancer cell looks different from a white one. We have a 41 percent higher mortality rate than white women. We have a 39 percent higher recurrence rate of breast cancer than white woman, which is crazy. KOTB: So, with her new home, her new fiance and her new way of life came a new purpose, a nonprofit called Touch: The Black Breast Cancer Alliance. FAIRLEY: I wanted to change the game on how the world thinks about black women and breast cancer. I want to advance the science. I want to stop the dying. I wanted to bring pharmaceutical companies to the table to say, deal with this. Help us. KOTB: 11 years after she was told she was going to die, Ricki is still cancer free and has been able to watch her oldest daughter get married and have a family of her own. FAIRLEY: I work for my granddaughters. I don`t want them to ever think about this disease. I don`t want them to have to talk about it. I don`t want them to -- I don`t want it to be in their existence. KOTB: As for her younger daughter, Haley, Ricky got her wish and watched her graduate college. They now work side-by-side to help other women going through the unthinkable, HALEY BROWN, DAUGHTER OF RICKI FAIRLEY: Seeing my mom firsthand, being sick and dealing with all the things that come with it. And now just the things that even come with survivorship. Just being a support system for these women has been a large part of my mission. And so, what I`m trying to do now for the breast cancer community is also create that safe space. KOTB: Looking back, Ricki has advice for her younger, busier self. FAIRLEY: Your piece is non-negotiable. Take care of yourself, check your breasts, give yourself a minute, give yourself a pause. It`s OK to say no. KOTB: And that she sits with her family, four generations of strong women, Ricki`s mission is clear. FAIRLEY: I`m a miracle. I know I`m a miracle. I shouldn`t be here. So many women that with --that had what I had didn`t make it. And I know that God left me here to do this work to be an advocate for other women. It`s my purpose. (END VIDEOTAPE) KOTB (on camera): Ricki, I mean, we are in awe of you. Your purpose came with that horrible diagnosis. A huge change. You made so many changes that you`re probably too afraid to make your whole life. What -- was there ever a point of trepidation? Should I divorce my husband, change all these things because of this -- of what happened to you? FAIRLEY: No. There was no trepidation. I knew -- I knew in my spirit that I had to save my life. And I just went for it. I didn`t even think twice about it. And people said, are you crazy? are you sure you should do all this at one time? Do you want to think about it? I said, no, I have to go now. HAGER: You know, the best thing about this is that you had the second life and you`re using it to help other women. You -- those statistics that we heard in the piece are unacceptable. You could have just read those and thought, OK, but instead, you`re fighting them. And that just seems like an incredible mission. FAIRLEY: I work for my granddaughters. I don`t want them to ever think about breast cancer, and we have a lot of work to do to save black women. And I don`t -- I don`t want anybody to die of breast cancer. But we deserve mortality rate parity. KOTB: Well, I thought what you said after the diagnosis was like you, the doctor, me, God, medicine, whatever, we all do -- we`re all going to have to work together on this one. You sound like your faith was unshakable throughout. FAIRLEY: It was. I -- you know, faith is my spiritual gift. I know that God left me here to do this work. And I`m on a mission to try to change how we think about it. HAGER: Well, Ricki, we are impressed with you if that`s not obvious. But also, Thrive Cosmetics, they told us they were so inspired by the work that you do to eradicate black breast cancer. But guess what, they`re donating $10,000 to Touch to continue the efforts that you put in in everything you do. FAIRLEY: Oh, wow, that`s so awesome. HAGER: Will that be able to make a difference? FAIRLEY: That will be awesome. You know, we have this movement called When We Trial. Whenwetrial.org to educate black woman about clinical trials, so we can get better drugs, so I will put it to work today. HAGER: Oh, awesome. Ricki, we love you. KOTB: You`re unbelievable. You`re unbelievable. Wow, what a gift for us. Thank you so much. HAGER: Thank you. Thank you. Thank you so much. FAIRLEY: That`s such a blessing. Thank you so much. KOTB: Wow, for us too. HAGER: How brave and awesome is Ricki. We love everything she`s doing especially for the black breast cancer community. KOTB: Yes, she is an inspiration. HAGER: Coming up next, the author and poet whose book is on Hoda`s nightstand. We talked about him earlier, Yung Pueblo, after this. (COMMERCIAL BREAK) [10:33:11] HAGER: TODAY Show is all about people who lift us up through their positivity and light. And one of those people is bestselling author, Diego Perez. KOTB: You probably know him by his pen name, which is Yung Pueblo. His words have brought me and millions and millions of others comfort and wisdom when we`ve needed it the most. And recently, Donna caught up with him as he released his newest book, check it out. (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) DONNA FARIZAN, NBC PRODUCER (voice over): If you`ve ever scrolled on social media, you may have already come across the words of Yung Pueblo. Diego Perez is the poet behind the pen name, inspiring readers with wisdom, like, "realize how short the walk is from gratitude to happiness." And "manage your reactions, but do not suppress your emotions." Since he first began sharing his words of wisdom in 2014, Yung Pueblo has connected with over 2 million followers. And has written two New York Times bestselling books of poetry on topics like self-love, growth, and relationships. When you first started posting your writing, what was your intent? YUNG PUEBLO, AUTHOR, LIGHTER: I wanted to write about healing being possible. This hopefully inspires someone else out there who also needed to find a way to heal themselves. FARIZAN: Diego and his family emigrated from Ecuador to Boston, Massachusetts, when he was four years old. PUEBLO: My mom, she worked cleaning houses, my dad worked at a supermarket. So, we were really stuck in a poverty trap. And then, I think a lot of that tension just got embedded inside of me as well. When I got to college, I could not deal with any tension that was coming up inside of me, I would quickly try to hide it with, with drugs, with smoking, with going to more parties. [10:35:02] What was the breaking point for you? PUEBLO: It was right after college. This time I pushed my body to the edge. And I took, you know, an assortment of different drugs. I felt like my heart was going to explode. I ended up talking to a doctor after that episode. And she told me, and said -- but I described to her sounded like a mild heart attack. FARIZAN: How has being first generation American affect your overall outlook of life, especially in that point? PUEBLO: The first thought is my parents. I saw the immense sacrifice that they made to just give us the chance at a better opportunity. I felt like I was giving all of that up by just filling myself with more and more pleasure just so that I can run away from my pain. I knew that the only way out was to start telling myself the truth. FARIZAN: In 2011, Diego started taking small steps toward building positive habits. FARIZAN: And meditation gave you the clarity and creativity to write and share. PUEBLO: Definitely. I mean, I was never creative before meditating, you know. And I didn`t go into meditating to become more creative. When the mind becomes lighter and it`s not as burdened by past hurt that you carry, this creativity bubbles up. Diego`s poems have been liked and shared 1,000s of times. And in his newest book titled, Lighter, Diego shares his own journey and advice on how to achieve personal transformation. What do you hope is the biggest takeaway for people who come to you and look to your words? PUEBLO: I hope they take away inspiration. It`s really possible to transform your life. It`s really possible to sort of take that big leap forward in your own evolution. (END VIDEOTAPE) HAGER: Oh my gosh. What an incredible journey. Our conversation with Yung Pueblo, right after the break. (COMMERCIAL BREAK) [10:40:45] KOTB: Before the break, we introduce you to someone whose books I`ve been reading poet and bestselling author, Diego Perez, who goes by the name Yung Pueblo. HAGER: After some difficulties with alcohol and drugs, he found his way to a life of light and inspiration. We got to chat with Diego about his new book, Lighter. PUEBLO: Totally. I had no idea. I never saw myself as a creative person. But honestly, after I did about three silent 10-day courses, I felt that creativity bubbling up. And I felt my intuition really telling me, you know, it`s time to write. Even though you`re not fully healed, even though you`re not fully wise, you know, you have a long way to go. But just write about healing being possible, because I noticed a significant differences in my mind. HAGER: You know, it`s so interesting, because so many of us are kind of covering pain. PUEBLO: Yes. HAGER: Like -- and I love that you have said, it`s OK to feel -- PUEBLO: Totally. Yes. HAGER: It`s OK to have those emotions, and you have to. KOTB: Well, we, Jenna, and I love your quotes. And we`ll just share a couple of them. And just maybe talk a little bit about them. KOTB: Yes. PUEBLO: If you start allowing that to burn away through some process or another, then you`re going to notice a burst of creativity happening in your life. HAGER: Yes. HAGER: OK. HAGER: It`s a really nice way to wake up with a text from you, and via Hoda. The undeniable radiance of someone who is not afraid to grow, to be free, and thrive. PUEBLO: Yes, I mean, I think it`s something that it`s pretty common. When people start deeply healing themselves, they radiate in a different way. Because that`s often what happens is that something difficult situation arises, and your old self will want to show up as opposed to how you want to intentionally show up in the present. KOTB: You know what`s funny? There was a woman who was just on with Andrew Lloyd Webber , and she walked through, and she was like, hey, I just want to say something to you. And she looked at me, and say, I just want to let you know, I`ve been thinking about you and praying for you. And as I looked at her, I felt like this incredible moment. And it was something that wasn`t concrete. I didn`t know her well. It was just -- it was that. It was like she was alive. She had something inside of her that was like luminous to me. And I was like I`m still dazzling. When she left, I was like, wait, where are you going? Because she had to leave, it was time to go. But people do give that off. Here is what we`d like to -- Maturity is knowing that when your mood is down, you should not trust the - - you should not trust the way you see yourself. HAGER: Yes. KOTB: Like it`s a bad moment, not a bad life? (CROSSTALK) HAGER: Yes. PUEBLO: Yes. I mean, that`s a really important one because as soon as your mood goes down and your emotions feel heavy, you`ll want to just jump into self-critique, and you`ll start telling yourself things that are totally untrue, like, you haven`t actually gotten that far, or, you know, you`re just like, sort of building this narrative that isn`t based on reality at all. You know, it was hard seeing my parents go through this immense challenge of trying to keep our family afloat. And we were just -- you know, like I said before, we were stuck in a poverty trap. And it was quite difficult for us to come out of it until I became older until my brother became older, my little sister and now we can support ourselves, help our parents as well. And I think my parents are just they`re really grateful that the gamble paid off for all three of us. Because coming to United States it`s -- HAGER: Yes. PUEBLO: You know, it`s a bit of a risk and but it worked out for us. KOTB: Well, I have your book by my bedside, it`s one of those you can open up read one beautiful line and go to sleep and sleep really well. So -- HAGER: She actually goes to bed with your words in her head every night. KOTB: Yes. PUEBLO: Wow. HAGER: And then make her feel lighter. PUEBLO: That`s a big honor. KOTB: Big for me too. Thank you. HAGER: And then make her feel lighter. And I think if you want that light, it`s here. KOTB: Yes. And you got to get the book, Lighter. And also, your other two books are amazing. I like all three, but get this one because it`s new. (END VIDEOTAPE) KOTB: By the way, since that segment aired Yung Pueblo`s book Lighter reached number one on the New York Times bestsellers list. AMANI SHAH, CEO, SECOND SERVE: I think more could supply tennis because it`s a phenomenal way to build character. AYANNA SHAH, PRESIDENT, SECOND SERVE: Tennis has taught me so many lessons and I think the biggest one is learning how to push through obstacles. AMANI SHAH: When I was 10 years old was when I really fell in love with the sport. AYANNA SHAH: The relationships that I`ve built through tennis have been just amazing. AMANI SHAH: Historically, tennis has been deemed an elitist sport because of its very high-cost entry. AYANNA SHAH: Second Serve redistributes new and gently used tennis equipment all around the world. Our mission is to create greater access, inclusion, and diversity within the sport. One of my personal favorite donations was to a young girl in Nigeria named Nana Rosie (PH). UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: I started playing tennis since I was three years old. AMANI SHAH: Nana spends four to five hours every day playing tennis and her dedication is really an inspiration for us. HAGER: Ayanna and Amani tap teams across the U.S. to make this all happen. AMANI SHAH: Our team has grown to over 90 different high school team members all across the U.S. We`ve been able to redistribute over 20,000 items in over 26 states and 14 different countries. EMMA HIGUCHI, COO, SECOND SERVE: What I was drawn to is it was a -- it`s a youth-led organization. We always have monthly meetings. DIANNA, ORANGE GLEN HIGH SCHOOL STUDENT: At first I couldn`t really hit but now I can do like everything. PRATT: Now she`s competing. She`s our number one player. Second Serves` mission of enhancing the lives of underserved children by fostering a love for tennis is inspirational and empowering, to support that mission Athleta is donating 100 girls` tennis dresses to Second Serve. headline: TODAY WITH HODA & JENNA for Dec 26, 2022, NBC
story_text: (COMMERCIAL BREAK) [10:00:17] HODA KOTB, NBC NEWS ANCHOR (voiceover): Today, get ready to be inspired. Donna shows up at the door of a beloved neighbor and gives him the ultimate sweet surprise. Plus, writer and poet Yung Pueblo. How his millions of followers are learning and healing from his every word. And the breast cancer survivor whose personal journey is touching and saving the lives of countless women. JENNA BUSH HAGER, NBC NEWS ANCHOR (voiceover): It`s TODAY WITH HODA -- KOTB: -- & JENNA. It all starts right now. HAGER: It all starts right now. KOTB (on camera): Hey, guys, happy day after Christmas. It`s Monday, December 26th. We hope that you all had a very merry one and a happy one. All the wrapping paper the bows and all that stuff tucked away. HAGER (on camera): Waking up with family still in the house. It`s -- what were they called this day in the U.K.? Boxing Day? KOTB: Boxing Day? They do? HAGER: Yes. I`m not sure why. KOTB: Oh, just like to decorative -- HAGER: But let`s celebrate Boxing Day. Why not? KOTB: OK. I like that. HAGER: And we`ve got an amazing show today that`s going to leave you feeling inspired and feeling good. Just as this day should. KOTB: Oh my God, this is -- this is our kind of show. HAGER: It sure is. KOTB: Because we love -- loves -- love things that feel like that. HAGER: Wait, in fact, can you just talk about the way you start your day? And the way you end your day? Because Henry is reading a book called Think Like A Monk by Jay Shetty. KOTB: Jay Shetty, yes. HAGER: And he says a lot of people think about the morning routine, but people forget about the end. KOTB: You know what`s funny? The morning routine I packed with inspirational readings and quotes and prayers and writing in my journal and all these kinds of things at night. I usually read and we have Yung Pueblo on today, a couple of lines from his book. And just before I close my eyes. Like last thing in, last thing in. I also try to say -- usually you think of like three things you`re grateful for. Yes, but a twist on that and this sounds vain, but it isn`t. Three things I appreciate about myself. Now, think about for right now, just freeze for a second. In this moment, what are three things you appreciate? Not that you`re grateful for? So, what is it that you`ve done that you appreciated? And it`s only for you, you`re not bragging. But what did you -- what have you done so far that you appreciate? And sometimes they`re small things like I gave my kids space, so that they could say what they wanted to say and then I received? OK, that`s the thing. And so, that`s the way -- HAGER: Yes. Or the way you handle situations. KOTB: Yes. Yes. HAGER: Yes, it`s so -- it`s so interesting, because I think we don`t even realize the negative stuff we say to ourselves, which is constant. Why did you do that? Why did you do that for? Why did you -- KOTB: I`m telling why (INAUDIBLE) should -- HAGER: You shouldn`t have said that. KOTB: Yes. HAGER: But -- so imagine just filling that time with? Oh, look, what you did there. You know, saying nice things. And I think it really does make a difference. KOTB: You know, Michelle Obama`s book that`s been out for a little bit is so beautifully written. But she talks about in one part, how we have a rectangular-sized shield that we put between us and the world. And she`s talking about the phone. HAGER: Oh, interesting. KOTB: And she says, what we`re doing every day is we are missing micro connections. You`re in the line at the bank, but I`m playing Candy Crush, so I don`t even look up to say hello, or I`m here and I`m doing something small. What your day -- she talked about how every day a micro connection and actually matters. It shows that we`re -- we may be different, but we`re human. But if you`re -- if there`s something in your ears and something in front of you, because people keep saying why are we drifting further apart? Tiny interactions that we would normally have. HAGER: Thank you. Yes. KOTB: Please, hi on the street. HAGER: The kind of smile that kind of makes you feel good. KOTB: Yes. Yes. HAGER: Wait, do you know -- so, when I first went back to work after having Mila, she`s 9, so about nine years ago, I got assigned the story. And I swear, it was like some sort of gift. Because the story was all about how basically kids are feeling like they`re not interesting. There was this doctor at Harvard who was studying what this -- what this does to a child. So, pretend you`re saying, Mommy, mommy -- KOTB: Hey, mom, mom, I want to tell you something. No, mom, mom, mom? HAGER: Hear. Hear. Hear. So, the words -- KOTB: Right. This is more important. HAGER: This is more important than this. KOTB: Than you. Than you. HAGER: And it was the best gift because what I realized is I was putting emphasis on work everything -- KOTB: I got to get this deal. Very important. HAGER: -- and you`ll (INAUDIBLE) instead of looking into my baby`s eye. KOTB: Yes. HAGER: And well, it`s not true. I mean, no mom thinks this is more interesting than their child. KOTB: Or, we don`t even realize -- we think how of just doing one quick thing, just one quick thing. HAGER: Anyway, that`s -- that could be a New Year`s resolution for a lot of people out there, and it`d be for mine. KOTB: Yes, yes. Me, too. [10:05:05] HAGER: OK. So, there`s research that recently was published in the Economic Times. It says humor at work actually accelerate creativity, motivation, and promoting productivity. KOTB: You know what, here`s the funny thing. I`m sitting next to this one. So, here`s the funny thing about you. Sometimes, I worry as we`re sitting here, because the things you say are so crazy and funny that I`ll just lose it instantly. But here`s the funny thing. I feel like there are ways -- there are ways of connection. HAGER: Yes. KOTB: For us, we have it. I think we have a deep kind of spiritual connection. But when you make me laugh, I feel so weirdly and crazily connected. Like I am -- sometimes I think about what you say much later in the day, and I`ll literally just be like, and goes what, I got nothing. It was something -- I can`t even explain. HAGER: You called me the other day. And you go, all I have to say is pirate and hung up. KOTB: You know why? Because I thought I was wearing a pair of cute black pants, black boots, but they didn`t meet in the middle. So, Jenna goes, hey, pirate. And literally, I was -- I just laughed, but that`s the whole thing. They say, it`s the whole thing. If you have them laughing, you have them listening. HAGER: That is such a good one. KOTB: And teachers who are -- yes, teachers who are -- who make kids laugh, kids lean in, they listen. HAGER: Totally. But laughing also is so much fun. I feel like that`s -- I mean, I`m coming up with all my New Year`s resolutions. Somebody, write this down. KOTB: What is it? HAGER: My other New Year`s resolution is to laugh more. KOTB: Yes. How? HAGER: Like why are we too busy? I mean, we laugh a lot because that`s our -- KOTB: Because we have -- and we also have space too. If we didn`t, if we were rushing through, you know, the whole -- HAGER: Rushing and doing this, and -- here`s your paper. Like, laugh instead, right? KOTB: Get in the next segment. I know. HAGER: Why don`t we just laugh more? KOTB: Yes, we do. HAGER: I mean, we do. In life, why don`t we -- KOTB: We all, collectively. OK, shall we see this video that`ll make us feel good. HAGER: Yes, yes. All right, this is the father of a bride in Jersey. So, the wedding videographer mic`d up the dad for his big walk down the aisle. So, let`s take a listen. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) UNIDENTIFIED MALE: Nice and slow, honey. Look at his face. You see nothing but smiles. I love you, you know? Take care of her. Give me a hug, too. You`ll be fine, kiddo. I`ll be always by your side. You`ll never be alone, OK? (END VIDEO CLIP) KOTB: Oh my gosh. HAGER: There were so few words yet they were so beautiful. KOTB: We were talking about laughing. HAGER: It`s good, now we`re crying. But you know what I think about crying? If you`re crying, you`re listening, too. KOTB: Yes, yes, yes. It works for both. All right, coming up, if you love a surprise we got a good one for you. HAGER: And Donna shows up unannounced to surprise a beloved neighbor right after this. (COMMERCIAL BREAK) [10:10:00] HAGER: Now to our series, "KNOCK KNOCK SURPRISE!" And this is a surprise that`s going to fill your heart, for sure. KOTB: Yes. So, a few months ago, a viewer wrote in to tell us about her incredible neighbor of 20 years. His name is Ernie Mann. He lives in Rensselaer, New York. So, we sent Donna there to surprise him with something we knew he`d love. Check it out. DONNA FARIZAN, NBC NEWS HOST: This is so exciting, ladies. I`m here with Amy Mooney who nominated Ernie for National Good Neighbor Day. We`re walking up to his door right now. I`m going to leave you right there, Amy, OK? And I`m going up. I am -- we were hiding in the bushes for quite some time, a little bit nervous of what was going to happen, and how he`s going to react. Amy said that he`s going to be in shock. So, I`m going to knock on the door right now. And hopefully, Ernie will come out and be surprised. We can`t wait. There`s a crowd of over 30 here with us. This neighborhood loves him so much. And I don`t know how he`s going to react, but I`m hoping he`s going to be happy. So, let`s see what Ernie has to say. We`ve knock knocked the doors. Hi, Ernie, surprise! Ernie, come on out here. I`m Donna -- I`m Donna from the TODAY SHOW. And you are live. Come on over here with me, Ernie. It`s nice to meet you. You are so beloved as you can feel and see. And I don`t know if you know this, Ernie, but we can go right here. It is National Good Neighbor Day today. And we wanted to honor you because you are a pillar of this community. Ernie`s sense of humor can be summed up in a card that our daughter received at Johns Hopkins Hospital, he sent her a beautiful get well card and signed it Derek Jeter . FARIZAN: Well, thank you for all that you do. You`re such a great representation of not only calm but a good neighbor. MANN: Thank you so much. FARIZAN: And you know, I wanted you to put the earbuds in one more time because I heard Ernie that you are a big Yankees fan. Is that right? MANN: Yes, that`s true. FARIZAN: So, well, in honor of that, I think there`s a member of the team that wanted to say hello to you if that`s OK, let`s take a listen. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) NESTOR CORTES: Nestor Cortes here with the New York Yankees . I just want to congratulate you on being a good neighbor. [10:20:00] (COMMERCIAL BREAK) HAGER: All morning long, we`re celebrating people whose stories inspire us to live our very best life. KOTB: Breast cancer survivor Ricki Fairley is one of those people. FAIRLEY: I work for my granddaughters. I don`t want them to ever think about breast cancer, and we have a lot of work to do to save black women. story_text: (COMMERCIAL BREAK) [08:00:00] HODA KOTB, NBC NEWS TODAY, CO-ANCHOR: It`s 8:00 on "TODAY." Coming up, flu fears. New concerns over medication shortages as cases spike from coast to coast. Let`s talk about Brittney Griner. We don`t want to miss the moment here, Andrea. She has been freed after nearly 10 months. Can you talk about the type of conditions she may have been kept in? I know at the very end there she was sent to a notorious penal colony in Russia. MITCHELL: Exactly. At the beginning of November after her appeal was lost, she was taken from the detention jail where she had been at least more accessible to occasional visits from US embassy officials and taken to this penal colony. And the conditions, we understand, were terrible. That the rule that they were fed, not nutritious, no hot water, one bathroom for as many as 80 women prisoners, very little exercise. And this woman is six foot nine (inaudible) had already been kept in a cell that was way too small for her. She`s missed, you know, an entire season 10 months of physical fitness and of conditioning, and of her career at the peak of an athlete`s life and career. So she has suffered immeasurable loss. We`re just hoping when she gets to that medical facility in San Antonio that the wonderful doctors who have taken care of all of our service members for so many years of conflicts, that they will know exactly what to do about PTSD, about whatever else she may be suffering from, and about getting back in shape. KOTB: And it`s worth kind of underscoring why she was arrested in the first place. They originally said that she was charged with smuggling drugs. And was she was contending that she just had some cannabis oil that she had medical permission to use for some of her ailments. So that was the genesis of why -- GUTHRIE: In the context at the very moment that Russia was launching its war in Ukraine. So many people, Andrea, feel she was swept up in geopolitics. MITCHELL: Absolutely, it was February 17th when they were about to launch the war in February 24th. And the fact is it was less than a gram. There was no testimony. And I watched all of the trial, no testimony in any of these events that it was more than, you know, less than a gram of cannabis oil, medically prescribed by the physicians, the sports doctors in Phoenix. So there`s no question that she was not doing anything that would warrant this. In any case, even if there weren`t -- if she weren`t being held hostage geopolitically, there`s no excuse at all. KOTB: And it`s also, Andrea, worth noting this is exactly what she said when she was in trial. I never meant to hurt anybody. I never meant to put in jeopardy the Russian population. This is what she had to say after the conviction. I`ve never meant to break laws here. I made an honest mistake. I mean, that`s what she contended. We have Peter Alexander at the White House. GUTHRIE: Peter at the White House and I want to talk about the Whelan family because the statement, which I said is quite lengthy and very nuanced, very generous of course to Brittney Griner. But also it`s tough on the administration, past and present, saying that the family wishes it had been more assertive to get Paul`s release. Does that work continue or is this just a dead end? Russia saying we want you to give us a spy, the USA we don`t have any spies, and that`s the end of it? ALEXANDER: Well, the US war continues as the President himself indicated in his remarks earlier today, but as you see they are facing a brick wall in terms of the Russian Federation right now, their unwillingness to turn over Paul Whelan, who you`ll remember was picked up back in 2018. He is a US businessman, but notably, he is a former US Marine. And it`s on that basis that Russia has been making its case. The US says wrongfully that he was there serving as a US spy. The US has repeatedly denied that. We are now hearing from some of the officials here as this news is breaking. They are saying this is a big day. It is a great day they say but it would sure be a lot better in the words of one of these officials if Paul was coming home as well. So that`s what makes this particularly bittersweet right now. And we should note, I mean, this is the President ultimately who signed off on this. But Victor Bout, he is a significant prisoner that the US had in custody. As we have said a convicted arms dealer, the merchant of death, Savannah, as you noted earlier. There were conversations in the back and forth that took place over the course of the last several months where the Russians appear to have expressed interest into one of their citizens who was an assassin, who was being held in Germany by the German government . But that was a nonstarter in the course of the back and forth. [08:55:20] But as Andrea indicated, at the end of the day, when the Russians said they would give up Brittney Griner and Brittney Griner, the president of United States made the decision to go with it. GUTHRIE: All right. Peter, thank you very much. This has been NBC News Special Report covering the release of Brittney Griner. And we`ve learned this morning she has been traded, as Peter mentioned, for a notorious Russian arms dealer who had been convicted and served about three quarters of his sentence, Victor Bout. That trade has secured her release. She is on route to San Antonio where we understand she`ll be receiving medical treatment. KOTB: And it was nice to see her wife, Cherelle, up there at the podium saying that at this moment, although there`s still a lot going on, she`s going to take this moment to pause and smile. headline: The Today Show for December 8, 2022, NBC
story_text: (COMMERCIAL BREAK) [08:00:00] HODA KOTB, NBC NEWS TODAY, CO-ANCHOR: It`s 8:00 on "TODAY." Coming up, flu fears. New concerns over medication shortages as cases spike from coast to coast. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: There`s hardly anything to choose from. (END VIDEO CLIP) KOTB: Coming up, what you can do to ensure your family is prepared this flu season. Plus, breast cancer breakthrough. The just-released study sparking hope for women with breast cancer who want to start a new family. What the promising new data shows about a safe path forward. And Garten`s variety. The Barefoot Contessa herself, Ina Garten, joins us for a full hour to help spruce up our holiday tables, from a new spin on some tasty treats to becoming the host with the most. Plus, a glimpse into some of our most treasured traditions. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) CROWD: Three, two -- yahey. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: Blast off. (END VIDEO CLIP) KOTB: We`ve got a fun-filled hour ahead with a few surprises along the way. Today, Thursday, December 8, 2022. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: Best friends. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: And "TODAY" super fans. CROWD: From Parkersburg, West Virginia. CROWD: From Pullman, Washington. CROWD: And Lynwood, Illinois. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: From Hagerstown, Maryland. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: Celebrating our 25th anniversary. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: Friends for 20 years. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: From El Paso, Texas. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: Here with my grandson. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: From Mechanicsville, Virginia. CROWD: Hello from Woodbine, Iowa. CROWD: And Cincinnati, Ohio. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: Celebrating Vicky`s birthday. CROWD: From Baton Rouge. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: Here to experience a magic. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: Of Christmas in New York. CROWD: From Mizpah, Minnesota. (END VIDEO CLIP) KOTB: Welcome back. How do we say thank you for coming out -- SAVANNAH GUTHRIE, NBC NEWS TODAY, CO-ANCHOR: I know. KOTB: -- every morning? This crowd, it`s like six people thick. It`s a big crowd. We cannot wait to get outside and visit with everybody in just a bit. But what do you say we get to our news at 8:00? CRAIG MELVIN, NBC NEWS ANCHOR: Yes. KOTB: An early surge in flu cases is sending more Americans to the hospital and it`s actually causing pharmacies to run out of both prescription and over-the-counter treatments. NBC Sam brock has the latest on how long this might last and what you should do in case your drugstore shelves are empty. Sam, good morning. SAM BROCK, NBC NEWS CORRESPONDENT: Yes. Hoda, good morning. The mere fact that the flu season has arrived weeks in advance, as you said, has put parents in quite a crunch, pretty much across the board from antibiotics to antivirals. It`s true in Coral Gables, Florida, where I am, in San Francisco, California, Detroit, Michigan. All over the country. Now, the owner of University Pharmacist here tells me that amoxicillin right now, she has, about, maybe four or five patients worth of supplies left here. This is so important, it`s so critical because it`s the preferred antibiotic for kids. It`s a little bit milder, fewer side effects. That`s just one example. She wants to order more, cannot right now. Check out the store shelves. When it comes to decongestants, you see some Mucinex but the rest of the shelf here is empty. Robitussin, Sudafed they were down here, that`s gone as well. As far as anti-inflammatories for kids, Tylenol and Advil, there`s empty spaces on the shelf for that as well. All of it is unavailable. Now, the ASHP is a pharmacy group that tracks short supplies for drugs. They have right now, Hoda, some 260 drugs nationally that are short at the moment that includes Tamiflu, which is the most popular drug for treating the flu for kids, certainly, for adults as well. The issue with Tamiflu says one of their manufacturers, they have enough supply. They said it`s available for pharmacies to buy, but the owner here tells me it now cost three times of what it did just a few weeks ago. So, that anecdotally, is something that we`re seeing on the ground. This problem could go on for a number of weeks, well into the holidays. One of the advice -- pieces of advice doctors have for you, make you`re your pediatricians office contacts the pharmacy ahead of time to see if they have a drug in stock and to ask if there`s a viable alternative if there`s not. But parents right now are having to get creative as they go through this period where everybody is getting sick. Hoda, back to you. KOTB: Yes, happening in my neighborhood, too. All right. Sam Brock for us. Sam, thank you. GUTHRIE: For the first time in four decades, journalists and other employees at " The New York Times " are staging a large-scale walkout. The 24-hour strike by more than 1,000 members of the news gilded New York started just after midnight. The union says it lost patience with contract talks that have gone on for two years. A spokesperson for the "The Times" denied the talks were at an impasse and said it was disappointing that the union had taken what she called an extreme action. Negotiations have stalled over wages and remote work rules. MELVIN: A new study has found that women who`ve been treated for breast cancer may be able to pause their follow-up medications long enough to have a baby. After treatment, patients often take drugs to suppress their hormones for up to 10 years, but those drugs can also make it hard to conceive. [08:05:00] The new research led by Dr. Ann Partridge looked at how to balance the need for drug therapy with the desire to complete a family. And it found that within three years of pausing their medications, women had no greater risk of their cancers returning than those who stayed on the drugs, and about two-thirds were able to conceive and have a child. GUTHRIE: Well, grownups, who can`t recall third grade English lessons, can probably still sing every word of the "Schoolhouse Rock" cartoon that aired on Saturday mornings in the `70s and `80s. Well, George Newall, the man who helped create those classis tunes has passed away. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: Conjunction junction what`s your function. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: Hooking up words and phrases and clauses. (END VIDEO CLIP) GUTHRIE: I mean, we`re just singing it right here. KOTB: Yes. Uh-huh. MELVIN: Uh-huh. GUTHRIE: Those cartoons had a generation of kids about math and science and civics and grammar. Newall was an advertising pro. He composed all of those songs including "I`m Just a Bill on Capitol Hill." Remember that one? KOTB: Uh-huh. GUTHRIE: "Three is a Magic Number", he got the idea when a colleague with children asked about putting multiplication tables to music. George Newall was 88 years old. What a legacy. KOTB: Wow. Indeed. Wow. All right. Guys, would you like a little "Morning Boost"? GUTHRIE: Yes. MELVIN: Yes. KOTB: You got it. As you probably know, a white elephant party, it`s when you get together with your friends and you exchange silly gifts, usually just for kicks. So, Baylor University volleyball player Lauren Briseno never imagined she would -- what she would unwrap during their white elephant party that her coach hosted for the team. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) LAUREN BRISENO, BAYLOR UNIVERSITY VOLLEYBALL PLAYER: Hear ye, hear ye. It is with great exclamation that this proclamation be read. Due to unwavering diligence and determination for relentlessness and execution of incredible skills at the highest levels. For you (ph) of this year proclamation has hereby earned yourself a full scholarship. (END VIDEO CLIP) MELVIN: Oh, wow. GUTHRIE: Wow. KOTB: Lauren is a sophomore, by the way. She was a walk-on on the volleyball team. That was a surprise scholarship. She said she was eternally grateful. I mean, you think you`re getting one of those white elephant gifts. GUTHRIE: I know. KOTB: And you get one of that. GUTHRIE: Exactly. It sure beats the fridge magnet or whatever. MELVIN: Yes. GUTHRIE: All right. KOTB: Let`s go to NBC`s chief White House correspondent Peter Alexander with reaction there. Hey, Peter. PETER ALEXANDER, NBC CHIEF WHITE HOUSE CORRESPONDENT: Hey, Hoda and Savannah, good morning to you. We want to pull back the curtain a little bit about what we know happened already earlier this morning. As you just heard from the President earlier this morning, President Biden joined in the Oval Office by Cherelle Griner, who you just heard from, as well as the Secretary of State Tony Blinken and the Vice President Kamala Harris , who you see there were able to speak with Brittney Griner by phone. And then later Cherelle Griner, Brittney Griner`s wife, was able to have a private conversation by phone with her wife from the President`s study. So the question now is, where does she go? Senior administration officials are telling NBC News that Brittney Griner is being flown to a military medical facility in San Antonio for care and treatment effectively to make sure that she is physically well and to check on her. You can imagine the mental and physical ordeal that Griner would have had over the course of nearly 10 months behind bars. She was there first attain February 17th of this year. We are told that Cherelle Griner will be flying to San Antonio where she will have the first opportunity to greet her wife. But for the White House, this is a major diplomatic achievement. But as you note, it does come with some significant frustration, the inability to be able to get Paul Whelan home as well. Whelan, a US businessman, a former US Marine remains detained in Russia. We`re told by senior officials here that the US did everything in its power to try to bring Whelan home as well. But the Russians made it very clear that it was going to be Brittney Griner or no one. The US continues to deny that Whelan was a spy, but his espionage case, Savannah and Hoda, at this point, the Russians are not willing to turn Whelan over. Back to you. It was his trade that secured the release of Brittney Griner this morning. headline: What We Learned From Voters In This Week`s Elections About The Issues That Really Matter To Them And Where The Country May Be Headed From Here
story_text: [08:15:00] WILLIE GEIST: On election day, all of the polls, the punditry, the focus groups, and the tea leaves give way to voters. Energized by a swirl of issues, inflation, abortion, crime, immigration, and the very foundations of democracy, Americans turned out in near record midterm numbers to make a loud statement about what they`re seeing in the country and what needs to change. NBC News Capitol Hill Correspondent Ali Vitali looks closer in our "Sunday Focus". (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) ALI VITALI, NBC NEWS CAPITOL HILL CORRESPONDENT (voiceover): They were the midterms that few saw coming. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: What happened to the red wave, Congresswoman? VITALI (voiceover): History defying results. BIDEN: We lost fewer seats and House representatives in any democratic president`s first elected midterm, at least 40 years. VITALI (voiceover): Near record turnout and a twist in where the competitive seats really were. Dems holding on in red states like Kansas. While losing key seats in blue New York. REP. SEAN PATRICK MALONEY (D-NY): I don`t like to lose, but my opponent won this race. And he won it fair and square. VITALI (voiceover): The economy and inflation, the top issue for voters, and a weak point for Democrats who struggled to offer a clear response. But issues like abortion and threats to democracy acted as a dam to the previously predicted red wave for Republicans. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: I`m out to say where democracy. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: I don`t think that a body of strangers should tell us what our choices should be. VITALI (voiceover): In crucial states like Michigan and Pennsylvania, abortion rights surpassed inflation as voters` number one concern, allowing Democrats to notch key governor and Senate race wins and quiet gains on the state level. Dems not losing a single state legislative chamber for the first time in nearly 90 years. Back in Washington, Republicans now grappling with how it could have gone so wrong. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: Look, I`m frustrated that it didn`t turn out well for us. VITALI (voiceover): From once predicting a more than 20-seat margin in the House of Representatives to just being happy with a majority. REP. KEVIN MCCARTHY (R-CA): What`s was our mission? To win the majority, to stop Biden`s agenda, and fire Nancy Pelosi . All of that is accomplished. VITALI (voiceover): Maybe, but if Republicans do take the House, it`ll be very slim margins. Giving all members more power. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: I think it`s wonderful because everybody`s voice needs to be considered. [08:20:00] VITALI (voiceover): And GOP Leader Kevin McCarthy. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: Oh, I think there`s some questions about leadership. VITALI (voiceover): His future as house speaker now thrown into flux. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: I expect there will be a challenge. VITALI (voiceover): But amid a week of surprises, one important traditional hallmark, candidates who lost saying so. TIM MICHELS (R-WIS) GUBERNATORIAL CANDIDATE: Unfortunately, the math doesn`t add up. I just called Governor Evers and conceded. I wish the Evers family well. VITALI (voiceover): Not necessarily a given. With nearly 300 election deniers on the ballot and a former president insisting they make election denialism a central focus. KARI LAKE (R-AZ) GUBERNATORIAL CANDIDATE: Trump won, you`re right. VITALI (voiceover): That said, more than half of election denying candidates won their races, many coming to Congress now in 2023. And in the aftermath, Republicans also reckoning with the Trump of it all. Many of his hand-picked candidates lost. DONALD TRUMP , FORMER U.S. PRESIDENT: Well, I think if they win, I should get all the credit. And if they lose, I should not be blamed at all. VITALI (voiceover): While pro-democracy candidates won in key states. KELLY: No one party has a monopoly on good ideas. VITALI (voiceover): One of the Democrat`s strongest voting blocs, Gen Z. young voters showing up in record numbers. Rallying around things like student loan forgiveness. Among them, 25-year-old Maxwell Frost who won his election in Florida, making him the first Gen Zer elected to Congress. CROWD: Maxwell. Maxwell. VITALI (voiceover): And in a midterm election full of firsts, another. A record $17 billion spent on campaigns and ads. All for the country to wake up Wednesday pretty much how it went to bed on election night, divided down the middle. (END VIDEO CLIP) GEIST: And Ali joins me now live. Ali, good morning. It`s great to see you. So, after the stunning midterm elections, there`s been a lot of talk about Republicans walking away from Donald Trump , but we`ve heard that before. VITALI (on camera): Yes. GEIST: And the former president made it very clear again this week, he will not go quietly or perhaps at all. VITALI: Yes, that`s right, because Mr. Trump is expected to announce another run for president this week down at Mar-a-Lago. But it comes as the party that he`s controlled for the last six years has spent the last week actively pondering a future or as "The New York Post" said, a defuture without him. One of the names that keeps coming up for 2024 is Florida Governor Ron DeSantis . But we know that former V.P. Mike Pence , former Ambassador Nikki Haley, former Secretary of State Mike Pompeo , also others, they all likely have their eyes on the presidential prize this coming cycle. And while Mr. Trump`s had a bad political week, we have seen this time and again, Willie, Republicans end up going back and sticking by the former president. So, time will tell if this moment is actually any different. Willie. GEIST: Yes, see you January 6th for that. VITALI: Yes, exactly. GEIST: Meanwhile, we wake up this morning Democrats in control of the Senate. And as Steve Kornacki told us again last night, the house still very much in play. VITALI: Yes. GEIST: Extraordinary. Ali, thank you very much. Coming up next a new "Sunday Sitdown" with Daniel Radcliffe on the fun of playing "Weird Al" Yankovic in a new movie and the rocket ride of being "Harry Potter". And then a life well-lived, the pioneering journalist who broke down the locker room door for the women who came after her. And as we head to break, our photo of the week. The iconic Dolly Parton performing at last weekend`s Rock and Roll Hall of Fame induction ceremony in Los Angeles. After initially saying she did not think belonged in that hall, Dolly finally relented to the fans and accepted the honor. She even wrote and performed a new song for the occasion called "Rockin`". Dolly joined in this year`s class by Duran Duran, Eminem, Lionel Richie, Carly Simon, among others. Congratulations to Dolly, our national treasure. (COMMERCIAL BREAK) [08:25:00] (LOCAL NEWS) (COMMERCIAL BREAK) [08:30:00] (LOCAL NEWS) (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) CECILY STRONG, ACTRESS: The Maricopa County officials are incompetent. And it`s my belief that the election is rigged and the results should be thrown out. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: It sounds like new numbers coming in which has you taking a narrow lead over Katie Hobbs . STRONG: Which is why I have always said, this is democracy. Trust the system. Trust the voters. (END VIDEO CLIP) GEIST: That is Cecily Strong as Arizona Republican Gubernatorial candidate Kari Lake on last night`s new episode of "Saturday Night Live." Legendary comedian Dave Chappell hosted the show with musical guest Black Star. END Content and programming copyright 2022 NBCUniversal. ALL RIGHTS RESERVED.
