headline: Today for October 27, 2022, NBC
story_text: (COMMERCIAL BREAK) [07:00:16] SAVANNAH GUTHRIE, NBC NEWS ANCHOR: Good morning. It`s Thursday. Big developments overnight in two key races that kind of decides who`s in charge in Washington. HODA KOTB, NBC NEWS ANCHOR: With just 12 days to go until the midterms, we`re going to break it all down for you. It is October 27th. This is Today. New accusations, another woman comes forward claiming Herschel Walker urged her to have an abortion. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: I do not believe that Herschel is morally fit to be a U.S. senator. (END VIDEO CLIP) KOTB: While in Pennsylvania, John Fetterman addresses his debate performance. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) LT. GOV. JOHN FETTERMAN (D-PA), SENATOR CANDIDATE: During that debate wasn`t exactly easy. (END VIDEO CLIP) KOTB: We got it all covered. Crisis mode, hospitals nationwide being forced to take drastic measures to handle the tripledemic surge of flu, COVID, and RSV. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) UNIDENTIFIED MALE: Not only are there a lot of sick kids right now, there`s no place for them to go. (END VIDEO CLIP) KOTB: Just ahead, the new message from health officials all families need to hear. Breaking overnight, a new wave of protests in Iran, despite authorities intensifying a brutal crackdown, this morning the powerful scenes playing out across the country. Under pressure, Tesla reportedly facing a criminal investigation over its autopilot claims after a string of high profile crashes. So has the popular automaker misled consumers about how safe their cars really are? Those stories, plus, members only. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: Contrary to popular belief, you can be any age to join AARP. (END VIDEO CLIP) KOTB: From AARP to AAA, the surprising clubs you can sign up for to save big. And feeling lucky. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) UNIDENTIFIED MALE: Here are tonight`s winning numbers. (END VIDEO CLIP) KOTB: With no winner overnight, the Powerball jackpot jumps to a whopping $800 million, one of the largest prizes ever now up for grabs. Today, Thursday, October 27th, 2022. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: From NBC News, this is Today with Savannah Guthrie and Hoda Kotb live from Studio 1A in Rockefeller Plaza. KOTB: Well, good morning. It is so good to see you, happy that you`re here joining us. It is a Thursday morning. GUTHRIE: Well, you got it lined up if you want to get those Powerball tickets. The drawing is this weekend so you have time to get your tickets but jackpots up to 800 million. KOTB: It is. We`re going to have a lot more on jackpot fever coming up. But we`re going to start with another big countdown. We`re talking about the one to the midterm. GUTHRIE: Yes, 12 days to go now, and the spotlight is intensifying on two major races in Georgia and Pennsylvania. What happens there could impact the lives of every American. KOTB: Here`s what`s at stake, the balance of power in the Senate and the direction of key issues from the economy to abortion rights to rising crime rates, NBC`s senior Washington correspondent Hallie Jackson has the very latest for us. Hey, Hallie, good morning. HALLIE JACKSON, NBC NEWS SENIOR WASHINGTON CORRESPONDENT: Hey Hoda, hey Savannah. You have laid out the stakes and it is crunch time now, right, for candidates in these really important really close races with big guns like former presidents in both parties set to hit the campaign trail in the coming days. And the focus today turning to Georgia, where there`s a new abortion allegations surfacing, and one of the country`s most closely watched matchups. (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) JACKSON (voice-over): With less than two weeks to go this morning, the future of the Senate could hang on to key states with neck and neck races in Pennsylvania and Georgia, where there`s now another twist, Republican Herschel Walker who`s campaigned on an anti-abortion platform now denying a new allegation from a second woman who says Walker pressured her to have an abortion in the early 90s. HERSCHEL WALKER (R-GA), SENATOR CANDIDATE: What I`m saying, this is a lie and I`ve said it once and I`ve moved on my campaign. JACKSON (voice-over): The anonymous woman sharing her voice only came forward in a Zoom press conference arranged by Attorney Gloria Allred. The accuser saying after she became pregnant in 1993, Walker encouraged her to have an abortion, adding she first couldn`t go through with the procedure, but that Walker encouraged her to go back driving her to a Dallas clinic where she had the abortion. The woman explaining why she`s speaking up now. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: I am a registered Independent and I voted for Donald Trump in both elections. I do not believe that Herschel is morally fit to be a U.S. senator. JACKSON (voice-over): NBC News has not verified her allegations and the woman did not provide evidence Walker was involved in her abortion. WALKER: I`m done with this foolishness. JACKSON (voice-over): The Republican candidate and former football star also denied allegations earlier this month from another former girlfriend who says Walker paid for her abortion in 2009. In a statement the campaign for Walker`s opponent, Senator Raphael Warnock says Walker has a problem with the truth, a problem answering questions, and a problem taking responsibility for his actions. That match up, very close with recent polling showing Warnock leading by just five points. And in another closely watched race in Pennsylvania a tossup with polls ranking Democratic Lieutenant Governor John Fetterman and Republican candidate Dr. Mehmet Oz within the margin of error. [07:05:11] FETTERMAN: During that debate wasn`t exactly easy, you know, I knew it wasn`t going to be easy after, you know, having a stroke after five months. JACKSON (voice-over): Fetterman appearing at a campaign rally in Pittsburgh after raising $2 million, his team says, in the hours after his one and only debate against Republican Mehmet Oz. Fetterman facing questions about his at times halting debate performance with lingering auditory processing issues after a stroke five months ago. Oz also on the campaign trail hammering the issue of crime and on defense against a new Democratic ad highlighting his debate comments on abortion. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: This is who Dr. Oz wants in charge of women`s health care decisions. MEHMET OZ (R-PA), SENATOR CANDIDATE: I want women, doctors, local political leaders, local political leaders. (END VIDEOTAPE) GUTHRIE: Meanwhile, Hallie, the President hitting the campaign trail today, what do you expect? JACKSON: He is all about the economy, Savannah, in this kind of closing argument here trying to highlight his administration`s record on something we know that voters care about the economy plus cost of living. The top issue that voters say matters to them come Election Day. The President is going to be at Upstate New York to argue that Democrats economic policies are better than Republicans, even as many GOP candidates have pointed to high inflation in their midterm campaigns. You`ve also got the president`s cabinet fanning out across the country too. All of it is part of this full core press ahead of Election Day. Savannah? GUTHRIE: Twelve days to go. Hallie Jackson, thank you. And we turn now to growing concerns over the dangerous tripledemic of viruses nationwide flu, COVID, and the respiratory illness, RSV. With cases surging, some hospitals even in areas of warmer weather, are running out of beds. NBC national correspondent Gabe Gutierrez is inside Phoenix Children`s Hospital this morning with more. Gabe, good morning. GABE GUTIERREZ, NBC NEWS NATIONAL CORRESPONDENT: Savannah, good morning. It`s only October but doctors here and across the country are dealing with patient numbers that they usually don`t see until much later in winter. And overnight we met one mother who barely heard of RSV until she ended up here with her newborn son. (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) GUTIERREZ (voice-over): This morning, the latest wave of child respiratory illnesses is spreading prompting more concerns of a tripledemic this winter. In Arizona, RSV cases are up 344 percent over a typical season. CHEYENNE SHIELDER`S (ph), SON DIAGNOSED WITH RSV: Terrifying, this is serious illness. You know, with him being this young. He doesn`t have an immune system to fight it off. GUTIERREZ (voice-over): Cheyenne Shielder`s (ph) two-month-old son Ryder (ph) was in the hospital overnight. (on camera): What would you tell other parents? SHIELDER: Look up the symptoms of RSV and trust her gut to because I was on the border about coming or not to the hospital. And I feel like I probably should have come a little bit sooner. GUTIERREZ (voice-over): Last year and now this year, Phoenix Children`s Hospital has been dealing with an unusually high number of RSV cases, though the facility is not at capacity, it`s bracing for a rough winter DR. WASSIM BALLAN, PHOENIX CHILDREN`S HOSPITAL CHIEF OF INFECTIOUS DISEASES: COVID-19 combined with a potentially bad influenza season and now we`re seeing RSV going up at the same time, that obviously makes us concerned that we might get into this triple pandemic situation. GUTIERREZ (voice-over): This year, even western and southern states with warmer temperatures are seeing a significant rise in RSV and flu cases. In Arizona, 87 percent of pediatric hospital beds are occupied, in Texas 91 percent, Seattle Children`s tells NBC News it`s at 200 percent capacity in the ER. DR. ASHISH JHA, WHITE HOUSE COVID-19 RESPONSE COORDINATOR: Under normal circumstances, about 90 percent of kids end up getting RSV at least once, by the time there are two. Because of the pandemic, some of the kind of standard patterns have been disrupted so we`re seeing a lot of RSV at once. GUTIERREZ (voice-over): Parents now worried sick across the country from San Diego where Fernanda Costanarez (ph) is caring for baby Alejandra (ph). FERNANDA COSTANAREZ (ph), DAUGHTER DIAGNOSED WITH RSV: She was struggling to breathe. She was struggling breathing. And we got scared because she had no color at all on her skin. GUTIERREZ (voice-over): To Washington, D.C. where three-year-old Izzy Banki (ph) is recovering. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: Nobody wants to like hold their kid down and hold a mask on their face. And so she`s screaming and trying and trying to rip the breathing tubes out. And that breaks your heart as a parent. (END VIDEOTAPE) GUTIERREZ: And while COVID cases are trending downward nationwide, right now, there are concerns about new strains this winter. And of course, Savannah, concerns about that flu season that is already hitting many states hard around the country. Savannah? GUTHRIE: All right, Gabe Gutierrez, thank you. KOTB: Meantime, new unrest is rocking Iran with massive protests across the country more than a month after a young woman`s death while being held by the nation`s morality police. Some of those demonstrations turned deadly, emitted ongoing crackdown and that`s led to new sanctions from the United States, NBC`s chief international correspondent Keir Simmons has been following this story for us. Hey Keir, good morning. [07:10:00] KEIR SIMMONS, NBC NEWS CHIEF INTERNATIONAL CORRESPONDENT: Hoda, good morning to you. And we`re just getting more incredibly impactful video from the city of Mahabad in north western Iran. Take a look at this. This is a just this morning. You can see protesters targeting a building there. Later they seem to be throwing stones there. Looks like there is tear gas. The Kurdish rights group that posted this video says a number of government buildings have been taken over and that it`s also rounds the funeral of a man who was shot dead during protests yesterday. (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) SIMMONS (voice-over): This morning, a powerful image seen around the world. A young woman not wearing a headscarf stands on the roof of a car hands in the air as crowds attempt to reach the grave of Mahsa Amini. And near the cemetery, this video from an independent Kurdish human rights organization, captioned the resistance is glorious. Huge numbers across Iran determined to mourn and to protest the death of the 22-year-old, marking 40 days after she died in the hospital, the morality police targeting her for allegedly violating the country`s strict clothing code. In the capital of Tehran, clashes with the security forces and the sound of gunfire. In Mahsa`s hometown, they shouted women, life, freedom. And these demonstrators daring to chant freedom, freedom, enough of the despotism. Then images like this one, smoke rising told them another violent crackdown there. Reports say live rounds were used and tear gas. The Iranian authorities switching off the internet in the city. But a semi official news agency reporting at least 10,000 demonstrated. Thousands of miles away the White House announcing sanctions targeting more than a dozen Iranian officials. KARINE JEAN-PIERRE , WHITE HOUSE PRESS SECRETARY: Our message to Iran is very, very clear, stop killing your people and stop sending weapons to Russia to kill Ukrainians. SIMMONS (voice-over): A dramatic change from earlier this year when the Biden administration was trying to negotiate a nuclear deal with Iran. But this morning, there is no sign of compromise in Tehran and no backing down by these young female protesters and the many men out on the streets in support. (END VIDEOTAPE) SIMMONS : And just underscoring how incredibly tense it is in Iran, Hoda, a news of a shooting that was not related to the protests, 15 worshippers were killed, ISIS claiming responsibility for that. The government blaming foreign terrorists. It just emphasizes how incredible it is that these protesters are coming out on the streets day after day to support Mahsa Amini. KOTB: Yes, and worth repeating, too, that as you said, it`s not just women on those streets, it looked like equal numbers of men that we were seeing in those videos all with the same cause. All right, Keir Simmons for us in London. Kier, thank you. GUTHRIE: Back home, we`ve got new concerns about energy bills this winter. We haven`t even handed out the candy to trick or treaters. But in recent weeks, a lot of us have gotten that early taste of the cold and it doesn`t bode well for what`s to come. NBC`s Tom Costello over in the Bronx with that story this morning. Tom, good morning. TOM COSTELLO, NBC NEWS CORRESPONDENT: Hi, Savannah, we are at an oil terminal facility here in the Bronx. So oil comes out of this facility and into homes across the Northeast. And millions of people use heating oil to heat their homes in the Northeast leading oil stocks right now, the lowest in decades. But there is no talk of rationing. It doesn`t matter if you heat your home with heating oil, gas, or electricity, you`re going to pay more to stay warm this winter. (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) COSTELLO (voice-over): From the Northeast and Midwest to parts of the south, Mother Nature has already given millions of us a sneak peek at what`s ahead. And this morning, the forecast for America`s collective wallet this winter may also be a bit frigid. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: It`s a very, very high bill. COSTELLO (voice-over): Across the board, energy costs are expected to be higher than last year. The federal government expects the biggest jumps for customers who use heating oil or natural gas to stay warm up, 27 and 28 percent. Two factors are driving the spike the global market affected by Russia`s war in Ukraine and OpEx plan to slash production of crude oil. The supply of heating oil in New England is also about a third of where it typically is. BRIAN DEESE, NATIONAL ECONOMIC COUNCIL DIRECTOR: We are operating right now at unacceptably low inventory levels. COSTELLO (voice-over): Still, and this is important, experts say that is not cause for concern. CHRIS HERB, CONNECTICUT ENERGY MARKETERS ASSOCIATION PRESIDENT: Supply is tight. That is undeniable. We have enough fuel to supply people`s needs at this time. And for over a century, our industry has never failed. COSTELLO (voice-over): Right now, the cost for a gallon of heating oil is about 5.70 per gallon. That`s up more than $2 from last year with eight states paying even more. DONNA HUBER (ph), RHODE ISLAND RESIDENT: There are people that are going to have to choose between feeding their families or heating their home. And that`s scary. You know, it`s really scary. COSTELLO (voice-over): Experts say the best ways to say, check windows for leaks and seal or replace if needed. Adjust your thermostat when you`re sleeping or out of the house. And schedule routine services to maintain your heating systems. [07:15:05] UNIDENTIFIED MALE: This will heat about 2,000 square feet. COSTELLO (voice-over): Donna Huber (ph) in Rhode Island is among many Americans looking for alternatives to stay warm. Recently installing a wood stove in her home. HUBER (ph): I bought three quarts of wood for under $800. If I wanted to heat my house solely on the wood, that would take me through the season. That`s less than half of a tank of oil. (END VIDEOTAPE) GUTHRIE: Tom, there are also local programs that people can turn to for help. COSTELLO: You know, this is important, every state has Home Energy Assistance Programs, so if you have trouble paying your bill, and the bills are going to get expensive this winter, turn to those programs. And you might even check with your own utility company to see if they offer assistance. And by the way, if you can pay your bill, if it`s no problem, and you can round off, you know, most states offer that option, roundup your bill to help those in need, this may be the win or two offer an extra dollar to help those in need. Savannah? GUTHRIE: Tom, it`s a great idea, round up. Tom, thank you very much. KOTB: All right, 7:15 time to cut to the chase. You did not win the big prize in last night`s Powerball. story_text: (COMMERCIAL BREAK) [07:00:16] SAVANNAH GUTHRIE, NBC NEWS ANCHOR: Good morning. It`s Thursday. Big developments overnight in two key races that kind of decides who`s in charge in Washington. HODA KOTB, NBC NEWS ANCHOR: With just 12 days to go until the midterms, we`re going to break it all down for you. It is October 27th. This is Today. New accusations, another woman comes forward claiming Herschel Walker urged her to have an abortion. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: I do not believe that Herschel is morally fit to be a U.S. senator. (END VIDEO CLIP) KOTB: While in Pennsylvania, John Fetterman addresses his debate performance. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) LT. GOV. JOHN FETTERMAN (D-PA), SENATOR CANDIDATE: During that debate wasn`t exactly easy. (END VIDEO CLIP) KOTB: We got it all covered. Crisis mode, hospitals nationwide being forced to take drastic measures to handle the tripledemic surge of flu, COVID, and RSV. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) UNIDENTIFIED MALE: Not only are there a lot of sick kids right now, there`s no place for them to go. (END VIDEO CLIP) KOTB: Just ahead, the new message from health officials all families need to hear. Breaking overnight, a new wave of protests in Iran, despite authorities intensifying a brutal crackdown, this morning the powerful scenes playing out across the country. Under pressure, Tesla reportedly facing a criminal investigation over its autopilot claims after a string of high profile crashes. So has the popular automaker misled consumers about how safe their cars really are? Those stories, plus, members only. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: Contrary to popular belief, you can be any age to join AARP. (END VIDEO CLIP) KOTB: From AARP to AAA, the surprising clubs you can sign up for to save big. And feeling lucky. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) UNIDENTIFIED MALE: Here are tonight`s winning numbers. (END VIDEO CLIP) KOTB: With no winner overnight, the Powerball jackpot jumps to a whopping $800 million, one of the largest prizes ever now up for grabs. Today, Thursday, October 27th, 2022. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: From NBC News, this is Today with Savannah Guthrie and Hoda Kotb live from Studio 1A in Rockefeller Plaza. KOTB: Well, good morning. It is so good to see you, happy that you`re here joining us. It is a Thursday morning. GUTHRIE: Well, you got it lined up if you want to get those Powerball tickets. The drawing is this weekend so you have time to get your tickets but jackpots up to 800 million. KOTB: It is. We`re going to have a lot more on jackpot fever coming up. But we`re going to start with another big countdown. We`re talking about the one to the midterm. GUTHRIE: Yes, 12 days to go now, and the spotlight is intensifying on two major races in Georgia and Pennsylvania. What happens there could impact the lives of every American. KOTB: Here`s what`s at stake, the balance of power in the Senate and the direction of key issues from the economy to abortion rights to rising crime rates, NBC`s senior Washington correspondent Hallie Jackson has the very latest for us. Hey, Hallie, good morning. HALLIE JACKSON, NBC NEWS SENIOR WASHINGTON CORRESPONDENT: Hey Hoda, hey Savannah. You have laid out the stakes and it is crunch time now, right, for candidates in these really important really close races with big guns like former presidents in both parties set to hit the campaign trail in the coming days. And the focus today turning to Georgia, where there`s a new abortion allegations surfacing, and one of the country`s most closely watched matchups. (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) JACKSON (voice-over): With less than two weeks to go this morning, the future of the Senate could hang on to key states with neck and neck races in Pennsylvania and Georgia, where there`s now another twist, Republican Herschel Walker who`s campaigned on an anti-abortion platform now denying a new allegation from a second woman who says Walker pressured her to have an abortion in the early 90s. HERSCHEL WALKER (R-GA), SENATOR CANDIDATE: What I`m saying, this is a lie and I`ve said it once and I`ve moved on my campaign. JACKSON (voice-over): The anonymous woman sharing her voice only came forward in a Zoom press conference arranged by Attorney Gloria Allred. The accuser saying after she became pregnant in 1993, Walker encouraged her to have an abortion, adding she first couldn`t go through with the procedure, but that Walker encouraged her to go back driving her to a Dallas clinic where she had the abortion. The woman explaining why she`s speaking up now. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: I am a registered Independent and I voted for Donald Trump in both elections. I do not believe that Herschel is morally fit to be a U.S. senator. JACKSON (voice-over): NBC News has not verified her allegations and the woman did not provide evidence Walker was involved in her abortion. WALKER: I`m done with this foolishness. JACKSON (voice-over): The Republican candidate and former football star also denied allegations earlier this month from another former girlfriend who says Walker paid for her abortion in 2009. In a statement the campaign for Walker`s opponent, Senator Raphael Warnock says Walker has a problem with the truth, a problem answering questions, and a problem taking responsibility for his actions. That match up, very close with recent polling showing Warnock leading by just five points. And in another closely watched race in Pennsylvania a tossup with polls ranking Democratic Lieutenant Governor John Fetterman and Republican candidate Dr. Mehmet Oz within the margin of error. [07:05:11] FETTERMAN: During that debate wasn`t exactly easy, you know, I knew it wasn`t going to be easy after, you know, having a stroke after five months. JACKSON (voice-over): Fetterman appearing at a campaign rally in Pittsburgh after raising $2 million, his team says, in the hours after his one and only debate against Republican Mehmet Oz. Fetterman facing questions about his at times halting debate performance with lingering auditory processing issues after a stroke five months ago. Oz also on the campaign trail hammering the issue of crime and on defense against a new Democratic ad highlighting his debate comments on abortion. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: This is who Dr. Oz wants in charge of women`s health care decisions. MEHMET OZ (R-PA), SENATOR CANDIDATE: I want women, doctors, local political leaders, local political leaders. (END VIDEOTAPE) GUTHRIE: Meanwhile, Hallie, the President hitting the campaign trail today, what do you expect? JACKSON: He is all about the economy, Savannah, in this kind of closing argument here trying to highlight his administration`s record on something we know that voters care about the economy plus cost of living. The top issue that voters say matters to them come Election Day. The President is going to be at Upstate New York to argue that Democrats economic policies are better than Republicans, even as many GOP candidates have pointed to high inflation in their midterm campaigns. You`ve also got the president`s cabinet fanning out across the country too. All of it is part of this full core press ahead of Election Day. Savannah? GUTHRIE: Twelve days to go. Hallie Jackson, thank you. And we turn now to growing concerns over the dangerous tripledemic of viruses nationwide flu, COVID, and the respiratory illness, RSV. With cases surging, some hospitals even in areas of warmer weather, are running out of beds. NBC national correspondent Gabe Gutierrez is inside Phoenix Children`s Hospital this morning with more. Gabe, good morning. GABE GUTIERREZ, NBC NEWS NATIONAL CORRESPONDENT: Savannah, good morning. It`s only October but doctors here and across the country are dealing with patient numbers that they usually don`t see until much later in winter. And overnight we met one mother who barely heard of RSV until she ended up here with her newborn son. (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) GUTIERREZ (voice-over): This morning, the latest wave of child respiratory illnesses is spreading prompting more concerns of a tripledemic this winter. In Arizona, RSV cases are up 344 percent over a typical season. CHEYENNE SHIELDER`S (ph), SON DIAGNOSED WITH RSV: Terrifying, this is serious illness. You know, with him being this young. He doesn`t have an immune system to fight it off. GUTIERREZ (voice-over): Cheyenne Shielder`s (ph) two-month-old son Ryder (ph) was in the hospital overnight. (on camera): What would you tell other parents? SHIELDER: Look up the symptoms of RSV and trust her gut to because I was on the border about coming or not to the hospital. And I feel like I probably should have come a little bit sooner. GUTIERREZ (voice-over): Last year and now this year, Phoenix Children`s Hospital has been dealing with an unusually high number of RSV cases, though the facility is not at capacity, it`s bracing for a rough winter DR. WASSIM BALLAN, PHOENIX CHILDREN`S HOSPITAL CHIEF OF INFECTIOUS DISEASES: COVID-19 combined with a potentially bad influenza season and now we`re seeing RSV going up at the same time, that obviously makes us concerned that we might get into this triple pandemic situation. GUTIERREZ (voice-over): This year, even western and southern states with warmer temperatures are seeing a significant rise in RSV and flu cases. In Arizona, 87 percent of pediatric hospital beds are occupied, in Texas 91 percent, Seattle Children`s tells NBC News it`s at 200 percent capacity in the ER. DR. ASHISH JHA, WHITE HOUSE COVID-19 RESPONSE COORDINATOR: Under normal circumstances, about 90 percent of kids end up getting RSV at least once, by the time there are two. Because of the pandemic, some of the kind of standard patterns have been disrupted so we`re seeing a lot of RSV at once. GUTIERREZ (voice-over): Parents now worried sick across the country from San Diego where Fernanda Costanarez (ph) is caring for baby Alejandra (ph). FERNANDA COSTANAREZ (ph), DAUGHTER DIAGNOSED WITH RSV: She was struggling to breathe. She was struggling breathing. And we got scared because she had no color at all on her skin. GUTIERREZ (voice-over): To Washington, D.C. where three-year-old Izzy Banki (ph) is recovering. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: Nobody wants to like hold their kid down and hold a mask on their face. And so she`s screaming and trying and trying to rip the breathing tubes out. And that breaks your heart as a parent. (END VIDEOTAPE) GUTIERREZ: And while COVID cases are trending downward nationwide, right now, there are concerns about new strains this winter. And of course, Savannah, concerns about that flu season that is already hitting many states hard around the country. Savannah? GUTHRIE: All right, Gabe Gutierrez, thank you. KOTB: Meantime, new unrest is rocking Iran with massive protests across the country more than a month after a young woman`s death while being held by the nation`s morality police. Some of those demonstrations turned deadly, emitted ongoing crackdown and that`s led to new sanctions from the United States, NBC`s chief international correspondent Keir Simmons has been following this story for us. Hey Keir, good morning. [07:10:00] KEIR SIMMONS, NBC NEWS CHIEF INTERNATIONAL CORRESPONDENT: Hoda, good morning to you. headline: Democrat John Fetterman And Republican Dr. Mehmet Oz Face Off
story_text: [07:00:17] HODA KOTB, NBC NEWS ANCHOR: Good morning. It`s Wednesday, all eyes were on Pennsylvania overnight. SAVANNAH GUTHRIE, NBC NEWS ANCHOR: Yes. The first and only Senate debate there with control of Congress hanging in the balance. It is October 26th, this is Today. Center Stage, Democrat John Fetterman and Republican Dr. Mehmet Oz face off on the issues. JOHN FETTERMAN (D), PENNSYLVANIA SENATE CANDIDATE: My campaign would fight for Roe v. Wade. MEHMET OZ (R), PENNSYLVANIA SENATE CANDIDATE: John Fetterman picks everything to an extreme and those extreme positions hurt us all. GUTHRIE: And ongoing concerns over Fetterman`s fitness to serve. FETTERMAN: I had a stroke, he`s never let me forget that. GUTHRIE: This morning the candidates in their own words and the takeaways in one of the nation`s most important midterm contests. Inside the Rampage, new details on the gunman behind that deadly school shooting in St. Louis, with a letter found in his car is revealing about a possible motive, and the stories of bravery now emerging. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: I really credit my students a lot because even with the gunshots that close, they did not scream. GUTHRIE: That harrowing firsthand account just ahead. Cooling Off, housing prices falling fast after soaring to record highs. So is now the best time to buy, and what does it mean if you`re in the market to sell. We`ll break it down. All of that plus, Chaos and Controversy. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: Miss USA is Texas. GUTHRIE: The Miss USA pageant embroiled in scandal. Some contestants claiming it`s rigged. The organization`s president now suspended and an investigation underway. The very latest straight ahead. And breaking news, what scientists are now saying about whether you really need to rake those leaves and it could make your weekend a lot more enjoyable. Today, Wednesday, October 26, 2022. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: From NBC News, this is TODAY with Savannah Guthrie and Hoda Kotb live from Studio 1A in Rockefeller Plaza. GUTHRIE: Good morning, everybody. Welcome back to TODAY. It is Wednesday morning, nice to have you along with us. This raking story, you want to get back those hours of your childhood raking leaves, don`t you? KOTB: Can you imagine -- you go remember all the time your parents said you got to go out and rake the leaves and stuff them into hefty bags. Who knew that we didn`t have to do that? GUTHRIE: Science is saying something different this morning. We`ll get to that. KOTB: Yes. We got a busy morning a lot to get to including we`ve got some rare good news. It`s tied to the economy at least if you`re planning to buy a house. GUTHRIE: Yes. Prices are now going down at a record rate. Tom Costello is going to have everything we need to know. KOTB: Of course, we will begin with last night`s big debate in Pennsylvania. GUTHRIE: This was highly anticipated not only because of questions concerning Democrat John Fetterman`s health after his stroke six months ago, but also because this race could decide which party controls the Senate. And that will affect every single American come next year. We`ll show you how it all played out. Let`s start this morning with NBC`s Dasha Burns in Harrisburg. Dasha, good morning. DASHA BURNS, NBC NEWS CORRESPONDENT: Savannah, good morning. This debate was highly anticipated not just by voters here in Pennsylvania but people across the country. It`s an extremely tight race, just a couple of points separating these candidates in the polls. And in a battle against one of the most familiar faces on American television, many tuned in to see how Fetterman would fare after suffering a stroke earlier this year, and the stakes could not have been higher. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) BURNS (voice-over): In a race that could help decide the balance of power in Congress, Pennsylvania Democrat John Fetterman and Republican Mehmet Oz neck and neck in the polls finally face to face on the debate stage. FETTERMAN: I`m running to serve Pennsylvania. He`s running to use Pennsylvania. OZ: John Fetterman picks everything to an extreme and those extreme positions hurt us all. BURNS (voice-over): Fetterman acknowledging what he called the elephant in the room, the stroke that nearly killed him five months ago. FETTERMAN: I had a stroke, he`s never let me forget that. And I might miss some words during this debate, mush two words together. I`m also fighting for any forgotten community all across Pennsylvania. They ever got knocked down that had to be -- to get back up. And I`ve made my entire career dedicating to those kinds of pursuits. BURNS (voice-over): Fetterman using closed captioning to assist with auditory processing battling Dr. Oz. FETTERMAN: It`s about supporting and helping young earners -- excuse me, young students to give them a break. headline: The Today Show for October 26, 2022, NBC
story_text: [07:00:17] HODA KOTB, NBC NEWS ANCHOR: Good morning. It`s Wednesday, all eyes were on Pennsylvania overnight. SAVANNAH GUTHRIE, NBC NEWS ANCHOR: Yes. The first and only Senate debate there with control of Congress hanging in the balance. It is October 26th, this is Today. Center Stage, Democrat John Fetterman and Republican Dr. Mehmet Oz face off on the issues. JOHN FETTERMAN (D), PENNSYLVANIA SENATE CANDIDATE: My campaign would fight for Roe v. Wade. MEHMET OZ (R), PENNSYLVANIA SENATE CANDIDATE: John Fetterman picks everything to an extreme and those extreme positions hurt us all. GUTHRIE: And ongoing concerns over Fetterman`s fitness to serve. FETTERMAN: I had a stroke, he`s never let me forget that. GUTHRIE: This morning the candidates in their own words and the takeaways in one of the nation`s most important midterm contests. Inside the Rampage, new details on the gunman behind that deadly school shooting in St. Louis, with a letter found in his car is revealing about a possible motive, and the stories of bravery now emerging. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: I really credit my students a lot because even with the gunshots that close, they did not scream. GUTHRIE: That harrowing firsthand account just ahead. Cooling Off, housing prices falling fast after soaring to record highs. So is now the best time to buy, and what does it mean if you`re in the market to sell. We`ll break it down. All of that plus, Chaos and Controversy. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: Miss USA is Texas. GUTHRIE: The Miss USA pageant embroiled in scandal. Some contestants claiming it`s rigged. The organization`s president now suspended and an investigation underway. The very latest straight ahead. And breaking news, what scientists are now saying about whether you really need to rake those leaves and it could make your weekend a lot more enjoyable. Today, Wednesday, October 26, 2022. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: From NBC News, this is TODAY with Savannah Guthrie and Hoda Kotb live from Studio 1A in Rockefeller Plaza. GUTHRIE: Good morning, everybody. Welcome back to TODAY. It is Wednesday morning, nice to have you along with us. This raking story, you want to get back those hours of your childhood raking leaves, don`t you? KOTB: Can you imagine -- you go remember all the time your parents said you got to go out and rake the leaves and stuff them into hefty bags. Who knew that we didn`t have to do that? GUTHRIE: Science is saying something different this morning. We`ll get to that. KOTB: Yes. We got a busy morning a lot to get to including we`ve got some rare good news. It`s tied to the economy at least if you`re planning to buy a house. GUTHRIE: Yes. Prices are now going down at a record rate. Tom Costello is going to have everything we need to know. KOTB: Of course, we will begin with last night`s big debate in Pennsylvania. GUTHRIE: This was highly anticipated not only because of questions concerning Democrat John Fetterman`s health after his stroke six months ago, but also because this race could decide which party controls the Senate. And that will affect every single American come next year. We`ll show you how it all played out. Let`s start this morning with NBC`s Dasha Burns in Harrisburg. Dasha, good morning. DASHA BURNS, NBC NEWS CORRESPONDENT: Savannah, good morning. This debate was highly anticipated not just by voters here in Pennsylvania but people across the country. It`s an extremely tight race, just a couple of points separating these candidates in the polls. And in a battle against one of the most familiar faces on American television, many tuned in to see how Fetterman would fare after suffering a stroke earlier this year, and the stakes could not have been higher. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) BURNS (voice-over): In a race that could help decide the balance of power in Congress, Pennsylvania Democrat John Fetterman and Republican Mehmet Oz neck and neck in the polls finally face to face on the debate stage. FETTERMAN: I`m running to serve Pennsylvania. He`s running to use Pennsylvania. OZ: John Fetterman picks everything to an extreme and those extreme positions hurt us all. BURNS (voice-over): Fetterman acknowledging what he called the elephant in the room, the stroke that nearly killed him five months ago. FETTERMAN: I had a stroke, he`s never let me forget that. And I might miss some words during this debate, mush two words together. I`m also fighting for any forgotten community all across Pennsylvania. They ever got knocked down that had to be -- to get back up. And I`ve made my entire career dedicating to those kinds of pursuits. BURNS (voice-over): Fetterman using closed captioning to assist with auditory processing battling Dr. Oz. FETTERMAN: It`s about supporting and helping young earners -- excuse me, young students to give them a break. BURNS (voice-over): But experiencing some stumbles throughout the debate particularly during an exchange over fracking challenged by the moderators for past contradictory comments. FETTERMAN: I do support fracking and I don`t -- I don`t -- I support fracking and I stand and I do support fracking. [07:05:03] BURNS (voice-over): Fetterman says he`s fit to serve citing a letter from his doctor, but he would not commit to releasing his full medical records. FETTERMAN: I believe if my doctor believes that I`m fit to serve, and that`s what I believe is appropriate. BURNS (voice-over): The celebrity TV doctor never directly addressing Fetterman`s health but saying this during an exchange on education. OZ: Visited vocational schools. I`ve been answered but John, because obviously, I wasn`t clear enough for you to understand this. BURNS (voice-over): One point where Oz has not been clear how he`d vote on a 15 week abortion ban introduced by Republican Senator Lindsey Graham . OZ: I want women doctors, local political leaders, letting the democracy that`s always allowed our nation to thrive, to put the best ideas forward so states can decide for themselves. BURNS (voice-over): A clear difference from his opponent. FETTERMAN: My campaign would fight for Roe v. Wade, and if given the opportunity to codified into law. BURNS (voice-over): Oz also trying to court moderate undecided voters. But it was former President Trump`s endorsement that helped get him onto the Republican ticket here. MODERATOR: Donald Trump has supported you. He has endorsed you. Why won`t you fully commit to supporting him in 2024? OZ: Oh, I do. I would support Donald Trump if he decided to run for president. (END VIDEOTAPE) BURNS: And, Savannah, speaking to media after the debate, the Fetterman spokesperson said the campaign was thrilled with his performance saying he won "countless exchanges against Oz." And we asked the Oz spokesperson what the Republican meant when he said that decisions about abortion should be made between "a woman or her doctor and local political leaders." The campaign responded that he is "prolife" with exceptions for rape, incest and the life of the mother. And, Savannah, voters that we talked to overnight said that they wish they`d seen more substance and fewer attacks, Savannah. GUTHRIE: All right. Dasha Burns leading us off, thank you. Let`s turn to NBC`s Hallie Jackson. You watch the debate as well, Hallie. I mean, John Fetterman said the elephant in the room was his health, his recent stroke, his fitness to serve, how did it play in the room? HALLIE JACKSON NBC NEWS CORRESPONDENT: So I talked to some folks are in the room. I was on the phone with a campaign advisor right after the debate last night, Savannah. And here`s where I think it`s coming down at this point for Democrats, who are largely acknowledging that, yes, John Fetterman , it`s very evident, is clearly still recovering from a stroke. There were accommodations made, as Dasha talked about, the closed captioning, to be able to have him conduct this debate. But I will say that there is a sense among people close to the lieutenant governor that voters will understand that he had a health issue, that he is recovering, that he is putting himself out there. They`re going after Oz for the line about abortion access being between a woman, a doctor and local political leaders. I would expect to see some potential attack ads on that in the coming days. But he also talked with Democratic allies, Savannah, who questioned whether it will actually help that Fetterman was on the debate stage and questions overall on both sides of the aisle on how this is going to move the needle for Pennsylvania voters. This is such a close race. Every vote will matter in his race. It has bigger stakes nationally. And there is still a question mark of how voters will respond and react. GUTHRIE: And on the issues, we saw some themes play out that have obviously been -- it`s kind of a microcosm of what`s happening in other races where Republicans are hitting hard on the economy and crime, Democrats turning to abortion and we saw that last night. JACKSON: It was on full display, Savannah. You`re totally right. When you look at, for example, the abortion access, the answer from Oz. When you look at how Oz went after Fetterman on crime and the economy, we are seeing that not just in Pennsylvania. But you look at other debates that were happening overnight in places like New York, for example, where crime in the economy were also issues that Republicans were really trying to hit hard on Democrats. These are issues that are going to matter to voters in the next 13 days before Election Day. You saw them on stage and they`re going to continue to play out over the next two weeks. GUTHRIE: All right. Hallie Jackson, thank you very much. KOTB: Supreme Court Justice Samuel Alito says that leak of the draft opinion to overturn Roe vs. Wade endanger the life of justices. Those comments came last night during an event at the Heritage Foundation . Alito says the leak was "a great betrayal of trust," and it put targets on their backs. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) SAMUEL ALITO , SUPREME COURT JUSTICE: The leak also made those of us who were thought to be in the majority and support of overruling Roe and Casey targets for assassination because it gave people a rational reason to think they could prevent that from happening by killing one of us. (END VIDEO CLIP) KOTB: In May, the Supreme Court martial launched in an investigation to identify the leaker. No findings from that probe have been made public. GUTHRIE: Also this morning, new details are emerging from the investigation into that deadly high school shooting in St. Louis. Police say a letter left behind is shedding light on what may have led a former student to carry out that attack. NBC`s Emilie Ikeda has more on the story joins us from St. Louis. Emilie, good morning. EMILIE IKEDA, NBC NEWS CORRESPONDENT: Savannah, good morning. Investigators say one of the most revealing pieces of evidence was found in the suspect`s car, a hand written note where the teenage gunman called himself an isolated loner.
