headline: Today for October 20, 2022, NBC
story_text: (COMMERCIAL BREAK) [07:00:16] SAVANNAH GUTHRIE, NBC NEWS ANCHOR: Good Thursday morning from Washington and New York. Our top story, all eyes once again on Ukraine. HODA KOTB, NBC NEWS ANCHOR: Tension there building after new attacks and new threats. It is October 20th. This is Today. Leave immediately, this morning, thousands of residents in southern Ukraine being forced to flee their own homes. Mass evacuations underway after a warning of imminent attacks and martial law declared by Vladimir Putin . And this morning, mounting concern over power outages ahead of a harsh winter, we`ll have the very latest and a live report straight ahead. On the road, President Biden hits the campaign trail today in the closely watched battleground of Pennsylvania. Can he move the needle for the undecided voters with less than three weeks to go? Feeling the freeze, another day of bitter cold across much of the country, parts of the south waking up two record lows, but Al says, hang in there, a big warm ups on the way. They`ll have your full forecast. Consumer alert, the new warning from police after a string of robberies in cities across the country tied to popular online marketplaces. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) CMDR. RODNEY G. HILL, CHICAGO POLICE DEPARTMENT ENGLEWOOD DISTRICT: Nine times out of 10, if you see a deal that is too good to be true, it is. (END VIDEO CLIP) KOTB: This morning what you need to know before you click. Those stories, plus, "The Crown" and the controversy. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) UNIDENTIFIED MALE: It is with regret, the Prince and Princess of Wales are separating. (END VIDEO CLIP) KOTB: The growing backlash against the hit show`s upcoming storyline. Why an Oscar winner wants it to come with a disclaimer and how "The Crown`s" creator is responding. And smash hit. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) UNIDENTIFIED MALE: At the wall looking up, see you later. (END VIDEO CLIP) KOTB: The Astros defeat the Yankees in game one of the ALCS while the Padres rally to tie up their series with the Phillies in a game for the record books. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) UNIDENTIFIED MALE: Aaron Nola against Austin Nola, little brother against big brother. (END VIDEO CLIP) KOTB: The battle of the brothers going down in history, today, Thursday, October 20th, 2022. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: From NBC News, this is Today with Savannah Guthrie live from Washington, D.C. and Hoda Kotb live from Studio 1A in Rockefeller Plaza. KOTB: Well good morning. Good to see you. So happy you`re joining us on a Thursday morning. Savannah is joining us in D.C. And SG, can you imagine being the mom and dad you`re like, I`m cheering for both my sons. You go, no you go. It`s got to be a tough one. GUTHRIE: I know. Yes, moms are always like, no, I don`t have a favorite. No really, I don`t. Well, a lot more of those highlights in just a bit. Plus nearly two thirds of the country waking up to another morning of bitter cold, I know you`re feeling it there in New York, here Washington too. Record low temps expected in the south today. Al is tracking it and he has some good news on when it`ll feel a little more like fall. KOTB: But we are going to start this morning in Ukraine where new evacuations are being ordered. It comes as residents are being told to charge their devices after drone strikes knocked out key power stations, rolling blackouts now common. And this is just as the brutal Ukraine winter is approaching. NBC`s Cal Perry is in Ukraine for us. Cal, good morning. Give us the latest. CAL PERRY, NBC NEWS CORRESPONDENT: Hey, good morning to you, Hoda. Fresh strikes overnight, the target once again that vital energy infrastructure of Ukraine. It is what has prompted the mayor here to tell people turn off your electricity, save power. All the while as you mentioned, the bitter cold from the winter has arrived, the temperatures plunging overnight, all the while the strikes continue across Ukrainian cities. (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) PERRY (voice-over): This morning, the people of Kherson are caught in the middle. Thousands in the port city that has been under Russian occupation for months, now being ordered to evacuate by Russian installed leaders. Some getting text messages that read, dear residents, evacuate immediately. There will be shelling of residential areas by the armed forces of Ukraine. The evacuations and apparent reaction to Ukraine`s counter offensive in the region, recapturing villages and farmland in recent weeks, Ukrainian officials accusing Russia of trying to create hysteria. It comes on the same day Russian`s President Putin declared martial law in the four Ukrainian regions currently occupied by Russia. I have signed a decree, he said, introducing martial law into these four entities of the Russian Federation. Under the order Russia can, it says, legally seize Ukrainian homes and property, move civilian populations and create local militias, meaning Moscow may try to force Ukrainians to fight against their own country. JOE BIDEN, PRESIDENT OF THE UNITED STATES: It seems his only tool available to him is to brutalize individual citizens in Ukraine. PERRY (voice-over): From Mykolaiv and the south to Kyiv and the north, the Russian bombardment continues. In just over a month, at least 239 drones have been shot down by air defenses, according to the Ukrainian military. The ones that make it past those air defenses are frequently striking infrastructure targets, 30 percent of power plants have been destroyed. [07:05:17] Other times, civilians pay the price. Here in the capital of Kyiv, eight dead in 24 hours, all the while the threat of a nuclear attack looms. Children drill in a nearby school here in Kyiv. And while bulletproof vests are necessary on the battle front, swim caps and goggles must do here on the home front. (END VIDEOTAPE) PERRY: Now Ukraine is asking countries around the world to help with its air defense system. Israel the latest to offer hands saying it will help provide that very important early alert system. But holding back on the ammunition needed to actually shoot down the drones. Officials here are hoping to get that from the United States. Hoda? KOTB: We`re counting those young kids with swim caps and goggles, it`s just -- it`s also unsettling. Thank you so much. We appreciate your report there. Let`s move on back here at home. We`ve got another morning of cold temperatures and a lot of the country, record setting in parts of the South. Let`s bring in Mr. Roker to get a first check of the forecast. Good morning, Al. AL ROKER, NBC NEWS ANCHOR: All right, good morning, Hoda. Good morning, everybody. The good news is if you are one of the 76 million people under these frost advisory, freeze warnings, we`ve got some relief coming for you, so hold on. For this morning though, Memphis 39 degrees, Tallahassee right now 32, Orlando 55 degrees, Norfolk 39. But we are going to see a little bit of a change. For today though, it is going to stay cold but we are going to see a little relief. But for today, about 12 degrees below average in Buffalo behind where the Jetstream dips to the south. We`re looking at Pier 75 degrees, that`s 15 degrees above normal, Boise, Idaho 77. For tomorrow, those temperatures still a little on the chilly side from New York, Charlotte on into Jacksonville. But the warmth is coming, Little Rock 81, San Antonio 86, Dallas, it`s going to be 88 degrees. And as we get into early next week, temperatures moderate, look at this, we`ll be in the 60s in New York right on into early next week, 70s in Raleigh and in Cincinnati, Chicago as well. And hot springs Arkansas into the 80s. We have that record warmth out west, record cold in the east. However, it`s because of this jet stream that`s really been amplified. The good news is if you`re here in the east, we`re going to see a flip, cooler air with rain and snow, which is good news for Seattle and Portland. They have right now the worst air quality in the world because of all the heat and the wildfires. They`re going to see temperatures drop 10 to 25 degrees below normal here in the East, much warmer as we get into next week with temperatures 10 to 20 degrees above normal. So Savannah, we`re all getting some good news back to you. GUTHRIE: All right, I like that Al. Thank you. Well, this morning, new data is out. And it reveals more about the effects of inflation on families all across this country, and the Federal Reserve`s efforts to get it under control. This is some top business leaders are voicing big concerns about the months ahead. NBC`s Tom Costello here with us in Washington tracking it again. Not good news that we`re hearing from business leaders. TOM COSTELLO, NBC NEWS CORRESPONDENT: Not good news. And we`ve been talking for months about persistent sky high inflation. And now, the head of one of the country`s biggest banks, Goldman Sachs is warning about a possible volatile period as we head into 2023. Listen, when Goldman talks, people listen, for the average family, there`s less concern right now about whether we are entering a recession or already there, but rather, when will things improve and how do we cope right now. (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) COSTELLO (voice-over): From Main Street, USA to Wall Street, Americans are still staring down red hot inflation that shows no signs of cooling off. Now some top executives are warning of potentially tough times in the months ahead. DAVID SOLOMON , GOLDMAN SACHS CEO: I think it`s a time to be cautious. That doesn`t mean for sure that we have a really difficult economic scenario. But in the distribution of outcomes, there`s good chance we could have a recession. COSTELLO (voice-over): And Amazon founder, Jeff Bezos , also issuing a warning earlier this week tweeting, the probabilities in this economy tell you to batten down the hatches. With less than three weeks before the midterm elections, President Biden denies that the move to continue tapping into the nation`s emergency oil supply is politically motivated, calling on oil companies to increase production and their refining operations. BIDEN: You still make a significant profit. Your shareholders will still do very well. And the American people catch a break they deserve and get a fair price at the pump as well. COSTELLO (voice-over): But gas is just one part of the global inflation picture. In the U.K. inflation is running even hotter, above 10 percent. Food up a staggering 14.6 percent while the average American family now spends nearly $450 more per month to buy the same goods as last year. The head of the country`s largest retailer, Walmart , tell Savannah it`s hitting people in different ways. [07:10:00] GUTHRIE: Do you feel like consumers are hitting that point where they`re done paying those high prices? JOHN FURNER , WALMART U.S. CEO: I think it depends on the personal situation that consumers are in, really different depending on where you are around the country. COSTELLO (voice-over): For Stephanie Lane`s (ph) family of six living off a single income in Pennsylvania, it`s meant cutting back across the board. STEPHANIE LANE (ph), PENNSYLVANIA RESIDENT: It`s a hard pill to swallow when you have to really change everything you`ve done. And do it everything differently because you can`t afford it. COSTELLO (voice-over): Despite the challenging times, Stephanie (ph) says she and her family are looking forward. LANE (ph): We don`t know when it`s going to get better. But I do know it will. I have faith that it will. (END VIDEOTAPE) GUTHRIE: Tom, we`ve been talking so much about the Fed`s interest rates hikes and how it`s going into effect. And sometimes it takes time to see if they`re working. We`re already seeing some leading indicators right now turning up and affect in the economy. COSTELLO: Last week, you and I talked about a lagging indicator. The unemployment rate is a lagging indicator of what the economy is like right now. We have a new leading indicator, this is concerning. New home building fell 8 percent last month, the lowest since the earliest days of the pandemic, that`s a concern. Mortgage rates, of course, now up to 7.2 percent on a 30 year, that`s double in a year. As a result, existing home sales, we expect are going to be sliding dramatically when we get that data in and price is expected to fall dramatically. All of that is not good for the economy. GUTHRIE: All right, Tom, thank you so much. And, of course, another big focus here in Washington, the midterm elections, which is 19 days to go. Early voting already underway, President Biden is hitting the campaign trail in the battleground of Pennsylvania today. And that brings us over here to Kristen Welker, who`s been covering politics, of course. Well, let`s start here with gas prices. We talked to Tom about the economy, gas prices, is a leading indicator, both economically and politically for the White House. KRISTEN WELKER, NBC NEWS CHIEF WHITE HOUSE CORRESPONDENT: That`s absolutely right. And there`s no doubt that there`s a lot of concern about gas prices, which have ticked up a bit over the past month. They`re down significantly, though, from their high in the summer over $5 a gallon. Yesterday, President Biden announced they`re releasing another 15 million barrels from the Strategic Petroleum Reserve. But look, this is really the tail end of an announcement that was made several months ago to release 180 million barrels. And Savannah, it`s not clear it`s going to have a big impact on gas prices. What it does is it allows the President to make the case that he is working on this issue, which 44 percent of Americans say is their top issue right now heading into these midterms. I talked to the White House Chief of Staff Ron Klain , what`s the first thing he does every morning? Check gas prices. And it underscores, Savannah, the fact that what happens in November could very much be determined by the price of the pump. GUTHRIE: Yes, because it`s something that absolutely everyone feels and it creates a ripple through the economy. Let`s talk about the issue of abortion. Democrats thought they had a lot of momentum with that issue right on the heels of the Dobbs decision in June. Now, it doesn`t seem that it`s having as much of a sway with independent voters. WELKER: That`s right. And you look at the swing that we`re seeing among independent women in particular, who said that they favored Democrats in September. Now, huge swing over to Republicans, you saw abortion as an energizing factor in races in Kansas in special election in New York in the primaries, but I think Democrats are concerned that they need to be having a broader appeal. You saw President Biden talking about the issue of abortion earlier this week. He said remember, basically the outrage that you felt on the day that Roe v. Wade was overturned, trying to turn back the clock in essence, Savannah, but there`s a real awareness and I think a message from the White House. Yes, we need to talk about abortion. But we need to talk about issues including the economy and crime that voters care about in this election cycle, too. So that`s why the President is going to be in Pennsylvania talking about infrastructure today, for example. GUTHRIE: Yes, the polls have shown that the Republicans appeared to have some momentum going into these midterms. The control of the Senate, control of the House is on the table, Pennsylvania, where the President will be today is a key Senate race and it`s tight. WELKER: It`s very tight. It`s basically a statistical dead heat, Savannah. And what`s notable about the President stop in Pennsylvania today, he`s going to be talking about infrastructure. And here you can see these polls between John Fetterman and Dr. Oz. He`s going to talk about infrastructure and then hold a fundraising event with John Fetterman . So not the typical rally that you would usually see a President hold in these closing weeks of a campaign. Why? Well, his approval ratings are low. And I think a lot of Democrats are concerned that he will hurt, he will hinder them instead of helping them. And so that`s why I think you`re not seeing these traditional rallies. But I spoke to an administration official who said, look, the bottom line is, we think it`s more effective to have him out talking about things like infrastructure, talking about things like abortion, gas prices, the things that he has worked on, instead of basically shouting at a crowd. They point to Obama, they point to Trump, they say, look, they had big losses in their midterms as well. So they don`t necessarily see that as an effective strategy. They`re also saying he will be holding typical events getting closer. GUTHRIE: All right, Kristen Welker here in Washington with me. Thank you so much. Hoda to 14 minutes after the hour, I`ll send it over to you. [07:15:01] KOTB: All right, thank you SG. Now to the rising health concern for families across the country just as flu season is getting underway, doctors are seeing an alarming rise in cases of RSV. Now that`s a common respiratory illness that`s left some children in need of hospitalization. So the surge, so severe one Children`s Hospital in Connecticut is now using temporary units to handle their patients and is considering asking for national help. So what is going on? What`s causing it? Why now? NBC News medical contributor Dr. Natalie Azar is here with everything we need to know. Well, first of all, that sounds scary what`s happening in Connecticut. Let`s break it down. Tell us about RSV. And why is it exploding in this moment? DR. NATALIE AZAR, NBC NEWS MEDICAL CONTRIBUTOR: Right, so Hoda, so RSV is a typical seasonal respiratory virus, right? It is, by the time children are two years old, most of them will have been infected with RSV. But it does and it can cause a close to 60,000 hospitalizations every year in children. And the majority of people, it causes a mild cold like illness. So we`re talking runny nose, a low grade fever, a cough, sneezing. KOTB: How long does it last? AZAR: Usually lasts about one to two weeks, sometimes the symptoms can peak at day five. KOTB: OK. AZAR: But in certain individuals, when it goes from the upper respiratory tract into the lungs, it can actually cause more severe disease. And I think it`s very important, especially for caregivers out there of young ones who can`t communicate, the symptoms of more severe disease would be things like poor feeding, irritability, wheezing, or shortness of breath. Those are the kinds of symptoms and signs that you`d want to reach out to your pediatrician immediately. KOTB: So sometimes you wouldn`t know if your child has a cold or has this but either way, like, how do you treat it? What do you suppose to give them? AZAR: Well, that`s the thing. And so you mentioned a very good point, it`s actually indistinguishable, you know, from cold or flu or things like a COVID, you would actually need to get tested. You have to get tested, though in the doctor`s office, there are no home tests for this. In terms of treatment for the majority of people, the treatment is supportive. So that means rehydrating, managing the airway. There is a treatment, however, for people who are at risk, and that group includes premature infants, kids under the age of six months, heart lung problems, weakened immune systems, older folks. It`s a monthly injection that can actually prevent severe disease. KOTB: Just a last quick thing. There was a headline in -- here in New York that said COVID cases in some pockets of New York were up 20 percent. Is that a bellwether? Are we expecting like this big bounce in numbers? AZAR: Right, Hoda. So we`re talking about new strains, and they are descendants of the Omicron strain. This is not unexpected. This is what we expect the virus to do. At this point, it doesn`t appear that it`s causing more severe disease. But remember, more infections could lead to more hospitalizations, and then the convergence of flu. We worry about hospital capacity and of course, cases of lung COVID. So we`re certainly keeping an eye on it. KOTB: And that 20 percent is pretty alarming even in -- AZAR: It`s a pretty significant doubling time. That`s what`s making experts concerned. KOTB: All right, Dr. Azar, thank you. We appreciate it. It is 17 minutes after the hour. Hello, Craig. CRAIG MELVIN, NBC NEWS ANCHOR: Hello, good morning, Hoda. Good morning Dr. Natalie as well and good morning to you. October best part of the year for baseball fans, major league baseball playoffs underway right now. The Houston Astros came out swinging in game one of the ALCS. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) UNIDENTIFIED MALE: Drive into right, well hit, Judge on the run, and Chas McCormick, opposite field home run. (END VIDEO CLIP) MELVIN: And there you have it. Chas McCormick with Houston second home run of the inning there, they would go on to beat the Yankees four to two. Game two is tonight. Over to the National League now, the San Diego Padres scoring five runs in the fifth inning to take the lead there. They would hold on to that lead to win it, eight to five. That series all tied up at one game apiece. There was some history made in that game as noted at the top of the show here, Phillies pitcher Aaron Nola is facing his brother Austin Nola, who is a catcher for San Diego. You see their parents looking on there to the farm, right. It`s the first time in MLB postseason history that a pitcher faced his brother at the plate. Austin Nola getting the big RBI single there. That was smart the Padres in the fifth inning. And I heard you and SG in the top of the show about which, you know, as a parent watch. KOTB: -- you do, you know, who -- MELVIN: I`ll tell you who`s the favorite child, it`s Austin, the oldest child is always the favorite. KOTB: But, you know, I was just -- I was thinking of Peyton and Eli Manning`s mom and dad. How many times have they watch their two kids and there were one point they were in the Super Bowl together. It`s like, oh my, oh my, oh my. GUTHRIE: And guys, I was like either they put the split screen up of the parents so it`s like the brothers and the parents have to keep the neutral face, like game face. Yes, we like everyone. KOTB: Look at them, I can`t the jerseys, I see a Phillies Jersey maybe the mom`s got a Padres on. MELVIN: But if you look at the Phillies jersey, it looks like he`s got a Padres jersey on underneath and a Padres hat. KOTB: OK. All right, fair enough. Let`s go guys, time for the weather. Mr. Rocker we`re talking about some brutal cold. [07:20:01] ROKER: Although, Craig, I hope Sibby is not watching. MELVIN: I hope she`s not either. That`s just -- ROKER: -- you said the older is the favorite. MELVIN: Not in my house. Not in my house. ROKER: Nice clarification. I`ll do what I can to help you. MELVIN: Thank you. Anyway, for today, we do have that fire risk continuing in the western plains. So we`re watching that sunny and warm out west. It`s going to be another gorgeous day. They do really need the rain. We`re going to look at that in the next half hour and easing chill coming into the East. So that`s good news there. We`re going to get to your local forecast in the next 30 seconds. (COMMERCIAL BREAK) (LOCAL NEWS) ROKER: And that`s your latest weather. You know it`s cold when we got the hand warmers out. KOTB: SG, I got hand warmers in here, girl. GUTHRIE: Oh my gosh. But you know who`s happy Craig Melvin, he likes it when that thermostat is breezing cold. KOTB: Exactly. MELVIN: Fall and winter in 1A. KOTB: All right, coming up, it`s a big hit. But Kelly Cobiella, we got some controversy surrounding the upcoming season of "The Crown ." Tell us about it. KELLY COBIELLA, NBC NEWS ANCHOR: That`s right, Hoda. In fact Oscar winner Dame Judi Dench is now joining a chorus of critics calling some depictions in the new season, cruelly unjust. We`ll take a look at what all the controversy is about and also what the show`s creator is saying coming up. GUTHRIE: Well, that`s a good one. We`ll find out about that. Also, guys, if you buy or sell stuff online don`t want to miss this story, especially as we`re heading into the holidays, the new warning about criminals using popular sites to find their next victims. We`re going to break down the red flags to look for and give you advice for staying safe. But first, this is Today on NBC. (COMMERCIAL BREAK) MELVIN: Still ahead, the inspiring high school football player making sports history with her touchdown. [07:24:41] KOTB: Indeed. But first, your local news. (COMMERCIAL BREAK) (LOCAL NEWS) (COMMERCIAL BREAK) (LOCAL NEWS) (COMMERCIAL BREAK) (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) [07:30:18] UNIDENTIFIED MALE: Let`s please welcome the 2022 Caregiver Champion, it is not a better word to describe her, Savannah Guthrie. GUTHRIE: Thank you hidden heroes for this beautiful honor. And thank you most of all to caregivers for the privilege of knowing you. (END VIDEO CLIP) KOTB: We are back. Boy, that was beautiful. I have even seen the whole speech and I`m in. This is the reason Savannah is in D.C. She was honored with this year`s Caregiver Champion Award. And as Tom Hanks said, there`s no better descriptor than that. That was at the Elizabeth Dole Foundation`s heroes and history makers gala. Savannah, what a night, man, I mean, that looks beautiful. We`re so proud of you. GUTHRIE: Well, it was so cool. I mean, the caregivers were out in force. They just -- it was their special night. And I think we raised a lot of money for a really great cause. Senator Elizabeth Dole was there. This is her mission that she started 10 years ago. And coming up, we`re going to introduce you to the very first, so I call her the original kind of the OG caregiver that met Mrs. Dole in the hospital at Walter Reed 11 years ago and told the story of her experience. And boy that got Mrs. Dole on a mission and that mission is going strong. We`ll have more on that coming up. MELVIN: Maybe become such an important part of that mission, so more on that coming up in just a few minutes put. But right now, a check of your 7:30 headlines on this Thursday morning. Former President Donald Trump answering questions under oath yesterday in a defamation lawsuit that was brought by a writer who claims that Trump raped her in the mid-1990s, the deposition gave E. Jean Carroll`s lawyers a chance to interrogate Trump about the assault allegations, as well as statements he made in 2019 when she told her story publicly for the first time, Trump has called Carroll`s allegation quote, a hoax and a lie. KOTB: Less than three weeks after Hurricane Ian destroyed Florida Sanibel Island causeway, the bridge reopened yesterday. It was initially scheduled to reopen at the end of this month but crews worked around the clock to get the repairs done ahead of schedule. That entire road was completely washed out by floodwaters late last month. Crews used more than 8,000 loads of dirt, 2,400 loads of rock, and 4,000 tons of asphalt to finish those temporary repairs. KOTB: Wow, incredible. All right, in New York City tradition getting ready to make its return. Oh yes, the Radio City Rockettes, they`re busy gearing up for the Christmas Spectacular. This year, the show is promising new songs, new dances, new costumes, new everything and with all the old traditions, the Radio City Christmas Spectacular runs November 18th through January 2nd, it`s always on our list of things we do every single year. GUTHRIE: And I was enjoyed it when they come to the plaza as well to give us a little preview. Now to one of the most popular shows on Netflix and the growing controversy around it, Savannah, we`re talking about that Emmy winning drama "The Crown ." GUTHRIE: Yes, we all love it. Fans go crazy for waiting for next season. But this morning some prominent figures from the worlds of politics and Hollywood are publicly criticizing the series for how it depicts the royal family this season. NBC`s Kelly Cobiella is at Buckingham Palace with more on that. Kelly this got a lot of eyebrows raised. COBIELLA: It does. And you know this has come up in the past and Adam -- and Netflix has always been adamant that this show is fictitious but as they deal with more recent history, controversial times in the royal family like the marriage and divorce of Charles and Diana, some are saying it just hits too close to home for an already grieving royal family. (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) COBIELLA (voice-over): This morning as anticipation builds for the fifth season of "The Crown ." UNIDENTIFIED MALE: This has become an all-out war. COBIELLA (voice-over): Sensitive storylines now sparking new backlash in wake of Queen Elizabeth`s passing last month. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: But for Prince Charles bared his soul to the nation. COBIELLA (voice-over): The new season is controversial because it will focus on Prince Charles and Princess Diana`s divorce as well as her death. In an open letter to the "Sunday Times," Oscar winning actress Dame Judi Dench calling on Netflix to place a disclaimer on the series, writing in part, the time has come for Netflix to reconsider for the sake of a family and a nation so recently bereaved. Dench who describes herself as a great believer of artistic freedom, calling this series, cruelly unjust, adding, the closer the drama comes to our present times, the more freely it seems willing to blur the lines between historical accuracy and crude sensationalism. The Times disclosing despite Dench`s close relationship with the royal family, she has not been prompted to write the letter. [07:35:05] UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: I don`t often get into a fight. But when I do I want to win. COBIELLA (voice-over): Netflix describes the series as a fictional dramatization inspired by real events. In a statement of variety, creator Peter Morgan responding to the recent criticism, writing in part about King Charles in the royal family, I have enormous sympathy for a man in his position, indeed, a family in their position. Netflix also confirming to The Sun this week that it will not show the exact moment of Diana`s death in the series. The two actors who portrayed Charles and Diana in the new season, defending the show amid the scrutiny. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: To a certain responsibility towards these characters. COBIELLA (voice-over): Elizabeth Debicki who will play Diana also calling the amount of research and caretaking in the production, immense. Photos of Debicki and the upcoming seasons have gone viral recently with her striking portrayal of the people`s Princess. Matt Smith, who played Prince Philip in the first two seasons, revealing to Savannah and Hoda last month that at least one royal watches "The Crown," Prince Harry . MATT SMITH, ACTOR: And he rocked up to me, and he went, granddad. KOTB: Granddad? SMIT: Yes, he watched the show. He watched the show. (END VIDEOTAPE) COBIELLA: We`ve reached out to Netflix , Judi Dench, and to Buckingham Palace we heard from Buckingham Palace this morning, Savannah, they said no comment. GUTHRIE: Well, Kelly, I mean, speaking of Prince Harry , this is coming at a time when the royal family is anticipating more projects, including his memoir, that could certainly cause some drama. COBIELLA: Yes, it`s a sensitive time for a lot of reasons. First of all, we`re in the first few weeks of King Charles`s reign. He`s waiting, riding a wave of goodwill right now, this period depicted in "The Crown " that goes back to a time when his popularity hit rock bottom. And then on top of that, as you mentioned, a couple of projects coming out Prince Harry`s memoir and also the Netflix docu series by Harry and Meghan and we don`t know much about either one of those projects and what`s in them. Guys? GUTHRIE: All right, Kelly Cobiella, at her post at Buckingham Palace. Kelly, thank you. KOTB: All right guys, still ahead. The powerful new message that pop star Christina Aguilera is sending to young girls, with a new take on one of her biggest hits. MELVIN: First though, Vicky Nguyen is here with a new warning for everyone using those wildly popular online marketplaces to buy or sell, right, Vic? VICKY NGUYEN, NBC NEWS SENIOR CONSUMER INVESTIGATIVE CORRESPONDENT: Good morning. Yes indeed, a bargain hunters beware, police are warning that criminals are targeting would be buyers. You think you`re showing up to get a great deal, but it could be a trap. What you need to know to stay safe. That`s coming up next on Today. (COMMERCIAL BREAK) [07:42:21] KOTB: We`re back 7:42 with Today`s Consumer Confidential, it`s our series that we do around this time each morning and we focus on everything that`s impacting your bottom line. MELVIN: Yes, this morning, an urgent warning for people who use some of the really popular sites to buy and sell things online. Authorities say criminals, criminals are on those sites as well and they`re looking for victims. KOTB: Yes, NBC`s senior consumer investigative correspondent Vicky Nguyen is here to tell us how we can sit stay safe. Hey, Vic. NGUYEN: Hey. Good morning, Hoda and Craig. Those online marketplaces they sell everything from clothing to cars. Here`s how it works. You see something you want, you agree to meet up with cash to make that purchase. But police say beware, it can be a bait and switch. (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) NGUYEN (voice-over): For holiday shoppers in a season of high inflation, online marketplaces can be a great place to find bargains. Unfortunately, police a peer to peer sites like Facebook marketplace and OfferUp are also being used by scammers and violent criminals. HILL: Nine times out of 10, if you see a deal that is too good to be true, it is. NGUYEN (voice-over): Chicago police are investigating dozens of robberies over the past few months. The suspects using online listings to lure in would be buyers. HILL: The offenders will contact them via cellphone and tell them to go to another location. And when they go to that area, four multiple offenders will show up, display guns and take not only the money that they have in their pockets, but sometimes vehicles, watches, and wallets that type of thing. NGUYEN (voice-over): It`s a trend law enforcement officials say has been growing nationwide. In Houston, police releasing this video of a robbery earlier this year. They say the suspects posed on Facebook marketplace as potential car buyers. In Florida and Detroit, similar cases of suspects accused of robbing individuals selling Air Jordans and iPhones. Authorities say criminals are most likely to target high end items like designer purses, all-terrain vehicles, scooters, Apple iPads, and watches. To stay safe, officials they always use safe exchange locations, including in some cities inside the lobby of a police station. (on camera): And the police are OK with that? HILL: That`s what we want them to do. Especially now, the holidays are quickly approaching, we don`t want anyone to trade their safety for a great deal. NGUYEN (voice-over): Experts say online marketplaces are also targeted by hackers and scam artists who use fake accounts and listings to steal your money. Common red flags include the seller refusing to meet in person or let you see the item before purchase. The seller`s profile shows the same item look catered in different states, the seller asking for gift cards instead of cash. Facebook says it takes the threat of scams seriously and has specialized detection tools and trained enforcement and review teams working to remove bad actors from the platform. [07:45:16] OfferUp says it also has a team of investigators who looked to remove bad items and users from its site and provides in-app tools for identity verification. Facebook also allows users to set up a meeting plan within the app that can be shared with a group of trusted friends, all to ensure your hunt for deals doesn`t put you in danger. (END VIDEOTAPE) KOTB: Wow, we could always use one more way to protect ourselves, what do you have? NGUYEN: Yes, Hoda, when it comes to buying anything online, if you are going to use a payment method, always use your credit card because that offers another layer of fraud protection and of course, if you`re seeing a deal that is way below market, that`s your first red flag. And when you`re doing this in person, police say, anytime you feel something is off, trust your gut, leave, get out of that situation. KOTB: Right. They can tell you, meet around the corner then you should not. All right, thank you Vic. MELVIN: Thank you, Vic. Mr. Roker, it looks like a relatively quiet day in the weather. ROKER: It really is. We`ve got that still pesky low pressure system now over Canada brings some light snow and rain around the Great Lakes. But we`re not looking at a risk of thunderstorms anywhere in the country. It is rare to see that and not unusual during winter but we like it. We`re also looking at those cool temperatures through the Great Lakes on into the Northeast, warming up as we get out west. We`ll see that change later in the week. For the day, today, sunny and warm out west, easing chilly conditions here in the East, sunshine from the plains down to Texas. That`s what`s going on around the country. Here`s what`s happening in your neck of the woods. (LOCAL NEWS) ROKER: That is your latest weather. Guys? KOTB: All right, Al, thank you. All right, coming up next, guys, you`ll like this one. Pick your favorite flavor. We`re talking about pop tarts, the great debate over pop tarts, what`s yours? We`re going to talk about it and ours coming up right after this. ROKER: Not PopStart? MELVIN: Pop tart. KOTB: No, pop tarts. I gave you another, you said, you didn`t like it. Let me guess Joe, you`re going to come out and say the chocolate unfrosted. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: What am I, an idiot? UNIDENTIFIED MALE: What are you going to say then? S`mores. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: S`mores are good. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: They`re good. And as you saw that thing quickly devolved into an epic emotional clash, one of the host commented on the video saying, I still haven`t recovered from this and might never. So we decided we`re going to continue the debate. Savannah, do you have a pop tart at your house over there? GUTHRIE: Yes, I love pop tarts as you guys know. They actually found some here in Washington. This is frosted cherry. I would say like strawberry or raspberry, I`m going to be controversial. I don`t like it, I like unfrosted. (CROSSTALK) KOTB: I thought I heard you say you like unfrosting. GUTHRIE: In coming, I like unfrosted. KOTB: Don`t at me. (CROSSTALK) ROKER: It`s OK, whatever you like. KOTB: OK. Mine is blueberry by far frosted. Also I`d like to eat around the edges to get rid of the part that`s no good and then get in. GUTHRIE: The edges are the best part. ROKER: Toasted or untoasted? story_text: (COMMERCIAL BREAK) [07:00:16] SAVANNAH GUTHRIE, NBC NEWS ANCHOR: Good Thursday morning from Washington and New York. Our top story, all eyes once again on Ukraine. HODA KOTB, NBC NEWS ANCHOR: Tension there building after new attacks and new threats. It is October 20th. This is Today. Leave immediately, this morning, thousands of residents in southern Ukraine being forced to flee their own homes. Mass evacuations underway after a warning of imminent attacks and martial law declared by Vladimir Putin . And this morning, mounting concern over power outages ahead of a harsh winter, we`ll have the very latest and a live report straight ahead. On the road, President Biden hits the campaign trail today in the closely watched battleground of Pennsylvania. Can he move the needle for the undecided voters with less than three weeks to go? Feeling the freeze, another day of bitter cold across much of the country, parts of the south waking up two record lows, but Al says, hang in there, a big warm ups on the way. They`ll have your full forecast. Consumer alert, the new warning from police after a string of robberies in cities across the country tied to popular online marketplaces. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) CMDR. RODNEY G. HILL, CHICAGO POLICE DEPARTMENT ENGLEWOOD DISTRICT: Nine times out of 10, if you see a deal that is too good to be true, it is. (END VIDEO CLIP) KOTB: This morning what you need to know before you click. Those stories, plus, "The Crown" and the controversy. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) UNIDENTIFIED MALE: It is with regret, the Prince and Princess of Wales are separating. (END VIDEO CLIP) KOTB: The growing backlash against the hit show`s upcoming storyline. Why an Oscar winner wants it to come with a disclaimer and how "The Crown`s" creator is responding. And smash hit. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) UNIDENTIFIED MALE: At the wall looking up, see you later. (END VIDEO CLIP) KOTB: The Astros defeat the Yankees in game one of the ALCS while the Padres rally to tie up their series with the Phillies in a game for the record books. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) UNIDENTIFIED MALE: Aaron Nola against Austin Nola, little brother against big brother. (END VIDEO CLIP) KOTB: The battle of the brothers going down in history, today, Thursday, October 20th, 2022. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: From NBC News, this is Today with Savannah Guthrie live from Washington, D.C. and Hoda Kotb live from Studio 1A in Rockefeller Plaza. KOTB: Well good morning. Good to see you. So happy you`re joining us on a Thursday morning. Savannah is joining us in D.C. And SG, can you imagine being the mom and dad you`re like, I`m cheering for both my sons. You go, no you go. It`s got to be a tough one. GUTHRIE: I know. Yes, moms are always like, no, I don`t have a favorite. No really, I don`t. Well, a lot more of those highlights in just a bit. Plus nearly two thirds of the country waking up to another morning of bitter cold, I know you`re feeling it there in New York, here Washington too. Record low temps expected in the south today. Al is tracking it and he has some good news on when it`ll feel a little more like fall. KOTB: But we are going to start this morning in Ukraine where new evacuations are being ordered. It comes as residents are being told to charge their devices after drone strikes knocked out key power stations, rolling blackouts now common. And this is just as the brutal Ukraine winter is approaching. NBC`s Cal Perry is in Ukraine for us. Cal, good morning. Give us the latest. CAL PERRY, NBC NEWS CORRESPONDENT: Hey, good morning to you, Hoda. Fresh strikes overnight, the target once again that vital energy infrastructure of Ukraine. It is what has prompted the mayor here to tell people turn off your electricity, save power. All the while as you mentioned, the bitter cold from the winter has arrived, the temperatures plunging overnight, all the while the strikes continue across Ukrainian cities. (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) PERRY (voice-over): This morning, the people of Kherson are caught in the middle. Thousands in the port city that has been under Russian occupation for months, now being ordered to evacuate by Russian installed leaders. Some getting text messages that read, dear residents, evacuate immediately. There will be shelling of residential areas by the armed forces of Ukraine. The evacuations and apparent reaction to Ukraine`s counter offensive in the region, recapturing villages and farmland in recent weeks, Ukrainian officials accusing Russia of trying to create hysteria. It comes on the same day Russian`s President Putin declared martial law in the four Ukrainian regions currently occupied by Russia. I have signed a decree, he said, introducing martial law into these four entities of the Russian Federation. Under the order Russia can, it says, legally seize Ukrainian homes and property, move civilian populations and create local militias, meaning Moscow may try to force Ukrainians to fight against their own country. JOE BIDEN, PRESIDENT OF THE UNITED STATES: It seems his only tool available to him is to brutalize individual citizens in Ukraine. PERRY (voice-over): From Mykolaiv and the south to Kyiv and the north, the Russian bombardment continues. In just over a month, at least 239 drones have been shot down by air defenses, according to the Ukrainian military. The ones that make it past those air defenses are frequently striking infrastructure targets, 30 percent of power plants have been destroyed. [07:05:17] Other times, civilians pay the price. Here in the capital of Kyiv, eight dead in 24 hours, all the while the threat of a nuclear attack looms. Children drill in a nearby school here in Kyiv. And while bulletproof vests are necessary on the battle front, swim caps and goggles must do here on the home front. (END VIDEOTAPE) PERRY: Now Ukraine is asking countries around the world to help with its air defense system. Israel the latest to offer hands saying it will help provide that very important early alert system. But holding back on the ammunition needed to actually shoot down the drones. Officials here are hoping to get that from the United States. Hoda? KOTB: We`re counting those young kids with swim caps and goggles, it`s just -- it`s also unsettling. Thank you so much. We appreciate your report there. Let`s move on back here at home. We`ve got another morning of cold temperatures and a lot of the country, record setting in parts of the South. Let`s bring in Mr. Roker to get a first check of the forecast. Good morning, Al. AL ROKER, NBC NEWS ANCHOR: All right, good morning, Hoda. Good morning, everybody. The good news is if you are one of the 76 million people under these frost advisory, freeze warnings, we`ve got some relief coming for you, so hold on. For this morning though, Memphis 39 degrees, Tallahassee right now 32, Orlando 55 degrees, Norfolk 39. But we are going to see a little bit of a change. For today though, it is going to stay cold but we are going to see a little relief. But for today, about 12 degrees below average in Buffalo behind where the Jetstream dips to the south. We`re looking at Pier 75 degrees, that`s 15 degrees above normal, Boise, Idaho 77. For tomorrow, those temperatures still a little on the chilly side from New York, Charlotte on into Jacksonville. But the warmth is coming, Little Rock 81, San Antonio 86, Dallas, it`s going to be 88 degrees. And as we get into early next week, temperatures moderate, look at this, we`ll be in the 60s in New York right on into early next week, 70s in Raleigh and in Cincinnati, Chicago as well. And hot springs Arkansas into the 80s. We have that record warmth out west, record cold in the east. However, it`s because of this jet stream that`s really been amplified. The good news is if you`re here in the east, we`re going to see a flip, cooler air with rain and snow, which is good news for Seattle and Portland. They have right now the worst air quality in the world because of all the heat and the wildfires. They`re going to see temperatures drop 10 to 25 degrees below normal here in the East, much warmer as we get into next week with temperatures 10 to 20 degrees above normal. So Savannah, we`re all getting some good news back to you. GUTHRIE: All right, I like that Al. Thank you. Well, this morning, new data is out. And it reveals more about the effects of inflation on families all across this country, and the Federal Reserve`s efforts to get it under control. This is some top business leaders are voicing big concerns about the months ahead. NBC`s Tom Costello here with us in Washington tracking it again. Not good news that we`re hearing from business leaders. TOM COSTELLO, NBC NEWS CORRESPONDENT: Not good news. And we`ve been talking for months about persistent sky high inflation. And now, the head of one of the country`s biggest banks, Goldman Sachs is warning about a possible volatile period as we head into 2023. Listen, when Goldman talks, people listen, for the average family, there`s less concern right now about whether we are entering a recession or already there, but rather, when will things improve and how do we cope right now. (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) COSTELLO (voice-over): From Main Street, USA to Wall Street, Americans are still staring down red hot inflation that shows no signs of cooling off. Now some top executives are warning of potentially tough times in the months ahead. DAVID SOLOMON , GOLDMAN SACHS CEO: I think it`s a time to be cautious. That doesn`t mean for sure that we have a really difficult economic scenario. But in the distribution of outcomes, there`s good chance we could have a recession. COSTELLO (voice-over): And Amazon founder, Jeff Bezos , also issuing a warning earlier this week tweeting, the probabilities in this economy tell you to batten down the hatches. With less than three weeks before the midterm elections, President Biden denies that the move to continue tapping into the nation`s emergency oil supply is politically motivated, calling on oil companies to increase production and their refining operations. BIDEN: You still make a significant profit. Your shareholders will still do very well. And the American people catch a break they deserve and get a fair price at the pump as well. COSTELLO (voice-over): But gas is just one part of the global inflation picture. In the U.K. inflation is running even hotter, above 10 percent. Food up a staggering 14.6 percent while the average American family now spends nearly $450 more per month to buy the same goods as last year. The head of the country`s largest retailer, Walmart , tell Savannah it`s hitting people in different ways. [07:10:00] GUTHRIE: Do you feel like consumers are hitting that point where they`re done paying those high prices? JOHN FURNER , WALMART U.S. CEO: I think it depends on the personal situation that consumers are in, really different depending on where you are around the country. COSTELLO (voice-over): For Stephanie Lane`s (ph) family of six living off a single income in Pennsylvania, it`s meant cutting back across the board. STEPHANIE LANE (ph), PENNSYLVANIA RESIDENT: It`s a hard pill to swallow when you have to really change everything you`ve done. And do it everything differently because you can`t afford it. COSTELLO (voice-over): Despite the challenging times, Stephanie (ph) says she and her family are looking forward. LANE (ph): We don`t know when it`s going to get better. But I do know it will. I have faith that it will. (END VIDEOTAPE) GUTHRIE: Tom, we`ve been talking so much about the Fed`s interest rates hikes and how it`s going into effect. And sometimes it takes time to see if they`re working. We`re already seeing some leading indicators right now turning up and affect in the economy. COSTELLO: Last week, you and I talked about a lagging indicator. The unemployment rate is a lagging indicator of what the economy is like right now. We have a new leading indicator, this is concerning. New home building fell 8 percent last month, the lowest since the earliest days of the pandemic, that`s a concern. Mortgage rates, of course, now up to 7.2 percent on a 30 year, that`s double in a year. As a result, existing home sales, we expect are going to be sliding dramatically when we get that data in and price is expected to fall dramatically. All of that is not good for the economy. GUTHRIE: All right, Tom, thank you so much. And, of course, another big focus here in Washington, the midterm elections, which is 19 days to go. Early voting already underway, President Biden is hitting the campaign trail in the battleground of Pennsylvania today. And that brings us over here to Kristen Welker, who`s been covering politics, of course. Well, let`s start here with gas prices. We talked to Tom about the economy, gas prices, is a leading indicator, both economically and politically for the White House. KRISTEN WELKER, NBC NEWS CHIEF WHITE HOUSE CORRESPONDENT: That`s absolutely right. And there`s no doubt that there`s a lot of concern about gas prices, which have ticked up a bit over the past month. They`re down significantly, though, from their high in the summer over $5 a gallon. Yesterday, President Biden announced they`re releasing another 15 million barrels from the Strategic Petroleum Reserve. But look, this is really the tail end of an announcement that was made several months ago to release 180 million barrels. And Savannah, it`s not clear it`s going to have a big impact on gas prices. What it does is it allows the President to make the case that he is working on this issue, which 44 percent of Americans say is their top issue right now heading into these midterms. I talked to the White House Chief of Staff Ron Klain , what`s the first thing he does every morning? Check gas prices. And it underscores, Savannah, the fact that what happens in November could very much be determined by the price of the pump. GUTHRIE: Yes, because it`s something that absolutely everyone feels and it creates a ripple through the economy. Let`s talk about the issue of abortion. Democrats thought they had a lot of momentum with that issue right on the heels of the Dobbs decision in June. Now, it doesn`t seem that it`s having as much of a sway with independent voters. WELKER: That`s right. And you look at the swing that we`re seeing among independent women in particular, who said that they favored Democrats in September. Now, huge swing over to Republicans, you saw abortion as an energizing factor in races in Kansas in special election in New York in the primaries, but I think Democrats are concerned that they need to be having a broader appeal. You saw President Biden talking about the issue of abortion earlier this week. He said remember, basically the outrage that you felt on the day that Roe v. Wade was overturned, trying to turn back the clock in essence, Savannah, but there`s a real awareness and I think a message from the White House. Yes, we need to talk about abortion. But we need to talk about issues including the economy and crime that voters care about in this election cycle, too. So that`s why the President is going to be in Pennsylvania talking about infrastructure today, for example. GUTHRIE: Yes, the polls have shown that the Republicans appeared to have some momentum going into these midterms. The control of the Senate, control of the House is on the table, Pennsylvania, where the President will be today is a key Senate race and it`s tight. WELKER: It`s very tight. It`s basically a statistical dead heat, Savannah. And what`s notable about the President stop in Pennsylvania today, he`s going to be talking about infrastructure. And here you can see these polls between John Fetterman and Dr. Oz. He`s going to talk about infrastructure and then hold a fundraising event with John Fetterman . So not the typical rally that you would usually see a President hold in these closing weeks of a campaign. Why? Well, his approval ratings are low. And I think a lot of Democrats are concerned that he will hurt, he will hinder them instead of helping them. And so that`s why I think you`re not seeing these traditional rallies. But I spoke to an administration official who said, look, the bottom line is, we think it`s more effective to have him out talking about things like infrastructure, talking about things like abortion, gas prices, the things that he has worked on, instead of basically shouting at a crowd. They point to Obama, they point to Trump, they say, look, they had big losses in their midterms as well. So they don`t necessarily see that as an effective strategy. They`re also saying he will be holding typical events getting closer. GUTHRIE: All right, Kristen Welker here in Washington with me. Thank you so much. Hoda to 14 minutes after the hour, I`ll send it over to you. [07:15:01] KOTB: All right, thank you SG. Now to the rising health concern for families across the country just as flu season is getting underway, doctors are seeing an alarming rise in cases of RSV. Now that`s a common respiratory illness that`s left some children in need of hospitalization. So the surge, so severe one Children`s Hospital in Connecticut is now using temporary units to handle their patients and is considering asking for national help. So what is going on? What`s causing it? Why now? NBC News medical contributor Dr. Natalie Azar is here with everything we need to know. Well, first of all, that sounds scary what`s happening in Connecticut. Let`s break it down. Tell us about RSV. And why is it exploding in this moment? DR. NATALIE AZAR, NBC NEWS MEDICAL CONTRIBUTOR: Right, so Hoda, so RSV is a typical seasonal respiratory virus, right? It is, by the time children are two years old, most of them will have been infected with RSV. But it does and it can cause a close to 60,000 hospitalizations every year in children. And the majority of people, it causes a mild cold like illness. So we`re talking runny nose, a low grade fever, a cough, sneezing. KOTB: How long does it last? AZAR: Usually lasts about one to two weeks, sometimes the symptoms can peak at day five. KOTB: OK. AZAR: But in certain individuals, when it goes from the upper respiratory tract into the lungs, it can actually cause more severe disease. And I think it`s very important, especially for caregivers out there of young ones who can`t communicate, the symptoms of more severe disease would be things like poor feeding, irritability, wheezing, or shortness of breath. Those are the kinds of symptoms and signs that you`d want to reach out to your pediatrician immediately. KOTB: So sometimes you wouldn`t know if your child has a cold or has this but either way, like, how do you treat it? What do you suppose to give them? AZAR: Well, that`s the thing. And so you mentioned a very good point, it`s actually indistinguishable, you know, from cold or flu or things like a COVID, you would actually need to get tested. You have to get tested, though in the doctor`s office, there are no home tests for this. In terms of treatment for the majority of people, the treatment is supportive. So that means rehydrating, managing the airway. There is a treatment, however, for people who are at risk, and that group includes premature infants, kids under the age of six months, heart lung problems, weakened immune systems, older folks. It`s a monthly injection that can actually prevent severe disease. KOTB: Just a last quick thing. There was a headline in -- here in New York that said COVID cases in some pockets of New York were up 20 percent. Is that a bellwether? Are we expecting like this big bounce in numbers? AZAR: Right, Hoda. So we`re talking about new strains, and they are descendants of the Omicron strain. This is not unexpected. This is what we expect the virus to do. At this point, it doesn`t appear that it`s causing more severe disease. But remember, more infections could lead to more hospitalizations, and then the convergence of flu. We worry about hospital capacity and of course, cases of lung COVID. So we`re certainly keeping an eye on it. KOTB: And that 20 percent is pretty alarming even in -- AZAR: It`s a pretty significant doubling time. That`s what`s making experts concerned. KOTB: All right, Dr. Azar, thank you. We appreciate it. It is 17 minutes after the hour. Hello, Craig. CRAIG MELVIN, NBC NEWS ANCHOR: Hello, good morning, Hoda. Good morning Dr. Natalie as well and good morning to you. October best part of the year for baseball fans, major league baseball playoffs underway right now. The Houston Astros came out swinging in game one of the ALCS. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) UNIDENTIFIED MALE: Drive into right, well hit, Judge on the run, and Chas McCormick, opposite field home run. (END VIDEO CLIP) MELVIN: And there you have it. Chas McCormick with Houston second home run of the inning there, they would go on to beat the Yankees four to two. Game two is tonight. Over to the National League now, the San Diego Padres scoring five runs in the fifth inning to take the lead there. They would hold on to that lead to win it, eight to five. That series all tied up at one game apiece. There was some history made in that game as noted at the top of the show here, Phillies pitcher Aaron Nola is facing his brother Austin Nola, who is a catcher for San Diego. You see their parents looking on there to the farm, right. It`s the first time in MLB postseason history that a pitcher faced his brother at the plate. Austin Nola getting the big RBI single there. That was smart the Padres in the fifth inning. And I heard you and SG in the top of the show about which, you know, as a parent watch. KOTB: -- you do, you know, who -- MELVIN: I`ll tell you who`s the favorite child, it`s Austin, the oldest child is always the favorite. KOTB: But, you know, I was just -- I was thinking of Peyton and Eli Manning`s mom and dad. How many times have they watch their two kids and there were one point they were in the Super Bowl together. It`s like, oh my, oh my, oh my. GUTHRIE: And guys, I was like either they put the split screen up of the parents so it`s like the brothers and the parents have to keep the neutral face, like game face. Yes, we like everyone. headline: TODAY for October 18, 2022, NBC
story_text: (COMMERCIAL BREAK) [07:00:16] SAVANNAH GUTHRIE, NBC NEWS ANCHOR: Good morning. It`s Tuesday. Hope you have those winter coats handy. HODA KOTB, NBC NEWS ANCHOR: Yes, and in several cities, they`re already breaking out the snow shovels. It is October 18th. And this is Today. Deep freeze, nearly 100 million people waking up to brutally cold temperatures from Colorado to New England all the way down to Florida, some places in between coping with the earliest snowfall in years. It`s going to be a long winter. We are alive where the flakes are falling and Al will have your full forecast. Breaking overnight, cities across Ukraine facing a new barrage of Russian airstrikes, this time, cutting power and water supplies to tens of thousands of civilians, the very latest in a live report from the front lines. Growing concern, an Iranian athlete in the international spotlight after competing in a high profile event without her hijab, so was it a show of support for women protesting on the streets back home, her new message overnight and what she`s facing as she returns to Tehran. Three weeks to go, with the midterms fast approaching candidates from coast to coast clashing in closely watched debates overnight, just ahead, we will break down the key races where they stand and the biggest issues on the minds of voters. All that, plus, burgers, tacos, fries, oh my, those sky high prices now hitting a staple for millions of Americans, fast food, what you need to know and how to save on your next meal. And just for kicks, the Los Angeles Chargers use a big Monday night rally to collect your field goal. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) UNIDENTIFIED MALE: The kick is good. And the Chargers win it in overtime. (END VIDEO CLIP) KOTB: And knock off the Denver Broncos in a nail biter, today Tuesday, October 18th, 2022. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: From NBC News, this is Today with Savannah Guthrie and Hoda Kotb live from Studio 1A in Rockefeller Plaza. KOTB: Well, good morning. Good to see you. It`s a Tuesday morning. We`re so happy that you`re with us. GUTHRIE: Oh, yes, and burr, that cold snap affecting much of the country, we started talking about it yesterday. Well today, it`s here. KOTB: More specifically it is here. The snow really whipping up this morning in northern Michigan near the shores of Lake Superior and while it may not be snowing where you live, the chances are it is getting cold. GUTHRIE: Yes nearly 100 million Americans under frost and freeze warnings this morning with that winter like weather extending from Colorado all the way up and down the East Coast. KOTB: And that early Cold is a cause for concern for many Americans who are already bracing for higher heating costs. Al is standing by. He`s got his forecast. But first, NBC`s Maggie Vespa joins us now from a snowy Michigan. Maggie, we can`t believe what we`re seeing in there. MAGGIE VESPA, NBC NEWS CORRESPONDENT: I know guys, good morning. This is crazy, right? You wouldn`t know it based on this snow globe of a live shot. But we are less than a month into fall right now. And obviously this looks like a winter wake up. And to be clear, we`re in the Negaunee, Michigan like Upper Peninsula Michigan, so a dusting of snow this time of year is not unusual. But look at our handy dandy tape measure. Here in Negaunee, we`re at roughly eight inches and counting. And again, this chill is not just affecting the Midwest, this cold snap is stretching all the way to Florida. (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) VESPA (voice-over): Overnight, fall quickly turning to winter in the Midwest. (on camera): Is a part of this painful given that we`re like mid-October? UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: It`s going to be a long winter. VESPA (voice-over): And early season storm dumping more than a foot of snow in northern Wisconsin and Michigan. And making for a treacherous drive in Indiana. The weight of the heavy snow knocking out power to tens of thousands, Monday, and causing trouble for plows. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: We have hard times for our plows to get through because the trees are hanging over the roads. VESPA (voice-over): Autumn leaves blanketed in white as Chicago saw its first flurries of the season. The October chill bringing the first freeze of the season to 89 million people this week. Today Kansas City Omaha and dozens of other cities waking up to record breaking cold as low as the teens. Americans forced to crank the heat just as heating bills are expected to hit a 10-year high. The frigid blast arriving nearly a month ahead of schedule and also surging south, sending temperatures tumbling from Tennessee to the Florida Panhandle this week. Alabama and Mississippi set to feel even colder than Boston Wednesday. While in South Carolina farmers are scrambling to harvest before the frost. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: It isn`t fun to lose crops. We will harvest what we can and we`ll continue to harvest tomorrow. VESPA (voice-over): A change of season and a taste of winter come early. (on camera): What is it looks like this when your trip trick or treating? UNIDENTIFIED MALE: I`m going to freeze my butt off. (END VIDEOTAPE) [07:05:03] VESPA Yes, guys, the stakes are high. And for reference, by the way, the first day of winter isn`t until December 21st. And for those of you down south, it sounds like you`ll be waking up to your coldest morning tomorrow morning, your coldest temperature is tomorrow morning. The good news is it sounds like you won`t need those jackets for long. Hoda, I`ll send it back to you. KOTB: All right, Maggie Vespa for us, Maggie, thank you. GUTHRIE: She`s got all the gadgets in her tricks. And Al has got even more. AL ROKER, NBC NEWS ANCHOR: I know she doesn`t have a big wall like this. GUTHRIE: Yes, come on. ROKER: But we can show you all that snow that`s going to be coming in and it`s going to be hanging around a bit. We`re going to talk about that later. But let`s get to that cold. Right now it`s 22 in Des Moines, 39 in Cincinnati, Fort Smith, Arkansas at 40 degrees, Pittsburgh 38. The Jetstream dips down to the south the eastern half of the country. Out west, they`ve got some record warmth in the Pacific Northwest. But for this afternoon, only 46 in Detroit, that`s 14 degrees below average, Memphis 53, 20 degrees cooler than average, Knoxville 50, that`s 10 degrees cooler. And then tomorrow morning, we look for possible records in Raleigh Savannah, Knoxville, Tupelo, Little Rock Tulsa, on into Austin and Baton Rouge. However, we will see temperatures start to temper just a bit as we move toward the end of the week by Friday at 60 in New York City, 68 in Cincinnati on Friday, Memphis will be 77. And by next week, we`re going to flip the script, out west colder than average. And here in the east, it`s going to be warmer than average. So just hang in there. Good news is coming guys. GUTHRIE: Yes. KOTB: Cool. All right, Al, thank you. Breaking overnight, a new wave of attacks across Ukraine, explosions have been felt across the capital of Kyiv and other cities, even as the death toll rises from yesterday`s barrage of Russian strikes. NBC`s chief foreign correspondent Richard Engel has the very latest. Hey, Richard, good morning. RICHARD ENGEL, NBC NEWS CHIEF FOREIGN CORRESPONDENT: Good morning, Hoda. Russia is now attacking Ukrainian cities daily and with impunity. This was the main flower market here in the city of Mykolaiv was hit by a Russian missile overnight. And just down the street, Russia attacked an apartment building killing at least one person according to Ukrainian officials. And Ukrainian say by attacking sites like these that have no military value, Russia is trying to break the Ukrainian spirit. (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) ENGEL (voice-over): Russia is flattening Ukraine, one market at a time. Death by a thousand cuts. For Irina Shipchenko (ph), whose flower shop was destroyed overnight in Mykolaiv, what Russia is doing is nothing less than state terror. We clean up and continue living. What else can we do and we will win, she says. Over the last two weeks, Russia has intensified attacks on Ukrainian cities, claiming to be destroying the country`s infrastructure and its ability to wage war. But Russia is firing directly on civilians attacking an apartment building overnight in Mykolaiv, too. Officials say Russia launched a guided missile, killing one person. The strikes came hours after an airplane mysteriously crashed in Russia. State media reporting that a pilot on a training mission took off from an occupied part of Ukraine and ejected, the aircraft smashing into a building and killing four Russians. Ukrainians wonder if it was an accident or sabotage from within. President Putin personally dispatched investigators to the scene. Discontent is growing in Russia after the Kremlin imposed the draft, rounding up conscripts across the country. And with precision weapons in short supply, Moscow is increasingly relying on Iranian made dive bomber drones, launching them in swarms at Ukrainian cities including Kyiv with deadly effect. Overnight in his daily address, President Zelenskyy called for more air defenses. Secretary of State Blinken condemned Iran for supplying Russia with weapons. The United States gives Ukraine billions of dollars in military support, but not long range weapons, trying to find a perhaps impossible balance of supporting Ukraine without antagonizing Moscow excessively. In a sign, both sides seemed to recognize this will be a long war. Russia and Ukraine exchanged prisoners 108 Ukrainian women for captured Russian soldiers in a one to one swap. (END VIDEOTAPE) ENGEL: Over the last several days, we`ve been talking a lot about how Russia is using those Iranian made drones. The drones are highly effective. They have a long range but they don`t carry very much explosive power. Certainly not enough to cause damage like this or to dig a crater in the ground anything like this. You see it can even expose the city`s earlier foundation. And President Zelenskyy today commenting on this attack says it is more evidence why his country needs better air defenses. And he wants Russia to be held accountable. Hold? [07:10:14] KOTB: All right, Richard Engel for us there in Ukraine. Richard, thank you. GUTHRIE: There is international concern this morning for the safety of an Iranian athlete after she represented her country in a recent climbing competition without wearing the customary hijab. NBC`s Meagan Fitzgerald has that story for us this morning. Meagan, good morning. MEAGAN FITZGERALD, NBC NEWS CORRESPONDENT: Savannah, good morning. Elnaz Rekabi competed on Sunday with what appeared to be a headband her hair uncovered which is a violation of Iran strict dress code. Now this morning, an apology on her Instagram page, but there`s still growing concern for her safety. (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) FITZGERALD (voice-over): This morning, concerns for a young female Iranian athlete after she competed without wearing a hijab. Elnaz Rekabi, a prominent rock climber, took part in a competition in South Korea this weekend, notably climbing with her head uncovered. In the past, Rekabi has worn the traditional headscarf while climbing. The hijab has been a focus of recent extraordinary protests in Iran, sparked by the death of 22-year- old Mahsa Amini who was detained by the morality police for breaching the dress code. She died three days later. Women across Iran have protested by cutting their hair and appearing in public with their heads uncovered. After the appearance in South Korea, Rekabi is headed home. The Iranian embassy in Seoul tweeting she departed yesterday. Human rights groups have been concerned about pressure she may face from authorities. MAHMOOD AMIRY-MOGHADDAM, DIRECTOR OF NGO IRAN HUMAN RIGHTS: I think they will put her under tremendous pressure. There is fear of torture, ill treatment, psychological pressure. They want to set an example both for other athletes in the same situation and also for the Iranian girls so that they don`t get a role model in Elnaz. FITZGERALD (voice-over): Rekabi this morning posting on Instagram that her job had issues before she was called to climb. While the statement was posted on her account, the circumstances under which he was posted remain unclear. Now back in Iran, the regime has been under pressure as protests led by young women continue, many watching Rekabi`s returned to the country with concern. (END VIDEOTAPE) FITZGERALD: Now the International Federation of sports climbing says it`s in contact with Rekabi. They also say they`re in contact with the Iranian Climbing Federation. They released a statement that I want to read to you. They say athlete safety is paramount for us. The IFSC fully supports the right of athletes, their choices, and expression of free speech. But Savannah, of course, this is a story that we`re going to be watching closely. GUTHRIE: All right, Meagan Fitzgerald, thank you very much. And we turn now to the midterms with just three weeks to go early in person voting is now underway across a number of stakes. And at stake, control of the Senate and the House. And on the minds of voters major issues like the economy, crime, abortion rights. NBC`s national political correspondent Steve Kornacki is here with some of the things we`re watching three weeks out. And let`s start right there with the issues that voters say matter to them. And what that`s telling us about what might happen here and these elections. STEVE KORNACKI, NBC NEWS NATIONAL POLITICAL CORRESPONDENT: Yes, interesting, Savannah. We`ve talked so much all year about the economy and inflation being important issues. How about this? This is a " New York Times " poll brand new here asking voters what`s the top issue on your mind this election? I haven`t seen it this dramatic in a poll. Add the economy and inflation together. That is 44 percent. We`re getting close to half of all respondents in this poll saying that`s their top issue. Nothing else even cracks 10 percent right now. And we`ve talked about the Republicans when it comes to the economy and inflation having a pretty clear advantage in the polls. GUTHRIE: And that brings us to the next question on the poll. They call it the generic ballot, you know, they just asked, would you like a Republican or a Democrat to control Congress? And there`s been some movement here. KORNACKI: Yes. And typically, this has been a pretty good indicator of where things end up in midterm elections. So this is the average of the generic ballot right now. And you can see the Republicans with a lead here. That is a 2.2 point lead for Republicans now. It`s close, generally speaking, but we were here a week ago taking you through the generic ballot. And a week ago, this number was inside of one point. You had that inflation news over the last week certainly didn`t help the Democrats. And it does seem that as the economy moved to center stage, Republicans are improving their chances here. GUTHRIE: And a few weeks ago, it was the Democrats who had the advantage there. So you see the momentum in these final weeks. Let`s talk about the issue of crime, not high on the list of voters concerns and yet it seems to be making an impact in certain races. KORNACKI: It`s fascinating because we showed you the top issue voters have, crime doesn`t rate high there, doesn`t mean it`s not on their mind. So let`s show you a place where I think it is having an impact. This is Wisconsin, one of the key Senate races, Ron Johnson to term Republican incumbent. He leads in the polling average over his Democratic challenger. Now Johnson has been leaning heavily on crime. [07:15:00] Interesting poll that came out of Wisconsin this week they asked things a little bit differently. They basically asked, are these issues important to you? That`s what`s being asked here. Inflation tops the list. But look at crime. It`s close to 90 percent. And I think also striking, abortion is under 80 percent. Republicans running heavily on crime, Democrats running heavily on abortion, and it looks like in this Wisconsin race, crime may have more resonance than abortion does. GUTHRIE: Making a big difference in Pennsylvania Senate race as well, it appears. But let`s talk about Georgia, because it may just be Georgia, Georgia, Georgia to quote our friend Tim Russert. That might be the decision maker in terms of who controls Congress. KORNACKI: Yes, I mean, again, we saw this two years ago, Georgia is a runoff state. If nobody gets 50 percent and here`s that Senate race, Raphael Warnock , Herschel Walker , Warnock leading but nobody had 50. If nobody cracks 50, it`s a December 6th runoff, could have control of the Senate on the line. They did have a debate last Friday. We`re waiting to get a readout from some polls haven`t really seen it yet if that change anything there. GUTHRIE: Real quickly, the governor`s race is interesting because it doesn`t look like people are at least telling pollsters they`re going to vote straight down party lines. KORNACKI: We thought this type of voter was extinct, the split ticket voter. But look in Georgia, Brian Kemp , the Republican governor, pretty comfortably ahead outperforming the other Republican, Herschel Walker . What pollsters say they`re seeing here is there`s a suburban voter outside Atlanta who doesn`t like Biden, doesn`t like the Democrats but also doesn`t like Donald Trump . And, you know, Brian Kemp went to political war with Donald Trump and he survived in that voters eyes. Kemp`s OK. Walker`s got some convincing to do. GUTHRIE: We`re going to be spending a lot of time together, Steve Kornacki as we get close to election day, thank you so much. Hoda? KOTB: All right guys, let`s turn to Monday Night Football. Four quarters not enough for the Chargers and Bronco so the game went into OT and this is how it ended. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) UNIDENTIFIED MALE: That`s good. Scott puts it down. That`s good. The kick is good. And the Chargers win it in overtime. (END VIDEO CLIP) KOTB: There you go. That was just in Hopkins, a fourth that field goal of the night, his foot was hurting but he kicked it anyway. The Chargers win it 19 to 16. Plenty of sunshine though. And record highs into the Pacific Northwest today with even more sunshine. That`s what`s going on. We`re going to get to your local forecast in the next 30 seconds. (COMMERCIAL BREAK) (LOCAL NEWS) ROKER: And that`s your latest weather. Guys? KOTB: All right, Al, thank you. Still ahead, the search for the winners of a lottery jackpot where the half a billion dollars, and Kerry, one of those tickets sold in a city that was so hard hit by Hurricane Ian.
