headline: TODAY for October 18, 2022, NBC
story_text: (COMMERCIAL BREAK) [07:00:16] SAVANNAH GUTHRIE, NBC NEWS ANCHOR: Good morning. It`s Tuesday. Hope you have those winter coats handy. HODA KOTB, NBC NEWS ANCHOR: Yes, and in several cities, they`re already breaking out the snow shovels. It is October 18th. And this is Today. Deep freeze, nearly 100 million people waking up to brutally cold temperatures from Colorado to New England all the way down to Florida, some places in between coping with the earliest snowfall in years. It`s going to be a long winter. We are alive where the flakes are falling and Al will have your full forecast. Breaking overnight, cities across Ukraine facing a new barrage of Russian airstrikes, this time, cutting power and water supplies to tens of thousands of civilians, the very latest in a live report from the front lines. Growing concern, an Iranian athlete in the international spotlight after competing in a high profile event without her hijab, so was it a show of support for women protesting on the streets back home, her new message overnight and what she`s facing as she returns to Tehran. Three weeks to go, with the midterms fast approaching candidates from coast to coast clashing in closely watched debates overnight, just ahead, we will break down the key races where they stand and the biggest issues on the minds of voters. All that, plus, burgers, tacos, fries, oh my, those sky high prices now hitting a staple for millions of Americans, fast food, what you need to know and how to save on your next meal. And just for kicks, the Los Angeles Chargers use a big Monday night rally to collect your field goal. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) UNIDENTIFIED MALE: The kick is good. And the Chargers win it in overtime. (END VIDEO CLIP) KOTB: And knock off the Denver Broncos in a nail biter, today Tuesday, October 18th, 2022. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: From NBC News, this is Today with Savannah Guthrie and Hoda Kotb live from Studio 1A in Rockefeller Plaza. KOTB: Well, good morning. Good to see you. It`s a Tuesday morning. We`re so happy that you`re with us. GUTHRIE: Oh, yes, and burr, that cold snap affecting much of the country, we started talking about it yesterday. Well today, it`s here. KOTB: More specifically it is here. The snow really whipping up this morning in northern Michigan near the shores of Lake Superior and while it may not be snowing where you live, the chances are it is getting cold. GUTHRIE: Yes nearly 100 million Americans under frost and freeze warnings this morning with that winter like weather extending from Colorado all the way up and down the East Coast. KOTB: And that early Cold is a cause for concern for many Americans who are already bracing for higher heating costs. Al is standing by. He`s got his forecast. But first, NBC`s Maggie Vespa joins us now from a snowy Michigan. Maggie, we can`t believe what we`re seeing in there. MAGGIE VESPA, NBC NEWS CORRESPONDENT: I know guys, good morning. This is crazy, right? You wouldn`t know it based on this snow globe of a live shot. But we are less than a month into fall right now. And obviously this looks like a winter wake up. And to be clear, we`re in the Negaunee, Michigan like Upper Peninsula Michigan, so a dusting of snow this time of year is not unusual. But look at our handy dandy tape measure. Here in Negaunee, we`re at roughly eight inches and counting. And again, this chill is not just affecting the Midwest, this cold snap is stretching all the way to Florida. (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) VESPA (voice-over): Overnight, fall quickly turning to winter in the Midwest. (on camera): Is a part of this painful given that we`re like mid-October? UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: It`s going to be a long winter. VESPA (voice-over): And early season storm dumping more than a foot of snow in northern Wisconsin and Michigan. And making for a treacherous drive in Indiana. The weight of the heavy snow knocking out power to tens of thousands, Monday, and causing trouble for plows. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: We have hard times for our plows to get through because the trees are hanging over the roads. VESPA (voice-over): Autumn leaves blanketed in white as Chicago saw its first flurries of the season. The October chill bringing the first freeze of the season to 89 million people this week. Today Kansas City Omaha and dozens of other cities waking up to record breaking cold as low as the teens. Americans forced to crank the heat just as heating bills are expected to hit a 10-year high. The frigid blast arriving nearly a month ahead of schedule and also surging south, sending temperatures tumbling from Tennessee to the Florida Panhandle this week. Alabama and Mississippi set to feel even colder than Boston Wednesday. While in South Carolina farmers are scrambling to harvest before the frost. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: It isn`t fun to lose crops. We will harvest what we can and we`ll continue to harvest tomorrow. VESPA (voice-over): A change of season and a taste of winter come early. (on camera): What is it looks like this when your trip trick or treating? UNIDENTIFIED MALE: I`m going to freeze my butt off. (END VIDEOTAPE) [07:05:03] VESPA Yes, guys, the stakes are high. All right so back out here live, again, we have this handy dandy thermometer now. And you can see it`s right around freezing, so just hold it up for the snow to keep piling up. And for reference, by the way, the first day of winter isn`t until December 21st. And for those of you down south, it sounds like you`ll be waking up to your coldest morning tomorrow morning, your coldest temperature is tomorrow morning. The good news is it sounds like you won`t need those jackets for long. Hoda, I`ll send it back to you. KOTB: All right, Maggie Vespa for us, Maggie, thank you. GUTHRIE: She`s got all the gadgets in her tricks. And Al has got even more. AL ROKER, NBC NEWS ANCHOR: I know she doesn`t have a big wall like this. GUTHRIE: Yes, come on. ROKER: But we can show you all that snow that`s going to be coming in and it`s going to be hanging around a bit. We`re going to talk about that later. But let`s get to that cold. As you can see stretching from the Rockies all the way to the northeast down to Mobile, Alabama, almost 90 million people impacted by frost advisories, freeze watches and warnings. Right now it`s 22 in Des Moines, 39 in Cincinnati, Fort Smith, Arkansas at 40 degrees, Pittsburgh 38. The Jetstream dips down to the south the eastern half of the country. Out west, they`ve got some record warmth in the Pacific Northwest. But for this afternoon, only 46 in Detroit, that`s 14 degrees below average, Memphis 53, 20 degrees cooler than average, Knoxville 50, that`s 10 degrees cooler. And then tomorrow morning, we look for possible records in Raleigh Savannah, Knoxville, Tupelo, Little Rock Tulsa, on into Austin and Baton Rouge. However, we will see temperatures start to temper just a bit as we move toward the end of the week by Friday at 60 in New York City, 68 in Cincinnati on Friday, Memphis will be 77. GUTHRIE: Yes. KOTB: Cool. All right, Al, thank you. Breaking overnight, a new wave of attacks across Ukraine, explosions have been felt across the capital of Kyiv and other cities, even as the death toll rises from yesterday`s barrage of Russian strikes. State media reporting that a pilot on a training mission took off from an occupied part of Ukraine and ejected, the aircraft smashing into a building and killing four Russians. He leads in the polling average over his Democratic challenger. Now Johnson has been leaning heavily on crime. KORNACKI: We thought this type of voter was extinct, the split ticket voter. headline: Conversation With Elizabeth Heiskell About Her Breast Cancer Journey
story_text: HODA KOTB: We are back. 8:13. The "Pink Power TODAY". And this morning story hits close to home for us. SAVANNAH GUTHRIE: Yes, our beloved "TODAY" food contributor Elizabeth Heiskell was diagnosed with stage two breast cancer this past summer. KOTB: Like a lot of women this can happen, too. She was in the best shape of her life. She has no family history. She says breast cancer wasn`t just -- well, not on her radar. Elizabeth, we love you. You are here with us. ELIZABETH HEISKELL, " TODAY" FOOD CONTRIBUTOR: Yes. KOTB: We are going to talk to you in a second. OK. But first, let`s check out her story. ZAP: We have a cure for breast cancer now and that is catching up early and young women don`t have that luxury. We`re not being screened annually. ANN PARTRIDGE, YOUNG AND STRONG PROGRAM FOR YOUNG ADULTS WITH BREAST CANCER: We think that`s because young women are more likely to not be screened. And so, their tumors are bigger by the time we find them. THOMPSON: Dr. Ann Partridge directs Dana-Farber`s program for young women with breast cancer. PARTRIDGE: They tend to present with more aggressive types of breast cancer. story_text: [07:00:00] (COMMERCIAL BREAK) KRISTEN WELKER, NBC NEWS ANCHOR: Good morning, thanks for starting your weekend with us. Georgia is on the minds of voters everywhere with the Senate candidates facing off in their first and likely only debate last night. PETER ALEXANDER. NBC NEWS ANCHOR: The high-stakes race there could decide control of the Senate. It`s October 15. This is "TODAY." (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) ALEXANDER (voiceover): A Bruising Night In The Peach State, Georgia`s Democratic Senator Raphael Warnock face to face with his Republican challenger Herschel Walker , the two battling one another on everything from the economy to policing. Walker`s own personal life also under scrutiny with questions whether he paid for an ex to have an abortion. HERSCHEL WALKER , REPUBLICAN SENATE CANDIDATE, GEORGIA: I`ll be a senator that protects life. And I say that was a lie and I`m not backing down. ALEXANDER: Demanding Answers. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: I think I heard three or four gunshots, UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: OK. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: I hear people screaming. ALEXANDER: New 911 calls released overnight reveal the chaos and confusion during a shooting rampage that left five people dead in Raleigh, North Carolina. A 15-year-old suspect in custody as policed and grieving family members try to figure out why this tragedy happened. Cat Scratch Fever. Some conservative political candidates and elected officials under fire this morning for spreading the false claim that schools are providing kitty litter boxes for students who identify as cats, this morning, dissecting misinformation. All that plus there`s no Hogwarts without Hagrid. ROBBIE COLTRANE, SPANISH ACTOR: Rubeus Hagrid, keeper of keys engravings at Hogwarts. ALEXANDER: Robbie Coltrane, the actor best known for playing the lovable giant in the Harry Potter movies died on Friday at 72. How his co-stars are remembering him? Today, Saturday, October 15, 2022. ANNOUNCER: From NBC News, this is "TODAY" with Peter Alexander and Kristen Welker. (END VIDEOTAPE) ALEXANDER: Welcome to today. Thanks for joining us on this Saturday morning. I think there is a generation of kids and dare I say adults who feel like they grew up with that gentle half-giant Hagrid. Robbie Coltrane is going to be missed. WELKER: He sure is. Those who knew him described him as boisterous and eccentric. And we will look back at his life at his legacy. Yes. Well, we do have a lot to cover this morning, especially in the world of politics with questions swirling about whether former President Trump will answer that subpoena to appear before the January 6 committee Mr. Trump did respond with a scathing letter slamming the committee but never actually said if he would appear. Meantime, the Republican Senate candidate in Georgia backed by President Trump, Herschel Walker , appeared on stage with incumbent Democratic candidate Raphael Warnock for their only debate overnight. ALEXANDER: Georgia is one of at least three crucial battleground states with very high-stakes Senate races at stake there. They could determine whether the Democrats retain control or if the Republicans will take it away. So we want to begin this morning with NBC`s Ellison Barber. She`s in Savannah with a wrap-up of last night`s big showdown, Ellison, good morning. ELLISON BARBER, NBC NEWS CORRESPONDENT: Good morning, Peter. This is a closely watched race. This debate was highly anticipated. This morning, both campaigns are declaring victory. It wasn`t just Herschel Walker`s first time debating Senator Warnock, it was his first time debating ever, which led to some fiery moments on the debate stage. (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) BARBER (voiceover): Incumbent senator Raphael Warnock and Republican candidate Herschel Walker trading blows on a range of topics in their first and likely only debate. RAPHAEL WARNOCK , DEMOCRATIC SENATE CANDIDATE, GEORGIA: He says no exceptions, even in the case of rape, incest, or the life of the mother. I think that`s extreme. BARBER: Walker, who once said he`d support an all-out ban on abortion, attacking Warnock for being a pastor who supports abortion rights. WALKER: And instead of aborting those babies, why you`re not baptizing those babies? BARBER: Clarifying his current stance. WALKER: I support the Georgia heartbeat bill because that`s the bill of the people from Governor Kim. And I said that has exceptions in it. BARBER: And denying accusations that he paid for the mother of one of his children to have an abortion. WALKER: And I`ll be a senator that protects life. And I say that was a lie and I`m not backing down. BARBER: Throughout the debate, Warnock tried to emphasize his work in Washington. WARNOCK: I pass the single largest tax cut, contrary to what my opponent is suggesting for middle and working-class families in American history. BARBER: And paint Walker as unqualified. WARNOCK: I`ve never pretended to be a police officer. And I`ve never -- I`ve never threatened a shootout with the police. [07:05:00] BARBER: Walker pulling out what appeared to be some sort of badge only to be admonished by the moderator. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: You have a prop. WALKER: Yes. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: That is not allowed, sir. WALKER: It is. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: I asked you to put that prop away. BARBER: Walker tried to focus on the economy. WALKER: You have to blame this administration and Senator Warnock because, within two years, disinflation has gotten worse. BARBER: And tie Warnock to a president whose approval rating among Georgia voters is 37 percent. WALKER: Can you tell me why he voted with Joe Biden 96 percent of the time if he was standing for Georgia? BARBER: Every topic, Georgia voters have the final word, and early voting begins Monday in a race that could determine which party controls the United States Senate . (END VIDEOTAPE) BARBER: In Georgia, a candidate has to pass a 50 percent threshold in order to avoid a runoff. In recent polling, Walker and Warnock are in a statistical tie, Peter, Kristen. ALEXANDER: Just a few weeks away until those crucial midterms. Ellison Barber there in Savannah, Georgia, Ellison, thank you. WELKER: And this morning, there`s new drama surrounding the legal battles of former President Trump on the Mar-a-Lago documents case. The Department of Justice is asking a federal appeals court to throw out the appointment of the Special Master who`s looking at the classified records cease during the search. This, as Mr. Trump, has yet to say whether he will comply with a subpoena to appear before the January 6 committee. ALEXANDER: NBC`s Monica Alba is here with us in studio with the latest on all of it. Monica, good morning. MONICA ALBA, NBC NEWS WHITE HOUSE CORRESPONDENT: Good morning, Peter and Kristen. Donald Trump responded to the January 6 committee`s unanimous subpoena with a lengthy letter of baseless election claims but didn`t say whether he`d actually comply with the request. And it`s not the only open question for the former president, now facing another legal twist in a separate investigation. (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) ALBA (voiceover): This morning, it`s up to a federal appeals court to decide if it should stop the work of an independent reviewer known as a special master evaluating thousands of documents seized at former President Trump`s Mar-a-Lago state. The Justice Department filed a brief on Friday, arguing there`s no legal basis for an outside review. The latest legal development, as lawmakers wait to see whether the former president might appear before the January 6 committee which plans to subpoena him in the coming days. REP. LIZ CHENEY, (R-WY): We are obligated to seek answers directly from the man who set this all in motion. ALBA: Mr. Trump hasn`t said whether he will, either way, instead releasing a scathing 14-page statement Friday, full of falsehoods and disproven claims of widespread election fraud, repeating that he won certain states in 2020 that he clearly lost and including photos of the crowd at the Stop the Steal rally he headlined on January 6. In the letter to Chairman Bennie Thompson , the former president also defended the rioters as great American patriots and called the January 6 committee a witch hunt of the highest level. Just hours after the panel showcase never before seen video featuring congressional leaders of both parties huddled together pleading for the National Guard to be deployed as the attack unfolded. SEN. MITCH MCCONNELL, (R-KY): Get in there in one hell of a hurry, you understand? SEN. CHUCK SCHUMER , (D-NY): We need them there now whoever you got. ALBA: The new footage film by Speaker Nancy Pelosi`s daughter Alexandra, a documentary filmmaker. In another exchange -- REP. NANCY PELOSI , (D-CA): Hi, Mr. Vice President. ALBA: Speaker Pelosi reaches then-Vice President Mike Pence , expressing her concern for his well-being. PELOSI: I worry about you being in that Capitol building. Don`t let anybody know where you are. (END VIDEOTAPE) ALBA: Now, it`s still possible the committee could subpoena the former vice president. They haven`t rolled that out yet. But there`s not that much time left for the group to do its work since it could be disbanded if Republicans take control of the House in the next midterm elections. Next step, the committee will finish its final report and that is expected to be released sometime in December, Peter, and Kristen. WELKER: All right a lot to watch, Monica. Thank you. Good to see you. ALBA: Great to be with you. ALEXANDER: On November -- excuse me, a North Carolina community is grieving and looking for answers this morning after the latest mass shooting in this country that killed five people. The suspected gunman is just 15 years old. NBC`s Priscilla Thompson is in Raleigh with more. Priscilla, you spoke to the fiance of one of the victims, what did he tell you? PRISCILLA THOMPSON, NBC NEWS CORRESPONDENT: Yes. Peter, Kristen, good morning. headline: Behind The Scenes Of Carrie Underwood`s Epic New Tour
story_text: SHEINELLE JONES: I am excited for this. So, this morning, we have a "TODAY" exclusive. A first look at what to expect when country superstar Carrie Underwood hits the road for her Denim and Rhinestones tour. It`s her first in three years since she took me back stage in South Carolina where it all kicks off. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) CARRIE UNDERWOOD, SINGER: It`s a good time. A lot of hard work has gone into the show and very, very proud of it. People are going to have fun. JONES (voiceover): It`s been a few years since a Carrie Underwood tour has made its way across the country. And no one seems more excited than the superstar herself.\\ JONES (on camera): What is the one thing you miss about touring? UNDERWOOD: The crowds. I love to sing. When I`m on stage, I feel like I am at home. And just to feel the energy from people and you look out at all these seats and every single person that is there. JONES (voiceover): The eight-time Grammy winner embarking on a 43-stop arena tour, kicking it all off with a huge show in Greenville, South Carolina. And yours truly is given an all-access pass. JONES (on camera): This gives me like the feels. UNDERWOOD: It`s pretty awesome. It looks bigger. I feel like from up here. JONES: From here? UNDERWOOD: Yes. JONES (voiceover): The stage for her "Denim and Rhinestones" tour lit in dramatic purple will include pyrotechnics and even Carrie performing some high-flying aerial stunts. UNDERWOOD: I am always looking to do things I`ve never have done before. JONES (on camera): Like fly? UNDERWOOD: Like fly. JONES (voiceover): Carrie, taking a page out of her CMT Awards performance. UNDERWOOD: And it`s important to me to make sure like everybody gets a good view. So, we want to figure out some cool ways to get from point A to point B. JONES (on camera): How exciting is that? JONES (voiceover): It`s all part of her goal to bring something new to the arena tours. UNDERWOOD: I want everything to feel different. I don`t want somebody to be like, no, I saw a Carrie Underwood show, you know, four years ago and I`m good. JONES (voiceover): Something definitely worth the price of admission, Carrie`s stunning wardrobe. JONES (on camera): Like this is -- UNDERWOOD: It`s a lot. There`s a lot going. JONES: It`s amazing. Look how beautiful it is. UNDERWOOD: The last part is adding more rhinestones. JONES: I don`t know if you could add any more rhinestones. UNDERWOOD: You always can. I mean -- JONES (voiceover): But something no amount of rhinestones can replace, Carrie`s time with her kids on the tour and at home. [09:35:00] UNDERWOOD: They will be out to visit. This tour, I`m going home a lot more than I ever have before. There is a way to get me home even if it`s just for the day. JONES (on camera): So, are your kids aware of what mommy does? I mean, they`ve been on tour with you before but they are young. UNDERWOOD: I feel like Israel who is seven and a half, he is becoming more aware that it`s not normal, probably because of people around him. So, he`ll go to school and somebody will be, like, I saw your mom on TV last night. JONES (voiceover): One of the Carrie`s few must-haves, a mobile gym. JONES (on camera): This is good. Do you ever work out to your own music? UNDERWOOD: No. JONES: No. UNDERWOOD: It`s weird. JONES (voiceover): A U.S. arena tour, a long way from Carrie`s "American Idol" days. JONES (on camera): Let me take you back. UNDERWOOD: Yes. JONES: It was in 2005. I was a reporter in Tulsa, Oklahoma, and I had the assignment to meet you at the door. The whole town was going nuts because a local girl made it on "American idol." And you walked in and your hands were like -- and I grabbed your hand. I was like, are you ready? If you look at this picture, like this girl right here, do you remember what you were feeling in those early days? UNDERWOOD: At that point, it was all very new, very fresh. And I am, like, OK, you know, let`s enjoy this and have fun and, you know, keep trying to, you know, move forward, but it could all go away at any second. And I think it`s kind of important to treat everything like that, you know, because it just makes you grateful. So, I still -- I`m waiting for the moment where I`m like feeling like I belong. JONES: Are you kidding me? JONES (voiceover): And while I had her, I just had to ask. (MUSIC PLAYING) JONES (on camera): One of your fellow "American Idol" winners, you know, Kelly Clarkson, does her Kellyoke. Have you heard her sing "Before He Cheats?" UNDERWOOD: I have. I have. I feel like she`s one person that you`re like, please, don`t sing my song because you`re going to make me look bad. JONES: Are you joking? You all are both like powerhouses. (END VIDEO CLIP) JONES: That`s funny. I was asking her, you know, if she stays in touch with some of the -- you know, the folks who she, you know, was on "Idol" with years ago. And she has -- great. She says she still talks to Simon, you know, that whole thing. DREYER: Oh, that`s great. JONES: One thing I will say about Carrie is she is so humble and it`s not lost on her. Because I`m like, oh, my god, look at all these clothes and look at all of this. And she is like, yes. You know, she just -- it keeps it -- DREYER: It seems like it hasn`t gone to her head. JONES: Not at all. DREYER: She`s walking around like, can you -- JONES: She is still saying, can you believe it? DREYER: Yes. JONES: I know. DREYER: That`s great. JONES: The tour kicks off tomorrow and tickets are on sale now. There will be pyrotechnics. She flies, as we talked about. She even -- she`s like, I am humble and even -- SOBOROFF: I want to see you get up on the flying thing. JONES: I loved it. Yes. ROKER: Oh, yes. DREYER: With that old hairstyle. JONES: Exactly. DREYER: Yes. JONES: Exactly. DREYER: All right. Coming up, another icon is here with us in studio. She`s -- SOBOROFF: There she is. DREYER: Stella McCartney . You`re going to fashion, family and so much more, right? STELLA MCCARTNEY , FASHION DESIGNER: Absolutely. DREYER: OK. When we come back. SOBOROFF: Don`t go anywhere. JONES: Gorgeous. Gorgeous. SOBOROFF: Nice done. Nice walk off. (COMMERCIAL BREAK) [09:40:00] JONES: We have our life therapist here. She`s also -- SOBOROFF: Really have a good time JONES: -- a fashion royalty with us this morning here in studio. SOBOROFF: Stella McCartney has made a name for herself designing clothes for celebrities like Meghan Markle , Amal Clooney, Beyonce Johnson, so, so many more. DREYER: She launched her brand in 2001, pioneering animal free and ecofriendly fashion. ROKER: And Stella joining us now fresh off her Paris fashion show. JONES: Yes. ROKER: Good morning, Stella. JONES: Good morning. STELLA MCCARTNEY , FASHION DESIGNER: Hi. SOBOROFF: Good to see you. MCCARTNEY: Good morning. ROKER: So, you made this a part of your mission, you know, sustainable ecofriendly. I mean, Bella Hadid`s Met`s dress in the Paris fashion show you making a big splash. How important is that to you and why did you decide so early on? I mean, you were really ahead of the curve on this. MCCARTNEY: You know, I grew up on an organic farm in England as a vegetarian and I basically wanted to be a fashion designer and I was lucky enough to be one and I thought, I can`t compromise my ethics for my career. I don`t want to kill animals. You know, billions of animals get killed for handbags and shoes and leather jackets. So, I was like, I can`t do that. I need to find an alternative. And it started there really. And, you know, the best thing about today is that actually doing sustainable fashion and being ethical and conscious is actually on trend. JONES: It`s in. SOBOROFF: That`s true. MCCARTNEY: Which is a miracle. JONES: Right. DREYER: Is it hard to do? MCCARTNEY: It`s impossible to do. DREYER: Yes. MCCARTNEY: It`s a miracle that I am here today. It`s really, really hard. You know, you have to work with your suppliers so deeply. But it`s this kind of sexiest thing, I think, in fashion. It`s the future of fashion. I think if people don`t start adopting this way of working, then, you know, they`re going to go out of fashion pretty quick. JONES: Yes. SOBOROFF: Thanks in no small part to everything that you have done. And Al mentioned, by the way, at Paris Fashion Week, I want to ask you about that because saw your dad was there, your sister Mary was your photographer. MCCARTNEY: Yes. SOBOROFF: A real family affair. How was it? You guys have a good time? You guys always go together as a group? MCCARTNEY: No. I mean, I`m always there. But, you know, my dad is a busy guy. So, when he can come, I`m always so excited. And, you know, family, the most important thing, right? Let`s face it. Family and friends. And, you know, the fashion industry is a tough cookie and to have your family there supporting you. You know, my family happened to be fabulous. So, it adds a little diamond. SOBOROFF: Understatement. JONES: That`s fair to say. SOBOROFF: I saw -- speaking of your dad, that he posted -- he is almost 80 and he`s doing -- still doing head stands. Here it is. ROKER: Wow. SOBOROFF: Wait. Guys, look in the corner of the TV screen. He is watching MS and there a teaser for our documentary series. So, shout out -- JONES: Oh, look at that, Jacob. SOBOROFF: Shout out to Mr. McCartney. JONES: So, that`s why you -- MCCARTNEY: There you go. SOBOROFF: Do you do that too? MCCARTNEY: I will be sending a check in the post. SOBOROFF: Yes. Thank you very much. MCCARTNEY: And you are going to owe him a couple of pounds. SOBOROFF: Are you a head stander? MCCARTNEY: Yes, I can do the head stand. SOBOROFF: Really? MCCARTNEY: But my dad is very religious about it. He does eye exercises. You know, I mean, he just headlined Glassenbury (ph) a couple of months ago. JONES: Yes. MCCARTNEY: A week after turning 80 to 250,000 people. So, he must be doing something right. JONES: I love it. MCCARTNEY: Should all we do one now? SOBOROFF: No. No, thank you. JONES: You know what, earlier this year you were awarded -- somebody in my ear goes, yes, please. Are you joking? MCCARTNEY: Yes. JONES: Earlier this year you were awarded the CBE. So, it`s the Commander of the Order of the British Empire by the late Queen Elizabeth. MCCARTNEY: I know. SOBOROFF: Amazing. JONES: For your services to fashion and sustainability. Your father, of course, is knighted. And you also designed the dress that Meghan Markle wore at the queen`s funeral? MCCARTNEY: I did. JONES: What an honor. [09:45:00] MCCARTNEY: Yes. Well, you know, it is a real honor, actually. It`s funny. I don`t know. You know, it`s hard to not kind of pinch yourself when these things happen. And yes, I have another award coming up. I`m really excited. I`m -- ROKER: Do tell. SOBOROFF: Tell us about it. MCCARTNEY: It`s the -- oh, God. This is when I stop -- start to -- like that. SOBOROFF: Tell us, tell us. MCCARTNEY: It`s the other after the CBE. DREYER: The Next One? MCCARTNEY: Is Next One. JONES: That`s -- so, Next level up, so this week? MCCARTNEY: The Next. I am going up as opposed to going down, which is a good thing. DREYER: So, what is your title then? MCCARTNEY: Don`t ask me. I`m terrible. I am like the worst person in the world. DREYER: Oh, we don`t know. We were talking to America. We don`t know any of this. MCCARTNEY: You can put it out audience. You can have the community search of what I am going to be next. ROKER: Wow. MCCARTNEY: You guys, you can win a Stella McCartney plant-based handbag. How about that? SOBOROFF: Oh, really? MCCARTNEY: If one of you tells us. DREYER: Can I submit an answer? I wouldn`t mind that. MCCARTNEY: You can do it. SOBOROFF: I`ll start Googling. JONES: I know. DREYER: Let`s also talk about your skin care line. This too keeps the environment in mind. I mean, it`s got to be just as hard to do in the skin care industry as well. MCCARTNEY: Oh, God. Yes. It`s really, really tough. You know, there are so many less ingredients, really, when you`re trying work in a sustainable and natural way. But my new skin care range is coming soon. It`s coming here. And I`m so excited. JONES: I can`t wait. MCCARTNEY: I am so proud of it. It took me three years to do. It doesn`t harm animals. It doesn`t harm the planet. It`s refill-based. So, that`s really, really exciting. SOBOROFF: Oh, that`s -- MCCARTNEY: You know, with -- JONES: It`s the way of the future. ROKER: That`s -- everybody is doing that. JONES: Yes. MCCARTNEY: And it`s great. You can throw in your bag. It`s delicious. Like -- and I think the best thing about what I tend to do in luxury fashion and sustainability is you shouldn`t compromise in any way the quality and the luxury element of what you -- you know, you`re investing in. So, the skin care feels like luxurious, it smells delicious and it`s just the results are amazing. DREYER: And yet, your skin is. MCCARTNEY: And yet, it`s learning to nature. DREYER: I`m so close to you right now and your skin is -- MCCARTNEY: Yes. Look at that. Look at that. Smell that. ROKER: OK. That`s not a little creepy. OK. JONES: I love it. ROKER: Stella, it is always great having you here. JONES: Thank you so much. MCCARTNEY: Thank you for having me. SOBOROFF: Good to see you. MCCARTNEY: Thank you so much. SOBOROFF: Let`s do some head stand. MCCARTNEY: I love doing it. JONES: Well, up next, we are sticking with the fashion and beauty theme. We`re going to show you some smart products to add to your routine, like a chill pill for your face. That sounds good. I need a chill pill for my face. SOBOROFF: I could use that. JONES: We`ll be right back. (COMMERCIAL BREAK) [09:50:00] DREYER: This morning, we are upgrading our beauty routines with smart products designed to make our lives a little easier. And here to help us is Julee Wilson, Cosmopolitan`s beauty editor-at-large. Good morning. JONES: Good morning. JULEE WILSON, COSMOPOLITAN`S BEAUTY EDITOR-AT-LARGE: Hi. How are you? ROKER: Hey, Julee. SOBOROFF: Hey, Julee. JONES: I love it when you come. WILSON: I just love being here. DREYER: Well, we love having you. And we`re starting off with blush. WILSON: Yes. DREYER: Because blush, I feel like you go with the wrong color, you are kind of throwing things off. WILSON: Yes. But this one is super smart. It`s from Youthforia. It`s green, you see here. DREYER: Yes. WILSON: But when you put it on your skin, it works with your skin`s natural pH. And it turn -- look it. Do you guys see this? It actually turns color. DREYER: And it will be a different color on me? WILSON: And it`s buildable. You see how it`s turning color? ROKER: It`s like a chameleon. WILSON: Yes, it`s amazing. So, it`s super smart. DREYER: And mine goes more pink. WILSON: Yes. It`s clean. You can sleep in this. ROKER: How do it know? WILSON: The creator -- DREYER: It`s like a mood blush. WILSON: Yes. It`s like a mood blush. It`s so cool. JONES: I love it. WILSON: Clean formulation. You can sleep in it. It has like -- DREYER: Look at that. There are different colors. WILSON: I know. DREYER: So interesting. JONES: Mind blown. All right. Let`s talk about this. Some folks, you know, we are looking to firm and smooth and all the good things. SOBOROFF: As Julee already told me, I didn`t use this. WILSON: Yes. So, I don`t know if you`ve ever heard of nuFACE. You probably seen their bigger devices. This one is super smart because it is on the go. You can put this in your bag. And basically, it`s a microcurrent device. So, it doesn`t -- you don`t like feel it. ROKER: It`s not like killing flies. WILSON: I mean, you can feel it. You can feel it vibrating, but you -- it pretty much it erases fine lines and wrinkles. SOBOROFF: Come on. Here, give me one. Give me one. WILSON: Hello. It`s working -- SOBOROFF: Pass one down. WILSON: It`s working the muscles of your face. And so, it`s toning. It`s smoothing. It`s clearing out lines. I mean, it`s genius. DREYER: How often do you need use it? WILSON: You can use it once or twice a day. DREYER: OK. Just -- WILSON: And I love a device that gives you instant gratification, not one that you have to keep using it and I`ll see the effects over a few weeks. DREYER: Oh, you look so much younger. headline: TODAY WITH HODA & JENNA for October 14, 2022, NBC
story_text: (COMMERCIAL BREAK) (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) [10:00:16] HODA KOTB, NBC NEWS ANCHOR (voice over): Today, a Hollywood star who is doing it all, actress, entrepreneur, musician and mom, Zooey Deschanel. HAGER: Smack in the middle of October. KOTB: Halfway to Halloween. HAGER: Yes, halfway to Christmas. No? But we`re closer. KOTB: Don`t you love a Friday? HAGER: It`s feeling like fall in the northeast. KOTB: I know. Have you looked at the leaves yet? HAGER: Yes. KOTB: You did? HAGER: Did you look at the leaves? KOTB: I saw them the other day. HAGER: They`re changing. KOTB: Sometimes you get busy and you miss the most obvious thing in the world. HAGER: Don`t miss -- by the way, they`re right behind you. KOTB: They`re changing. HAGER: They`re right behind us and they`re changing but yes, a Friday feeling. KOTB: Yes, we hope you guys -- we hope you guys have a great weekend, savor and linger. Let your weekend last. HAGER: And look at the leaves. KOTB: Roll it out. Yes, enjoy. All right, so, there is a gentleman in his 40s who is turning heads because he looks fine like wine. HAGER: OK, we`re talking about Chris Pine. He has a new hairdo. KOTB: OK, look at his before picture. HAGER: Which was kind of blonde. KOTB: Shoulder length. HAGER: Blondish. KOTB: But if you look deeply into the picture on the left, it`s very gray with blonde ends. HAGER: Yes. KOTB: And he decided he was going to just kind of -- HAGER: Go for it. KOTB: Go for it. HAGER: Shave it all off. KOTB: OK. Wow. What do you think of -- do you think that is? HAGER: First of all, he`s not my favorite Chris. I know there`s a lot of Chris`s. Who`s your favorite again? KOTB: I can`t remember. HAGER: There`s so many. KOTB: There`s too many Chris`s. There`s so many. HAGER: There`s too many Chris to even count. But anyway, now with that hairdo, he`s in the top two, or three. KOTB: He`s moved. He was that (INAUDIBLE). HAGER: I don`t know who else there is. There`s Chris Hemsworth. There`s Chris Stapleton. KOTB: Chris Pratt. HAGER: Chris Pratt. Anybody else from -- Chris Evans. KOTB: Chris Evans, of course. Chris Hemsworth. HAGER: There`s a lot of Chris`s. KOTB: There`s so many. Wouldn`t you hate to be a Chris? There`s just too many cute ones. HAGER: Kris Kringle. KOTB: OK, you`re really getting weird as usual. HAGER: Yes, I feel like Chris was that name that I always named my Ken Doll. It was either Chris or Chad. You know in the 90s -- 80s, 90s. KOTB: Chad was very bougie (PH). HAGER: Right? Yes, bougie. Chad with the thing around his neck. KOTB: Right. Tying the sweater. Who wore sweaters like that? HAGER: In the 80s. KOTB: Drape it. Did you do that? HAGER: No. KOTB: Did you wear chinos? Do you know what chinos are? HAGER: Khakis? KOTB: Yes, they`re like khakis. HAGER: I mean, my mom might have dressed me but I don`t think anybody would have called me bougie if they saw my baby picture. I was (INAUDIBLE) were about to size is too small and like a huge t-shirt. KOTB: Do you remember -- do you remember one of your first day of school outfits? Do you remember liking that or whatever? Do you remember what those outfits were you were like, it`s the first day? HAGER: I remember always towards the end of August wanting to like plan out my outfits, being excited about it. But I didn`t ever have any way to do it. So, I`d look through the Archie comic books and see what Veronica was wearing. I like Veronica, did you? KOTB: Yes, I love the Archie comics. I don`t know that I ever looked at Veronica and say I want to wear her outfits. HAGER: I look at her outfits and I`d like circle them. But the saddest part is they would never come to fruition. You know, it was like my -- would I wear this on the first day? KOTB: Isn`t that cute? HAGER: But our mom didn`t really. KOTB: My mom loved to pick out our outfits. I remember an orange vest with an orange long color and an orange skirt. Thinking I was wow. And I remember walking like, does everybody see me? HAGER: Wow. KOTB: Because I thought that was really something. I remember the feeling. HAGER: I wish I had this picture and maybe you`ll do. I remember a mustard yellow shirt with a kilt and a tie that I believe my sister made a matching tie for my cat. But it was like mustard yellow and a mustard yellow tie. And I had glasses. KOTB: Glasses. We all had glasses. HAGER: And it just was a terrible look. KOTB: I just feel like the more I think about those of us who went through all those different phases, compared to now, I just think -- [10:05:03] HAGER: It gets better later. KOTB: It gets greater later. No, but people who had a more difficult childhood have a more -- have an easier adulthood I think. I think you go through a lot. And you`re like, oh, that`s nothing. I`ve been through that. I`ve had that. HAGER: Well, I mean, I look at pictures of myself in fourth grade with a full mustache. And I`m like, where did that hair go? I mean, I know I waxed it for a period of time. KOTB: You did? HAGER: Not on fourth grade, but later, you know, and I`m just like, wow, you know? KOTB: I know. Anyway, if you`re going through an awkward stage, or if your kids are, just hang on. HAGER: Yes, totally. KOTB: Hang on. HAGER: It gets greater later. KOTB: Debbie Smith said that, greater later. HAGER: But if you`re not looking, put your banana down. KOTB: Upside down, curve down. HAGER: Honey, I hope you`re putting your banana down. Leave your banana down. KOTB: Can you imagine if you`re just grocery shopping and then suddenly and you -- HAGER: I don`t think people really do this. KOTB: Nobody does. OK, next. HAGER: People are too busy. KOTB: This is a good one. You`re aware of this one. HAGER: I am not aware of this one. KOTB: No, you were aware of the concept. HAGER: You`re talking to me? KOTB: Of the concept. HAGER: OK. Evidently if there`s an upside down pineapple. Upside down -- upside down. What does upside down means? KOTB: It means that the pointy stuff is down. HAGER: OK, upside down pineapple, that means you`re in a couple. But you`re still actively looking. KOTB: What`s the pineapple? HAGER: Evidently, a pineapple signifies that you`re -- KOTB: Why would you know that? HAGER: I only know it because I have a pineapple light. KOTB: Like a nightlight? Like a real light? HAGER: A chandelier. I know. OK, don`t make fun of me. KOTB: No, I`m not, I`m just curious. HAGER: I have a pineapple thing and somebody -- lamp. Well, a pineapple lamp means that you could be looking for extracurricular. KOTB: OK. KOTB: No, they`d be like, did you drop this in my cart? I think it would be you`re thinking it`s like some hot gesture and they`re like, this is my cart lady. You`re like, oh, sorry. Can you imagine? Coming up next, a social media challenge from none other than Ricky Gervais. HAGER: Oh, I`m scared. We`re going to scroll through this week`s best viral videos and post, after this. headline: Embattled Republican Senate Candidate Herschel Walker Defiant In The Face Of New Accusations From The Ex-Girlfriend Who Claims He Paid For Her To Have An Abortion
story_text: KRISTEN WELKER: All right, well, now to several new twists and what is arguably the most closely watched Senate race of next month`s midterm elections. Overnight, Georgia`s Republican Senate candidate Herschel Walker , speaking out to NBC News and standing by his claims that he didn`t know an ex-girlfriend had an abortion more than a decade ago. This is the same woman now says Walker wanted her to have a second abortion years later but she refused. NBC`s Allie Raffa is following all of these developments from Atlanta for us this morning, Allie, good morning to you. [07:10:00] ALLIE RAFFA, NBC NEWS CAPITOL HILL CORRESPONDENT: Kristen, good morning. Democrats controlled the Senate by just the thinnest of margins and keeping that hold could easily come down to this crucial Peach State Senate race where in just a few days has gone from too close to call to downright roiled in allegations. (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) RAFFA (voiceover): This morning, all eyes on Georgia, the crucial Senate race between Trump-back to Republican Herschel Walker and incumbent Democratic Senator Raphael Warnock roiled in controversy after bombshell allegations this week by The Daily Beast that Walker paid for a former girlfriend`s abortion in 2009. And a New York Times report Friday that Walker pressured this same woman to have another abortion two years later, but she refused. headline: Republicans Rally To The Defense Of Georgia Senate Candidate Herschel Walker Facing Devastating Abuse Accusations From His Own Son And A Report He Paid For An Ex-Girlfriend`s Abortion
story_text: HODA KOTB: Meantime, the midterms just over a month away and a firestorm has erupted in a key Senate race in Georgia. Herschel Walker , the former football star now Republican nominee denying a report that he paid for his ex-girlfriend`s abortion. NBC`s Kristen Welker joins us with details on this sordid tale. Hey, Kristen, good morning. KRISTEN WELKER, NBC NEWS CHIEF WHITE HOUSE CORRESPONDENT: Hi, Hoda, good morning to you. Well, campaigns always brace for the possibility of an October surprise. Well, here it is in the critical Senate race in Georgia with a new controversy surrounding Republican Herschel Walker . Now GOP sources are telling NBC News that leading senators are preparing to stand shoulder to shoulder with him on the airwaves and on the campaign trail. But will it be enough with just five weeks until the midterms? (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) WELKER (voice-over): This morning Republicans are closing ranks around former football star Herschel Walker , their embattled Senate nominee in Georgia, a swing state that`s critical to Republicans fight to win control of the Senate. After "The Daily Beast" reported Walker in 2009, urged to then girlfriend to get an abortion after he got her pregnant, then reimbursed her for the procedure and sent her a get well card. Walker who says he wants to ban abortion after 15 weeks without exceptions, is denying the allegation. H. WALKER: It is a flat out lie. I can tell you right now, I never asked anyone to get an abortion. I never pay for an abortion. WELKER (voice-over): "The Daily Beast" says the woman asked not to be identified citing privacy concerns, adding she backed up her story by providing the get well card from Walker, an abortion clinic receipt, and a bank receipt with an image of a $700 check signed by Walker. NBC News has not independently verified the documents. CHRISTIAN WALKER, HERSCHEL WALKER`S SON: Everything has been a lie. WELKER (voice-over): Walker is also facing fierce criticism from his own son, Christian, a budding conservative influencer who says the family urged him not to run quote, because we all knew some of his past. C. WALKER: Family values people. He has four kids, four different women, wasn`t in the house raising one of them. He was out having sex with other women. Do care about family values? WELKER (voice-over): Herschel Walker later tweeting, I love my son no matter what. Walker is locked in a tight race with incumbent Democratic senator Raphael Warnock who won a special election by just two percentage points last year. Many Republicans are rushing to Walker`s defense led by former President Trump who`s endorsed him now saying Walker is being slandered and maligned by Democrats. It`s not the first controversy to rock his campaign. He`s falsely claimed he was a member of law enforcement and acknowledged fathering three children out of wedlock. Walker`s ex-wife has accused him of holding a gun to her head and threatening to kill her in incident Walker has blamed on his struggle with mental health. (END VIDEOTAPE) WELKER: Now his challenger again incumbent Democratic senator Raphael Warnock, not directly responding to the controversy. Instead, he`s stressing his long standing support for abortion rights. The big question here, will all of this make a difference? It`s just too soon to tell. But in close races like this one, even a few votes in either direction, could have an impact. Hoda? KOTB: Yes, those are some stunning allegations there. Kristen Welker for us there in Washington. Kristen, thank you. GUTHRIE: Former President Trump has taken his battle over those documents seized at his Florida Country Club, all the way to the Supreme Court filing an emergency request, Mr. Trump asking the court to declare that the 103 classified documents should be reviewed by that independent observer, the special master. Well, the government is arguing that even the special masters should not see those classified documents that were kept at Mar-a- Lago because of national security. The emergency request is being handled by Justice Clarence Thomas , who has given the Department of Justice until Tuesday afternoon to respond. headline: Conversation With Clea Shearer, About Her Breast Cancer Journey
story_text: [08:10:00] CRAIG MELVIN: We are back. 8:12 with "Pink Power TODAY". Our special series for breast cancer awareness month. And this morning, this morning we`re checking in with our friend Clear Shearer. SAVANNAH GUTHRIE: Yes, "The Home Edit" co-founder was diagnosed with breast cancer earlier this year and she has decided to share every step in her journey, including her recent milestone of finishing chemo. HODA KOTB: Yes, throughout it all, though guys, there`s been a group of women she`s been leaning on. They talk every day but they had never met face to face until two days ago. They`re amazing women. They all came together from all across the country for a very special conversation. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) CLEA SHEARER, "THE HOME EDIT" CO-FOUNDER: Look, all of your toys are so accessible. KOTB (voiceover): Clea Shearer finds joy in being a helper. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: Will you guys help me? JOANNA TEPLIN, "THE HOME EDIT" CO-FOUNDER: I can`t get up there fast enough. SHEARER: Yes. TEPLIN: Like, show us the closets. SHEARER: Yes. KOTB (voiceover): She`s created a career out of it. Taking on clutter and organizing people`s lives as one half of "The Home Edit" team. SHEARER: Hey, guys. So, by now you probably read or heard that I have breast cancer. KOTB (voiceover): But after she shared her breast cancer diagnosis earlier this year, Clea found herself asking for help from those who personally knew the fight she was facing. SHEARER: As you`re going through something so brutal, like chemo, everyone in your life wants to help, but there`s nothing quite like someone who`s actually been through it or going through it at the same time. KOTB (voiceover): A friend connected her to Maria Boschetti, a three-time breast cancer survivor who lives in California with her husband. The 42- year-old, who works in public relations, was first diagnosed when she was just 25. SHEARER: She`s taken so many copious notes. So, if I just say -- if I whip out any side effects she`s like, boop, boop, boop -- KOTB (on camera): Got it. SHEARER: -- page eight. She`s like, you`ll get over that real soon. KOTB (voiceover): Amy Jethway was 42 years old when she found a lump while on vacation with her boyfriend. The biotech sales account manager diagnosed with breast cancer just weeks after Clea. Their mutual friend passed along Clea`s number to Amy who lived hundreds of miles away in New Jersey. KOTB (on camera): These are strangers? People you`ve never met. SHEARER: I`ve never met them. KOTB (on camera): Just on text. Hey, girl? SHEARER: Well -- yes, literally. And I -- there are some of, you know, these women I talk to every day. If not every day, every week, and, you know, just to check in. They`re like my dear close friends. KOT (voiceover): A community connected through tough times. Dear friends who have never met. Meeting up in person for the first time. KOTB (on camera): Well, I think it`s a good time to meet them because it`s fun to text, but it`s more fun to see people in person. [08:15:00] SHEARER: Oh. Oh, my God. AMY JETHWAY, BREAST CANCER SURVIVOR: I can`t believe we get to see you. You`re real. You`re real. Oh, my God. SHEARER: It`s so good to see you. JETHWAY: I`m going to cry. Oh, my gosh. You`re so tall. KOTB (on camera): This is so cool in this moment to be sitting here. SHEARER: I can`t believe. KOTB (on camera): First of all, you haven`t met in person yet you -- SHEARER: No. Oh, my God. KOTB (on camera): -- but you know each other intimately. What did you think, Maria, when you first started connecting with Clea? MARIA BOSCHETTI, BREAST CANCER SURVIVOR: I was shocked she was so positive, right? Because it`s a terrifying time in your life. You were wanting to talk about it. You had questions but also you were -- wanting to help others. KOTB (voiceover): Others like Amy. JETHWAY: I reached out to you during your fourth AC -- SHEARER: Yes. JETHWAY: -- when you felt really horrible. SHEARER: Yes. JETHWAY: And she was so available to me. Like, that was really overwhelming to me because I was about to start my chemo journey. KOTB (voiceover): Did that make you scared or did that make you prepared? JETHWAY: I was so grateful for how open you were and how honest you were about things because if this is what`s going to happen to me, then this is going to happen. I wound up having a very different reaction with my fourth. SHEARER: I know. I was, like, so sorry. I scared you. KOTB (on camera): Oh, you were like, I`m cool. SHEARER: She was like, fine. JETHWAY: Yes. SHEARER: Meanwhile, this whole time I was, like, guys brace yourselves. It`s going to be awful. JETHWAY: Like, it aches everywhere. KOTB (voiceover): Clea`s openness about her hair loss empowering Amy as she started to lose her own. JETHWAY: I told my boyfriend, I`m going to shave this. Like, we`re -- we can do this. We can take this head on. And kind of, whatever parts of the journey you can own, you now, that`s something I got from you. KOTB (on camera): That`s important -- that`s something you got from Clea? JETHWAY: Yes. KOTB (on camera): What is that? JETHWAY: Like, owning what you can in the journey. KOTB (on camera): Were you reluctant, Clear, because there are parts that you want to share and then there are parts you want to keep. But it sounds like you were very -- SHEARER: Oh, I don`t keep much to myself. KOTB (on camera): You don`t? SHEARER: No. Hoda, you know me. I am a barrier soul kind of girl. KOTB (on camera): Yes. SHEARER: Not only did I tell everything pretty much to these ladies but, I mean, I would also tell our Instagram followers what was going on. And it made me feel understood, you know. And it`s also nice not to feel like an anomaly. KOTB (on camera): When you`re having a crummy day, you need someone who gets it. How important has that been, Maria, to have that? BOSCHETTI: It`s so important. I -- you know, I was so young the first time I was diagnosed. And I didn`t have anybody to talk to. You don`t process those emotions when you don`t have someone to talk to or ask question and that friendship. And now, you know, I was just texting Clea last night. I feel like you are this light of sunshine that`s even bringing the last eight years back in me. SHEARER: I`m sorry about that. KOTB (on camera): By the way -- BOSCHETTI: Don`t make me cry. I`m not a pretty crier. KOTB (on camera): But that`s so beautiful. That`s a really important point. BOSCHETTI: Yes, yes. KOTB (on camera): It like -- sometimes feelings lay dormant. SHEARER: Yes. JETHWAY: Yes. BOSCHETTI: Yes. KOTB (on camera): Until someone says, let`s unearth those. KOTB (voiceover): Clea, Maria, and Amy finding strength in each other and finding peace in the small things. KOTB (on camera): Everybody has their spot where they go to when they want to just, like, cleanse and clear and you all are walking in mine. This is Central Park. What`s your place, Clea? Where do you -- SHEARER: My back porch. KOTB (on camera): Your back porch? SHEARER: I have a chair. I read there. I listen to the rain there. I greet my kids after school there. KOTB (on camera): Uh-huh. SHEARER: I just -- it makes me so peaceful. KOTB (on camera): What about for you, Amy? JETHWAY: I have my one bench right on the Hudson -- SHEARER: Oh, that`s so nice. KOTB (on camera): Yes. JETHWAY: -- and that just go out. KOTB (on camera): Doing meditation, Maria, or anything that like -- BOSCHETTI: Yes. KOTB (on camera): You`re a meditator? BOSCHETTI: Yes, meditation and beach. KOTB (on camera): Meditation and beach? BOSCHETTI: Yes. KOTB (on camera): All right. So, this is a sisterhood. SHEARER: Yes. KOTB (on camera): This is something that you believe, Clea, is not for this moment. SHEARER: Uh-huh. It`s for life. KOTB (on camera): How do you know? SHEARER: You go through life and certain people enter it for a reason. I consider you one of those people, too, Hoda. Because I don`t lose friends. I only make them. So, we`ve been through something really incredible together. And also, and a little earth shattering. KOTB (on camera): Yes. SHEARER: A lot earth shattering. So, you`re stuck with me. KOTB (on camera): We`re stuck with clea. (END VIDEO CLIP) GUTHRIE: Wow. KOTB: So. sweet. And by the way, if you wonder if that friendship`s rear - - real, they`re planning a vacation October together. Also, Joanna, you know, Clea`s partner, was standing in the background the whole time. Weeping. Weeping. Like these friendships, the new old friendships or old friendships are all keeping her in. She also said about her hair, she talked about it. She said it`s very kind of peach fuzzy. She`s like, I`m not sure if I`m going to cover it. I think I might just -- finally, I`m free of all that stuff. SHEINELLE JONES, NBC NEWS 3RD HOUR OF TODAY, CO-HOST: I think she looks beautiful. GUTHRIE: She has posted this week, actually, about her -- why she was wearing a wig to her kids` pickup. KOTB: Yes. GUTHRIE: She didn`t want to embarrass them. KOTB: Yes. GUTHRIE: And -- this is going to make me cry. Then her daughter said, mommy, you don`t embarrass me, I think you`re beautiful. So, she started -- yes. And you took them to your special place -- KOTB: Yes. GUTHRIE: -- in Central Park when you went through breast cancer? KOTB: Yes, that was my spot. It was very calming to me. It`s like -- you know, there`s no green space here but that was mine. So, I used to go there and feel very peaceful. And everyone had their little spot where they felt the warm hand. So, it was beautiful. I want to say thank you, of course, to Clea. She`s amazing and Maria and Amy. We also want to thank the Kent, that`s a beautiful space in New York. We had a great conversation there. So, we want to say thank you to them. MELVIN: That was wonderful. GUTHRIE: I`m so weepy today. MELVIN: That was wonderful. KOTB: All right. Mr. Roker, take us away. ROKER: Oh, special. OK. Guys, well, we are looking at a rainy, windy day here in the northeast and parts of New England. Sunshine through the southeast on into the Gulf where it will be nice and warm. Even up to the Great Lakes, we`re looking at a flood risk through the southwest. We`re going to continue to track that. And beautiful sunshine from Seattle to San Diego. [08:20:00] That`s what`s going on around the country. Here`s what`s happening in your neck of the woods. (LOCAL NEWS) ROKER: Don`t forget, if you`re heading out the door, head out to "TODAY" show Radio Sirius XM Channel 108. But right now -- KOTB: What time is it? ROKER: -- best time of the morning. GUTHRIE: All right. ROKER: In for Carson. KOTB: Come on, Sheinelle. JONES: We have good stuff for you this morning. KOTB: OK. We`re ready. JONES: OK. headline: Conversation With Clea Shearer, About Her Breast Cancer Journey
story_text: [08:10:00] CRAIG MELVIN: We are back. 8:12 with "Pink Power TODAY". Our special series for breast cancer awareness month. And this morning, this morning we`re checking in with our friend Clear Shearer. HODA KOTB: Yes, throughout it all, though guys, there`s been a group of women she`s been leaning on. They talk every day but they had never met face to face until two days ago. They`re amazing women. TEPLIN: Like, show us the closets. SHEARER: Yes. KOTB (voiceover): She`s created a career out of it. Taking on clutter and organizing people`s lives as one half of "The Home Edit" team. SHEARER: Hey, guys. So, by now you probably read or heard that I have breast cancer. KOTB (voiceover): But after she shared her breast cancer diagnosis earlier this year, Clea found herself asking for help from those who personally knew the fight she was facing. So, if I just say -- if I whip out any side effects she`s like, boop, boop, boop -- KOTB (on camera): Got it. SHEARER: -- page eight. She`s like, you`ll get over that real soon. KOTB (voiceover): Amy Jethway was 42 years old when she found a lump while on vacation with her boyfriend. The biotech sales account manager diagnosed with breast cancer just weeks after Clea. If not every day, every week, and, you know, just to check in. They`re like my dear close friends. KOT (voiceover): A community connected through tough times. Dear friends who have never met. Meeting up in person for the first time. KOTB (on camera): Well, I think it`s a good time to meet them because it`s fun to text, but it`s more fun to see people in person. [08:15:00] SHEARER: Oh. KOTB (on camera): First of all, you haven`t met in person yet you -- SHEARER: No. Oh, my God. KOTB (on camera): -- but you know each other intimately. headline: How To Identify Your Personal Breast Cancer Risks And The Steps You Can Take To Reduce It
story_text: [09:10:00] SHEINELLE JONES: We are back with our "Pink Power" series to mark the start of Breast Cancer Awareness Month. And this morning, we have a checklist of important information all women need to know from risk factors to screening and more. So, joining us now is Dr. Marisa Weiss , director of breast radiation oncology at Lankenau Medical Center in Pennsylvania. And Dr. Weiss is a breast cancer survivor herself. So, she certainly knows of what she speaks. Good morning to you. DR. MARISA WEISS, CHIEF MEDICAL OFFICER AND FOUNDER OF BREASTCANCER.ORG: Good morning. JONES: So, you and I we were just talking, it was 12 years ago. DR. WEISS: Yes. 12 years ago. JONES: That you were diagnosed? DR. WEISS: Yes. I am very grateful. I benefitted from early detection. And I am here today to share important information to help save other lives. JONES: I love that. So, with that, let`s dig in and get right to it. How do women assess their personal risk for breast cancer? I am hearing about women who have no family history getting breast cancer. DR. WEISS: Exactly. So, breast cancer is the most common cancer to affect women and 75 percent of the time, there is no family history. JONES: 76 percent? DR. WEISS: Yes. No inherited gene abnormality. But if you do have in your family breast cancer, ovarian cancer, prostate, melanoma in your family, you could be at higher risk of breast cancer because of an inherited gene. JONES: OK. DR. WEISS: So, that`s why it`s so important to share that information with your doctor, to assess your risk, you know, to take and make a plan to lower your risk. JONES: Absolutely. What do you mean by background? DR. WEISS: And consider genetic testing. JONES: OK. DR. WEISS: Background, well, you heard from Katie Couric about dense breast tissue? JONES: Yes. DR. headline: How To Identify Your Personal Breast Cancer Risks And The Steps You Can Take To Reduce It
story_text: [09:10:00] SHEINELLE JONES: We are back with our "Pink Power" series to mark the start of Breast Cancer Awareness Month. And this morning, we have a checklist of important information all women need to know from risk factors to screening and more. So, joining us now is Dr. Marisa Weiss , director of breast radiation oncology at Lankenau Medical Center in Pennsylvania. And Dr. Weiss is a breast cancer survivor herself. So, she certainly knows of what she speaks. Good morning to you. DR. MARISA WEISS, CHIEF MEDICAL OFFICER AND FOUNDER OF BREASTCANCER.ORG: Good morning. JONES: So, you and I we were just talking, it was 12 years ago. DR. WEISS: Yes. 12 years ago. JONES: That you were diagnosed? DR. WEISS: Yes. I am very grateful. I benefitted from early detection. And I am here today to share important information to help save other lives. JONES: I love that. So, with that, let`s dig in and get right to it. How do women assess their personal risk for breast cancer? I am hearing about women who have no family history getting breast cancer. DR. WEISS: Exactly. So, breast cancer is the most common cancer to affect women and 75 percent of the time, there is no family history. JONES: 76 percent? DR. WEISS: Yes. No inherited gene abnormality. But if you do have in your family breast cancer, ovarian cancer, prostate, melanoma in your family, you could be at higher risk of breast cancer because of an inherited gene. JONES: OK. DR. WEISS: So, that`s why it`s so important to share that information with your doctor, to assess your risk, you know, to take and make a plan to lower your risk. JONES: Absolutely. What do you mean by background? DR. WEISS: And consider genetic testing. JONES: OK. DR. WEISS: Background, well, you heard from Katie Couric about dense breast tissue? JONES: Yes. DR. WEISS: Putting you at higher risk, you might need extra test to find it. Also, black women are more likely to get breast cancer at younger ages at more advanced stages and have a more serious type of breast cancer. Jewish women are more likely to inherit an abnormal breast cancer gene. And age, our risk goes up as we grow older. But keep in mind, 20 percent of breast cancers happen before the age of 50. JONES: My goodness, which is why screening is so important. DR. WEISS: So important. Absolutely. MARTIN-BROOKS: Speaking of that, Dr. Weiss, earlier detection. DR. WEISS: Absolutely. MARTIN-BROOKS: And we talked a little bit about this in the green room. So, I have a history in my family. DR. WEISS: Yes. MARTIN-BROOKS: They told me 45 you start, this was five years ago. Now, is it 40? When should you start for these yearly mammograms? DR. WEISS: Yes. I say, please, everyone, get your yearly mammograms starting at age 40. And if you have -- MARTIN-BROOKS: Even if you don`t have family history? [09:15:00] DR. WEISS: If you don`t have family history, that`s right. And if you let things slip and slide because of the pandemic, call today to schedule your appointment. You also want to make sure that you get a comprehensive breast exam by your doctor or nurse practitioner once yearly and then, examine yourself on a regular basis just to make sure that you know what`s normal, what may have changed. And if you are at extra risk because of a strong family history, an inherited gene, or many you have dense breast, you might need extra tests like adding an ultrasound to your mammogram, then getting an MRI six months later and then, repeating that overtime. MARTIN-BROOKS: It`s really important information. DR. WEISS: It really is. Hey, Al. ROKER: So, Dr. Weiss, what should women be looking for, you know, when you talk about self-exams, things like that? DR. WEISS: Yes. Well, as it turns out, most breast cancers don`t produce signs or symptoms. They are found by mammography. But people regularly feel things or see things like a lump or an area of thickening in the breast or the armpit, area of swelling or a bulge or the skin might be dimpled or retracted, you might notice a nipple discharge or you might have, let`s say, pain or discomfort in the breast. If you have any of those symptoms that are new and persist, check them out. Call your doctor. Don`t wait. You want to find breast cancer as early as possible when it`s most treatable. ROKER: OK. DR. WEISS: Thank you. MELVIN: Dr. Weiss, what are some things that folks who are watching or listening can do to reduce the risk? DR. WEISS: Yes. Well, the good news is the same steps that reduce your risk of breast cancer improve your overall health. MELVIN: OK. DR. WEISS: Like getting to and sticking to a healthy weight, exercising regularly, even 10 minutes a day makes a big difference. You want to eat mostly a vegetarian-based diet with like meat, chicken, fish more as a sideshow. And then, reduce your alcohol use, since the more you drink, the higher the risk. And stop smoking because it increases the risk for all kinds of things. I say start with one step, then go to a next step. And before you know it, you will be in a healthier place. MELVIN: So, let`s just say you go to the doctor, you get the diagnosis. You get the dreaded C word. DR. WEISS: Yes. MELVIN: You hear it. DR. WEISS: Yes. MELVIN: Life is not over. How do you manage that part? DR. WEISS: It can really make -- I mean, I have been there. I am a doctor and a patient as it were. Well, it`s so important to get answers to your medical questions to reduce uncertainty and to know what to expect. Put your questions and concerns on a list and put the most important ones on the top and call, e-mail or text your doctor to get answers to your questions. Hey, don`t try to do it all. We women carry the weight of the world on our shoulders, right? So, delegate and reach out for help with like childcare, grocery shopping, you know, housework, all the things that don`t matter as much. Save your precious energy for your treatment. MELVIN: Lean on your friends and family. DR. WEISS: Absolutely. MELVIN: I want to ask you, you mentioned something a few moments ago, I want to follow up on. DR. WEISS: Yes. MELVIN: Genetic testing. Who should consider that? DR. WEISS: Anyone who`s got breast cancer who is -- can be -- can get genetic testing. But if you`re diagnosed at age 50 or younger, if you have a history of ovarian cancer in the family, there are men in the family with breast cancer, there`s a history of breast, ovarian, pancreatic cancer, melanoma, you should ask to get genetic testing. MELVIN: OK. DR. WEISS: If you`re of Jewish background, you should ask for genetic testing. MELVIN: OK. ROKER: And you mentioned men, doctor. DR. WEISS: Exactly. If you are a man who gets breast cancer, you are more likely to have an inherited genetic mutation, like BRCA1 and BRCA2. And you want to make sure, if there are any men in the family -- because men get breast cancer just as -- not as often as women, like about 1 percent of the time, but that goes along with higher risk of an inherited gene abnormality. ROKER: All right. MELVIN: Thank you. JONES: It`s important that we`re talking about it.; MELVIN: Thank you so much. DR. WEISS: Thank you. JONES: Dr. Weiss, thank you. DR. WEISS: You`re welcome. JONES: And for more information on breast cancer awareness, we put so much on our website. Just go to today.com/health. MELVIN: When we come back, former ambassador to the United Nations and governor of the greatest state in the country, South Carolina, Nikki Haley is here like. We`re going to talk about leadership, we`re going to talk about powerful women and of course, we`ll also talk about 2024. ROKER: Well, she lives in New York State, which is -- anyway. Then multi- talented actor and producer Kate Del Castillo is joining us in studio to talk about bringing back her international hit series. "3rd Hour of TODAY" will be right back live from New York State. (COMMERCIAL BREAK) [09:20:00] JONES: We are back on this Monday morning. And we are reminded of a famous quote, this is from Margaret Thatcher . She said, if you want something said, ask a man. If you want something done, ask a woman. MELVIN: Former South Carolina governor, former ambassador to the United Nations under President Donald Trump , Nikki Haley took that advice to heart. In fact, it`s the basis of her new book. There`s the title, "If You Want Something Done...: Leader Lessons from BOLD WOMEN." In the book, she profiles that obstacles and accomplishments of 10 powerful women throughout history and weaves them in with her own story. And the former ambassador joins us this morning. Good to see you again. JONES: Good morning. NIKKI HALEY, FORMER SOUTH CAROLINA GOVERNOR, FORMER AMBASSADOR TO THE UNITED NATIONS UNDER DONALD TRUMP AND AUTHOR: Great to be with both of you. MELVIN: Welcome back. Welcome back. I just told you in the green room, I started reading the book this weekend. It`s a fantastic concept. We`re going to dig into the book in just a moment. But let`s start with -- because, I mean, the reality as you write this book about accomplished women and there has been some talk, perhaps you have heard, 2024, that maybe this accomplished woman would for president of the United States. I know you have said you haven`t made a decision. How are you going to decide? What factors will you consider and what`s your timetable? HALEY: Well, I mean, I think, first of all, our focus is November. You know, everybody`s looking at the November elections and I have been all over the country working on that. And then, after, you know, the first of the year, Michael and I will sit down. We`ll figure out if there is a place for me. If there is a place for me, I`ve never lost a race, I am not going to start now. We will put 1,000 percent in and we will finish it. If there`s not a place for me, I have fought for this country as long as I can remember and I will do it until my last breath. MELVIN: And you -- I think you said last spring that if your former boss, Former President Trump, if he does decide to run, that you will sit this one out, you won`t run. Is that still the case? And if so, why? HALEY: I mean, we`ll see if he runs. You know, we`ll see if he runs. He hasn`t said that he is going to run. And so, you know, we will make a decision after the first of next year and figure it out. MELVIN: Would you ever run against him? HALEY: It`s not something I think about. I was proud to serve with him in the administration. It`s something that, you know, I can tell you that I`m thrilled with the accomplishments we did together. We had a great working relationship. But right now, we will see what he does. JONES: You have been very involved in the midterm elections this year. As you know, some Republicans, you know, the candidates running have denied the results of the election. Do you think that`s a disqualifier? HALEY: Well, I mean, I think that the candidates I`m helping, they are really focused on the economy. They are very focused on crime. They are focused on education. Those are the things people are talking about. [09:25:00] I mean, do I think that the elections were real? Yes. Do I think that Joe Biden is the president? Yes. Unfortunately, I am not happy with that, but that is what it is. And the candidates that we`re talking about, real people, they are talking about the fact that it cost more money to go to the gas station, and that`s how they go to work. It cost more money at the grocery store, and that`s how they feed their family. JONES: So, they deny those election results though, you don`t think that`s a disqualifier? HALEY: I don`t know that I`ve talked to anyone that`s denied the election results. Everybody that I`m helping acknowledges the fact that the elections, you know, were real. MELVIN: Let`s talk about the book. What was the impetus? How did it come about? HALEY: You know, it`s -- this is a book about ordinary women that did extraordinary things. And if you are a parent, you know that if you raise strong women, they become strong -- if you raise strong girls, they become strong women and strong women become strong leaders. And so, I was a fan of Margaret Thatcher . And loved how she was very confident in herself. She believed in Britain but believed had herself. And then, when I went to the United Nations, I learned more about Jeane Kirkpatrick, who was my predecessor. And she was someone who was unapologetic about loving America. But then, I met people like Nadia Murad, who was in Iraq. She was part of the Yazidi community. They were overtaken by ISIS. She was gang raped. She was -- her family died and she came out, won the Nobel Peace Prize, fought for her community. Or people like Cindy Warmbier, where, you kno, her son, Otto Warmbier, we know was tortured in North Korea. But you find these stories that are just fantastic of women who had sheer will and knew that they were meant for great things, and they deserve to be in the room. And I hope that this is a reminder to every parent who has a child that we want those kids to know they deserve to be in the room. If you are someone who has had a female mentor or a leader, give them this as a thank you and say, thank you for believing in me. And these are inspirational stories. MELVIN: One of the things I found interesting in the book is this idea -- and I never knew this -- you, throughout the course of your career, you send notes to women who inspire you. Who have you sent notes to? HALEY: I mean, you know, any time I see a woman make a leap. You know, I think I sent one to the head of the New York Stock Exchange. I send it to the first female head of city. You know, I just sent it to the new female anchor at Fox News.
