headline: An Exclusive Interview With Katie Couric
story_text: HODA KOTB: All right, meantime, we are marking the start of breast cancer awareness month with a story that hits close to home. SAVANNAH GUTHRIE: Yes, our friend Katie Couric is with us. She has long been a cancer advocate using her platform, including her time here at Today to inform and educate the public. Well now she`s gone from cancer advocate to cancer survivor. (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) GUTHRIE (voice-over): Last week in a personal essay on the Katie Couric Media website she wrote, June 21st was the first day of summer, my eighth wedding anniversary, and the day I found out I had breast cancer. Like more than a third of women, Katie, was not up to date on her annual screening writing, had the pandemic given me a skewed sense of time? Had it messed with my memory? Six months overdue, Katie, went in for a mammogram and a breast ultrasound noting something suspicious in her left breast. Her doctor did a biopsy and it was cancer. After having a lumpectomy and 15 days of radiation, Katie, is sharing her story to educate others and once again save lives. In 2000, two years after her husband, Jay Monahan, died of colon cancer, Katie aired her own colonoscopy right here on Today. As a result, there was a 20 percent increase in screenings with the University of Michigan dubbed, the Couric effect. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: Katie that smile right here please. GUTHRIE (voice-over): Now, she`s on a mission again. (END VIDEOTAPE) GUTHRIE: And she`s right here with us. Hi, Katie, it`s so good to see you. COURIC: Hi, look at us all in pink. GUTHRIE: We are in pink. We got the memo. It is breast cancer awareness month. And the first question has to be, how you`re feeling? How are you doing? COURIC: I`m feeling great. I`m just getting over a cold. That`s why I wouldn`t give you all a hug this morning to protect you but I`m feeling just fine. You know, I finished radiation last week. They said it made you tired. I was actually not too tired from it. I had a lumpectomy in July. And my next stop I go on something called aromatase inhibitors which suppress estrogen because I have a hormone receptor positive, HER2 new negative tumor that they removed when I had my lumpectomy. But I just feel super lucky that it was diagnosed when it was that I went even though I was late that I went when I did. KOTB: Can you take us back because I think I mean, you are a cancer advocate, obviously but it`s a whole different ballgame when you go in, you think you missed your mammogram by six months, which is probably like most people at home right now. So you went in for your checkup? Tell us about that moment. COURIC: Well, I went in with my phone camera and I was going to share it with my followers and people who read my newsletter and go the website to say don`t forget, I forgot, I don`t want you all to. So when my rady -- breast radiologist Susan Rossmann said, can you turn off your phone? I was like, uh-oh, what does that mean. And she said I think there`s something we really need to biopsy and I want to do it today. [07:35:11] So I thought, oh, my God, you must be kidding me. And then which I found out the next days, she called me, I was pretty stunned. And I think those words, it`s cancerous or you have cancer, do stop you in your tracks. But she told me it was treatable. We needed to have a plan. So I went from feeling shocked to not that shocked, given my family`s history, and the, you know, and to relieved because my exposure to cancer with Jay and Emily and my mother in law, Carol Monahan, you know, they were all advanced, and the prognosis was really tough. So, I felt so grateful, honestly. And that`s why I`m so thrilled to be able to talk to you all about the importance of screening. And I know, Hoda you know about that, because Hoda and I had, you know, you have the same kind of tumor I had when you were in your 40s. When you talk about early detection, it was so funny, because when I was diagnosed here, I remember I sat with Corvo, David Corvo. And I told him what had happened. And he said, I`m going to tell you something. I said, OK. He said, I know a lot of friends who have breast cancer, and they all have one thing in common. And I said, what`s that? He said, they`re still here. And that was about just like, for you and for me to once you get the early detection, some of it, then it just becomes, now it`s medical. COURIC: Right, exactly. And there have been so many strides made. KOTB: Yes. COURIC: But likes -- I mean, as you said, a third of all women, I didn`t even know that number, didn`t get screened during COVID. And a lot of screening places shut down. I think our, the cadence of our lives changed. And I think we just got off track. And that happened to me as well. GUTHRIE: Before we get into some of the particulars, because I know you are a woman on a mission, and you have a really important message. I just, I immediately thought of Carrie and Ellie, your daughters, they`re in their 20s now. COURIC: Yes, Ellie is 31, if you can believe it, yes. GUTHRIE: You know, they experienced so much loss at a young age, you know, their father, their grandmother, their aunt? And I`m sure it was, that was a hard call to make even knowing that you, you know, had a really good prognosis. COURIC: Yes, it was -- I was nervous about it. I waited a few days, so I could process and really understand what we were dealing with and I FaceTime each of them. And Ellie is in LA. And Carrie never calls me back, so I basically had to FaceTime both of them. She`s here in New York. And, I told them, but I was very reassuring. But I saw in their faces, you know, it`s just hard to deliver that news, no matter how you do it. But, you know, I assured them that I was going to be fine. And Carrie came with me, when I got my lumpectomy, when I was being wheeled into the operating room. She was singing the "Arms of an Angel." She`s so funny. But anyway, but they`ve been incredibly supportive. And of course, I was worried about that. But again, just so grateful that they caught it early enough, so it could be treated. And by the way, you know, even when it`s at later stage than mine, I`m stage 1-A, there are so many treatments available. And a lot of women are living with breast cancer. But we need to do better. We need to come up with better treatments, and we need to get more women screened, I was surprised to see only 70 percent of women actually get breast cancer screening. And that number went down to 65 percent during the pandemic, but I think it`s probably went even lower. KOTB: Here`s a weird thing that we just saw on the American Cancer Society website. It says, and I think we have a graphic, women 55 and over should switch to mammograms every two years. They`re kind of giving you that window. You don`t need to go each year, you can go every two. COURIC: Yes, I mean, I think the recommendations have been all over the map. I mean, I`m not a doctor, and I`m trying to play one on T.V. but, you know, I think people should go every year. headline: Today for September 29, 2022, NBC
story_text: (COMMERCIAL BREAK) [07:00:16] SAVANNAH GUTHRIE, NBC NEWS ANCHOR: Hi everybody. It`s Thursday. Millions in Florida waking up to catastrophic damage from Ian. HODA KOTB, NBC NEWS ANCHOR: Yes, the full impact being revealed as the sunrises this morning. It is September 29th. This is Today. Path of destruction, massive flooding and power outages as Ian barrels across Florida crashing ashore as one of the strongest hurricanes to ever hit the state. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: All the sudden I felt something and then heard like a train coming right to the house. (END VIDEO CLIP) KOTB: Nearly 3 million people in the dark, the devastating storm surge leaving entire neighborhoods underwater, homes and cars floating down streets. This hospital swapped from above and below, losing part of its roof, its ground floor flooded, crews still carrying out emergency rescues on land and at sea. We`re live across the state with complete coverage and what millions need to know as the threat moves up the East Coast. Get out, the urgent security alert for all Americans in Russia to leave the country immediately. And the new warning that anyone there with dual citizenship couldn`t be drafted into the Ukraine war, we`ll have the very latest. Breast cancer battle, well wishes pouring in for Katie Couric this morning after she revealed her diagnosis. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) KATIE COURIC, AMERICAN JOURNALIST: Thank you all for your support. (END VIDEO CLIP) KOTB: Just ahead, her decision to speak out and what she wants all women to know. Those stories, plus, historic blast. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) UNIDENTIFIED MALE: Judge keep the left field. This could be it. See you. (END VIDEO CLIP) KOTB: Yankee`s superstar Aaron Judge crushes his record tying 61st homerun of the season, cementing his place among baseball royalty. Today, Thursday, September 29th, 2022. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: From NBC News, this is Today with Savannah Guthrie and Hoda Kotb live from Studio 1A in Rockefeller Plaza. KOTB: Good Thursday morning. So happy you`re joining us today. Good to see you. GUTHRIE: Yes. The sun is coming up in Florida and we`re getting a closer look now at the widespread devastation left behind by Ian. KOTB: Yes, there are two major concerns right now there, the flooding of course and the power outages. Nearly 3 million people across the state woke up this morning and could not turn the lights on, no electricity. GUTHRIE: Ian made landfall yesterday as a major category four packing 150 mile an hour winds and causing massive storm surges across Florida`s Gulf Coast. KOTB: So right now, Ian is making its way east toward the eastern side of Florida. We have a live look at some of the conditions going on. This is Orlando. And while the storm did weakened overnight, it still remains a serious threat. GUTHRIE: Yes, it`s a rain story there. And then once Ian heads away from Florida, it is expected to then curve back toward the Georgia, South Carolina coastlines impacting millions across the South in the coming days. KOTB: Yes, we got it all covered for you this morning. We`re going to start off with NBC`s Sam Brock. He is in Venice, Florida. That`s just north of where Ian made landfall. Hi, Sam, what`s the assessment this morning? SAM BROCK, NBC NEWS CORRESPONDENT: Yes, Hoda, Savannah, good morning. It is terrifying to think what we`re going to see in the light of day. I was just talking to a police officer here in Venice. They resume search and rescue operations at 2 o`clock this morning looking for critically injured people. But he said look, I got to warn you, block to block, there`s dead wire, there`s live wire. As you look behind me right now, you`ll see splintered signs and power lines down all through here. Now when East Naples guys, there were 30 rescue missions yesterday as the urgent efforts right now are underway to find those imperiled by Ian. (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) BROCK (voice-over): It`s devastation that was predicted with the grim reality of this storm`s warped power defies imagination. Ian now with tropical storm hit the coast as a fierce hurricane shredding homes apart and Placida, Florida, tearing off roofs and splintering trees. While in the Tampa area, extremely causing this tree to crash through a home. In one of the hardest hit areas, Fort Myers, there were storm surges nearly seven feet high, nearly double the previous record more than 20 years ago. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: Oh my God. BROCK (voice-over): The massive surge of water leaving entire communities completely underwater. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: Do you want me to come out? BROCK (voice-over): Roads looking more like the ocean for block after block. Ian packed catastrophic 150 mile an hour winds knocking out power to more than 2 million customers. GOV. RON DESANTIS (R-FL): We have seen life threatening storm surge as was predicted. We`ve also seen major flooding, but that`s going to rank as one of the top five hurricanes to ever hit the Florida peninsula. BROCK (voice-over): This team of emergency responders unable to respond, a massive wall of water swamping their fire truck. [07:05:06] UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: Now we have a truck issue and the guys are pushing the truck out of the bay. BROCK (voice-over): In Port Charlotte, hospital staff working through the storm to protect patients. Other first responders struggling to help those in need, unable to start rescues until after life threatening conditions subsided. Despite repeated warnings to leave, some people did not or could not evacuate. They found themselves stranded by a 12 foot storm surge. Mark and Elizabeth living in an apartment in Venice Island, Florida but at the last minute, grab their air mattresses and hunker down in this Sarasota office when her boss offered it to them. (on camera): Here you are with air mattresses in an office space. Your home is 50 or 100 miles away. But you consider yourself lucky. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: We are. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: Yes. BROCK: Is that because you`re saved from the storm? UNIDENTIFIED MALE: Yes, yes, because somebody helped us. BROCK (voice-over): Others stayed behind in the flood zone, trying to help those who were unable to leave. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: I want to help the people in here because they`re good people here in paradise. BROCK (voice-over): This morning, the destruction left behind by this massive blow from Mother Nature is just starting to come into focus. (END VIDEOTAPE) KOTB: Well, hats off to those first responders, all those helpers out there, Sam. There were some viral images in Tampa that were just shocking. It was actually Tampa Bay, and it looked dry. It looked like you could walk on it. People were taking video and pictures of it. What`s the after effects there? BROCK: Yes, so here`s the deal, Hoda, you`re seeing all this water being really sucked out. It`s called negative storm surge. And the reason behind it, you have counterclockwise winds and hurricanes. So on the northern edge of the eye wall, the water was being pulled out of Tampa Bay, into the Gulf of Mexico. The problem with this, Hoda, is the fact that it can then refill when wind directionality change. And it can happen in a matter of minutes. So if you see this, it might be tempting to go out there on the sand and check it out. Don`t do it for your own safety. Hoda? KOTB: All right, Sam Brock for us there in Venice, Sam, thanks. GUTHRIE: Yes. These conditions can change in a split second, the water has finally stopped rising in Fort Myers. But this morning, the impact of the catastrophic flooding there is being felt across the city. And joining us now Fort Myers Mayor Kevin Anderson. Mr. Mayor, good morning. We`re glad to have you on the phone with us this morning. Have you been able to assess damage? I know it`s still early there. What`s your sense of how bad it was? MAYOR KEVIN ANDERSON, FORT MYERS, FL: We haven`t had a full assessment obviously with the sun just coming up, but it is pretty bad. I`m standing on a floating concrete dock. I`m down in the River District of downtown. The problem is the dock is in the middle of an intersection, a block, two blocks away from the water. This is about a piece of concrete that weighs a ton. And it was moved this far away. It shows you how powerful the waters were last night. KOTB: I know one of the things, that`s most concerning in a moment like this is what happened to the people who decided to stay or who were left behind. Have you guys been able to conduct rescues? Do you know how many people are still out there and in need of your help? ANDERSON: We would estimate several dozen people who stayed behind were in need of some assistance. Our teams have been working on that. I`m happy to report at this time. I`ve been not -- I haven`t been told of any loss of life in the city. Now keep in mind, we have a metropolitan area and there may be some outside, but inside the city there`s been no reports to my knowledge. GUTHRIE: Fort Myers more or less took a direct hit, Mr. Mayor, what`s your sense of how this compares to other storms that Fort Myers has experienced? ANDERSON: I came here in the mid 70s. I was on the police department for almost 25 years, so a lot of storms here. This is by far the worst storm I have ever witnessed. They`re watching the water from my condo in the heart of downtown, watching that water rise and just flat out all the stories on the first floor. It was heartbreaking. KOTB: Boy, for -- Mayor for you who`s been there all those years and seen so many storms come and go to take a direct hit. So what is the plan now, like walk us through what will happen this morning and the days ahead? ANDERSON: So the first thing we need to do is make sure the roads are passable. And they`re safe. We do have a curfew in place for next 48 hours until we get a handle on everything. Once we get the roads cleared, you know, FPL will start working on the electricity. Our teams will be out there going through the neighborhoods trying to make sure people are safe, getting assistance, anyone who needs it. We`ll start working on getting the other utilities up and functioning getting cleaned up. We`ve gotten some great support pledge by the President and the governor. So I think I`m optimistic it`s going to be a long recovery but nonetheless we`re going to recover because Floridians are very resilient. [07:10:13] GUTHRIE: They are indeed. Mr. Mayor, thank you so much. Kevin Anderson of Fort Myers, you know, it`s going to be a busy day, so we thank you for your time. KOTB: All right, let`s -- ANDERSON: Thank you. KOTB: Thank you. Let`s turn now to Bill Karins. He`s been tracking the path of destruction where it`s heading and what it`s left behind, hey. BILL KARINS, NBC NEWS METEOROLOGIST: Yes, good morning. So we`ve been showing you where all the worst has been as far as the storm surge went, that was the Fort Myers area, Bonita Springs all the way down to Naples. Overnight, we`ve still had a lot of heavy rain. Our NBC affiliate in Orlando and meteorologists were saying in Kissimmee, there`s been houses with homes with one to two feet of water in them. The little McIver River in Seminole County located right about here is one foot over record flood stage. So again, there`s still problems and still water going into homes right now because of this situation. And look at Daytona Beach. A wind gust of 69 miles per hour, so this is down to a tropical storm, but it is not a pleasant morning in Volusia County, Flagler County heading up there to Jacksonville. That`s where the storm surge is going to be coming in during the day today. So even though it`s a weekend storm, there still could be some significant problems. And then it may actually intensify a little bit on its way up tomorrow in between Savannah and Charleston here to South Carolina, we may actually get landfall that either a strong tropical storm or as a hurricane tomorrow afternoon. And of course, we`re going to get heavy rain in this area, winds could gust possibly up to 70 miles per hour. And that way we could be dealing with some more power outages, guys, in this area too. And storm surge problems, which we`ll explain more about during the show today. GUTHRIE: All right, Bill, thank you. And as we`ve come on the air President Biden has officially declared the state of Florida, a major disaster. So that opens up funding and a lot of help hopefully today. NBC Nightly News anchor Lester Holt rode out the storm overnight in Bradenton just south of Tampa Bay. Homes there flooded, the area`s airport badly damage too. Lester, good morning, the view from where you sit. LESTER HOLT, NBC NEWS ANCHOR: Well, Savannah, I went out to with my trusty flashlight a little while ago surveying the immediate area around us. There appears to be no major damage here. We spoke when heard from the mayor of Sarasota a while ago. He was venturing outside his home for the first time, saw plenty of damage. He`s not aware of anything catastrophic. But certainly during the night, we can hear this thing howling, ultimately dying down now. The rain has stopped and we`re feeling relative breezes after what we saw and went through yesterday. But we`re all OK. KOTB: Yes, difficult night for a lot of people. Lester, a lot of people spent the night in shelters. I`m sure they have tons of concerns about their homes. What are you hearing from them? HOLT: Yes, we went to a shelter a few hours before the eye wall came ashore and talked to people who made that choice. They`d heard the predictions. A lot of them thought it was a no brainer, immediately went into shelters. We talked to officials there who were very concerned that while they did have a number of people, they didn`t have nearly as many as they expected. And that`s why there`s a bit of trepidation this morning as the sun comes up here. You heard from one of the other mayors the sense of what they`re going to find now in the light of day in some of these neighborhoods. One couple of we talked to said they lived in a trailer home, very worried obviously about their neighborhood, the vulnerability. They decided to get out but so many of their neighbors did not. So that will be the big focus today, trying to get to those folks who rode it out and make sure they`re OK. GUTHRIE: All right, Lester, thank you. And of course, we`ll see you tonight on nightly news from Florida. I mean, bears (ph) repeating this is in the top five of strongest storms ever to hit the U.S. KOTB: Yes, that`s an incredible statistic. And as Bill mentioned, the worst of Ian now passing through Central Florida, seeing some heavy rain, strong winds, hitting Orlando, Blayne Alexander, is there, Blayne, good morning, what are you seeing? BLAYNE ALEXANDER, NBC NEWS CORRESPONDENT: Well, Hoda, you can see just here in our live shot, just how powerful these winds are. In fact, we just spoke with an officer who said, not too far away from here, there was a tree that came down into a motel. But by far the real concern here is the rain and of course, the concerns over flooding. Just here in the Orlando area, we saw about a foot, more than a foot of rain overnight. Now to put that into perspective, that`s more than double the amount that this area typically sees in the entire month of September. And that`s what`s leading to incredible images like these. I think we can show you this. We`ve got a video from one of our affiliates, our local reporter, Tony Atkins with our affiliate WESH 2, actually rescued a woman who was stranded in her car in floodwaters. She told our affiliate that she was a nurse trying to drive to work. She was swept away by the flood. Unbelievable pictures of him actually carrying her on his back to safety. And officials believe that as this rain is expected to continue here, it`s only going to see, we`re only going to see more pictures like that. In fact, just north of where we are, we`re already getting more reports of rescues having to occur with people stranded in cars on an on ramp to a highway. We`re also getting reports of water coming into some businesses here in the Orlando area. Now the other wrinkle really that a lot of officials are watching is of course Orlando is known for its theme parks, it`s known for Disney , some for SeaWorld , Universal , all of those parks have been shut down at least through the end of today. But there were a number of people who already came into town, hoping to kind of take advantage of some of the clearer days toward the beginning of the week. [07:15:20] Well, now they`re being told to shelter in place in their hotels, as the storm has continued -- continuing to blow through. Guys, we`re expecting to see rain at this same speed and the same intensity of wind until at least noon if not later, guys. KOTB: All right, Blayne, thank you. I mean, hats off to that WESH reporter for helping that nurse. But hats off to that nurse who was getting in her car and driving to work to help people, so, wow. GUTHRIE: Incredible sight. KOTB: Yes. GUTHRIE: -- puts her on his back, I mean just incredible. KOTB: Wow. MELVIN: Thanks for helping the helper. KOTB: Yes. All right, let`s welcome in Craig. CRAIG MELVIN, NBC NEWS ANCHOR: Hey, Hoda, Savannah, good morning. Good morning to you as well. Obviously the storm has brought air travel across much of Florida to a total standstill. This morning, that is having a ripple effect for passengers all over the country. NBC`s Tom Costello is at Reagan National Airport with that part of the story. Tom, good morning. TOM COSTELLO, NBC NEWS CORRESPONDENT: Good morning, Craig. I just checked 2,000 flight cancelations right now nationwide, but the vast majority are flights going into or out of Florida as you would expect. story_text: (COMMERCIAL BREAK) [07:00:16] SAVANNAH GUTHRIE, NBC NEWS ANCHOR: Hi everybody. It`s Thursday. Millions in Florida waking up to catastrophic damage from Ian. HODA KOTB, NBC NEWS ANCHOR: Yes, the full impact being revealed as the sunrises this morning. It is September 29th. This is Today. Path of destruction, massive flooding and power outages as Ian barrels across Florida crashing ashore as one of the strongest hurricanes to ever hit the state. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: All the sudden I felt something and then heard like a train coming right to the house. (END VIDEO CLIP) KOTB: Nearly 3 million people in the dark, the devastating storm surge leaving entire neighborhoods underwater, homes and cars floating down streets. This hospital swapped from above and below, losing part of its roof, its ground floor flooded, crews still carrying out emergency rescues on land and at sea. We`re live across the state with complete coverage and what millions need to know as the threat moves up the East Coast. Get out, the urgent security alert for all Americans in Russia to leave the country immediately. And the new warning that anyone there with dual citizenship couldn`t be drafted into the Ukraine war, we`ll have the very latest. Breast cancer battle, well wishes pouring in for Katie Couric this morning after she revealed her diagnosis. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) KATIE COURIC, AMERICAN JOURNALIST: Thank you all for your support. (END VIDEO CLIP) KOTB: Just ahead, her decision to speak out and what she wants all women to know. Those stories, plus, historic blast. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) UNIDENTIFIED MALE: Judge keep the left field. This could be it. See you. (END VIDEO CLIP) KOTB: Yankee`s superstar Aaron Judge crushes his record tying 61st homerun of the season, cementing his place among baseball royalty. Today, Thursday, September 29th, 2022. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: From NBC News, this is Today with Savannah Guthrie and Hoda Kotb live from Studio 1A in Rockefeller Plaza. KOTB: Good Thursday morning. So happy you`re joining us today. Good to see you. GUTHRIE: Yes. The sun is coming up in Florida and we`re getting a closer look now at the widespread devastation left behind by Ian. KOTB: Yes, there are two major concerns right now there, the flooding of course and the power outages. Nearly 3 million people across the state woke up this morning and could not turn the lights on, no electricity. GUTHRIE: Ian made landfall yesterday as a major category four packing 150 mile an hour winds and causing massive storm surges across Florida`s Gulf Coast. KOTB: So right now, Ian is making its way east toward the eastern side of Florida. We have a live look at some of the conditions going on. This is Orlando. And while the storm did weakened overnight, it still remains a serious threat. GUTHRIE: Yes, it`s a rain story there. And then once Ian heads away from Florida, it is expected to then curve back toward the Georgia, South Carolina coastlines impacting millions across the South in the coming days. KOTB: Yes, we got it all covered for you this morning. We`re going to start off with NBC`s Sam Brock. He is in Venice, Florida. That`s just north of where Ian made landfall. Hi, Sam, what`s the assessment this morning? SAM BROCK, NBC NEWS CORRESPONDENT: Yes, Hoda, Savannah, good morning. It is terrifying to think what we`re going to see in the light of day. I was just talking to a police officer here in Venice. They resume search and rescue operations at 2 o`clock this morning looking for critically injured people. But he said look, I got to warn you, block to block, there`s dead wire, there`s live wire. As you look behind me right now, you`ll see splintered signs and power lines down all through here. Now when East Naples guys, there were 30 rescue missions yesterday as the urgent efforts right now are underway to find those imperiled by Ian. (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) BROCK (voice-over): It`s devastation that was predicted with the grim reality of this storm`s warped power defies imagination. Ian now with tropical storm hit the coast as a fierce hurricane shredding homes apart and Placida, Florida, tearing off roofs and splintering trees. While in the Tampa area, extremely causing this tree to crash through a home. In one of the hardest hit areas, Fort Myers, there were storm surges nearly seven feet high, nearly double the previous record more than 20 years ago. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: Oh my God. BROCK (voice-over): The massive surge of water leaving entire communities completely underwater. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: Do you want me to come out? BROCK (voice-over): Roads looking more like the ocean for block after block. Ian packed catastrophic 150 mile an hour winds knocking out power to more than 2 million customers. GOV. RON DESANTIS (R-FL): We have seen life threatening storm surge as was predicted. We`ve also seen major flooding, but that`s going to rank as one of the top five hurricanes to ever hit the Florida peninsula. BROCK (voice-over): This team of emergency responders unable to respond, a massive wall of water swamping their fire truck. [07:05:06] UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: Now we have a truck issue and the guys are pushing the truck out of the bay. BROCK (voice-over): In Port Charlotte, hospital staff working through the storm to protect patients. Other first responders struggling to help those in need, unable to start rescues until after life threatening conditions subsided. Despite repeated warnings to leave, some people did not or could not evacuate. They found themselves stranded by a 12 foot storm surge. Mark and Elizabeth living in an apartment in Venice Island, Florida but at the last minute, grab their air mattresses and hunker down in this Sarasota office when her boss offered it to them. (on camera): Here you are with air mattresses in an office space. Your home is 50 or 100 miles away. But you consider yourself lucky. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: We are. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: Yes. BROCK: Is that because you`re saved from the storm? UNIDENTIFIED MALE: Yes, yes, because somebody helped us. BROCK (voice-over): Others stayed behind in the flood zone, trying to help those who were unable to leave. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: I want to help the people in here because they`re good people here in paradise. BROCK (voice-over): This morning, the destruction left behind by this massive blow from Mother Nature is just starting to come into focus. (END VIDEOTAPE) KOTB: Well, hats off to those first responders, all those helpers out there, Sam. There were some viral images in Tampa that were just shocking. It was actually Tampa Bay, and it looked dry. It looked like you could walk on it. People were taking video and pictures of it. What`s the after effects there? BROCK: Yes, so here`s the deal, Hoda, you`re seeing all this water being really sucked out. It`s called negative storm surge. And the reason behind it, you have counterclockwise winds and hurricanes.
